https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: André Janones descarta assumir ministério e decide continuar na Câmara
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Redação
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
O deputado federal reeleito André Janones (Rede-MG) afirmou que não aceitará assumir nenhum ministério no quarto mandato do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT). A declaração foi dada em entrevista exibida no domingo (1º) no “Fantástico”, da TV Globo, e reforçada em mensagens enviadas pelo parlamentar aos seus apoiadores nas redes sociais.
“Eu não vou aceitar nenhum ministério. Está cravado. Não vou ser ministro do governo Lula. Vou continuar na Câmara dos Deputados representando o povo”, declarou o parlamentar. O nome de Janones passou a ser cotado para comandar a área de comunicação digital do governo federal ou assumir a Secretaria de Comunicação Social (Secom) após sua atuação na mobilização de militantes digitais durante o segundo turno das eleições.
Em áudio divulgado no canal de WhatsApp “Exército do Lula”, espaço criado por ele e que reuniu mais de 10 milhões de inscritos durante a campanha, Janones explicou as razões de sua decisão. O deputado argumentou que a nomeação para um cargo no primeiro escalão traria limitações institucionais que prejudicariam sua atuação política na internet.
“Em um ministério, eu fico preso em burocracias, em cumprir reunião, em fazer isso, em fazer aquilo, em assinar papel. Eu não fico solto. Existe uma liturgia do cargo que me impede de ser um guerrilheiro. Então eu preciso estar livre, eu não posso ter amarras”, afirmou o parlamentar aos seguidores.
Janones sustentou que conseguirá contribuir de forma mais efetiva para a governabilidade do governo petista atuando a partir do Poder Legislativo, sem os impedimentos formais impostos pela rotina de uma pasta ministerial.
Reeleito para o seu terceiro mandato com 78.780 votos em Minas Gerais, o deputado confirmou que permanecerá filiado à Rede Sustentabilidade e que manteve conversas com o presidente reeleito para definir a gestão do canal digital construído durante o processo eleitoral.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Lula garante que não vai extinguir programas sociais e critica ‘mentirosos de sempre’
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Redação
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
O presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) garantiu, neste domingo (1º), que nenhum programa social será extinto em seu próximo governo, que vai de 2027 a 2030. Reeleito para o quarto mandato, Lula afirmou que vai cumprir tudo o que prometeu na campanha, sem retirar direitos conquistados pela população.
“O que pode acontecer é a gente criar novos programas sociais ou melhorar aqueles que já estão [funcionando]”, declarou o presidente em vídeo publicado em seu perfil no Instagram.
Na gravação, Lula rebateu informações falsas que circularam nas redes sociais após o segundo turno, realizado no último dia 25. “Não acredite nos mentirosos de sempre, que vivem tentando vender desgraça e infelicidade para o nosso povo”, disse.
O presidente atribuiu a onda de desinformação ao período em que esteve afastado das aparições públicas. “Em uma semana que eu fiquei sem falar, a mentira tomou conta deste país outra vez”, lamentou.
Nos dias seguintes à eleição, circularam nas redes boatos sobre a proposta de fim da escala 6×1 e sobre supostos cortes no Bolsa Família. Na quarta-feira (28), o governo federal desmentiu as publicações e reforçou que os programas seguem em funcionamento.
Recuperação da voz
Lula explicou que precisou se preservar depois da eleição para recuperar a voz, desgastada pela rotina intensa de campanha. A rouquidão voltou a aparecer nos últimos meses, e o presidente vem sendo acompanhado por uma fonoaudióloga. Em 2022, ele passou por um procedimento para retirar uma lesão superficial na corda vocal esquerda.
“Estava sem voz durante a semana inteira. Fiz muito trabalho para me recuperar e estou me recuperando […] Estou bem de saúde, a voz melhorou e logo, logo, quero voltar a percorrer o Brasil para visitar cada estado e agradecer, olhando nos olhos de vocês que foram para as ruas e mantiveram o funcionamento da democracia brasileira”, afirmou Lula, que recebeu mais de 64,2 milhões de votos no segundo turno.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Finados: lei amplia olhar e sensibilidade para vontades antes da morte
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Luiz Claudio Ferreira
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
Os convidados serviam-se de cerveja gelada e brindavam com sorrisos-lágrimas nos olhos. Da caixinha de som, os sambas se alternavam.
A música inspirava os abraços entre os familiares e os amigos de Regina Célia Pinheiro, que morreu, em Brasília, aos 77 anos, em setembro de 2021, vítima de um problema cardíaco.
Cada palavra sobre ela era motivo de brinde naquele velório incomum. “Foi muito emocionante”, recorda a filha, Marcia Pinheiro, de 51 anos.
Era a homenagem no formato como a carinhosa matriarca queria. Amada por tanta gente, mais de 160 pessoas apareceram para a despedida.
Entre os presentes, o marido, o comerciante aposentado Antonio Pinheiro Neto. Eles eram casados há mais de 50 anos. Mesmo com a dor, as cinzas do corpo de Regina foram plantadas em uma área pública junto a uma mangueira.
Dois anos depois, Antonio morreu de câncer, aos 80 anos. O velório também foi especial, com bebidas mais quentes e muito refrigerante, tal como o antigo comerciante gostaria que fosse.
Suas cinzas estão enterradas junto às da esposa, na mesma mangueira, próximo ao local onde moravam. Conversar sobre morte, luto e despedida não era tabu na casa deles. Muito pelo contrário.
Foi com esse caminho aberto, em dias em que estavam todos saudáveis, que conversavam sobre como, em caso de adoecimento, ninguém concordaria em prolongar a vida de forma artificial. De fato, entubações, por exemplo, que não representariam chance de salvar os pacientes foram rejeitadas pelos filhos.
“Sempre escutamos a vontade deles”
Segundo uma das filhas do animado casal, a psicóloga Márcia Pinheiro, conversar sobre a partida fortaleceu a família em vida.
“Nós não persistimos porque sempre escutamos muito a vontade deles. A gente sempre conversava sobre isso”, recorda a filha emocionada.
No caso da mãe, por exemplo, a família fez a opção de não continuar com o tratamento da hemodiálise quando não havia mais possibilidade de recuperação.
“Conversávamos sobre esses temas, não no momento do leito de morte. A gente conversava como uma convicção de vida”, diz a filha.
Legislação avançada
O respeito ao desejo da pessoa foi celebrado em uma lei (Lei n° 15.378/2026) publicada neste ano e que, na prática, criou o Estatuto dos Direitos dos Pacientes no Brasil. A legislação estabelece direitos como autonomia, consentimento informado e acesso ao prontuário.
Segundo a pesquisadora e assistente social goiana Clisciene Magalhães, a lei vai ao encontro dos ideais de dignidade humana e representa um grande avanço para o país.
Ela é autora do livro “Antes de morrer: diretivas antecipadas de vontade”.
O trabalho chegou à segunda edição e traz discussões pertinentes ao tema e um guia de como lidar com a morte e o luto. “Esse é um tema historicamente cercado de tabu e desinformação no Brasil”, afirma a pesquisadora.
Segundo a lei, as diretivas formam a “declaração de vontade escrita sobre os cuidados, os procedimentos e os tratamentos que o paciente aceita ou recusa, a qual deve ser respeitada quando ele não puder expressar livre e autonomamente”.
Para a autora, as vontades não podem ser expressas por terceiros no calor da emoção que envolve o fim da vida.
Garantias de direitos
A assistente social, que atua também na rede de saúde pública do Distrito Federal, explica que as diretivas antecipadas de vontade ganharam força de lei e garantem aos cidadãos o direito de decidir antecipadamente sobre os próprios cuidados de saúde no fim da vida. Ela queria que esse tema fosse tratado de forma simples e acessível a todos os públicos.
Como profissional da rede pública, ficou sensibilizada em observar que pessoas acamadas e sem consciência não tiveram a chance de se manifestar de como gostariam de ser cuidadas.
A lei expressa, por exemplo, que paciente tem o direito “a cuidados paliativos, livre de dor, e de escolher o local de sua morte”. Além disso, os familiares do paciente devem ser apoiados para lidar com aquele momento.
A autora do livro pondera que garantir a diretiva de vontade parte da ideia de um cuidado humanizado e representa autonomia e dignidade.
Por outro lado, ela explica que as equipes multiprofissionais devem ser treinadas também para ter cuidado ao informar paciente e familiares sobre não haver mais possibilidade de cura. “Promover a saúde não é só o cuidado biológico”.
Banco de informações
Clisciene Magalhães defende que as diretivas de vontade deveriam ser catalogadas e aplicadas no sistema eletrônico do Sistema Único de Saúde. Assim não iria se tornar uma discussão específica para quando a pessoa está na situação terminal.
“É preciso sensibilizar a sociedade para esse tema. Ninguém sabe a hora que vai adoecer. É importante que todos nós possamos nos manifestar sobre como devemos ser tratados para um momento de doença terminal e incurável”. A lei tornou essa decisão pública. “Qualquer papel serve de registro”, destaca.
Nessa sensibilização, a assistente social diz que as pessoas deveriam prestar mais atenção a esses temas. “A pessoa tem o direito de escolher com quem quer estar no momento de cuidado, o cheiro do quarto. Tem o direito de se manifestar também sobre a despedida”.
A pesquisadora argumenta que a lei não pode estar restrita a quem tem mais recursos.
“Para a gente evoluir mais, é preciso que o país promova esse banco de informações para que todos nós possamos registrar publicamente [nossas vontades].”
Despedida
Um dos capítulos do livro trata sobre o codicilo – documento particular de última vontade, mais simples e menos solene do que um testamento tradicional, que trata dos temas do pós-morte. A pessoa tem o direito de expressar como quer sua despedida e também o que será feito do corpo.
A assistente social recomenda também que os familiares ajudem para que esse momento seja sensível e sincero, para que nem o paciente nem os mais próximos se sintam isolados.
“As crianças costumam ser excluídas. Isso pode gerar um trauma no processo de perda. Isso é uma violência. Não explicam para ela o que está acontecendo com aquele familiar”.
Na casa da família de Marcia Pinheiro, não foi assim. Por mais difícil que tenha sido a perda dos mais velhos, a família inteira ficou unida, incluindo a participação dos mais novos.
“Foi sempre muito natural. Foram momentos muito difíceis, mas também foi muito bonitos. A gente conseguiu ver muita beleza em tudo. A gente ria, a gente chorava…”, afirma entre pausas de saudades.
Saudades
As cinzas da mãe foram depositadas pelo pai junto à mangueira que ele comprou e plantou.
Depois, foram as cinzas dele que foram colocadas pelos filhos. A árvore ainda está em crescimento. Não é ainda gigante como a saudade que ficou na família.
Sem combinar, a família costuma visitar aquele espaço para sorrir, chorar e se abraçar como nas despedidas do velório.
Não há ainda nada marcado para este Dia de Finados (2). Em uma das últimas vezes que visitaram a árvore, os filhos leram uma carta que Antonio escreveu.
“Eu viverei em meus sucessores. Em cada um, eu viverei nas suas virtudes, nas suas imperfeições, nos seus sorrisos, nas suas lágrimas, nos seus dissabores, nas suas vitórias, nas suas derrotas. Viverei na árvore que plantei, a mangueira'”.
A família visita a mangueira para celebrar. “As pessoas podem achar estranho. A gente fica lá na frente de uma árvore, conversando, rezando, lembrando… A gente sente a força deles”.
Na memória da família, o afeto, as discussões, as brincadeiras e a certeza de que estão bem unidos até depois do que equivocadamente se costuma chamar de final.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: ‘Our aim is that children are protected’: besieged West Bank school fortifies its defences against settler violence
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: William Christou and Sufian Abu Taha in al-Mughayyir
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
This year, parents in al-Mughayyir had to be persuaded to send their children back to school. Israeli settlers had killed five teenage students last academic year – one of them at the school gates.
To reassure parents, teachers of the public secondary school gave a tour of the facilities, which they had spent the summer break fortifying. Metal fences now towered over the schoolyard’s walls and the door had been replaced by a sturdy metal gate. A new wall shielded the classrooms from a hilltop where last academic year a settler had shot dead two people, including a student.
Al-Mughayyir, a town of about 3,000 people north-east of Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, is under a siege by Israeli settlers. Armed settlers regularly raid the village, assaulting residents, attacking homes and seizing livestock. Israeli soldiers set up checkpoints that prevent people from entering or leaving for hours at a time.
The school is isolated on the very edge of the village, close to its entrance. Settlers stage their raids around the school, attacking under the watchful eye of the Israeli military.
A single Israeli soldier stands at the entrance of the village, his rifle slung over his shoulder as he paces back and forth idly. It is he who decides who can come and go in the village. The excited shouting of schoolchildren playing can be heard from where he stands; the children’s voices echo across the otherwise quiet village, most shops shuttered despite it being a weekday.
Residents say the violence is part of a wider project to displace Palestinians from their land, one that has already driven smaller communities from their homes. Now, they fear the same tactics are being turned against an entire village in an attempt to make life so intolerable that residents leave.
“When the settlers began their attacks, they began in the Jordan valley area, displacing communities of farmers consisting of 10, 20 people. Now, they are trying to displace entire villages. What’s happening in al-Mughayyir is the beginning of this project,” said Ameen Abu Alia, the 54-year-old mayor of the town.
Abu Alia has watched as the number of settler outposts – small groups of Israeli shepherds who establish outposts near Palestinian communities – has multiplied around the town over the last three years. In 2023, there was just one settler outpost near the town. Now, there are 12.
Settlers now enter the town on a regular basis, shutting down roads, and harassing residents as they graze their sheep on fields next to the school and deeper in the village. Residents say that settlers steal sheep from villagers, provoking fights with residents who depend on livestock for their livelihood. When villagers resist they can be arrested, or killed.
In 2024, settlers attacked a home in al-Mughayyir. Waheed Abu Naim, a 37-year-old schoolteacher, rushed to help defend it, trying to push the settler away. The settler put a pistol to Abu Naim’s breast and squeezed the trigger. Abu Naim closed his eyes, but no explosion followed – the settler had already fired his last bullet.
The settler siege is a tactic seen in the West Bank before. Small settler outposts run by teenagers and a few adults have popped up around small Bedouin communities in the Jordan river valley since 2023 and engaged in a steadily escalating campaign of violence to make life intolerable for the Palestinians living there. In Ras ‘Ein al-‘Auja in the south Jordan valley, settlers drove out the last inhabitants of the community in January after they could no longer endure the constant attacks, in a pattern similar to what is now happening in al-Mughayyir.
Despite settlements being considered illegal under international law, the Israeli government has taken few steps to curtail steadily expanding settler violence, beyond issuing a few condemnations. Extremist ministers in the Netanyahu government have equipped settlers with guns and vehicles and the rate of settlement expansion has soared under the current government.
The settler outposts are not visible from al-Mughayyir but are present just beyond the arid hills that ring the village. Residents drive fast along the winding 1-mile road that leads into the town, wary of how exposed they are to settler attacks along the way.
Local people describe close cooperation between Israeli soldiers and settlers. They often see them talking as settlers enter the town, and soldiers provide protection for settlers, only intervening when they – not Palestinians – are under threat.
In early September two teenagers, Omar al-Nassan, 19, and Khalil Abu Alia, 16, were killed by settlers and Israeli soldiers as the pair tried to stop settlers from taking their sheep, Abu Alia said.
“The last theft was of 60 sheep in the centre of the village. Ten military vehicles came. They came into the centre of the village and laid siege to that area. They stole the sheep and opened fire on people,” said Abu Alia.
The Israeli military said that it entered the village to provide security for an Israeli civilian and police trying to retrieve livestock, and that it fired on “key instigators” when Palestinians threw stones at the soldiers.
The village’s olive groves remain unpicked, despite the arrival of the season’s first rains, which signal the fruit is ripe: villagers are wary of the settler violence they have seen accompany harvests in neighbouring villages. Settlers have carried out more than 170 attacks since the start of the harvest at the end of September, according to Yesh Din, an Israeli rights group.
While settlers attack residents, the Israeli military is placing increasing restrictions on villagers. Olive production is a key industry, but residents have been prohibited from harvesting without prior military approval. The military closes the only entry to the village for several hours a day, several times a week, preventing people from going to work and teachers from reaching the school.
The result has been a slow strangulation of people’s livelihoods. Already, three families have left the village to be closer to their work, fearful of the constant road closures.
“Someone who has no money is now forced to sell part of their flock, and end their involvement in farming and search for other work,” said Abu Alia.
At the secondary school, teachers have developed emergency plans for settler attacks and incorporated lessons on avoiding confrontations into their curriculum, trying to preserve a sense of normality for their students.
“The school’s aim is that when the children enter the school, and when they go home, they are protected,” said Bassam Abu Assaf, the 54-year-old principal of al-Mughayyir secondary school. “The amount of time we spend sitting is almost nonexistent. Our eyes are outside the school. We’re thinking, God forbid, there could be a settler attack against us.”
Despite the precautions, students’ educations have inevitably been disrupted. About 80% of the school staff live outside the village, and they are often prevented from entering the school by the Israeli military checkpoint. School is only in session for three days a week, and ends early so teachers don’t get caught by the road closure, which typically happens in the afternoon. Once, the Israeli army shot teargas near the school and the noxious fumes blew into the classrooms, with teachers powerless to stop it.
“Today there was news that settlers were present outside. Now, the student is sitting in front of you, but they’re not paying attention. He’s thinking about the danger that could come from the army, from the settlers. ‘Where are the settlers? Where is the army?’ That’s what he’s thinking about,” said Abu Naim, the teacher. His own brother was killed last April in a settler attack outside the school.
“You try as much as possible to make the student concentrate with you – but the educational gap becomes very large because of the number of days when the student can’t concentrate,” he said.
Abu Assaf, who attended the school he now heads, remembers a different childhood in the village, when children could roam freely through the surrounding hills.
“We could walk around, coming and going. Everything was open. We’d have fun, we’d barbecue. Now, the kids are stuck in their homes, seeing the world through their phones,” he said.
At noon the bell rang, marking the end of the school day. Students gathered in the yard as teachers peered over the gates to see if any settlers were about. Seeing none, they let the students out.
“There is a plan of displacement. But we will raise another educated generation regardless. Our aim is to confront these attacks through education,” said Abu Naim.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Eleições nos EUA podem limitar poder de Trump e influenciar ofensiva contra o Brasil
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Rodrigo Chagas
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
Os Estados Unidos vão às urnas na próxima terça-feira (3) para definir o controle do Congresso durante os dois últimos anos do governo de Donald Trump, do Partido Republicano. A disputa acontece em um cenário de baixa popularidade do presidente, aumento do custo de vida e desgaste provocado pela guerra contra o Irã. Uma eventual vitória do Partido Democrata poderá limitar a atuação do governo estadunidense, inclusive nas medidas adotadas contra o Brasil após a reeleição de Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT).
Os republicanos controlam atualmente a Câmara dos Representantes, com 218 deputados contra 214 democratas, e o Senado, com 53 das 100 cadeiras. Para conquistar a maioria em qualquer uma das casas, os democratas precisam de um ganho líquido de quatro assentos. As eleições realizadas na metade do mandato presidencial, renovarão todas as 435 cadeiras da Câmara e 35 das 100 que compõem o Senado, além de definir governos estaduais e cargos locais.
Uma pesquisa Reuters/Ipsos divulgada na segunda-feira (26) apontou que 47% dos eleitores registrados pretendiam votar nos democratas, contra 36% nos republicanos. A aprovação de Trump ficou em 32%, próxima do menor patamar de seus dois mandatos. A preferência nacional pelos partidos, porém, não determina diretamente a distribuição das cadeiras, decididas em disputas estaduais e distritais.
Para Zoe Alexandra, diretora de notícias do BreakThrough News, a queda de popularidade de Trump tornou-se um dos principais argumentos das campanhas democratas, que apresentam a disputa como uma avaliação popular do governo.
“Se os democratas conseguirem uma maioria nas duas casas, será um golpe duro para Trump e para o MAGA”, afirma Alexandra, em entrevista ao Brasil de Fato, em referência ao movimento Make America Great Again (Faça a América Grande de Novo, em inglês), que reúne parte importante da base política do presidente.
Stephanie Weatherbee, da coordenação da Secretaria da Assembleia Internacional dos Povos (AIP), observa que o partido que ocupa a Presidência costuma enfrentar dificuldades nas eleições de meio de mandato, especialmente quando há insatisfação com a economia.
“Surpreendentemente, a margem de vitória dos democratas não é tão grande. Seria de esperar que, dada a aprovação tão baixa de Trump, a diferença entre os que favorecem os republicanos e os democratas fosse maior em favor dos democratas”, afirma.
O que pode mudar para o Brasil?
Uma nova maioria na Câmara ou no Senado poderia ampliar a fiscalização parlamentar sobre as medidas adotadas pelo governo Trump contra o Brasil, especialmente as tarifas comerciais, as sanções contra autoridades brasileiras e o envolvimento estadunidense nas disputas políticas do país.
O governo Trump utilizou instrumentos comerciais e diplomáticos para pressionar o Brasil desde 2025, justificando as medidas como resposta ao processo judicial que condenou Jair Bolsonaro por tentativa de golpe de Estado e às decisões da Justiça brasileira sobre a atuação das plataformas digitais. Também manifestou apoio à família Bolsonaro durante a eleição presidencial deste ano.
A tensão voltou a crescer após a vitória de Lula sobre Flávio Bolsonaro (PL), no último domingo (25). Trump questionou a lisura do resultado, sem apresentar provas de irregularidades, e autorizou a entrada do senador e de sua família nos Estados Unidos. Flávio chegou a Miami na quarta-feira (28), depois de deixar o Brasil pela Argentina, apesar de uma determinação judicial para entregar seus passaportes.
A contestação do resultado brasileiro contrasta com as avaliações das missões internacionais que acompanharam a votação. A Organização dos Estados Americanos (OEA) divulgou relatório preliminar sobre o segundo turno em 27 de outubro, enquanto o Centro Carter também acompanhou o processo eleitoral.
O reconhecimento internacional do pleito é considerado pela diplomacia brasileira um elemento de fortalecimento da posição de Lula diante das pressões externas.
Democratas pressionam Trump
A acolhida de Flávio por Trump provocou reações de parlamentares democratas. Um grupo de 25 deputados enviou uma carta ao secretário de Estado, Marco Rubio, cobrando explicações sobre a concessão de vistos à família Bolsonaro e a eventual participação de autoridades estadunidenses na saída do senador do Brasil.
Os congressistas querem saber se o Departamento de Estado tinha conhecimento das investigações contra Flávio e da ordem judicial brasileira, além de questionarem o possível uso de recursos diplomáticos para facilitar sua viagem. Também pedem esclarecimentos sobre eventuais contatos com autoridades da Argentina e do Equador, países por onde o senador passou antes de chegar aos EUA.
Um relatório do Serviço de Pesquisa do Congresso dos Estados Unidos, atualizado também na quinta-feira, aponta que o Legislativo pode fiscalizar a utilização de sanções, tarifas, vistos e recursos de assistência externa pelo Executivo. Os parlamentares também podem propor restrições legais e orçamentárias a determinadas medidas.
O documento registra que o Senado aprovou, em outubro de 2025, uma resolução para encerrar a emergência nacional declarada por Trump em relação ao Brasil. A proposta ainda depende de tramitação na Câmara e enfrenta a possibilidade de veto presidencial.
As mudanças no Congresso poderiam, portanto, abrir novas frentes de pressão sobre a Casa Branca. Isso não significa que os democratas conseguiriam reverter automaticamente as sanções ou obrigar Trump a reconhecer o resultado eleitoral brasileiro.
Fontes ouvidas pelo Brasil de Fato no Itamaraty indicam que uma eventual maioria democrata em pelo menos uma das casas do Congresso poderá favorecer o Brasil, especialmente nas relações com as grandes plataformas digitais e nas negociações ambientais.
A avaliação nos bastidores do Itamaraty é de que a reeleição de Lula fortaleceu a posição diplomática do Brasil, permitindo preservar a estratégia adotada durante o tarifaço de 2025, quando Brasília manteve as negociações comerciais mesmo diante das sanções impostas pelo governo Trump.
A acolhida a Flávio ocorre em um contexto de endurecimento das operações do Serviço de Imigração e Controle de Alfândegas (ICE), responsável por prisões e deportações de imigrantes. A agência registrou quase 51 mil prisões em agosto, um recorde pelo terceiro mês consecutivo.
O próprio Alexandre Ramagem, ex-chefe de inteligência do governo Bolsonaro e foragido da justiça brasileira, foi preso pelo ICE, mas solto dias depois.
Para Zoe Alexandra, a autorização de entrada concedida ao senador brasileiro evidencia o tratamento diferenciado dado a aliados políticos de Trump, enquanto milhares de imigrantes enfrentam detenções e deportações. “É outro exemplo desse privilégio das elites e do desprezo pelo povo”, afirma.
Guerra e custo de vida pressionam Trump
A economia é uma das principais preocupações dos eleitores estadunidenses. Na pesquisa Reuters/Ipsos de outubro, 73% dos entrevistados avaliaram que o custo de vida estava seguindo na direção errada.
A guerra iniciada pelos Estados Unidos e por Israel contra o Irã, no fim de fevereiro, agravou as pressões sobre os preços da energia. Segundo estimativa do Pentágono obtida pela Associated Press, o conflito já teria custado US$ 47,1 bilhões ao país, sem contar com os prejuízos provocados pelos ataques iranianos a instalações militares estadunidenses.
Weatherbee alerta que o conflito também contraria as expectativas de parte dos eleitores que apoiaram Trump por suas promessas de reduzir os custos domésticos e evitar novos envolvimentos militares.
“Há uma insatisfação muito grande, inclusive dentro de uma parte da base do Partido Republicano, a parte que é mais de baixa renda, sobre o efeito da guerra e sobre a falta de políticas para reduzir a inflação e o custo do combustível e dos alimentos”, explica.
Os preços dos seguros de saúde, dos serviços médicos e dos medicamentos também aparecem entre as preocupações apontadas pela pesquisadora. Segundo ela, o descontentamento nessas áreas atinge os dois partidos, mas tende a pesar especialmente sobre os republicanos por controlarem a Presidência e o Congresso.
Alexandra relaciona a deterioração da economia à estratégia militar do governo estadunidense, mas destaca que a insatisfação com a política externa não começou com a guerra contra o Irã. As mobilizações contra o financiamento militar a Israel durante o genocídio palestino já haviam ampliado o debate sobre o envolvimento dos Estados Unidos em conflitos internacionais.
“Antes se dizia que o eleitor estadunidense não se importava com a política externa como tema das eleições. Hoje é um tema muito importante”, afirma.
A jornalista também cita as operações contra a Venezuela e o aumento da presença militar estadunidense na América Latina. Na avaliação dela, cresce a percepção de que as intervenções estrangeiras podem agravar crises migratórias que o próprio governo Trump utiliza para justificar sua política de deportações.
“Dizem que precisam deportar todas essas pessoas, mas, ao mesmo tempo, vão desestabilizar o continente para que haja mais fluxo migratório”, resume.
Até onde os democratas podem mudar os EUA?
Uma vitória democrata na Câmara permitiria ampliar investigações parlamentares, convocar integrantes do governo e exercer maior influência sobre a aprovação do orçamento. O controle do Senado também daria ao partido instrumentos para bloquear nomeações de autoridades, incluindo integrantes do Judiciário federal.
Trump manteria o poder de veto sobre projetos aprovados pelo Congresso, além de importantes atribuições executivas nas áreas de política externa, imigração e segurança nacional. Para derrubar um veto presidencial, seria necessária uma maioria de dois terços nas duas casas.
A guerra contra o Irã é um exemplo dessas limitações. Parlamentares podem tentar restringir o emprego das Forças Armadas por meio de resoluções baseadas na legislação sobre poderes de guerra, mas enfrentam obstáculos políticos e jurídicos para impor limites ao Executivo.
Weatherbee lembra que a utilização desse mecanismo dependeria não apenas de uma maioria democrata, mas também da capacidade de reunir apoio suficiente para superar um eventual veto presidencial. Uma diferença pequena de cadeiras entre os partidos tornaria essa tarefa particularmente difícil.
“É difícil imaginar que, se os democratas tiverem uma maioria pequena, conseguiriam pôr fim à guerra no Irã”, afirma.
A pesquisadora também lembra que o Partido Democrata sustentou o financiamento militar a Israel durante o governo de Joe Biden, inclusive nos momentos mais críticos da ofensiva israelense contra a população palestina.
Zoe Alexandra aponta dificuldades semelhantes para eventuais mudanças na política migratória. O Congresso já aprovou recursos expressivos para ampliar a estrutura federal de fiscalização, detenção e deportação, com verbas previstas para exercícios fiscais futuros. A mudança da maioria legislativa não eliminaria automaticamente esses recursos nem as atribuições do Executivo.
“Os democratas estão dizendo que podem retomar as duas casas e fazer mudanças reais. Mas, quando tiveram esse poder no passado, não fizeram isso”, critica.
Weatherbee destaca, ainda, a influência do financiamento empresarial sobre as decisões dos dois partidos. Ela cita como exemplo os setores farmacêutico e de seguros privados de saúde, cujas contribuições eleitorais tendem a dificultar a aprovação de políticas contrárias aos interesses dessas empresas.
Segundo levantamento divulgado pela Reuters, a publicidade política nos Estados Unidos já havia movimentado aproximadamente US$ 3,8 bilhões até outubro. O empresário Elon Musk destinou, sozinho, cerca de US$ 366 milhões ao apoio a candidatos republicanos, conforme registros de financiamento eleitoral.
A esquerda democrata
A disputa pelo futuro do Partido Democrata também passa pelo avanço de candidaturas vinculadas ao Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), organização que defende a ampliação dos direitos sociais, o fortalecimento dos sindicatos e o enfrentamento do poder econômico das grandes corporações. O grupo apoia 131 candidatos nas eleições de novembro, dos quais dez disputam vagas na Câmara dos Representantes.
Nas eleições primárias, candidaturas socialistas derrotaram parlamentares democratas tradicionais, como Melat Kiros, de 29 anos, que venceu Diana DeGette, deputada há quase três décadas pelo Colorado. Em Nova York, Darializa Avila Chevalier derrotou Adriano Espaillat, enquanto Claire Valdez conquistou a indicação democrata para uma cadeira aberta. Há expectativa de crescimento na atual representação, que tem duas cadeiras na Câmara.
Stephanie Weatherbee considera que essa disputa revela uma dificuldade dos democratas em enfrentar o avanço da extrema direita. “É importante notar que os democratas, tanto nesta eleição como em outras, estão mais focados em minimizar a força potencial de candidatos mais progressistas, de esquerda, como os candidatos do DSA, do que em minimizar o crescimento da extrema direita”, afirma.
A pesquisadora também chama atenção para os obstáculos à participação eleitoral, como as leis que exigem documentos específicos de identificação para votar e o gerrymandering, prática de manipulação dos limites dos distritos eleitorais para favorecer determinados partidos.
Em 24 estados, os eleitores precisam apresentar documentos com fotografia, exigência que, segundo organizações de defesa dos direitos eleitorais, pode dificultar a participação de pessoas pobres e integrantes de minorias.
Segundo ela, os republicanos promoveram essas mudanças ao longo de décadas, enquanto os democratas não organizaram uma resistência suficientemente consistente. As regras podem prejudicar desproporcionalmente a representação de comunidades negras, latinas e de baixa renda, dependendo de sua aplicação em cada estado.
“Esse processo é muito antigo, vem acontecendo ao longo dos últimos 20 anos e esse é o caráter verdadeiramente antidemocrático dessa eleição”, conclui.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live.title: US midterm elections 2026 live: Americans go to the polls in referendum on Trump’s agenda
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live.author: Chris Hippensteel and Lucy Campbell (now); Yohannes Lowe (earlier)
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live.text:
What is being decided in the midterms and why do they matter?
David Smith
The US Congress has two chambers: the House of Representatives and theSenate. Both must approve federal legislation before it can become law and both play important roles in overseeing the executive branch.
The House is elected every two years, meaning all 435 voting seats are contested at every congressional election. The Senate has 100 members serving staggered six-year terms, so roughly a third of its seats are up for election every two years.
This year’s ballot includes:
All 435 seats in the House of Representatives. Republicans are defending a narrow majority, with Democrats needing a net gain of four seats to take control.
35 seats in the Senate. Thirty-three seats are up in regular elections, along with two special elections in Florida and Ohio to fill the remainder of terms that were vacated early. Republicans currently hold 53 seats, against 47 held by Democrats and independents who caucus with them. Democrats need to gain four seats to secure a majority.
39 governorships. Voters will choose governors in 36 states and three US territories.
Thousands of state legislative seats, as well as local offices, judicial contests and ballot measures on issues including taxes, abortion rights and voting rules.
The elections for Congress will determine which party controls Congress for the final two years of Trump’s second term. The governorships and state legislative contests will shape policymaking closer to home, from education and reproductive rights to taxation and the administration of elections.
The midterms have a long history of punishing the occupant of the White House. The president’s party has lost House seats in 18 of the past 20 midterm elections, a 90% rate of loss that stretches back to 1946.
Speaking to reporters after casting his ballot in Michigan, Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers denounced what he called “vicious” Democratic attacks on Haley Stevens, the former Democratic primary candidate who abandoned her party to endorse him in the eleventh hour before the midterms.
“Obviously I’m disappointed in how vicious they’ve been,” Rogers told reporters assembled in a parking lot “But I think that speaks to who the modern Democrat party is.”
Rogers continued: “Here’s somebody who said ‘I voted Democrat all the way down the list, except for one person who I think is too extreme for our state.’ That’s country over party. They ought to celebrate her courage and encourage her to continue being a Democrat rather than trying to throw her out of the party.”
“I’ve never seen such viciousness online.”
Stevens, the erstwhile challenger of Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed, broke with her party to endorse Rogers over the weekend, after a renewed public break with El-Sayed over an issue that fiercely divided them in their primary race: US support for Israel.
The line to vote at Burbank Early Childhood School in Columbus, Ohio grew long as hundreds of people filed into the polling site to vote throughout the morning.
Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican candidate for governor, voted at the site alongside his wife, Apoorva Ramaswamy. He said before entering the school:
At the start of this day, if I have one suggestion to those who are deciding how to vote today, vote for the person who can actually make your life better. Vote for the person who you believe in your heart of hearts is actually going to make your family’s life better.
This election, especially for the role of governor, comes down to who’s going to allow your family to live a better life.
He added, “Our work begins tomorrow morning”.
After filing into the building, Ramaswamy and his wife stood in line with other voters.
Some voters experienced minor issues as they tried to cast their ballot. “My voting machine didn’t work, and I was standing next to Ramaswamy and thought that was kind of ironic,” said Andrea, a Columbus native.
Several other voters turned around when they saw the line. “I’ll try again in the afternoon,” said John Pearson.
On election day, Georgia resident Bunny Calloway tells our colleague George Chidi about her hopes for AI regulation and expresses concerns about misinformation and the possibility of people not honoring the outcome of the midterm results.
Two days of torrential downpours gave way to a brighter morning in south Florida, where voters took advantage of the brief respite to show up at soggy polling stations in what officials said were encouraging numbers.
At Ramblewood elementary school in the Fort Lauderdale suburb of Coral Springs, Curt Tiefenbrun, president of the local Democratic club and a water district candidate, dodged an early shower to greet a “receptive” line of voters when the polls opened at 7am.
“We had a pretty good turnout this morning before everybody had to go to work. They’re very enthusiastic as they accept our voter guide, and we’ve seen a lot of Democrats come out. We’re really happy with that,” he said.
Sunday it rained for hours and people were coming out to vote. All of us were standing out there wearing our ponchos, handing out guides. It was fun to see everybody come out and really participate.
Florida election officials released early voting figures on Tuesday showing registered Republicans in the state returned over 250,000 more ballots than Democrats - 1.49 million to 1.21m. Democrats are hoping in-person turnout on Tuesday, together with support from hundreds of thousands of independent voters and Republicans disillusioned with their party, will help them overcome the deficit.
Tiefenbrun said Democratic turnout in early voting was “extremely encouraging” compared to what he saw in 2024 and 2022. “We’re hoping we can stay above the fray, so to speak, on this final day, election day,” he said.
Polls are set to begin opening in Alaska, which is hosting the competitive Senate race between Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan and Mary Peltola, his Democratic challenger.
The race has been complicated by revelations that Peltola’s campaign allegedly recruited another man named Dan Sullivan to join the race, hoping to peel ballots away from the incumbent. While the tactic wasn’t clearly illegal, it’s prompted calls from the Trump administration to toss out the results if Sullivan doesn’t win out, and to investigate Peltola’s campaign for potential criminal violations.
A federal judge recently denied a Department of Justice request to block the race’s certification, and the state of Alaska – itself investigating Peltola – assured the court that ballots were designed to minimize confusion. But we’ll learn over the coming days just how many votes the imposter Sullivan will receive – and if it’s enough to sway the outcome of a crucial contest.
Trump tells Fox he'll slash aid to Israel by end of this year
In an interview with Fox & Friends this morning, in which he made a meandering final pitch to Americans voting in the 2026 midterm election, Trump said that he had agreed with Benjamin Netanyahu to cut off $4 billion of US military aid to Israel.”
“Bibi Netanyahu and I have made a deal,” Trump said. “We give Isreal $4 billion a year, and we made a deal months ago that we’re stopping. And they’re fine with it, because, you know, they’ve become a very successful country. They don’t need it. And we won’t be paying anymore to Israel.”
Trump said that the deal came at the insistence of Netanyahu, whose political future is in doubt following an Israeli election that failed to deliver the longtime prime minister a clear majority.
US ties to Israel, the country’s conduct in Gaza, and the conflict with Iran have become major issues in the 2026 midterm election.
‘Call me senator after tomorrow’: Democrat Abdul El-Sayed mocks Trump in final rally – video
Michigan’s Democratic Senate nominee, Abdul El-Sayed, mocked Donald Trump and rallied supporters alongside senator Elizabeth Warren in Detroit, in a final push for votes before Tuesday’s midterm elections. Progressive El-Sayed is seeking to hold an open seat for Democrats against Republican Mike Rogers, who received a last-minute endorsement from Democratic congresswoman Haley Stevens.
A leading abortion rights group has endorsed Troy Jackson, the Democratic Senate candidate for Maine, while attacking the record of his Republican opponent, Senator Susan Collins.
Mini Timmaraju, president of the advocacy group Reproductive Freedom for All, hailed Jackson - who was formerly an opponent of abortion - for “evolving” on the issue at a last-minute canvassing event in Scarborough. At the same time, she attacked Collins for trying to depict herself as “pro-choice”, saying she had voted to confirm the conservative US Supreme Court justice, Samuel Alito, who was the author of the 2022 court ruling that overturned the historic Roe versus Wade decision that guaranteed the right to an abortion. Jackson has repeatedly criticised Collins’ 2018 vote to confirm another conservative justice, Brett Kavanaugh, who subsequently voted to overturn Roe v Wade.
Timmaraju said Jackson’s election was vital to counteract a Trump administration plan to be “hand-off on abortion post-midterms” that she said would make it easer to dismantle state protections.
“We know the Trump administration has plans for a few weeks from now to reverse on abortion, to make it harder to get,” she said. “If we do not put Troy Jackson in the Senate, we won’t have that protection in Maine, where so many Mainers get access to abortion through the mail, through Telehealth.
“There are so many ways to ban abortion, by going around the states, and that is what the Trump administration is extremely interested in.”
Doug Emerson, a self-described activist, parked his car, festooned with slogans protesting the Trump administration’s policies, outside the office of Senator Susan Collins in Portland, Maine’s biggest city.
Emerson said he wanted to bring the attention of Maine voters to what he described as Collins’ tacit collusion with Donald Trump’s most extreme actions, despite her image as a moderate, independent-minded Republican cultivated over five terms as the state’s senator.
“We can’t change things unless we alter the demographics of the current Congress,” said Emerson. “I’m not sure Mainers are paying close enough attention.”
Astronauts For America, an alliance of more than 100 former Nasa explorers, has written an election day open letter to US voters reminding them of the importance of their vote in defending constitutional principles against threats to democracy.
“Federal authority is not a license for any president or federal agency to take over state election administration,” the letter, also signed by ther non-partisan, pro-democracy groups National Security Leaders for America and Leadership Now, said.
“Regardless of political party or personal beliefs, every American should be able to trust that elections are conducted according to the law, every lawful vote is counted, and the results are determined through established legal procedures - not political pressure or the arbitrary exercise of power.”
Astronauts For America, which includes astronauts from almost every generation of US spaceflight from Apollo to the space shuttle, recently completed a nationwide tour of college campuses urging young and first-time voters to ensure their voices are heard.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ru.title: Russian Teenager Detained After Posting Neo-Nazi Threats on TikTok, Targeting Moscow Museum
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ru.author: Hikmat Mohammed
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ru.text:
The US embassy in Moscow put a warning on its website Saturday, alerting US citizens of “a credible threat of a mass casualty event” at the Tsaritsyno Museum Reserve in Moscow. The palace museum and large park reserve are 10 miles from the Kremlin.
Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) said it followed the warning from US officials and detained a teenage boy on suspicion of planning a terrorist attack, reports Bloomberg.
The Russian state-run news agency Tass reported that the teenager had been posting videos on TikTok holding an automatic weapon while wearing tactical gear and a balaclava. He simultaneously posted photos of the Tsaritsyno with the caption “I found a place.” According to the FSB, the teenager was engaging with neo-Nazi content on Telegram and had made a “significant number of search queries regarding past terrorist acts, mass murders, and other violent acts.”
As a result of the threat, scheduled events at the museum were canceled and tight security measures were put in place. Baza, the Russian investigative Telegram channel, reported that the venue was evacuated on Saturday, cutting an organ concert short with about 10 minutes left, as well as canceling a concert dedicated to folk traditions of the North Caucasus region.
“The above-mentioned items of clothing and accessories were found at the detainee’s residence, and his communications devices contained a TikTok account used to post threats, a subscription to a neo-Nazi channel on the Telegram messenger,” the FSB said in a statement. “We are grateful to the American side for the information provided.”

https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/israe.title: Israeli prison guards ‘shot prominent Palestinian detainees nine times’
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/israe.author: MEE staff
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/israe.text:
Israeli prison guards ‘shot prominent Palestinian detainees nine times’
Israeli prison guards shot and wounded prominent Palestinian detainee Hassan Salameh nine times last month, his fiancee and a prisoners' rights group have said.
The assault on Salameh, 55, came after National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir stormed his cell and filmed himself threatening to kill him.
The Palestinian Prisoners’ Society (PPS), which monitors the conditions of Palestinian detainees, said it received information about the assault following a visit to Salameh by a lawyer on Monday.
Information provided to the group and Salameh’s fiancee, Ghufran Zamel, indicated that he had been severely beaten and shot nine times.
The type of ammunition used and the precise circumstances of the shooting remain unclear.
New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch
Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
Israeli prison guards have recently stepped up the use of rubber-coated bullets against prisoners, firing at them from close range inside their cells.
The practice has caused severe injuries and potentially irreversible harm, according to rights groups.
PPS said Israeli restrictions on prison visits had prevented the lawyer from obtaining further details.
“This has raised serious concerns about the prisoner's fate and underscores the urgent need to disclose the circumstances of the incident and guarantee his physical safety,” the group said.
Zamel told local media that Salameh was beaten before Ben Gvir's visit and after he left. An Israeli force stormed the cell, subjecting him to a severe beating, including blows to the face, before firing nine bullets at him.
Three days after the assault, Salameh was taken to have his injuries photographed. He was then returned to his cell without medical treatment and given only painkillers, despite the injuries he had sustained, Zamel said.
According to Zamel, Monday's visit by the lawyer confirmed that Salameh was still suffering from the effects of the assault and remained in poor health. He appeared visibly exhausted.
PPS said the attack came amid what it described as a campaign targeting prominent Palestinian prisoners, which goes “beyond repression and punishment” and places their lives at risk.
“Prisoner leaders are facing various forms of physical and psychological torture, systematic crackdowns and public threats to kill them made by Israel's far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben Gvir,” the group said.
“The continuation of these policies, alongside restrictions on visits and the absence of independent oversight, paves the way for further violations and deprives prisoners of even the most basic protection.”
Escalating abuse
Born in the Khan Younis refugee camp in southern Gaza in 1971, Salameh became involved in Palestinian resistance against the Israeli occupation after the outbreak of the First Intifada in 1987.
He later became a leading figure in the armed wing of Hamas, the al-Qassam Brigades. In 1996, Israel convicted him of orchestrating several bombings that killed and wounded scores of Israelis.
Salameh said the attacks were carried out in response to Israel's assassination of Hamas bombmaker Yahya Ayyash earlier that year.
He was sentenced to 48 life terms and has spent a total of 14 years in solitary confinement since his imprisonment 30 years ago.
In September, Ben Gvir posted a video showing himself in Salameh’s cell, surrounded by security guards, as he told him that he wanted to "execute" him.
The minister also vowed to ensure prisoners such as Salameh were "put to death" if he became defence minister.
Palestinian prisoners, particularly prominent figures such as Salameh, have long faced abuse by Israeli prison authorities.
However, reports of abuse have escalated since the Gaza war and genocide began in October 2023. Several rights groups have accused Israeli prison authorities of widespread torture, physical assaults, sexual violence, starvation, medical neglect and humiliation of prisoners since then.
Last month, Physicians for Human Rights Israel and the Public Committee Against Torture in Israel said they had collected 21 testimonies documenting what they described as a “dangerous practice” of prison guards firing rubber-coated bullets at prisoners from close range.
In one incident, an Israeli prison guard seriously wounded a Palestinian prisoner by firing rubber-coated bullets at his testicle. His right testicle was “completely crushed” and had to be surgically removed.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/hi.title: Pace’s Marc Glimcher Responds to Reported Financial Loss, High Museum of Art Former COO Sentenced to Prison for Embezzlement, and More: Morning Links for November 3, 2026
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/hi.author: Hikmat Mohammed
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/hi.text:
To receive Morning Links in your inbox every weekday, sign up for our Breakfast with ARTnews newsletter.
Good Morning!
- Pace CEO Marc Glimcher responded to ARTnews about reports of financial losses and the gallery’s direction.
- Brady Lum, former COO of the High Museum of Art has been sentenced to one year in federal prison.
- For the first time, lawmakers in Italy are examining a new bill to facilitate the restitution of art and cultural items looted between 1933 and 1945.
The Headlines
KEEP UP THE PACE. Pace CEO Marc Glimcher responded to ARTnews about reports of financial losses and the gallery’s direction. “Everything is turning,” Glimcher said over the phone, noting a “record” Art Basel Paris last month, “sellout shows” helping business get back in the black and a new location expansion in Europe coming “fairly soon.” Last week, Pace published its accounts with Companies House, showing significant losses in turnover for 2024 and 2025. Glimcher said: “We did a balance sheet shift, which appears to be a loss because we’re changing around the way we invest money and take money from other units and let the money flow through each unit independently.” He added that the 50 artists dropped by the gallery in June “were not artists that we had a super active engagement with,” and “it wasn’t benefiting them or us.” He is also working on moving into a new space in London, to be decided. “When we have the space and announce it, it’s going to make a lot of sense to everybody,” he said.
DOING TIME. The High Museum of Art’s former COO, Brady Lum, has been sentenced to one year in federal prison, followed by one year of supervised release, for embezzling over $600,000 from the museum by tampering with invoices and approving personal purchases, announced Georgia’s United States Attorney’s Office. “Lum brazenly pilfered hundreds of thousands of dollars from a beloved civic institution to pay for his high-end guitars and other personal items,” said US Attorney Theodore S. Hertzberg. “His appalling breach of trust damaged not only the High Museum but also the larger art community,” he added. Lum served as Atlanta’s High Museum of Art COO from January 2, 2019, to December 9, 2025. He has paid back the full, stolen $607,688 to the museum, plus another $500,000 to cover costs the museum spent to uncover his own crime.
The Digest
Lawmakers in Italy are examining a new bill to create a committee that will research provenance and facilitate the restitution of art and cultural items pillaged by Nazis and Italian police between 1933 and 1945. [The Art Newspaper]
A city council in New South Wales will not exhibit Phil Buehler’s “Wall of Tears” installation memorializing the names of children killed in Gaza, due to cited safety concerns. [The Guardian]
In an interview pegged to a new limited-edition collaboration with watchmaker Hublot, Jeff Koons said: “I never think about price. I know I’m associated with very valuable things, but it’s not something I think about. I believe in the value that things have for humanity, in a conceptual way. In the knowledge and care they reflect.” [El País]
Despite turmoil at the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, its prestigious annual Kennedy Center Honors celebration for lifetime achievement is pressing forward, awarding the likes of pop singer Paul Anka, playwright David Mamet, actor Andy Garcia, and country singer Barbara Mandrell. [The New York Times]
An unknown, intimate drawing by Duncan Grant of Vanessa Bell, the English artist and sister of Virginia Woolf, was discovered amid research for Tate Britain’s forthcoming show on Bell and Grant. [FAD Magazine]
The Kicker
ART WANTED, DEAD OR ALIVE. Thanks to an inventive “WANTED” campaignby the Musée des Beaux-Arts d’Orléans in France, aimed at tracking down hundreds of WWII-era looted artworks, one painting has just been found, reports Le Journal des Arts. The stolen painting by Dutch artist Willem Cornelisz Duyster, titled Le Buveur, was located at an auction house in Switzerland and is expected to be restituted to the museum shortly. Its owner purchased the painting in the 1990s, agreed to hand over the artwork, and said they had not known of its problematic provenance. In June 1940, Nazis attacked the city of Orléans, burning an annex of its fine arts museum, known as the Musée Paul Fourché, which was subsequently almost entirely ransacked, likely by people on both sides of the conflict. Some 350 paintings from Europe, dating back to the 16th century, were lost.

https://www.middleeasteye.net/opinion/ho.title: How an election defeat triggered a carnival of racism against Palestinians
https://www.middleeasteye.net/opinion/ho.author: Lubna Masarwa

How an election defeat triggered a carnival of racism against Palestinians
A day before the Israeli elections, I was walking through a well-heeled, leafy neighbourhood in West Jerusalem, five minutes from President Issac Herzog’s official residence.
I was on my way to interview an expert on Palestinian citizens of Israel, who were expected to vote in large numbers for the first time.
Three children - they could not have been more than seven or eight - jumped off the slides in a playground and ran towards me.
One of them asked whom I was going to vote for. A funny question, I thought, coming from kids.
I told them I would vote for the Joint List. The leader of the group asked, “What is the Joint List? Is it Bibi?” I said no, without explaining that it was an Arab bloc of parties.
New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch
Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
The kid said: “So you’re not voting for Netanyahu?”
I said no. He spat at me, and the other two gave me the middle finger.
They must have thought I was a Jew defecting from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s camp. I wondered what they would have done if they knew I was Palestinian.
Kids spitting at a middle-aged woman didn’t seem to bother any of the passersby.
To liberal Zionists, this election was a debate about the boundaries of Israeli democracy, and whether it could include us as Arabs.
Wherever you look in the streets and highways, you will see neon signs, stickers, or big election billboards warning Jews about Palestinians
But the more I think about it, something far deeper is going on than mere hatred of a minority group, deeply entrenched though that is. The reaction to 7 October merely brought it out into the open.
Wherever you look in the streets and highways, you will see neon signs, stickers, or big election billboards warning Jews about Palestinians, and calling openly for more occupation, expulsion and deportation.
Palestinians who live in the city have to hold their breath if they want to live with this reality. They have no right to complain against another sticker calling on them to be killed or expelled.
It’s not just in every debate in this election campaign. You can hear it in small conversations in the street: “We will not sit with the Arabs.”
All the discussion is about how to build coalitions without the votes of the Arabs.
Palestinians vote for survival
Three Israeli political parties ran on platforms that openly support the deportation, displacement and expulsion of Palestinians - even those with Israeli citizenship.
Bezalel Smotrich, the finance minister and head of the Religious Zionism party, has made “Judaising” the Galilee and Negev regions of Israel, where many Palestinians citizens live, a key feature of his election campaign.
All of this was orchestrated by the person who by rights should be Israel’s outgoing prime minister, Netanyahu, but who continues as its caretaker.
Haaretz analysed Netanyahu’s social media activity on election day. Every second post by the prime minister was against Arabs, laying the groundwork for claims about the integrity of the vote.
The response of Palestinian citizens of Israel, who make up a fifth of the population, was immediate. They flocked to the polls, gaining an unheard-of 19 seats, and became the third-largest parliamentary bloc after Likud and Yashar.
Those who had boycotted elections for their entire lives went to vote for the first time.
This was not some sudden revelation. Every Palestinian understood that they were only part of Israel as window dressing, to make it look democratic, but with no meaningful ability to change their lives. In the past, just over half of them voted.
The genocide in Gaza did not end there. It could well continue in Israel itself
But this time, it was different.
The Palestinians of Israel know that what happened in Gaza, and is continuing to happen in the occupied West Bank, could happen to them too.
Israel committed genocide and got away with it. This vote is a survival vote; an expressed, very existential fear.
Palestinian sociologist Ameer Fakhoury told Middle East Eye: “The moment your existence becomes the central concern, the very meaning of citizenship changes. A citizen, in the substantive sense, should not have to engage in politics simply to avoid death.
“This is not how citizenship is supposed to function. When survival becomes the dominant motivation, the boundaries of ordinary political participation collapse. The symbolic and substantive meaning of citizenship is fundamentally undermined.”
Such a result in a “normal” democratic country would have ended with the opposition winning.
But not in Israel. Netanyahu’s initial loss became an orgy, a festival of racism against Palestinians.
No good or bad Arabs
Channel 12 News reported that on election day and its aftermath, there was a 400 percent rise in racist discourse against Arabs on social media, as Arabs were accused of stealing the elections.
Ayala Hasson, the veteran journalist of Israel’s public broadcaster, Kan 11, claimed, without any proof, that some of the 19 newly elected Knesset members from the Palestinian-led parties, Ra’am and the Joint List, “transferred money to Hamas”.
Hasson, a pro-Netanyahu journalist, also questioned the integrity of the elections, saying that Palestinian voters received envelopes with money as part of an illegal voter mobilisation campaign.
It doesn’t really matter what your politics are. The fact that you are an Arab is proof enough of your guilt.
Mansour Abbas, the leader of Ra’am, has openly adopted a Zionist agenda by acknowledging the Jewish state and calling for national service.
He received the same treatment. This means that even Palestinians who strip themselves of their national identity cannot be part of a political system designed for Jews only.
The same thing happened to Lucy Aharish, an Arab journalist married to an Israeli Jew who served as a combat soldier in the reserves during the genocide in Gaza.
Aharish was savaged by prominent figures in Likud.
Itzik Bonzel, a Likud candidate, posted on Facebook: “You can walk around our streets as much as you like, but merely living among us does not make you Israeli in any way, and you will never be part of us, nor part of the people of Israel.”
Aharish is an opponent of the Palestinian national cause. Bonzel said she was “a foreign body, without any real roots in this land, and you will never be an Israeli”, concluding with a threat: “Know your place.”
Arabs in Israel can no longer ignore the fact that for large groups in Israel, possibly now the majority, there are no good or bad Arabs. It matters not who goes over to their side.
For them, Palestinians are illegitimate and should be expelled from the Jewish state.
The genocide in Gaza did not end there. It could well continue in Israel itself - and this should not be ignored by the Palestinian leadership.
I was asked in an interview with a Canadian radio station whether I thought Palestinians would vote again in future elections. Did this result inspire them?
For a moment I was taken aback by the stupidity of this question.
“I am not inspired, I am terrified,” I replied.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Judge orders Iowa to permit Satanic Temple holiday event at state capitol
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Michael Sainato
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
A federal judge ordered state officials in Iowa on Monday to permit a local Satanic Temple organization to hold a holiday event in the rotunda of the state capitol after years of denying the group’s application.
The religious organization and Iowa Republican state officials have been in a legal battle over the group’s applications to hold a holiday event at the state capitol in recent years.
Republicans in Iowa, who currently control the governorship and majorities in the state house and senate, have cited the capitol building’s policies prohibiting gratuitous violence and obscene displays as justification for denying the applications.
According to the office of the attorney general, Brenna Bird, state Republicans intend to appeal the federal judge’s decision.
The Satanic Temple and Iowa chapter leader filed a lawsuit in August, alleging discrimination from former and current state officials.
Chief District Judge Stephanie M Rose stated in her court order that the group was likely to succeed on its free speech claim and ordered the current director of the Iowa department of administrative services to approve the holiday event application within seven days.
The Satanic Temple (TST), which was founded in Salem, Massachusetts, in 2013, characterizes itself as a “non-theistic religious organization” that advocates for secularism and emphasizes separation from the Church of Satan founded in 1966.
The Satanic Temple argues it does not believe in Satan, rather arguing it uses Satan as a symbol to protest against religious authoritarianism.
“Satan is a symbol of the Eternal Rebel in opposition to arbitrary authority, forever defending personal sovereignty even in the face of insurmountable odds,” the Satanic Temple’s website states. It adds: “Satanists adhere to the principles of individual sovereignty and the rejection of tyrannical authority.”
In December 2023, the group had a religious holiday display in the Iowa state capitol, but it was vandalized by a Christian military veteran. The Turning Point founder, Charlie Kirk, pledged $10,000 to the accused vandal’s legal defense. The following year, the Satanic Temple’s application for a holiday display and event was denied.
“State officials have made it clear that they denied TST permission to hold events in the Capitol rotunda because they disagreed with their religious viewpoint,” said Shefali Aurora, ACLU of Iowa staff attorney, in a statement on the court order. “It is a foundational principle that the government cannot restrict speech in this way, favor one religion over another, or discriminate against religious groups because they don’t agree with them.”
The group said its proposed holiday event would include costumes of the European folklore character Krampus, caroling, coloring for children and ornament making. In its denial of the application, state officials cited sticks included in the costumes that could be used as weapons and policies meant to protect children who might be present in the public space.
Judge Rose wrote that the state officials’ arguments did not justify the denials, noting the argument that the character Krampus might scare children was “not a permissible basis for excluding speech” and the argument about the sticks included with the costumes “cannot justify denying the entire event”.
The Iowa department of administrative services and the Republican governor, Kim Reynolds, have not yet commented on the court order.
In 2023, Governor Reynolds stated in response to the group’s holiday display at the state capitol, “like many Iowans, I find the Satanic Temple’s display in the Capitol absolutely objectionable. In a free society, the best response to objectionable speech is more speech, and I encourage all those of faith to join me today in praying over the Capitol and recognizing the nativity scene that will be on display – the true reason for the season.”

https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.title: UK Supreme Court to hear landmark appeal over Palestine Action ban
https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.author: Katherine Hearst
https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.text:
UK Supreme Court to hear landmark appeal over Palestine Action ban
The British government will defend its decision to ban Palestine Action at the UK Supreme Court, in a landmark case that continues to test the boundaries of British counterterror legislation, freedom of speech and the right to protest.
The appeal, which begins on Wednesday and is expected to last two days, comes amid mounting civil unrest and police crackdowns across Britain in relation to the ban on Palestine Action.
A portion of the proceedings will be heard in secret because of the national security nature of the evidence.
Over the weekend, police arrested hundreds of demonstrators outside the US Embassy in London and Edinburgh for holding placards that read “I oppose genocide, I support Palestine Action.”
Since the government banned Palestine Action in 2025, the six-word statement has become a rallying cry and led to 4,000 people facing arrest under Britain’s Terrorism Act, including human rights lawyers, elderly activists and holocaust survivors.

https://www.aljazeera.com/gallery/2026/1.title: In Pictures: US midterm elections in 20 photos
https://www.aljazeera.com/gallery/2026/1.text:
In Pictures
In Pictures: US midterm elections in 20 photos
Voters, parents, and campaigners share the spotlight in a crucial election set to reshape US political direction.
Americans head to the polls on Tuesday in midterm elections that will decide control of Congress and determine how much pressure President Donald Trump faces for the rest of his term.
After two years of unified Republican control, Democrats are fighting to reclaim both the House of Representatives and the Senate, while Republicans work to defend their narrow majorities and protect Trump’s agenda on immigration, the economy and the courts.
These 20 photos capture the pulse of this deeply polarised contest – from crowded polling stations and get-out-the-vote drives to last-minute campaign stops – offering a glimpse of voters at the booths and parents with children in tow across the country, all playing their part in a race set to shape the direction of American politics for years to come.

https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/uk-su.title: UK Supreme Court to hear landmark appeal over Palestine Action ban
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/uk-su.author: Areeb Ullah
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/uk-su.text:
UK Supreme Court to hear landmark appeal over Palestine Action ban
The British government will defend its decision to ban Palestine Action at the UK Supreme Court, in a landmark case that continues to test the boundaries of British counterterror legislation, freedom of speech and the right to protest.
The appeal, which begins on Wednesday and is expected to last two days, comes amid mounting civil unrest and police crackdowns across Britain in relation to the ban on Palestine Action.
A portion of the proceedings will be heard in secret because of the national security nature of the evidence.
Over the weekend, police arrested hundreds of demonstrators outside the US embassy in London and in Edinburgh for holding placards that read “I oppose genocide, I support Palestine Action”.
Since the government banned Palestine Action in 2025, the six-word statement has become a rallying cry and led to 4,000 people facing arrest under Britain’s Terrorism Act, including human rights lawyers, elderly activists and Holocaust survivors.
New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch
Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
The ban has also raised questions about whether it breaches the right to free speech, following Irish novelist Sally Rooney's books being withdrawn from sale in the UK after she expressed support for the direct action group.
After the ban, Palestine Action co-founder Huda Ammori launched a legal appeal that has moved through England’s highest courts and led to legal ping-pong:
- July 2025: The British government banned Palestine Action under UK terrorism laws, criminalising membership and public support for the group.
- February 2026: The UK High Court delivered a landmark victory to campaigners, ruling that the government’s proscription was unlawful and represented a disproportionate interference with human rights.
- June 2026: The Court of Appeal overturns the High Court decision, restoring the terrorism designation.
- August 2026: The Supreme Court justices grant Palestine Action co-founder Huda Ammori permission to launch a final appeal.
Lawyers representing Ammori will argue over the next two days that using counterterrorism laws to designate a direct action group targeting arms suppliers sets a dangerous precedent which criminalises political dissent.
In written submissions to the Supreme Court, Ammori’s legal team noted that the Home Office assessed that less than one percent of Palestine Action’s “direct action protest activities over five years fell within a definition of terrorism”.
Raza Husain KC, for Ammori, said that only three out of 385 actions carried out by Palestine Action over a five-year period were assessed as meeting the definition of terrorism under part of the Terrorism Act.
'Total destruction'
Husain added the ban has led to “the total destruction of a protest group which enjoyed widespread support from across civil society”.
Human rights groups and international observers, including UN special rapporteurs, also submitted written statements, which warned the ban sets off a chilling effect across civil society.
The British government, meanwhile, will continue to defend its position, and remind the Supreme Court that the Court of Appeal rejected Ammori’s attempt to portray Palestine Action as a “non-violent direct action protest group”.
In written statements to the Supreme Court, James Eadie KC, the government's standing counsel, notes: “The principles applied by the Court of Appeal in allowing the Secretary of State’s appeal were long-standing, settled, and orthodox.
“The Court of Appeal made no error of law. Their conclusions of fact were plainly justified on the evidence before them.”
Jewish groups, including the Community Security Trust and Jewish Leadership Council, also submitted evidence to the court, in support of the ban, claiming the proscription protects Britain’s Jewish community.
Earlier this year, UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the proscription of Palestine Action had inadvertently led to "grannies and vicars" being arrested for terror offences.
"I don't think anyone's intent was to have those people criminalised," Miliband told LBC News.
“But obviously the Supreme Court has got to look at this issue and obviously it’s something we keep looking at as government.”
