https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.title: ‘The output of a lunatic asylum’: what the Bloomsbury group can tell us about mental health
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.author: Amie Corry
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.text:
‘As an experience,” Virginia Woolf wrote in 1930, “madness is terrific and not to be sniffed at … In its lava, I still find most of the things I write about.”
Woolf’s 1941 suicide by drowning in the River Ouse, her pockets weighted with stones, is usually framed as evidence of her tortured genius. But a new exhibition at Charleston in Lewes radically excavates this narrative while challenging ideas about mental illness.
Curator Hazel McMichael describes the Bloomsbury group as a “case study for looking at a mad community”. She explains: “We wanted to look at how aspects of psychiatry and psychoanalysis were echoed in the group’s everyday lives and art.”
Aligning with the “mad pride” movement of the 1990s, the exhibition reclaims the word “mad” as a point of pride and political identity, much like “queer” or “crip”. McMichael’s aim is not to deny the tragedy of Woolf’s suicide, which followed at least two other attempts, but to ask: mad according to who?
Woolf’s mental health issues were not anomalous in her circle, but her treatment – mainly private care at home – meant she could continue working. Meanwhile her peer, the artist Helen Coombe, studied at the Royal Academy and enjoyed early success, but her career dissolved on her admittance to the Retreat, an asylum in York where she spent the last 26 years of her life. Coombe was the wife of the critic and (much lesser) painter Roger Fry. In 1910, Fry curated the seminal exhibition Manet and the Post-Impressionists at Grafton Galleries, London, which was roundly accused by critics of being “the output of a lunatic asylum”.
Charleston displays paintings from that exhibition alongside rarely seen examples of Coombe’s work, including exquisite designs for stained glass and a drawing of a female Narcissus (a recurring, psychoanalytically informed motif in the show). In 1883, Coombe petitioned the RA to allow women to study partially draped figures. When Vanessa Bell, Woolf’s sister, began her studies there in 1901, she directly benefitted from Coombe’s activism. Bell’s prolific output is the subject of a forthcoming exhibition at Tate Britain, alongside Duncan Grant, her friend, lover and co-owner of Charleston, the Bloomsbury group’s countryside base. You can’t help but think: what might have become of Coombe without institutionalisation?
Photographs of the Retreat show light-filled rooms and displays of patients’ handicrafts. In correspondence with Coombe’s doctor, Fry pushed for the integration of colour and art in the treatment of patients. It’s a far cry from an 1897 image of the crowded women’s dining hall at St Pancras Workhouse, where Bell’s servant Mary Elizabeth Wilson ended up following a period of severe mental disturbance. We know of Wilson because of Bell’s comedic account of her life – “Mad Mary” – which Bell read aloud to the inner echelons of the Bloomsbury group in 1921 at the Memoir Club. Woolf’s diaries also refer to Wilson’s “servant’s hysteria”.
Wilson’s presence adds welcome nuance to the ever popular Bloomsbury story, which often celebrates the group’s revolutionary spirit without acknowledging the privilege that facilitated it: access to “a room of one’s own” and magnificent homes such as Charleston. But Wilson’s story remains secondhand. “Madness is often an invisible phenomenon,” McMichael says, “haunting objects in ways that are difficult to pin down”.
Contemporary responses brilliantly plug these gaps. An installation by the Mad Heritage Collective, a group with experience of mental illness and neurodivergence who co-produced the exhibition, features a text composed of cut-up extracts of Bell’s “Mad Mary” essay. Louisa Fairclough’s sound piece, The World Went Out of Tune With Itself, viscerally recreates the artist’s seven-year experience of psychosis. Discordant electronica made, Fairclough explains, “from within madness”, is layered with notes recalling obsessive, paranoid thought patterns.
While the tortured genius narrative casts Woolf as exceptional, mental illness recurred in her family. Among hundreds of family photos of Woolf’s siblings, only two survive of her half-sister, Laura Stephen. A hazy photograph of a girl, head downturned to obscure her features, evokes a haunting absence when displayed alongside handsome oil paintings of Woolf and other celebrated relations.
Another photograph was taken on Laura’s admittance to Earlswood Asylum in 1893, aged 22. McMichael notes: “Patients were photographed in formal attire, which appeared to dignify them, but the doctors in charge used patient portraits to document facial features for racial classifications.”
Laura was diagnosed with hereditary “imbecility” because her grandmother had attempted suicide. But her Earlswood case notes describe her repeating the words “bed”, “boys” and “family”, suggesting a link to the sexual abuse we know Woolf and Vanessa Bell suffered at the hands of their older half-brothers.
The notion of inherited madness prompted complex conversations among the research groups at Charleston. McMichael notes that while many “found solace in the potential genetic roots of neurodivergence, others wanted to focus on how pathologised ways of thinking, feeling and acting are responses to a maddening world”.
The subject also evokes the Bloomsbury group’s often overlooked history of eugenic attitudes, which the show addresses head-on. The economist John Maynard Keynes, a frequent Charleston guest, was vice-president of the Eugenics Society. “Only healthy seed must be sown!” blares a 1930s Society poster. Woolf wrote horrifyingly in 1915 of encountering an “ineffective shuffling idiotic” group of learning-disabled adults who she declared should “certainly be killed”.
The Bloomsbury group didn’t just experience mental illness, they were at the forefront of changing ideas around it in Britain. Adrian and Karin Stephen, Woolf’s brother and his wife, were prominent psychoanalysts. The Hogarth Press, founded by Woolf and her husband Leonard, published Freud’s Complete Psychological Works under James Strachey’s editorship.
Strachey – a sometime lover of Maynard Keynes – made the consequential decision to use the Latin “ego” and “id” for Freud’s German “das Ich” (I) and “das Ees” (it). This, says McMichael, “transformed self-explanatory language into clinical jargon, shaping the way we think about consciousness.”
The group’s extraordinary output was also impacted by therapeutic encounters. TS Eliot started writing The Waste Land in 1921 following a breakdown, and while undergoing treatment from Roger Vittoz in Lausanne. Diagrams illustrate Vittoz’s technique of “brain control”, which focused on sensory experience, simple repeated movements and exercises. The academic Matthew Gold’s revelatory work argues that the fragmentary, rhythmic echoing in The Waste Land (birdsong is “twit twit jug jug”) were a product of Vittoz’s methods as well as existential dissolution.
Whatever the medical profession has us believe, psychiatric labels reflect social attitudes. Homosexuality, for example, was classed a “mental disorder” for the majority of the 20th century. In keeping with Charleston’s spirit, Mad Bloomsbury leaves space to celebrate transgression from norms. Duncan Grant’s naked Spanish Dancer costume was worn with wig, heels and painted face at a typically fabulous looking Charleston party. Grant’s painted jigsaw of a rosy, spanked bottom also features, alongside tender 1970s portraits of young queer friends Grant found late in life through Brighton’s Gay Liberation Front.
The exhibition’s quieter moments speak to non-medical methods of managing distress. McMichael says: “We talked of how fundamental animals and nature are to being able to function in our day-to-day lives.” Grant’s portraits of beloved pets join Vanessa Bell’s sketches of a woman and her dog, made for the cover of Woolf’s 1933 novel Flush, which was inspired by the spaniel Vita Sackville-West gifted Woolf. The writer’s cross-stitched tapestry handbag nods to Woolf’s comment in a 1912 letter to Leonard: “knitting is the save of life.”
In exploring the Bloomsbury group’s relationships to mental health, the exhibition expands our understanding not only of a fascinating milieu, but of the mind and its diverse workings.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/3.title: Very cold war: Who’s attacking Europe’s supermarket freezers?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/3.text:
Very cold war: Who’s attacking Europe’s supermarket freezers?
Cold stores in supermarkets across Europe have been targeted in a cyberattack with no clear culprit.
Supermarket refrigerators and freezers across Europe have been targeted by a cyberattack that raised the temperature of internet-linked units, destroying and damaging large quantities of food.
On Monday, fridges and freezers at more than 100 shops in several European countries ran hot. Cyberattacks on supermarkets began last month, when hundreds of French supermarkets were left with spoiled food and damage to units which had overheated, costing millions of euros.
So far, it remains unclear why hackers targeted the supermarkets, but attacks have spread across the continent and even to the United States.
Here’s what we know:
Which countries in Europe have been targeted?
On Monday, several supermarkets in Europe were affected, including the following:
- Dutch supermarket operator Delhaize said dozens of its shops in Belgium and Luxembourg were hit by an “IT incident”.
- French retailer Carrefour said about 15 of its 700 Belgian locations were hit by refrigeration problems.
- The Colruyt group, which runs Spar stores in Belgium as franchises, said five of its shops were affected.
- Swedish Coop said cooling systems at seven of its 800 stores were affected, with disruptions ranging from complete shutdowns to partial operation.
- Swedish furniture retailer IKEA, which also operates restaurants at its stores, said one site in Mons, Belgium, had been affected by a cyberattack.
- De Laet & Van Haver, the Belgian butchery chain, said the temperature in its fridges at its store in Hove, south of Antwerp, was raised as high as 18 degrees Celsius, ruining meat worth about 15,000 euros ($16,764).
- The food wholesaler Musgrave said a cyber-incident affected refrigeration systems in 13 of its SuperValu stores in Ireland.
- In October, hundreds of French supermarkets suffered cyberattacks, spoiling tonnes of food, causing fires and melting parts of refrigeration units.
What has happened in the US?
In August, freezers at a market in Fort Huachuca, an Army base in Arizona, went into defrost mode, spoiling all the frozen food they contained, according to a post on Facebook by the base.
The same month, the naval station in Newport, Rhode Island, reported on Facebook that its refrigeration system was affected, leaving only dry goods were available for purchase.
The Pentagon considered the freezer malfunctions on the military bases to be a suspected hack, the Reuters news agency reported late last month, citing four officials close to the matter.
One official said Pentagon investigators were communicating with the French authorities about the issue.
How are cyberattackers targeting fridges and freezers?
Hackers can access the controls of fridges and freezers which use internet software and raise their temperature in order to spoil frozen food.
In some cases, hackers have increased the temperature of appliances to as high as 50C (122F) in European supermarkets, causing them to melt or even catch fire.
Awais Rashid, a professor of cybersecurity at the University of Bristol in the UK, explained that many supermarket refrigeration systems which are remotely managed and, often by third parties, have not been given necessary software updates to prevent hackers.
“In line with established cyber security practices, these systems should be managed via secure networks. However, this is not the case in these incidents and they are accessible on the Internet,” Rashid told Al Jazeera.
“A remote managing party can access a web server on the controller to configure the system including temperature changes and maintenance. There are known vulnerabilities in several controllers (many of which are past their end of life),” he said.
Rashid added that vulnerabilities include “easily guessable” passwords, which would mean anyone could gain access.
Why are hackers doing this?
The motive behind the attacks is unclear, but authorities believe it may be a deliberate attempt to disrupt food supplies.
On Monday, the European Commissioner for Agriculture and Food, Christophe Hansen, said the attacks on fridges were a “deliberate attempt to disrupt” the bloc’s food supply and to undermine consumer confidence.
He added that while “food security is not currently at risk … the food waste and impact on businesses are real”.
Rashid said that while there are few details about who may be behind the attacks or what their motives are, it is likely that these are “the motive here is likely disruption”.
“This has financial impacts on the supermarkets but also societal impacts in terms of security of the food supply chain. Critically, this risks undermining trust in infrastructures on which people rely daily,” he said.
Who is behind the attacks?
On Monday, Belgium’s prosecutor’s office announced that it had opened a criminal investigation into the latest fridge cyberattacks. But so far, no one has taken responsibility.
Theories have emerged linking state actors to cyberattacks generally, with North Korea most recently accused of being behind last week’s $6.3bn Binance cryptocurrency heist, which forced the crypto group to freeze accounts.
European intelligence officials have also warned that Russia is escalating its shadow war on the continent amid the ongoing conflict with Ukraine, with cyberattacks among the methods it uses.
On Tuesday, the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre warned that Britain needs to be prepared for an artificial intelligence (AI)-powered cyberattack on its critical national infrastructure within the next two years.
“By 2028, it is highly likely that Russia, China and other nation states will routinely use AI-cyber to achieve their geopolitical goals, with the UK facing an increase in scale and speed of sophisticated cyberattacks,” the NCSC said in a report.
The report comes shortly after the UK launched its “Be Ready” campaign, calling on citizens to stockpile enough tinned food, bottled water and cash to last three days in the event of a cyberattack or national emergency.
Rashid said that as our infrastructure becomes increasingly digitised, the risk of disruption from cyberattacks, especially “cyber-physical infrastructures such as refrigeration systems”, has risen.
“However, we should also note that a lot of our digital infrastructures operate safely everyday because good security practices enable that. The world works because cyber security works effectively. So it is important that all businesses follow good cyber security practices,” he said.

https://www.humanite.fr/medias/benoit-de.title: Après 34 ans, Groland c’est (presque) fini
https://www.humanite.fr/medias/benoit-de.author: Caroline Constant
https://www.humanite.fr/medias/benoit-de.text:
Après 34 ans de bons et loyaux services, la communauté grolandaise quitte Canal +. Ce qui signe la fin d’une aventure télévisuelle aussi loufoque que créative, aussi satirique qu’ancrée dans son temps.
Le 12 décembre prochain, le Conseil des ministres de Groland se réunira pour la dernière fois, en prime et en clair, sur Canal +. Benoît Delépine l’a annoncé ce mardi 3 novembre chez Léon, un bistrot-restaurant routier en formica jaune et nappes à carreaux rouges et blancs, où l’aventure Groland a commencé en 1990.
Pour cette dernière édition, histoire de ne pas faire « l’année de trop », Benoît Delépine promet un festival de mauvais goût loufoque. Chaque ministre rassemblé autour du personnage de président Emmanuel Micron (Raphaël Jimenez) parlera de son secteur d’activité.
Benoît Delépine a choisi, par fidélité, de tenir cette conférence dans ce bistrot, où une plaque a été déposée, « avec le nombre de verres qu’on a bus ici, qui dépasse un peu le millier, le nombre de sandwichs rillettes cornichons qu’on a bouffé également », sans compter les castings, réalisés sur place.
Un dernier épisode après être allé « le plus loin possible »
Il raconte qu’au départ, personne n’a cru à Groland. Y compris à Canal +, où le directeur des programmes Alain de Graef a ri de bon cœur avant de décréter : « c’est drôle mais la France n’est pas prête ».
Avec ce dernier épisode, en fin de tournage, l’équipe, estime être allée « le plus loin possible ». S’arrêter, estime Benoît Delépine, « ce n’est pas seulement une fatigue », mais aussi un principe de réalité : « Il y a aussi des gens qui s’en vont, je parle bien sûr de Christophe Salengro notre président (décédé en 2018). La semaine dernière encore, un de nos auteurs fétiches, Franck Benoît, s’en est allé. D’autres sont partis à la retraite comme Francis Kuntz ou Jules Edouard Moustic. » Il estime qu‘« une forme d’énergie s’en est allée avec eux ».
Au plus près de celles et ceux qui créent
L’Humanité a toujours revendiqué l’idée que la culture n’est pas une marchandise, qu’elle est une condition de la vie politique et de l’émancipation humaine.
Face à des politiques culturelles libérales, qui fragilisent le service public de la culture, le journal rend compte de la résistance des créateurs et de tous les personnels de la culture, mais aussi des solidarités du public.
Les partis pris insolites, audacieux, singuliers sont la marque de fabrique des pages culture du journal. Nos journalistes explorent les coulisses du monde de la culture et la genèse des œuvres qui font et bousculent l’actualité.
Aidez-nous à défendre une idée ambitieuse de la culture !
Je veux en savoir plus !

https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.title: Federal judge dismisses Trump lawsuit seeking Harvard admissions data
https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.author: Michael Sainato
https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.text:
A federal district court judge dismissed a lawsuit on Monday filed by the Trump administration seeking individual applicant records from Harvard, finding the government failed to meet procedural requirements before filing the lawsuit against the university.
Judge Myoung J Joun did not rule on the merits of the case, rather he granted a request from Harvard to dismiss the case on procedural grounds, finding that the justice department failed to demonstrate it took necessary steps to seek voluntary compliance before moving for judicial enforcement.
The justice department filed the lawsuit against Harvard in February 2026, seeking records and claiming Harvard had “thwarted” and “slow-walked” a federal civil rights review by delays and failure to meet deadlines for record requests.
The Trump administration has sought the records to ensure Harvard ceased using affirmative action in admissions.
Last week, Harvard released admissions data showing the enrollment of Black students at Harvard fell for a third straight year, to 9.3% for the class of 2030, down from 18% in the class of 2027.
“A deadline and a threat to sue, standing alone, do not necessarily demonstrate compliance with the regulatory voluntary-compliance process where the agency seeks to enforce disputed demands for extensive information,” Joun wrote in his opinion.
He also found the Department of Education failed to follow proper procedural steps prior to folding its admissions investigation into the lawsuit filed by the Department of Justice.
Harvard has maintained it provided more than 2,000 pages of documents without divulging personal individual records, which it states are privileged information. Lawyers for Harvard have argued the Trump administration prematurely abandoned negotiations with the university in favor of a retaliatory campaign against Harvard.
In August 2026, the same federal judge dismissed the Trump administration’s antisemitism lawsuit against Harvard, in one of the Trump administration’s many efforts against Harvard that has included freezing federal funds and attempting to revoke Harvard’s ability to accept international students.

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.title: Who is goalkeeper Owono and will he be punished after De Miguel’s death?
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.text:
Who is goalkeeper Owono and will he be punished after De Miguel’s death?
Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono is at the centre of a social media storm after the death of Tenerife’s Jesus de Miguel.
Jesus Owono has become a global figure overnight after the goalkeeper’s challenge led to the death of Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel.
The 30-year-old died in hospital in Santa Cruz on Tuesday morning after suffering a cardiac arrest in the wake of a high challenge by Andorra goalkeeper Owono in stoppage time of Monday’s La Liga 2 game.
Owono received a straight red card for his challenge and has since received criticism from around the world for his part in the tragedy while local police are reported to have begun an investigation into the incident,
Who is Jesus Owono?
The 25-year-old goalkeeper was born in Bata, Equatorial Guinea, but moved to Spain’s Basque Country as a child.
His first club was Antiguoko, a youth club in San Sebastian, at the age of eight, but after moving on to Real Sociedad, he played for the Basque Country’s representative side at under-16 level.
He joined Alaves in 2017 and worked his way through the youth ranks before making his first-team debut in a 1-1 draw against Real Sociedad in January 2022, becoming the first international born in his country to appear in La Liga.
He went on to make 20 appearances in the league and Copa del Rey but spent last season on loan with La Liga 2 side Andorra, keeping six clean sheets in 20 league games before earning a permanent move in August and signing a two-year deal.
Owono made his Equatorial Guinea debut shortly after turning 18 in March 2019 and has gone on to represent his country 46 times, playing every minute of their three group games in the 2025 AFCON edition and both their AFCON 2027 qualifiers against DR Congo and Sierra Leone in September.
How did Owono react to the collision?
After colliding with De Miguel in the centre circle, Owono did not turn back to look at his opponent on the ground but immediately began walking towards the touchline, anticipating the red card which Manuel Angel Perez Hernandez swiftly brandished.
However, as he walked off, after exchanging a handshake with teammate Nacho Quintana, he turned back as medical staff were beckoned frantically onto the pitch and jogged to join players surrounding De Miguel as he lay prostrate on the turf.
He remained on the field until he was led away by club officials and down the tunnel at the same time that De Miguel was being rushed off the field at the opposite end of the stadium on a stretcher to a waiting ambulance, with videos posted online showing Tenerife fans in the stands chanting ‘assassin’ at Owono for his part in the incident.
Why has Owono received online abuse?
The reaction to Owono’s challenge on De Miguel is that it was widely considered reckless and using excessive force.
The keeper was standing well outside his area as 10-man Andorra piled on late pressure, seeking to complete an unlikely comeback from 2-0 down with just seven minutes of normal time remaining.
When the ball was cleared by Tenerife from the edge of their own box in the air towards the halfway line, De Miguel looked favourite to have a clear run on goal, leading Owono to sprint forward and jump to challenge him in the air before the ball bounced, with his knee appearing to strike De Miguel in the chest and head.
Some social media users have called for a life ban from football and criminal charges to be filed against Owono, while others have flooded his own profile with racist abuse, insults and comments of “murderer”.
Could Spanish football authorities punish Owono?
Yes, and they almost certainly will.
The Spanish Football Federation’s Disciplinary Code suggests a suspension of four to 12 matches for players found to have committed violent conduct during play, resulting in serious injury.
An investigation into the events surrounding De Miguel’s death will assess the challenge and the context in which it was made before determining the punishment.
Can a footballer be charged with negligent manslaughter?
While a severe sporting punishment seems inevitable, many football fans are suggesting that criminal charges should also follow.
Reports in the local media in Tenerife on Tuesday afternoon say The Homicide Group of the National Police in Santa Cruz is already investigating the circumstances of De Miguel’s death.
The death of a player due to an act on the field in the midst of a match is, thankfully, incredibly rare, and there are no precedents established in a tragic case like this.
The question of charges is likely to be determined by whether Owono’s challenge meets the threshold of criminal negligence.
Article 142 of the Spanish Penal Code distinguishes between manslaughter due to gross negligence and manslaughter due to less serious negligence.
Gross negligence, if proven, can carry a prison sentence of up to four years, while the lesser charge carries a fine calculated over three to 18 months.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/3.title: Trump says US will stop giving Israel aid after year-end
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/3.text:
Trump says US will stop giving Israel aid after year-end
Military aid to Israel and campaign contributions from Israel’s backers to US candidates have animated political debate.
US President Donald Trump says he made a deal with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that Washington would no longer be providing funding to Israel after the end of this year.
“Now, as far as paying Israel, Bibi Netanyahu and I have made a deal that we give Israel $4bn a year, and we made a deal months ago that we’re stopping,” Trump told Fox News’ Fox and Friends after voting in the midterm elections began.
“We’ve already agreed that by the end of this year we won’t be paying Israel. Now we’ll help Israel if they need it.”
It was not immediately clear what form of aid Trump was discussing.
Trump cited Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, a vocal critic of US support for Israel, in his rationale.
“Why should we suffer the slings from lunatics like an El-Sayed when they don’t need it? It’s a bad, it’s a bad talking point,” Trump said, adding that the Israeli prime minister had proactively sought the aid cut-off.
“Can I be honest with you, [Netanyahu] brought it up, he said, ‘I think it would be appropriate if we do not receive aid’, because he understands this is one of their points of contention.”
The US Department of State did not immediately respond to an Al Jazeera request for comment. There was no confirmation of the move by Israel’s foreign minister or Netanyahu’s office.
Hot button issue
“Talk about a November surprise,” said Al Jazeera’s Kimberly Halkett, reporting from the White House, attributing the move to a desire to undercut criticism of US policy towards Israel both from progressive Democrats like El-Sayed and critics from within his own Make America Great Again movement.
“But there’s a very important distinction to note,” she added. “The money is appropriated by Congress; Trump can’t end this aid unilaterally. What’s unclear is whether this is a last-minute attempt to get votes or whether or not this could be a tangible change.”
Military aid to Israel, and US political campaign contributions from Israel’s backers to candidates, have been a flashpoint for both Democrats and Republicans this year.
US public support for Israel has fallen since Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began in 2023, especially among Democrats.
A Quinnipiac University poll in June found 48 percent of voters and 66 percent of Democrats believe the US is too supportive of Israel, up from 16 and 20 percent, respectively, when the question was asked in 2017.
‘Isn’t going to change results’
A provision in a bill passed by Congress in July tied the US and Israeli militaries far more closely together, deepening cooperation on weapons research, production and technology.
The United States-Israel Defense Technology Cooperation Initiative appeared as Section 219 in the fiscal year 2027 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), the annual US defence policy bill.
It passed a roughly party line vote carried by majority Republicans despite warnings from some voices on both sides of the aisle that it could compromise US sovereignty.
Harsh public criticism of Israel by US political leaders in recent years marks a dramatic shift from decades of staunch bipartisan backing.
The US House of Representatives defeated an amendment to cut off aid to Israel in July, despite nearly half of Democrats supporting it, reflecting a growing rupture between US progressives and Israel over its war on Gaza.
The House voted 314 to 104 to defeat the measure, offered as an amendment to a State Department spending bill by outgoing Representative Thomas Massie of Kentucky, an outspoken Republican critic of US policy in the Middle East.
“Amazing how being on the verge of Republicans getting wiped out in the midterms changes hearts and minds,” another Trump opponent, former Republican Congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene, wrote on X.
“Trump getting permission from Netanyahu to end annual aid to Israel isn’t going to change today’s election results.”

https://www.humanite.fr/politique/ile-de.title: « Bouclier de sécurité » en Île-de-France : un nouveau revers pour Valérie Pécresse
https://www.humanite.fr/politique/ile-de.author: Simon Guichard
https://www.humanite.fr/politique/ile-de.text:
Le tribunal administratif doit statuer, dans les jours qui viennent, sur la légalité du dispositif sécuritaire mis en place par la présidente LR d’Île-de-France. Dans ses conclusions consultées par « l’Humanité », le rapporteur public estime que la région n’est pas compétente pour subventionner des drones et des armes létales destinés aux agents municipaux.
Valérie Pécresse va-t-elle à nouveau se casser le nez sur son « bouclier de sécurité » ? Cinq ans après le début de la procédure contestataire, la justice administrative devrait définitivement enterrer dans les jours qui viennent le « bouclier de sécurité » de la région Île-de-France. Ce dispositif, créé en 2016 et doté d’un budget de 11 millions d’euros par an, vise à subventionner l’achat d’équipements – notamment des drones, mais aussi des armes létales – à destination des polices municipales.
Des subventions illégales, selon le groupe de la Gauche communiste, écologiste et citoyenne (GCEC) au conseil régional. Associé à la Quadrature du Net, association de défense et de promotion des droits et libertés sur Internet, le groupe GCEC avait déposé en février 2022 un recours devant le tribunal administratif de Montreuil, estimant que la sécurité est une compétence régalienne et non régionale.
Un mois plus tôt, le préfet de région alertait d’ailleurs sur les risques légaux de ce dispositif. Pour ses services, « aucun texte ne peut fonder juridiquement le subventionnement par le conseil régional de l’équipement des polices municipales. Le conseil régional n’est donc pas compétent pour accorder ce type de subvention ».
Dans ses conclusions, consultées par l’Humanité, le rapporteur public préconise l’annulation de plusieurs délibérations relatives au bouclier de sécurité, au motif que « le financement des équipements des forces de sécurité et de la vidéoprotection des communes ne (peuvent) se rattacher à aucune des compétences de la région ». Le rapporteur public préconise aussi l’annulation d’une subvention de 794 euros versée en 2022 par la région à la ville de Nangis (Seine-et-Marne) pour financer l’achat d’armes pour la police municipale, pour les mêmes raisons. Dans la majorité des contentieux, le tribunal administratif suit l’avis du rapporteur public.
Pécresse joue la montre
Le 1er juillet 2025, le rapporteur public avait déjà conclu à l’illégalité du dispositif, largement musclé en 2021, au moment où Valérie Pécresse se lançait dans une campagne présidentielle calamiteuse, achevée avec 4,8 % des voix.
Au lendemain de cette audience devant le tribunal administratif de Montreuil, la présidente de région répondait à sa manière, en convoquant 150 maires au Conseil régional pour vanter son « bouclier de sécurité » et annoncer le dépôt d’une note en délibéré pour répondre aux conclusions du rapporteur public.
Une méthode visiblement efficace puisque le tribunal avait suspendu la mise en délibéré de la décision issue de cette audience. « Valérie Pécresse a mis la pression de tous les côtés pour essayer de gagner du temps, analyse la conseillère régionale d’Île-de-France et présidente du groupe GCEC Céline Malaisé. Finalement on aura perdu beaucoup de temps pour un dispositif illégal. »
Depuis, la majorité de droite présidée par Valérie Pécresse a reconnu en creux l’illégalité de son « bouclier de sécurité ». Le 23 septembre dernier, son groupe Île-de-France Rassemblée (IDFR) a déposé un vœu, pressant le gouvernement d’accélérer le parcours législatif de son projet de loi pour élargir les compétences des polices municipales – notamment en matière d’usage des drones -, aujourd’hui au point mort. Le délibéré est attendu dans les prochains jours.
Oui, on s’en doute : vous en avez assez
Voir ces messages d’appel au don, ça peut être pénible. Nous le savons. Et on doit bien vous avouer que nous préférerions ne pas avoir à les écrire…
Mais voilà : c’est crucial pour l’Humanité. Si ce titre existe toujours aujourd’hui, c’est grâce au financement régulier de nos lectrices et lecteurs.
- C’est grâce à votre soutien que nous pouvons exercer notre métier avec passion. Nous ne dépendons ni des intérêts d’un propriétaire milliardaire, ni de pressions politiques : personne ne nous dicte ce que nous devons dire ou taire.
- Votre engagement nous libère aussi de la course aux clics et à l’audience. Plutôt que de chercher à capter l’attention à tout prix, nous choisissons de traiter les sujets que notre rédaction juge essentiels : parce qu’ils méritent d’être lus, compris, partagés. Parce que nous estimons qu’ils vous seront utiles
À l’heure actuelle, moins d’un quart des lectrices et lecteurs qui viennent plus de 3 fois sur le site par semaine nous aident à financer notre travail, par leur abonnement ou par leurs dons. Si vous voulez protéger le journalisme indépendant, s’il vous plaît, rejoignez-les.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: Brazil publishes first global ‘roadmap’ for phasing out fossil fuels
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Fiona Harvey Environment editor
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
All countries can start to break their dependence on fossil fuels now without needing to wait for new technologies or economic changes, Brazil’s government has said ahead of a global climate summit.
Brazil, the host of last year’s UN climate conference, set out the world’s first global “roadmap” for phasing out fossil fuels on Tuesday, showing that countries could boost their economies and pull people out of poverty while breaking the link with coal, oil and gas.
But Joeri Rogelj, a professor of climate science and policy at Imperial College London, said that although the Brazilian roadmaps represented a step forward, they were limited. “The roadmaps are valuable but fall short of clearly indicating the pace of change needed by including no timeline or key benchmarks,” he said.
“Because of this omission, they still leave much to be imagined about what is needed to achieve the Paris agreement’s ultimate goal: limiting global warming to well below 2C, and preferably to 1.5C, to avoid dangerous climate harm.”
André Corrêa do Lago, Brazil’s president of the Cop30 summit, said the roadmaps were intended to help move the annual UN Cops away from their previous focus on negotiating global agreements to tackle the climate crisis, and on to implementing the targets that had already been agreed. Cop31 takes place in Antalya, Turkey, this month.
“They are documents of implementation,” Corrêa do Lago told the Guardian in an interview. “There is a different group of people that negotiate and that implement. The problem we’ve had at many Cops is to think that the same people who negotiate might also need to coordinate the implementation – this is not the case.”
He said the roadmaps should be taken up by ministries of finance, transportation, energy and infrastructure to work on how they could be implemented in each country.
Brazil hosted the Cop30 summit last November in the coastal city of Belém, in the Amazon rainforest, where a bitter dispute broke out over whether the final set of resolutions should include pledges on fossil fuels. As a compromise, the presidency agreed to produce two roadmaps, one on “transitioning away from fossil fuels in energy systems in a just orderly and equitable manner” and the other on halting and reversing deforestation.
These roadmaps are separate from similarly named plans from governments that met after Cop30 at a conference in Santa Marta, Colombia, in April, to discuss the transition away from fossil fuels. At that conference, nearly 60 countries formed a new “coalition of the willing”, separate to Cops, to set out their own national roadmaps to phase out fossil fuels. Several countries have since produced national plans, including Germany, France and the Netherlands.
The roadmaps produced by governments under the Santa Marta initiative are much more specific and prescriptive than Brazil’s, as each of those is written by the national government responsible for implementing the policies recommended.
The Brazilian roadmaps only set out steps that are possible. They are not binding, they contain no deadlines or milestones for actions, and they leave it to countries themselves to “diagnose” their degree of dependence on fossil fuels and select steps to reduce it.
“Every country will have a different rhythm [for moving away from fossil fuels] – it’s very important to concentrate on the diagnoses of countries’ circumstances,” Corrêa do Lago said. “Based on these diagnoses, they can choose their levers [of policy] and implement the transition.”
Among the steps Brazil suggests is for oil and gas producers to urgently cut the flaring and venting of gas from extraction sites. Methane is a greenhouse gas 80 times more powerful than carbon dioxide, so this would have an immediate impact. Other steps are for countries to reduce their subsidies to fossil fuel use or production, and building up renewable generation.
The roadmap on deforestation notes the large sums that are expected to be needed to help poor countries with heavily forested areas such as the Amazon, the Congo rainforests and south-east Asian tropical forests that are under threat from fires and palm oil exploitation.
About $300bn is likely to be needed every year for forests by 2030, and $500bn a year by 2050, according to the roadmap, citing UN figures. The current amounts available fall far short at about $85bn a year.
At Cop30 last year, Brazil set up the Tropical Forest Forever Facility, a fund aiming to preserve forests, which raised about $7bn from various countries including a £400m loan from the UK.
The deforestation roadmap also notes the importance of regulating trade between forested countries and consumer countries. At present, there are few trade checks to stop unscrupulous companies from selling goods from deforested areas.
In some cases, deforestation has appeared to be condoned or encouraged by local or even national administrations. Indonesia is being sued by civil society groups for “gross negligence” over the record-breaking fires over the last few months that have cleared swathes of forest and destroyed wildlife habitats, most likely to be replaced by palm oil plantations.
Brazil was able to publish the roadmaps after its president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, won a fourth election term just over a week ago. In the last four years under Lula, deforestation rates have fallen by about 70%. His defeated opponent Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the jailed ex-president Jair Bolsonaro, had been expected if elected to return to his father’s policies of rampant exploitation of the Amazon rainforest.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/3.title: Iran commander sets out five conditions for regional security
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/3.text:
Iran commander sets out five conditions for regional security
Mediator Qatar says the US and Iran are studying proposals to resume negotiations and that it was ‘hopeful’ of an agreement.
The chief of staff of Iran’s armed forces has laid out five conditions for what he calls a roadmap to lasting security, as Qatar said it was “hopeful” that Tehran and Washington could reach a deal paving the way for future negotiations, despite overnight US strikes on Qeshm Island.
Major-General Ali Abdollahi’s plan calls for an end to hostilities on all fronts, including Lebanon and the Gaza Strip, the complete lifting of sanctions and the unfreezing of Iranian assets and war reparations, Iran’s Tasnim news agency reported on Tuesday.
The plan also calls for recognition of Iran’s sovereignty over the Strait of Hormuz, and a guarantee against future aggression under a regional security framework for West Asia.
The plan comes as Qatar steps up mediation efforts amid fears the US-Israel war on Iran, launched in late February, could escalate after the midterm elections in the United States on Tuesday.
Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman Majed al-Ansari said in his weekly briefing in Doha on Tuesday that a Qatari delegation held a meeting with Iranian officials in Tehran for more than three hours on Monday, before returning to Doha that evening. Both sides are now reviewing Qatar’s proposal, he said, with mediators exchanging proposals between them in real time.
“If there were no glimmer of hope, there would be no negotiations,” al-Ansari said, adding that Qatar would not speculate on whether an agreement or a military escalation was more likely.
He warned that any escalation, whether attacks on Iranian territory or on shipping, “will have an impact on the negotiations”, and said continuing the Qatari-Pakistani mediation remained a priority. He reiterated that freedom of navigation in Hormuz was nonnegotiable, referring to Doha’s condemnation of the targeting of the Qatari tanker Al-Mayda.
Reporting from Tehran, Al Jazeera’s Resul Serdar Atas said mediators were aiming to avert a new round of fighting.
He said a Qatari delegation visited Iran on Friday in response to a letter to Iran from US Vice President JD Vance, and an Iranian delegation travelled to Qatar the following day.
“The Qataris are trying to mediate with Iran, not on a peace deal, but on a framework to restart the negotiations,” he said. Of Monday’s brief visit, he added: “The reading is that the Qataris carried a message to Tehran and immediately left after that.”
“The main issue is the mistrust between the two parties,” Atas said. “The Iranians say that twice previously the US attacked them when they were engaged in diplomacy. That’s why they’re asking for concrete steps, such as lifting sanctions, removing the naval blockade, returning frozen Iranian assets and letting Iran sell oil on the global market.”
US officials reportedly said the military carried out limited strikes on Qeshm Island on Monday that did not amount to a resumption of major combat operations, saying Iran had tried to target a US aircraft and the attack took out the launcher.
One official called it “a defensive measure for Iranians using surface-to-air missiles against US assets”. IRNA reported five explosions on the island, with more blasts heard in Bandar Lengeh. President Donald Trump had said on October 8 that the US would not attack Iran before the midterm elections.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Tuesday it downed two US MQM-170 reconnaissance drones south of Qeshm and destroyed an MQ-9 drone east of the strait.
Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran’s lead negotiator, said, “The ball is in America’s court to prevent war.”
Tehran’s Hamshahri newspaper reported that Iran had updated its target bank to include US bases and infrastructure in Europe.
On Tuesday, Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei said on X that Washington’s response to Iran’s demands needs to be explicit and convincing.
“America’s response to Iran’s rights and demands was not convincing,” he said.
Rezaei added that the United States’ response “must fully and explicitly address Iran’s seven conditions and act upon them; only in this case will the Strait of Hormuz be reopened”.
Zeidon Alkinani, the founding director of the Arab Perceptions Institute, said both sides remained open to diplomacy.
“Diplomacy and force are running in parallel,” Alkinani told Al Jazeera. “The diplomatic channel is alive – it has always been since March, but there hasn’t unfortunately been a fundamental breakthrough.”
Vance had said on Monday he was optimistic about reaching a negotiated settlement.
However, Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said on Tuesday Iran was neither waiting for the outcome of US midterm elections nor shaping its policies around them.

Saudi Pro League postpones matches after Asian Cup rescheduling
League delays matches after revised Asian Cup dates create ‘additional flexibility in the domestic football calendar’.
Matches in Saudi Arabia’s premier football league scheduled for the coming week have been postponed after the rescheduling of the AFC Asian Cup 2027, the Saudi Pro League (SPL) says.
“The decision comes as part of a wider review of the 2026-27 league fixture schedule, with the revised Asian Cup dates creating additional flexibility in the domestic football calendar,” the SPL said in a statement on Tuesday, two days before the start of the match week.
The postponement of the Asian Cup until December next year was announced earlier in the day after recent attacks on the kingdom. The 24-team continental tournament had been due to take place from January 7 to February 5.
Asian football’s governing body announced the decision after “extensive discussions and close consultation with the Local Organising Committee (LOC) of the AFC Asian Cup Saudi Arabia 2027 and the Saudi Arabian Football Federation (SAFF)”.
The tournament will now run from December 23, 2027, to January 21, 2028.
An attack on Riyadh’s international airport last month killed at least 13 people and wounded more than 300. Yemen’s Houthis claimed responsibility for the deadliest attack in Saudi Arabia in more than a decade. Further attacks on the airport in the span of a week killed at least five more people.
“New dates for matchweek 13 will be announced once the review is complete.”
The SPL has rescheduled several domestic league games this season for logistical reasons, and last month’s AFC Champions League Elite clash in Riyadh between hosts Al-Nassr and Emirati side Al Wasl was postponed due to a threat of missile attacks.
Kickoff was delayed after Saudi Arabia’s Civil Defence issued a safety warning 15 minutes before the scheduled start time.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Citizen-led ballot initiatives seek to limit electricity firms’ political donations in Michigan
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Tom Perkins
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Two citizen-led ballot initiatives seek to rein in Michigan’s powerful electric utilities as residents say politicians have failed to address pressing issues around controversial datacenters, high energy rates and poor electric reliability.
On Tuesday, voters statewide will consider a nation-leading ban on political donations by the state’s deeply unpopular regulated utilities. At the same time, organizers in Ann Arbor, one the state’s largest cities, are proposing to banish utility giant DTE Energy by municipalizing the grid. It would establish a public power company to deliver energy.
The two initiatives are not coordinated, but are borne out of increasing frustration over energy delivery and datacenters. The citizen-led campaigns represent test cases that could help gauge the US public’s appetite for structural change in the nation’s politically powerful utility industry, and what is legally possible, organizers say.
DTE and Consumers Energy are among the nation’s largest utilities, and serve about 80% of Michigan’s customers. They have supported dark money non-profits, Pacs and front groups to attack the proposals, while their allies among city of Ann Arbor leadership have filed a last minute lawsuit to stop the public power initiative.
If voters approve either proposal, a bitter legal fight is virtually guaranteed. The utility-aligned group opposing the political spending ban, Protect MI Free Speech, has claimed the initiative violates free speech protections under the Citizens United ruling that struck down limits on companies’ donations to candidates. But the proposal’s architects say they have figured out a way around Citizens United.
Regardless, the initiatives underscore the broader, growing discontent with many of the nation’s large utilities, said Karlee Weinmann, a researcher with the utility industry watchdog, Energy and Policy Institute.
“What we’re seeing on a number of levels is the utilities’ political influence operations begin to break down under the weight of this public outrage over high bills, poor service, and lack of accountability, and I think both initiatives are reflective of that in their own ways,” Weinmann said.
Michigan consistently ranks among the nation’s worst in terms of frequency and length of outages, federal data shows. Each year, DTE and Consumers propose steep rate hikes, and they ally themselves with unpopular datacenters because the energy-hungry facilities demand fossil fuel resources that are profitable to utilities.
The problems in Michigan “are a microcosm of the nation”, said Christy McGillivray, the Michiganders for Money Out of Politics executive board co-chair. She said voters understand that political spending is a root cause of the problems – 93% of legislators took utility industry money in a recent session.
Optimism is high as the Ann Arbor public power initiative appears to have momentum, and recent polling found broad bi-partisan support statewide for the political spending ban, with 71% of respondents backing it.
“There’s so much energy and momentum behind this,” McGillivray said. “Pay-to-play politics keeps elected officials from actually tackling what voters really want, which is real solutions to the cost of living and utility bills, and they won’t if utilities keep bankrolling their campaigns.”
State Proposition 2 would prohibit regulated gas and electric utilities, or companies with more than $250,000 in government contracts, from making political contributions. It would also block executives and their immediate family members, as well as other people with close connections to the companies, from making donations.
In Ann Arbor, Proposal E would establish a new board to direct and manage the establishment of a city-owned electric utility. That utility, after a second vote, would replace DTE Energy as the city’s electric supplier.
Brian Geiringer, the executive director of Ann Arbor for Public Power, said that DTE is unpopular in Ann Arbor because of, among other reasons, the unreliable service, general resistance to clean energy and a lack of accountability. The appeal in the public utility model lies in the direct, democratic control over an essential service, he said. “The question of whether a private, shareholder corporation or publicly owned entity that you’re a part of is in control of your electricity – that is an extremely poignant question at this moment,” Gerringer said.
In a statement to the Guardian, Katie Carey, a Consumers Energy spokesperson, noted that the campaign against utility spending and their environmental nonprofit allies, also take dark money.
The proposal “won’t eliminate money in politics – it will simply shift influence away from Michigan companies and toward wealthy national donors and special interests, similar to the dark money funders of their ballot proposal”, Carey wrote. “Meanwhile, local employers and their employees risk being sidelined.”
DTE and Protect MI Vote, its affiliated anti-Proposal 2 group, did not respond to requests for comment. But Protect MI Vote told the Detroit News: “This is not over on November 3. We believe … this is going to go on for years. And it’s going to cost a lot of money to protect people’s first amendment freedoms.”
A confluence of frustrations
DTE and Consumers are “regulated monopolies” with full control over their service territories, but their broad level business decisions, such as rate increases, decisions about grid maintenance and clean energy plans, must be approved by state regulators.
Consumer advocacy groups allege that the Michigan public services commission, which regulates the utilities and is led by governor appointees, has largely allowed the companies to prioritize shareholder and industry interests over residential customers’ needs.
DTE for decades failed to adequately keep up with replacing ageing equipment, tree trimming maintenance and other grid maintenance, industry experts have said. That left the grid vulnerable to strong storms.
Many of the problems originated under GOP leadership, and in 2023 Democrats took full control of the state government for the first time in 40 years, ushering in new hope that the party would rein in the utilities. That did not happen.
GretchenWhitmer, the state governor, and Democratic leadership received huge amounts of donations from DTE and Consumers, and every piece of legislation opposed by the utilities died.
Residents have lost confidence that either party can solve these issues, McGillivray said. She spent a day earlier this year at the state Republican party’s nominating convention and a No Kings rally, and got the same response at each. “They were excited about it, they wanted to learn more,” McGillivray said. “It gives me hope.”
Establishment Democrat and Republican political support for an onslaught of datacenter proposals helped crystallize the bi-partisan opposition to the utilities. As an intense battle raged last year over a Whitmer- and Donald Trump-backed datacenter being built just outside Ann Arbor, the governor appeared to tell an Oracle executive: “We’re used to people telling us no and doing it anyway.” That drew outrage.
The legal battles ahead
In Ann Arbor, the city has for nearly a decade opposed the public power proposal, and instead implemented a Sustainable Energy Utility (SEU). It allows the city residents to generate rooftop solar or community clean energy. But DTE still owns and maintains the grid and sets the rates, which public power advocates say are main problems.
The city also installed a former DTE executive to run the SEU, which drew questions from clean energy advocates. The city’s lawsuit filed this week claims that Ann Arbor for Public Power has proposed a city charter amendment, when a new utility actually requires a full charter revision.
“We must be winning,” Gerringer told local media when he learned of the lawsuit. He said that Michigan’s attorney general has already found that their proposal only requires a charter amendment, not a full revision.
Meanwhile, the ban on utility political spending was intentionally designed to survive a legal challenge that invokes Citizens United. It is modeled after state laws elsewhere that prohibit companies that have government contracts, or which work closely with governments, from making political contributions. Instead of singling out utilities, the new proposal targets all companies with at least $250,000 in state contracts.

https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.title: ‘Les the bare-handed beekeeper asked if he should put them on his face. I said: Sure!’ Holly Lynton’s best photograph
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.author: Interview by Chris Broughton
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.text:
‘Les didn’t wear gloves as he needed to be able to feel the bees so he didn’t crush them. He looks like something out of The Odyssey’

The jumping-off point for my Bare Handed series was a bird becoming trapped in the netting around the raspberry bushes in my backyard. It made me think of the problem humans have interacting with the natural world. How do we navigate obtaining food and the other things we need while still being good stewards of the land? I’d seen work by photographers demonstrating how Big Agriculture was destroying the environment. I wanted to find people who took a respectful approach, tried to work in tandem with it, but who might be in a fearful or dangerous situation.

I approached Les, the man in this picture, after speaking to the director of an exhibition space in Albuquerque, New Mexico, who had hired him to remove a feral beehive from his tree. I’d already tried to photograph another beekeeper who wore a full protective suit, but he might as well have been an astronaut. With Les, I was able to stay nearby and work with him over three days. The first couple involved straightforward documentary pictures of him tending his hives. Then, on the third day, his apprentice Amber showed up to help.

Les had the queen bee in a cage in his shirt pocket and asked Amber to take it out. Wherever the queen is, the rest of the colony will swarm. There’s a picture I made where Les and Amber are joined together by bees, and that was my “ah ha!” moment. Amber took out the queen and placed her in Les’s hand, which is where the bees went next. He looked at me with his hands full of bees and said: “Should I put them on my face?” I said: “Sure!”

Les slowly moved his hands up to his face. Bees don’t like hair, which is why they’re not in his beard or the top of his head. He closed his eyes for a few minutes, and I photographed. Afterwards, he said: “You know, I couldn’t hear anything but the buzzing.” I don’t think he’d ever done that before. People sometimes have their own ideas, which I just go with. One of the reasons I like spending some time with them is that when they’re engaged in work, it’s almost like watching a dance and waiting for the right gesture.

Les didn’t wear gloves when handling the bees. He said he needed to be able to feel them so he didn’t crush them, and that it was too hot to wear a suit. I wore a shirt that buttoned up tight at the wrists and tried wearing a beekeeper’s veil, too, but I abandoned that after finding it hard to focus through the mesh. I did get a bee buzzing in my ear and had to walk away until she let up.

I was using a medium-format analogue camera, and the bees were also landing on my hands while I was looking through the lens. I could feel them but not see them. That was disconcerting, but Les advised me just to move slowly, as he did. That worked: I didn’t get stung.

For a while, the photograph of Amber and Les joined together by bees was the one I preferred. I was worried people would find the bees on his face over the top. The themes of the project were quickly reinforced when I photographed wolves in a sanctuary with their trainers, and then went out with a family of catfish noodlers in rural Oklahoma. “Noodling” involved them catching these fish with their bare hands – even though they can weigh 45kg and really fight back. I realised none of these people had any fear. They were all experts at whatever it was they were doing, and for them this was a spiritual, meditative practice. That became the focus for the series.

Before I started taking photography classes, I planned to be a psychologist and a writer. But what I love about photography is that you can create ambiguous narratives, a multilayered story in a single frame. A lot of my work references cultural memory. Rather than straight documentary, I’m aiming for something more mythic, and gestures that happen spontaneously can sometimes seem to reference a certain myth or biblical allusion. This photograph leans more towards Greek mythology, even if it doesn’t directly reference an exact story. Les isn’t Odysseus but, like him, he elects to hear rather than protect himself, which makes him feel like he’s a part of The Odyssey, somehow.

High point: High points occur when my photographs are both made and shown. When photographing, a high point is when everything aligns – the light, content, composition – and I create an unanticipated image that transcends the moment. One that elicits allusion, mystery and wonder. In terms of exhibitions or publications, it’s often what is recent. In the past few years, institutions as varied as the Nelson-Atkins Museum in Kansas City and Bristol Cathedral in England have exhibited my work. I’m thankful that institutions have enabled people from many different backgrounds and perspectives to see my photographs. Talking with viewers and hearing their reactions has been a real gift. My book Bare Handed, published by L’Artiere, was another high point.

Top tip: Right now, the quest for authenticity instead of artifice feels crucial, and what I’d urge photographers to undertake. I’d also say there is no such thing as too much curiosity (even though some people might make you think so). Don’t be afraid to change your mind about what you are working on, the meaning behind it or how to go about it. Reframing is what I like to call it. Follow your intuition. And find the joy in the practice of making work and being creative. Difficult moments will occur, and ones that feel like failures, but it’s the journey, not the end goal.

https://theintercept.com/2026/10/27/la-c.title: The Elon Musk Funder Trying to Sway the Race for LA’s Top Lawyer
https://theintercept.com/2026/10/27/la-c.author: Jonah Valdez
https://theintercept.com/2026/10/27/la-c.text:
A DSA-backed California prosecutor who helped force Meta to pay a historic $17 billion settlement this year is on a glide path to become the top lawyer for Los Angeles — unless a tech investor cozy with Elon Musk can spend enough to stop her.
San Francisco resident John Hering has sunk more than $1.25 million into an effort to defeat Marissa Roy, a deputy attorney general at the California Department of Justice endorsed by the LA chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America, and to support John McKinney, a county prosecutor running an uphill general election campaign. It’s a heavy injection of cash from a single individual in a local race for a little-known office, but it pales in comparison to Hering’s private-sector spending: In 2022, his investment firm Vy Capital pumped $700 million into Musk’s takeover of the company then known as Twitter and $300 million into his tunnel-construction Boring Company.
A co-founder of the cybersecurity company Lookout, Hering is spending in line with the tech industry in which he’s long been invested. While the city attorney’s office is commonly used as the city’s defense against litigious residents, the office also carries the power to mold legislation, enforce state law, such as labor protections, and take on corporations and the federal government in court. Roy has vowed to wield the office’s regulatory muscle against corporations — including Big Tech.
“Monopolies and Big Tech are things that [Roy] sees as an opportunity to wage battle against,” said former LA City Councilmember Mike Bonin, who has not endorsed either candidate. “If I were Big Tech, I would certainly think, ‘OK, well, this is someone who is a potential threat.’”
Hering, who did not respond to The Intercept’s request for comment, is part of a group of tech titans backing McKinney. Others include the founders of Ring, Tinder, and Boingo, and investors in Anthropic, Anduril, and SpaceX, who have collectively put more than $1.9 million into pro-McKinney committees. A group called “Committee to Expand the Middle Class Candidate” — backed by the property rental tech giant Airbnb — donated an additional $4.2 million to a committee supporting McKinney.
To help get McKinney through the June primary election, Hering and fellow tech investor Diego Berdakin poured more than $1 million into another committee. Over the past month, Hering’s general-election spending group, Neighbors for John McKinney, has been paying for TV and online ads and mailers that play up McKinney as “a lifelong Democrat” and “100% anti-MAGA.”
The same can hardly be said for the group’s top funder.
After giving to Hillary Clinton’s failed 2016 presidential bid and Democratic candidates like Beto O’Rourke, Hering donated $41,300 to the Republican National Committee and $500,000 to Musk’s America PAC in 2024 to support Donald Trump’s run for president. He has publicly praised Musk’s chaotic purge of the federal government through his so-called Department of Government Efficiency program and called the world’s richest man an “American hero” for offering to pay TSA salaries during the spring government shutdown. In 2025, Hering and Ring founder Jamie Siminoff, who has also donated to Neighbors for John McKinney, attended a White House dinner where Trump hosted dozens of high-profile Silicon Valley figures. The pro-McKinney group is also funded by billionaires Rick Caruso, a failed LA mayoral candidate, and Ron Burkle, a Democratic megadonor.
Earlier this cycle, Hering, who listed San Francisco as his residence in campaign finance documents, also waded into the LA mayoral election — boosting right-wing reality star Spencer Pratt.
Tech industry spending in LA’s elections arrives amid a midterm cycle where Big Tech and artificial intelligence have doled out millions of dollars to exert influence in congressional and state races across the U.S. as lawmakers grapple with how to regulate the industries. Musk, for example, has dropped more than $442 million into the midterms, including more than $70 million in his political action committee, America PAC, in October alone. And in state Assembly and Senate races across California, tech and AI executives have spent more than $29 million, according to Tech Equity Action, a political nonprofit that lobbies to craft tech-related legislation while advocating for workers’ rights.
California Gov. Gavin Newsom gave big AI companies a scare last month, when he signed a slate of bills protecting workers from AI overreach, like limiting its use to terminate or discipline workers, banning employers from using AI to surveil employees in bathrooms, and assuring that human healthcare workers will have the final say on patient care decisions.
The tech industry had fought hard to kill the bills, and while Newsom did offer the industry some concessions, labor organizers say the new laws offer them an opportunity to expand local worker protections, too.
In LA, Roy has said she would use the city attorney’s office to fight for workers against losses in potential wages, promising that she would go after “large corporations and big tech companies” that “misclassify workers as independent contractors to avoid paying them minimum wage and providing benefits,” according to her campaign website. She also spoke against companies who are increasingly using automation “to evade regulations and eliminate jobs.”
Tech leaders may view a city attorney with an appetite for regulation as “existential to their business model,” said Brian Justie, a researcher at the UCLA Labor Center who was part of the coalition that pushed for the bills.
“What happens in California sets a precedent and serves as a blueprint for the rest of the country,” Justie said. “And so if you’re a Big Tech, you really need to have a certain outcome come to pass here to avoid ripple effects elsewhere.”
For his part, McKinney has blasted Roy for her desire to “turn the city attorney’s office into the country’s largest public interest law firm” as out of touch with what LA voters want. However, voters across the U.S. have increasingly expressed opposition to the expansion of artificial intelligence and the construction of data centers. Roy’s campaign has shown a willingness to lend an ear to growing AI anxieties.
“Billionaires don’t want to answer to the working people, consumers, and communities they exploit,” Roy said in a statement to The Intercept. “But as Los Angeles’ City Attorney, I intend to hold them, their corporations, and the MAGA Republicans that permit their behavior accountable — that’s why they’re spending on someone who won’t.”
McKinney did not respond to The Intercept’s request for comment.
Ads put out by Neighbors for John McKinney assert that McKinney would “take on crooked landlords.” The committee’s website said he would fight for tenant’s “legal protections” against things like “illegal eviction.” But among the committee’s biggest funders is the Santa Monica-based real estate firm, Douglas Emmett Properties, which attempted to carry out one of the largest mass evictions in LA history until it was overruled by a judge. Douglas Emmett donated $250,000 to Neighbors for John McKinney in late September.
Neighbors for John McKinney has also funded attack ads against Roy that paint her as an inexperienced attorney who is weak on crime and has “extreme DSA” positions. The ads cite an article by the conservative California Post, a West Coast spinoff of the New York tabloid, that claimed she had supported a freeze on prosecuting misdemeanors, which she denies.
McKinney campaigns in the mold of law-and-order candidates, pledging to address homelessness and public safety by prosecuting misdemeanors, touting closer relationships with police, and promising to revive a neighborhood prosecutor program. Other California tech-supported efforts have echoed the same — like when tech leaders in the San Francisco Bay Area fueled a successful effort to oust progressive District Attorney Chesa Boudin.
But the LA city attorney’s office holds limited criminal enforcement power, Bonin pointed out. He suspects the tech investment in the LA race is more concerned with potential civil litigation, and he thinks that if voters make that connection, it could spell an issue for the campaign.
“Voters are concerned about Big Tech, they’re certainly concerned about AI, they’re concerned about the influence of — I don’t think you can describe it any other way — 21st-century robber barons,” said Bonin, who now runs the Pat Brown Institute for Public Affairs at California State University, Los Angeles. “Income inequality is a big issue in Los Angeles, so if they make the connection that this funding is symbolic of the agenda that McKinney will pursue … then it becomes more of an issue.”
Roxana Tynan, senior advisor of the Los Angeles Alliance for a New Economy, called the amount of Big Tech money being spent in the race “outrageous.” As she and other labor rights groups gear up for a fight for more worker AI protections in LA — like expanding safeguards to include temporary and gig workers, and banning employers from using AI software to collect sensitive worker information — she said she hoped people would follow the money being poured into the race and the influence that a few figures look to exert on the city.
“These are people who really believe that not only can they buy elections,” Tynan said, “but that they deserve to buy elections.”
Correction: October 29, 2026
This story has been updated to correct Roxana Tynan’s title.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.

https://gothamist.com/news/police-search.title: Police search several blocks in Canarsie after dead man’s body found
https://gothamist.com/news/police-search.author: Charles Lane
https://gothamist.com/news/police-search.text:
Police closed several blocks in Canarsie to search the area after a man’s badly decomposed body was found Friday morning.
Officers responded to a 911 call around 9:20 a.m. in the area of East 93rd Street and Avenue L, where they found an unconscious and unresponsive man, police said. EMS pronounced him dead at the scene.
Police officials said the man's body was badly decomposed. They have not disclosed the man’s identity or announced what caused his death.
Police closed Avenue L between 93rd and 95th streets on Friday, and officers went store to store looking for surveillance video.
Erwin Fairweather, who works in the area, said he was passing by at around 9 a.m. when he saw a sanitation truck, bags on the ground and a crowd of sanitation workers and residents gathered.
"They were discussing back-and-forth," Fairweather said. "How did it get here?"
Police have not said precisely how the body was found.
Fairweather called the discovery disturbing.
"That's awful," he said.

https://gothamist.com/news/ny-unemployme.title: NY unemployment recipients brace for delays during system upgrade
https://gothamist.com/news/ny-unemployme.author: Jon Campbell, Carol Chen
https://gothamist.com/news/ny-unemployme.text:
Nearly everyone who interacts with New York’s decades-old unemployment benefits system agrees it’s in need of a major makeover.
That’s why advocates for those receiving benefits are largely pleased that the state Department of Labor is beginning an overhaul of the system on Monday. It’s a painstaking process that will require the state to migrate more than 5 billion business records to a new apparatus in a move that promises to make the byzantine apparatus more user-friendly.
But the massive changeover comes with a major snag: The state will shut down the entire unemployment system for several days. It’s a dramatic move that means tens of thousands of people could see their payments delayed for at least a week.
Jean Stevens, director of the benefits law project for Volunteers of Legal Service, a Manhattan-based nonprofit that offers free legal advice to those navigating the unemployment system, said the temporary pause is “a huge concern for most of the people we’re talking with.”
“They're really struggling to get by and they really rely on these benefits,” Stevens said. “They really need them to pay their bills, to pay for gas, to put food on the table. So every week is really important to them.”
About 106,000 people claimed unemployment benefits totaling $67.6 million for the week ending Oct. 17, according to state Department of Labor data. Of those, 50,206 — or 47% — were from New York City.
It’s easy to see why the unemployment system needs an upgrade.
The interface is outdated, doesn’t work on smartphones and is only active during certain hours of the day. Calls to the help line are known to drop during peak hours. In certain instances, businesses are required to fax — yes, fax — information in. And the technology on the system dates back to the 1970s and 1980s, with some functions requiring a key punch — a long obsolete data processing tool — to operate.
The new system is expected to fix all of that and be easier to use, allowing people to certify for benefits on their phone or tablet with a more modern interface. It’ll also include a feature that will allow anyone to check the status of their claim without having to call in. State Labor Commissioner Roberta Reardon calls it the “pizza tracker.”
The whole thing has cost the state about $188 million to build and implement, according to the Department of Labor.
The upgrade has been in process since at least 2017 and has had significant fits and starts. Most notably, it was disrupted by the COVID-19 pandemic — a period of time that saw the unemployment system grind to a near-halt under the weight of more than 1 million claims for benefits in March and April 2020.
“The build has taken a very long time, but we are ready,” Reardon told Gothamist. “And when we go live, this will be a significant upgrade. This is the largest transition of [an unemployment insurance] system ever in the United States.”
The shutdown is scheduled to begin at 5 p.m. Monday and last for nine to 12 days, according to the state Department of Labor.
The state is encouraging people to file for their weekly unemployment benefits before the Monday shutdown to avoid a delay in payment, at least for the first week. The pause will not result in anyone losing their benefits; they can certify for back payments after the new system comes online.
”If you're already collecting and you certify before 5 p.m. on Nov. 2, that claim will be processed as usual and your money will land in your bank account probably by the end of that week,” Reardon said.
But those who rely on the payments say that even a temporary delay could force them to make difficult financial decisions in a time where they’re struggling to find work.
After a short-term pain, there's going to be a long-term gain.
Magaly Irizarry, who has been collecting unemployment since May, said a delay will “affect me tremendously” because she’s relying on the benefits to meet her credit card and mortgage payments. She said she’ll try to certify before the shutdown to avoid that.
“I think they should have another way of us getting our payment,” said Irizarry, who spoke with Gothamist at the Bronx Workforce1 Career Center. “They should have another way of us certifying.”
Kenneth Johnson, who was at the Bronx career center and has just begun receiving unemployment benefits, said the shutdown could mean he pays his bills late.
“I won’t be able to certify right then and there,” he said. “If there's a bill that's due, it’ll just have to wait until I get the money.”
Reardon said the Department of Labor considered migrating to the new system in parts. That move would’ve required a series of shorter shutdowns, rather than one longer one. But ultimately, Reardon said the all-at-once approach was determined to be the best option.
Gov. Kathy Hochul said she, too, questioned whether the shutdown was necessary. But she said she’s convinced it’s “the only way we can do the proper transition from the old system to the new.”
