https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Governo Lula quer aprovar PEC da Segurança Pública sem incluir redução da maioridade penal
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Redação
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
O governo Lula vai trabalhar para aprovar a Proposta de Emenda à Constituição (PEC) da Segurança Pública sem incluir a redução da maioridade penal. A orientação foi anunciada nesta terça-feira (3) pelo ministro da Secretaria de Relações Institucionais (SRI), José Guimarães, horas antes da votação no plenário do Senado, marcada para as 16h.
“A posição do governo, depois de avaliar todas as possibilidades, é que nós vamos votar a PEC tal como veio da Câmara dos Deputados”, afirmou Guimarães a jornalistas no Palácio do Planalto. O ministro disse que o governo não se opõe a discutir a maioridade penal, mas defende que o tema tramite em outra proposta. “Separa e trata em outro projeto. Essa discussão está posta no governo, mas não dá para misturar”, declarou.
A posição foi fechada em reunião de líderes governistas no Planalto, convocada para alinhar a base antes da votação. Segundo Guimarães, a emenda alternativa apresentada pelo líder do PT no Senado, Camilo Santana (CE), que reduziria a maioridade para 16 anos apenas em crimes hediondos, será retirada. “O governo está unido e coeso nessa posição”, garantiu o ministro.
‘Jabuti’ na PEC
A estratégia do Planalto é evitar que a PEC volte à Câmara. Se o Senado alterar o texto aprovado pelos deputados, os trechos modificados precisam passar por nova análise, o que atrasaria a promulgação. A PEC é considerada pelo governo etapa necessária para a criação do Ministério da Segurança Pública, promessa de campanha de Lula.
“Trazer o debate da maioridade penal para o âmbito dessa PEC é o que a gente chama de corpo estranho à PEC. Não que não seja um debate que precise ser feito, mas não no âmbito de uma PEC da Segurança, que é algo muito mais estruturante do sistema”, argumentou a líder do governo no Senado, Teresa Leitão (PT-PE).
Para barrar as mudanças, o relator da PEC, senador Rogério Carvalho (PT-SE), vai rejeitar as emendas sobre o tema. “O relator Rogério Carvalho vai emitir o seguinte despacho: os temas relativos à redução da maioridade penal tramitarão em PEC autônoma e serão despachados para a proposta que já está sendo debatida na Câmara dos Deputados e que tem calendário próprio para apreciação”, explicou o líder do governo no Congresso, Randolfe Rodrigues (PT-AP).
A saída apontada pelo governo é a comissão especial instalada na Câmara em julho para discutir a maioridade penal. O colegiado deve apresentar relatório até o início de dezembro.
Oposição insiste
A oposição, porém, não recuou. Depois de reunião de líderes com o presidente do Senado, Davi Alcolumbre (União-AP), o líder da oposição, Rogério Marinho (PL-RN), confirmou que vai manter o destaque. “Vamos manter o destaque, porque é de interesse de quase 80% da população brasileira. Espero ter votos”, disse.
A emenda de Marinho reduz a maioridade penal de 18 para 16 anos como regra geral e para 14 anos em crimes hediondos, tortura, tráfico de drogas, terrorismo e participação em organizações criminosas. Para entrar na PEC, o texto precisaria de ao menos 49 votos, três quintos do Senado, em cada um dos dois turnos. O governo afirma ter votos suficientes para derrubá-la.
O impasse já havia levado Alcolumbre a retirar a PEC da pauta em 15 de outubro, às vésperas do segundo turno. A redução da maioridade ganhou força na campanha, quando Flávio Bolsonaro apresentou proposta sobre o tema. A emenda de Camilo, articulada como resposta, dividiu a bancada petista e enfrentou resistência na base social da esquerda. Na época, o PT chegou a desistir de inserir a redução no texto. Lula declarou depois ser favorável à redução em crimes hediondos, mas defendeu que o assunto fosse tratado separadamente.
Aprovada pela Câmara em março, a PEC prevê a integração entre União, estados, Distrito Federal e municípios no combate ao crime organizado. O texto inclui o Sistema Único de Segurança Pública (Susp) na Constituição, amplia as atribuições da Polícia Federal e da Polícia Rodoviária Federal (PRF) e endurece as regras para líderes e integrantes de facções e milícias.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/3.title: South Carolina shrimpers weigh costs, vote in crucial US midterms
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/3.text:
South Carolina shrimpers weigh costs, vote in crucial US midterms
Shrimpers worry about fuel costs, tariffs and Trump’s proposed cuts to the agency that provides vital weather data.
Mount Pleasant, South Carolina – For Mark Marhefka, the weather can be the difference between a profitable fishing trip and a dangerous one.
As a shrimper and fisherman for 49 years, Marhefka relies on forecasts, weather buoys and data from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) to decide when it is safe to take his boats offshore. With storms and warm water temperatures disrupting this year’s fishing season, he worries that President Donald Trump’s proposed funding cuts could further reduce the services fishermen depend on.
“They’ve already started cutting back on NOAA, and they’re looking to do more in this next fiscal year,” Marhefka, who owns Abundant Seafood, told Al Jazeera. “It’s definitely something that we need to fight against.”
Since Trump returned to office in January 2025, NOAA has lost roughly 20 percent of its workforce, according to an analysis of federal employment data. The administration’s proposed 2027 budget would cut funding for ocean monitoring and terminate a programme supporting regional ocean observations.
But the weather is only one of the pressures facing South Carolina shrimpers as they head to the polls on Tuesday for the US midterm elections.
Rising fuel prices, equipment costs and competition from imported shrimp are weighing on people who make their living from the water.
Marhefka believes Democrats could address these pressures better than Republicans.
“Fuel costs have doubled since Trump has been back in office,” said Marhefka. “I voted Democrat because I really think Annie Andrews is going to help South Carolina.”
At an election-eve rally in Charleston on Monday, the state’s Democratic Senate candidate, Annie Andrews, sought to appeal to voters like Marhefka, arguing that her campaign would address the financial pressures facing coastal communities.
“I’m fighting for a South Carolina that we can afford,” Andrews said to the crowd. “I’m fighting to lower the damn diesel for our farmers and our fishermen and our shrimpers.”
Although shrimpers make up a small share of South Carolina’s electorate, their concerns raise bigger questions about the cost of doing business and retirement planning.
John Henry Middleton, an 81-year-old fisherman who has been shrimping for about 50 years, is an undecided voter. He says he is frustrated with both parties, arguing that politicians make promises but fail to work together on issues affecting common people.
“I want to see them get together and work for the good of the people,” he told Al Jazeera.
His concerns as he heads to the ballot box on Tuesday include the cost of living and whether he will have enough money to support himself in retirement. He said he has paid taxes and worked for decades, but still has to work at 81.
Kevin S, who declined to give his last name, works at Geechee Seafood on Shem Creek and said he plans to vote Republican on Tuesday. He said many people in the fishing industry lean Republican because they see government regulation as an obstacle to making a living.
“It’s a pretty regulated industry. A lot of red tape, a lot of extreme permits,” he told Al Jazeera, adding that some fishing permits can cost thousands of dollars.
Kevin added that rising fuel prices have increased the cost of running his business, but he doesn’t closely follow the factors driving those increases.
When asked whether the war in Iran was contributing to higher prices, he said he didn’t know enough about the issue to say. Instead, he pointed to Trump’s efforts to increase domestic energy production as a reason he thinks Republicans are better placed to address fuel costs.
He also believes many blue-collar workers share this view, but emphasised that industry support for Republicans does not necessarily mean enthusiasm for the party.
“I just don’t really trust Democrats as much to make the best financial decisions,” he said. “It’s not that a lot of people love the Republican Party. It’s more of a lesser of two evils.”
‘Not lavish living’
The pressures facing shrimpers are also evident in the dwindling number of businesses around Shem Creek, a historic fishing area near Charleston. Cindy and Taylor Tarvin, co-owners of Tarvin Seafood, estimate that only about eight shrimpers remain in the area. They say the decline reflects how difficult it has become to make a living in the industry.
“Younger captains can make a living, but not a lavish one,” Cindy Tarvin told Al Jazeera.
The Tarvins said their diesel costs rose sharply this year. They started the year paying $2.71 per gallon (3.78 litres), but by late September they were paying $5.99 per gallon. The American Automobile Association (AAA) reported that South Carolina’s average retail diesel price reached a record $6.17 that month.
Maintenance and equipment costs have also risen, adding to the financial strain on boat owners.
“There will always be a demand for watermen and what they produce. What scale they’re able to do it at is the big question,” Taylor Tarvin told Al Jazeera.
The Tarvins agree that one of the biggest challenges is the volume of imported shrimp entering the US market. Shrimp from abroad is often sold at lower prices, making it difficult for domestic fishermen to compete.
They said the influx of imports has contributed to falling prices and razor-thin profit margins, forcing some local boats out of business.
The competition extends well beyond South Carolina. According to the Southern Shrimp Alliance, the United States imported 1.59 billion pounds, or about 721,000 tonnes, of frozen warmwater shrimp in 2025, a 2 percent increase from the previous year.
In July 2026, the Trump administration imposed additional tariffs of 10 to 12.5 percent on imported shrimp from major suppliers including India, Ecuador, Indonesia, Vietnam and Thailand.
Trump’s tariffs on imported shrimp initially raised hopes among domestic shrimpers that foreign products would become more expensive and local catch more competitive. But the Tarvins said they have yet to see a meaningful benefit in the prices they receive, and are unsure whether they ever will.
There is another complication. Tariffs on imported steel, aluminium and products made from those materials have increased the cost of maintaining boats.
“So all of the pieces and parts that go into keeping a fishing boat running and keeping the equipment replaceable are affected by tariffs,” Cindy said.
For Marhefka, rising costs are part of a broader frustration with the country’s direction. He says he tries not to discuss politics often, but has heard growing frustration from those who voted for Trump and feel their circumstances have worsened.
“I just don’t think that we can go and handle another two more years of this,” he said. “We’re just getting squeezed too hard.”

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Violência menstrual é violação de direitos humanos e exige mobilização social, alerta especialista
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Afonso Bezerra
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
A falta de acesso a absorventes, a ausência de saneamento básico e o silenciamento sobre a menstruação configuram uma forma estrutural de violência de gênero no Brasil. Essa é a síntese para a criação do Almanaque Saúde Menstrual da Girl Up Brasil, lançado na última quinta-feira (29).
Em entrevista ao É de Manhã, da Rádio Brasil de Fato, Munar Malek, gerente de projetos da organização, defende que a pauta precisa ultrapassar a noção tradicional de pobreza menstrual para alcançar o conceito amplo de dignidade. Segundo Malek, o conceito foi estruturado a partir da escuta de quase 200 jovens ativistas do país. “A violência menstrual é uma violência de gênero que está conectada com a menstruação. Quando o horizonte que a gente tem é o da dignidade menstrual e ele não é cumprido, nós estamos diante de uma violência e de uma violação de direitos, se a gente compreende o menstruar enquanto direito humano”, explica.
Além do desabastecimento de insumos higiênicos, o problema se manifesta na negligência médica e na desconsideração de dores crônicas ou incapacitantes, como as causadas pela endometriose, que chegam a afastar meninas das salas de aula. O desinteresse histórico em investigar a dor feminina perpetua estigmas e atrasa diagnósticos.
“As dores das mulheres não foram desconsideradas ao longo da história. Muito pelo contrário, elas foram consideradas histeria, loucura, exagero. A gente tem dois polos muito opostos, que são da desconsideração da dor enquanto algo legítimo e da consideração da dor enquanto algo ligado a um corpo feminino histérico, no sentido de um corpo que inventa dores”, avalia Malek.
Para romper com o isolamento provocado pelo tabu, a Girl Up aposta na educação e na informação qualificada para adolescentes, famílias e educadores. “Combater o tabu menstrual é primordial para a gente avançar nas discussões que nós temos sobre o menstruar”, destaca.
A estratégia de conscientização também ocupa os espaços públicos com ações lúdicas voltadas às infâncias, incluindo o lançamento da mascote Maria Menarquinha, na avenida Paulista, em São Paulo (SP). A personagem utiliza metáforas simples, como o derretimento do gelo e a metamorfose da borboleta, para introduzir a menstruação como um processo natural de transformação do corpo sem assustar as crianças.
“A gente procura criar autonomia no sentido de possibilitar essas conversas a partir da linguagem infantil e combater as surpresas e as violências que vêm quando a menstruação não é conversada desde o começo”, argumenta.
Para ouvir e assistir
O É de Manhã vai ao ar de segunda a sexta-feira, às 7h da manhã, na Rádio Brasil de Fato, 98.9 FM, na Grande São Paulo, com transmissão simultânea também pelo YouTube do Brasil de Fato.

https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.title: Darfur survivors vow to tell story of those killed after Sudan camp attacks
https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.text:
Darfur survivors vow to tell story of those killed after Sudan camp attacks
Survivors of attacks on displacement camps in Darfur recall the lives they built, and the violence that forced them to flee.
In a small house in Omdurman, Hassan Saber Jumaa, a senior administrator at the Zamzam displacement camp in Sudan, sat on a simple wooden chair. He scrolled through his phone, looking for any photograph he might have of Zamzam, which is near el-Fasher, the capital of North Darfur, and once sheltered hundreds of thousands.
He found nothing. Jumaa explained that his old phone was looted during last year’s attack by Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces on the camp. Pointing to the bare walls around him, Jumaa said that all he has left are his memories of the camp, and the people who once called it home.
Zamzam, established in 2004, was home to generations of people displaced by western Sudan’s Darfur war, which began in 2003 and continued for nearly two decades. Alongside Abu Shouk camp and al-Salam camp, Zamzam formed part of one of Darfur’s largest concentrations of displaced people.
Jumaa recalled a bustling community, with its market open every day, and children walking to school.
Zamzam memories
Zamzam continued as a refuge for civilians until Sudan’s current war, which began in 2023. The RSF, fighting the Sudanese Armed Forces and its allies, captured the camp in April 2025, after months of attacks. Famine had been confirmed in the camp in August 2024.
Mukhtar Musa, a survivor of the assault, watched the community he knew descend into starvation and violence. He said restrictions on the movement of goods had exhausted food supplies, leaving some residents with little choice but to eat animal feed and peanut shells.
Umm Kulthum Ali Saleh described the months before the final attack as the hardest of her life. The RSF siege on Zamzam stopped goods from entering. She searched for food every morning, and recalled seeing women cooking grass and mixing mud with flour to bake bread.
Saleh believes the blockade was not merely a military measure, but a deliberate way to weaken the camp’s residents in advance of the final offensive, and Zamzam’s fall.
Brutal military offensive
On April 11, the RSF launched a three-day assault using cars, camels, and horses, burning straw homes and health facilities.
A United Nations Human Rights Office report documented at least 1,013 civilians killed, including 319 who were summarily executed in homes, markets, schools, clinics, and mosques. The report documented other abuses, including rape, gang rape, sexual slavery, and other forms of sexual violence, particularly targeting the Zaghawa community.
Musa was a witness to some of those mass killings, and said he saw RSF fighters kill civilians while chanting religious slogans. He described seeing bodies scattered around the main market and near schools, and said fighters continued pursuing civilians along roads leading out of the camp.
Saleh also recalled seeing bodies littering the roads, with only chickens, donkeys, and sheep wandering among the abandoned buildings.
The attack forced tens of thousands to flee Zamzam, with many remaining in the el-Fasher area, and others fleeing south to Tawila and Dar al-Salam.
The violence continued to engulf el-Fasher and its surrounding displacement camps over the following months.
With Zamzam under its control, the RSF launched an attack on el-Fasher in August 2025, and soon captured the Abu Shouk camp.
The UN Human Rights Office said at least 40 displaced people were killed inside Abu Shouk, while 19 others were injured. The International Organization for Migration reported that at least 500 residents fled the camp that day.
The RSF captured el-Fasher itself on October 26, 2025. More than 6,000 people are believed to have been killed in the attack, in el-Fasher as well as on escape routes out of the city. The UN found that RSF fighters targeted civilians, including members of non-Arab communities, and committed acts amounting to war crimes.
The RSF has previously denied targeting civilians in Zamzam and el-Fasher, while acknowledging that some fighters committed abuses.
The survivors of Zamzam, al-Shouk, and el-Fasher focus on bearing witness to the tragedy they faced.
Jumaa said the destruction of Zamzam marked not the end of the violence, but the beginning of another wave of displacement.
For him, the camp survives in the memories of those who once lived there – even as they are now displaced elsewhere.
Musa, meanwhile, said he cannot forget the first days of the siege, and the bodies he saw on the streets.
“Whoever survives must tell the story of what happened,” Musa said.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: Trump’s troubles with Iran could open the door to China
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Amy Hawkins Senior China correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
China has held a flurry of meetings with Gulf leaders in a sign that Beijing is stepping up its diplomatic efforts in the Middle East.
The diplomatic salvo comes before a highly anticipated meeting between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping when the US president is expected to attend the Apec conference in Shenzhen, China, on 18 and 19 November.
Xi held talks with Haitham bin Tariq, Oman’s sultan, in a historic state visit to Beijing on Monday.
President Xi’s foreign minister, Wang Yi, met Saudi Arabia’s national security adviser, Musaad bin Mohammed Al Aiban, and the deputy secretary of Iran’s national security council, Ali Bagheri Kani.
Haitham’s trip to Beijing is the first time that an Omani head of state has visited China since the two countries established diplomatic relations nearly 50 years ago. According to a Chinese readout of the meeting, Xi warned that the Middle East should not become an arena for “great power rivalry and geopolitical conflicts”.
He said: “China has always been actively committed to stopping conflict and promoting peace, and hopes to contribute wisdom and solutions to resolving the regional security dilemma.”
Wang said after his separate talks that China was willing to “play a constructive role in helping the region emerge from the shadow of the pandemic and achieve lasting peace and stability”. In his meeting with Bagheri Kani, Wang said China supported Iran “in safeguarding its sovereignty and security”. According to China, the Iranian official said his country looked forward to China “playing a more important role in international and regional peace”.
When the US and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran in February, China was credited with pushing Tehran toward ceasefire talks in Pakistan, bolstering its status as a regional mediator.
Beijing’s influence in the Middle East is “no longer what it used to be”, said Shen Dingli, a Shanghai-based scholar of international relations. But he added: “Given China’s increased investment and trade in the region … its influence cannot be ignored.”
As the war has dragged on, China’s diplomatic efforts have been muted. Its biggest economic leverage over Iran is the fact that it buys about 90% of the Middle Eastern country’s crude oil exports. Between April and June, it slashed its crude imports by 30%, with the total in June plunging to the lowest level in a decade. That saved the global economy from a major spike in inflation. According to some estimates, China’s cut in oil imports shaved $30 or more off barrel prices of Brent crude, a global benchmark.
Beijing has otherwise done little to broker peace in the Middle East. That is partly because it does not see the conflict as being its responsibility to resolve. In March, Wang said the war “should never have happened” and that the US and Israel would find “no popular support” for the strikes.
China is also a beneficiary from the damage that the fighting has done to the US’s global reputation.
According to findings published in July by the Pew Research Center, a Washington-based thinktank, China is now viewed more favourably than the US in a majority of 36 countries surveyed.
The pain caused by the long-term disruption to the strait of Hormuz, the waterway through which much of the world’s oil and gas flows, also poses a risk to China’s economy. Shortages of energy cause inflation, which risks reducing global demand for Chinese goods.
Tehran and Washington are locked in intensive talks to reach an agreement, which could include reopening the strait. Trump has repeatedly threatened to renew military action against Iran after Tuesday’s midterm elections in the US, a move which would cause alarm in Beijing.
Trump’s desperation to reach a deal in the Middle East may also provide an opportunity for China to present itself as a regional peacemaker, bolstering Xi’s status before their meeting. Beijing brokered a detente between Saudi Arabia and Iran in 2023 but since then its diplomatic impact in the region has been limited.
Shen said China’s desire to improve diplomatic relations with Middle Eastern countries as well as the US were “mutually reinforcing” trends.
China’s foreign ministry spokesperson, Mao Ning, said on Monday that China would send special envoy Zhai Jun to Iran, Oman and Saudi Arabia in early to mid-November.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: North America’s most widely distributed game bird is under threat
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Stephen Starr in Greene county, Ohio
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Every November, hundreds of hunters descend on four designated wilderness areas in southern Ohio in pursuit of the elusive ruffed grouse.
But not this year.
Dispersed across an enormous range from the southern Appalachian mountains to Alaska, the ruffed grouse is one of the most popular game birds in North America. But for the first time since 1937, no open permits have been issued to the public to hunt ruffed grouse in Ohio due to falling numbers.
“Roadside drumming surveys suggest grouse numbers remain quite low across the species’ range in eastern and southern Ohio,” says Mark Wiley, forest gamebird biologist for the Ohio department of natural resources.
Actual ruffed grouse numbers are not recorded in Ohio, but hunters conducting drumming counts, which can provide a broad estimate, have fallen to less than 1% of the rate recorded in the early 1980s.
Six years ago, ruffed grouse was added to Indiana’s state endangered list, where it is thought to survive in just 12 counties. That state’s hunting season closed in 2015. Four years later, ruffed grouse hunting ended in New Jersey for similar reasons.
While the bird is famously tough and able to withstand winter storms that many other bird species struggle with, habitat shortages and the growing distribution of West Nile virus, a disease that’s carried by mosquitoes that feed on blood, are taking a toll.
Detected in more than 320 species of birds, raptors and corvids are especially susceptible to West Nile virus. In 2023, dozens of hawks fell sick from the virus in northern Colorado after heavy early summer rain. Birds in general are thought to be favorite targets of the white-dotted mosquito.
While prolonged freezing winter conditions typically prevent mosquitoes from migrating north, warming temperatures and milder winters caused by human-activated climate change mean that may no longer be the case.
“We’re seeing a shift in both altitude, with the mosquito moving farther north, and also topography-wise, that it’s moving into upland, mountainous areas where the higher elevations of New York and Pennsylvania have been strongholds for grouse,” says Karl Malcolm of the Ruffed Grouse Society, a conservation and advocacy organization.
“I wasn’t surprised by the decision [in Ohio to close open hunting this year]. The long-term storyline here is one of decline of the species.”
An analysis of data by Climate Central, a nonprofit news organization, found that the Ohio valley and north-east regions of the US have experienced a greater increase in “mosquito days” – days with an average relative humidity of 42% or more and daily minimum and maximum temperatures ranging between 50F (10C) and 95F (35C) – than any other region in the country since 1979.
What’s more, infected birds can also serve as a virus amplifier, passing the virus on to other mosquitoes not previously infected by it.
For rural communities that depend on income from hunters, the struggles facing the ruffed grouse could be particularly damaging. Hunting is worth almost $2bn to Ohio’s economy, the overwhelming majority of which stays in rural communities. The majority of ruffed grouse hunting was centered in the state’s Appalachian counties, a region with some of the lowest income levels in Ohio.
Biologists at the Ohio division of wildlife say that while they don’t have specific figures for the economic impact of ruffed grouse hunting on rural communities, between 1993 and 2014, the number of licensed hunters pursuing the bird fell from 13% to two per cent.
Wisconsin, Michigan and Minnesota are home to the largest populations of ruffed grouse in the country, but they are also states that have experienced some of the highest levels of warming between 1970 and 2025, according to reports.
Northern Wisconsin is known as the ruffed grouse capital of America, and a 2022 study by the Wisconsin department of natural resources found that hunting the bird alone generated about $7.5m in economic output.
In Park Falls, Wisconsin, Terry and JoAnn Ides have been offering guided grouse and woodcock hunts on local rolling swamp forests since the 1970s. Each fall, the family works with around 100 clients and right now, the couple says they are not concerned about West Nile virus affecting the birds their business runs on.
“We sent in a lot of samples to be tested for West Nile, and we really weren’t a hotspot here,” says Terry. “I don’t consider that to be a problem.”
However, the first recorded case of the virus in Wisconsin this year was in a wild bird found in a county an hour’s drive from Park Falls.
What’s more, there have been signs that changeable weather has influenced local birds’ behavior. JoAnn says that warm temperatures this fall have kept birds high in the trees, where they use the passing wind to keep cool, making it harder for hunters to track them on the ground.
About the same size as a bantam chicken, on spring mornings, the male ruffed grouse can be heard in woods “drumming” their wings against their chests while perched on a log. The dozen grouse species of birds known to live in North America are notoriously wild and difficult to breed in captivity.
With habitats across 38 US states and all Canadian provinces, ruffed grouse numbers are also struggling in the eastern US due to ageing woodland topography: the bird thrives in open spaces of young tree growth, which is in increasingly short supply as forests across Appalachia and the midwest mature.
The amount of birdlife in the country’s eastern forests has fallen by 27%, according to a report by the Cornell Land Trust Bird Conservation Initiative.
Part of the problem, says Malcolm, who has a doctorate degree in forest and wildlife ecology, is that the wider population no longer has a strong relationship with the outdoors, or understands that conservation and hunting in fact work hand in hand.
“We’re getting to a point in human history where people don’t have that same direct connection to the landscape and a lot of folks have a sense that the only thing you can do with nature is either leave it alone or mess it up,” he says.
“The reality is there are a lot of things we can do that make the land healthier.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: US voters share why they cast their ballots – from frustration with Trump to affordability concerns
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Robert Tait in Portland, Maine, Joseph Gedeon in Dearborn, Michigan, Ed Pilkington in Anchorage, Alaska, and George Chidi in Atlanta, Georgia
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
In the battleground state of Maine, Todd Cox, 63, has supported the state’s incumbent Republican senator Susan Collins not once, but twice, in previous elections. Not this time.
On Tuesday, Cox, a technology professional, cast his vote for Collins’ Democratic challenger Troy Jackson – driven not by pressing local issues, but broader concern “for the direction the country is going in”, he said.
“We definitely haven’t become kinder and gentler under this administration,” Cox told the Guardian. “There’s a lot of bullying that goes on. It goes back to affordability. It’s the war in Iran – that shouldn’t be happening. It’s the disregard for the rule of law. It just seems like they’re thumbing their nose at it.”
As millions lined up to cast their ballots nationwide, the question looming over Tuesday’s US midterm elections – with control of US Congress and key checks and balances on Donald Trump at stake – was just how many Americans felt the same way.
There were signs of high turnout in this election, with 435 seats in the House of Representatives, 35 of 100 seats in the Senate, 39 governorships and thousands of state legislative seats up for grabs, as well as many local contests and ballot measures on issues including taxes, abortion rights and voting rules.
To win control of the US Senate in Washington, Democrats must flip four Republican-held seats and retain all of those currently held by the party. They meanwhile need a net gain of just three seats to obtain a majority in the House.
In interviews with the Guardian across the country, voters cited affordability concerns, Trump’s war on Iran and his administration’s aggressive crackdown on immigration as among the key issues that had driven them to cast their votes. Lines formed outside polling stations in key states including Texas and Maine.
In Maine, a steady stream of voters entered the Merrill auditorium polling station in Portland’s busy downtown district in mid-morning, leading to queues of up to half an hour to cast a ballot, according to organizers.
“I’m concerned about ICE raids that have been happening here in Portland,” said Maple Razsa, 55, a global studies professor at Colby College in Waterville. “The political system is just run amok at this point.”
There was still robust support for Trump’s party, however. “I voted straight Republican,” said a 63-year-man in Maine, who declined to give his name. “I don’t know much about the issues, but I’m not ready to throw away Israel yet. I don’t really see the war in Iran as a real war. What have we lost? Dozens. We lose hundreds and thousands in these wars and if they have a nuclear bomb, we’re going to have a nuclear war anyway.”
In Georgia, where heated races for the Senate and governor are playing out, David Boy, an attorney from Johns Creek, voted for Republicans yesterday despite his staunch antipathy for the president. “I don’t like Trump. I’ve never voted for him,” he told the Guardian. “I want to go to my deathbed saying I never did.”
But these are midterm elections – not presidential – and he looked beyond his view of the current occupant of the White House in a bid to elect candidates he believed would act on the issues he cared about.
“I’ve got school-age kids, so making sure the schools are good for them,” said Boy. “Taxes. I’m in the prime earning years right now, so paying taxes … and then also for me, personally, my faith and integrity and moral issues. And then, I want things to be run well. Honestly, I want our government to be run efficiently and effectively.”
These remain divided times. Jason Griffin, an engineer from Johns Creek, Georgia, told the Guardian he was specifically motivated to vote for Democrats on Tuesday by Trump. “I used to like the policies of most of the Republicans,” he said.
Others were driven by local concerns. “Michigan is in a dumpster fire,” Sona, a Dearborn resident in her 60s who declined to give her last name, said of another key swing state that both parties have chased on the path to controlling the Senate. She voted Republican.
Sona described herself as a lifelong conservative who opposes abortion and is concerned about “transgenderism”, specifically transgender athletes in women’s sports – an issue Republicans have sought to hammer in recent months. She also pointed to wages she said run about $10,000 below those in neighboring states, and to high electric bills.
In Alaska, another battleground state, Republican voter John House had a mixed assessment of Trump. “He talks too much, but he’s done so much for us,” he told the Guardian. But House, 62, a carpenter living and working in Anchorage, had no time for the Democrats. “You’d be a damn fool to vote Democrat,” he declared. “We’ll go backwards.”
Many voters took a different view. Chaunice Carr, 27, cast her vote for Mary Peltola, the Democratic senate candidate in Alaska – an action she described as “insanely important” to her. “There are a lot of bad things happening in Alaska, in the world. A lot of violence. ICE raids, people being deported in horrid ways. I’m hoping that today we can start to get that violence out of our lives.”
Juanita Cupa, also voted for Peltola. Prices are up, and life is tough. She spends $120 every two weeks filling up her truck, which she can’t do without in Alaska’s snowy wilderness. She is so hard up that she has had to move back in with her parents. “I’m living check to check.”
She was no fan of Trump, either. “He is spreading hatred, racism,” said Cupa, 30. “His leadership is disgusting – the way he talks about women, and human life.”
Alaska has been roiled in recent days by a report Peltola’s that campaign was behind an effort to recruit another candidate on the ballot called Dan Sullivan, with the same name as her Republican opponent. Peltola has denied any knowledge of such a scheme on the part of her campaign.
“It’s just been a lot of foolishness around this, on both sides,” said Cupa, with a weary shrug. “We’re all ready for it to be over.”

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.title: US tech stocks recover after selloff spooks investors over AI spending
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.author: Lauren Aratani
https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text:
US tech stocks made a recovery on Tuesday afternoon after a selloff spooked investors over AI spending.
Tuesday’s midterm elections didn’t appear to have a huge impact on Wall Street, though investors are predicting Democrats get at least a majority in the House and potentially gain seats in the Senate, which could lead to more AI regulation.
The S&P 500 was up 0.37% at market closing on Tuesday, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq increased 0.83% for the day. The Dow dropped 0.38% following a 1.9% dip in Apple’s share price after the company released a worse-than-expected margin forecast due to the higher cost of memory chips.
Nvidia picked up a 2.3% gain after dropping over four sessions, while fellow chipmakers Advanced Micro Devices, Broadcom and Micron Technology also jumped Tuesday.
Tuesday marked the end of a brief selloff of AI and tech stocks that started last week, with the Nasdaq in October experiencing its largest monthly decline since March 2025. The Nasdaq had ended on Monday in correction territory, dropping 10% from its 6 October record close.
Small drops in oil prices, amid potential new negotiations with Iran and Russia, also eased investors. Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, dropped to $103 a barrel on Tuesday, down from $117 a barrel at the end of October.
While many Americans say frustration with the higher cost of living will be a major factor in their vote on Tuesday, Wall Street has continued to soar off investments in AI, particularly the chips and infrastructure used to power the technology. The S&P 500 is up 10% for the year so far, while the Nasdaq and the Dow are up 9% and 7%, respectively.
Analysis from CNBC of post-midterms market performance from 1980 to 2024 showed the market tends to pick up after an election. Wall Street is often jittery before an election, when results are uncertain, but recover once results are settled.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Minnesota voters leave ‘I Voted’ stickers at memorial sites for Alex Pretti and Renee Good
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: José Olivares in Minneapolis
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Minnesota voters left “I Voted” stickers on memorial sites for Alex Pretti and Renee Nicole Good, the two US citizens killed by federal immigration officials earlier this year.
Pretti, a 37-year-old intensive care unit nurse at the Veterans Affairs medical center in Minneapolis, Minnesota, and Good, a writer and mother of three, were killed during a large-scale immigration enforcement operation in the Minneapolis region in January.
Donald Trump’s aggressive and violent mass deportation campaign has been a key issue for voters across the country during this midterm cycle, and has played a large part in Minnesota’s election.
“I knew Alex Pretti,” said a retired physician who worked with Pretti and asked only to use his first name, Arne. “I just knew that he was a competent nurse – a really, really liked guy. And he was assassinated.”
Arne left his “I Voted” sticker at the memorial site and choked up when speaking about his vote, Pretti and when federal immigration officials killed him.
Another voter, Mike F, who withheld his last name for privacy reasons, left his sticker at Good’s memorial site: “I felt like my vote felt a little bit more in touch with some of the things that happened earlier this year in the city,” he said. “So I felt like it was just the right thing to do – to come pay some respects and attach my vote to what happened here.”
At the end of 2025 and early this year, Minnesota became a central target for the Trump administration. Federal immigration officials descended on the area during “Operation Metro Surge”. Community groups organized rapid response teams throughout the city to prevent officials from arresting immigrants, and the situation escalated after Good and Pretti were killed.
Many groups involved in the immigration rapid response work have since shifted their attention on to the elections. In Minnesota, voters are choosing a Senator and governor, as well as House candidates.
“The country has humiliated itself by putting in a bad man, a very, very bad character,” Arne said of the president. “Today is a chance for America to say whether they support this kind of thing.”
If they don’t oppose it, “then fuck America”, he added.
In a primarily Somali neighborhood elsewhere in Minneapolis, the Rev Shandon Klein, a progressive pastor from the Park Avenue United Methodist church, said she was “keeping a watchful eye over the polling place just to make sure I’m a non-anxious presence that’s available here and just ensuring that everybody has access to voting.
“There’s a general, just, feeling of empowerment and really excited to get out there and vote,” Klein said.
So far, no federal law enforcement officials have been spotted, despite threats by the Trump administration to deploy them to voting sites.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Midterm elections 2026: how are votes counted and when will we know the results?
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Rachel Leingang
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
There’s no simple answer as to when US voters will know the results of the midterms.
Elections are managed locally throughout the US, and it’s different in each state. Sometimes, if a race isn’t close, there’s a near-instantaneous sense of who won. In more contested races, it can take many hours, days or even weeks.
This year, all 435 members of the House of Representatives are up for re-election, and 33 Senate seats are up for grabs. The governor’s offices of 36 states are on the ballot, as well as countless other statewide and legislative races. That’s not to mention local councils and school boards.
The lag between voting and knowing results can lead to an information vacuum and uncertainty that partisan actors may exploit to spread lies about stolen elections. Donald Trump, who has denied the results of his 2020 loss and other elections when he hasn’t liked the results, has tried to assert federal control over elections, which the courts have rebuffed. But election officials are on guard for potential interference in election processes this year.
Here’s what you need to know about how votes are tabulated and when we may expect to know the results.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: US midterm voting goes smoothly with only a handful of issues nationwide
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Auzzy Byrdsell in New York
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Voting in US midterm elections took place relatively smoothly nationwide on Tuesday, with only a handful of reported issues as tens of millions of voters cast their ballots.
With control of the US Congress in the balance, glitches at polling locations were minimal as Americans lined up to vote.
In Westchester county, New York, voting machines were unable to scan as many as 250,000 ballots at 332 polling locations. Some machines did not accept paper ballots.
At a news conference, the Westchester county executive, Kenneth Jenkins, stressed that people were still able to vote, and would be directed to use emergency ballots, which would be placed in sealed orange bags and counted later.
Parts of Westchester county are within New York’s closely watched 17th congressional district, where Republican Mike Lawler is in a close race to hang on to his seat.
In Kansas, a polling place ran out of ballots. Officials cited a county clerk error resulting in 100 paper ballots being ordered instead of 100,000.
In Georgia, officials requested permission to rescan more than 1,000 early votes as a result of malfunctions with two scanners – one which was run over by a wheelchair, according to WSB-TV.
Another southern state, Mississippi, reported a late-opening precinct; voting machines being temporarily down; state agency websites experiencing accessibility issues; and voters verifying registration status.
In Tennessee, voters raised concerns with touch screen voting machines that reportedly selected Republican candidates when voters attempted to select Democratic candidates.
Like Westchester county in New York, some polling locations in Tennessee and Oklahoma resorted to using emergency bins for ballots that had complications. They will be counted on Tuesday after polls close. Technicians were dispatched across the country to polling locations that were reporting problems.
In North Carolina, the state board of elections will decide on extending voting time by four hours in counties where technical difficulties affected voting. The board announced that the release of election results would be delayed from 7.30pm to 8.30pm.
Minor voting issues occurred in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, (where primary voting had issues as well), due to poll worker error, which has been the subject of recent litigation. Massachusetts also experienced minor technical difficulties in four precincts, but officials said they were rectified this morning.

https://theintercept.com/2026/10/27/flav.title: The Bolsonaro Family Playbook: Lose, Cry Fraud, and Run to Trump’s America
https://theintercept.com/2026/10/27/flav.author: Andrew Fishman
https://theintercept.com/2026/10/27/flav.text:
“I never thought about leaving the country,” Flávio Bolsonaro, a Brazilian senator and son of the deposed, disgraced leader, told his 16 million Instagram followers on Monday. It was the day after he lost the presidential election to President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva by a margin of more than 4 million votes.
Flávio promised to stay in Brazil to “organize the opposition” during Lula’s next term.
“I’m the last obstacle to the Workers’ Party’s plan to destroy the country,” Flávio warned, referring to the party of Lula, who defeated his father four years earlier.
A few hours later, he left his mansion in Brasilia and sought asylum in the U.S. The Trump State Department told The Associated Press that it will grant him and his family visas.
“I didn’t take sides, but it looked like another rigged election,” President Donald Trump told reporters on Monday, echoing Flávio’s election night talking points without providing any credible evidence that casts doubt on Lula’s come-from-behind victory — even as Flávio’s own party put out a statement acknowledging the results later that day.
It is no coincidence that the Trumps and the Bolsonaros are so fond of each other. Their modus operandi is nearly identical.
Both wrap themselves in the rhetoric of patriotism and moral righteousness, while treating their political offices as personal get-rich-quick schemes. And, when their lies finally catch up with them, you can be sure that they will jump ship to save themselves first and abandon their followers.
The affinities become obvious when you watch Bolsonaro, his failsons, and co-conspirators all end up in Trump’s America, where Flávio is about to join his brother, and in the denialism and violence that follow their failures.
Coups and Flight Risks
Flávio Bolsonaro’s election denial and hasty escape are his version of Trump’s infamous January 6 speech: Rile up the troops to do your dirty work and get the hell out of the way.
It’s not the first time a Bolsonaro ran this playbook. After Jair Bolsonaro became the first modern Brazilian president to lose a reelection bid, he refused to attend the January 2023 inauguration ceremony. Instead, he also fled to the U.S., staying in a Minions-themed children’s bedroom in the Orlando, Florida, home of retired UFC fighter José Aldo.
A week later, on January 8, the ex-president’s allies laid siege to the capital, Brasília, vandalizing Congress, the presidential palace, and the Supreme Court, as foot soldiers in a larger coup plotted to overthrow the Lula government. Nearly four decades of Brazilian democracy was only spared when key military leaders blinked before they could finish the job.
Jair Bolsonaro eventually returned to Brazil and was sentenced to 27 years in prison for leading the plot, which included a plan to assassinate Lula, Vice President Geraldo Alckmin, and Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes. Allies, including top military brass, were also convicted. Jair remains under house arrest — widely thought to be pinning his hopes for freedom on a Flávio presidency that wasn’t to be.
Flávio, however, will not be lonely in the States. His brother, former Brazilian Congress member Eduardo Bolsonaro, just received green cards for his family and is living in a $1.2 million McMansion in Southlake, Texas, in the Dallas-Fort Worth area, as we revealed in The Intercept Brasil earlier this year. Eduardo, who is a regular on the Trumpworld circuit, was sentenced in absentia to four years and two months in prison for lobbying the U.S. government to interfere in his father’s trial.
Flávio, too, seems poised to receive news of his own prison sentence while sitting on a couch in a Texas suburb. In May, our reporting at The Intercept Brasil put the first nail in the coffin of his presidential campaign when we published chat logs and audio recordings of the senator negotiating $24 million — and being wired $10 million — from disgraced billionaire banker Daniel Vorcaro, who is a sort of Brazilian cross between Charles Ponzi and Jeffrey Epstein.
The payments, wired to a U.S. account, were supposedly meant to finance “Dark Horse,” a biopic about Jair Bolsonaro starring Jim Caviezel. Brazilian Federal Police, though, have already poked holes in Flávio’s story as they investigate whether the money was actually used to bankroll Eduardo’s treasonous lobbying of the Trump administration to sanction Brazil and help his brother’s electoral chances.
Flávio is also being investigated for his alleged ties to a billion-dollar money-laundering scheme through an online betting company run by Willer Tomaz. The two are not only close friends but also business partners. Flávio even had unfettered access to one of Tomaz’s offshore bank accounts. You will not be surprised to learn that Tomaz left Brazil in August and is now living in Miami.
Police argued that, after losing the election, Flávio would pose a flight risk, especially in light of his closest associates’ recent actions. They asked the Brazilian Supreme Court to order Flávio to turn over his passport, which is permitted under Brazilian law. A top justice granted the request and, when the deadline passed, canceled the senator’s travel documents.
By then, Flávio was already on his way to the U.S.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/3.text:
UK’s King Charles expresses ‘sorrow’ in Antigua over slave trade
Caribbean nations call for reparations as King Charles stops short of issuing an apology for colonial-era slavery.
King Charles III has said at the official opening of the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) in Antigua and Barbuda that the transatlantic slave trade fills him with “horror” and “the most profound personal sorrow”.
The British monarch said on Tuesday that the slave trade “still casts a shadow over these [Caribbean] islands and other members of our Commonwealth”, and that the Royal Navy had played “a leading role” in ending it.
“We cannot change the actions of those who came before us,” Charles said. “We can, however, learn from the past.”
The king said he was seeking ways to address the wrongs by improving access to education, investing in jobs, encouraging trade among Commonwealth countries and pushing for climate resilience.
He ended the speech short of the apology that many Caribbean and African countries had hoped for. He offered no measures to address the economic and social damage of slavery.
Buckingham Palace had said the king would not issue a formal apology for slavery during his Caribbean tour, which also took him to the Bahamas and Guyana.
Guyanese President Mohamed Irfaan Ali said in an interview that an apology should be the king’s next step.
The dispute surfaced at the last Commonwealth summit in Samoa in 2024, when leaders called for discussions about reparations despite opposition from then-British Prime Minister Keir Starmer.
Last week, current British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the UK was open to a formal apology, while ruling out financial reparations.
Burnham, writing in The Guardian, said he wanted “to express my sorrow and regret for the pain and suffering of so many millions of people”.
He also proposed leading a programme of debt restructuring to help the Commonwealth’s poorest countries.
Ahead of Charles’s speech on Tuesday, a small group of protesters outside the venue held signs reading “Acknowledge the wrong. Commit to repair.”
“Technically, we’re free, but mentally a lot of us aren’t,” said Shana Michelle, from Antigua. “You have to apologise, yes. That is where we start with the repair.”
Leaders, including Burnham, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, were among those in attendance on Tuesday.
The Commonwealth has 56 member nations. Antigua and Barbuda Prime Minister Gaston Browne said, “No nation should be forced to mortgage its future simply to survive its present.”

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/10/.title: The High School Hunt: A Guide to NYC’s Complex Admissions Process
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/10/.author: Amy Zimmer, Chalkbeat
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/10/.text:
This story was originally published by Chalkbeat. Sign up for their newsletters at ckbe.at/newsletters
Applying to high school in New York City is daunting: Eighth graders can choose from 700 programs in 400 schools across the five boroughs.
Last year, of roughly 68,000 eighth graders who submitted applications, 58% of those were offered a seat in their top choice; 82% received one of their top three choices.
There’s still time left to build your list — and you add as many schools as you’d like. Applications are due Dec. 4, with offers expected to be sent after 3 p.m. on March 3, 2027.
Some families have already spent months researching their options. Others might not know where to begin.
Here’s a guide to help with the basics. (And here are tips on how to dive into a school’s data.)
NYC high schools broken down by the numbers
Even though the application process is citywide, there are still roughly 20 large comprehensive high schools that guarantee spots for students who live within a certain geographic zone around their campuses. Another six give priority to students living in their zone. (You can find out if you are zoned for any schools through the city’s MySchools platform.)
That said, New York City schools have a larger share of selective schools than other districts across the nation. Nearly 130 programs screen students based on seventh grade GPAs in core subjects. Another 30 also use essays and interviews.
Screened schools sort students into groups for priority, with those in group 1 earning a GPA in the top 15% of their class or an average of at least 94.67 in their core courses last year.
More than 75 programs require auditions or art portfolios. Nearly 50 programs have a specific language requirement.
About 80 schools are open enrollment, meaning they have no priorities and are just based on your lottery number. (See below about lottery numbers.)
The vast majority of programs — about 400 — use the Education Option, or Ed. Opt., admissions method to create balanced classes, targeting a third of its seats for those in the high category (with a seventh grade average of 89.24 or higher), the middle category (78.67 to 89.24), and the low category (an average below 78.67).
Eight schools base admissions solely on the Specialized High School Admissions Test, or SHSAT, and the application process for these schools, along with the audition process for LaGuardia High School of Music and Art and Performing Arts, is completely separate from the rest of the application process. And if you get into one of these schools, you will also get an offer to another school through the regular admissions process.
Finding your lottery number
Before you build your application, you should know your Education Department-assigned random number, or lottery number. You can find it by signing into your NYC MySchools account, which is the portal through which you will submit your application.
When you click “edit profile,” you can scroll down to find the 32-character hexadecimal string of numbers and letters. The first two digits or letters are the most helpful, with priority moving from 0-9 and then from A-F.
A random number beginning with 0 means an applicant will have a relatively high priority; an applicant whose random number starts with an F will have the lowest priority.
The random number is essentially used as a tiebreaker when there are more applicants per seat in a given priority group.
If you don’t know how to log in to MySchools, reach out to your child’s guidance counselor.
Some students have higher priority at certain schools
Nearly 60 schools — 35 of which are screened programs — are part of the city’s “Diversity in Admissions” program, setting aside a portion of seats for students from low-income families, English language learners, or other underrepresented groups. When you find your lottery number in MySchools, it should also tell you whether you are eligible for these seats.
Schools also set aside a certain number of seats for students with disabilities. That means that applications from students with individualized education programs, or IEPs, who spend at least 20% of their week receiving special education instruction, are considered in a different pool than general education students.
How to understand your chances of getting into a particular school
MySchools includes last year’s applicant-to-offer ratio for general education students as well as for students with disabilities. For example, Eleanor Roosevelt High School, a coveted school on the Upper East Side that gives priority to families living in Manhattan, had 30 applications per seat for general education students and four applications per seat for students with disabilities.
MySchools also has a helpful tool illustrating your odds: Once your MySchools account is active — and shows your “tiered” groups for screened schools, ED Opt group, random number, and any other priority designations — you will be able to search schools and see a graphic with three bars, showing whether you have a high, medium, or low chance of getting into a particular program.
A parent-created search platform called NYC-SIFT, the Search Information Finder Tool, can also show your chances once you input your information. The SIFT tool includes a trove of other data and school tour information.
(You will not, however, be able to see your chances for schools that require essays, exams, or other additional measures.)
Make sure to create a balanced list
Education Department officials advise students to rank schools in order of preference.
You can list an unlimited number of schools on your application, but make sure your list is balanced with not only “reach” schools, where your odds might be slim, but also with some schools that you have a higher likelihood of getting a seat. In fact, before you submit your application, the Education Department will flag your application if you only include screened schools.
About 3% of last year’s applicants were placed in schools that were not on their list, according to Education Department data.
Also, if you don’t get your top choice through the regular admissions process, you will be on the waiting list for all of the schools you listed above the school where you received an offer.
What else to consider
It helps to decide what it’s important to your eighth grader. Is a short commute or a one-seat subway ride important? Is access to certain academics important, such as advanced math or theater? Do you want a school with a more traditional approach to academics or one that focuses more on project-based learning? What about clubs and sports teams? How important is homework load? Do you want a large school that has an array of courses and extracurricular activities or a smaller one that might have more personalized attention but not have a full array of activities?
Some of these questions can only be answered by touring a school. While it can be challenging to make time for tours — some are during the school day, some are at night or on weekends — it’s important to see at least some of your top choices and get a feel for the building, commute, and neighborhood.
What’s so special about the specialized high schools?
For the city’s eight schools that require the specialized high school admission test, or SHSAT, students must register to take the exam by Oct. 30. The test will be administered in middle schools and K-8 schools during the school day on Nov. 18. Other students can take the exam at central Education Department locations on Nov. 14 or Nov. 15.
Last year, about 26,100 eighth graders took the SHSAT, and about 4,000 test takers received offers.
Because the eight schools — often seen as a ticket to elite universities and a way into the middle class — admit relatively few Black and Latino students, many integration advocates have pushed for changes to the admissions process.
But research reveals some of the effects of attending these schools might be overblown. One study, looking at specialized high school graduates between 1994 and 2013, found no evidence that those students were more likely to enroll in college, complete college, or attend an especially elite institution than comparable students from other high schools. Another study found that students who just made the cutoff for Brooklyn Tech were actually 2 percentage points less likely to graduate from a four-year college.
Amy Zimmer is the bureau chief for Chalkbeat New York. Contact Amy at azimmer@chalkbeat.org. Chalkbeat is a nonprofit news site covering educational change in public schools.

Hi!
We did not have a newsletter last month (we were on summer break), so it’s about time for an update! Below you’ll find our latest news, cartoon collections, and the most popular cartoons of the month. Enjoy! And no newsletter is complete without promoting our other newsletter, our daily editor’s choice.
Cartoon Movement at the Dutch Journalism Festival
The Dutch Journalism Festival (Nederlands Journalistiek Festival) is taking place on September 18 and 19 in Deventer, the Netherlands. The two-day festival features panels, workshops, movie screenings and live journalism. Cartoon Movement is also present with the workshop we delevoped for DELIAH: The Importance of Humour for Democracy: Good Humour versus Bad Humour
Unfortunately, the workshop is already fully booked. If you are interested, we did a similar workshop at the International Journalism Festival in Perugia in April, which was recorded:
Also, if you are planning to visit the festival, several Dutch cartoonists will be drawing live on Saturday to see who can make the best cartoon.
The state of democracy, in cartoons
The Kettering Foundation has published a collection of international cartoons with different perspectives on democracy. The collection, with cartoons from 19 renowned cartoonists, was put together by Tjeerd Royaards (cartoonist and editor-in-chief at Cartoon Movement), Terry Anderson (executive director at Cartoonists Rights), and Patrick Gathara (2026 CFK Global Fellow).
