https://gothamist.com/news/it-is-a-crime.title: 'It is a crime!': Upper West Side owl lovers outraged after rooftop work wrecks nest
https://gothamist.com/news/it-is-a-crime.author: Carol Chen
https://gothamist.com/news/it-is-a-crime.text:
Politicians, police and wildlife officers flocked to an Upper West Side apartment building Friday in an urgent effort to stop work on a rooftop water tower where a beloved family of seven barn owls had nested.
The two owl parents and five fledglings have turned heads since the family was first spotted on West 75th Street in early October. But on Thursday, some owl admirers noticed workers had disturbed the nest while removing the roof of the water tower for repairs. Video from onlookers showed a worker apparently using a torch, which sent smoke up into the nest.
Bird lovers were alarmed, contacted the authorities and believed the owls would get a reprieve from further disturbance. The owls are protected under the Migratory Bird Treaty Act.
But on Friday, the owl lovers — including state Sen. Erik Bottcher and Manhattan Borough President Brad Hoylman-Sigal — were stunned to see a worker back up on the water tower.
“The first time in probably a century we have nesting barn owls,” said Rita McMahon, the director of the Wild Bird Fund. “How could you do that to them?”
Birders said the fledglings had returned to the rooftop last night and were being fed by their parents, though they were no longer hunkering down in their nest, which was mostly destroyed. They desperately tried to prevent any further disturbance to the owls’ abode.
“You’re violating federal law,” Hoylman-Sigal yelled, banging on the building’s front door.
“They wouldn’t let us in,” he said, adding that the building manager saw them coming and ducked into the elevator.
The politicians worked the phones. Bottcher said he called Mayor Zohran Mamdani and his staff. “Any wrong movement could send these owls to their deaths,” Bottcher said.
Hoylman-Sigal said Department of Environmental Conservation officers headed to the construction company’s office in Long Island City to serve cease-and-desist papers. New York Road Runners has canceled a drone show planned for Friday night to avoid disturbing the owls, he added.
By the afternoon, environmental conservation and NYPD officers entered the building and spoke with the workers on the roof. The repairs seemed to be paused again and workers were seen leaving the building.
“I am shocked that this work even proceeded this morning at all,” NYC Bird Alliance executive director Jessica Wilson said.
Efforts to reach the landlord and management company of the building near Central Park West were unsuccessful.
Wilson feared the second day of construction had pushed the young owls away from the site, leaving them to starve without the help of their parents.
McMahon said the family of owls had scattered, with some perching on air conditioners and windowsills on nearby buildings. The young can fly but have not learned to hunt, and they need several weeks with their parents to pick it up, she said. “First they fly, then they learn how to be an owl,” she said.
She asked the Wildlife Conservation Society and the Cornell Lab of Ornithology for advice on a replacement roost box for owls that are nearly grown. Volunteers were inquiring with nearby buildings that might be willing to host the roost and keep people away from the roof for a few weeks.
The raptor lovers were heartbroken.
Kathryn Russell, 63, an Upper West Side resident who took up birding during the pandemic, said the work could have waited until the young birds left.
“Put up with the noise for three more weeks and let the birds do their thing and get out of here,” she said.
Mary Ann Zovko, a birder who lives on West 82nd Street, said she had come to watch the owls many nights. “It is a crime,” she said. “You can’t destroy a nest with living birds.”
Wilson said the fledglings will fly around the Upper West Side for the next few weeks. She asked people to keep their distance, skip flash photography and avoid loud noises.
“We all need to protect them,” she emphasized.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Justice department funds research into gender dysphoria and violent crime in latest anti-trans effort
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Abené Clayton
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
The US Department of Justice is funding research aimed at exploring whether there is a link between gender dysphoria and violent crime.
Last month, the National Institute of Justice (NIJ), the research arm of the justice department, said it would grant up to $1m for studies into the frequency and type of violence committed by people who have been diagnosed and treated for gender dysphoria.
The notice comes as the Trump administration has aggressively sought to curtail the rights of transgender people in the US, limiting their access to healthcare and identification documents with their correct gender identity on them. It also comes more than a year after the administration has cut funding to research into hate-fueled and extremist violence.
The Trump administration has repeatedly sought to falsely portray transgender people as more likely to commit extremist violence, said Wendy Via, the co-founder and CEO of the Global Project Against Hate and Extremism (GPAHE). By doing this, the administration diverts attention from violence driven by far-right extremist ideologies such as the “great replacement” theory, which several high-profile shooters have cited in their manifestos, she added.
“What the administration is doing is very dangerous,” Via said.
Experts and LGBTQ+ advocates call these attempts to link trans people and violence “pseudoscience”, because they depart from a growing body of academic literature showing that it is impossible to link a single characteristic, such as race, political affiliation or gender, as the prime reason for violence. Instead, researchers say the most common thread between most high-profile attackers is not their identity, but their views, which often include racism, homophobia, misogyny and nihilism.
That has not stopped public speculation around the role gender identity plays in violence.
After conservative activist Charlie Kirk was shot and killed in September 2025, rightwing influencers argued that the suspected shooter was motivated in part by what they call “transgender ideology”, a term often used by those on the right to falsely suggest that being trans is a political ideology, not an identity.
The idea that being trans or that being an ally to trans people represents a dangerous political ideology was included in a White House counter-terrorism report this year. Part of its counter-terrorism approach is to address leftwing violence and “transgender ideologies”.
The vast majority of mass shootings in the US have been carried out by cisgender people, although transgender and non-binary people have committed some mass shootings, including ones at Annunciation Catholic school in Minneapolis, Club Q in Colorado Springs, and Tumbler Ridge elementary school in British Columbia in Canada. In these cases, transgender shooters shared characteristics of modern high-profile mass shooters, such as idolizing other killers and online radicalization.
“We don’t know exactly why a person decides to commit mass violence, because they’ve all had things in their lives that have led them to it,” Via said. “Being trans or being straight likely doesn’t have anything to do with it.”
The NIJ’s new funding priorities will shift attention away from the dangers posed by far-right extremists and toward trans people, said Zane McNeill, a staff attorney with Lawyers for Good Government.
“I see it as a part of this larger apparatus to distract from who’s propagating the violence,” McNeill said. “It’s also about weaponizing funding decisions. They’ve been undermining projects while diverting taxpayer dollars for far-right pseudoscience.”
The NIJ is not the only part of the government trying to find links between transgender people and violence. The Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) recently published the report, Where the Clinic Meets the Movement: Does Gender Ideology Arm Left-Wing Authoritarian Psychology?
The report was commissioned by HHS and authored by researchers from Rutgers University, the Manhattan Institute and the Network Contagion Research Institute. It’s based on a survey of about 1,200 adults in the US and suggests that people who receive or support gender-affirming care are more likely to support political violence.
Last month, McNeill sent a letter to HHS requesting several corrections to the report, and argued that it violated the agency’s own guidelines. McNeill and other researchers are trying to obtain access to the survey data so they can offer their own analysis.
“This research is so flawed that it should not be published,” McNeill said. “It’s obvious that it’s extremely biased.”
The NIJ and the institutions affiliated with the HHS report did not respond to the Guardian’s request for comment.
In a statement to the Guardian, HHS press secretary Grace Davis Jamison said that the department’s report will help the government better understand how “political radicalization develops”.
“The findings should be evaluated based on the evidence, and under the Trump administration, HHS will not shy away from asking important questions to protect the health and safety of the American people,” she said.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Millions of Americans crippled by medical debt despite relief efforts
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Eric Berger
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Some of the millions of Americans who collectively owe billions of dollars for medical expenses have seen their debt forgiven in recent years, and there has been a dramatic uptick in aid this year.
But the relief still only covers a small fraction of the outstanding balance and is just a stopgap measure that does not solve the fundamental problem: people in the US get into serious financial trouble because they can’t afford the healthcare they need, experts say.
“Addressing the affordability crisis in healthcare is what will ultimately get at the heart of the issue,” said Mary Shannon, director of Care Over Collections, a non-profit that educates patients who receive bills about their options.
In 2024, people in the United States owed at least $220bn in medical debt, according to KFF, a non-profit health research group. About 14 million people owed more than $1,000, and 3 million owed more than $10,000.
“Costs are very high, and some people have no health insurance, so when they get sick or injured or need healthcare, they have no way to pay the extremely high charges,” said Emma Wager, KFF senior policy analyst.
Even people with insurance often have high deductibles or high cost-sharing provisions in their plans, which means they could still find the bills unaffordable, Wager said.
Patients often fall behind in their payments. In 2024, 21% of US households had a past-due medical bill, according to the journal Health Affairs Scholar. In 2021, more than half of the bills sent to collectors were for medical care, according to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.
Undue Medical Debt, founded in 2014 by former debt collection executives, helps address the problem by purchasing large portfolios of debt from healthcare organizations and collection agencies at a steep discount. According to the organization, a $1 donation erases about $100 of medical debt.
The organization does not take requests from individuals, but people who earn four times the federal poverty level or less, or with medical debt that is 5% or more of their annual income, are eligible.
Undue Medical is not alone in helping people pay for their medical care. For example, Dollar For, another non-profit, allows patients to apply for financial assistance to forgive or reduce their medical debt and has provided more than $117m, according to the organization. The HealthWell Foundation helps with prescription copays and insurance premiums and deductibles, among other expenses.The Community Service Society of New York has successfully advocated for state legislation like the Fair Medical Debt Reporting Act, which prohibits hospitals and providers from providing consumer reporting agencies information about a patient’s medical debt.
Undue Medical gets its funding from private donors and state and local governments. For example, in Illinois, the state provided $10m to Undue Medical, which used the funds to provide more than $1.1bn in medical debt relief for its residents, according to the state.
Unlike when people get those nausea-inducing bills from providers, recipients get surprise notices informing them that their debt has been absolved.
The organization states that it has provided $53.3bn in medical debt relief. About half of that was provided this year. The organization attributes that spike to its investment in technology that allows it to process files more quickly and its increased partnerships with governments.
“I am hopeful everyone that receives a letter feels more comfortable going back to the doctor and getting the care that they need and are not scared about the financial consequences,” said Allison Sesso, president and CEO of Undue Medical.
Still, Sesso acknowledges that the financial assistance is a “stopgap for people that need help today”.
“We have set up a system that incentivizes profits over people,” Sesso said.
To affect change upstream, providers must do more to make patients aware that they offer financial assistance, advocates argue.
For example, in Missouri, almost all general hospitals offer free or discounted care but less than a quarter of adults said they received information about the programs from a provider, according to a 2025 study from the Missouri Foundation for Health and the Lown Institute.
States are working to increase financial assistance for patients who need it. Federal law requires non-profit hospitals to establish a financial assistance policy but does not specify any minimum eligibility requirements; eighteen states have gone further and required all hospitals – including for-profit ones – to offer financial assistance with minimum eligibility standards, according to the Commonwealth Fund, a non-profit that studies health care issues.
Six states also have “presumptive eligibility” laws, which require hospitals to screen patients to determine whether they qualify for assistance and, if so, proactively erase the debt, KFF Health News reported.
The Biden administration also passed a rule that banned the inclusion of medical debt on credit reports, but the Trump administration and trade groups asked a federal court to block the measure, which a judge did.
But 16 states prohibit or restrict the inclusion of such debt on credit reports, according to the Commonwealth Fund.
“It has a major impact on people’s credit ratings,” said Sara Collins, Commonwealth Fund senior scholar for expanding coverage and access. “People have healthcare problems that are not their fault, and yet they are being saddled with medical debt because they don’t have the coverage to pay it off.”
In 2019, Tiffany Miller was just 26 weeks pregnant when she went into labor. Her daughter, Brie, spent more than three months in the neonatal intensive care unit and then required physical and occupational therapies. Even though Miller, a mental health caseworker, had insurance, she still accumulated more than $2,000 in debt.
“I’m a very faith-based person, so I had just been praying a lot because a lot of this debt was on my credit report,” said Miller, 40, who lives in Aurora, Illinois.
In May, she received a letter from Undue Medical informing her the debt had been erased.
She thought it was a scam but did some research and learned it was real. Meanwhile, Brie is now a healthy seven-year-old.
Harris said: “It just felt like those financial weights that have accumulated over the years, like a couple of them were taken off.”

https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/iran-.title: Iran says US ceasefire proposal 'insufficient' as strikes are reported on Qeshm Island
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/iran-.author: MEE staff
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/iran-.text:
Iran says US ceasefire proposal 'insufficient' as strikes are reported on Qeshm Island
Iran cast doubt on the chances of a deal with the US on Tuesday, after the US carried out air strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island, with the fate of last-minute negotiations between the two sides uncertain.
The air strikes, which occurred late on Monday, came after US President Donald Trump said he did not plan to attack Iran after the midterm elections and voiced hope for a deal. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said an agreement could be reached and that the government was “authorised” to renew a truce.
However, on Tuesday, the head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, Major General Mohsen Rezaei, rejected an offer passed to Tehran from Qatari negotiators.
“America’s response to the demands of the Iranian nation was insufficient. They must fully and explicitly address Iran's seven conditions and act upon them; only in this case will the Strait of Hormuz be reopened,” he said on X.
Last-minute negotiations to avert what officials and analysts in the region say could be a return to full-scale war took place against the backdrop of US air strikes on Qeshm Island, a strategic place that Iran has used as it attempts to assert control over the Strait of Hormuz.

The Wall Street Journal, which first reported the strikes on Qeshm, said the US was deliberately keeping the attacks quiet to reduce the risk of escalation. One US official described the strikes as “defensive” in the report.
According to the report, in one exchange, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps fired a surface-to-air missile at a US warplane, which fired back in self-defence. Another strike occurred after the US intercepted a missile fired from Qeshm at a commercial vessel.
Iran also said it downed a US MQ-9 Reaper drone and two Lucas drones near the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday.
Parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said the ball was in Washington's court after Tehran had delivered what he described as a "strong and rational response” to the proposal conveyed by Qatar.
"The enemy seeks to force the Iranian nation into submission through threats and military action, but they are sorely mistaken; Iran will not submit," Qalibaf said.
Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said on Monday that Tehran has a seven-step proposal for a diplomatic solution that could be implemented in two days.
The plan would call for the US to end its blockade on Iranian ports, Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz waterway, a US waiver on Iranian oil sales, the cancellation of new sanctions on Iran, and then talks on the nuclear file.
The US and Iran agreed to a ceasefire in the spring and then signed a 14-point memorandum of understanding to advance talks, but it was never implemented. The talks collapsed in part over the US’s reluctance to agree to Iran controlling traffic in the Strait of Hormuz.

https://gothamist.com/news/nycha-says-it.title: NYCHA says it's removed asbestos found at Brooklyn’s Marcy Houses
https://gothamist.com/news/nycha-says-it.author: Giulia Heyward
https://gothamist.com/news/nycha-says-it.text:
The city says that there are no more traces of asbestos at Brooklyn’s Marcy Houses.
A steam leak left asbestos-laden residue on some of the exterior walls at 502 and 504 Marcy Ave., part of the New York City Housing Authority complex in Bedford-Stuyvesant.
NYCHA and the city Department of Environmental Protection visited the site on Thursday after some residents said they had been complaining for weeks.
Some buildings also lost heat and hot water because of the issue.
The city said it has relocated four of the 23 households residing near the asbestos-laden walls until Oct. 31, while another household opted to stay with family.
The city also confirmed that all 24 air monitors installed in the apartments along the affected wall tested negative for asbestos on Friday.
Similar tests at the daycare, management office and exterior of Buildings 4 and 17 also tested negative.
The city also restored heat and hot water at four of the affected buildings on Thursday around 11:30 p.m., followed by the remaining five buildings just after midnight.
While residents have already received notices about the negative test results, the city said it will continue to test all exterior areas in the complex for asbestos.
"To date, all air monitoring test results have been negative for asbestos, including exterior and interior apartment testing, and air monitoring of exterior areas will continue until remediation is complete,” NYCHA spokesperson Andrew Sklar said.
The city’s environmental protection department has already cleaned up the sidewalk, cars and building facade at Brooklyn’s Marcy Houses, but has yet to finish the courtyard.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s office did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the matter.

https://gothamist.com/news/a-violent-hat.title: A violent hate crime claimed one NYC man's marathon dream. A year later, he's taking it back.
https://gothamist.com/news/a-violent-hat.author: Brittany Kriegstein
https://gothamist.com/news/a-violent-hat.text:
When Daniel Cho crosses the finish line of this year’s New York City Marathon, he’ll join more than 18,000 first-time runners to do so.
But this time last year, he was part of a very different statistic.
Cho was standing on the platform of the Bowery J/Z train station at around 4 p.m. on Oct. 29, 2025. He was on his way to collect a racing t-shirt for his first-ever marathon from a non-profit group he was helping to raise money for low-income Asian youths.
A stranger approached him on the platform and punched him in the face, shouting a racist slur. Cho ended up on the train tracks.
“I turned around to look if there was a train coming. [The tunnel] was pitch black, and so I said, ‘OK, get it together, and you're gonna be able to figure it out,’” Cho said.
He climbed back onto the platform, called 911, and gave the police a detailed description that helped them quickly catch his assailant. But in an instant, Cho, 46, became one of more than 29,800 people who would experience a serious physical assault somewhere in the city in 2025.
The arrest of his perpetrator was only the beginning of Cho’s mental and physical journey toward recovery. With multiple fractures to his right cheekbone, nerve damage along his eye socket and only four days to go before the race, doctors told him to cancel his marathon bid.
In the months that followed, he’d endure surgery to install a titanium plate in his face, log hours of work with a therapist to overcome lingering post-traumatic stress disorder, and shuttle to acupuncture treatments to tackle persistent numbness.
In early spring, Cho decided he was ready to run again — and hoped to take another shot at New York City’s iconic race.
“ Both marathon training and recovery from violence, or just a crime, ask for the same things: resilience, motivation, mental fortitude,” he said. “So I've been able to redefine that strength.”
While many of the city’s major violent crimes have declined significantly this year, felony assaults — the kind of attacks that leave people with serious injuries — have remained confoundingly high. According to the most recent NYPD data, there have been 165 more felony assaults reported citywide this year than the same time period last year, bucking the decreases in other kinds of offenses.
The same man who punched Cho was allegedly involved in four other anti-Asian attacks that same day, according to Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg. So far this year there have been 548 felony assaults in transit, up from 490 at this time last year; an 11% increase.
The MTA declined to comment on Cho’s attack or on the spike in assaults on its system.
Cho, who works for the New York City Campaign Finance Board, was originally running the marathon to raise money for Apex for Youth: a nonprofit headquartered in Manhattan’s Chinatown that provides resources and mentorship to young Asian Americans from low-income backgrounds. Now, he said, he is also running to raise awareness about the prevalence of similar attacks, to spread hope to other survivors, and to reclaim his sense of safety and community in the city he loves.
“I was running for kids who are learning to trust this city to nurture and protect their futures. And then I had to learn to trust the city again myself with every commute, with every subway ride,” he said.
Cho’s message to other survivors is to treat recovery like marathon training: a long process with ups and downs, twists and turns, progress and setbacks.
“Find your own healing journey,” he said. “Don’t be afraid to tell your story…and my last thing is, create space for that intentional rest.”
On marathon day, Cho said he is most looking forward to “taking it all in,” “finding joy in the struggle,” and seeing his wife and two kids at mile 14. He said the race provides a unique opportunity for people from all walks of life to find common ground with strangers.
“ New York is a place for everyone, like nowhere else in the world, and the city belongs to all of us,” he said. “Hopefully we can lift each other up.”
This story has been updated to clarify the item Cho was collecting and the nature of his attack.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: Mamdani, Schools Chief Face ‘Backlog of Tough Decisions’ With Enrollment in Free Fall
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Michael Elsen-Rooney, Chalkbeat
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
This story was originally published by Chalkbeat and is the third story in a three-part series. Read parts one and two here. And keep Chalkbeat’s valuable education coverage at the top of your feeds by clicking here and checking the box next to their name.
Nearly a year into his administration, Mayor Zohran Mamdani has not shared a vision for addressing many of the pressing challenges facing the New York City school system.
One of the most urgent is the small-schools crisis, driven by years of declining enrollment.
It’s a crisis that past administrations have allowed to fester — and one that some district leaders and principals say Mamdani and his schools chancellor, Kamar Samuels, could make a defining feature of their education agenda. By closing and merging schools, Samuels and Mamdani could cut costs, expand academic opportunities for vulnerable students, and help integrate students from different backgrounds, proponents argue.
But it remains to be seen whether the Mamdani administration is willing to spend the time and political capital necessary to close and merge schools at scale — and in the face of likely pushback from families and educators.
“The city must choose between managing quiet decline — or leading a bold, community-driven project of renewal,” wrote Marielys Divanne, a longtime education leader and former adviser under Mayor Eric Adams, in a report released last year.
The number of schools with fewer than 250 students — the size under which Education Department leaders say it’s difficult to offer a robust education — has multiplied eightfold over the past 25 years, from 42 to 335, a Chalkbeat analysis found.
Meanwhile, enrollment in public schools is in free fall. The K-12 student population in public schools is down 187,000 over the past 12 years to 790,000 due to birth rates falling and families leaving the city. It’s projected to fall almost as much in the decade to come.
“The challenge now is that there is such a backlog of tough decisions,” said Karin Goldmark, a former deputy chancellor who oversaw school closures and mergers under de Blasio. “The sheer volume of action required means superintendents and principals will have to do heavy lifting.”
Samuels indicated earlier this month that he doesn’t want to create a systemwide plan to reduce the number of schools. He said he prefers that future plans to consolidate schools come from communities rather than top down. He launched working groups in five districts to develop community-driven plans and promised to expand those groups citywide. Officials haven’t yet offered a timeline for that work.
In recent weeks, superintendents have floated proposals to close at least two underenrolled schools, a high school in Harlem and a middle school in the South Bronx, Chalkbeat has learned.
“The data shows that schools with larger enrollment can offer more advanced coursework, more enrichment like arts and sports, and more opportunities our students deserve,” Education Department spokesperson Nicole Brownstein said. “At the same time, every school community is unique, and this work must be led locally.”
Easy To Open, Hard To Close: The Origins of the Small-Schools Crisis
The problem the city faces now is, in some ways, one of its own making.
When Mayor Michael Bloomberg opened hundreds of new schools in the early 2000s, he promised a marketplace that would increase choice for families while weeding out the weakest schools.
Bloomberg’s market-based reforms, however, didn’t work as envisioned because in practice it has been easier for the city to open schools than to close them.
“What’s happened is an embrace of the marketplace on the front end of the process but an unwillingness to pull the thread through on the back end,” said Jennifer Jennings, a sociology professor at Princeton University who recently published a book on the history of New York City’s high school admissions system.
Multiple mayors have failed to meaningfully address the small-schools problem.
De Blasio, who believed in shuttering low-performing schools only as a last resort, closed and merged some schools, but those efforts slowed when the COVID pandemic hit in 2020. The Adams administration largely delegated decision making about consolidating schools to local superintendents and opened new schools to try to recover from the enrollment nosedive that began in the pandemic.
The resulting system has been costly.
Since 2010, the number of principals has grown 11% to 1,610, while the number of assistant principals jumped 31% to 3,518, according to data provided to Chalkbeat by the Independent Budget Office.
In 2020, de Blasio introduced an emergency policy called “hold harmless” to keep school budgets steady even as they lost enrollment. Every mayor since, including Mamdani, has continued that policy, spending a total of almost $2 billion.
From Crisis to Opportunity: Why Some Educators Say Mergers Offer a Path Forward
Some community members say mergers can be less disruptive than closures because students and staff stick together instead of dispersing across many schools.
They can also, in some cases, foster integration if officials deliberately merge schools with different student populations — an approach Samuels embraced as a superintendent of diverse districts in Brooklyn and Manhattan.
He often points to Arts & Letters 305 United, the Brooklyn school where he oversaw a merger of a largely Black, high-poverty and underenrolled elementary school with a more affluent, white and oversubscribed school, as an example of what’s possible.
Samuels described the school today as “truly integrated.” Arts & Letters 305 United — which is now a little more than one-third Black and one-third white — is outperforming citywide averages in math and reading and is attracting families at a time when the district’s enrollment has declined, he said at a recent town hall.
Some parts of the school system cannot be easily integrated when it comes to race or family income. But there is potential for integrating students with different academic needs.
That was the case when Health, Education, Research Occupations High School, or HERO, in The Bronx merged in 2021 with the School of Hospitality and Tourism, a tiny and struggling school on an adjacent campus, said HERO Principal Kristin Cahill.
Hospitality and Tourism had 173 students, fewer than half of whom graduated on time and only 15% of whom enrolled in college. At HERO, 90% of students graduated on time and often left high school with an associate degree and training for careers in healthcare and education.
HERO benefited too, Cahill said. The merger allowed the school to grow from about 500 students to more than 700.
And while joining the two schools didn’t significantly change their racial and socioeconomic makeup, it ensured a “critical mass” of advanced students in every class. That allowed teachers to make their courses more challenging, which ultimately benefited all students, Cahill said.
Cahill believes mid-sized high schools like hers can be a template for the city by preserving the benefits of small schools while bringing some of the variety that larger high schools offer.
“This is a model that students and families can get excited about, while providing a pathway out of segregation and dwindling school size,” Cahill recently wrote in policy recommendations she hopes will inform Mamdani’s education agenda.
School Mergers and Closures Could Face Uphill Battle
To make a dent in the small-schools crisis, Samuels would have to potentially consider dozens of closures or mergers at once. But to win the approval of the Panel for Educational Policy, or PEP, the body that votes on school consolidation plans, the city must approach each proposal with enough care to make community members feel heard, current and former officials said.
It’s a challenge that has vexed past administrations.
“The amount of time and attention required at the leadership and staff levels to do even one school closure or merger makes it unfeasible to do at scale,” said Dan Weisberg, the former first deputy chancellor under Adams who oversaw closures and mergers for four years.
Adriana Alicea, a Queens parent and the chair of the PEP’s committee on school utilization, said the panel wants to see evidence that officials have gotten to know a school community beyond its enrollment numbers, have considered alternatives to closure and have ensured students who are displaced get access to more opportunities.
“The more you’re in the community, the more you understand the little nuances, and that goes a long way,” she said.
When school communities feel unheard and mobilize fierce opposition, Alicea said, there is an “expectation” that the Education Department will withdraw the proposals before they reach a PEP vote. That happened last spring with plans that Samuels helped draw up as a superintendent to close three small middle schools on the Upper West Side.
Goldmark, the former deputy chancellor under de Blasio, said it’s valuable to seek community buy-in, but the city can’t expect full support for every proposal.
Samuels, she said, is “highly skilled at cultivating consensus whenever possible, and in the past he’s also shown a willingness to press forward without it if needed to serve students better.”
Alicea, for her part, believes it’s possible to address the small-schools crisis at scale without sacrificing community collaboration.
“It is possible for us to do both,” she said. “It is possible to make grand sweeping changes and to let the community be the ones holding the broom.”
Michael Elsen-Rooney is a reporter for Chalkbeat New York, covering NYC public schools. Contact Michael at melsen-rooney@chalkbeat.org

https://taz.de/Frontex-Luftueberwachung/.title: Frontex-Luftüberwachung: Spähflüge für die libysche Küstenwache
https://taz.de/Frontex-Luftueberwachung/.author: Christian Jakob
https://taz.de/Frontex-Luftueberwachung/.text:
Frontex-Luftüberwachung: Spähflüge für die libysche Küstenwache
Eine Forschungsgruppe hat nachgewiesen, dass die Europäische Küstenwache verstärkt das Mittelmeer ausspäht – und so das Abfangen von Geflüchteten ermöglicht.
Um 5.24 Uhr am Morgen des 12. November 2024 startete ein von der EU-Grenzschutzagentur gechartertes Flugzeug mit dem Rufzeichen „Osprey 2“ von der Insel Lampedusa zu einem Überwachungsflug. In den folgenden Stunden überflog es ein Gebiet im Mittelmeer, in dem der EU-Staat Malta für die Seenotrettung zuständig ist. Dabei sichtete es ein Boot mit 23 Menschen. Dessen Motor war ausgefallen, die Insassen hatten deshalb einen Notruf abgesetzt. Kurze Zeit später beobachteten Seenotretter, wie ein Schiff der libyschen Küstenwache die Menschen innerhalb der maltesischen SAR-Zone – kurz für Search and Rescue Zone – an Bord nahm und nach Libyen brachte.
Einer am Dienstag veröffentlichten Untersuchung der Forschungsgruppe Liminal von der Universität Bologna zufolge ist Frontex immer häufiger an der gewaltsamen Rückführung von Migrantinnen und Migranten nach Libyen und Tunesien beteiligt. Demnach haben von Frontex-Flugzeugen und -Drohnen gewonnene Positionsdaten zwischen August 2018 und Oktober 2024 nachweislich das Abfangen und Zurückdrängen von mindestens 611 Flüchtlingsbooten mit 33.107 Menschen ermöglicht.
Rund 150.000 Menschen sind nach Zählung der UN-Migrationsorganisation IOM seit 2020 von libyschen Milizen auf dem Mittelmeer aufgegriffen und nach Libyen gebracht worden, etwa ebenso viele nach Tunesien. 2026 zählt die IOM bisher allein über 17.200 sogenannte Interceptions nach Libyen. Die Menschen werden dort unter „unmenschlichen und inakzeptablen Bedingungen inhaftiert“, so die IOM.
Die Auswertung von Flugtracking-Daten habe laut Liminal einen Anstieg der Einsatzstunden von Frontex-Flugzeugen im zentralen Mittelmeer von 469 Stunden im Jahr 2019 auf mindestens 5.253 Stunden im Jahr 2023 gezeigt. Das Frontex-Budget für die Luftraum-Überwachung sei von 11,7 Millionen Euro im Jahr 2018 auf 278,6 Millionen Euro im Jahr 2026 gestiegen. Die jüngste Ausschreibung der Agentur für Luftüberwachungsdienste vom Juni 2026 habe für einen Zeitraum von zwei Jahren ein Volumen von über einer halben Milliarde Euro.
Teil der „Pushback-Maschine“
Mit einer interaktiven Onlineplattform namens „Aerial Bordering“ hat Liminal den Aufbau einer umfangreichen Flotte privat betriebener Flugzeuge und einer Drohne nachgezeichnet, deren Videoaufnahmen in Echtzeit an die Frontex-Zentrale in Warschau übertragen werden können.
Die meisten Daten liegen demnach für das Jahr 2021 vor. In dieser Zeit gingen mindestens 36 Prozent aller dokumentierten Abfang-Aktionen auf See auf Sichtungen durch Frontex-Flugzeuge zurück.
„Die Luftüberwachung ermöglicht es Frontex, das zentrale Mittelmeer lückenlos im Blick zu behalten und sich gleichzeitig seinen rechtlichen Verpflichtungen zur Rettung der Menschen an Bord und zu ihrer sicheren Ausschiffung in Europa zu entziehen“, sagt Giovanna Reder vom Liminal. Reder spricht von einer „Pushback-Maschine“ die das Abfangen von Menschen auf See und ihre gewaltsame Rückführung nach Libyen und Tunesien möglich mache.
Die Luftoperationen von Frontex hätten es der libyschen Küstenwache ermöglicht, ihre Abfangaktionen auf ein deutlich größeres Gebiet auszudehnen – bis weit in die maltesische Such- und Rettungsregion hinein. Frontex ermögliche so Gewalt gegen Geflüchtete. „Zugleich profitieren Rüstungsunternehmen finanziell und in ihrer öffentlichen Legitimität, obwohl sie an schwersten Verbrechen beteiligt sind“, sagt Lorenzo Pezzani, Professor an der Universität Bologna, der Liminal leitet.
Frontex verweist auf das Völkerrecht
Seit Jahren steht der Vorwurf im Raum, Frontex würde mit der libyschen Küstenwache kooperieren. Dabei wird diese von mafiösen Milizen kontrolliert und hat in der Vergangenheit in internationalen Gewässern Schusswaffen gegen europäische Seenotretter eingesetzt.
Frontex erklärt, es arbeite „in keiner Weise mit den libyschen Behörden zusammen“. Allerdings stießen Frontex-Flugzeuge innerhalb der Zone des Mittelmeeres, in der Libyen für Rettungseinsätze zuständig sei – der sogenannten SAR-Zone – „häufig auf überfüllte Boote in Not.“ In diesen Fällen werde „gemäß dem Völkerrecht“ die libysche Rettungsleitstelle über die in Not geratenen Boote informiert. Seit Jahren berichten NGOs aber von Fällen vor allem in der maltesischen SAR-Zone, in denen Frontex oder andere europäische Institutionen trotzdem die libysche Küstenwache rufen – um zu verhindern, dass die Menschen nach Europa gelangen.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. So viele unterstützen freiwillig und regelmäßig. Noch nicht dabei? Werden Sie jetzt Teil der Community! Jetzt unterstützen

A group of senior Israeli ex-military officials helped Palestinian farmers on Tuesday to harvest olives, in a gesture of solidarity amid an upsurge in extremist settler violence targeting Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.
"When I see what is going on here, when I see these guys come... and hit women and kids, it reminds me of stories from my parents from the time when the Jewish people suffered," said former Major General Eyal Ben-Reuven, who compared the settler attacks to pogroms.
Ben-Reuven said he began organising a group of around 30 senior military officials - including six generals - several months ago, following an increase in settler violence that many Palestinians say is enabled by the Israeli military.
"Occupation is the main problem of Israeli society. I believe we must deal with it. We cannot ignore it. We must try to solve it together with the Palestinians," said former Colonel Doron Meinert.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/3.text:
Michigan US Senate race: Rogers, El-Sayed urge turnout for critical race
Democratic hopeful Abdul El-Sayed faces a slew of last-minute Islamophobic attacks as he seeks to unseat Trump-backed Republican candidate Mike Rogers.
Michigan voters are casting their ballots in a charged, closely watched race that could make Democrat Abdul El-Sayed the first Muslim in the United States Senate and help decide control of the chamber.
Mike Rogers, his Republican opponent, cast his ballot at a polling station in White Lake, Michigan hours after polls opened. El-Sayed had already had his vote submitted and counted through an absentee ballot before Election Day.
The two candidates seek to fill the seat of retiring Democratic Senator Gary Peters. A final New York Times/Siena poll placed El-Sayed 11 points ahead of Rogers going into the election.
Polls opened at 7am local time (12:00 GMT) and close at 8pm (01:00 GMT on Wednesday). If the race is close, it may not be called until later on Wednesday. The US Department of Justice has announced that election monitors will be present at the polls in Michigan and all 50 other states, a first in US history.
El-Sayed, a Muslim born to Egyptian parents, is the former head of Detroit’s health department and has campaigned on progressive policies such as Medicare for All.
Rogers, a former congressman and close ally of US President Donald Trump, is seeking to come back after a narrow loss to a Democrat in a 2024 Senate race.
Democrats need to gain four seats in Tuesday’s midterm elections to wrest back the Senate from Republicans and rein in Trump. The race is also seen as a test of whether a progressive who openly criticises Israel can win in a swing state.
Both candidates made a final push on social media as voting got under way.
“It’s time. It’s up to us to show the country what’s possible. The world is watching,” El-Sayed wrote, sharing an upbeat campaign video that features former US President Barack Obama.
Rogers posted a video that featured interviews with supporters, one of whom called El-Sayed an “extremist”.
“We have a state to save”, the post read.
Democratic Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer gave a firm endorsement of El-Sayed after casting his own ballot in New York’s race.
“There are millions of Michiganders whose number one issue is getting their costs down,” said Schumer.
“Abdul El-Sayed is … talking to the people about those issues and doing things about them … He is going to win tonight because he’s talking about what Michiganders care about.”
‘One vote’
The El-Sayed campaign’s final days were overshadowed by a rift with Congresswoman Haley Stevens, a fellow Democrat whom El-Sayed narrowly defeated in a primary election in August.
On Sunday, Stevens endorsed Rogers, saying she was “choosing country over hate” and capping off a weeks-long row about El-Sayed’s opposition to US support for Israel.
Stevens is a staunch supporter of Israel, and the pro-Israel lobbying group the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) spent more than $30m backing her against El-Sayed. A majority of her large donors lined up to support Rogers after her loss, channeling $9m into a Republican group that supports him, according to The New York Times.
El-Sayed, by contrast, has accused Israel of genocide in Gaza and argued that US aid to Israel would be better spent at home.
Asked by NewsNation on her way in to vote for Rogers whether her change in support was worth it, Stevens replied: “Absolutely. Voting is always worth it, right?”
Senate leader Schumer, who had initially backed Stevens, was asked whether her defection could hand the election to Republicans. “Haley Stevens is one vote,” he replied.
Islamophobic attacks
El-Sayed, the Michigan-born son of Egyptian immigrants, has faced persistent attacks on his faith. Republican Party ads have sought to link him to “terrorism” and radicalism, with Trump joining in the inflammatory rhetoric.
The US president has repeatedly called El-Sayed a “jihadist” and a “nasty guy”, mocking his name and repeating an unfounded, widely circulated Republican claim that he belongs to the Muslim Brotherhood.
Hours before polls opened, Trump once again took aim at El-Sayed, this time in a post on his Truth Social platform.
“Abdul El-Sayed Hates Jews and Hates Blacks. Don’t feel bad, he also Hates Whites. Only fools would vote for him in the Michigan race for the U.S. Senate! He will, 100%, do you in! VOTE FOR MIKE ROGERS,” Trump wrote.
The US president also mentioned El-Sayed in a Fox News interview early on Election Day, when he said annual US financial aid to Israel should stop at the end of 2026.
“Why should we suffer the slings from lunatics like an El-Sayed when they [Israel] don’t need it?” he said.

Yemen’s internationally recognised government has accused Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), as well as Lebanon’s Hezbollah, of deploying 21 experts to help the Houthis plan and direct military operations in the country.
Interior Minister Major-General Ibrahim Haidan said in a statement on Tuesday that 14 members of the group are from the IRGC and seven from Hezbollah.
The experts’ roles show that foreign involvement has moved from financing, arming and training to “direct supervision and participation in planning and managing operations and building military capabilities”, said Haidan.
The statement added that eight of the experts are in Hodeidah, four in Sanaa, four in Saada, two in Hajjah, two in Amran and one in the coastal city of Khokha.
It listed their specialities as including command and control, ballistic missiles and drones, electronic warfare, smuggling military components, coordinating naval operations and choosing commercial ships as targets, developing explosive-laden boats and autonomous submarines, and training fighters in mine-laying and siege tactics.
Haidan warned that the activities “threaten shipping in the Bab al-Mandeb strait and the Red Sea” and could transfer military expertise to other armed groups.
He called on the international community to designate the Houthis a “terrorist” organisation, dismantle their financing and arms networks, and enforce the arms embargo under United Nations Security Council resolutions 2216 and 2624.
The statement comes as Yemeni armed forces and fighters loyal to the government battle the Houthis in five provinces, after the group seized the western Red Sea coast and the Bab al-Mandeb area in September.
The resumption of fighting has shattered a relative quiet brought by a 2022 ceasefire that followed a lengthy civil war which first erupted in 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa.
In 2015, Saudi Arabia entered the war at the head of an international coalition aimed at restoring Yemen’s internationally recognised government.
The government has long claimed the IRGC is supporting the Houthis, while Tehran insists the Houthis act independently. The Houthis acknowledge their alliance with Iran but have long denied being an Iranian proxy, while Hezbollah has previously rejected having a role in Yemen’s war.
Saudi Arabia, whose airports and oil facilities have come under Houthi attack in recent weeks, has accused Iran of encouraging the escalation.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Democrats aim to retake Senate from Republicans as Americans go to polls
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Chris Stein in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Republicans are defending their majority in the US Senate against resurgent Democrats, who believe voters’ dissatisfaction with Donald Trump will put them back in control of Congress’s upper chamber.
The president’s opponents notched two early wins, with the Associated Press calling Georgia’s Senate race for Jon Ossoff, the incumbent who appears to have easily won a second term in a state that voted for Trump in 2024.
In New Hampshire, Democrat Chris Pappas will succeed outgoing senator Jeanne Shaheen, according to the AP, defying Republicans’ hopes for an upset win in a state known for its independent streak.
Democrats were also re-elected or kept hold of Senate seats representing Virginia, Delaware, New Jersey, Illinois, Rhode Island and Massachusetts, all blue states they were expected to win.
Democrats lost their majority in the Senate in 2024, when voters re-elected Trump and gave his Republican allies 53 seats in Congress’s upper chamber. The party must win at least four seats to regain control, which would give them a potent tool against Trump for the final two years of his presidency. Not only could they block the president’s bills and issue subpoenas to investigate his administration, but they could also reject his nominees to the federal judiciary – including the supreme court.
At the outset of his presidency, it appeared difficult to believe that the minority party would have much of a shot of regaining control in the midterms – most senators set to face re-election represented solidly red or blue states, giving Democrats few offensive opportunities.
But Trump’s approval ratings have fallen sharply since his inauguration, fueled by dissatisfaction over his handling of the economy, and the all-important cost of living. His decision to attack Iran has also proven unpopular with voters, as has his hardline implementation of immigration law.
To flip the Senate, Democrats initially named as their best bets races in Maine – the only state that voted for Kamala Harris and had a Republican incumbent on the ballot – North Carolina, Ohio and Alaska.
As sentiment towards Trump worsened, the party believed their candidates had a shot at winning in Texas, Kansas, Iowa and South Carolina – all red states Trump won by double digits.
In a sign of Republican concern that a “blue wave” could sweep their Senate majority away just two years after it was created, Trump spent the final weeks before the midterms campaigning in places like Kansas, South Carolina and Texas, where his party usually romps to victory.
Republicans have their own targets, namely Democrats attempting to defend seats they hold in states that had broken for Trump two years ago, or that Harris carried by slim margins. This group included Minnesota, New Hampshire, Michigan and Georgia, though Republican candidates have already lost in two of those states.
A poll by the New York Times and Siena University published Sunday found Democrats leading in five battleground states surveyed, and statistically tied in a sixth. But other surveys have found Republican candidates ahead, while some Democrats vying for important seats have been dealing with drama and scandal in the closing days of the race.
Last week, the New York Times reported that Alaska Senate candidate Mary Peltola’s campaign collaborated with Democratic operatives to recruit a candidate with nearly the same name as her opponent, the incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan. The state’s governor has ordered a criminal investigation into the allegation, while the US Department of Justice filed a suit to block the election’s certification if Sullivan loses, though a federal judge recently dismissed it.
In Michigan, tensions between Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed and congresswoman Haley Stevens, whom he defeated in the primary, erupted into open conflict after she endorsed his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers. Stevens said she objected to El-Sayed’s stance on an advertisement by an outside group that blamed the rising cost of living on US support for Israel, but Democrats accused the four-term congresswoman of “betrayal”.

https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/n.title: Citizen Kim by Jonathan Van Meter review – Kardashian under the microscope
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/n.author: Rebecca Nicholson
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/n.text:
The magazine writer Jonathan Van Meter profiles very famous people for extremely glossy publications. He was responsible for the notorious 1990 interview in which supermodel Linda Evangelista said she wouldn’t wake up for less than $10,000 a day, and in recent years, he has interviewed Taylor Swift, Michelle Obama and Lady Gaga for American Vogue. In 2019, he wrote a cover story, also for Vogue, on Kim Kardashian, the reality TV star turned businesswoman turned criminal justice activist, and one of the most famous women in the world. In the lengthy acknowledgments to this book, he describes receiving a phonecall from her after the piece had been published. “There’s no better feeling in the world than when someone gets you,” she told him. He replied by telling her that he was going to write a book about her, “whether you like it or not!”
Spoiler alert: she liked it. And the concept underlying the book can be justified: Kim Kardashian really has transformed celebrity culture. Her family, broadcasting their lives for years, came to define contemporary reality television, beginning with Keeping Up With the Kardashians in 2007 and continuing to the present day with The Kardashians. She saw the potential in social media and used it to her advantage from its inception. Last year, her clothing line, Skims, was valued at $5bn (£3.75bn). Van Meter notes that despite her ubiquitous presence, there has been “a dearth of well-written profiles and shrewd cultural analysis” about the phenomenon of Kim K.
But what is promised and what is delivered are not exactly the same. Early on, Van Meter references Kant and the academic Timothy Morton, and later, he invokes Joan Didion’s writing on Hollywood. But any attempts at cultural analysis, shrewd or otherwise, quickly fall away in favour of a more traditional in-depth biography, its wheels greased by regular, intimate access to the Kardashians and many of Kim’s closest friends and colleagues.
Van Meter visits his subject often, at her many homes and places of work. They talk over snacks and coffee. Kim may be in her pyjamas or a bathrobe, having just got out of the shower. At one point, she does away with the formality of clothing entirely. “I looked up from my phone and she was entirely naked. Neither of us flinched,” he writes, describing a day spent with her at a photoshoot. This is intended to suggest candour, though inevitably it implies a lack of critical distance. At the end, in the acknowledgements, he thanks her for her “time, but more so, your trust”.
Van Meter notes that Kim does not like to dwell on the bad stuff, nor does she seem particularly inclined towards introspection. What more is there to say about her life that has not already been televised? Ironically, her views on the family’s show may be the most fascinating part of this book. Doing television has been good for them, she says, “because we’re not going to leave an episode unfinished” – by which she means that arguments are almost always resolved, because they have to be, for the shape of the TV narrative. Public and private are one and the same.
At its best, the book does expose some of the Kardashian family’s gothic underbelly. In 1995, Kim’s mother and father found themselves on opposing sides of the OJ Simpson murder trial (Kris Jenner supported her best friend Nicole Brown’s family during the trial, while her ex-husband, the late Robert Kardashian, was on Simpson’s legal team). For a while, Kim’s teenage boyfriend was TJ Jackson, nephew of Michael, whose own family lore is horrifying and unique. Her school days are likened to the movie Clueless, but there is a touch of Bret Easton Ellis in there, too.
There is some reflection on the sex tape that propelled Kim into the public eye (it has left her with “a lot to prove”, she says). Van Meter offers a pop-psychology analysis of why she seems to gravitate towards “lost boys”, and she talks about her marriage to Kanye West, albeit with respect and restraint. She describes a move away from a more materialistic worldview after being robbed at gunpoint in Paris, in 2016. The book ends with speculation that she might run for political office. “I am so flattered,” she responds, and leaves the prospect open.
There are moments of camp extravagance. One chapter begins, “Did the trouble start with not one, but two boob jobs?” Van Meter namedrops Anna Wintour, Oprah Winfrey and his own tennis coach. But elsewhere, the narrative swoons and fawns. Kim’s private jet is “a shade of nudey grey,” we learn. “Which is so me,” she says. It is also so this book. The Kardashian aura must be strong, because reading this evokes the same sensation as watching their show: it is seductive, hypnotic, but possessed of a sleight of hand that turns everything beige.

https://theintercept.com/2026/10/28/main.title: Trump Vows to Send Election “Monitors” to Maine After Far-Right Conspiracies Spread
https://theintercept.com/2026/10/28/main.author: Noah Hurowitz
https://theintercept.com/2026/10/28/main.text:
With voters set to cast ballots in two critical races that could help determine control of both chambers of the U.S. Congress, fears of potential voter suppression are running high in Maine.
Officials in the state have prepared for months against the possibility of election interference from federal officials, and the state remains on high alert in the run-up to the general election on November 3.
Training materials for law enforcement officials in the state, obtained by The Intercept through a public records request, were updated this year for the elections to include explicit references to federal statutes barring armed federal agents from polling sites.
In an interview with the New York Times this week, Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows said the inclusion of such references was a direct defense in response to the fearmongering around election integrity from President Donald Trump and his administration.
“This is the first time ever that we have had to engage in scenario planning to safeguard against potential federal interference in elections,” Bellows said. “It seems like the federal government is now adversarial to the states.”
Bellows’s office offered up the training slideshow, which cites a U.S. law that bars armed civil or military officers from posting at voting sites, to law enforcement personnel in the run-up to Maine’s primary election in June and again in the lead-up to the general election on November 5.
Nationwide, Democratic officials have expressed fears that the Trump Administration might weaponize U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement or other federal agencies to undermine the rights of voters. In New York, state Attorney General Letitia James issued a reminder to voters that federal officials may not “police the polls,” and the Arkansas chapter of the NAACP called out the assignment of federal election monitors to two counties in the state as potential intimidation.
The Trump administration, meanwhile, has sounded the alarm about the alleged scourge of non-citizens on the voter rolls, sending agents from the FBI and ICE’s Homeland Security Investigations division to probe alleged fraud. A handful of people in California, New York, and North Carolina have been indicted for allegedly voting as non-citizens, but a review of similar cases by the Washington Post found that such cases were often the result of honest mistakes.
In Maine, worries about federal interventions at polling places flared when — following a slew of social media videos from Trump allies suggesting that fraud is already taking place among the state’s Somali American community — a local outlet reported that the Department of Justice would be sending election monitors to the state.
Jon Fetherston, a journalist with the far-right Maine Wire, which is funded by conservative megadonor Leonard Leo, was seen following people in and around an early voting site at Lewiston City Hall and aggressively questioning them. (The Maine Wire did not immediately respond to a request for comment.)
Critics said the moves were tantamount to voter harassment, but Maine Wire editor-in-chief Steve Robinson later defended them as an act of election transparency. Robinson, who has led a crusade against what he alleges to be a network of fraud in the state’s Somali American community, questioned the role of interpreters tasked with helping “jobless Somali bums” cast their ballots.
In the wake of the Maine Wire controversy in Lewiston, Bellows confirmed to the Maine Morning Star that a wave of federal election monitors would be headed to polling sites in Lewiston and Portland.
The Department of Justice on Tuesday confirmed to The Intercept that it intends to send election monitors to Maine for Election Day, but did not elaborate or respond to specific questions about where the monitors were to be sent.
“We will have around 1,000 monitors in counties throughout the United States, but we will not share the full list until Election Day,” a Justice Department spokesperson told The Intercept in an email Tuesday. “All monitors must meet the same legal and ethical requirements, including that they not interfere with the voting process. Every monitor has the same role: observe for potential violations of federal law and report concerns to the Department, which the Department will review after Election Day and act where appropriate.”
Robinson did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Collins Takes Right-Wing Bait
With Maine a key battleground state for control of Congress — Democratic challenger Troy Jackson is seeking to topple long-serving GOP Sen. Susan Collins, and the Democratic House candidate Matt Dunlap is seeking to best former Gov. Paul LePage in Maine’s 2nd Congressional District — temperatures are running high in the state.
Progressives in Maine worry that even without a robust federal presence at voting places — whether monitors are armed or not — activist campaigns like the one undertaken by the Maine Wire journalists could pose a potential threat to voters’ rights.
“Basically, if you were walking into City Hall and you were Black, you could expect to have this guy come up to you with his phone and ask you all sorts of rude and obviously racist questions,” said Ben Chin, co-director of the progressive Maine People’s Alliance. “We’re trying to encourage everyone to come out to vote, but it makes sense why that might give people pause. You hear a guy like that is outside a polling location, it’s reasonable to wonder, ‘Should I go down there right now?’”
In a statement to The Intercept, Bellows said the state and the city of Lewiston were taking steps to ensure that voters could cast a ballot free of harassment.
“We have received complaints about the intrusive filming, photography, and harassment of voters in the City of Lewiston by political operatives,” Bellows told The Intercept in a statement. “All voters should be able to exercise their right to vote without feeling watched, questioned, or harassed, and we take these allegations seriously, particularly when it appears that voters were targeted for no other reason than their race or ethnicity. We understand the City of Lewiston has taken steps to address the problem, and we will continue to monitor the situation.”
Collins, meanwhile, took the Maine Wire’s reporting seriously after Fetherston asked the senator at a campaign event about the role of interpreters, which he and the Maine Wire cast as “electioneering.”
“I’m unaware of those allegations, but certainly only Americans should be voting in American elections,” Collins said. “And it is troubling to me if people are being accompanied into voting booths and handling ballots in a way that is not sanctioned by law.”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
