https://taz.de/Roman-von-Milada-Souckova.title: Roman von Milada Součková: Der Ausweg aus dem poetischen Labyrinth
https://taz.de/Roman-von-Milada-Souckova.author: Claudia Lenssen
https://taz.de/Roman-von-Milada-Souckova.text:
Roman von Milada Součková: Der Ausweg aus dem poetischen Labyrinth
Der neugegründete Verlag dimidium mundi verlegt fast vergessene Schriftstellerinnen neu. Nun erscheint der Coming-of-Age-Roman einer Prager Avantgardistin.
Schriftstellerinnen schreiben meist biografisch-psychologisch, Schriftsteller konfrontieren die Welt dagegen gern mit ihrer literarischen Experimentierlust, zumindest wenn sie sich auf dem Weg zum männlichen Genie fühlen. So weit das immer noch gültige Klischee, das allerdings seit Jahrhunderten von vielen Frauen kreativ unterlaufen wird. Wir kennen sie nur nicht, weil sie vergessen und aus dem Kanon verdrängt sind.
Nicht erst Virginia Woolf, Gertrude Stein und Ingeborg Bachmann haben mit Erzählperspektiven, Zeitsprüngen und Mischformen jongliert, um ihre Skepsis gegenüber dem falschen Versprechen auszudrücken, realistische Romane würden die Welt, wie sie ist, eins zu eins abbilden.
Obwohl jedoch immer wieder vergessene Schriftstellerinnen neu aufgelegt werden und sich beispielsweise der Aviva Verlag konsequent um die Wiederentdeckung vor allem von jüdischen Autorinnen vor dem Kahlschlag durch das Naziregime verdient macht, braucht es auch heute Initiativen wie www.lueckenliste.de, auf der Interessierte aus dem Literaturbetrieb und der Wissenschaft ihre Hinweise auf vergessene Schriftsteller_innen teilen. Ziel ist nicht weniger als die Sichtbarkeit der Hälfte der (literarischen) Welt.
Der Roman
Milada Součková: „Amor und Psyche“. Aus dem Tschechischen von Doris Kouba. dimidium mundi, München 2026, 320 Seiten, 26 Euro
dimidium mundi, ein von Zarifa Mamedova in diesem Jahr in München neu gegründeter Verlag, zeigt mit seinem aus dem Lateinischen entlehnten Namen an, dass er sich genau diesem Ziel verpflichtet fühlt, die Hälfte des literarischen Kanons für Autorinnen der Weltkultur zu erobern.
Kam im Frühjahr als Debüt der Roman „Die Lust am Manne“ (1928) der österreichisch-ungarischen Schauspielerin, Autorin und Filmregisseurin Olga Wohlbrück heraus, folgt mit „Amor und Psyche“ (1937) nun ein früher Roman der hierzulande (bis auf die 1998 und 2010 edierten Romane „Der unbekannte Mensch“ und „Bel Canto“) viel zu wenig bekannten tschechischen Schriftstellerin Milada Součková.
Avantgardistische Künstlerzirkel
Geboren 1898 in Prag als Tochter eines Bauunternehmers, besuchte Milada Součková das Prager Minerva-Gymnasium, das erste Mädchengymnasium Österreich-Ungarns, dessen pädagogisches Programm auf die freie Entfaltung und Emanzipation der Schülerinnen – darunter die Journalistin und zeitweise Kafka-Gefährtin Milena Jesenská – ausgerichtet war.
Ihr naturwissenschaftliches Studium in Prag und Lausanne schloss Milada Součková 1923 mit einer Doktorarbeit über „Das Seelenleben der Pflanzen“ ab. In der lebendigen Prager Kulturszene der seit dem Ende des Ersten Weltkriegs gegründeten ersten tschechoslowakischen Republik schloss sich Milada Součková den avantgardistischen Künstlerzirkeln der Stadt an, heiratete den Maler Zdenek Rykr und veröffentlichte Gedichte, Reiseberichte über Südeuropa und die zunehmenden politischen Bedrohungen der Epoche in literarischen Zeitschriften.
Als Mitglied der Gruppe 42, einer tschechischen Künstlergruppe, die bis zu ihrem Verbot durch das kommunistische Regime 1948 bestand, teilte Milada Součková das Misstrauen der Avantgarde gegenüber den konventionellen Formen des realistischen Romans. Inspiriert von Marcel Prousts monumentaler Erinnerungsarbeit über die goldene Ära des Bürgertums bis 1914 und angeregt durch André Gides Roman „Die Falschmünzer“ (1925), einer Geschichte schwuler Jugenderfahrungen in wechselnden Erzählperspektiven, begann die Schriftstellerin, sich mit dem Lebensgefühl ihrer politisch wachen Generation auseinanderzusetzen. Die überkommenen literarischen Mittel erklärte sie für nutzlose Fossile, untauglich, um den Wirbel ihrer in Fragmente zerfallenden Erfahrungswelt zu beschreiben.
Herausfordernde Coming-of-Age-Geschichte
„Amor und Psyche“ ist eine fein gesponnene, in Teilen herausfordernde Coming-of-Age-Geschichte im Umfeld junger Frauen aus dem Prager Bürgertum – weder konkret autobiografisch grundiert noch psychologisch als oberflächliches Angebot zur Identifikation erzählt. Das Mädchen Augustina und die Erzählerin verstricken sich in ein amüsiertes, vom Ringen um Nähe und Distanz bestimmtes Spiel um Augustas Tagebuch, das von ihrer Liebe zu der von beiden angebeteten Lehrerin Alsbětă handelt.
Im zweiten Teil des Romans spiegeln sich die Wünsche und Träume der Mädchen aus anderer Perspektive im Tagebuch der Erzählerin. Der dritte Teil, ein poetisches Labyrinth der Erlebnisse beider Mädchen und weiterer Figuren aus ihrem Kosmos, treibt die Fiktion auf die Spitze, sodass das Spiel der Tagebuchfragmente wie eine Parodie auf das Genre wirkt, komödiantischer als beispielsweise in dem ikonischen queeren Film „Mädchen in Uniform“.
Eine Göttin am literarischen Horizont, wie es Psyche, die Braut des Gottes Amor in Apuleios' berühmter Novelle aus dem 2. Jahrhundert, wird, scheint Augusta nicht zu werden – oder doch? Das göttlich-ingeniöse Selbstbild des literarischen Schreibens und seiner Spitzenvertreter ist in Milada Součkovás Augen in Zeiten grundstürzender Disruptionen in Zweifel zu ziehen.
Die Schriftstellerin verlor ihren im Widerstand gegen die NS-Besatzung engagierten Mann, als er sich der Verhaftung durch Suizid entzog. Sie wurde im Prag der Nachkriegszeit zur Außenseiterin, als sie 1945 als Kulturattaché der zweiten tschechoslowakischen Republik nach New York wechselte und 1948 nach der kommunistischen Machtübernahme in den USA blieb. Bis zu ihrem Tod 1983 wirkte sie als Bohemistin und Literaturtheoretikern in Harvard, Chicago und Berkeley, unterstützt vom Netzwerk der tschechisch-amerikanischen Community um Roman Jacobsen, den Linguisten und Freund aus Prager Zeiten. Die englische Übersetzung ihrer Werke kam nicht zustande.
Zarifa Mamedova beweist Mut, mit „Amor und Psyche“ den Weg ihres anspruchsvollen Verlagsprogramms vorzuzeichnen. dimidium mundi plant weitere Neuentdeckungen von Schriftstellerinnen, auch aus anderen, bisher zu wenig bekannten historischen Buchkulturen aller Kontinente. Wie die Bücher von Olga Wohlbrück und Milada Součková werden auch die kommenden Editionen Grafiken von der Hand junger Künstlerinnen enthalten, deren Originale man online über das zweite Standbein des Verlags erwerben kann.

https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.title: Carrie at 50: Brian De Palma’s fiery masterpiece still has the power
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.author: Jesse Hassenger
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.text:
Often when a pop culture figure, whether real or fictional or somewhere in between, is described as an eternal teenager, it refers to an image of youthful vitality. Carrie White, the wallflowery, telekinetic, sort-of heroine at the center of Stephen King’s book and its multiple adaptations, is a sadder case. She’s forever a teenager because until recently, every version of the story ends with her demise – a turn that would qualify as a spoiler if not for the universal familiarity of her story, or the fact that the book heavily implies her fate within the first 30 pages or so.
That fate is poised to change with Mike Flanagan’s TV series, which was recently renewed for a second season (though even then, there’s still plenty of room for poor Carrie to die young). The new show updates and expands the story of the 1974 novel, taking its inspiration from a combination of 2020s social trends and details from the original text. In other words, it’s a new adaptation, not a remake of the Brian De Palma film from 1976. As such, it’s the first truly successful version of Carrie in half a century. (Previous iterations popped up in a 1999 movie sequel, a 2002 miniseries and another film in 2013.) It’s arguable, however, that the reason such a high-profile new version of Carrie exists in 2026 is that first film, which was released 50 years ago on 3 November.
In fact, King’s book was not a bestseller when it first came out in 1974. His subsequent novel, Salem’s Lot, sold better out the gate in 1975; Carrie didn’t hit the New York Times bestseller list until December 1976, in paperback form. This was a month or so after the release of De Palma’s film, which had become an unexpectedly strong holiday-season hit. Though a willowy Sissy Spacek wasn’t a precise match for King’s description of Carrie as a more full-figured and less ethereal teenager (nor was her mid-20s age a match for Carrie’s teenage status), the image of her drenched in blood, wide-eyed with shellshocked vengeance at the film’s prom-set climax became indelibly associated with the simple story.
De Palma’s film is even more streamlined than King’s novel. It retains the basic structure – the first half taking place over a week or so leading up to the high school prom, the second following that evening, where Carrie is unexpectedly crowned queen before suffering a planned humiliation, followed by an extremely brief survey of the aftermath – as well as many of the book’s details and some of its dialogue. But King also intersperses excerpts from various (fictional) outside texts written after the story’s deadly climax, both hinting (sometimes more than hinting) at the carnage to come and filling in various backstories and flashback anecdotes about Carrie White, her telekinetic powers and her religious fanatic mother Margaret (Piper Laurie in the movie).
Without these digressions, De Palma’s film seems ruthlessly efficient, especially compared to the recent series. While King’s imaginative array of academic explorations, magazine articles and fake tell-alls lend the proceedings a slight detachment (if a frequently mournful one), De Palma uses his pure-cinema immediacy to put the audience into the movie’s hair-trigger adolescent-hothouse atmosphere. That most of the actors were actually well into adulthood only makes their aggression pop more. Some have accused De Palma’s opening sequence, where the camera tracks around a girls’ locker room in anticipation of the famous inciting incident where Carrie gets a late-onset period and is terrorized by her cruel classmates, of crossing the line into lasciviousness. But when his camera lands on a showering Carrie White, alone with her thoughts and a vaguely sensual look on her face, De Palma keys into all that is discomfortingly intimate about the story, fraying at that image immediately when Carrie notices her menstrual blood and panics.
That raw-nerve discombobulation is a hallmark of the film, which traffics in familiar settings (high school, teenagers in cool cars, a glittery dance) while making them feel distorted and intense. To this end De Palma makes heavy use of split-diopter shots, a camera-lens trick that creates the ability to sharply focus on objects in the foreground and background simultaneously, with a blurry, out-of-focus line separating the two. In an English-classroom scene, for example, De Palma keeps popular, cheerful Tommy (William Katt) in closeup while Carrie, quietly besotted with the poem he wrote for class, remains in focus several rows behind him. They’re occupying the same space, but Carrie – bedeviled by her classmates, yes, but also the haranguing of her impossible-to-please, God-fearing mom – looks impossibly distant, too.
Later, after repentant popular girl Sue (Amy Irving) has Tommy, her boyfriend, ask Carrie to prom to give her a taste of social acceptance, De Palma’s camera follows the not-quite-couple to the dancefloor. As they dance in circles, the camera rotates around them, which in conjunction with the colorful lighting creates a dizzying, carnival-like effect. It’s a lead-up to a classic De Palma uncorking, where vengeful mean girl Chris (the terrific Nancy Allen, who later married and divorced De Palma) dumps a bucket of pig’s blood on to poor Carrie, unleashing the girl’s nascent telekinetic powers. An entire gymnasium’s worth of students suffers her split-screened, fiery wrath, with Psycho-style string stings accompanying the bursts of power. (It’s probably not a coincidence that the main location has been rechristened Bates high school by Alfred Hitchcock-loving De Palma.)
Watching De Palma’s treatment of this sequence soon after Flanagan’s is striking: in part because De Palma’s version is scarier (while Flanagan’s somewhat mitigates Carrie’s participation), and in part because it’s so evocative without the torrents of dialogue that Flanagan favors. There are about 15 minutes from Carrie’s prom-queen coronation to her arrival back at home to have it out with her mother that involve only incidental chatter. For that matter, there isn’t a whole lot of dialogue in the ensuing final 15 minutes, either. This does mean that both King’s book and Flanagan’s series have a bit more nuance to various characters. The 1976 movie portrays the world around Carrie as both beautiful and unceasingly harsh; her moments of respite, even joy, have a pleading quality. That quality only makes Spacek’s performance – Oscar-nominated, alongside Laurie’s – all the more heartbreaking. In the end, the White house collapses on to Carrie and her mother; it crumbles from her psychic powers, but she seeks cover all the same, toting her lousy mother’s body with her, surrendering to her power as uncontrollable.
De Palma can’t resist one last sting that wouldn’t make much sense in the book: a dreamy scene where Sue visits the razed site of the White house, whereupon a bloody arm bursts out of the ground and grabs hold of her, before she awakes screaming in fright. This could be read as a cheap horror-movie trick to rattle audiences just a little more on their way out the door, or a nasty rebuke to Sue’s mother who claims a doctor said Sue will probably forget all about the Carrie White incident in time. Fifty years later, though, it feels most like an acknowledgment of how this particular version of Carrie has lingered in the public imagination as a nightmare reflection of the adolescent experience. Flanagan brought Carrie White into the 21st century, but she didn’t have to travel far to get here.
- Carrie is available to watch on Amazon Prime in the US, UK and Australia

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: From the US midterms to the hard right in Britain, empathy has become a dirty word in politics | John Harris
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: John Harris
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Towards the end of the summer, the Tory-Reform defector Robert Jenrick authored an op-ed piece for the Daily Telegraph about the seemingly impossible economics of rising benefits bills because of mental ill-health. In his capacity as Reform’s Treasury spokesman, his task was to big up its plans to cut 25% of so-called welfare spending by 2030, and thereby tackle what he called the state’s “suicidal empathy”.
Straight away, I wondered where this most opportunistic politician had borrowed that phrase from, and instantly found out: a book with the same title, published this year by the Canadian academic Gad Saad, whom the dust jacket describes as having particular expertise in “the use of evolutionary psychology in marketing and consumer behaviour”. It comes with an endorsement from Elon Musk. “Western civilisation is doomed unless the core weakness of suicidal empathy is recognised and actions are taken that are hard but necessary for survival,” says the world’s richest man. “All of Gad’s books, including this one, are great.”
Unfortunately, Suicidal Empathy is not great. It is, in fact, a baggy mess, glueing together absurd straw men (“suicidal empathy can cause people to care more about rapists and other felons than their victims”) to familiar arguments about immigration, Covid lockdowns and whether the word “imbecile” is offensive. One of its most head-turning claims is that the west’s supposed embrace of degenerate woke-ism is largely traceable to the fact that “women are much more likely to succumb to such emotional and ideological capture”. At a push, its most useful function is as a meandering guide to the soup of ideas simmering in the minds of hardcore Maga voters as they prepared for this week’s midterms.
There is a huge amount of this stuff around, crystallising the philosophical core of Trumpism and its adherent movements across the world – roughly, the idea that might is right and compassion is for wimps. We are now well beyond the culture wars and the US right’s long history of (to put it politely) Christian revisionism, and into the very serious prospect of a decisive western moral counter-revolution that may already be under way. That’s certainly the intention of the slew of voices responsible for podcasts, social media posts and other Maga potboilers – witness 2024’s Toxic Empathy: How Progressives Exploit Christian Compassion, by the Christian podcaster Allie Beth Stuckey, or last year’s The Sin of Empathy: Compassion and its Counterfeits, by the rightwing pastor Joe Rigney.
But here’s the crucial thing: the same moral push is also supported by alarming numbers of regular people. According to polling by the Public Religion Research Institute, while 84% of registered US Democrats support the proposition that empathy helps build a healthy society, only 54% of Republicans agree. Perhaps most strikingly, to quote from the survey’s accompanying blurb: “White evangelical Protestants are the only religious group in which a majority does not agree that empathy is a foundational moral value (42%). Instead, a majority (54%) say empathy can be dangerous.”
Much the same seems to be true of that possible Trump successor, JD Vance – a Catholic convert who now has the rare distinction of having locked horns with two popes. In April, Leo XIV plainly decried the US’s attacks on Iran, insisting: “Anyone who is a disciple of Christ, the Prince of Peace, is never on the side of those who once wielded the sword and today drop bombs.” Vance’s response? “I think it’s very, very important for the pope to be careful when he talks about matters of theology.” Only a few months before, the vice-president insisted his “old-school” notion of Christian compassion descended in priority from “your family”, “your neighbor” and “your community” to “your fellow citizens in your own country”. Then and only then, he said, could you “focus [sic] and prioritize the rest of the world”.
Soon after, our era’s most pre-eminent moral philosopher was interviewed by the podcaster Joe Rogan. “The fundamental weakness of western civilisation,” said Musk, “is empathy, the empathy exploit.” Progressives, he said, have set themselves on “exploiting a bug in western civilisation, which is the empathy response”.
At that point, I went straight back to one of my favourite modern books: the classicist and historian Tom Holland’s bestseller Dominion, that brilliant history of Christianity and its global impact that illuminates how an emphasis on what we now call empathy (the word was only created in 1908, as the English translation of the German “Einfühlung”, or “in-feeling”) was one of that religion’s philosophical revolutions.
“Across the Roman world,” Holland writes, “wailing at the sides of roads or on rubbish tips, babies abandoned by their parents were a common sight.” Such everyday barbarism was also reflected in official attitudes to poor, disabled and infirm people – until a moral up-ending began with Rome’s conversion to Christianity under Constantine. As Holland writes: “Every week in churches across the Roman world, collections for orphans and widows, for the imprisoned, and the shipwrecked and the sick had been raised … Entire systems of social security had begun to emerge.” But there was an additional element of this sea change – which, in a modern context, stands in sharp contrast to everything from ICE detention camps to Musk’s vandalism of USAID and the 700,000 deaths it is reckoned to have already caused. As Holland puts it, “divine love for the outcast and derelict demanded that mortals love them too”.
No one would claim Christian countries and institutions stuck to those ideas in the centuries that followed, but the modern US is surely now moral light years away. And there is a British story here, too, bound up with the changes brought to our politics by Margaret Thatcher – who was raised as a strict Methodist, and occasionally blurted out quite remarkable opinions about Christian teaching and questions of morality: in January 1980, for example, she claimed that “no one would remember the Good Samaritan if he’d only had good intentions; he had money as well”.
In this and so many other respects, she was way ahead of her time, opening the path to the kind of moral contortions we hear not just from Jenrick, but both his new comrades in Reform and his former Tory colleagues. Some have gone even further: let migrants drown, they say, while others accuse the lifeboat service – the lifeboat service! – of complicity in a supposed invasion of untouchables, barely pausing for breath before they mourn the decline of “Judeo-Christian culture”. In the States, a proper Republican drubbing on Tuesday might give the anti-empaths the kind of shock they deserve, but Musk’s power and influence alone shows that it will take a lot more than a single round of election results to really push them back. Meanwhile, all over the world, compassion, kindness and other such virtues gather a thick layer of dust, like old hymn books in a long-deserted church.
- John Harris is a Guardian columnist

https://www.humanite.fr/monde/dereglemen.title: Les bonnes affaires de Tony Blair : comment l’ex-premier ministre britannique veut réformer l’UE au profit des États-Unis
https://www.humanite.fr/monde/dereglemen.author: Lina Sankari
https://www.humanite.fr/monde/dereglemen.text:
L’ancien premier ministre travailliste britannique garde une influence considérable grâce à son institut. Il propose une thérapie de choc pour l’Union européenne qui vise, au nom de la puissance, à y rétablir l’influence de Londres, au profit des États-Unis.
Tony Blair n’a plus de mandat, mais il a des idées. Et quelques leviers pour les imposer. Premier ministre travailliste britannique entre 1997 et 2007, il reste pour beaucoup le symbole de l’aplaventrisme depuis l’intervention militaire britannique en Irak en 2003, aux côtés de George W. Bush.
À l’époque, la « relation spéciale » avec Washington présentait un intérêt manifeste pour le locataire du 10, Downing Street en ce qu’elle lui permettait de garder ses distances avec Bruxelles. Mieux, il n’a cessé de plaider pour l’élargissement de l’Union européenne (UE) pour mieux affaiblir certains membres historiques récalcitrants à l’atlantisme, dont Paris.
Puis en 2004, il voit dans l’accueil de dix pays de l’Est au sein du cercle européen une manière de reléguer la Russie au rang de puissance de second ordre : « Nous nous réjouissons en effet de cette étape historique qui mettra un terme aux divisions artificielles de la guerre froide », écrit-il dans une tribune intitulée « Mon Europe », publiée par Le Monde.
Depuis, le Brexit est passé par là et l’influence du Royaume-Uni sur les affaires du Vieux Continent a perdu de sa superbe. Mais Tony Blair n’a visiblement pas renoncé à la sienne. C’est aujourd’hui...

Dès 2017, le chef de l’État a méthodiquement écarté les confédérations de travailleurs tout en réprimant les mouvements sociaux. Depuis la mobilisation unitaire de 2023, le locataire de l’Élysée n’arrive pas à se défaire de la contestation et des mots d’ordre syndicaux.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: America has been witnessing the worst speeches in presidential history | Ted Widmer
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Ted Widmer
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
In a sense, history has already been made. We do not know the result of the election yet, but over the last two months, Americans have endured the worst speeches ever given by a president of the United States.
It is far from a simple matter to adjudicate – there have been so many bad speeches over the years, going back the founders, some of whom dreaded speaking in public. George Washington’s inaugural address did not begin promisingly, with a halting first sentence: “Among the vicissitudes incident to life, no event could have filled me with greater anxieties than that of which the notification was transmitted by your order, and received on the 14th day of the present month.”
But it feels like we have entered new territory, with speeches that are far worse than convoluted, or dull. Instead, they are routinely overflowing with vitriol against perceived enemies, groundless predictions of victory, and delusions of grandeur.
At their best, they can offer a form of entertainment to the Maga supporters who still line up, in dwindling numbers. At their worst, they provide evidence of a president whose faculties are failing him.
It used to be vitally important for any White House speechwriter, under any previous administration, to factcheck a speech, because it would be unthinkable to state a known falsehood in a presidential address. Now, it is impossible to rely on anything communicated from the most powerful office in the world, whether in the torrent of rally speeches now ending, or in the ceaseless drip of social media posts every night.
Donald Trump has succeeded in lowering the bar even further than where it was in his first term, or even in the first year of his second term.
In the past, a White House would routinely put every presidential utterance on its website, believing it to be in the interest of the American people. But the current gatekeepers refuse to put Trump’s rally speeches online, as if conscious that they are lowering the dignity of the office. Instead, they must be read in other places.
The media has reported with some bemusement on the strangeness of Trump’s 28 rallies, but the problem is more serious than that. Many of the speeches make little sense. The president often loses his way.
In North Carolina, Trump told the story of Mike Dukakis and Willie Horton twice in the same speech. There are non-sequiturs (“only a Hispanic could survive that fall”). Or threats to rename oceans and rivers. Or boasts about the “freaking fortune” the oil industry is making from the Iran war. Or casual pardons issued to polluters from the stage (making one lucky recipient “as clean as a newborn baby’s ass”).
As that comment suggests, it has been a race to the bottom. There has been a lot of profanity (in Ohio, he said: “We’re going to win, and we’re going to win big. And we’re going to shove it up their ass.”) At other times, he has referred (repeatedly) to the firmness of Jon Husted’s posterior.
Then there are the insults to foreign countries (“Norway sucks”) political rivals and Robert DeNiro (“a moron”). The juvenile nicknames: Talafreako, Annie Trannie, Dumocrats. The taunts to hecklers (“shut up, loser!”), who are coming out in ever greater numbers, drawn to the spectacle of this bonfire.
It is not simply that Americans have a president who, as if defensive, brags about acing his cognitive tests (“I’m a freaking genius”). There is also the absence of any moral leadership of any kind, on issues ranging from our foreign policy to domestic concerns.
We rarely hear of defending democracy; instead, we have seen a palpable decline in US support for Ukraine, and last week offered refuge to an election-denier, Flávio Bolsonaro, who lost by more than 4m votes to Lula. Our own elections have been under constant attack, even before they can be held. We declare “ceasefires” that are routinely ignored. We have no idea what the plans are for Iran.
This is the American Carnage that was promised in Trump’s 2017 inaugural. It goes far beyond mere rhetorical chaos; instead, it threatens the irreversible decline of the presidency itself, and the great nation it is supposed to represent. It’s a striking setback during a year that was supposed to be all about celebrating America’s 250th birthday and the enlightened ideas enshrined within our founding creed, the Declaration of Independence.
The founders anticipated some of these problems – Washington warned that the “baneful effects” of excessive partisanship would “enfeeble” the nation. His successor, John Adams, worried that the country would only be as moralistic as its leaders. In 1798, he wrote: “Avarice, Ambition and Revenge or Galantry, would break the strongest Cords of our Constitution as a Whale goes through a Net.”
Of course, they also wanted “energy in the executive”, as Alexander Hamilton put it in Federalist 70, and to be fair, it does require a lot of energy to speak for nearly two hours at a rally. But is that serving the interests of the nation, or even of the Republican party?
It could be argued that the Trump brand is now so toxic that it does more harm than good for a candidate to appear at a rally with him. The wheels are coming off the bandwagon.
Historians often debate the best presidential speeches; they rarely worry about the bad ones. In fact, many have been failures.
William Henry Harrison’s inaugural address in 1841 was so long (8,445 words) that it essentially killed him (he died not long after delivering it). James Buchanan refused to take a stand on slavery in 1857 and promised to “cheerfully accept” the dreadful Dred Scott decision. Jefferson Davis (not quite a president) promised “no aggression upon others” shortly before the Confederacy attacked Fort Sumter, launching the American civil war.
The 20th century brought more duds. Barry Goldwater’s convention address in 1964 has often been cited as an embarrassing example of extremist rhetoric, attacking international communism as well as the US government. But a close reading indicates many passages that appear downright calm compared with the constant fusillades of the Trump rallies.
Goldwater called for “the flowering of an Atlantic civilization, the whole of Europe reunified and free, trading openly across its borders” and offered a definition of his party that was eminently reasonable: “Balance, diversity, creative difference – these are the elements of the Republican equation.”
Richard Nixon had well-known problems with the truth, and, like Trump, hated his enemies. But a casual glance at his rally speeches in the fall of 1970 show nothing like the invective of 2026 – simply cautious statements about balancing the budget, offering tax relief, and restoring law and order.
It will take time to heal from the nonstop airing of grievances over the past two months – the Festivus Campaign of 2026. The next two years may be difficult in Washington, with a lot of blaming and shaming if the Republicans perform as poorly as expected. But if early indications are accurate, there will be a far greater balance in Washington, and that is a beginning.
In other ways, too, democracy has been making a comeback, with surprising victories for progressive campaigns in Brazil and Serbia, and elegant speeches delivered in the last few days by the leaders of those causes, Lula and Radomir Sajčić.
They do not demonize their opponents; they simply accept the challenges of building peace and prosperity at home, promote unity and promise to get to work for the people.
In the final weeks of 2026, it would be difficult to think of a better way to vindicate the long-ago promises of the Declaration of Independence, that a better day is possible for a people willing to role up their sleeves and work together.
- Ted Widmer, a former White House speechwriter, is the editor of American Speeches, and the recently published The Living Declaration: A Biography of America’s Founding Text, both published by the Library of America

La France insoumise place la santé au cœur de son projet pour 2027. Son plan, dévoilé en exclusivité par l’Humanité, entend réduire les inégalités d’accès aux soins et limiter la place des intérêts privés, avec une question centrale : comment soigner tout le monde ?
C’est un invariable des enquêtes d’opinion : les années passent et la santé figure systématiquement parmi les premières préoccupations des Français. Hormis les sympathisants LR, tous les électorats placent, d’après un sondage Toluna Harris Interactive publié fin septembre, cette thématique dans leurs cinq priorités de l’élection présidentielle.
« C’est le sujet numéro un, avance même le député LFI Hadrien Clouet, qui a coordonné le programme de Jean-Luc Mélenchon avec sa collègue Clémence Guetté. Le journaliste, écrivain et documentariste réalise son premier long métrage de fiction. Une famille française, porté par un financement participatif, raconte la Seine-Saint-Denis, celle où il vit, loin des clichés.
Du gros matos envahit le petit trois-pièces. Une quinzaine de personnes s’affairent, courent dans tous les sens. « Ça va ? Tu veux un thé ? » Nadir Dendoune passe une tête. En repasse une autre cinq minutes plus tard. « Un café ? » On lui sourit. « Non, non. Toujours rien ! » Il s’excuse. Assure qu’à la pause déjeuner, il sera plus tranquille. Assise à table, face à un imposant buffet, l’actrice Hiam Abbass attend le coup d’envoi. Nadir se marre. « Ça tombe bien que l’Huma soit là, on va tourner la scène où Djamila, le personnage principal, se sert du journal pour éplucher des carottes. »

Révulsée par son éphémère expérience au sein du service de presse de l’armée israélienne, Ayelet Kroizer vient d’être nommée porte-parole de l’ONG « Breaking the Silence ». Avec l’intention revendiquée de rompre la chape de plomb entourant les exactions dans les territoires occupés.
« L’heure est venue de dire la vérité sur l’occupation. » C’est par ces mots que l’ONG israélienne Breaking The silence a souhaité la bienvenue sur X à sa nouvelle porte-parole Ayelet Kroizer. Une recrue qui a valeur de symbole retentissant pour l’organisation créée en 2004, dont la mission est de « briser le silence » pesant autour des soldats israéliens de retour à la vie civile.
Et pour cause, le parcours et la liberté de parole revendiquée par la jeune femme née dans un environnement ultra-orthodoxe, révulsée par son éphémère expérience en tant que porte-parole de l’armée israélienne, tranchent au sein d’une société acquise aux discours déshumanisants frappant les Palestiniens. Ayelet Kroizer, qui explique n’avoir « jamais été douée pour (se) taire face aux injustices », a en effet long à en dire.
« Exposée à la réalité en Cisjordanie et à Gaza »
« Au sein du service de presse de Tsahal, j’ai été exposée à la réalité en Cisjordanie et à Gaza, et à la manière dont Tsahal choisit de présenter cette réalité au public », raconte, sur son compte X, celle qui a vu de l’intérieur la fabrique du mensonge.
Les exemples, concrets, cités par la jeune femme font écho aux voix qui dénoncent depuis trois ans l’instrumentalisation de l’attaque terroriste du 7-octobre pour justifier le génocide en cours : « J’ai vu comment le mot » terroriste « est accolé même à des Palestiniens innocents », a encore dénoncé Ayelet Kroizer, qui exhorte : « Si vous avez servi pendant la guerre, ne vous taisez pas non plus. »
Pour une information libre sur la Palestine
Nous avons été l’un des premiers médias français à défendre le droit des Palestiniens à disposer d’un État viable dans le respect des résolutions de l’ONU. Et nous avons inlassablement défendu la paix au Proche-Orient. Aidez-nous à continuer de vous informer sur ce qui se passe là-bas. Grâce à vos dons.
Je veux en savoir plus !

https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.title: They fell in love on The Simpsons and married in real life. Meet the French Homer and Marge
https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.author: Hannah J Davies
https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.text:
The Simpsons is the biggest cartoon comedy in the world, with suburban couple Homer and Marge at its heart. From their beginnings as high-school sweethearts to the travails of married life, they’re an unbreakable pair. Gag-heavy as it may be, it’s also a series with plenty of sentimental plots, from Homer giving up his beloved Duff beer for a month to prove his love to Marge, to Marge composing a heartfelt poem to a dying Homer (miraculously, he makes it through his sushi-induced food poisoning).
Not even the temptations of a brunch-loving bowling instructor called Jacques or a doughnut-guzzling redhead called Mindy could get between them. Plus, of course, they enjoy the occasional “snuggle” (even on a miniature golf course … ).
Now in its 38th season, The Simpsons has also been a huge hit across the globe, meaning hundreds of international actors have voiced this much-loved couple. Among them are Philippe Peythieu and Véronique Augereau, who – as well as playing Marge and Homer in the French dub of The Simpsons since 1990 – met through the show and ended up getting married.
“Matt Groening called us the second most famous couple in the history of animation,” says Peythieu. “There were the actors who voiced Minnie and Mickey Mouse [the late Wayne Allwine and Russi Taylor], and then there was us. Meanwhile in Los Angeles, he said, everyone he worked with was getting divorced …”
The pair record their scenes together with a director in a Paris dubbing studio over 10-12 days a year. But clearly The Simpsons is a 365-day-a-year commitment, from appearances at galas and conventions to the gifts they receive from adoring fans. Both are adamant that they wouldn’t carry on without the other, which means a definite non to AI taking over in the future. “We’re not for artificial intelligence – we’re for artistic intelligence!” says Augereau. There will always be roles that require a human soul, she adds, and – for Peythieu and Augereau – this role has given them each a soulmate to boot.
Do you remember meeting for the first time?
Philippe Peythieu: We met at a casting call in 1989 – it was only six months after The Simpsons had debuted in the US, so it wasn’t a success there yet. We auditioned, and then six months later – by fax – we found out we had got the roles.
Véronique Augereau: Philippe and I didn’t know each other well at all. When we were trying out, we crossed paths in the hallway at the dubbing offices and greeted each other but we were just colleagues – we weren’t even friends at that stage. There’s a video of us at a wrap party for the first series and we’re just walking right past each other, not even speaking, let alone stealing any glances!
PP: Voilà, that’s how this beautiful story began. The recording process brought us closer together, since we were working in the darkness of the studio, and so we became more than friends … We had to be very discreet in the beginning, because this was a professional setting, but eventually word got out and we were inseparable from that point on. As for the series, we never imagined it would last so long. But the success also contributed to the success of our relationship.
VA: In terms of what actually attracted us to each other, it’s hard to say, but I think the atmosphere around the recording sessions helped – there was always a friendly, funny vibe. Personally, I find the show and the storylines extraordinary, and incredibly intelligent. I think we really loved this show and were enthusiastic about it from the get-go. We liked the spirit of the series, and that humour that could be quite biting.
What do Homer and Marge love about each other?
VA: Marge isn’t a fan of Homer’s over-the-top antics, but deep down she knows that he is her one and only love in life. Ultimately, she has a lot of tenderness and affection for this man, whom she knows is devoted to her and to their children. He is completely in love with his family – even if he doesn’t remember his children’s names all the time …
PP: Through the seasons there have been rifts, but every time they’ve found their way back to each other. If you look at the film [The Simpsons Movie, released in 2007], Marge decides to leave Homer, but ends up forgiving all of his foolish mistakes in the end. Their love grows stronger – they’re able to separate then find each other again.
VA: A critic in France, Romain Nigita, actually wrote a book called Les Simpson ou le paradoxe du donut intemporel (The Simpsons, or the Paradox of the Timeless Doughnut), to which we wrote the preface. [The book is about the show’s relationship with time, and how it never changes yet always seems relevant.] He writes about Marge and Homer’s first meeting in high school – Homer smoking in the bathroom with Barney, Marge burning her bra at a feminist protest, before the pair cross paths at the high-school prom. That’s when Homer says: “I’m sure we were meant to be together. Usually when I have a thought, there’s a lot of other thoughts in there ... something says yes, something says no ... But this time, there’s only yes! How can the only thing I’ve ever been sure about in my life be wrong?”
When did you realise this was a love story for the ages?
VA: Across all of these seasons (we will soon be dubbing season 38), this couple is still standing!
PP: Despite his doubts, his worst gaffes and the tests of time, Homer is certain of one thing: Marge is the love of his life!
What have been your favourite romantic moments between them?
VA: We love the bedroom scenes when they’re in their room with the lights off and you can only see their eyes moving around.
PP: Those scenes that can be a bit cheeky but they’re handled very well – the show addresses sexuality but with a lightness of touch, affection and humour.
Is there anything you wish Marge and Homer did differently?
PP: When you’re this hooked on The Simpsons, it’s hard to be critical of the show. It would also be difficult to rewrite its history – it’s a show that has defined an era. Besides, we love these characters unconditionally, so whatever they do we would always forgive them! Homer also resembles us – I think, as a man, I’m a bit like him, and he’s a bit like me in some ways. What you see is what you get with Homer, and yet he still manages to surprise us …
VA: I don’t love the Halloween specials, personally.
PP: She finds them scary. There was a Halloween episode where they sent up The Shining – I loved that one.
What is your real relationship like off camera?
VA: We share the same values in life and move forward together, bound by a very strong connection.
How romantic are you in real life?
VA: We often stroll down the street arm in arm, and people always say, “Hello, lovebirds!” or – if I’m alone – “Oh, not with your husband today?” I don’t want to say that people have this idealised vision of us, but when we meet fans at conventions they always say the same sorts of things to us too. Whether in The Simpsons or in real life, it seems that many people see us as this devoted couple that they enjoy spending time with.
PP: We’ve had the opportunity to meet Matt Groening and the team several times, and they’ve always told us that the French version is one of the best, because we’ve understood the spirit of the series, and the fact that we’re husband and wife has added that little extra something to it.
What has been the most intense fan reaction to Marge and Homer?
VA: People tell us, you were the soundtrack to our childhood. Fans will tell us that we represent this perfect couple in their eyes – every Saturday night we were in their homes, on their TVs, so for some people we were almost like surrogate parents.
Did you keep something from set that reminds you of Marge and Homer?
VA: It’s not from set, but at a charity gala in Switzerland we were given a huge portrait of Marge as a Playboy bunny [a callback to the episode The Devil Wears Nada].
PP: I’ve lost count of the amount of times I’ve been given doughnuts.
What can Marge and Homer teach us about love?
PP: What they teach us is that – come what may – it’s all about this strong bond that they have. It’s a bond that’s almost indestructible despite life’s difficulties and the differences that sometimes come between them.
VA: They show us that love is about forgiveness.
PP: And accepting the differences between both people.
VA: You have to be on the same page in life too … with us, we have the same tastes, like contemporary art, food …
PP: We’re bon vivants! We love life. We rarely argue, and if we do it’s usually about trivial things.
VA: That’s why it’s lasted all these years – we’ve been together nearly as long as The Simpsons!

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Trump says US will end military aid to Israel by the end of this year
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Andrew Roth
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Donald Trump has said that the US will end military aid to Israel at the end of this year in a surprise election day announcement that appeared to be targeted at voters sceptical of US support for Israel and the war in Gaza.
In a phone interview with Fox News as voting began on Tuesday morning, Trump said the US would cut nearly $4bn (£2.96bn) in military aid to Israel because “they don’t need it.”
“We were giving them $4bn … But it gets cut off at the end of the year,” he said.
Trump also indicated that he had decided to end the aid – which he claimed would be replaced by arms sales to Israel instead – because it had become a popular criticism of US foreign policy led by outspoken candidates including the Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed.
“Why should we suffer the slings from lunatics like El-Sayed when they don’t need it?” Trump said. “It’s a bad talking point.”
During the interview, Trump claimed that the abrupt ending of aid was proposed by Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu. “We give them $4bn of things and money, and they don’t need it,” he said. “And I was approached by Bibi Netanyahu, and we’ve been talking about it for a couple of years because it’s a lot of money.”
Netanyahu had previously suggested tapering off US military aid to Israel over the next decade, but Trump’s announcement on Tuesday would significantly accelerate that timeline.
Israel received most of the approximately $3.8bn in 2025 as Foreign Military Financing grants that allow the country to buy US military hardware including F-35 fighter jets. Another $500m was given for joint missile defence programmes.
Trump’s announcement on Tuesday appeared timed to affect the outcome of the midterm elections, where US foreign policy and support for Israel have played an unusually important role in key races, including the Michigan senatorial race where El-Sayed is running against Republican Mike Rogers. He would become the country’s first Muslim senator if he is elected.
A Quinnipiac University poll released in September showed that 48% of Americans believed that the US was too supportive of Israel, and other recent polls have shown a historic shift away from US support for Israel and Netanyahu’s government.
Anger over the humanitarian crisis in Gaza has helped usher in a wave of progressive Democratic candidates including El-Sayed, and Trump’s vice-president JD Vance has openly accused Israel of trying to sabotage US negotiations with Iran. In a June interview with the New York Times, Vance said of Israel’s foreign policy: “You can’t just kill your way out of solving every single national security problem that you have.”
During his Fox News interview, Trump spoke warmly about Netanyahu and also boasted about his own popularity in Israel. “If people ever got tired of me in the US, I’ll move to Israel and become prime minister,” he said.

https://www.theguardian.com/wellness/202.title: ‘The nipple touch of doom’: what is sad nipple syndrome and what causes it?
https://www.theguardian.com/wellness/202.author: Ivana Rihter
https://www.theguardian.com/wellness/202.text:
Some say it feels like a sudden burst of anguish; others liken it more to homesickness. The sudden onset of a sinking, upsetting feeling due to nipple stimulation is anecdotally known as Sad Nipple Syndrome (SNS), and for Sandra, it can be triggered by something as commonplace as putting on a shirt.
“I was probably a child when I first noticed: ‘Why does touching my nipple make me sad?’” says the 28-year-old. The sensation seemed to happen at random, and without the words to describe it, she kept it a secret. It wasn’t until college that she worked up the courage to Google it. “I realized I wasn’t crazy,” she says.
There are many others like Sandra (who, for privacy, has asked to use a pseudonym). Breastfeeding mothers, queer lovers and cis men alike have all sought an explanation for this phenomenon.
What is Sad Nipple Syndrome (SNS)?
Sad Nipple Syndrome is often discovered in private. People describe it as a sudden dysphoria (a profound state of unhappiness or uneasiness) that follows nipple stimulation. It is often resolved within a couple of minutes, but can cause confusion and disruption.
I spoke to four people who experience SNS, and each described similar negative feelings. Sandra described it as “dread, a nostalgic sadness or the feeling of a bad memory”. Salma Zaky, a New York-based comedian who has talked about her SNS on stage, says she can “tell if a woman has gone through it – they’ll light up or clap”. Zaky likens it to a mix of homesickness or nostalgia.
For Sandra, the most common trigger is a light, unexpected touch when changing clothes or towel drying. Its intensity can vary depending on the circumstances. For instance, if she triggers the feeling on her own with light touch, “the negative feelings tend to persist for more than just a few seconds,” says Sandra. If there is sustained friction with her clothing, she sometimes feels “deep grief”.
Their sentiments are echoed in thousands of online posts asking whether anyone else experiences the “nipple touch of doom”. In the absence of a formal clinical diagnosis, most people’s understanding of Sad Nipple Syndrome has come from word of mouth or chatter online.
“Reddit was helpful in just being like: ‘Oh, I’m not an insane person,” says Zaky. “Other people feel this too.”
What do scientists think is happening in SNS?
SNS is not an official medical diagnosis, and scientific research remains in short supply. That said, awareness is growing, even among researchers and medical practitioners.
As with many conditions that primarily affect women’s intimate or hormonal experiences, there is not much medical curiosity, funding or research. “While there is no explanation yet, we can assume that the hormone oxytocin is somehow involved, since nipple stimulation leads to its release,” says Dr Vladimír Kraus, PhD, Department of Gynaecology and Obstetrics at Pavol Jozef Šafárik University.
Oxytocin is often referred to as the “love hormone”. Largely responsible for bonding and increased emotional connectivity, it is triggered by physical touch like hugging, massage or sex, and also after uterine contractions during childbirth or breastfeeding. When it comes to its role in SNS, Kraus theorizes that “some subtle changes may cause the [oxytocin signaling pathway] to go haywire and [could] be responsible for the surprisingly prompt and very negative feeling experienced”.
There are no SNS-specific studies, but there are two more well-studied conditions that are similar enough to help us understand it. The first is dysphoric milk ejection reflex, or D-MER, which occurs during breastfeeding. It is an emotional response to the milk letdown, the moment where milk starts flowing out of the milk duct. People commonly describe the sudden rush of emotion as homesickness, sadness, loss of hope, worthlessness, shame and guilt, according to Alia Macrina Heise, an international board-certified lactation consultant and an expert on D-MER in Naples, New York. “It is disruptive to the duration of lactation and to the mother’s experience of breastfeeding and bonding,” she says.
SNS and D-MER present identically, and are also similar to post-coital dysphoria, says Heise. While SNS and D-MER are focused on nipple stimulation, the negative feelings people experience with post-coital dysphoria occur after the hormonal spike of orgasm. Anyone who has one of these conditions “will describe the embodied emotional sensations basically exactly the same way, even though the cause and the trigger is different”, says Heise.
The prevailing theory is that these three conditions involve a “hormonal cocktail inside the body”, says Heise.
The two most relevant hormones are prolactin and dopamine. This cocktail Heise refers to affects every human in a multitude of ways. “Prolactin and dopamine have a known relationship inside the human body – male, female, breastfeeding, not breastfeeding, in sexual arousal, in orgasm,” says Heise. Prolactin also contributes to weight control, immunoregulation, stress adaptation and maternal behavior.
Meanwhile, dopamine drives the brain’s reward system, playing a key role in movement, pleasure, desire, motivation and thinking. “Dopamine is often called prolactin’s gatekeeper,” explains Heise. In order for prolactin to flow into the body, dopamine has to allow prolactin through in order to complete one of its many jobs.
It’s possible that what happens in SNS, D-MER and post-coital dysphoria has to do with the way prolactin and dopamine go about their daily duties. One possible explanation is “inappropriate dopamine activity”, says Heise, who first heard a colleague mention SNS in the 2000s. “With dopamine being a mood stabilizer, that inappropriate activity is causing a mood destabilization that lasts for a very short amount of time.”
There is a growing body of research focused on D-MER, but to truly understand these conditions, we need more specialized studies. Without a clearer picture, sufferers are left feeling alone and “crazy”. Even if they work up the courage to ask their doctor about it, most medical professionals don’t have enough experience with these conditions to recommend treatment.
Techniques for reducing the severity of symptoms are mostly experimental. “One of the tricks that we’ve found helps the most by also targeting the dopamine system is cold therapy,” says Heise, who’s worked with thousands of breastfeeding mothers with D-MER. “Mothers drinking ice water or putting cold wraps around the back of their neck and cooling down their face and mouth receptors before letdown significantly eases the symptoms because it increases prolactin levels.” But whether this trick works for people with SNS is unknown.
How does SNS affect people?
Unexplained physical phenomena can be confusing and distressing, especially when they involve intimate body parts. The impact of SNS goes beyond the brief sensations, to shame and confusion over what they might mean.
Without formal answers from the medical community, many have developed theories about the causes, including forgotten sexual trauma, questions about one’s sexuality and marital doubts. These unfounded explanations can do real harm.
Kraus says SNS has rarely come up in his practice, but those who experience it often feel concerned “about their mental state or fear that they don’t like their partner or sex”.
As with all sexual preferences or personal boundaries, clear communication is key, experts say. It may also feel challenging or personal for partners of people who experience SNS.
“This isn’t about you, and it isn’t rejection,” says Dr Jennifer Lincoln, a board-certified OB-GYN and author in Portland, Oregon. “Talk about it outside the bedroom, agree on a signal to pause or change what’s happening, and let the person with the reaction lead.”
It can be tricky to bring up something you might not even know the name for, feel ashamed of or confused by. But talking about it can be helpful.
“Even just naming [Sad Nipple Syndrome] helps a lot, because many people think they’re going crazy – or with D-MER, that they are a bad mother,” says Lincoln. Similarly, shame can arise when SNS leads to negative experiences during sex and intimacy.
“I just avoid any nipple stuff during sex now, and it’s completely fine,” says Zaky.
“It pretty much has not impacted my sex life at all,” says Sandra. “I think the hardest part was simply feeling like a weird freak, and having a reaction that can’t be explained.”
Ivana Rihter is a writer in Chicago whose work has appeared in Vogue, Vanity Fair, Slate, Nylon and more

Sur le logo révélé ce 3 novembre lors d’une conférence de presse, un nom : « Angoulême bande dessinée ». https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: What made Haley Stevens turn on el-Sayed? | Judith Levine
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Judith Levine
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
“Did you talk to anyone? Did you have a long night of the soul? Were you up all night? ... Did you have a dream?”
Interviewing the Michigan US representative Haley Stevens on CNN on Sunday, Anderson Cooper was casting about for explanations. What caused the Democrat’s radical change of heart between a Saturday night promise to her House colleague Debbie Dingell that she would stand with the Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and a public endorsement on Sunday morning of his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers?
All Cooper could get from Stevens was her bruised feelings at el-Sayed’s “anger and lack of kindness”. El-Sayed disinvited her from a campaign event at a Black church with the South Carolina representative Jim Clyburn. She went to another Black church and sat with Rogers.
Stevens told Cooper she has “a whole heck of a lot of love for the Democratic party”, and that she “was just trying to help this campaign and stand up for people who felt hurt”. Democrats from the Senate minority leader, Chuck Schumer, to the Vermont senator Bernie Sanders lambasted her. Half of her own staff resigned in disgust.
It’s hard not to psychoanalyze Stevens. She evinces equal measures of titanic self-absorption and midwestern self-abnegation, masculine arrogance and feminine people-pleasing. While imperiling what might be the last chance Congress has to contain a rampaging Donald Trump, she insists that she’s just one voter, who is “not trying to upset anyone”. In televised interviews about this very serious matter, she smiles a lot. Is she being deceitful, or just deluded?
Maybe Stevens inherited this confusion from her mother, who declared herself proud of her daughter for “standing up for her values … [and] for the Democratic Party”. Dingell, who has condemned Stevens’ betrayal, allowed that she is nevertheless “worried” about her friend as “a human being”. Others have raised questions about the influence of her fiance, who backed Rogers before she did.
Stevens now joins the quisling caucus with Senator John Fetterman, Democrat of Pennsylvania, who made a video appearance at Trump’s Republican convention in September, in which he denounced socialism and praised his fellow Pennsylvania senator, Republican David McCormick.
As with Fetterman, there is one issue that triggers Stevens to act in ways that are destructive both to herself and her allies: Israel. Fresh from endorsing El-Sayed after her primary loss, she told the Jerusalem Post that “anti-Zionism” is a “hate movement” so powerful it can “break down civil society”.
Fetterman has said that official Democratic opposition to Israel’s policies would be the “red line” whose crossing would force him to leave the party.
Unlike Fetterman, who has received nothing from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, Stevens has debts to Aipac, which spent at least $30m in attack ads against El-Sayed during the primary and added $9m to support Rogers in October. Maybe she was counting on more of Aipac’s largesse in her political future, imagining she had one.
Stevens cannot stop obsessing about El-Sayed’s various anti-Israel and antisemitic supporters, who act independently from him and his campaign. But she expresses no discomfort with her new guy’s unpalatable champions, including the Trump-loving gang leader-turned-preacher Lorenzo Sewell, who calls Islam a “death cult” and El-Sayed an “Islamist jihadist”, and the Texas oil billionaire Tim Dunn, who once told the Jewish Republican Texas speaker of the House that only Christians should hold leadership positions. Of a $23m campaign war chest, Dunn donated $5m.
At some point in history, Zionists and anti-Zionists had reasonable political differences. But in 2026, when the world, including the UN, confirms that Israel is committing genocide and when a win for the US president’s party augurs a plummet into full-on fascism, Stevens’ betrayal of the Democrats suggests a kind of political madness, Israel derangement syndrome.
- Judith Levine is a frequent contributor to the Guardian. Her Substack is Today in Fascism

https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.title: Jon Stewart on Haley Stevens’s betrayal in Michigan: ‘The most diabolical episode of Fargo I’ve ever seen’
https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.author: Guardian staff
https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.text:
On the eve of the US midterm elections, late-night hosts mocked Donald Trump’s lack of focus on the campaigns, a scandal in the Alaska Senate race and Haley Stevens’s about-face in Michigan.
Jon Stewart
With only one day to go until the midterms, “it’s closing arguments time,” said Jon Stewart on Monday evening, “and today, the president took to the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool to make his final case to the voters.”
But instead of talking about the election, Trump instead droned on about his reflecting pool renovations, bragging about “this massive piece of pool”.
“That was the president of the United States, on the day before the midterms, choosing to make a speech at the reflecting pool to talk about the reflecting pool,” the Daily Show host marveled. “No symbolism, no metaphors, just straight-up pool maintenance. That was Donald Trump’s ‘I had it cleaned’ speech, if you will.”
But while Trump’s priorities were, as Stewart put it, “badly misplaced”, Democrats “appear in position for a wave election” in the House and Senate “as long as the remaining couple of days before the election are bombshell-less, drama-free, non-earthquakey”.
And then there’s Michigan, where the Democratic congresswoman Haley Stevens switched her endorsement at the 11th hour away from the progressive who defeated her in the primary, Abdul El-Sayed, to the Republican Mike Rogers. “We all knew there was drama in Michigan when Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed defeated Haley Stevens in a contentious primary for the Democratic nomination, but Stevens has always been very clear as to their shared goal of defeating Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers,” said Stewart before several clips of Stevens criticizing Rogers as a “nightmare” Trump Republican who would not stand for Michigan voters.
And yet on Sunday, Stevens posted a video endorsing Rogers seemingly filmed in her car.
“Is her car in a ditch? Is she endorsing Mike Rogers after getting in a car accident?” Stewart wondered. “Real quick, before I lose consciousness, I am endorsing the nightmare.’
“What the fuck happened?” he added. “This is like the most diabolical episode of Fargo I’ve ever seen.
“What could have driven Haley Stevens into the arms of the Rogers campaign?” he asked, before a clip of Stevens alongside Rogers, complaining that she was not invited to any of El-Sayed’s campaign events.
“That says why you’re mad at Abdul. But not why you’re for Rogers,” Stewart said. “Rogers is, hold on, let me find the word, a nightmare, who is against every principle you’ve worked for your entire career.
“I mean, at least say you were visited by three ghosts who convinced you that it turns out people don’t need health insurance,” he added. “This can’t really be about getting your feelings hurt.”
Jimmy Kimmel
“More than 57 million Americans have already cast their ballots,” said Jimmy Kimmel on Monday evening. And “Trump made his closing arguments. He chose to do that in front of his ill-fated reflecting pool. What better way to reassure the public that they are in good hands than in front of a pool you’ve repeatedly botched to the tune of $16m?
“Donald Trump, the man who famously promised to ‘drain the swamp’, made his last stand at the site of his own man-made swamp, standing victoriously in front of this hard-won pond like the soldiers who triumphed at Iwo Jima,” he joked.
The president spoke beside the pool for over an hour, and “many are calling it his Pettysburg address,” Kimmel quipped. “He blamed Joe Biden and Obama for everything that happened to the pool before he was there. He said he’s giving serious thought to renaming the pool after himself – which, that’s a nice idea. He ranted about bermuda grass and topsoil and his construction projects and the ballroom, James Comey, rusty pipes. He had visual aids. And then he stripped down to his diapers and did a pretty impressive cannonball into the shallow end of the thing.
“Somehow, the ‘Energizer Dummy’ managed to blabber his way through 30 rallies over the past 32 days,” he added. “And with the campaign for control of Congress at the 2-yard line, Trump is laser-focused on the issues that matter most.”
Seth Meyers
In the final stretch until the midterms, “Trump isn’t really hitting the campaign trail,” said Seth Meyers on Late Night. “He’s just kinda falling on it with a big ol’ splat, like a birthday cake hitting the pavement facedown.
“Execution isn’t what he and his buddies are worried about,” he continued. “Don’t focus on the insane things he’s saying. Focus on how hard he’s working and how little he’s sleeping.”
According to Trump, “no president has ever worked so hard on a midterm”, as he’s “working like a dog”.
And yet the president canceled several campaign rallies that were supposed to be held this weekend in Kansas and Iowa. “The dude’s done 30 rallies in less than two months, and suddenly he’s canceling during the final climactic weekend?” Meyers laughed. “That’s like sprinting the first 26 miles of the New York City marathon and then calling an Uber for the last thousand feet.”
Meyers then switched tack to a bombshell New York Times report from the Alaska Senate race. According to the investigation, Democrat Mary Peltola’s campaign helped recruit an independent candidate named Dan Sullivan as a spoiler in her race against a different Dan Sullivan.
“Wow, I am shocked. It pains me to say this, but I have to call balls and strikes: this is very fucking funny,” said Meyers. “I mean, fuckin’ A, they finally did it: the Democrats finally did something as dirty as the Republicans.
“I mean, it’s not systematically lobbying state election officials to send alternate slates of electors to Congress as part of an illegal scheme to undermine a presidential election and then storming the Capitol, shitting in the rotunda and threatening to kill Mike Pence dirty, but it’s still pretty dirty,” he added.
“Both parties do stuff like this,” Meyers noted. “The difference is, this time, the Democrats were actually good at it.”

https://taz.de/Debatte-in-der-Linksfrakt.title: Linksfraktion in Berlin: Vanessa Emde provoziert weiter
https://taz.de/Debatte-in-der-Linksfrakt.author: Stefan Alberti
https://taz.de/Debatte-in-der-Linksfrakt.text:
Linksfraktion in Berlin: Vanessa Emde provoziert weiter
Die umstrittene Linkspartei-Abgeordnete kommt zur Fraktionssitzung in Begleitung von Hannah Bruns, gegen die ein Parteiausschlussverfahren läuft.
„Ich bin die Begleitung von Frau Emde“, stellt sich die geschätzt 30-Jährige an der Sicherheitsschleuse des Abgeordnetenhauses vor. Die Frau, die mit der umstrittenen Linkspartei-Abgeordneten Vanessa Emde anschließend die Treppenstufen hoch in den 3. Stock und in den Fraktionssitzungssaal 311 geht, ist Hannah Bruns. Gegen sie ist ein Parteiausschlussverfahren im Gange.
Bruns ist eine zentrale Stimme in der Landesarbeitsgemeinschaft (LAG) Palästinasolidarität innerhalb der Linkspartei, ihr wird israelbezogener Antisemitismus vorgeworfen. Dass Emde, von deren Rauswurf aus der Linksfraktion die SPD eine Koalition abhängig macht, ausgerechnet Bruns zur Fraktionssitzung am Dienstagnachmittag mitbringt, gilt als Provokation. Besser gesagt: als weitere Provokation.
Erst am Wochenende hat Emde beim Landesparteitag der Linkspartei gegen die eigene Partei demonstriert. Dort war sie vor der Tagungshalle bei einer Gruppe von einigen Dutzend Demonstranten zu finden, deren Motto lautete: „Gewählt für Palästina. Verraten für den Senat“. Bei der Kundgebung forderte Emde Vergesellschaftung und Palästinasolidarität und beendete ihre Rede mit den Worten: „Yalla, yalla, Klassenkampf! Freiheit für Palästina!“
Fraktionsmitarbeiter hielten es am Dienstagnachmittag für möglich, dass Emde Bruns als Mitarbeiterin angestellt haben könnte. Bestätigen ließ sich das bis Redaktionsschluss nicht: Bruns reagierte auf Medien-Ansprache nicht, Emde hatte schon im Parlamentseingang Fragen der taz nicht beantworten mögen.
Ein Ausschluss benötigt eine Zweidrittelmehrheit
Vor Sitzungsbeginn ging Fraktionssprecher Thomas Barthel davon aus, dass der Vorstand um Elif Eralp und Tobias Schulze an diesem Nachmittag keinen Ausschlussantrag gegen Emde ankündigen würde. Das muss laut Fraktionssatzung mindestens eine Woche vor Diskussion und Abstimmung des Antrags passieren.
Ohne Antrag ließe sich Emde nicht in der Sitzung kommenden Dienstag ausschließen und wäre damit auch in der nächsten Plenarsitzung des Abgeordnetenhauses am 12. November noch Mitglied der Linksfraktion. Offen ist weiter, ob die für einen Ausschluss Emdes nötige Zweidrittelmehrheit zustande kommt.
Das würde die Frage aufwerfen, wie lange sich die SPD als potenzieller Koalitionspartner – Montag haben Gespräche über ein Bündnis begonnen – diesen Zustand gefallen lässt. Ihr Landesvorsitzender und Fraktionschef Steffen Krach hatte vorige Woche in der Talksendung „Markus Lanz“ für den Fall eines Emde-Verbleibs in der Koalition gesagt: „Dann werden wir keine Koalition haben.“
Nach gut einer Dreiviertelstunde mussten Mitarbeiter und Gäste kurz vor 15 Uhr den Sitzungsraum 311 verlassen. Dann wollte die Fraktion über „Personalfragen“ sprechen, hieß es.
Nach Ende der Sitzung gab es keine offiziellen Stellungnahmen. Fraktionssprecher Thomas Barthel bestätigte jedoch der taz, dass kein Ausschlussantrag gegen Emde eingebracht wurde. Jetzt soll offenbar erstmal die Partei am Zuge sein. Wie das konkret heißt, ist unklar – klar ist nur, Emde bleibt einstweilen Teil der Fraktion.

https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.title: Lupin is back! Omar Sy is ridiculously watchable and effortlessly charming as a blindingly brilliant thief
https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.author: Paul F Verhoeven
https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.text:
If you’re not watching Lupin, you’re missing out on one of the most charming, thrilling and twisty capers of all time. Netflix’s adaptation of the popular French drama first hit our screens back in 2021 and it is the most wildly ambitious – and successful – to date. The brilliant writing, terrific ensemble cast and the effortless charm and panache of its lead actor, Omar Sy, make it ridiculously watchable.
The series is based on the adventures of Arsène Lupin, conceived by the French author Maurice LeBlanc. In France, Lupin is an almost totemic cultural figure. LeBlanc penned 24 books about the definitive gentleman thief in his lifetime, the first being 1907’s Arsène Lupin, Gentleman Cambrioleur. And the 119-year-old character is everything readers crave: suave, mysterious and cunning, with an unerring ability to run circles around law enforcement.
In the Netflix series, which is now in its fourth series, Assane Diop (Sy) is a blindingly brilliant thief who has modelled himself after his hero – Lupin.
“We grew up with him,” Sy says, speaking to me via Zoom about Lupin. “We had shows, we had so many movies … the Japanese anime from when we were kids and, of course, the books, so it really was all around us.”
Diop is a fresh take on the Lupin legend. “It was very natural and organic for me to think about maybe having my own vision of this character,” Sy says. “Because I’d always been watching him, you know? I wanted to create my version of him.”
During the interval between the show’s seasons, France experienced a real-life museum heist, though perhaps not one worthy of a master thief like Diop.
“Actually, I was so surprised to see that happen,” Sy says, grinning. “Seeing people try, and then really do it, you know? It took me a lot of time to process and really believe it happened.
“And when that passed, I was a little bit … well, feeling a little bit guilty that I could have inspired something like that. And after that, at some point, you become very cynical … like, hey, maybe it’s a good advertisement for the show?”
What makes the series so appealing is how analogue Diop’s schemes feel. There are smatterings of tech involved but by and large the capers are classic thievery, rife with deceptively simple misdirects. One of the tools in his arsenal? Good old-fashioned disguises.
“Lupin is my best toy,” Sy says, “because I get to play a character … who plays characters, you know? I always have this picture of putting a mirror in front of another mirror – there are infinite doors opening, it’s endless. There are so many things you can do with him. That’s why we have four seasons, and we could do 10 more! He’s so inspiring, and he’s such a joy to play.”
Sy caught the world’s attention with his leading role in The Intouchables, becoming the first black actor to win France’s coveted César award for best actor in 2012. Since then he has become colossally famous – and instantly recognisable.
Would he ever wear one of Diop’s disguises in public? “No, but it’s not that far from the truth!” he says. “The FX guy I work with, for the prosthetics on the show, we started to talk about one mask we could work on that I can put on my face and go to a concert, [take] the metro and all of that … we really started to talk about it very, very seriously.”
The first three seasons of Lupin are fascinatingly propulsive in that they tell one long, protracted story with ever-increasing stakes. In the books, Lupin flits in and out of strangers’ lives. In the show, Diop finds himself fighting an uphill battle as the odds stack up against him.
Season four opens with him facing public notoriety, a nemesis with a grudge and nobody in his corner to back him. Will Lupin ever go straight? Give up his perilous life of crime?
“I love the fact that all the characters besides him and the audience, the viewers, know that that will never happen,” Sy says. “And I’m so happy for that, because the audience is always completely with us and it’s also very, you know … touching, that he really tries, you know? He really wants that, to escape his life of crime, but everyone knows that will never happen.”
It’s mind-boggling that Lupin is as consistently excellent as it is. There not a single wasted minute of screentime. And even if you’ve seen it already, and know how Diop pulls off his increasingly complex schemes, a rewatch from the beginning will give you a newfound appreciation for the dazzling cleverness of it all.
“Putting back on the coat and being on set was really a relief for me,” Sy says, laughing. It’s a relief for us too.
- Lupin is available on Netflix in Australia, the UK and the US. Find more recommendations of what to stream in Australia here

https://taz.de/Foerderung-neuer-Gaskraft.title: Förderung neuer Gaskraftwerke: Saurer Apfel

https://taz.de/Foerderung-neuer-Gaskraft.text:
Förderung neuer Gaskraftwerke : Saurer Apfel
Wer elektrische Sicherheit gewährleisten will, kommt an fossilen Kraftwerken nicht vorbei. Der Stromverbrauch ist von den Netzen nicht zu schaffen.
N atürlich ist die aktuelle Entscheidung bitter, wenn man die Energiewirtschaft zügig auf Klimaneutralität umrüsten will: Da werden nun fossil betriebene Kraftwerke gefördert und sie werden laut Ausschreibungsbedingungen noch bis mindestens 2046 in Betrieb sein. Dass die Anlagen ab 2045 klimaneutral, also ohne Ausstoß von CO2 laufen sollen, ist bei der ganzen Geschichte nur ein schwacher Trost.
Trotzdem muss man, so schwer es fällt, konstatieren: Willkommen in der Realität! In der industriellen Produktion, im Wärmemarkt und im Verkehr soll das gesamte Leben mit großem Pomp elektrifiziert werden – und plötzlich stellt man fest, dass der viele Strom gar nicht in der gewünschten Stetigkeit verfügbar ist. Sei es, weil Wind und Sonne gerade schwächeln, oder sei es, weil der Strom grundsätzlich zwar irgendwo vorhanden ist, aber wegen fehlender Netze nicht dort ankommt, wo der Kunde ihn braucht.
In der gesellschaftlichen Debatte sind nun einfache Lösungen gemeinhin schnell gefunden: Dann muss man eben die Netze ausbauen. Und man muss mehr Speicher bauen. Alles richtig. Doch mit dem projektierten Anstieg des Stromverbrauchs werden die Netze in den kommenden Jahren beim besten Willen nicht mithalten können. Der Bau von Infrastruktur dauert eben in einem dicht besiedelten Land. Und die Speicher? Die wirken netztechnisch allzu oft wie schlichte Verbraucher und scheitern somit ebenso am fehlenden Netzanschluss.
taz debatte
Die taz ist eine unabhängige, linke und meinungsstarke Tageszeitung. In unseren Kommentaren, Essays und Debattentexten streiten wir seit der Gründung der taz im Jahr 1979. Oft können und wollen wir uns nicht auf eine Meinung einigen. Deshalb finden sich hier teils komplett gegenläufige Positionen – allesamt Teil des sehr breiten linken Meinungsspektrums.
So bleiben aus rein physikalisch-technischer Sicht für die kommenden Jahre nur zwei Optionen. Entweder man baut steuerbare Kraftwerke, die einspringen, wenn die erneuerbaren Energien nicht ausreichen. Oder aber es müssen sich zumindest größere Stromverbraucher damit abfinden, dass die gewünschte elektrische Leistung nicht jederzeit gesichert ist. Es ist eine Frage der Ehrlichkeit: Wer gegen fossile Kraftwerke ist – und dagegen zu sein, dafür gibt es gute Gründe –, muss sich aber auch fragen lassen, welche Einschränkungen er dafür zu tragen bereit ist.
