https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/n.title: Juan Atkins built a cybernetic future for music – but invested it with humanity
https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/n.author: Whitney Wei
https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/n.text:
Juan Atkins, the originator of techno who died on 31 October, spent his lifetime translating a fascination with the future into sound.
He was the oldest of the founding fathers of techno known as the “Belleville Three”, along with his junior high school friends Kevin Saunderson and Derrick May. He was the first of the trio to buy a Korg MS-10 synthesiser, and also taught the others how to DJ on turntables. His work in the duo Cybotron alongside Rik Davis was the sonic blueprint that sketched out what later became known as techno – indeed, he is the one who gave the genre its name. Without Atkins, and the way he empowered those around him, electronic music certainly would not exist in its current form today.
After moving from his birthplace of Detroit to nearby Belleville, Michigan, Atkins holed himself up in his bedroom, toiling away for hours creating drum kicks. “I more or less knew I was doing stuff that was not the normal thing to do,” he said in a Red Bull Music Academy interview in 2017.
As a teenager in the 1970s he wouldd listen to The Midnight Funk Association, a five-hour late-night radio programme by DJ Charles “The Electrifying Mojo” Johnson, which opened with the space-age introduction of The Landing of the Mothership before braiding together selections from Prince, Michael Jackson, Parliament-Funkadelic, the B-52s, the Human League and Atkins’s biggest influences, Yellow Magic Orchestra and Kraftwerk. Atkins was a conduit for a particular moment in musical and technological history: able to draw from this increasingly accessible globalised pool of music, and put those influences to bear on musical hardware that just a few years earlier would have been the wildly expensive preserve of universities or computing companies.
Atkins also loved anything about space, time travel, UFOs, religiously consuming TV shows such as Star Trek and Lost in Space, and the books of HP Lovecraft and Isaac Asimov. Three texts in particular defined the extraterrestrial reach of his sound: Childhood’s End by Arthur C Clarke, and Future Shock and The Third Wave by Alvin Toffler. The latter two were how he initially developed a bond with Davis at Washtenaw Community College in Ann Arbor, Michigan, as they discussed Toffler’s idea of the third wave, a way of living that would come after agrarian and industrial societies. Inspired by Toffler, Atkins deployed words such as Metroplex, the name of his record label which evokes a sprawling future city, and Cybotron, the name of his duo with Davis which calls to mind a brutally efficient robot who may or may not be benign.
He also applied Toffler’s idea of “techno rebels” to music – those people who wield technology for their own creative empowerment; a third option between destructive luddites and uncritical techno-optimists. Atkins reportedly rejected Derrick May’s suggestion to label their music “hi-tech soul” on the Virgin Records compilation that introduced the propulsive Detroit sound to the UK. Instead, the compilation was titled after one of Atkins’ tracks on it, Techno Music, and that became the name of a whole global movement.
Crucially, and like his hero Toffler, Atkins wasn’t naive or needlessly optimistic about the impact technology would have on the future, even if it was giving him the means to make a totally new style of music. Living in and near Detroit, where the city’s car manufacturing industries had badly decayed by the 1980s, Atkins had a front row seat to see how an industrial society could become obsolete and end up far from a techno-utopia.
In the 1996 Arté documentary Universal Techno, he is filmed against the backdrop of post-industrial Detroit, explaining: “The general attitude here with the powers that be is that industry must die to make way for technology … I think that we probably wouldn’t have developed this sound in any other city in America … There is a certain atmosphere here that you can’t find in any other city that lends to the technological movement.” Detroit’s mayor Mary Sheffield paid tribute after his death: “Today, millions of people dance to music that traces back to him and to our city. That is a Detroit story: genius, grit, and invention, from neighbourhoods the world too often overlooked.”
Atkins’ music, born from Detroit’s urban discord, found a shared spiritual home in 90s Berlin after the fall of the Wall. Dimitri Hegemann, founder of the Berlin club and record label Tresor, tells me that Atkins – alongside other US midwest visionaries such as Jeff Mills and Robert Hood – gifted the then fragile German capital a new soundtrack for the reunification of east and west. “His music was actually the sound of freedom,” Hegemann says.
For more than four decades after his earliest innovations, Atkins produced and performed his music worldwide, most recently in 2026 at the 30th anniversary of Amsterdam Dance Event and the Motor City’s own home-grown electronic celebration Movement festival. Laurens Von Oswald, nephew of Moritz Von Oswald – one half of Borderlands, the 2013 duo with Atkins – collaborated with Atkins to revive Cybotron in 2023 after 28 years away, resulting in the singles Maintain the Golden Ratio and Parallel Shift. In remembering Atkins, he says: “It’s particularly heartbreaking losing a man who gave the future its sound, knowing how much of his own future was still unwritten.”
Von Oswald emphasises the “magnitude” of the oeuvre Atkins created, saying it was “as though he’d travelled somewhere the rest of us hadn’t been and returned with something to show us”.
Atkins was a prophet of modern music. Thirty years ago, he foresaw both the overwhelming challenges and endless possibilities of an era he deemed the impending “techno age”. The key, as he found, was not relentless technology for its own sake, but a means of returning to emotion and finding our way back to what makes us human. “They make these synthesisers and keyboards with functions to allow you to get as close to a human feel as they possibly can,” he once said. “I think this is the beauty of Detroit: we were able to put that emotion into our music.”

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Trump’s midterm campaign has distilled his vile message | Sidney Blumenthal
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Sidney Blumenthal
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Far from veering off his track, Trump in his ceaselessly vile midterm campaign statements has attained an optimal level of Trumpism. He has distilled the raw elements of misogyny, racism and nativism to the purified essence of his political philosophy.
The Republican candidates and his vice-president have followed him down the trail of “defining deviancy down”, as explained by Daniel Patrick Moynihan, in his essay in The American Scholar in 1993, about lowering the bar to make abnormal criminal behavior seem normal, coping through denial of its obvious presence, and through that process trivializing “the manifest decline of American civic life”.
Moynihan wrote:“Here is a theory that clearly implies that there are circumstances in which society will choose not to notice behavior that would be otherwise controlled, or disapproved, or even punished.”
Trump’s disinhibition has been on neon display. In nearly every public speech he has delivered in the last month, he has spewed profane or vulgar language. He has directed his obscenities at Democrats, “dumb sons of bitches”, to whom he is going to “shove it up their ass”, but also called Norway a “shithouse country” for not awarding him the Nobel peace prize.
Trump used to hold up Norway as a model Nordic country as opposed to the “shithole countries” of Africa and Haiti. He has lately been confusing his racial disparagement with his personal peeves and forgetting that his trademark denigrating word is “shithole”, not “shithouse”.
Wielding his vulgarity, Trump has refined Maga without excuses. His animus springs from a deep well of resentment, in the beginning considered enticing forbidden fruit by TV talkshow hosts who gave him $2bn in free airtime in 2016. His rants are little different in substance, even if they now are rancid. In escalating his hyperbole, he fails to realize that such excesses have now become self-discrediting.
Alienating Latinos with his ICE roundups, the young men of his now tattered manosophere and working-class swing voters who believed he would benefit them economically, his supposed 2024 coalition is long gone with the wind. He’s down to his last resort.
At his Republican mini convention in September – for a minimum $25,000 attendance fee; $89,000 for a picture with Trump – he demanded that the paying customers raise their right hands to recite after him: “I pledge, to the greatest president in the history of the United States, that loves us so much he can’t even breathe, that I will go out with my family, my friends, I’ll do it any way, I don’t care if I’m registered or not, I’m going try and cheat like hell …”
The bounder from Queens who frenziedly sought the approval of the Manhattan elites, but whose own clownishness and bankruptcies curdled his dearest desire, has risen on inciting his Maga minions against these specters of elitism.
Yet now, the more he gets his Maga followers to dance to YMCA, and show ever greater devotion in the face of self-evident failure, the more his condescension for them leaks out. “I could say the stupidest things, and you’d clap me,” he said on 11 October in Tennessee to a Maga crowd that immediately burst into applause.
Trump’s routine and flagrant lies about his Iran war, as if he attacked out of necessity because Iran was on the verge of developing a deliverable nuclear weapon, are now accompanied by his proposal to rename the strait of Hormuz “the Trump strait”, which he has frequently been calling the “Hormone strait”, perhaps in the recesses of his mind a conflation.
He hails the “greatest” economy, and promises $5,000 to everyone “if the Republicans win”, his unfulfillable lies a series of false incentives.
Trump tosses out the allure of his ridiculous bribes almost as an aside to get to the red meat. On 27 October, after deriding the Democratic candidate for the Senate from Texas falsely as a vegan, Trump yelled: “I love the meat! Ahhh, I love it! Look!” while he rapidly jerked his hand back and forth from his mouth and grunted, closely resembling either clumsily eating a sausage or an act of fellatio.
This disturbing act followed his weeks-long obsession with men’s “asses”, repeated more than a half-dozen times across four states beginning when he leeringly declared about the Republican candidate for the Senate from Ohio Jon Husted on 12 October: “I don’t do this with men very often. I started examining his body … And I looked, and I watched up and down, and I looked at his ass … ”
His hankering for the aesthetics of men’s asses was matched with his expressions of contempt for women’s professional status whether they were Democratic candidates or members of the press. He told female journalists they were “fake”, “dumb”, should “be quiet” and to one: “Your whole outfit is fake, and so are you.”
He referred to the Democratic candidate for the Senate from South Carolina, Annie Andrews, a pediatrician and public health expert, as “Annie Trannie”, and to the Democratic candidate for the Senate from Florida, Angie Nixon, a state representative, as a “very low IQ person” and someone “who can’t speak or think properly”. She is in fine company as the ninth prominent Black official, from Kamala Harris to the supreme court associate justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, whom Trump has called “low IQ”.
These insults are for Trump simply commonplaces. He has reached new territory, however, with his defense of the ad produced by Vivek Ramaswamy, the Ohio Republican candidate, that charged his opponent Amy Acton, a physician and former director of the Ohio department of health, with lying about being raped repeatedly as a 12-year-old girl by her stepfather. In fact, the records show that she was a victim.
In effect, the ad was a cloaked defense of pedophilia. Trump called it “hitting pay dirt”, while JD Vance slammed the ad’s Republican critics for “whining”.
Trump neatly recapped his nostalgic Roy Cohn-era Red Scare, nativism and bigotry in his attacks on Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate for the Senate from Michigan, labeling him a “jihadist lunatic”, a communist and “on the side of the terrorists”. Trump told a Maga crowd to “send him back to where he came from”.
El-Sayed, born in Michigan, was already back where he came from. JD Vance came to Michigan to prove his superiority as a man of the people and an intellectual at the same time to falsely assert that El-Sayed “says not only should we have sharia law, but if you criticize it you’re a white supremacist”.
Mike Rogers, the Republican candidate in Michigan, insistently and falsely claimed that El-Sayed had “pledged his support to the Muslim Brotherhood” and adhered to “this radical Islamic agenda”.
In Kansas, the Republican senator, Roger Marshall, facing a tough challenge from Adam Hamilton, the Democratic candidate and pastor of the largest United Methodist congregation in the country, accused Hamilton of pedophilia: “He pushes drag shows for kids … is that grooming? Yeah, he probably is grooming.”
Perhaps the most pathetic descent of the Republican candidates to validate their credentials in Trump’s cult of personality through imitation was the wan effort of Darline Graham Nordone, whom Trump had induced into the Senate seat in South Carolina left vacant by the death of her brother, Lindsey Graham.
Utterly unprepared for the position, floundering like a broken-winged sparrow, she introduced Trump at a rally on her behalf, by calling her opponent Annie Andrews “batshit crazy”. She had managed to eke out “batshit” to please Trump.
On 27 October, Trump stumped at a rally in Texas for Ken Paxton, the scandal-ridden Republican candidate for the Senate, dangling his $5,000 promise if Republicans win.
“You’ll be my guest at Mar-a-Lago,” Trump said. “The problem is that for $5,000, the most you’ll be able to buy is a hamburger and maybe a small dessert. I’m not even sure you could buy that. No, don’t go there. That’s not a good place if you’re price-conscious.”
And so, Trump mocked his followers and their economic plight, for which they cheered and laughed.
Four days later, Trump staged a lavish jungle-themed Halloween costume and drag party at Mar-a-Lago, with tables spread with caviar and king crab as the “trick-or-treat”, flashing green strobe lights, performers hanging from the ceiling, dancers in full-body spandex animal print leotards, face-painted guests in drag style, some with reptilian headdresses, a live miniature pony and a caged zebra. The House speaker, Mike Johnson, and attorney general, Todd Blanche, were among the revelers.
On 20 April 1945, on the night of Hitler’s last birthday, as the Red Army closed in on Berlin, Hitler held a staid little party with Heinrich Himmler and Hermann Goering after which they fled the capital. Above the Führerbunker, in the Old Reich Chancellery, the staff and officers remaining broke into stores of champagne, played jazz records and held a wild hedonistic party.
An annoyed Hitler trying to sleep below sent an aide up to order them to shut off the phonograph and stop the party. But the Führer’s command was disobeyed. The end was near.
As the Mar-a-Lago Halloween drag party reached a fever pitch, Donald Trump burst in wearing his blue suit and red tie, and flapping open his jacket.
“I came as Donald Trump,” he announced. “I had 10 minutes … rich people spend nine hours getting ready.” He raved with pride: “Look at all my rich members. They spent all day getting ready. Look at these guys.” And he danced to YMCA.
- Sidney Blumenthal, former senior adviser to Bill Clinton and Hillary Clinton, has published three books of a projected five-volume political life of Abraham Lincoln: A Self-Made Man, Wrestling With His Angel and All the Powers of Earth. He is a Guardian US columnist and co-host of the Court of History podcast

https://www.theguardian.com/news/ng-inte.title: ‘I perfected deception’: My secret life as a relapsed alcoholic | Meghan O'Gieblyn
https://www.theguardian.com/news/ng-inte.author: Meghan O'Gieblyn
https://www.theguardian.com/news/ng-inte.text:
I am finding it very hard to write about my return to drinking. This is unexpected, given that I spent more than 10 years identifying as an alcoholic and narrating, from the podiums of church basements, the most shameful and unflattering moments of my life. The story of how you initially fell into addiction is comparatively easy to tell, because it’s widely understood that nobody chooses to become an addict, that it’s something that sneaks up on you and takes hold gradually, usually when you are too young to know better, and that quitting is an uphill battle against denial and the difficult work of coming to admit to yourself that there is a problem.
It’s much harder to tell the story of how you convinced yourself to return to a habit that you had already pushed to its limit, a habit from which you’d been free for more than a decade.
I was not under the delusion that my drinking was contextual, that my 20s had been a particularly dark time, and that things would be different in my late 30s. People had suggested this over the years – people who were not addicts themselves and who saw a commitment to lifelong abstinence as a rather extreme response to the ordinary rough patches that people experience, especially in their youth, especially when there has been a disruptive life event, like the loss of my Christian faith.
People who are not addicts seem to put a lot of stock in context, perhaps because their own drinking fluctuates according to the ups and downs of life, and because they experience alcohol as a wave of relaxation or mild euphoria that softens the world’s rough edges, not as a bolt of religious rapture that makes you want to sell all your possessions and hole up in a cave with your one precious pearl, which is how it is for those of us who were born with this disease.
So how did I convince myself to return to drinking? For a long time, I did not even understand that there was an argument taking place. There was only the hypothetical, the mental game I played to pass the time, the idle fantasies. Each bar I passed became part of the game. It got a silent vote of yes or no, depending on whether I could see myself drinking there or not. I decided I could not sit at a bar – it had to be a table. And I could not order the drink, which is to say that I could not audibly request it. This was something I only understood the first time I allowed myself to imagine the scenario in detail. I could not say the words aloud. I could not hear myself say them. It could only happen if there was a deli case next to the register, or, as I’d once glimpsed, rushing through an unfamiliar airport to make a connecting flight, self-serve taps where you could pay at an automated station.
At some point, these hypotheticals bled into planning, but the threshold between those two mental states was so subtle I did not recognise it until I’d passed over. And even then, I failed to see it as a real threat. The hypothetical was a firmly contained grammatical structure, one that was relegated to the mind, which is, as everyone knows, unreal.
Wasn’t this what I’d come to believe? I’d recently published a book about AI and human consciousness and had spent that year speaking on panels with people who insisted that our minds were fundamentally computational and determined, conclusions that were not so different, on their surface, from the meditation lectures I’d been listening to about the illusory nature of the self. It occurred to me that the whole notion of “sobriety” was a narrative construct I’d been imbuing for years with reality and substance, as though it were a concrete facet of my identity, as though there were a “self” to be sober.
This line of thinking, I can see now, rested on a crucial (and perhaps deliberate) misapprehension of these teachings. The point of recognising the “unreality” of thoughts was to avoid getting caught up in their seductive logic. I had drawn from the lectures the inverse conclusion: that if my thoughts were not real, then they could not possibly hurt me or have any effect on the real world. And if selfhood was just a story, then I could tell that story however I liked.
I was in Helsinki for work that December – a month that is, at that latitude, almost entirely swallowed by darkness. It was 15 below zero most mornings, and my eyes watered so constantly from the cold that I now remember the city as a blur of light: candles flickering in the windows of oyster bars, the green pulse of mastheads gliding into the harbour. In the mornings, magnificent plumes of pink smoke billowed out of chimneys, and during the slender hours of daylight, all the buildings were cast in a rose-coloured light that seemed to belong to both dawn and dusk. The Christmas market was set up in the middle of town, and many of the tents sold cups of glögi, the traditional mulled wine, in large metal vats.
I was doing some shopping on my last night, wandering from booth to booth, encased in my parka, looking at the wooden nativities, the long taper candles, the meat pastries. Some of the tents offered glögi in both alcoholic and non-alcoholic varieties. I was very cold. I reached for my wallet, approached one of the vendors and ordered a glass of the non-alcoholic kind. The woman behind the table did not hear me, or did not understand my pronunciation. “Which one?” she asked in English. She picked up the small chalkboard sign on which the two alternatives were listed, and when I pointed, I found my finger gravitating, without hesitation, towards the other option. It was a split-second decision, a reckless act.
That’s how it felt as I paid for the drink and took it, my heart pounding.
I told myself it was a misunderstanding. I walked towards the bin to throw it away, but before I did, I took off the lid and drank half of it, maybe more. Then I left the market and walked two blocks to a restaurant. It was there, at the entrance to the restaurant, that I felt it, though it was not euphoria or religious rapture. It wasn’t even pleasant. I felt blurry and slightly confused. I ate, and the fogginess subsided, then turned into an awful depression.
I walked back to the hotel in the cold, consumed with a Sunday-evening emptiness that I had not felt in years. It would go away if I drank more, I thought. But the strangest thing was that I did not want more. I felt precisely the way I’d heard “normal” drinkers describe feeling after a single drink: tired, sedated, eager to reclaim their clarity of mind with a coffee or a glass of water. Eleven years had passed. All my cells had since replaced themselves. Maybe it was in fact unreasonable to think I would respond the way I had in my 20s, when I was lost and miserable. I had lived for 11 years in fear of that supposed inevitability, which some part of me must have known was not the truth, but one of the many necessary fictions on which I’d built my new life.
I did not plan to drink again after that night. I had no desire to do so, and I had given up looking for the deli kiosks and self-serve taps at airports. But then, quite suddenly, a new loophole appeared, one that fate itself supplied: QR codes. Seemingly overnight, they were bolted to every table and printed on the backs of menus, initiating the miracle of contactless service that allowed you to order without speaking your sin aloud.
I was flying out of Nashville one morning, a brilliantly sunny February day that felt like spring. I’d arrived at the airport three hours before my flight and found myself, immediately after passing security, at a restaurant with QR codes on the table. A seating area below some skylights. Pop music from the previous decade over the speakers. I sat at the table and ordered a burger and a glass of white wine. The first one went straight to my head. I ordered a second before my food arrived. That was when it happened. Then or just after I’d started the third.
When I tell this story at meetings, I don’t linger on this moment, but instead flash forward several hours to the layover at O’Hare, where I switched to vodka and ended up on my knees in the women’s bathroom, vomiting into a toilet that kept flushing automatically because my head was triggering the sensor. In meetings, I talk about how I almost missed my connecting flight, and I recall the waves of shame, relief and disappointment I felt later that night, when my husband picked me up from the airport and it became clear that he did not suspect anything.
I do not talk about that moment in Nashville, finishing my second or beginning my third, when I noticed for the first time the late-morning light that fell from the skylights, purely and simply, on to the surface of my table; the warmth that came down and lifted me out of my life, out of time, and placed me in a chamber where I could see everything from a position of cosmic indifference, a perspective that captures how life must look from the vantage of eternity, where it’s possible to see how the totality of a person’s temptations, digressions and errors contribute to the compositional beauty that makes up a life. I thought about all the rules I’d made and almost laughed at how silly and stupid they were, how they belonged to the fearful, small-minded part of myself who was deluded about what really mattered, and for whom I felt enormous compassion, the way you do for a child, because even the delusions were beautiful and belonged to the expansive order of the composition.
I do not talk about this moment at meetings because I would be guilty of romanticising and elevating an act of reckless self-destruction – and also, more importantly, because words are but resounding gongs and clanging cymbals, because it is impossible to describe in language that singularity where time dissolves, and all utterance fades into light, and which entirely consumed me that morning as I sat alone, dumbstruck in the winter sunlight, wondering how on earth I had ever consented to give this up.
The following nine months were, objectively speaking, the most boring period of my entire history with alcohol. They were also the purest and most perfect. There was nothing standing between myself and the bottomless freefall of bliss. I was not trying to prove anything. I was no longer under the delusion that I could control it; the only objective was to contain it. The experience was very nearly ascetic. I limited myself to airports and hotel rooms. I never spoke to anyone, except to request the cheque or to ask, at the hotel desk, where the ice machine was, though even these small transactions were minimised by the digital interfaces that had suddenly gone up everywhere, and which appeared to have been designed specifically for people in my position, people who had slipped between the cracks of their lives and were entirely content to remain in the cracks, unobserved by the world of conscience and daylight.
I did speak to my husband, on the phone and sometimes in person, on the days when I came home not yet entirely clear. These conversations caused a great deal of anxiety, though the anxiety did not arrive until the next day, an anvil of terror and guilt as soon as I woke up, because in the moment I had been floating 10,000 miles above my body.
I had spent a decade of my life – a formative decade, the first of adulthood – perfecting the art of dissemblance, and I fell back into the groove of these tactics through sheer muscle memory. It was like riding a bicycle. Arriving home an hour before he returned, I knew instinctively to get into the bath – an old trick, one that offered a rationale for flushed cheeks, plus the tub created a barrier, as did the fragrant suds, to the smell of alcohol leaving the pores.
Each binge was a controlled explosion, safely contained from the rest of my life. I reasoned they were hurting no one, and it’s true that for a while there were few consequences. Or perhaps I am cursed with “euphoric recall” – the inability to remember the lows with the same vivid resolution as the highs. I do remember the vomiting, both during and after.
It made a difference, whether it was during or after. During was not entirely unpleasant: you kneeled and opened your mouth and your body took it from there – there was nothing to it. And you always felt better afterwards, empty and slightly more sober, ready to drink more. It was a cleansing that literalised the central promise of the intoxicated mind: that every error could be undone, that all the tapes could be reversed, that all would be well.
After was a different story. The body still took over, but it was with churning, mechanical violence – or perhaps the problem was that the mind on those wretched mornings was not willing to play along, was not able to let go and surrender to the process. You tasted everything coming up, there was no way to avoid it, and it was not the blameless liquid that had escaped so easily the night before, but all the filth that had festered in your stomach for hours, the shame of whatever you had eaten and forgotten you had eaten before passing out. The clear afterbirth that followed, pure stomach acid that burned the back of your throat and tasted like death itself, acid you had to cough to get out.
And that was not even the end of it, because there was also the empty heaving, the eternity during which you sat on the cold tile floor, praying it was over, occasionally spitting fire into a wad of toilet paper, conscious the whole time of how close you were to death, grateful only that you did not see any bile.
There was so much to be grateful for during those months. I had forgotten about this, how any period of dissolution brings you into such close proximity to the gratuitous abundance of human kindness. I had experienced it throughout my 20s: the cab driver who picked me up when I was passed out on a kerb, drove me to the address on my licence, carried me up the stairs to my apartment and laid me on the couch, where he left me unharmed. The pharmacist who could have reported me for trying to fill an expired script (the date changed by one number), and who instead saw that I was shaking with withdrawal and told me to meet her outside, where she slipped me two pills and the number of a local detox centre. The woman who stopped at my table in the rehab cafeteria, where I was sitting alone, sobbing, and told me it would get better, her voice so full of calm authority that I assumed she was a doctor or a therapist, or perhaps an angel, and whom I discovered later was a patient who’d been admitted only three days before me.
The dangers this time around were not as extreme, but I was still frequently the recipient of baffling acts of compassion. The woman at the airport bar who paid my tab when I realised I was about to miss my flight. The flight attendant who brought me aspirin when I was vomiting in the aeroplane toilet. The librarian who was so entirely forgiving when I cancelled the virtual panel she had organised on the morning it was supposed to take place, and who may or may not have bought my line about a stomach virus.
These were not heroic acts, but the kindness was so entirely undeserved – in fact, the opposite of what I deserved – that it felt like grace in its most intense form, the grace of the reformers, unmerited favour “given to the most undeserving and unworthy”, as Luther said. We should all pity those perpetually capable, functioning adults who have never experienced this grace, which is among the rare miracles of this life.
One afternoon, as I was boarding a flight, I received a voicemail from the teenage son of one of my mother’s friends. I had not spoken to this kid – I still thought of him as a kid, though he was now 18 – for several years, but I’d heard through the family grapevine that he had just completed his second or third stint in rehab. His voice in the message was sullen and compulsory; it was clear that his mother had given him my number and urged him to call. But when I called him back, soon after arriving on the east coast and checking into my hotel, I was surprised to hear real desperation in his voice.
He’d been sent to rehab this last time, he said, after an overdose that may or may not have been a suicide attempt – he was not totally sure himself – and had been thrown out of the institution for smuggling in pills. He was now back at home with his mum, trying to go to recovery meetings. There were lots of people his age who were excited about sobriety, but he did not feel that way. He said that he could not picture his life without drugs and alcohol, that it was the most depressing thing he could imagine. There was an exhaustion in his voice that seemed to belong to someone much older, not a child who had his whole life ahead of him.
I listened for a long time and then said everything I knew to say: I told him that I loved alcohol more than anything, more than any person or thing, more than God. I said the thing about addiction is that it demands everything; no sacrifice is ever enough. I said that he could have this one luminous thing, or he could have everything else, which is to say every experience, every possibility, all the ups and downs that make up a life. I said these things and meant them. I truly believed, as I sat there on the floor of my hotel room, looking out at the freezing rain, that his life would be better if he could stay on the right side of that equation, just as mine had been better for doing so. I also, at the same time, believed that if I wanted to choose the single luminous object over a rich and full life, it was my business.
He asked how long I had been sober.
Eleven years, I said.
How hard it was during that year to say that number out loud! My whole life had become a lie, though so long as I remained in the realm of language and narrative, as opposed to the inflexible mathematics of time, it was easy to believe that nothing had changed. The story of my life was one I had been telling for more than a decade, and I believed it was strong enough to sustain private infractions. Or perhaps the point of the infractions was to discover how much the story could sustain. As far as everyone in my life was concerned, including even my husband and my closest friends, I was the same person I had always been – a person who could be counted on to keep an extra set of keys to your house, or to be named the godmother to your child, or to offer wise counsel to a kid who’d just got out of rehab.
I don’t pretend to remember exactly what I was thinking during this time, or all the convoluted ways I rationalised my actions to myself, but I do remember the fundamental inability to buy into the reality of my secret life, and the inarticulate conviction that so long as the official version of my life continued without hiccup, that was what counted. I felt like a marine crustacean whose shell remained on shore, a solid proxy for its being, while the animal inside slithered off into the sea.
This is an edited extract from Will and Attention, published by Little, Brown. To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.title: Caleb Williams and new arrival Jeffery Simmons power Bears past sputtering Seahawks
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.author: Agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text:
Caleb Williams threw a touchdown pass on the opening drive and Jeffery Simmons delivered just what Chicago needed on defense as the Bears beat the host Seattle Seahawks 34-17 on Monday night.
Williams was extremely efficient for the Bears (6-2) against one of the NFL’s stingiest defenses, committing no turnovers, taking just one sack and throwing for 247 yards while completing 71% of his passes.
Williams’s play helped set up three short touchdown runs by D’Andre Swift and that proved to be more than enough against Sam Darnold and the Seahawks (4-4), thanks to the impact Simmons had on the defense.
Acquired last week from Tennessee for a package that included two first-round picks, Simmons took little time to make a big impact on a defense that had lacked difference-makers.
He had a sack on the opening drive, added another tackle for loss and finished with six tackles and a pass defended as Chicago held Seattle to 252 yards and one third-down conversion on 11 tries.
“I’m so excited to be a Chicago Bear man,” Simmons told ESPN. “This is just the beginning. We’ve got some stuff to clean up but it’s a good football team and I’m happy to be a part of it.”
The reigning champion Seahawks lost for the third time in four games and are now looking up at the NFC playoff standings. They can ill afford many more slip-ups. The loss ended a 30-game streak for Seattle in the regular season and playoffs – the fourth longest for any team in the Super Bowl era – of not losing by more than four points.
Darnold went 17 of 34 for 188 yards and two touchdowns for Seattle, but his interception in the fourth quarter set up Swift’s third touchdown that made it 34-17 with 4:41 to play.
The Seahawks struggled once again to run the ball despite their trade last week for three-time All-Pro guard Quenton Nelson and the return of Zach Charbonnet and Jadarian Price from injures. Seattle ran for just 81 yards.
The Bears started off well against Seattle’s stout defense by putting together a 17-play drive on their opening possession. They took the lead when Williams threw a one-yard touchdown pass to Luther Burden III. Chicago added two more field goals in the first half and built the lead to 20-9 in the third quarter with another efficient touchdown drive that ended with a one-yard run by Swift.
The Seahawks were bottled up by Simmons and the Bears for almost the entire first half before Darnold connected with Jaxon Smith-Njigba on a 43-yard touchdown pass with 30 seconds left in the second quarter.
Things looked bleak for Seattle when Jason Myers had a 33-yard field goal blocked in the opening minute of the fourth quarter. But DeMarcus Lawrence forced a fumble by Colston Loveland on the next possession that set up Darnold’s seven-yard touchdown pass to Cooper Kupp, and Seattle converted the two-point attempt to make it 20-17.
The Bears answered with another touchdown drive and put the game away after Darnold’s interception.
Swift rushed 27 times for a game-high 69 yards, and Loveland and Burden each made seven receptions. The Seahawks had entered the game with an NFL-best .711 winning percentage on Monday Night Football (32-13).

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.title: Wolff hails world champion Antonelli as role model in blast at F1’s ‘entitled moaners’
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.author: Giles Richards in Mexico City
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text:
The Mercedes team principal, Toto Wolff, has described his Formula One world champion Kimi Antonelli as a new kind of racing driver who represents the future of the sport, comparing him scathingly to what he called some of the entitled moaners on the grid and declaring “selfless, ruthless” drivers now dead to F1.
Antonelli secured his first world title in Mexico City on Sunday, at 20 years old becoming the youngest F1 champion in only his second season in the sport. The Italian’s attitude, enthusiasm and sense of fair play have been notable in a revelatory season for a driver so young and Wolff believes he has proved to be a gamechanger in more ways than one.
Wolff said: “This notion of win at all costs, selfish, opportunistic, ruthless for your own benefit, that model of racing driver has died. We have a new champion that represents values: humility, integrity, loyalty, respect. Being himself. He should be a role model for many other young drivers.
“He should be a role model for the few entitled ones in Formula One. The endless moaners on the radio. The ones that complain, the ones that crash. Look at this kid of 20 years and then think what you can do in order to improve. That’s the message to these kids.”
Wolff did not name the targets of his ire but his comments will be lost on no one and clearly he believes Antonelli, who has been with Mercedes since he was 12, is an excellent example.
Antonelli sealed the title with his third-place finish in Mexico, after a season where he has been on top throughout but has driven clean. Fellow world champions including Lewis Hamilton, Max Verstappen and Lando Norris offered similar plaudits to the young driver who has bested them and his Mercedes teammate, George Russell, roundly beaten by the Italian this year, has acknowledged his honest and fair approach to racing.
Wolff went further in stating that the most senior figures in the sport felt Antonelli embodied what they wanted in Formula One drivers, including Stefano Domenicali, the F1 chief executive, and the president of the FIA, Mohammed Ben Sulayem.
“That is how the FIA, that Mohammed, that Stefano, that I would want to see racing drivers in the future,” Wolff said. “That is modern Formula One. Kimi represents the modern Formula One driver, because of those values, not only because of his talent. The talent is there with everyone. But you got to be a good person too and he has demonstrated that you can beat everyone out there by being a good person.”
Before Wolff had raised the subject in Mexico, Antonelli had already expressed his desire to retain his sense of self, even as world champion. Now entitled to put the No 1 on his car next season, he said he would instead retain his current No 12. Antonelli chose it because of his admiration for Ayrton Senna who used it early in his career with Lotus between 1985 and 1987 and when he won his first title in 1988 for McLaren.
“I’ll stay with No 12 because obviously it’s a very special number for me but also it’s a way for me to stay grounded, to stay humble,” Antonelli said when asked if he would adopt the champion’s No 1. “I feel like by keeping No 12, it allows me to have a new point where to start and build on everything again and try to improve.”
After what was clearly a hugely moving experience in taking the title, Antonelli, was raised aloft on the podium after the race by Verstappen and Hamilton, two greats of the sport who finished in first and second in Mexico, which the 20-year-old said he would treasure and immortalise.
“I will definitely frame that picture and put it in my house,” he said. “It’s just an incredible moment. To see so much respect from two incredible drivers in the history of the sport is truly special that will live and will always be remembered.”

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/podcast/.title: ‘Idosos agora têm vez’, diz Tânia Maria, de 79 anos, que está no elenco de Yellow Cake
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/podcast/.author: Conversa Bem Viver
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/podcast/.text:
O longa-metragem “Yellow Cake”, dirigido por Tiago Melo, estreia em 26 de novembro no circuito comercial de cinema de todo o país. Já exibido em festivais nacionais e internacionais, o filme é uma ficção científica sobre meio-ambiente e a interferência estrangeira na exploração de minério no Brasil.
Na história, um grupo de pesquisadores pretende usar as reservas de urânio do município de Picuí, no sertão da Paraíba, para criar um modo de combate ao Aedes aegypti, mosquito responsável por transmitir dengue, zika e chikungunya. O plano, no entanto, escapa ao controle, e uma cientista brasileira busca então formas de evitar uma catástrofe.
Tânia Maria — que ficou conhecida por sua participação em “Bacurau” e pela personagem Sebastiana em “O Agente Secreto“, filmes de Kleber Mendonça Filho — interpreta nessa nova produção dona Rita, uma moradora da cidade.
Em entrevista ao programa Conversa Bem Viver, da Rádio Brasil de Fato, a atriz convida as pessoas a irem ao cinema: “Esse filme ensina tanta coisa. Se a gente prestar atenção, é um filme e tanto. Convido todo o povo em geral para assistir no cinema ‘Yellow Cake’ e dá uma nota para a dona Rita. Eu quero que todos gostem.”
Aos 79 anos, Tânia Maria aproveitou a fama alcançada com seus trabalhos no cinema para publicar um vídeo nas redes sociais convocando as pessoas de mais de 70 anos (que não têm mais a obrigação de votar) a marcar presença nas urnas neste segundo turno das eleições presidenciais no Brasil.
“Quando deu 8 horas, eu já estava na boca da urna para dar o meu voto. Nós vamos esperar pelos novos? Não! Nós que temos experiência é que temos que escolher. Eu sempre votei, nunca perdi nenhuma eleição. Enquanto eu entender, eu conhecer os números, eu voto”, relatou a atriz.
Tânia também faz uma participação especial da série “Delegado”, que estreou no dia 30 de outubro, no Canal Brasil e no Globoplay. Drama policial brasileiro regado de humor, acompanha a chegada de um jovem ingênuo ao comando de uma delegacia em Recife, capital de Pernambuco.
Ao comentar como tem sido engrenar uma carreira como atriz depois das 70 anos, Tânia Maria diz que quer ainda mais produções para o futuro. “Os velhos é que estão fazendo sucesso no Brasil, é bom demais! Os idosos agora têm vez, agora que minha vida começou, quero que venham muitos filmes para trabalhar.”
Conversa Bem Viver

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Republican Ashley Moody defeats progressive Angie Nixon in Florida Senate race
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Richard Luscombe in Miami
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Ashley Moody fended off a challenge from Angie Nixon, a democratic socialist, to win Florida’s special election and retain her seat in the US Senate.
It was the first election win for the Republican, who was appointed by Florida’s governor Ron DeSantis in January 2025, when Marco Rubio became US secretary of state. Moody will serve the remainder of his term until the 2028 election.
Polling in the run-up to Tuesday gave Moody a clear but narrow advantage, which Nixon sought to close and overcome with the support of prominent progressive Democrats.
Both Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez rallied last month with Nixon in central Florida, an immigrant-heavy section of the state where the Trump administration’s harsh detention and deportation policies have proved unpopular.
The contest was also a gauge of whether Florida remained reliably Republican, after the party built a 1.5 million-voter advantage in registrations, or if Democrats – shut out in statewide races for a decade – had made progress towards restoring Florida’s lost status as a key battleground.
Moody, during campaign appearances, focused on denouncing Nixon as a “socialist”, and portrayed her alignment with the Democratic Socialists of America as evidence she was intent on defunding the police and the US military, abolishing prisons and supporting unchecked immigration and noncitizen voting.
Moody lauded Trump’s immigration policies but, mindful of the president’s strong disapproval ratings over the Iran war and high gas prices, largely refrained from praising him personally.
Nixon campaigned vigorously on affordability and corruption in politics, frequently referring to Moody’s role as Florida’s attorney general in the so-called Hope Florida scandal, in which DeSantis’s administration diverted a $10m Medicaid payout to political committees.
“I don’t want to abolish prisons, because I want Ashley Moody in one of them,” she said in an interview that provided one of her campaign’s most viral moments.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Democrat Chris Pappas wins New Hampshire Senate race to become first out gay senator
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Shrai Popat
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Chris Pappas, the four-term Democratic congressman, has won New Hampshire’s US Senate race, protecting the open seat from a Republican flip in a closely fought contest against John Sununu, the former senator.
Pappas, 46, is a centrist voice in the US House who has at times broken with his party on major legislation. He focused his Senate campaign on serving as a bulwark against the Trump administration, which is unpopular in the Granite State. Pappas will be the first out gay man to serve in the US Senate.
The race became a late source of anxiety for Democrats, with Pappas, a moderate, locked in a neck-and-neck battle with Sununu to succeed Jeanne Shaheen, the retiring Democratic senator.
Pappas secured endorsements from several prominent Democrats and portrayed Sununu, who once called Donald Trump a “loser”, as a faux moderate who would ultimately rubber-stamp the president’s agenda. Pappas sought to capitalize on the Trump administration’s low approval ratings, highlighting a range of unpopular policies on the campaign trail, from the war against Iran to Medicaid cuts included in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
Meanwhile, Sununu – who represented New Hampshire in the Senate before losing his seat in 2008 – pitched himself as an independent-minded candidate. He worked to put distance between himself and Trump, despite securing the president’s endorsement. Sununu criticized the war in Iran, accused the administration of not doing enough to support Ukraine and even claimed in a recent campaign ad that he had “never met” the president.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Democrats look poised to win House control in midterm elections after two turbulent years of Trump
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Sam Levine
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Democrats are winning competitive US House races and are expected to flip the US House of Representatives after two tumultuous years of Donald Trump’s second presidency. A change in House control would give Democrats a perch to conduct robust oversight of the administration for its final two years.
Republicans currently hold 218 seats in the House and Democrats have 214. (There is one vacancy in a Republican seat and one vacancy in a Democratic seat, and one Republican member switched his party affiliation to independent.) Democrats need to flip just three seats to gain control of the House.
All members of the House run for re-election every two years. To have a majority in the House, a party must control at least 218 seats. While there is still some uncertainty about how many seats Democrats could gain, the non-partisan Cook Political Report predicts Democrats will pick up 15 to 25 seats, which could give them anywhere from 230 to 240 seats in the House.
The Center for Politics at the University of Virginia, another forecaster, lists 239 House seats in Democrats’ favor.
Traditionally, the president’s party performs poorly in the midterms – held midway through the president’s four-year term. Republicans are facing significant headwinds this year with Trump’s approval rating hitting record lows. The war in Iran also remains deeply unpopular and gas prices remain extremely high.
Gaining a majority in the House would give Democrats control of the body’s committees and the ability to subpoena documents and witnesses as part of investigations. Democrats have signaled they will investigate Trump’s family business, immigration enforcement, matters related to Jeffrey Epstein, and Robert F Kennedy Jr’s handling of vaccine procedures and recommendations, among other issues.
If Democrats retake the House, Hakeem Jeffries, a Democrat from Brooklyn first elected in 2012, is expected to become speaker. The 56-year-old would be the first Black speaker in US history.
Democrats are expected to take control of the House despite an unusual and aggressive effort by Republicans to redraw congressional districts before the election to their advantage.
At the request of Trump, Republicans in Texas, Florida, Missouri and other Republican-led states redrew their districts to add more GOP-friendly ones. After the supreme court issued a landmark ruling significantly weakening a key provision of the Voting Rights Act, lawmakers in Alabama, North Carolina and Tennessee redrew their maps to eliminate districts where Black voters had been able to elect a candidate of their choosing.
But the political environment is so unfavorable to Republicans that Democrats could win races in the Alabama and North Carolina districts that were redrawn. Some GOP-friendly districts added in Texas also appear winnable for Democrats. Overall, Republicans may only pick up a handful of the districts they redrew to their advantage.
The first polls closed in Indiana and Kentucky at 6pm ET, with more states following mostly hourly after that. Results in Kentucky’s sixth district will be closely watched, as Democrat Zach Dembo, a Navy veteran and former prosecutor, leads Republican Dr Ralph Alvarado, whom Trump has backed, for the open seat. The Cook Political Report rates the race as a toss-up despite a partisan lean towards Republicans.
Polls closed across Florida at 7pm ET; there are also several competitive House races in the state, even in districts that state Republicans recently redrew in their favor. Democrat Kathy Castor, for example, won in a district that includes Tampa that was redrawn to be more favorable to Republicans. Had the district been in place in 2024, Trump would have won it by 11 points. The Cook Political Report rated the race as one of the most competitive this cycle.
Democrat Jared Moskowitz also won a highly competitive race in Florida’s 25th congressional district that Republicans redrew in their favor. Democrat Pia Dandiya also won the election in the newly drawn 22nd congressional district that heavily favored Republicans. That means Democrats have triumphed in three of the four Florida districts that Republicans redrew in their favor earlier this year.
In North Carolina, Democrat Jamie Ager won in the 11th congressional district in the western part of the state, flipping it in Democrats’ favor. The district is currently represented by Republican Chuck Edwards, who dropped his re-election bid after an ethics committee report found he sexually harassed staffers.
In New Jersey, Republican representative Tom Kean Jr was ousted by Democrat Rebecca Bennett. Kean disappeared from public view for three months earlier this year without explanation.
Representative Debbie Wasserman Schultz easily won re-election in Florida’s 20th district, which is heavily Democratic, according to the AP.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/4.title: Keisha Lance Bottoms makes history as Georgia’s first Black woman governor
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/4.text:
Keisha Lance Bottoms makes history as Georgia’s first Black woman governor
Bottoms, who formerly advised ex-President Joe Biden, beat Republican Rick Jackson.
Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms has made history as the first Black woman elected governor in the United States.
The former Atlanta mayor emerged victorious over her billionaire opponent, Republican Rick Jackson, who spent more than $200m of his personal fortune in an attempt to succeed popular outgoing Republican Governor Brian Kemp.
Bottoms, an adviser to former US President Joe Biden, was propelled to victory in part by the state’s significant Black voting bloc, which turned out in large numbers during early voting.
During the campaign, she faced Republican attempts to characterise her time as mayor as a crime-ridden decline for the state’s largest city.
“It’s a longstanding playbook to paint Atlanta as this big bad place,” Bottoms told the Associated Press news agency.
Bottoms’s win marks the third consecutive time that Georgia Democrats have nominated a Black woman for governor. Stacey Abrams lost in 2018 and 2022 to Kemp, who is leaving office in January after eight years due to term limits.

https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.title: “This Election Was a Defeat for Lies”: Read Lula’s Inspiring Victory Speech
https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.author: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva
https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.text:
“I doubt that Russia, China, or the United States has an army as victorious as the army of democracy of this country,” the president told his supporters.

On Sunday, Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won a record fourth term in office, defeating far-right challenger Flávio Bolsonaro. After his victory was declared, Lula addressed a cheering crowd of supporters in São Paulo. Here are some excerpts from that speech, as translated by longtime Nation contributor Greg Grandin.

I wanted to thank the Brazilian people for their generosity, those who stayed with me through the length of this runoff. I want to thank the generosity of the young, who took to the streets to defend democracy. I want to thank the elderly. I know that many of them were urged on by their grandchildren to vote for me. People with cancer, people with limited mobility, with other kinds of illness. And you went to vote. It will be very important to assure them that their vote was worth it, that it will safeguard democracy in this country.

I want to thank society as a whole, which is the real winner of this election. This is an election in which we prevailed over outside interference, especially by digital platforms, which we are going to have to regulate. We need to understand that crime in the digital world will be treated as crime in the real world. We can’t have monstrous, giant companies earning millions and billions, paying no taxes to this country, and trying to influence electoral results.

This election was a defeat for denialism, a defeat for lies. And I confess that every time there was a debate, I felt embarrassed, because I’ve debated with a lot of people. I’ve taken part in many elections. I meet every year with the G20, the BRICS, the G7. I meet every year with the leaders of the world. And we discuss the world’s main issues. But I never thought I’d come face to face with the genuine representative [Flávio Bolsonaro] of paramilitary power in this country. I never imagined someone could lie so much, so shamelessly, as if there weren’t a single cell of humanity inside him. It all seems fake….

I was stunned to see the enthusiasm of people singing the Independence Anthem…in a demonstration that this country does not accept being anyone’s backyard.…

This election taught me many lessons. I can assure you that we are going to change the way this country is governed. We’re going to have the people take a greater part in decision-making. And digital communication is going to get a very large place in my government.…

I won’t allow my words to be interpreted in bad faith. I won’t. I’ll say what I think and what I do. One of the things that motivated me most in these elections was not letting those people win so they could privatize our public health system.

Again, I will say that having won the election, we no longer have an adversary. I will govern for all Brazilians. In my coming term, I am going to focus on caring for our elderly, who are have given us life. Women will be treated with much more respect by Brazilian public policy. All religions will be respected on equal terms.…

Whatever anyone’s faith and spirituality, it is the responsibility of the secular state to guarantee full religious freedom, so that people can practice their faith fully. We will continue our revolution in Brazilian education. We will achieve universal full-time high school. We will universalize the student savings program so that no young man or woman drops out of school because they have to work. We’ll teach more math, more engineering. Because I don’t want to depend on Chinese or US artificial intelligence. I want to create a Brazilian one. We have to take advantage of the energy potential of a country that may have the greatest renewable energy capacity, to bring here the data centers we need, so that our data is stored in Brazil. ….

We will move Brazil from being a developing country to a developed one, through investment in the digital economy, the green economy, and the creative economy. This country will be built not by me—because many of the things I’m mentioning here I know little about—but by you. We will the people’s creative potential so as to stop being a peripheral country.… We are going to show the world how to handle climate policy. This year is the first time we’ve managed to reduce deforestation four years in a row….

This country is ready to be built. I won’t use the words “national unity,” because that phrase doesn’t always fit this country. But I want you to know: As far as it depends on me, this country will be civilized. This country has a Constitution. Nobody is obliged to like the president-elect, but he was elected to govern for everyone, based on respect for the Constitution and on his relationship with Congress.…

I want to say I have great pride. First, because I am the only president of the Republic, a metalworker without a university degree, elected four times democratically…. We had Roosevelt, who was elected four times, but he couldn’t finish his final term because he had a very serious illness. Now, I won’t want another term but I’m going to finish this term in full.… So I want to thank God, and thank you, the men and women of this country. These elections were about honor, nationalism, democracy and the future you want. I’ve never won an election in the first round, but I’ve never lost in the second. I’m 81 years old. The day after tomorrow, the 27th, I turn 81. And I want to make a commitment in front of the press and in front of you: I’m going to have the best term any president has had in this country’s history. You can be sure. I’ll dedicate 20, 24 hours a day to making this the country everyone dreams of. A country where people know they can go to sleep and wake up with peace of mind….

I doubt that Russia, China, or the United States has an army as victorious as the army of democracy of this country. A hug to the soldiers, men and women, of our army.

Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva is the president of Brazil.

https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.title: Lessons From Lula’s Historic Victory
https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.author: Benjamin Fogel
https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.text:
The Brazilian left has stopped the right-wing wave in Latin America. Now it has four years to work out a succession plan.

After three of the most intense weeks in the history of Brazilian politics, Luiz Inácio “Lula” da Silva will be president again. Though he lost the first round of the presidential election earlier this month, he went on to win a historic fourth term, finishing 4.4 million votes ahead of Flávio Bolsonaro, the crooked oldest son of former president and convicted coup plotter Jair (the final tally was 51.79 to 48.21 percent). If it wasn’t clear before, it is now: Lula is the greatest popular leader of his generation and one of history’s most gifted politicians.

Flávio has predictably refused to concede, but Lula’s margin of victory was twice as large as his 2022 margin over Jair—and unlike his father in 2022, Flávio does not have the power of the presidency to try to stop Lula from taking office. Some of his closest allies have already fled to Miami, and his brother Eduardo, a former federal deputy who exiled himself to Texas a few years ago, suggested on a podcast last week that Flávio should join him in the United States.

Flávio ran a weak second-round campaign, as scandal after scandal broke almost daily. Together, they tied him and his closest allies to organized crime, money laundering, social security fraud, the gambling lobby, and the largest banking fraud in Brazilian history. He also alienated many voters by acting as if he were already in government, announcing bizarre cabinet appointments and unpopular policies. During the debates, his attempts to first troll Lula and then to pose as a statesman both backfired.

Lula’s victory has not only stopped the wave of right-wing victories crashing across Latin America, but it also marks a major setback to Imperial Miami’s project for the region, encapsulated in the so-called Donroe Doctrine. Indeed, it is the most significant defeat for the far right internationally since Donald Trump won a second term in 2024. It was a victory against the odds: Lula won an astonishing 10 million–plus new votes in the runoff after losing to Flávio by 2.2 million votes on October 4 (47.03 percent to Lula’s 45.16). And he did it despite coordinated attempts to sabotage his campaign by Big Tech, the United States, the president of Brazil’s Electoral Court, elements of legacy media, and one of the most powerful online disinformation machines ever assembled.

The result will reverberate well beyond Brazil’s borders. The country has the largest economy and population in Latin America, and it has often been credited with the potential to become a major power—not only because it is blessed with critical minerals but also because it has the capacity to withstand bullying, tariffs, and economic warfare from the United States. That power is why even the right-wing governments of its neighbors—with the exception of the increasingly delusional Javier Milei—have already acknowledged Lula’s victory. Trump has so far stayed silent.

What, then, can the left elsewhere learn from Brazil? First, we now have an answer to the question I posed in a piece for Jacobin before the second round: whether “the politics of the street are enough to counter some of the effects of social disintegration.” The answer is a resounding yes: The politics of the street still matter.

The day before the October 25 runoff saw perhaps the two largest rallies in the history of Brazil: Close to a million people, myself included, joined Lula on Copacabana Beach in Rio, and likely well over a million occupied the entirety of Avenida Paulista, the main thoroughfare in São Paulo, the most populous city in the Americas. There were also significant rallies in all of Brazil’s other major cities, midsize cities, and even small towns. Getting people on the street doesn’t just provide an antidote to the virus of political despair; it can still mobilize voters.

Second, this is the first election I have witnessed in which the left won the online battle—despite Big Tech, particularly Meta, tilting the algorithm toward the far right. Credit for that goes mostly to a centralized online army—Lula’s Army—of 10.8 million people, organized through a WhatsApp channel in less than three weeks and commanded by the Julius Caesar of Brazilian social media, Minas Gerais Federal Deputy André Janones. The general not only turned the algorithm against the far right but also reclaimed symbols of Brazil such as the national football team’s jersey (by sending his followers on missions like posting a selfie on Instagram on a Saturday at 9 am wearing it) and made the trademarked “L” hand sign for Lula.

In this war, Janones had help from a new generation of Brazilian left-wing politicians who launched their own offensives on social media. Among them were Homeless Workers’ Movement leader Guilherme Boulos, who also serves in Lula’s cabinet as minister for the presidency; Brazil’s Marxist-Leninist answer to Hasan Piker, Pernambuco Federal Deputy Jones Manoel; and the 21-year-old Minas Gerais Workers’ Party Federal Deputy Ana Elisa Silva.

The contrast with the right is instructive. Bolsonarismo’s Militant Digital Party—as political scientist Marcos Nobre describes it, drawing on the work of Paolo Gerbaudo—is largely organic and decentralized, led by a host of political entrepreneurs who run their own online pyramid schemes (as the philosopher Rodrigo Nunes outlines in his new book Anatomy of Disintegration). It operates largely out of public view, through covert networks and individualized algorithms, and is flush with dirty money from the online gambling industry, organized crime, and various other scams.

According to Nobre, it has a hard-line base of around 25 percent of voters and has swallowed up the old rent-seeking parties of the centrão (big center) by way of a conventional party apparatus. Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party is now the dominant force in both the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate. Those gains have come not at the expense of the left, which actually increased its representation in Congress, but of old-school authoritarian, center-right, and slightly more democratic machine parties.

The left took the opposite approach. By centralizing communications and messaging, it reached not only undecideds but also those who abstained in the first round or cast null ballots, and even more than a few Flávio supporters. The result was a historic jump in turnout. The upshot is that if the left is to launch a digital counterattack against the far right, it needs to centralize communications and create a welcoming online space for alienated and isolated people looking to do more than shout into the void.

While Lula is a generational leader produced by a world-historic movement of the working class—and Janones is a digital commander who could only have emerged in Brazil—this victory still offers invaluable lessons for a left that wants not just to play defense against the far right but to go on the counterattack, combining the politics of the street with a centralized online army.

None of this will make Lula’s job easy. Governing Brazil with a Congress controlled by the far right will be an enormous task, and we can expect repeated attempts, backed by the United States, to contest the results. After all, Jair Bolsonaro was convicted of plotting a failed coup after the last election—a plot that, among other things, would have involved the assassination of Lula.

Benjamin Fogel is the head of publications at the Alameda Institute and a contributing editor at Jacobin.
