Progressives elsewhere have no reason to let up the pressure for broad sanctions and a total arms embargo. Nevertheless, they can take inspiration from the many Palestinian (and a few Jewish) citizens of Israel, who by voting for the Joint List have expressed their steadfastness — sumoud — in the struggle for democracy, justice, and peace.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.title: Chris Ofili brings story of Laure—the Black model painted by Manet—in from the margins at Turin exhibition
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.author: Gareth Harris
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.text:
The UK artist Chris Ofili is rewriting the canon in a new show launching in Italy, giving one of Édouard Manet’s most famous figures—Laure, the Black model depicted in Manet’s Olympia (1863)—her own place in art history.
For the latest edition of Beyond the Collection curatorial initiative at the Pinacoteca Agnelli in Turin (30 October-4 April 2027), Ofili presents new works inspired by Laure including a large-scale painting, a watercolour and a series of drawings.
“[The exhibition] means questioning who has written our history and the exclusions involved,” said Sarah Cosulich, the director of the Pinacoteca Agnelli, at a press briefing. “Art historians rewrite history in their own way but Ofili brings this imaginative approach,” the exhibition curator Pietro Rigolo tells The Art Newspaper (Rigolo is also chief curator and head of collection at Pinacoteca Agnelli).
Among the works on view is Manet’s Portrait of Laure (La Négresse), around 1862, which is drawn from the Pinacoteca Agnelli's collection and has been renamed (the piece was originally entitled La Négresse).
“Ofili starts with this idea of giving back to this woman her name and her identity, giving her a story and presence,” Rigolo says. “Nobody has objected to the name change [of the work],” he adds.
Ofili’s large-scale painting, Saint Laure (2026), is the same size as Manet’s Olympia, in which Laure brings flowers to a nude, reclining Parisian courtesan. In his piece, Ofili turns Olympia’s body into a desert landscape which runs along the base of the work, shifting “Laure from the margins to the centre”, an exhibition statement says.
For the work, “Ofili looks to Italian and religious art—in particular depictions of angelic figures and artists such as Giotto and Fra Angelico (Beato Angelico)—and he also looked to an Italian movie called Io Capitano [2023],” Rigolo adds. Io Capitano follows two young Senegalese cousins on their journey from West Africa to Italy. “There is a debate in Italy about migration—this [Ofili] project is grounded in what is happening in Italy now,” Rigolo says, referencing the ongoing political issue polarising European countries. Ofili bases his depiction of Laure in particular on the film’s unnamed character known as “woman in the desert”.
Ofili’s new works also draw on the research of Denise Murrell, a curator-at-large at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York. Murrell has reshaped the role of the Black female figure in Modern art in her studies, as in the exhibition Posing Modernity: The Black Model from Manet and Matisse to Today, which opened at Columbia’s Wallach Art Gallery in 2018. “From the outset, Ofili said he wanted to involve Murrell [who contributes to a scholarly booklet accompanying the show],” Rigolo says.
The new season of exhibitions at the Pinacoteca Agnelli also include a retrospective dedicated to the 20th-century Greek-Italian painter and polymath Alberto Savinio, the brother of Giorgio de Chirico who played a fundamental role in the development of Metaphysical art (30 October-4 April 2027).
Next year, Ofili’s largest solo exhibition in London since his Tate Britain show in 2010 will open at the Hayward Gallery (7 September-9 January 2028). It will survey three decades of his practice and feature key works from the 1990s alongside his latest paintings.
- Laure. Chris Ofili & Édouard Manet, Pinacoteca Agnelli, Turin, Italy, until 4 April 2027

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.title: After seven years, Hirshhorn Museum opens Hiroshi Sugimoto-designed sculpture garden
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.author: Angelica Hankins
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.text:
When the Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden opened in 1974 in Washington, DC, The New York Times called it “the capital’s newest cultural treasure”. Likening the Hirshhorn to a René Magritte picture, reporters drew out the “juxtaposition of man and nature with architecture”, the seamless melding of light and form, indoors and out, that sets apart its collection of Modern and contemporary art.
On 31 October, the Hirshhorn is scheduled to unveil a new cultural treasure: its $68m renovated sculpture garden. The project has been years in the making, designed by the Japanese artist Hiroshi Sugimoto—who also redesigned the museum’s lobby in 2018. The reorganised 1.3-acre space, with its 30,000 new plants and trees, draws on the architect Gordon Bunshaft’s original design. This is part of a broader transformation at the museum, including renovations to the plaza and building infrastructure.
Featuring 60 works—21 of them from the 1974 installation—the renovated garden includes five entrances, east and west overlooks and an underground passageway of stainless steel. Sugimoto describes its mirrored finish as “reflecting the garden and the people moving through it, an experience in itself—one that is continually transformed by the interplay of light, nature and the visitors”.
I decided a Japanese dry-stone wall would serve as a symbolic link between the ancient and the modern Hiroshi Sugimoto
The walkways and alcoves are delineated using stacked-stone walls, each hand-selected and arranged by the artist. “Bunshaft was deeply influenced by the stone gardens of medieval Japan,” Sugimoto tells The Art Newspaper. “Inspired by this, I decided a Japanese dry-stone wall would serve as a symbolic link between the ancient and the modern, providing the perfect backdrop for the museum’s Modernist sculptures.”
The garden’s opening follows years of controversy. Sugimoto’s early vision for the space was met with criticism. In 2021, Charles A. Birnbaum (the president and chief executive of the Cultural Landscape Foundation) said that the stacked-stone plan “fundamentally disrupts” the garden’s Modernist design and the “artistic intent” of Bunshaft and the landscape architect Lester Collins.
Adjustments to Sugimoto’s initial design were made five years ago, according to the Hirshhorn, after a public consultation process as well as meetings with the National Capital Planning Commission and the Commission of Fine Arts. In 2022, the museum hosted a groundbreaking ceremony with Jill Biden. “I was amazed by the backlash,” Sugimoto said at the time.
Today, Birnbaum stresses that the Hirshhorn’s “landscape architecture is an art form” and urges the museum to “afford it the same curatorial oversight, care and respect as the rest of the material collection”.
A sense of calm
Sugimoto’s practice is meditative, rooted in a close study of the natural world. “There is an 11th-century Japanese garden manual, Sakuteiki, which tells us to ‘listen to the voices of the stones’,” he says. Each stone has its own character, weight and direction. He adds: “My task is not simply to place it, but to discover where it already wants to be; precision comes from listening carefully enough to find that inevitable position.”
This sense of balance is felt throughout the garden. With benches for quiet reflection and shaded, out-of-the-way recesses, the lawns encourage deep focus, an attentiveness to and a delight in the play of forms. “It’s not just about looking at art,” says Aaron Seeto, the Hirshhorn’s deputy director, “but about looking at it as the garden itself is changing.”
Sculpture in the space is arranged chronologically. The east garden includes a cast of Auguste Rodin’s poignant The Burghers of Calais (1884-89), its six figures weighed down and their necks bound in a darkened procession. Nearby is Henri Matisse’s The Backs I-IV (1909-31), a series of abstracted nudes in bronze relief, their angular silhouettes catching the light.
Henry Moore’s King and Queen (1952-53) is one of five works by the artist on view. It depicts a pair of seated figures, their faces abstracted, the curve of their shoulders liquid smooth. “Joseph Hirshhorn was one of Moore’s closest friends and one of the most significant collectors of his work,” says Godfrey Worsdale, the director of the Henry Moore Foundation. (Joseph Hirshhorn owned 55 sculptures by Moore, and Hirshhorn’s fourth marriage took place before a cast of the artist’s Upright Motive No. 1: Glenkiln Cross.) Worsdale applauds the renovated garden for offering “unfettered access to Moore’s work for new generations”.
In the west garden, home to new commissions, stands Yoshitomo Nara’s Sentinels of Stillness series (2025)—three monumental heads, fashioned from aluminium and coated in brilliant white paint. Following the Tōhoku earthquake and nuclear disaster in 2011, Nara found himself unable to paint and instead took to sculpting. The physicality of modelling clay served as a kind of healing for him.
Liz Larner’s 6 (2010-11), meanwhile, is a cuboid of stainless steel in deep ochre, lavender and white—the tendril-like lines seeming to expand and contract as if suspended in air. The work is a kind of “variable in space”, says Larner, who is absorbed by the mathematical concept of x (the unknown). Following in the tradition of the Surrealist artist Meret Oppenheim, Larner explores the indefinable, “the variable of a variable, the changing perspectives that don’t ossify”.
Comparably fluid is Raven Halfmoon’s Dancing at Dusk (2024), a neighbouring work of cream, coppery-red and slate-grey travertine. Halfmoon, a citizen of the Caddo Nation, gestures to violence and strength, pairing the themes in a work of banded-stone—her first in the medium—trimmed with a line of crosses. There is a kind of solemnity to the piece, the composite visage resolute, meeting the world as it is.
That pathos carries over to KAWS’s 14ft bronze SHELTER (2026), reminiscent of a mother and child—their eyes crossed out, their modelling soft, even tender. It is a warm embrace, the two encircled by an overhanging elm tree.
There is a stillness to the Hirshhorn’s new garden space, a sense of calm in the otherwise fast-moving capital city. “I hope people will experience a different sense of time in the garden,” Sugimoto says. “The sculptures, stones, trees, water and the changing light all exist on different clocks. The garden allows us to slow our own clock enough to become aware of these differences.”

https://gothamist.com/news/calif-judge-c.title: Calif. judge cites 'mountain of evidence' ICE racially profiled Latinos, drawing NY notice
https://gothamist.com/news/calif-judge-c.author: Herb Pinder
https://gothamist.com/news/calif-judge-c.text:
New York civil rights activists are applauding a judge’s findings in California that there was “a mountain of evidence” showing Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents racially profiled Latinos in the Los Angeles area, in violation of constitutional protections against unreasonable searches and seizures.
Amy Belsher, director of Immigrants Rights Litigation at the New York Civil Liberties Union, said the findings in the much-watched Central District of California case “confirms that ICE has an unconstitutional policy of stopping people based only on the color of their skin.”
She added, “We don’t live in a ‘show me your papers’ country. That’s why we have challenged that same unlawful policy on behalf of New Yorkers (in court filings) — because the Constitution protects all of us from unlawful stops and detentions.”
U.S. District Court Judge Maame Ewusi-Mensah Frimpong issued a temporary order, dated Oct. 23 and made public on Thursday, barring ICE and other federal officers from stopping people “just because they look Latino or because they look Latino and working class.”
Concluding plaintiffs challenging the arrest "will likely prevail" in the ongoing litigation, the judge issued a temporary order barring the government from enforcing “their policy and practice” of making enforcement stops based on racial stereotyping and which lack the required “individualized, particularized assessment,” based on reasonable suspicion, that the people being stopped are in violation of U.S. immigration law.
The Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to a Gothamist request for comment. The LA Times reported that the Trump administration was appealing the order – a follow up to an earlier directive from the same judge that also sought to rein in ICE agents making enforcement stops in California. That measure was ultimately blocked by the Supreme Court in an emergency order.
The LA Times quoted a Justice Department official who said Frimpong’s new order would hinder immigration enforcement.
Frimpong’s directive applies only in the Central California district, but it addresses longstanding charges brought by immigration advocates and civil rights attorneys across the country that ICE agents, including in New York and New Jersey, have engaged in racial profiling in furtherance of the Trump administration’s mass deportation initiative.
Frimpong concluded the plaintiffs, including immigrants’ rights groups and Latino individuals who were stopped by federal authorities, cited a “mountain of evidence” showing agents “routinely make detentive stops of individuals because those individuals appear Latino or Latino and working class.”
Relying in part on body-worn camera evidence, the judge’s opinion referenced dozens of instances where federal officers “explicitly use apparent Latino race” as a basis of stopping and detaining people, without the officers’ asking or securing any additional information.
The stops included people in a wide range of circumstances: Latinos dressed in work clothes; Latinos present at low-wage job sites, including car washes; and Latinos riding bicycles or driving their children to school. She also cited evidence, in support of her findings, of officers using racial slurs and "dehumanizing language" in referring to those they stopped.
“The Court’s order makes clear that Latino workers have the right to go about their lives without being detained because of the color of their skin,” Lauren Michel Wilfong, staff attorney with the National Day Laborer Organizing Network and co-counsel for the plaintiffs, said in a statement.
Wilfong added, “This win was made possible by the Plaintiffs and dozens of class members who spoke truth to power to expose DHS’s unlawful actions and safeguard our fundamental rights.”

https://jacobin.com/2026/10/trump-netany.title: The Iran War Might Soon Get Catastrophically Worse
https://jacobin.com/2026/10/trump-netany.author: Branko Marcetic
https://jacobin.com/2026/10/trump-netany.text:
The Iran War Might Soon Get Catastrophically Worse
It looks increasingly likely Donald Trump may try a reckless escalatory bombing campaign against Iran after the midterms. And it looks increasingly likely it will backfire terribly.
Between all the action around next week’s midterms and Donald Trump’s meddling in Brazilian politics, it’s easy to forget there’s a war going on. But sure enough, Trump’s war on Iran is still humming in the background, and every indication is that it could flare up in a terrible new way very soon.
According to multiple reports, Trump has been planning a renewed attack on Iran that is likely to be launched after the midterms, though according to the Wall Street Journal, the president had not yet firmly decided whether he’ll go through with it. The renewed attack, the Journal reports, would be a “short, intense war” that would hit Iranian infrastructure, its munition arsenal, and its nuclear sites, or at least that’s what sources have told the US press. Sen. Chris Murphy, who has been briefed on some of the attack plans, has called them “insane” and said they would lead to “the likely destruction of our commitment to the rule of law,” which suggests something potentially broader and even more extreme.
Funnily enough, a month before any of this reporting was published, Quincy Institute Executive Vice President Trita Parsi had predicted to me that Trump was likely to do this, as a way of trying to end the war on his terms. “Trump has come to a space in his mind in which he believes that he has already tried everything. He’s tried diplomacy. He’s tried sanctions. He’s tried limited war,” Parsi said in mid-September.
“The only thing he hasn’t tried is all of those different military threats he issued early on, but never exercised: taking out the desalination plants, taking out Iran’s energy infrastructure, taking one of the islands in the Persian Gulf. I think after the midterms, that is what he’s going to try.”
Trump has, not surprisingly, been egged on in this by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who in the lead-up to the Israeli election this week repeatedly vowed to restart the war against Iran and “overthrow” the remnants of the regime there. But according to the Israeli press, Netanyahu went beyond merely pushing for war: he actively looked to start one with a planned attack on Iran that he was ultimately talked out of. As Netanyahu openly said this week on Twitter/X, he and Israel had a narrow “window of time” to act — specifically, “another two years of Trump to finish the work in Iran.”
Netanyahu’s obvious attempts to spark renewed war with Iran briefly became an election issue in Israel, when one of his opponents announced he had requested a treason investigation into the prime minister over his “pressuring the heads of the security establishment to take steps that could create a miscalculation vis-à-vis Iran,” and trying to “drag the state of Israel into war on the eve of elections.” Netanyahu has a history, especially over the past three years, of using war as a means of keeping himself in power, and it’s not hard to see how a war with Iran — particularly one he could sell as being started by Tehran — could give him a popularity boost.
Netanyahu’s efforts to do this may not have worked out for the moment, but the currently deadlocked Israeli election result, combined with Trump’s preexisting plans to restart the war as soon as a week from now, could give him another shot at it. If Netanyahu’s opposition remains unable to form a government, he will stay on as caretaker prime minister until the next election, by which point a US war with Iran may well have provided a shot in the arm to his far-right coalition.
Playing With Fire
But however “insane” and brutal this latest US bombing campaign turns out to be, it’s unlikely to give Trump what he wants: for Tehran to soften its demands and take a deal that’s worse for them and better for him.
Trump’s actions — including his repeated violation of agreements and diplomatic protocols, and the sneak attack that killed scores of Iranian officials at the start of the war — have thoroughly delegitimized Iran’s moderates and placed the country firmly in the hands of hard-liners who oppose negotiations, and some of whom do things like move to impeach the country’s more pro-diplomacy foreign minister.
These hard-liners believe that any deal Iran strikes with Washington is pointless, because Trump or his successor will just rip it up later regardless. The hard-liners are convinced the only way to ensure both the state’s and the country’s survival is to inflict such costs on the United States and its political leadership that they’ll leave their country alone. They are also, ironically, now looking seriously at actually pursuing a nuclear weapon — a pursuit Iran’s previous supreme leader had, it turns out, been the main roadblock to, until Trump dropped a bomb on his house in February and killed him.
Trump still reportedly hopes that using military force will this time stop Iran from making a bomb. But that idea is likely to run into the same problem as before: namely, that Iran’s buried nuclear sites are basically unreachable, even by the largest bombs the United States can drop on them, so he would need to launch a risky ground operation to extract the enriched material that still wouldn’t be guaranteed of success. Look at how costly the vastly less complicated effort to recover a single pilot in April proved, and you start to get a sense of the difficulty with this idea.
Meanwhile, Iran’s new hard-line leadership is willing to absorb (or more accurately, willing to let the Iranian people take) a tremendous amount of pain to achieve this, as they have demonstrated. Years of preexisting suffering under US sanctions and a rally-’round-the-flag effect that has seen anti-government dissent evaporate means life in Iran is persisting in the face of widespread shortages, nearly 90 percent inflation, and at least $270 billion worth of destroyed infrastructure.
So what would a “short, intense war” on Iran actually do, then? Besides the human toll on ordinary Iranians just trying to live their lives, it would likely mean even worse blowback on everyone else, the United States included.
Like Trump, Iran’s leaders have military cards they haven’t played yet, and they are openly threatening much worse retaliation this time if they’re attacked again. Iranian officials have threatened to make the war “longer and in a wider geographical area,” and to inflict a “devastating impact” on energy markets, aiming to shove the world into outright recession and create a large-scale refugee crisis. Surrounding oil facilities, ports, pipelines, refineries, power grids, and even desalination plants have been mentioned as targets.
This would be devastating for — and in the case of power grids and desalination plants, existentially threatening to — life in the Gulf states, whose economies have already been battered by the war. This is why a host of Iran’s neighbors, including Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey, have been desperately holding talks with Tehran to try to stop what might be the most devastating round of an already regionally destructive war, so far with no tangible results.
But it’s not just Iran’s neighbors who will bear the brunt of this. Iran’s leaders specifically named as targets the undersea cables that carry internet traffic and the trillions of dollars of infrastructure in the region that the US artificial intelligence industry relies on, including data centers. That industry, which Trump is heavily relying on to prop up the US economy, is already showing serious signs of strain in the face of mounting financial losses and growing investor skepticism. Major damage to critical infrastructure and resulting market disruption risks adding further strain on an industry that many already fear is a bubble waiting to pop. In its recent initial public offering prospectus, AI firm Anthropic specifically mentioned the fact that “armed conflict” could damage or destroy data centers and other infrastructure as one of its risk factors, a warning that other industry players have made.
More ominously, a senior Iranian security official has also named “US political targets” as potentially fair game. Recall, too, that Iran is widely believed to be the culprit behind months of cyberattacks on a variety of US infrastructure, including water systems. If either of these is part of Iran’s next retaliatory move, it would not only cause intense chaos and suffering for the US public but potentially trigger a dangerous escalation spiral.
Vice President J. D. Vance has reportedly now reached out to Iran’s hard-line top security chief to resuscitate peace talks. Given everything laid out above, this would be wise.
The Choice Is Clear
The trouble is that the two parties here remain a canyon apart. Iranian leadership views it as effectively suicide to budge from the terms they agreed to earlier this year, while Trump has been led to view those terms as a personal humiliation, so he keeps trying and failing to bomb or blockade his way to a more favorable deal after the fact. There is also the wild card of Netanyahu, who has already more than once tried to single-handedly torpedo a Trump-Iran deal by bombing Lebanon and violating one of Iran’s core demands.
The White House now is certain that Iran is on the brink of capitulation, and all it will take is one more push to get it there. In reality, Trump is dealing with an Iran that is more dangerous and less likely to capitulate than ever: not because it has a nuke, but because years of Trump’s own foolish policy choices have turned it into an adversary that sees itself as having nothing to lose — and is acting like it, which is why Iranian leaders are effetively threatening that if they go down, they will take the entire region as well as the global economy with them.
Trump and the people around him are looking at next week’s midterms as the moment they will be unshackled from political constraints, freeing them to take the reckless, escalatory measures they were reluctant to take before for fear of voter backlash. If they were smart, they would treat it as freeing them instead to take the deal they had already agreed to, and to just swallow the inevitable political point-scoring and cries of “capitulation” that are, sadly, now just standard whenever any president tries to end a war.
But it is clear that there is a dearth of voices around the president that are inclined to tell him this. It is increasingly likely that Trump soon takes a step that will prove even more terrible for the country, for his political party, and his own legacy.

https://gothamist.com/news/nypd-says-bro.title: Bronx e-bike fire that killed a boy has claimed 3 more lives, NYPD says
https://gothamist.com/news/nypd-says-bro.author: Amanda Rozon
https://gothamist.com/news/nypd-says-bro.text:
The death toll from a deadly e-bike fire continues to rise, police said, after two teenage boys and an adult woman have now died alongside Zion Maine, the boy killed earlier this week in his family’s Bronx apartment.
Fire officials said the battery on an e-bike ignited just before 1 a.m. Wednesday in the kitchen of the family’s 11th-floor apartment. The bike was stored near the front door and blocked the family’s exit.
Maine died at a nearby hospital, city officials said. His father, Courtney Maine, 37, was in stable condition Saturday. The three others hospitalized were Maine’s two sons and his partner Syida Adams, but police did not confirm their identities Saturday.
Tayesha Aiken, 41, has lived in the Patterson Houses, a public housing complex in Mott Haven, for a decade. She said Zion was “loved in the community.”
“Praying and crying is all I’ve been doing,:” she said earlier this week. “I think that’s all we really can do at this point is pray.”
Carol Chen contributed reporting.

https://gothamist.com/news/donald-trump-.title: Donald Trump looms over New York attorney general’s race
https://gothamist.com/news/donald-trump-.author: Jon Campbell, Walter Wuthmann
https://gothamist.com/news/donald-trump-.text:
Few people have gotten under President Donald Trump’s skin quite the way New York Attorney General Letitia James has.
The Democratic attorney general has long been one of the president’s chief antagonists, suing the Republican’s administration more than 80 times since she took office in 2018 while becoming a frequent target of his ire on social media and at rallies.
Now, James has made her battles with Trump a central part of her campaign to win another four years in office.
“As I travel all throughout the state of New York and even the country, individuals thank me for standing up and protecting the interest of New Yorkers,” James said in an interview with Gothamist. “They thank me for recognizing that no one is above the law and that we do not bow to kings.”
But if she’s to win on Tuesday, she’ll have to overcome a challenge from Republican Saritha Komatireddy, a former federal prosecutor who has accused James of being “obsessed with national politics” and politicizing an office that should remain apolitical.
James, the former New York City public advocate who previously served as a city councilmember from Brooklyn, first rose to the attorney general’s office in the middle of Trump’s first term in 2018.
Since then, she has become a legal thorn in the president’s side.
Her lawsuits against the Trump administration — often leading a coalition of Democratic attorneys general from other states — have targeted the president’s actions on everything from immigration enforcement to Medicaid funding to housing grants.
She’s also targeted the president’s business, winning a civil fraud judgement against the Trump administration in 2023 that found it engaged in a scheme to inflate the value of its real-estate holdings to obtain better rates on loans.
But the fraud judgement ultimately became a mixed bag for James. It initially came with a $500 million disgorgement penalty, which a mid-level appeals court later threw out in its entirety. The case remains tied up in the Court of Appeals, the state’s highest court.
Trump’s Department of Justice, meanwhile, tried to prosecute James for alleged mortgage fraud on a home occupied by a family member in Virginia. A court threw out the indictment.
James said her legal clashes with Trump are a sign that she’s willing to take on powerful people when their interests clash with those of New Yorkers. She said voters have responded warmly to her legal battles with Trump.
Komatireddy, meanwhile, has tried to keep the focus of her campaign on James, not the president.
The Republican has said she voted for Trump but has emphasized that she worked in the U.S. Attorney’s Office for New York’s Eastern District under three presidents — Trump, Barack Obama and Joe Biden. She also served as chief of staff to the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration under Biden.
“I've always protected New York and protected Americans by working with Democrats and Republicans and for Democrats and Republicans,” Komatireddy said in an interview with Gothamist. “I have no problem doing that. Not everything has to be partisan.”
Komatiredddy said she would reorganize the attorney general’s office to have more of a focus on crime and fraud — two areas where she says James has been lacking.
“ This is just about having competent government,” she said. “People are tired of elected officials using the office for their own personal benefit instead of the benefit of New Yorkers, and I'm actually here to make New Yorkers' lives better for all of us.”
Komatireddy has experienced a fundraising bump following her lone debate with James earlier this month, when the Republican’s aggressive, direct critiques of James landed several clips that bounced around certain corners of the internet. Those clips were further boosted by Trump, who praised Komatireddy’s performance on his Truth Social platform without mentioning her by name.
In the 11 days following the debate, Komitareddy raised about $500,000, not counting public matching funds. In the three months prior to that, she raised about $700,000, according to state disclosure records.
“I'm walking down the road in [the New York City Columbus Day] parade and people are reaching out to shake my hand, shouting out saying, ‘You did a great job. I'm voting for you,'” Komatireddy said. “Someone came up to me and said, ‘Can I donate to your campaign?’”
James, meanwhile, says Komatireddy’s focus on street crime shows a fundamental misunderstanding of the job.
The attorney general’s office has traditionally focused on civil issues, not local crimes. Under James, that has included work obtaining financial settlements from opioid manufacturers and distributors for their role in the opioid crisis, as well as from Facebook and Instagram parent company Meta to settle claims that they intentionally got kids hooked on the social-media platforms.
Local district attorneys, on the other hand, are generally charged with prosecuting crimes like assault, theft and drug trafficking.
“If she's interested in being a district attorney, I would urge her to pick one district attorney — there are 62 of them — and run against them,” James said.
Some legal experts are skeptical of Komatireddy’s pitch to use the attorney general’s office to prosecute more street crime, too.
“You really do need local knowledge and experience in order to do that brand of policing and that brand of prosecuting,” said Steven Wasserman, a longtime criminal defense attorney who teaches at John Jay College of Criminal Justice. “This is not a great idea.”
Ben Max, the program director at New York Law School's Center for New York City and State Law, said Komatireddy would have some “leeway” to follow through on her campaign promise if she were to be elected.
Max said Komatireddy could target organized crime that crosses jurisdictional boundaries. The attorney general can also follow up on referrals from state agencies and the governor’s office.
Regardless of its feasibility, Max argued Komatireddy’s creative pitch and disciplined messaging have propelled her from relative obscurity.
“She has undoubtedly made something of a name for herself coming out of nowhere in this race,” he said.
The early voting period runs through Sunday in New York. Election Day is Tuesday.

https://gothamist.com/news/how-formerly-.title: How formerly homeless New Yorkers are helping others get off the streets
https://gothamist.com/news/how-formerly-.author: Karen Yi
https://gothamist.com/news/how-formerly-.text:
Outreach worker Felipe Ramos said one of the hardest parts of his job is seeing himself in those he helps: the people sleeping on New York City's streets.
Ramos has also cycled through homelessness, incarceration and a history of mental illness. But he said his past is now his superpower as he crisscrosses Manhattan every day, trying to get New Yorkers to come inside.
“We can say to our clients, ‘Hey, I know exactly what you're feeling. … I'm actually going to feel it with you in this moment, and then when you're ready, we're going to come up with a detailed plan to get you out of this feeling,’” he said.
“It's probably the most genuine form of connection that we can build.”
Ramos is part of the Neighborhood Navigators program, started by the Manhattan district attorney’s office to bring street homeless New Yorkers inside and prevent them from entering the criminal justice system. The Mamdani administration this year awarded the program $1.25 million in funding as it develops a citywide plan to combat homelessness.
It’s part of a growing citywide effort to interrupt the cycle of New Yorkers moving between the street, the hospital and the shelter system. Nearly 5,000 people slept in parks, subway stations or the street this year — the highest number recorded in more than a decade.
“It’s far more powerful to get people who have walked in these shoes,” Manhattan DA Alvin Bragg told Gothamist. “And recognize the significance of what that individual engagement means to them because they know what it meant to them.”
The city’s street outreach system can be uncoordinated, leaving groups working in silos or overwhelming the very people they’re trying to help, advocates said. It’s why elected leaders and other stakeholders are calling on the city to streamline its approach and double down on programs that show results.
Bragg said the Neighborhood Navigators approach is different because it hires workers with similar experiences to form closer relationships with chronically homeless people and because of the amount of time workers spend with those they help, including accompanying them to appointments or doctor’s offices.
“Instead of, ‘What's wrong with you?’ We ask, ‘What happened to you?’” said Rocio Santos, program director of the Neighborhood Navigators.
“Looking them in their face, taking the time to [say], ‘Hey, how are you? We noticed you don't have shoes. Is there anything that we can support you with?’”
Bragg said his office decided to start its own street outreach program after realizing people were falling through the cracks between various providers and city agencies. He said he ultimately wants to prevent people from ever landing in court.
The DA’s office hired nonprofit The Bridge to implement the program in certain neighborhoods in 2024, using forfeiture funds. More than 175 people have been placed in housing since.
“Sometimes the navigators will be with someone for an entire day, just making sure that they get into their housing placement or to an inpatient substance use treatment program,” said Lauren Curatolo, a deputy division chief at the Manhattan DA's office.
The program works in certain areas of the city including Central and East Harlem; Chinatown and the Lower East Side; Washington Heights and Inwood; and Midtown West, Hell's Kitchen and Chelsea.
Barbara Blair, president of the Garment District Alliance, said the Neighborhood Navigators “do a good job of following people” from point A to point B. She said the business improvement district also hired the navigators to perform outreach in the area.
“I don't want you dumping someone off at the hospital and then you don't hear from them again, you don't see them again until they're back on the street,” Blair said.
In one case, the Neighborhood Navigators helped a 58-year-old Harlem man get his public benefits reinstated, staying with him at the city’s benefits office all day. In another case, they were able to connect a 67-year-old living in Lower Manhattan to a supportive housing unit in less than three weeks. The man also received a psychiatric evaluation and medication to remain stable.
Ramos said the Neighborhood Navigators have a good reputation among people living on the street and that helps them make inroads. So if they say they’ll pick someone up from the hospital at 6 a.m., they’ll be there at 6 a.m.
“Recovery isn't comfortable, but it's attainable. So being willing to listen to them and being able to hold their hand through the hard parts is what'll continue to make things systematically better,” he said.
The group does not have access to the city’s database of engagements between outreach workers and homeless people. Only providers contracted by the Department of Homeless Services do, and that can make collaboration with other groups difficult.
But the Navigators said they create networks in each neighborhood. They know whom they can lean on for substance abuse programs, shelter, medical care or mental health.
“ We brought the personal back into this type of work,” said Santos. “We're able to pick up the phone at any given point and reach those individuals that could support and help our clients.”

https://jacobin.com/2026/10/trump-gop-mi.title: Preparing for MAGA’s Worst on Election Day
https://jacobin.com/2026/10/trump-gop-mi.author: Stephanie Luce
https://jacobin.com/2026/10/trump-gop-mi.text:
Preparing for MAGA’s Worst on Election Day
Donald Trump and the GOP are wildly unpopular going into the midterms, but they have few scruples about interfering in election results. Leftists should be prepared to operate in a broad front with liberals and others to stop that from happening.
Imagine this: Election Day comes and goes. Democrats turn out big and flip a few seats, some by close margins. Forces opposing the increasingly authoritarian drift of the United States breathe a sigh of relief.
Before the results are even called, however, Donald Trump declares in a wave of Truth Social posts that Democrats have cheated, the results are fraudulent, and those responsible will be prosecuted and persecuted. By the next day, the claims have spread to congressional Republicans, who vow to seek justice — and, in some cases, vengeance — for the supposed voter fraud.
Protesters take to the streets in several cities, demanding that all votes be counted. They call on their representatives to stand behind voters’ democratic wishes. The protests spread, and on November 6, Trump claims that protesters in several cities have gotten out of hand and broken windows. He then declares that Iran has engaged in cyber election interference, thereby invalidating the results of the vote. Trump announces he will send in the National Guard and invoke the Insurrection Act to defend the country against these incursions.
Is this scenario likely? It’s hard to say. The midterms are shaping up to be a rout of the Republicans, with Trump and his party facing nearly unprecedented unfavorability and losses so great that even his normal bluster and lies about stolen elections won’t be able to hold his diminishing base. In Brazil this week, Flávio Bolsonaro floated a Trumpian trial balloon by claiming the presidential election was stolen by the Workers’ Party’s Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, but the nearly 4.5-million-vote margin that Lula won by made such mendacity absurd, and Bolsonaro has since fled the country for Miami.
But given the antidemocratic drift of the United States over the past decade and since Trump’s second election in particular, this scenario is far from impossible. Indeed, parts of it, like Trump’s denial of the election results, seem all but assured. And as the president feels his mandate in the country (and perhaps his own mental health) slipping away, who knows what a newly desperate Trump will do.
He would not be alone in taking such steps. Scholars who study authoritarianism call them an “authoritarian playbook”: a set of similar steps leaders like Flávio Bolsonaro’s former president father Jair, former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán in Hungary, and Recep Tayyip Erdoğan in Turkey have taken to consolidate power. It includes going after critics through investigations and harassment, installing loyalists, expanding federal powers, crushing dissent, and deploying military forces on their own citizens.
The Trump administration has been moving through the playbook at record speed, from firing federal workers to Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) shootings to the attacks on Rep. Ilhan Omar. Unions, community and faith organizations, immigrant rights groups, and lawyers have resisted and slowed the attacks, but that hasn’t stopped Trump. His administration has already taken steps to undermine the 2026 midterm elections, attempting to restrict mail ballots, purge voter rolls, and mess with ballots in Alaska. They plan to send ICE to the polls. And Rep. Tim Burchett (R-TN) has announced plans to try to block the seating of democratic socialist Darializa Avila Chevalier, the likely next House member from New York’s Thirteenth District, while MAGA is building the legal case to do exactly that.
The task for socialists is not to vote and defend elections in order to return to the status quo, but to defend basic democratic norms while putting forth a vision of a different future. Lots of people care about elections and will be looking for answers if things go wrong. Socialists cannot sit on the sidelines. We need to challenge racist gerrymandering and minoritarian institutions like the Supreme Court and Senate to weaken the stranglehold of the authoritarian right on the federal government in order to have the opportunity to advance reforms that can establish new social and economic rights. Attacks on elections are tied to attacks on our rights to organize and protest, our rights to independent media, and our rights to engage in the democratic institutions we fought hard to create.
And for a growing share of the socialist movement, contesting for governing power via elections is a key part of the strategy. The Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) are set to send seven, and potentially as many as ten, members to Congress; their strategy depends on fair elections that get those members seated so they can build a bloc that pushes for transformative demands.
We can’t develop a full plan ahead of time, but we can develop our planning skills under crisis. National organizations and some unions have already been training people on potential election scenarios through versions of “tabletop exercises” where organizers role-play different scenarios and develop strategy and tactics together. The more we practice, the easier it might be to respond when a crisis hits.
One possible scenario to come out of next week’s election is a state of confusion, where vote counting is challenged or stopped in a state or two, and courts are going back and forth about what to do. This would be similar to what happened in 2000, when the initial presidential vote count in Florida showed George W. Bush beating Al Gore by only 1,784 votes. Gore called for a recount in some counties, including Miami-Dade. Republican operatives moved quickly to send in staffers to protest outside the recount, eventually rushing the doors and attacking people, resulting in the recount being called off. After more back-and-forth, the case went to the Supreme Court, which called for an end to the recount.
Rather than protesting, Democratic Party leaders, including Gore (who would have won in a full recount), accepted the loss. This time around, we need to be ready to respond to ballot and legal confusion without waiting for courts to decide.
If we have another Florida-type scenario, such as Republican operatives refusing to count all the ballots in Texas, then socialists and all our allies need to be ready to fight back. People around the country, whether in blue, red, or purple states, can fill the streets and pressure their representatives, especially Democrats, to demand that every vote is counted. Legal observers and traditional election groups are working to protect voter registration, ensure access to polls, and prepare legal challenges. No Kings will be ready to call for mass peaceful marches. May Day Strong is preparing for economic disruption if needed, examining how people can undermine the corporate pillars that are supporting Trump’s authoritarianism.
There are billionaires and corporations directly profiting from surveillance, ICE contracts, war, and deregulation: they have a material interest in Trump’s success. Some billionaires, such as Peter Thiel and Elon Musk, go beyond that and have an ideological commitment to authoritarianism of various forms. Using the full toolbox of boycotts, sit-ins, slowdowns, walkouts, and strikes, how can we best target the billionaires and corporations who are enabling and profiting from authoritarianism, like Amazon and Jeff Bezos, and how can we encourage others, like Jamie Dimon at JPMorgan Chase and Delta Air Lines, to defect from the authoritarian coalition by making it too costly to stay?
A Broad Front
Working in a broad front, a wide range of political actors who may oppose Trump’s antidemocratic measures but disagree with us on most everything else, to defeat authoritarianism can be simple on the one hand, because there is one unifying task: build the biggest “we” possible to defeat MAGA. But broad front politics get complicated fast. It means working with mainstream Democrats who often seem more intent on destroying DSA than MAGA. It might mean working with anti-Trump Republicans, who see socialists as the second-biggest threat after authoritarians. And it requires being in alignment with a whole host of organizations that can be annoying or disruptive or way too verbose.
Working in a broad front requires patience, education, and skill. But it also opens up the space to work with millions of people who are newly engaged by the real threat MAGA poses to their lives or jobs.
As Ash-Lee Henderson reminds us, 89 million people didn’t vote in 2024. People are angry about the cost of living, and many want and need big changes, from Medicare for All to reliable transit to an end to war. The Democratic Party has made little to no effort to acknowledge these 89 million and their frustrations, leaving the job to socialists or right-wing extremists.
To stay anchored in a broad front, socialists need nested strategies: a short-term strategy to block the authoritarian right and a longer-term strategy to build the Left. We can do that by emphasizing the capacities we need to build no matter the task: democratic participation, mass training and education on the issues that matter, door-knocking and talking with coworkers, organizing unions and mapping workplaces. We’ll need these skills to defend the midterm results; if we can do them well, we’ll connect with thousands of new people joining the fight — and be in stronger shape to shift from defense to offense.
Since the start of the second Trump administration, many unions, DSA chapters, and community organizations have had to develop the ability for rapid response against the federal government’s attacks on our neighbors. We have called protests against federal workforce union busting, developed mutual aid networks to support immigrants, and trained ourselves in direct action.
By getting more organized at a block-by-block level, we can prepare for the possibility of Republicans seriously contesting the results of our elections and make sure we are ready to organize more workers who know that we need a real voice not just in our workplaces but in our political system too. Building these muscles puts us in better shape for actions in 2028, including influencing the presidential primaries and election, and a potential May 1, 2028, national strike.
Our tasks: Vote. Get trained on noncooperation and strike readiness. Sign a pledge to defend the elections through targeted actions on corporations and elected officials. If things get messy, be ready to help coworkers and neighbors make sense of the moment and invite them into the organizations that are fighting for a better world.

https://citylimits.org/en-harlem-residen.title: En Harlem, residentes de vivienda pública van de puerta en puerta con la candidata al Congreso Avila Chevalier
https://citylimits.org/en-harlem-residen.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/en-harlem-residen.text:
Share This Article
“Hay mucho por hacer en nuestra comunidad”, afirmó Barbara Williams, una activista de 78 años y residente de las torres Polo Grounds de NYCHA. La candidata de la DSA, Avila Chevalier, que en junio desbancó al veterano titular del distrito, “parece ser esa persona, por lo que dice y por lo que he leído sobre ella, que va a estar a la altura”.
Este artículo se publicó originalmente en inglés el 29 de octubre. Traducido por Daniel Parra. Read the English version here.
Este reportaje se produjo en colaboración con Factchequeado.
Barbara Williams, una activista comunitaria de 78 años y residente de vivienda pública en las torres Polo Grounds en Harlem, pasó la tarde del sábado llamando a las puertas de sus vecinos junto a la candidata al Congreso Darializa Avila Chevalier, que se perfila como ganadora en la carrera por representar al distrito 13 de Nueva York.
Avila Chevalier, una socialista demócrata respaldada por el alcalde Zohran Mamdani, logró una importante victoria política al ganar las elecciones primarias de junio (y desbancar al representante Adriano Espaillat, que llevaba cinco mandatos en el cargo y fue el primer dominicano-estadounidense en formar parte de la Cámara de Representantes de Estados Unidos).
Se enfrentará al candidato republicano Jomo Manuel Williams en las elecciones generales de la próxima semana (la votación anticipada ya está en marcha). Manuel Williams, que se presentó a las elecciones al Concejo Municipal en 2021 y a la presidencia en 2008, no respondió a los intentos de City Limits por ponerse en contacto con él.
“Hoy estoy aquí para asegurarme de que los residentes estén inscritos en el censo electoral”, declaró a City Limits lla activista Williams, quien reside en Polo Grounds Towers desde 1988.
Desde hace más de una década, forma parte de Community Voices Heard Power (CVHP, por sus siglas en inglés), un grupo de defensa política que impulsa políticas que promueven la justicia racial y económica y respalda a candidatos que hagan lo mismo.
El grupo, que colabora estrechamente con los residentes y los líderes de los inquilinos de la Autoridad de la Vivienda de Nueva York (NYCHA), anunció su apoyo a Avila Chevalier para representar al distrito, que incluye Harlem, Hamilton Heights, Washington Heights y zonas del noroeste del Bronx.
Según los datos del censo, la mitad de los residentes del distrito se identifican como hispanos y casi una cuarta parte son negros.
Williams, junto con unos 50 residentes de vivienda pública y miembros de la comunidad, se reunieron en las torres Polo Grounds con Avila Chevalier para un acto de “movilización electoral” organizado por CVHP el sábado 24 de octubre, que era el último día en que los neoyorquinos podían inscribirse para votar en las elecciones generales del 3 de noviembre.
Allí, Avila Chevalier habló con los residentes sobre sus ideas para preservar la vivienda pública y también visitó sus hogares para conocer los problemas cotidianos a los que se enfrentan diversos problemas de deterioro causados por el atraso en el mantenimiento de la Autoridad de la Vivienda de Nueva York (NYCHA), que asciende a 78.000 millones de dólares.
“Hay mucho por hacer en nuestra comunidad”, afirmó Williams, y añadió que Avila Chevalier “parece ser esa persona, por lo que dice y por lo que he leído sobre ella, que va a estar a la altura”.
Una de las primeras viviendas que visitó Avila Chevalier pertenecía a Mary Andrews, una residente de 82 años que mostró unas baldosas desconchadas, placas de yeso dañadas y grietas manchadas de moho en el techo de su cuarto de baño. Andrews, que contó que había sufrido recientemente un ictus, está preocupada por la inhalación de moho y por la lentitud con la que se realizan las reparaciones.
Otra residente describió problemas recurrentes de fontanería, entre los que se incluye que su bañera se inunde de agua.
“A menudo hablamos de estos problemas estructurales de forma muy abstracta, pero cuando se les añade la historia de una persona, la situación se vuelve más urgente”, declaró Avila Chevalier a City Limits.
“Para poder defender esta problemática en el Congreso, para mí es importante poder decir que conocí a la señora Andrews y que ella me mostró el estado de su cuarto de baño”, afirmó. “Para las personas que viven con las consecuencias de esto día tras día, ya es urgente, y eso debe reflejarse en las instituciones que tienen el poder de cambiar las cosas”.
A la hora de otorgar su respaldo, los dirigentes de CVHP afirman que buscan candidatos que den prioridad a la vivienda y a las comunidades con bajos ingresos. La organización ofrece apoyo político, formación y respaldo a candidatos de la ciudad de Nueva York, Westchester y dos condados del valle del Hudson.
En esta campaña electoral, el grupo invitó a más de 50 candidatos de 25 circunscripciones a solicitar su respaldo y, entre ellos, el grupo respaldó a seis candidatos para las elecciones generales.
En la ciudad, esos candidatos son Avila Chevalier, la exconcejala Diana Ayala, que se presenta para representar al Distrito 68 de la Asamblea en East Harlem, y Grace Lee, una diputada que se presenta al Senado estatal para representar al Distrito 27 del Bajo Manhattan.
CVHP tiene en cuenta varios factores antes de otorgar su respaldo, según la directora ejecutiva del grupo, Juanita Lewis. Entre ellos se incluyen las estrategias de los candidatos para involucrar a la comunidad, así como su capacidad para ser elegidos y su disposición a colaborar en políticas que apoyen a las comunidades de bajos ingresos y a la clase trabajadora.
También se incluyen entrevistas presenciales entre los candidatos y el personal de CVHP —“gente que hace preguntas difíciles”, señaló Lewis—.
Se evalúa cómo piensan los candidatos convencer a sus colegas del Congreso para que apoyen leyes que beneficien a los residentes de viviendas públicas —especialmente en la ciudad de Nueva York, que cuenta con el mayor número de viviendas públicas del país— y qué grado de conocimiento tienen sobre la financiación de su campaña.
“Todos nuestros miembros han pasado por la experiencia de estar a uno o dos sueldos de preguntarse cómo van a pagar el alquiler”, dijo Lewis. “Queremos entrar en el aspecto político. Esa es la razón principal por la que queríamos que ocuparas ese cargo”.
Lewis afirmó que los miembros del grupo se identificaron especialmente con el enfoque de Avila Chevalier en la preservación de la vivienda pública, la financiación de reparaciones urgentes y la mejora de la seguridad de la comunidad.
Uno de esos miembros es Darique Warren, quien se mudó a las Torres Polo Grounds en 1999, cuando tenía 11 años. Según contó, en aquel momento los residentes estaban orgullosos del edificio, pero a medida que las condiciones se deterioraban, observó cómo sus vecinos se iban desanimando. Mencionó problemas como los intercomunicadores y las puertas rotas, entre otros aspectos relacionados con la seguridad.
“Hoy en día, lo principal es animar a la gente a votar y recordarles por qué es importante”, declaró Warren a City Limits. “Queremos acudir a los políticos y no limitarnos a decir que lo estamos pasando mal, sino pedirles que, por favor, hagan esto, aquello y lo otro por nosotros”.
Warren afirmó que le atraen las ideas de Avila Chevalier para financiar NYCHA, entre las que se incluye el apoyo a la Ley del Nuevo Pacto Verde para la Vivienda Pública (Green New Deal for Public Housing Act), que invertiría hasta 234.000 millones de dólares en un plazo de 10 años para convertir todo el conjunto de viviendas públicas del país en viviendas con cero emisiones de carbono. La ley fue propuesta por la diputada Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (Nueva York), la diputada Delia Ramírez (Illinois) y el senador Bernie Sanders (Vermont), y el actual diputado Espaillat también es copatrocinador de la legislación.
Avila Chevalier se opone a los esfuerzos de NYCHA por convertir sus propiedades al programa de la Sección 8, incorporando a empresas de gestión privadas para que se hagan cargo de la gestión de las urbanizaciones, al tiempo que se financian reparaciones de gran envergadura, incluyendo fondos a los que la autoridad de vivienda no puede acceder por sí misma.
“Ella ha mencionado el uso de fondos estatales y municipales, la conservación de las viviendas y la colaboración con coaliciones como las voces de sus electores”, dijo Warren. “Tenemos la intención de mantener una relación positiva con ella y su equipo, y lo veo como algo recíproco.”
Para otros miembros de la CVHP, Lewis explicó que “la cuestión más importante que se planteó en torno a la vivienda pública para nuestra gente gira en torno a su protección y conservación, y cómo se llevaría a cabo”.
“Si afirmas que la vivienda es una parte importante de tu programa, no puedes olvidarte de este enorme conjunto de viviendas”, señaló Lewis refiriéndose a NYCHA.
“La vivienda pública es el hogar de trabajadores, cuidadores y personas que hacen funcionar la ciudad y el país”, añadió. “Es hora de que surja una nueva historia y una nueva narrativa en torno a la vivienda pública”.
Lewis también señaló que “el entusiasmo de Avila Chevalier por querer venir a llamar a las puertas con nosotros en las viviendas públicas, y acudir a los encuentros con los ciudadanos para escuchar las opiniones de la gente sobre la vivienda pública, son algunas formas interesantes en las que podría convertirse en una defensora de la vivienda pública en el Congreso”.
Los residentes de las Torres Polo Grounds reconocieron y expresaron su apoyo a Avila Chevalier mientras recorría los pasillos llamando a las puertas, y ella describió esos momentos como “realmente surrealistas”.
“Hay mucho entusiasmo”, declaró a City Limits. “Durante gran parte de la campaña estás con la cabeza agachada trabajando, y luego llegan esos momentos en los que te das cuenta de que estamos abriéndonos paso y de que estamos construyendo el poder colectivo necesario para luchar en el Congreso”.

https://www.propublica.org/article/snap-.title: After Millions in Stolen SNAP Benefits, Trump Administration Moves to Fight Theft
https://www.propublica.org/article/snap-.author: Eli Hager
https://www.propublica.org/article/snap-.text:
The Trump administration this week announced an overhaul of the nation’s food stamp payment system, aimed at modernizing benefit cards to protect families from electronic theft. The move comes a week after ProPublica published an investigation showing how $470 million in Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, benefits were stolen from recipients last year alone, in large part because these cards are technologically outdated.
ProPublica’s story highlighted victims’ experiences and examined repeated failures by Congress and the U.S. Department of Agriculture to upgrade Electronic Benefits Transfer, or EBT, cards nationally. ProPublica’s reporting was shared around the department, according to two USDA officials.
The new proposed rule, officially issued by the USDA’s Food and Nutrition Administration on Friday, has been in the works since 2023 — but it was continually delayed until now. Reasons included understaffing at the USDA, especially in the wake of the Department of Government Efficiency’s cuts last year, and a backlog of other regulations that the White House budget office had prioritized. White House and USDA officials did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the sudden shift.
Read More
The rule will mandate that all 50 states transition from EBT cards with just a magnetic stripe on the back — which are easy for criminals to skim data from — to ones with digital microchips, which credit and debit cards have had for more than a decade, and tap-to-pay technology. Other changes include creating new federal “SNAP EBT Operating Standards” to be revised on an ongoing basis, so that the feds and states together can do a better job of keeping up with best practices in the credit card industry and the changing tactics of fraudsters.
A handful of states have already transitioned to chip cards on their own, including California, where the theft of SNAP and other public benefits was reduced by 83% in two years after the technology was adopted. But more than 40 states haven’t added chips, and hundreds of thousands of lower-income Americans continue to show up at grocery store checkout lines only to find that their food assistance for the month has been drained by thieves. NPR and other news outlets have also recently reported on this crisis.
Members of the public, including state SNAP administrators and grocery store owners who may have logistical questions about how to overhaul their EBT systems, now have 60 days to submit comments on the new USDA regulation; these will be reviewed by agency officials before the rule is formally enacted. After that, states will have two years to switch to chip cards, although their ability to meet that deadline will depend on several factors. For one, many are budget-strapped right now, due in large part to the fact that President Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act slashed states’ funding for administering their SNAP programs — dollars that they could have used to upgrade their EBT systems and print and mail out the new cards.
Multiple current and former FNA officials, as well as state program administrators, told ProPublica that they are worried the agency is mandating expensive changes for states but that Congress so far has shown little sign it will provide federal funding for the chip card transition. As ProPublica reported last week, the Senate’s version of this year’s Farm Bill includes money for this purpose, but the House version does not; Democrats and Republicans remain at loggerheads about overall SNAP spending, and it is unclear what will happen. The estimated total federal and state cost of the changes is $283 million, as compared with the more than $600 million in SNAP and other benefits that are stolen from existing cards every year.
Still, the mandate that all states implement chip EBT cards “is a big deal for low-income households,” said Justin King, a longtime safety net advocate who is now the policy director for Propel, a company that helps SNAP recipients access their benefit information. He added that he was “legit surprised” by the administration’s decision.
“Theft rings don’t care about state lines. You’re just squeezing a balloon if you update one state at a time,” King said of the prospect of individual states continuing to gradually adopt chip cards without a federal requirement. “A national standard means there’s nowhere left to go” for the criminals, he said.
For the moment, at least, there are signs that the Trump administration’s posture toward this issue has shifted more broadly. On Wednesday, while barnstorming in Ohio for Republican candidates, Vice President JD Vance (whose roles include serving as the administration’s “fraud czar”) called a press conference and made a point of emphasizing that low-income families are often the victims of SNAP fraud.
This was at odds with how Vance has portrayed the problem in the past. “There are people who have Lamborghinis who currently receive SNAP benefits,” he has previously said, in a typical comment. For ProPublica’s previous article, research reporter Gabriel Sandoval reviewed dozens of speeches, social media posts and press accounts of statements made by Vance and other Trump officials, and found that they have consistently portrayed SNAP recipients as the perpetrators of fraud.
Vance also took a startlingly different tone this week toward the food stamp program itself. In his 2016 memoir “Hillbilly Elegy,” which first propelled him to fame, he wrote that SNAP recipients in Kentucky and Ohio “live off of government largesse”; he said that people in that part of the country are largely “hardworking, except of course for the many food stamp recipients who show little interest in honest work.”
But this week from the stage in southern Ohio, he said, “Step back for a minute and realize that the [SNAP] program is one of the most important social service programs that we have in the United States of America.” He went on at length: Food stamps ensure that “all of our fellow citizens, particularly children, are able to have a full belly at the end of every single night, that regardless of whether they can pay for a meal, we don’t let American children and American families go hungry. That is one of the most important and sacred things that our tax dollars go to.”
The White House and Vance’s press office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on his rhetorical about-face.
Vance then had Attorney General Todd Blanche and other top officials give more details on multiple recent SNAP theft prosecutions. These included several ongoing EBT card skimming cases in Oregon in which criminal groups had allegedly pilfered the SNAP account numbers and PINs of legitimate beneficiaries and then used that data to buy bulk quantities of goods like energy drinks and baby formula — which the scammers resold for over $3 million. This is exactly the type of case that ProPublica reported on last week.
“The simple reality is that it is actually a very tough thing to go through a [grocery store checkout] line with kids,” Vance said. “To present that card, to expect to be able to take that food home to your family, to be able to cook it and provide a meal for your kids, and to be told that because of the theft of a fraudster, that you are being rejected. And there are hundreds of thousands of families all across our country, all across the state of Ohio who have had that experience.”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.title: The name of a 3,500-year-old Egyptian dog depicted in a tomb painting has been revealed—and it has a unique link to the god Anubis
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.author: Garry Shaw
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.text:
A researcher has identified the previously unknown name of an Ancient Egyptian dog, painted in the tomb of a noble 3,500 years ago. The name, Duaty, is the first to feature an epithet of the canine-headed god Anubis, raising fresh questions about the role of dogs in Ancient Egyptian society.
“The name is entirely unique among the known corpus of dog names from Egypt,” the archaeologist Chelsea Kaufman of Johns Hopkins University, United States, tells The Art Newspaper. “We only know about 100 dog names from Egypt, several of which are duplicates, but Duaty is entirely new.”
The tomb, located in a necropolis at Luxor, 500km south of Cairo, had previously been investigated by Egyptologists, but the dog’s name, Duaty, couldn’t be read without modern digital imaging software.
Ancient artisans painted three dogs in User’s tomb. Each wears a collar and sits upright beneath User’s chair. Egyptologists had already read the names of two of these dogs: one was Kenii, “Strong One” and the other was Maaty, which means “Trusty”. But the third remained anonymous.
When re-examining photographs of this tomb scene, Kaufman noticed that there was a faint painted inscription above the third dog’s head. She then used digital imaging software to enhance the blue pigment in these faded hieroglyphs, which made it possible to read the name more clearly.
Kaufman’s investigation, published in The Journal of Egyptian Archaeology, revealed that the dog’s name, which means “He-of-the-Underworld”. This is usually an epithet of Anubis, a god associated with the dead and funerary rituals.
“The significance of the name remains an open question,” Kaufman says. “It’s tempting to interpret it as a direct reference to Anubis, but we just can’t be certain this was the intention. It is worth considering that the name alludes to the dog having already died by the time the tomb was painted, but of course this remains speculation.” The dog’s painted presence and name meant, however, that he would survive after death, and enjoy the food and drink that Egyptians offered to the dead in the tomb.
Duaty also differs from the other dogs in the tomb, and every other dog in Egyptian art, by his unique coat pattern, which is red and rippled—intriguingly similar to the clothing worn by User above.
Speaking to The Art Newspaper, the Egyptologist Salima Ikram, who was not involved in the study, says of the discovery: “Pets, particularly dogs, are often shown in Egyptian tomb paintings. Dogs are frequently named, unlike cats, which are called the male cat or the female cat. On the whole, pets are shown as a record of actual companion animals of the deceased, but they might have alluded to the gods as well, such as Anubis, Re, Bastet, and Hathor, with only Anubis being evoked by canines.”
Kaufman meanwhile says it is an extraordinary feeling to have made this discovery. “As far as I know, I am the first person in 3,500 years to read Duaty’s name. We spend so much time studying the people of ancient Egypt, but as someone who is passionate about dogs, it is an honour to give Duaty some of his identity back as well.”
