https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/4.text:
Democrats win control of House and Senate: Key US midterms takeaways
First Democratic senator in Kansas for nearly a century, first Muslim in the senate – key Democratic wins in the midterms.
Democrats have won control of Congress after flipping Republican-held House and Senate seats in Texas, South Carolina, Iowa, Michigan and Kansas in the midterm elections.
The results are being seen as a major rebuke to US President Donald Trump’s Republicans, who were previously in control of both houses of Congress.
All 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 of the Senate’s 100 seats were contested in Tuesday’s elections, including special elections in Florida and Ohio to fill the seats vacated by Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Vice President JD Vance.
Voters in 36 states also elected governors, as well as state legislators and local officials.
Counting continued throughout Tuesday evening and night in the US. Results in some races may, however, not be known until Wednesday or later.
These are the key takeaways from this year’s US midterms:
This is the biggest win for the Democrats since the 1990s
Democrats have won 228 seats in the House of Representatives so far, according to the Associated Press’s tally, and are leading in 34 others. That means they could end up with in excess of 260 seats in the House, the party’s biggest strength since 1990, when the Democrats won 267 seats in the lower chamber.
The Republicans held 220 seats in the House after the 2024 elections, while the Democrats had 215.
In the Senate, the upper chamber of Congress, Democrats have won 54 seats and are leading in another, while the Republicans have won 44 seats and are leading in one. To control the Senate, a party needs 51 seats. In the 2024 midterm elections, the Republicans had a majority with 53 seats, while the Democrats won 47 seats.
The Democrats have not had such a clear majority in the Senate since 2008, when the party won 56 seats in the slipstream of Barack Obama’s historic first presidential election.
Amid governors leading in each state, Democrats now have 28 governors, while 20 governors are from the Republican Party. Races in two states currently remain uncalled. Following the 2024 midterms, 27 governors of states were Republican while 23 governors were Democrats.
Not all seats have been called, and Democrats are projected to win more, but they have already flipped 25 seats in the House of Representatives from the Republicans – more than the 21 they took in 2008 when they last held the largest majority in Congress.
Several historic wins for Democrats
They include the following:
Trump loses both houses of Congress
This is the first time in 20 years that a Republican president has lost control of both houses of Congress, after George W Bush in 2006.
But Trump’s losses are far deeper than Bush’s: In the 2006 midterms, the Republican strength in the House went down from 232 to 202, while the party’s numbers in the Senate fell from 55 to 49.
This time though, the party is projected to fall short of 180 seats in the House, and is not expected to win more than 45 seats in the Senate.
In the House, in 18 of the 20 midterms held from 1946 to 2022, voters have taken House seats away from the party in power. The average loss was 26 seats across both houses. Only Bill Clinton’s Democrats in 1998 and George W Bush’s Republicans in 2002 bucked that trend by gaining seats or holding them all.
In the Senate, the governing party has lost seats in 13 of the 20 midterms since 1946 but lost overall control of the chamber in only six: 1946, 1954, 1986, 1994, 2006 and 2014.
In the current midterms, while President Trump’s name was not on the ballot, he regularly urged voters to imagine that it was, and the results are seen as a verdict on his presidency.
Michigan elects Senate’s first Muslim
Abdul El-Sayed, a former public health official, has defeated Mike Rogers for senator after a fierce Michigan battle, becoming the first Muslim ever elected to the US Senate.
President Trump has repeatedly targeted El-Sayed, even calling him a “jihadist”.
“He would be the only senator that will have to go through a metal detector before he’s allowed to go into the Senate,” Trump said during a campaign rally in Michigan.
In his victory speech, El-Sayed said: “America’s greatness is not about ignoring our flaws; it’s the courage that we have to correct them.
“We don’t need to be great again. We need to embrace that thing about us that has always made us great: the will to be more perfect,” he said.
“And right now that means taking on the corporations and the billionaires’ special interests who rigged the system against us,” El-Sayed said.
A record for Black women in the Senate
Democrat Juliana Stratton’s win in the Senate race in Illinois marks the first time in US history that three Black women will be in the Senate at the same time.
Stratton will join Senator Lisa Blunt Rochester of Delaware and Senator Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland, who were not up for re-election.
Meanwhile, among governors, Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms has made history as the first Black woman elected governor in the US.
The former Atlanta mayor emerged victorious over her billionaire opponent, Republican Rick Jackson, who spent more than $200m of his personal fortune in an attempt to succeed popular outgoing Republican Governor Brian Kemp.
First Native American state governor
Democrat Deb Haaland has made history as the first Native American woman elected governor of a US state, according to The Associated Press news agency’s projections.
Haaland, a former US interior secretary and member of the Laguna Pueblo, defeated Republican Gregg Hull, a former mayor of Rio Rancho, to lead New Mexico.
First Democratic senator to serve in Kansas in 94 years
Democratic US Senate candidate Adam Hamilton has defeated Republican incumbent Roger Marshall in Kansas.
The highly competitive contest between Hamilton, a Methodist pastor, and Marshall stunned political observers given the state’s long history of Republican wins. A Democrat has not won a Senate seat in Kansas since 1932.
“We’re always told to not talk about politics or religion but this is one time we’re trying to save our democracy. The next two years are a pivotal time for our country,” Hamilton had said on Monday.
The race in Kansas was considered consequential to control of the US Senate.
First Democratic senator in Texas in more than 30 years
Democrat James Talarico has defeated Republican Ken Paxton to win the US Senate race in Texas, the first time a Democrat has won state office since 1994.
“The people of Texas were my slingshot,” he told a crowd in Austin in his victory speech. “And tonight, we defeated Goliath.”
Talarico, a member of the Texas House of Representatives, centred his campaign on portraying Paxton as the face of a corrupt political system that allows billionaires to wield outsized political power.
The Democrat’s argument was supercharged after Elon Musk, the world’s richest man and Texas resident, became a key donor in the race.
Talarico also tried to woo moderate Republicans and independents put off by Paxton.
Democrats hold on to California governor
Xavier Becerra, a Democrat who ran on his decades of experience in public office, will take over from California Governor Gavin Newsom as the next governor of the nation’s most populous state.
“If anyone wants to come after California or any one Californian, they better be ready for a fight,” Becerra said on Tuesday night in front of a crowd near Sacramento, according to a report by The Associated Press.
Becerra has become the first Latino elected governor in a state where 40 percent of the population is Hispanic or Latino.
Trump’s endorsements widely lost
Trump had asked voters to pretend he was on the ballot in the midterm elections.
He also endorsed candidates in South Carolina, North Carolina, Texas, Michigan and others, who were defeated by the Democrats.
In South Carolina, which had not elected a Democratic senator since 1998, Trump backed Darline Graham. But Democrat Annie Andrews won the seat.
In North Carolina, Trump had endorsed former national Republican campaign official Michael Whatley, who was beaten by Democratic Governor Roy Cooper.
In Texas, Trump promoted Attorney General Ken Paxton. But Democrat Talarico won the race.
Then in Michigan, Former US Representative Mike Rogers, Trump’s choice in Michigan, was defeated by Democrat El-Sayed.
Speaking to Fox News, Trump said: “I think the Democrats did a good job. I really do. I think they did a good job. They fought hard.”
He added that there was a “mood in the air” and said, “I shouldn’t feel guilty.”
Opinion polls got it right, for once
Opinion polls ahead of the midterms had pointed to Democrats having a good night and winning the House and possibly the Senate.
But some pre-election polls were also cautious in calling it a complete win for Democrats since polls in the recent past have been off the mark.
Polling in the US began with newspapers collecting local opinions in the 1880s. Predictions have often been right, historically.
But in more recent years, they have often been horribly wrong.
In 2016, opinion polls correctly predicted the popular vote for Hillary Clinton, but also had her winning the presidency, comfortably, in states like Pennsylvania, Michigan and Wisconsin, which Trump ultimately won. Their forecast of Clinton winning the Electoral College was also proved wrong.
Polls were off in 2020 again, when COVID-19 restrictions greatly limited surveys. Most polls correctly predicted that Joe Biden would win the Electoral College and national votes. But they significantly overestimated support for Democrats by an “unusual magnitude”, according to the American Association for Public Opinion Research (AAPOR), while undercounting voters backing Trump.
Then, in 2022, polls got it wrong the other way – for the midterm elections. Some polls suggested that Republicans would sweep the House and Senate that year. In the end, the race was much closer, at least in the Senate, where neither party won a majority. Democrats ended up gaining narrow control with 51- 49, with the support of independents who caucus with them. Republicans, as predicted, won the House 222 – 213.
Then, in the 2024 presidential election, public opinion polls had predicted a neck-and-neck race between Donald Trump and Vice President Kamala Harris. Yet eventually, Trump cruised to a comfortable victory, defying most polls.
But this year, opinion polls have been in track with voter’s opinions, with many saying they voted for change.
Gary Colbert, who cast his ballot on the west side of Detroit, lamented the rise in fuel prices due to the US-Israel war on Iran, and added that Trump and “his cronies” are negatively affecting people’s lives, “and they don’t care”.
His wife, Shirley Colbert, said “some changes need to be made” to address the cost-of-living crisis.
“I’m going with the Democrat; I’m not going to go with Republicans because we have one of those in office right now, and we see what’s going on not just in Michigan but across the United States,” she told Al Jazeera.
Texas voter Monique Orellana, 46, had a message for every candidate regardless of party: “Do your job!”
“I would vote for Republicans if I felt they were going to do what they said they were going to do. Right now I’m not feeling it,” she told Al Jazeera.
“It’s name-calling and stuff like that. They don’t ever give anything about their policies. It’s just like ‘Talafreako’ [a nickname for Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico coined by his Republican opponent, Ken Paxton, and adopted by US President Donald Trump] and all of that,” she said
“Trump said he wasn’t going to start a war, and he did anyway. And he said he was going to fix the price of groceries on day one. They went up anyway. I still don’t know why they started this war and why it’s still going. But right now it’s just hope,” she added.

De l’« espoir » et une « leçon » : la gauche a célébré ce mercredi 4 novembre le revers cinglant imposé par les démocrates au président américain Donald Trump lors des élections de mi-mandat, en le comparant avec le Rassemblement national, qui a lui rejeté tout parallèle.
La candidate écologiste à la présidentielle Marine Tondelier s’est réjouie d’une « défaite historique » du dirigeant républicain après son deuxième mandat « apocalyptique ». « Mais ce qui vient de se produire aux États-Unis ces dernières années est un avertissement pour la France. Si notre pays porte au pouvoir le RN l’année prochaine, il connaîtra le même destin tragique que les États-Unis », a-t-elle écrit sur X. Elle a accusé le RN, donné en tête dans les sondages, d’être aussi « fasciste », « corrompu », « climatosceptique » et « incompétent » que Donald Trump. « Les États-Unis ont payé deux fois pour voir. Puisse cette leçon nous servir », a-t-elle dit.
Le candidat social-démocrate Raphaël Glucksmann y a lui vu « la victoire de la démocratie et de la décence ». « Il n’y a aucune fatalité en politique et ce sursaut démocrate est un message d’espoir pour tous ».
Au-delà des États-Unis, la gauche veut voir un vent favorable à sa famille politique dans les récents résultats électoraux, notamment la réélection de Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva au Brésil. « Partout dans le monde, c’est la mobilisation populaire qui permet de faire reculer l’extrême droite », s’est satisfait le coordinateur national de La France insoumise, Manuel Bompard. « En France aussi, nous le ferons ». « Quelques jours après l’éclatante victoire de Lula au Brésil, le recul de Netanyahou, voici la vague démocrate aux États-Unis », s’est enthousiasmé de son côté le premier secrétaire du Parti socialiste Olivier Faure.

Aipac and the Michigan Senate race: How the Israel lobby became toxic
"A lobby is like a night flower: it thrives in the dark and dies in the sun.” So said Steve Rosen, former foreign policy director of the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac) in a memo to a fellow staffer. Rosen would later be fired amid a major scandal involving espionage in passing classified US information to Israel.
Rosen was correct about the danger to a lobbying organisation that publicity poses. But in December 2021, Aipac decided to test that theory by creating two political action committees (Pacs) that enabled it to take part directly in political campaigns.
The results were mixed, and Aipac recently announced that it was closing one of the Pacs it had set up.
Aipac had been an advocacy organisation, promoting Israel’s interests, but it did not fund campaigns directly, nor did it endorse or fund political candidates.
In many ways, that made it more effective. It could do things like issue a congressional report card which rated every member of Congress’s support of Israel. Then other groups that were actual Pacs could use those reports to decide which candidates they should be contributing to.

Brasilien verschärft Haftregeln für Bandenchefs
Kriminelle Banden haben in Brasilien großen Einfluss. Nun sollen ihre Anführer unter strengeren Bedingungen ihre Strafen verbüßen.
Brasilia. Anführer krimineller Banden in Brasilien sollen künftig verpflichtend in Hochsicherheitsgefängnissen untergebracht werden. Zudem soll ihnen der Wechsel in einen weniger strengen Haftmodus erschwert oder ganz verwehrt werden, wie aus einer vom Senat verabschiedeten Verfassungsreform hervorgeht. Kriminelle Organisationen verfügen in Brasilien über erheblichen Einfluss, viele Bürger fühlen sich unsicher.
Die Reform war ein zentrales Vorhaben von Präsident Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, der nun ein eigenständiges Ministerium für öffentliche Sicherheit schaffen will. Bei der erst vor wenigen Tagen abgehaltenen Präsidentenwahl gehörte die innere Sicherheit zu den wichtigsten Wahlkampfthemen.
Die Reform sieht zudem vor, Vermögen aus kriminellen Aktivitäten leichter einziehen zu können. Außerdem soll sie die Zusammenarbeit zwischen Bund, Bundesstaaten und Kommunen im Kampf gegen die organisierte Kriminalität verbessern und die Rolle der Bundesregierung stärken.
Brasilien verfügt bereits über fünf vom Bund betriebene Hochsicherheitsgefängnisse. Dort sitzen besonders gefährliche Straftäter unter strengeren Bedingungen als in gewöhnlichen Haftanstalten ein. So leben Gefangene in Einzelzellen und haben nur eingeschränkte Besuchsmöglichkeiten.
Lulas unterlegener Herausforderer Flávio Bolsonaro hatte im Wahlkampf mit einer harten Sicherheitspolitik geworben und auch einen Ausbau der Hochsicherheitsgefängnisse versprochen. Der Sohn des derzeit unter Hausarrest stehenden Ex-Präsidenten Jair Bolsonaro, der trotz eines gerichtlichen Ausreiseverbots nach seiner Wahlniederlage in die USA gereist war, wollte fünf weitere Hochsicherheitsgefängnisse bauen lassen und 500.000 weitere Haftplätze schaffen. dpa/nd

Bei uns muss niemand zahlen, um informiert zu sein. Klingt nach einem schlechten Geschäftsmodell? Ist es auch. Aber uns sind unabhängiger Journalismus und Teilhabe für alle wichtiger als Profit. Journalismus kostet trotzdem Geld: Recherche, Druck und all die Menschen, die ihn machen. Deshalb sind wir auf dich angewiesen. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/4.text:
Israel vote results confirmed as election commission rejects fraud claims
Netanyahu’s allies refused to back the result, as President Herzog began talks on who should form the next government
Israel’s Central Elections Committee has certified the results of last week’s parliamentary elections after finding no evidence of fraud, a blow to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s efforts to discredit the vote.
Speaking at the official results ceremony at President Isaac Herzog’s residence, Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg said those casting doubt on the election results pose “a real danger” to Israel’s democracy.
The elections committee said a review of 9,069 polling stations found no irregularities that compromised the integrity of the election or changed its results. Its acting director, Dean Livne, said every complaint had been examined individually and the results accurately reflected voters’ choices.
In the committee’s five-member presidium, representatives of Yesh Atid and Blue and White voted to ratify the results, while Likud and Shas abstained. The chair, Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, cast the deciding vote.
Netanyahu and his allies have repeatedly claimed, without evidence, that Arab-led parties “stole” the election, possibly with foreign help.
After the vote, the internal security agency Shin Bet told the committee that intelligence pointed to widespread foreign funding and influence operations involving “thousands of people and possibly more”, The Times of Israel reported. Law enforcement sources told Haaretz daily, they were unaware of any operation of that size.
The Shin Bet is reportedly seeking to question four Arab politicians, but has not given prosecutors evidence regarding three of them. Likud accused Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara of blocking the interrogations. In turn, she effectively accused Shin Bet chief David Zini, a Netanyahu appointee, of undermining the rule of law, according to The Times of Israel.
National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir called on Zini to arrest all Arab party leaders and question them in Shin Bet cells, even without the attorney general’s approval. He also demanded a freeze on certification and on forming a government. “The elections were stolen, the results are fraudulent, foreign countries interfered,” Ben-Gvir wrote on X, adding that his far-right Otzma Yehudit party would therefore vote against approving the results.
Likud legislator Amit Halevi resigned from the committee. He alleged that some lawmakers “bought their seats with bribe money” and that the vote reflected “the choice of the rulers of Qatar, Iran or Turkey”.
Haaretz reported that Likud had weighed refusing to recognise the results altogether. Such a move would be unprecedented in Israel, and would likely be swiftly overturned by the courts. Sohlberg rejected a Likud demand to discuss the results before certifying them, writing that no party, “however distinguished or senior”, could withhold their publication. He has said even if foreign interference were confirmed, it would not undermine the overall result. Qatar has rejected claims that it funded Arab-led parties, calling them disinformation.
The results were submitted to President Isaac Herzog on Wednesday. He will then hold two days of consultations with party leaders before choosing the candidate best placed to form a coalition. In a break from custom, The Times of Israel reported that President Herzog will meet with the smaller parties first, starting with Religious Zionism, followed by Shas and Yisrael Beytenu. It’s expected the remaining factions will meet with the President on Thursday, ending with Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar and, finally, Likud.
The Netanyahu-led bloc won 53 seats, while Eisenkot’s got 48, and the Arab-led parties Ra’am and the Joint List secured a record 19. Neither could attain the majority – 61 seats – needed to govern. The deadlock raises the possibility of a unity government or an alliance between Eisenkot and Arab-led parties. If no one is able to form a governing coalition, Israel would hold another election early next year.
Yesh Atid leader Yair Lapid said the Democrats’ victory in the US Congress in the midterm elections had ruled out a unity government led by Netanyahu, a close ally of President Donald Trump.
“Israel cannot afford to let him remain prime minister,” Lapid wrote on X.

https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.title: The Greatest review – Amazon’s sturdy Muhammad Ali series is a tale told too many times
https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.author: Andrew Lawrence
https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.text:
The Greatest is a new limited series that repackages the life of Muhammad Ali for generations born too late to remember when the sporting icon was the world’s most famous man, or too lazy to seek out one of the many books written about his boxing rise, his exile from the sport for refusing the draft, his improbable late-career comeback and his steely resilience in the face of a seismic Parkinson’s diagnosis. That this TV adaptation comes from Amazon is both a stroke of vertical integration and an indictment of a viewing public whose patience for source material wears thinner with every scroll.
The Prime Video drama says it’s based on “the life of Muhammad Ali”, a credible claim given the extent to which Ali’s cultural ubiquity made him a public figure of eminent domain. The first-ever “authorized scripted series” also has the backing of Ali’s widow, Lonnie, who serves as an executive producer. But the show clearly takes its direction from the definitive tome authored by Muhammad Ali’s brother, Rahaman Ali. The younger brother was a lifelong sparring partner, sharing a room in their childhood Kentucky home and remaining a prominent member of his entourage until the champ’s death in 2016, aged 74 – an occasion for global mourning.
This eight-part series, though, harks back to the epoch before he publicly declared himself a Black Muslim, when Muhammad Ali was a rising pugilist known as Cassius Clay Jr. It focuses tightly on the four-year period between Clay’s light-heavyweight gold at the 1960 Olympics in Rome and his heavyweight title victory over Sonny Liston at age 22, a world-stopping upset that brought household fame and infamy.
Showrunner Ben Watkins tries to have it both ways, with Clay as the star and younger brother Rudy as his equally compelling sidekick – the Watson to his Holmes. But in reaching for compromise, Watkins underscores how novel his series might have been, how much fresher the time-worn Ali story could have felt had it been told from the point of view of the lesser light in the great man’s shadow.
Without a shift in perspective to chew on in the hourlong episodes, viewers who already know the story or lived through it will be left obsessing over the accuracy of the show’s details and, more urgently, how closely the actors come to the true characters they’re portraying. Up-and-comer Kai Parham has some leeway to take emotional chances as Rudy, a character little known even to Ali’s biggest fans. Omari Hardwick, of Power fame, is a dead ringer for Cassius Clay Sr and brings a Ghost-like coolness to the father’s conflicted feelings over his namesake breaking through the social barriers that have kept the older man in check. Michael Ealy as Malcolm X is a casting choice no one will see coming from Think Like a Man or The Perfect Guy – but he handles the role with understated aplomb. But even that casting surprise pales in comparison to Hav Plenty’s Hill Harper as the honorable Elijah Muhammad.
Jaalen Best, however, is in the unenviable position of launching his career by showing he can shuffle, brag and look as pretty as the champ after Will Smith’s Oscar-worthy portrayal and Eli Goree’s estimable follow-up in One Night in Miami. Alas, Best doesn’t set himself apart. Watkins’s scripts and direction often leave him drowning in angst and self-doubt – as if the bombastic self-confidence and narcissism that came to define Ali were just an obvious mask for deeper insecurities. Self-delusion was his original superpower, after all, and self-actualization the second.
All the while, the fight choreography lacks real punch; the scenes in the ring aren’t half as jarring as the moments at home with Clay Jr and his mother, Odessa (The Hateful Eight’s Dana Gourrier), whose chemistry occasionally veers from standard mama’s boy territory towards the downright Freudian. The bouts don’t generate much suspense, either. Viewers coming to Muhammad Ali’s story fresh have the show’s title as a dead giveaway. The Greatest? A loser? Of course not. Not until he met Joe Frazier at the Garden in 1971, anyway.
That’s not to say The Greatest doesn’t win some rounds. The soundtrack’s needle drops, rather than its original score, betray Shawn Carter’s production influence – in a good way: the snippet of Donny Hathaway’s I Believe to My Soul morphing into Wu-Tang’s One of These Days. And Snowfall’s Amin Joseph absolutely steals the show as Liston – the deeply flawed belt holder who would have made a worthy protagonist for his own dramatic series.
And therein lies the problem with Hollywood’s boxing fix: when it isn’t reheating the classic underdog yarn, it’s recirculating the same old stories about Rocky, Muhammad Ali and Mike Tyson – as if boxing hasn’t overflowed with some of the wildest testaments to the human spirit through the ages. The rise of Cassius Clay Jr may be the most hallowed of them all, but Rudy as Watson would have given it a timeless resonance. Rahaman, who died last year aged 82, receives a dedication in episode seven.
In the end, the Prime Video series should go down on the cards as a missed opportunity. The book, any book, would be time better spent.

De l’« espoir » et une « leçon » : la gauche a célébré ce mercredi 4 novembre le revers cinglant imposé par les démocrates au président américain Donald Trump lors des élections de mi-mandat, en le comparant avec le Rassemblement national, qui a lui rejeté tout parallèle.
La candidate écologiste à la présidentielle Marine Tondelier s’est réjouie d’une « défaite historique » du dirigeant républicain après son deuxième mandat « apocalyptique ». « Mais ce qui vient de se produire aux États-Unis ces dernières années est un avertissement pour la France. Si notre pays porte au pouvoir le RN l’année prochaine, il connaîtra le même destin tragique que les États-Unis », a-t-elle écrit sur X. Elle a accusé le RN, donné en tête dans les sondages, d’être aussi « fasciste », « corrompu », « climatosceptique » et « incompétent » que Donald Trump. « Les États-Unis ont payé deux fois pour voir. Puisse cette leçon nous servir », a-t-elle dit.
Le candidat social-démocrate Raphaël Glucksmann y a lui vu « la victoire de la démocratie et de la décence ». « Il n’y a aucune fatalité en politique et ce sursaut démocrate est un message d’espoir pour tous ».
Au-delà des États-Unis, la gauche veut voir un vent favorable à sa famille politique dans les récents résultats électoraux, notamment la réélection de Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva au Brésil. « Partout dans le monde, c’est la mobilisation populaire qui permet de faire reculer l’extrême droite », s’est satisfait le coordinateur national de La France insoumise, Manuel Bompard. « En France aussi, nous le ferons ». « Quelques jours après l’éclatante victoire de Lula au Brésil, le recul de Netanyahou, voici la vague démocrate aux États-Unis », s’est enthousiasmé de son côté le premier secrétaire du Parti socialiste Olivier Faure.

https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/israe.author: MEE staff

Israel's Shin Bet arrests activist amid incitement over Palestinian electoral gains
Israeli security forces arrested prominent Palestinian political activist and journalist Abd Abu Shahadeh on Tuesday, amid incitement against Palestinian citizens of Israel following their historic electoral gains in last week’s elections.
Abu Shahadeh, a Palestinian citizen of Israel, was taken from his home in Jaffa around midnight and transferred to an undisclosed location, according to news outlet Arab48.
Around 15 security personnel, including masked officers, stormed the house, arresting Abu Shahadeh in front of his two children. They also seized electronic devices and several books.
Police confirmed that the case was under investigation by the Tel Aviv Central Unit and Shin Bet, Israel’s domestic intelligence agency. A court subsequently issued a publication ban, citing a “security-related investigation”.
Abd Abu Shahadeh heads the elected Islamic Council in Jaffa and is a member of the editorial board of the Arab 48 news website. He is also a regular contributor to Middle East Eye’s opinion section.
New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch
Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
The arrest comes amid a wave of incitement against Palestinian citizens of Israel following their record voter turnout and electoral gains in last week’s elections.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party claimed the elections had been “stolen” by Palestinian parties, citing allegations of foreign interference.
Opposition figures have accused Likud of attempting to undermine the election results by exaggerating the allegations.
Palestinian-led parties denied the accusations.
Israel’s Central Elections Committee certified the election results on Wednesday, saying it had found no evidence of irregularities that undermined the integrity of the election or affected the outcome.
On Tuesday, Shin Bet chief David Zini, an ally of Netanyahu, was seeking to question the leaders of Palestinian-led parties under caution.
Those targeted included United Arab List leader Mahmoud Abbas, Ta’al leader Ahmed Tibi and Balad leader Sami Abu Shehadeh.
Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara blocked the request to interrogate the Palestinian lawmakers, publicly stating that citizens and elected officials could not be questioned without proper evidentiary grounds.
Attempt to 'steal' elections
Sami Abu Shehadeh said on Wednesday that Abd Abu Shahadeh’s arrest formed part of an effort by Netanyahu and Zini to “steal the elections”.
“Abd’s arrest is part of a broader campaign of arrests, interrogations and threats against political activists, designed to undermine the election results through the weaponization of the police and the Shin Bet,” the politician said.
“None of this will change one simple fact: Netanyahu lost the election, thanks to Arab citizens who turned out in massive numbers and kicked him out.”
He described the “abduction” as a serious crime but said it would not deter Palestinian citizens.
“We will not be intimidated, and we will not let them steal the election,” he added.
The Shin Bet claimed on Wednesday that it had gathered intelligence pointing to widespread foreign funding intended to influence the election results.
However, security sources told Haaretz they were unfamiliar with the Shin Bet’s claims of operations involving “thousands of people” and “huge sums” in the investigation.
One source pointed to Zini’s declaration on election day that the vote was secure.
“If huge sums were flowing in, it should have been thwarted,” the source said.
The allegations emerged after Palestinian-led parties won a record 19 seats in the 120-member Knesset, dealing a major blow to Netanyahu’s coalition.
The prime minister’s bloc won 53 seats, down from 64 in the 2022 elections, leaving him unable to form a majority government with the same parties. The opposition bloc also fell short of the numbers needed to secure a majority, resulting in political deadlock.
Netanyahu’s allies have since accused Palestinian citizens of stealing the election through foreign funding.
National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir called on Zini to arrest all Palestinian party leaders and interrogate them “in Shin Bet basement cells”.
“The election was stolen here in the State of Israel,” Ben-Gvir said.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120363.title: USA-Wahlen | Demokraten gewinnen US-Kongresswahlen
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120363.author: Oliver Kern
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120363.text:
- Politik
- USA-Wahlen
Demokraten gewinnen US-Kongresswahlen
Die Opposition übernimmt die Mehrheiten im Senat und Repräsentantenhaus. Für US-Präsident Donald Trump sind das empfindliche Niederlagen.
Die Wähler in den USA haben gesprochen, und ihre Botschaft war laut und klar: Sie sind alles andere als einverstanden mit der Richtung, in die Donald Trump das Land geführt hat. Der Präsident selbst stand zwar am Dienstag nicht zur Wahl, seine Republikanische Partei hat jedoch empfindliche Niederlagen bei den Midterms genannten Zwischenwahlen einstecken müssen.
Im Senat verloren die regierenden Republikaner den vorläufigen Ergebnissen von Associated Press (AP) zufolge mindestens sechs Sitze an die oppositionellen Demokraten und damit die Mehrheit in dieser Kammer des Kongresses. Die Zahl von nun mindestens 51 von 100 Sitzen könnte in den kommenden Stunden und Tagen sogar noch steigen, wenn die letzten Stimmen in den weiterhin umkämpften Bundesstaaten Alaska, Mississippi und ausgezählt sind.
Obwohl zum Beispiel in Kalifornien an der Westküste noch tagelang Stimmen ausgezählt werden, steht bereits fest, dass die Demokraten auch das Repräsentantenhaus gewonnen haben. Laut Berechnungen der TV-Sender CNN und NBC werden sie dort eine Mehrheit der insgesamt 435 Sitze erringen. Denn schon früh in der Nacht deutscher Zeit hatten sie den Republikanern mehr als die erforderlichen drei Mandate abgenommen. Letzten Hochrechnungen zufolge könnten sie sogar rund 250 Sitze besetzen – nichts Geringeres als ein Erdrutschsieg. Damit übertrafen die Demokraten sogar noch die bereits rosigen Umfragen vor der Wahl.
Bereits um 2:29 Uhr stand fest, dass Roy Cooper als erster Demokrat seit 2008 einen Senatssitz in North Carolina gewonnen hatte. »Es war ein harter Kampf. Wir wussten, dass sich die reichsten Leute des Landes in Washington die Taschen auf unsere Kosten vollstopfen. Die Korruption schadet allen hier. Und ihr habt heute laut und deutlich gesagt: Das muss enden«, sagte der ehemalige Gouverneur seinen Anhängern in der Siegesrede.
Siege in konservativem Kernland
Es war der erste Bundesstaat der Wahlnacht, in dem die Opposition triumphierte, obwohl Donald Trump hier vor zwei Jahren bei der Präsidentenwahl noch siegreich gewesen war. Drei Stunden später waren drei weitere Bundesstaaten hinzugekommen, womit auch der Senat endgültig in die Hand der Opposition fiel. »Das ist eine massive Zurückweisung von Donald Trump, und zwar im ganzen Land«, kommentierte Barack Obamas ehemaliger Berater David Axelrod auf CNN.
Auf der Ebene der Bundesstaaten könnten sich die Demokraten erstmals seit der Präsidentschaft von Barack Obama auch eine Mehrheit der Gouverneursposten sichern. Dies hätte durchaus Auswirkungen auf die Präsidentschaftswahlen in zwei Jahren. Von Republikanern regierte Staaten hatten zuletzt immer wieder Wahlgesetze verabschiedet, die vor allem links wählende Bevölkerungsgruppen (junge Menschen, Schwarze, Latinos) von der Abstimmung fernhalten sollen. Dies hat offenbar 2026 nicht gefruchtet und dürfte unter den neuen Mehrheitsverhältnissen noch schwieriger werden.
Die Demokraten gewannen am Dienstag nicht nur in ihren üblichen Hochburgen, sondern auch tief im konservativen Kernland: Texas, wo Elon Musk mehr als 200 Millionen Dollar für die Kampagne des schließlich unterlegenen Senatskandidaten Ken Paxton verschleuderte, sowie Kansas und South Carolina sind wohl die bedeutendsten Staaten, die den Republikanern teilweise erstmals seit 1932 (Kansas) abgenommen werden konnten. Damals war selbst der heute 80-jährige Trump noch nicht geboren. Hier punkteten die Demokraten zumeist mit eher moderaten Kandidaten wie Adam Hamilton, ein Methodisten-Pastor aus Kansas. In Texas wird James Talarico erster demokratischer Senator seit 1988.
Historische Siege für schwarze Kandidaten
Auch die linken Kandidaten, die von den Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) unterstützt worden waren, konnten einige Siege einfahren. Allen voran der Progressive Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, der sich in den vergangenen Wochen einer islamophoben Hasskampagne vonseiten seines Gegners und Präsident Donald Trump persönlich hatte erwehren müssen. Eine weitere Hoffnung auf eine Sensation blieb jedoch aus: In Florida konnte die DSA-Kandidatin Angie Nixon die Amtsinhaberin Ashley Moody nicht vom Thron stoßen, auch wenn sie ihr mit knapp 47 zu 50 Prozent der Stimmen näher kam, als es viele Experten prognostiziert hatten.
Die Demokratin Keisha Lance Bottoms wurde derweil die erste schwarze Gouverneurin in den USA überhaupt und das auch noch im Südstaat Georgia. »Das ist ein historischer Moment«, sagte Politikwissenschaftler und CNN-Kommentator Van Jones. »Schwarzen Frauen wie ihr wurde in den letzten Jahren immer wieder sprichwörtlich ins Gesicht geschlagen. Doch sie hat weitergekämpft. Das ist ein enormer Durchbruch, denn es zeigt: Wenn man auf schwarze Frauen setzt, kann man gewinnen.« Ein Hinweis darauf, dass die Niederlage von Kamala Harris im Präsidentschaftsrennen 2024 unter anderem mit ihrem Geschlecht und ihrer Hautfarbe begründet worden war.
Die ehemalige Bürgermeisterin von Atlanta war jedoch nicht die einzige, die am Dienstag Geschichte schrieb. Ihr Parteikollege Chris Pappas aus New Hampshire wird der erste offen schwul lebende Mann im US-Senat sein und der Republikaner Byron Donalds der erster schwarze Senator aus dem Südstaat Florida. Zudem wird Demokratin Gina Hinojosa als erste Latina Gouverneurin von Texas.
Sollte der bisherige Minderheitenführer Hakeem Jeffries von seinen Kollegen Anfang Januar dazu bestimmt werden, könnte er zudem der erste schwarze Sprecher des Repräsentantenhauses werden. »Heute beginnt das große amerikanische Comeback. Das Volk hat gesprochen. Überall im Land. Sie haben genug vom Extremismus und von der Korruption. Sie wollen, dass der Kongress für sie arbeitet. Genau das werden wir ab Januar tun«, rief er seinen Anhängern zu. »Die Kosten sind zu hoch für viel zu viele Menschen. Wir werden für Kleinstädte, Großstädte und Dörfer kämpfen, damit für jeden Amerikaner das Leben wieder bezahlbar wird. Das ist eine Wechselwahl. Und wir werden für einen Wandel sorgen. Milliardäre wollten den Kongress kaufen, doch die Amerikaner haben gezeigt: Amerika steht nicht zum Verkauf.«
Damit werden die Demokraten die legislative Agenda im Land bestimmen. Da Donald Trump jedoch weiterhin Präsident bleibt, kann er mit seiner Vetomacht alle Gesetze blockieren, die von den Demokraten in den kommenden zwei Jahren beschlossen werden. Letzteren bliebe immerhin noch eine neue Kontrollmacht durch die Möglichkeit, Untersuchungsausschüsse einzuberufen und Minister vorzuladen. Vor allem aber hat der Kongress die Budgethoheit und könnte beispielsweise dem Verteidigungsministerium die wichtige Finanzierung des Iran-Krieges vorenthalten. Ob es so weit kommt, steht jedoch noch in den Sternen.
Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf
Bei uns muss niemand zahlen, um informiert zu sein. Klingt nach einem schlechten Geschäftsmodell? Ist es auch. Aber uns sind unabhängiger Journalismus und Teilhabe für alle wichtiger als Profit. Journalismus kostet trotzdem Geld: Recherche, Druck und all die Menschen, die ihn machen. Deshalb sind wir auf dich angewiesen. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro.
Spende einmalig oder regelmäßig, jeder Betrag zählt. Damit nd bleibt.

In Pictures
Photos: US Democrats celebrate winning control of Congress
Democrats flipped seats that had long been held by Republicans in a wave of historic leadership firsts.
Democrats have seized control of the United States Congress, winning the Senate and the House of Representatives in a nationwide rebuke of President Donald Trump that is expected to slow the final two years of his term.
In a series of historic firsts, the first Black female governor, the first openly gay male senator, the first Muslim senator, and the first female Native American governor have all won office, securing landmark victories in a vote that delivered resounding gains for the Democratic Party.
The sweeping Democratic gains in Tuesday’s election hand the opposition significant power to block legislation, open wide-ranging investigations into Trump’s administration, and challenge his judicial and senior government appointments.
The results reflect deep public anger over rising living costs, tariffs, and Trump’s confrontation with Iran, which has driven up fuel prices and amplified frustration with an already deeply unpopular president.

https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: ‘A true icon of the hair industry’: celebrity hairstylist John Frieda dies aged 75
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: Caroline Davies
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
John Frieda, the celebrity hairstylist who launched his own bestselling hair product range, has died aged 75.
In an Instagram post, his salon wrote: “It is with heavy hearts that we share the news that our dear John passed away peacefully … surrounded by his family.
“John was more than a mentor to us; he was a true icon of the hair industry. He was the person who taught us everything, believed in us, and made us better.
“His talent and passion touched so many, and his legacy will live on in every single one of us. We will continue to do him proud. Our thoughts are with John’s family and everyone who loved him. Rest in peace, John. You will be forever in our hearts.”
The London-born businessman, whose father was a hairdresser and whose grandfather was a barber, styled celebrities ranging from Twiggy and Jackie Kennedy Onassis to Scarlett Johansson, Madonna, Nicole Kidman and Diana, Princess of Wales.
He created the famous “Purdey” hairstyle – a statement bowl cut – for Joanna Lumley in 1976 for her role in The New Avengers TV series, and opened his first salon that same year, aged 25.
He went on to launch the popular Frizz Ease hair care line and open salons around the world. He also styled for British Vogue and Harper’s Bazaar
Frieda married his first wife, the Scottish singer known as Lulu, in 1977. They had one child, Jordan Frieda.
Frieda moved to the United States in 1990 to focus on his growing hair care brand, and his relocation contributed to the end of the marriage.
He met his second wife, Avery Agnelli, widow to an heir of the Fiat car company, in 2002 and they married in 2019. They had two children together, Jackson and Leyla, and Frieda was stepfather to her daughter, Asia Agnelli Lagrange.
Agnelli Lagrange shared a series of photos of them together on Instagram, writing: “Sadly my J has passed away. Today we lost the best man to ever exist. I share this because I know he touched the lives of so many.”
The cause of death has not been made public.
Born Alan Howard Frieda in Kenton, Middlesex, he began his career at London’s House of Leonard salon and adopted the name John because another stylist at the salon was also named Alan.
In the 1980s he worked with the American hair care executive Gail Federici to create his own product line, and he launched Frizz Ease in 1988 and his Sheer Blonde line in 1998.
Among those paying tribute on social media was Jo Wood, the model, TV personality and the wife of the Rolling Stones guitarist Ronnie Wood. She said: “Oh No… that’s so sad. When I was 16 and John worked as an assistant at Leonards, he would do my hair. He was so great… we would go to the pub after… but I couldn’t drink. RIP John it was lovely to know you.”
Cetera Lamb, the creative director of Frieda’s London salon, said: “The industry has lost a true legend, a real maverick in hairdressing. For 50 years, he led our wonderful salon, leaving behind an incredible legacy of passion, creativity, vision and outstanding hairdressing.”
In 2002, Frieda sold his hair care company to the Japanese conglomerate Kao in a deal valued at $450m. He retained ownership of five salons: two in London, two in New York and one in Los Angeles.

https://taz.de/Portraet-der-Kuenstlerin-.title: Porträt der Künstlerin Susanne Ahner: Das Gedächtnis in den Dingen
https://taz.de/Portraet-der-Kuenstlerin-.author: Katrin Bettina Müller
https://taz.de/Portraet-der-Kuenstlerin-.text:
Porträt der Künstlerin Susanne Ahner: Das Gedächtnis in den Dingen
Susanne Ahner arbeitet oft mit dem, was übrig bleibt im Alltag. In Berlin ist ihr „Marmorpalais“ im Verein der Berliner Künstlerinnen zu sehen.
Stein wiegt schwer. Aber nicht bei Susanne Ahner. Da sind es nur kleine Zettelchen, lapidar an die Wand geklebt, die eine Typologie der Marmor-Gesteine verzeichnen, mit Herkunft und Farben genannt, etwa: Namibian Green/grün/Namibia. Dieser grüne Marmor könnte durchaus dabei sein in den Bruchsteinplatten, die Ahner auf dem Fußboden im Projektraum des Vereins der Berliner Künstlerinnen 1867 (VdBK 1867) verlegt hat: allerdings nur im fotografischen Abbild, als quadratische Fotokacheln.
Die Bilder machte die 1960 in Bremen geborene Künstlerin in ihrem Elternhaus. Beide Eltern waren Bildhauer mit guten Kontakten zu Steinlieferanten. Vieles in ihrem Haus, das die Mutter Ingeborg Ahner-Wiese Ende der 1950 Jahre entworfen hatte, legten sie mit eigener Hand an, wie die Fußböden aus den Bruchstücken, Resten der Marmorindustrie.
Die Arbeit mit den Resten, dem Übriggebliebenen, mit Fundstücken des Alltags: Das ist ein entscheidendes Element im Werk von Susanne Ahner. Sie werden zum Material der Erinnerung, aber auch zur Verknüpfung von Vergangenheit und Gegenwart. Im Projektraum des VdBK 1867 nehmen die Fotofliesen die Anordnung des vorhandenen grauweißen Marmorbodens auf, noch aus der Zeit, als hier ein Antiquitätenladen war.
Die Ausstellung
Susanne Ahner, „Marmorpalais“, im Projektraum des Vereins der Berliner Künstlerinnen 1867, bis 22. November 2026
Minimalistisch ist die Ausstellung und legt eine ironische Distanz ein zum opulenten Titel – „Marmorpalais (Himmel und Hölle)“ –, der an das Versprechen von Repräsentation und Luxus erinnert, das mit Marmor verbunden ist. Dazu passt ein müde und braun gewordener Lorbeerkranz an der Wand. Als er noch grün war, 2002, war er ein Requisit bei der Verleihung des Marianne-Werefkin Preises, den Ahner vom VdBK 1867 erhielt.
In ihrem Umgang mit den Resten liegt etwas von Demut und Respekt gegenüber den alltäglichen Dingen. Sie reflektiert damit, wie wir uns unsere Welt gestalten, setzt Zäsuren im beschleunigten Verbrauch der Ressourcen und würdigt dabei nicht zuletzt die Ästhetik, die in funktionaler Gestaltung steckt.
Seit vielen Jahren arbeitet Ahner mit der Künstlerinnengruppe Endmoräne, die jedes Jahr Orte im ungewissen Übergang zwischen Vergangenheit und Zukunft bespielt, eine verfallende Papierfabrik in Eberswalde etwa, ein leerstehendes Gutshaus, einen ehemaligen Bahnhof. Fast immer findet Susanne Ahner dort etwas Zurückgelassenes, ein leicht zu übersehendes Detail, mit dem sie dem Ort Geschichten und Stimmen gibt.
1986, sie hatte ihr Bildhauerstudium an der Hochschule der Künste gerade abgeschlossen, erhielt sie für sechs Monate ein Stipendium für Paris. Das war eine Zeit der Befreiung von Erwartungen, von den Bildhauer-Eltern und vom figürlichen Programm. Dort, erinnert sie sich, begann sie Umgebungen zu erkunden, den Materialien ihre Geschichten abzulauschen.
Gedenken ohne Pathos
Susanne Ahner ist in vielen Zusammenschlüssen von Künstlerinnen aktiv, die ihre Ausstellungen selbst organisieren, Förderungen beantragen, an eigenen Plattformen arbeiten: eben im VdBK 1867, auch in der Gedok, bei Endmoräne. Sie hat an der Universität der Künste in Berlin und in Erfurt gelehrt.
In Berlin hat sie seit Beginn der 1990er Jahre an vielen Wettbewerben für Kunst am Bau und Gedenken im öffentlichen Raum teilgenommen. Realisiert wurde etwa in Berlin-Pankow der elegant geschwungene Schriftzug „Garbaty“, der an den jüdischen Firmengründer der Garbaty-Cigarettenfabrik erinnert. Er war in sozialer Hinsicht ein vorbildlicher Arbeitgeber.
Dazu gehört in Potsdam-Babelsberg der Willi-Frohwein-Platz: Willi Frohwein war ein Auschwitz-Überlebender, der als Zeitzeuge an Berliner Schulen von Ausgrenzung, Verfolgung und dem Leben in Konzentrationslagern erzählte und die Jugendlichen mit seinem Ton zu packen wusste. Sätze von ihm sind in die Begrenzungen des Platzes eingelassen und in hohe Stuhlformen. Die Buchstaben sind ausgestanzt, beim Lesen sickert die Umgebung in die negativen Formen.
Diesen Gedenkort, der zum Weiterforschen anregt, hat die Künstlerin zusammen mit Schüler:innen des Bertha-von-Suttner-Gymnasiums entwickelt. Teil davon ist eine Website, auf der man die Stimme Frohweins, der 2009 starb, noch einmal hören kann. Bei diesen Arbeiten ist die Erinnerung Auftrag, den Susanne Ahner ohne Pathos und mit zurückhaltenden Formen aufnimmt.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. So viele unterstützen freiwillig und regelmäßig. Noch nicht dabei? Werden Sie jetzt Teil der Community! Jetzt unterstützen

‘Complicit’: World Medical Association criticised for rejecting calls to suspend Israel
The World Medical Association (WMA) is facing strong criticism for refusing to suspend the Israeli Medical Association (IMA), despite documented allegations of complicity by Israeli doctors in the torture of Palestinian detainees and abuses committed in Gaza.
A petition signed by 6,500 medical personnel from the IMA Out! campaign, a coalition of health advocacy groups, was presented to the WMA General Assembly in Rotterdam, the Netherlands, last month, calling on the international body to expel the IMA.
Hundreds of doctors also took part in protests as the General Assembly was convening, with some carrying a shroud bearing the names of 18,000 Palestinian children who have been killed during Israel’s genocide in Gaza.
Doctors argue that the IMA has failed to uphold core standards relating to medical ethics, and that they are complicit in serious violations of human rights against Palestinians, including failing to penalise Israeli doctors who may have overseen the torture of Palestinian detainees and the deaths of Palestinian healthcare workers in Israeli prisons.
The Hind Rajab Foundation (HRF), a group seeking justice for war crimes, crimes against humanity and human rights violations committed by Israel against Palestinians, also filed a complaint last month to the International Criminal Court (ICC), urging it to investigate whether Israeli doctors, as well as the IMA and officials from Israel’s ministries of health and defence, have been involved in the torturing of Palestinians.

It is the first time that a WMA member has been referred to the ICC.
Dr Jonathan Fluxman, a retired British GP of Jewish heritage and organising member of the IMA Out! campaign, attended the protests in Rotterdam.
“Both the WMA and IMA are refusing to investigate multiple reports by numerous human rights agencies that were sent directly to them relating to the torture and murder of healthcare workers,” he told Middle East Eye.
“This goes back 30 years - the WMA has been burying reports about Israeli torture.
“They are behaving in the same way as the US and British governments, by allowing Israel to get away with a genocide. In my view, the WMA is complicit in the IMA’s involvement in this.”
‘Carte blanche’ to Israel
Dr Fluxman believes that the WMA should immediately initiate an investigation into the potential involvement of IMA members in the torture, abuse and deaths of Palestinian detainees.
“This is about defending medical principles and the application of them,” he said.
“It raises very serious questions about the WMA’s role as the international guardian of medical ethics, and we understand that a number of national medical associations remain very concerned about the situation.”
‘It raises very serious questions about the WMA’s role as the international guardian of medical ethics’
- Dr Jonathan Fluxman, retired British GP
The WMA was established in 1947 to uphold medical ethics following the Second World War, after doctors from Nazi Germany were found to have participated in war crimes.
One hundred and eighteen countries are currently represented within the international body.
Each member country must adhere to WMA codes of practice, including its 1975 Declaration of Tokyo, which states that doctors must not participate in torture and have a duty to call it out.
The last time an association was suspended was in 1976, when South Africa was blocked from attending two general assemblies due to doctors being complicit in torture during the apartheid.
The first attempt to hold the IMA accountable for the alleged participation of Israeli doctors in the abuse of Palestinian detainees came in 2009, when 725 physicians from 43 countries presented findings by human rights groups to the WMA, which that year was holding its general assembly in Tel Aviv.
At the time, the president of the IMA, Yoram Blachar, was also president of the WMA - he rejected allegations that Israeli medics were complicit in torture, describing them as defamatory.
In 2016, 71 UK-based doctors again urged the WMA to suspend the IMA, but it refused.
The Israeli association represents over 90 percent of doctors in Israel. Its current president, Zion Hagay, chairs the WMA’s socio-medical affairs committee, while its chief executive officer advocate, Leah Wapner, serves in several advisory roles, including on the WMA’s finance and planning, socio-medical affairs, and medical ethics committees.
Dr Fluxman believes that the international body is protecting the IMA.
“What has 30 years of inclusion and dialogue led to? Things have got worse, and the IMA has been given carte blanche to do whatever it wants,” he said.
Around 1,700 healthcare workers have been killed by Israel since October 2023.
South African push to expel IMA
The call for the IMA to be suspended from the WMA was led by the South African Medical Association (Sama) last year.
Sama’s motion failed to secure the majority that was needed to get the WMA to consider expelling the Israeli group. Instead, the WMA passed a resolution calling on the Israeli government to protect healthcare and health workers in Gaza, and asked all its members to issue public statements condemning attacks on hospitals and medical personnel.
The IMA has remained silent on this, however.
Dr Mvuyisi Mzukwa, the chairman of Sama, told MEE his group had decided to take its own approach against the IMA.
“We were the first medical association to formally cut ties with the IMA,” he said.
This was followed by the British Medical Association and the Turkish Medical Association.
“We also withdrew from the WMA’s Taipei Working Group on ethics because it is chaired by an Israeli medic. It is hugely problematic that the IMA is part of the WMA’s leadership structures, given the allegations surrounding them,” Mzukwa said.
“As a world body, the WMA’s name is being tarnished by the presence of the IMA, and they should have suspended them until these controversies are resolved.
“It is a huge indictment on the WMA. The international body must be clear about the principles it stands for.”
Dr Mzukwa explained that he had been planning to arrive earlier at this year’s General Assembly in order to rally other members of the WMA to join the call for the IMA to be boycotted.
However, he and most of his South African colleagues could not attend because of visa issues.
“I had applied on time, but for some reason the visa ended up being sent to Pretoria rather than Durban, where it usually goes, and there was no way I could have collected it in time for the General Assembly,” he said.
“I have my suspicions about why this might have happened. I was planning to give a speech at the General Assembly and was prepared to put my head above the parapet to call for the IMA to be expelled.
“It’s not beyond the realms of possibility that there could have been some intel on me to try to prevent me from attending.”
MEE contacted the Netherlands’ Ministry of Foreign Affairs for comment but received no response by the time of publication.
Mzukwa has been vocal in his criticism of Israel’s genocide in Gaza. His stance aligns with that of the South African government, which brought a case to the International Court of Justice in 2023 accusing Israel of committing genocide.
Dr Mzukwa also told MEE that Sama, the IMA and the WMA had held a meeting at the end of July about the case of Dr Hussam Abu Safiya, a Palestinian paediatrician and former head of Kamal Adwan Hospital in Gaza, who has been detained by Israel since December 2024 and subjected to brutal beatings.
“We raised concerns about the lack of access to Dr Abu Safiya, the denial of medical treatment for him and uncertainty around his condition,” Dr Mzukwa explained.
“The IMA told us they had requested the Israeli authorities to carry out medical examinations and allow external physicians into the prison where Dr Abu Safiya is being held, but we weren’t shown any evidence to support this - this was a red flag for us.”
‘A buttress of the Israeli state’
Derek Summerfield, an honorary senior lecturer at King’s College London who has researched and campaigned on the psychiatric impact of the detention and torture of Palestinian prisoners in Israel, has been calling on the WMA to expel the Israeli association for almost two decades.
“We’re dealing with two ethically corrupt bodies - the WMA and the IMA - and are appealing to one to do something with the other one - but the WMA has long since sold out,” he told MEE.
‘We’re dealing with two ethically corrupt bodies - the WMA and the IMA - and are appealing to one to do something with the other one - but the WMA has long since sold out’
- Dr Derek Summerfield, King’s College London
“There is a long-established body of evidence on Israeli doctors’ complicity in torture suites, and these days they are even more present there, and participate directly.
“The IMA is an example of the disgusting way in which doctors can behave - they are shielding doctors’ involved in Israel’s genocide on Gaza, and it’s outrageous that they’re a full member of the WMA.
“The IMA really is the buttress of the Israeli state.”
Dr Fluxman has also raised concerns about how the IMA’s ethical policy allows for exemptions from the WMA’s principles.
“It is their policy to allow Israeli doctors to compromise fundamental ethical principles and defer to military and security officials over the provision of healthcare and protection of health personnel,” he said.
“It also means they are in breach of the WMA’s position on medical neutrality.”
The IMA has consistently remained silent amid ongoing attacks on healthcare facilities in Gaza, as well as the targeting of healthcare workers.
In fact, it has frequently sought to challenge criticism of Israel’s actions by international medical associations.
At this year’s WMA General Assembly, the IMA installed banners outside the convention, calling on medical associations not to boycott them and asking them to remember the 7 October 2023 attacks.
In November 2023, IMA’s president, Professor Hagay, refused to call for a ceasefire and justified Israeli military strikes on hospitals in Gaza, arguing that Hamas fighters needed to be “rooted out of terror bases”.
That month, 81 Israeli doctors signed a letter supporting the bombing of hospitals, something which the IMA refused to condemn, contravening WMA principles on the protection of healthcare settings and health workers.
Furthermore, Dr Liav Goldstein, a senior member of the IMA’s ethics bureau and chief medical officer of the Israeli Prison Service, has approved the starvation diet imposed on thousands of Palestinian prisoners after 7 October by the national security minister Itamar Ben Gvir.
The IMA’s attempts to safeguard the reputation of the Israeli state were also laid bare when in May 2024, Hagay wrote to the Israeli Prison Service about the death in prison of Dr Adnan al-Bursh, a Palestinian surgeon who was head of the orthopaedic department at Al-Shifa Hospital in Gaza City.
After a highly critical British Medical Journal article about the circumstances surrounding Dr Al-Bursh's death, Professor Hagay wrote: “We would appreciate any information that could help us refute this claim, which, needless to say, causes significant harm to Israel’s standing and image worldwide.”
Torture camp
Whistleblowers from Sde Teiman, an Israeli military base in the Negev desert that was converted into a detention camp at the start of the Gaza genocide, have documented the systemic abuse and torture of Palestinian detainees there, including the denial of medical treatment by Israeli medics.
Accounts describe prisoners being held naked, shackled and forced to wear nappies instead of being allowed to use a toilet.
Some have also had to undergo amputations, often without anaesthesia.
'The WMA must answer why an association that provided institutional cover for torture is still welcome at its table'
- Dyab Abou Jahjah, Hund Rajab Association
The centre has been used to detain thousands of Palestinians from Gaza, the majority of whom are civilians, including healthcare and humanitarian workers, who are being held under the so-called “unlawful combatants” law, which has been used to strip detainees of basic legal protections and enable their detention without charge or trial.
Several individuals have died while being held there.
IMA ethics board director Yossi Walfisch dismissed accusations of ill-treatment and said prisoners at the camp were receiving “appropriate medical care”.
Dr Al-Bursh was held at Sde Teiman before being taken to Ofer Prison, where he died. While in prison he was brutally beaten, tortured and repeatedly raped, according to testimonies of released Palestinian prisoners who had met him.
The Hind Rajab Foundation said evidence shows that medical participation in torture and abuse at the camp was structural.
Dyab Abou Jahjah, director general at HRF, said: “Israeli physicians abandoned their neutrality when they agreed to treat patients in chains and erase what was done to them.
“The WMA must answer why an association that provided institutional cover for torture is still welcome at its table.”
If IMA members are found to be complicit in this, it would violate the WMA’s code of practice, values and guidelines, as well as international humanitarian law, Abou Jahjah said.
The WMA told MEE: “Inclusion sits at the core of the WMA's identity. Patients remain our focus, alongside the protection of health personnel, including physicians, wherever they serve.
“Our members, including the Israeli Medical Association, regularly call out injustices and violations of medical neutrality even when their own governments are involved.”
MEE also contacted IMA but received no response by the time of publication.

From education to housing protests, Palestine’s flag spreads across Europe
Symbols such as the flag and keffiyeh represent anti-colonial struggles but some question their use amid mass demonstrations.
The Palestinian flag and traditional keffiyeh scarf have been regular appearances at recent demonstrations across Europe over housing, education and the cost of living.
Palestinian symbols were also displayed in Northern Ireland, where a decades-old standoff risked reigniting historic grievances.
Kenny Pierre Agboton, from the Free University of Brussels for Palestine platform, says the use of the Palestinian flag in demonstrations is a nod to anti-colonialism and anti-repression struggles.
“From climate change to liveable Earth, the Palestinian issue becomes the crossroad for every fight we have, at least in Western Europe,” he told Al Jazeera.
He said that engaging in a political struggle is a political choice that values education over “giving arms to the military”.
His association is in contact with like-minded groups at other universities in Belgium and “we usually give one flag to each association” during nationwide demonstrations.
Across the border, France is witnessing nationwide rallies that began over faults within the education system.
High school students, backed by university and teacher associations, trade unions and some politicians, are demanding more affordable, higher-quality education, upgraded schools, smaller classes and more teachers. And some have done so while carrying the Palestinian flag or wearing the keffiyeh.
‘Global system organising attacks on our rights’
Alice Cohen-Morzadec, spokesperson for the French Student Union and a regular protester, views the flag as a symbol of the daily struggles in the occupied West Bank and Gaza and broader global inequalities.
“As young people, high school or university students, we know that these demonstrations are not just about our own situation; it is about a global system that is organising attacks on our rights,” she said. “It is a broader movement against world capitalism and colonialism system.”
Some politicians support using the symbols, too.
Nelson Mandela wore the keffiyeh in 1990. In 2006, then-Spanish Prime Minister Jose Luis Rodriguez Zapatero of the Socialist Workers’ Party briefly wore one after a young Palestinian reportedly placed it around his neck.
“What’s wrong with a citizen taking to the streets with a Palestinian flag?” said Mario Furore, an Italian member of the European Parliament from the Five Star Movement, which belongs to The Left parliamentary group. “Should we really be outraged by this, when the Israeli government is accused of genocide in Gaza and continues to massacre Palestinians in the West Bank? We mustn’t make the mistake of relativising everything,” he said.
“Since October 7, 2023, Israeli operations have caused tens of thousands of Palestinian deaths, nearly 80,000 according to some estimates. This fact alone should put things into perspective.”
But the anti-colonial messaging of the students or the realpolitik of some politicians does not resonate in every country with a protest movement.
Fatos Lubonja, an activist and writer who spent 17 years in prison during Albania’s communist rule, said he is one of the few who has carried the Palestinian flag or worn a keffiyeh during anticorruption demonstrations in his Muslim-majority country over the past four months.
He said that in Albania, some see the Palestinian struggle alongside issues related to Muslims. And Muslims are equated with the Ottoman Empire.
“We were liberated from the Ottomans. The Ottomans were considered as occupiers with whom we lived with a long time. The narrative was that we were coming back to Europe, returning to our roots,” he said.
“Being a Muslim for Albanians during communism means you had to be emancipated, that we wanted to be [a] Westerner, part of NATO. That is why Albanians, even today, are very pro-American and, of course, being pro-American means you also have to be pro-Israel,” he said.
Seeing the Palestinian cause and flag waved at European demonstrations is not to everyone’s liking, especially since some violent protesters have also brandished Palestinian symbols.
Palestinian writer and researcher Waddah Abu Jamea, writing in Al Majalla magazine in October, described discomfort watching on.
“Palestinians consequently find themselves expected to condemn the thief while thanking the student or academic who raises their flag. They watch as the flag’s original meaning disappears behind a cacophony of competing causes and agendas. They see it enlisted in struggles over identity, immigration, religion and security. At the same time, their own story, like the Palestinians’ collective national cause, fades into the background amid the growing politicisation of solidarity,” he wrote.
“The flag has crossed borders, but those borders remain closed off to Palestinians. It has entered universities and institutions while schools in Gaza have been destroyed, depriving Palestinian children of access to education. It flies above demonstrations in Paris, while Palestinians in the West Bank are denied the freedom to carry it in protest against killing, imprisonment, and siege.”
Some sent blunter messages to the student protesters.
Janine di Giovanni, a journalist and the head of The Reckoning Project, which documents war crimes, was visiting the West Bank on October 18 when she posted about the French protesters on her Facebook page.
She said that as she lives in Paris and has worked in Palestine for more than 30 years, she understands the root of the European protests.
“But I am writing this from the West Bank, where I document what is happening to Palestinian families during the olive harvest,” she wrote. “Every day there is violence. … So I ask you, gently: please don’t link your struggle to Palestine.”
“Not because yours doesn’t matter, but because they are not the same. Palestinians are fighting for something more basic: the right to live freely and safely on their own land. When the two are conflated, it blurs what is happening here and gives those who already misunderstand both causes an easy excuse to dismiss them, or to see only violence. Fight for your future. It is worth fighting for. But let Palestine’s story be told on its own terms.”

De l’« espoir » et une « leçon » : la gauche a célébré ce mercredi 4 novembre le revers cinglant imposé par les démocrates au président américain Donald Trump lors des élections de mi-mandat, en le comparant avec le Rassemblement national, qui a lui rejeté tout parallèle.
La candidate écologiste à la présidentielle Marine Tondelier s’est réjouie d’une « défaite historique » du dirigeant républicain après son deuxième mandat « apocalyptique ». « Mais ce qui vient de se produire aux États-Unis ces dernières années est un avertissement pour la France. Si notre pays porte au pouvoir le RN l’année prochaine, il connaîtra le même destin tragique que les États-Unis », a-t-elle écrit sur X. Elle a accusé le RN, donné en tête dans les sondages, d’être aussi « fasciste », « corrompu », « climatosceptique » et « incompétent » que Donald Trump. « Les États-Unis ont payé deux fois pour voir. Puisse cette leçon nous servir », a-t-elle dit.
Le candidat social-démocrate Raphaël Glucksmann y a lui vu « la victoire de la démocratie et de la décence ». « Il n’y a aucune fatalité en politique et ce sursaut démocrate est un message d’espoir pour tous ».
Au-delà des États-Unis, la gauche veut voir un vent favorable à sa famille politique dans les récents résultats électoraux, notamment la réélection de Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva au Brésil. « Partout dans le monde, c’est la mobilisation populaire qui permet de faire reculer l’extrême droite », s’est satisfait le coordinateur national de La France insoumise, Manuel Bompard. « En France aussi, nous le ferons ». « Quelques jours après l’éclatante victoire de Lula au Brésil, le recul de Netanyahou, voici la vague démocrate aux États-Unis », s’est enthousiasmé de son côté le premier secrétaire du Parti socialiste Olivier Faure.

https://taz.de/Krachende-Niederlage-der-.title: Krachende Niederlage der US-Republikaner: Riesenklatsche, unsichere Zukunft
https://taz.de/Krachende-Niederlage-der-.author: Bernd Pickert
https://taz.de/Krachende-Niederlage-der-.text:
Krachende Niederlage der US-Republikaner : Riesenklatsche, unsichere Zukunft
Bei den Midterms in den USA gewinnen die Demokraten beide Kammern des Kongresses zurück. Es ist ein deutliches Votum gegen die Politik Trumps – der nun noch gefährlicher wird.
D ie US-Amerikaner*innen haben Präsident Donald Trump und der von ihm dominierten Republikanischen Partei in den Zwischenwahlen eine derartige Klatsche verpasst, dass selbst die sonst so wortgewaltigen US-TV-Kommentatoren kaum Worte dafür fanden. Die Demokraten haben den Republikanern weitaus mehr Sitze im Repräsentantenhaus und im Senat abgenommen, als nötig gewesen wäre, um die Kontrolle über beide Kongresskammern zu übernehmen.
Selbst in tief republikanischen Staaten konnten die Demokraten gewinnen oder zumindest republikanische Amtsinhaber ins Wackeln bringen. Nur zwei Jahre nach Trumps überragendem Wahlsieg gegen Kamala Harris hat eine große Mehrheit der US-Amerikaner*innen von diesem Präsidenten die Nase gestrichen voll. Oder zumindest: Von den Ergebnissen seiner Politik. Nicht wenige, die Trump 2024 gewählt hatten, sagten Reporter*innen vor der Wahl in die Mikrophone, sie seien über Trumps gebrochene Versprechen enttäuscht: Die Senkung der Lebenshaltungskosten und die Absage an neue Kriege sind Trumps inflationstreibender Zollpolitik und dem benzinpreiserhöhenden Krieg gegen den Iran gewichen.
Und die Abschiebung „illegaler“ Migrant*innen fanden viele ebenfalls nur so lange erstrebenswert, bis vermummte Bewaffnete auftauchten, die Nachbarn verschleppten und der Wirtschaft die Arbeitskräfte wegnahmen. Die Wahlergebnisse dieser Nacht bedeuten auch, dass doch keine Mehrheit der US-Amerikaner*innen komplett gefühllos und verrückt geworden ist.
Markiert also diese Wahl tatsächlich das Ende des Trumpismus in den USA und in der Republikanischen Partei? Nicht bei einem wie Trump. Jeder andere Präsident würde bei so einem Ergebnis zur lahmsten aller lahmen Enten, würde sich vielleicht in ein paar außenpolitische Initiativen flüchten, bei denen der Kongress kaum Mitspracherecht hat und ansonsten aus dem Weißen Haus beobachten, wie in seiner Partei um die Nachfolgekandidatur gekämpft wird.
Das ist für Trump nur schwer vorstellbar – freiwillig wird er das Rampenlicht jedenfalls nicht verlassen. Es ist vielmehr zu vermuten, dass er, je enger ein demokratisch kontrollierter Kongress ihn einzuhegen versucht, auch den letzten Rest an Respekt für Regeln und Gesetze verliert und umso wilder und wütender um sich schlägt. Das kann im übrigen auch Europa treffen, Kuba, den Nahen Osten, ganz sicher die Ukraine.
Es wird eine der großen Fragen werden, ob die Wahlklatsche jetzt endlich zu einem Aufwachen der Republikaner führt, um nicht als Partei mit Trump unterzugehen. Dazu braucht es aber Führungsfiguren, die den Widerspruch wagen. Der erzrechte Kulturkämpfer Ron DeSantis, abtretender Gouverneur von Florida, hat gerade erste Schritte in die Richtung gemacht, indem er sich traute, die hohen Benzinpreise Trumps Krieg im Iran anzulasten. Aber ob da noch mehr kommt, ist ungewiss.
Die Demokraten ihrerseits haben einerseits innerparteiliche Machtkämpfe vor sich, und nicht nur über die Frage der Präsidentschaftskandidatur 2028. Sie haben so umfassend gewonnen, dass sich daraus kaum ableiten lässt, ob nun linke, progressive oder doch eher zentristische Ansätze erfolgversprechender sind.
Und: Sie müssen sich sehr genau überlegen, was sie mit ihrer neuen Macht in Washington anstellen wollen. Es wird sehr schnell der Moment kommen, an dem Trumps Regelverstöße ein Ausmaß annehmen, dass eine demokratische Führung des Repräsentantenhauses glauben wird, kaum anders zu können, als ein weiteres Amtsenthebungsverfahren einzuleiten – eine zutiefst unpopuläre Maßnahme auch bei vielen, die jetzt demokratisch gewählt haben.
Trump hat alles daran gegeben, die Machtkompetenzen in Washington weiter Richtung Weißes Haus zu verschieben. Aufgabe der Demokraten muss es sein, zumindest wieder ein effektives Gegengewicht aufzubauen. https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/uae-i.author: Elis Gjevori
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/uae-i.text:
How the UAE-Israel-Morocco threat pushed Algiers to send troops to Niger
An Algerian military convoy arrived in Niger last Friday, marking the country's first deployment of forces abroad since 1973, when it supported Egypt in its war against the Israeli occupation of the Sinai peninsula.
The deployment marks a major departure from Algeria’s longstanding policy of principled non-intervention. It follows Algiers’ decision to send four fighter jets to Niger on 30 August to thwart an attempted coup against President Abdourahamane Tiani.
Although the North African state opposed the 2023 coup that brought Tiani to power, Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune now appears willing to offer the beleaguered leader a much-needed lifeline.
Tiani requested the deployment. Speaking on Sunday, Algerian Senator Belkacem Boulghiti said the troops would protect economic infrastructure and oil facilities belonging to Algerian companies.
Algeria is “not sending our soldiers to wage war in Niger”, Boulghiti added.
