Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
Retired senior Algerian diplomat Amar Belani offered a clue to Algiers’ thinking in an article published in October.
Belani described growing instability in the Sahel, including Niger, as part of a “destabilisation strategy actively involving the United Arab Emirates, Morocco, Israel and certain French proxies”.
Continuing instability in Niger would “directly threaten Algerian interests” and hinder the Nigeria-Niger-Algeria trans-Saharan gas pipeline project, he added.
Security imperative
Zine Ghebouli, a visiting fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations (ECFR), told Middle East Eye that the situation in the region “is imposing new security imperatives on Algiers and the necessity to secure its strategic interests, particularly in the energy sector”.
This evolving regional situation includes an increasingly strong presence of the United Arab Emirates, with which Algeria severed diplomatic relations in September after “exhausting all means to preserve bilateral relations”.
'Algeria has accused the UAE of being responsible for bloodshed across the region and views the Emirati role as destructive'
- Zine Ghebouli, visiting fellow, ECFR
The Algerian foreign ministry said it had repeatedly warned Abu Dhabi over its “hostile actions”, devoting significant effort to “drawing the attention of the Emirati side and warning it of the grave consequences that may result from its regrettable and unjustified behaviour”.
“Despite these numerous warnings, the United Arab Emirates has persisted in these actions, which have reached a point where they can no longer be considered acceptable or tolerable within the framework of relations between two sovereign states, or remain unanswered,” the statement added.
“The fact that Algiers took the plunge to break relations proves that Emirati manoeuvering was deemed by Algerian authorities as explosive and irreconcilable,” Ghebouli said.
The UAE’s regional interventions and partnership with Israel have drawn growing opposition from governments across the region. Sudan broke ties with Abu Dhabi over its documented funding and fuelling of the country’s bloody civil war.
Somalia, Libya and Yemen have also accused Abu Dhabi of threatening their territorial integrity through its support for rival armed groups and separatist forces.
“For Algiers, Abu Dhabi’s diplomatic, financial and military support to several actors in the region from Libya to Sudan and the Sahel serves divisions,” Ghebouli said.
“Algeria has accused the UAE of being responsible for bloodshed across the region and views the Emirati role as destructive. Also, the Emirati lobbying and pressures on regional actors to expand the Abraham Accords was another point of discord,” he added, referring to the normalisation deals with Israel and Arab states, including Morocco.
In recent years, the UAE has intensively cultivated relationships with the Sahel’s military regimes through high-level diplomacy, gold trading and investment.
In May 2025, Emirati minister Sheikh Shakhboot bin Nahyan met the leaders of Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger to discuss cooperation in economic development, energy and other sectors. Mali’s government explicitly included security among the subjects discussed.
“The Sahel has long been considered as an extension of Algerian national security and Algiers now is actively acting based on that,” said Ghebouli.
“Current geopolitical shifts and all that entails in regards to rivalry with and interventions of foreign actors mean that new tools, such as a show of presence including at the military level, are no longer a taboo and will be utilised to draw and reinforce Algeria’s redlines,” he added.
Competing energy corridors
Eastern Libya’s de facto ruler, Khalifa Haftar, presents another concern. The UAE backs Haftar, who commands the Libyan Arab Armed Forces (LAAF).
His military expansion towards the corridors connecting Libya and Niger has heightened Algerian concerns about Emirati influence along its southern flank.
'By securing Niger, Algeria is protecting its own answer to the Morocco-UAE axis'
- Dr Fatiha Dazi-Heni, senior political scientist at Irsem
“Algeria has had a poor relationship with the Haftar family for several years, and the mutiny in Niger in the last days of August illustrated it,” Jalel Harchaoui, a Libya analyst affiliated with the Royal United Services Institute, told MEE.
Haftar’s son Saddam supports Mahamoud Sallah, a Nigerien opponent of Tiani.
“Saddam Haftar and the Algerian state are on opposing sides,” Harchaoui said of Niger.
“That being said, observers mustn’t assume that Algeria is intervening in Libya. Its current effort is to deploy troops on Nigerien soil, so its mission relates to what happens inside Niger: maintaining security within a framework that will become clearer over the coming days and weeks,” he added.
Turkey’s rapprochement with Haftar in October could help Algeria consolidate its foothold in the Sahel. Ankara and Algiers maintain close diplomatic relations and share interests in Libya and Sudan, potentially giving Algeria a back channel to Haftar.
Rabat is also making overtures to the Haftar family, according to reports. Lieutenant General Khaled Haftar, another of Khalifa Haftar’s sons and chief of the general staff of the eastern Libyan forces, paid an official visit to Morocco last month.
Separately, energy and economic interests also underpin Algeria’s approach to Niger.
Algeria’s national energy company Sonatrach, the Nigerien government and the Nigerian National Petroleum Corporation are jointly developing a 4,000-km pipeline to carry Nigerian gas through Niger and Algeria and onwards to Europe.
“The troops are meant to protect energy installations, notably Sonatrach’s oil projects and the corridor of the Trans-Saharan Gas Pipeline”, said Dr Fatiha Dazi-Heni, a senior political scientist specialising in the Arabian Peninsula at Irsem in Paris and Sciences Po Lille.
Morocco is promoting a rival pipeline along an Atlantic route, drawing on the same Nigerian gas reserves to supply the same European markets.
Crucially, the UAE has agreed to support the Nigeria-Morocco pipeline financially and technically.
“Niger is the one country the overland route cannot bypass. By securing Niger, Algeria is protecting its own answer to the Morocco-UAE axis. Rabat and Abu Dhabi clearly have an interest in the Atlantic route prevailing, and Israel indirectly through its partnership with Morocco,” Dazi-Heni told MEE.
“Algeria’s traditionally cautious strategic culture” now reflects “the new strategic constraints it faces”, she added.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/4.text:
Indonesian president’s chief of staff dismissed over alleged wiretapping
Government says Listyo Sigit Prabowo may have committed ‘treason’ after he is arrested, accused of wiretapping top officials’ phones.
The Indonesian president’s chief of staff has been fired for what the government says could be “treason” after he allegedly wiretapped phones with the help of two other serving police officers.
President Prabowo Subianto dismissed Listyo Sigit Prabowo on Wednesday, a day after police announced his arrest over allegations that he had illegally wiretapped phones belonging to several high-profile individuals, including the president and cabinet ministers.
Two other senior police officers were also arrested, including Ahrie Sonta Nasution, head of the legal division of the Indonesian National Police, according to local media.
“This was, of course, carried out by certain rogue individuals, and we are also of the view that what was done may already fall into a category that can be considered an act tending towards treason,” presidential spokesperson Prasetyo Hadi said on Wednesday.
“It also tends towards acts that endanger state interests and the safety of the nation’s leadership, including the safety of the head of state,” he said.
The unauthorised wiretapping allegedly took place from last year to this year while Listyo was serving as chief of the National Police, a position he held for five years before becoming the president’s chief of staff last month.
The suspects are also accused of trying to conceal their actions by ordering the deletion of files containing intercepted communications last month.
Yusril Ihza Mahendra, Indonesia’s senior minister for legal affairs, said the motive behind the alleged wiretapping has not yet been determined.
The operation was conducted “without any legal basis or without any investigative or inquiry process in accordance with applicable laws”, according to Asep Safrudin, the top detective in the National Police.
Also on Wednesday, the Indonesian military deployed more than 20,000 soldiers in the capital, Jakarta. It did not say whether the deployment was linked to the arrests.
Indonesian armed forces spokesperson Major-General Muhammad Nas said the troop movement was standard procedure for maintaining national security and territorial integrity.
“Troop deployments are a normal occurrence,” Nas said, adding that the military “must always be prepared to protect the entire nation and safeguard the integrity of the Republic of Indonesia”.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Democrats aim to sweep most US governor elections after wins in key states
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Stephanie Kirchgaessner
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Voters across the US have elected Democrats to lead many of the biggest states in the nation, marking a sea change in traditional Republican strongholds such as Georgia and Texas in what could have a profound effect on Donald Trump’s remaining term and the 2028 presidential election.
From Keisha Lance Bottoms’ victory in Georgia, making the former Atlanta mayor the first Black woman to be elected governor of any state, to Amy Acton’s win in reliably red Ohio, the results represented a repudiation of Trump, rank corruption in Washington and the power of billionaires to shape American politics. Democrats aimed to win a majority of governorships in the US, something they have not done since the 2006 midterm elections.
One of the biggest prizes of the night was the Texas governorship, with Democratic state representative Gina Hinojosa unseating Republican incumbent Greg Abbott in a stunning upset. Hinojosa will be the first Latina governor of the state, and the first Democrat elected to the Texas governorship in 30 years.
Like Hinojosa’s win, considered unthinkable in the aftermath of Trump’s 2024 victory in Texas, Lance Bottoms’ win in Georgia against billionaire Rick Jackson also represented a stunning flip of a Republican stronghold, where the GOP has held the governor’s office and both chambers of the state legislature for more than 20 years.
In Ohio, Democrat Acton defeated Republican Vivek Ramaswamy. The campaign drew national attention after Ramaswamy’s campaign aired a much-maligned ad featuring Acton’s estranged mother, who lost custody of her children after her husband was accused of sexually abusing Acton as a child, sharply criticizing her daughter. Acton is the first Democrat elected governor in the state since 2006, and the first woman elected governor of Ohio.
Iowa Democrat Rob Sand pulled off an upset against Republican Zach Lahn, marking a major step towards the party rebuilding its standing in a state that has voted for Donald Trump three times and where the GOP has dominated state politics in recent years.
And in Wisconsin, Democrat David Crowley defeated Republican Tom Tiffany to become the state’s first Black governor. Crowley, who withdrew from the race only to rejoin at the urging of the outgoing Democratic governor, Tony Evers, overcame a massive fundraising gap to win the governorship.
With about a third of the votes still to be counted in Arizona and Alaska, Democrats Katie Hobbs and Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins had wide leads in those states.
Democrats also racked up gubernatorial victories in Pennsylvania, where popular incumbent Josh Shapiro handily defeated Stacy Garrity, and New York, where Kathy Hochul sailed to re-election. Democrat Deb Haaland was elected governor of New Mexico, making her the first Native American woman to win a governorship, while Xavier Becerra, also a Democrat, became California’s first elected Latino governor.
In Florida, Byron Donalds, Republican congressman and a strong Trump ally, edged out the former Republican turned Democrat David Jolly, becoming the Sunshine state’s first Black governor.
While media attention has focused intensely on the battle to control the US Congress, and whether Democrats could not only flip the House of Representatives but also win most of the Senate, upsets in gubernatorial races in traditionally Republican states could reset the map before the 2028 presidential contest.
Most of the so-called swing states that help determine who wins the White House – including Michigan and Wisconsin – are among the 36 states electing governors in Tuesday’s midterm elections.
The first two years of Donald Trump’s second term as president have underscored the roles Democratic governors play in serving as a bulwark against Trump’s most excessive policies, including by filing lawsuits and other executive actions. While rules differ state by state, some governors appoint election officials who oversee elections, and can sign legislation to protect voter rights.
Republicans have held a majority of governorships since the 2010 election.

De l’« espoir » et une « leçon » : la gauche a célébré ce mercredi 4 novembre le revers cinglant imposé par les démocrates au président américain Donald Trump lors des élections de mi-mandat, en le comparant avec le Rassemblement national, qui a lui rejeté tout parallèle.
La candidate écologiste à la présidentielle Marine Tondelier s’est réjouie d’une « défaite historique » du dirigeant républicain après son deuxième mandat « apocalyptique ». « Mais ce qui vient de se produire aux États-Unis ces dernières années est un avertissement pour la France. Si notre pays porte au pouvoir le RN l’année prochaine, il connaîtra le même destin tragique que les États-Unis », a-t-elle écrit sur X. Elle a accusé le RN, donné en tête dans les sondages, d’être aussi « fasciste », « corrompu », « climatosceptique » et « incompétent » que Donald Trump. « Les États-Unis ont payé deux fois pour voir. Puisse cette leçon nous servir », a-t-elle dit.
Le candidat social-démocrate Raphaël Glucksmann y a lui vu « la victoire de la démocratie et de la décence ». « Il n’y a aucune fatalité en politique et ce sursaut démocrate est un message d’espoir pour tous ».
Au-delà des États-Unis, la gauche veut voir un vent favorable à sa famille politique dans les récents résultats électoraux, notamment la réélection de Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva au Brésil. « Partout dans le monde, c’est la mobilisation populaire qui permet de faire reculer l’extrême droite », s’est satisfait le coordinateur national de La France insoumise, Manuel Bompard. « En France aussi, nous le ferons ». « Quelques jours après l’éclatante victoire de Lula au Brésil, le recul de Netanyahou, voici la vague démocrate aux États-Unis », s’est enthousiasmé de son côté le premier secrétaire du Parti socialiste Olivier Faure.

Morning update
Good morning Middle East Eye readers,
Here are the latest developments:
- Iranian media is reporting that Tehran is not planning to attend talks with the United States, after President Donald Trump ordered US negotiators to travel to Pakistan on Monday, just days before a ceasefire in the Middle East expires.
- US President Donald Trump acknowledged that the war on Iran played a role in Republicans' losses in the midterm elections . "I think a part of it was Iran, but at the same time people understood the importance of what I've done with Iran," he said during an interview with Fox News. In another interview with The New York Times, the American president said he was willing to accept the results of the midterm elections.
- Iran's chief negotiator in talks with the US Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said that Americans voted "NO TO WAR" after Democrats routed Republicans in the midterm elections. "Conscience or the cost of living, Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message," Ghalibaf wrote in a post on X.
- Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said four "rogue" oil tankers were destroyed after htting naval mines while trying to traverse a route in the Strait of Hormuz that is considered prohibited. The incident occurred south of the waterway, with the statement adding that IRGC forces also intercepted two other vessels.
- Israeli opposition leader Yair Lapid has accused supporters of Benajmin Netanyahu's government of attempting to "crush" Tel Aviv's democracy. "What we are seeing tonight is an attempt to crush democracy and steal the election with the help of government plants in the security system," he said in a post on X. "This is a direct threat to our democracy from people who are unwilling to admit defeat," Lapid added.
- Speaking to the Financial Times, US President Donald Trump indicated that are no immediate plans to strike Iran. "I'm ready, we're ready. We're locked and loaded if we need to go, but there may be no reason for it," he said. "We seem to be getting everything we want," Trump added, referring to negotiations with Iran.

Syrians see Israel as biggest regional threat, followed by Iran: Survey
Some 97 percent of respondents to the Arab Opinion Index for Syria say Israel threatens security and stability in the Middle East.
Most Syrians view Israel as the greatest threat to the security of their country and the region, with Iran a distant second, according to a new nationwide survey.
The poll, conducted by the Doha-based Arab Center for Research and Policy Studies and the Arab Center for Contemporary Syria Studies, published its results on Monday.
The Arab Opinion Index for Syria 2026 found that 61 percent of respondents named Israel as the main threat to Syria, while Iran was named by 20 percent, Turkiye by 6 percent and the United States by 5 percent.
Asked about the Arab world as a whole, 58 percent of respondents named Israel as the main threat, unchanged from last year. Meanwhile, the share naming Iran as the main regional threat doubled from 12 percent in 2025 to 24 percent.
Some 97 percent said Israel threatens the security and stability of the Middle East, up from 78 percent a year earlier. The percentage of those who said the same about Iran rose from 74 to 93.
Israel has seized territory in southern Syria since the fall of Bashar al-Assad in December 2024. About 96 percent of respondents said Israel is working to destabilise Syria and 86 percent said it is driving separatist tendencies.
Almost 80 percent oppose recognising Israel, up from 74 percent in 2025, and 74 percent oppose any agreement that does not return the occupied Golan Heights. Respondents were split on direct talks between Syrian and Israeli officials: 41 percent said they serve Syria’s interests and 49 percent said they do not.
Al Jazeera interviewed residents on the streets of Damascus ahead of the Israeli elections last month. One of them, Jihad el-Hamwi, said Israel’s approach to Syria was unaffected by the change of government.
“In my opinion, Israeli policy does not change when the ruler changes, because it is an expansionist policy,” he said. “Just as it has expanded into Syria, Palestine, Lebanon and other countries, its aim is expansion, not a change of ruler.”
Another resident told Al Jazeera, “The Israeli elections only ever bring in a ruler who is unjust, who does not even recognise the rights of his neighbours, and who has absolutely no connection to international norms.”
On the US-Israel war on Iran, 80 percent of survey respondents said Iranian missile strikes on Israel were justified, with 74 percent saying Iranian strikes on Arab countries, other than US military bases, were not. Three-quarters said Washington had waged the war on Israel’s behalf.
The survey also points to growing support for pluralism: 76 percent agreed that democracy, despite its problems, is better than other systems, up 16 percentage points from last year. Three-quarters said a democratic system with political pluralism and a separation of powers was best for Syria. No alternative, including rule by Islamic law without elections, drew more than 9 percent.
About 87 percent of respondents said no one should question the patriotism of people who oppose government policy, a 20-point increase.
Views of the country’s direction were mixed. Half said Syria was heading the right way, citing the end of the former government, the release of detainees and the lifting of sanctions, but 35 percent disagreed.
The survey comes nearly two years after al-Assad was toppled in an offensive led by opposition fighters, ending more than five decades of his family’s rule.

De l’« espoir » et une « leçon » : la gauche a célébré ce mercredi 4 novembre le revers cinglant imposé par les démocrates au président américain Donald Trump lors des élections de mi-mandat, en le comparant avec le Rassemblement national, qui a lui rejeté tout parallèle.
La candidate écologiste à la présidentielle Marine Tondelier s’est réjouie d’une « défaite historique » du dirigeant républicain après son deuxième mandat « apocalyptique ». « Mais ce qui vient de se produire aux États-Unis ces dernières années est un avertissement pour la France. Si notre pays porte au pouvoir le RN l’année prochaine, il connaîtra le même destin tragique que les États-Unis », a-t-elle écrit sur X. Elle a accusé le RN, donné en tête dans les sondages, d’être aussi « fasciste », « corrompu », « climatosceptique » et « incompétent » que Donald Trump. « Les États-Unis ont payé deux fois pour voir. Puisse cette leçon nous servir », a-t-elle dit.
Le candidat social-démocrate Raphaël Glucksmann y a lui vu « la victoire de la démocratie et de la décence ». « Il n’y a aucune fatalité en politique et ce sursaut démocrate est un message d’espoir pour tous ».
Au-delà des États-Unis, la gauche veut voir un vent favorable à sa famille politique dans les récents résultats électoraux, notamment la réélection de Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva au Brésil. « Partout dans le monde, c’est la mobilisation populaire qui permet de faire reculer l’extrême droite », s’est satisfait le coordinateur national de La France insoumise, Manuel Bompard. « En France aussi, nous le ferons ». « Quelques jours après l’éclatante victoire de Lula au Brésil, le recul de Netanyahou, voici la vague démocrate aux États-Unis », s’est enthousiasmé de son côté le premier secrétaire du Parti socialiste Olivier Faure.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/4.title: GOP’s redistricting gamble backfires in Florida as Democrats hold ground
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/4.text:
GOP’s redistricting gamble backfires in Florida as Democrats hold ground
Trump’s party dealt a setback as the Republican bid to tilt Florida’s House map falters on a strong night for Democrats.
The Democratic Party has won several United States House of Representatives seats that Florida’s Republican-led legislature redrew to favour the GOP in a redistricting effort.
In a sweeping result reflecting Democrats’ broader midterm election victory, Kathy Castor held Florida’s 14th congressional district, which swung nearly 16 percentage points towards Democrats compared with its 2024 presidential vote.
Democratic first-time candidate Pia Dandiya won the 22nd district, and Jared Moskowitz retained the 25th.
Notably, the race between incumbent Darren Soto and Republican challenger Dan Green in Florida’s 9th district remained the closest of the four, with Soto holding a slim lead as the final votes were counted on Wednesday.
The wins add to a wave of Democratic victories across the nation, in an election widely cast as a referendum on President Donald Trump. Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress, including at least 54 Senate seats, a major setback for Trump that could provide a significant check on his power in his final two years in office.
Florida’s returns also offer another measure of the electoral headwinds facing Republicans this election cycle, despite tilting the district map in their favour to make several seats more Republican-friendly.
Longtime Trump ally and outgoing Florida Governor Ron DeSantis and the state’s Republican-controlled legislature redrew Florida’s congressional map in April, seeking to bolster the party’s chances of retaining control of the US House.
The move formed part of an unprecedented nationwide Republican effort to secure a structural advantage ahead of the midterms by reshaping the boundaries of congressional representation.
The revised boundaries gave Trump’s party a lead in four Democratic-held districts: the 9th, 14th, 22nd, and 25th, and were explicitly engineered to compress the state’s Democratic delegation in the US House.
Under the new map, signed into law by DeSantis in May, Trump would have carried three of the four districts by double-digit margins during his 2024 presidential campaign, and the fourth by roughly 9 percentage points.
At the time, some had argued that redrawing the map may backfire on Republicans, diluting the party’s strongholds and tightening margins at a time when Trump’s approval ratings had dipped to an all-time low amid the economic knock-ons of the US-Israel war on Iran.
Redistricting is the process of redrawing electoral boundaries, usually after the US census every 10 years, to account for population shifts and ensure districts maintain roughly equal populations.
The boundaries determine which voters are grouped together to elect a representative to the US House.
Because the party in power in a state legislature often has a hand in drawing the map, the process can be used to give one party an electoral advantage – a practice known as gerrymandering.
Following tit-for-tat map re-drawings, Republicans hoped to net at least 13 seats nationally, though polling had suggested their gains may be much more muted.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Democrats’ blue wave and a bad night for Trump: key US midterms takeaways
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Ariana Baio
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
- 1. The blue wave Democrats saw their hoped-for “blue wave” become reality by flipping seven Senate seats, more than two dozen House seats and expanding the number of Democratic governors. Shortly after polls closed, Democrats saw winning streaks in closely watched Senate races. Before midnight, the Associated Press had declared Democrats would hold the majority in Congress’s upper chamber. Less than two hours later, they secured the House. With control over both chambers, Democrats gain the authority to push back on Trump’s agenda. Tuesday evening’s results were sweeping, with states and districts that voted for Trump two years ago abandoning the president’s allies in the midterms. Even Republican incumbents running in comfortably red areas, such as Florida, were locked in close races with Democrats.  In one of the most closely watched races of the night, the Democrat Abdul El-Sayed won in Michigan in the face of a largely Islamophobic campaign against him.
- 2. Republicans suffer historic losses The Democrats’ win was underscored by Republicans’ historic losses across the country. For the first time in 94 years, a Democrat won a Senate seat in Kansas, with Adam Hamilton defeating Roger Marshall. Republicans lost a South Carolina Senate seat for the first time in nearly 30 years when Dr. Annie Andrews defeated Darline Graham – the sister of the late senator Lindsey Graham and a close ally of Trump. James Talarico, a progressive Democratic newcomer, defeated Ken Paxton, the state’s conservative attorney general, in Texas’s Senate race, ending Republicans’ 38-year streak. Iowa and North Carolina also had not elected a Democratic senator since 2008.
- 3. Trump walks back claims to be on the ballot After suffering major losses, Trump asserted he “wasn’t on the Ballot” but “would have won IN A LANDSLIDE” if he was – a reversal from his request that voters act as though he was. For weeks, Trump had encouraged supporters to vote as though he was a candidate on the ballot, in the hopes of generating support for Republicans. But on Tuesday night, he dismissed concerns that the midterm results were a reflection of that. “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE! Thank you for your attention to this matter,” Trump said. He reiterated his claim to the New York Times, saying: “I wasn’t on the ticket, and because I wasn’t on the ticket, we couldn’t get enough people out to vote.” The US president, who has a long history of making false election fraud claims, also told the newspaper he was “absolutely willing” to accept the results of the midterms.
- In the lead-up to the election, polls indicated Democrats were poised to win the House and possibly the Senate, with Democratic candidates holding narrow leads over Republicans in competitive Senate races. But pre-election polls were more reserved about Democratic candidates’ prospects, in part due to the failed predictions over the 2024 presidential election. In the Kansas Senate race, pre-election polls indicated Hamilton had a small lead over Marshall. But pollsters from the Washington Post warned that the prediction could be misleading because Democratic voters were more likely to respond than Republicans.
- 5. Trump’s handpicked candidates lose In another example of voters’ rebuke of Trump, the US president’s handpicked candidates in key races lost their bids to Democrats. Historically, candidates endorsed by Trump perform well in primaries and general elections. But this time around, those candidates could not convince voters to cast their ballot for them. In the Texas Senate race, Paxton lost even after securing Trump’s support in a contentious primary. In the South Carolina Senate race, Darline Graham failed to defeat Annie Andrews, even after Trump elevated Graham to take over her late brother’s seat and campaigned for her heavily. Trump chose Michael Whatley to fend off the Democrat Roy Cooper in North Carolina’s Senate race, but he failed to do so.

https://taz.de/US-Midterm-Wahlen/!622718.author: Hansjürgen Mai
https://taz.de/US-Midterm-Wahlen/!622718.text:
US-Midterm-Wahlen: Die Demokraten räumen auch in Texas ab
Es ist eine historische Nacht in dem konservativen Bundesstaat. Der bibelfeste Talarico holt den Senatsposten, die bisher eher unbekannte Hinojosa das Gouverneursamt.
Die blaue Welle, die in der vergangenen Wahlnacht bei den Midterms durch die Vereinigten Staaten zog, hat auch in Texas nicht haltgemacht. Mit James Talarico haben die Demokraten zum ersten Mal seit 1988 wieder eine Senatswahl in dem christlich-konservativen Bundesstaat gewonnen. Noch überraschender als der Sieg Talaricos kam der Erfolg von Gina Hinojosa, die im Rennen um das Gouverneursamt den republikanischen Amtsinhaber Greg Abbott besiegte. Hinojosa wird damit zur ersten Latino-Gouverneurin in der Geschichte des Bundesstaates.
Für die Demokratische Partei galt Texas lange Zeit als Luftschloss. Immer mal wieder stand sie knapp vor einem Sieg – aber am Ende blieb er doch unerreichbar. Dass es nach Jahrzehnten jetzt doch geklappt hat, ist auf mehrere Gründe zurückzuführen.
Ein skandalfreier Demokrat wird Senator für Texas
Im Senatsrennen trat mit Talarico ein charismatischer, bibelsicherer Landespolitiker ohne Skandale an. Sein republikanischer Kontrahent, der texanische Justizminister Ken Paxton, war das genaue Gegenteil. Ein von US-Präsident Donald Trump installierter, skandalgeplagter Politiker, dessen eigene Partei versucht hatte, ihn des Amtes zu entheben. „Heute Abend haben wir Goliath besiegt“, sagte Talarico vor einer jubelnden Menge auf seiner Wahlparty in Austin. Er bezeichnet sich selbst als progressiver Christ und trat mit dem Versprechen an, Korruption zu bekämpfen und die Lebenshaltungskosten zu senken.
Sein Sieg ist ein schwerer Schlag für die Republikaner und für Trump selbst. Trump und seine Verbündeten pumpten Millionen Dollar in den Wahlkampf; bei Wahlkampfveranstaltungen griff der Präsident Talarico zudem häufig an und stilisierte ihn dabei zu einem landesweiten Sinnbild für die Demokraten.
Talarico selbst konzentrierte seinen Wahlkampf auf wirtschaftliche Themen und die Korruption. Und legte sich dabei mit dem reichsten Mann der Welt, Elon Musk, immer wieder an. Dieser hatte Millionen in die Wahlen in Texas investiert, um republikanische Kandidaten zu unterstützen. Im Wahlkampf erklärte Talarico, dass die größte Spaltung in den USA „nicht zwischen links und rechts“ verlaufe, sondern „zwischen oben und unten.“
Vor allem Latino-Wähler in Texas, die vor zwei Jahren noch für Trump gestimmt haben, haben aufgrund der wirtschaftlichen Situation sowie dem Vorgehen der Einwanderungsbehörde ICE der republikanischen Partei vermehrt den Rücken gekehrt. „Sie mussten miterleben, wie ihre Nachbarn oder Angehörigen abgeführt, abgeschoben oder verhaftet wurden“, sagte Stephanie Guerra aus San Antonio der taz.
Im Vorfeld zeigten die Umfragen, dass es für Talarico ein knappes Rennen sein würde. Nach den bisher ausgezählten Stimmen liegt er nun aber mit elf Prozentpunkten vor Paxton.
Erste Latino-Gouverneurin für Texas
Anders war die Ausgangslage für Gina Hinojosa. Sie ist ebenfalls eine texanische Abgeordnete, doch im Gegensatz zu Talarico fehlten ihr der Bekanntheitsgrad und die Unterstützung der demokratischen Parteizentrale.
Es gelang ihr jedoch, einen populistischen Wahlkampf zu führen. Sie kritisiert den Ausbau von Rechenzentren für künstliche Intelligenz sowie die Korruption in der Politik. Amtsinhaber Abbott – der seit Jahrzehnten eine feste Größe in der texanischen Politik ist und für seine vierte Amtszeit als Gouverneur kandidierte – schien seine Herausforderin unterschätzt zu haben.
„In Texas ist alles größer – auch die Überraschung über diesen Sieg. Wir haben heute Abend die Welt verblüfft. Mit dem typischen texanischen Kampfgeist zeigen wir, dass alles möglich ist“, sagte Hinojosa nach ihrem Sieg. Als Gouverneurin des Bundesstaates mit der zweitgrößten Einwohnerzahl nach Kalifornien kann sie nun die Bundespolitik beeinflussen.
Abbott hatte dies in der Vergangenheit mit seiner konfrontativen Immigrationspolitik gezeigt: Unter dem demokratischen Ex-Präsidenten Joe Biden installierte er etwa physische Barrieren, schickte Sicherheitskräfte an die Grenze.
„Wäre Greg Abbott, der Gouverneur von Texas, in den letzten sechs Monaten seiner politischen Laufbahn nicht zu einem RINO (Republican in Name Only) geworden, hätte er nicht verloren“, kommentiert allerdings Trump dessen Niederlage.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. US midterm elections 2026: Abdul El-Sayed becomes first Muslim elected to Senate
Progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed won a highly coveted Michigan Senate seat on Wednesday, and will become the first Muslim to serve in the upper chamber of Congress come January.
El-Sayed declared victory with 80 percent of votes counted, showing him in a comfortable 51.8 percent lead compared to his Republican opponent Mike Rogers at 46.2 percent.
The Associated Press declared El-Sayed the winner at 2:27 am EST (7:27 GMT)
"I am so proud and honored to stand here as your senator-elect," Sayed said in an energized victory speech, where he said he was able to overcome Islamophobic slurs aimed at him by US President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance.
"To all the parents who struggled to explain [to their kids] why the president openly mocked someone for their name or how they pray, let them know tomorrow that the bad guys lost," he said to cheers and applause.

Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
"They want an America that is too small for some of us. We know that America is big enough for all of us," he added.
US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed celebrated his victory by taking on Aipac and the special interests that poured millions into trying to defeat him https://t.co/Wd2L9m9qdC
— Middle East Eye (@MiddleEastEye) November 4, 2026
Sayed, smiling and responding to lively applause specifically called out Vance and Trump.
"JD, habibi, there is this delicious irony in the fact that you're constitutionally obligated to swear me in in January," he said.
To Trump he said: "Donald, I know you struggle with my name, so after JD swears me in in January, you can just go on and call me Senator".
Sayed's victory marks a watershed moment in US political history.
'We don't want our money sent to do apartheid or genocidal war,'
Abdul El-Sayed
A progressive who shocked the party establishment when he narrowly defeated Haley Stevens, who was backed by pro-Israel lobbying groups, in the August Democratic primary, Sayed was endorsed early by the Senate's leading voice on progressive issues, Bernie Sanders of Vermont.
Sayed specifically challenged the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac) and other pro-Israel lobbying groups that spent tens of millions of dollars against him.
"To Aipac who spent $42 million against us. Thank you for giving me the opportunity to beat you twice," he said.
"They try to call you hateful if you believe that Palestinian kids should get to grow up in the land of their forefathers without being murdered by our tax dollars," he said. "If you believe in equal rights for peace, diginity and self-determination that's not hate, it's love," he said.
"We want our taxes spent here...we don't want our money sent to do apartheid or genocidal war," he said.
That race proved so pivotal that half a million more Democratic voters showed up to the polls than in previous primary races, which typically see low turnouts, Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel said at the time.
In the later stages of his campaign, Sayed received the backing of former President Barack Obama, who remains one of the most popular figures among the party establishment.
Who is Abdul El-Sayed?
The 42-year-old's full name is Abdulrahman Mohammed El-Sayed. He is married to an Indian-American doctor and has two daughters. When he graduated from the University of Michigan and gave the commencement address in 2007, the event's keynote speaker, former President Bill Clinton, praised his oratory skills at the podium.
The Michigan native then earned a medical degree from Columbia University and led the public health departments in Detroit and Wayne County before launching what was seen as a long-shot bid for the US Senate in 2025.
But it wasn't his first time.
In 2018, Sayed unsuccessfully sought the governorship of Michigan, but he managed to lay the foundations for his vision for Medicare-For-All: the establishment of a national health insurance programme in the US.
As private insurance premiums have skyrocketed in the US since then, that policy proposal grew increasingly popular among those on the left and the right, as did Sayed's criticism of the closeness of the US-Israel relationship - an approach that was very similar to that of the highly popular New York City mayor, Zohran Mamdani.
Sayed has repeatedly said that he has never met with corporate lobbyists, and in both his campaigns, he raised money only from individual donors rather than corporations.
'He's different'
Unlike Mamdani, however, Sayed was not endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America, as he sought the support of his party's centrists in a volatile swing state like Michigan.
He appeared on as many television networks, podcasts, and social media influencer accounts as he could, in a bid to reach as many segments of the American public as possible, regardless of political affiliation, Sayed often said.
But he was also met with such a disproportionate amount of media scrutiny that he inadvertently became better known - and perhaps more appealing - to voters than his opponent, former Republican Congressman Mike Rogers.
Rogers, who was not under the microscope in the same manner, was endorsed by President Donald Trump at a time when the president's approval ratings were at an all-time low.
Trump has repeatedly called Sayed "a Communist loser who hates Jews and Israel", and insisted that he would only call him "Mohammed" because that's what the majority of Muslims are called, Trump said.
Republicans also cast doubt on his allegiance to the US Constitution, claiming he had ties to the Muslim Brotherhood because of statements his half-sister once made.
There is no known evidence tying Sayed to the group, which has no central hub and was not designated as a terrorist organisation in the US until Trump sanctioned three of its political branches last year.
Sayed said in August that the focus on his name and identity is "the only play they got" against him.
"It's like, wow, he's different," he said of Republican attacks.
"That's the best you got? You can't actually talk about what you want to do? My name is not raising your gas prices. My name is not taking us to war. My name is not the reason you can't afford your groceries."

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/4.title: ‘Rejecting hate’: Abdul El-Sayed wins Senate seat despite racist attacks
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/4.text:
‘Rejecting hate’: Abdul El-Sayed wins Senate seat despite racist attacks
The progressive Democrat defeats Republican Mike Rogers to win Michigan seat to become first Muslim senator-elect in US history.
Detroit, Michigan — Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed has defeated his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, to win the United States Senate seat in Michigan, overcoming a campaign of anti-Muslim attacks spearheaded by President Donald Trump.
With the victory on Tuesday, El-Sayed is set to become the first Muslim senator in US history. He will be sworn in on January 3 .
Maya Berry, executive director of the Arab American Institute (AAI), said Republicans had turned anti-Arab and anti-Muslim tropes into a pointed strategy against El-Sayed — one that eventually did not work.
“The electorate rejecting that bigotry is tremendous, I would argue, for every little boy named Abdul, every little girl named Zainab, every little kid named Bobby, because the reality is, at the end of the day, we’re talking about whether this country supports an inclusive democracy or not,” Berry told Al Jazeera.
After winning a hard-fought primary in August that saw the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) spend more than $30m against him, El-Sayed, a critic of Israel’s policies, was subjected to an avalanche of unfounded accusations — including that he is a “jihadist” — by Trump and other Republicans.
El-Sayed, a former public health official, campaigned on expanding government-funded healthcare to all Americans, getting money out of politics, and addressing the affordability crisis.
The Democrat has also accused Israel of carrying out a genocide in Gaza and called for investing money currently spent on foreign wars to instead fix local issues.
The final days of the campaign were rocked by El-Sayed’s former primary opponent, Democratic Congresswoman Haley Stevens — a staunch Israel supporter — endorsing Rogers.
El-Sayed’s win helps Democrats regain control of the Senate, but for many of his supporters, it means far more than a single seat in the upper chamber of Congress.
Throughout Election Day on Tuesday, voters in Michigan told Al Jazeera the election could determine the direction of the state and the country for years to come.
For Democrats, the vote was about rejecting Trump’s agenda and defeating the racist rhetoric from the president and his allies.
Republicans not only used Islamophobia against El-Sayed, but also invoked Arab-Black tensions to try to peel off African American voters from the Democratic coalition.
Michigan is home to a large Arab American community.
Trump seized on that narrative, saying that any Black or Jewish person who backs El-Sayed is “crazy”.
But early election results show that El-Sayed performed well with Black voters in Detroit.
Gary Colbert, who was casting his ballot on the west side of Detroit, denounced Trump’s comment about Black voters.
“Everybody kind of knows he’s the true nut. He says any and everything,” Colbert told Al Jazeera.
Colbert — who lamented the rise in gas prices due to the Iran war — added that Trump and “his cronies” are negatively affecting people’s lives, “and they don’t care”.
Trump, who is struggling with low approval ratings, told supporters in Michigan last month to vote as if he was on the ballot.
On Tuesday, Frank Espinosa, a teacher who was volunteering at a voting station in Southwest Detroit — home to a large Latino community — said protecting immigrants from Trump’s crackdown is a priority for voters in the city in this election. The Trump administration has targeted immigrant communities across the country by deploying Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers on the streets, tasked with arresting allegedly undocumented migrants. Dozens of people have been shot, and several of them killed — including American citizens protesting against what they see as reckless methods of enforcement.
“I think the number one thing we want is ICE out of our streets,” Espinosa told Al Jazeera.
“We also want the end to foreign wars. I know my students want their gas bills to be better. We want affordability all across our city, not just at the gas pump, but at the grocery store as well.”
He added that the campaign targeting El-Sayed’s Muslim faith and Arab identity is “incredibly disheartening”.
“I also know that Detroit is better than all of that, and I think that there’s a lot of noise outside of our state, outside of our city. But here, I know Detroiters will ultimately do the right thing and ultimately vote Abdul for Senate,” Espinosa said.
In neighbouring Dearborn, a Detroit suburb known as the Capital of Arab America, the vote — for many — was about the right to belong to the US.
Ali Baleed Almaklani, a leader in the Yemeni American community, said the anti-Muslim campaign motivated the Arab and Muslim community to increase its political participation.
“We are sick and tired and the American people are generally sick and tired of all this hate,” Almaklani told Al Jazeera.
“He’s talking about healthcare, about the economy, about the issues that are hurting people, and on the other side all they talk about is ‘terrorism’ and baseless accusations about the Muslim Brotherhood.”
Dearborn saw a high voter turnout on Tuesday, with lines stretching across polling stations.
Several voters told Al Jazeera they are responding to bigotry through the ballot box.
In an animated, expletive-laden interview, Dearborn voter Mike Mohammed criticised the Republican-led campaigns to paint Arabs and Muslims, including El-Sayed, as foreigners.
“We’re more American than them. I’m more American than any of them m************. I grew up here. I went to this school,” he said, pointing to the elementary school where the voting was taking place.
Sally Howell, an emeritus history professor at the University of Michigan-Dearborn who pioneered academic research about Arab American communities, said El-Sayed’s victory shows that the American people want change.
“This change also includes a rejection of hate in politics, especially anti-Muslim hate,” Howell told Al Jazeera. “And it includes a recognition of the value of Palestinian lives alongside those of Americans, immigrants, and so many others. For the Arab community in Michigan, it means people can wake up in the morning knowing that their contributions to the American body politic will be acknowledged, their voices heard and welcomed, their labour rewarded.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: US voters rebuke Trump as Democrats win control of Congress in ‘blue wave’
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Ed Pilkington in Anchorage, Alaska
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Donald Trump has been dealt a devastating blow to his authority in a night of crushing defeats in the midterm elections, which saw his Republican party stripped of control of the Senate and the House as his handpicked “Maga” candidates were swept away by a blue tsunami.
The president spent weeks before the election pleading with the American people to pretend he was on the ballot. He may now rue that tactic: the American people took him at his word, and delivered him a bloody nose of historic proportions, flinging his presidency into lame duck status.
He appeared last night to have changed his mind, declaring on social media: “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!”
As the night progressed, one shock followed the next. Top of the list was Texas, the state that has come to epitomise the iron fist of modern Republican rule.
In a seismic shift, James Talarico became the first Democrat to be sent by Texas to the US Senate since 1988. A Democratic dream of flipping the state that has been frustrated in countless previous cycles finally came to pass.
The Presbyterian seminarian used his faith combined with a stringent call for economic justice to undermine 30 years of Texas Republican rule. In the process he took down Trump’s controversial pick, the scandal-ridden state attorney general, Ken Paxton, despite hundreds of millions of dollars poured into the race by Republicans, including funds from Elon Musk.
“Against big money and big odds we took our power back,” Talarico said in his victory speech. He slammed the negative campaign that had been waged by his opponent, which he said amounted to the “final howls of a dying establishment, the death rattle of a status quo that knows its days are numbered”.
In a double whammy, out too went Greg Abbott, the titan of Texas Republican politics. He was ousted by Gina Hinojosa, who becomes the first Democratic governor of Texas in 36 years.
Her elevation to the state’s highest office as its first Latina governor stands in itself as a repudiation of the Trump administration. The brutal mass deportation campaign unleashed by ICE against Hispanics in Texas was one of Trump’s most resounding own goals, as it pushed away droves of voters who had backed him only two years ago.
In Michigan, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, the doctor and progressive insurgent, made history in winning the closely watched Senate race, defeating the Republican Mike Rogers and becoming the country’s first Muslim senator.
His opponent and detractors, including Trump, led a largely Islamophobic campaign against him, often pointing to his name and faith, including the president alleging he was a “jihadist” and that he would need to walk through a metal detector to get into the Senate.
“They want an America that is too small for some of us,” El-Sayed said. “We know that America is big enough for all of us.”
The pattern of stunning Republican defeats was repeated across the country, from the East Coast through the plains, and even deep into the American South. It amounted to a withering rebuke of Trump’s broken promises, economic follies, and war with Iran at a time when many American families are struggling to put food on the table and gas in their tanks.
The list of astounding results extended to Kansas, a state that until recent days lay well beyond even the most optimistic Democrats’ wildest fantasies. Adam Hamilton, a mega-church pastor, becomes the first Democrat to win a US Senate seat in the state in 94 years.
He throws out Roger Marshall, the incumbent, who became a poster boy for Republican callousness when it was revealed he had sued 700 of his own patients for failing to pay him their medical bills when practising as a doctor.
Among the most jaw dropping results of the night was the victory of Annie Andrews, a Democratic pediatrician, in the deeply conservative southern state of South Carolina. She defeated Darline Graham, the late Trump loyalist Lindsey Graham’s sister, marking the first time South Carolina has sent any Democrat to the Senate since 1998.
Trump had personally persuaded Graham to stand for election in her brother’s seat. She had her misgivings, aware of her lack of experience which she fatally exposed during an election debate in which she said that national security was “not my thing”.
In Maine there was another shock when just before 1am Susan Collins conceded to Democrat Troy Jackson, letting go of a Senate seat she had held for almost 30 years.
Trump spent the night watching his party’s disaster unfold on a White House TV set. He was reportedly fuming.
Though he is unlikely to admit it publicly, the extent of the personal drubbing he experienced on Tuesday night cannot be exaggerated. A political leader who appeared over the past 10 years to have a unique touch that protected him from the perils that befall mortal politicians had waved his magic wand, and this time nothing happened.
A prediction made by leading pundits just a few days ago now appears to hold substance: Tuesday night may come to be seen as marking the end of the Trump era.
It was a night in which the American people spoke more loudly and clearly than many had anticipated. As such, it could also have enormous implications for Trump’s final two years in office, and with it the immediate future of the US and the world.
Hakeem Jeffries is now poised to become the first Black speaker of the House in US history. “America is back,” he said on Tuesday night. “Today begins the great American comeback. The American people have spoken all across the land, from sea to shining sea, and made clear they have had enough of the extremism and corruption.”
Democrats flipped critical Republican House seats across the country, extinguishing some already dwindling GOP seats in places such as New York and New Jersey, and scoring upsets in deep red districts in states from Tennessee to Texas.
They also scored a string of victories in districts that Republicans redrew to their advantage earlier this year.
From January, the incoming Democratic caucus will enjoy a majority whose final numbers have yet to be finalised but not its whopping scale. So emboldened, they have indicated they will use their newly-acquired oversight and subpoena powers aggressively to investigate the most egregious of Trump’s excesses.
That includes the president’s financial enrichment of himself and his family, which Democratic leaders have said amounts to corruption.
The incoming Democratic majority is also likely to hit the White House with a blizzard of war powers resolutions designed to pressure Trump to end his war with Iran. Democratic leaders are preparing to challenge his tariffs regime, work to rein in ICE and its mass deportation efforts, and move to reinstate cuts to Medicaid, healthcare subsidies and other welfare benefits.
Pete Hegseth, the combative defense secretary, is also in Democratic crosshairs.
With the Senate also under their control, Democrats will have the power to block many of Trump’s judicial and cabinet appointments. They are unlikely though to be able to pass major legislation, given the 60-vote filibuster, but they will want to be seen trying to bring sustenance to hard-up working people.
“Five words for the American people,” the Democratic Senate leader Chuck Schumer said. “Relief is on the way.”
Trump has already made clear that he intends to block any Democratic-initiated legislation by wielding what he called “tremendous powers”. To ram the point home, Trump released a photo of a red Maga hat on Tuesday night, with the word Maga replaced with “VETO”.
Despite such characteristic bluster, Trump will find it hard to argue away a night of unrelenting terrible results. As John King, the CNN political analyst, put it, “this is the collapse of the president’s party on live TV”.
Alarm bells for the Republicans began ringing early in the night, with Jon Ossoff winning re-election to his Georgia senate seat shortly before 8pm on the east coast. That the Democrat swatted away his Trump-endorsed challenger Mike Collins so comfortably, in a state which the president won two years ago, set the compass needle in for what was to come.
Less than half an hour later, still chillingly early in the evening for Trump and his party, Democrats picked up the first of four senate seats they needed to retake the upper chamber. Former governor Roy Cooper defeated another Trump chosen one, the former national Republican party chairman, Michael Whatley.
Such a convincing win is likely further to elevate Ossoff in the hearts of Democrats as a potential 2028 presidential candidate. He proved himself during the campaign to be a fearsome debater, fundraising juggernaut, and savvy social media operator – three skills that Democrats will be desperately seeking in two years’ time as they look to prevent a Trump successor in the White House.
There were implications too from Tuesday night for a leading Republican contender for the 2028 presidential race, JD Vance. The incumbent senator in the Ohio seat he vacated when he became Trump’s vice-president, John Husted, was another one to bite the dust when he was defeated by the former Democratic senator, Sherrod Brown.
Like Texas, Ohio also experienced a double whammy. In addition to the Senate seat, the governor’s mansion also fell to the Democrat Amy Acton. It was another astonishing blow for a Trump-endorsed candidate: Vivek Ramaswamy who alienated many voters when he released one of the most contentious election adverts in recent memory featuring Acton’s estranged mother from whose custody she had been removed when she was 12.
“Ohio has chosen unity and decency over division and hate,” Acton said at her party HQ. “The healing begins today.”

À la veille de la mobilisation du 5 novembre, l’intersyndicale a déposé un recours pour contraindre la préfecture de police de Paris à statuer sur le tracé de la manifestation. Cette offensive judiciaire dénonce une tendance nationale : de Lyon à Toulouse, les autorités s’appuient sur le spectre du 17 octobre pour éloigner les cortèges des hypercentres, ravivant les tensions autour du maintien de l’ordre et de la garantie constitutionnelle du droit à manifester.
Le bras de fer se déplace donc aussi sur le terrain judiciaire. L’intersyndicale (CFDT, FSU, Solidaires, FO, CGT, UNEF) a choisi de saisir le tribunal administratif en référé. L’objectif est clair : forcer la préfecture de police de Paris à abattre ses cartes avant mercredi 14 heures concernant le tracé demandé entre Bastille et Concorde. Les organisateurs redoutent un arrêté d’interdiction ou de modification de parcours publié à la toute dernière minute, une manœuvre qui les priverait de la possibilité de contester la décision devant un juge....

https://taz.de/-Nachrichten-im-Ukrainekr.title: +++ Nachrichten im Ukrainekrieg +++: Ukraine trifft Logistikzentrum von russischem Onlinehändler
https://taz.de/-Nachrichten-im-Ukrainekr.text:
+++ Nachrichten im Ukrainekrieg +++: Ukraine trifft Logistikzentrum von russischem Onlinehändler
Kyjiw hat mit Drohnen ein Versandzentrum eines russischen Internethändlers angegriffen. Trump zeigt sich mit Blick auf die anstehenden Friedensgespräche optimistisch.
Ukraine trifft Logistikzentrum von russischem Onlinehändler
Die Ukraine hat in der Nacht erneut eine Filiale eines großen russischen Internethändlers angegriffen. Die Mitarbeiter eines Logistikzentrums von Ozon in der südrussischen Teilrepublik Adygeja seien wegen eines Drohnenangriffs evakuiert worden, berichtete die staatliche russische Nachrichtenagentur Tass unter Berufung auf das Unternehmen. In dem Zentrum sei ein Feuer ausgebrochen. Nach vorläufigen Angaben gab es keine Verletzten. Die Angaben konnten zunächst nicht unabhängig überprüft werden.
Die Ukraine hat in den vergangenen Wochen verstärkt Versandzentren der russischen Online-Riesen Wildberries und Ozon zerstört oder beschädigt. Das Land wehrt sich seit Februar 2022 mit westlicher Hilfe gegen eine russische Invasion und greift in seinem Abwehrkampf seit mehreren Monaten systematisch auch weit entfernte Ziele in Russland an.
Derweil machte US-Präsident Donald Trump in der britischen Financial Times deutlich, er sei optimistisch, dass die Friedensgespräche zwischen der Ukraine und Russland Fortschritte machten. „Ich glaube, beide Seiten sind an dem Punkt angelangt, an dem sie sagen: Lasst uns eine Einigung erzielen“, sagte er. Nächste Woche Dienstag und Mittwoch finden unter Vermittlung der USA in den Vereinigten Arabischen Emiraten die ersten direkten Gespräche zwischen der Ukraine und Russland seit Langem statt.
Am Dienstag hatte Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz den ukrainischen Präsidenten Wolodymyr Selenskyj in Berlin getroffen. Beide pochten darauf, dass die Europäer an den anstehenden Gesprächen zur Beendigung des russischen Angriffskriegs beteiligt werden müssten. Deutschland ist der wichtigste Unterstützer der Ukraine.
Selenskyj schrieb am späten Abend auf der Plattform X, er habe Bundespräsident Frank-Walter Steinmeier für die umfassende Unterstützung Deutschlands gedankt. Europa bezeichnete er als wichtigen Bestandteil, den Friedensprozess voranzutreiben. (dpa)
Russland greift wieder mehrere ukrainische Regionen an
Russland hat in der Nacht wieder zahlreiche Landesteile der Ukraine angegriffen. Dabei seien zwei Kraftwerke in den Regionen Kyjiw und Schytomyr getroffen worden, teilte das russische Verteidigungsministerium auf dem Kurzmitteilungsdienst Telegram mit. Zudem sei ein Frachtschiff nahe der Hafenstadt Odessa attackiert worden. Ukrainischen Behörden zufolge gab es weitere Angriffe in den Regionen Poltawa, Dnipro, Kirowohrad und Riwne sowie auf die Hauptstadt Kyjiw. Auf der von Russland annektierten Halbinsel Krim kam es nach einem Unfall zu Stromausfällen, Einzelheiten dazu lagen zunächst nicht vor. (rtr)
Melania Trump kündigt Treffen mit Ukrainern und Russen an
First Lady Melania Trump hat nach ihrer Vermittlung einer Waffenruhe in der russisch besetzten Frontstadt Oleschky ein Treffen mit Vertretern der Ukraine und Russlands im Weißen Haus angekündigt. Sie persönlich werde die Repräsentanten von zwei Nationen zusammenbringen, die sich aktiv im Krieg befinden, teilte das Weiße Haus mit.
Zudem werde Melania Trump am Donnerstag um 11.00 Uhr Ortszeit (17.00 Uhr MEZ) über die Oleschky-Waffenruhe sprechen. Es wurden keine Angaben gemacht, welche Ukrainer und Russen an der Begegnung teilnehmen sollen. Ukrainische Medien meldeten unter Berufung auf eigene Quellen, dass aus Kyjiw der Menschenrechtsbeauftragte Dmytro Lubinez und der Fraktionschef der Präsidentenpartei, David Arachamija, nach Washington reisen werden. Die russische Seite sollen demnach Lubinez’ Kollegin Jana Lantratowa und Kremlunterhändler Kirill Dmitrijew vertreten.
Das Weiße Haus schrieb die Vermittlung der begrenzten Waffenruhe im Süden der Ukraine der Präsidentengattin zu und sowohl Russland als auch die Ukraine bedankten sich bei ihr. In einer gemeinsamen Rettungsaktion wurde in der vergangenen Woche die Ausreise zahlreicher Menschen aus der Trümmerstadt Oleschky ermöglicht – sie konnten dabei wählen, ob sie in die Ukraine oder nach Russland wollten. Auch humanitäre Hilfsgüter wurden in die Stadt gebracht. (dpa)
Kanadas Premier: Russland nicht zu Eishockey-Junioren-WM
Der kanadische Premierminister Mark Carney hat kategorisch ausgeschlossen, dass eine russische Eishockey-Auswahl an der U20-Weltmeisterschaft am Jahresende in Kanada teilnimmt. Damit stellte sich Carney klar gegen eine Entscheidung des Internationalen Sportgerichtshofes CAS, der eine Wiederzulassung russischer Teams an Eishockey-Turnieren genehmigt hatte.
Solange Russland und sein Verbündeter Belarus den „illegalen und ungerechtfertigten schrecklichen Krieg“ gegen die Ukraine unterstützten, würden keine ihrer Athleten für ihre Länder in Kanada antreten, sagte Carney am Rande des Gipfeltreffens der Commonwealth-Staaten am Dienstag (Ortszeit). „Wenn Sie also insbesondere nach der Junioren-WM fragen – dort werden die Russen nicht sein“, fügte der kanadische Regierungschef hinzu. Umsetzbar wäre dies durch die Verweigerung von Visa. Zuletzt hatten die Niederlande russischen Turnerinnen die Einreise für die Weltmeisterschaften in Rotterdam verwehrt.
Kanadas Eishockey-Verband dankte der Regierung in einer Mitteilung für die starke Position, die Sportler und Offizielle aus Russland und Belarus davon abhalte, unter ihren nationalen Symbolen an internationalen Sportveranstaltungen in Kanada teilzunehmen. Die Junioren-WM findet vom 26. Dezember 2026 bis zum 5. Januar 2027 in Edmonton und Red Deer in der kanadischen Provinz Alberta statt. Zu den bislang zehn Teilnehmern zählt auch die deutsche U20-Auswahl, nicht aber die russische.
Zuvor hatten nach Eishockey-Weltmeister Finnland auch Schweden, Dänemark, Norwegen und Lettland angekündigt, nicht gegen Russland anzutreten. Der tschechische Verbandspräsident befürwortete ebenfalls einen Boykott. Die finnische Stadt Turku hatte angekündigt, nicht mehr als Mitausrichter der für den Jahreswechsel 2027/2028 angesetzten U20-WM zur Verfügung zu stehen, wenn Russland teilnehmen sollte.
Die nächste Weltmeisterschaft der A-Mannschaften ist für den 14. bis 30. Mai 2027 in Düsseldorf und Mannheim geplant. Dafür wäre Russland spielberechtigt, nachdem der Sportgerichtshof CAS einer Berufung des russischen Eishockey-Verbandes gegen den Weltverband IIHF auf Wiederzulassung stattgegeben hatte. Der Deutsche Eishockey-Bund prüft derzeit, ob er die WM ausrichten kann und beschäftigt sich eigenen Angaben zufolge auch mit der Option, sie zurückzugeben. Ein Regierungssprecher hatte angekündigt, die Bundesregierung werde sich über mögliche Folgen des CAS-Urteils zeitnah mit dem DEB austauschen. (dpa)
