https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/4.text:
Key takeaways from the 2026 midterm elections in California
Democrats easily hold on to governor’s office and are on track to notch up wins in key congressional races.
While votes are still being counted in California, a handful of important races in the midterm elections have already been called or are pointing firmly in one direction.
Despite its status as a reliably Democratic stronghold, the Western state has played a dynamic role in Tuesday’s United States elections, acting as a testing ground for questions as varied as partisan redistricting and tax measures targeting billionaires.
Let’s take a quick look at some of tonight’s results:
Democrats ahead in key races
While vote-counting was still under way, Democratic candidates have pulled decisively ahead in several contests seen as must-wins for the party’s effort to take control of the US House of Representatives.
To boost the party’s chances, voters a year ago approved a partisan redistricting measure promoted by Governor Gavin Newsom to net Democrats five additional seats in the US House.
One such race took place in the state’s 22nd Congressional District, located in the agriculture-rich Central Valley.
Progressive educator Randy Villegas celebrated the results of the race on Tuesday night as the Democrat held a commanding lead of about 30 percentage points over Republican incumbent David Valadao.
Democratic candidate Marni von Wilpert is also ahead in the 48th district, located in Southern California near San Diego, where she is leading Republican Jim Desmond by about 20 points.
While those advantages are considerable, The Associated Press news agency has not yet officially called those races.
Progressive Aisha Wahab is also firmly ahead in her race against Melissa Hernandez, a fellow Democrat, in the 14th district.
Wahab overcame substantial spending by pro-Israel groups to defeat the establishment-aligned Hernandez in a special election in September. She is now on track to win a full term in that seat.
With her previous victory, Wahab became the first person of Afghan ancestry elected to Congress.
In the San Francisco Bay Area, moderate Democrat Scott Wiener is leading progressive rival Connie Chan in a race for the seat of retiring Representative Nancy Pelosi, the powerful former Democratic House speaker. Wiener has a lead of about 10 points with 50 percent of the vote tallied thus far.
Republicans face another bruising defeat in gubernatorial race
While Republicans across the country have laboured to turn California into a symbol of liberal dysfunction, voters in the state remain unconvinced that conservatives offer a better alternative.
The gubernatorial race was called for the Democratic candidate, former state Attorney General Xavier Becerra, immediately after the polls closed.
Becerra’s Republican rival, British political commentator Steve Hilton, had argued that years of unbroken Democratic domination had resulted in sky-high prices and public disorder.
But his bid to underscore cost-of-living issues by holding campaign events where he offered discounted petrol fell flat at a time when many voters blame President Donald Trump’s war on Iran for eye-watering prices at the pump.
Becerra’s victory comes more than five years after Republicans tried to dislodge Newsom through a recall election that failed by a margin of more than 20 points.
In the past, Republicans could console themselves that if they remained in electoral purgatory in the most populous US state, their Democratic rivals were likewise locked out of power in conservative strongholds such as Texas.
Tuesday’s losses will sting a bit more after a series of shock wins by Democrats in states that can usually be counted on to deliver easy wins for Republicans, including Texas.
Uncertainty over some ballot measures
While some results have come in quickly, tight contests over some of the state’s ballot measures, or policy questions put directly before voters, have yet to be called.
Proposition 40, which would institute a one-time tax on the net worth of billionaires in the state to help fund programmes such as healthcare and education, is trailing with about 44 percent of the counted votes in favour and 56 percent against.
The measure won support from progressive figures, such as Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Ro Khanna, but prompted a deluge of spending from wealthy donors and companies to oppose it.
The Associated Press has announced that Proposition 39, which would have instituted voter ID laws sought by conservatives, has been rejected by voters.

https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/n.title: A Life in Fragments by Marina Litvinenko review – intimate testimony of Putin’s poisonous regime
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/n.author: Luke Harding
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/n.text:
Among the many images of violence that might be used to define Putin’s chilly reign, one stands out. The photo of the Russian dissident Alexander Litvinenko – gaze defiant, lying in intensive care – taken in November 2006. Litvinenko had met with visitors from Moscow: they poisoned his tea with radioactive polonium. A public inquiry concluded that Putin had “probably” approved the hit, sending two clownish assassins to carry it out.
The London deathbed picture featured in newspapers across the world. It was a powerful symbol of what post-millennial Russia had become: a cruel and vindictive place, ruled by a paranoid KGB tsar. Litvinenko was its ill-fated prophet. He was the target, he told British detectives, of a vengeful mafia state. If unchecked, Putin would start a war in which millions would die, he warned presciently.
Twenty years after these lurid events, Litvinenko’s wife Marina has told her own story in a memoir. Her book, co-written with Emily Fairbairn, is a moving act of reclamation. In it, she brings her dead husband back to life – not as a tragic figure, hurtling towards a grisly public doom, but as a real and vibrant person. Instead of Litvinenko we get Sasha: a loving partner, softie dad and incorrigible optimist, who always saw the best in people.
Throughout, she rejects the label of widow. She describes the word as reductive, saying: “I never felt comfortable with it.” Instead of embracing her victim status, Marina decided to continue her husband’s battles. Her chief opponent was the Kremlin, which covered up its crime and shamelessly celebrated Litvinenko’s killers. One of them, Andrey Lugovoy, became a parliamentary deputy and fixture on state television.
A more surprising adversary was David Cameron’s coalition government. The justice secretary at the time of the murder, Chris Grayling, refused her legal aid, while home secretary Theresa May turned down her request for a public inquiry. May said this might harm international relations – in other words, annoy Moscow. The policy was grubby and short-sighted. May only relented after a Russian missile downed Malaysia Airways flight MH17 over eastern Ukraine, killing all on board.
Giving evidence at the 2015 inquiry, held in the high court, Marina described her husband’s awful cancer-like decline. Her book contains new poignant details. The evening after meeting Lugovoy and his accomplice Dmitry Kovtun at the Millennium hotel, Litvinenko fell violently ill. “Marina, I don’t feel good. Maybe I’ve been poisoned,” he told her. Admitted to hospital, his condition was wrongly diagnosed as a stomach bug.
It took three more agonising weeks before the British establishment realised Litvinenko had ingested a small nuclear bomb. Belatedly, an MI6 contact, “Martin”, rushed to his bedside. Marina opposed the deathbed snap and an accompanying statement accusing Putin of Litvinenko’s murder. Later she acknowledged the photo was effective. “Sasha’s hard gaze seemed to say, I will never be silenced,” she writes.
After his death doctors allowed her to touch his body. “I was able to kiss him and touch his skin with my bare hand. Despite all the medicine, he smelt like Sasha,” she records. Amid her grief, there were bureaucratic episodes. An “officious woman” rang up demanding payment of council tax. “My house is radioactive and the subject of an ongoing police inquiry,” Marina said. “I’m afraid the bill is still overdue,” the official replied.
There was little in Marina’s background that suggested she would become a campaigner for justice and scourge of craven politicians. She grew up in Moscow, the daughter of factory workers. One clue was her childhood habit of questioning her teachers and authority. Her mother, Zinaida, pleaded with her to toe the line, a necessary survival tactic in the USSR. “I had a childish belief in truth and fairness,” Marina recalls.
A talented dancer, she took lessons at a KGB club. There she was allowed to watch Disney and Charlie Chaplin movies prohibited for ordinary citizens. Her first marriage to a fellow ballroom dancer ended in divorce. She met Sasha at her 31st birthday party. He was “boyishly handsome”, she writes, with high cheekbones and “full, almost feminine lips”.
Sasha, she discovered, slotted easily into social situations. His remarks were sharp and funny. He told her he was an “oper”: an operative detective investigating the dark world of organised crime, and about to be divorced. They fell in love and Marina became pregnant. Soon afterwards they married, spending idyllic summers with their little son Anatoly at a dacha near the Russian capital.
Litvinenko was working for the FSB, the KGB’s domestic successor. The moment of crisis arrived in 1997 when he was told to kill the influential oligarch Boris Berezovsky. Sasha refused, tipped off his victim and held a press conference with other officers, denouncing their illegal order. As Marina notes: “Doing the right thing was his driving force.” It was a brave act. And, he understood, one that would bring awful retribution.
Putin, the FSB’s new boss, singled out Litvinenko for exemplary punishment. He was suspended and then incarcerated in Lefortovo, the FSB’s gloomy prison. Marina and Sasha wrote each other daily letters, maintaining the “invisible thread” that connected them. He was freed, rearrested and bailed. In 2000 Litvinenko slipped out of Russia and told Marina to go on holiday to Spain. Reunited in Turkey, they escaped to London.
Initially homesick, Marina adapted to her new British life. From here, her tale proceeds with grim irony. After the family received political asylum, Sasha “bounced off the walls of our flat”, exclaiming “we’re safe”, she writes. Of course, they weren’t. Former colleagues rang Litvinenko from Moscow, and warned: “Remember what happened to Trotsky.” Russian diplomats buzzed their front door, which was later hit with a petrol bomb.
Putin’s apparent pursuit of his enemies continued even after Litvinenko’s death. In 2013 Berezovsky was found hanged at his ex-wife’s Berkshire mansion. Marina does not believe he killed himself, the finding of British police. The same evening, there was a break-in at her apartment. The thief stole Sasha’s old laptop, hidden at the back of a cupboard, and Marina’s computer containing files relating to the polonium investigation.
There were further personal blows. Marina found a new companion, Alexei, a brilliant Russian chemist based in Berlin. It was, she writes, the coming together of two adults, with few expectations beyond a desire to enjoy each other’s company. They talked often of Sasha. Their romance was cut short when Alexei was diagnosed in 2018 with terminal cancer, dying shortly afterwards.
During the same bitter period, Marina’s mother was gravely ill. She urged her daughter to ask Putin for forgiveness and to return home. This was impossible: most likely the regime would prevent her from leaving Russia, and use her as a propaganda pawn. She was unable to attend her parents’ funerals. A friend retrieved childhood photos from her mother’s untouched flat, which were seemingly left as “bait”.
A Life in Fragments is the testimony of an extraordinary woman. Marina emerges from its pages as plucky and dogged, as well as kind and empathic, with an unerring sense of right and wrong. She was in western Ukraine in 2022 when Russia sent in its army. She believes Putin is a “tyrant on a par with Stalin” and that his habit of silencing critics will ultimately fail. “Sasha might be gone but his voice lives on in me. His fight is my fight,” she writes.

https://www.humanite.fr/societe/justice/.title: Un policier condamné à un an de prison avec sursis pour des violences commises sur deux adolescents et racontées par un journaliste infiltré
https://www.humanite.fr/societe/justice/.author: La rédaction
https://www.humanite.fr/societe/justice/.text:
Le gardien de la paix de 38 ans, Marc F., a été condamné à un an de prison avec sursis, mardi 3 novembre, par le tribunal correctionnel de Paris, pour des violences aggravées sur deux mineurs. Des violences qui avaient été mises au jour par Valentin Gendrot dans son ouvrage « Flic » paru en 2020, fruit de son infiltration au sein de la police.
Le récit de son infiltration au sein de la police a été un témoignage choc, ses répercussions judiciaires ont abouti ce mardi 3 novembre, six ans après la parution de son ouvrage. Dans son livre Flic, paru en 2020, Valentin Gendrot a décrit les « tabassages », les insultes racistes et homophobes, mais aussi le manque de moyens, les suicides et le mal-être des policiers dans un commissariat de l’est parisien, où il a passé six mois comme adjoint de sécurité. C’est un policier de ce commissariat qui a été condamné à un an de prison avec sursis, mardi 3 novembre, par le tribunal correctionnel de Paris, pour des violences aggravées sur deux mineurs.
Le gardien de la paix de 38 ans, Marc F., était jugé pour des violences commises sur deux frères, en avril 2019. Les « petites claques humiliantes » données au cadet lors d’un contrôle vont déclencher la colère du grand frère, qui est interpellé pour s’être interposé, a rappelé la présidente. Selon la procureure, il aurait ensuite reçu, « enfermé entre quatre murs » dans la voiture, « coup de poing sur coup de poing », puis un nouveau coup à son arrivée au commissariat.
Désormais pilote de drone à la préfecture de police de Paris, le fonctionnaire a refusé de se remettre en question lors de l’audience : « C’est de l’action-réaction, c’était proportionné », a-t-il affirmé, jugeant par ailleurs « brodé » et « romancé » l’ouvrage du journaliste, auquel il reproche de donner « l’impression qu’on est tous des racistes, misogynes, (…) violents, ce qui n’est pas le cas », dit-il se réfugiant derrière un « jargon » et « des blagues ».
Un « faux » procès-verbal
Les violences n’ont pas été rapportées dans le procès-verbal d’intervention, qualifié de « faux » par le journaliste Valentin Gendrot, qui a assisté à sa rédaction. Après l’interpellation, le gardien de la paix avait déposé plainte pour outrage et menaces aggravées contre l’aîné des deux frères. Le jeune homme reconnaît avoir injurié le policier, en réponse aux insultes et aux coups reçus, selon sa déposition lue au tribunal.
Plusieurs épisodes de violences racontés au fil des pages du livre Flic n’ont pas pu être corroborés par l’enquête, « faute d’identification » des personnes concernées, des migrants le plus souvent. Mais ces accusations intéressent néanmoins les trois juges. « J’ai appris par hasard la tenue de cette audience », a de son côté expliqué Valentin Gendrot à l’AFP, regrettant de ne pas avoir eu la parole.
Au moment de la sortie de son livre, ce dernier témoignait d’une violence systémique auprès de l’Humanité, et non pas de dérapages isolés : « Un seul policier qui a dérapé embarque toute son équipe dans une action délictueuse pour le protéger. À aucun moment, il n’a été question de briser cette omerta. Tant que la minorité de policiers violents ne sera pas sanctionnée, ce système perdurera », racontait-il alors dans nos colonnes à propos de l’affaire jugée mardi.
« Tout ce que je veux, c’est que les enfants soient protégés par la police », a pour sa part expliqué mardi la mère des deux frères, absents de l’audience car ils ne souhaitaient pas, selon elle, se replonger dans cette histoire.
Avant de partir, une dernière chose…
Contrairement à 90% des médias français aujourd’hui, l’Humanité ne dépend ni de grands groupes ni de milliardaires. Cela signifie que :
- nous vous apportons des informations impartiales, sans compromis. Mais aussi que
- nous n’avons pas les moyens financiers dont bénéficient les autres médias.
L’information indépendante et de qualité a un coût. Payez-le.
Je veux en savoir plus

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/4.title: Who determines Iran’s fighting and negotiating position amid US threats?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/4.text:
Who determines Iran’s fighting and negotiating position amid US threats?
Iran is on the brink of a new escalation with the US, but negotiations are continuing.
Tehran, Iran – Negotiations to prevent a further outbreak of war between Iran and the United States are being held, but the stagnant process has highlighted who holds power within Iran’s government.
President Masoud Pezeshkian, a relative moderate, said on Monday that his government had been given “certain powers” by Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei regarding the negotiations with the US.
Pezeshkian, who has come under fire from hardliners opposed to any deal with Washington, did not give any details about what authority this entails.
His comment followed efforts by mediators, including Qatar and Pakistan, to prevent new US strikes on Iran. There have been strong indications of an impending major escalation in the conflict, which began with US and Israeli air strikes on Iran on February 28, which killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and other top Iranian officials.
Since then, the balance of power in Iran has increasingly shifted towards the commanders of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and other security-minded officials.
“I think the key point is that any agreement must have the backing of the security-military establishment in Iran,” Sina Toossi, a senior fellow at the Center for International Policy, told Al Jazeera.
The political analyst added that this is especially true given that negotiations now concern not just the Iranian nuclear programme and sanctions but also the broader security arrangements emerging from the war, including control over the Strait of Hormuz and guarantees against renewed attacks.
Iran has put forward a seven-point plan it demands the US abide by to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Iranian authorities said decision-making on the war and negotiations takes place through a concerted approach within the framework of the institutions of the government.
Those institutions include the office of the supreme leader and the Supreme National Security Council (SNSC). Military and security figures and bodies are prominent in all of them.
Mojtaba Khamenei’s office said he met with top military commanders, including IRGC chief commander Ahmad Vahidi, to give them directives on how to handle US threats of all-out war.
Khamenei said Iran’s armed forces should respond immediately and without geographical restrictions against any threat and expand their list of US and Israeli targets in case the war escalates.
Ultimately, important decisions, such as ending the war, are decided by the supreme leader, but the SNSC – which includes representatives from the armed forces, ministers from the government, and the heads of parliament and the judiciary – votes on them first.
Who holds more sway now?
By law, Iran’s president is also the head of the SNSC, but the position of the secretary has recently held more weight due to his role as a central coordinator for top national security files.
That position has been occupied since early August by Mohsen Rezaei, a former IRGC commander-in-chief who has never held public office.
When US Vice President JD Vance wrote a letter to Tehran last week, he addressed it to Rezaei, not the president or Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran’s parliament speaker, who has also acted as its chief negotiator in recent months.
Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said Rezaei, not Ghalibaf, would respond to the letter if he chooses. But he also pointed out that Ghalibaf had not been removed from the position of chief negotiator.
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and his deputies, including Kazem Gharibabadi, also remain among the main government figures for maintaining contact with mediators and pursuing diplomacy through the United Nations and international bodies.
Ghalibaf had steered talks that led to the signing in June of a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with Washington, which briefly paused the war and lifted a maritime blockade imposed against southern Iranian ports by the US military.
But it fell apart after Tehran accused the US of violating several provisions of the deal, including on the Strait of Hormuz, and the IRGC launched attacks against three vessels attempting “unauthoritsed” transits.
The US military then escalated its own strikes on Iran, reimposed the blockade and introduced new sanctions on Iran. A larger number of ships in the Strait of Hormuz were then hit by explosions, and Iran’s military was believed to be behind the attacks.
The MoU’s downfall prompted discussions about the power dynamics within Iran’s government. For months, local and international media and analysts speculated about who ordered the attacks and what their implications were. Some US media quoted sources as saying hardline factions within the establishment directed the attacks on shipping.
In early August, Pezeshkian said he would have preferred the MoU had continued, adding, “A team should have been formed to address violations rather than to fight.”
In mid-October, IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebbi said hitting the three ships was no rogue action and there was coordination with unspecified higher authorities.
“It is not possible for someone to ignore military hierarchy and take action of their own accord on an important issue like war between two or several countries. This is by no means possible,” he said.
Mohebbi characterised the attacks as a “decisive response” to the violations by the US, which had previously launched attacks during negotiations.
He accused Washington of violating the MoU by establishing an alternative shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz near Oman and taking other steps.
“It appears that noncommitment and violation of treaties exist as an unwritten doctrine among the governing body of the US,” Mohebbi said.
Official conditions for a deal
In the current mediated talks with the US, some of Iran’s demands amount to a return to the MoU along with better sequencing and some additions to guarantee a potential future deal would last longer.
Rezaei told state television he detected a positive change in tone in the message sent by Vance, but Iran’s security chief has so far left it unanswered because Iran’s primary conditions have been clearly communicated through mediators.
Tehran seeks an end to the US naval blockade, lifting of oil and other sanctions, release of its funds frozen abroad, reduction in the US military deployment in Iran’s periphery and a halt to fighting on all fronts, including in Lebanon.
In the Strait of Hormuz, Iranian authorities have been united in saying they want to enforce sovereignty and expect Washington to recognise an Iran-Oman deal that establishes shipping routes for a partial reopening.
Decision-makers in Tehran have insisted those preliminary conditions must be fulfilled before negotiations move to a next phase that would also deal with Iran’s nuclear programme.
In a statement on Tuesday, Ali Abdollahi, chief of staff of the armed forces, said “Iran’s roadmap for sustainable security” includes relying on “security measures from within West Asia” as well as guarantees of nonaggression.
Political analyst Toossi said he wouldn’t necessarily interpret the different roles of Rezaei, Ghalibaf and Pezeshkian as evidence of competing centres of power.
“Rather they seem to reflect a division of responsibilities within a centrally coordinated process under Khamenei,” he said.
Iran’s leaders appear determined not to repeat the perceived mistakes of previous negotiations with US President Donald Trump’s administration when it made concessions or relied on US assurances only to face renewed pressure and military attacks.
“Tehran now wants Washington to fulfil its commitments before making concessions of its own, including on arrangements that would formalise Iran’s role in managing the Strait of Hormuz,” Toossi said. “This presents a formidable obstacle, even as both sides have compelling reasons to avoid another war.”
He said the fact that Iran has offered to shorten the timeline for reopening the strait to two days shows a tactical concession although it does not resolve larger issues.
“The real sticking point is not how quickly Hormuz reopens; it’s who controls the terms under which it stays open. Unless the two sides can bridge that fundamental disagreement, shortening the reopening timeline alone is unlikely to produce a breakthrough,” Toossi said.

https://www.humanite.fr/-/-/mes-lasers-s.title: « Mes lasers spatiaux destinés à interférer dans les élections n’ont pas fonctionné » : battu, Elon Musk ironise sur les élections
https://www.humanite.fr/-/-/mes-lasers-s.text:
De l’« espoir » et une « leçon » : la gauche a célébré ce mercredi 4 novembre le revers cinglant imposé par les démocrates au président américain Donald Trump lors des élections de mi-mandat, en le comparant avec le Rassemblement national, qui a lui rejeté tout parallèle.
La candidate écologiste à la présidentielle Marine Tondelier s’est réjouie d’une « défaite historique » du dirigeant républicain après son deuxième mandat « apocalyptique ». « Mais ce qui vient de se produire aux États-Unis ces dernières années est un avertissement pour la France. Si notre pays porte au pouvoir le RN l’année prochaine, il connaîtra le même destin tragique que les États-Unis », a-t-elle écrit sur X. Elle a accusé le RN, donné en tête dans les sondages, d’être aussi « fasciste », « corrompu », « climatosceptique » et « incompétent » que Donald Trump. « Les États-Unis ont payé deux fois pour voir. Puisse cette leçon nous servir », a-t-elle dit.
Le candidat social-démocrate Raphaël Glucksmann y a lui vu « la victoire de la démocratie et de la décence ». « Il n’y a aucune fatalité en politique et ce sursaut démocrate est un message d’espoir pour tous ».
Au-delà des États-Unis, la gauche veut voir un vent favorable à sa famille politique dans les récents résultats électoraux, notamment la réélection de Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva au Brésil. « Partout dans le monde, c’est la mobilisation populaire qui permet de faire reculer l’extrême droite », s’est satisfait le coordinateur national de La France insoumise, Manuel Bompard. « En France aussi, nous le ferons ». « Quelques jours après l’éclatante victoire de Lula au Brésil, le recul de Netanyahou, voici la vague démocrate aux États-Unis », s’est enthousiasmé de son côté le premier secrétaire du Parti socialiste Olivier Faure.

https://taz.de/Ausstellung-ueber-Kuenstl.title: Ausstellung über Künstlerkolonien: Wir essen Salat, ja, wir essen Salat
https://taz.de/Ausstellung-ueber-Kuenstl.author: Jan Feddersen
https://taz.de/Ausstellung-ueber-Kuenstl.text:
Ausstellung über Künstlerkolonien: Wir essen Salat, ja, wir essen Salat
Eine Ausstellung im Berner Kunstmuseum widmet sich Künstlerkolonien. Sie zeigt die ländliche Welteroberung und schlägt damit den Bogen ins Heute.
Der Titel der Freitag im Berner Kunstmuseum eröffneten Ausstellung ist, alles in allem, gut gewählt: „Reise in die Freiheit“. Liegt die Betonung auf dem Touristischen, Weltinteressierenden – oder auf der Bewegung aus Zwängen und Konventionen hinaus? Der Kunsttempel wurde 1879 als – quasi – architektonische Machtgeste der avancierenden bürgerlichen Klassen erbaut. Zeitgleich entstanden die Künstlerkolonien, denen die Schau gewidmet ist, etwa auf Capri oder am Monte Verità. Erobert zur Blütezeit der bürgerlichen Klassen lagen sie weit weg von den Akademien der ästhetischen Produktionen in den Hauptstädten.
Die Überschrift hätte auch „Reise in die Selbstbestimmung“ lauten können, womöglich war dies zu kompliziert. Worauf es anzukommen hat, ist die Bewegung selbst, das Reisen in Unbekanntes. Über 60 Gemälde zeigt diese Ausstellung – und sie sind allesamt mit Orten und Landschaften verbunden, die Idyllen fantasieren lassen – keine aus den Fugen knallenden Städte wie Kopenhagen, Berlin, Rom oder London.
Die Kunstorte waren schwer erreichbar, man musste sich mühen, zu ihnen eine Reise zu unternehmen, dort gar zu bleiben, Quartier zu nehmen, Bilder zu malen. Capri als Trauminsel vor Neapel, nur mit schaukelnden Booten erreichbar; der Monte Verità im schweizerischen Tessin, kaum wegsam dorthin oberhalb des Lago Maggiore; Skagen, ein tristes Fischerdörfchen an der Spitze Jütlands, karg und, als die ersten Künstler:innen kamen, als Platz für sie nur denkbar, weil eine kleine Eisenbahnlinie durch sandige und eher ja gräuliche Landschaften dorthin angelegt worden war.
Ein alternatives Leben
Aber die Künstlerscharen waren Kolonisten, für sie stand außer Frage, dass sie ein alternatives Leben dort haben wollten, viel Pionierarbeit war nötig, aber Zeit und Mittel waren ja vorhanden, so gut wie alle Kunstmenschen waren irgendwie familiär vorgepampert.
Vieles, was heutzutage als bürgerlicher Lifestyle gang und gäbe ist, fand dort erste Zeichenhaftigkeit. Atemübungen gegen Krankheiten, Gymnastik zur Erspürung der Körper, vegetarische Nahrungsexperimente, Experimentelles in sexuellen Hinsichten, offene Ehen, der Feminismus und das Ausleben queerer Lüste – die Lebensreformbewegung, wie diese historische Vorläuferin zur grünalternativen Bewegung genannt wurde, hatte im 19. Jahrhundert ihre ersten Aufbrüche im Kunstmilieu.
Bei den Frauen insbesondere: In Skagen oder auf dem Hügel oberhalb Asconas zu leben hieß auch, auf einschnürende Korsetts verzichten zu können.
Andererseits gab es immer auch Hohn und Spott auf die Aussteiger:innen, etwa als 1905 der Anarchist und Schriftsteller Erich Mühsam nach einem Besuch auf dem Monte Verità dichtete, „ein alkoholfreies Trinklied“: „Wir essen Salat, ja, wir essen Salat / Und essen Gemüse früh und spat. / Auch Früchte gehören zu unserer Diät./ Was sonst noch wächst, wird alles verschmäht.“
Suche nach der Echtheit
Die Gemälde sind von den Kurator:innen Livia Wermuth und Andreas Schwab gut gewählt – Letzterer nah Bern lebender Autor des Buches „Zeit der Aussteiger. Reise zu den Künstlerkolonien von Barbizon bis Worpswede“, faktisch die Inspiration zu dieser Schau und zugleich ihr Katalog. Gut, dass beide sich entschlossen, zu den Bildern jeweils Texte als Fact-Checking-Instanzen beizustellen und sie nicht hinter einem QR-Code verschwinden zu lassen: Die Künstler:innen nahmen die realen Einwohner in den Dörfern als Objekte ihrer Gemälde – wie aber war es, jenseits künstlerischer Fantasien, um die echten Leben der, nun ja, Ureinwohner bestellt?
So sehr aber der Blick auf Authentizität, auch echte Echtheit geeicht scheint, so bleibt etwa auch das Bild eines jungen Mannes bei seiner Tätigkeit am Fischernetz rätselhaft: Wann wo auch immer war je ein junger, körperlich von keiner Alterung berührter makelloser Mann bei seiner Tätigkeit nackt zu sehen? Oder wann, wie auf einem Gemälde aus Capri, lief eine junge Frau mit einer Hälfte ihres Oberkörpers barbusig durch die Gassen? Oder was mag sich der Maler einer Gruppensituation von Fischern im Meer gedacht haben, als er diese mit lächelnden Mienen auf die Leinwand brachte?
Liegt da nicht, keineswegs kompliziert, eine Art von Lust auf Exot:innen vor? Oder musste dies ästhetisch so gezeigt werden, weil die pure, arbeitsplackerische Dokumentation auf dem Markt der Gemälde in den Metropolen wenig Anklang gefunden hätte? Wenn schon nichtbürgerliche Menschenobjekte – dann doch wenigstens ob ihres Loses, körperlich brutal hart arbeiten zu müssen, mit gewinnenden Mienen.
Der Clou scheint nur, und die Ausstellung sagt dies auch in ihren instruktiven Begleittextchen, dass kurz nach der „Entdeckung“ dieser Orte, besonders auf Capri und in Skagen, deren Ureinwohner begannen, aus den (was sie ja faktisch waren) Touristen selbst Kapital zu schlagen: als Dienstpersonal, mit Postkartenständen, mit Restaurants und all dem Gewerbe, das sich überall inzwischen einstellt an Orten, die auf den bucket lists der Weltbewohner stehen: Da muss man hin …
Hot Spots ihrer Zeit
Denn, abgesehen vom Monte Verità, der im Tessiner Tourismusmarketing keine Rolle spielt, sind diese Künstlerkolonien in gewisser Weise Hot Spots ihrer Zeit geworden: Sehens- und Besuchswürdigkeiten jenseits offizieller Museumsarrangements. Wer wüsste in heutiger Zeit schon über Worpswede Bescheid, hätten sich dort nicht Paula Modersohn-Becker, Rainer Maria Rilke und Heinrich Vogeler eine Zeit lang niedergelassen? Eben: ein geografischer Alptraum ohne Liebreiz mitten in Mooreslandschaft.
Dass die Ausstellung in Bern ohne die genretypischen fame holder wie die eben Genannten auskommt, ist von inhaltlich starkem Reiz. So lenkt niemand von den Berühmtheiten vom eigentlichen Thema ab: die Freiheit, sich von Konventionen wegzubewegen, sich zu trauen, nicht alternativlos zu denken, auch zu scheitern, anders als rund um und in den Kunstakademien zu Luft zu kommen, und sei es landwirtschaftliche.
Diese feine, recht eigentlich unbeabsichtigte Wechselwirkung zwischen Kolonisierung von übersehbaren Örtlichkeiten und den Nützlichkeiten der neuen Gäste für die ursprünglichen Bewohner dieser Landschaften hatte vielleicht noch einen anderen Effekt, auch dies legt die Ausstellung nahe: die Geburt der Instagramabilität interessanter Weltgegenden.
Künstler:innen und ihre Gemälde, die als erste klassische Kunstwerke – die Fotografie als Genre war gerade geboren – wie Werbung für Land und Leute jenseits der eigenen Metropolenbubble funktionierten. Dass das auch viel mit Exotismus, Welteroberung ohne Krieg und Vernutzung angeblich ursprünglicher Lebensweise zu tun hatte: egal. Für die Ureinwohner, so sieht es auf vielen der gezeigten Bilder aus, war die zunächst sachte Invasion ihrer Gäste weltnäherbringend.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: What can Democrats actually do now they have won Congress?
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Guardian staff
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Democrats have flipped the US Senate and House of Representatives in a massive rebuke of Republicans and Donald Trump’s agenda. With Democrats majorities in both chambers, the final two years of Trump’s presidency will look markedly different from the first half. But what can Democrats actually do with with congressional power?
What can Democrats do with a House majority?
After a string of wins in Republican districts across the country pushed Democrats past the 218-seat threshold needed to capture a majority, Hakeem Jeffries is poised to become majority leader and Republicans will lose their ability to pass legislation through the chamber without Democratic support. A Democratic majority can launch investigations into the administration, demand documents and testimony and subject senior officials to sustained congressional scrutiny.
They might also come under pressure from their support base to impeach Trump for a third time.
What can Democrats do with a Senate majority?
The Senate confirms cabinet officials, ambassadors and federal judges, including supreme court nominees. A Democratic majority can block or delay many of Trump’s appointments and force the White House to negotiate over legislation.
What will Democrats investigate?
Political reporter Joseph Gedeon laid out the most consequential investigations Democrats could launch. Here are a few of the investigations:
- The family business: Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House oversight committee, has ranked Trump family corruption first on his list of priorities, while Representative Jamie Raskin has requested information on the business dealings of Trump son-in-law Jared Kushner and son Donald Trump Jr.
- Epstein and the emails: Thanks to a tag-team effort by Representatives Ro Khanna and Thomas Massie, the Department of Justice was forced to release millions of files related to Jeffrey Epstein last year. But off the bat, the justice department blew the legally mandated deadline to disclose the files. Then it released only about 3.5m pages of the 6m in its possession; it said it had deemed the rest duplicates. And there has been bipartisan consternation about heavy redactions in some places, and the apparently accidental disclosure of the names of victims in other places. The justice department is now facing a lawsuit from journalist Katie Phang over many of these issues. Even under a Republican-controlled Congress, the oversight committee under its GOP chair, James Comer, has been a rare spot of bipartisan comity, with members of both sides routinely (but not always) acting in concert to subpoena witnesses and hold them in contempt when they don’t cooperate. Expect that to continue in any new Democratic Congress.
- The Pentagon and the war: Jason Crow, a Colorado congressman who sits on the armed services and intelligence committees and co-chairs the House end corruption caucus, says he will start with the Pentagon, citing reports of defense money steered toward companies linked to the Trump family.
- Impeachment: Jeffries says Democrats have ruled nothing out regarding impeachment this time around, while the current Republican House majority leader, Steve Scalise, predicts an attempt on “Day 1”.
What did the Democrats do last time they flipped the House under Trump?
In 2018, halfway through Trump’s first term, the Democrats flipped the House of Representatives in a sweeping blue wave. House committees quickly launched dozens of inquiries into his businesses, his handling of the Russia probes and possible conflicts of interest.
Just over a year after the 2018 midterms, after months of leftwing calls for impeachment, the House voted mostly on party lines to impeach Trump.
Democrats had accused Trump of pursuing a scheme to cheat in the upcoming presidential election by pressuring Ukraine to manufacture bad news about Joe Biden and then blocking congressional oversight. Trump was later acquitted in the Republican-controlled Senate on both articles of impeachment.
In 2021, Trump was impeached – and acquitted – a second time for inciting the January 6 attack on the US Capitol.

https://taz.de/Digitalisierung-des-Heere.title: Milliardengrab Bundeswehr: Mit dem USB-Stick an der Front
https://taz.de/Digitalisierung-des-Heere.author: Cem-Odos Güler
https://taz.de/Digitalisierung-des-Heere.text:
Milliardengrab Bundeswehr: Mit dem USB-Stick an der Front
Projekt D-LBO ist das Codewort für ein Milliardengrab der Bundeswehr. Und dann sind Soldat*innen mit Geräten aus dem Technikmuseum unterwegs. Na dann gute Nacht!
E s gibt im Bundeswehr-Kosmos Themen, die Menschen aus unterschiedlichen Lagern in ihrer Rage vereinen. Kriegsgegner*innen, das Verteidigungsministerium, Abgeordnete, Soldat*innen und sogar Rüstungslobbyist*innen sind auf ein Problem wütend, das sich hinter einer Abkürzung verbirgt.
Falls Sie Boris Pistorius mal auf einem E-Roller sehen, sich aber nicht sicher sind, ob das gerade wirklich der Verteidigungsminister war, machen Sie den D-LBO-Test! Rufen Sie ganz laut: Herr Pistorius, wie steht es um die Digitalisierung der landbasierten Operationen beim Heer? Zuckt er gefährlich zusammen, haben Sie richtig gesehen. Falls nicht, war es nur Armin Laschet.
Bei dem Vorhaben handelt es sich um eines dieser Milliardengräber in der Bundeswehr, die alle sechs Monate für einen hysterischen Aufschrei sorgen und dann wieder zwischen Beschaffungsamt und Verteidigungsministerium vergessen werden. „Wir sind auf einem guten Weg“, ist der Satz, der meist zu hören ist, wenn es, vereinfacht gesagt, darum geht, das Heer für Einsätze mit dem Internet zu verbinden.
Wie immer ist dieses Projekt voller Abgründe – es scheint, dass das Verteidigungsministerium bereitwillig in jedes einzelne hineingestürzt ist. Nachzulesen sind diese Eskapaden in meiner stets beruhigenden wehrtechnischen Gute-Nacht-Lektüre „Europäische Sicherheit und Technik“ (ESUT): Obwohl bereits 2016 ein softwarebasiertes Funksystem zur Verfügung stand (dessen Entwicklung die Bundeswehr in Auftrag gegeben hatte) und das Verteidigungsministerium im Jahr 2018 die Digitalisierung der Landstreitkräfte als „entscheidend“ für die vernetzte Operationsführung bezeichnete – tat das Beschaffungsamt was?
Genau, es bestellte im Jahr 2021 30.000 analoge Funkgeräte. Das Problem, dass die Geräte auf dem technischen Stand der 80er-Jahre waren und nicht mehr gebaut wurden, weil sie nirgendwo mehr nachgefragt wurden, wurde für die Bundeswehr gern gelöst – es kostete nur 600 Millionen Euro.
Eine Weinwanderung mit dem Beschaffungsamt
Während Soldat*innen also weiterhin munter mit Geräten aus dem Technikmuseum unterwegs sind, geht das Verteidigungsministerium mutig voran – zumindest finanziell. Gepampert mit dem neuen Sondervermögen bewilligte der Bundestag im Dezember 2022 einen Rahmenvertrag für internetfähige und abhörsichere Funkgeräte für 2,9 Milliarden Euro. Dabei sollten allein die ersten 20.000 Funkgeräte 1,35 Milliarden Euro kosten.
Gleich nachdem dieser Auftrag vergeben war, muss die zuständige Abteilung im Koblenzer Beschaffungsamt zu einer zehnmonatigen Mosel-Wanderung aufgebrochen sein. Nur so kann man erklären, was danach passierte: Als die Firma die bestellen Funkgeräte lieferte, war man bei der Bundeswehr so überrascht darüber, dass man sie erst einmal einlagern musste. Das ist kein Scherz!
Niemand hatte sich Gedanken über den Einbau der Funkgeräte in die Fahrzeuge gemacht. Pistorius wies die Verantwortung dafür von sich. „Der Auftrag ist erteilt worden im Dezember, also vor meiner Zeit. Ich wäre davon ausgegangen, dass man sich vor der Bestellung, aber mindestens mit der Bestellung Gedanken macht, wie die Integration erfolgt“, sagte er Ende September 2023.
Heute, drei Jahre später, ist die Umstellung immer noch eine so große Baustelle, dass eine Umrüstung der Fahrzeuge im Heer erst für Ende 2030 geplant ist. Laut einem Fachmagazin erfolgt bis dahin der Datenaustausch zwischen digitalisierten und nicht digitalisierten Einheiten in Gefechtssimulationen per USB-Stick. „Man muss sich das sehr rustikal vorstellen: Ein Soldat kam mit einem USB-Stick, übergab ihn der Besatzung des Schützenpanzers, und diese speiste die Daten ein“, heißt es bei ESUT. Na dann, gute Nacht!

https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.title: Ukraine: Time to End the War
https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.author: Robert L. Borosage, Katrina vanden Heuvel
https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.text:
For both Russia and Ukraine, the war has taken a staggering toll and poses an ever-greater danger of spreading.

It is long past time to bring the brutal war between Russia and Ukraine to an end. Now, just as both countries seem open to serious negotiations, Donald Trump perversely seems intent on giving peace a bad name.

Even as his amateur emissaries—real estate investors Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law—launched separate discussions with Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky and Russia’s Vladimir Putin, Trump decided to tilt the board for Putin. He lashed out at Zelensky, saying Ukraine needed a new president. For domestic midterms consumption, he announced an “energy ceasefire” that neither combatant had heard of, temporarily approved the purchase of Russian diesel oil, and shelved the intensified sanctions contained in legislation he had signed. He delusionally claimed that “Russia, frankly, had been fine on Ukraine. They haven’t been doing much,” even as Russia’s attacks on Ukraine intensified. Witkoff risibly hailed Putin as a “humanitarian,” while salivating over economic deals that the United States could cut with Russia when the war ends. Trump embraced Putin’s suggestion of a tripartite summit—Putin, Xi, and Trump—to settle the war, although Trump said it should focus on nuclear weapons, not Ukraine.

Delivery of defensive Patriot missiles paid for by the Europeans has been mysteriously held up. And although Trump denied that he was responsible, Ukraine suffered sudden restrictions on its use of Starshield, the Starlink satellite program vital to providing early warning of Russian missile attacks, restrictions that Elon Musk claimed only the White House could order.

Not surprisingly, these actions spurred outrage in Europe and condemnation in the US, even echoed by some Republican senators. They also inevitably triggered the Trump derangement syndrome that muddles liberal analysis. The New York Times editorial page indicted Trump for “helping Mr. Putin wage war,” and called on the West to “continue to punish Mr. Putin, the oligarchs who support him, and Russia’s war-making economy,” ignoring the terrible price Ukrainians are paying. At stake, the Times intoned, is “whether the West can rally to protect democracy and innocent lives,” although the Times carefully noted that in this “defense of democracy,” only Ukraine should put troops and civilians at risk, and Europe should bear most of the cost.

Hillary Clinton weighed in, painting Trump once more as “a willing Putin puppet,” warning that “Putin’s not going to stop with Ukraine.” She charged that Trump wants to “divide the world: He gets the Western Hemisphere, Putin gets Russia and Europe, and Xi Jinping gets the rest of the world,” a fantasy that makes the unlikely assumption that Trump would accept the smallest piece of the world and ignores European and other nations that might have something to say about the division. In contrast, the popular liberal historian Heather Cox Richardson scorned Russia as a “minor economic player whose military is flailing at its attempt to absorb its neighbor,” charging that Trump is “openly embracing Putin and is working to destroy the strongest and most successful alliance in human history to cement that partnership, apparently with an eye to enriching himself.”

Trump’s scorn for our allies and solicitude for strongmen like Mr. Putin and Xi Jinping are notorious. And his brazen use of his office to enrich himself is contemptible. Offering bribes to Putin while undermining Zelensky is more likely to undermine than facilitate negotiations.

That said, the understandable fury at Trump’s antics should not blind us to reality. This is a war that needs to come to an end.

For both Russia and Ukraine, the war has taken a staggering toll. Russia has suffered an estimated 1.5 million casualties; Ukraine, 500,000. Both find it harder to replace the losses. A million Russians have fled the country, disproportionately the most educated and skilled of the young. Over 20 percent of the Ukrainian population has been displaced, with over 5 million leaving the country. The Russian Navy has been driven out of the Black Sea; the key Ukrainian port of Odesa, center of its grain trade, has been shut down. Ukraine, with 80 percent of its power generation and 90 percent of its food logistics infrastructure destroyed, faces a brutal winter. Russia is suffering far greater damage than Putin would have imagined. Recent attacks on its oil industry have shut down some 30 percent of its refining capacity.

With continued oil sales to China, India, and other countries, Russia has managed to avoid a recession. Ukraine’s economy has been devastated, its GDP down by a quarter since the war began, its survival utterly dependent on European assistance. The World Bank estimated the cost of rebuilding Ukraine to be $588 billion over a decade even before the most recent devastating Russian missile and drone attacks.

And the war poses an ever-greater danger of spreading. Ukrainian drones striking St. Petersburg have been reported as traveling through or being launched from NATO countries. European allies warn of an escalating Russian “hybrid war,” with suspicious drone sightings and arson at Starlink hubs. Germany has called the threat of Russian sabotage of troop facilities “significant.”

Riots are spreading across Europe, a reaction to rising economic pain significantly worsened by the sanctions that cut off Russian oil and the renewed European military buildup, topped by the soaring energy prices resulting from Trump’s Iranian debacle. Ukraine requires ever more aid just as European economic turmoil makes that ever more difficult.

The assumption in the European and American foreign policy commentariat that Putin is on his last legs, and that with renewed aid and weaponry Ukraine can win the war, is both fantasy and folly. Fantasy because it ignores the reality that Ukraine verges on collapse; folly because, were Putin facing defeat, it would increase the peril of a wider war that no rational person would risk. Nor does the hysteria that Putin will take on NATO after Ukraine make sense: Ukraine has exposed Russia’s weakness, not its strength, and inflicted a steep price for its aggression.

Polls show majorities in both Russia and Ukraine are open to peace negotiations. Both Putin and Zelensky have accepted the need for negotiations, and preliminary talks have begun.

With Russia occupying nearly 20 percent of Ukraine, any settlement will be painful. The inescapable reality is that Mark Milley, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, was right in 2022, after Ukraine had repelled the initial Russian invasion, when he urged Ukraine to “seize the moment” and negotiate. After all the casualties and destruction, the settlement will be worse now than it would have been then.

Still, we would be well advised not to allow Donald Trump’s biliousness to give peace a bad name. What’s needed instead is a global movement for ending the war. The European allies now bearing the brunt of the cost of sustaining Ukraine should help lead the negotiations, bringing expertise and experience to an American team that badly needs it. The countries that ignored US sanctions—China, India, and others—should join the push for a negotiated settlement.

Zelensky, first elected as a peace candidate, has led a courageous resistance. Now he needs even more courage to lead the country to a settlement before it is completely destroyed.

Robert L. Borosage is a leading progressive writer and activist.

Katrina vanden Heuvel is editor and publisher of The Nation, America’s leading source of progressive politics and culture. An expert on international affairs and US politics, she is an award-winning columnist and frequent contributor to The Guardian. Vanden Heuvel is the author of several books, including The Change I Believe In: Fighting for Progress in the Age of Obama, and co-author (with Stephen F. Cohen) of Voices of Glasnost: Interviews with Gorbachev’s Reformers.

https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.title: How the End of “Roe” Is Reshaping Medical Care: A Q&A With Alice Miranda Ollstein
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.author: Amy Littlefield
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
In her new book Side Effects, the Politico reporter shows that the impact of abortion bans goes far beyond reproductive health care.

In her new book “Side Effects,” the “Politico” reporter shows that the impact of abortion bans goes far beyond reproductive health care.

Alice Miranda Ollstein covers the politics of abortion as a reporter for Politico. But as she traveled the country reporting on the fallout from the Supreme Court’s decision to overturn Roe v. Wade in 2022, Ollstein began to hear another drumbeat in the background. “[O]ver the course of writing hundreds of articles, as I interviewed patients, doctors, pharmacists, researchers, and others impacted by the new restrictions, I saw how such laws were also eroding the quality and availability of health care—and not just reproductive health care,” Ollstein writes in her new book, Side Effects: How Abortion Bans Impact Everyone’s Health (published by The New Press this October).

In her book, Ollstein uncovers how the harmful consequences of abortion bans stretch well beyond miscarriage management, maternity care, and contraception, as well as, of course, delaying or outright denying care to those seeking abortions. Everyone from veterans suffering the effects of war to chronically ill patients seeking care for debilitating pain are affected by these laws. The Supreme Court’s Dobbs decision has sent ripple effects across the healthcare landscape, shaping where clinicians live, how they train, what drugs they prescribe, and how they conduct medical research. “No part of the healthcare system went untouched by Dobbs,” Ollstein told me. I interviewed her recently about the findings in her book, and as the midterms approach, I also took the opportunity to ask her about how abortion will affect the elections in November.

I’ve edited our conversation for clarity and length.

Amy Littlefield: Let’s start with an area of medicine impacted by Dobbs that is fully related to reproductive health care—contraception. How did banning abortion affect access to contraception?

Alice Miranda Ollstein: There are so many contradictory trends in the contraception space right now. You have, on the one hand, more demand than ever for contraception, including permanent contraception, because people are more afraid of an unintended pregnancy that they would not be able to terminate. On the other hand, there is reduced access. Some of that is due to the blurring of the line between what is an abortifacient and what is a contraceptive. There’s been a lot of misinformation about that, from official state government entities and circulating online. That has led to certain forms of contraception being excluded from government programs [and] government coverage. In some cases, universities that are state-run stopped providing certain forms of contraception because they were unsure if it would violate their new state abortion ban. A lot of it was in the immediate aftermath of Dobbs, but some of it still continues to this day.

AL: Let’s talk about some areas of healthcare that are less intuitively connected to abortion. How do abortion bans impede medical research, including into conditions totally unrelated to abortion?

AMO: One example is that the abortion pill mifepristone has a lot of potential, being studied in the United States and around the world, for treating certain cancers and all kinds of other conditions. I met a researcher in Florida who found that this medication had a miraculous impact on older veterans who had debilitating mental and physical impacts from Gulf War Syndrome, which is caused by being exposed to toxic chemicals in Operation Desert Storm. This medication that right now is only authorized for abortions made a huge difference for them, but because of state bans, that research got delayed and there were all these hurdles, and so veterans still cannot access this medication that could really help them. I met another researcher who was trying to study mifepristone’s impact on breast cancer, and she ended up abandoning the study altogether because she was based in a state with a near-total abortion ban and was afraid of losing access to the medication midway through the study.

AL: In the book you tell the story of Tara Rule, a New York woman who had debilitating cluster headaches, whose doctor balked at prescribing medication that could have alleviated her symptoms because the drug could cause birth defects. Can you talk about this trend?

AMO: I was really struck by the trend of people with chronic illnesses who were not pregnant, were not planning on being pregnant, in some cases physically could not get pregnant, and they were still being denied medication they really depend on because either that medication was a potential abortifacient or that medication could cause birth defects if you become pregnant while you’re taking it. What was wild to learn about is that this was happening [all] around the country right after Dobbs. It was happening in states with bans and in states with abortion protections. It was happening to people with lupus, Crohn’s, rheumatoid arthritis, Ehlers-Danlos. Sometimes it was the doctor who refused to prescribe it; sometimes it was a pharmacist who refused to fill it, and sometimes it was the insurer who refused to cover it. When Tara Rule was posting on social media about this, which went viral at the time, she started hearing from so many other people saying, ‘Hey, this happened to me, too.’

AL: Some stories of women dying while suffering miscarriages when providers delayed giving care have gotten lots of media attention. But there are other fatalities we have heard less about —like that of an Indiana woman who died when her ectopic pregnancy ruptured and she had to travel further for care because her local hospital’s labor unit had recently shut down. What does her death show about how hard it is to document deaths from abortion bans?

AMO: You’re seeing labor and delivery units around the country close, and a lot of that is economic, but in some instances the hospital themselves publicly say that the state abortion ban is a factor in losing doctors and not being able to maintain access. Doctors are also just more fearful and hesitant to treat pregnant women who are going through literally anything. Even if somebody comes in from a car accident, there’s just so much fear of accidentally seeming like you maybe caused an abortion, or you didn’t document it right. These delays can be deadly in some circumstances. It’s hard to prove causality, and I think that it’s especially challenging because the state entities that are supposed to make those determinations, these mortality maternal mortality review committees, their work has been made a lot harder by bans, and in certain states they have been censored. They’ve been fired and replaced. The reports have been delayed. I’m thinking in particular of Georgia, Texas, and Idaho. All had major disruptions of their maternal mortality review committees, and those are the committees that are supposed to go through every death during pregnancy, birth, and the postpartum period, and determine what caused it. That’s information that could save lives in the future.

AL: Another story from your book that has stayed with me is that of Samantha Casiano, who learned during her 20-week anatomy scan that her fetus had a lethal birth defect called anenchephaly. But she lived in Texas and couldn’t afford to leave her four kids to travel out of state for an abortion. Talk about her story and what it shows about the overall message of your book.

Even though the whole thesis of my book is that everyone is impacted in some way by abortion bans, some people are clearly more impacted than others, and low-income women of color are, in a lot of circumstances, being impacted the most. I reported on women in Texas who received diagnoses later in pregnancy that their fetus had a medical condition that was incompatible with life. The upper-middle-class white women I met had the financial resources, the job flexibility, the family support to leave the state and get an abortion in another state and come back. I’m not saying that they had it easy. It was very, very difficult emotionally and physically. But you compare that with what happened to Samantha Casiano, who did not have the financial resources to be able to leave the state, and she ended up carrying to term her fetus that had anencephaly, and it died in her arms four hours after birth, gasping for breath, turning purple. It was so traumatic for Samantha that when she testified in court about it as part of a lawsuit by the Center for Reproductive Rights, she actually vomited on the witness stand, just reliving that trauma. I really think about her and what differences class and other divisions can cause.

AL: One of the most compelling parts of the book is your reporting on how the Dobbs decision has politicized doctors in new ways. Can you talk about that?

AMO: A lot of abortion providers were already very politically active. They were part of lawsuits. They were outspoken. Often, they felt like they had to be. But what I saw happen after Dobbs is that all of these other doctors who never performed an abortion themselves—many of them didn’t even treat women of reproductive age—they saw the spillover effects on their own work and thought, “I really need to get involved.” I talked to neurologists, rheumatologists, oncologists, pediatricians, ER doctors, just across the medical system, and you had this happening at the individual level, where individuals were speaking out more, participating in some of these political campaigns, running for office themselves in some cases, joining lawsuits. But they also lobbied their medical societies, either state or national, to take stronger stands on access to abortion than those groups ever had in the past.

AL: How do you see abortion shaping the way that people vote this year?

AMO: There are four states where abortion is going to be directly on the ballot. That obviously brings it more top of mind in Idaho, Missouri, Nevada, and Virginia. But it’s been coming up in the Maine Senate race, where the Democratic challenger has been hammering Susan Collins over her vote to confirm the Supreme Court justices who overturned Roe, and that has become one of her bigger liabilities. There is polling [showing] that people do care about abortion as an issue, and they want candidates to talk about it, and they say they’re more likely to support a candidate who supports abortion access. But when people are asked to rank issues, it does not rank in the very top, along with things like being able to afford groceries, for instance. There are glimmers of signs that it is still a potent issue. I was interested to hear James Talarico in Texas give a pretty full-throated support for abortion rights, and that is in a tough race in a very conservative state. I don’t think he would have said that if he didn’t think it was a message that resonated with a lot of people.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Inside the Fight to Protect the Youth Vote
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Sena Chang
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Republican-led efforts threatening young people’s rights to the ballot have sparked efforts to protect the youth vote across college campuses.

In response to increasing federal attempts to limit ballot access, lawmakers, students and college administrators are mobilizing to safeguard young people’s access to voting.

More than 80 percent of eligible voters aged 18 to 29 in key battleground states said that they “probably” or “definitely” plan to vote in the upcoming midterm elections, according to a recent survey. Despite this enthusiasm, deep concerns remain that thousands of student voters may be thwarted from casting their ballot come November by an absence of polling sites on college campuses.

On October 15, the first day of in-person early voting in North Carolina, more than 100 students walked 40 minutes to the Guilford County Courthouse to cast their ballots after a Republican-majority state board of elections denied requests for early voting sites at two Greensboro universities.

The students, from North Carolina A&T State University, the largest historically Black university in the country, and the University of North Carolina at Greensboro, had access to on-campus early voting during the 2024 election. While dozens of students advocated for adding the two polling sites, the sites were ultimately denied in January, with the board citing low turnout.

“Honestly, it took me back to the same fight that our ancestors were fighting years and years ago in the ’60s,” North Carolina A&T senior Tatiana James, the president of the university’s NAACP chapter, told The Nation. “Today, it’s the same fight, it’s just dressed up differently.”

In 2024, the closest polling site on campus was located at the Dudley Memorial Building, which features a statue of the Greensboro Four—the four Black students from North Carolina A&T who staged a sit-in at a segregated Greensboro lunch counter during the civil rights movement in 1960. “That’s literally the history of A&T. That’s our significance,” James, who is currently mobilizing students on campus to vote early, said.

At North Carolina A&T and college campuses across the nation, Republican-led efforts that threaten young people’s rights to the ballot have sparked efforts to protect the youth vote across college campuses. In an analysis of 35 states offering in-person early voting in 2020, 74 percent of college campuses lacked in-person voting options on campus, and over half of American college students did not have any voting option on campus.

Threats to youth voting rights extend well beyond the absence of on-campus polling locations. Restrictive residency and voter-ID requirements disproportionately burden young voters, who often move frequently and may lack accepted identification, especially in states that do not accept student IDs. Young people also face a disproportionately high risk of provisional ballot rejections and late mail ballots. For first-time voters already juggling coursework, jobs, and navigating an unfamiliar electoral system, these barriers can make casting a ballot especially difficult, experts said.

“For the first time since the Voting Rights Act was passed in the 1960s, we have millions of Americans headed to the polls without clear federal protections to enforce voting rights,” Rebekah Caruthers, the CEO of the Fair Elections Center, told The Nation. She noted that such threats could disproportionately impact young voters, potentially affecting a significant segment of the electorate; nearly 50 million people between the ages of 18 and 29 are eligible to vote in November.

In Texas, the majority-Republican Tarrant County Commissioners Court cut the number of polling places by nearly a third, from 316 in the previous midterms to 224. This included the elimination of four early voting locations on college campuses, including two places at Tarrant County College campuses and another at the University of Texas at Arlington.

“If you combine the [UT Arlington] student population, the faculty, and the staff, that’s about a population of 60,000, and no polling locations except the closest one a mile and a half away,” Janet Mattern, the president of the League of Women Voters of Tarrant County, said. Mattern and her team are offering options for low-cost transportation to the polls in the county.

“If it happens in Tarrant County, it can happen in other places too,” Mattern said.

This April, New Hampshire joined 10 other states in eliminating student IDs as a form of identification. Washington voters aged 18 to 25 faced the highest rate of challenges to their mail-in ballots from 2020 to 2025, according to a recent study. And in Greensboro, North Carolina, the student polling site now located at the county courthouse is “still really inaccessible to students,” according to Olu Rouse, the cofounder and codirector of Protect Ours North Carolina.

“You have to cross multiple highways and main streets to get to the site by walking,” Rouse told The Nation. “For first-year students who do not have cars, this has always been a concern, and why we pushed so hard for an on-campus early voting site,” he said.

The threats facing young voters are not confined to the local level, experts warned. In Washington, Republican lawmakers have pushed to overhaul voter registration requirements through the SAVE America Act, which passed the House earlier this year. The proposed bill requires Americans to present proof of citizenship to election officials when registering to vote for the first time, whenever they update their registration following a change of name or address—measures that could disproportionately impact low-income youth and youth of color.

Although the bill has stalled in the Senate, similar measures have gained traction in state legislatures. Since 2024, 12 states have joined Arizona and Georgia by enacting laws similar to the SAVE Act.

The broader topic of voting rights has also reached the Supreme Court. In April, the justices ruled in Louisiana v. Callais that Louisiana’s effort to create a second majority-Black congressional district amounted to racial gerrymandering that was unconstitutional. The decision also narrowed the circumstances under which the Voting Rights Act can justify race-conscious redistricting.

“We saw it as the last attack, the last takedown of the Voting Rights Act,” Selasi Tagbor Morales, communications manager at the Alliance for Youth Action, said. “That was very much a decision that was a product of this administration,” she said.

These federal actions could have a chilling effect on young voters this November, Molly Metz, a first-year student at Penn State and the president of the university’s NextGen chapter, explained. Speaking in her personal capacity, Metz pointed to President Trump’s unfounded claims of voter fraud associated with mail-in voting and the administration’s rhetoric on election interference as possible deterrents to voting.

“I think a lot of people are also afraid to even go in person to vote,” Metz said. “It is a really scary thing to do in a climate where ICE might be there and monitor the polls, as has been threatened.” Though the administration has denied that it will send ICE agents to the polls, advocacy groups are remaining cautious.

In response to increasing federal attempts to limit ballot access, lawmakers, students, and college administrators are mobilizing to safeguard young people’s access to voting.

Last month, Senator Elizabeth Warren reintroduced the Youth Voting Rights Act of 2026, which, among other measures, would require on-campus polling stations, expand voter registration at public colleges and universities, and allow preregistration before young people turn 18. Representative Nikema Williams introduced similar legislation in the House last year.

“Young people have a constitutional right to vote, and no politician should be allowed to stand in their way. With Trump and Republicans pushing voter suppression policies and on-campus polling sites being shut down nationwide, we must act now to protect young voters ahead of the midterms,” Warren told The Nation. “The Youth Voting Rights Act will break down barriers to the ballot box and make sure young people have a fair say in the future of our country.”

These various obstacles put in the way of youth political participation collectively reveal a “constellation of abridgements of the right to vote on account of age,” said Yael Bromberg, the architect of the Youth Voting Rights Act and an American University law professor. “They may look like rollbacks to the availability of offering student identification where voter-ID requirements are in place, or continued inconsistencies with equal access to vote by mail,” Bromberg said.

At Bard College, new students stop at a voter registration booth before getting their room keys. Massive student-led outreach campaigns are also conducted, among a host of other efforts to mobilize young voters. “Colleges should not be neutral on democracy,” Jonathan Becker, the acting president of Bard College and co-editor of “Youth Voting Rights: Civil Rights, the Twenty-Sixth Amendment, and the Fight for American Democracy on College Campuses” with Bromberg, said. “The foundations of American higher education are informed by a belief in engaged citizenship—that is a through line in American higher education since the revolution, and voting, as the most foundational of democratic rights, is one they should be supporting.”

One of the biggest barriers to youth voting has been a lack of information, according to Metz. “If the process becomes any bit difficult, it becomes increasingly harder to motivate people who may be on the fence about voting,” she said, pointing out that many students do not know how to start a mail-in ballot away from home or format their dorm addresses. “It’s an objectively confusing process, and it’s hard to blame them when the system is not really set up with college students in mind.” Approximately 40 percent of 18-to-24-year-olds in the nation are enrolled in college, and these young voters could help play a decisive role in closely contested states such as Maine and New Hampshire.

Ahead of the midterms, Alabama A&M student Kelvin Edwards is constantly sending e-mails urging voting as part of the campus’s civic engagement and voter registration team. A combination of tabling events, civic engagement game nights, and a planned “March for Midterms” is energizing a majority of students to show up to vote, according to Edwards.

“Groups like [NextGen America] are doing everything in their power to provide pathways [to voting],” Arianna Jones, the executive director of NextGen America, said. “The big thing for me is that young people take hold of their own futures and step into that power and recognize the fact that no one would be fighting this hard to take it away from them if it wasn’t worth it.”

Sena Chang is a student at Princeton University and a 2026 Puffin Writing Fellow for The Nation. Her work can be found in The Daily Princetonian, Teen Vogue, and LAist.

https://hellgatenyc.com/chantz-rivera-wa.title: He Did It! He Walked From the Bronx to San Francisco!
https://hellgatenyc.com/chantz-rivera-wa.author: Hell Gate
https://hellgatenyc.com/chantz-rivera-wa.text:
On Tuesday, more than 2,500 miles and 149 days after he began walking on foot across the country, Bronxite Chantz Rivera made it to San Francisco. 
He left his dishwashing job in May with the goal of getting to the Pacific Ocean. Before that, he had only left the five boroughs twice in his life.
"The inspiration behind the trip was just free will, you know," Rivera told us last month from Ely, Nevada. "Just gotta experience life, be free." 
Late capitalism has drastically lowered the stakes for this kind of cross-country, identity-seeking journey. You have a $50,000 Sprinter van, an email job, and an Instagram account—we're supposed to give a shit? 
In contrast, Rivera's trip seemed ill-planned, spur-of-the-moment, mildly dangerous. That is to say: He left for the right reasons, and he has both the discipline to endure thousands of miles across this country's often-hostile highways and the uncynical heart to appreciate it all.   
Despite having been stopped by the police and having his stuff stolen the moment he walked into California, Rivera was in good spirits when we spoke to him on Wednesday evening.
This interview has been lightly edited and condensed for clarity.
