https://gothamist.com/news/november-has-.title: November has 3 meteor showers and the best chance to see Uranus
https://gothamist.com/news/november-has-.author: Rosemary Misdary
https://gothamist.com/news/november-has-.text:
Every week in November has a dazzling night sky headliner for fall stargazers.
“November has meteor showers that tend to be a favorite,” said Jackie Faherty, astrophysicist at the American Museum of Natural History. “This month is a good time to see planets, especially Saturn and Jupiter.”
Shooting stars
On Nov. 4-5, the Southern Taurids will peak with about five meteors per hour. That number might sound small, but the meteors are exceptionally bright, slow-moving and long-lasting. The shower often produces fireballs, which are as luminous as some of the brightest celestial objects. During the peak, there will be a crescent moon, which means skies will be darker and more ideal for spotting the streaking lights.
“Even in the city, some of these meteors will be bright enough that you'll be able to see them,” said Bart Fried, a member of the American Astronomical Society.
The Northern Taurids peak about a week later, on Nov. 12-13, yielding the same display of dazzling light as the Southern Taurids. During that evening, viewing conditions are good because of the low light from the crescent moon.
“These are bright enough that if you catch it anywhere in your field of view, your eyes snap right to it,” Fried said. “Don't worry about having to stare in the right spot. There is no right spot.”
The third and final meteor shower of the month, the Leonids, peaks Nov. 17-18 with around 15 shooting stars per hour. The moon will be at about half its illumination, which will make the sky brighter, but not impossible to see a meteor. Stargazers should head to darker spots in the city, such as Floyd Bennett Field.
“ Your best viewing for the Leonids will be from midnight until dawn after the moon sets,” Fried said.
Supermoon
The moon will appear up to 14% larger and 30% brighter on Nov. 23-24. The phenomenon is called a supermoon, when the moon is at or near its closest position to Earth in its oval-shaped orbit. When at this point, also called perigee, it appears larger and brighter.
A supermoon comes about three to five times per year. The next supermoon, which lands on Christmas Eve, will be the brightest, largest and final one of the year.
The planets
It will be possible to spot half of the planets in the solar system with the naked eye.
Jupiter, appearing in the southeast section of sky, is currently the brightest planet. For most of the month, Mars will be close to the gas giant. New Yorkers can see the red planet in the evening skies starting this month.
Golden-hued Saturn is also visible in the southern section of the sky. For views of the rings, stargazers will need binoculars or a telescope.
While looking for the rings, it’s a good time to find Uranus. The greenish-blue dot is the coldest planet in the solar system, and the second-farthest from the sun. The average temperature is about -320 degrees Fahrenheit. The seventh planet from the sun will be at opposition on Nov. 25, which means it’s at its closest distance to Earth on its roughly 84-year orbit around the sun.
Fried recommends using a planetarium app in order to locate Uranus before pointing a telescope or binoculars at the sky. At around midnight, the ice giant will be at its highest point in the sky, right overhead.
“With a 4-inch telescope, you can find Uranus with no problem,” Fried said. “It’s reasonably bright. It’s not visible to the naked eye, but it is visible in binoculars if you know where to find it.”
Early risers can catch a glimpse of Venus, which was the brightest object in the night sky during the summer. At this time of year, the solar system's hottest planet is referred to as the morning star.
Fall Constellations
As the weather cools, the constellations are continuing to shift with the seasons. This month, Orion the Hunter shines prominently along with his two dogs, Canis Minor and Canis Major.
Despite the city’s formidable light pollution, these constellations are easily discernible from the dissonance. Orion has a famous line of three stars that form his belt. Sirius, the dog star, is the brightest star in Earth’s night sky. The star is part of Canis Major.
Right near Orion, the bright stars of Gemini are also visible, Castor and Pollux.
“Gemini is a really good constellation to look for right now,” Faherty said. “You can see Castor and Pollux from New York City high in your sky towards the zenith.”

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/cruse-biogra.title: Harold Cruse, the Loneliest Black Radical Intellectual
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/cruse-biogra.author: Alan Wald
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/cruse-biogra.text:
Harold Cruse, the Loneliest Black Radical Intellectual
Harold Cruse’s Crisis of the Negro Intellectual became an instant classic and helped found the field of African American studies. His writing brimmed with erudition and insight, but his fragile ego and personal grudges left him isolated.
Harold Wright Cruse (1916–2005), my colleague at the University of Michigan for decades, may have been the most flamboyantly paradoxical radical intellectual ever to roam our institution’s halls. An astonishing autodidact with a wealth of knowledge about cultural and political history, Cruse authored a foundational work in black studies: The Crisis of the Negro Intellectual: A Historical Analysis of the Failure of Black Leadership (1967). Now, two decades after his death, a short, pacy biography by Villanova University theologian and Africana studies scholar Vincent W. Lloyd titled Harold Cruse: Critic, Writer, Teacher captures many of Cruse’s idiosyncrasies to present a riot of contradictions.
Cruse, a high school dropout with no college degrees, was recruited to the Michigan history department one year after the publication of Crisis, which quickly became a standard classroom text, often cited alongside Frantz Fanon’s The Wretched of the Earth (1961) and The Autobiography of Malcolm X (1965). Cruse’s book was a six-hundred-page tome bursting with insight and erudition but also ornery opinions about racial integration, black nationalism, and communism, not to mention uncharitable generalizations about women, Jews, and Caribbean immigrants. These were voiced, on and off the page, with absolute certainty and self-righteousness.
His most scathing criticisms were aimed at leading African American activists and thinkers, and his style stood out for his penchant for hurling rhetorical grenades. His targets included civil rights organizations such as the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) and Martin Luther King Jr’s Southern Christian Leadership Conference, which he saw as “motivated by selfish class interests, because the main objective of the Negro middle class is a status and a social position approximating . . . the great Anglo-American middle class.” But more often, such “Cruse missiles” were launched at the very black leftists I was teaching and admired.
Richard Wright, for example, my cultural lodestar since high school, was depicted, in language redolent of far-right Judeo-Bolshevik conspiracy theories, as “so ideologically blinded by the smog of Jewish-Marxist nationalism that he was unable to see his own clearly.” Lorraine Hansberry, James Baldwin, and Paul Robeson were part of a long list under fire for naiveté and a lack of independent, sophisticated thought. Hansberry, Cruse said, was the “Joan of Arc of People’s Integration,” and Baldwin “a rather innocent and provincial intellectual.” Robeson’s 1958 autobiographical manifesto, Here I Stand, was described as “a weak, muddled, sentimental book, suffused with innocent idealism and lacking a single paragraph of original thought on Negro problems.”
Cruse’s overall literary legacy, consisting of three books and numerous essays, left an erratic track record: a baffling mix of acuity, wide reading, personal grudges, and dubious hot takes. He used Marxist terminology but was not a Marxist, for he saw the United States as a battleground of competing racial and ethnic groups more than a conflict between economic classes. He advocated black self-determination, but at the center was culture, not land, and his notion of culture was black art, theater, literature, and media, not the less elitist anthropological definition. For Cruse, Harlem was to be the center of black autonomy, even as over 90 percent of the black population lived outside Harlem with a vastly different cultural experience.
Most problematic, as the late Trinity College Professor Jerry Gafio Watts observed in Heroism and the Black Intellectual (1994), is that he “wanted to frame the issues of black intellectual life and politics along a rather simpleminded axis between black nationalism and integrationism.” It was a questionable either-or version of the old race and class debate that still roils the Left in new forms.
Cruse’s belief that black Americans should operate as an organized ethnic interest group to bargain for power failed to challenge the capitalist foundation of American society. Was there no way for a fight for cultural self-determination, racial pride, and democratic rights against a racially oppressive system to blend with class struggle, aiming at a society with economic and social justice for all? Lloyd even speculates that, until the end of his life, Cruse wrestled with the question: “What if separate but equal was not such a bad thing?”
Portrait of a Person
Lloyd’s approach to Cruse is more that of a storyteller than a historian. His focus is on the portrait of a person, not on defending or disputing Cruse’s political theories. Through a narrative based on numerous interviews and some original documentation, we soon learn that there were many Harold Cruses. That’s because Lloyd makes every effort “to allow the people who knew Cruse to speak for themselves.” People’s perceptions of memorable individuals vary by age and context, and the man who ultimately emerges from Lloyd’s portrait was not to everyone’s taste.
As an authoritative spokesperson for a particular brand of African American self-determination in the 1960s and ’70s, Cruse was both adored by acolytes and despised by those with whom he differed or whom he had offended. Many, including me, admired his ambition, his ability to pose challenging questions, and his desire to promote African American intellectual thought. We liked that he didn’t pitch softballs but were flummoxed by shortcomings in his thinking — too many grandiose claims followed by superficial analysis.
Lloyd himself is less drawn by any agreement with Cruse’s stances than by what he sees as the “critical dimension” and “spirit” of Cruse’s thought. Nevertheless, for those of us who knew Cruse, all this was complicated by how to negotiate a personal relationship with an imposing figure marked by a titanic but fragile ego.
In five chapters, Lloyd offers a rather chatty survey that begins with Cruse’s working-class family background in Virginia, his hardscrabble youth with relatives in Harlem, and his military service in World War II. Then come a half-dozen years in the Communist Party USA (CPUSA) as a journalist and librarian, followed by life as a Greenwich Village bohemian with literary aspirations in theater and fiction. Cruse next shifts into black nationalist activism and social criticism with the Liberator Magazine and the Freedom Now Party. When Crisis becomes a national publishing sensation, he is hired as a visiting black studies instructor at the University of Michigan. He retires fifteen years later as a full professor, an “elder,” and something of a legend.
Lloyd’s is a kind of magpie method, with proleptic leaps from the outset, but it proves surprisingly helpful in certain areas because, previously, only uneven source material had been available for many facets of his subject’s life. Lloyd knows how to distill the essential from the inessential and never allows archival minutiae to submerge the core concern.
Moreover, Lloyd is no slouch in the revelation department. Cruse was ostentatious about name-dropping and telling tales of his army experiences in North Africa and Italy, as well as his 1960 trip to Cuba sponsored by the Fair Play for Cuba Committee. But he was mostly tight-lipped about his personal and emotional past. This left some of us wondering how dark his secrets might be.
As it turns out, most of Cruse’s closeted skeletons are the familiar human ones — a love life Lloyd can’t untangle and some problematic episodes with alcohol. On the other hand, there is the revelation from Freedom of Information Act records that Cruse “named about a dozen of his former [Communist] party associates as Communist Party members” to the FBI, even as he would later deny any such cooperation. Sometimes not all the facts in a person’s life are convenient, and often the lies we tell about the past seem necessary to live in the present. Still, this is a whopper that will leave many of his acquaintances with the taste of ashes in their mouths.
Otherwise, what Lloyd unravels is a long life with many loops, interludes, and repetitions. At times, it’s something of a detective story as he tries to figure out whether Cruse was ever legally married, whether he abandoned a son in Europe, and whether the sweep of Cruse’s career reads more like a rise and slide than a rise and fall. After a twenty-year wait and many false starts, his final book, Plural but Equal: A Critical Study of Blacks and Minorities and America’s Plural Society, appeared in 1987. Instead of a late-life powerhouse performance, it was judged to add little to his thesis that the United States was a society of competing ethnic blocs, and it has been effectively out of print for nearly four decades.
We learn about many elements of Cruse’s baroque personality — highly complex, dramatic, extravagant, and emotionally intense. With ramrod posture and a face often set in a dignified pose, he projected brooding bitterness and the aura of a man who felt personally wronged. At Michigan, he seemed to swing between episodes of immense energy and passion and periods of existential rumination, with students both benefiting and suffering. Through it all, Lloyd is remarkably nonjudgmental. He rightly seems to accept the mysteries of the shadowlands of human motivations. He has no desire to canonize a saint and recognizes that Cruse was somewhat intoxicated with his own sense of self-importance. I would also add that, intellectually, Cruse was the type who always needed to have a foil.
The Boundary Crosser
For me, the arc of Cruse’s life felt awe-inspiring. A true boundary crosser, he was catapulted from plebeian marginality to superstar fame, mainly through ulcer-producing hard work and an authentic, self-authored identity that I associated with my own Marxist-existentialist aspirations. Lloyd, however, shows that certain fortuitous friendships (a Jewish couple with publishing connections) and political coincidences (a black student revolt at the University of Michigan) also helped his rise.
Yet despite our fundamentally different political orientations, some of us on the Left were attracted to Cruse’s intellectual stridency, not to mention the exciting charge of his transgressive opinions. Attacking orthodoxies and stomping on taboos — what’s not to like? After all, I, too, was working on a book-length call to arms for a new approach based on a critical reassessment of the Left’s past record on culture and intellectuals. That my focus was on Jews, and that I was Jewish, never seemed to be a problem for him, despite his oft-expressed wariness of Jewish Marxist intellectuals.
Moreover, having read much C. L. R. James and George Breitman’s 1967 book, The Last Year of Malcolm X, I was open to the idea of an independent black liberation movement as a vanguard catalyst that did not need to subordinate itself to a conservatized white working class. To be sure, I was hardly an expert on the chameleon ideology of nationalism, but I sympathized with anti-colonialism and opposed expansionist and chauvinistic nationalism. One could be suspicious of any claims of nationalist belonging and yet reject the facile stereotype of all varieties of nationalism as equally essentialist and ethnocentric.
I felt most politically at odds with Cruse on the centrality of intellectuals, ultimate economic goals, and the black movement’s relationship to the white working class. As for his treatment of the CPUSA, my own research had convinced me that one can be correct about its Stalinist politics but wrong about almost everything else. Cruse had grossly misrepresented both the sincerity and the impact of the CPUSA members’ commitment to anti-racism, and in this regard Crisis read too much like a pulpy novel of revenge.
Lloyd’s interview findings match my own experiences with Cruse. I first met him at events sponsored by Michigan’s Center for Afroamerican and African Studies in 1975, just after his brief term as an early director. After several discussions about his CPUSA experiences, he gave me an autographed copy of a long and remarkable course description for “Marxism and the Negro Question,” a class he took at the CPUSA’s Jefferson School in the late 1940s. Then, in the fall of 1979, he requested a favor: Would I take over some reviewing assignments he had promised the socialist newspaper In These Times? This would start with James Baldwin’s new novel Just Above My Head (1979), which he found “unreadable.” As an untenured nobody, I was quite flattered, and this review led to eight more, on writers such as Hansberry, W. E. B. Du Bois, and my fellow English department member Gayl Jones.
For the next fifteen years, during which time he officially retired in 1984, we continued our association, although I mainly queried him for information on his CPUSA comrades with little reciprocal curiosity. Then, in the spring of 1992, I invited the emeritus Cruse to address two sessions of a seminar I had organized on the cultural left in the 1950s; the plan was to juxtapose chapters of Crisis against one of Cruse’s objects of criticism — the novel Youngblood (1954) by the pro-Communist leader of the Harlem Writers Guild, John Oliver Killens. Cruse seemed pleased, and I opened the first class with a fulsome introduction, including a biographical sketch with highlights of his career that I thought he might have been too modest to mention himself. To my surprise, the discussion that ensued around Killens was stilted and relatively unproductive.
When I met with Cruse afterward, he gave me a sharp dressing-down; nothing I had said was inaccurate or disrespectful, but he had wanted to represent himself, not have me do it for him. This was followed by a letter explaining that he would not return to the seminar, but for a different reason: “To be honest, I never finished reading Youngblood after it was published. For me, the novel possessed no literary merit.” Sheesh, I thought, why didn’t he say that in the first place?
Lloyd’s biography, however, discloses a history of similar behavior — walking offstage, hanging up mid-conversation, and precipitously dumping a graduate student — and I likely got off easy. Just four months later, we were back in dialogue. He wanted to learn what I had heard about Van Gosse’s book in progress about the Fair Play for Cuba Committee, although he did manage to stick in an admonishment about my allegedly teaching Youngblood as a “masterpiece.”
The point is that Cruse had an unsleeping vigilance for any possible slight, which was a significant element in his alienation from the CPUSA. As Lloyd reveals, Hansberry and others he saw as an insider group under CPUSA control rebuffed his aspirations to write for the theater in the 1950s. And as Lloyd convincingly argues, “Cruse’s ideas . . . grew out of Cruse’s life.” But too much of it was a synthetic certainty about the motives and achievements of a bricolage of black communist cultural dupes: “White intellectuals are unoriginal, imitative, and puerile, and black intellectuals are brainwashed by the whites.”
Throughout his writing, he hammers this theme like Vulcan, rolling over it relentlessly from new angles — casting would-be African American radical intellectuals as betrayed by West Indians, manipulated by Jews, and undermined by black women. No wonder one of Cruse’s most impressive legacies has been highly sophisticated, well-researched refutations, starting with the concluding section of Winston James’s Holding Aloft the Banner of Ethiopia: Caribbean Radicalism in Early Twentieth Century America (1999).
The longer one ponders Cruse, the more enigmatic his beguiling strangeness becomes. Yes, he was always available for discussion and consultation, yet this seemed tethered to a thirst for adulation. His inner life is not my story to tell, and he had a perpetually inscrutable aura. I quickly saw I would never be the yin to his yang — far from it. It was hard not to sense that his personality contained many combustible elements that, mixed at high velocity, might explode. I, and probably many others, handled him with kid gloves. But did I ever actually see him for who he was?
Perhaps the crucial insight comes from a private letter to his mother that Lloyd quotes early in his biography: “I have grown up mostly alone. I have always been forced to be reliant on no one but myself.” Simone de Beauvoir, among others, has written about the deep emotional isolation that comes from complete self-reliance, but surely the price is tenfold for a working-class African American like Cruse aspiring to literary fame. His may superficially resemble the familiar radical individualism of those of us who reject what we believe are prepackaged identities handed down by others. But for Cruse, it was a new and self-owned identity agonizingly forged in the crucible of a white-racist and class-divided society.
Cruse was no doubt as guilty as the rest of us at times in acquiescing to opportunistic acts of self-preservation. At Michigan, although he taught pioneering and successful classes, he was no ally in the activist campaigns against South African apartheid and US intervention in Latin America. He sneered at most campus activism. If he was not the leading man, he wasn’t going to play a supporting role.
Moreover, his anti-communism fed Cold War myths, and many of his attitudes about gender were retrograde even by the standards of his generation. Although commonly regarded as a black cultural nationalist, he was hypercritical of the movement’s leaders and a splinter in its toe as well. Nevertheless, he is hardly alone among his generation in being disoriented by the Stalinist experience, and I see his obsessive writing as testimony to an undying struggle to define his own life and create his own meaning. The loneliness of the black radical intellectual was perhaps the most direct price he paid for this autonomy.

https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-council-t.title: NYC Council to scrutinize snow removal plans as winter approaches
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-council-t.author: Catalina Gonella
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-council-t.text:
The leaves are still falling, but New York City lawmakers are already talking about clearing snow.
The City Council’s sanitation committee will take a closer look at how the city prepares for winter storms and snow removal on Monday, after two major winter storms buried streets and sidewalks earlier this year and lingering low temperatures kept piles of snow frozen for weeks.
Lawmakers will also consider a bill requiring the city’s Department of Sanitation to keep and publish snowplowing records on its PlowNYC website. Right now, the site lets New Yorkers see the last time their block was cleared of snow, but it doesn’t keep historical data.
In a memo supporting the bill, primary sponsor Councilmember Ty Hankerson said the legislation would give New Yorkers greater transparency during and after snowstorms.
“Snow plows are often a contentious issue, with accusations that certain parts of New York receive many more snow plows than others,” Hankerson wrote. “As the City navigates this issue, it must do so with all of the relevant data publicly available to everyone.”
The hearing comes as federal forecasters predict a warmer-than-average winter in New York City, partly due to El Niño, a weather pattern linked to warming Pacific Ocean waters. But meteorologists have said a major snowstorm is still possible.
Last winter was particularly brutal, bringing prolonged cold and heavy snowfall to the city.

https://gothamist.com/news/the-best-day-.title: 'The best day of the year': Inside Clinton Hill's 'mile nine' NYC marathon party
https://gothamist.com/news/the-best-day-.author: Stephanie Keith
https://gothamist.com/news/the-best-day-.text:
For Danielle Strle, Marathon Sunday in New York City is “the best day of the year.”
Strle, 45, chief product officer for the satirical news site The Onion, came dressed as a banana to cheer people on as they dashed by.
She was among thousands of revelers packed into the brownstone-lined streets of Brooklyn's Clinton Hill, near mile nine of the 26.2-mile route, for one of the city's most exuberant marathon watch parties.
Strle said the "Mile Nine" party along Lafayette Avenue in Clinton Hill has been going on for 23 years. And she's been part of it since the beginning.
"We kind of started it by accident," she said.
In the early days, locals would pass out bodega sandwiches. Now, "we’ve upgraded to a grill. We have waffles. We have egg sandwiches. We have coffee. We’ve got orange juice," she said. "We’ve just gotten bigger and bigger every year."
"Nobody was having parties on the end of the block when we started doing this," she added. "It’s the best block for the marathon party spectator scene."
This year's marathon kicked off the morning after Halloween and many revelers appeared to show up in their Halloween costumes from the night before. Strle was one of many dressed up like the potassium-rich snack favored by endurance athletes.
Some 60,000 runners participated in the race, which winds through all five boroughs before finishing in Central Park.
A few blocks down the marathon route, another party convened around Emmanuel Baptist Church. Around 11 a.m., the church choir came out to serenade the runners, while a grill had been set up to serve barbecue.
On Sunday, nearly all the runners lagged far behind Andreas Almgren of Sweden and Sheila Chepkirui of Kenya, the men's and women's winners, who both finished the marathon in just over two hours.
But winning was hardly the point for most participants, and certainly not for the spectators cheering them on.
“It’s a real triumph of the human spirit,” said Strle.

https://gothamist.com/news/mta-should-el.title: MTA should eliminate some jobs to prepare for budget woes, watchdog writes
https://gothamist.com/news/mta-should-el.author: Stephen Nessen
https://gothamist.com/news/mta-should-el.text:
In less than four years, the MTA could be looking at a nearly $900 million funding shortfall as spending outpaces fare revenue, according to a new analysis from the Citizens Budget Commission, which recommends cutting the workforce to close the gap.
The budget watchdog recommends sweeping job cuts to positions that it argues technology has made obsolete. The budget commission suggested the MTA allow its trains to run with just one worker, instead of two.
Train lines that have new computer-based signals, like the L and the 7, are already fully automated, as are the announcements on the trains. While the conductor opens and closes the train doors, the operator has few other duties, which include hitting a button every 20 seconds to signal they are alert. The budget commission cited the operator’s limited responsibilities as a sign the job could be cut with no impact to service.
Eliminating operator jobs on the L and 7 lines could save $36.5 million a year, according to the report. If the agency moved to phase out two people operating trains across the system, it could save $500 million a year.
The agency is in the process of installing new signals on other lines like the A, C, E, F, G, M and R lines. For now, those lines still require two people to run the trains.
The suggestion from the Citizens Budget Commission comes at a sensitive time as Transport Workers Union Local 100 negotiates a contract with the MTA for its 40,000 subway and bus workers. The MTA is expected to release its financial plan for next year in the coming weeks, which will include a 4% fare and toll increase. The board will vote on that plan in December.
“The same recommendations have been coming down for dozens of years, so there's nothing new about it,” said Transport Workers Union of America President John Samuelsen. “It's essentially a recommendation to balance alleged deficits that the MTA has off the backs of working people.”
Last year, the state legislature tried to enshrine a requirement of two MTA workers on each train into law, but Gov. Kathy Hochul vetoed the bill, leaving open the possibility that one-person train operations could happen in the future.
“Legislatively mandated staffing prevents the MTA from modernizing — as technology and best practices continue to improve — and realizing the efficiency and financial benefits,” the Citizens Budget Commission's report argues.
The Citizens Budget Commission acknowledges the MTA has become more efficient in recent years, saving a reported $576 million this year through what the agency calls “operating efficiencies.” But the report argues that without cutting labor and healthcare costs, the MTA faces a $300 million budget gap next year that will grow to $900 million by 2030. The budget commission estimates its recommended reforms could save $2.5 billion annually.
Other recommendations include streamlining fare collection on the commuter railroads by checking tickets prior to boarding, reducing the need for someone to walk through the train. The Citizens Budget Commission argues cutting more than 1,000 jobs on Metro-North and the Long Island Rail Road could save $380 million annually.
The report also recommended MTA retirees pay more in healthcare premiums, which could bring in an additional $315 million a year.
Samuelsen countered that many laborers, ironworkers, track workers, and crane operators in the MTA get paid less than their peers in the private sector, but accept that because of the generous retirement benefits.

The Vilcek Foundation has announced the twelve recipients of its 2026 grants, totaling $212,000. Founded in 2000 by Czechoslovakian immigrants Jan and Marica Vilcek, the New York–based nonprofit to date has awarded more than $9.6 million in prizes to individuals and over $7.6 million in grants to organizations in its drive to promote the arts and sciences and bring attention to the contributions of immigrants to American society.
The dozen nonprofit organizations making up this years’ cohort of grantees were chosen from among nearly two thousand open-call applicants—representing a 46 percent increase over the inaugural, 2025 cycle. Winners were selected based on level of innovation, depth of community engagement, and the potential for lasting impact.
“Immigrants are essential to the fabric of the United States, yet their contributions are often overlooked or undervalued,” said Vilcek Foundation president Rick Kinsel in a statement. “The Vilcek Foundation is proud to partner with organizations that elevate immigrant voices and drive tangible impact within their local communities.” Kinsel noted that this year, the organization extended the geographic reach of its grantmaking, “with recipients in eight new states, bringing us closer to supporting local, regional, and national nonprofits enacting meaningful change across the country.”
A full list of winners is below:
- Bemis Center for Contemporary Arts, Omaha, NE ($20,000)
- Radio Boise, Boise, ID, ($20,000)

- Rhode Island Latino Arts (RILA), Providence, RI ($15,000)
- Voices Jackson Hole, Jackson Hole, WY ($12,000)

News
On October 30, culture workers at the Venice Biennale went on strike in solidarity with a national general strike in Italy, and similar protests by dockworkers at over 110 ports all across the world. According to reporting by Ocula, the global strikes called for an end to the use of ports for transporting arms—art workers also issued demands for better living and working conditions.
More than 25 unions across six continents backed the organizing movement, per Reuters. Demonstrations were initially planned across Italy, France, Greece, Spain’s Basque Country, Turkey, and Morocco but spread to India, Cyprus, Brazil, Austria, Mexico, and Uruguay. The strikes were organized by a group called ‘No Harbour For Genocide.’
As per a statement on the group’s website, organizers called for an “immediate end to the genocide of the Palestinian people and all imperialist wars,” the prevention of arms, troops, and munitions transport through participating ports, and health, safety, and job security safeguards for workers.
In Venice, artists, gallery attendants, and cultural workers closed down pavilions and marched from the Campo Santa Margherita to Rialto. The march was part of a strike organized in conjunction with the Art Not Genocide Alliance (ANGA) and Biennalocene.
ANGA stated in an Instagram post that the strike was organized in “solidarity with dock workers around the world who have downed tools to block the passage of ships carrying military material to Israel and with students across Italy who fight for the right to education and against the war economy pursued by the Meloni government.”
Around 20 national pavilions were either fully or partially closed as part of the strike, including those of the UK, Japan, Austria, the Bahamas, Brazil, Canada, Denmark, Finland, India, Ireland, Japan, Korea, Lebanon, Malta, New Zealand and the Netherlands. This is the latest in a string of protests that have rocked the biennale this year, including a strike on May 8, organized to protest Israel’s participation.

https://gothamist.com/news/ny-opens-heap.title: NY opens HEAP applications to help pay for heating costs
https://gothamist.com/news/ny-opens-heap.author: Louis C. Hochman
https://gothamist.com/news/ny-opens-heap.text:
The state has opened applications for the regular Home Energy Assistance Program, which can help provide up to $1,086 to low- and middle-income households for help with heating costs.
The benefits can pay for fuel, or for heating and cooling equipment. Specific benefit amounts can vary based on factors including income, household size, heating source and whether a family includes a vulnerable member. A family of five could make up to $7,948 per month and qualify for assistance.
The state increased the benefit amount this year in response to rising costs of heating oil and kerosene, state officials said in announcing the program. The benefit for heat with oil, kerosene, or propane has been increased by $90 to $990. The amount for heat with wood, pellets, and coal has increased by $65 to $700.
Applications opened Monday for people not automatically enrolled in the program because of their enrollment in other social benefit programs.
Applications can be submitted online or through the mail, or at at departments of social service. New York City residents can apply through the Access HRA portal.
State officials urge those seeking benefits to apply as soon as possible, as they’re awarded on a first-come, first-serve basis, and are only awarded until funding runs out. Payments are made directly to vendors for the expenses.
The state will also open applications for emergency HEAP benefits — for people in danger or running of out of fuel or having services shut off — on Jan. 4.
In October, the state opened applications for the Heating Equipment Clean and Tune benefit, to help both with the cleaning of primary heating equipment as well as chimney cleaning, minor repairs and installation of carbon monoxide detectors or programmable thermostats. Benefits for that program can be up to $500.
Older adults can contact Offices for the Aging or the NY Connects helpline at 1-800-342-9871 for help applying and navigating benefits.

https://gothamist.com/news/heres-what-dr.title: Here’s what drove NYC gas prices higher and whether relief is on the way
https://gothamist.com/news/heres-what-dr.author: Ramsey Khalifeh
https://gothamist.com/news/heres-what-dr.text:
The cost of living is top of mind for most New Yorkers — and the price of gas this year is playing a big part.
After the U.S. and Israel launched strikes on Iran starting in February, global gas prices rose as the geopolitical makeup of the Middle East created a strain on oil tankers traveling through the Strait of Hormuz. That passage typically carries more than 20% of the world’s oil trade.
The conflict is impacting New York, which already pays more for gas compared to states like Texas and Louisiana, located closer to oil production and refineries.
But according to Patrick De Haan, who leads petroleum analysis at the gas price monitoring platform GasBuddy, New Yorkers can expect gas prices to lower in the coming weeks as the winter season approaches. The big caveat: The Trump administration doesn’t ramp up attacks on Iran after the midterm elections.
“ Generally, we do see gas prices fall most years in the autumn. [It’s] a combination of Americans that start to stay closer to home and aren't driving as much in colder weather now that the summer is kind of behind us,” De Haan said. “As well as a seasonal switch over to cheaper winter gasoline, which happens every year in September.”
According to the platform’s own data, New York City’s average gas price in the last week — based on a survey of more than 1000 stations — is $4.37 per gallon. A year ago, the city's average price was $3.10 per gallon.
This year has been nothing but ordinary for diesel prices as well. De Haan said targeted airstrikes over the summer of oil refineries in Russia by Ukraine in the ongoing war between the two European nations have peaked diesel prices.
“ Diesel prices in the last month have set new records in just about every U.S. state,” he added.
The underlying effect of higher diesel prices on the everyday New Yorker — who relies on public transportation — is on the MTA’s balance sheet.
Transit agencies like the MTA typically ink longer-term fuel contracts and lock in pricing for months at a time to supply their buses or a crop of their diesel-powered work repair trains. While the influx in global diesel prices might not affect the transit agency now, De Haan said a future with prices staying high could.
“The higher cost of diesel will eventually likely cause these agencies to have some imbalances in their budget and whether or not they raise fares or they somehow find revenue to offset that somewhere else is up to the respective agency,” De Haan said.

https://hyperallergic.com/a-midterm-elec.title: A Midterm Election Guide for Artists and Arts Workers
https://hyperallergic.com/a-midterm-elec.author: Valentina Di Liscia
https://hyperallergic.com/a-midterm-elec.text:
A Midterm Election Guide for Artists and Arts Workers
Issues touching on arts funding, censorship, AI regulation, and more are at stake for the country’s cultural sectors across key Senate, House, and Gubernatorial races.
Midterms are tomorrow, marking the first nationwide election since President Donald Trump started his second term in the Oval Office. In the wake of Trump’s financial and ideological crackdowns on Smithsonian, unapproved pet projects around the US Capitol, devastation to cultural landscapes through border construction, and dozens of other policies targeting history and heritage, many will be lining up at the polls with arts and culture policies on their minds.
Because Congress ultimately decides appropriations for federal arts entities, such as the National Endowment for the Arts, control of the House and Senate is incredibly important for the cultural sector. (Republicans currently have narrow majorities in both chambers.) From artists running for Congress, like Claire Valdez in New York and musician Bobby Pulido in Texas, to longtime culture advocates like Angie Nixon in the Senate race, we zeroed in on some of the key campaigns to watch in the United States if you care about artistic freedom, affordability for artists, and cultural funding.
We've organized this guide into three sections: Senate, House, and Gubernatorial races. Click through each section below.
Rebecca Schiffman and Lisa Yin Zhang also contributed to this guide.
Senate Races
Michigan
Democrat Abdul El-Sayed leads Republican Mike Rogers by an average of five points in one of this election cycle’s most-anticipated races. El-Sayed, an epidemiologist and the former head of the Detroit and Wayne County health departments, has been subject to repeated racism and culture war tirades over his Muslim faith and criticism of Israel by Rogers and President Trump throughout his campaign. Rogers, a former FBI agent and United States Representative, was endorsed by Trump in July 2025 and has received major funding from pro-Israel lobbying groups during this election cycle.
Here’s what you should know.
- At the center of Abdul El-Sayed’s platform is “Medicare for All,” which he co-authored a book guide on with Micah Johnson in 2021. This is particularly relevant for artists, among whom only 84% have access to health insurance, according to a 2023–25 survey by the National Opinion Research Center. El-Sayed also believes “unions are one of the most important bulwarks for the dignity of work in a moment when AI is coming for a lot of that.” He has been a member of the National Writers Union, the SEIU (Service Employees International Union), the AFT (American Federation of Teachers), and the Michigan-founded UAW (United Auto Workers), which represents workers at museums including Manhattan’s Museum of Modern Art and the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston.
- Mike Rogers has routinely aligned with President Trump on key issues. Encore, a local Michigan performing arts news outlet, notes that “his congressional majority is the one that proposed zeroing out the federal arts education funding,” making his contrast with El-Sayed’s across-the-board pro-educational funding initiatives “not subtle.” Also in opposition to his Democratic opponent, Rogers has fiercely fought Medicare for All proposals and has consistently battled against UAW in Congress.

https://gothamist.com/news/buzzer-beater.title: Buzzer beater? MTA vows to turn this SoHo pit into a basketball court in 30 days.
https://gothamist.com/news/buzzer-beater.author: Liam Quigley
https://gothamist.com/news/buzzer-beater.text:
A Downtown Manhattan basketball court that’s been in MTA construction purgatory for four years is set to reopen at the end of November, according to transit officials.
The refreshed Grand Canal Court at Sixth Avenue will feature new benches, a water fountain, upgraded lighting and fencing. The courts were ripped up in 2022 so workers could build a new substation that provides electricity to trains.
The MTA said in a December 2022 statement that the project would be complete by the end of 2024. Signage at the site states the project should have been done by April 2026.
Now, the MTA and parks department say the project will actually be done by the end of November — though making that deadline may require a buzzer beater.
The site was abuzz with activity Thursday. Crews were still working in pits below the street shored up with timber. The site has not yet been paved and none of the new amenities — or the basketball court and hoops — have been installed.
“We look forward to welcoming the community back to Grand Canal Court with an upgraded space for New Yorkers to come together, stay active and enjoy the game,” Alberto Roldan, the parks department borough commissioner, wrote in a statement.
The budget for the project was $45 million in 2014, but now it's nearly doubled to $83.7 million, according to MTA records. The agency blamed a host of issues for the increase, including unforeseen utility work.
The worksite is surrounded by litter, and straphangers must squeeze through a narrow passage to reach the Canal Street subway station entrance at Sixth Avenue.
John Underwood, 68, a retired city worker who has walked by the site for decades, was skeptical it would reopen soon.
“It might open in a year or two,” he said. “I had even forgotten it was a basketball court.”
The wedge-shaped parkland was created by Sixth Avenue’s southern extension in the 1930s, said Andrew Berman, executive director of local civic group Village Preservation.
“These little oddly shaped lots along Sixth Avenue have been surprisingly popular and resilient recreational spaces over the years,” he said.
Not everyone wants the basketball court back. An online petition to replace it with a dog run has 2,200 signatures.
Berman compared the shifting demands to bocce courts in Manhattan giving way to ballfields and playgrounds. “Sometimes longtime uses disappear,” he said.
Herb Tam, an organizer with the Chinatown Basketball Club, remembered teenagers spilling from the Canal Street station and nearby schools to play ball at the park.
Tam said a closed park changes the feel of the whole block. “When you have live parks, the whole neighborhood around the park feels safer, he said.
“I can’t imagine our court closing for even, like, a month… let alone how long the courts over at Canal and Sixth Avenue have been closed,” he said.
“If I was one of the regulars, I probably would’ve found other places to play already.”

https://gothamist.com/news/nycs-school-p.title: NYC's school PTA fundraising gap is growing, mirroring broader racial disparities
https://gothamist.com/news/nycs-school-p.author: Joe Hong
https://gothamist.com/news/nycs-school-p.text:
Parent teacher associations may conjure images of read-a-thons and fun runs, where grandparents and relatives pledge to pay their grade schooler for every page they read or lap they jog. And of course, there’s the iconic PTA bake sale.
But in New York City, PTA fundraising efforts vary from hawking homemade muffins and pastries for a few hundred dollars to running sophisticated, self-sustaining nonprofits that operate like small businesses and take in millions in revenue.
P.S. 29 in Cobble Hill, Brooklyn, raised about $2 million in donations and revenue, more than any other school last year, according to data from the Department of Education. In second place was P.S. 158 on Manhattan's Upper East Side, which raised $1.7 million. Both schools enroll between 600 and 700 students. New Explorations into Science, Technology & Math, a K-12 school on the Lower East Side, which enrolls about 1,600 students, came in third, raising $1.4 million.
Each school in the city is required to have a parent association. In total, they reported nearly $70 million in revenue and savings in the 2024-25 academic year, which helped their schools pay for beneficial after-school enrichment programs, field trips, support staff and in some cases even building maintenance.
“We find evidence that PTA money above and beyond any public resources actually do boost achievement in reading and math,” said Brittany Murray, an education professor at Davidson College who researches PTAs. “But it tends to help those that are more affluent.”
PTAs in many of the city’s low-income neighborhoods are far less flush with cash, with some parent groups reporting donations of just a few hundred dollars or nothing at all. A comparison with demographic data reveals sharp racial disparities in which students benefit the most from parent fundraising that have only grown since the COVID-19 pandemic.
Last year, schools serving more white students outraised those that primarily serve Black children 5-to-1.
The findings come as the Mamdani administration is under increased pressure to address segregation and inequality in the city’s education system.
On the whole, PTA funds ultimately made up a small amount compared to the city education department's overall $41 billion budget. And the city makes an effort to offset the detrimental effects of poverty on education by providing other sources of money for schools in underprivileged neighborhoods.
Nicole Brownstein, a spokesperson for New York City Public Schools, pointed to the city’s Fair Student Funding formula, which channels more money to schools with large concentrations of poverty, students with disabilities and English learners. The city also provides money for these schools to expand arts education.
“We recognize that funding capacity reflects differences in community resources and fundraising capacity – that is why we are consistently working to strengthen our Fair Student Funding formula, meeting schools and students where they are,” she said.
But experts in education policy say even that additional money is not enough, and that while PTA fundraising is a lifeline for many schools, the wide gaps in fundraising can worsen inequality and are yet another symptom of a segregated school system that has come under fresh scrutiny since the start of the school year. Last month, New York Times journalist Nikole Hannah-Jones detailed her daughter’s experience with inequality and segregation in the city’s school system, renewing calls to address long-standing disparities.
“When you have places that are highly economically segregated and racially segregated, then you're gonna see vast differences in the schools that can fundraise,” said Murray. “It exacerbates inequality.”
Anita Baier, a PTA president at P.S. 8 in Brooklyn Heights, said PTAs do more than fundraising. She said they play an essential role in planning events for families and connecting parents within the community But she said much of their work is unfortunately focused on raising money to pay for necessities the city does not provide, like after-school programs and support staff.
“Not only do we need more funding, we need predictable and adequate funding year over year so parents are not always having to be on alert and step up to plug these gaps,” Baier said.
Racial and geographic disparities
The five boroughs are home to more than 1,200 parent associations. And yet just 15 PTAs accounted for a third of the $70 million raised and saved by parent associations last year. Those in Manhattan had the highest average revenues last year, over $200,000. But the top funded parent groups were scattered across both Manhattan and parts of Brooklyn.
Gothamist used PTA financial data and student demographic data from the Department of Education to calculate how much a typical student, depending on their race, benefits from PTA fundraising. The average white student in the 2024-25 school year benefited from$254 in PTA money. For the average Black student, the amount was just $46.30. Of the 15 schools that raised more than $1 million, only two have Black enrollment above 4%.
Take P.S. 8 in Brooklyn Heights, where 69% of enrollment was white and 3% was Black over the course of the last school year. Only 1-in-8 students at the elementary school came from low-income households, compared to a citywide average of nearly 3-in-4 students. The school raised $1.3 million and ended the year with $844,000 in the bank after expenses.
At the top earning school, P.S. 29 in Cobble Hill, 69% of grade schoolers were white. According to the education department’s data, the school had just six Black students, and 13% of pupils overall came from low-income households. Out of the $2 million the school raised in total, it ended the 2024-25 year with over $1.1 million after expenses.
Contrast that with P.S. 399 in Brooklyn’s Flatbush neighborhood, where 66% of students are Black, and P.S. 43 in the Bronx’s Mott Haven neighborhood, where 78% of students are Latino. Over 95% of students at both schools come from low-income households, among the highest concentrations of poverty in the city. Their PTAs each raised less than $1,000 last year.
None of the parents at the school’s parent association, or those at several other low-fundraising PTAs, responded to requests for interviews.
Claire Mackevicius, an education professor at the University of Oregon who researches parent teacher associations across the country, said affluent parents are often blamed for those wide fundraising disparities. But she said they’re merely plugging holes in school systems that are struggling to provide enrichment programs, pay for tutoring and keep class sizes down.
“ I want to be clear that sort of onus and burden is not on the committed and hardworking volunteers in the PTA organization itself,” Mackevicius said. “Our public schools are underfunded, full stop.”
She said the chasm between rich and poor PTAs is instead a reflection of broader disparities, and that elected officials and policymakers have grown complacent about inequality and segregation in schools. By some measures, school segregation in the city has worsened since the 1990s, with students of color more likely today to be attending a school with fewer white students.
Murray, the Davidson College professor, said segregation has worsened in part because New York City’s parents can choose to send their children to middle and high schools outside of their neighborhoods. And a PTA that raises more money is another factor that makes certain schools more attractive than others in the eyes of some parents.
“It's this kind of circular problem,” she said. “It’s really hard to disentangle the segregation piece and the school choice piece.”
How PTAs spend
The Department of Education’s rules for PTAs, known as Regulation A-660, allow parent fundraising to support a variety of personnel and services at schools. PTAs can pay for specialized, supplemental teachers who rotate into different classrooms throughout the school day, or staff who work during after-school or weekend programs. This includes academic support like tutoring or homework help, as well as enrichment and extracurricular activities, such as science and math clubs or art classes.
After-school programs are a big component of what some PTAs provide, and some parent associations hire a staff member to oversee those services. That might mean managing a contract with a company that provides art, music or dance lessons.
What PTAs can’t do is cover classroom teachers for core subjects like math, science, English and history.
New York City Public Schools does not collect and publish detailed data on how PTAs spend their money. But a review of some tax filings show that many of the PTAs that raise hundreds of thousands of dollars each year generate revenues by collecting fees from families attending after-school programs. Most of those revenues typically go back into staffing those programs.
According to tax filings for P.S. 8’s PTA, the organization spent $526,000 in 2024-25 on its after-school program, including $146,000 for the program’s staff salaries. Other costs included paying third-party vendors who come with their own staff and curriculum, according to PTA Co-President Amélie Walker-Yung. The fees collected from families for after-school and extracurricular programs and clubs amounted to $991,000.
Walker-Yung said the after-school program regularly changes its offerings based on what parents and students want. Clubs and activities range from chess and STEM-based programs to drama, dance and sports. She said her son is currently taking a comic-book drawing class.
Gothamist’s analysis found a $200 difference on average in how white students benefit from PTA fundraising compared to Black students.
“ It doesn't sound like much,” Murray said, but it can be spent in “highly impactful” ways. A field trip or an after-school program that fosters an interest in science or technology can pay off in the long run, she said.
“ When you accumulate that across the whole school, that can make a big difference,” she said. “Whether it's supplies, whether it's grants for teachers, whether it's field trips, that goes a long way across a school building.”
Her research shows that the PTAs that raise enough money to afford additional programs and activities are most likely to be in white, affluent neighborhoods.
P.S. 29’s PTA in Cobble Hill spent $1.6 million on its after-school program, which included $700,000 for staff. Additional money went to staff training, supplies and insurance. The program in turn raised $1.5 million in fees, according to tax filings. Some of the instructors in the after-school classes are also classroom teachers at the school. The PTA also covers training for teachers in the program.
After-school offerings at P.S. 29 change periodically, said Kasey Noziska, one of the school’s PTA presidents. Students have taken classes in cooking, fashion design and understanding the stock market. Parents pay from $25 to over $100 per session, depending on whether the class needs extra materials or equipment, which is a bargain compared to private school programs in the area. Noziska said the PTA offers financial assistance for families who can’t afford it.
In addition to academic and artistic enrichment, the after-school programs fulfill a more basic parental necessity: childcare.
“It started because there was a huge need for childcare after school, and there weren’t many affordable options,” said Noziska. “And there wasn’t a real diversity of options catering to children’s interests.”
For schools without PTA-funded after-school programs, the city operates 900 free programs across the five boroughs.
PTA tax filings for some schools include more detail than others: P.S. 158’s PTA on the Upper East Side spent $39,000 on a fifth grade trip and $10,600 on the school yearbook. Records also show the PTA supported a “photo day” to the tune of $5,900.
Other PTA tax filings are more vague. Take Stuyvesant High School, the highly selective high school that integration advocates criticized for admitting just three Black students this school year. Its PTA provided $841,253 in grants to the school for “additional funding for various departments, educational & extracurricular programs” while also earning $32,000 in “investment income.” What those investments were are not detailed in the association’s tax forms and PTA leaders at Stuyvesant High did not respond to emailed questions about either of these amounts.
PTA funding vs. public funding
Hannah-Jones’ New York Times magazine article about her family’s experiences with school segregation and disparate educational outcomes in Brooklyn has reignited calls to fix what advocates say is a broken system.
Education policy experts have urged Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who campaigned on expanding free childcare, to propose a more robust plan for addressing systemic inequality and increasing funding for the city’s public schools.
PTA fundraising dollars make up a fraction of the overall amount of money received from local, state and federal sources. On average, the city already spends roughly $35,000 each year per student, according to education department data, far more than other large school districts, with the bulk of that funding coming from city coffers. It’s an increase of about 34% from pre-COVID 19 pandemic levels. Nearly 40% of that budget is spent on K through 12 education. Another third or so goes to employee benefits and pensions, along with debt payments.
The Department of Education gives each school the same amount per pupil, but then adds supplemental funding that depends on a student’s grade level, academic need and household income.
At P.S. 29 in Brooklyn, where the PTA raised $2,886 per student during the last school year, the school received about $17,000 per pupil in public funding.
But at P.S. 307, the elementary school where Hannah-Jones enrolled her daughter in 2014, the funding sources are essentially flipped. It received $42,000 in public, per-pupil funding in 2024-25. The school’s student body is 46% Black, 35% Latino and 10% white. About 85% of students come from low-income households. The school’s PTA did not report any fundraising income in 2024-25.
And at P.S. 44 in the Bronx, the PTA raised just $332 in total last year, less than $2 per pupil. It was among the lowest of PTAs that reported at least some income. A third of the students are Black, 67% are Latino and nearly all students come from low-income households. The school received $35,000 in per pupil funding from the city, state and federal governments.
Both P.S. 307 and P.S. 44 benefit from additional city funding that goes to schools serving more students from low-income households. They also get additional federal dollars, known as Title I money, allocated to schools serving high-poverty communities. The funding is designed to pay for extra teachers, additional curriculum and after-school tutoring to help counteract the ways poverty can prevent students from doing well in school.
Some parents at high-fundraising PTAs say differences in public spending make PTA fundraising necessary to provide critical parts of a “well-rounded education.”
“We’re not a Title I school, so we get significantly less money from DOE,” said Noziska at P.S. 29. “There are a lot of things necessary for our children, like arts, that DOE does not provide enough for us to fund.”
But Murray, the Davidson College professor, urged caution when drawing comparisons between PTA fundraising for schools in more affluent neighborhoods and extra city and federal support for schools in low-income neighborhoods designed to level the playing field.
“I don’t think that takes into account just how much it costs to educate a student that is poor,” she said. “Money matters, especially for students with the greatest needs.”

Your Midterm Guide to Voting for the Arts
We rounded up key races and where candidates stand on culture funding, AI, and more.
Happy Election Day. Today, voters across the country are casting their ballots on races that could not only impact the balance of power in Congress, but also decide the future of democracy in the United States. If you’re an artist or cultural worker, there are several key states to watch, where issues including arts funding, artistic freedom and censorship, and the incursion of AI on creative professions are now at stake. We compiled a dedicated Midterm Election Guide highlighting House, Senate, and Gubernatorial races that may prove decisive for arts and culture, especially as Trump and his allies ramp up their attacks on history, heritage, and diverse communities.
But as we’ve always emphasized here at Hyperallergic, the policies that most benefit artists are also what benefit the majority: affordable healthcare and housing, a better education, the right to speech and expression. Candidates including Claire Valdez in New York and Jonathan Nez in Arizona have voiced that very sentiment in interviews with us as part of our robust coverage ahead of the Midterms over the last six months — we’re re-sharing many of those articles below.
One last note: We’re only able to produce our in-depth, unbiased reporting because we are completely independent, not beholden to donors or investors. Please consider supporting us as a member so we can continue this work. And, should you feel so inspired, we love seeing your “I Voted” selfies … :)
GET OUT THERE!!!
—Valentina Di Liscia, senior editor
A Midterm Election Guide for Artists and Arts Workers
Midterms are tomorrow, marking the first nationwide election since President Donald Trump started his second term in the Oval Office. In the wake of Trump’s financial and ideological crackdowns on Smithsonian, unapproved pet projects around the US Capitol, devastation to cultural landscapes through border construction, and dozens of other policies targeting history and heritage, many will be lining up at the polls with arts and culture policies on their minds.
Because Congress ultimately decides appropriations for federal arts entities, such as the National Endowment for the Arts, control of the House and Senate is incredibly important for the cultural sector. | Valentina Di Liscia, Phillip Pyle, Anna Lee, and Rhea Nayyar
