https://theintercept.com/2026/10/31/trum.title: How Trump Destroyed South Africa’s Effort to Slow HIV Transmission
https://theintercept.com/2026/10/31/trum.author: Steven W. Thrasher, Afeef Nessouli
https://theintercept.com/2026/10/31/trum.text:
This story was supported by the Pulitzer Center and the Fund for Investigative Journalism.
JOHANNESBURG, SOUTH AFRICA — When it opened in early 2024, Engage Men’s Health Clinic served as a free, one-stop shop for sexual health, gender-affirming medical care, and HIV prevention, testing, and treatment. Located within a short distance of seven universities, it was a place where many college students came before “they’d even had sex for the first time,” a former worker told The Intercept. This made Engage a “high-impact” clinic for distribution of the HIV prevention drug PrEP.
The building, on a tree-lined stretch of Reserve Street in Johannesburg, was adorned with the logo for the President’s Plan For AIDS Relief, or PEPFAR; a rainbow-colored mural of Simon Tseko Nkoli, the gay anti-apartheid activist who helped start one of Africa’s first Pride celebrations and who died of AIDS in 1998; and a sign for USAID saying the site was a gift “from the American people.”
Today, it would be very hard to get help here, despite the welcoming-but-outdated signage. The clinic, once staffed full-time by professionals, closed abruptly during the first hours of the second Trump administration. Its replacement, an unrelated volunteer clinic called USpace, is open a mere four hours a week. They can do HIV tests here. But they have no HIV treatment, HIV prevention, or gender-affirming medication to distribute.
South Africans account for about a fifth of the 41 million people living with HIV around the world. Out of a population of nearly 64 million, some 8 million people in South Africa are living with HIV, which is roughly 1 in 8. Managing their healthcare is a matter of international concern and requires global coordination and an immense local network. In a nation with such high rates of HIV, public health workers can’t just wait for people to walk into clinics; they must proactively go to them.
Yet over the last year and a half, this crucial work has been stymied. By Jacqueline Pienaar’s count, HIV prevention groups have lost track of approximately 20,000 people with HIV in the Johannesburg and Pretoria region alone since U.S. President Donald Trump came back to the White House. “It used to be if someone didn’t show up to get their medication, you’d go to them,” said Pienaar, a principal investigator and global health specialist at the Aurum Institute, an NGO that offers medical care and contact tracing for the region’s massive HIV-positive population.
For years, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention funded her work. Many of her patients were homeless, unemployed, and extremely poor. If they are unaccounted for and unmedicated, their viral loads will spike, all but assuring large transmission increases in a country that is already home to 20 percent of the world’s HIV-positive population.
With U.S. funding vanished, South Africa now finds itself at risk of unmitigated HIV spread.
Now, at organizations like the Aurum Institute, interviews with Pienaar and other workers reveal how funding cuts have devastated the care apparatus. Employment in HIV care and prevention has become precarious, and resources to slow HIV transmission are increasingly scarce. As elsewhere in the world, this is creating a crisis of unemployment for Black LGBTQ+ workers, which itself creates higher risk for HIV. Gender-affirming care, which is a crucial tool for preventing HIV, has disappeared almost entirely.
Until the second Trump administration, the United States government sent a bit more than half a billion dollars a year to the Republic of South Africa. Of the $580 million the U.S. sent in 2024, 78 percent ($455 million) went towards HIV/AIDS.
But this money from America was hardly charity or lacking in self-interest. Because viruses know no borders, what happens with AIDS in the country with the most infections affects everyone on Earth. Controlling HIV in South Africa makes the entire world safer by preventing the emergence of dangerous viral mutations, reducing the global burden of infectious diseases, and strengthening health systems that detect future pandemics. Because viruses mutate rapidly when allowed to replicate unchecked, poorly controlled epidemics anywhere pose a direct threat to global health security.
South Africa also leads the world on another important front: medical research to address HIV. The republic is home to more clinical trials than any other country for seeing how medications of all kinds (including Covid vaccines) impact those with HIV. The profits of American drug companies depend on South Africans undergoing research trials.
And after a year-and-a-half of dialing down HIV funding and only allowing it with many caveats which have caused major harm, the United States announced in June — during America’s LGBTQ+ Pride Month — that it will end all HIV funding in South Africa.
The ramifications of this will be felt globally for years to come.
They are already being felt by the millions of South Africans for whom HIV care has become harder and harder to find. And the effects are most severe for those already on the margins of South African society: those already living with HIV/AIDS, immigrants, trans women, and the poor, including thousands of newly unemployed HIV prevention workers.
On January 20, 2025, Trump signed two executive orders: 14169, “Reevaluating and Realigning United States Foreign Aid,” and 14168, “Defending Women from Gender Ideology Extremism and Restoring Biological Truth to the Federal Government.”
Within hours of Trump taking the oath of office, the vast majority of workers for OUT LGBT Well-Being, which ran the Engage clinic, were told not to come in to work the next day nor to even open their work laptops again. According to one, 82 of 86 workers were let go. They would become part of the one-third of South Africans who are already unemployed.
Trump executive order 14155 formally pulled the U.S. out of the World Health Organization in January 2026. Trump’s cuts came after the outgoing administration of President Joe Biden reportedly failed to pay some $130 million in 2024 WHO dues, leaving the organization with a $1.9 billion gap. As a consequence, WHO implemented a 30 percent reduction in its workforce.
South Africa’s response to HIV has been shaped by its two most famous citizens: Nelson Mandela and Elon Musk.
Mandela, the first president of the republic, played a large role making sure combating AIDS was part of national policy, even guiding the writing of gay, lesbian, bisexual and even trans rights into the constitution (the first constitution in the world to do so). Musk, for his part, can take credit for exacerbating the plague.
During Trump’s first term, with Musk merely cheering from the sidelines, U.S. funding for LGBTQ+ health and HIV did not decrease significantly, at home or abroad. But ahead of Trump’s second term, it was Musk who first recommended a U.S. “government efficiency commission” to Trump in 2024, planting the seeds for what was to come.
HIV funding nationally and globally have plummeted in Trump’s second term through cuts largely enacted at the behest of Musk’s short-lived Department of Government Efficiency. (These have been paired with an immigration policy so racist, over the last six months, literally the only refugees to enter the U.S. have been white South Africans.)
Musk quit just a few months into his tenure in 2025, before DOGE shut down entirely. He reportedly took a swath of DOGE data with him, saw his wealth skyrocket, and became the world’s first trillionaire. Reporting on mathematical projections about how many people have been or will be killed by the U.S. Agency for International Development, or USAID, cuts he pushed have ranged from hundreds of thousands to about 10 million to even tens of millions. (When Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., accused Musk of executing “a death sentence for an estimated 4.5 million children around the world,” Musk threatened to sue him.)
But not all harm results in immediate, quantifiable fatalities. HIV-related deaths usually take many years to occur, and South Africans who die of HIV, or due to an increasingly transphobic healthcare system, are unlikely to be mourned in any numerically comprehensive database.
In South Africa, being trans is not a crime — it’s legally protected thanks to its 1996 constitution shaped by Mandela. And yet, as one trans HIV-prevention worker put it, “we have rights for trans women only on paper.” Because trans care was largely being financed largely by USAID, PEPFAR, and CDC research, when U.S.-money disappeared, trans care went away — along with a lot of the much-needed HIV prevention for everyone.
In South Africa, LGBT Pride celebrations happen in the fall to connect gay history to the September 24 Heritage Day national holiday.
At last year’s Soweto Pride in the all-Black township where Winnie Mandela once lived, there were no corporate sponsors and zero presence from the U.S. Embassy or any U.S.-based NGOs.
It was here The Intercept first met Sibonelo Ncanana Trower, the worker at OUT LGBT Well-Being which had run the now-shuttered Engage clinic. He and his partner were wearing matching rainbow sweaters. Nearly nine months after being laid off, he was still looking for work — and it was one of his first times going to a gay event.
Though he was no longer getting paid, Sibonelo still was doing a lot of public health work for free, out of a sense of communal responsibility.
“If you go on Grindr — and I don’t suggest that you do, it’s too dangerous,” Sibonelo said, “you will see many of my former colleagues offering services.” People who had been trained as social workers and peer educators to provide care to sex workers were now working as sex workers. In an email to The Intercept, Sibonelo said he is back to working at OUT as of early June.
As the festivities continued, the almost entirely Black crowd danced to a mix of hip hop, rap, and dance hall on a grass field, bordered on one side by tents. Under the banner “The Queer Nation Has No Borders,” a group of volunteers and workers at the SafePlace International tent welcomed LGBTQ+ migrants and refugees and offered help for finding housing and work.
While Europeans are routinely worried about African refugees trying to cross the Mediterranean to Greece or Italy, SafePlace explained that most migrants in Africa are not trying to leave the continent at all — and most queer and African migrants fleeing legal persecution head down to South Africa. They try to go south because they’ve correctly heard that South Africa is legally good for queer Africans and that they can claim asylum. But they also come because they’ve heard — rather incorrectly — that South Africans welcome migrants. (In recent decades, migrants have faced great hostility in South Africa, especially in the lead-up to 2025’s G20 summit in Johannesburg, which Trump boycotted, and in increasingly bold xenophobic protests in 2026.)
Mpho is a lesbian from rural South Africa, and she spoke about a kind of refugee status few Westerners consider. Mpho explained that people who come from within South Africa to Cape Town, Durban, Pretoria or Johannesburg are often called immigrants, for their distinct cultures, languages (South Africa officially has 12 languages), and understandings of sexuality, gender, and being intersex. She herself knew she was different; but in her township, where there is not constant connectivity with mass media, she didn’t know anyone like her until she came to a big city.
Masi has had an even more challenging route. He is a trans man born in Zambia who made his way to South Africa, after surviving an arranged marriage and a community shunning.
Mpho and Masi have both known trans people who have experienced extreme body dysmorphia, including trans men who have started to have periods again once they lost access to hormone replacement therapy due to the Trump–Musk cuts. They know someone who has gone into the public health system, had their doctor leave the room in the middle of a genital exam — and then return with a group of colleagues to laugh at their body.
This has led to a wave of depression and suicides among their friends. Masi has made the difficult decision to only “socially transition.” He has chosen to dress and live as a man without hormonal or surgical intervention, because he does not want to begin any process that he can’t finish, or which could be taken away from him for any time.
A few days later, Masi and Mpho drove into Johannesburg in a car early on a Saturday morning, decked out in “the queer nation has no borders” swag. With them was Mandi, a trans woman from Uganda. While Mandi waits for surgeries she plans to have, she has found a way to get estrogen — and stay on it — despite “the cuts.”
The three friends were on their way to perform an “Act of Kindness,” a part of SafePlace’s program where queer and trans people perform service projects which confer dignity upon each other. (SafePlace is privately funded, and like other privately funded NGOs, its work and workers are stressed in trying to meet the profound additional need in the wake of U.S. and WHO cuts.) Masi, Mpho, and Mandi would be serving lunch at a shelter for displaced queer women in the Vaal area, south of Johannesburg.
Mandi grew up assigned as a boy but knew she liked other boys. Uganda only made being gay a capital offense in the last couple of years, but it has been illegal in various forms since at least 2014. As in many places, Mandi’s legal problems did not come from random government surveillance; rather, she kissed a friend, whose parents found out, who told their school, who told the authorities, who arrested them both. This, in turn, outed Mandi to her family, who threw her out on the street. (She has never seen them again.)
Eventually, she made her way 5,000 kilometers by land to South Africa.
Mandi had an idea that South Africa “accepted people like me,” and while living on the streets of Cape Town (and then in the back of a restaurant where she did unpaid labor), someone pointed her to SafePlace. They found her a home, helped her get healthcare, and supported her in starting to live as a woman.
After crossing the Mandela Bridge, the roads shifted from highway to unpaved, red-clay-earth roads. They arrived in the Vaal and approached Orange Farm, an area well known to AIDS researchers for its high prevalence of HIV and for hosting many research studies, including the world’s first trial to see how circumcision could affect rates of HIV transmission.
Mpho, Masi, and Mandi pulled up to a nice home, double wide in size, which had a rainbow flag on its fence. This was the shelter where they’d be serving lunch.
The group set up a precarious gas stove in the garage and began cooking massive amounts of chicken, vegetables, and pap, the South African grain dish that is akin to Cream of Wheat in America or polenta in Italy.
Before the meal, Mandi got up in front of important community elders from the neighborhood and told her story. She implored them that the most important thing about having an LGBTQ+ child is to not kick them out and to stay connected. As a cautionary tale, she warned them that her elders now wanted her to return to Uganda to take care of them in old age — even after they’d abandoned her.
Gwendolyn Dube lives in the Orange Farm section of the Vaal, in a tin-roofed shack with no running water or electricity, not far from the Steve Biko Elementary School.
At 35, she has lived with HIV for more than 20 years; she was infected when she was raped as a child. She was among the first cohort of South African children to receive antiretroviral medication, or ARVs, in the early 2000s.
For many years, she received free medical care and ARVs at a clinic across the street from Eyethu Orange Farm Mall. It encompasses many buildings across a large campus, and its rooms are simple and very crowded. A small pride flag hangs on a poll beside the South African flag — both are at half mast, for no discernible reason.
While this is not officially an HIV clinic, Orange Farm has one of the highest rates of HIV anywhere in the world, and HIV is part of most medical care here. In a room with racked, connected plastic chairs like a bus terminal, signs read: “Are you or your child on ARVs? Do you know your VIRAL LOAD?”
Moving through the hall full of hundreds of mothers with children carried on backs in baby wraps, Gwendolyn recalled how difficult it’s become to get medicine. She used to get three months of treatment at a time, then two, then one. Then she was told there was no file for her.
“I think they say that when they’re overworked,” she said.
One of the workers behind the check-in desk told The Intercept that things have gotten much harder since the cuts: “We don’t turn people away. But we don’t have enough staff. People will come here and wait for 8, 10, even 12 hours — and sometimes they don’t even get to see someone about what they need.” (For people living in abject poverty, the loss of a day’s earnings can be devastating — especially if they have HIV and have to face this risk regularly.)
Another clinic worker shared that since the cuts, many visiting healthcare workers on U.S.-funded grants not only left, but also took their equipment with them.
The nurses of the clinic move with a military precision, even wearing military rank epaulets on their shoulders. The head of them is the “matron,” who, when asked by The Intercept, denied that they’ve run out of any medication, or that they turn people away (a claim Gwendolyn and others disputed). The matron conceded that sometimes people have to wait so long “they will leave” — and maybe don’t come back. She acknowledged that the clinic doesn’t always have the specific medication people need when they need it. She also bemoaned that it’s hard to keep staff, burnout and turnover are high, and that her mobile teams, which would go out into the townships, are severely limited.
“I used to send teams out every day,” she said. “Now, it’s maybe once a week.”
Shon, a Black trans woman living with HIV, is still working at the Aurum Institute — at least for now. Unlike at the shuttered Engage clinic in Johannesburg, some staff remain in Aurum’s Pretoria office, but they decreased in number. As a result, Aurum is offering fewer services and steering patients to the public health system, where trans people receive little necessary care.
Aurum used to be a “one-stop shop” for trans women, Shon said. But now, after the cuts, doctors visits are no longer free and hormone drugs aren’t available at Aurum’s popular Pop Inn clinics. “The ladies do come to get [HIV medication], others come to get PrEP, but they cannot get hormones,” Shon said. “They’re told to go to a public clinic,” but “they don’t know anything about trans women!” Shon added that patients will be addressed with derogatory and incorrect terminology at such locations.
The stigma is too high to go to a public clinic, so Shon goes to a private doctor herself, when she can afford it. But getting hormones is now tough. While patients aren’t being blackmailed as they are in Uganda, “a pharmacist might say, ‘What do you need this for? No, I’m not giving it to you for that. I have other patients who really need it,’” Shon said.
Trans women are struggling, Shon said, recalling how she knew two “who were suffering from depression. One couldn’t take hormones, became really religious,” stopped hormones, and became suicidal. Another was suffering from liver problems after buying hormones on the contraband market, without the supervision of doctors.
Whenever transgender patients are taking contraband hormones via syringes which might not be sterile, they are being exposed to increased risks of contracting HIV and hepatitis — all because DOGE cuts took sterile medical care away from them.
Amid the devastating cuts to global HIV care, a potential breakthrough treatment is just beginning to reach patients. Lenacapavir, a new medication, promises to prevent HIV for six months with just one injection. But it comes with a prohibitively expensive $28,000-a-year price tag, making it out of reach for those who need it most.
Recently, the Global Fund for HIV, Tuberculosis, and Malaria struck a deal with pharmaceutical company Gilead Sciences to produce the shot for $40 in limited quantities. Small amounts are headed to South Africa.
At an outdoor cafe under a massive tree in the picturesque city of Cape Town, Fatima Hassan, a legal and HIV scholar, blasted the pilot study coming to the republic.
The government’s approach was “making the same mistake” of excluding those who were most affected: sex workers and men who have sex with other men.
The plan is to bring a one-time shipment of 40,000 doses — a woefully inadequate number for a country of more than 60 million people where about 1 in 5 adults is living with the virus is living with the virus.
Worse, only a tiny fraction — 5 percent, or 2,000 doses — is to be set aside for testing on men who have sex with men.
None are going to be set aside for sex workers.
And another problem: So many of the people who would be needed to distribute lenacapavir to the people who need it most — to the gay college students who used the shuttered Engage clinic on Joburg’s Reserve Street, to the trans women who went to the Pretoria Pop Inn clinic — have been fired. Without those workers, can South Africa even distribute the medication?
Steps from the cafe, within sight of well-appointed apartments topped with electrified razor wire and the Desmond Tutu Health Foundation, there is a shantytown of cardboard-and-wood dwellings, home to some 100 Black adults without anywhere else to live.
A conservative estimate means that probably at least 20 of them were living with HIV, if not more.
And because of Trump and Musk, the people who used to find them and treat them have been fired — and are at higher risk of HIV themselves.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.title: New book charts American artist’s lifelong devotion to the South Seas
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.author: Christoph Irmscher
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/10/.text:
This is a book about a love affair, one that ran so deep it yielded thousands of watercolours, hundreds of oil paintings and three illustrated books. The painter Robert Lee Eskridge (1891-1975) first visited the South Seas in May 1927, when his ship pulled into the harbour of Papeete, Tahiti. Seeking respite from the grey skies and bone-chilling winters of Chicago, he was instantly smitten and kept returning to the South Seas, eventually making his home in Honolulu, Hawai’i.
Little in Eskridge’s early life had predicted that infatuation. Born in Philadelphia, he attended the Art Institute of Chicago, studied in Paris with the Cubist painter André Lhote, and travelled across Europe for three years. His style, fusing Art Deco patterns with a form of relaxed realism, won him gigs as an illustrator and artist, culminating in a high-profile commission to produce murals for the lobby of the newly rebuilt Palmer House hotel in Chicago. On the eve of his departure for Tahiti, he chose Marco Polo as his subject. (The murals were painted over in 1966.)
Honouring rich traditions
Falling in love with the South Seas is not a unique experience. Names like Herman Melville, Robert Louis Stevenson and Paul Gauguin conjure lush tropical forests, foam-crested waves lapping pristine beaches, and carefree Islanders performing hula dances: a vision inevitably darkened by the damages wrought by colonialism. The Islanders Eskridge painted, unlike Gauguin’s, are not immobilised by the artist’s desire to project meaning into them. They are walking, working, dancing, fishing and making music, living fully in the present even as they honour their rich traditions.
Eskridge’s enthusiasm for Islander culture finds a perfect match in biographer Cook’s enthusiasm for Eskridge. While the more lyrically effusive passages in this volume might not appeal to everyone, the lavish illustrations drawn from multiple collections and the excellent captions help us understand the breadth, range and sophistication of a supremely adaptable painter who deserves to be better known. (Regrettably, some images—of the lost Chicago murals, for example—are AI-produced).
Eskridge’s paintings, whether they show bustling street scenes or re-create rituals he witnessed, vibrate with life. As a young man, he was entranced with Sandro Botticelli’s The Birth of Venus (around 1485, in the Uffizi Gallery), and that painting’s revelatory spirit lingers on in Eskridge’s bright, luminous colours or in the way he arranges groups of people around a central figure or an activity.
His training under Lhote shapes the cascading abstract forms Eskridge uses in the background of works such as Stone Fishing (around 1930, Gallery Hawaiiana). In this ancient Polynesian fishing practice, men use ropes with stones to herd leaping fish into shallower waters—a communal effort as well as an occasion for individual daring, represented here beautifully by the young man in the middle, who jumps to grab a fish from the air. A later masterpiece is Hilo Wharf (around 1949, Honolulu Museum of Art), a harbour scene, in which Eskridge blends shirtless workers and the bodies of gigantic tuna fish, some already packed up, into an intense drama of shapes, colour and movement.
Since Eskridge treated the Islanders and their culture with respect, they accepted him as one of their own
Since Eskridge treated the Islanders and their culture with respect, they accepted him as one of their own, Cook tells us. They even asked Eskridge to represent them at the Chicago World’s Fair in 1933. Invitations followed to provide Hawaiian-themed murals for the McCoy Pavilion in Honolulu’s Ala Moana Park and, later, to design clothes for the Hawai’ian label Paradise Sportswear.
Always one to defy expectations, Eskridge, at age 64, married Helen Gebhardt and settled in Olympia, Washington. But the Islands kept calling. He died in April 1975 at a hotel in Honolulu named, appropriately, Hale-kulani, “house befitting heaven”.
• C.J. Cook, Robert Lee Eskridge, South Pacific Dreams Publishing, 344pp, 509 col. illust., $59.95 (hb), published 11 August
• Christoph Irmscher is a critic and biographer

https://apache.be/2026/10/23/westerse-do.text:
Na een kurkdroge zomer met hitterecords, is de kou eindelijk gearriveerd. Normaal is het tijd om te cocoonen en te vertragen. Helaas lijken we dit niet te mogen – de zondagsrust is op sterven na dood. En staat onze feed nooit stil, onze gsm nooit af en consumeren we meer dan we kunnen verteren. Een ware overdaad zonder einde, die de beeldspraak van een zondvloed oproept.
In 1524 voorspelde de astroloog Johannes Stöffler een zondvloed. Wie het kon, bouwde een ark. De vloed bleef echter uit. Vijfhonderd jaar later zien we techmiljardairs bunkers bouwen in Nieuw-Zeeland en op Hawaï, terwijl ze ons waarschuwen dat AI de mensheid kan uitroeien. Het einde der tijden is terug van nooit weggeweest.
Vandaag verkopen AI-labs het verhaal dat enkel zij de ondergang kunnen voorkomen, en dus onbelemmerd moeten doorgaan
Angst die zich projecteert op een onzekere toekomst of ‘eindtijdangst’ is zo oud als beschaving zelf. Rond 1200 voor Christus stortte de bronstijdwereld in. Ugarit brandde, het Hettitische rijk verdween, handelsroutes vielen weg. Wie erbij was, moet gedacht hebben dat de wereld ophield. De wereld hield niet op, maar het handelssysteem transformeerde. Veel autonome Fenicische steden overleefden deze ineenstorting, omdat ze niet van één paleis afhingen maar van handel en netwerken. In de brokstukken werd het alfabet en ijzer verspreid.
Na de Zwarte Dood, die een derde van Europa wegvaagde, verdwenen de lonen niet. Integendeel, ze stegen, en het feodalisme kende zijn eerste cruciale scheuren.
En ook de millenniumbug bleek uiteindelijk onschuldig omdat er hard was gewerkt aan het voorkomen van problemen én omdat consultants de dreiging ervan bewust hadden opgeklopt om er een fortuin aan te verdienen. Apocalyptische verhalen en opgeklopte angst zijn zelden neutraal of rationeel, maar wel al te vaak instrumenteel.
De middeleeuwse kerk verkocht aflaten tegen de angst voor het vagevuur. De IT-consultants van 1999 verdienden aan de angst dat computers op 1 januari 2000 zouden vastlopen. Vandaag verkopen AI-labs het verhaal dat enkel zij de ondergang kunnen voorkomen, en dus onbelemmerd moeten doorgaan. Wie de apocalyps voorspelt én bezit, wil vooral geen democratisch toezicht maar een hemels mandaat.
End times fascism
Naomi Klein en Astra Taylor noemden dat onlangs end times fascism in hun gelijknamige boek. Ze beschrijven daarin een elite die het vermeende, toekomstige maatschappelijke instorten al heeft ingecalculeerd en kiest voor ontsnapping in plaats van herstel. Net zoals een binaire machine heeft deze tech elite duidelijk geen menselijke moed en zijn ze zich niet bewust van het belang van gezonde frictie, tegenspraak en tegenmacht.
Econoom en auteur Yanis Varoufakis liet dan weer zien waarom angst zo goed past bij technofeodalisme. Want wie bang is, sluit zich aan, betaalt en past zich aan. Angst maakt de mens voorspelbaar of om het meer in zijn jargon te verwoorden: een horige.
Onder het huidige doemdenken (en doemscrollen) zit nog iets anders. Elke generatie voelt haar tijd als uniek en versneld. De middeleeuwse kroniekschrijver, de negentiende-eeuwse persoon voor wie de trein de ruimte “vernietigde” of de telegraaf de communicatie versnelde ervaarden allemaal wat wij nu ook voelen: de perceptie van versnelling. Elke dag is er iets nieuws: een nieuwe doorbraak en een nieuwe calamiteit. Wie de tijd niet meer neemt om te vertragen en te verteren, ervaart elke nieuwigheid als breuk, en een breuk lijkt altijd op het einde.
Zaaien, wachten, oogsten
Ondertussen is doem voor veel mensen geen toekomstscenario maar realiteit. Voor Gaza, Soedan en de Sahel is de breuk al decennia daar. Het dominante doemverhaal hier daarentegen is een westers en klassengebonden luxeproduct dat ons aangesmeerd wordt. En we slikken het als zoete broodjes.
Wie de tijd niet meer neemt om te vertragen en te verteren, ervaart elke nieuwigheid als breuk, en een breuk lijkt altijd op het einde
Dat betekent niet dat de risico's of problematieken verzonnen zijn. Klimaatontwrichting, een nieuwe wereldorde en machtsconcentratie zijn reëel. Maar we dienen ons bewust te zijn van wie het verhaal erover schrijft en hoe we met angst en met een veranderde wereld omgaan. Na de ineenstorting van de bronstijd overleefden niet de bunkerbouwers, maar de gemeenschappen die water, handel en kennis bleven delen. Zij die niet meegingen in de waan(zin) van de dag.
We kunnen een zekere toekomst niet garanderen, maar we moeten wel weigeren dat angst ons regeert. Want blijvend versnellen, wat de psychosomatische reactie is op angst, leidt uiteindelijk tot burn-out en accidenten. En dat zijn zaken die enkel lucratief zijn voor wie kapitaliseert op spreekwoordelijke pleisters op de wonde: supplementen en optimalisatietools, verzekeringen, of andere industrieën die niet verdienen aan de oorzaak, maar aan het gevolg. Een versneld lichaam is een klant. Een lichaam dat tijd krijgt, is een burger.
De bunkerbouwer koopt zekerheid en betaalt met zijn rust. Wie kanalen graaft, kent geen garantie, maar wel een ritme: zaaien, wachten, oogsten. Dat ritme is geen luxe maar moed en het is de voorwaarde om te gedijen.

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/02/r.title: Report: NYPD’s Dangerous Increase In High-Speed Pursuits Did Not Decrease Crime
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/02/r.author: Sammy Sussman
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/02/r.text:
The NYPD’s decision to increase high-speed vehicle pursuits under Mayor Eric Adams led to more crashes, injuries and deaths — and didn’t even drive down crime, according to a new study.
The department increased its pursuits 25-fold in 2022, as Streetsblog previously reported, from around eight pursuits per month to 200. The increase had no tangible impact on crime beyond larger national trends — but it did cause roughly 675 more collisions, 355 additional injuries and seven additional fatalities, according to the researchers.
“It’s a lot of innocent lives,” said Justin Nix, a professor at the University of Nebraska at Omaha and co-author of the study, “The Fast and the Spurious — A Causal Evaluation of NYPD’s Pursuit Policy, 2022–2025.”
“One-third of the people who are getting injured or killed are other people — drivers, pedestrians — who didn’t even decide to flee [police].”
The researchers used city crime statistics to look at the effects of the increase, and subsequent decrease, in pursuits. They focused on three specific categories of crimes — collisions, robberies and gun violence — while factoring in national trends. Their analysis found one immediate effect: crashes increased and then decreased, as did resulting injuries and deaths, based on changes in agency policy.
But the researchers saw no noticeable changes in robberies and gun violence.
“Pursuit escalation produced clear and attributable collision harms while providing no credible evidence of crime reduction,” Nix wrote with his co-author John Hall.
The researchers used a value-of-life analysis — a common, if macabre, method of criminological data analysis that essentially puts a price tag on injuries, deaths and property damage – to calculate at what point the toll of increased pursuits would be mitigated by decreases in crime.
Ultimately, they found that New York’s crime levels were nowhere near the level needed for the new pursuit policies to justify the overwhelming costs in terms of collisions, injuries and deaths. Instead, they found that the NYPD unleashed costly harms on city residents in exchange for purely imaginary crime-reduction benefits — in other words, the top brass’s decision to increase these pursuits came at a shocking net loss to public safety.
“Agencies should require affirmative evidence of crime-prevention benefits before expanding pursuit authority,” the authors wrote in implicit criticism of the NYPD after studying their actions from 2022 to 2025.
The study noted that the initial decision to increase pursuits was made unofficially, seemingly in late 2022.
“People thinking they can take off on us? Those days are over,” Chief of Department John Chell told reporters at the time — an indication that he had ordered his cops to be more aggressive with their cars.
By August 2023, then-Chief of Department Jeffrey Maddrey released a memo formalizing the department’s pursuit policy, which remained just vague enough to maintain the Chell-initiated trend: pursuits could continue for non-violent crimes, but they should be terminated when “the risks to uniformed members of the service and the public outweigh the danger to the community if suspect is not immediately apprehended.”
Police leaders across the country often argue that pursuits serve as a crime deterrent. But previous research has found that roughly 30 percent of police pursuits end without a successful apprehension. And suspects choosing to flee police are overwhelmingly young, male, intoxicated and unlicensed — characteristics associated with a “weakened deterrence perception” and “impaired risk assessment.”
Under fire as chases rose dramatically under Chell and Maddrey, the NYPD revealed in 2024 that around two-thirds of its pursuits began as simple car stops for traffic offenses — and 25 percent of the 2,278 chases “resulted in some combination of a collision, property damage, or physical harm,” the NYPD told Streetsblog.
Around a dozen of the pursuits resulted in fatalities — including Amanda Servedio, who was killed in Astoria in 2024 by a driver who was not suspected of a violent crime fled the cops.
Commissioner Jessica Tisch reversed the Chell-Maddrey initiative and codified NYPD policy in 2025, restricting chases to serious crimes, discouraging pursuits near schools and playgrounds and shielding cops from criticism or discipline if they chose to terminate a pursuit because of safety concerns. The department’s pursuit numbers quickly declined, though they remain slightly higher than where they were before the 2022 escalation.
Nix noted that this quick reversal was abnormal, and it allowed researchers to study how pursuits affected crime numbers both as pursuit numbers went up and as they came back down — making the statistically significant changes in crashes, and the lack of change in crime numbers, even more apparent.
“If we observed an effect,” Nix said, “we would obviously expect to see the opposite when the policy changed again.”
The NYPD did not respond to multiple messages seeking comment for this story.
Sammy Sussman joined Streetsblog in May 2026 as law enforcement reporter after successful stints at New York Focus and The New York Times. In 2019, he interned on a team that won a Pulitzer.

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/02/w.title: Would A One-Way Conversion Fix Brooklyn’s Grand Street Or Make It Worse?
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/02/w.author: Sophia Lebowitz
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/02/w.text:
Two cyclists on a tandem bike are forced into traffic on Grand Street. Photo: Sophia Lebowitz
Grand in name only.
The frequently blocked Grand Street bike lane in Brooklyn is one of the worst in the city — but advocates are raising early concerns that a nascent proposal by the city could be worse than the current dysfunction.
The Department of Transportation has been soliciting feedback for a plan to convert Grand Street into a one-way eastbound street and nearby Metropolitan Avenue, also currently two-way, into one-way westbound with a new protected bike lane.
Street safety advocates in the area worry that converting the currently two-way streets to one-way will create two faster roadways, thanks to having two traffic lanes in one direction. A conversion without traffic calming on side streets, parking reform, a road diet and maintaining two-way bike infrastructure wouldn’t improve anything, one advocate said.
“I think the most likely outcome with a one-way is two travel lanes on both streets,” said Brent Bovenzi, an organizer with North Brooklyn Open Streets who lived on Grand Street for four years. “That would encourage more speeding, especially at night. And Grand Street has so many bars. I just don’t see how that’s going to make the street safer.”
The idea of a one-way conversion of the two busy truck routes was first discussed formally at a Street Improvements Workshop in 2023. Industrial and manufacturing businesses in the area, who are represented by Evergreen Inc., want two-lane traffic on both streets, teeing up a future conflict with street safety advocates. Both streets are designated “local truck routes,” meaning trucks use them to get to inter-borough destinations.
“Both of those streets actually have manufacturers and industrial businesses directly on them. But more broadly those streets are truck routes,” said Leah Archibald, the executive director of Evergreen. “This really affects all of the businesses in the area because they do rely on trucks in and trucks out.”
Grand Street is a bustling commercial corridor. There are copious bars, coffee shops, grocery stores, clothing stores and gyms. Those who live in the area can pretty much get anything done on the street. One study suggests that two-way traffic could contribute to that vibrancy.
The study, conducted in 2017 by the Transportation Research Board, found that multi-lane, one-way streets have higher rates of traffic collisions and contribute to “degradation and erosion of community.”
Another 2019 study by researchers at Penn State and ETH Zurich found that two-way streets offer more redundancy to drivers which could come in handy if routes are blocked, and that two-way streets with prohibited left turns can be even more efficient. One-way networks, the study finds, are only the best option in “a few” scenarios because “they force vehicles to travel the longest distances on average.”
Grand Street’s high concentration of businesses means many will want a voice in the design process. Storefront businesses on the corridor between Union and Bushwick avenues are represented by the Grand Street BID, which is supporting a one-way conversion idea, for now.
“We’re really focused on safety and streets that work for everyone in East Williamsburg,” said Francesca Bruce, the Grand Street BID’s executive director. “I think that we are cautiously optimistic. We support [a one-way conversion] in theory because we haven’t necessarily seen a feasible alternative that accounts for all users.”
Eyes on Grand Street
All stakeholders Streetsblog spoke with said that Grand Street’s current design leaves much to be desired.
“Everyone agrees that what we have now is suboptimal,” said Archibald.
The eastbound side has concrete barriers, but breaks in the protection allow trucks and cars to double park, trapping cyclists in.
And the westbound side’s parking protected design is frequently blocked by construction and is much narrower than the new bike lanes that the DOT has been installing in Manhattan.
“It’s almost impossible to go from Union Avenue to Bushwick Avenue without having to leave the bike lane at some point,” said Bovenzi.
The further east, the worse it gets, with the lane essentially disappearing past Bushwick Avenue due to the industrial businesses using it as an extension of their garages.
Grand Street is not only a mess for cyclists, but bus riders on the Q59 and Q54 routes are forced to crawl through traffic.
The city has classified both Grand Street and Metropolitan Avenue as “Vision Zero Priority Corridors,” which means they are especially dangerous. In 2025, there were 103 reported crashes on the Grand Street corridor DOT is studying, injuring 26 cyclists and eight pedestrians. On the corresponding stretch of Metropolitan, there were 50 reported crashes injuring two cyclists and five pedestrians.
Looking ahead
Bovenzi said that everything he has seen so far makes him worried that the DOT will still prioritize vehicle movement with its new plans. “The outreach crews, the teams from DOT that were on Grand and Metropolitan, they talked a lot more about improvements to traffic congestion than anything else,” he said.
He also noted that because of the density of restaurants on Grand, many delivery workers are riding up and down the corridor at all hours. If the bike lane was changed to one-way, it would likely encourage “salmoning,” or riding the wrong direction, from workers picking up food and those commuting from further east in Bushwick to Manhattan.
“If you move one of the bike lanes all the way to Metropolitan Avenue [four blocks away], people are not going to do that. People are going to salmon,” Bovenzi said. “You’re going to make it harder for delivery stuff. You’re going to make harder for any commuters that are beyond the L train commuting shed too, which is a whole lot of people.”
The DOT collected about 1,500 responses via a survey, which closed on Sept. 30, and got another 200 responses on a feedback map. The DOT also conducted focus groups, did on-street outreach and had feedback sessions with local stakeholders, a spokesperson told Streetsblog. The agency is now analyzing the results of the outreach and has not yet proposed any formal plan.
“DOT is working closely with the community to develop a proposed redesign of Grand Street and Metropolitan Avenue that improves safety and better protects New Yorkers on these streets, while providing more space for New Yorkers on all modes of transportation,” said spokesperson Will Livingston. “We are currently reviewing the feedback we’ve collected, and we look forward to sharing our findings in the coming months.”

live Midterms: Historischer Sieg in Georgia
Bei den Zwischenwahlen in den USA geht es nicht bloß um die Mehrheit im Kongress. Auch Gouverneure und Landesparlamente werden neu gewählt. Die US-Midterms im Liveticker.
Am 3. November finden in den USA Zwischenwahlen statt (engl.: „Midterms“). Hier entscheidet sich, ob US-Präsident Donald Trump weiterhin auf die Gefolgschaft von beiden Kammern des Kongresses zählen kann. Alle 435 Abgeordneten des Repräsentantenhauses und rund ein Drittel des Senats werden neu gewählt.
Doch es geht noch um mehr: 36 von 50 Gouverneursposten stehen zur Wahl, und in allen 50 Bundesstaaten werden die Landesparlamente neu gewählt. Aufgrund der verschiedenen US-Zeitzonen haben die ersten Wahllokale nach deutscher Zeit um 1 Uhr nachts geschlossen, die letzten schließen um 7 Uhr am Mittwochmorgen.
Mit ersten Ergebnissen ist schon in der Nacht zu rechnen. Wann die Mehrheitsverhältnisse im Kongress feststehen, ist unklar – dies kann bei engen Ergebnissen auch Tage dauern.
03.22 Uhr: Historischer Sieg in Georgia
Die Demokratin Keisha Lance Bottoms gewinnt in Georgia und wird erste afroamerikanische Gouverneurin der USA. In Florida gewinnt der Republikaner Byron Davis, ebenfalls Afroamerikaner. Das sind zwei schwarze Gouverneure im tiefen Süden.
03.20 Uhr: Guten Morgen, guten Abend!
Es ist 21.20 Uhr in Washington und New York. Wir beginnen den Liveticker.
🐾 Wer? Wann? Was? Wie?
Die Zwischenwahlen am 3. November können entscheidend sein für die Zukunft der USA. Aber was passiert da genau? Amerika-Redakteur Bernd Pickert erklärt im Überblick, worauf es ankommt.
🐾 Wann gibt es welche Ergebnisse?
In den USA geht es nicht nur um die zwei Kammern des Kongresses. Auch zahlreiche Gouverneursposten und Landesparlamente werden neu gewählt. Wann gibt es welche Ergebnisse? Die wichtigsten Fragen und Antworten zur Wahlnacht.
🐾 Was macht Trump, wenn er die Wahlen verliert?
Sollten die US-Demokraten die Kongresswahlen gewinnen, können die Republikaner einiges sabotieren. Manche Tricks sind illegal – manche schlicht bizarr. US-Korrespondent Sebastian Moll zum schlechtesten aller Verlierer im Weißen Haus.

UK: Dozens arrested outside Supreme Court hearing on Palestine Action ban
Lawyers representing the co-founder of Palestine Action have argued that the direct-action group has never advocated for violence against individuals, as the campaign to overturn its designation as a terrorist organisation by the UK government reached the Supreme Court.
Speaking on the first day of the two-day hearing, Raza Husain KC, representing Huda Ammori, opened proceedings and said that less than one percent of the group’s protests met the legal definition of terrorism.
"It’s not the label that's important – it’s the substance. Palestine Action has never advocated violence against individuals and follow a similar vein to the Suffragettes who were not peaceful... are part of the tradition [and] proven right by history and venerated.
“The uncontroverted evidence shows moreover that [the] Suffragettes, anti-war groups, environmental groups, animal rights protesters all used tactics similar to or more extreme than Palestine Action, yet they were not regarded as terrorists or proscribed,” said Husain.
The barrister noted that the Suffragettes are now widely celebrated despite using tactics like arson and bomb attacks in the cause of campaigning for the right to vote for women.

Ammori’s legal team also emphasised that the ban on Palestine Action had impacted the group’s right to freedom of speech and protest, noting that it created a “chilling effect” on British society.
“Filton marked a watershed moment - [the activists] were arrested as terrorists and treated as such,” said Husain.
“That came as a shock to the movement.”
The Supreme Court hearing comes after judges granted an appeal following the government's successful proscription under anti-terrorism laws.
It marks the group's final attempt to appeal the ban after going through several courts to reach this stage.
Outside the court, dozens of activists risked arrest for holding signs that quoted posts from Sarah Helm, former journalist and wife of national security adviser Jonathan Powell, who caused an uproar after publicly criticising the ban on Palestine Action.
Last month, Helm posted “God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action” after books by Irish author Sally Rooney were withdrawn from sale in the UK because of her support for the group.
Protesters customised the signs by swapping out “authors” for descriptors that reflected their personal identities or professions, including “Jew”, “physiotherapists”, “son of a Holocaust survivor”, “gardeners” or “normal people”.
Among the 25 people arrested by the police for holding the placards were actor Alfie Enoch, who starred in the Harry Potter movies, and Massive Attack musician Robert Del Naja.

Donald Trump says that Vance's comment about Iran war kneecapping Republicans in catastrophic midterms is 'largely true'
Donald Trump responded to JD Vance’s comments today that the war in Iran was ultimately the reason behind the catastrophic Republican losses in the House and Senate in this year’s midterms.
“I think it’s largely true because it drove the gasoline up a little bit short term,” Trump said. “But at the same time … I’d have to do it again because long term, it’s the only answer.”
The president said that he felt the decision to begin the conflict was unavoidable. “I thought the oil would go up a lot more,” Trump said. “You have no choice. You have to do it. You can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon.”
Trump once again insisted that if he were on the ballot Republicans would have won their races, which in many cases they lost to Democrats in historic landslides.
“They just couldn’t transfer that love,” Trump said. “There was such love at those rallies. It was incredible. We weren’t able to transfer the love to candidates.”
Donald Trump didn’t give a clear answer about whether he knew JD Vance was going to post about the Iran war costing Republicans control of Congress.
“I know how he feels about it. I think it was. I think it was fine. I thought it was good,” Trump said, while remaining belligerent about his decision to start the conflict. “I can tell you that as far as that war is concerned, I would have done nothing different.”

Florida’s governor, Ron DeSantis, moved quickly today to position himself among the leading pack of 2028 Republican presidential hopefuls by attacking party colleagues who lost seats in the midterms bloodbath.
Bucking the national trend, but just barely, Florida voters elected Republicans to the US Senate and governor’s mansion yesterday, achievements DeSantis boasted were because of his eight-year term as governor that ends in January.
“People can look at Florida and show how you can deliver big results and how you can build a durable coalition,” he told a press conference in Tallahassee.
“Why did Florida hold up? Why were we able to hold the line? The answer is we’ve built up a record of achievement. We’ve earned trust from our voters that even in the worst situation that you can imagine politically, we were able to prevent the worst from happening here,” he said.
DeSantis had harsh words for Republicans in Washington who he said failed to deliver campaign promises, including releasing the Epstein files and cleaning up corruption.
“We ran as Republicans on saying we need to do that, and then you actually have people in the Congress voting against release when the attorney general said she had all this horrific stuff on her desk and that people were going to be held accountable,” he said. “It’s untenable when you have people trading stock. Why don’t they ban congressional stock trading? It would be a breath of fresh air.”
DeSantis’s run for the 2024 presidential nomination, won by Donald Trump, ended in humiliation when he dropped out early. Speaking to reporters today, he said he would “talk about anything we’re doing” in terms of the 2028 contest after he is termed out of office on 5 January.
Analysts see DeSantis as all but certain to run again. In a blistering podcast interview yesterday, he attacked Trump’s handling of the Iran war, the economy and the president’s second-term immigration crackdown.
Top House Democrat says party will hold hearings and pass regulations on AI, datacenters
Ted Lieu, a California representative and vice-chair of the House Democratic caucus, said that Republicans had made a mistake by failing to regulate AI while they controlled Congress – and that Democrats would step in to change that.
“Two things will change next term,” Lieu said. “We will hold public hearings on AI. We will pass legislation, reasonable guardrails, on AI.”
Democrats, Lieu said, would specifically take a closer look at guardrails around the building of new datacenters, after the breakneck pace of construction for those facilities drew the bipartisan ire of communities around the country.
That pledge sets Democrats up for a potential showdown with Donald Trump, who has vowed to veto any Democrat legislation and who has harshly criticized the idea of reining in AI development.
Trump avoids speaking about stunning Republican losses in first public event post-midterms
Donald Trump is addressing members of the press for the first time since Republicans lost control of Congress in a stunning midterm defeat.
The president has yet to mention Democrats flipping seven Senate seats and securing 229 seats in the US house, with more victories expected.
Instead, Trump has focused on speaking about his East Room ballroom project, the new helipad on the White House lawn and his various “beautification” projects around Washington DC.
Pressed on whether the Democratic House caucus would pursue the impeachment of Donald Trump upon assuming a majority in the chamber, Hakeem Jeffries seemed to downplay the possibility
“I haven’t had a single member of the House Democratic caucus talk to me about impeachment,” Jeffries said to a group of reporters. “We’ve been relentlessly focused on affordability and accountability.”
Still, Jeffries did assert that a Democratic-controlled House of Representatives would assert its authority to rein in the Trump administration.
“The days of the House of Representatives functioning like a wholly owned subsidiary of the Trump administration are over. House Democrats are going to lead a Congress that does serve as a check and balance on an out of control executive branch.”
Asked separately whether he would consider investigating or impeaching Pete Hegseth, Trump’s Defense Secretary, Jeffries responded dismissively – “Is Pete Hegseth still around?” – before moving on to the next question.
Hakeem Jeffries said that neither he nor Chuck Schumer has spoken with Donald Trump since Republicans’ brutal defeat in the 2026 midterm elections.
“I have not heard from President Trump,” Jeffries told a group of reporters. “It is my understanding that leader Schumer has not heard from President Trump.”
Democrat Christina Bertrand Hines flips red Michigan House district
Democrat Christina Bertrand Hines has flipped the solidly Republican 10th congressional district in Michigan, which is now held by John James – who lost his governor’s race to Democrat Jocelyn Benson.
Bertrand Hines beat her Republican challenger, Michael Bouchard, for control of the district, which a GOP representative has held for more than a decade.
Hakeem Jeffries: Democrats have been handed a mandate 'to make life more affordable'
Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, the House minority leader and soon-to-be speaker of the House, Hakeem Jeffries, characterized the midterm election results as a “stunning rebuke of Maga extremism.”
“Mike Johnson was correct,” Jeffries continued, referencing the now-outgoing Republican House speaker. “The polls were wrong. It wasn’t simply a blue wave, it was an American tsunami.”
In his remarks, Jeffries highlighted what he said would the party’s main priority now that it has control of legislative branch. The American people, Jeffries said, had tasked House Democrats with “a relentless effort to make life more affordable”.
That included, Jeffries said, reversing cuts to Medicaid, extending Affordable Care Act tax credits, undoing Trump’s tariff regime and ending Trump’s “reckless and costly war of choice” with Iran.
Mississippi US Senate race still on knife's edge with 96% of votes counted
The US Senate race in Mississippi is still on a knife’s edge, with Democrat Scott Colom leading Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith by just 43 votes, with 96% of the final votes counted.
If he’s successful, Colom would be the first Democratic senator that Mississippi has sent to Washington since 1982.
We’ll be keeping an eye on the final result, which would be the eighth Senate flip for Democrats in this astonishing midterm election, and in a state which Donald Trump carried by 22 points in 2024.

Danish students join European protest wave against education funding cuts
Danish government proposes scrapping allowance scheme for students from wealthier families.
Thousands of young people in Denmark have demonstrated against a government plan to cut student stipends under a decades-long allowance scheme, adding to a wave of youth unrest across Europe.
Organisers said up to 13,000 students marched from Copenhagen’s city hall square to parliament over proposed cuts to free up funds for defence spending on Monday, under the banner “Enough is Enough”.
The rally echoed student protests in France that spread to other European countries in recent weeks, and that morphed into wider grievances over the cost of living and housing crises impacting young people across the continent.
Student associations said some 40,000 students were on strike at 57 schools across Denmark over the proposed cuts.
Since 1970, all students enrolled in schools or university in Denmark over the age of 18 have automatically received the student allowance regardless of their parents’ income.
Students currently receive 1,154 kroner ($173) a month for those who live with their parents, and 7,426 kroner ($1,116) for those who live on their own.
Under the new government proposal, the allowance would be abolished for students living with parents earning over 700,000 Danish kroner ($105,248).
Only students living with parents earning between 419,589 kroner ($63,087) and 700,000 kroner ($105,248) a year would be eligible for the allowance, with stipends staggered based on their parents’ income.
Heavy police presence
Copenhagen police were out in force during the demonstration.
Thousands of young people chanted “Broken Promises” and carried signs reading “Save SU”, the Danish acronym for the student allowance, “Less Support, Less Educated” and “Don’t Cheat the Young”.
“In Denmark, we get funding and economic support for getting an education, and we’re very proud of this,” said one protest organiser, Danish High School Students Association president Oscar Tonsberg Hoffmann.
He told AFP that it would be wrong to dismantle “one of the world’s strongest educational systems”.
Kieran Hindshaw, a 23-year-old agronomy student, said he felt betrayed by the government.
“I’m infuriated that we finally get a supposedly ‘red’ government in Denmark that includes the left parties … we get cuts to our welfare and to the economies of young people whilst they’re funding corporate tax reductions and warfare,” he said.
The Higher Education Ministry said around 14,000 students are expected to lose their stipends, and some 8,000 would see it reduced.
The government has also proposed that unemployment benefits for recent university graduates be paid only to those who have worked during 18 of the last 24 months of their studies.
Industry Minister and Social Liberal Party leader Martin Lidegaard has meanwhile said the cuts “are not pleasant decisions”.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: The Guardian view on the US midterms: joy for Democrats, a rout for Republicans and a reprieve for democracy | Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Bitter experience made Democrats wary of believing that the blue wave predicted by polls would materialise. What arrived was not just victory but a rout: control of Congress and a Republican wipeout. It was an astounding humiliation for a president whose political brand is power. Donald Trump won it back in 2024 by promising voters lower prices and no foreign wars. He lost it by launching an illegal conflict that hit them in the pocket and imposing hefty tariffs too. He urged voters to pretend that he was on the ticket and they delivered a verdict that could not have been more damning.
Two years ago, retaking the House looked like a genuine fight for Democrats, and the Senate a long shot. On Tuesday, they needed to flip four more seats to gain a 51-seat Senate majority. Within hours of polls closing, they had 54, with two more races in the balance, and had easily passed the 218 seats needed for a House majority. This appears to be the biggest congressional landslide since 1976, in Watergate’s aftermath.
What was stunning was not only that Democrats claimed deep red states like Kansas, but that they did it so decisively. Mr Trump carried South Carolina by 18 points in 2024; Annie Andrews beat her rival for the Senate by almost five points. James Talarico won by 12 points in Texas, which the president carried by nearly 14 points. Democrats also flipped governorships, winning their first gubernatorial majority for two decades.
Two years after Kamala Harris’s crushing defeat by Mr Trump – and having watched even greater chaos and cruelty wreaked in his second term – Democrats are rightly rejoicing. Tuesday night delivered abundant new talent and a generational shift too. The first black and native American women and first out gay man will take their seats in the Senate. Yet the party remains unpopular and the battles over its future are just beginning. For progressives, Abdul el-Sayed’s senate win in Michigan is proof that they can win in purple states. But the scale of Democratic victory gives Hakeem Jeffries – poised to become the first black House speaker – a greater cushion against justified and necessary pressure from the left.
Simultaneously, a Republican faultline over whether to embrace Trumpism or move away from it is yawning. Mr Trump picked candidates (disastrously) and campaigned vigorously – yet seemed strangely detached. Republicans have genuflected to him because he wins. A growing number now believe that they can only win by facing him down – but fear being crushed in the process.
Strikingly, Democrats – notably the senator Jon Ossoff who was easily re-elected in Georgia – successfully tied the affordability crisis to corruption. They will use their newly gained power in Congress to pursue accountability, though Mr Trump’s executive overreach and refusal to accept legislative constraints are unlikely to shift. A vengeful and erratic president who is now wounded and wants to change the narrative may in some ways be more dangerous at home and abroad – notably on Iran.
At least, faced with results “too big to rig”, Mr Trump had to say that he would accept them. The Republican campaign hit new lows, but election officials (including Republicans) pushed back against voter-suppression efforts. Gerrymandering proved ineffective – with black voters turning out in response, and Latino voters whom Republicans counted on swinging back towards the Democrats. So did culture war attacks, vile bigotry and personal smears and a huge spending advantage. This was a bad election for Elon Musk and other big tech donors, with a voter revolt against datacentres and cronyism. It was not just a defeat for Republicans and a good day for Democrats, but a critical victory for democracy itself.

Netanyahu bet on Trump – but both lost
Alongside scramble to form ruling coalition, Israel’s political establishment grapples with US voter rejection of White House ally and own contribution towards it.
US President Donald Trump and his Republican party’s resounding midterm defeat has left many in Israel, particularly on the political right, grappling with the scale of the rebuke to those seen as their closest allies in Washington.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has repeatedly sought to portray himself as almost uniquely qualified to maintain the unflinching support of Trump, who returned to the White House last year promising, among others, to not start “stupid foreign wars that never end”.
Yet in late February, Trump joined Netanyahu in ordering a joint military campaign against Iran, prompting immediate Iranian retaliation and raising the spectre of an all-out regional war. With the prospect of renewed hostilities looming, both leaders exchanged effusive endorsements in the build-up to Tuesday’s US congressional election and Israel’s parliamentary vote last week, calling upon the other’s electorate to head to the polls to support their ally.
The moves, however, seem to have either backfired or missed the mark dramatically.
Netanyahu’s right-wing coalition finished the October 27 electoral race with just 53 seats, far shy of the 61 needed to form a government. Trump’s party, meanwhile, lost control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate to Democratic challengers who made sweeping inroads into traditionally Republican territory, including the strongholds of Texas and Kansas.
“Obviously, what we have witnessed is a historic political tsunami that amounts to a total repudiation of Trumpism, so it’s certainly broader than one issue,” Shibley Telhami, of the University of Maryland and director of the Critical Issues Poll, said of the US midterm results. “But foreign policy was central, especially the Iran war and US backing of Israel, as Americans tie these to pocketbook issues,” he added.
The US is Israel’s staunchest diplomatic and military backer. Over the years, it has repeatedly used its United Nations Security Council veto to block dozens of resolutions critical of Israel, including several motions calling for an end to the genocidal war against the Palestinians in the Gaza Strip.
At the same time, it has been providing Israel with at least $3.8bn in military aid annually, allowing it to acquire the cutting-edge US weaponry that has granted it military superiority across the region – assistance, however, that is carrying an increasingly high political cost.
Polling overseen by Telhami a week ago found that a majority of people in the US believed that Israel had influenced the Trump administration’s decision to instigate the costly and protracted war with Iran. The survey indicated that Washington’s close relationship with Tel Aviv had become more of a liability than an asset for many in the electorate, Telhami noted, “with most saying specifically Israel would be a factor in their vote. An even larger majority said the Iran war, which they tie to Israel, would impact their vote”.
‘Tail wagging the dog’
While Trump acknowledged the Democrats’ midterm win, and reluctantly conceded that the war on Iran was partly to blame due to its impact on energy prices, Netanyahu has spent the days since his own electoral defeat questioning the results.
Over the past week, the Likud party leader has falsely accused foreign powers of illegally boosting the vote for Israel’s Arab-led parties and cited his victory among Jewish voters as the basis for a national government. In his most recent echo of Trump’s reaction to his own loss in the 2020 US presidential election, Netanyahu even threatened not to recognise the certification of the results.
But as Israel enters a period of coalition wrangling, its political establishment also has to grapple with the routing of its White House ally and its potential culpability in it.
On Wednesday, key opposition figure Yair Lapid said almost all of Netanyahu’s actions since the vote, including his call for the internal security service Shin Bet to investigate the leaders of the Arab parties, in conjunction with the US election results, had rendered the prime minister politically noxious.
With voting still ongoing on Tuesday, Trump said in a TV interview he had made a deal with Netanyahu that the US would no longer be providing funding of “$4bn a year” to Israel after the end of 2026. While details remain scarce, the timing prompted speculation that Trump’s comments were part of a bid to stave off public anger over his administration’s support for Israel and a time of mounting domestic economic pressure.
“There’s a degree of denial inside Israel as to the depth of the change that is taking place in the US,” former Israeli government adviser Daniel Levy told Al Jazeera, caveating that while Israel itself may not have been on the midterm ballot, the sense of the “tail wagging the dog” in how Netanyahu’s relationship with Trump was perceived, certainly was.
“Most palpable was, of course, the effect of the Iran war,” said Levy. “Part of that is the Israeli role in dragging a gullible president into another calamitous Middle East military adventure.”
The war also brought a sense of clarity to the US public over their country’s relationship with Israel and the electoral cost of launching further wars in the Middle East, he added.
That the US’s full-throated support for Israel may be shifting in the face of growing international isolation might as well be on the minds of Israel’s opposition leaders as they weigh their coalition options. Netanyahu may be reviled by some within the US Democratic Party, but his relationship with Trump could still give him the political space to foment a new push for escalating the war against Iran, the political consequences of which could even see him once more able to set the agenda, Levy suggested.
“Netanyahu’s hand will now be weaker in trying to achieve that, but it should not be dismissed altogether – certainly not with a wounded Trump at the helm,” he said.
For Alon Pinkas, a former Israeli ambassador and consul general in New York, the relationship between the US and Israel had reached “a real inflection point, the consequences of which I don’t think much of Israel has either the imagination or education to truly understand”.
Much will depend on the Iran war and Trump’s reaction to the dramatic rejection of him and his policy agenda at the polls, Pinkas said, which could see him either escalate the conflict or seek an agreement that might appease Congress.
Either way, the future ties between the US and Israel had fundamentally changed, he argued.
“Even with all the speculation that the ending of the $3.8bn grant was some kind of quid pro quo to satisfy the US public, there was still no mention of the access to the weaponry that’s part of that grant,” said Pinkas.
“The money, Israel could probably live without; the weaponry, it depends upon – but there was no mention of that,” he added. “There was no mention of any future strategic agreement. It’s all just in the air.”

Presidential hopeful Vance appears to question Iran war after polls debacle
Vance cited trusted pollster saying Iran war, Israel ties were top of mind for Trump voters swinging to Democrats.
Vice President JD Vance has blamed the war on Iran for his party’s withering midterms defeat, suggesting that the conflict may not have been worth ceding control of the US Congress to Democrats.
“The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” he wrote in a lengthy post on X. “If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so.”
“Everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.”
Vance, a likely 2028 presidential candidate and heir apparent to Trump’s Make America Great Again movement, has been a key negotiator with Iran as the two countries search for a way out of the conflict, which has dented their economies and pushed global fuel prices up.
His statements on Tehran have been more dovish than those of other key members of the administration, and his post-election note appears to mark the closest he has yet come to publicly diverging from his boss on an issue that looks set to dog Republicans as the war continues.
Citing a pollster he describes as “one of the smartest people I know”, Vance said he was told ending the Iran war and “changing our relationship with Israel” were two of the top four answers given by Americans surveyed who had voted for Trump in 2024 but were planning to vote for Democrats in the 2026 midterms.
In stark contrast, Trump said, in the wake of the rebuke at the ballot box, that he had no regrets about launching the conflict.
“I did the right thing. I would have done it again,” he told the Wall Street Journal.
