https://www.propublica.org/article/brent.title: In a Newly Drawn District, Black Voters May Get a Representative Who Spent Years Undermining Their Interests
https://www.propublica.org/article/brent.author: Wendi C. Thomas
https://www.propublica.org/article/brent.text:
Reporting Highlights
- Undermining Voters: As state senator, Brent Taylor passed laws that superseded the will of Memphis voters. Now he wants to represent them in Congress.
- Overruling Elected Officials: Voters elected Democratic District Attorney Steve Mulroy, who rejected a tough-on-crime approach to public safety. Taylor’s laws have restrained his authority.
- Harming Black Memphians: Laws restricting how county judges set bail and reversing limits on police traffic stops disproportionately harm Black residents, studies show.
These highlights were written by the reporters and editors who worked on this story.
Not two weeks after the Tennessee legislature carved Memphis into three congressional districts this spring, in a move designed to eliminate Democratic representation, Republican state Sen. Brent Taylor made his electoral expectations clear in a photo posted on social media.
Taylor and U.S. Rep. Tim Burchett, a fellow Republican, sat side by side on the U.S. Capitol steps. “My friend Tim Burchett showing me the dadgum ropes,” Taylor wrote in a Facebook post.
On May 7, the same day that the new districts were approved, Taylor had announced his bid to represent the redrawn Congressional District 9, which for more than four decades had stood as the state’s sole majority Black district. During that time, it covered mostly the Memphis area; it now stretches across half the state and is majority white.
Taylor, 58, already has a track record with many of the voters he is now seeking to represent in Washington, D. C.: In his nearly four years as a state senator, he has taken steps to strip authority from local officials elected by many of those same voters. With the backing of a Republican supermajority, Taylor, who is white, pushed through half a dozen laws that superseded the power and priorities of local politicians.
Around the country, state legislatures from both parties have used preemption laws to control local governments. That tactic has been embraced by Republican-dominated statehouses in recent years as a way to restrict the ability of Democratic-led cities to enact policies state leaders disagree with, including protections for civil rights, public health and workers.
Memphis has long struggled with high rates of violent crime that have begun to fall only in the last couple of years. This is where Taylor focused his legislative efforts. He led the charge to prohibit judges from considering a defendant’s ability to pay when making bail decisions. He has tried to oust Steve Mulroy, the first Democrat elected as Shelby County district attorney in 25 years, and pushed through legislation authorizing the state to review every decision made by his office. And he co-sponsored a law that voided the Memphis City Council’s ban on police stops for minor traffic infractions, which had been passed after the 2023 beating death of Black motorist Tyré Nichols.
The question of how to keep communities safe has drawn divergent political approaches in Memphis — from Mulroy’s focus on rehabilitation as part of his effort to lower violent crime, to Taylor’s emphasis on aggressive prosecution and incarceration. Those approaches can mean very different experiences for the people of Memphis, which makes up most of Shelby County. Some elected officials and criminal justice experts warn that the laws Taylor has championed will embolden police to detain drivers without justification and the criminal justice system to lock up more people for longer periods in the already overcrowded county jail, where more than 65 people have died since 2018.
“I think he’s very dangerous for Shelby County, and he’s going to be very dangerous for the Ninth District if he gets elected,” said former Shelby County General Sessions Court Judge Bill Anderson, referring to how Taylor’s policies could especially harm Black men. Anderson retired in May 2025 after clashing publicly with Taylor over bail reform measures. (Anderson supported them; Taylor opposed them.)
Taylor is favored to win because of redistricting by Tennessee Republicans after a U.S. Supreme Court ruling in April made it harder to challenge gerrymandering that dilutes the Black vote. The Mississippi native, who lives in an antebellum-style mansion in a tiny and heavily white community east of Memphis, has loaned his congressional campaign $1.5 million. The candidate made millions after selling his funeral home businesses to a private equity firm.
Taylor’s opponent is state Rep. Justin J. Pearson, a 31-year-old Black Democrat who has taken a very different approach to what the district needs. Pearson has called for addressing the root causes of crime by improving schools and economic opportunities instead of a singular focus on incarceration. He first made national headlines for his role in stopping the construction of an oil pipeline in a Black Memphis neighborhood. He is also one of two Democratic legislators expelled by the Republican supermajority after leading a protest calling for gun control following a 2023 school shooting. With deep family roots in southwest Memphis, Pearson has positioned himself as the better fit for the historically Democratic Ninth Congressional District. He has also received support from national Democrats and has outraised Taylor in campaign donations.
Taylor, who declined to be interviewed for this story, has said that the laws he has championed prioritize public safety. He did not respond to detailed questions.
But John Pfaff, a professor at Fordham School of Law who has studied how state preemption laws impact prosecutors, said tough-on-crime laws like the ones Taylor helped pass have historically been “a form of social control against disliked minority groups” under the guise of public safety. 
Non-urban voters, Pfaff said, “do feel, however incorrectly, sort of victimized by expanding civil rights” that urban voters choose. While these voters cannot cast ballots in city elections, he said, they have another path by which to exert power: “If the suburbs and rural areas control the governor’s mansion and the state legislature, they then can use their power there through preemption laws that finally tell Memphis what they want Memphis to do.”
Prohibiting Limits on Police Traffic Stops
In January 2023, the month Taylor took office, the nation was shaken by video of violent policing in Memphis.
A street surveillance camera and police body cameras captured what happened after undercover Memphis police officers pulled over 29-year-old Nichols just a few blocks from his mother’s home. For three minutes, officers repeatedly punched the unarmed man in the face, hit him with a baton and kicked him as he screamed for his mom. Nichols would die from his injuries in the hospital three days later.
After pressure from Nichols’ family and community organizers, the Memphis City Council unanimously passed an ordinance in April of that year barring police from pulling motorists over for minor traffic violations, such as a broken tail light, as a pretext for investigating an unrelated, more serious crime. Research shows that these stops are disproportionately used to detain Black drivers, undermine the public’s trust in police and create unnecessary police encounters that can turn deadly. 
Taylor, who had been in the state Senate for a few months when the city ordinance passed, said it made the public less safe by limiting the potential for police to investigate more serious crimes. The next year, he and state Rep. John Gillespie, a Shelby County Republican, sponsored legislation that prohibited local government from curbing law enforcement’s ability to conduct traffic stops, effectively undoing Memphis’ ordinance.
Nichols’ mother, RowVaughn Wells, pleaded with lawmakers to drop the bill. Speaking on the Senate floor, Taylor responded, saying that as a funeral home director, he empathized with the Nichols’ family, but “we can’t let that empathy, Mr. Speaker, cloud our judgment in protecting 7 million Tennesseans.”
Taylor’s intervention suggests “that Memphis voters don’t know what their best interests are,” said Martavius Jones, who was chair of the Memphis City Council when the city ordinance passed. “What we were trying to do would not jeopardize the safety of anyone — not even in Memphis, but much less the rest of the population of Tennessee.”
Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee, a Republican, told reporters before signing the law that no one should limit police in their enforcement methods and officers should be held accountable for their actions.
“I think what’s most important for us to remember is that we can give law enforcement tools,” Lee said, “but we’ve got to hold law enforcement to a standard of using those tools appropriately, where there’s an appropriate interaction with the public.”
Eight months after Tennessee lawmakers passed Taylor’s preemption bill, the U.S. Department of Justice released its investigation of the Memphis Police Department, finding that its aggressive traffic enforcement had harmed Memphians. The Justice Department recommended that the city limit the use of pretextual stops. Such police activity enabled the “regular use of excessive force with impunity” and unlawfully discriminated against Black residents, the Biden administration’s report said. When President Donald Trump took office in 2025, his Justice Department retracted those findings.
Over the last year, law enforcement has ramped up the use of such stops, especially in immigration enforcement, as Trump’s Memphis Safe Task Force — a collection of more than two dozen state and federal law enforcement agencies, including the National Guard — descended upon the city. Taylor supported the effort, testifying before the U.S. Senate days before it began that the task force would “succeed in doing the hard work to infiltrate gangs and arrest more routine criminals.”
Unprecedented Scrutiny of a District Attorney
Since his first year in the state Senate, Taylor had also been working to displace the decision-making authority of another locally elected office: district attorneys, especially Mulroy, one of Tennessee’s two Democratic county prosecutors. Taylor called him a “far-left zealot” who “has the potential to make the scourge of violent crime even worse.”
In 2023, Taylor sponsored a law that transferred the power to review certain death penalty cases from county prosecutors, who are elected, to the state attorney general, who is appointed by the state Supreme Court. While the law applied statewide, it disproportionately impacted Shelby County, where half of the state’s 40 death row prisoners were prosecuted. The law, Mulroy said at the time, “effectively disenfranchises the voters” who chose their district attorney.
Taylor would go on to further weaken Mulroy’s office following Trump’s 2025 deployment of his crime task force to Memphis. As arrests soared, Taylor worked to place the district attorney’s decisions under unprecedented scrutiny, saying he wanted to ensure that the prosecution of task force cases was as aggressive as the task force itself.
One new law, co-sponsored by Taylor, authorized the state attorney general to review every case that comes through Mulroy’s office, including those that stem from arrests made by Trump’s task force, “to ensure the proper administration of justice necessary to protect the safety of the community.” The dispositions of each case, along with bail recommendations, would be reported to legislative leaders.
Republican state Rep. Andrew Farmer, who introduced the bill in the House, noted that it is designed to ensure that “all crimes that deserve to be prosecuted are prosecuted.”
Mulroy is “just going to have to work harder and ensure that people are continuing to stay safe,” Farmer said on the House floor. “We want Memphis to continue on the path that it’s going — up.”
The state’s district attorneys general conference, led by Republican former District Attorney Stephen Crump, opposed an early version of the bill, which would have applied to district attorneys across the state, because it could lead prosecutors to second-guess their decisions. He dropped his objections after the bill was narrowed to apply to only Mulroy.
That law has another provision aimed at Mulroy as well: If he declines to prosecute specific categories of crime, the state attorney general can ask the state Supreme Court to intervene by installing a temporary district attorney who would then decide whether to prosecute. Taylor has long sought to limit Mulroy’s authority, and the provision would be a way to do so. Mulroy said the effect would be “an unelected shadow DA operating in parallel to the duly elected DA.”
“Prosecutorial discretion and prosecutorial independence is a key fundamental part of our criminal justice system,” Mulroy said. “It’s clear under both the text of the Tennessee constitution and Tennessee Supreme Court case law, and this bill does great violence to those principles.”
Taylor co-sponsored a second law, passed in May, that requires Mulroy’s office to report to the state and the U.S. Department of Justice within 10 business days every time it has entered into a plea deal, or dismissed or lowered the charges on a felony offense that resulted from a task force arrest.
“Memphis residents deserve confidence that the significant investments being made to combat violent crime are matched with accountability at every level of the justice system,” Gillespie, who co-sponsored the bill in the House, said at the time.
Taylor argued the reporting requirements were necessary to give the federal government an opportunity to prosecute cases Mulroy dismissed. In a post on X and a statement made before the U.S. Senate Judiciary Committee, he called Mulroy “the weak link” in the task force’s efforts. He’s also claimed, without evidence, that Mulroy refuses to prosecute crimes.
In a rebuttal, Mulroy noted that more than 40,000 defendants are prosecuted by his office each year.
Mulroy has sued to stop both laws, claiming they are unconstitutional because they unfairly single out Shelby County and create an administrative burden. The lawsuit is pending in state court. Meanwhile, Mulroy has objected to his staff spending time on the reporting requirements, which he called “pointless busywork.” 
Mulroy’s election in 2022 as the county’s first Democratic district attorney in more than two decades came on the heels of a year with a record number of homicides. But Republicans’ tough-on-crime approach had grown unpopular with voters, and Mulroy vowed to be an alternative. He promised to deprioritize the prosecution of low-level offenses such as marijuana possession and shoplifting; emphasize rehabilitation such as drug treatment, mental health counseling and job training; and establish a unit to examine the validity of convictions.
One of the people who campaigned for him was William Arnold, who had spent nearly seven years in state prison before his conviction was dismissed following examination by a Davidson County conviction review unit. The community organizer said he saw Mulroy’s candidacy as a way to “support someone who could help Memphians in a different way.”
To see Mulroy’s power being muted by Taylor is disheartening, Arnold said. But that is not surprising to him, given how the state legislature has long treated the predominantly Black city, including replacing the Memphis Shelby County Schools’ elected board with a state-appointed one.
Bail Calculator Scrapped
Among the preemptive legislation Taylor has sponsored, a 2023 effort stood out: the dismantling of a bipartisan effort to ensure Shelby County’s bail practices did not discriminate against poor people, who are disproportionately Black.
Under state law, magistrates are to “impose the least onerous conditions” when deciding bail and should set bail “as low as the court determines is necessary” to assure the defendant returns to court.
But in practice, hundreds of people were being detained at the Shelby County Jail simply because they couldn’t afford bail, according to Just City, a Memphis criminal justice reform organization, which along with the American Civil Liberties Union threatened to sue the county in 2021 for violating existing state law. Being jailed while awaiting trial can cause arrestees to lose jobs and child custody, the organizations argued.
In August 2022, the organizations and county officials — including Mulroy’s predecessor, Republican District Attorney Amy Weirich — agreed on a new bail order that included an “ability to pay” calculator.
That tool quickly drew Taylor’s ire, and by the following January he had co-sponsored a bill to kill it, characterizing the calculator in a Senate Judiciary Committee meeting as a way of “essentially asking defendants how much money they happen to have in their pocket so that they can make bail.”
The bill’s supporters said judges should prioritize public safety when deciding whether to release defendants. “There is blood running in the streets of Memphis today because they’re letting people out,” state Rep. William Lamberth, a Republican, said on the House floor.
State law requires judges, when setting bail, to consider several factors, including a defendant’s financial condition. And Josh Spickler, executive director of Just City, said that’s exactly what the tool helped judges do.
Under Taylor’s law, however, “the defendant’s ability to pay shall not be considered.”
“That tied our hands as judges,” Anderson, the former Shelby County judge, said in an interview.
A 2025 University of Memphis study found that the median bail amount increased after Taylor’s law took effect. And the law’s impact falls hardest on Black residents, Anderson said, because they are more likely to be low-income and make up a disproportionate share of Shelby County jail occupants.
“To those of us in the system, it’s obvious what he’s doing,” said Anderson, who resigned in 2025 with six years left of his eight-year term. “He called them reform acts, but they’re not reform.”

https://www.propublica.org/article/zohar.title: Cybersecurity CEO Indicted for Allegedly Scamming Millions From Ransomware Victims
https://www.propublica.org/article/zohar.author: Renee Dudley
https://www.propublica.org/article/zohar.text:
A Florida man who was the subject of a 2019 investigation by ProPublica was indicted last month on federal charges that he defrauded clients of his ransomware data recovery firm.
According to the Justice Department, the man, Zohar Pinhasi, told customers he could recover their encrypted files without having to pay hackers, when, in reality, he paid the ransom and charged victims a hefty fee on top.
The indictment mirrors the findings from ProPublica’s 2019 article “The Trade Secret,” which centered on Pinhasi and his scheme. The outlet found that the ransomware victims were being harmed twice: once by the hackers, who locked their targets’ files and demanded ransom, and a second time by MonsterCloud, Pinhasi’s Florida-based data recovery firm, which misled its clients about not paying ransoms.
“By falsely claiming to decrypt ransomware without paying off the ransomers, the defendant re-victimized his clients while extracting a hefty profit for himself,” U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella said in an Oct. 7 press release. “Our Office will vigorously prosecute ransomware attackers who prey on Americans from across the world and those who cynically profit from their criminal activity.”
When ProPublica published its story in 2019, ransomware was growing into one of the world’s most pervasive cyberthreats. Hackers locked the data of governments, schools and businesses, holding the decryption key for a ransom payment, which they usually demanded in bitcoin and other types of difficult-to-trace cryptocurrency.
ProPublica’s reporting focused on how U.S. industries, from data recovery firms like MonsterCloud to insurance giants that cover ransom payments, all fueled the extortion economy. Ransomware remains a widespread threat today, and the threat to national security has grown as hackers linked to hostile foreign governments are believed to use ransomware as a cover for espionage. The prevalence of AI tools is also making it easier for attackers to spread ransomware.
Pinhasi, who went by the alias Zack Green, told ProPublica in 2019 that MonsterCloud never promised clients that their data will be recovered by any particular method. “How we do it, it’s our problem,” he told ProPublica. “You will get your data back. Sit back, relax and enjoy the ride.” He called MonsterCloud’s data recovery methods a “trade secret.”
Pinhasi hung up when reached on his cellphone this month. A message left with a representative at MonsterCloud’s office phone number and a message left with his attorney were not returned. A spokesperson for the U.S. Attorney’s Office said Pinhasi pleaded not guilty to the federal charges.
In its 2019 investigation, ProPublica interviewed MonsterCloud’s clients and ransomware experts and found that in certain cases the firm must have paid ransoms on behalf of clients. MonsterCloud’s services were particularly popular with local law enforcement agencies, who are loath to engage with or pay criminal hackers. Several interviewed by ProPublica at the time said they chose MonsterCloud to help them recover from ransomware because they believed the firm would never pay a ransom.
Pinhasi, who described himself to ProPublica as a former IT security intelligence officer for the Israeli military, said in 2019 that MonsterCloud handled up to 30 calls a day and had about 20 employees in South Florida as well as extensive global contacts.
Federal investigators found that, over the course of the scheme, Pinhasi allegedly charged clients more than $19 million and paid more than $8 million in ransom payments. In one example, Pinhasi made a ransom payment of about $8,200 but charged the client about $150,000. If convicted, he faces up to 20 years in prison.
In the Justice Department’s October press release, an FBI official said Pinhasi had “turned the victim’s crisis into his own profit center. This deception is unacceptable, and the FBI is committed to ensuring accountability for those who choose to victimize the very people who trusted them for help.”
The Justice Department did not address ProPublica’s 2019 finding that one of the FBI’s own was among Pinhasi’s associates at MonsterCloud. John Pistole, a former deputy director of the FBI under Robert Mueller, was prominently featured in a promotional video on MonsterCloud’s homepage. “Police departments, government agencies, hospitals, small business and Fortune 500 firms trust MonsterCloud to help recover from attacks and protect against new ones,” Pistole said in the video. “MonsterCloud’s proprietary technology and expertise protects their professional reputations and organizational integrity.”
Pistole was not mentioned by name in the Pinhasi indictment.
In 2019, Pinhasi touted MonsterCloud’s ties to law enforcement as evidence of its integrity. Pistole, who also headed the Transportation Security Administration under President Barack Obama, was listed on MonsterCloud’s website as the only member of its “Cyber Security Advisory Council.”
Pistole did not respond to a request for comment for this story. In a 2019 interview, he said he became acquainted with Pinhasi after MonsterCloud reached him through a speaker’s bureau and that MonsterCloud paid him indirectly through that group. He said Pinhasi scripted his testimonial and that he was well aware that in most cases — including MonsterCloud’s — the only way to decrypt data locked by ransomware is to pay the hackers. “That’s the business model as I understood it,” Pistole told ProPublica at the time. “Based on my experience and knowledge, ransom is paid and they facilitate the best practices moving forward.”
A spokesperson for the U.S. Attorney’s Office declined to comment on Pistole’s connection to MonsterCloud.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/nationalizat.title: Public Ownership of Key Economic Sectors Is Popular
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/nationalizat.author: Chance Phillips
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/nationalizat.text:
Public Ownership of Key Economic Sectors Is Popular
A new poll shows significant support for nationalization of health care, railroads, and artificial intelligence among Democratic voters. Public ownership can be part of a winning pitch for addressing the cost-of-living crisis.
Democratic voters overwhelmingly support the public ownership and operation of several key industries. At least one of the Democratic politicians who want to win the party’s next presidential primary should take note.
A poll I recently commissioned from the Center for Strategic Politics found that a supermajority of Democratic voters support public ownership and operation of health care and the electrical grid. A slight majority supports public ownership of the nation’s railroads. And far more voters said they would support public ownership and operation of artificial intelligence than opposed it.
Per other polling conducted back in June, Bernie Sanders’s proposal to partially nationalize AI companies is also incredibly popular across the political spectrum. Maybe it’s the number of socialists holding public office now, or maybe it’s the Trump administration’s habit of demanding stakes in private companies, but public ownership isn’t all that taboo anymore. Not if you trust the polls.
And at least in American politics, polling has been having a moment for the last few years. Political consultants and talking heads are paid handsomely to tell politicians and partisans of both parties that they really need to consult the latest polls before deciding how they’ll campaign.
Besides the inherent issues with such an approach, polling is usually a poor way to find a novel policy proposal or a topic that candidates could win a campaign by bearing down on. Asking hundreds or thousands of prospective voters a battery of questions quickly becomes quite expensive, and while the marginal cost per question isn’t especially high, most polls focus on policy areas that are already salient. Ergo, we don’t see many polls that directly ask whether voters would support nationalizing parts of the economy, aside from questions about Medicare for All. But we do know that nationalization can be very popular.
Across gender, age group, ethnicity, and political leaning, and across polls, the economy or the cost of living is by far the issue cited most frequently as deciding Americans’ votes. Even when socialization doesn’t have any real ideological appeal for voters, pitching public ownership as a cost-of-living measure has proven to be politically effective. Just look at New York.
The poll I commissioned showed that grocery stores are one of the industries Democrats are least interested in taking into public ownership, but piloting municipally owned groceries was a key platform plank of the wildly successful Zohran Mamdani mayoral campaign. It polled quite well during the campaign and, despite significant pushback, is one of the campaign promises that Mamdani is currently working to keep.
Calls for a larger public stake in or full public ownership of other industries are far more likely to be political winners: thanks to the Hugging Face hack and similar fiascos, the public is increasingly concerned about recent developments in artificial intelligence. The war with Iran and increased demand are driving up electricity prices across the United States. And private health care and health insurance are just inherently disastrous.
Right now, Democratic voters still haven’t fully lined up behind any of the major presidential hopefuls. The largest bloc across almost every poll says it will support Kamala Harris, but a half-dozen other candidates are also polling relatively well. Most notably, democratic socialist Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez usually ends up in the top tier of serious contenders.
The poll results suggest that a properly motivated political entrepreneur could benefit from the American cost-of-living crisis quite easily. Just call to nationalize the industries that Americans want to see nationalized. If, as Substacker Matthew Yglesias suggests, the politically minded “should encourage candidates to embrace popular progressive causes,” then we should encourage candidates to embrace nationalization.
Now, maybe ambitious Democrats should not call for the nationalization of restaurants, but at a minimum, the government taking a leading role in the rapidly developing AI sector and large swaths of the private health care system appears overwhelmingly popular. As a vision to rally around, it would at least help secure them the nomination.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Fifth generation Indian weaver launches luxury cashmere brand
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: The Art Newspaper
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Mujtaba Kadri’s family has produced cashmere for five generations and his atelier in Srinagar, the largest city in Kashmir, is just 50m away from where his great-grandfather had his own. “I’ve been involved since I was a child,” Kadri says. His spinners and weavers are still based exclusively in Srinagar, mostly women working from home. Hand spinning creates a slightly uneven texture in the fibre, which leaves tiny air pockets once it is woven. It is this that makes the fabric both very light and incredibly warm.
Kadri studied at university in Mumbai but returned immediately to his home city, albeit with a more international outlook. “Our cashmere is the finest quality, which means its micron count is always below 14.5,” Kadri says. “I knew it had potential in foreign markets.” He went on to work with Carolina Herrera, Oscar de la Renta and Marni, making custom-ordered textiles. Later, he met Mary-Kate and Ashley Olsen, and collaborated closely with their label, The Row, when they launched their home line.
He is now launching the Kadri brand, using his own name, in outlets including London’s Dover Street Market. On sale will be scarves, blankets and other home and fashion accessories. “I’ve wanted to do this for a long time,” he says. Designs are developed in a small Paris studio where the creative team includes colour specialist Maeva Elfassi. “Colour can be the element that cashmere brands get wrong,” Kadri says.
Hand-woven cashmere is expensive due to the rare raw materials, from a special breed of goats in the Jankan region, and its time-consuming production. A shawl, which sells for $1,000, will go through 12 processes, undertaken by a number of artisans, and takes 40 days to make. “It really is slow fashion,” Kadri says. But more importantly, for him, it is a way to sustain a community where weaving has always been a way of life.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: A Van Gogh hidden away for over 50 years and a vibrant Cezanne harlequin: our pick of the November auctions
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Carlie Porterfield
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Vincent van Gogh, Châtaigniers
en fleurs (1890)
Legendary: The Blaquier-Arrieta Collection Evening Auction, Sotheby’s, 18 November
Estimate: in the region of $180m
Vincent van Gogh painted Châtaigniers en fleurs (blossoming chestnut trees) during the final weeks of his life, having just moved to the French village of Auvers-sur-Oise after spending the previous year in a psychiatric asylum in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence. Initially he took to painting with a renewed optimism at his surroundings and work. The painting at hand depicts flowering chestnut trees blooming into a blue sky, with women passing through with parasols and Japanese-inspired dress. Châtaigniers en fleurs is expected to fetch in the region of $180m, Sotheby’s says. The artist’s current record at auction is $117.2m, set by Christie’s New York in November 2022 during the Paul Allen sale with Verger avec cyprès (orchard with cypresses, 1888). Châtaigniers en fleurs has not been seen in public since entering the Argentinian Blaquier-Arrieta collection in 1975.
Paul Cezanne, Arlequin (1888-90)
Legendary: The Blaquier-Arrieta Collection Evening Auction, Sotheby’s, 18 November
Estimate: Around $120m
Arlequin is a rare appearance on the market of one of Paul Cezanne’s paintings from his harlequin series, modelled on his son, Paul, and inspired by Mardi Gras parades from the artist’s childhood in Aix-en-Provence, France. It is one of only four such examples, according to Sotheby’s. When the painting was unveiled at Sotheby’s in London, it was the first time it had been seen in public since 1975, when it was acquired by the sugar magnates Carlos Pedro Blaquier and Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier. Before it entered their collection in Argentina, it belonged to legendary dealers like Ambroise Vollard, Paul Durand-Ruel and Paul Rosenberg. It also hung for two decades at Merton Hall in Cambridge, the then-family home of the British branch of the Rothschild family. Another version of the painting is part of the collection of the National Gallery of Art in Washington, DC. If it exceeds its estimate, Arlequin could set an artist record at auction. The most valuable Cezanne to sell at auction was a view of his beloved Sainte-Victoire mountain, for $137.79m, at Christie’s New York in 2022 during the sale of Paul Allen’s collection.
Man Ray, Le Baiser (around 1930)
Collection Roger Therond, Christie’s, Paris, 13 November
Estimate: €250,000 to €350,000
Man Ray’s Le Baiser (the kiss) comes from the collection of Roger Therond, the journalist and longtime editor of Paris Match, whose holdings included photographs by some of the leading artists of inter-war Paris. Therond was particularly drawn to Man Ray, whom he nicknamed “the Frenzied One”. In Le Baiser, two figures are captured in ambiguous poses, leaving the relationship between the two sitters deliberately unclear. According to Christie’s, Therond encouraged his children to look at the photograph from a distance and imagine different possibilities and circumstances for the subjects. The sitter on the left side is the American photographer Lee Miller, who began her career as a fashion model and later worked as a correspondent for Vogue during the Second World War. Miller was one of the first journalists to arrive at the Dachau concentration camp after its liberation in 1945, and recorded some of the most haunting photographic evidence of the Holocaust. She famously posed for a photo while bathing in Adolf Hitler’s personal bathtub at his Munich apartment.

https://gothamist.com/news/stabbing-of-b.title: Stabbing of Brooklyn runner believed to be ‘random attack,’ NYPD says
https://gothamist.com/news/stabbing-of-b.author: Ben Feuerherd
https://gothamist.com/news/stabbing-of-b.text:
NYPD detectives believe the stabbing of a young woman who was jogging along a running path in Brooklyn was a random attack, the department’s chief of detectives said Monday.
An unknown attacker stabbed Katie Suarez, 28, in the neck as she was running on the path on Shore Parkway near Bay 17th Friday evening. She was critically injured in the attack and remains hospitalized. No arrests have been made.
“As of right now, it appears it was a random attack,” Chief of Detectives Joseph Kenny told reporters. “ Nobody else would've known that she was running there at that particular time.”
On the night of the attack, Suarez was doing her usual routine, Kenny said. She left work at a nearby bank at about 6:35 p.m., changed into athletic gear, met up with her mother who took her work outfit, and then set off for her run.
Her father had also just left work and was planning to meet up with both of them at a nearby Wendy’s restaurant and give them a ride home after Suarez finished her jog, Kenny said. At about 7:56 p.m., her father called Suarez to find out when she would arrive, and she told him she was about half a mile away and would be there soon.
When she didn’t arrive on time, the father set off to look for her on the path. At 8:16 p.m., he found her unconscious under a tree, bleeding from the neck, Kenny said.
The path where she was attacked is a stretch of running and biking track that is not covered by surveillance cameras, Kenny added. The path runs along the water from a pier in Bay Ridge to a large shopping center in Bath Beach. It’s often crowded with runners, bikers and fishermen.
Police are trying to recover any surveillance footage that may have been recorded by a food cart that was parked near the crime scene, Kenny said. Police are asking any drivers who may have passed through the area on the Belt Parkway around that time to contact them in case they have dashcam footage of the attacker.
Police are offering a reward of $10,000 for anyone who comes forward with information about the stabbing that leads to the attacker’s arrest.

https://gothamist.com/news/nypd-investig.title: NYPD investigating bullying as possible motive in Bronx teen's killing
https://gothamist.com/news/nypd-investig.author: Charles Lane
https://gothamist.com/news/nypd-investig.text:
NYPD detectives are investigating whether bullying played a role in the fatal shooting of a 15-year-old Bronx student last week, but say the city Department of Education won't provide information about the alleged bullying without a subpoena.
“Unfortunately, they’re not willing to give us that information without a subpoena, so we’re going through proper channels to get that information,” NYPD Chief of Detectives Joseph Kenny said Monday, four days after the shooting.
Kenny said detectives have not yet named any suspects in Frimpong’s death.
Javits’ father, Thomas Frimpong, has said two students fought with his son at Dreamyard Preparatory School a few days before the shooting, and that both were suspended. Kenny called it “one aspect that we’re looking at as well as some others.”
Spokespeople for the DOE and the school did not immediately respond to questions about the NYPD’s request for information or whether the department needed a subpoena.
Investigators are also weighing other possibilities, including whether the killing resulted from a robbery, or whether Javits was thought to be someone’s rival, he said. But, he added, “We’re not going to discount the bullying angle here.”
So far, police have found nothing that indicates Javits was involved in gang activity, the chief said.
“Seems like he was just a very good kid,” he said. “ He would voluntarily leave his phone at home because he wanted to concentrate on his schoolwork.”
Three people, hooded and wearing surgical masks, were in Crotona Park well before Javits came along Thursday morning, Kenny said. When they walked up on him, Javits ran, the chief said.
“All three gave chase, and these cowards shot him in the back,” Kenny said.
Javits dropped his backpack as he ran, and someone else stole it, police said. It has not been recovered.
The three attackers then went back and picked up the shell casings, the chief said. “So they knew exactly what they were doing.”
After the shooting, all three jumped a subway turnstile and got on a southbound 5 train, and police tracked them to Manhattan, according to Kenny.
In a statement Friday, the education department said it was making counseling and other support available to students, families and staff, and “supporting NYPD as they investigate.”
Students at DreamYard Preparatory School held a walkout and a memorial for Javits on Monday, Kenny said.
In a survey this school year, most students said they felt safe in or near the school — including 84% who said they felt safe traveling between home and school — according to data from the DOE published by the NYC SIFT platform. Students’ overall impression of safety at the school was slightly lower than the citywide average at other public schools.
Thomas Frimpong said Monday morning that a detective had visited the family Sunday night and said police would go to the school Monday morning. “But we haven’t heard back from them today,” he said.
The chief said detectives have been in constant contact with the father, who has the lead detective’s cell number.
On Saturday, Mayor Zohran Mamdani said President Donald Trump had agreed to grant a visa to Javits’ mother, who lives in Ghana, so she can travel to New York.

https://gothamist.com/news/nypd-officers.title: NYPD officers shoot man after exchange of gunfire outside Bronx deli, police say
https://gothamist.com/news/nypd-officers.author: Giulia Heyward
https://gothamist.com/news/nypd-officers.text:
NYPD officers shot a man in the Bronx on Monday afternoon after he fired at them, police said.
The shooting occurred around 3:20 p.m. near Bainbridge Avenue and East 194th Street in the Bronx, police said. The NYPD advised the public to avoid the area near 2657 Bainbridge Ave. and expect road closures and delays.
Police said Victor Soto, 49, had been involved in a dispute with several people inside Sammy Gourmet Deli, where he pulled out a firearm and pointed it at people inside, causing them to duck for cover.
The man then left the deli and began walking northbound with the gun in his hand, slamming it against the deli's glass window, according to police.
The NYPD said two officers arrived at the scene and ordered the man to drop the gun. Police said he ignored their commands and instead pointed the firearm directly at the officers.
This led to "an exchange of gunfire between the officers and the subject," according to NYPD Assistant Chief Aneudy Castillo, who spoke at a news conference Monday evening.
"As the subject is discharging his weapon, he is continuing northbound and firing behind him in broad daylight with civilians in the area," Castillo said.
Officers shot the man and took him into custody, police said. Soto was hospitalized in stable condition and is expected to survive, according to Castillo.
Attorney information for Soto was not immediately available.
Castillo said the incident was captured on police body cameras and surveillance cameras both inside and outside the deli. He said police also relied on eyewitness accounts in describing what happened.
The NYPD's Force Investigation Division is reviewing the shooting.

https://gothamist.com/news/washington-sq.title: Washington Square Park snowball thrower gets community service for pelting NYPD
https://gothamist.com/news/washington-sq.author: Walter Wuthmann
https://gothamist.com/news/washington-sq.text:
An influencer accused of criminal assault for pelting an officer with a snowball during a viral Washington Square Park snowball fight earlier this year will have his case dismissed for community service.
Manhattan prosecutors on Friday agreed to toss the charges against Gusmane Coulibaly, 28 — AKA “Diaper Man” — if he completes 20 hours of community service for the Parks Department.
The plea deal marks the end of a chapter in the snowball-gate saga. The social media-fueled showdown between a rowdy crowd and police officers sparked a broader debate about Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s approach to public safety. Mamdani downplayed the incident as “a snowball fight,” while NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch called the incident “disgraceful” and “criminal.”
Even Gov. Kathy Hochul weighed in, saying it was “never acceptable to throw anything at a police officer, full stop.”
The NYPD put out wanted photos for four men in connection with the snowball fight following a historic blizzard that dumped 20 inches of snow on the city. Officers arrested Coulibaly a few days later.
Prosecutors in Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s office declined to pursue assault charges, instead charging Coulibaly with misdemeanor obstructing government administration and a harassment violation.
Both charges will be dismissed if Coulibaly completes the community service hours. In a prepared statement to the court Friday, prosecutors said, “We believe this disposition is appropriate and consistent with this defendant’s conduct that day.”
Police union officials disagreed.
“We’re not surprised that we’re getting weak justice in this case, because DA Alvin Bragg and Mayor Mamdani made sure of that from the beginning,” Hendry said in a statement. “By downplaying this attack on police officers, the mayor and DA gave this individual a free pass to keep causing chaos on our streets.”
Hendry had appeared at Coulibaly’s arraignment in February, alongside about a dozen uniformed officers.
A second suspect, 18-year-old Eric Wilson, was arrested in March after turning himself in. Wilson pleaded guilty to non-criminal harassment charges in April in exchange for community service, according to the Manhattan DA’s Office.
Coulibaly has continued to have run-ins with police since the snowball fight.
Police arrested Coulibaly on Oct. 8 for allegedly attempting to rob a street vendor in East Harlem. Officers accused Coulibaly of lifting his shirt “to reveal the handle of a firearm in his waistband,” court records show. Coulibaly has pleaded not guilty.
In a video posted to his “Diaper Man” Instagram page on Oct. 22, Coulibaly appears to be arrested by NYPD officers after driving an e-scooter on a sidewalk.
“Took the cops on a lil troll run,” the caption reads.
Coulibaly did not respond to an inquiry. His attorney declined to comment.

https://hyperallergic.com/the-indian-pav.title: The Indian Pavilion in Venice Asks: What Is Home?
https://hyperallergic.com/the-indian-pav.author: Avedis Hadjian
https://hyperallergic.com/the-indian-pav.text:
The Indian Pavilion in Venice Asks: What Is Home?
"Geographies of Distance" offers a polysemous reading of home during a period of accelerated urbanization in India.
VENICE — The Indian Pavilion at the 61st Venice Biennale is to visual art what minor tones are to music: striking notes that invite contemplation and convey depth. Geographies of Distance: Remembering Home interprets the Biennale’s theme, “In Minor Keys,” through the rich diversity encompassed by India's name. The exhibition offers a polysemous reading of home in a country where time and space are measured on a vast scale, bringing together disparate experiences of place, memory, distance, and belonging.
The exhibition represents all of India: from the sun-baked earth of the southern state of Tamil Nadu to the stepped architecture of Ladakh in the north, to houses at the foot of the Himalayas, and to the ghost of a Delhi long succumbing to bulldozers. Enormous flowers hang from the ceiling, standing in for gardens and their most distinctive inhabitants, a tribute to their prominent place in Indian private, public, and sacred life. A mesh of bamboo canes evokes a widespread construction technique in the East, symbolizing new cities rising above older urban landscapes.
“I would characterize the pavilion and the work of the five artists as a reflection on identity and belonging in a period of accelerated change,” said Amin Jaffer, curator of Geographies of Distance. “[It] proposes the idea that home is not solely a physical place we inhabit but a condition that we carry with us.”

https://hyperallergic.com/as-politicians.title: As Politicians Break Promises, This Public Artwork Keeps Them
https://hyperallergic.com/as-politicians.author: Anna Gallagher-Ross
https://hyperallergic.com/as-politicians.text:
As Politicians Break Promises, This Public Artwork Keeps Them
Paul Ramírez Jonas debuted his participatory artwork “Public Trust” months before Trump was first elected. A decade on, it feels more urgent than ever.
Last month, Paul Ramírez Jonas invited the people of Toronto to sit down with a stranger in a public space, make a promise, swear on it, see it spelled out on a large-scale marquee, and then memorialize it in a one-of-a-kind contract they kept. One of hundreds of such vows was: “I promise to disagree better.”
Ramírez Jonas’s participatory public artwork “Public Trust,” presented by The Bentway (where Anna Gallagher-Ross directs programming), was commissioned and first showcased by Now + There (founded by Kate Gilbert and later renamed the Boston Public Art Triennial) in 2016, months before Donald Trump was elected as president.
“Public Trust” was the Now + There’s first project, a labor of love for its one-and-a-half-person team, and has since set the standard for its commissions. The promises made by everyday Bostonians — often similar in their commitments to family or self-improvement but coming from very different walks of life — were juxtaposed with daily headlines, including promises by politicians, corporations, weather forecasters, and more. This intermingling of commitments, both personal and authoritative, invites us to reflect on the power of our words, participation, and role in the democratic process. Ramírez Jonas often quips that he would like this project to one day become irrelevant.
Ten years later, in the lead-up to our municipal election in Toronto, we could think of no better project to invite people to reflect on the power of their words and their participation. Why does the simple act of sitting across from a stranger and making a promise feel more important than ever?

https://taz.de/Wiener-Akademie/!6223209/.title: Wiener Akademie: Wie die Kunst verwaltet wurde
https://taz.de/Wiener-Akademie/!6223209/.author: Uwe Mattheiß
https://taz.de/Wiener-Akademie/!6223209/.text:
Wiener Akademie: Wie die Kunst verwaltet wurde
Eine Ausstellung der Wiener Akademie der bildenden Künste versucht die Geschichte des Widerstreits von Akademie und Avantgarde neu zu erzählen. Klappt das?
Akademismus hat in der Kunst keinen guten Ruf. Sind vorgefundene Regeln und Wissensbestände nicht zunächst Fesseln der individuellen Schöpfung, die jenseits von Reproduktion ihre Regeln erst hervorbringt? Dennoch ist seit dem 16. Jahrhundert der bevorzugte Ort dieser wundersamen Wandlung von Fremd- zu Selbstbestimmung die Akademie. Sie generiert Wissen, etabliert Kunst als autonome Sphäre. Zugleich haftet ihr der Verdacht an, gewonnene Autonomie wieder herrschaftsförmig zu kanalisieren.
Unter dem Titel „Der große Michelangelo ist tot!“ rekapituliert die Wiener Akademie die Geschichte der Institution und ihrer Feinde in 15 Stationen von der frühen Neuzeit bis in die Gegenwart. Die vom Kunsthistoriker und Kulturtheoretiker Helmut Draxler kuratierte Schau bezieht die ausstellende, Wissen produzierende Institution selbst in die Bewegung der Reflexion ein.
300 Jahre nach Erstellung ihrer Statuten kann die Akademie aus ihrer Sammlung zum Wandel von Organisation und Lehre vieles beitragen. Exponate obsoleter Methoden wie Kopien und Gipsabgüsse werden zum kuratorischen Asset, stehen gleichrangig neben Originalen, historischem Material, Kommentaren und zeitgenössischen Arbeiten.
Die Ausstellung
„Der große Michelangelo ist tot! Avantgarde und Akademismus“. Akademie der bildenden Künste Wien, Gemäldegalerie, bis 22. August 2027
Der Gegensatz von Akademie und Avantgarde ist nicht mehr der unendliche Streit von Alt und Neu, nicht mehr das Erbe historischer Avantgarden nach ihrem Scheitern und ist auch etwas anderes als die Dialektik einer Entfaltung der Ausdrucksmöglichkeiten.
Kunst als symbolische Kategorie
Draxler relativiert mit der Ausstellung den Antagonismus, ohne der Auseinandersetzung die Schärfe zu nehmen, und wählt die Figur des Widerstreits, der sich weder in der Synthese aufheben noch nach einer gemeingültigen Regel entscheiden lässt. Dieser Streit erst konstituiere „Kunst als symbolische Kategorie“, zeige, was mit der Kunst in ihrer Gegenwart möglich sei.
Alles beginnt am Grab Michelangelos um 1564. Die Florentiner hatten seinen Leichnam insgeheim aus Rom überführt. Zur Nachfolge des „Göttlichen“ bedürfen gewöhnliche Sterbliche einer Lehre zur Vermessung der Welt und einer Institution, die dieses Wissen verwaltet. Giorgio Vasari, Architekt, Maler und in seinen „Viten“ früher Vertreter einer Kunstgeschichtsschreibung, initiiert die Accademia del Disegno. Sie gibt der Kunst ein theoriegeleitetes Verständnis und Wirkungsmacht im entstehenden absolutistischen Staatswesen.
Die Erforschung des Sichtbaren gewinnt das Potenzial eigenständiger geistiger Schöpfung in den Disziplinen Malerei, Skulptur und Architektur. Vasari ist zugleich verantwortlich für das städtebauliche Programm seines Fürsten Cosimo I. Neu ist der Effizienzgedanke. Künstler der Akademie würden, so Vasari, das Niveau der Meister der Hochrenaissance kaum erreichen, sie in der Quantität ihrer Produktion aber mehrfach übertreffen.
Das monarchische Prinzip
Die Pariser Akademie treibt ein knappes Jahrhundert später die Rationalisierung des Kunstbegriffs und die Verklammerung mit den Interessen des merkantilistischen Staatswesens auf die Spitze. Sie etabliert Wettbewerbe, mit ihren conférences ein diskursives Format und erste Formen von Kunstkritik. Unter den Auspizien des Königs soll die Autonomie des Künstlers das monarchische Prinzip verkörpern.
Die neue Anbindung an den Staat verleiht Unabhängigkeit von einstiger Willkür feudaler und kirchlicher Auftraggeber wie von einem über den Markt vermittelten Geschmack. Später, Ende des 18. Jahrhunderts, war die Wiener Akademie eine Art Kunstbehörde vom Zeichenunterricht bis zum Bauwesen.
Wer Kunst konsekriert, darüber wird von nun an gestritten. Im Aufwind bürgerlicher Emanzipation spotten die Karikaturen William Hogarths der Vorliebe des englischen Adels für dunkel gefirnisste Glattmalerei kontinentaler Vorbilder. Der Einschnitt der Französischen Revolution mit der zeitweiligen Abschaffung der Pariser Akademie bleibt nur eine kurze Episode. Nachhaltiger auf den Lehrbetrieb wirken die antiakademischen Tendenzen der Romantik.
Individuelle Selbsterkundung
Mit der Rückkehr der Nazarener und anderer, die sich zuvor mit großer Geste absentiert hatten, etabliert sich in Gestalt der Meisterklasse institutionelle Hierarchie in einer neuen personalisierten Form. Für den Akademiegegner Gustave Courbet ist die Meister-Schüler-Beziehung später ein Selbstwiderspruch. Künstlerische Entwicklung ist ihm nur als individuelle Selbsterkundung denkbar.
Der Avantgarde als Kunst gelingt immer nur die temporäre Unterbrechung des Betriebs. Als Bewegung gegen die Institution Kunst bekämpft sie zur Überwindung der Trennung von Kunst und Lebenspraxis gerade jene Autonomie, deren symbolisches Mehr sie für den Fortschritt in die Waagschale wirft. Der Begriff wird mehrdeutig, unter seiner Dachmarke formieren sich ästhetische, kunstbetriebliche und politische Geltungsansprüche, die keineswegs gleichsinnig voranschreiten.
Gegenpositionen gehen aus der Akademie selbst hervor, neue Bewegungen breiten erfolgreich ihre Curricula aus. Im Katalog zur Ausstellung verfolgt Sabeth Buchmann die Wirkung der Reformpädagogik des Bauhauses, die den Fokus vom Werk auf die Selbstreflexion im Schaffensprozess lenkt, bis hinein in die Sprachspiele gegenwärtiger konzeptueller Kunst.
Der „Düsseldorfer Akademie-Krach“
In seinem Text über den „Düsseldorfer Akademie-Krach“ in den 1960er Jahren verweist Hans-Jürgen Hafner darauf, dass der Protest von Studierenden nicht überkommenem Akademismus galt, sondern exponierte Vertreter der Moderne traf. Einige Aktivisten kehren im Rückgriff auf eine neue figurative Malerei an die Akademie zurück, etwa Jörg Immendorff als Professor.
Das Konzentrat einer Akademiegeschichte hinterlässt der Gegenwart Fragen nach dem stillen Rückzug des Staates. Das Interesse an Repräsentation durch Kunst gehört weitgehend der Vergangenheit an, ebenso eine gesellschaftspolitische Reformagenda, in deren Windschatten das Feld lange Zeit expandierte.
Die neue Indifferenz untergräbt als Effizienzgebot für einen schlanken Staat langfristig auch die Finanzierungsgrundlage der Akademien. Welche Argumente können ihre partiell dem Primat der Ökonomie enthobene Praxis dagegen noch behaupten?
Entfesselte, globalisierte Märkte stellen das Spekulationsobjekt Kunst ununterscheidbar neben andere Luxusgüter. Löst am Ende der Geschichte der Avantgarde das Kapital unverhofft deren Forderung ein, die Trennung von Kunst und Lebenspraxis zu überwinden? Die Frage, wer Kunst konsekriert, wird neu gestellt. Funktionen und Institutionen des traditionellen Betriebs – Kritik, Museum, Akademie – werden damit nicht obsolet, sie drohen zum Dekor im Dienst der Verwertung zu werden.

Abkommen mit den USA: Grönland gibt grünes Licht
Das grönländische Parlament hat für das Sicherheitsabkommen mit den USA gestimmt. Wenn Dänemark zustimmt, kann die Vereinbarung in Kraft treten.
dpa | Das grönländische Parlament hat grünes Licht für ein neues Sicherheits- und Verteidigungsabkommen mit den USA gegeben. Bei einer Abstimmung am Dienstag stimmte der Nachrichtenagentur Ritzau zufolge eine Mehrheit für die Vereinbarung, die US-Präsident Donald Trump, die dänische Ministerpräsidentin Mette Frederiksen und der grönländische Regierungschef Jens-Frederik Nielsen im September am Rande der UN-Generalversammlung in New York unterzeichnet hatten. Demnach sprachen sich 16 Abgeordnete für das Abkommen aus, sieben enthielten sich. Gegenstimmen gab es nicht.
Nun steht noch die Zustimmung des dänischen Parlaments aus. In Kopenhagen ist ein Votum für den 19. November angesetzt. Wenn die USA auf diplomatischem Weg über die Ergebnisse der beiden Abstimmungen informiert sind, kann das Abkommen endgültig in Kraft treten.
Was steht in dem Abkommen?
Die Vereinbarung modernisiert und ergänzt ein bereits seit 1951 existierendes Verteidigungs-Abkommen Dänemarks mit den USA. Sie setzt einen mindestens vorläufigen Schlussstrich unter den Konflikt um die Arktisinsel, den der US-Präsident angezettelt hatte. Trump hatte in der Vergangenheit mehrfach mit der Annexion Grönlands gedroht und sein Vorgehen mit Sicherheitsinteressen begründet. Nach der Unterzeichnung der Vereinbarung hatten sich alle drei Parteien als Sieger gefeiert. Aus dänischer und grönländischer Sicht sind die Zugeständnisse ein geringer Preis. Die Souveränität wird nicht angetastet.
Durch das Abkommen aus dem Jahr 1951 haben die USA ohnehin schon recht großen militärischen Spielraum auf der Arktisinsel. Aktuell unterhält das US-Militär dort aber nur noch eine Militärbasis, die für Raketenabwehr und Radarüberwachung wichtige Pituffik Space Base im Nordwesten Grönlands. Der Deal erlaubt den Amerikanern, diese zu modernisieren und ihre Aktivitäten dort zu erweitern. Außerdem sollen die USA zunächst zwei weitere Verteidigungsstandorte aufbauen dürfen.
Was hat Trump davon?
Zudem räumen Dänemark und Grönland den US-Streitkräften große Bewegungsfreiheit auf der und um die Arktisinsel ein. Dagegen soll kein Nicht-Nato-Staat ohne die Genehmigung der drei Parteien Militäranlagen in Grönland errichten dürfen. Auch bei Investitionen begrenzt der Deal den Einfluss von Staaten – oder Investoren aus Staaten -, die weder Nato-Mitglieder oder -Partner noch EU-Mitglieder sind. Das kommt Trumps Wunsch entgegen, Chinas und Russlands Einfluss in der Region einzuschränken.

https://taz.de/Buecher-ueber-Drogen-und-.title: Neue Bücher über Drogen und Verbote: Dem Irrsinn nahe
https://taz.de/Buecher-ueber-Drogen-und-.author: Ambros Waibel
https://taz.de/Buecher-ueber-Drogen-und-.text:
Neue Bücher über Drogen und Verbote: Dem Irrsinn nahe
Drogen sind überall, nicht zuletzt an der Supermarktkasse. Der Soziologe Robert Feustel schreibt in seinem Buch aufrüttelnd über Rausch und Angst.
Was ist das Hauptproblem des Mannes, der schlafend, bewusstlos oder tot vor mir auf dem eiskalten Pflaster liegt? Wenn wir der herrschenden Erzählung folgen, dann ist es nicht seine Obdachlosigkeit, nicht seine Armut, Krankheit, Verwahrlosung und existenzielle Verlassenheit. Es ist seine – hier unterstellte – Drogenabhängigkeit.
So würde ich die zentrale These von Robert Feustels Buch „Der verbotene Rausch: Wie Drogen zum Problem wurden“ zusammenfassen, das der Autor selbst kein Pamphlet, aber durchaus eine „Streitschrift“ nennen möchte.
Man könnte auch sagen: Das Ganze der Erzählung über Drogen ist das Unwahre – zumindest, wenn wir auf die Prohibition, auf die Illegalisierung bestimmter und den völlig selbstverständlich legalen Gebrauch anderer Drogen Bezug nehmen.
Verbote erzeugen Probleme
Disqualifizieren würde sich jedenfalls, wer dem in Leipzig als Sozialwissenschaftler und Autor lebenden Feustel unterstellte, er verkenne oder verharmlose Drogen. Das tut er nicht: Nicht im Buch, nicht im Gespräch in einem Leipziger Backshop und schon gar nicht in seinem anschließenden Vortrag „Die Erfindung des Drogenproblems“, den er vergangenen Mittwoch im Rahmen des Studiums universale zum Thema „Regeln & Brüche“ vor gut 60 sehr gut unterhaltenen und am Ende kluge Fragen stellenden Zuhörenden an der Uni Leipzig hielt.
Aber fangen wir mit dem an, was unumstritten ist: „Gerade die repressive Verbotspolitik stellt systematisch jene Probleme erst her, die dann von unterschiedlichen Institutionen gelöst werden sollen“, schreibt eben nicht nur Feustel.
„Der verbotene Rausch“ und „Katerland“
Robert Feustel: Der verbotene Rausch: Wie Drogen zum Problem wurden, Kohlhammer 2026, 22 €.
Georg Schumerus: Katerland: Wie wir den Alkohol feiern, aber Menschen mit Abhängigkeit ausgrenzen und wirksame Alkoholpolitik verschlafen, Beltz 2026, 22 €
Pragmatisch gesagt: Der von angekokelter Alufolie umgebene, leidende Mensch vor meiner Haustür hätte schlicht ein existenzielles Problem weniger, wenn er sich die Substanz, die er konsumieren möchte – großes Fragezeichen, klar – auf legalem Weg besorgen könnte.
Und die globale Gesellschaft könnte Billiarden in Armuts- und Suchtbekämpfung stecken, die heute ein Polizei- und Justizapparat sich angeeignet hat, dessen Arbeitsresultate nicht einfach fragwürdig sind, sondern absurd: Illegalisierte Drogen, die so aufwändig bekämpft werden, sind erstens überall und werden zweitens immer billiger.
Reale Verfallsgeschichten
Was auch einen technologischen Grund hat: „Auf dem großen Marktplatz der Drogen bestimmt inzwischen die Chemie das Geschehen“, hat ein italienischer Experte dieses Phänomen in der taz benannt.
Dieser totale Krieg gegen die Drogen hat aber neben seiner totalen Wirkungslosigkeit einen, wie Feustel es nennt, „mythologischen Raum“ geschaffen, dem mit Argumenten schwer beizukommen ist. Man spürt das nicht zuletzt an den eigenen Widerständen, an den Mythen, aber eben auch an den erlebten und erzählten Verfallsgeschichten der Drogenbiografien im unmittelbaren Umfeld.
Feustel geht es dem folgend nicht zuletzt um „Drogenwissen“. Er schreibt: „Das in weiten Teilen irreführende und zugleich wirkmächtige Drogenwissen steht größtenteils stabil wie ein Boxer mit ausgeprägten Nehmerqualitäten. Hier und da hat er ein paar Kratzer, mehr nicht. Wenn ich etwa in Debatten erwähne, dass die Unterscheidung von ‚harten‘ und ‚weichen‘ Drogen irreführend ist, schlägt mir im Regelfall Irritation und souverän ablehnendes Kopfschütteln entgegen.“
Lesung "Gegen Abend kein Speed"
Multimediale Lesung von Robert Feustel und Nancy Grochol aus "Der verbotene Rausch"
am 6.11. in Dresden, kosmotique, 19.30 Uhr
am 20. 11. in Leipzig, "Ilses Erika", 20.00 Uhr
„Dasselbe gilt, wenn es darum geht, dass auch Heroin erst nach längerem Konsum körperlich abhängig macht und der Entzug weniger problematisch ist als bei Alkohol. Wer es also wagt, die Selbstverständlichkeiten des Drogen- und Suchtwissens anzuzweifeln (ohne Risiken und problematische Konsummuster zu leugnen), könnte entweder selbst high oder dem Irrsinn gefährlich nahe sein. Das Unwissen über das, was als Droge umschrieben wird, sitzt ähnlich tief wie die Angst davor.“
Nun ist Angst nichts grundsätzlich Schlechtes, zumindest dann nicht, wenn sie realitätsbezogen ist. Es ist gut, Angst zu haben, wenn ich eine Substanz zum Konsum angeboten bekomme, deren Zusammensetzung und Wirkung ich nicht einschätzen kann. Etwas ganz anderes ist die von der Gesellschaft projizierte Angst vor dem Rausch.
Die häufigste Behinderung
Feustel schreibt, der unterstellte „Motor der Sucht“ sei „der Wiederholungszwang, den der mindestens latent irre Rausch auslöst“. Das dahinter stehende Menschenbild ist eines des Verdachts: Wenn die Mittel zum Rausch zur Verfügung stehen, dann ballern wir uns nicht nur umgehend gnadenlos zu, sondern können auch gar nicht anders, als jede Gelegenheit zu ergreifen, uns wieder zu bedröhnen, was dann letztlich das organisierte Zusammenleben zerstört.
Diese Geschichte erzählen wir uns, während die Realität, wie sie der Direktor der Klinik für Psychiatrie und Psychotherapie am Uniklinikum Leipzig, Georg Schumerus, in seinem ebenfalls aktuellen Buchs „Katerland“, beschreibt, so aussieht: „FASD ist in Deutschland die häufigste angeborene Behinderung“, also die Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder.
„Es werden Kinder geboren, die ihr Leben lang darunter leiden, dass sie in der Schwangerschaft Alkohol ausgesetzt waren“, einer überall verfügbaren und beworbenen Droge, die steuerlich gepampert wird – die Biersteuer wurde zuletzt 1993 erhöht, von 8 Cent pro Liter auf 9 Cent, eine super großzügig inflationsunabhängige Besteuerung. Übrigens: Wird Bier teurer, bleibt die Steuer trotzdem gleich.
Trotz dieser staatlichen Drogenverordnung ist das Land aber noch nicht abgesoffen. Zu jeder durch Alkohol verursachten Elendsgeschichte gehört die Vorstellung, wie elend alles wäre, wenn Alkohol illegalisiert würde; und natürlich, wie viel besser man die Volksdroge Alkohol regulieren könnte. Und zu jeder Elendsgeschichte illegalisierter Drogen gehört die Vorstellung, wie viel Leid gemindert oder vermieden werden könnte, wenn wir aufhören, Menschen in die Unterwelt zu verbannen und zu quälen.
Robert Feustel öffnet mit seinem populär, und nicht ohne seine Thesen einhämmernde Wiederholungsschleifen, geschriebenen Buch eine Tür, durch die wir als selbstbewusste und mitfühlende Gesellschaft hindurchgehen müssen. Um uns endlich den zentralen Problemen widmen zu können: Obdachlosigkeit, Armut, Krankheit.

Paris, Toulouse, Lille, Marseille, Lyon en passant par Rouen ou Montpellier, l’intersyndicale a décidé de passer outre les interdictions de cortège dans les centres-villes ce jeudi 5 novembre par les préfets. « l’Humanité » fait le point.
À quelques heures de la journée de grève et de mobilisation nationale du jeudi 5 novembre à l’appel de la CFDT, la CGT, FO, UNSA, FSU. L’intersyndicale appelle le gouvernement et les préfectures à respecter le droit de manifester devant les interdictions qui se multiplient et les cortèges seulement autorisés à défiler loin des centres-villes dans plus d’une vingtaine de départements.
La secrétaire générale de la CGT, Sophie Binet, déplore « un moment extrêmement grave avec une dérive autoritaire très dangereuse du gouvernement ». De Marseille à Paris, en passant par Toulouse, Le Havre ou Annecy, l’Humanité fait le point sur les autorisations des préfectures ville par ville.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: PL oficializa candidatura de Rogério Marinho à presidência do Senado para destravar anistia a golpistas
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Redação
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
O PL oficializou nesta quarta-feira (4) a candidatura do senador Rogério Marinho (PL-RN) à presidência do Senado para o biênio que começa em 2027. Em reunião com cerca de 30 senadores em Brasília, o líder da oposição evidenciou que a principal motivação da disputa é abrir caminho para o projeto de anistia aos condenados pela tentativa de golpe de Estado, entre eles o ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro, condenado pelo Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) em setembro de 2025.
“O Congresso Nacional vai nos dar condição de destravar a pauta e vamos permitir que o projeto da anistia seja apreciado”, afirmou Marinho durante o encontro.
O senador vai enfrentar o atual presidente da Casa, Davi Alcolumbre (União-AP), que tenta a recondução. Alcolumbre já declarou que a anistia a golpistas não é assunto de interesse dos brasileiros e chegou a articular um texto alternativo, restrito à redução de penas e sem alcançar Bolsonaro.
Voto aberto e recado ao STF
Na entrevista coletiva após o lançamento, Marinho defendeu mudar as regras da eleição para a Mesa Diretora, hoje feita por voto secreto. Segundo ele, a votação aberta permitiria ao eleitor acompanhar a posição de cada senador e evitaria o que chamou de estelionato eleitoral. “Voto aberto é extremamente recomendável e necessário, mas vamos avaliar de que forma podemos fazer”, ponderou.
Enquanto a regra não muda, aliados do senador discutem uma estratégia para que parlamentares de direita anunciem publicamente em quem vão votar.
Marinho também tentou desvincular a candidatura da ofensiva bolsonarista contra ministros do STF, embora tenha deixado a porta aberta para pedidos de impeachment. “Evidente que não seremos candidatos com o tema de impeachment de quem quer que seja. Somos candidatos defendendo a Constituição. Se algum ministro do STF cometer crime de responsabilidade, não seremos omissos, mas não vamos antecipar ou fazer juízo de valor”, declarou.
Revanche de 2023
Não é a primeira vez que Marinho tenta comandar o Senado. Em 2023, a pedido de Bolsonaro, ele concorreu contra Rodrigo Pacheco (PSD-MG) e perdeu, com 32 votos. Ao relembrar a derrota, o senador reclamou de ter sido excluído, junto com a bancada do PL, da distribuição de postos nas comissões. “Os vencedores não fizeram gestos, não nos permitiram participar das comissões. Se ganharmos, vamos tratar de forma diferente. Vamos respeitar a democracia e a dissidência”, prometeu.
Durante o evento, Marinho homenageou Flávio Bolsonaro (PL-RJ), de quem coordenou a campanha presidencial. Derrotado por Lula no segundo turno, Flávio não reconheceu o resultado e deixou o Brasil rumo aos Estados Unidos.
O lançamento reuniu também nomes de fora do PL, como o senador Hamilton Mourão (Republicanos-RS) e os senadores eleitos Guilherme Derrite (PP-SP) e Deltan Dallagnol (Novo-PR). O Novo, que terá três senadores, anunciou apoio formal à candidatura. Já o PL terá a maior bancada da Casa a partir do ano que vem, com 28 parlamentares, mas ainda está longe dos 41 votos necessários para vencer entre os 81 senadores. Marinho, no entanto, diz já contar com mais de 40 apoios.
Direita dividida
O principal obstáculo do senador está no próprio campo. A senadora Tereza Cristina (PP-MS), ex-ministra da Agricultura de Bolsonaro, mantém candidatura própria e aposta no trânsito com o Centrão para se viabilizar. Na avaliação da oposição, duas candidaturas de direita favorecem Alcolumbre.
Marinho afirmou que conversou com a senadora na manhã desta quarta e que os dois devem buscar um nome único mais adiante. “A Tereza tem toda a legitimidade para ser candidata. Conversamos pela manhã. Ela naturalmente vai tentar viabilizar sua candidatura e, em momento oportuno, vamos convergir”, disse.
O líder do PL no Senado, Carlos Portinho (RJ), saiu em defesa da ex-ministra diante de ataques vindos da própria direita. “Queria lamentar alguns posicionamentos da direita sobre a Tereza Cristina. Ela sempre esteve em todas as nossas reuniões com Rogério Marinho. É nossa aliada”, criticou.
Alcolumbre, por sua vez, já reúne o apoio das direções de União Brasil e PP, que formam uma federação, além de MDB, PSD e PT.
