https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.title: Lions’ Jack Campbell making progress on movement in upper body after injury during game
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.author: Guardian sport
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text:
Detroit Lions linebacker Jack Campbell says he has regained some movement in his body after sustaining a serious neck injury during his team’s win over the Minnesota Vikings on Sunday.
The 26-year-old was treated for nine minutes on the field after making a tackle during Sunday’s game. Players from both teams were visibly distraught as Campbell received medical attention before he was taken for further treatment at a hospital in the Detroit area.
In a statement on Wednesday, Campbell said he is making progress in his recovery. “I’m incredibly encouraged by the progress I’ve made in such a short period of time. I have full movement in my lower body, and I’m continuing to make progress with movement in my upper body,” Campbell, who remains hospitalized, said in the statement. “I know there’s still work ahead, but I remain very optimistic. I’m taking things one day at a time, staying positive, and focusing on getting better.”
On Monday, Lions coach Dan Campbell paid tribute to the former first-round pick’s contributions to the team.
“I don’t even know if I can put it into words. You get voted captain, that says a ton, especially with this group of guys. He earned every bit of that. He’s trustworthy. He’s dependable. He’d give you the shirt off his back,” said Dan Campbell. “He’s just all heart, all effort. And just an unbelievable person. Down to earth. Very genuine. There’s not a man on this team that doesn’t respect Jack Campbell and care about him.”
Campbell was named an All-Pro last season and is in his fourth year in the league. In May, he signed a four-year contract extension with the Lions worth $81m.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Get ready habibis, Abdul El-Sayed’s ‘shawarma law’ is coming to the US | Arwa Mahdawi
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Arwa Mahdawi
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Repeat after me: yallah. YAH-luh. This versatile Arabic word means everything from “hurry up”, to “come on” to “speak to you later”. If you add a “bye” at the end, the meaning shifts to “please shut up, fool” or “speak soon friend,” depending on your intonation.
Next up: wallah. wa-LAH. Again, the definition changes depending on context and cadence. It can mean everything from “no way!” to “I swear to God.”
What exactly am I doing here? Helping to prepare you for the Arab and Muslim takeover of the US, of course. Now that Abdul El-Sayed, the son of Egyptian immigrants, is going to become the first Muslim senator in the US, it’s only a matter of time before everyone is going to say “yallah bye” to western civilization.
“I hope everyone is learning Arabic,” Laura Loomer, the informal Trump adviser and rightwing personality announced on X Tuesday night. Don’t worry, habibti, if people won’t learn by themselves, we’ll send them to re-education camps. And after that, we’re going to make good on El-Sayed’s threat to implement “shawarma law”.
Forgive me, I know El-Sayed’s victory over Mike Rogers in Michigan has been extremely difficult for Islamophobes and anti-Arab racists to come to terms with, particularly since it comes hot on the heels of Zohran Mamdani’s Muslim takeover of New York. So I would like to send everyone mourning the midterms my thoughts and sharia prayers.
Poor old Loomer, in particular, seems in need of prayers at this time; she is having a very public crisis of faith. “If God is in charge, why did he let our country get taken over by Muslims and communists?” she tweeted on Tuesday night. She then fired off almost 100 other X posts lamenting the “Islamic communist takeover” of the US and calling for a “full Muslim ban”.
Loomer is a professional racist and self-described “proud Islamophobe”, so it’s not surprising that she’s short-circuiting over a highly accomplished brown man getting elected to the Senate. But it’s worth stressing that plenty of more “respectable” people have been foaming at the mouth about El-Sayed and the handful of other Arabs and Muslims who were elected in the midterms. This morning, CNN asked the newly victorious Texas Democrat James Talarico if he was prepared to stand up to El-Sayed, stating “there are a lot of things he believes in that you might not share”. Last week, David Frum, a senior editor at the Atlantic, urged Democratic leadership to “curb the ugliest instincts of a Senator el-Sayed”. On Monday, James Kirchick, a former contributing writer to the Atlantic, called El-Sayed an “Islamist”.
You know what I think all these El-Sayed haters are struggling so much with? The fact that Michigan’s incoming senator, who had to deal with a torrent of vile racism throughout his campaign, including from his own party, didn’t water down his identity or his beliefs in order to get elected. He didn’t try to whiten his name or make himself seem less Arab or Muslim. He didn’t bow to demands that he condemn extremists who have nothing to do with him, or lean into a “politics of appeal”. He won by being himself. And in his victory speech he made sure to inform his detractors that he was going to continue being himself.
“My name is Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed,” the progressive Democrat said, before going on to poke fun at Republicans in a victory speech peppered with Arabic words. “Up until right about now, you might have noticed I always say “inshallah”, or “God willing”, whenever the outcome of this race was mentioned. But today, tonight, we can turn that inshallah into alhamdulillah. For the rightwing ops, that just means “praise be to God,” OK?”
El-Sayed continued his Arabic lesson with a jab at the vice-president. “JD, habibi, there is this delicious irony in the fact that you’re constitutionally obligated to swear me in in January.” (Habibi means “my love” and habibti is the feminine form of the word.)
In a country as diverse as the US it shouldn’t be a big deal to hear an Arab-American politician use Arabic in a political speech. But after decades of dehumanisation – dehumanisation so ingrained that New York Times columnists can casually compare Arabs to bugs and a congressman can compare Muslims to dogs – those few words of Arabic felt incredibly powerful.
Also powerful: the fact Michigan’s newest senator used his speech to call out the genocide in Gaza and the abuse directed at everyone who cares about it. “See, they try to call you hateful if you believe that Palestinian kids should get to grow up in the land of their forefathers without being murdered by our tax dollars,” El-Sayed said. “Michiganders, we want our taxes spent here, for schools here, and healthcare here, and infrastructure here. We don’t want our money sent to do apartheid or genocide or war.”
Not so many years ago, a speech like this by a newly elected senator called Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed would have been unthinkable. Strategists and pollsters would have said it was political suicide to support Palestinians, use Arabic in your speeches, and campaign as a proud Arab American.
But while anti-Arab racism and Islamophobia is still pervasive, things are slowly changing. Attitudes towards Israel have dramatically shifted, thanks to the genocidal war on Gaza. Meanwhile, Arabic words and Arab culture have slowly been infiltrating US culture. Drake named one of his 2026 albums Habibti. New York magazine had a cover piece about the Swana (south-west Asia and north Africa) scene in the city called Habibi city. The Palestinian comic Mo Amer has a show on Netflix. US rapper Macklemore just wrapped up a Free Palestine tour.
The right is still doing everything it can to try to paint El-Sayed as scary and divisive. “Abdul El-Sayed used victory speech to taunt ‘enemies’ rather than heal divisions after ugly campaign,” a New York Post headline blared, for example. But it is not divisive to refuse to pander to racists; to refuse to try to prove your worth to people who fundamentally see you as worthless. El-Sayed has realized that what the establishment likes to call “civility” is really just servility. He refused to play by the old rules and, alhamdulillah, he has won. The right may have their pitchforks out, but shawarma law is coming.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Will the Progressive Insurgency in NY-17 Oust MAGA Loyalist Mike Lawler?
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Joan Walsh
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Local progressive groups have turned out a huge ground game to support Democratic nominee Cait Conley, despite her centrist leanings.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries with Cait Conley, Democratic candidate for NY-17, during an early voting rally on the first day of early voting for the midterm election in Peekskill, New York, on October 24, 2026.

“When you take on Mike Lawler, you take on organized labor,” Teamsters president Sean O’Brien told New York 17th Congressional District voters at a rally for Lawler in Westchester County last week. It was a false, even brazen claim: The state AFL-CIO backs the Republican Lawler’s Democratic challenger, Caitlin Conley. So do the Communications Workers of America, SEIU1199, local teachers’ unions, and many other labor groups who are, as usual, supporting the Democrat in the race.

That didn’t stop O’Brien. And he wasn’t chastened by the fact that Conley would be the first female special operations veteran from New York in the House of Representatives when he told her, condescendingly, it’s time “to put your helmet on and button your chin straps, it’s a full contact sport.”

Here’s the thing: Conley would seem to sleep with her helmet on. Given the reservations I’ve heard about her from progressive voters over the last year, the main one is that she can be reserved, not at all warm or fuzzy, and is by progressive standards a little bit hawkish. She comes off as the Army veteran she is. But in the district, no one doubts Conley’s bravery or readiness for battle. Conley snickers at the Teamster leader’s braggadocio in a phone call with me a few days later. “I love how people who never left the comfort of their couch after 9/11 want to talk about hard fights.” She regularly talks about how she vowed as a teenager to join the military after the 2001 attacks.

Lawler is a MAGA loyalist who has on occasion broken with the president. But in a district that voted for Kamala Harris two years ago, that may no longer be a winning record. So he plays up his differences with Trump, and his support from Democrats and union members, and he hopes he can get by Conley that way.

He may not. Conley beat two popular, progressive female rivals in the June primary, and some of those women’s supporters are still a little bitter over what they perceive as establishment Democrats’ behind-the-scenes support for the military veteran, who had no local political record, over two local politicos, Rockland County legislator Beth Davidson and Tarrytown Village Trustee Effie Phillips-Staley, who have served their communities legislatively for years. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries didn’t prove to be the biggest draw when he appeared in Peekskill with Conley October 24. A crowd of maybe 200 people, many of them union members, milled about along the Hudson River and applauded, especially when Conley introduced him as “Speaker Jeffries” (his fervent wish). But elsewhere that day, Peekskill was teeming with activism, as the many local groups who’ve emerged in the district used the next-to-last election-season weekend to gather, train volunteers and canvas.

The paradox of Conley’s race is that if she wins, the centrist will at least partly owe her victory to a progressive insurgency that came together after Lawler’s 2024 victory vowing to defeat him with a Democrat. Many didn’t get their chosen candidate in the June primary, but they’re still hard at work. As Phillips-Staley herself told me, “What we are all aligned on, from the left to the moderate within the Democratic party, is that Mike Lawler needs to go.”

Most polls show Democrats winning the House, but Conley’s race is important. New York cost Democrats the House in 2022, losing five blue seats, when the party nationwide only came up short by four. This year’s primaries saw a lot of lefty victories in the Manhattan area–three DSA members, plus reliable progressives Brad Lander and Micah Lasher–but they’ll all win next week. Upstate near Conley, centrist liberal incumbents Pat Ryan and Josh Riley look safe. It’s Conley, plus somewhat vulnerable Democratic centrists Tom Suozzi and Laura Gillen on Long Island, and an unlikely Democratic victor in Elise Stefanik’s former seat, Democrat Blake Gendebien, who will make Tuesday night interesting.

NY 17 is a diverse district, with multiracial, fairly Latino Peekskill, Sleepy Hollow, and Tarrytown; still pretty white segments of Rockland, Putnam, and Dutchess Counties, plus miles of Westchester cities and towns, some of which are still 1960s alabaster, but most are not. Roughly 20 percent of the district is Jewish, and Conley’s self-described “balance” on Israel—some consider her to be rabidly pro-Israel—is helping the Democrat with many voters, but not with the energetic pro-Palestine left. “This is where I have been consistent, and as someone who has been to war, the last thing I want to see is more human suffering,” she tells me. “I do believe we have to get to a two-state solution, where there’s equal safety, security, and sovereignty for Israel and Palestine. And that America should be pushing to deliver on that and not just give it lip service.” Although Conley has opposed some Democratic moves to limit sales of weaponry to Israel, she insists that she “will criticize the Netanyahu administration or any administration I believe is doing the wrong thing for Israel and America.”

About half of the district’s voters are either veterans, law enforcement officials, or public employees (Conley’s mother was a postal worker). Conley’s military experience, as well as her family’s public service, resonates with many voters in the area. A white progressive volunteer told me she found that Conley’s military service was a draw to some Latino voters, and Phillips-Staley, whose mother is from El Salvador, said she wasn’t surprised. “My dad was a military veteran, and Latino cultures can sometimes be a little conservative, and that’s fine.”

Conley says her military service is a cross-racial, cross-party draw. “I have shown that I’m willing to do the right thing for this country in our community, even when it’s hard, even when it’s dangerous, I’m willing to put my life on the line, to protect this country and fight for our future. And there is a degree of trust that comes with that,” Conley told me in our interview.

“I’ve had Republicans come up to me and say, ‘I’ve never voted for a Democrat, but I’m voting for you because you’re a veteran.’”

Even though I could find plenty of progressives in the district with reservations about Conley—hey, I write for The Nation—virtually everyone I met united behind her, post-primary. Some believe they are helping her most by focusing on the low-propensity voters, low-income and/or Latino, that the Conley campaign may miss as it focuses on getting registered Democrats back in line, plus adding some independents and Republicans. Other progressives are focused on winning back Democrats who’ve fallen for Lawler’s bipartisan shtick. Another key group of voters to reach will be those who’ve been alienated by the party’s shenanigans in recent congressional races.

A Democratic seat since 1986, New York 17 elected progressive Mondaire Jones in 2020. But redistricting put DCCC head Sean Patrick Maloney, the representative in New York 18, in the newly drawn 17 for 2022, pushing Jones out of the race. Jones wound up moving to and running in New York 10, a lower Manhattan and Brooklyn district, against Working Families Party’s Yuh-Line Niou, and both progressives lost to the self-funding Levi’s family tycoon and liberal lawyer Dan Goldman. Maloney, widely accused of ignoring his own race to raise money for Democrats in Europe that October, lost to Lawler by 1,800 votes. When Jones ran again in NY-17 in 2024, the party was split, Lawler had made inroads with Democrats, and, despite Kamala Harris winning the district at the top of the ticket, Jones lost to Lawler by a depressing 24,000 votes.

After what many in the district call “the Mondaire mess”—and to be fair, Jones didn’t mainly make the mess—local progressives came together in a coalition of roughly 35 groups, known as the CD 17 Community Coalition. “The DCCC had run these last two campaigns and lost,” says its director, Tina Volz-Bongar. CD 17 Community Coalition committed to building a ground game that the DCCC had failed to create. Local progressives, including 20 small Indivisible chapters plus local nonprofits, got organized in 2025 and have been meeting almost weekly since. “People say we live in a purple district, but that’s because Democrats don’t come out to vote,” Volz-Bongar adds. In fact, the district has a one-point Democratic voter registration advantage, and is rated a toss-up by The Cook Political Report. But judging by demographics, it should be bluer than it is. The diverse coalition behind Conley is trying to figure out why it’s not.

So on the same Saturday that Jeffries visited Peekskill, the CD 17 Community Coalition hosted “Free Democracy Donuts and Coffee” events at the city’s public and Section 8 housing complexes. Working Families Party members were out knocking doors. In addition, Canvassing Connectors, a deep-canvassing group based in Peekskill, partnered with Plus One, which focuses on voters linking up with friends and neighbors over meals, for an open house at a local café. Plus One has found it challenging to meet its gathering goals, cofounder Emily Simoness tells me. “But once people actually do the work, they are thrilled, and they’re reminded of our shared humanity, and that we have more in common than the algorithm might tell us,” she says. “I really feel like part of how we get back to being a civil society is by being in person together.”

Canvassing Connectors likewise emphasises longer-term relationships and in-person gatherings. “We’ve been telling people we canvass that ‘we’re gonna have a party,’” Canvassing Connectors cofounder Ellen Chapnick told me, when she invited me to join them at the café. “Well, this is the party!” Food and Water Action sponsored a Stop Data Centers rally just before Jeffries’s waterfront gathering. You couldn’t walk the streets of the small, quaint Peekskill downtown that bright Saturday without spotting someone working to elect Conley.

Conley says she’s grateful for all the help. Despite ideological differences, she didn’t perceive her primary as a bitter one. “We shared a lot more than we differed on. And how we make a positive impact on people’s lives has to be our focus.” True to her brand, Conley added that she wasn’t only focused on Democrats but making a place in her coalition for independents and Republicans. Phillips-Staley, endorsed by the Working Families Party, also said the female candidates made common cause before the primary was over. “We could have been a lot nastier to each other. But for the most part all the candidates got along pretty well. Because we understood—and we said it repeatedly during the primary—that the mission is to defeat Mike Lawler. What we said in many debates and in many forums is that we would all be running against him in the general.” And so they are. The WFP endorsed Conley once she won the primary.

Even this late in the game, the polls are too close to call. The last Emerson College poll had Conley up by two points, within the margin of error. The good news for the Democrat was that Lawler was on target to lose some of the Democratic support he won away from Mondaire Jones in 2024. That year, according to Emerson, 20 percent of Democrats supported Lawler; this year it’s down to 12 percent, while Conley is grabbing 10 percent of Republicans, and Jones just 4 percent “Had Democrats stayed on the side of the Democratic Party, Mike Lawler would not have won,” Phillips-Staley told me. She is nonetheless working hardest on unaligned, low-propensity Latino nonvoters.

Canvassing Connectors is focused on much the same voters as Phillips-Staley, especially Latinos. Ellen Chapnick is proud of “El Equipo,” the group’s Spanish-speaking canvassers, who can quickly turn out to help English speakers work with Spanish speaking voters. “You know, they’re used to having an experience where people knock on their door, ‘Oh, you don’t speak English. I’m so sorry. Well, here’s a Spanish language flyer,’” she told me. “That doesn’t work too well.They don’t feel like they have a voice. But we can have a 10-, 15-minute conversation with them in their own language, and often what happens is they’ll say, ‘Oh, you should talk to my children. You know, you should talk to my sister-in-law.’”

Chapnick was ecstatic when we met in Peekskill that Saturday: She had just met two Republicans who’d decided to vote for Conley. That hadn’t happened to many progressives while out knocking doors, though some told me they felt the campaign dynamics shifting, especially as Donald Trump stayed out on the trail (though not in New York), talking about the physique of Ohio Senator Jon Husted as well as GOP rapper Nicki Minaj while lying about inflation and the Iran War. Speaker Mike Johnson visited Lawler’s district a couple of days after Jeffries did, and insisted local and national polling is wrong.

“It feels like 2024 to us,” Johnson told a press gaggle in Rockland County’s Orangeburg October 26. “The polling is wrong. They are trying to suppress and depress Republican turnout in the elections. The polling has underestimated the Republican vote by an average of 4 percent. Don’t believe the polls. People are not responding to polls anymore in increasing numbers.” But Johnson also praised Lawler for supporting Trump’s One Big Ugly Bill, which gave tax cuts to the wealthy and will lead to Medicaid and SNAP cuts to lower-income and working-class District 17 residents.

Conley may win over some progressives with her pledge to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, an issue on which Jeffries joined her in Peekskill. “Every day Pete Hegseth is in that seat, we are less safe,” she told me.“This man is single-handedly destroying our military institutions and driving out our best military leaders. The man needs to go.” Jeffries, not known for ideological fire and brimstone, told the Peekskill crowd he plans to “run Pete Hegseth out of town” if and when Democrats take the House.

Meanwhile, Phillips-Staley keeps working for Conley. “I see Cait’s role, and the way her campaign is structured, is to try to keep those Democrats [who voted for Lawler in 2024] in line with the Democratic Party, to try to retain them, to deny him victory.”

But she adds, “Unfortunately, that kind of message doesn’t work with a progressive base, but what does work is the truth that Mike Lawler is catastrophic for our democracy, right? We keep hammering home to remind people that harm reduction is real, and we have to deny him power. Not only do I want to see Mike Lawler go, I want to see communities that have been disenfranchised by the Democratic Party, standing up, using their power and firing Mike Lawler. That’s why I’m in it.”

Joan Walsh, a national affairs correspondent for The Nation, is a coproducer of The Sit-In: Harry Belafonte Hosts The Tonight Show and the author of What’s the Matter With White People? Finding Our Way in the Next America. Her most recent book (with Nick Hanauer and Donald Cohen) is Corporate Bullsh*t: Exposing the Lies and Half-Truths That Protect Profit, Power and Wealth In America.

https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.title: How the Serbian Student Movement Is a Victory for Organizing Power
https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.author: Ivana Nikolić Hughes
https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.text:
In Serbia, the students may have discovered a formula for rescuing democracy through nonviolence and commitment to collectivism. Students everywhere should take note.

When I first came to the United States, as a foreign exchange student from former Yugoslavia in 1994, I didn’t come only because I dreamed of studying science at some of the world’s best universities. To my 17-year-old self, being in the US meant arriving in the birthplace of democracy, a place where human rights and individual freedoms were sacrosanct. At the time, the country I had grown up in was not just falling apart but doing so violently. Combined with the earlier repressive decades of Tito’s Communist government, however gentler they may have been relative to what went on in the Soviet bloc, made coming to America about more than a hope of a better education or personal life.

The irony was not lost on me when I learned that the Serbian student movement, which had challenged the rule of Aleksandar Vučić, a strongman who ruled the country for 14 years, won a parliamentary snap election outright. Standing on the corner of Broadway and 72nd Street in New York City and reading the news with tears in my eyes, I absorbed that democracy had won in my homeland, just as my adopted country is struggling to hold on to its own hard-won democratic experiment, 250 years in the making. But perhaps the Serbian example, novel in a number of ways, can give hope not only to the people of Serbia, who have collectively suffered long enough, but to all who have watched in fear as democratic standards and ideals erode across the globe.

The first time Serbia had multiparty elections in December of 1990, still as part of the Federal Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia, my mother took me along to the polling station at my school, just across the street from our apartment building. Inside the voting booth, she handed me the pen (I was 14!), knowing how much I cared about the historic turn towards democracy.

That election was a huge leap for democracy in Serbia, although one that followed the playbook of existing democracies. What the Serbian student movement has just accomplished is arguably more significant. Students began protesting in November of 2024, following a tragic accident in Novi Sad, the second-largest city in the country, where the awning of a newly renovated train station collapsed, killing 14 people instantly and injuring three more, two of whom died in the coming weeks and months. The protesters saw the disaster as a symbol of overwhelming corruption at multiple levels, both in the way in which funds for infrastructure projects had been distributed, and in how accountability for the tragedy was sought. Their demands for justice and responsibility quickly turned into an indictment of Vučić’s one-man rule.

What happened over the next two years was extraordinary. Students set up blockades of universities across the country, which eventually led to the suspension of the entire educational system, including K-12, for many months. Peaceful protests took place in Belgrade and across the country, with students frequently walking tens and even hundreds of kilometers from different towns to attend such protests. Once they reached a city, they would be welcomed with open arms by citizens of all stripes. Videos and images of these arrivals were powerful not the least because they were reminiscent of the spirit of “liberation,” that came with the partisan army kicking the German occupying forces out of Serbian towns in the fall of 1944.

Three essential features of the student movement emerged over time. Although this was at times very challenging, the students kept the protests peaceful. Nonviolence was essential to garnering and maintaining the support of the population, which began backing the students in larger and larger numbers. Secondly, the movement from the very beginning had no leaders, among the students themselves or the existing opposition politicians. They understood that in an authoritarian system, individuals were uniquely vulnerable to intimidation, legal action, and personal attacks. By maintaining a level of anonymity for those calling the shots, as well as truly running a grassroots movement, the students ensured continuity of their efforts. Finally, when it came time to form the parliamentary list of 250 candidates, they didn’t nominate themselves or existing opposition politicians but rather people from all walks of life, including professors, engineers, journalists, economists, and even a former NBA basketball player, Dejan Bodiroga. The number of candidates on the student parliamentary list with a PhD is a staggering 160 out of the total 250. The candidates were selected through student assemblies (known as plenums), followed by broad consultations and collective decision-making.

Contrary to what some Western media outlets and politicians are saying, the student movement and the government it has selected are not choosing sides in the geopolitical sphere. Their platform clearly states that the new government will not issue sanctions on Russia (which wouldn’t impact anyone but Serbia itself), putting the questions of joining the European Union (EU) in the background, in the great tradition of Yugoslavia’s role in founding the Non-Aligned Movement. In fact, the party that explicitly called for aligning with the EU and NATO won just 3 percent of the vote. Significantly, the new government is also committing to banning all arms exports to nations in military conflicts, including Israel, Russia, and Ukraine. Such an anti-war stance is much needed in today’s conflict-mired world.

Student movements should be seen as the purest expression of our democratic ideals. One should not have to agree with whatever students may be protesting for to think that young people coming together to pursue something bigger than themselves ought to be viewed as positive. The future after all, is theirs.

In Serbia, the students may have discovered a formula not only for finding their own voice but for rescuing democracy through nonviolence, persistence, and commitment to collectivism. Students everywhere should take note.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: How the Midterms Will Test Our Desire for  Real Accountability
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: David Faris
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Sure, a Democratic win next Tuesday would be a relief—but we still need to repudiate all facets of MAGA authoritarianism.

Prresident Donald Trump addresses a midterms rally in Mobile, Alabama.

By now there’s little left to say about what might happen in Tuesday’s midterm elections. Democrats seem all but assured of taking the House of Representatives according to experts, but the outcome in the Senate could be anything from a modest Democratic gain of two or three seats to a heretofore unimaginable wave that leaves Democrats with 55 or 56 seats. This latter scenario would include wins in places like Kansas and South Carolina that weren’t even on the radar a few months ago.

Without diminishing the obvious importance of Democrats’ reclaiming control of Congress, the stakes of Tuesday’s elections are as much existential as they are practical. Substantive Democratic gains in reliably Republican states and districts would serve as confirmation that the breathtaking, two-year display of self-dealing, cruelty, and ineptitude we have just lived through carries a penalty larger than the standard thermostatic midterm backlash. If it doesn’t, Republicans will rightfully conclude that they can get away with just about anything, as long as their next president doesn’t start a stupid war.

After all, it’s not particularly earth-shattering that swing states like North Carolina would go blue this year. Wins there and in Maine, together with holds in purple states like Georgia and Michigan, wouldn’t suggest by themselves that a tectonic political shift is under way. They’re closer to the outcomes you’d expect in a normal, pre-Trump midterm election, when voter sentiment shifts against the party in power enough to give the out party the advantage in many competitive districts and states.

It is the Senate contests in more sharply Republican-leaning states like Ohio, Iowa, Texas, and Alaska, as well as in House districts that Trump carried by double digits that are the real test of the American electorate’s tolerance for abusive authoritarianism and rank corruption. The outcomes there will serve as a measure of whether negative polarization is a force so strong and resilient that it has warped the ability of voters to make informed judgments and hold their representatives accountable.

In the House, Democrats can build a majority of 232 seats without winning a single seat in a district that Trump carried by 10 or more points in 2024. If you had asked anyone on the left in, say, April 2025 whether they would be happy with a 17-seat gain in the House and a 232–203 majority, they would have replied with an exuberant, justified yes—especially if they knew that Republicans would make the prospect even harder by ordering fresh, Supreme Court–assisted gerrymanders in a series of red states.

But here, as in the Senate, the test of whether America is truly rejecting Trumpism will be how many seats Democrats can win deep in Trump territory. Given the sheer level of depravity on display from the Trump administration, failing to win a significant number of the hardcore Trump districts now in play will be not just disappointing but soul-crushing.

It will be satisfying, for example, if Democrat Brian Poindexter wins Ohio’s seventh district, which Trump carried by 11.1 points in 2024 and where incumbent GOP Representative Max Miller has been credibly accused of horrific acts of domestic violence by multiple women. But the GOP candidate shouldn’t have to be a physically abusive, misogynist dirtbag for Republican-leaning voters to support a Democrat amid the rampant authoritarian corruption of today’s GOP. Trump’s dreadful policy record and consistently unconscionable conduct in office should be enough to warrant dismissal of any congressional Republican who spent the past two years obsequiously surrendering constitutional power to Trump and his MAGA putsch—which, to be clear, would be all GOP incumbents on Capitol Hill.

ICE’s reign of terror alone should be enough to persuade even committed Trump voters to change their minds. Trump’s masked federal agents have terrorized both big metropolitan areas and rural communities, violently seizing tens of thousands of undocumented immigrants, the vast majority of whom had committed no serious crimes. These public renditions, often carried about by sadists in a repressive apparatus funded more lavishly than the Manhattan Project and glorified by unapologetic white nationalists in the Department of Homeland Security, are a permanent stain on America’s pretensions to be governed by laws and not men. These vicious brownshirt raids have inflicted extraordinary trauma on immigrant families and communities, led to the unlawful detention of hundreds of American citizens, and caused the tragic deaths of innocent noncitizens as well as dissenting US citizens like Renée Nicole Good and Alex Pretti.

The blatant corruption of the president himself is also grounds for broad and deep repudiation of his party in a functional republic. Trump continues to nakedly manipulate the stock market by selling access to his market-moving social-media posts and then conducting thousands of transactions whose sheer brazenness makes the phrase “insider trading” seem like a polite euphemism.

Trump has also corrupted the president’s pardon power by effectively selling freedom to oligarchs and partisan allies and turned American foreign policy into a tool to enrich himself and his circle of oligarchs. For the crime of living in a blue state, he has withheld relief from people whose lives were destroyed by natural disasters, and he has not been subtle about it.

Even Republicans who support dramatically lower levels of immigration to the United States should oppose a secret police force whose members can commit violent crimes on camera in front of hundreds of witnesses and never face any kind of accountability. Even those who believe, for example, that facilitating Somali immigration to the United States was a mistake should be disgusted and chilled by the GOP’s racist, menacing rhetoric and actions against Somalis, including the preposterous raid on the home of Representation Ilhan Omar (D-MN).

Trump voters who agree with many of his economic and social policies should be able to see that a president’s exploiting his office for the enrichment of himself and his family is disqualifying. Diehard Republicans should likewise grasp that the abuse of federal money and power to punish the citizens of states who withheld their support from the ruling regime a recipe for the eventual dissolution of the republic—-as, on the other side of the ledger, are Trump’s repeated promises to bribe citizens who give the GOP their support in this election.

Pick your issue, and you’ll almost certainly find conduct that is an affront to human decency or the rule of law—-and usually both. There’s the vindictive and inhuman assault that the Trump administration has conducted against the small and vulnerable trans minority; the wanton, illegal air strikes against boats suspected of drug trafficking; the bizarre threats of violence against long-standing democratic allies like Canada and Denmark; and the illegal, unprovoked war against Iran that started with the murder of schoolchildren and the country’s head of state and has turned into a geopolitical and economic calamity. This is to say nothing of the myriad abuses and public fleecings carried out by Trump’s coterie of fanatical MAGA allies in and around his cabinet, from Elon Musk’s illegal DOGE reign of destruction to Russell Vought’s deep-state machinations to punish applicants for scientific grants who don’t toe the party line.

The Nation would have to build its own data center to host a full accounting of this administration’s misdeeds. The names of congressional Republicans up for election this year who have done anything at all to push back on this bacchanal of abuse and crime, on the other hand, could fit on the back of a cocktail napkin.

If the characterization of these threats as “existential” seems overblown, it bears reminding that we are in this position only because we flunked a very similar test two years ago. Whatever motivated someone to vote for the disgraced Trump in 2024, be it the price of eggs or resentment against the Biden administration’s immigration policy or even just the boredom of affluence, there should have been little doubt about what he intended to do with a second term. Throughout that election cycle, Trump barnstormed around the country loudly promising mass deportations, partisan vengeance, ruinous tariffs, and vindictive persecution. The Supreme Court even drove home the apocalyptic stakes of that year’s election by granting American presidents almost monarchical power in its stupendously wrongheaded executive immunity decision, Trump v. United States.

Rarely has the American electorate faced such a stark choice between the rule of law and the whims of an aspiring autocrat. And yet here we are. Living through the second Trump administration has been like feeling, in the memorable phrasing of New York Times columnist Michelle Goldberg, “the air go out of an entire social order.” That’s the net result of a sustained campaign of eager MAGA capitulation led by elites in tech, law, academia, the judiciary, and the media. So it’s down to the electorate, again, to do the job that those tasked with defending the Constitution could not.

Democratic wins in unexpected places like South Carolina, which Trump carried by 18 points in 2024 and where a gold-standard New York Times/Siena College poll on Wednesday found a tie between Republican Darline Graham Nordone and Democrat Annie Andrews, would send an unambiguous message to the forces of Trumpism: that there is actually a line and they have crossed it, and that another electoral walloping awaits them in two years if they continue to empower authoritarian impunity in Washington.

It’s true that even a resounding Democratic win on Tuesday may mean nothing more than that these awful people that we have now twice put in charge of the country have at long last alienated enough voters to be thrown out on their ear. It could also be the case that it was mostly inflation and spiraling energy costs putting some of these races in play, and they will snap back to being GOP strongholds in a year or two. Still, such losses would be unspinnable, even by the talented propagandists that populate the MAGA media universe.

On the other hand, modest gains or, God help us, a failure to capture either chamber of Congress would send an unambiguously grim message—that an electorally decisive plurality of the American people likes violent, corrupt authoritarianism, wants more of it, and indeed enjoys being governed by hapless gutter racists, lazy podcasters, and moneyed rapists. They’d also effectively be saying that they don’t care how incompetent and negligent their leaders are, so long as the libs are being owned and the right people are getting hurt.

David Faris is a professor of political science at Roosevelt University and the author of It’s Time to Fight Dirty: How Democrats Can Build a Lasting Majority in American Politics. His writing has appeared in Slate, The Week, The Washington Post, The New Republic, and Washington Monthly. You can find him on Bluesky at @davidfaris.bluesky.social.

The fight over the California billionaire wealth tax ballot initiative has been covered largely as a state tax and budget issue, but that is too narrow a lens. At its core, this fight over the health and well-being of millions of Californians is about democracy.

In a democracy, there is a simple principle: Voters decide, not the people with the most money. Today, that principle is under extraordinary strain. The 170 biggest-spending billionaire families have already contributed a record-breaking $1.7 billion to the 2026 midterm elections. Elon Musk, now the world’s first trillionaire, has spent more than $480 million to bend the outcome toward his own financial and political interests. Billionaires are deploying unprecedented sums to drown out the voices of ordinary voters, and they are proving a hard truth: We can have a government of, by, and for billionaires, or the people, but we cannot have both.

The fight over Prop 40—which would impose a one-time 5 percent tax on the net assets of billionaires to provide healthcare, as well as food assistance and education, to millions of Californians—is Exhibit A in the threat that runaway extreme wealth poses to our society. Californians overwhelmingly support taxing the ultrarich. So, instead of persuading voters differently, a handful of billionaires have spent the past year trying to stop them from voting at all.

§ First, they tried to price democracy out of reach, driving up the cost of signature collection to keep the Billionaire Tax Act off the ballot;

§ When that failed, they tried to buy the company collecting the signatures; and

§ When that failed, they bankrolled two poison-pill measures, Props 41 and 42, designed to confuse voters, undermine Prop 40, and shield their fortunes from taxation permanently.

Now they are flooding the airwaves with misinformation, pouring more than $429 million into anti-wealth-tax efforts—more than Musk spent in the 2024 presidential election that landed him influence to grow his wealth to trillionaire status. And as a recent report shows, the billionaires complaining about Prop 40’s one-time 5 percent tax have seen their wealth surge by an average of 65 percent during the past 20 months and have paid only 0.26 percent of their wealth in state income taxes over five recent years. But the opposition’s playbook has nothing to do with morality or the merits. It is about whether concentrated wealth can override the will of the majority and drown out our votes.

That is why this fight matters so much for California and the nation. For people who spend more than $330 million and barely notice, this is a pilot program. If it works, every billionaire in America learns the lesson: When voters want something you don’t, then you obstruct, confuse, and outspend them until they give up. We cannot let that become the playbook. And the stakes will only grow as artificial intelligence threatens to concentrate wealth and power in the hands of these very tech bros on a scale the world has never seen.

A democracy responsive to the many rather than the few requires policies that check the wealth and power of the ultra-wealthy, starting with taxing the largest fortunes. California voters have the first chance to show it can be done.

The question on the ballot in California is not just about taxes. It is about who governs. Let’s answer it clearly: The people do.

John Bonifaz is a constitutional attorney and the cofounder and president of Free Speech For People, a national nonprofit public interest organization dedicated to defending our democracy and our Constitution across the country.

Christina Livingston is executive director of the Alliance of Californians for Community Empowerment Action (ACCE Action) and chair of the California Working Families Party. She has over two decades of experience organizing at the intersection of racial and economic justice.

The five questions this year range from what to do with small, publicly-owned properties to how the city should plan for its financial future via the rainy day fund.
Early voting is underway in New York City, which will continue through Sunday, Nov. 1, and residents will have their final opportunity to vote on Election Day Tuesday.
In addition to races for governor, State Senate and State Assembly, the backs of New Yorkers’ ballots will give them a chance to approve or reject several proposed changes to New York City’s Charter.
The five questions this year range from what to do with small, city-owned properties to how the city should plan for its financial future via the rainy day fund.
Several bundle multiple changes into a single question. The Mamdani administration—which convened a Commission on Government Efficiency (COGE) earlier this year to draft the measures—is pushing them as a way to a “faster government” and to remove bureaucratic red tape. But critics have raised concerns with some of the proposals.
City Limits put together this guide detailing each question, which hundreds of thousands of voters have weighed in on already.
Proposal 1: Revocable consents and public space
When a business wants to construct, operate, or maintain “a structure on, over, or under New York City’s public streets and sidewalks,” it needs to have a revocable consent, approved by the city’s Department of Transportation (DOT).
A revocable consent is a permit to use public spaces, such as sidewalks or roadways, for a long list of structures, like accessibility ramps and lifts, benches, utility poles, planters, bike racks or kiosks, the city’s Commission on Government Efficiency (COGE) explained.
Proposal 1 asks voters if they want to include applications for outdoor dining sheds and sidewalk cafes in the standard revocable-consent process. These currently require a separate, longer approval process with extra steps.
“Restaurants can wait many months, sometimes losing an entire outdoor dining season and the revenue and jobs that come with it,” said Andrew Rigie, executive director of the NYC Hospitality Alliance, a not-for-profit trade association that represents bars and restaurants and supports the ballot measure.
According to COGE, the proposal would replace the required public hearing and newspaper advertisements for revocable consent applications with an online portal, where the public could review and comment on pending applications.
The Center for Independence of the Disabled in New York (CIDNY) and Common Cause New York, a nonprofit watchdog, criticized this element of the plan, saying it comes at the expense of “public participation and legislative oversight.”
But Rigie counters that the streamlined process still preserves “opportunities for community and elected official input,” calling it “a commonsense reform.”
“New York City can protect the public interest while making it easier for neighborhood restaurants to open outdoor cafés and serve their customers,” he said.
Under the proposal, the city could still revoke a permit if it needs to regain the public space. Community boards could still hold hearings, and DOT could decide a hearing is needed when public comments demand it.
“If it passes, it would cut the outdoor dining application process by about 75 percent from eight months to two months, saving small businesses time and money,” COGE’s Executive Director Ann Cheng said.
“It would also cut down the process for building accessible ramps, like ADA accessible ramps, by about two months, and similarly save time and money,” Cheng added.
Proposal 2: Changes to city contracting
Proposal 2 combines several elements. It would authorize the Procurement Policy Board (PPB), which sets rules for city contracting and procurement, to come up with a new pre-contracting form for certain businesses and nonprofits that provide goods and services to city agencies.
It addresses one of the city’s conundrums: that city agencies often find it very difficult to make purchases, while contractors face a complicated system that can cause delays.
The ballot proposal would authorize the PPB to amend the pre-contracting questionnaire—which both small and large companies seeking city contracts must complete, no matter the sum involved in the deal—for efficiency. It would require the board to meet regularly (at least once every three months) to develop the new form.
If this measure passes, PPB could adapt the questionnaire to better reflect the type or size of the contracts in question, COGE explained, and as in any new rule, the public would be able to comment on the proposed changes.
The city estimates that streamlining the questionnaire requirements would save up to 30 days in the contracting process, from its current average of roughly 13 months.
The measure would also reduce the workload for city agencies when it comes to annual reporting requirements on planned client-services contracts.
Instead of having to write a preliminary report, hold a hearing, and then write a final report, as the current process requires, agencies would just issue their reports each year, giving a heads-up to the vendor community about what contracts they plan to issue, the Mayor’s Office of Contract Services explained.
An additional subsegment in this proposal would make permanent a state provision (expected to sunset in 2030) that allows the city to provide online public notice and collect public comments on contracts.
Other provisions would allow the mayor to delegate certain approvals for noncompetitive contracts over $5 million to agencies, with the approval of the agency’s commissioner.
Proposal 3: Street safety projects, city-owned small lots, and office leasing
Proposal 3 combines three different measures: street safety, city-owned property, and office leasing.
This proposal tries to streamline the city’s process for building new street safety infrastructure, while keeping community input and engagement requirements in place.
Currently, when the Department of Transportation (DOT) is planning “major transportation projects“—like bike and bus lanes that affect four consecutive blocks or 1,000 feet, whichever is less—it is required to consult with four other agencies: the NYPD, Fire Department, Department of Small Business Services, and the Mayor’s Office for People with Disabilities. Certain subunits within those agencies have to sign off on the plans, in very specific ways.
If Proposal 3 passes, DOT would still have to consult with those four agencies, but without the requirement for sub-agencies to weigh in. Instead, it would be up to each agency’s leaders to decide which of their own units or subunits to consult, COGE explained.
The Center for Independence of the Disabled in New York (CIDNY) said they support this ballot proposal, calling it “common-sense efficiency reforms.”
The measure would also allow the DOT to move forward on projects at the same time that it notifies local community boards and elected officials, instead of after, when there’s a situation of immediate need, like street changes made in response to crash and safety data. Supporters say it would protect new bike and bus lane plans from being delayed or blocked by lawsuits, saying opponents often take advantage of mistakes and technical errors in the interagency consultation process to lodge legal challenges.
The city has 1,500 surplus lots, according to the Department of Citywide Administrative Services (DCAS), and City Hall says about 6 percent of them would fall under the 10,000-square-feet category that could be sold.
Under Proposal 3, plans for these lots would no longer undergo the Uniform Land Use Review Procedure (ULURP), the city’s public approval process for certain development projects, and instead go through the new Expedited Land Use Review Procedure (ELURP), which compresses the seven-month review timeline to 90 days.
The Municipal Art Society (MAS) of New York criticized the measure, not only for sausaging “three loosely connected proposals” into one ballot question, but because they say it fails to address “two of the city’s essential needs: open space and affordable housing.”
“New York City’s public land is one of its most valuable—and finite—resources,” MAS Communication Manager Viviane Eng said via email sent to City Limits. “Once sold or transferred, it can be difficult or impossible to reclaim. Decisions about its future must be guided by a comprehensive, long-term vision for the public good, not simply by short-term revenue opportunities.”
A spokesperson for COGE, Jimmy Wyderko, said the proposal would still maintain two key steps of the process for selling city-owned land. The “proposal does not change the public auction requirement nor the land use requirements on the new purchaser (i.e., if the new purchaser wants to build something beyond as-of-right, they would need to go through a ULURP),” Wyderko said in an email.
Marcel Negret, Regional Plan Association’s director of land use, said the current rules make these small lots less attractive to potential developers, at a time when the city is trying to facilitate as many new apartments as possible to address the housing shortage.
“One way to look at it is like putting them [these lots] in a better market position,” Negret said.
COGE officials said the measure would reduce the administrative burden to sell small lots.
Another part of this ballot proposal would remove City Council and the City Planning Commission approvals when the city leases office space for government employees. Currently, the city notifies the local community board and the borough president about such leases, followed by a public hearing and a vote at the City Planning Commission, and then the City Council.
Instead, the Department of Citywide Administrative Services commissioner would provide the community board, local council member, and borough president with a notice of intent to acquire the new office space ahead of time. Then the city would need to notify the Council and comptroller.
Proposal 4: Moving waterfront permitting and building permitting
Proposal 4 would create a one-stop, centralized online construction permitting hub, overseen by the Department of Buildings (DOB), for applicants looking to do construction on an apartment or storefront, or to build affordable housing. COGE says this would give applicants an easier route to getting construction permits than the current process, which requires the involvement of dozens of different city agencies. 
The DOB would have until 2030 to get the hub running. If passed by voters, it would also allow additional DOB staff to approve certificates of occupancy. 
Another point of this proposal would transfer responsibility for waterfront construction permits from the Department of Small Business Services to the Department of Buildings, where the expertise lies, officials and advocates explained.
“Right now, the process can be confusing,” said Tyler Taba, Waterfront Alliance director of policy and government affairs. “Moving that responsibility to DOB is a practical step toward reducing confusion, delays, and unnecessary costs for waterfront projects.”
Proposal 5: Setting a goal for the city’s rainy-day fund
Through a 2019 ballot proposal, New Yorkers took the first steps toward creating a “rainy day” fund to help the city fill budget gaps during economic downturns.
The city’s existing fund, formally known as the Revenue Stabilization Fund, has nearly $1.7 billion in it. But there are no specific goals for how much the city should be saving with it.
If Proposal 5 is approved, the city would set a savings target for the fund at 12 percent of prior-year tax revenue. But that doesn’t mean the city will contribute that 12 percent all at once: the Office of Management and Budget (OMB), in consultation with the comptroller and the public, would be required to develop a plan by May 2027 that would outline when the city needs to contribute and if so, how much in a given year.
The city will contribute every year as long as that criteria is met, until the 12 percent threshold is reached. Once it hits that goal, the city no longer has to contribute to the fund, but still could if officials choose to. “That is like the city’s savings account, and so it would establish a target of 12 percent of the city’s prior year tax revenue, in order to work towards long-term fiscal stability,” Cheng said.
Good government groups like Reinvent Albany and The Citizens Budget Commission (CBC) are urging people to vote “no,” on Proposal 5, saying it doesn’t do enough to force the city to beef up its financial reserves.
“Voting no on Proposal 5 does not oppose strengthening the Rainy Day Fund. It is a vote declaring the status quo is not good enough, and the city should do better,” CBC President Andrew Rein wrote in an Op-Ed in October.
Comptroller Mark Levine’s office put out a report in April suggesting that a 16 percent reserves target would suffice to help the city weather an “entire below-trend period” like a recession.
