Participating exhibitors at Art Basel Paris are demanding compensation for the fair closing two days early on October 23 due to security concerns over planned protests the next day. The fair was scheduled to take place from October 23-25 with VIP previews occurring in the days leading up.
As per Artnet News, the Comité Professionnel des Galeries d’Art (CPGA), an industry group representing over a quarter of the exhibitors, wrote an open letter on October 28 with their demands addressed to Karim Crippa, director of Art Basel Paris. In the letter, which was reviewed by Artnet News, CPGA wrote: “The decision to close the fair was made by Art Basel Paris, and by Art Basel Paris alone.”
The letter described the decision as one that caused “profound incomprehension,” among dealers and other exhibitors. This cost them two days of business, which, as per the dealers, warranted “fair compensation.”
Although many dealers suspected that the fair would be closed on Saturday, the decision to remain shut on Sunday came as a surprise. Dealers also told ARTnews that they were informed of the closure at 3:30 p.m. on Thursday. As a result, they had little time to decide whether to pack up or hold tight until things calmed down in Paris.
The letter added that other fairs such as Design Miami Paris, AKAA, and Offscreen stayed open on Sunday. Signed by CGPA president, Philippe Charpentier (co-founder of the Paris gallery Mor Charpentier) the letter featured the signatures of 14 other dealers, including Michel Rein, Christophe Gaillard, Nathalie Obadia, Jocelyn Wolff, and Magda Danysz.
Additionally, CGPA also noted in the letter that it had a more collaborative relationship with Art Basel Paris’s earlier management. CGPA later told Artnet News that Christopher Miles from France’s Ministry of Culture is organizing a meeting to discuss the demands between Art Basel Paris, CGPA, and GrandPalaisRmn, which operates the Grand Palais, the fair’s venue.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: Mamdani Admin Intervenes on Eviction, a First Use of New Deed Fraud Law
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Samantha Maldonado
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
For the first time, Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s administration used a new law to intervene on behalf of a Brooklyn family facing eviction they say is because of deed fraud.
But the move may not have worked.
A city lawyer filed papers Friday to try to prevent the impending eviction of a family in order to examine a possible underlying case of deed fraud or theft related to the historic Crown Heights brownstone where they live.
But a Brooklyn housing court judge declined to grant the stay, writing in a filing that two courts had already litigated the deed theft allegations.
An eviction could take place as soon as this week. The City Law Department is evaluating next steps, according to spokesperson Nick Paolucci.
The family, including Helen “Queen Afua” Robinson and her grown children Sherease and Ali Torain, have been fighting to keep their home for over a decade. They alleged their late grandmother Ida Robinson, who purchased the home with her husband in 1968, was a victim of deed theft.
“After all this time, I was hoping for something totally different and unfortunately this happened,” said Sherease Torain on Sunday evening from her stoop, where over 30 locals gathered to speak about the situation and plan to stop a possible eviction by physically blocking the home.
“It really breaks my heart that I started this in my 30s, now I’m in my 40s , and I’m not too far away from my 50s,” she continued. “This is what it does to you — it steals time and that’s something you can never get back.”
The ongoing saga has played out across multiple lawsuits over the years, as the family tried to reclaim the property deed and the current recorded owner of the home attempted to kick them out. In the past, local tenant organizers have kept watch over the stoop to prevent previous eviction attempts — and at one point, helped the family re-enter the home after the owner changed the locks.
New Law to Halt Eviction
The Friday filing marked the first time city lawyers had intervened in court to halt an eviction related to possible deed theft under a state law. In 2023, state lawmakers had updated the law to allow for government entities to motion for a stay — to prevent eviction — in order to investigate matters where deed theft or fraud may have taken place.
Philip Schaffroth, the chief of detectives at the Office of the New York City Sheriff supported the request for a stay, as the city Department of Finance’s Bureau of Investigation looks into a claim of deed fraud. The Mayor’s Office of Deed Theft Prevention referred the case to the finance agency’s investigators in September, Schaffroth wrote in court documents.
He said the investigation would include a records review, interviews of the parties involved and subpoenaing bank records.
The law states that if a government motions for a stay, the court “shall issue a stay” of the proceeding in the face of an ongoing investigation. But a Housing Court judge, Javier Ortiz, did grant the request
“Any new investigation constitutes futility of process with an inevitable and obvious conclusion,” Ortiz wrote.
Edward Mostoller, director of the Homeowner and Consumer Debt Advocacy Project at the City Bar Justice Center who is not involved in the proceedings, said he was “surprised” by the judge’s decision to not grant the stay.
“Like with many newly instituted legal protections for consumers and homeowners, it will take efforts to educate our courts to promote greater awareness and a more uniform (and proper) interpretation of these new laws,” Mostoller wrote in an email.
Disputed Deed
The dispute over the deed stems from a deal Ida Robinson appears to have made in 2015. Property records show she sold the home to an LLC, which transferred the property to another LLC and then to Menachem Gurevitch, who is the owner according to current property records.
Robinson and her family became tenants in the home. They have alleged in court documents that the deed was forged. Gurevitch, who is associated with the companies Mandy Management and Netz Capital Management, moved to sue the family for eviction, but they have continued living in the home.
Gurevitch and his lawyer did not respond to an emailed request for comment and in a brief call, Gurevitch’s attorney Pamela Smith declined to comment. In court papers, they have denied the family’s allegations. In a letter to the court after the city filed its paperwork, Gurevitch’s attorneys called the move “an eleventh hour ploy” to delay eviction.
Previously, both the New York Attorney General’s office and Brooklyn District Attorney’s office have investigated the matter regarding the brownstone. Neither office brought criminal charges.
Deed theft happens when the title to a home is stolen without the homeowner’s approval or knowledge. It can involve forgery, fraud or other tricks. A lawyer who examined the case in 2022 — whom Attorney General Letitia James referred to the family — determined the situation could be a “foreclosure rescue scam,” a scheme where an entity claims to help a property owner who is behind on their mortgage but exploits them instead.
Deed theft has been an ongoing issue in New York City, especially in gentrifying Black and brown communities where home values have skyrocketed. Elderly people have long been targets for predatory real estate schemes.
Deed theft burst into the national spotlight in the spring when Councilmember Chi Ossé was arrested while protesting an eviction of a family at a Bedford-Stuyvesant brownstone, about a mile north of the Crown Heights home at the center of the Robinson’s fight.
Ossé — along with Inez and Charles Barron, both former members of City Council and the state Assembly — appeared at the stoop of the Crown Heights home Sunday evening.
Editor’s note: This article previously stated that Ida Robinson had once fallen behind on her mortgage. It has been updated and corrected.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: High Stakes and High Costs: NY Voters Hit the Polls as Hochul Faces Blakeman
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Katie Honan
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
New York City voters head to the polls Tuesday after a surge in early voting, capping a high-stakes campaign where affordability was one of the defining issues.
More than 690,000 voters had cast their ballots in New York City since early voting opened Oct. 24, up from more than 432,000 in the 2022 governor’s race.
Gov. Kathy Hochul, a Democrat, is hoping not just for a win but a more definitive victory than the one she eked out four years ago, focusing on affordability amid cost-of-living increases.
Her Republican challenger, Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman, has positioned himself as the savior of a state he says is overrun by crime and sky-high taxes.
The race, and Hochul’s possible margin of victory, will be closely watched by Mayor Zohran Mamdani and his team as they prepare to push the next governor to raise taxes on the wealthy to fund housing and childcare in New York City.
Both candidates spent the weekend on the stump, criss-crossing the state to urge voters to the polls.
Blakeman campaigned throughout the city and Long Island, telling supporters at a rally Saturday in Middle Village in Queens that “help is on the way.”
“I feel like a winner,” he told The City Reporter about the days heading up to Tuesday’s election.
Hochul was joined by top Democrats including Mayor Mamdani, who accompanied her at the Queens Night Market on Saturday and watched a Buffalo Bills game at an Astoria bar on Sunday, alongside Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.
The governor was confident that she’d sail to victory on Tuesday, just like her beloved Bills.
“When you’re focusing on affordability and what we can do to help lift up New Yorkers, that is the message that is resonating,” Hochul said during the game.
Late Polls Boost Hochul
A late October poll by Marist University found Hochul was up 11 points against Blakeman, with 4 percent of voters undecided. A Siena University poll had Hochul up 14 points.
The biggest issue for voters is the economy and cost of living, according to an October Quinnipiac University poll. That’s shown in ads from both of the candidates, with Blakeman focusing on increases under Hochul.
At Blakeman’s rally Saturday in Middle Village, U.S. Army soldier Juan Nieves, 32, said his top priority was safety.
“I you don’t have law and order, we would have nothing,” he said.
Peter Kauffmann, a Democratic strategist, said Hochul’s re-election campaign was notably stronger than her 2022 effort, and with more emphasis on voter concerns.
“It’s great to see that she’s actually responding to issues that people care about, she seems really focused,” he told The City Reporter.
Hochul’s relationship with Mamdani has also energized her campaign and voters, even if Blakeman has tried to use it against his opponent.
“I think they will continue to govern well with one another,” Kauffmann said.
State Attorney General Letitia James is also up for re-election, and has been challenged by Republican Saritha Komatireddy, a former federal prosecutor.
Recent polling showed James up by at least 15 percentage points.
The state Comptroller Thomas DiNapoli also faces Republican Joseph Hernandez, who ran for New York City mayor last year.
New York City voters will also decide on five ballot proposals that the mayor says will, if passed, cut bureaucracy around how the city builds bike and bus lanes, contracts with small businesses and sells and leases some properties.
Democrats across the country are hoping to reclaim the House of Representatives and the Senate with pivotal races in states like Texas, Maine and Michigan. The issues nationally match those in New York City: the rising cost of living, which is felt acutely in the five boroughs.
If Democrats prevail nationally, two Brooklynites could wind up running Congress: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer. (New York City’s House races were largely decided in the June Democratic primary. Schumer and Democratic Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand are not up for reelection this year.)
A recent AP-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll found just 25% of polled adults approved of how President Donald Trump was handling the economy — down from 32% in July.
L. Joy Williams, the president of the New York State NAACP Conference of Branches, said affordability is the biggest issue “across the board.”
“I don’t think it matters in terms of race, ethnicity,” she said.
“Even though wealthier people are making money hand over fist, everybody else is not. That’s what’s driving people.”
Kristin de Guzman, a marketing strategist, met Hochul outside the Chambers St. stop on West Broadway on Monday, sharing that she’d voted for the governor the day before. As a small business owner, she was focused on the cost of living.
“I think she’s done a great job,” de Guzman said. “We care about the economy and affordability, like everybody on the planet.”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Californian Michelin-starred restaurant serves up book on the art of hospitality and farming
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: The Art Newspaper
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Kaiseki is a type of Japanese dining offering up multiple courses that together form one long and delicious experience. This is precisely what is on offer at SingleThread, a three-star Michelin restaurant in California’s Sonoma Wine Country, so it’s perhaps no surprise that its proprietors, Kyle and Katina Connaughton, describe themselves as storytellers. But SingleThread is also a 24-acre farm, and a five-room inn, and works closely with nearby ranchers who rear the meat it uses. It’s a multi-volume affair.
Now, all its wisdom, history, instructions for ikebana flower arranging, planting diagrams for the kitchen garden, and a number of recipes are gathered together in one book. As with its restaurant ethos, it’s a publication that assumes you have a great deal of time and inclination to spare: there’s an entire section on the negi onion.
On the other hand, if you’re unlikely to visit Sonoma any time soon, or don’t fancy joining a months-long waiting list, this book is a treat. The photography is stunning and, unlike a ten-course meal—which, however delightful, can feel like being held hostage and will cost a bare minimum of £500—you can dip in and out at leisure in the comfort of your own home.
• SingleThread, DK Alpha, £50 (hb)

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/03/t.title: Tuesday’s Headlines: Empire State Wilting Edition
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/03/t.author: Gersh Kuntzman
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/03/t.text:
Just in time for today’s election, Transportation Alternatives has put out a new report revealing that Department of Transportation projects take too long to go from public presentation to completion.
The group reviewed all bike lane projects announced between 2022 and 2025, and found that an average of 527 days passed between that presentation and completion, which is a lot of time when you consider that it famously took 410 days to build all 102 floors of the Empire State Building nearly a century ago.
Setting aside whether the bike lane vs. Empire State Building comparison is apt (it’s not) — 527 days is a very long time between telling a community board the plan and finishing said project. Yes, there’s usually an intermediate step — defending the plan against the inevitable (and inevitably fruitless) lawsuit — but it still takes too long to make roadways safe.
During those long interregnums, people have been injured and killed, as the group points out:
On Tremont Avenue in the Bronx, safety improvements proposed in June 2024 were not completed until September 2026. In that time, 17 New Yorkers were seriously injured on the street.
On Third Avenue in Brooklyn, safety improvements proposed in 2023 have yet to be installed. Since 2022, three pedestrians have been killed, and 14 people have been seriously injured.
In Sunset Park, safety improvements proposed in 2020 have still not been installed. In 2025, two elderlywomen were killed while walking in separate incidents on Seventh Avenue.
“Red tape is killing New Yorkers,” said Ben Furnas, the group’s executive director. (For another reminder of why timely safety projects are important, check out Erik Engquist’s tweet below):
Delays were also an issue in a report issued last week by Comptroller Mark Levine, whose office that more than half of restaurants that received outdoor dining licenses since the program began in March 2024 waited more than 19 months for approval — far longer than the Department of Transportation’s eight-month timeline.
The good news? DOT started doing a much better job in 2026, after the swearing in of a new mayor. Before that, DOT submitted roughly 29 permits per month to the Comptroller’s office, but starting in February 2026, that number rose to an average of 228 permits per month, rising to 475 permits in July 2026.
“While this increase represents meaningful progress, it does not erase the lengthy delays experienced by applicants or establish whether the program can consistently deliver timely approvals going forward,” Levine’s office wrote. “As of mid-June, when data was collected as part of this investigation, only one roadway application filed in 2026 had resulted in a license within six months. DOT was still working through large numbers of older applications, and 2,115 applications remained pending.”
The takeaway from both these reports: We need city government to be more nimble so that it can better serve the public. Fortunately, there are two referenda about that on today’s Election Day ballot (we’ve covered them, and Gothamist and The City Reporter did yesterday, too): Proposal 1 will make it easier to open outdoor dining setups. And Proposal 3 will cut down the time it takes for the city to redesign roadways for safety.
As a non-profit, we’re not allowed to endorse candidates, but we can endorse ideas — and both of these proposals have our support (as well as the support from the more-eloquent Open Plans). In any event, please vote and remember to turn over your ballot for the referenda. (And find your polling place here.)
In other news:
Game on? When will the MTA restore the basketball court near our office? (Gothamist)
Non-starter: The Citizens Budget Commission is already putting it out there that the MTA should cut some jobs to save money. (Gothamist)
Mayor to ICE: Stop using our parking lots. (NY Times, NYDN)
Subway ridership soared during the Marathon on Sunday. (NYDN)
The plutocratic populists at the New York Post are at it again: an editorial board that believes that congestion pricing is a “tax” on the middle class now want you to believe that they care about bus riders. Fact: The Post’s editors don’t care about bus riders; they just want to undermine public faith in transit so that less public money is allocated to transit, starving it further and serving their larger anti-urban agenda of encouraging more car ownership and use.
Case in point: The Post thinks the PATH train is too expensive. Now do cars, Rupert!
And, finally, in case you missed it, here’s Streetsblog’s Sammy Sussman and Henry Beebe-Center getting to the bottom of the car-filled bridle path in Central Park:
Tabloid legend Gersh Kuntzman has been with New York newspapers since 1989, including stints at the New York Daily News, the Post, the Brooklyn Paper and even a cup of coffee with the Times. He's also the writer and producer of "Murder at the Food Coop," which was a hit at the NYC Fringe Festival in 2016, and “SUV: The Musical” in 2007. He also writes the Cycle of Rage column, which is archived here.

Brady Lum, the former chief operating officer of Atlanta‘s High Museum of Art, has been sentenced to one year in federal prison for stealing more than $600,000 from the institution. He previously pleaded guilty to the charges in July. Before his sentencing, Lum paid full restitution to the museum and reimbursed $500,000 of its legal and investigative fees.
The disgraced former COO joined the High Museum in January of 2019 and resigned in December of 2025. He started to siphon money from the institution in September of 2019, and continued until the discovery of fraud in November of 2025. He used doctored invoices and used his power to approve transactions for personal purchases, and used accounting adjustments to spread his expenses across multiple cost centers. He utilized the money he embezzled to purchase high end guitars, music lessons, and woodworking equipment. The Justice Department found that Lum had received more than seven hundred reimbursements from the museum, most of them under $1,000.
U.S. District Judge Michael L. Brown sentenced Lum to one year in prison, followed by one year of supervised release. Lum took a plea deal, which involved paying full restitution of $607,688.18 to the High Museum. “We expect leaders of one of our communities’ historic institutions to serve as stewards, not loot it,” said Marlo Graham, Special Agent in Charge of FBI Atlanta, in a press release from the US District Attorney’s Office of Northern Georgia. “Brady Lum manipulated internal processes to steal hundreds of thousands of dollars. The FBI is committed to uncovering and stopping this kind of greed and fraud.”

https://gothamist.com/news/medicaid-is-c.title: Medicaid is changing. We want to hear from NYers about what's ahead.
https://gothamist.com/news/medicaid-is-c.author: Caroline Lewis
https://gothamist.com/news/medicaid-is-c.text:
Sweeping federal changes are coming to Medicaid in January, potentially creating new hurdles to maintaining health coverage for the more than 6 million New Yorkers the program insures statewide.
City and state officials, community groups and healthcare providers say they are working to prevent people from losing health coverage as a result of upcoming eligibility changes. But many New Yorkers on Medicaid are still figuring out what this means for them. Some are already in the process of renewing their insurance for the coming year.
If you’re a New Yorker on Medicaid, Gothamist wants to hear from you about your questions, concerns and experiences navigating these changes. We also want to hear about why Medicaid is important to you.
People who work in healthcare or are helping New Yorkers on Medicaid navigate these changes are also welcome to respond.
If you live in the New York City area and could be affected by the upcoming Medicaid changes, please fill out this response form.
Under the new rules, adults under 65 will need to prove they are either working 80 hours a month, doing equivalent amounts of community service, attending job training programs or enrolled in school at least part-time.
Many New Yorkers will be exempt from these requirements, however. That includes people with certain medical conditions, disabled veterans and parents of children under 14. State health officials are also seeking an exemption for Bronx residents because of the borough’s high unemployment rate.
But the new rules will also require more frequent recertifications and paperwork to prove eligibility — and some policymakers and healthcare providers worry that could put Medicaid coverage at risk even for those who still qualify.

https://gothamist.com/news/a-typo-a-miss.title: A typo. A missing screw. These are the small snags keeping NYC families in shelters.
https://gothamist.com/news/a-typo-a-miss.author: Karen Yi
https://gothamist.com/news/a-typo-a-miss.text:
Roxy Shweky’s job is to make sure New York City apartments pass their inspections. Once they do, families living in city shelters can use housing vouchers to move into them.
Shweky works for the housing nonprofit Anthos Home, acting as a liaison between the landlord, tenant and the city.
During a recent tour of a Brooklyn apartment that had already failed twice, she showed an inspector the smoke detector that needed to be moved closer to the bedroom and the electrical outlet that needed grounding. Then he noticed a tiny detail on a kitchen window frame. On a metal bracket where there should be two screws, there was only one.
The apartment failed again. Shweky would need the landlord to make the fix before the apartment could get the OK for a family to move in.
“We all care deeply about households moving into quality, safe, dignified housing,” said Chris Mann, vice president of public policy and strategy for WIN, the city’s largest provider of family homeless shelters and supportive housing.
“But the complexity doesn't need to be this way.”
New York City’s cityFHEPS housing vouchers are a lifeline for people trying to leave the homeless shelter system. But getting city approval for a voucher can be a serpentine process — where one wrong move can mean starting over.
Housing advocates said even the smallest issue — like a burned out light bulb during an apartment inspection or a typo on a form — can delay a family moving out of a shelter and into an apartment by weeks. The pitfalls can happen at nearly every step of the process: from the moment a household applies for rental assistance, to finding an available unit, to the nearly 70-100 pages of paperwork and forms the city requires before giving a final OK.
“ We're talking about people's lives,” Mann said. “Every day in shelter is a day too long for a family.”
Housing advocates said the municipal voucher program is unnecessarily convoluted, trapping New Yorkers who desperately need a place to live in shelters for too long.
The Mamdani administration has announced a series of changes to speed up the process and said it’s already cut down the number of days it takes an application to be reviewed.
Nicholas Jacobelli, a spokesperson for the Department of Social Services, which administers the vouchers, said the administration has “taken numerous steps to cut the red tape required for New Yorkers to move out of shelter and into stable housing. We continue to test new mechanisms to further expedite these processes with the goal of housing New Yorkers more quickly.”
He said the city reduced how often applications from shelter residents are returned from 94% to 58% and cut down the number of times an application is returned prior to its approval by more than half. City officials also launched a new pilot to make move-ins for shelter residents into housing much faster by working directly with landlords.
But nonprofit groups and shelter providers said there’s still more to fix, and the stakes are high: A record number of New Yorkers are residing in city shelters every night as the rate of available apartments remains historically low.
Several bills introduced by City Council members aim to streamline parts of the system, like requiring city officials to approve or deny voucher applications within 15 days. The city said it now takes an average of 24 days to approve or deny an application, down from 28 days in the past. Applications are usually returned over missing, incorrect or incomplete forms, according to the Department of Social Services.
Jackie Mallon, chief operating officer for Anthos Home, a nonprofit focused on getting shelter residents into housing quickly, describes a process reminiscent of the board game Chutes and Ladders.
“There are a lot of points in the process where you could be stuck, have to go back to the beginning and start all over, and it's frustrating and difficult,” Mallon said. “It's just incredibly hard to do it on your own.”
Erin Dalton, the social services department's commissioner, said during a recent city council hearing the agency needed to balance making inspections faster while making sure the apartments taxpayers are subsidizing are safe.
She said once a person is found eligible for a voucher, it takes an average of nearly 8 months, or 236 days, for a family to move into a unit. City officials said the dearth of affordable housing and the city’s 1.4% of empty apartments can make the search process longer.
About 14,200 people are currently in shelter who have been found eligible for a voucher and are authorized to look for an apartment, city officials said.
Growth and savings
The CityFHEPS voucher program is one of the largest municipal voucher programs in the country.
More than 74,000 households rely on the program that’s expanded due to high demand. Recipients pay no more than 30% of their income toward rent. The city covers the rest.
With federal cut backs to rental assistance programs and only modest state rental aid, the vouchers are the primary way New Yorkers are able to leave the city’s homeless shelters.
But even as the city is pushing reforms, some efforts have backfired. Earlier this year, the Mamdani administration announced it would make the $1.2 billion program more efficient and save $500 million by cutting back how much it pays brokers and landlords.
In April, officials began checking to make sure the city wasn’t overpaying rents — an initiative that resulted in even more delays.
The new review process meant what used to take two days began taking an average of 53 days, according to Jade Vasquez, director of policy and research at WIN.
“ You don't want to overpay city dollars to landlords that are overcharging. But the process just seems very burdensome,” Vasquez said.
In September, the city moved the new rent review requirement to after a tenant moves into the unit to avoid further delays. But the change only applies to rent stabilized units. Market-rate units continue to experience move-in delays, providers said.
“It's like a half of a solution,” Vasquez said.
Repeat inspections
Housing advocates said inspections can be the most onerous part, setting back move-ins by months over issues that are often minor. Inspections are done by nonprofit partners, with the harder ones conducted by the Department of Social Services — and based on a strict checklist.
“Water temperature has to be between 120F and 128F. If it's too low, it won't pass. If it's too high, it won't pass,” said Shweky, housing unit readiness and repairs specialist at Anthos Home.
According to the Department of Social Services, 44% of inspections it conducts fail, with the top causes due to water temperature, electrical outlet deficiencies, missing or unlabeled apartment numbers, window guard and bracket violations or fridge and freezer temperature failures.
“ The porridge has to be exactly the right temperature for it all to magically be ready,” said Laura Lazarus, cofounder and CEO of Anthos Home.
Landlord and developer Iser Shepherd said the process can take so long that units are sitting vacant for months.
“Everyone gets frustrated. The tenant wants to know, the management wants to know. The landlord's getting furious like, ‘I'm not getting any response. Let me get another tenant,’” he said.
“Landlords, they want to accept vouchers. They just want to have a way that 's easy to do.”
City officials said they piloted a fast track inspection process that will expand next year.
Reams of paperwork
After a person is found eligible for a voucher, finds an apartment, gets the unit approved by the city and collects all necessary paperwork, everything is submitted to the city in a package.
The complete application includes forms like the last 30 days of income for everyone in the household over 18 years old, a letter from the homeless shelter, a checklist for the unit’s conditions, and a lease agreement. All of it can number as many as 100 pages.
Mann said a typo on the paperwork sent to the city — such as the apartment written as both 1A and A1 — can mean rejection, and having to resubmit everything again.
And if along the process, an applicant’s income changes by more than $125 a month, then they have to resubmit their pay stubs to the city so they can recalculate the budget.
Mario Vega, program director of operations for Anthos Home said since many applicants are hourly workers, just a couple work shifts can trigger the lengthy process
“I can't imagine a participant being able to do any of this without the support of their shelter worker or … us.”
Social services officials said homeless shelters are budgeted to have one housing specialist that can help with housing applications for every 40 residents, though not all shelters have one. Officials said all shelter staff should know how to navigate the housing voucher process.
Three case managers
Kelvin Wallace, 65, spent 11 months in a homeless shelter as he scrambled to figure out how to move out with a housing voucher. He said he worked with three different case managers in that time.
“I had to submit my application [on] at least three different occasions with three different case managers,” he said.
The challenge for him was figuring out whether he was even eligible for a voucher and being able to see the status of his application.
“ You have to reset each and every time,” a case manager changes, he said. Wallace said his case was ultimately referred to Anthos Home which helped him get an apartment in four months.
“I feel comfortable that I'm here. I'm on solid ground,” he said.

https://gothamist.com/news/ballot-proble.title: Ballot problems in Westchester: Lawler v. Conley race results could be delayed
https://gothamist.com/news/ballot-proble.author: Ben Feuerherd
https://gothamist.com/news/ballot-proble.text:
Voting on Election Day hit an early snag in Westchester County Tuesday as issues with voting machines were reported throughout the county, according to a statement from the county’s Board of Elections.
The board in statement initially said a paper thickness problem prevented the devices from accepting ballots. In a subsequent statement it removed mention of the paper issue. Voters' ballots will be counted, the board said, but delays may occur.
Westchester is ground zero for the marquee congressional race between Republican Rep. Mike Lawler and Democratic challenger Cait Conley.
The agency strongly suggested that voters remain in line and cast their ballots in spite of the technical difficulties. They said once ballots are filled out, they will be placed in emergency ballot bags, which will be secured and monitored by poll workers.
The ballots will be counted later in a way consistent with election procedures, the statement said. The statement said every eligible vote will be counted despite the snafu.
Aside from Congress, Westchester County, just north of New York City, could be a critical swing county in a number of races, including the gubernatorial election.
Lawler tweeted about the issues Tuesday morning, encouraging his supporters to remain in line.
“Every ballot will be counted,” he wrote. “Stay on line and vote. Do not leave the polling place without voting.”
His challenger, Cait Conley, similarly encouraged voters to stay at the polls and said the issue was being handled and resolved in a bipartisan way.
“The Polls are open and operational, and every vote cast will be counted. Please stay in line and have your voice heard as they work to resolve the issue,” she said on social media.
This is a developing story and may be updated.

https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.title: 'The Muppets Take Manhattan' in Queens and more November films in NYC
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.author: Emma Stefansky
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.text:
It’s a dark and misty night and one man prowls the streets dressed in a creepy mask and a swirling cape. It’s Hugo Weaving from “V for Vendetta!” And he’s ushering in the month of November with a classic action movie that reminds us all of the power of a cool monologue and an even cooler sword.
This month at the movies, New York is playing host to aliens, Muppets, ambitious directors, and families big and small as the onset of the holiday season has us all thinking about finding home wherever we are. Whether you’re staying close by or launching into outer space, there’s no better place to do it than at the movies.
"V for Vendetta"
Remember, remember, the 5th of November, especially when it comes to re-releases of classic dystopian action movies. This month brings the 20th Anniversary of “V for Vendetta,” adapted from the Alan Moore comic (with a script by the Wachowski sisters) about the price of revolution in a totalitarian society. Starring a high-kicking Hugo Weaving wielding a Guy Fawkes mask and a big sword alongside an iconically bald Natalie Portman, the memorably stylized movie invokes the English revolutionaries’ 1605 Gunpowder Plot to spin a tale of rebellion against a system that no longer works in the favor of the people. Better brush up on your V-words.
Participating AMCs, Nov. 1-5
"Wild Horse Nine"
Eighteen years after his feature-length debut “In Bruges,” Irish director Martin McDonagh returns to his unique brand of spy comedy with “Wild Horse Nine,” starring John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell as CIA operatives dispatched to Easter Island mere days before the 1973 Chilean coup d'etat. The constantly bickering pair wrestle with their inner demons and their mounting disillusionment with international destabilization while the shadows of the island’s giant heads loom.
Angelika Film Center, opens Nov. 5
"Crooklyn"
“Crooklyn” is perhaps Spike Lee’s most personal film, a semi-autobiographical family portrait of a Bedford-Stuyvesant household in the summer of 1973. Told mainly through the eyes of the family’s young daughter Troy Carmichael (Zelda Harris), the film stars a cast of colorful Brooklynites doing what they can to get by. These days, the movie is mainly celebrated for its soundtrack of hits from the 1960s and ’70s, including The Jackson 5’s “ABC” and The Chambers Brothers’ “Time Has Come Today.”
"Everytime"
When a shocking tragedy befalls a teenage girl, what remains of her family — her mother, her younger sister, and her boyfriend — find themselves immersed in the surreality of grief in the modern age, where the dead remain semi-present via a digital realm of photographs, videos and Minecraft islands. Determined to regain some sense of normalcy, the fractured family unit goes on their pre-planned vacation to the Spanish island of Tenerife, resulting in a reality-bending climax that must be seen to be believed. “Everytime” is the third feature film by audacious Austrian director Sandra Wollner, an exploration into the hidden connections between death, grief, and technology.
Film at Lincoln Center, opens Nov. 6
"News from Home"
When Belgian director Chantal Akerman was 21, she moved to New York City for two years, from 1971 to 1973, and later returned in 1976 to capture footage of the places where she’d lived, worked and taken walks. These long takes of NYC streets, subway stations, and the Staten Island Ferry make up her avant-garde documentary “News from Home,” scored with a voiceover of Akerman herself reading the letters her mother sent to her while she was living there. This underseen gem is as much a snapshot of NYC in a bygone era as it is a depiction of all-too-familiar parental anxiety that hits after your children leave the nest.
"Hermia & Helena"
While in New York on an artist’s residency, an Argentine theater director intends to put on a Spanish translation of William Shakespeare’s fantasy play “A Midsummer Night’s Dream.” One of director Matías Piñeiro’s ambitious series of films loosely inspired by the Bard’s works, “Hermia & Helena” charmingly follows protagonist Camila (Agustina Muñoz) on her romantic and artistic exploits, casting a who’s-who of fellow international creators (French director Mati Diop, American director and critic Dan Sallitt) in supporting roles.
Metrograph, Nov. 8. There will be a Q&A with director Matías Piñeiro following the opening day screening.
"Cloverfield"
New York is rivaled only by Tokyo in the getting-invaded-by-giant-monsters department, and the visceral 2008 found-footage sci-fi horror movie “Cloverfield” took that competition to new heights. When a going-away party is interrupted by an alien invasion, a group of friends must make their way through the city and avoid getting crushed in the mysterious creature’s destructive wake. We all remember where we were when we first encountered the nausea-inducing digital shaky cam with which the movie’s cast of screaming twentysomethings captured a giant extraterrestrial monster’s rampage across Manhattan. (In a cheeky “Cloverfield”-esque twist, though it was shot to emulate a cheap handicam, IFC’s screenings of the movie will be on 35mm.)
IFC Center, Nov. 13, 14
"The Muppets Take Manhattan"
Making it in New York isn’t easy, not even for the Muppets! When the troupe of charming performers put on a variety show for their college’s graduating class, their classmates’ cheers inspire them to take it all the way to Broadway. But showbiz isn’t all song and dance, and Kermit, Miss Piggy, and their pals soon find out that producing a show in the heart of New York City isn’t as easy as it seems. “The Muppets Take Manhattan” is a glowing ode to NYC, featuring a fabulous array of cameos from stars like Joan Rivers, Elliott Gould, and the inimitable Liza Minnelli.
MOMI Redstone Theater, Nov. 21 and 22
All of a Sudden
A director of a Parisian memory care nursing home whose efforts to humanely train the staff lead to frustration and burnout. A Japanese playwright whose diagnosis with terminal cancer hasn’t stopped her from putting on a play in the city. When their worlds collide by happenstance, the two women’s lives instantly mesh, bonding through meditative conversations about healthcare, mental illness and philosophy. “All of a Sudden” is Japanese director Ryusuke Hamaguchi’s first French-language film, a celebration of life in the face of overwhelming despair.

https://gothamist.com/news/2026-midterm-.title: 2026 Midterm Election Day is here: What to know in NY and NJ
https://gothamist.com/news/2026-midterm-.author: Verónica Del Valle, Brittany Kriegstein, Brigid Bergin, Mike Hayes
https://gothamist.com/news/2026-midterm-.text:
Polls are open across the country today as voters cast their ballots in elections that will decide the balance of power in Congress, along with several high-profile races for governor and other races down-ballot. The midterm election is often considered a referendum on the party in control of the White House. But with spiking costs at the grocery store and gas station, the cost of living has consistently ranked among the top concerns of voters.
Shrey Panda of Fort Greene voted during his morning run Tuesday and said, like most Americans, that affordability was top of mind.
"It's very expensive here and I think in the country," Panda, 33, said before going in to vote. "I think the economy is always going to be number one."
In New Jersey's 7th Congressional District, Republican Rep. Tom Kean Jr. is fighting for his political life against Democratic challenger Rebecca Bennett who leads most polls in the race. But Dean Seda, a DJ with DJ's at the Polls, was spinning some tunes at a polling site in the district Tuesday morning, to give the electoral fight a more festive atmosphere.
"It's a unique opportunity to be a part of a very important day in New Jersey and the U.S.A.," Seda, 35, said, adding he's part of a national initiative at thousands of polling sites across the country, "to provide a little more of an energetic environment at the polls."
What to know today
Polls open at 6 a.m. in New York and New Jersey on Tuesday.
Find out where your Election Day poll site in New York is here. Polls close at 9 p.m.
Find out where your Election Day poll site in New Jersey is here. Polls close at 8 p.m.
What if I have a mail ballot?
In New York, you can complete your mail ballot and drop it off at your county Board of Elections office or any poll site open on Tuesday. Your mail ballot will count if the Board of Elections receives it by Election Day, or it arrives within a week of Election Day but has a postmark of Election Day. The United States Postal Service does not always apply a postmark the day an item is received, so it may be too late to put a ballot into the postal mail to ensure timely delivery.
In New Jersey, you can drop off mail-in ballots at a secure drop box or your county Board of Elections office. You can find a drop box location in your county here. For those returning ballots via mail, ballots must be postmarked no later than Election Day at 8 p.m. and received no later than six days after the election. Note: Polling sites DO NOT accept vote-by-mail ballots.
What is on the ballot in New York?
New York voters will choose their governor, state attorney general, state comptroller, along with federal and state legislative representatives.
Read more about the candidates in our New York voter guide.
What about New York City specifically?
In New York City, voters will also be asked to decide five ballot questions. A guide to the ballot questions is here.
Who is on the ballot in New Jersey?
Congressional races are dominating this year’s election cycle in New Jersey. You can find our early voting guide here.
First-time Democratic nominee Rebecca Bennett is attempting to unseat Republican Rep. Tom Kean in New Jersey’s 7th Congressional District in what’s expected to be New Jersey’s most competitive midterm race.
Unlike some other rising Democrats in the state, like progressive Rep. Analilia Mejia and Dr. Adam Hamawy, Bennett has run as a middle-of-the-road Democrat in a typically conservative district that has leaned Republican since 2020. The 39-year old former healthcare executive and Navy helicopter pilot has focused on affordability issues like rising costs for gas, grocery, childcare and healthcare. Read more about her attempt to court independent and Republican voters in the red-leaning district in North Jersey.
Kean, the political heir of one of the Garden State’s most well-known political dynasties, is seeking a third term in Congress. The 58-year old Republican is the son of a popular former governor and served in the state Legislature for nearly two decades. He is running in the shadow of President Donald Trump’s sinking poll numbers in the state and has faced lingering questions about a 100+ day absence from Congress earlier this year when Kean was hospitalized for serious depression.
Who else is running in New Jersey?
In the closing days of the midterm season, the race in South Jersey’s 2nd Congressional District has emerged as a surprisingly close contest between four-term incumbent Republican Rep. Jeff Van Drew and Democratic challenger Zack Mullock, a small-town Jersey Shore mayor from Cape May. Early voting showed Democrats building a large lead in the vote heading into election day.
Democratic congressional candidates Rep. Analilia Mejia, first-time candidate Dr. Adam Hamawy, and Rep. Nellie Pou are all expected to be victorious Tuesday in districts around the state, according to political analysts like Cook Political Report and Decision Desk HQ. Republican Rep. Chris Smith is also favored to win a 24th term in New Jersey’s ruby red 4th district.
Democratic Sen. Cory Booker is also heavily favored to win a fourth consecutive term amidst rumors he’s teeing up a run for president in 2028.
Are federal law enforcement or immigration agents allowed at poll sites?
No. Federal law enforcement officials are not legally allowed at poll sites. Every New York City poll site does have NYPD officers assigned to it under state law.
If a voter has a problem in New York or New Jersey, the person can call 1-866-OUR-VOTE to speak with a volunteer with the nonpartisan Election Protection hotline.
This story has been updated with additional information.

https://gothamist.com/news/how-to-spend-.title: How to spend $20M in East Williamsburg? A discussion begins.
https://gothamist.com/news/how-to-spend-.author: Willow Higgins
https://gothamist.com/news/how-to-spend-.text:
The East Williamsburg section of Brooklyn is wrestling with an enviable question: How to spend a $20 million grant from Albany?
Last summer, the neighborhood won the money through the governor’s Downtown Revitalization Initiative, which funds capital projects to spur economic development in commercial corridors.
Community members and organizations have been asked to submit project proposals to help decide how the money is spent. Applications close on Wednesday. Those close to the initiative say it’s a tricky question in a community with so many divergent needs.
The neighborhood has become a destination for wealthy families looking to raise their children, and young people seeking a version of the cool, creative Williamsburg that its namesake to the west once was. East Williamsburg is also home to generations of residents who have managed to stay, mostly in rent-regulated and tenant-protected sites.
City leaders in charge of allocating the grant funding are trying to identify projects that will serve the entire community, not just those who patron the new fancy restaurants and night clubs.
“Navigating the demands of the neighborhood … is really challenging,” said Francesca Fernandez Bruce, the president of the Grand Street Business Improvement District and leader on the project. “It’s a hard line to walk in terms of balancing and making sure that everything is inclusive.”
Bruce said neglected infrastructure and aging public spaces are a concern, especially when residents can shop online instead. Low foot traffic was the paramount issue merchants said they were concerned about in a neighborhood needs assessment published this spring.
“East Williamsburg is a really great example of a community that has in many ways been underserved for a really long time, both from a design and a financial perspective,” Bruce said.
Tree canopy and open green space in the neighborhood is some of the smallest in the city, according to a report published alongside the request for proposals. Summers are desolate, she said, and winters are dark.
“ At 4 p.m. in the wintertime you can't really walk down [the street] because cause there's no sidewalk lighting,” Bruce said. “People don't feel safe to go shopping, and that hurts our mom and pops.”
But, she said, a few simple fixes could make a big difference.
Theresa Middleton, now 53, said she agrees.
Middletown said she has lived in the same apartment in East Williamsburg since she was a child. The rent stabilized unit was passed down by her parents.
She said it’s the only reason she can still afford to live in the neighborhood.
“I wouldn't be able to pay it, between light, gas,” Middleton said. “It's hard nowadays, especially with the cost of everything, trying to make ends meet.”
With all the new wealth in the neighborhood, she said she’s surprised that there’s not more open places for people to just hang out. She hopes the new grant funding can change that.
“It’s peaceful,” she said. “It's a good place to raise a family. There is a future there. There really is.”
A neighborhood identity crisis
The neighborhood’s own name makes some New Yorkers scratch their heads.
Alberto Valentin, who leads the Graham Street BID, told Gothamist that local lore is that East Williamsburg’s name was popularized by developers trying to take advantage of Williamsburg’s brand – which, before it became one of the most costly places to live in the city, was a hot spot for artists and hipsters.
If it’s true, the developer’s trick worked. More than a decade later, the neighborhood has clearly gone through what Valentin calls the “g-word” – otherwise known as gentrification.
Bistros with no available reservations in sight, wine bars and luxury towers are now plentiful. The average one-bedroom apartment in the neighborhood, according to Rent Hop, an apartment rental website, is about $4,700 a month.
Farther east, the area is industrial, where warehouse clubs, some cramming in thousands of sweaty bodies at a time, are peppered among powerplants and manufacturing facilities.
Leah Archibald, the executive director of Evergreen Exchange, a nonprofit that represents the industrial and manufacturing community, said that “all the cool stuff migrated east,” after “Williamsburg proper” became home to luxury chains like Chanel and Hermès.
But, East Williamsburg, too, has become whiter, more affluent and more expensive to live, according to data published along with Downtown Revitalization Initiative’s request for proposals.
As of 2024, the number of non-white residents of East Williamsburg have declined since 2010, according to the report. The neighborhood's median household income rose 50% over the same period, to more than $82,000 — higher than the average for Brooklynites.
But there are still pockets of people living in poverty, said Antonio Reynoso, the Brooklyn borough president, and gentrification may have already maximized their displacement.
There are about six public housing developments in the same general area, he said, and “no one from those housing developments is going anywhere.”
The key, he said, will be to make the area inhabitable for the different demographics who now call the neighborhood home.
“ People assume that because of the gentrification, that there are no more poor people,” Reynoso said.
East Williamsburg, Reynoso said, is now lined with fancy bars and restaurants for what he calls “ a very specific demographic that has a lot of expendable cash.”
But the thousands who live in public housing or tenant protected units don’t necessarily benefit from that kind of development, he said.
The changes, Reynoso said, “are not supporting the longer term residents in the neighborhood.”
He said he hopes an influx in money for neighborhood improvements will change the script.
“ We feel like we can build an environment that is both fruitful and economically prosperous, while not forgetting that we have a large population of poor people that still need services as well,” Reynoso said.
The $20 million question
So how’s the money going to be spent?
“That’s the $20 million question,” Bruce said. The wish list for potential neighborhood improvements to East Williamsburg is long.
The planning committee Downtown Revitalization Initiative will ultimately decide from the project proposals that community members have thrown in the ring – and a consultant will help tweak the projects to make sure they are feasible.
Bruce and Reynoso said they’re particularly interested in projects that improve public space: efforts like adding more green space and better lighting, outdoor dining areas, turning cul de sacs into small parks, and sprucing up the existing parks with more trees, better benches, dog runs and lending libraries.
Only so much can be done with the money, Reynoso said, but he said he hopes the grant will open the floodgates for additional investment.
“ I expect the city to be big-time partners with us for this,” Reynoso said. “ I expect that at least $40 million to come down on this project once it's all said and done.”
As for Middleton, she said that the hopes from longstanding community members are simple.
“People just want to live decent and comfortable,” Middleton said. “They don't want that stress … Should I pay my rent, my light, or put food on the table for my children? They just want to be in peace and live. That's, that's all we hear.”

https://hyperallergic.com/fernando-calvi.title: Fernando Calvillo, Beloved Fixture of Oklahoma's Art Community, Dies in Train Crash in Spain
https://hyperallergic.com/fernando-calvi.author: Anna Lee
https://hyperallergic.com/fernando-calvi.text:
Fernando Calvillo, Beloved Fixture of Oklahoma's Art Community, Dies in Train Crash in Spain
“He embraced people wholeheartedly, recognized what they needed, and connected them with opportunities and with one another,” said Calvillo’s colleague.
Fernando Calvillo, an esteemed artist and leader in Oklahoma City's arts community, died in a high-speed collision between two trains in the province of Toledo, Spain, on Wednesday, October 28. He was aboard with his husband, Lawrence Naff, who is expected to recover from serious injuries at a local hospital.
The crash, which Spanish Transport Minister Óscar Puente attributed to computational failure and human oversight, claimed the lives of at least 68 other people and comes just nine months after another crash in southern Andalusia in Spain, which claimed the lives of 46 people. Puente resigned today, November 3, after a congressional session regarding rail safety.
Calvillo was declared a missing person until the Mexican Foreign Ministry and the Oklahoma Visual Arts Coalition (OVAC), where Calvillo worked as the director of community relations, confirmed his death in separate statements on Monday, November 1.

https://hyperallergic.com/exhibition-as-.title: Exhibition as Living Archive: the 1950s Baghdad Modern Art Group in the UAE Today
https://hyperallergic.com/exhibition-as-.author: NYU Abu Dhabi
https://hyperallergic.com/exhibition-as-.text:
Exhibition as Living Archive: the 1950s Baghdad Modern Art Group in the UAE Today
All Manner of Experiments: Legacies of the Baghdad Modern Art Group, Curated by Nada Shabout, on view at the NYU Abu Dhabi Art Gallery through January 3, 2027
The Baghdad Modern Art Group was established in 1951 by two of Iraq’s most influential artists, Jewad Selim (1919–1961) and Shakir Hassan Al Said (1925–2004), and grew to engage many of Iraq’s leading artists, architects, poets, and more. Together, they sought to develop a new art form, one that negotiated a time of globally inflected modernism from Baghdad, an Abbasid city (est. 762 CE) that traces its lineage to the ancient civilizations of Mesopotamia. In All Manner of Experiments: Legacies of the Baghdad Modern Art Group at NYU Abu Dhabi Art Gallery, Dr. Nada Shabout brings together the artists from this circle, as well as those whom its work influenced, both at the time and in the following generations, until today.
After the Kingdom of Iraq’s formation in 1932 as an independent state, Iraqi artists explored the new parameters of the secularized, modern society that was emerging following Britain’s maneuvering to dismantle the Ottoman Empire. Artists questioned the ability of traditional “Islamic art” practices to present their contemporary realities, searching for a more effective visual language. In this context, modern art provided a conduit for exploration and was perceived by Iraqi artists as a global space of shared humanity.
Various artist groups launched initiatives to convey the importance of national representation through culture, which included promoting the modern art movement in Iraq. This period set the stage for Iraq’s so-called golden age of the 1950s: a time of maturation for a generation of artists pivotal in initiating rigorous standards of art theory and practice, thus charting new possibilities for future generations.
The experimental ethos of the group continues to resonate today beyond Baghdad to direct and connect contemporary Iraqi artists around the world to each other.
Featured artists include Faraj Abbo, Sadik Kwaish Alfraji, Himat Mohammad Ali, Rasoul Alwan, Suad al-Attar, Qahtan Awni, Dia al-Azzawi, Bogus Bablanian, Amar Dawod, Ghassan Ghaib, Faiq (Faeq) Hassan, Mohammed Ghani Hikmat, Jabra Ibrahim Jabra, Rand Abdul Jabbar, Fouad Jihad, Saadi Al Kaabi, Ardash Kakafian, Salma Khoury, Hanaa Malallah, Mahmoud Obaidi, Widad al-Orfali, Khalid al-Rahal, Kareem Risan, Miran al-Saadi, Mahmoud Sabri, Naziha Salim, Nizar (Nazar) Salim, Shakir Hassan Al Said, Delair Shaker, Jewad Selim, Lorna Selim, Walid Siti, Ismail Fattah (Al-Turk), Madiha Umar, Khalil al-Ward, and Nazar Yahya.
The exhibition’s curator Dr. Nada Shabout has published widely on modern and contemporary Arab and Iraqi art and has curated numerous exhibitions. She has joined NYU Abu Dhabi as a senior investigator at al Mawrid Arab Center for the Study of Art and as a visiting professor of art history. She is the founding president of the Association for Modern and Contemporary Art from the Arab World, Iran, and Turkey (AMCA) and founding director of the Modern Art Iraq Archive (MAIA).
The exhibition is on view at the NYU Abu Dhabi Art Gallery through January 3, 2027.
Learn more at nyuad.nyu.edu

Just one week after the Pace Gallery reported 35.5% losses, CEO Marc Glimcher has announced that the gallery is looking for new London outpost, as it put its Hanover Square location on the market in June.
Pace published its 2024 accounts with Companies House, the British government’s business register, last week. The filing was ten months late, and showed a turnover of $67.7 million. Shortly after, it published its 2025 accounts, with turnover dipping 2.6%, to $65.9 million. Pace’s UK registered company, The Pace Gallery Limited, is an umbrella company for all of its operations, excluding their Tokyo and US locations.
Glimcher told ARTnews in an interview that the gallery had a record art fair at Art Basel Paris and sellout shows of young artists. “We did a balance sheet shift, which appears to be a loss because we’re changing around the way we invest money and take money from other units and let the money flow through each unit independently,” said Glimcher to ARTnews. “We’re in a process of keeping those units a little more autonomous and self-sufficient; to do that, you have to shift the balance sheet.” Glimcher told the outlet that Pace will never close in London and that it is already looking at new locations.
The gallery laid off 50 staffers and dropped 50 artists from its roster this year. According to Glimcher, these artists were not artists the gallery had a “super active engagement with.”
“We have had an extremely profitable year already in Los Angeles. The things we’ve done are already bearing fruit, and they’re bearing fruit because the market has substantially changed,” he said. “What we’re doing in London, when we have the space and announce it, it’s going to make a lot of sense to everybody.”

https://hyperallergic.com/guadalupe-rosa.title: Guadalupe Rosales’s Portable Archive of East LA
https://hyperallergic.com/guadalupe-rosa.author: Carolina A. Miranda
https://hyperallergic.com/guadalupe-rosa.text:
Guadalupe Rosales’s Portable Archive of East LA
In two new books, the artist weaves her archive of photos, ephemera, and flyers into the story of ’90s Chicanx youth culture, tracing both a personal and collective coming-of-age.
If someone had described Los Angeles youth culture in the late 1990s, they might have invoked towheaded surfers, Sunset Strip hair bands, Beverly Hills teens, and the graffiti-soaked clubs that harbored New Wave and punk. Thanks to Guadalupe Rosales, our view of that time is now much more expansive.
Since 2015, the Los Angeles artist has collected the stories of the city’s Chicanx and Latinx youth — in particular, women and girls — via a pair of wildly popular Instagram pages, @veteranas_and_rucas and @map_pointz, which have become a collective archive of pre-internet adolescent life in the ’80s and ’90s. Big hair. Lined lips. Body-hugging tanks and baggy jeans. Not to mention the party flyers bearing titles like “Bad Influence” and “Titty Juice,” with their irreverent promises of liberation.
Over the years, Rosales has displayed this ephemera in imaginative ways, often in architectonic environments that pulse with the energy of nocturnal gatherings. In her installation for In Minor Keys, the international exhibition at the 61st Venice Biennale, infinity mirrors edged with neon are embedded with artifacts and suspended on a steel structure evoking the form of a SoCal bungalow.
A new project, however, finds the artist presenting her archive in more intimate ways. East of the River: A Memoir of Los Angeles Girlhood, published this fall, assembles many of the photos, flyers, news clips, and testimonials that followers have sent her for more than a decade. To that, she adds her own photographs and experiences, relaying the poignant story of her Eastside upbringing and the ways in which revelry with friends offered a respite from troubles both at home and in the larger city: the 1992 uprising, growing anti-immigrant sentiment, and gang violence. The latter claimed the life of her beloved cousin, Ever Sánchez, who was killed at a party in 1996. “It took me years to forgive those who took his life,” she writes, “but eventually I was able to turn the grief into altars and memorials and storytelling.”

The Kennedy Center Honors, the marquee event of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, will celebrate a host of performers on December 7, even while the institution is at the center of legal and political fights.
This year’s honorees are country star Barbara Mandrell, singer and onetime teen idol Paul Anka, actor Andy Garcia, music producer David Foster, and playwright David Mamet. The Kennedy Center Honors began in 1978, and for the first time in its history, the gala ceremony will be held off-site, at the Capital One Arena in downtown Washington, DC, instead of at its traditional venue, the Opera House at the Kennedy Center.
The move is the result of months of turmoil surrounding the institution, beginning in 2025, when Trump stacked the board with loyalists, who then voted to add his name to that of the center’s. Officials then closed the building, citing the need for a $257 million renovation project. Although a court ruled the addition illegal, the announcement of this year’s honorees still bore Trump’s name, according to the New York Times.
The Times also reports that lawyers for Representative Joyce Beatty of Ohio, an ex officio member of the center’s board who is suing to block the closure of the center, have cited documents that show that its shuttering is intended to hide its decline under Trump’s stewardship. She argues that trustees voted to close the center under financial pressure, after artists and patrons fled, and out of fealty to the president.
“Defendants are shuttering the Kennedy Center to hide the ongoing mismanagement of this once vibrant institution and to placate its current chairman,” they wrote in the filing.
The filing contains text messages from Donna Arduin Kauranen, the center’s former chief financial officer, about a conversation between a conversation between trump allies Jennifer Fischer, the board’s vice chair, and Howard Lutnick, the secretary of commerce. In one message, Arduin Kauranen, referring to Fischer, writes, “She said we are broke and borrowed money to pay the bills.”
Lawyers from the Justice Department, which is representing the center in court, have argued that given the “severe structural deficiencies,” closure the building “was the only responsible option.”

The organizers of the India Art Fair have named more than 120 participants in its eighteenth iteration, set to run February 4–7, 2027, at the NSIC Exhibition Grounds in New Delhi. Among the returning international galleries are Galleria Continua, neugerreimschneider, Sundaram Tagore Gallery, Whitestone Gallery, and David Zwirner. India’s Nature Morte, whose founder, Peter Nagy, died last month, will be present, alongside well-known Indian galleries Chemould Prescott Road, DAG, Experimenter, Jhaveri Contemporary, and Vadehra Art Gallery.
The fair will welcome a cadre of fresh faces this year: Delhi’s Pristine Contemporary, Gallery XXL, and Gallery Vayu are all making their debuts, as are London’s Chilli, and the Opera Gallery, which has sixteen outposts worldwide.
“The 18th edition of India Art Fair reflects the remarkable energy and ambition of South Asia’s artistic landscape today” said fair director Jaya Asokan in a statement. “What makes our 2027 fair particularly exciting is the momentum we have built through our year-round programming across the country.”
The fair promises an expanded Design section featuring both established and emerging studios, and will center the relationship among art, craft and design practices, while the Focus section will highlight works by artists including Rina Banerjee, Sameer Kulavoor and Ketaki Sarpotdar.
Among the projects and interventions planned for the fair are Jitish Kallat’s architectural reworking of his 2015 work Here After Here After Here, which will see him cover the fair’s exterior with highway signs; a large-scale outdooor Birender Yadav installation presented by the Kiran Nadar Museum of Art, and a textile work by December Design honoring Jaipur’s three hundredth anniversary, presented by the City Palace Museum.
The India Art Fair was founded in 2008 in New Delhi. It is owned by Montgomery Arts, which runs regional art fairs including Hong Kong’s Art Central, Shanghai’s Photofairs, Taipei Dangdai, Sydney Contemporary, Singapore’s Art SG, and Yokohama’s Tokyo Gendai. Plans for a Mumbai iteration were scrapped ahead of its planned 2025 launch and to date have not been revitalized.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/mu.title: Nearly Everyone Is Concerned About How Museums Use AI in Exhibitions, Survey Says
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/mu.author: Alex Greenberger
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/mu.text:
A new survey suggests that the broad majority of US museum visitors are worried about how AI is used in the production of exhibitions and marketing materials, mirroring an anxiety about AI that proliferates widely today.
The American Alliance of Museums‘s 2026 survey showed that just 9 percent of respondents accepted the use of AI in museum shows. Nineteen percent were unbothered by the notion that AI could used for brainstorming but not exhibition texts, meanwhile, and 29 percent said they felt no reservations about the usage of AI to write emails sent by museum officials.
Forty-three percent of respondents said they expected humans to “develop all content from museums, including exhibitions, emails…everything.”
AI is not yet widely used to produce exhibitions. But a New York Times report from this past weekend revealed that a handful of forthcoming shows will incorporate it, though not always in the form of wall texts. For one, the Smithsonian’s National Museum of Asian Art will involve AI in a VR recreation of James McNeill Whistler’s Peacock Room for its version of a Tate-organized retrospective for the artist.
The AAM survey also addressed the issue of museum attendance, a perennial concern since the onset of the pandemic in 2020, which limited visitorship to such a degree that many institutions have still struggled to bounce back. The survey did not explicitly tackle the amount of visitors each institution receives annually, but it did suggest a new problem in its place: the issue of repeat visitation.
“In the six years since the pandemic began, this repeat visitation has leveled off into a lower ‘new normal’ that seems to reflect enduring changes in behavior,” the survey said. “In other words, it’s not whether people are visiting museums that’s causing attendance shortfalls; it’s how often.”
In more positive terms, the survey noted that, where museums previously saw their audience “to be whiter, older, and more educated than Americans on average,” now there are signs this is changing.
Per the survey, “only 47 percent [of museum visitors] hold a college degree, only 35 percent are white (not Hispanic or Latine), and only 26 percent are 60 or older. In fact, white respondents are the most likely to report “never” visiting museums (while Asians and Asian Americans are the most likely to report visiting), and adults over 60 are the least likely of any age/life stage group to have visited in the past year (while parents or guardians of minor children are the most likely).”
And the public appears to want to museums to remain inclusive, even as the current Trump administration seeks to change that. “While younger people and liberals show the most inclusive attitudes, the majority of all age segments and the majority of conservatives still fall on the side of inclusion,” the AAM survey said.

https://taz.de/Rohstoffboom-in-Brasilien.title: Rohstoffboom in Brasilien: Ein Dorf wehrt sich
https://taz.de/Rohstoffboom-in-Brasilien.author: Alice de Souza
https://taz.de/Rohstoffboom-in-Brasilien.text:
Rohstoffboom in Brasilien: Ein Dorf wehrt sich
Im brasilianischen Bundesstaat Bahia haben Anwohner ein Gesetz gegen Bergbau durchgesetzt. Dennoch gehen die Erkundungsarbeiten weiter.
Zunächst tauchten plötzlich Fremde in der Gegend auf. Sie kamen mit dem Auto, hielten mitten auf der Straße und sammelten Sand ein. Später begannen sie, Grundstücke zu betreten und Markierungen auf dem Gelände anzubringen. Schließlich sprachen die Bewohner*innen der ländlichen Gebiete von Itarantim, einer Stadt im Südwesten des brasilianischen Bundesstaates Bahia, die Unbekannten direkt an. Diese wollten Bohrungen auf ihren Grundstücken durchführen und boten dafür etwas Geld und zahlreiche Versprechungen.
„Sie erweckten den Eindruck, als hätten sie etwas so Wertvolles wie Erdöl gefunden“, erzählt der 43-jährige Juliano Coelho, Bewohner und Vorsitzender der Gemeindevertretung von Corgão in Itarantim.
Euromérica-Workshop
15 Journalist:innen aus 12 Ländern Lateinamerikas nehmen am Workshop „Euromérica“ der taz panterstiftung teil. Es geht um Chancen und Herausforderungen des EU-Mercosur-Abkommens und die lateinamerikanisch-europäischen Beziehungen. Am 5. 12. erscheint dazu eine Beilage in der taz, am 9. 12. gibt es einen öffentlichen Talk in der taz Kantine. Alle Texte finden Sie hier.
Die Fremden waren gekommen, um nach jenen Rohstoffen zu suchen, die derzeit als neuer Reichtum der Welt gehandelt werden: kritische Mineralien und Seltene Erden. Als die Bewohner*innen verstanden, worum es ging, beschlossen sie, sich gegen die Erkundungsarbeiten in ihrer Region zu organisieren.
Gemeinsam erarbeiteten sie ein Gesetzesvorhaben und setzten dessen Verabschiedung durch. Es verbietet sämtliche Erkundungs- und Bergbauaktivitäten auf ihrem Territorium. Angesichts der zunehmenden Spekulation mit Rohstoffvorkommen in Brasilien, das nach China über die zweitgrößten Reserven an Seltenen Erden weltweit verfügt, kämpfen die Menschen in Itarantim nun darum, dass ihr Gesetz auch tatsächlich eingehalten wird.
Ein Jahr Widerstand
Das im August 2025 vom Stadtrat einstimmig verabschiedete und nur zehn Tage später von der Stadtverwaltung unterzeichnete Gesetz stellt die sechs Gebirgszüge der Gemeinde unter Schutz. Sie gelten fortan als Natur-, Landschafts- und touristisches Erbe und sind vor Aktivitäten mit hohen Umweltauswirkungen wie dem Bergbau geschützt.
In Brasilien können Bürger*innen einer Gemeinde selbst einen Gesetzesvorschlag in den Stadtrat einbringen, ohne dafür auf die Unterstützung eines Abgeordneten angewiesen zu sein. Dieses in der Verfassung verankerte Recht setzt allerdings voraus, dass mindestens fünf Prozent der Wahlberechtigten der Gemeinde den Vorschlag unterstützen.
Als Bewohner der Gemeinde Água Vermelha bemerkten, dass Fremde für Bergbauprojekte ihr Land betraten, begann im August 2024 eine breite Mobilisierung für das spätere Gesetz. Die Menschen errichteten eine Protestblockade, um von dem Erkundungsunternehmen Cacto Consultoria Erklärungen zu den geplanten Arbeiten zu verlangen. Die Aktion endete damit, dass die Mitarbeiter des Unternehmens das Gebiet verlassen mussten.
Daraufhin formierte sich Widerstand unter Kleinbauern und -bäuerinnen, ländlichen Vereinigungen, Lehrkräften und religiösen Gemeinden gegen die Erkundung des Schwermetalls Niob und Seltener Erden. Bewohner*innen aus Stadt und Land schlossen sich zusammen und gründeten eine Bürgerkommission für Umweltfragen. Sie sammelten schnell die nötigen Unterschriften, organisierten Aufklärungsveranstaltungen sowie zwei Demonstrationen.
Schlüsselrolle für Brasilien
Die Nachfrage nach Rohstoffen für die Energiewende und Digitalisierung hat Brasilien in eine strategisch wichtige Position im globalen Wettlauf um Bodenschätze gebracht. Die Vorkommen an Niob, Naturgraphit, Nickel und Seltenen Erden sowie das Potenzial zur Förderung von Kupfer, Lithium und Silizium könnten dazu beitragen, die Abhängigkeit der USA und der Europäischen Union vom chinesischen Rohstoffmarkt zu verringern.
Brasilien fördert beispielsweise mehr als 90 Prozent des weltweit produzierten Niobs. Das Mineral ist auch einer der Gründe für die Erkundungsarbeiten in Itarantim. Zugleich ist das Land bereits ein bedeutender Rohstofflieferant für ausländische Märkte. Eine Studie der brasilianischen Agentur für Exportförderung und Investitionen (ApexBrasil) zeigt, dass die Europäische Union 2025 insgesamt 37,6 Prozent der brasilianischen Exporte von neun kritischen Rohstoffen abnahm: Kupfer, Niob, Silizium, Nickel, Lithium, Graphit, Seltene Erden, Phosphat und Kalium.
Laut der Studie könnten europäische Regulierungsrahmen und spezielle Förderprogramme wie der Critical Raw Materials Act (CRMA), die Global-Gateway-Initiative und die European Raw Materials Alliance (ERMA) Brasilien zu einem wichtigen Partner bei der Diversifizierung europäischer Rohstofflieferanten machen. Ein formelles Abkommen über die Rohstoffversorgung wie mit anderen lateinamerikanischen Ländern gibt es zwar nicht. Die EU spricht jedoch von einer bereits etablierten Zusammenarbeit mit Brasilien in diesem Bereich.
Die internationale Nachfrage schlägt sich unmittelbar in den Erkundungsaktivitäten vor Ort nieder. Ziel ist es, die Förderkapazitäten auszuweiten. Nach Angaben der brasilianischen Bergbaubehörde ANM verfügt Itarantim über 158 erteilte Genehmigungen zur mineralischen Erkundung. 44 davon betreffen Niob und Seltene Erden.
Vertiefung historischer Konflikte
Itarantim liegt in Bahia, einem der brasilianischen Bundesstaaten, die im Zentrum des Wettlaufs um Seltene Erden und kritische Rohstoffe stehen. Bis Juli 2026 entfielen 37 Prozent der mehr als 2.700 Bergbauverfahren zu Seltenen Erden in Brasilien auf Bahia.
„Die Anträge auf Flächen für die mineralische Erkundung und den Abbau überschneiden sich in weiten Teilen mit den Gebieten indigener und traditioneller Gemeinschaften“, erklärt Valdirene Rocha, Professorin am Bundesinstitut für Bildung, Wissenschaft und Technologie von Bahia. Ihr zufolge verschärft der Wettlauf um Rohstoffe die historischen sozialökologischen Konflikte in der Region. „Diesen Projekten liegt eine kapitalistische Logik zugrunde, die auf Profit ausgerichtet ist“, meint Rocha. „Sie stehen im Widerspruch zu den Formen des Zusammenlebens mit den Territorien, für die die Menschen lange gekämpft haben.“
