https://apache.be/2026/10/23/advocatenko.title: Advocatenkosten voor deontologische raad wegen op journalistiek
https://apache.be/2026/10/23/advocatenko.author: Steven Vanden Bussche
https://apache.be/2026/10/23/advocatenko.text:
Journalisten en media worden geconfronteerd met dure advocatenbureaus die mensen bijstaan tijdens de behandeling van deontologische klachten voor de Raad voor de Journalistiek. Die verregaande juridisering jaagt journalisten en media, klein én groot, op kosten terwijl hun verzekering hiervoor niet tussenkomst.
Eind vorig jaar onthulde Apache hoe twee Belgen verdienen aan een omstreden Congolese belasting op het gebruik van een mobiele telefoon. Journalist Thibault Coigniez achterhaalde hoe de Antwerpse diamantair Philippe Heilmann en de Brusselse zakenman Jérôme Spaey met hun bedrijf 5C Energy een lucratief contract sloten met de Congolese overheid. Het contract zelf blijft tot op heden een Congolees staatsgeheim.
Heilmann was niet opgezet met de publicatie. De Antwerpse diamantair werd nochtans tijdig gecontacteerd voor een weerwoord, zijn reactie werd in het artikel verwerkt en ook nog eens integraal gepubliceerd onderaan het artikel.
De Raad stelde geen inbreuken vast op het principe van waarheidsgetrouwe berichtgeving, maar jaagde Apache wel op kosten
Begin 2026 eisten advocaten Olivier Sasserath en Herman Croux verregaande aanpassingen aan het stuk. Via een ingebrekestelling dreigden Heilmanns advocaten met een schadeclaim. De diamantair diende ook een klacht in bij de Raad voor de Journalistiek, die zich buigt over het deontologisch handelen van journalisten en media. Het bedrijf 5C Energy stuurde tot slot een Recht van antwoord dat Apache, hoewel er geen juridische verplichting was, integraal publiceerde.
Aangezien Heilmann geld veil had om het gespecialiseerde Brusselse advocatenbureau MVVP op Apache af te sturen, zag de redactie zich genoodzaakt ook een advocaat te raadplegen. Na heen-en-weer geschrijf tussen advocaten en een hoorzitting, besliste de Raad voor de Journalistiek om de klacht van tafel te vegen. De Raad stelde geen inbreuken vast op het principe van waarheidsgetrouwe berichtgeving, maar jaagde Apache wel op kosten.
Doe een gift op BE55 5230 8045 8444 (met vermelding ‘STOP SLAPP’) of via onze giftenpagina.
Geen alleenstaand geval
Eerder dit jaar diende een gepensioneerde politieman via zijn advocaat klacht in tegen Humo en een journalist. De politieman werd eind jaren 90 van het Dutroux-onderzoek gehaald. In een commentaarstuk wees journalist Douglas De Coninck erop dat de agent destijds een verband zag tussen de bende rond Dutroux en twee Franse gangsters die opdoken in het onderzoek naar de Bende van Nijvel. De journalist handelde onafhankelijk, meende de Raad, en had geen “kwaadaardige bedoelingen” zoals de voormalige politieman opwierp.
Freddy Kempeneer, hoofdredacteur van Persinfo.be, een nieuwssite die regionaal nieuws uit het Pajottenland, de Zennevallei en de Denderstreek brengt, werd dan weer verrast door de aanwezigheid van een advocaat tijdens de hoorzitting. De klager, een schepen die zonder omgevingsvergunning verbouwingswerken liet uitvoeren, bracht Kempeneers niet op de hoogte dat een advocaat zijn belangen zou verdedigen.
“Ik voelde me daardoor benadeeld, te meer er ook geen beroepsmogelijkheid is tegen uitspraken van de Raad”, zegt Kempeneer. “Had ik dat geweten, dan zou ik me ook laten bijstaan door een advocaat. Dat die advocaat daar plots stond, was voor mij ook intimiderend.” De klacht bleek grotendeels ongegrond, op een feitelijk element en te weinig responstijd voor wederhoor na.
Er zijn het afgelopen anderhalf jaar nog meer voorbeelden gepasseerd waarbij advocaten de klagers bijstonden, maar finaal bot vingen bij de Raad: bij een klacht van een opgepakte verdachte crypto-oplichter over berichtgeving bij HLN en een gesanctioneerde deurwaarder bij opiniesite Doorbraak.be.
Niet gedekt door verzekering
Charlotte Michils, algemeen secretaris van de Vlaamse Vereniging van Journalisten (VVJ) merkt op dat een procedure voor de Raad voor de Journalistiek laagdrempelig en gratis is. De zaak komt pas voor de Raad wanneer er geen minnelijke schikking getroffen kan worden.
Karl van den Broeck: “Voor die éne zaak moest Apache ruim 5.000 euro ophoesten, terwijl het dossier feitelijk onderbouwd was en op een deontologisch correcte manier afgewerkt”
“Als de ene partij een advocaat in de arm neemt, is het niet onlogisch dat ook de andere partij dat overweegt”, zegt Michils. “De aanwezigheid van een juridisch professional brengt immers de nodige techniciteit in het dossier waardoor het meer tijd en middelen vergt om je te verdedigen. Voor minder kapitaalkrachtige partijen kan dat een probleem zijn.”
Omdat de Raad van de Journalistiek geen schadevergoedingen toekent, dekt een verzekering burgerlijke aansprakelijkheid ‘beroep en uitbating’ juridisch advies en bijstand bij de Raad voor de Journalistiek niet.
“Dat zorgde ervoor dat Apache voor die éne zaak ruim 5.000 euro moest ophoesten, terwijl het dossier feitelijk onderbouwd was en op een deontologisch correcte manier afgewerkt”, zegt Karl van den Broeck, hoofdredacteur van Apache. “We betreuren die manier van werken en maken ons daarover ook zorgen.”

https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.title: The Punk-Rock Appeal of the Women’s Pro Baseball League
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.author: G’Ra Asim
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
The new competitive circuit captures the energy and DIY spirit of punk, while promoting a surprisingly sturdy vision of civic belonging.

Ashton Lansdell of the Los Angeles Queens celebrates after scoring against the San Francisco Firebells in game two of the Women’s Pro Baseball League Championship.

Cultic ecstasy seizes my body. I leap to my feet from a sitting position and thrust my hands skyward like someone who got the Holy Ghost in church. Like a contagion, the same behavior ripples across the aisle I’m sitting in. About a quarter of the way across the crowded baseball stadium, the vector peters out. Either the people roughly 10 rows away don’t notice our spirited efforts to sustain a wave across the entire crowd, or they just don’t feel like participating.

“Those guys suck, dude,” our wave leader groans. “They need to get with the program!”

It’s no less than the sixth time that this person has hectored our section to start an ill-fated wave. To the chagrin of the visibly exasperated spectators around him, he has not lost hope.

I’m in the stands for game three of the Women’s Professional Baseball League’s best-of-five inaugural championship series. The Los Angeles Queens are up two games to none on the San Francisco Firebelles, and another Queens win will secure the championship. The WPBL website boasts that “for the first time in 70 years, the best women baseball players in the world are competing on a professional stage.” Players hail from across the United States and 11 other countries. The league’s first-ever regular season began a few weeks earlier on August 1, 2026. Each squad in the league played all the other teams five times, for a total of 15 regular season games in a triple round-robin format. For now, there are four teams in the WPBL, two of whom have already been eliminated: the Boston Hunters and the New York Heights. All the games are played in impartial Springfield, Illinois. Watching teams named aspirationally after major markets compete in the neutral territory of flyover country feels like a provisional unity of these States, in a way it’d be hard to approximate by other means.

I’ve taken a road trip from St. Louis, Missouri, where I live, to Springfield, which I’m not sure I’ve heard of before now. Despite the city’s claim to fame as the adult home of Abraham Lincoln, it wouldn’t have surprised me to find the Klan posted up in the stadium parking lot. Along with my intrepid companions Jesse and Doc, I bought tickets online the night before the game, but pickings were slim. Three successive seats in the same row weren’t available. We bought a pair that were right next to each other and a third ticket a few rows behind those two. Our plan was to barnstorm the end of one row and dare anyone to challenge our claim. A group of white fans to our left look like they want to. They gawk over their shoulders at us like schoolyard extras in a Ruby Bridges movie. I almost hear my antebellum-era ancestors assembling into a bluesy chorus of telltale woe and foreboding.

When we pulled into Springfield half an hour ago, my eyes settled on a chain restaurant I’d never seen before.

“Taco Gringo?” I blurted. “Sounds a little too White Power for my taste. Is it really a selling point that gringos are back there making the tacos?”

“I don’t think the gringos are making the tacos,” Doc had joked. “They’re probably just cracking the whip.”

Though most of my teenage years and young adulthood took place on the East Coast, I’m a native St. Louisan. The MLB’s St. Louis Cardinals are our dominant sports franchise, so naturally my earliest baseball memories were formed at Busch Stadium. I’ve had difficulty rooting for the home team since the police killing of Ferguson teenager Mike Brown in 2014. That year, social media was awash in clips of mobs clad in Cards regalia spitting and cursing at Black Lives Matter protesters. It’s likely that there’s some overlap between the folks at the ballpark with me now and those justice-averse Cardinals fans. But here, as supporters of a new league, it feels like we have a clean slate.

Well, sort of. I can’t help but suspect that some percentage of the enthusiasm that radiates throughout Robin Roberts Stadium today is traceable to the 2023 NCAA women’s college basketball final, in which Caitlin Clark’s Iowa Hawkeyes fell to Angel Reese’s LSU Tigers. The widely watched showdown between two highly marketable and racially polarizing players sparked a surge in public interest in women’s sports. There is no competitive storyline Americans relish more than a clash between a Great White Hope and what they perceive as an uppity Black antagonist, and apparently the fervor is gender neutral. That revelation doesn’t exactly brighten the forecast for our crumbling empire, but it does boost the overall flashbulb wattage of women’s sports.

Here at game three of the WPBL’s inaugural championship series, fans carry signs with slogans like “I drove 300 miles to be a part of HERSTORY.” There is a palpable shared sense that the one thing better than being on the right side of history is cheering history on while you’re sitting by its third base line.

A strict, masc-of-center auntie in her 50s or 60s seated to my right foretells the outcome of each at-bat.

“That’s an out!” she yells sometimes, leaning back in her seat with her arms crossed as a fly ball lingers over second base.

“That’s a hit,” she claims other times, as soon as she hears the crack of the bat.

Growing up a baseball fan in the 1990s Midwest, I tracked the traditional box score stats in the paper every morning before school. Before the Moneyball movement, baseball diehards assessed player performance via straightforward statistical categories like batting average, fielding percentage, and runs batted in. These were the numbers you would see on the back of a baseball card. Starting in the early 2000s, those traditional statistics were phased out in favor of advanced analytics. Where sportscasters once narrated home runs by bellowing things like, “Busting out the whooping stick!,” they instead began to pepper the broadcast with references to math nerd esoterica like launch angle, spin rate, and exit velocity.

Look, I love Neil deGrasse Tyson. Physics has its place. But I doubt I’m speaking only for myself when I say I tune into baseball games to watch swaggering leviathans swing clubs at projectiles and hammer them to the moon. The shift in how baseball is discussed and understood is a microcosm for how the digital age has muddied the distinction between information and meaning. I appreciate that the experts can contextualize the game with such an impressive volume of information. This stern auntie’s play-by-play—which more than compensates with passion for what it lacks in data—strikes me as far more meaningful. The subtext of her commentary is that she’s been waiting for a league like this one for most of her life, and she’s not going to take one iota of action for granted.

Typically, yearning for baseball’s salad days would mark me as retrograde. In this case, I’m quite sure appreciating WPBL for its contrasts with MLB makes me a part of the vanguard. That said, I hesitate to position the WPBL as somehow morally superior to other professional sports leagues. Women’s sports are more often instrumentalized as battlegrounds in the culture wars than treated as legitimate ends in themselves. Moralizing is boring, and watching some of Earth’s most talented and tenacious people push their bodies to their limits in the name of autumnal glory is a good time. At least as much as we need an endless hermeneutics of ball, we need an erotics of ball.

Being taken out to this ballgame and taken out to the crowd also feels more poignant at a cultural moment defined by atomization. When things like, say, the venerable practice of wearing headphones when listening to media in public have fallen out of favor, any symbiosis between strangers feels like a sign of great respect in our culture. That’s what makes me realize why being absorbed into a fandom that’s both salutary and scintillating is so comforting, so familiar. The WPBL is the new punk rock.

As a millennial pushing 40, I’ve been a punk rocker much longer than I wasn’t one. I’m in two actively recording and gigging bands right now; I threw my first house show in my parents’ basement to celebrate my 15th birthday. Punk is about building the reconciled world in miniature and making its qualities infectious. Organizing a scene in your town is a small insurrectionary act—lining up a single domino that might, and sometimes does, kick-start a massive cascade.

A lot of the viral content about being an aging punk or emo kid focuses on nostalgia, as if the upshot of belonging to a forward-thinking subculture is to perseverate on the past. But the skills and instincts that we honed in VFW halls, garages, and church basements are just as easily applicable to the pursuit of gender equity in professional sports. Why settle into being a mark for the contrived cash grabs of your local Emo Nite when you could sublimate your ennui and residual angst into supporting a likeminded subculture like the WPBL instead?

Everyone who spent their teens and 20s working for street teams, orchestrating circle pits and Walls of Death, and tucking show flyers under windshield wipers can channel their punk-rock past in helping to secure the WPBL’s future. In 2018, Vice published a satirical article asking, “What Kind of Punk Dude Over 30 Are You?” The article joked that thirtysomething punks have a limited menu of acceptable hobbies and interests that they can cultivate to stave off the creep of cultural irrelevance. As I ponder the high jinks I might get up to as an over-40 punk, WPBL zealotry presents a compelling case.

Punks are better known for throwing bricks than laying them, but jury-rigging alternative structures is a big part of what we do. Whether we’re debuting a zine, a new band, or a DIY show space, we’ve always taken a distinct pride in supporting something precisely because it’s fledgling yet fertile, burgeoning and brimming with promise. The slightly grating wave whisperer here at the game reminds me of the dutiful mosh mentors I grew up with in the punk scene. They trained members of the audience to pick up anyone who fell down while slam dancing, reminded us to choose opportune and safe moments for our stage dives, and urged us to pass the hat for touring acts even when there wasn’t much money to go around. A movement isn’t only held together by the headliners—it’s also sustained by the energized, anonymous folks who dole out unsolicited marching orders, and those who roll with them even as we roll our eyes.

As the innings accumulate, I’m brought back to the beer-soaked stages and sweat-streaked floors where I cut my teeth. The early days of a punk band’s ascent are traditionally viewed as innocent, less cynical, driven by a genuine love of the game. Likewise, since legal gambling is now largely coextensive with professional sports, watching professional baseball for its own sake is a return to a simpler time. Cheering and jeering abound, but no one here is screaming about their parlay, or frantically refreshing the FanDuel app.

Much like navigating the street parking outside a makeshift venue or house show, figuring out where to leave the whip near the stadium was a riddle. My friend Jesse ended up pulling her SUV onto a muddy strip of grass next to some train tracks nearby. The demand for women’s professional baseball for the moment outpaces the real estate set aside for its patrons. We figured Springfield was still adjusting to the influx of fans from other cities, and strict parking enforcement would be unlikely. On his way to the ticket line, a man in a Chambray shirt and jeans looked back at our car and grinned impishly.

“Looks like a parking spot to me!” he declared, flashing us a thumbs-up. A nascent iteration of the American pastime foments the same constructive lawlessness as Warped Tour or the Fest.

A newfangled women’s baseball league and a punk scene both recall the architectural principle of flex space—a term that describes any versatile, adaptable, lightly zoned area in a commercial building. Some rooms or settings are designed for specific purposes. The construction of the room circumscribes how the room can be used. By contrast, flex space is meant to be pliable enough that occupants can customize it to suit the fluctuating needs and aims of their business. The punk scene and the WPBL are both flex spaces where norms can shift in real time. They’re both underground pockets that can slip the generally totalizing yoke of unfettered capitalism. In these flex spaces, the conditions of possibility are developed and implemented on the fly.

This includes a temporary suspension of the “customer is always right” ethos that otherwise guides American commerce. Jesse ventures into the bowels of the stadium to brave the concession line in the third inning. By the top of the fifth, she still hasn’t returned. I hop out of my seat and pace the stadium corridors until I find her in line, where an interminable trail of sweaty, hungry WPBL supporters are being surprisingly civil about the slow, disorganized food service. Jesse herself mentions being on the verge of becoming hangry, but exercises some commendable and not totally characteristic restraint. It’s as if the entire concession line is down for the cause. They know the WPBL is an embryonic but well-intended enterprise that calls for a level of patience and indulgence that the more established sports institutions may not require.

The phrase “social construct” penetrated the mainstream during the height of what is now derisively described as Woke 1, those pathbreaking days from early 2014 to 2021 when American culture seemed more mutable and benevolent than it has felt since. Whenever I heard gender, sexuality, or race described as social constructs, I always wondered why we couldn’t consciously build some new, more humane structures from scratch. Where was the social construct factory? Who among us might put on their hard hat and start hammering out frameworks meant to shelter rather than subjugate? In the stands at a WPBL championship game, I feel that construction effort commence.

It turns out the crowd of murmuring, staring white folks in the section next to us were actually marveling at Doc’s service animal, a preternaturally adorable toy Australian shepherd. Dogs are the ultimate social lubricant. When paired with baseball, they form a diversion powerful enough to neutralize racial reticence.

“His name is Dodger,” Doc tells a middle-aged white couple behind us. “The energy here almost reminds me of Dodger Stadium.”

“You’ve been to Dodger Stadium?” the husband breathes, as if Doc had seen the gates of Valhalla. I don’t directly observe this conversation, since I was wary that eye contact with the couple behind us would prolong the engagement. So I imagine Doc adjusting her sunglasses and tossing her fabulous Afro as she says, “Yeah, I’m originally from LA. The Dodgers are my favorite team. Where are you guys from?”

“We’ve seen Bush Stadium and Wrigley Field,” goes the husband.

It’s not quite an Obama-era beer summit, but it is a quiet coalescence of coastal elites and heartland dwellers, a glimmer of baseball’s potential to patch up tattered social fabric. The moment recalls the words of legendary folk-punk troubadour Frank Turner. Addressing the crowd at an Amityville Music Hall solo show in 2025, he explained how and why a punk performance—like a WPBL game—is always more than meets the eye.

“If we all do our parts, we will achieve two things. The first of which is, we’ll make a cool noise. And arguably, that’s what this is all about. But the other thing we’ll do is demonstrate a point which is important to me. Which is that live music, rock ’n’ roll, folk music, punk rock—whatever name you wind up calling this—is not about raised pieces of flooring and backstage passes and tour buses and egos and all that stuff. It’s about bringing people together. It’s about a room full of strangers who leave as friends, a room full of strangers who achieve something together that’s more than the sum of their parts, thereby demonstrating to themselves and to the rest of the world that we can be a community if we choose to be one.”

Doc, Jesse, and I rocked up to the ballpark expecting the Los Angeles Queens to close out the series with a 3–0 sweep. San Francisco had other plans. They overpowered the Queens from the jump, racing out to a commanding seven-to-nothing lead in the second inning and not letting up. Attendance at the decisive victory of a best-of-five series would certainly be more historic, but San Francisco’s fighting spirit won the crowd over. We all needed reminding that no deficit is too daunting if you come out swinging. A few weeks later, a sitting president will casually fantasize aloud about sacrificing two major Californian cities to the war against Iran. For now, we’re galvanized by the collective exercise of manifesting a future where the San Francisco Firebelles’ smoking baseball bats are as American as smoking gun barrels.

During a seventh-inning stretch, the wave’s most vocal advocate finally sees his wish fulfilled. The wave breaks out on the side of the stadium opposite ours. Our section exults and keeps it going when it reaches us. As fireworks shimmer across the late-summer sky, the glass ceiling feels like a piñata visibly starting to give way, sprinkling rewards that will only multiply if we all keep swinging on target. I’m filled with enough goodwill and forbearance to consider stopping at Taco Gringo on the way home.

G'Ra Asim, a writer and musician, is an assistant professor of creative writing at Washington University in St. Louis. His latest book is 99 Problems Finding the 1: a love story (sort of).

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Where with a little bit of luck—and a ton of grassroots organizing—decency has a fighting chance.

You can see it in the polls, which show Rob Sand, the Democratic state auditor running for governor, consistently ahead of Republican Zack Lahn, in a state where the outgoing incumbent, MAGA Republican Kim Reynolds, was reelected by a 19-point margin four years ago—and where Donald Trump beat Kamala Harris by over 13 points.

You can see it in Dubuque, where hundreds of protesters gathered for a No Kings rally before Trump’s visit to the state earlier this month. And in Sioux City, where 12 percent of the city’s residents are foreign-born, and in Des Moines, where thousands of demonstrators turned out at the State Capitol in the spring, and where the most recent protest, on October 17, was focused on encouraging early voting.

I first saw it for myself in late July in Guthrie Center, a town of about 1,500 people spread out along the South Raccoon River. This was the second day of RAGBRAI, the 53rd running of the Des Moines Register’s Annual Great Bicycle Ride Across Iowa. Invented by John Karras, a feature writer for the paper, and columnist Don Kaul, as a stratagem to get their employer to pay for a newsman’s holiday, the pair invited readers to join them for a weeklong bicycle jaunt across the state. Some 300 riders turned up back in 1973—of whom 114 stayed the distance.

This year there were 20,000 of us at the start in Onowa, a town that claims the widest Main Street in the country, but whose chief attraction these days is the Blackbird Bend Casino, operated by the Omaha tribe of Nebraska, and which boasts 350 electric slot machines—but no table games. After dipping our rear wheels in the waters of the Missouri River (the ceremonial start to every RAGBRAI) our route climbed over 3,500 feet, and 59.3 miles, to Harlan, where the temperature briefly hit triple digits. The road to Guthrie Center the next day brought an even greater number of hills—by the end of the day, several riders could be heard cursing whoever had assured them Iowa was flat—with the heat index reaching 110 degrees.

The Iowans on the ride were not surprised; indeed, many wore jerseys with the slogan “Iowa: Flat as a waffle.” But after pedaling under the blazing sun for hours between cornfields on one side of the road and soybeans on the other, without a stick of shade between them, it was a great relief to come into the shade and think about politics. The topic would have been on my mind anyway—I’d been given my first lessons in prairie populism by David Leshtz and Jeffrey Cox, co-editors of The Prairie Progressive, back in 2015 when the two of them were all in for Bernie Sanders. Jeff died in 2020, but Dave keeps up the fight, and it was partly his influence that made me say yes when a Vermont friend asked me if I’d ride RAGRAI with him. But I’d also brought along a native informant from Brooklyn.

I met Peter Hedges because we shared a physical therapist in Cobble Hill, and after weeks of groaning side by side every Thursday, we began to talk and discovered a shared passion for movies and left politics. Peter is a playwright and screenwriter by trade; when I asked him if he’d written anything I might have seen, he said “I wrote the screenplay for What’s Eating Gilbert Grape.” Turns out he wrote the novel, too. Peter was born and raised in West Des Moines, where he graduated from Valley High School. And that’s where the story gets interesting.

Because it turns out that Ashley Hinson, the Trump-endorsed candidate to replace retiring MAGA loyalist Joni Ernst, is also a graduate of Valley High. Back in the spring, a bipartisan group of Hinson’s former teachers joined with Valley High alumni to form Iowans for Decency, a PAC dedicated to marshaling local grassroots opposition to the Republican’s campaign—months before Josh Turek had even secured the Democratic nomination. Peter was already deeply involved, so when I asked him if he might want to come along on RAGBRAI, I didn’t have to twist his arm. “My brother rode RAGBRAI, and my cousin, and I always wanted to do it. But I never did.”

What I was thinking about in Guthrie Center—once my brain stopped boiling—and kept thinking about all the way to the finish line in Dubuque, was the way his fellow Iowans responded to Peter, who wore an “Iowans for Decency” jersey during the daytime, and a “What’s Eating Iowans?” purple T-shirt in the evening, when he’d turn up at the local high school to talk to the theater kids, or at the town library for the Iowans for Decency Listening Tour.

It wasn’t the issues that were surprising: the devastating effect of Trump’s tariffs on farm incomes, the price of gas and diesel, fear for their sons and daughters sent to fight Trump’s wars of choice, or the way, thanks to Big Ag dumping chemicals into the water table, Iowa has seen a sharp rise in cancer diagnoses (even while rates keep falling elsewhere in the country). What I kept hearing, and seeing, was some kind of limit being reached. It wasn’t exactly a prairie fire of populist enthusiasm—though Turek, who was politicized by his experience as a person with spina bifida navigating the American healthcare system, does describe himself as a “prairie populist.” (Sand, the Democratic nominee for governor, describes his politics as “radical centrist populism.”)

But then, in a state that sent Tom Harkin to the House for five terms and then to the Senate for five more terms, the Democratic Party brand is still sufficiently toxic for Sand’s yard signs to use green and orange rather than blue; I saw hundreds of them as I rode east across the state, without any idea which party the candidate was in.

So while Iowa may lack the high-stakes ideological drama of Abdul El-Sayed’s race in Michigan, or the presidential potential of Jon Ossoff’s expected triumph in Georgia, I’m going to be keeping my eyes on Iowa, where with a little bit of luck—and a ton of grassroots organizing—decency has a fighting chance.

D.D. Guttenplan is a special correspondent for The Nation and the former host of The Nation Podcast. He served as editor of the magazine from 2019 to 2025 and, prior to that, as an editor at large and London correspondent. His books include American Radical: The Life and Times of I.F. Stone, The Nation: A Biography, and The Next Republic: The Rise of a New Radical Majority.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Elie Mystal
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
In this week’s Elie v. U.S., our justice correspondent asks why the media is obsessing over Obama’s Cheesecake Factory joke while largely ignoring allegations of Trump’s sexual assaults. Plus: Republicans prepare to cry election fraud.

Donald Trump and future wife Melania pose with Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell.

The president of the United States of America has been accused of rape. Again. The president of the United States has been accused of rape in a report issued by the Democrats of the House Judiciary Committee, as part of their ongoing investigation of Donald Trump’s ties to Jeffrey Epstein. The president has been accused of raping two women, one when she was as young as 13, and sexually assaulting three more. They are among 11 women who provided evidence or testimony that Trump “abused, assaulted, and even raped numerous women alongside, and in coordination with, the most infamous sex trafficker in history.”

I have been made to understand that many people do not know about the Judiciary Comittee report—and the fact that five women have accused Trump of sexual assault while in or near the presence of noted pedophile Jeffrey Epstein. I have been made to understand that this is because the mainstream media finds former president Barack Obama’s comments about the [checks notes] Cheesecake Factory more worthy of their attention than the current president’s abuse of multiple women.

If asked, mainstream media types would no doubt argue that the lack of coverage of these latest rape allegations stems from the fact that previous rape allegations failed to “move the needle.” Trump’s sexual misconduct (both alleged and litigated) is “baked in” to people’s understanding of the man. People either won’t believe the charges or won’t care—or else they do believe the women and do care and vote accordingly—but everybody knows what he’s been accused of, generally speaking at least.

I find this line of argument unadulterated bollocks that reveals the deep failure of our mainstream media. It is news when the president is credibly accused of rape. It is important news. While I, too, don’t think these latest sexual assault accusations will materially change the national conversation about Trump or his presidency, that is not an excuse for ignoring, downplaying, or skipping over brutal allegations that he repeatedly assaulted women, including minors.

Journalists cannot decide what other people think is important. Their job is to illuminate what they think is in the public interest. I think reporting on rape allegations levied against the president of the United States is in the public interest. And since I think that, it really doesn’t matter if the public agrees with me.

With that in mind, I, unlike people who work for Bari Weiss, read the Judiciary report. Here are some of the allegations:

Next week, the Republicans are going to lose. I don’t know precisely which ones or by how much: I suspect that Democrats will retake the House; there’s certainly a chance they will retake the Senate. But no matter how things shake out, it’s very likely that the Republicans will emerge from the election with less political power than they went in with.

That’s not surprising. This is a midterm election, and the party in power in the White House usually loses seats in the midterms, just as a matter of course. And we can expect those losses to be exacerbated when the president in power is deeply unpopular, the economy is in the tank, and the country is engaged in a pointless war that it’s not even winning. The laws of political physics say the GOP is supposed to lose next week, and quite badly.

But the Republicans, at least the ones most devoted to the Trump cult, likely have no idea they are about to lose. That’s because Trump and the white-wing media have been feeding them a steady diet of lies, priming them to believe that the only way Democrats could win is if there is election fraud. Their reasons for doing this are clear: If Trump’s base thinks their loss is due to fraud, they will likely support the most antidemocratic measures Trump takes to hold on to power over the will of the people. If they really believe Trump, at least some of them will turn to violence to support his antidemocratic efforts.

A new study from The Washington Post illustrates the complete saturation of the white-wing media by this false electoral narrative.

Nearly 600 high-profile, right-wing social media accounts, podcasts and other online media have published more than 7,000 statements questioning the election’s integrity so far this year, a Washington Post analysis found. That messaging has, in particular, pushed overstated claims that noncitizens are on voter rolls and that mail-in ballots enable widespread fraud—themes that are twice as prevalent as they were during the 2024 election cycle, The Post’s analysis found.

Look, losing can be a shock in the best of times, but when you are priming your audience to think that a loss could happen only through massive cheating and fraud, and that audience has already shown an appetite for violence when it doesn’t get the electoral outcomes it would like, you are playing with fire.

Trump, of course, wants there to be a fire if his party loses. He needs it. He can’t challenge the election if most people agree that his party lost fair and square. He is trying to sow distrust in the system, because distrust is a crucial precondition to violent overthrow of the system.

One wouldn’t expect any particular candidate to tell their supporters, “Hey guys, we’ll probably get our ass kicked tomorrow, but let’s show up and rock the vote anyway.” Candidates need to engender a sense of hope, even if it’s false, until the end.

But one would expect the media to do the work of preparing people to confront reality. What’s the point of all this inane horse-race coverage if it’s not even going to prepare people for the reality of losing?

Unfortunately, the door swings both ways. There isn’t a nefarious conspiracy about how Trump rigged this election that I’d dismiss out of hand at this point. If the GOP pulls off a series of “close” victories in majority-minority precincts because votes didn’t materialize or vanished into thin air, I’m going to be ready to take to the streets myself.

There is no trust left in the electoral system, on either side. Republicans have been actively trying to undermine it, but I’m not sure what Democrats can do to restore it.

The Department of Justice preemptively sued Alaska to delay certification of the results in the Senate race there because there are two candidates running with the same name. The New York Times then Columbus’d the story, reporting that one of the candidates was likely a plant from the Democrats meant to cause confusion among Republican voters.

The thing is, the Times had trouble remembering the most important legal fact of the story: that all of this was litigated, in Alaska, in June, all the way up to the state Supreme Court. That’s what I wrote about. I explained that Republicans had already objected to the other guy with the same name as their incumbent and lost. I explained that the only reason the DOJ is bringing this up again, in October, is to cause confusion and sow distrust in the election, as well as ask for a remedy so antidemocratic that it cannot be allowed.

As I mentioned, the mainstream media is more concerned with President Obama’s comments about the Cheesecake Factory than with the credible rape allegations against Donald Trump. For those who somehow missed it, Obama said, “He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory.”

Cheesecakegate has inspired a raft of terrible takes, but none worse than the one from the whole-ass editorial board of The Wall Street Journal, which blared: “Obama Goes Socialist, Scorns Cheesecake.” The editorial criticized Obama for, among other things, being condescending toward Middle America with his slam on the Cheesecake Factory.

That last point requires some explanation. The Cheesecake Factory was founded in Beverly Hills, California, which is about as far from “Middle America” as you can get without getting wet. While it now has franchises across the US, it’s mainly an overpriced mall hub that is most popular on the coasts. It’s essentially a diner for people who don’t have access to good diners and don’t mind paying an outrageous premium for diner food. Only a WSJ editor could think that this kind of high-end schlock represents “Middle America.”

I lived in Indiana for 13 months. The chain-store diner-food option was Steak ’N Shake. Applebee’s was another contender. In places I don’t feel safe driving through, the equivalent is Cracker Barrel. There is no place I know of where the Cheesecake Factory’s (shitty) cheesecake represents a thin slice of Americana.

In any event, Trump allegedly sexually assaulted five people while in or near the company of Jeffrey Epstein. Obama made a joke about interior design. If you cannot correctly order the relative political importance of each of those stories, you deserve to dine at the restaurant of your choice with Saddam Hussein in Hell.

https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.title: The Eviction Kings Are Being Sued
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.author: Thomas Birmingham
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
Corporate landlord American Landmark admitted that its business model priced tenants out. Now, former tenants have filed a class-action lawsuit against the company.

In January of 2025, recalling the eviction that had made him homeless, Diron Kelly told me his corporate landlord had left him living through “a nightmare.”

He said American Landmark, owner of his Charlotte, North Carolina, apartment and some 30,000 others, had a “bully” business model—from raising his rent by some $400 while forcing him to pay fees for frivolous amenities to jumping at the chance to take him to court once his pockets ran dry. “They really messed everything up,” he said.

But starting last week, it’s now Kelly taking the real estate giant to court. On October 20, he filed a class-action lawsuit against the company in an attempt to prove that not only does its model—first revealed by The Nation and Type Investigations in a piece last year—violate North Carolina law but it has left thousands of similar “nightmares” in its wake.

At stake are the likely millions of dollars that the suit alleges American Landmark illegally coerced out of current and former tenants like Kelly.

The lawsuit, filed by Halperin Petersen & Mikkilineni LLP, the North Carolina Justice Center, and Kelly Guzzo, PLC in the US District Court for the Middle District of North Carolina, focuses on a state that has been an epicenter in American Landmark’s network of mega-complexes throughout the South. When I traveled to Charlotte last year, I learned that American Landmark had filed evictions against at least 450 residents over a six-month period, and my interviews with dozens of American Landmark tenants revealed how the company had engineered a system to price Kelly and his neighbors out.

Even American Landmark CEO Joseph Lubeck admitted when I spoke to him that the company’s “modeling” assumes that 45 percent of existing tenants will “move out” after American Landmark takes over: “a number of people are not going to be able to afford what we do.”

Kelly’s case, which is seeking additional plaintiffs, asks for restitution for any tenant who has lived in one of American Landmark’s roughly 3,000 apartments in the state since October 20, 2022. “During their tenancies,” the complaint reads, “Defendants have charged Plaintiffs thousands of dollars in unlawful, deceptive, and unfair fees.”

When reached by e-mail, Lubeck wrote, “American Landmark strongly denies all of the specious claims in the suit, which is clearly an attempt to extort money and rooted in antisemitism, like your previous coverage.”

According to the complaint, American Landmark weaponized mandatory “junk” fees to arbitrarily raise its tenants’ monthly costs by upwards of $100 per month. Kelly’s attorneys claim that American Landmark universally implements these fees—described as a “profit center”—in its North Carolina homes.

In 2025, 18 American Landmark tenants told me their first bill from the company surpassed what they believed they should have owed—thanks to the mandatory fees. Though Lubeck acknowledged at the time that he was “sure there are cases where people don’t know what they sign,” he told me that the fees were “disclosed up front and in writing.” In his e-mailed comment on the lawsuit, he again emphasized that “we provide full and fair value for all our residents and for all services, all of which are clearly spelled out and explained in their contracts and welcome packages.”

These underhanded fee structures are an epidemic for modern renters. As private-equity firms and large conglomerates take over more and more US real estate, tenants are losing out on hundreds of millions of dollars through junk fees every year, according to the National Consumer Law Center (NCLC). These fees, especially in cities like Charlotte, disproportionately burden Black and brown tenants. But a 2025 NCLC report found that states have begun pushing back, with at least 20 adopting laws restricting junk fees in some form. In Minnesota, for example, landlords must include mandatory fees in the publicly advertised cost of their apartments.

In December 2025, the country’s largest property manager, Greystar, agreed to refund tenants $23 million after the Federal Trade Commission sued the company for advertising rentals at “deceptive prices” that “excluded several fixed, mandatory monthly fees.” Kelly’s class-action hopes to build on that national precedent.

“In Mecklenburg County alone, more than 50,000 families faced eviction last year,” Peter Gilbert, director of litigation at North Carolina Justice Center, said in a press release. “These deceptive and unlawful fees are one of the primary drivers of evictions as landlords squeeze tenants past their breaking point.”

Specifically, the complaint alleges that the fees violate North Carolina’s Unfair and Deceptive Trade Practices Act. After American Landmark took over, Kelly and his neighbors soon received an approximately $100 monthly fee for cable and Internet. Though Kelly’s lease, the complaint alleges, describes this package as “additional rent,” the details are buried in one of many lease addendums, and the nonnegotiable cost far exceeds what tenants could find on the open market.

What’s more, American Landmark disconnects the service when tenants fall behind on payments and “continue to charge the Technology Fee even though the tenant is not receiving the service,” the complaint reads. Then, American Landmark “impose[s] a $75 or more fee to “reconnect” the services that they have disconnected.”

“In at least one month, Mr. Kelly was charged over $160 in Technology Fees and Reconnect Fees when his service was not connected,” the complaint reads.

The Nation and Type Investigation’s 2025 investigation found that the technology package was anathema among American Landmark tenants. For that piece, I spoke to Stephen Tuju, one of Kelly’s former neighbors, who e-mailed complaints about the surprise $75 reconnection fee to his property managers. The company inexplicably responded that it would “adjust” the fee to $25.

In my conversation with Lubeck last year, he confirmed that the company disconnects the technology package when tenants pay late. In Tuju’s case, “it’s possible someone made a mistake,” Lubeck said, but “everything is established and fair across the board.” But the new lawsuit alleges that not only does Kelly’s lease authorize only a $25 reconnection fee but that the company nonetheless habitually demands tenants pay $75 or more for it, as it did to Tuju.

Once Kelly fell behind on payments, he allegedly encountered a “cascade” of additional fees American Landmark contrives from the eviction filing process. Under North Carolina law, landlords can charge tenants for court filing and processing fees, as well as up to 15 percent of a tenant’s overdue balance to help cover the cost of eviction attorneys. But Kelly was allegedly once charged “approximately $1,000 in Attorney or Legal Fees on a balance of less than $2,000,” according to the complaint.

Twice in 2023, per the complaint, American Landmark pressured Kelly to pay legal fees associated with evictions the company had never even filed in court. Less than a year later, Kelly became homeless.

Kelly’s attorneys analyzed thousands of North Carolina court records and found that over 40 percent of the tenants American Landmark files evictions against will incur another eviction attempt in the future. Each new case brings new fees. “In 2025 alone,” the complaint alleges, “over fifty tenants went through this cycle four or more times.”

“That’s why I’m still trying to play catch-up,” said Christopher Dawkins, a tenant I met in Charlotte in 2025, of these legal fees. He told me American Landmark charged him around $300 for each of his four eviction cases. “I got kids, too. When you got a lot going on, every dollar counts.”

Not content to have just kicked Kelly out, American Landmark, the complaint alleges, is also violating the state’s Debt Collection Act: Kelly “continues to receive collections notices from a third-party debt collector acting on behalf of [American] Landmark attempting to collect all illegally charged fees.”

Most of Kelly’s supposed debt, the complaint reads, comes from an “early termination” fee. After the company evicted him, American Landmark charged Kelly nearly $3,000 as a penalty for leaving the company unable to collect rent from him through the rest of his now-voided lease agreement.

The complaint alleges that American Landmark tenants “are given no notice” of this “immoral, unethical, oppressive, and unscrupulous” fee “prior to their eviction.”

“I feel like they’re predatory,” Jeff Schuman, a tenant who was evicted in March 2025 from an American Landmark property in Jacksonville and was similarly hounded by a collections agency, told me last year. “They can put a person out on the street with no recourse. I was like, ‘I don’t have anywhere to go and have a small child.’ It was one of the worst experiences I’ve had in my life.”

The scale of the American Landmark eviction machine that chews up tenants like Kelly and Schuman far outpaces state and national norms. As The Nation and Type Investigations reported last year, in one six-month period, the company filed 82 evictions for every 100 units at one Charlotte complex, and after American Landmark bought Kelly’s building in 2022, the company began filing evictions four times more often than the previous owner.

Kelly’s attorneys found a similar pattern: Though landlords statewide filed 12 evictions per 100 units during the 2025–26 fiscal year, American Landmark on average filed 50.

“Red states are very landlordist,” Gil Rushinek, board chair of American Landmark’s parent company, said in a 2024 podcast. In addition to North Carolina, the company owns buildings in Florida, Georgia, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas, and Virginia, all of which have Republican-controlled legislatures. “In free-market capitalism, there are few protections for the tenant. If you want to evict a tenant in New York, you will have a lot more of a challenge than evicting a tenant in Florida,” Rushinek continued. But North Carolina is the only American Landmark locale with a Democratic governor and attorney general, and the chief justice of the lawsuit’s district court was appointed by President Barack Obama.

The case now enters an uncertain period of months, if not years, of litigation. In addition to millions in damages, Kelly’s attorneys are asking for certification of each of their proposed classes of exploited tenants and a jury trial.

Were the lawsuit to yield a substantial payout, the impact could also reverberate internationally, because, as the Nation/Type Investigations 2025 investigation revealed, American Landmark is wholly owned by the Electra Group, an Israeli conglomerate with extensive ties to both illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank and the Israel Defense Forces (IDF).

Since these ties were first reported, the Electra Group has remained on the United Nations Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights database of over 200 companies that do business in the illegal settlements. Electra’s business is centered on making it easier for Israelis to commute to and from the settlements by constructing tunnels and roads and operating bus lines on stolen Palestinian land.

Meanwhile, “the IDF is a major client,” the CEO of another Electra subsidiary said on a 2024 earnings call, after the IDF had already killed tens of thousands of Palestinian civilians in Gaza. “We stand shoulder to shoulder with them in facing challenges and fulfilling missions. We are likely the only supplier that can say we’ve expanded our areas of deployment.… This is a great source of pride for us.” In a podcast appearance the same year, Rushinek described American Landmark as a “big winning card” for the conglomerate.

The class-action lawsuit, should it eventually force American Landmark into a settlement, could therefore result in a payout to tenants like Kelly of revenue that may otherwise have been funneled into the Electra operation that is playing an active role in the displacement and genocide of Palestinians.

But in the meantime, as of the filing of the complaint, Kelly still does not have a place of his own. American Landmark continues to haunt his life—through a belligerent collection agency and the eviction staining his record—despite their throwing him out of his apartment some 29 months ago.

It’s a vision of what may someday befall Paula Hindman, the case’s other named plaintiff.

She retired from decades of program directing at Piedmont Community College in 2022, just three months before American Landmark bought her building in Hillsborough. Eventually, “the fees at my apartment became so expensive that I went back to work part-time,” she said in a press release. She joined the ranks of the tenants I met over and over again when I traveled to Charlotte last year who were on the brink of being priced out for good. Most of them have since been evicted.

So it’s with Hindman and all of American Landmark’s current and future tenants in mind that the complaint is also seeking “injunctive relief,” a court order that would require American Landmark to permanently change its practices in the state. That means no more mysterious charges. No more collection agency calls.

No more North Carolina tenants wrung out to their last dollar.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Jeet Heer
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Wreckers like Haley Stevens are probably the GOP’s last hope of avoiding a wipeout on Tuesday.

Making political predictions is always a fool’s errand—particularly these days, when polls are becoming increasingly unreliable and sometimes even fraudulent. But there are still plenty of signs pointing to a strong Democratic Party victory in Tuesday’s midterms. Democrats appear to be in pole position to recapture the House of Representatives, and have a real chance to gain control of the Senate—something that seemed all but impossible until relatively recently.

We can tell which way the wind is blowing by the fact that Republican super PACs are bailing out of states like North Carolina—which was expected to be a marquee battleground this year but now seems all but lost to the GOP—and moving funds to bolster candidates in even redder states such as Texas and Iowa.

The Trump administration has also noticed how bad things are going, and is flailing accordingly. On Thursday, the White House announced that President Trump was canceling planned rallies in Kansas and Iowa, replacing them with tele-rallies. This news was telling on a number of levels. The very fact that Trump was headed to deep-red states like Kansas and Iowa was a sign of trouble. In more successful years such as 2016 and 2024, he ended his campaigns by going to genuine swing states such as Michigan, Wisconsin, and Pennsylvania, even making daring jaunts into New York.

Then, on Friday morning, the White House suddenly reversed course and said Trump would be holding the rallies after all. Perhaps Trump was stung by the implication of his previous decision to cancel—it sent the message that Republicans didn’t want to be seen with an unpopular president, and that Trump himself wanted to avoid the stink of being part of a losing campaign—or perhaps this was simply yet another sign of the chaotic, strategy-free nature of Trump’s approach. Not surprisingly, pundits such as Nate Silver and David Wallace-Wells are predicting that we may be watching the beginning of the end of the Trump era.

The president is clearly off his game. When he was at the peak of his political power, Trump would focus on issues that had genuine salience: immigration, the economy, and foreign policy. To be sure, he’d often muddle this message with his personal grievances and gloating, but he still had a coherent agenda. But in 2026, as Jonathan Lemire notes in The Atlantic, Trump’s message has become unusually muddled:

This time around, Trump’s primary rationale for why voters should support the GOP, as best I can tell, is that the affordability crisis is a “hoax,” Bill Maher is a “loser,” and Senator Jon Husted of Ohio has a nice physique. That easy-to-mock message has been accompanied by a staggering number of missteps. Just for starters, he’s belittled the impact of his stalled war with Iran, sided with Russia as it continues to pummel Ukrainian cities, defended an attack ad from the GOP candidate for Ohio governor that repulsed other top Republicans, downplayed high energy prices while boasting that U.S. oil and gas companies are “making a freaking fortune,” embraced AI as the nation turns against it, obsessed over White House construction projects, and spent a lot of time talking about handsome men, Husted being just one.

Trump seems to be engaged not in a campaign of persuasion, but a massive public crack-up And he’s not the only one. Prominent GOP candidates like Ohio gubernatorial nominee Vivek Ramaswamy and Texas Senate nominee Ken Paxton are also melting down. Ramaswamy is still dealing with the fallout from his disgraceful ad featuring the estranged mother of his Democratic rival, Amy Acton. The truly sordid nature of the ad became clear when it was revealed that Acton’s mother was homeless and deeply troubled, having lost custody of her children after she sided with a husband accused of abusing them. Ramaswamy first doubled down on the ad—but, on Thursday, he yielded to massive backlash and pulled it from the air. As for Ken Paxton, he’s being plagued by so many personal and ethics scandals that even stalwart Republicans such as political strategist Karl Rove won’t endorse him.

The one glimmer of hope Republicans have is that elite Democrats seem equally addicted to self-sabotage. Indeed, this election has often felt like a competition to see which party can inflict the most damage on itself.

In Michigan, Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed has been dogged by the sore-loser behavior of centrist Democrats who can’t abide the fact he won the primary. In particular, his defeated rival Haley Stevens keeps trying to extract political concessions from El-Sayed rather than letting him unite the party against Republican Mike Rogers.

Representative Haley Stevens of Michigan, who lost to Dr. Abdul El-Sayed in a bitter Democratic primary for Senate in August, has grown increasingly critical of him as the election draws near, injecting unusual intraparty tensions into the final days of a pivotal midterm contest.

While Ms. Stevens reiterated Wednesday night that she plans to vote for Dr. El-Sayed, she did so through seemingly gritted teeth in a televised interview just hours after her fiancé said that he would be voting for former Representative Mike Rogers, Dr. El-Sayed’s Republican rival. She also called on Dr. El-Sayed to denounce an ad from an outside group that she has argued amounts to “fear-mongering about Israel,” and to take down an ad from his campaign featuring Tucker Carlson.

On Thursday, Stevens seemed to partially relent in her undermining of the Democratic nominee by agreeing to campaign with El-Sayed.

Stevens’s actions are rooted in the internal Democratic Party rift over Israel/Gaza. Stevens is strongly pro-Israel, notoriously saying that “Israel comes to me in my dreams.” And she has company when it comes to undermining El-Sayed. On Thursday, former House speaker Nancy Pelosi went on a podcast and said El-Sayed’s comments on Israel were “concerning.” She added, “This new person in Michigan, we’ll see if he gets elected to the Congress.”

What makes Stevens’s antics particularly despicable is the fact that El-Sayed, like other Muslim candidates, has been subjected to vicious Islamophobia by the Republicans. At a rally in Michigan on Sunday, Trump said, “I’m here to keep a jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member from becoming a United States senator. If Abdul and the Democrats win, they will open the floodgates and invite hordes of jihadists to our shores, creating a nightmare of violence and terror until you cannot even have a Christmas.”

Writing in The New Republic, Perry Bacon rightly notes that Stevens’s behavior follows the pattern of centrist Democrats’ “attacking and undermining a compelling Muslim candidate who is also a target of the right.” In 2025, centrist Democrats similarly tried to kneecap Zohran Mamdani, both when he was running for mayor of New York and even after he won the party’s nomination. As Bacon points out, “A Democratic Party that won’t fully accept Muslim candidates isn’t a party that actually practices the principles of democracy, diversity, inclusion, pluralism, and multiculturalism that it preaches.”

Not all Democratic Party self-sabotage is ideological. Some of it is merely motivated by standard dirty tricks, as in the scandal engulfing Alaska Senate candidate Mary Peltola. On Wednesday, The New York Times reported that Peltola’s team worked to recruit a third-party candidate named Dan J. Sullivan so as to create confusion on the ballot with the current Republican governor, Dan S. Sullivan. John F. Kennedy’s campaign made the exact same maneuver in 1946 when he ran against a rival named Joseph Russo. The campaign found a ringer with the same name, and Kennedy sailed to victory.

Still, even if a dirty trick has a storied pedigree, it’s a dirty trick. Peltola might still win the election, but she’s surely alienated some voters.

The good news for the Democrats is that it’s hard to beat Donald Trump in a self-destruction competition. Trump ran in 2024 on a platform of avoiding more wars and focusing on fixing the economy. As president, he launched a disastrous war against Iran, which is creating a new affordability crisis. When it comes to shooting yourself in the foot, Trump remains undefeated.

Jeet Heer is a national affairs correspondent for The Nation and host of the weekly Nation podcast, The Time of Monsters. He also pens the monthly column “Morbid Symptoms.” The author of In Love with Art: Francoise Mouly’s Adventures in Comics with Art Spiegelman (2013) and Sweet Lechery: Reviews, Essays and Profiles (2014), Heer has written for numerous publications, including The New Yorker, The Paris Review, Virginia Quarterly Review, The American Prospect, The Guardian, The New Republic, and The Boston Globe.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Bernie Sanders Is Leaving It All on the Field in the Final Days of the Midterms
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: John Nichols
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
The senator is mounting a relentless, urgent campaign to stop Trump, elect progressives, and transform US politics.

Bernie Sanders speaks in support of Wisconsin Democratic congressional candidate Rebecca Cooke during a rally at the W.R. Davies Student Center on October 25, 2026 in Eau Claire, Wisconsin.

Eau Claire, Wisconsin—Bernie Sanders was up bright and early on a windswept, late October Sunday morning for the 17th stop on a month-long, nationwide campaign swing in anticipation of Tuesday’s midterm elections. But he wasn’t up any earlier than the overflow crowd that had come to see him in this western Wisconsin city of 69,421. By the time the independent senator from Vermont and two-time Democratic presidential candidate took the stage at the University of Wisconsin–Eau Claire student center, voters from the nation’s ultimate swing district had filled every seat and were crowding against the walls, sitting on the floor, and spilling into the hallways at the far end of the sprawling space. Amid the sustained applause that greeted his arrival, Sanders gestured to the back of the room and half-joked, “We’ve got to knock down the door there. We’ve got a lot of folks.”

That was it for small talk. The senator launched into an appeal for Rebecca Cooke, a 38-year-old Wisconsin congressional candidate whom he endorsed more than a year ago. Cooke welcomed Sanders with an introduction that hailed him as “our champion for the working class for decades” and “one of the last people in Congress that still has a spine, that is willing to stand up [to] special interests, and continues to put people first.”

“In my view, this is the most important midterm election in the modern history of our country, or maybe the history of our country,” Sanders told the crowd. “And what Rebecca’s race is about—and the reason that I am here—is that the time is long overdue for us to hold the most dangerous president in the history of the United States accountable. But it’s not only holding Trump accountable. It is an understanding, and I know Rebecca has campaigned on this relentlessly, [that it is possible] to create an economy that works for all people—not just the one percent.”

Democratic campaigns across the country have relied a good deal on surrogates this year, with much attention paid to late-stage campaign stops by former president Barack Obama, former vice president Kamala Harris, and potential 2028 presidential contenders such as New York US Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, California US Representative Ro Khanna, and former transportation secretary Pete Buttigieg. But no one has done it with quite the consistent messaging and strategic focus that Sanders has brought to the campaign trail. The senator, whom polls frequently identify as the most popular sitting elected official in the United States, began talking about the midterms shortly after Trump’s second inauguration, and used his 2025 “Fighting Oligarchy” tour of Republican red districts and states to argue that the 2026 election would offer a historic opportunity to transform American politics, place checks and balances on the White House, and strike a blow for governance by the people rather than wealthy elites.

Now, with the November 3 elections just days away, and an onslaught of billionaire-funded spending to prop up the flailing Republican effort to keep control of Congress, Sanders has been relentlessly making his closing argument to voters nationwide. In the past few weeks, he has attracted thousands of organizers, activists, and curious voters to events from Maine to California, on a tenacious schedule that is every bit as ambitious in its goals as any candidate or party leader’s. He told the cheering crowd in Eau Claire that this is the moment to “revitalize American democracy” by replacing Trump-aligned Republicans like Wisconsin US Representative Derrick Van Orden with working-class Democrats such as Cooke.

Sanders delivered a similar message the night before in Duluth, Minnesota, where an even larger crowd packed a school gymnasium to hear his pitch for Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party US Senate candidate Peggy Flanagan—a progressive who, like another Sanders endorsee, Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, beat a more politically cautious, AIPAC-aligned Democrat in the primaries and is now locked in a fall contest that could define control of the Senate. “I am so grateful that you’re on Team Peggy,” Flanagan said in her introduction of Sanders, “because the coach of our team is here!”

After making early endorsements of working-class candidates in House and Senate races—many of whom faced primary fights—Sanders has used digital platforms to participate in dozens of organizing calls, virtual canvass launches, and livestream conversations to ramp up support for Democratic contenders. And he has shown up, often repeatedly, for rallies with candidates such as Flanagan and Cooke. This unflagging, “all-hands-on-deck” energy has Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison describing the 85-year-old senator as the great progressive movement builder of our time.

“Bernie is shifting the ground, giving people hope,” says Ellison, who campaigned with Sanders and Flanagan in Duluth.

So far this month, Sanders has appeared at 20 major events in seven states. He’s been in Maine for Senate candidate Troy Jackson, in Florida for Senate candidate Angie Nixon, in Texas with Congressional Progressive Caucus chair Greg Casar for that state’s Democratic ticket, in California for multiple congressional candidates (as well as for the campaign in support of an ambitious ballot proposal to tax billionaires) and—just this week—in Michigan for three major events with El-Sayed.

At these stops, which often take him far from the well-trodden paths of American politics, Sanders does more than deliver a standard stump speech. He asks people in the crowds to talk about the issues that matter to them, and then he launches into deep discussions about those issues—data centers and artificial intelligence, single-payer healthcare, how economic inequality threatens the health and well-being of low-income Americans, and the desperate need for the Democratic Party to abandon deference to corporate donors and deliver for working-class Americans. “I’m fighting the two-front war. The first of the two fights is ending Republican control of the House and the Senate, and holding Trump accountable. But the second issue is having the Democratic Party do what the American people want it to do,” Sanders explained in an interview in Eau Claire. “I think you heard an example of that today. This is not New York City. We’re in Eau Claire, Wisconsin. All over the country, people understand that we need bold action to address the needs of the working class, that we need to take on the oligarchs, that healthcare is a human right.”

Sanders hasn’t just been donating his time. He’s also been donating his money and his team. The senator has joined online fundraising appeals to raise more than $3 million for the grassroots campaigns of endorsed candidates in states across the country. He has dispatched full-time staffers to work on the ground in key states such as Minnesota, Florida, and Michigan. And he has transferred roughly $2.3 million from his own committee—including $1,250,000 to support El-Sayed, more than $300,000 to help Nixon in Florida, more than $300,000 to Flanagan’s Democratic Farmer Labor Party in Minnesota, $100,000 to Troy Jackson’s Maine Senate run, and thousands more to boost the Senate bids of Democrats Sherrod Brown in Ohio and Scott Colom in Mississippi and independent Dan Osborn in Nebraska, and the congressional bids of Michigan Democrats Will Lawrence and Donavan McKinney—with an eye toward helping organize on-the-ground, in-person campaigns that counter the massive spending by billionaires and special-interest groups on television ads backing Republicans.

“Any progressive movement that’s going to be successful has got to have some people who are fulfilling the function that Bernie’s filling right now,” says Ellison. “A candidate like Abdul El-Sayed needs help. Bernie’s in a position to help. And he does help. He comes to it in a meaningful way, and brings people with him, and puts us in a position [to mount a stronger campaign] for somebody who is overtly talking about putting money in your pocket, getting money out of politics and Medicare for All. That’s a huge thing. That’s an enormous thing.”

For his part, Sanders says, “This is a debate about the very fabric of American society — whether we remain a democratic society or [become] an authoritarian society, where we engage in endless wars or not, where we have a government that vaguely represents the needs of working families or one that is totally owned by the oligarchs. So, yes, I worry very much about the future of this country if Republicans retain control of the House and Senate, and I’m doing everything I can to prevent it.”

And the best way to prevent it, he says, is by returning to the grassroots and campaigning face-to-face with people in places like Duluth and Eau Claire.

“What I have always believed is that, at the end of the day, the way you win elections is by grassroots activism,” says Sanders. “People like Rebecca are winning elections—she won the primary, and hopefully she’ll win the general—because of the grassroots support that she has. People going out, knocking on doors, talking to their neighbors. I know that sounds very old-fashioned. But I, a thousand times over, prefer to invest in that vision and work with those types of people, rather than putting stupid ads on television that cost a fortune.”

John Nichols is the executive editor of The Nation. He previously served as the magazine’s national affairs correspondent and Washington correspondent. Nichols has written, cowritten, or edited over a dozen books on topics ranging from histories of American socialism and the Democratic Party to analyses of US and global media systems. His latest, cowritten with Senator Bernie Sanders, is the New York Times bestseller It's OK to Be Angry About Capitalism.
