https://www.propublica.org/article/midte.title: Trump Has Tried to Exert More Control Over Elections. Here Are the Key Findings From Our Reporting.
https://www.propublica.org/article/midte.text:
Ahead of next week’s midterm elections, President Donald Trump has systematically demolished institutional guardrails that prevented him from overturning the 2020 presidential election, ProPublica’s reporting has shown.
Trump has empowered his loyalists to try to transform the voting process. He launched an unprecedented — and largely unsuccessful — effort to find noncitizen voters. And he tried to restrict mail-in voting.
Our reporters have spent much of this year covering Trump’s efforts to exert more federal control over elections. Here are five takeaways from their reporting.
1. The Trump administration has sought greater federal control over elections.
In April, Doug Bock Clark and Jen Fifield reported on Trump’s efforts to “take over” the midterm elections, detailing how the administration has discarded or diminished endeavors across the federal government to protect the voting process or block foreign interference. Those efforts have included cutting staff on election-related teams at federal law enforcement agencies and finding ways to exert greater federal control over voting.
Our reporting led by Peter Elkind revealed that the Trump administration harnessed Homeland Security Investigations’ personnel, technology and legal authority to try to back up Trump’s unproven claim that illegal voting by noncitizens is tilting elections toward Democrats. Administration officials insisted the effort spearheaded by HSI was producing meaningful results. Our analysis of Justice Department data found, as of May, 41 alleged noncitizens were charged with voting illegally or other election-related crimes. Earlier this month, CBS reported 156 people have been charged since the beginning of the second Trump administration.
“Paper Trail” Podcast
Learn more about this story on ProPublica’s podcast “Paper Trail.”
As part of that effort, the Justice Department has demanded states turn over unredacted voter rolls, which contain confidential information on millions of Americans and have historically been managed by states. Since September 2025, the department has sued 30 states and the District of Columbia for the confidential data. Wary of federal overreach, state officials — including some Republicans — have fought back, and so far every DOJ lawsuit that’s been decided by a federal judge has been dismissed. (The Trump administration has appealed most of its losses to federal appeals courts and has said it will consider taking its fight to the Supreme Court. A Justice Department spokesperson said its “attorneys are skilled, principled advocates who argue every case honestly and in good faith.”)
In a March executive order, Trump instructed the U.S. Postal Service to create new regulations for mail voting. The rules would have put the Postal Service in the unprecedented role of deciding whether to send or deny the delivery of voters’ mail-in ballots. The Supreme Court in September blocked the rules, at least until after November.
The Trump administration has said its actions will make U.S. elections fairer and more secure — and keep those prohibited from voting, such as noncitizens, from doing so. Spokespeople for the DOJ and Department of Homeland Security emphasized that their departments are focused on ensuring elections are free and fair, and that they are working closely with the states to achieve those goals. Contentions to the contrary, they say, are false.
2. Trump has pushed out career officials — and is coordinating with a conservative grassroots organization to transform elections.
At least 75 nonpartisan career officials who’d held roles at federal agencies related to election integrity and safety have been fired or left the government.
Two dozen Trump appointees — including many from the election-denial movement — have been hired. Ahead of the midterms, current and former government officials and election security experts have expressed concerns that once-fringe actors who’ve espoused debunked conspiracy theories about elections are now in positions to control the narrative around the voting process. (A DHS spokesperson said it hires “experts with diverse backgrounds who go through a rigorous vetting process.”)
At least 25 administration appointees have close ties to Cleta Mitchell, a lawyer who leads Election Integrity Network, a grassroots conservative group focused on transforming America’s voting system. This month, Clark profiled Mitchell — and detailed how, despite not holding a formal role in the White House, she’s played a key role in shaping the Trump administration’s elections agenda. The White House has appointed her associates to help hunt for noncitizen voters and investigate accusations of voting fraud in 2020. (Mitchell declined multiple requests to speak with ProPublica, but wrote in an email: “You’re my opponent. … You’re never going to write in any objective, non-judgmental way about the election integrity movement.”)
Help Us Report on Key Election Issues
ProPublica’s reporters are on the lookout for what’s going right and what isn’t. We’re monitoring voter suppression and interference, election observers and poll watchers, extremism tied to the election, and ICE activity at the polls. Have you seen something?
Mitchell, who played a role in helping Trump challenge his loss in the 2020 presidential election, has been leading efforts to pass state and federal iterations of the SAVE Act. The 2026 version of the bill, known as the SAVE America Act, would require voters nationwide to provide proof of citizenship to register and present a photo ID to vote, and would compel states to turn over their voter rolls to DHS. Trump has repeatedly called the measure his top legislative priority, but it has been blocked in the Senate.
In July, Trump also pushed out the remaining members of the bipartisan Election Assistance Commission, a four-member board designed to be evenly split between Republicans and Democrats that sets standards for state voting systems. (At the time, a White House official wouldn’t confirm the moves but said the president “reserves the right to remove individuals that may not be totally aligned with the important task of securing America’s elections and ensuring every legal vote is counted.”)
3. Trump officials asked a cybersecurity agency to secretly acquire a voting machine — and hack it.
A few months into Trump’s second term, political appointees at DHS asked its Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency to procure a voting machine, hack it and report the findings so they could be given to the White House, two former administration officials with knowledge of the request told Clark and Andy Mannix.
CISA employees told the political appointees their request was impossible, in part because the agents capable of pulling off such an operation had just been laid off by Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency. (One of Trump’s first actions when he returned to the White House was to dismantle the agency’s election security work.)
Though not acted on, the request shows how the Trump administration has tried to use the agency for its own ends while draining it of resources for one of its critical missions: protecting the nation’s voting systems. Since CISA became an agency in 2018, it has come to provide crucial support to thousands of local election officials grappling with increasingly sophisticated attacks.
But some state election officials said CISA provided them with little help as they planned for the 2026 midterms. And other state authorities told Clark and Mannix that they no longer trusted the agency and feared it had been compromised by the Trump administration. (A DHS spokesperson told us in April the “claim that DHS has a broken partnership with states and made our elections less secure is simply false.”)
DHS did not respond to questions for our October investigation, but a DHS spokesperson previously told ProPublica that the changes at CISA were in response to “a ballooning budget concealing a dangerous departure from its statutory mission,” which included “electioneering instead of defending America’s critical infrastructure.” A White House spokesperson declined an interview request but said, “President Trump has done more than any other President to ensure we have free and fair elections.”
4. The White House floated an idea that would’ve shut down virtually all mail-in voting.
The White House initially proposed a change for the Postal Service that would’ve been even more disruptive than the rule the Supreme Court rejected in September.
As Fifield and Elkind reported, the Trump administration suggested all ballots be delivered through certified mail, meaning voters would need to be home to sign for delivery of their ballots. The Trump administration dropped this plan after the USPS said it would be too difficult to execute. It instead proceeded with the executive order that would’ve forced postal workers to serve as gatekeepers, deciding which ballots would be delivered and which wouldn’t.
In an emailed statement, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis denied the administration had interfered improperly with the Postal Service, an independent agency whose governance structure is specifically designed to protect it from political influence.
The Supreme Court’s order in September means that voting by mail can proceed as planned for the midterms, with states left to decide the rules for mail-in ballots.
5. The Postal Service’s cost-cutting measures have led to delays and more rejected ballots in rural areas.
Amid the increased attention on the Postal Service’s role in elections, a ProPublica analysis found that delays resulting from the agency’s cost-cutting measures in recent years have endangered the validity of ballots cast in rural areas.
The Postal Service has consolidated processing of first-class mail into regional hubs, and the agency cut the frequency of mail pickups in half at many post offices 50 miles or more from those processing plants. The changes often added a day or more to delivery time and pushed back postmarking, an official mark confirming an envelope has been received by the Postal Service.
Across five states where the best data was available — Washington, California, Ohio, North Carolina and Oregon — the delays during this year’s primary elections have had the most substantial effect in areas that voted for Trump in 2024.
Postal Service leaders say such delays are less likely in the Nov. 3 general election because of “extraordinary measures” the agency puts in place for these votes, when there’s typically far more turnout.

https://apache.be/2026/10/26/hoe-servisc.title: Hoe de Servische studentenbeweging uitgroeide tot verkiezingsoverwinnaar
https://apache.be/2026/10/26/hoe-servisc.author: Simon Clément
https://apache.be/2026/10/26/hoe-servisc.text:
Wie vandaag de faculteit Filosofie in het Servische Novi Sad binnentreedt, merkt nog weinig van de blokkade die er maandenlang standhield. De Studentenlijst groeide hier uit tot de grote volksbeweging tegen de regering en de overheidscorruptie die afgelopen zondag (25/10) de verkiezingen won. Verdwijnen Vučić en zijn aanhangers na de nederlaag van dit weekend helemaal van het toneel?
Gejuich op de straten en pleinen in Servië gisteren (25/10): de Studentenlijst, die al twee jaar lang tegen het beleid van president Aleksandar Vučić protesteerde, heeft de parlementsverkiezingen gewonnen.
Deze lente trok fotograaf Simon Clément naar Servië om er de lokale verkiezingen te volgen, toen de studentenbeweging zich voor het eerst als politieke partij positioneerde.
Deze fotoreportage werd in juni 2026 gepubliceerd in Apache Magazine.
Op 1 november 2024 stortte een pas vernieuwd afdak van het treinstation in Novi Sad volledig in na een renovatie, waarop de regering nalatigheid verweten werd. Zestien mensen kwamen om het leven.
“De eerste dag was er een van shock. Iedereen stuurde sms’jes naar hun geliefden om te vragen of ze veilig waren”, herinnert Jelena Kleut zich, hoogleraar mediastudies aan de faculteit waar de studenten in opstand kwamen. “De tweede dag kwam de leugen.”
President Aleksandar Vučić verklaarde daags na de ramp dat de overheid de overkapping nog niet had aangepakt – iets wat verklaringen van betrokken ingenieurs en beelden van de burgemeester en minister van Transport die het net gerenoveerde station inhuldigden, onmiddellijk tegenspraken. “En dus braken er op de derde dag protesten uit”, vertelt Kleut.
Op de nationale dag van de studenten zei de huidige minister van Informatie, Boris Bratina, nog dat “de politie het recht heeft om studenten te slaan en zelfs te doden”
Meer dan twintigduizend mensen verzamelden zich aan het station van de kleine stad om hun woede te uiten over het feit dat de overheid de verantwoordelijkheid voor de ramp zo vlotjes van zich afschoof. In amper een jaar tijd groeide het aantal manifestanten tot 160.000 à 300.000.
“Samen met duizenden anderen waren we aan het wachten op de studenten alsof we wachtten op Tito, de voormalige Joegoslavische leider”, zegt de oudere Marica geëmotioneerd.
Anderhalf jaar na de ramp aan het stationsgebouw ligt het puin er nog steeds bij alsof het gisteren gebeurd is, slechts omringd met enkele hekken, talloze brieven, herdenkingsbordjes en verwelkte bloemen.
Sinds de Servische Progressieve Partij (SNS) van Vučić in 2014 de macht overnam, glijdt het land alsmaar meer af naar een dictatuur. “In Servië is werkelijk iedereen intussen getroffen of benadeeld door zijn beleid”, hekelt student literatuur Marco.
“Wanneer er zoveel politieke gevangenen zijn, onafhankelijke journalistiek zwaar onder druk staat en de rechterlijke macht haar autonomie verliest, kun je Servië moeilijk nog een democratie noemen”, meent Kleut. “Ze zijn het pad aan het effenen voor een complete machtsovername na de volgende nationale verkiezingen. De strijd is nog lang niet voorbij.”
Medeplichtige van Milošević
In de eerste jaren van zijn politieke carrière was Vučić minister van Informatie onder het nationalistische bewind van Slobodan Milošević. Hij was medeverantwoordelijk voor het ontkennen, verbergen en goedpraten van Servische wreedheden in Bosnië, Kosovo en Servië zelf. Kritische journalisten golden als buitenlandse spionnen, terwijl gedode burgers als terroristen werden omschreven.
Onafhankelijke media konden nog maar moeilijk overleven. Die zorgwekkende trend van intimidatie duurt ook onder de huidige minister van Informatie, Boris Bratina, voort. Op 4 april, Dan studenata of nationale dag van de studenten, zei hij nog dat “de politie het recht heeft om studenten te slaan en zelfs te doden”.
Vooral de demonstraties en campagnes tegen de geplande lithiummijnen inspireerden de huidige studentenbeweging
In zijn jaarverslag van 2025 spreekt Human Rights Watch van onwettig gebruik van geweld tegen demonstranten, intimidatie, inbreuk op de privacywetgeving en onmenselijke omstandigheden in de gevangenissen.
Het beleg van Belgrado
Voor Serviërs is protest niets nieuws. In het laatste decennium alleen al lijkt er elk jaar wel een kleine of grote protestgolf over het land te spoelen. In 2016 tegen vermeende verkiezingsfraude, in 2018 de “Een van de vijf miljoen”-protesten, toen Aleksandar Vučić zei dat zelfs als er vijf miljoen mensen op straat zouden komen, hij niets zou veranderen.
Maar vooral de demonstraties en campagnes tegen de geplande lithiummijnen inspireerden de huidige studentenbeweging. In 2024 trokken meer dan 100.000 mensen de straten op tegen de geplande mijnen.
Er werden treinsporen geblokkeerd en net als de studentenbeweging genoot het protest heel wat steun bij de bevolking, zelfs bij de SNS-achterban. Door de massale druk werd het mijnproject tijdelijk stop-
gezet, tot ongenoegen van de EU, die het als strategisch belangrijk ziet.
“Eten, protesteren, plenum en slapen. En dat vijf maanden lang”
“Al die ervaring heeft de studentenbeweging geërfd en getild naar een nieuwe protestbeweging”, vertelt student Milica Klajn. Ze organiseerden bijna dagelijks wakes om slachtoffers van de ramp in het treinstation te herdenken. Terwijl het dodental klom, blokkeerden de studenten eerst 14, dan 15 en uiteindelijk 16 minuten lang de straat in alle stilte.
In december viel een knokploeg kunststudenten uit Belgrado aan. “Ik ging meteen naar mijn faculteit omdat ik hoorde dat er een plenum was (een open vergadering waarin op gedecentraliseerde manier wordt gedebatteerd, red.). Daar besloten we om onmiddellijk ook onze faculteit te bezetten”, zegt Tatjana, een student biologie in Belgrado. Al snel volgden andere universiteiten en faculteiten over het hele land.
Ook buiten de traditioneel politiek actieve faculteiten groeide de mobilisatie: in Novi Sad daagden meer dan 3.000 studenten op voor het eerste plenum van de ingenieursfaculteit. “Ik hoop echt dat onze blokkades een verschil hebben gemaakt. Ik heb er zo veel voor gegeven, ik leefde er praktisch. Eten, protesteren, plenum en slapen. En dat vijf maanden lang”, zegt Milica met een zucht.
Vervroegde verkiezingen
Zelfs gewelddadige ontzettingen en een lange zomervakantie kregen de geest niet meer in de fles. “Vučić dacht echt dat deze beweging, net als eerdere protestgolven, gewoon zou uitdoven. Maar doordat hij ons bleef aanvallen in de media, maakte hij ons juist nog strijdvaardiger”, zegt Tatjana lachend. Tot op vandaag staat het plenum centraal in de horizontale manier van organiseren van de studenten.
Ondertussen hebben ook burgers het concept overgenomen. In Novi Sad komen sympathiserende groepen periodiek bijeen en bespreken zij zowel hoe ze hun lokale buurt kunnen verbeteren als hoe ze de protesten kunnen ondersteunen. Hoewel deze aanpak zorgt voor brede betrokkenheid, brengt ze ook vertraging met zich mee: het kostte de studenten maanden om te beslissen om als politieke partij voort te doen.
Tot grote verbazing werd er gehoor gegeven aan de eis tot vervroegde nationale verkiezingen, die er voor het einde van 2026 moeten komen. Volgens sommige peilingen genieten de studenten alvast van een meerderheid: zo’n 58% van de bevolking zou op hen stemmen.
Met als eerste cruciale tussenstop de lokale verkiezingen in ongeveer tien districten, die de lakmoesproef zijn voor zowel Vučić als de studenten. Maar ze zijn op hun hoede. “Want eerlijk verlopen de verkiezingen in Servië allerminst”, stelt Tatjana.
Waar blijft Europa?
Het verbaast de studenten dan ook wel dat er bijzonder weinig steun uit Europa komt. “Vroeger had ik een geïdealiseerd beeld van Europa”, geeft Tatjana toe.
“Ondertussen vertrouw ik die instituties niet meer. Al te vaak primeren strategische belangen op mensenrechten. Het lijkt alsof ze een andere taal spreken als het gaat over Oekraïne en Rusland dan wanneer het Israël en Palestina betreft. Europa wil nog steeds ons lithium voor goedkope batterijen in militaire drones.”
“Ze zetten wel druk, maar lang niet genoeg”, vertelt Kleut. “In het voorjaar vroegen negen Europese parlementariërs Vučić nog om de mensenrechten te respecteren. De EU ziet dat Vučić de controle verliest, en maakt zich tegelijkertijd zorgen over toekomstige lithiumaanvoer. De EU vreest dat als de banden met Vučić worden doorgesneden, hij zich volledig tot Rusland en China zal wenden. Dan verlies je elk middel van druk en invloed. De studenten blijven wat op afstand van die grotere vraagstukken over de EU. Maar je kan zulke beslissingen niet blijven uitstellen.”
Als de toren valt
Tijana Nešić (63) was een van de duizenden vrijwillige observatoren die de lokale verkiezingen hebben gemonitord. Ze ging eind maart naar Kula, wat in het Servisch ‘toren’ betekent, een klein stadje met net geen 50.000 inwoners. Hier hebben de studenten ervoor gekozen om zelf deel te nemen aan de lokale verkiezingen, terwijl ze in andere steden de bevolking aanmoedigen om op de oppositie te stemmen.
Voor haar vertrek verklaarde Tijana: “Als we Kula winnen, valt de rest als een kaartenhuis in elkaar.” Wellicht is ze een van de oudste studenten die aan de protesten deelnamen. Tijana besloot op latere leeftijd terug te studeren en belandde zo midden in de studentenprotesten. “Wat de studenten vooral doen met hun protesten is de bevolking weer verenigen, en dat is net de grote angst van Vučić. Het geeft ons opnieuw hoop, ik zie het ook bij mensen van mijn generatie”, getuigt ze.
Biologiestudent Tatjana: “Vučić heeft ons alleen maar strijdvaardiger gemaakt”
En dat is voelbaar in Kula zelf. “De enige manier waarop Vučić de verkiezingen hier wint, is door ze te stelen”, meent Dayin, inwoner van Kula. Dat wantrouwen is verre van ongegrond. Enkele dagen voor de verkiezingen eind maart duiken er plots heel wat nieuwe bewoners op in de stad.
“’s Nachts lopen er mannen met maskers rond om mensen te intimideren en op een avond weerklonken schoten. Twee weken geleden werden we zelfs met de dood bedreigd”, vertelt Vladica Klajić, een student die opkomt bij de verkiezingen.
“Normaal stellen de lokale verkiezingen helemaal niets voor. Maar de voorbije twee weken is de president al twee keer campagne komen voeren en waren er bezoeken van ministers in elk naburig dorp. In de media is dit het enige waar ze het over hebben.”
Op de verkiezingsdag rijden grote bussen rond zonder nummerplaten en een grote groep motoren baant zich een weg door de stad naar de stembussen. Rond de middag verlaat een gemaskerde knokploeg het lokale voetbalstadion. Ze vallen omstanders, onder wie journalisten, aan met stokken en keren terug naar het stadion, waar ze politiebescherming genieten.
Klokslag 23.00 uur bindt Vučić er geen doekjes om: zijn SNS-partij heeft in Kula gewonnen. Nochtans zijn de meeste stemmen op dat moment nog niet aangekomen in het stadhuis om geteld te worden. Uiteindelijk behalen de studenten de hoogste score, maar geen meerderheid – die is voor de SNS en haar coalitiepartners.
“We hebben voor onszelf uitgemaakt dat we nu kalm moeten blijven en ons moeten focussen op de nationale verkiezingen. Het feit dat ze zoveel energie hebben gestoken om in Kula te winnen, toont duidelijk dat ze aan het panikeren zijn”, vindt Vladica. “Dat is het teken dat we goed bezig zijn.”
Ondanks hun eerste nederlaag op lokaal niveau heeft de Studentenlijst de parlementsverkiezingen gisteren (25/10) gewonnen. De partij werd gevormd door universiteitsstudenten, maar geen van hen stond daadwerkelijk op de lijst. De kandidaten waren weinig bekende experts, sporters, boeren en kunstenaars. Deze fotoreportage werd in juni 2026 gepubliceerd in Apache Magazine, voor de nationale verkiezingen.

https://www.cartooningforpeace.org/en/br.text:
Cartooning for Peace / Brazil alert: Brazilian cartoonist Gilmar, also known on social media as ‘Cartunista Das Cavernas’, is the target of online death threats	
14 october 2026
Since July 2026, Cartunista Das Cavernas has been receiving death threats on Facebook because of his editorial cartoons. These messages, which have become increasingly violent, have turned into explicit death threats. The cartoonist has received these threats via private messages, but also in the comments on his posts. One user even went so far as to post a doctored photo of the cartoonist, in which he is depicted with a bullet in his head. The cartoonist has filed a complaint with the São Paulo State Police for threats and verbal abuse.
Cartooning for Peace, which is closely monitoring the ongoing legal proceedings, expresses its concern over the death threats against the Brazilian cartoonist Cartunista Das Cavernas and strongly condemns the attacks and acts of intimidation against the Brazilian press, particularly in the context of the upcoming elections.

https://www.cartooningforpeace.org/en/pu.text:
Cartooning for Peace / Publication: La bascule du monde – Perspectives from photographers and press cartoonists	
Photojournalism and press cartoons are unique languages, whose dialogue offers visual echoes and converging perspectives. This graphic osmosis reveals the universality and complementarity of these two forms of image journalism, which have been weakened by fake news, artificial intelligence and the many threats to press freedom.
Co-edited by Cartooning for Peace and Emmanuelle Hascoët, exhibition curator, and supported by Amnesty International, which wrote the afterword, this book presents some sixty pairs of photographs and press cartoons, accompanied by a text by Pierre Haski, geopolitical specialist and president of Reporters Without Borders, and a joint interview with Kak, press cartoonist and president of Cartooning for Peace, and Guillaume Herbaut, award-winning photojournalist.

https://www.cartooningforpeace.org/en/ca.title: Cartooning for Peace at the Africa Facts Summit 2025 in Dakar
https://www.cartooningforpeace.org/en/ca.author: ADMIN-principal2026
https://www.cartooningforpeace.org/en/ca.text:
Cartooning for Peace / Cartooning for Peace at the Africa Facts Summit 2025 in Dakar	
From 1 to 2 October 2025, Cartooning for Peace (CFP) will participate in the 4th edition of the Africa Facts Summit organised by the independent fact-checking organisation Africa Check.
This year’s event is being held in Dakar, Senegal, and will bring together nearly 200 fact-checkers from across the African continent for two days of discussions, synergies and networking in the fight against disinformation.
On this occasion, Cartooning for Peace is presenting an exhibition in partnership with Africa Check, Zimfact and Balobaki. It is part of the ‘Cartooning for Africa Facts’ project, implemented with the support of CFI.
It is also an opportunity to showcase the Illustrated Fact-Checking Manual, produced as part of this project, to all the fact-checkers attending the summit.
Invited by Cartooning for Peace, Lassane Zohoré, an Ivorian cartoonist and member of the CFP network, co-founder and editor-in-chief of the newspaper Gbich!, as well as Senegalese cartoonists Odia and Tijan, are actively participating in the Summit by sketching the discussions and key issues as they arise. Their drawings thus help to raise participants’ awareness of the evocative power of press cartoons and to forge links between fact-checking and press cartoons.

https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.author: Jonathan Jones
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.text:
Exhibition of the week
A Call to Art 
  
If you feel you need to see another exhibition about William Morris and the pre-Raphaelites, get yourself to Cambridge for this exploration of late Victorian art and politics.
 
Fitzwilliam Museum, Cambridge, until 3 May
Also showing
The Night Journal 
  
Aisling O’Beirn, Wilhelmina Peace and more meditate on the night: what does it mean when the world goes dark? One for Halloween maybe.
 
CCA Derry until 19 December
Robert Rauschenberg 
  
A special display from the Artist Rooms collection of the great magician of found stuff, with an emphasis on his later work – was it a falling off, or seriously underrated?
 
Tate Modern, London
Móti Collective 
  
A collective of no fewer than 17 artists and designers who work in Orkney celebrates their 10th anniversary in a gallery evocatively placed on Stromness harbour.
 
Pier Arts Centre, Stromness, until 24 December
Wilhelmina Barns-Graham 
  
The Cornish landscape becomes a bony but ethereal abstraction in this modernist painter’s work.
 
Tate St Ives until 3 May
Image of the week
This image may share the unpretentious quiddity of Giorgio Morandi’s bottle paintings and the prismatic lucidity of Rodric O’Conor’s, but it is not an everyday still life. At the Venice Biennale, Lotus L Kang arranged 49 bottles of spirits in front of film reels of tidal mudflats and visualisations of birdsong, to reflect the Buddhist belief that a soul spends 49 days between death and rebirth. The images are now part of Kang’s shortlisted entry for the prestigious Deutsche Börse photography prize.
What we learned
The Bayeux tapestry has become a pop culture hit
An excellent survey of LS Lowry depicts northern England as a spirit-crushing dystopia
The Iranian photographer Hoda Afshar’s work is beautiful – and shocking
Fans swarmed San Francisco for a BTS star’s art exhibition
Masterpiece of the week
Autumn Evening by Henri-Joseph Harpignies, 1894
This painting is a reminder that art isn’t really a progression from old to new, a wave of movements displacing the past, but a great big fascinating mess, with artists at any one time working in many styles, including archaic ones. For this calming, eerily beautiful view of rusty-leaved birches against a bronzed evening sky was painted in the 1890s when Cézanne, Munch and Toulouse-Lautrec were building modernism – but Harpignies has absolutely no interest in that. This painting is not even touched by impressionism, which had started in the 1870s. Instead it is completely loyal to the artistic ideas of the painter’s youth. Born in 1819, Harpignies was a diehard classicist steeped in the light of Italy that he saw on his travels. This landscape has the same charm as finding a totally archaic bistro in a remote French village and eating its coq au vin as the sun goes down.
 
National Gallery, London

https://www.cartooningforpeace.org/en/a-.text:
Cartooning for Peace / A Cartooning for Peace exhibition at the European Court of Human Rights	
As part of the 75th anniversary of the European Convention on Human Rights and the 30th anniversary of the Human Rights Building, the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) will open its doors to the public on Sunday 21 September 2025.
This day will be an opportunity for visitors to discover the Palace of Human Rights and learn about the importance of the Convention: its history, the scope of the fundamental rights and freedoms it protects, its impact on individuals, as well as how the Court works, its field of activity and the challenges it faces.
Cartooning for Peace is presenting an exhibition designed especially for this anniversary, with the support of the ECHR. Through cartoons from around the world, it illustrates the main principles of this convention, which aims to protect human rights and fundamental freedoms at a time when they are under particular threat.

Cartooning for Peace / One-year anniversary of the unlawful arrest and “pre-trial detention” of Egyptian cartoonist Ashraf Omar	
Today marks a sad day for freedom of expression. It is the one-year anniversary of the unlawful arrest and “pre-trial detention” of Egyptian cartoonist Ashraf Omar.
On July 22nd, 2024, a Cairo activist, cartoonist, and translator named Ashraf Omar was taken from his home by plainclothes officers. Forty-eight hours elapsed before there was any official acknowledgment of his arrest or confirmation of his wellbeing or location.

https://apache.be/2026/10/23/klimaatvera.title: Klimaatverandering maakte hittegolf zeker in steden nog dodelijker
https://apache.be/2026/10/23/klimaatvera.author: Steven Vanden Bussche
https://apache.be/2026/10/23/klimaatvera.text:
Afgelopen zomer stierven in Europese steden meer dan 50.000 mensen door de hitte. Bijna twee op de drie van die sterfgevallen waren toe te schrijven aan de klimaatverandering. Britse wetenschappers brachten de hittedoden van de voorbije kwarteeuw in kaart. Ze publiceerden gedetailleerde ramingen voor 824 Europese steden, telkens met en zonder de invloed van de klimaatverandering.
Een groot deel van Vlaanderen verslikte zich vorige zondag (18/10) allicht in de koffie. Na een “wekenlange stilte” verkoos Annick De Ridder (N-VA) om in de gratis krant De Zondag “elke kritiek” op haar beleid te “pareren”.
Op de vraag of ze wakker ligt van de klimaatcrisis, antwoordde de Vlaamse minister van Mobiliteit en Openbare Werken laconiek: “Nee, ik lig daar niet wakker van. Ik ben een vooruitgangsoptimist. Dankzij onze innovatieve bedrijven zullen wij ook deze omslag maken.”
De Ridders kijkt vult de politieke stilte van premier Bart De Wever (N-VA). Hoewel afgelopen zomer zowat 3.000 Belgen meer stierven dan normaal, overal in Europa het ene na het andere hitterecord sneuvelde, én half oktober 60.000 mensen op straat kwamen voor een doortastend klimaatbeleid, houdt de premier de lippen stijf op elkaar wat betreft het klimaat.
Klimaatverandering duidelijke oorzaak
Wetenschappers van Imperial College London en London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine (LSHTM) publiceren vandaag (23/10) twee onderzoeksrapporten over hittedoden in het vakblad Nature Health.
De grote oversterfte is duidelijk gelinkt aan de aanhoudende hittegolven van afgelopen zomer, stellen ze. Die hittegolven zijn op hun beurt een waarneembaar gevolg van de klimaatverandering. Door de klimaatverandering komen hittegolven niet alleen vaker voor, ze duren ook langer en zijn intenser. Oudere mensen en mensen met een zwakkere gezondheid zijn de eerste slachtoffers.
De grote oversterfte is duidelijk gelinkt aan de aanhoudende hittegolven van afgelopen zomer
De twee studies zijn gebaseerd op complexe klimaatmodellen. Die koppelen de dagelijkse temperatuurmetingen aan gedocumenteerde sterfgevallen in verschillende leeftijdsgroepen. Daarbij houden ze rekening met factoren zoals geografie, bevolkingsdichtheid of de socio-economische situatie.
Op die manier konden de wetenschappers inschatten hoeveel mensen per dag stierven bij bepaalde temperaturen. Daardoor kunnen ze uiteindelijk ook becijferen hoeveel hittedoden er zouden zijn zonder de gevolgen van klimaatverandering.
In de eerste studie staan steden centraal. Die zijn interessant vanwege de grote bevolkingsdichtheid en het fenomeen van het hitte-eilandeffect. Afgelopen zomer betaalden de grote steden in Zuid- en West-Europa de grootste tol voor de hete temperaturen.
Parijs registreerde naar schatting het hoogste aantal hittegerelateerde doden, gevolgd door Rome, Londen en Madrid. Als we kijken naar het aantal doden per aantal inwoners domineren Italiaanse steden de statistieken en zit België in de middenmoot.
Pierre Masselot, statisticus en epidemioloog (LSHTM): "Toenemende hitte zal voor iedereen in Europa een probleem worden"
Noord-Europese steden zouden volgens de schattingen verhoudingsgewijs minder hittedoden kennen. Toch ligt het aandeel hittedoden in de totale sterftecijfers er hoog.
“De toenemende hitte zal voor vrijwel iedereen in Europa een probleem worden”, vat Pierre Masselot het probleem samen. Masselot is statisticus en epidemioloog aan de LSHTM en een van de onderzoeksleiders.
De naar schatting 50.000 hittedoden van afgelopen zomer in Europa, waarvan ruim twee derde toe te schrijven is aan de gevolgen van klimaatverandering, zijn een triest hoogtepunt deze eeuw. Dat blijkt uit de tweede studie.
De wetenschappers becijferden het aantal hittegerelateerde sterfgevallen in steden gedurende de afgelopen kwarteeuw, telkens voor de maanden juni, juli en augustus. Ze becijferden ook hoeveel hittedoden er zouden zijn zonder klimaatopwarming.
Dit artikel maakt deel uit van een project over hittegolven, gecoördineerd door het Urban Journalism Network en met steun van Journalismfund Europe.
Auteur: Peter Aldhous (Centre for Collaborative Investigative Journalism)
Grafische vormgeving: David Meidinger
Coördinatie: Hendrik Lehmann, Gaby Khazalová

https://www.theguardian.com/membership/2.title: ‘Some photos imprint upon us’: How our Saturday magazine puts together special issues about world-changing photographs
https://www.theguardian.com/membership/2.author: Gautam Malkani
https://www.theguardian.com/membership/2.text:
Can photographs still exert power in an age when millions of pictures are taken and shared every minute, and when a viewer’s first response is to question whether an image is even real?
Every few months, a team of editors on the Guardian’s Saturday magazine puts together a special photography package in print and digital formats. It features photographs that don’t just stop the scroll, they have also prompted the rewriting of history books. They are the kind of images that have changed the world in some way or radically shifted people’s perceptions.
Each issue has a particular theme. Earlier this month, the magazine featured photographs that have changed how we view masculinity – from a 1950 portrait of Marlon Brando in a white T-shirt to a paparazzi shot of David Beckham in a sarong and a bare-chested Vladimir Putin on horseback. Previous issues have focused on photographs that have reshaped sport, forced people to confront the reality of the climate crisis and upended the world of fashion.
Beyond the impact each image had back when it first came out, they still feel powerful and affecting today – reminding us how great photography can command a kind of reverence and stillness in the viewer. “Working on these issues, you realise that there’s something about the power of the images that’s elemental,” says Rebecca Liu, a commissioning editor on the Guardian’s Saturday magazine. “Some photos imprint upon us before we even can think about them. They just immediately hit our bloodstream.”
The first special issue featured protest images that have prompted social or political change. It was initially conceived as a one-off feature in 2022 amid protests in the US that year against the overturning of Roe v Wade and demonstrations against police brutality. But the feature resonated so strongly with readers that it spawned an occasional series.
That regularity means the process of putting the issues together is now fine-tuned, though not without its own drama and headaches. “Sometimes on the day of going to print we’re waiting on two or three final things to be confirmed,” says Rebecca. “It’s a massive act of organisation and coordination and a real collective effort with a lot of moving parts.”
Selecting which pictures to include involves tapping the collective minds of picture editors and journalists on the magazine and across the Guardian. Different colleagues will have different criteria. How to weigh up a photograph’s social or political impact against its technical importance to the medium? Should it be an image that, in itself, has changed the world or a photograph of a world-shifting moment?
“Everyone working on the magazine has a different take on it,” says Louis Siroy, the magazine’s deputy picture editor. “Some editors will ask how a particular photograph shaped society; what does it mean? Whereas I might be asking what are the important photographs or photographers that fit into that theme or category.”
For example, the first special issue about protest photography didn’t just include the famous image of a protestor standing in front of a tank in Tiananmen Square, it also included a less famous but equally powerful photograph of a boy sitting on the shoulders of relatives above the sea of soldiers’ helmets. Taken by the photographer Dario Mitidieri, the image was suggested by Louis. “That to me is a great photograph, and I was trying to bring something that wasn’t necessarily the image people are familiar with,” he says. “Hopefully these selections inspire people to value and appreciate the breadth and power of great photographs.”
By drawing on colleagues’ different perspectives and experience, each special issue sheds unique light on its theme. “So while the selection can’t possibly be comprehensive and definitive, it’s still authoritative,” says Rebecca.
Other images included in the initial protest photography issue include the famous picture of US athletes John Carlos and Tommie Smith raising their fists in a black power salute during a medal ceremony at the 1968 Olympics. There are also several photographs of protesters facing off against riot police or soldiers, including a powerful image of a young girl in Santiago, Chile, during a 2016 demonstration marking the anniversary of the country’s 1973 military coup.
One of the most time-consuming challenges involves obtaining the rights to publish the images. “Some of the greatest challenges involve finding the right copyright holder for some lesser-known photographs,” says Caroline Hunter, the magazine’s picture editor.
Even well-known photographs can present hurdles. “Sometimes you have to get permission from the subject of the photo as well as from the photographer, particularly when it comes to photos of celebrities or fashion,” explains Louis. “It can get really hard to track down the person you need. For instance, the masculinity special featured a famous second world war photo of a US aeroplane gunner that was taken by the photographer Horace Bristol, who is now deceased. It took some time to contact the photographer’s son Henri in California and explain the context in which we wanted to use the photo. And even when dealing with well-known photographers, it still involves negotiating the rights for editorial use rather than commercial use.”
Another challenge that can arise is the quality of the photographs. “We have to ensure the image is large enough or good enough quality to reproduce, especially for very old images that previously existed only as prints,” says Caroline. “Works by famous and art photographers often have specific rules around usage, so it’s important to ensure that we keep within their guidelines. We had a really good response from photographers after our recent photo special marking America at 250. I think this was because there were so many great, iconic images from seminal photographers.”
The team also has to decide the best layout for the print and digital editions – which images to give prominence to, how they might best fit together, and the range of black-and-white and colour images. Maggie Murphy, the magazine’s art director, experiments with different layouts, sometimes on a screen, sometimes with printouts strewn across the desks.
As well as the images, a huge amount of work goes into the words. Each special issue includes a short guest-written essay, and each photograph has an extended caption about that particular picture’s significance or backstory.
The journalists who are commissioned to write these captions undertake extensive research. For example, the masculinity issue includes a famous 1970 advertisement depicting a pregnant man, for which the journalist tracked down the original campaign’s photographer, who is now 98. “I encourage original interviews and research wherever possible,” says Rebecca. “We want the words to illuminate something about the picture and for people to learn things. That’s not something you necessarily have to do for a 150-word caption, but we want to do it because the editorial component is so important to us at the Guardian.”
Researching the captions also reveals something about the nature of photography. “It really shows the importance of not just taking an image at face value,” says Rebecca. “I’m always surprised by what you discover when you look into things. You might find a complicated backstory behind the person who is photographed – perhaps their ambivalence about being pictured, for instance.”
The same applies to the thought that goes into the introductory essays. The novelist Anne Enright wrote perceptively about how women are captured on camera, for better or for worse, in her introduction to an issue that featured photographs that have changed the way society sees women. “As you look at a Kardashian selfie, consider how many rules had to be broken to get her to this moment of self-commodification,” writes Enright.
The masculinity issue contains an accompanying essay by the poet and novelist Luke Kennard, who reflects on how the images seem to capture extremes of masculinity, with little in between: “To judge from our media, one would think we were either waifs or muscle-men… Even the bang average is barely represented.”
Rebecca noticed that gap in representation back when the team was initially selecting which photographs to include in the issue. “I remember thinking, where are the other male bodies? It was difficult to find any – at least with the quality and artistry that we look for in these stories. You’d Google the words ‘dad bod’ and you’d just get screenshots of Seth Rogen and grainy paparazzi shots of celebrities on the beach.”
The team is very mindful of the power of images to subtly reinforce or subvert people’s preconceptions. “Working on these issues makes us reflect on how much we subconsciously absorb images,” says Rebecca. “And how they feed into our imaginations.”

https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: Historian Lucy Worsley looks back: ‘The story of my life has been – the bookworm shall go to the ball’
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: Harriet Gibsone
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
Born in Reading in 1973, Lucy Worsley is a historian and TV presenter. She graduated with a first in history from Oxford, before completing a PhD in art history at the University of Sussex. Worsley spent 21 years as chief curator of Historic Royal Palaces, overseeing the Tower of London, Hampton Court and Kensington Palace, among others. She has presented numerous documentary series, including Six Wives, Royal History’s Biggest Fibs and most recently Victorian Murder Club. She lives in London with her husband. Her latest book, Queens and Kings: An Unusually Personal History, is out now.
This is me at the age of four. It was my career ambition to become a witch. My back-up options were spy and nun.
We were living in Canada at the time. Dad was an expert in cold places – glaciers and permanently frozen ground – and he was embarking on a year’s swap with an academic at the University of Ottawa. My mother made the costume for me to go trick or treating with the family across the road. In my basket are sweets and I look very pleased and very proud.
Because of my father’s job, we moved around a lot. I wasn’t naturally good at making friends, because I’m quite shy. New schools could be intimidating, but I always had a safe space when reading books. Whenever I ask my parents what I was like as a child, they say, “We don’t know, because you were always reading a book and not talking to us.” Deep down, I was a secret showoff. I was flamboyant when adopting somebody else’s clothes or character or persona.
Outside school I had Guides, played musical instruments and acted in plays. Nobody there knew I was an A-grade student, so I was able to pass for normal. But at my state school in Nottingham, I couldn’t hide. I was a weird little nerd, and my studiousness marked me out in a way that I didn’t have the social skills to conceal. Even though I was lonely, I soldiered on because of my political views. For example, the pupils were going to have a “wear what you like” day to protest about the teachers who were always going on strike. I disagreed, and thought the teachers should strike, so I went in my school uniform – a horrendously stupid choice as everybody laughed at me.
I always loved history, but my father, being a scientist, wanted me to take a different path. To please him, I chose science subjects for my A-levels. Halfway through, my mum said, “You’re not enjoying this. You need to do what you want to do, which is history.”
At university, I studied ancient and modern history. It was a period in which I went mildly off the rails: staying up late talking to people who were just like me, organising the rag parade, playing in orchestras, rowing and doing all the extracurricular activities. I didn’t work hard until the very end of my three years, as I was too busy having a lovely time.
As soon as I saw the advert for the role of chief curator at Historic Royal Palaces, I thought, “That’s my job!” It was a lengthy recruitment process, with interviews in different palaces, and at one point I got in a tizzy looking for the right entrance at the palace of St James. A sentry was standing in a box, so I said, “Please tell me where the right way is. I’m desperate.” He wasn’t allowed to talk to me, but in the end he took pity and rolled his eyes in the direction I should go.
The role was high-profile and there was an expectation of what someone doing that job would be like. Historically, it had been done by men, always of a certain seniority – people very much in command of themselves. By comparison, I was 29 years old, small and pale. I had bought a long, dark coat, which I thought made me look grown up. But my youth and inexperience eventually became my superpowers, because everybody could see there was something different about the way I was going to do things. I came to realise that my authority is in building a relationship of trust with the person I’m talking to, not making them think that I know more.
My TV career began when BBC Look North came to make a film about Bolsover Castle in Derbyshire, where I was working. We ended up spending the day together, with me showing them how they could tell the story. That night I was struck by how much I enjoyed the experience. I began appearing as an expert “talking head” on various shows, and in 2008 I did a show about Henry VIII. More followed. The world was changing – I wasn’t Simon Schama or David Starkey – and we were ready for more women to talk about history.
The struggle to look “authoritative” that I’d experienced earlier came up again in my TV career. I would get notes such as, “She needs to wear tailoring. She needs a dark coat.” It felt wrong. I am known for wearing costumes – using whatever it takes to tell a story. Like a primary school teacher, I have no dignity. But that is also the skill that is available to me. The dressing up might be considered frivolous by critics, but clothes tell us about hierarchy and social structures. They are also fun to look at, which is important when making TV.
Each day is different on set, but some are stranger than others. In one of my early shows, I was dressed as a medieval peasant foraging in the woods. My costume was a brown blanket. It was November and really cold, but I didn’t have the confidence to say, “This isn’t working for me.” In the end, I just burst into tears. Crying does work, but it’s better to speak up: I did a programme about the American Revolution once, and said to the producer, “I’d really like to be in the Independence Day procession that goes through Philadelphia on 4 July.” I imagined I’d be in a modest costume with buttons and a hat, maybe playing the cymbals. It turned out I was part of a twirling team and my costume was a skin-tight leotard. The rest of the team were 22-year-old girls. I got changed, but agreed with the cameraman that he would only shoot me from the neck up.
Being recognised is wonderful and terrible, as I’m a showoff but also shy. I’m capable of slipping through the streets of London in my baseball cap and glasses, but one in a thousand people have weirdly impressive facial recognition skills and clock me. Once a lady recognised me from my teeth alone. I also have a distinctive voice. Someone overheard me speaking in a swimming pool and said, “I know that voice!” I thought, “I’m naked, I’m dripping. I don’t want to engage with you just now, but thank you.”
The story of my life has been “the bookworm shall go to the ball”. I’ve had a wonderful career. But since turning 50, I’ve realised I work too hard. I’m endlessly asking myself, “Do you really love your work? Or is it just the capitalist patriarchy that’s making you think you love your work because that’s good for the economy?”
I don’t have the answers. But that’s the job of the historian. To ask the questions – and, for me, to put on the costumes. So has the girl in the photo grown up at all? Perhaps not.

https://www.propublica.org/article/borde.title: Tribal Leaders Warned Border Wall Construction Would Disturb Native American Remains. They Were Right.
https://www.propublica.org/article/borde.author: Ryan Devereaux
https://www.propublica.org/article/borde.text:
Lorraine Eiler stood in the blazing August sun, surrounded by reporters, to offer a warning. The Trump administration was racing to erect a second border wall across Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument, southwest of Tucson. If the bulldozers came, she said, they were bound to disturb the final resting places of her family and Hia-Ced O’odham tribal ancestors.
“People used to live here,” the 89-year-old said.
Fifteen days later, her fears were realized.
ProPublica has confirmed that Native American remains were unearthed in Organ Pipe amid soil overturned by border wall contractors.
The discovery, unreported until now, was made on Sept. 8, the National Park Service said in a statement. “Following established protocols, the University of Arizona conducted an assessment and confirmed that the remains are human and align with tribal cremation practices,” the agency said.
The Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act governs the steps agencies must take following an inadvertent discovery of Native American remains on federal land. Those steps include halting any activity that contributed to the discovery until tribal communities are consulted.
“The National Park Service is committed to respecting tribal rights and traditions,” the agency went on to say, adding that it was “working diligently to identify the culturally affiliated tribe and ensure the respectful return of the remains, so the tribe may observe their religious and cultural practices.”
Eiler was alerted to the discovery by a cultural affairs specialist with the Tohono O’odham Nation, a larger tribe whose reservation is east of Organ Pipe, and later by the Organ Pipe superintendent’s office. Her family discussed what to do next. Ultimately, they decided to hold off on reburying the newly unearthed remains until construction in the area stops, fearing the work will disturb more sites.
“Who knows what more will come up,” Eiler said in an interview. “They’re going to find remains wherever they dig.”
Customs and Border Protection contractors have bulldozed a wide swath of vegetation parallel to the international divide. The agency has fashioned staging areas for heavy equipment by knocking down, uprooting and attempting to transplant select specimens of the monument’s native plants. Eiler was told the remains were found by a park service archaeologist near the base of a saguaro cactus that was still standing.
In a statement, CBP said it was advised of the discovery six days after it was made, that its cultural resource specialists examined the area and found no other remains, and that “no additional construction has occurred at this location to date.”
The discovery comes amid tensions between the Department of Homeland Security and tribal communities in the Sonoran Desert. In April, border wall contractors bulldozed through a large, well-marked earthen etching, known as the Las Playas Intaglio, that was believed to be at least 6,500 years old. (CBP said the incident was accidental.)
Soon after, the department awarded a $1.3 billion contract for construction of a 62-mile border wall across the entirety of the Tohono O’odham Nation. The tribe is fighting the project in federal court and has erected “no trespassing” signs to keep border wall contractors off its land. As ProPublica recently reported, DHS has responded by deploying masked federal agents as escorts for its work crews and conducting aerial surveillance of tribal members. The head of CBP has justified the need for a wall by describing the reservation as “one of the most dangerous smuggling and trafficking corridors on the Southwest border.”
Verlon M. Jose, the tribe’s chairman, expressed gratitude that the park service had notified his office of the discovery, but mourned the fact that it was necessary.
“When you have mass destruction and disturbance of land taking place where there are clearly sacred sites, cemeteries and other areas of cultural importance, these types of discoveries are bound to happen,” Jose said in a statement. “Every time this happens it is a wound to the heart of all members of the Tohono O’odham Nation — these are our ancestors, our family members — whose remains are being desecrated.”
U.S. Rep. Adelita Grijalva, who appeared with Eiler and the chairman at the August news conference, blasted the government for failing to heed their warnings. “Tribal leaders and elders have warned DHS about the devastating consequences of bulldozing through their ancestral lands, beginning with the destruction of the Las Playas Intaglio,” she said in a statement. “For months, those warnings have fallen on deaf ears. Now, we are seeing exactly what they feared: sacred sites destroyed and ancestral burial grounds desecrated.”
James T. Watson, curator of bioarcheology in the Arizona State Museum at the University of Arizona, analyzed the remains recovered in Organ Pipe in the field.
While he was not authorized to discuss the details of his findings without park service approval, Watson said in an email that he confirmed the remains were human. The evidence suggested they were cremated in a manner consistent with precolonial practices in the region dating back 1,500 years, he wrote.
Under NAGPRA, the graves protection act, Native American remains inadvertently uncovered on park service lands must be immediately secured, Watson explained, and the superintendent of the jurisdiction must notify “all relevant lineal descendants” with “potential cultural affiliation or ancestral ties to the land.”
“Work in the immediate discovery area must remain suspended for at least 30 calendar days,” he wrote, while the park service consults with tribal representatives “to determine the disposition and physical treatment of the remains.”
In a region as rich with archaeological sites as the American Southwest, the inadvertent disturbance of Native American remains occurs with some regularity. What sets the discovery in Organ Pipe apart are the extraordinary powers the Department of Homeland Security wields to expedite wall construction in the borderlands.
Following the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, Congress passed the Real ID Act, which included a provision empowering the secretary of DHS to waive any law that might slow border wall construction. In the two decades since, DHS has invoked its powers 66 times, with 60 of those instances occurring under President Donald Trump’s two administrations.
When DHS uses this authority, it typically waives dozens of laws at a time. That was the case in 2019 when the department set its sights on Organ Pipe. A waiver issued by then-acting Secretary Kevin K. McAleenan set aside more than 40 of the nation’s most stringent environmental and cultural resource protection laws, including the National Environmental Policy Act, the Endangered Species Act, the Clean Water Act and others. Also on that list was the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act, the landmark 1990 law that acknowledged the nation’s long history of desecrating Native American burials and required that ancestral remains and cultural objects be returned to tribes.
In an internal 2019 report obtained by The Washington Post, park service officials identified nearly two dozen archaeological sites in Organ Pipe as at risk of damage or total destruction by government contractors.
Of particular significance is a desert oasis known as Quitobaquito Springs. Less than 200 feet from the international border, the springs provide one of the only reliable sources of groundwater and shade for miles around, and they were a longtime gathering place, grazing site and home for O’odham families.
“Archaeological evidence of human presence at Quitobaquito extends back thousands of years, at least to Archaic times,” the survey found, adding that the springs represent the “only known Hia C-ed O’odham village site in the United States.”
A park service report in 2024 noted that a cemetery at Quitobaquito holds the remains of at least two families, including Eiler’s, and 34 graves. Throughout the region, remains of 5,500 ancestors that were displaced have been made available for return to the Tohono O’odham Nation, according to ProPublica’s NAGPRA database.
“This sort of incident has happened numerous times across our homeland, and it’s always alarming to hear about a case from an O’odham point of view,” said David Martínez, a professor of American Indian and transborder studies at the University of Arizona and a member of the Hia-Ced O’odham and Akimel O’odham tribes, as well as the Gila River Indian Community.
“Those remains shouldn’t have been disturbed in the first place,” he said. “While there are protocols existing today to properly care for these remains, ultimately, whatever either the government or the corporate world is pursuing to build, we know that at some juncture that construction will continue, and it always leaves us feeling, I think, a little hollow.”
Today, Quitobaquito lies in the shadow of the border wall erected during Trump’s first term. Its construction required detonating explosives in the national monument, blasting apart an area called Monument Hill and outraging tribal leaders. According to Eiler, the remains recovered in September were not found at the springs, though government work crews are working in close proximity to the site.
This year, DHS hired Sundt Construction, an Arizona-based company, to build a second wall in the monument. The $443 million contract was finalized in May. (Sundt directed questions concerning the discovery of human remains on its job site to CBP.)
According to CBP, the 2019 waiver for Organ Pipe is still in effect, years after completion of the project that prompted it. A second waiver, exempting DHS from many of the same laws and applying to the national monument as well as a wildlife refuge to the west, was issued by Homeland Security’s then-Secretary Kristi Noem last year.
“Unfortunately, there is no end date to the effectiveness of the waivers,” said Dinah Bear, a Tucson-based lawyer who served for 25 years as a senior attorney in the White House’s Council on Environmental Quality under both Democratic and Republican administrations. What’s more, she added, “there’s nothing in the statutory language that ties the waivers to a particular project.”
The Department of Homeland Security’s waiver powers have been central to a high-profile legal fight over the department’s efforts to build a border wall through Big Bend National Park in West Texas, with a federal judge overseeing the case recently ordering a temporary halt to the project.
Borderlands advocates in Arizona are hoping for similar interventions. In Congress, Grijalva is preparing legislation to void existing waivers that have allowed DHS to disregard laws designed to protect tribal sovereignty, sacred sites and environmentally sensitive lands.
In the meantime, construction on the border continues. For Eiler, it’s not just the destruction in Organ Pipe that’s troubling. She sees the disturbance of tribal graves resulting from wall construction as reflective of a wider pattern of destruction across the border.
“It’s sad because it’s not only happening down there,” she said. “It’s happening all over the United States, and nobody’s saying much about it.”

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/california-s.title: 100,000 California State Workers Struck Last Month
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/california-s.author: Kari Thompson
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/california-s.text:
100,000 California State Workers Struck Last Month
State employees with SEIU Local 1000 recently went on a one-day strike across California. It was the first walkout in the history of the union, which represents about 100,000 workers ranging from accountants to custodians to nurses.
State workers went on a one-day unfair labor practice strike across California on October 21, with picket lines in Sacramento, San Francisco, Los Angeles, and other cities. They’re demanding better pay, affordable health care coverage, and flexibility to work from home.
This was the first strike in the history of Service Employees International Union (SEIU) Local 1000, which represents about one hundred thousand government employees, ranging from accountants to custodians to nurses at state offices, hospitals, and prisons.
They have been working without a contract since July 1. Some five thousand employees were excluded from striking.
Governor Gavin Newsom’s “return-to-office” mandate went into effect this past summer. It requires workers to be in the office four days per week — even though workers report there isn’t enough space for all of them.
Workers argue the return-to-office policy compounds the lack of pay increases. Being forced back into the office is “more than just a pay cut,” said Jonah Paul, who works for the Employment Development Department in Sacramento. ”It’s a huge reduction in quality of life.
“Telework is a stopgap for a lot of problems our society is not willing to address,” Paul said: “The cost of childcare and insane commutes. Telework becomes a catch-all solution for a grueling life.”
Zero Raise
Last year, Local 1000 agreed to a pay freeze to help the state meet a budget shortfall. This summer, however, workers were supposed to see raises. But they got zilch.
The union is asking for a 20 percent raise over three years to catch up, especially given increased state revenue over the past two years.
Though Local 1000 and the state have met several times to negotiate a new contract, the union says CalHR, the bargaining representative for the state, has not been negotiating in good faith. It filed unfair labor practice charges with the state Public Employment Relations Board against CalHR for delaying negotiations and failing to respond to proposals.
“When I first started working for the state ten years ago, for the most part CalHR would throw us a bone,” said Steward Giovanni Martinez, a state worker in Sacramento. “This is the worst bargaining cycle I’ve witnessed. They don’t want to budge on a lot of stuff. Newsom takes us for granted, and the people he’s appointed in CalHR are the same way.”
Under previous leadership, the union kicked in $1 million to help Newsom fight a recall campaign in 2021. Members question why a governor they supported doesn’t have their backs now.
Strike Schools
Members of Local 1000 have been organizing over the past few months to increase membership numbers. Activists have been approaching nonmembers at their own worksites to ask them personally to join the union and calling others on the phone.
Stewards did their best to increase communications across the membership, though they were hampered by limited updates from the official Bargaining Unit Negotiating Committee.
Paul said that three years ago, the local offered “strike schools” to members, but these were more about discouraging members from planning for a strike. This time, he said, strike schools emphasized that the decision to strike was one for members to make, building membership numbers along with enthusiasm for walking out together.
In a strike authorization vote held from September 9 to October 7, 96 percent voted “yes” to walk out.
On the final day of the vote, the union held informational pickets to encourage participation in the vote. One picket happened to be next door to a building where Newsom was giving a speech.
With just a half-hour’s notice, stewards and other union leaders managed to get members together to cover every entrance of the building and make enough noise that Newsom had to comment on it during his event.
Despite this pressure from members, there was no last-minute deal to avert the strike, as happened ten years ago under Governor Jerry Brown.
“For a lot of folks this is their first strike — this is mine,” Martinez said. “We didn’t want to walk off the job — we have a good relationship with our supervisors — but we had no choice.”
World’s Fourth-Largest Economy
Strike participation appeared strong, with thousands of workers joining rallies and marches in cities across the state. Striking workers in the state’s capitol shut down multiple blocks with a march from CalHR headquarters to the capitol building.
“I was up on the truck with our president and a few other folks, leading people to different rally points,” said Emily Ingram, a Department of Education worker in Sacramento. “All you could see in every direction was more people. It was a pretty powerful feeling.”
In Los Angeles, hundreds of workers rallied outside a state building. Arielle Mangabat-Lowe, who works at the Department of Toxic Substances Control, said she was surprised how many people showed up, after prior actions had only a few dozen participants. She reflected that it can be hard as an organizer to put so much work into the union without knowing whether other members will participate.
But being with others at the strike rally boosted her spirits. “The state of California is a terrifying employer — it’s the world’s fourth-largest economy. We showed up today anyways,” she said. “It’s cool to feel like you have a voice, especially in these times.”
“As someone who has been trying to get folks to join up, I think a lot of state workers are fired up,” said Martinez. “The energy is here. Where we go with it, that’s up to us as members and our leadership.”
The union continued to pressure CalHR after the strike. On October 27, about twenty members disrupted a CalHR event in Sacramento, distributing flyers and shouting a message to the crowd demanding that the state stop intimidating members and bargain fairly.
The two sides met for contract mediation on October 30, but they did not reach a deal. “We are continuing to prepare for another strike if needed,” Ingram said ahead of that meeting.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/02/mich.title: Abdul El-Sayed’s Race Has Been Defined Islamophobia. Will It Be Determined By It?
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/02/mich.author: Matt Sledge
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/02/mich.text:
As Abdul El-Sayed’s one-time primary opponent attempts to redirect closing arguments in the Michigan Senate contest to the topics of Israel and antisemitism, the Democratic nominee has entered the final stretch of the midterms against a barrage of bigoted attacks over his own race and religion.
President Donald Trump called him a “jihadist.” Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. went on a racist rant against Arabs. According to Michigan state Sen. Mallory McMorrow, a mailer went out showing El-Sayed’s face next to the World Trade Center’s Twin Towers.
“They are running the most bigoted, hateful, Islamophobic campaign I’ve ever seen,” McMorrow told a local TV outlet. McMorrow, who ran for the Democratic Senate nomination but dropped out before the August primary, is taking a far different tack than Rep. Haley Stevens, the Democratic primary runner-up who has spent the race’s final days painting El-Sayed as an angry antisemite and crossed party lines Sunday to endorse Republican contender Mike Rogers.
Rogers has sought to portray El-Sayed as anti-American and repeatedly tried to tie his opponent to the Muslim Brotherhood. He insists the attacks have nothing to do with faith. But that is exactly how many observers see them, including Muslim Republicans who have been disgusted by the rhetoric.
As the election draws to a close, the Islamophobic attacks have taken a backseat to Stevens’s claims of antisemitism — most prominently concerning a PAC ad that connected high grocery prices to U.S. spending on Israeli military aid — and a personal feud between the former primary opponents. And some of El-Sayed’s allies worry that the Muslim and Arab-baiting attacks will work. One recent poll found that 38 percent of Michigan voters said they would be less likely to vote for a Muslim candidate.
Michigan’s Muslim and Arab organizers have not been taking the attacks lying down, however. In interviews last month, two prominent leaders in Dearborn’s Arab American community described widespread excitement over the opportunity to vote for the man who would be the first Muslim in the U.S. Senate.
“It very much feels like when President Obama was running and his whole campaign was around like hope. That’s what it feels like,” Layla Elabed, the organizing director at Arab Americans for Progress, told the Intercept on October 8.
Elabed, the sister of Rep. Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich., was one of the key movers in the Uncommitted movement, which urged Michigan voters to withhold their votes from Joe Biden during the 2024 primary in protest of his support for Israel’s war on Gaza. The movement succeeded in making a statement, but also drew criticism from centrist Democrats for allegedly fracturing party unity.
Elabed’s current group is an evolution of the Uncommitted movement. Its canvassers have been knocking on doors to turn out support for El-Sayed and other candidates.
“I don’t think many people in Dearborn are surprised by Haley Stevens,” Elabed told The Intercept on Monday. “Arab American Democrats in Michigan have been sounding the alarm about her for years, warning our fellow Democrats about a pattern of putting political interests ahead of the people she was elected to represent.”
She believes the same coalition that came together for Uncommitted could help push El-Sayed over the top this election.
“Abdul has been able to really take a stand on all the issues that were really important to anti-war voters and anti-genocide voters,” she said. “It’s not a coincidence that that same coalition, that same base of Democratic voters are now all coming out to support us.”
Hers is not the only group seeking to mobilize Muslim and Arab voters, who make up a sizable slice of the Michigan electorate. The Arab American Political Action Committee has also endorsed El-Sayed. Its president, Osama Siblani, said there is widespread enthusiasm for El-Sayed in areas with dense Arab populations such as Dearborn.
Siblani compared El-Sayed’s potential victory to John F. Kennedy’s pathbreaking election as the first Catholic president.
“First of all, he’s qualified. Second of all, he’s saying the right things, he has a good agenda,” Siblani. “His opponent is an asshole. In addition to all of this, he is breaking the ceiling for our community and for other communities. That is a plus.”
The goal of the Arab and Muslim-baiting attacks from El-Sayed’s enemies is clear, according to Nazita Lajevardi, an associate professor of political science at the University of Michigan.
“Islamophobia is a tried and true strategy for garnering a candidate support and swaying the vote,” she said.
Yet it is also possible that the attacks on El-Sayed’s identity will lead to greater turnout in places like Dearborn, she said.
“I think scholarship would tell us that when political elites discriminate, that it does mobilize people into action. Past scholarship would say yes, it would, but it’s an open question,” she said.
Elabed agreed that the attacks are nothing new. “We’ve watched it play out time and time again,” she told The Intercept. Stevens’s about-face isn’t a major development, she said, “It’s that the rest of the Democratic Party is finally seeing what our communities have been saying all along. We weren’t wrong. We just weren’t being listened to.”
Siblani expressed a similar sentiment on Monday. “I’m not surprised, I’m disgusted,” he wrote of Stevens in a text message, attaching an emoji of a person vomiting.
Stevens’s choice to jump ship for the Rogers campaign appears to have galvanized El-Sayed’s base. His campaign announced a one-day fundraising record after his fellow Democrat pulled her endorsement on Sunday.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
