https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/03/b.title: Bronxites: Don’t Sacrifice Our Waterfront Access For Yet Another Amazon Warehouse
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/03/b.author: Dave Colon
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/03/b.text:
Bronx residents are calling on Gov. Hochul to block an Amazon contractor from converting a former New York Post printing plant into a last-mile warehouse they say would inundate the area with trucks and sacrifice a huge chunk of the borough’s waterfront.
Environmental activists with South Bronx Unite say that logistics giant Prologis, which builds warehouses across the city, wants to convert the dormant printing building — located in Port Morris across from Randalls Island — into a last-mile fulfillment warehouse.
Jeremiah Kane, a vice president at Prologis, met with representatives from South Bronx Unite on Oct. 6 and told them that the company planned to tear down the existing printing plant building and replace it with a last-mile warehouse. 
Prologis’s top tenant nationally is Amazon, according to its most recent Securities and Exchange Commission filing.
The South Bronx waterfront, meanwhile, already hosts a large Fresh Direct warehouse in the Harlem River Rail Yard, which abuts the lot right next to the former newspaper plant. Researchers from Columbia University blamed the Fresh Direct warehouse for increasing motor vehicle traffic after it opened in 2018. With 1,000 Fresh Direct diesel trucks driving through the neighborhood each day, residents are understandably hostile to the possibility of another truck-heavy logistics operation opening in the lot directly next door.
“There’s this feedback loop of ‘Oh well, there’s warehouses here, so it’s a great place to put another warehouse’ instead of ‘Oh there’s warehouses here maybe and 60,000 people live here, maybe we should like think about other other things we can do,'” said South Bronx Unite spokesman David Rosales.
Port Morris and Mott Haven are stuffed with warehouses, and the city government so far has failed to regulate their associated emissions and traffic impacts. One option for doing so is an indirect source rule, under which the city would use a points-based system to force  warehouse owners to electrify their fleets and shift some deliveries to cargo bikes.
Researchers with South Bronx Unite believe that New York state has an opportunity to stop the warehouse development because the state Department of Transportation owns part of the land beneath the Post building.
Originally constructed by the defunct New Haven Railroad, the Harlem River Yards stretch from Lincoln Avenue to slightly east of Willow Avenue. The Penn Central Railroad, which acquired the site from NHR in 1969, sold it to New York State DOT in 1982. Nine years later, the state leased the land to a real estate developer, The Galesi Group, which operates the property under a subsidiary known as Harlem River Yard Ventures. The Post building sits on a lot which includes the easternmost piece of the Harlem River Yards, plus a former MTA bus depot, which the state sold to Harlem River Yard Ventures in 1999.
Before anyone builds anything, South Bronx Unite wants the state to investigate whether it has any direct control over how the land can be used, and if it does, to block a new warehouse from materializing.
“There are restrictive covenants that are tied to the lease that give both the city and the state certain enforcement rights over the land, so an ask that we have for the state is to essentially confirm whether or not these covenants are still still active,” said South Bronx Unite’s energy and economic justice advisor, Zoe Voss Lee.
Lee encouraged the state make use of its cumulative impacts law, which legislators intended to dissuade developments if they add more pollution to historically polluted areas.
“Since the plan for this is to become a warehouse, we can anticipate that there will be significant numbers of trucks that will be brought to the area,” she said.
Rather than another warehouse, South Bronx Unite wants the city and state to open the Bronx Kill waterfront to the public. Rosales pointed to the fact that the state Department of Environmental Conservation has highlighted SBU’s own Mott Haven-Port Morris Waterfront Plan in its official Open Space Conservation Plan.
For the former Post facility, South Bronx Unite envisions a hub for community solar power and a green manufacturing and job-training space. Formerly industrial waterfront spaces — such as Brooklyn Bridge Park, the East River waterfront parks in Manhattan and Brooklyn, Hunter’s Point South and Brooklyn Marine Terminal — have experienced, or will soon experience, second lives as mixed-use neighborhoods. 
As the city has shifted so much of the waterfront away from warehouses and heavy industry, Bronxites while they haven’t received the same treatment.
“Brooklyn and Queens and Manhattan have started to move away from that a lot more, and it feels like in the Bronx it’s moving a lot slower,” Rosales said. “At the end of the day, this stuff comes down to the willingness to do it, the willingness to prioritize it, the willingness to fund it.”
The old Post building is a short walk away from the abandoned and crumbling E. 132nd Street Pier. That proximity has led South Bronx Unite to speculate whether Prologis will pitch the warehouse as part of the city’s “Blue Highways” program to move more freight around the city by boat. That could make the project more palatable to decision-makers, but EDC has already identified locations for that program, and none of them include the pier or anywhere else in the Harlem River Yards.
Lee noted that Kane, the Prologis executive, told the trade publication BisNOW that he was interested in using the Blue Highways program to roll trucks onto and off of boats, in contrast to using small vehicles or even cargo bikes or quad bikes. His comments raised the group’s hackles because they suggested Prologis’s plan would invite even more truck traffic.
“We had a call with Prologis, they were positioning this development as part of the Blue Highways program, but we know that this is not formally a part of EDC’s Blue Highways initiative,” she said. “With the roll-on, roll-off model of Blue Highways, it’s likely that there will be increased truck traffic around the places where the hubs or the last-mile warehouses are actually located.”
The activists oppose the E. 132nd Street Pier’s potential conversion to industry because it conflicts with their vision for opening the waterfront. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who subscribes to the same vision, allocated $1 million just this year to the city’s Department of Small Business Services, who can use the grant to put in oyster reefs, clean up the shoreline and eventually rebuild the pier to restore public access to the pier.
“A concern that South Bronx Unite has regarding the potential of this site being a blue highway, has nothing to do with the premise of blue highways, which of course make a lot of sense when it comes to moving trucks off the road,” said Lee. “It has to do with specifically the positioning of this warehouse and the fact that the site for barging would be the 132nd Street Pier, which has been a project that has been prioritized for public access to the waterfront.”
For now, New York State DOT does not consider itself a participant in the fight over the warehouse. An agency spokesperson said the potential project is entirely privately owned. “The State Department of Transportation can confirm that it owns a portion of Harlem River Yards and has a ground lease with Harlem River Yards Ventures (an affiliate of the Galesi Group) on that portion of property,” said New York State DOT spokesperson Rolando Infante.
A spokesperson for Prologis said the company has only looked at a site that includes completely private land. The company spokesperson also denied that it bought the former Post printing plant, and that it is planning on building a warehouse for Amazon on the site.
“Prologis is not currently under contract to buy the former New York Post printing plant,” said spokesperson Mattie Sorrentino. “We are evaluating the site, as we do other potential projects in the region. Prologis has studied maritime freight options at the site, but the site has not been selected for the Blue Highways program. We have been part of the regional business community for years, investing in the local economy. We have and will continue to grow relationships here and be a long-term partner.”

https://mondediplo.com/2026/11/11uzbekis.title: A chill in Uzbekistan's cultural spring
https://mondediplo.com/2026/11/11uzbekis.author: Maya Jaggi
https://mondediplo.com/2026/11/11uzbekis.text:
Behind the turreted façade of a Russian imperial tram depot in the tree-lined Uzbek capital, Tashkent, is the shock of the new: a sensuous spiral staircase in toffee-coloured terrazzo. A tunnel beneath the yellow-brick site opens into a stunning gallery space.
The Centre for Contemporary Arts (CCA) Tashkent, Uzbekistan’s first such permanent hub, opened this autumn, part of an ambitious cultural strategy in Central Asia’s most populous state (39 million people), now marking 35 years of independence. This derelict 1912 diesel power station, which supplied the region’s first trams, was restored by French architects Studio KO (designers of Marrakesh’s Yves Saint Laurent Museum). The Samarkand carpet and ceramic tiles in the upscale restaurant reinvigorate Silk Road artisanship almost lost in the gruelling labour of cotton plantations during tsarist and Soviet rule.
‘Artists are our ambassadors,’ Gayane Umerova, who commissioned the centre, told me over a lunch of modern Uzbek cuisine. A British Museum exhibition on Afghanistan sparked her ambitions for Uzbek culture, as a student in London. She leads the state-run Uzbekistan Art and Culture Development Foundation (ACDF), created in 2017 by President Shavkat Mirziyoyev during the ‘Uzbek spring’.
After the dictator Islam Karimov died in 2016, following a 27-year iron rule, Mirziyoyev’s reforms (from reining in the secret police to ending child labour) gave birth to a ‘New Uzbekistan’. Yet, if more open, the country remains authoritarian. Opposition parties are not tolerated in practice. President Mirziyoyev (previously Karimov’s prime minister) changed the constitution – so he could rule until 2037. Press freedom is ranked a dismal 147th out of 180 countries. Since 2021, ‘insulting the president online’ has been a crime. https://mondediplo.com/2026/11/10spain.text:
Isabel Rubio Pérez, a retired primary school teacher, still reminisces about Los Nietos, a small village south of the Mar Menor lagoon where she spent ‘the happiest moments’ of her childhood. A black-and-white photo album open on her lap, she recalled, ‘We used to spend hours swimming in the crystal-clear water.’ But these idyllic images belong to the past. The fishing village has been swamped by a now largely deserted seaside resort, and algae – the result of years of nitrate pollution – blanket much of the lagoon.
Located in the Murcia region in southeast Spain, the Mar Menor is the largest saltwater lagoon in Europe, measuring 135 sq km. It is separated from the Mediterranean by La Manga (the sleeve), a 22km-long sandbar covered in hotels and holiday apartment blocks. The lagoon’s drainage basin spans more than 1,500 sq km of former desert where vegetables now grow in polytunnels, irrigated by desalination plants and sustained by chemical fertilisers. In the sub-region of Campo de Cartagena, agriculture accounts for around 20% of the local economy.
Pérez, an activist with the environmental organisation Pacto por el Mar Menor (‘Pact for the Mar Menor’), told me that agriculture ‘generates millions of euros in exports, but we now know it’s responsible for the devastation of the lagoon.’ Urbanisation, along with the replacement of traditional terraced farming with large-scale intensive agriculture, has exacerbated water runoff. Pérez complained that ‘since the 1980s, scientists at the Spanish Institute of Oceanography have been warning of the risks of eutrophication in the lagoon – but as ordinary citizens, we didn’t realise what was happening.’

https://mondediplo.com/2026/11/09france-.title: The sordid secrets of fish farming
https://mondediplo.com/2026/11/09france-.author: Ian Urbina
https://mondediplo.com/2026/11/09france-.text:
On 6 March 2024 Pascal Goumain, president of Saumon de France, said his company’s salmon pens in Cherbourg are part of France’s food future. In an interview, he described plans to adapt the farm to climate change and pointed to official backing for expansion: ‘The French ministry of agriculture set an objective to farm 20,000 tonnes of salmon in France by 2030.’ In late 2025 he said, ‘We should be a leading aquaculture country, but we’re falling behind’.
The industry and government pitch for aquaculture in France has been straightforward: fish farming could meet growing demand for seafood while slowing the collapse of the oceans. ‘The quantities caught are not sufficient to feed consumers,’ former minister of the sea Annick Girardin said in 2021. Two years later, the planning high commission argued that in a context of climate change and overfishing, the ‘responsible development’ of aquaculture could expand supply without undermining the fishing sector. France is the European Union’s second-largest producer of farmed seafood by volume, after Spain.
Globally, the ocean-sustainability argument for fish farming – ‘grow more, so we can catch less’ – is one of the reasons that the $313bn aquaculture industry is currently the fastest-growing food sector, and why half of the seafood eaten around the world is now farm-raised rather than caught at sea.
There is a problem, though. Two thirds of global aquaculture grows species that are fed fishmeal, a protein-rich powder made from the very kinds of wild fish that aquaculture claims to be saving, thereby accelerating ocean depletion. That includes the most popular types of farmed seafood consumed in France – salmon, prawns, trout, sea bass, sea bream.

https://mondediplo.com/2026/11/08algeria.title: Neighbours, but still not friends
https://mondediplo.com/2026/11/08algeria.author: Pierre Daum
https://mondediplo.com/2026/11/08algeria.text:
There is still a railway track running across the border between Morocco and Algeria. Half buried and often hidden by thorny bushes, no train has travelled on it for 30 years. A rough trail runs alongside it, which we needed a dirt bike to navigate. Once we passed the last farm, the plain was empty: no more shepherds grazing their sheep.
We could see the border from about 100 metres away, a sturdy metal fence topped with barbed wire. Algeria lay on the other side. A wide trench behind the fence made the border seem more foreboding. Suddenly a man in uniform emerged from behind an embankment. ‘What are you doing here? It isn’t allowed!’ In our motorcycle gear we hoped we could pass for lost tourists.
We turned back, leaving the railway track to continue towards Maghnia, an Algerian city 10km away, and then on to Oran. But no sooner had we left the path than a Moroccan gendarmerie van forced us to dismount. A captain with a stern moustache stepped out, flanked by two adjutants. They checked our ID, making phone calls to the General Directorate for National Security.
As the checks dragged on we made conversation with the younger adjutant, asking him whether the Algerians were enemies. ‘Oh no, they’re our brothers! But the trouble is they don’t like us’. He told us that Algerians supported Senegal during the African Cup of Nations final, which was held in Rabat this January. ‘That’s not very friendly!’ The officer returned our papers, calling, ‘Welcome to Morocco!’ over his shoulder before getting back into his vehicle. From that point on the Moroccan police surveilled us for the duration of our reporting.
This scene took place a few kilometres north of Oujda, capital of the Oriental region of northeastern Morocco. The railway line running through the region was commissioned in the late 19th century to facilitate French penetration into Morocco; France established a protectorate there in 1912. Despite their country’s significant human and economic losses, Iran’s leaders remain inflexible in their direct and indirect negotiations with the US administration. A similar attitude was shown by Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, who took several years to accept the peace offered by Iraq that ended a conflict which claimed nearly a million lives between 1980 and 1988.
Iran is demanding that the US lifts its sanctions and blockades, returns financial assets seized by Western states and ceases all hostilities in the Middle East, especially in southern Lebanon and Gaza. https://mondediplo.com/2026/11/05drone.text:
Representatives from navies across Asia turned up in their smart dress uniforms in spring 2025 for IMDEX Asia (the International Maritime Defence Exhibition), held in a vast exhibition hall by Singapore’s Changi Airport. This biennial event provides a showcase for leading naval defence companies to exhibit their new technologies. Among them were the UK’s Rolls-Royce (propulsion systems for submarines and frigates), Israel’s Elbit Systems (sonar), Singapore’s ST Engineering (onboard electronic systems), the US warship manufacturer Lockheed Martin and Austria’s Schiebel, which makes the Camcopter S-100, an aerial tactical reconnaissance drone.
The German group Euroatlas was promoting its Greyshark – an eight-metre, 4.5-tonne propeller-driven underwater drone with a shark-like profile and pointed snout. It is designed for a wide variety of civilian and military roles ‘depending on the operator’s needs’, according to the sales reps on the stand. The Greyshark’s extended mission endurance of up to 16 weeks greatly increases its capabilities, which range from mapping the ocean floor to protecting underwater infrastructure and recovering abandoned munitions. The future belongs to machines like these, the reps told me, because ‘humans are gradually being replaced by autonomous technologies in the oceans’.
Humans have been exploring the depths since the second half of the 20th century, descending to over a thousand metres in submarines and other submersibles. Yet 80% of the ocean’s volume remains uncharted. Studying the seabed using crewed vessels is hugely expensive, time-consuming and dangerous, so progress has been painfully slow. All three obstacles could be overcome with the advent of drones, a term which in the maritime context covers a variety of robotic craft: tethered, remotely operated underwater robots; small surface vessels; and, in particular, autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs).

For Roberto Vannacci, Giorgia Meloni’s government is too timid
Italy: right, far right and even further right
With elections due next year, Giorgia Meloni’s far-right government risks being outflanked by Roberto Vannacci’s National Future party, which is pushing hard for ‘remigration’ and ‘traditional family values’.
Roberto Vannacci’s book Il mondo al contrario (The world turned upside down) came out in 2023. It offers opinions such as ‘Women should look after the family. Working won’t bring them fulfilment.’ ‘Dear homosexuals, accept it: you’re not normal.’ ‘A foreigner who does not assimilate to the culture of the host country is not an immigrant but an invader.’ The book’s success – Vannacci claims it has sold 300,000 copies – has turned its previously unknown author into a major media presence in Italy.
Vannacci, a paratrooper and former major general who commanded several Italian and NATO special forces missions in Iraq and Afghanistan in the 2000s and 2010s, is the new standard-bearer of the Italian far right but is currently suspended from the army until July 2027. The defence ministry has imposed this punishment on him twice, in February 2024 and July 2026, on the grounds that his publications violate the ‘principle of neutrality and impartiality of the armed forces’ and damage the institution’s ‘prestige and reputation’.
Matteo Salvini, leader of the far-right Lega and Italy’s deputy prime minister, recruited him to his party shortly before the 2024 European elections. But having won a seat in the European parliament, Vannacci left the Lega in February 2026, after several months of internal tensions, and announced he was launching his own party, Futuro Nazionale (National Future), which currently stands at 7-9% in the opinion polls.
Vannacci believes the rightwing coalition government led by Giorgia Meloni (Fratelli d’Italia, far right) is too timid, especially on immigration and the defence of the traditional family. He also disagrees with them over the war in Ukraine: he opposes both military support for Kyiv and sanctions against Russia.

‘What matters to me,’ French education minister Édouard Geffray told France Info on 6 October, ‘is that secondary school students are heard within a democratic framework. Last night I launched a platform where every student can contribute and explain their problems and expectations.’ But when journalists asked whether this was simply a repeat of the offer made to the Gilets Jaunes in early 2019, the minister seemed lost for words.
Back then, in an attempt to resolve that crisis, the government – supported by a consortium of consultancy firms and startups  – had launched a huge consultation exercise, also based on a digital platform. Right at the outset they warned they would only consider contributions submitted online. But, in fact, the authorities never responded to the exercise at all. They also spirited away the books of grievances compiled by rural mayors and the protesters who gathered at roundabouts. Since then, successive governments seem in fact to have gone ever further in the opposite direction in response to protesters’ demands for equality and democratic freedom.
The consultation on pension reform (2018-19) and the Citizens’ Convention on Climate (2019) illustrate how public participation in decision-making is generally confined to collecting views on decisions already taken by the authorities. These contributions are promptly disregarded when they prove too ‘subversive’.   Although the 2015 consultation on the proposed Law for a Digital Republic attracted 8,500 responses, it ultimately proved ‘pointless in substantive terms’, according to the Observatory on Digital Rights and Freedoms, because ‘the government adopted virtually none’ of the proposals ‘that had received the most support from Internet users’, notably the ones about free software. This was somewhat ironic, given that the law, by enshrining open public data and digital access for all, was supposed to get the country used to ‘civic tech’.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Former High Museum of Art executive sentenced to 12 months in prison for embezzlement
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Matthew Terrell
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Brady Lum, a former chief operating officer at Atlanta's High Museum of Art, was sentenced to 12 months in federal prison on Monday (2 November) for embezzling more than $600,000 from the institution. The sentencing comes as the High celebrates its centennial and its parent organisation, the Woodruff Arts Center, conducts a major corporate fundraising campaign.
Federal prosecutors said Lum diverted museum funds to pay for personal purchases, including guitars, music lessons and woodworking equipment. He concealed the expenditures through falsified invoices, reimbursement requests and accounting adjustments. The scheme began in September 2019, less than nine months after Lum joined the museum, and continued until its discovery in November 2025.
Lum paid full restitution of $607,688.18 to the High and voluntarily paid approximately $500,000 more to cover costs the museum incurred while uncovering and investigating his criminal activity.
During Monday's hearing, US District judge Michael L. Brown focused extensively on the deterrent purpose of sentencing. Although Brown said he did not believe Lum was likely to reoffend, he emphasised the court's responsibility to discourage similar financial crimes by others in positions of trust.
The judge acknowledged similarities between his own professional and socioeconomic background and Lum's, discussing how sentencing structures have historically been shaped by educated, professionally successful individuals whose circumstances resemble those of many white-collar defendants.
Brown also considered Lum's prompt restitution after the misconduct was discovered, distinguishing between voluntarily returning stolen funds before detection and repaying them after being caught. The latter, he indicated, carried less weight in assessing accountability.
Lum addressed the court and apologised for his conduct, expressing regret for disappointing his family and community. The gallery appeared to consist largely of relatives, friends and supporters of Lum.
Contacted for comment following Monday's sentencing, a spokesperson for the Woodruff provided the following statement: "We respect the court’s decision and remain focused on fulfilling our mission, responsibly managing our resources and connecting deeply with the audience we serve."
Both the Woodruff and the High declined to provide substantive information about financial safeguards introduced following Lum's misconduct, or whether they intend to publish a remediation plan addressing financial controls, governance reforms and oversight procedures.

https://citylimits.org/new-york-city-sna.title: New York City SNAP Participants Will Get Extra Funds for Fresh Produce in 2027
https://citylimits.org/new-york-city-sna.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/new-york-city-sna.text:
Share This Article
The city is expanding its Health Bucks program, which matches every $2 a SNAP participant spends on fruit and vegetables at farmers markets and other select vendors. The change comes as inflation and rising food costs has more households struggling.
With food costs on the rise, the city is expanding a program that offers low-income New Yorkers extra money to spend on local produce, the Mamdani administration announced Thursday.
Starting in January, participants in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, also known as SNAP or food stamps, will have greater spending power under the city’s Health Bucks program, which matches every $2 they spend at farmers markets and farm stands with coupons they can use to purchase additional fruits and vegetables.
The city is raising the daily Health Bucks cap from $10 to $14, meaning SNAP participants can qualify for an extra $4 a day for fresh produce at more than 100 locations across the city—what officials say will offer a boost to both households’ budgets and local farmers.
“Every day, New Yorkers walk into a store hoping prices haven’t gone up again,” said Mayor Zohran Mamdani said in a statement announcing the change. “As food insecurity rises, far too many families are forced to skip the fruits and vegetables.”
From 2021 to 2024, the number of city residents at risk of food insecurity—meaning their households sometimes or often struggled to afford food—increased by 18 percent, from 2.2 million to 2.6 million, according to Health Department data released last month.
For certain demographic groups, the numbers were even starker: some 59 percent of Latino and 50 percent of Black New Yorkers were at risk of being food insecure in 2024, the same report found, compared to 40 percent of the city’s population overall. Food insecure households were more likely to forgo fresh produce, the report found.
The city says it expects to distribute nearly $2.3 million in Health Bucks benefits next year with the expanded matching cap.
The change comes as inflation and rising food costs have more SNAP households stretching their monthly dollars to make ends meet. A recent Urban Institute analysis found that for many counties across the country, maximum SNAP benefits fall far below the average cost of a “modestly priced” meal in that area.
In Manhattan, for example, that average meal is approximately $6.07—109 percent more than the $2.90 per meal that a maximum SNAP benefit covers, the analysis found, one of the largest gaps in the country.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/pakistan-cli.text:
Life Beneath the Melting Glaciers
Remote mountain communities in northern Pakistan have contributed almost nothing to global warming, yet glacial floods are sweeping away their homes. Jacobin traveled to talk to the families who are rebuilding with little help from the state.
Bulbul Kaie remembers when summer in Hassanabad revolved around a stream.
The village lies in the mountains of Gilgit-Baltistan, a disputed territory in northern Pakistan bordering China, Afghanistan, and Indian-administered Kashmir. Kaie’s family would carry chairs down to the stream fed by meltwater from the glaciers above, where a cold breeze rose from the water. They would spend afternoons on its bank among orchards heavy with apricots and cherries.
“We would sit together, drink tea, and enjoy the sound of the stream until it got dark,” recounts the mother of four. “We used to look forward to summer. The sound of the water made us feel calm.”
Now summer brings dread. “We fear what will happen each year,” the fifty-year-old says.
Pakistan has more than thirteen thousand glaciers, one of the largest concentrations outside the polar regions, many of them in Gilgit-Baltistan. As climate change drives temperatures higher in these mountains, where warming is outpacing the global average, the ice melts faster and rain falls harder and less predictably. Cloudbursts — intense, localized downpours that experts say were virtually unknown here until recently — can now destroy a village in an afternoon.
Last year, Hassanabad was among dozens of villages across Gilgit-Baltistan hit by one of the region’s deadliest flood seasons in years. At least seventy-two people died, and more than a thousand homes were destroyed or damaged.
The floods destroyed half of Kaie’s home. She has yet to rebuild. “I’m only staying here because I have no resources to go elsewhere,” she says, her voice breaking. “I fear for my children’s lives and mental health.”
Kaie is one of thousands still trying to recover. Some live in tents or cracked houses they fear could collapse. Others have been moved onto bare government plots with no land to farm and no way to earn. Few can afford to start again, and the next disaster is rarely more than a season away.
The people living among these glaciers bear almost no responsibility for the greenhouse gas emissions driving global warming; Pakistan itself accounts for about 1 percent of global emissions. Yet it is among the countries most affected by extreme weather, and in its remote mountain communities, homes are being washed away, farmland is disappearing, and livelihoods are collapsing.
At the Glaciers’ Mercy
Behram Shah gathers cherries from a tree outside his Hassanabad home and carries them to the table in a woven basket. “We rely on the glaciers for everything,” says the seventy-six-year-old, who has lost about nine acres to floods in the past decade. “Our livelihoods, and even our drinking water, depend on them. We are completely at the mercy of these glaciers.”
Every spring, before the summer melt, villagers would gather at the watercourses to pray over the year’s flow, asking God for protection and enough water for the months ahead, Shah recounts. These days, few still make the journey.
“We used to see the glaciers as the source of our lives,” Shah says. “Now, because of the floods, we associate them with destruction.”
“The cycles that kept us in balance for centuries are being disrupted,” he adds. “All we can do now is pray and leave everything to God.”
Hassanabad sits in the Hunza Valley, in the Karakoram — one of four mountain ranges that meet in Gilgit-Baltistan and contain some of the world’s highest peaks. Its roughly 175 households are scattered across the mountainous terrain, clustered on either side of the stream and up the slopes. Most residents are Ismaili Muslims who farm fields and orchards passed down through generations.
Three miles above the village, the Shisper and Muchuhar glaciers, once branches of a single glacier, eventually drain into the same stream, which runs about four miles down the valley to join the Hunza River. Their meltwater feeds the irrigation channels that keep Hassanabad alive.
In 2018, the Shisper began to surge, exhibiting behavior of a type of glacier that can sit almost motionless for decades or centuries before suddenly lurching forward. It advanced nearly a mile, at one point moving nearly sixty feet a day, before pushing across the ravine and damming the stream draining the Muchuhar.
The lake that formed behind the ice burst four times in four years, sending floodwater down the valley that scoured the ground along the stream’s banks. The last, in 2022, swept away the Karakoram Highway Bridge, cutting Hunza off from the rest of the country for two weeks.
By last summer, the danger was supposed to have passed. The ice still lay across the ravine, says Sher Muhammad, a cryosphere scientist at the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development, but a wide tunnel had opened through it and water was flowing freely.
Then the heat came. One town in southern Gilgit-Baltistan hit 119 degrees Fahrenheit (48.3 degrees Celsius), its highest temperature in nearly three decades. Across the region, streams were already running high as unusually warm conditions accelerated snow and glacier melt.
Chunks of ice broke off and fell into the stream, blocking the flow, Muhammad says. Water accumulated behind the ice blockages until they failed, releasing the impound water downstream. It happened twice, in July and August, damaging houses and farmland, ripping out a section of the Karakoram Highway, and cutting the water supply to Aliabad, Hunza’s main commercial town, and nearby villages.
Over the years, dozens of homes in Hassanabad have been destroyed or dismantled before the floods could reach them.
The Floodwater Threat
What came before the floods, Kaie says, was not a roar. It was a silence.
“It’s very ominous,” she says, sitting on the floor of her home, cracks running down the walls. “The entire flow of water suddenly feels like it stops. And there’s silence for about half an hour.”
In those minutes, the family would run to the bank to see what was coming. If the water looked dangerous, Kaie would send the children uphill to a relative’s house and go back for whatever she could carry.
“When the floodwater comes, it is so strong,” she says. “It carries boulders the size of houses. If it reaches your home, it will pull it from its foundations.”
They have lived this way for years, fleeing when the water rises, returning when it drops. When I visited in August, the family had already fled several times that summer. Their fridge and other belongings were still at a relative’s house up the hill.
Last year’s floods were the worst this part of Hassanabad had seen, residents say. They tore through the orchards between Kaie’s house and the stream and destroyed half the home she and her husband had spent seven years building. The couple had sold most of their farmland to afford it.
She scrolls through her phone to a photograph from before: rows of fruit trees running down to the water. “It was a very beautiful home,” she says, holding up the screen. Outside, the same ground is dry and stripped bare.
Later, the highway was rebuilt. It had always run a couple of hundred feet below the houses until last summer’s flood swept away part of it. The rebuilt section was laid higher up the slope, directly in front of Kaie’s house.
Now cargo trucks hauling goods between Pakistan and China pass a few feet from her door. They shake the walls, rattle the windows, and widen the cracks. Dust hangs in the air.
Her twelve-year-old son sometimes wakes at night, hears the trucks, and thinks the flood has come back, she says. He runs outside, and the family has to find him in the dark.
“This constant uncertainty is causing a lot of psychological issues for my children,” Kaie tells me, her son sitting quietly beside her. “I try to calm them down and assure them they are safe, but they are still terrified of every sound.”
She wants to leave, but her husband drives someone else’s car for a living and does not earn enough to move elsewhere. And no one will buy a house in a village beset by recurrent floods.
“If someone came and gave us money, we would leave immediately,” Kaie says, sniffling back tears. “It feels like torture knowing any day the waters will return and destroy our home we worked so hard to build. And it’s not a question of whether it will happen again; it’s guaranteed.”
Other families have stopped waiting for the water. Each summer, they take their houses apart, carrying off beams, windows, and doors before the floods can claim them.
Around the stream, the floods have carved a deep canyon into the land, with another Hassanabad neighborhood sitting beside it. On a flattened patch scattered with debris, the remains of the area’s jamatkhana, the Ismaili house of worship and community gathering, lie among the stripped shells of dismantled homes.
Living on the Edge
Sultan Ali, seventy-five, an elder and community leader, walks me along the cliff, shouting whenever I get too close to the edge. “The ground is not strong here,” he warns. “It can collapse at any moment.”
He gestures at the canyon below. “You see all of this? This was the most beautiful part of our village,” he says, shaking his head.
Nearby, Dilshad Bano, fifty-three, has come to pick cherries on a plot she abandoned about seven years ago. Floods destroyed half her house in 2019. The family dismantled the rest. “It took many years and a lot of hard work to build that house; we used up all our savings,” she says, standing in the ruins. “Then all of it was gone in a single day.”
They have moved higher up the valley, to a house twenty-five minutes’ walk through the mountains from the nearest road. “When we have health problems, it becomes extremely difficult,” she tells me.
Bano and her brother-in-law, Muhammad Abbas, fifty-five, each received about $900 in government compensation a few years ago, they say. Abbas’s four-room house is now a strip of orange-painted wall at the edge of the drop.
“That money was a joke,” he says. “You can’t rebuild your life with that.” He took out a bank loan and built three rooms at the far end of the village on the only plot he could afford. It floods and erodes like everywhere else.
Beyond some compensation for affected families, officials have done little for Hassanabad, residents say. The state has evacuated families and sent food and medicine after each flood, and rebuilt the road and the bridge. But no one has been relocated, and residents say most of the assistance they received afterward — temporary shelters, food, and bathrooms — came from the Aga Khan Development Network.
“The government is not helping us,” Ali says. “They need to relocate these families because this is a very dangerous place to live. We’re mostly farmers and shepherds and don’t have the resources to rebuild after losing everything.”
There was supposed to be a warning, too. Hassanabad is one of two dozen valleys covered by GLOF-II, a UN Development Programme project with Pakistan’s climate ministry that installed weather stations, river gauges, and sirens across the north. During last summer’s floods, residents say, no sirens sounded.
Muhammad, who was in Hunza at the time conducting a training session attended by officials from the meteorological department who manage the monitoring station, says the sirens are triggered when the water level reaches a predefined threshold. The stream in Hassanabad did not reach the threshold required to trigger the siren, he says. Residents say the siren on the bridge was later swept away by the flood.
Villagers must rely on one another instead. On the hottest days, when the melt runs high, volunteers from the community post themselves along the stream. When they see dust rising from the ravine, a sign that water has broken loose upstream, they quickly warn residents.
“Despite all these disasters and uncertainties, we are more united,” Ali says. “We all realize we are in the same situation, and we only have each other.”
“My Enemy”
Nargisa Khatoon was married in a mud and stone house, with carved wooden beams, that had stood for two centuries. “It was beautifully decorated,” says the eighty-three-year-old.
Her family has lived for generations in Tokorkot, a village in the Nagar Valley across the Hunza River from Hassanabad. They were landowners under the mirs, the princes who ruled Nagar until Pakistan abolished the monarchy in the 1970s.
In 2022, a summer of debris flows struck part of the house and swept away most of the family’s land and trees. For two years, they slept outdoors in a garden beneath a tarpaulin rigged against the rain and sun, or with relatives when there was room, before building the small house Khatoon lives in now.
“I don’t like to remember that day,” she tells me, shuddering. “To see my home swallowed by the water, right in front of me. . . . I was shocked.”
For months after, fear kept the village awake. People walked the riverbank at night, watching the water, wondering whose house would go next. “I still have dreams about those days,” she says.
Khatoon grew up seeing the water as a blessing. It irrigated the fields and grew the walnut trees. “But after the floods destroyed everything around us, I became afraid of the water,” she explains, leaning against the side of her house.
“Now, I see it as my enemy.”
Unlike Hassanabad’s Ismailis, people here are Twelver Shia, the largest religious community in Gilgit-Baltistan. The village of a few dozen families sits where two waterways meet: the Hispar River and the Hopar Stream, which comes down from the glaciers of the Hopar Valley above. The village is hemmed in by flood-prone streams on either side and the river in front. Residents say there is nowhere to go.
The Hopar Stream had flooded now and then for as long as anyone could remember. But in the summer of 2022, extreme heat followed by heavy rain likely destabilized the Daranchi Glacier, according to a study published last year, sending more than twenty debris flows — torrents of water, rock, and mud — down the stream in a single month, a frequency the researchers called unprecedented.
Across Tokorkot and four other villages along the stream, at least twelve houses, schools, forty irrigation and water channels, bridges, and about seventy-five acres of farmland were swept away. The district administration sent some tents, according to residents, and families spent the rest of the summer in them.
When the floods returned last year, destroying a bridge and cutting the road to Tokorkot, families took shelter in the same tents. On the hottest days, families still leave for higher ground, carrying food and sleeping together in tents.
In Tokorkot, the fear is too much water. In the valley above, among farmers whose fields the glaciers feed, it is too little.
Qurban Ali has watched the ice vanish over his lifetime.
When the seventy-two-year-old farmer was young, his family worked fields low in the Hopar Valley, fed by meltwater from the Barpu Glacier. As the glacier thinned, its surface sank and the meltwater level fell with it, until the water dropped below the mouths of the irrigation channels that carried it to their fields. The family abandoned those fields and moved higher, onto land watered by the Daranchi — the glacier behind Tokorkot’s 2022 debris flows.
“The glaciers are going deeper underground day by day,” he says. “So we cannot reach and bring up the water.” Farmers say the Daranchi is thinning too. Satellite measurements show the glaciers here losing mass every year since 2000, with the heaviest losses at their lower ends, where farmers draw their water.
“Our entire life here revolves around the glacier water,” Ali tells me. “If there are no more glaciers, then there’s no more life.”
Hopar sits on a terrace of fields about 330 feet above the Bualtar glacier, known locally as Hopar. From a lookout at the head of the valley, its ice lies directly below, blackened with rock and dust.
When a geographer surveyed Hopar in the mid-1980s, its five villages and roughly four thousand people were irrigating some seven hundred acres of terraces through more than 180 miles of hand-dug channels, with more meltwater than the fields needed for most of the growing season.
Satellite records since 1993 show the snow and ice here shrinking by more than two-thirds, and researchers have also documented fields in the valley being cut off from their water.
But as the melting increases, the same valley is being hit by the floods that have torn through the rest of the region. Lower down, where families live and farm along the Hopar Stream, the water arrives all at once.
Left With Nothing
Rashida sits outside her tent and washes the family’s clothes by hand in water carried up from the Ghizer River, one of the region’s main rivers. It quickly turns brown with silt. She stops, takes a deep breath and wipes sweat from her forehead.
“At our home in the village, we had a washing machine and clean running water,” the thirty-seven-year-old says. “I’m not used to living like this.”
Rashida’s family has lived in this tent settlement since last year, when they were displaced from their village, Hakis Thingi, in the Gupis Valley of Ghizer district, in western Gilgit-Baltistan.
At about 3 a.m. on August 22, a glacial lake in the mountains above Talidas village, in the Raushan area, burst. Officials blamed high temperatures. Water poured down a side stream, triggering landslides on both sides of the valley and sending a powerful debris flow through Talidas, flattening it. The debris then blocked the Ghizer River.
For about six hours, the river stopped flowing as water backed up behind the blockage. By daylight, the ensuing lake was several miles long. Across six villages, the flood destroyed or damaged hundreds of houses and large tracts of land. It also submerged part of the only road connecting the area to the rest of the region.
No one, however, was killed. Shepherds high in the mountains spotted the flood coming and phoned down to the villages below, where trained volunteers moved families out before the water arrived.
About 80 percent of Talidas was destroyed. Upstream, the rising water swallowed houses in Hakis Thingi village and nearby settlements. More than three thousand people from 330 households were displaced — the second-largest displacement in Gilgit-Baltistan since the Attabad disaster in 2010, when a landslide dammed the Hunza River and submerged a string of villages.
A year later, the floodwater in the Raushan area still stretches across parts of the valley, rooftops jutting above its surface.
A resettlement site was built high in the mountains for some of those displaced from Talidas, isolated from the villages and services below. Residents say the government provided the land. The University of Lahore, a private university, funded the houses at about $720 each.
Around sixty-five homes were washed away in Talidas, but only some families were provided plots, residents say. The rest are staying with relatives or in tents.
About twenty-three families from Hakis Thingi, meanwhile, still live in a sprawling tent settlement across the river from their drowned village. Residents say the government has allocated each family about a twelfth of an acre, and aid organizations are providing materials for a one-room shelter with a kitchen and bathroom. But the families, who lost their land and livelihoods, must provide the labor themselves.
The barren plots are only big enough for the shelters, residents say, and they cannot farm because the surrounding land is government-owned. They have relied on private aid, which dried up at the start of this year, and on whatever daily work they can find in construction, farming, or local shops.
When I visited in August, not a single shelter was finished, and the entire community was still living in tents.
“My whole life is different now,” Rashida says, settling onto the ground inside the tent beside her husband.
Nowhere to Turn
In Hakis Thingi, each family had scattered plots planted with almonds, apricots, apples, cherries, and mulberries. They grew their own vegetables, kept cows for milk and sold dried fruit at local markets for the cash they needed for clothes, household goods, and school fees.
For Rashida, her children’s education mattered most. She says all of them did well at school. “Before, we could easily afford to send them to very good English-medium schools,” she tells me. “Now we have to ask [nongovernmental organizations] for help with the costs of government schools.”
“I used to have very big plans for them,” she adds, as her children pull back the front of the tent and peek shyly inside. “I believed they would all go to university.”
“Now I’m just worried about how to feed them each day.”
Residents here say living so close to the Ghizer River — the river that took their homes — also leaves them constantly frightened.
A couple of miles upstream, others never left. Their houses still stand on the edge of the lake. About twenty-four of their neighbors’ homes remain submerged, occasionally reappearing as the lake recedes. Water drains through a natural spillway in the debris and officials have declared the lake no longer a threat.
Zarnisa, sixty, and her husband, Abdul Qayum, eighty, have moved between their home and the tents for more than a year. Their house stayed flooded for about six months, only its roof visible. When the water fell in January, they returned; three months later, it rose again. A few days before I met them, the spillway had widened, the lake dropped and they went home again.
“We are always afraid,” Zarnisa says, guiding me to the edge of her small yard and pointing to the water just a few feet away. “Maybe in a few days the water will rise again, and we will have to flee.”
Zarnisa’s husband has fallen into depression after being repeatedly displaced from their only home. “He’s constantly having panic attacks,” she tells me. From their yard, the roofs of sunken homes rise above the water, a perpetual reminder of what will eventually happen again to their own.
“It gives me a lot of anxiety,” she says. More than her own house, however, she worries about the neighbors whose homes are already gone. “My neighbors were all like family to me. I’m always thinking about them and feeling sad.”
Those neighbors now live in tents on higher ground or in the homes of relatives. They have not been given plots or shelters. One of them is theity-five-year-old Zaibunisa. Her family owned three houses with shops attached, and she ran a small early education school for local children. All of it is now under the lake, along with their land.
“When the flood came, we didn’t have time to grab anything, not even our phones,” Zaibunisa says. “We were left with nothing but our lives.”
With no other land, she pitched a tent outside a relative’s house. “We feel stuck,” she tells me, standing outside the tent she shares with her husband and their three young children. “We need help.”
“No Safe Area”
About a week before the glacial flood, a different kind of disaster struck elsewhere in the Gupis valley.
In Khalti village, the ground is a field of boulders and rocks. “Nobody here had ever feared floods; this side of the valley has no glacier above it,” says Karim Beig, seventy-three, a village elder. “The danger, in living memory, was always avalanches.”
On August 14, cloudbursts hit thirty-seven locations across Ghizer. At least thirteen people died. These downpours can dump four inches of rain or more in an hour over an area just a few miles across, sending walls of water and mud down the slopes within minutes.
One hit Khalti. Residents say eight houses were destroyed in about ten minutes and about four more were damaged. Six members of one seven-person family died. Villagers who reached the wreckage say they heard a small boy crying beneath it and dug him out. Beig and his younger brother, also in his seventies, lost half their house and most of their orchards and land.
Beig leads me through the rubble, then crouches and motions for me to follow him down a crevice. A small backpack and other belongings lie beneath the debris, left behind by families whose homes were crushed by the rocks and floodwater.
Cloudbursts are a “very new phenomenon” here, explains Syed Najam Hassan, an assistant professor at Karakoram International University in Gilgit who uses satellite data to map the region’s glacial lakes. They are associated with the monsoon, which until recently rarely reached these altitudes.
Ghulam Rasul, former director general of the Pakistan Meteorological Department, says the mountains are warming faster than the plains below, strengthening the forces pushing the monsoon north. The Himalaya runs east to west, blocking its path. But toward the west, the wall of mountains ends, and the monsoon is now pushing through into the high Karakoram.
“Now we all feel exposed,” Beig says, balancing on one of the rocks scattered across the village. “Every night when it rains, no one can sleep. Some of us come outside and watch the clouds for any sign of what might happen.”
Communities here have read the signs of approaching glacial floods for centuries, but nothing passed down by their elders tells them what a cloudburst looks like before it comes. Even researchers struggle to predict them, Najam says. A village can be sitting under clear skies while a storm builds over the ravine above, with the water arriving half an hour later.
“Everything has changed since that day,” Beig says. “It’s like we’ve been invaded by something unfamiliar, something we don’t understand and that could attack us at any moment.”
Theses dangers extend throughout the region. “Across Gilgit-Baltistan, everywhere is at high risk,” Najam tells me. “With the climate changing, there is no safe area.”
While the water can eventually recede, the trauma cannot. Nargis Asad, who chairs the psychiatry department at Aga Khan University in Karachi and has studied the mental health of displaced people in Pakistan since the 2005 earthquake, says these communities are not recovering from a single disaster but living in a state of chronic exposure.
“When you are continuously exposed to a threatening situation, there is an ongoing state of worry and apprehension about an impending disaster that can come at any time,” Asad explains. “It becomes a very fearful existence, affecting your psychological, cognitive, and physical well-being.”
“Losing your livelihood and your source of income is also a real trauma,” she adds. “It is a major hit to your identity and creates a sense of helplessness, especially when it is land your family has lived on for generations.”
The toll is physical, too, she says: cardiac problems, disrupted sleep, and illnesses that emerge long after the flood has receded. And the effects can extend to the next generation. “When children live under constant fear, their learning capacity, sense of safety, and sense of trust are all affected,” she says.
At the camp for displaced families from Hakis Thingi, Sher Wali, ninety, sits in his worn tent with his wife, Jamali, sixty, grieving decades of lost work. “All my life, I worked to build on what my ancestors gave me, to give my children more than I had,” he says, his voice rough with exhaustion.
“I lived off the land and cows and had a happy life,” he continues. “But now our children don’t even have milk for their tea or any fruit to eat.” He points through the tent opening to the treeless land outside, the sun beating down.
At night, he takes stock of everything he lost in the floods. “I remember every section of my land, every fruit tree and every piece of property I no longer have,” he tells me. “It pains my heart, and I can’t sleep well.”
“I’m an old man. . . . my life is almost over,” he adds. “But I fear for future generations. Without land or jobs, I’m afraid many of our young people and children will just be left to die.”

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/03/ashl.title: Ashley Hinson’s Digital Chief Oversees Firm Paid Millions to Push Israeli Propaganda
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/03/ashl.author: Jacqueline Sweet
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/03/ashl.text:
The person in charge of digital strategy for the Senate campaign of Iowa Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson helps run a company that received nearly $10 million to influence Americans with pro-Israel propaganda.
In September 2025, Hinson — who is battling Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek in a tight race that could decide control of the Senate — tapped Abe Adams to lead her campaign’s digital efforts.
Adams is a co-founder and managing partner of Targeted Victory, a digital consulting firm that has been used by high-profile Republican candidates such as Ted Cruz and Marco Rubio. Targeted Victory shares an address and much of its staff with Targeted Communications Global — a related company with no discernible online presence. Both are subsidiaries of marketing company Stagwell Global.
Israel awarded Targeted Communications a $9.9 million contract in March 2025 focused on social media and paid advertising, documents show. By October 2025, the firm was at work pitching news content and guests on Fox News and CNN, and creating YouTube ads suggesting young Iranians have been educated to believe the “most sacred thing they do is stab a Christian in the heart.”
Hinson is endorsed by both President Donald Trump and the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, and has been supportive of Trump’s war in Iran.
A June 2026 Department of Justice FARA filing from Targeted Communications details much of the firm’s work for Israel. The document lists 10 registered foreign agents working on the Targeted Communications contract for Israel. Six of them are identified as Targeted Victory employees on the company’s website or their LinkedIn accounts. Adams is not named in the filing.
Hinson, Adams, and Targeted Victory did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Adams is not the only Hinson campaign adviser with ties to Targeted Victory and the Israel lobby. Hinson’s current deputy campaign manager, Addison Lavis, worked at Targeted Victory before serving as Hinson’s campaign manager in her 2023 congressional run. Lavis was previously an intern at AIPAC. Lavis did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Hinson has received more than $100,000 from AIPAC and related pro-Israel PACs in 2026, and as an Iowa state representative supported legislation that prohibited the state from working with any companies that boycott Israel.
Hinson’s political action committee has paid Targeted Victory more than $1.6 million this election cycle for digital consulting and ads — 27 percent of its total expenditures, according to Federal Election Commission filings.
Israel’s deal with Targeted Communications is part of a major public relations push that has pumped more than $100 million into swaying public opinion, particularly among young conservatives, back toward Israel.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?

https://hellgatenyc.com/2026-election-da.title: Hell Gate's 2026 Election Day Live Blog
https://hellgatenyc.com/2026-election-da.author: Hell Gate
https://hellgatenyc.com/2026-election-da.text:
Election day is finally here, and amid national chatter about the big blue wave, the balance of power in Congress could all come down to New York.
No pressure, right? Early voting numbers have reportedly slowed since 2025, particularly in the Commie Corridor, which saw a 34 percent drop in early voting this election, but early voting increased in majority Black districts across the city, including Central Brooklyn (a 50 percent jump) and parts of Southeast Queens. (By the way, if you live in New York City and procrastinated on voting—and who would do something like that, especially if they had to work overtime on election night, ha ha ha—here's where to find your polling site.)
Tonight, we will learn if North Country voters choose a dairy farming executive, Democrat Blake Gendebien, over a guy with an AI rap album that lobs Islamophobic slurs at Mayor Zohran Mamdani, Republican Anthony Costantino. We'll find out if Republican incumbent Mike Lawler can smirk his way past Democratic candidate Cait Conley in NY-17. We'll see if Governor Kathy Hochul prevails over Bruce Blakeman, the sentient haircut slash would-be militiaman who is taking a run at Albany from Nassau County, and whose name could have hypothetically been Blake Bruceman. And although we promise we're not actually putting any money on this, we're pretty sure we'll be witnessing Darializa Avila Chevalier, Claire Valdez, Brad Lander, and various leftist candidates across the city ride the Mamdani wave to electoral victory.
But before all that happens, Hell Gate will be doing our usual live blog dance: running all around the city all day, talking to voters, catching up with candidates, and generally taking the temperature on whether New Yorkers consider this weird and wild midterm to be a referendum on Trump 2.0. (And don't forget about those ballot proposals!)
We'll be updating this post all day and into the early evening with dispatches from the team. Then, we'll keep the party going on our LIVE Hell Gate Election Night 2026 Podcast. The live pod starts at 9 p.m. on the dot on our YouTube channel and at select watch parties around the city (including the one you throw at your apartment, if you're a real fan).
Until then, keep refreshing, and we'll keep reporting.
And don't forget to subscribe to Hell Gate to support independent worker-owned journalism, from live blogs like this one, to features, to columns and newsletters, to our podcast, to our events, and more! We can't do any of this without you.

This has been a midterm election cycle unlike any other. Wealthy donors spent staggering sums. Both parties moved to redraw congressional district lines. President Donald Trump and his allies relentlessly questioned whether the results could be trusted even before a single ballot was counted. At Trump’s direction, the Justice Department filed a lawsuit that said the federal government would contest any outcome in which Sen. Dan Sullivan, the Republican incumbent in Alaska, was not victorious.
Newsrooms, including ours, have tried to plan how we will cover an election in which the losing side refuses to accept the will of the voters. Was the Alaska lawsuit a single data point or a harbinger?
As we prepare to write about Nov. 3 and beyond, we find ourselves in the uncomfortable position of trying to game out what might happen in the future — not our strong suit. The record shows that journalists are pretty good at telling readers what happened, particularly if we have some time and some data to sift through, and much less good at forecasting the future.
Help Us Report on Key Election Issues
ProPublica’s reporters are on the lookout for what’s going right and what isn’t. We’re monitoring voter suppression and interference, election observers and poll watchers, extremism tied to the election, and ICE activity at the polls. Have you seen something?
And yet we have to plan. Over the past few weeks we have prepared our reporters and editors to cover every scenario we can imagine. None of us have forgotten the chaos of 2020 when Trump was urged by advisers to send the military to seize voting machines in states he had lost. The Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol as lawmakers gathered to certify Joe Biden’s victory underscored the sense that literally anything was possible in the aftermath of elections.
We will have reporters on the ground in 11 key states covering voting, with even more in Washington, D.C., and others on standby. Our reporters have detailed what experts will be watching. But elections are no longer confined to Election Day (early voting and voting by mail constitute a huge share of the electorate). And our plans for covering voting stretch back many months.
Over the past year, we’ve tried to use the techniques of accountability journalism to add new facts to this pivotal moment in American history.
We have focused considerable attention on the mechanics of elections, a once-arcane issue that has become a central aspect of the MAGA movement’s argument that Trump’s 2020 loss was “rigged” by his opponents. We examined how the Trump administration depleted the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, the arm of the federal government charged with safeguarding election systems. We discovered that Department of Homeland Security officials had asked CISA to obtain a voting machine and hack it without informing the manufacturer of any vulnerabilities found. The plan wasn’t acted on, but its existence made CISA employees fear they were being asked to take part in political interference. CISA and DHS didn’t respond to our questions, but a White House spokesperson said Trump “has done more than any other President to ensure we have free and fair elections.”
Another story looked at how delays resulting from the U.S. Postal Service’s cost-cutting measures endangered the validity of mail-in ballots in rural counties, typically Republican strongholds, during this year’s primaries. The Postal Service said such delays are less likely in the general election.
One of our most detailed election stories traced the career of Cleta Mitchell, a lawyer who spearheaded the legal attacks on the 2020 results. Mitchell leads a coalition of what she calls “election believers” — people who scour the voting results for errors that they believe point to larger conspiracies. Changes she’d hoped Trump could push through before the midterms, such as compelling states to turn over confidential voter information to the Justice Department, have been blocked by the courts. But she has nonetheless become the voice of a well-funded national movement, one which has the president’s ear. When Trump is weighing what to do in the aftermath of this week’s vote, our reporting strongly suggests that Mitchell will be among the people he listens to.
We asked to speak with Mitchell multiple times. She declined but told us in an email: “What we focus on is making sure the election process is accurate, transparent, and honest. The ONLY steps I’ve urged the Administration to take are those that will give the voters — ALL voters — confidence that the outcomes are correct.” A White House spokesperson said she has no official role in election policy but is an effective private advocate.
We have also spent time doing the traditional work of investigative reporting, looking closely at candidates’ records in public office. A newsroom like ours can’t cover every race, so we focus our resources on areas where we have particular expertise.
Our team in Texas has covered state Attorney General Ken Paxton for years, and we kept our focus once he announced he would run for the U.S. Senate. One story looked at his travels, revealing that only 1 in 6 of his nearly 1,000 out-of-state trips were linked to his official duties. Texas taxpayers paid $3.3 million for Paxton’s security detail to accompany him. (Paxton didn’t answer our questions, but his office said he “faced numerous security threats.”) That has become an issue in the Senate campaign.
Another opportunity arose from an investigation that was seemingly not related to the midterms: our examination of the Trump administration’s handling of the Justice Department. We began many months ago to look for promising cases that had been dropped and found out the FBI had been looking into pay-to-play allegations involving prominent Democratic and Republican members of Congress. The case included a bipartisan list of political figures such as Susan Collins, the Republican senator from Maine running in a closely contested race this year, and James Clyburn, a leading Democratic representative from South Carolina who’s also on the ballot this year.
Our first story revealed that Collins helped a little-known defense contractor win millions in federal contracts while the company’s CEO helped bankroll her 2020 reelection effort through a donation made via a shell company. Our second story revealed that the FBI was looking into interactions that Clyburn and Sen. Lindsey Graham, who died in July, had with the same contractor. Collins has denied all wrongdoing. “A donation would never cause Congressman Clyburn to increase his support for the donor’s request,” Clyburn’s office said. Graham’s communications director wrote that “any allegations of quid-pro-quo behavior … are simply false.” The FBI stopped examining the allegations after Trump purged the bureau. Our coverage likewise has become an issue in the Maine race.
We stand at a moment of uncertainty in our history as a democracy. Trump has made his willingness to smear news organizations an essential aspect of his appeal. He routinely insults reporters to their face and has attempted to ban some outlets from the White House and Air Force One because he didn’t like the stories they wrote about him. He has diverted hundreds of federal agents from their jobs fighting drug cartels and organized crime to search for evidence that noncitizens have illegally voted in federal elections. Hardly any were found.
I’m deeply reluctant to make any predictions about how all this will end. ProPublica prepared for an array of dire scenarios in November of 2024 that might arise from a close election. None of them came to pass as Trump decisively prevailed. A federal judge dismissed the Justice Department’s lawsuit to block the Alaska Senate race results over the weekend, and the Trump administration’s plans to appeal stand on shaky legal ground.
The one thing I know for certain is that we will keep digging into the story of what really happened in this election, whoever wins.

https://mondediplo.com/2026/11/01edito.title: France's widening revolt
https://mondediplo.com/2026/11/01edito.author: Benoît Bréville
https://mondediplo.com/2026/11/01edito.text:
Lucie and Robin have little to complain about at their secondary school in southern France - it has recently been refurbished and class sizes aren’t especially large. But on 17 October they joined a demonstration in solidarity with less fortunate students. ‘Even if things are OK for us in Rodez, it’s not like that everywhere, especially in the suburbs,’ they told a local news reporter.
This solidarity between school students from places with apparently little in common has mainly developed through social media, where there is much sharing of experiences, video clips and messages of support. It’s one of the distinctive features of the movement that has swept France since the start of this academic year. Another is that this mobilisation, unlike many previous ones, did not grow out of opposition to an education reform, but erupted suddenly, during an election year, in protest at the general deterioration of state education.
The same concerns crop up everywhere, in towns and suburbs large and small, from Créteil to Lamballe, Vaulx-en-Velin to Villefranche-sur-Rouergue, as well as in Paris, Marseilles, Mayotte (off the east coast of Africa) and French Guiana (South America): dilapidated, badly insulated school buildings, teaching posts unfilled, timetables full of gaps and ever-longer school days, the higher education web portal Parcoursup and its incomprehensible algorithm… Not to mention an increasingly bleak future, with artificial intelligence threatening jobs, climate change threatening the planet and the spectre of war threatening Europe.
It may seem surprising that secondary school students from the banlieues and rural areas should join forces after 15 years of relentless talk about France’s ‘territorial divide’, which has entrenched the idea of a gulf between the France of the big cities and ‘the periphery’, and between urban and rural youth.
