Fire in Soweto
Sazi Bongwe
16.06.2026Dispatch
On 16 June 1976, school students in the township of Soweto began to protest against the apartheid regime. The police set dogs upon them and opened fire. At least 176 were killed, sparking months of unrest and rebellion across the country. On the 50th anniversary of the Soweto Uprising, Sazi Bongwe returns to an iconic photograph from the massacre.
This piece first appeared in our exclusive newsletter for paying members. Join one of our three membership tiers to receive the newsletter.
Masana Samuel “Sam” Nzima was born in 1934, in Lilydale, a small village in what was then the Northern Transvaal and is now the province of Mpumalanga. He grew up on the farm where his father worked and his family lived. His father worked the land but did not own it: in a black rural community, a white farmer made his bread by black labour.
At school, Nzima marvelled as his teacher made pictures come out of a box. At once, he bought a Kodak Brownie; during school holidays, he travelled to Kruger National Park and charged tourists to take their portraits. At age 12, he was put to work on the farm, but after nine months he ran away to Johannesburg. There, he worked as a gardener and a waiter, until he freelanced his way to a full-time photojournalist job at The World in 1968. Eight years later, on 16 June, he took the photograph that proclaimed the true character of the apartheid regime to the world. He would spend decades struggling against various newspapers to own the photograph. Only 22 years after the Soweto Uprising would Nzima obtain the copyright.
I cannot say when I first saw the photo, and I cannot count how many times I’ve seen it. In my memory it is like a landmark, always there in the distance – or perhaps it is more like the landscape, an indelible feature of the distance itself. I know it well: the diagonal lines perfectly splitting the background into three gradations of light and dark. Against that background, the terrible verticality of the two upright figures, running. Lying across them, the cruel horizontal of the young boy, lifeless and yet not weightless. I know their names: Hector Pieterson, shot dead at age 12; Antoinette Sithole, his sister, afraid to look, not knowing where to look; Mbuyisa Makhubo, weary, realising, resolute, holding Hector in his hands. I know their hands: Mbuyisa’s right hand tightly clutching Hector’s left leg; Hector’s two hands, hanging loosely and downwards, towards the earth; and Antoinette’s right hand, raised upwards, combining with the awful expression on her face to say: this is unbearable.
The meaning of the photo has changed as I have, as the country around me has. As a child, I saw it in countless history textbooks; each black child, born free, was meant to see Hector Pieterson as what they might have been had history not happened. A 176 school children were shot dead by the apartheid police for protesting the inferior ‘Bantu’ education they were receiving – an education preparing them for nothing beyond manual labour. Now, here, in our classrooms, reading and writing, equal and free, we were to see ourselves as the fruits of those students’ civic labour. It was a perfect story – perfect for a picture book but not perhaps for the historical chronicle we were still living. Not by state law, but by the more iron laws of capital and class, the facts of educational impoverishment are still everywhere to see in South Africa.
So are the very facts and politics of language that lit the Soweto Uprising’s fuse. Already, come the 1970s, black students were being made to learn in a language that was not theirs. Black students left their Bantu languages, their mother tongues, at home to study in English; most of them adopted names that were not their own; Rolihlala Mandela was given the English name Nelson by a teacher on his first day of school. Then, in 1974, the apartheid regime added the insult of a decree instituting Afrikaans as the medium of instruction alongside English. Not content with dispossessing black South Africans of their land, the apartheid regime sought to dispossess them of their voice – of their very ability to learn how to use their voice. Afrikaans, so to speak, fell; but today it remains true that the black South African who is born must speak English to do or own anything in his country. Questions of land expropriation linger in South Africa; so too do questions of the language in which the future of the country will be expressed.
Every year when 16 June comes around, Nzima’s image is circulated. Discontented South Africans use the photograph to point to each new injustice, suggesting we have not come as far as we would have liked. The photo has become, in itself, a protest; its fate in South Africa (and elsewhere) is like that of Picasso’s Guernica – a painting with which Nzima’s photograph shares an uncanny resemblance.
Every week Guernica names a new atrocity, accuses a new war criminal. Guernica stopped belonging to Picasso a long time ago. It belongs to the world in common; by means of it, we come to know how terrible our world remains. And it is the same with Nzima’s photo. The continuing plight of poor black South Africans; the many post-apartheid massacres tied to the mining industry, from Marikana to Stilfontein; the quieter deaths in pit latrines or through curable diseases – Nzima’s photograph condemns them. Even 50 years later, South Africans cannot put Nzima’s photograph behind them – it is theirs, it belongs to them.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Mummy in Glasgow may be repatriated to Egypt following removal from display
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Gareth Harris
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
A mummy removed from display last month at Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum could be returned to Egypt. According to the Scottish newspaper The Sunday Post, Egyptian authorities have asked for the mummified remains of the priest Nekht to be repatriated.
Glasgow Life, the charitable organisation which operates the museum, confirmed to The Art Newspaper that it had received a request to send remains of Nekht back to Egypt. The organisation has not confirmed the origin of the request.
Last month, officials at the museum removed the coffin and mummified corpse of the ancient Egyptian priest from public view. A spokesperson for Glasgow Life said: “Glasgow Life Museums’ draft Human Remains Policy proposes human remains should only be displayed where there is documented and informed consent from the deceased individual or, in appropriate circumstances, their descendants. In the absence of such consent, we believe removing ancient Egyptian human remains from display is more respectful to the deceased individuals.”
The move comes after the International Council of Museums (Icom) revised its code of ethics in June, recommending the “inherent dignity” of human remains be upheld; Icom does not state however that all remains should be removed from display.
Meanwhile the Hunterian gallery in Glasgow confirmed to Museums Journal that it had covered an open sarcophagus containing the mummified remains of Lady Shep-En-Hor following an internal ethical review, although the sarcophagus itself remains on display.
The removal of the mummified remains at Kelvingrove and other museums feeds into current debate in the UK museums and heritage sector over the care and display of human remains. In response to the museum's policy on the lack of consent by the deceased, Stuart Robertson, the former director of the Charles Rennie Mackintosh Society in Glasgow, wrote on LinkedIn that “applying modern, 21st-century bureaucratic consent standards retrospectively to ancient history is an absurd and impossible standard. It completely undermines the educational mission of public museums”.
Last year, officials at the Manchester Museum asked visitors if the mummified remains of an Egyptian woman should remain on display. The mummy, known as Asru, was subsequently taken off public view.
“Asru now lies in the museum’s stores within her outer coffin, which will remain closed, but this is not intended to be her permanent resting place. We are thinking about how we better care for ancestors, in line with the wishes of the dead and of living communities,” says the museum's website.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/unions-worke.title: How Workers Can Govern in Zohran Mamdani’s New York
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/unions-worke.author: Nantina Vgontzas, Sanjay Pinto
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/unions-worke.text:
How Workers Can Govern in Zohran Mamdani’s New York
Pro-worker policy isn’t just about the government improving labor standards. Zohran Mamdani’s administration could empower workers to shape and enforce standards by training and organizing each other.
In Amazon’s vast logistics empire, warehouse workers and delivery drivers incur frequent injuries amid stringent performance monitoring and evaluation. The best data we have indicates that many workers are interested in organizing to improve their conditions, yet the same infrastructure used to relentlessly boost productivity is deployed to suppress collective action. Refusing to come to the table even when workers unionize, Amazon is looking to have traditional legal pathways for expressing worker voice abolished altogether — and its algorithmic systems given free rein.
Still, closer inspection reveals stirrings of dissent. Across Amazon’s global network, workers aware of their strategic position in the distribution process are contesting speedup and discipline. Through their mastery of government regulations and the company’s own operating procedures, they are challenging productivity write-ups, refusing unsafe work, and teaching their peers how to navigate Amazon’s increasingly automated managerial systems. They are developing a knowledge base that prefigures more democratic forms of shop floor governance.
Not only are these emergent practices of peer education crucial for strategies of labor renewal, but they can inform a parallel question that has gained traction in the last year — the question of mass governance. Amid a deepening global crisis of liberal democracy, the election of a socialist mayor in New York City has generated interest in not only representing the interests of working-class people but, moreover, expanding opportunities for them to govern the city their labor makes run. Thus far, mass governance initiatives have focused on cultivating engagement at the neighborhood and borough levels, such as through “Rental Ripoff Hearings” and participatory budgeting assemblies. Meanwhile, the workplace remains an underexplored site. Though the Mamdani administration has begun expanding state capacities to enforce labor standards, less attention has been placed on the role that workers can play in this process.
This essay builds a framework of mass governance out of workers’ daily struggles on the shop floor, focusing on peer education as a dual organizing and policy tool. Versed in legal rights, work processes, and relational dynamics, peer educators are uniquely positioned to cultivate shared insights about the harms stemming from employers’ exploitative practices and facilitate tactical experimentation aimed at eradicating these harms together with strategic reflection around transforming the power relations that give rise to them. We term this mode of engagement mass worker education: democratizing the production of knowledge in service of democratizing the production of goods and services. Recognizing the importance of intellectual exchange and political deliberation for worker empowerment, this framework envisions workers as not only enforcing labor standards but shaping them as well.
Following on the Mamdani administration’s expansion of resources for the NYC Department of Consumer and Worker Protection (DCWP) as well as its establishment of the Mayor’s Office of Worker Power (MOWP) and Office of Mass Engagement (OME), the essay considers leveraging this enhanced capacity to institutionalize a role for peer educators in implementing worker protections and building workplace organization. As an exemplary case, we explore the idea of NYC establishing a mass worker education program in parcel shipping operations across the metropolitan area. Administered in partnership with unions and community groups, the program would build training capacity among a corps of warehouse workers and parcel delivery drivers, strengthening their role in enforcing new laws that address harmful industry practices and cultivating broader cultures of workplace safety. We also consider forms of partnership between NYC and New York State that could expand the scope and extend reach of this worker training and legal coenforcement with increasingly nonunion workforces. Last, we discuss how such a program could empower workers to participate in mass assemblies shaping policy development around data collection, deployment of new technologies, and other pressing concerns, helping pave the way toward mass sectoral governance.
Labor Standards Enforcement and the Role of Peer Education
Government agencies around the country are building partnerships with worker organizations to enforce labor standards. Drawing on the knowledge that workers have about their industries and specific worksites, these efforts in coenforcement have achieved important gains in addressing legal violations.
At Amazon’s San Bernardino International Airport (KSBD) air hub in Southern California, for instance, workers organizing with Inland Empire Amazon Workers United have collected and shared information about the facility’s weak safety protections during extreme summer temperatures, leading to several government citations. This work comes on the heels of over a decade of worker education and organizing that has raised consciousness around heat safety in the Inland Empire’s booming warehousing sector and contributed to the passage of statewide heat illness prevention standards.
In response to another acute threat faced by workers — the rapid deployment of artificial intelligence technologies — California, New York, and other states have also begun enforcing new quota transparency laws in the warehousing sector. In 2024, the California Labor Commission fined Amazon almost $6 million for violating Assembly Bill 701, which requires warehousing employers to provide written notice of quotas on which they are evaluated. Here, too, worker knowledge and organization proved crucial to enforcement, with workers at ONT8 (Optical Network Terminal) and ONT9 fulfillment centers sharing information with the Labor Commissioner’s Office under the auspices of the California Strategic Enforcement Partnership.
Increasingly, Amazon is challenging these efforts at enforcing quota standards. In California, the company has appealed the Labor Commission’s citations by arguing that it does not use predetermined quotas to evaluate workers, while in New York, workers report that management has been able to sidestep new quota provisions by evaluating workers on the basis of their relative productivity — a tactic that makes injured and pregnant workers especially vulnerable to heightened work intensity.
In maintaining its de facto quota system, Amazon insists that the data it collects on workflows and then uses to train computational systems constitutes proprietary information. Even in jurisdictions with strong data protections like Germany, the company refuses to give works councils (elected workplace bodies that represent employees’ interests to management) access to datasets and algorithms managed by engineers often hundreds or thousands of miles away from the worksite — the very measures that would enable frontline workers to intervene more directly in the technical processes that shape their working conditions.
Government agencies around the country are building partnerships with worker organizations to enforce labor standards.
In challenging the separation that capitalist production engenders between the conception and execution of labor, peer education offers a potential antidote. At a recent workshop, workers from different Amazon divisions came together to analyze the impacts of AI and explore strategies for expanding worker voice in its design and deployment. As a collective exercise in knowledge production, the gathering showed what may be possible if workers are empowered to disrupt hierarchical information flows in the workplace and policymaking arenas.
Highlighting worker knowledge for policymaking purposes suggests wider implications concerning the intersection of labor renewal and mass governance. For the most part, legislation aimed at supporting efforts to revitalize the labor movement (e.g., the Protecting the Right to Organize [PRO] Act) has been focused on making it easier for workers to organize. As necessary as these measures are for expanding the associational capacities of the working class, they are insufficient for expanding its governing capacities. Unions serve as a potentially politicizing force within the workplace, but they largely operate within legal frameworks that regularize collective bargaining while muting shop floor contestation. These frameworks not only enshrine capitalist control over production but also shift the task of governing away from workers’ daily struggles. Workers can try to influence the policy process either through union representatives appointed to tripartite structures or by lobbying elected officials.
Mass worker education challenges this distinction, emphasizing the agency of workers in more directly shaping and enforcing their rights on the shop floor. We draw inspiration from the factory councils of interwar Europe, experiments with autogestion (self-management) in decolonized Africa and Asia, and the cordones industriales (industrial belts) and comunas (communes) at the heart of socialist projects in Latin America. More immediately, we look to occupational health movements that used peer education to expand popular sovereignty under a range of authoritarian politics of early neoliberalism. During the Brazilian military dictatorship, for instance, metalworkers used their firsthand knowledge of the sector’s acute injury crisis to expose the state’s cosmetic fixes, laying the groundwork for a disability rights movement that made key legislative advances after the fall of the junta. In the Indian state of Chhattisgarh, mine workers in the 1980s partnered with health professionals to train “barefoot doctors” and establish a people’s hospital that broke down hierarchies of expertise in the health sector. Meanwhile, during the Reaganite offensive in the United States, worker movements within the United Auto Workers (UAW) and Oil, Chemical, and Atomic Workers International Union (OCAW) used peer education to link health and safety organizing to broader questions of environmental justice.
Presently, we see this legacy extended by Amazon workers building power across the company’s global network. Through meetings organized by Amazon Workers International and other networks, worker representatives exchange information about hazardous work and bring this knowledge home to share with coworkers on the shop floor. Moreover, in refusing unsafe work during the pandemic and other emergencies, Amazon workers have been articulating a common vision of making company operations safer for themselves and their communities.
These examples illustrate the openings that exist for workers to build shop floor power and influence policy even in challenging conditions. Through spaces of collective experimentation and reflection, workers can confront the root of the harms they face — power relations embodied in the production process itself.
Instituting Mass Worker Education in NYC
In NYC, the Office of Labor Policy & Standards (OLPS), a division of the DCWP, has undertaken important legal enforcement measures in recent years. For example, following the 2010 passage of the New York Domestic Workers’ Bill of Rights, OLPS convened focus groups with nannies, cleaners, and home health aides across the city to discuss violations and other issues. A parallel set of efforts led to the 2017 formation of the We Rise Nanny Training program, through which a coalition of domestic worker organizations have partnered with the Worker Institute at Cornell University in developing a peer education program centering around rights awareness, workforce development, and organizing skills. The coalition has since expanded the program to cover other sectors, training hundreds of nannies, cleaners, and home health aides, as well as day laborers and farmworkers. New research shows that NYC, with its strong enforcement of the Domestic Workers’ Bill of Rights, has seen major improvements in job quality indicators such as overtime relative to the rest of the state.
These experiences highlight the importance of not only responding to legal violations after they have occurred but also promoting organizing strategies that shift larger workplace cultures. A mass worker education program could support legal coenforcement while also equipping workers with resources to exercise greater control over their conditions, addressing shop floor challenges before they become acute.
To illustrate what such a program could look like, we return to the example of warehousing and parcel delivery. With its rapid expansion amid the e-commerce boom, the industry has attracted growing public concern over its impacts on workers, residents, and the environment. Amazon’s invasive deployments of AI and other digital technologies have received particular scrutiny, spurring wider discussion among consumers and workers across a variety of industries. Building on existing legislation and organizing in New York, a program of mass worker education could strengthen governance of warehousing and parcel delivery and serve as a model for other industries.
Legislation passed at the state level over the past five years regulates production quotas and mandates that employers implement injury reduction plans. In 2025, worker and advocacy groups in New Yorkers for a Fair Economy (NYFE) — a coalition convened by the Alliance for a Greater New York (ALIGN) — turned attention to the question of how to implement this legislation effectively. Amazon Labor Union–International Brotherhood of Teamsters Local 1 (ALU-IBT Local 1), representing five thousand workers at the JFK8 fulfillment center in Staten Island, focused on raising awareness of these laws as part of its safety campaign. Following several worker summits and stakeholder meetings, ALU-IBT Local 1 partnered with the Athena Coalition and National Employment Law Project (NELP) to pilot a training around laws relevant to advancing health and safety in the workplace, body and hazard mapping, and formation of workplace safety committees. With support from the Consortium for Worker Education (CWE), ALU-IBT Local 1 has carried out additional training with shop floor leaders and is building a training center near JFK8.
At the city level, the NYFE coalition is currently mobilizing in support of the Delivery Protection Act (DPA), introduced by NYC Council Member Tiffany Cabán in September 2025. The legislation would require operators of last-mile delivery facilities to obtain business licenses from DCWP and directly hire delivery drivers (including those who have unionized with Teamsters Local 804 at Amazon delivery facilities DBK4 and DBK1 in Queens) rather than misclassifying them as independent contractors. Importantly, the legislation would require employers to grant access to an independent certified organization to conduct safety and rights training with workers and managers. Drawing on a recent study commissioned by the NYC Comptroller’s office that shows an increase in traffic crashes and injuries in areas near last-mile delivery facilities like the ones in Maspeth, Queens, advocates argue that promoting the safety of workers would also help to safeguard residents. “The impact goes far beyond us,” according to Luc Rene, an Amazon Teamster based at DBK4. “The endless churn of underpaid drivers creates congestion, pollution, and wear on city streets.” If the bill passes, DCWP could partner with members of the NYFE coalition to develop a coenforcement strategy that builds on work around recent state laws.
Focusing on the training provision, we draw on an insight common among many evaluations of union education programs, which shows that workers more readily incorporate lessons received through peer education as opposed to other forms of pedagogy. A particularly instructive example comes from a peer education program developed to address sexual harassment and violence in California’s janitorial industry, where a coalition of labor and anti-violence organizations created a framework for anti-sexual-harassment training by peer educators, known as promotoras, for janitorial workers across the state. The coalition, which included worker leaders, saw that managers and supervisors often enable or enact harmful behaviors themselves, and determined that trained janitors — particularly survivors of sexual violence — were best positioned to educate their peers about relevant rights and strategies. Coalition members went on to support the creation of the Ya Basta Center in Los Angeles, which has trained hundreds of janitor promotoras to provide peer training in workplaces across California. Drawing on trauma-informed methods originally developed by the East Los Angeles Women’s Center, janitor promotoras facilitate spaces where workers can establish the trust needed to share their stories. These healing spaces have given janitors the confidence to stand with each other in the workplace and speak up against harassment, often joining fights around other issues like wage theft as well.
In New York, working together with an enforcement agency like DCWP as well as key anchoring institutions like MOWP, OME, and CWE, members of the NYFE coalition could set up a training program akin to the promotora program in California. Focusing initially on enforcement of the DPA, the program could prepare a core of last-mile delivery drivers and warehouse workers — including those engaging with local unions — to deliver training around issues of misclassification and safety addressed by the legislation. Like the promotora model, employers across this industry would be required to grant access to peer educators, enabling the program to cover nonunion workforces as well. Through program evaluation, the city could develop an evidence base showing whether and how peer training impacts worker awareness of legal rights and the sense of efficacy workers have in exercising these rights. Drawing on the city’s increasing agency capacities as well as its growing movement of labor and community groups targeting Amazon’s abuses, such work could evolve into the development of a training center like the Ya Basta Center.
Over time, building on emergent city-state partnerships around childcare and other issues, a peer education program could train a corps of warehouse workers and parcel delivery drivers in promoting awareness and enforcement of the right to organize as well as health and safety laws that Amazon and other employers have been known to violate. Given employers’ use of tech-enabled worker surveillance strategies to enforce unsustainable work rates and impede worker responses, peer educators could draw connections between these individual and collective forms of disempowerment. By bringing together workers from different parts of the logistics sector, a mass worker education program could generate broader knowledge about the infrastructures undergirding harmful practices and foster dialogue about strategies for building worker voice across the supply chain. Moreover, linking worker and community safety, the program could also generate support for other legislative efforts.
A partnership between the city and state could assist with the development of this program in multiple respects. First, Albany could generate revenue for the peer education training center by imposing a “robot tax” on Amazon and other corporations investing in high levels of automation. Second, implementing and refining a peer education program at the city level would serve as a test case before expanding its reach across New York state. In California, labor and anti-violence groups leveraged a rich movement ecosystem in Los Angeles, the historic birthplace of the Justice for Janitors campaign, toward establishing the Ya Basta Center as a base for strengthening statewide rights enforcement. A peer education training center based in NYC could serve a similar function. Last and most ambitiously, the state and city could follow the example of work-sharing agreements between government agencies, establishing coenforcement powers between NYS Department of Labor (DOL) and NYC DCWP that promote accountability for serial law breakers and discourage harmful employer behaviors. For instance, current state law mandates annual worksite evaluations by state-appointed industrial hygienists (government officials who identify and control workplace hazards to protect public health). Employers are then required to take concrete steps to address whatever ergonomic risk factors are identified in the evaluations, but it has not been specified what steps employers would need to take to comply. Establishing coenforcement powers between NYS DOL and NYC DCWP would enable the city government to work with unions and other partners in establishing participatory structures.
From the Shop Floor to the Assembly
Recent years have seen numerous proposals calling for sectoral governance as a labor renewal strategy in New York and other parts of the country, including wage boards and tripartite bargaining structures. In their implementation, however, such developments often have been relatively detached from and at times contradictory to grassroots efforts to grow worker power. This disconnect weakens legal enforcement, hampers ongoing policy development that could be responsive to evolving worker needs and concerns, and limits possibilities for the kind of consciousness-raising work that can engender positive feedback loops between policy and organizing. This separation also constrains the capacity of workers to build direct associational power vis-à-vis employers, clients, and other holders of economic power.
In institutionalizing channels for workers to promote labor standards enforcement and shift broader workplace cultures, an infrastructure of mass worker education could amplify the capacity of frontline workers to meaningfully shape policy. Specifically, peer education could build on workers’ existing job-related knowledge to deepen understandings of industry dynamics and relevant policy debates; seed the formation of what ALU-IBT Local 1 leaders have called “tech governance councils,” which would combine strategic reflection on shop floor organizing with proposals for enhancing worker voice in technology deployment; and facilitate recruitment of workers into mass sectoral assemblies. These assemblies could provide a forum for workers from different worksites, occupations, and job titles to convene around developing citywide organizing and policy strategies. Such assemblies could deepen member engagement in areas where unions already have a foothold and provide a space for unions to continue deepening their coalitional relationships with other communities. Critically, amid continued employer attacks on legal rights to free association, mass assemblies could build networks of support for collective action in areas with little or no union density as well.
We end by returning to our opening vignette of Amazon workers resisting acute forms of digital surveillance. Amid growing interest in the regulation of data collection and computational systems, the framework we have proposed would anchor shop-floor governance practices, like the efforts of Amazon workers to teach each other how to navigate the company’s surveillance systems, in the insights of workers who encounter these systems daily. Moreover, in establishing a consistent feedback loop from the point of production to sectoral assemblies and the halls of state power, the policy process would be infused with ongoing experimentation, reflection, and refinement. As Big Tech and other corporate actors seek greater control over nearly every aspect of economic, social, and political life, the Mamdani administration has a historic opportunity to create agile policy mechanisms that can respond to this rapidly shifting terrain — moving from the shop floor up.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/03/demo.title: If Democrats Win, Thank the Left
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/03/demo.author: Jessica Washington, Noah Hurowitz, Akela Lacy, Matt Sledge
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/03/demo.text:
Democrats are on the verge of reversing their political fortunes. The party is heading into the midterm elections Tuesday under the kind of conditions campaign consultants dream of, after two years wielding hardly more power than a strongly worded letter.
Donald Trump has spent the erratic waning years of his presidency leading his party into a political wilderness by waging a deeply unpopular war on Iran and driving the cost of living ever higher. Republicans who enjoy a governing trifecta have tried to distance themselves from the party’s decision-making and its leader, a once-animating force who has turned himself into a liability. Poll after poll says the same: Democrats are poised to take control of one or both houses of Congress — and spend the next two years thwarting Trump’s agenda.
But after a primary season dominated by an ascendant left wing and a broader rejection of centrist politics, the question isn’t just whether Democrats win on Tuesday. It’s what kind of Democratic Party emerges on Wednesday morning.
“I really like the socialism aspects,” said Gibrel Said, a supporter of Abdul El-Sayed at his closing rally in Detroit Monday night. In the marquee contest serving as a referendum on the Democratic Party’s future, the Michigan Democratic Senate nominee espouses progressive politics and has often been associated with the the left’s agenda-setting socialists, though he doesn’t identify as one. His race has been rocked by the kind of left-versus-right identity crisis that presents a perennial challenge for Democrats.
“One, Medicare for All; two, how do we fund things that help us as constituents,” Said told The Intercept, ticking off things he appreciates about the candidate. Said, who lives in the Arab enclave of Dearborn, Michigan, especially praised El-Sayed’s willingness to buck party leadership and speak out on U.S.–Israel policy. “Instead of tiptoeing around the subject, he very adamantly says, hey there’s a genocide happening here, we shouldn’t send our money.”
Cycle after cycle, in state after state, an insurgent band of Democrats critical of the political establishment’s ties to corporate interests and its unflinching commitment to Israel has had to overcome the barriers erected by its own party’s centrist leadership. Both sides present themselves as the true representatives of working people: the centrists by arguing that more transformative ideas will scare off lower-information voters, the left by saying they represent the masses.
How much of this trickles down to actual voters? On Monday, The Intercept followed canvassers and spoke to voters in Michigan, Maine, and Texas, asking about which issues had permeated and taking the temperature of voter enthusiasm. Some rolled their eyes at the spats that have dominated the headlines, dismissing the idea that eleventh-hour backstabbing would make a difference. Others regurgitated right-wing misinformation. Many complained of too many campaign mailers.
“They’re wicked mean,” said Sharon McDonnell, a supporter of Troy Jackson, the Democratic Senate nominee in Maine. Speaking to The Intercept in the town of Yarmouth, she described one mailer that included a photo of Jackson chomping a cigar and describing him as “evil.” “It’s just nasty.”
In Maine, the party’s left flank seized power in the nominating process for the Democratic Senate candidate — then fought to hang onto it after onetime rising star Graham Platner flamed out after a sexual assault allegation (which he denies). With Jackson, a former state Senate leader, Maine now offers progressives one of two opportunities to test their message at the Senate level, where a candidate has to secure appeal statewide, not just in deep-blue House districts.
The other is Michigan, where the intraparty battle is still raging. Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., demolished her past attempts at fence-mending when she endorsed Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers on Sunday and abandoned El-Sayed, who beat Stevens in a Michigan primary that saw $30 million in outside spending from the super PAC for the American Israel Public Affairs Committee.
The dustup has had Democrats biting their nails and moderate party leaders making the cable news circuit to demand party discipline — this time, to scold a centrist. The party leads in the polls for 218 of the 435 seats up for grabs in the House of Representatives, but they need to perform well in seven key states — Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, and Texas, in addition to Maine and Michigan — if they want to win the Senate.
“I think she’s counterintuitively, perhaps, given people a reason to rally some more,” said Kathleen Britton, an El-Sayed supporter at the Detroit rally on Monday, of Stevens. “I really don’t think it’s gonna help Mike Rogers.”
Earlier that day, in a predominantly Black neighborhood of Detroit, a prominent Black supporter of El-Sayed preparing to knock on voters’ doors described Stevens’s endorsement as an “ego-driven statement.”
Mike Bland, the executive director of the Black Men Vote PAC, highlighted that Stevens made her public endorsement of Rogers in a Black church in Detroit. He doubted that Stevens, whose criticism of El-Sayed centers primarily on his skepticism of the U.S. relationship with the state of Israel, would be able to pull Black voters to Rogers, a conservative former House representative whose campaign has repeatedly peddled anti-Muslim tropes against El-Sayed.
“How can I say this without cursing? She used a Black church as a prop, and we have seen that time and time again,” Bland said. “Black folks aren’t stupid.”
Over the past month, El-Sayed has rallied with Barack Obama and Kamala Harris, the two most prominent Black politicians in America — and hardly radicals estranged from the establishment power center. At the same time that Stevens was making her endorsement of Rogers public, El-Sayed was attending a get-out-the-vote event at another church in Detroit. The two primary foes were supposed to appear together that day with Rep. Jim Clyburn, D-S.C.
One of the Democrats’ most coveted Senate pickups didn’t present much of an opportunity for the left in the primary, but it has still been characterized by intraparty animosity.
In Texas, where both Democratic Senate primary contenders espoused relatively moderate politics, outgoing Rep. Jasmine Crockett, D-Texas, has declined to campaign with state Rep. James Talarico, though she endorsed him after he beat her in the state’s March Democratic primary.
Talarico has been performing well with Latino voters, a massive voting bloc that helped fuel his primary victory. But Crockett — who, unlike Stevens, is Black — has suggested that Talarico has not done enough to excite Black voters, a demographic she carried in the primary. On a canvassing operation targeting Black voters in the Dallas–Fort Worth area on Monday, few Black Texans who spoke to The Intercept expressed excitement for Talarico. But most had already voted for him, saying they were motivated to do their civic duty.
Black voters frequently discussed concerns over affordability, gas prices, and homelessness. Canvassers told The Intercept they had heard some of those voters express concerns over their perception of Talarico’s policies toward transgender children, at times espousing blatant misinformation, such as the idea that Talarico supported arresting parents who refused to give their children gender-affirming surgeries.
“ I don’t stand for that,” said voter Jermiah Robinson, referring to her belief that Talarico pushed “sex-change” surgery for minors. Like many voters, she cited the cost of living as her most pressing issue. Robinson said she would “want to vote for him if he stands by his words, and he’s actually like ‘Yeah, I’ll help out as far as prices and everything.’”
Talarico appears to have improved his margins with Black voters in the final stretch. According to the Texas Politics Project at the University of Texas, Talarico is leading with 79 percent of the Black vote, signaling a significant increase in support from Black voters from just last month. The conventional wisdom suggests that he could barely ask for a better opponent than the scandal-plagued Republican candidate, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton.
In 2015, Paxton was indicted on felony securities fraud charges in Texas, in a case that dragged on for roughly nine years, and ended with Paxton being required to do community service and pay restitution. And in 2023, the Texas House of Representatives voted across party lines to impeach him as attorney general for alleged corruption and retaliation against whistleblowers.
Scandal kept rocking the race for Senate in Maine, where longtime Republican incumbent Sen. Susan Collins faces her toughest reelection challenge yet from Jackson. Before Jackson, who lost a race this cycle for the state’s Democratic nomination for governor, there was Platner, hailed early as a working-class champion who faced a series of personal scandals in his successful primary campaign. There was the revelation of a Nazi tattoo that he claimed not to understand until last October. There were crudely worded Reddit posts and stories of cruelty from women he’d dated. One former girlfriend’s allegations of sexual assault ultimately ended his campaign — and set off a scramble to find a replacement that progressives ultimately won by elevating Jackson.
By Monday, Mainers who spoke to The Intercept appeared exhausted by the lengthy, contentious, and expensive Senate race that has dominated the state.
“There’s a lot of fatigue. People are tired of it,“ said Charlie Dingman, who chairs the state Democratic Party. “I have had some conversations at doors with people that have led me to think that the extremely negative and extremely untruthful ads may be backfiring.”
Tyler Echard, in Norway, said he’d already cast an absentee ballot for Democrats down the ticket. He was disgusted with a deluge of political mailers and eager to stop seeing them pile up on his doorstep.
“The amount of mailers we get — just mailers, not just handed at the door but in the mail — especially from the Republican side, the amount of money is probably more than I will make in my lifetime, spent in this election,” Echard said. “At some point, we gotta get legislation because money’s just gonna run everything into the ground. I ain’t got it, so I can’t influence it.”
Frustration with the status quo in Congress could spell the end for Collins’s 30-year career in the Senate. On Monday, a University of New Hampshire poll found Jackson leading Collins by 4 percentage points. And in September, Collins found herself thrust into a scandal of her own, when ProPublica revealed that the FBI anti-corruption squad was investigating an alleged pay-to-play scheme between Collins and a donor eager to secure government contracts.
The Intercept later exposed that, alongside a series of campaign donations, defense contractors cozy with Collins had received lucrative carveouts in defense spending. (Collins has denied wrongdoing in all cases.)
But the incumbent senator has faced controversy and come out victorious before. And some Mainers doubt they’ll see change either way.
“I can’t vote for either side,” said a man, who declined to share his name with The Intercept, walking down a rural road in Norway with a hunting rifle slung over his shoulder. “You can’t trust neither of them.”
Noah Hurowitz reported from Yarmouth and Norway, Maine; Akela Lacy reported from Fort Worth, Texas; Matt Sledge reported from Detroit, Michigan.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Bill de Blasio

Hochul and Mamdani Teach Democrats a Vital Lesson in Party Unity
New York State’s governor and New York City’s mayor are illustrating how ideologically diverse Democrats can build winning coalitions.
To paraphrase a classic work, there is a specter haunting the Democratic Party, and its name is “socialism.” Or at least that’s what the mainstream American media would have you believe.
Whichever network I appear on, I’m sure to get a breathless question about the looming civil war between the progressive and moderate wings of my party.
It is treated as an article of faith that peaceful coexistence is an impossibility, and that any chance of unity will inevitably be subverted by the wily and newly empowered Democratic Socialists of America.
This narrative is oh-so-clean and fulfills the normal journalistic desire for conflict.
But the facts on the ground in 2026 suggest a far different reality, one that has been consistently developing over the last decade and that in truth offers new possibilities for the growth of the party.
The most powerful example is on display in my state: New York. Here, Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Governor Kathy Hochul have formed a mutually beneficial and strikingly cohesive alliance. In the New York context, we are getting an object lesson in the ways both wings of our party actually need each other.
On many of the issues that matter, it is Mamdani who often sets the tone ideologically and moves Hochul leftward, a phenomenon we will see more frequently around the country.
The recent adoption by the state legislature of a pied-a-terre tax for NYC—asking a little more from those with expensive second homes—is an example of a progressive policy that Albany would never have passed on its own but felt it had to because of the grassroots energy created by Mamdani’s movement.
To be clear, this is not an entirely new reality. When I was elected mayor in 2013 on a platform of higher taxes on the wealthy to fund Universal Pre-K, my campaign created inexorable pressure on then-Governor Andrew Cuomo to act.
The difference now is that rather than resisting Mamdani at every turn (which was my experience with Cuomo), Hochul understands that the best way to both win elections and to govern is with the mayor by her side.
The governor has taken positions on taxation and on Mamdani’s enlightened Universal Childcare Plan that she otherwise might not have. But instead of the sky falling for her politically because she worked with a democratic socialist, she is arguably in a stronger position to lead than ever.
In the run-up to today’s midterm elections, the Democratic Party’s Washington-based organs began to embrace the general election campaigns of progressive primary-winners in ways they wouldn’t have in the past. It may be grudging and not generous enough, but it has been happening.
DNC chair Ken Martin has more genuine affinity for the progressive wing than almost any of his predecessors, and Democratic congressional leaders Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries have clearly been changing their tune about the new voices emerging around them.
Have we seen a seamless and elegant transition to a new political reality? No, as has been illustrated by the drama surrounding defeated centrist Democratic Senate candidate Haley Stevens, and her late-stage withdrawal of support for the party’s nominee, Abdul El-Sayed.
But Stevens is the exception, not the norm. In most states, open warfare is rare. For the most part, the two tendencies are working together.
Even in Michigan, after arguably the nastiest primary fight in the nation, the vast majority of the mainstream Democratic establishment, led by centrist Senator Elissa Slotkin, quickly united behind El-Sayed. Indeed, Slotkin had been a steady and effective campaigner for El-Sayed.
Were there entirely practical motivations for Democrats such as Hochul and Slotkin to embrace unity and enlightened approaches to the 2026 campaign?
Absolutely!
But what’s striking is the growing recognition that moderates now need the energy and mobilization and new ideas that progressives bring.
And these examples also remind us that progressives can benefit from the resources (in Hochul’s case) and the access to important constituencies (in Slotkin’s case) that moderates often bring to the table.
Although I don’t want to overstate the notion that a productive modus vivendi is developing between the two wings of the party, it’s fair to say nationally there has been a striking change in recent years.
If 2016 was an extraordinary growth moment for the left because of Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders’s campaign for the Democratic presidential nomination, it also marked a low point for party unity. The Clinton campaign and the Democratic establishment simply couldn’t forgive Bernie’s audacity and didn’t want to embrace his movement. I had a front-row seat in Philadelphia as this huge mistake of arrogance and underestimation unfolded at that year’s Democratic National Convention. As I watched Bernie take the microphone and call for Hillary to be nominated by acclamation, I thought surely this was the beginning of the coalition we needed to win. But that fleeting moment was followed by a spurning of progressive ideas and energy that may well have cost Democrats the White House in 2016.

A scenario like that may not be unthinkable today, but it is much less likely.
Progressives have gained strength and won elections to such a degree that the Democratic mainstream now broadly understands they no longer have the party to themselves. Increasingly, they recognize that mainstream Democrats must work with the powerful movement that progressives have built.
Could this end up being a 1932- or 1964-like moment, when a new and bigger Democratic coalition developed accompanied by a more progressive vision?
It’s certainly possible, especially given the increasing openness of American voters to solutions that address the more glaring failures of the capitalist system.
As the discourse opens up, and proposals for real change begin to emerge, we Democrats should understand that Donald Trump—and the real threat of authoritarianism he poses—has inadvertently played a major role in sparking a long-overdue renewal in our party.
For while his disruption of the Republican Party has surely led it rightward—and badly damaged his party’s prospects in this midterm election season—his broader disruption of American politics, and of the American economy, has led to a disruption of the Democratic Party.
That disruption, along with decades of hard work by Sanders and the recent victories of a new generation of candidates, has brought Democrats closer to our New Deal and Great Society roots and begun to forge a party that is ready to win again. And when Democrats regain power, to build a future than does not just reject Trump but that builds a progressive future for our country.

https://www.propublica.org/article/ruido.title: I Was There to Document the Aftermath of Deadly Flooding. Then, It Started Raining.
https://www.propublica.org/article/ruido.author: Cengiz Yar
https://www.propublica.org/article/ruido.text:
Three summers ago, over Father’s Day weekend, my family and I went camping in the Lincoln National Forest, just a few hours drive north of our home in El Paso, Texas. It’s a beautiful area that’s long served as a getaway for the region, with skiing in the winter, and golf and hiking in the summer. My daughter played under the trees, and I rode my bike down mountain trails that, I noticed, seemed concerningly dry.
The next evening, after we left to drive home, two fires started in forests surrounding the town of Ruidoso, New Mexico, around 25 miles away from where we’d been. I watched horrifying videos online of fire lapping the mountains behind the village’s strip malls and parking lots. The fires were eventually suppressed by a combination of human effort and the late summer monsoon season. But when the downpour of rain hit the burnt landscape around Ruidoso, it created another problem: Recurring floods then ripped through town, damaging homes and infrastructure, and leading to emergency rescues.
The following summer, the scene repeated. On July 8, 2025, monsoon rain hit a burn scar and quickly swelled the Rio Ruidoso and its tributaries. Three people — two of them children — lost their lives.
Reporter Abe Streep, a member of ProPublica’s Southwest office, and I met in Ruidoso to report on what happened. Ruidoso is a place built on tourism, with a paid (rather than volunteer) fire department staff and its own disaster manager. How could two children and a man be swept to their deaths in a place that appeared equipped to handle such disasters?
In two stories ProPublica recently published, Abe answered those questions. He found that, after the 2024 fires, experts warned the town of increased flash flooding risks. Initially, local and state leaders considered a relocation plan for some homes and businesses that would get people out of harm’s way, but the project faltered. Instead, village leaders continued promoting tourism to the town, and the mayor even chastised residents for warning of floods on social media. Abe also reported that, while local and state officials insisted the emergency response to the flood was admirable, first responders say the three deaths could have been avoided. The responders told Abe that village leadership left them understaffed and inadequately equipped to contend with the flooding.
The Village of Ruidoso did not respond to detailed written questions about its emergency response, and it has not publicly released a report on rescue efforts during the flood. Reached by phone, the fire chief, Cade Hall, disputed our reporting but declined to provide specifics. Mayor Lynn Crawford has said protecting the village includes balancing public safety with tourism, the lifeblood of its economy. But in an interview last year, Crawford said to Abe and me: “Who’s to blame? I didn’t start the fire.”
My role as a photographer was to document Ruidoso as the story unfolded — to visualize the people and place at the center of it. It’s a role I’ve had countless times in my career, but this story hit unexpectedly close to home. I could imagine my own family caught unaware in a similar situation, trying to escape the El Paso summer heat but instead navigating an unfathomable disaster.
When Abe and I started reporting, we met people from the community and out of town who tried to help. I watched as New Mexico National Guard service members loaded sand bags into families’ cars, people prepared hot meals for those who had been displaced and volunteers handed out donated supplies from collection centers.
While we were reporting one afternoon, it started raining. Fear swept through me. Our phones lit up with flood warnings from the National Weather Service. We knew we should take them seriously.
Abe and I sought refuge in a local brewery perched high above the river basin. Before we knew it, the water from that thin little creek of Rio Ruidoso became a torrent. The rushing water rose quickly. It swept through the river valley right under the brewery, carrying what looked like trees and debris with it.
Still, I wanted to photograph the river up close. I left the safety of the brewery and let the heavy rain cover me as I moved closer to the river. As I made photos that afternoon and throughout the rest of the trip, questions about my own safety ran through my mind: Would the water keep rising? If it did, could I get to high ground? And, notably, would I have enough warning?
In hindsight, I realize these questions were largely about whether I could trust the systems in place to keep me and others safe. And as Abe kept reporting over the next year, the more those questions felt valid.
Last month, Abe and I traveled again to Ruidoso. The town felt lighter and less ominous. Much of the ruin had been removed or rebuilt. Grass and sagebrush sprouted on a burn scar. Tourists wandered around a lively downtown on a Friday afternoon. People seemed to be moving on from the terror of the previous year.
But Stephanie and Sebastian Trotter still carry the scars of the day. They lost their two children, Sebastian Rowan, 7, and Charlotte, 4, in the Ruidoso flooding.
There is now a memorial for them and Benjamin “Tim” Feagin, the third person who died, at the RV park where they had been camped. But I wanted to see for myself the places where each of them was found. I felt that making photos of those places could help people connect with the reality of their deaths as well as their lives. So, early one morning, I walked along the floodplain trying to find the locations Abe had shared with me.
I got to the bridge where a firefighter found Sebastian Rowan. There was no marker, no indication that anyone’s body had been found there.
Then I went looking for the area where Charlotte was found. I wandered under pine and cottonwood, through knee-deep grasses and wild sunflowers. Crows cawed overhead, and the early morning sun broke through the trees. I stood there for a while, admiring the beauty, awed by the sadness of the river’s trickle.

Speak the Wind
Hoda Afshar
08.04.2026Photo Essay
The wind, it is said, can possess a person.
In the islands of the Strait of Hormuz, off the southern coast of Iran, a distinctive local culture has emerged as the result of many centuries of cultural and economic exchange. Its traces are seen not only in the material culture of these islands but also in the customs and beliefs of their inhabitants.
Central to these is a belief in the existence of winds that may bring misfortune, principally in the form of illness, and a corresponding ritual in which a hereditary cult leader speaks with the wind in one of many local tongues to negotiate its exit.
Wider beliefs about these winds permeate the culture but are seldom openly discussed – perhaps out of fear that language might manifest the invisible.
While their exact origins are unclear, the existence of similar beliefs and practices in many African countries suggests that the cult may have been brought to the south of Iran from southeast Africa through the Arab slave trade – an account that agrees with that of many locals who hold that the winds themselves travel from Ethiopia.
For locals and visitors, too, these beliefs resonate with the surreal landscape of the islands – a topography marked by strange valleys and statue-like mountains that have been carved by the wind over many millennia.
This project documents the history of these winds and the traces they have left on these islands and their inhabitants – a visible record of the invisible seen through the eye of the imagination.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Why Mary Cassatt was more than just a painter of the 'modern Madonna'
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Annabel Keenan
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
As the centennial of the death of Mary Cassatt (1844-1926) brings renewed attention to the US-born Impressionist, a new publication challenges the image of her as a sentimental painter of mothers and daughters. In Cassatt Reconsidered, Mary G. Morton uses her expertise as a curator and head of French paintings at the National Gallery of Art in Washington, DC, to examine how the art world shaped Cassatt’s reputation, and posits a broader view of her within radical French Modernism.
The book coincides with major exhibitions on Cassatt, including at the Musée d’Orsay in Paris (until 31 January 2027), the Art Institute of Chicago (until 3 January 2027) and the New Britain Museum of American Art in Connecticut (7 November-14 February 2027). Looking closely at the artist’s work and framing her within the experience of women in a modern Paris, Morton shows why Cassatt deserves another look.
The Art Newspaper: What prompted your reassessment?
Mary G. Morton: I thought I knew enough about Cassatt until a 2014 exhibition at the National Gallery on Cassatt’s artistic pas de deux with Degas emphasising their radical technical experimentation. A few years later, an encounter with the PhD candidate Nicole Georgopulos transformed Woman with Sunflower (1905) in my mind from a generic mother and child image to a complex realist allegory, a kind of feminist manifesto responding to and supporting the contemporary suffrage movement. The public recognises Cassatt’s name but associates her with images of maternity. There is so much more to her art, to her story.
How did the art market contribute to the narrowing of Cassatt’s reputation?
Her dealer essentially marketed her as a painter of motherhood, the painter of the “modern Madonna”, hiring critics to write about her in this vein. And while he had success selling her work, the strategy did not serve her well in art historiography. Another dynamic is the burgeoning field of American art history in the 20th century, when Cassatt became an asset to curators as an Impressionist. In most major US museums, her work hangs with US artists, depriving her of the aesthetic context in radical French Modernism. She looks loud, garish, awkward, whereas if you put her with Degas, Renoir and Morisot, she fits in.
What would you like museums, scholars and the public to see differently about Cassatt?
It would be great if Cassatt could exit the limited box she has been put into. Cassatt was the most successful avant-garde artist of the 19th century to represent the lived experience of women in modern urban Paris. She created a fresh visual vocabulary for women’s interests and concerns, refusing the oppressive social norms of her class and producing an extraordinary body of work. Cassatt brings us women’s side of the story.
The primary aim of this book is to provoke readers who might be familiar with Cassatt as a misty-eyed painter of mothers and children to look again. My hope is that the book compels people into museums to find Cassatt’s art and experience what I have: brilliantly expressive, innovative objects that relay a unique vision of humanity and of women’s lives as they were lived more than 100 years ago.
• Mary G. Morton, Cassatt Reconsidered, Getty Publications, 208pp, $35 (hb)

Let Andreas Malm Speak
Britain has banned climate scholar and left-wing activist Andreas Malm from visiting the country. Following the ban on Hasan Piker, it points to an alarming repression of pro-Palestine speech in Britain.
Andreas Malm’s work has been among the most important of any scholar in any academic field over the past decade. His theoretical and strategic contributions have led developments in our understanding of the climate crisis’s basis in capitalism and fed debates about how to respond.
Yet last week, Britain’s Home Office banned Malm from entering the country, on the grounds that his “presence in the UK is not considered to be conducive to the public good.”
Malm had been due to visit London to speak alongside Palestine Action cofounder Huda Ammori at a Tribune magazine event, attend the academic conference Historical Materialism, and be interviewed by BBC Radio 4.
No specific reason was given for the ban. But it seems that the government’s decision is due to Malm’s principled opposition to the proscription of the direct-action network Palestine Action, officially labeled a “terrorist organization.” The move came a fortnight after publisher Faber & Faber announced that it would withdraw Sally Rooney’s novels from the UK market due to her support for Palestine Action, which means she is unable to collect revenue in the country. She too had fallen victim to the government’s silencing of free speech on Palestine, and to measures widely condemned by leading authors, artists, and public figures.
In June, American left-wingers Hasan Piker and Cenk Uygur had already been banned from entering the UK.
The decision by Andy Burnham’s government to ban Malm represents a further attack on the Marxist left. It denies ordinary citizens the opportunity to hear from someone who speaks and writes so clearly about the imminence of climate catastrophe, the horrors of Israel’s genocide in Gaza, and their entanglement.
It is surely no coincidence that these are the two areas in which Burnham’s government is failing resoundingly.
The ban on Malm comes in the same month that Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh approved the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea despite the Labour Party’s 2024 manifesto commitment to issue no new licenses for oil and gas.
It also comes just a few weeks after Burnham insisted that Labour could not work with Green councilors who failed to renounce their party’s policy holding that “Zionism is racism.” Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband’s recent emotive denunciation of Israel’s ethnic cleansing and settler violence does not do enough to stop the material support that the British state continues to provide to the genocide.
Malm is not an extremist from whom the British public needs protecting. His work is resolutely in the Marxist tradition but is cited widely by scholars across disciplines and spanning the political spectrum.
The Destruction of the Earth
Malm’s contributions are many. His seminal 2016 work, Fossil Capital, is perhaps the most important theoretical account of the historical entanglement of fossil fuel production in capitalism. The Progress of This Storm stakes out a clear position in ecological Marxist debates, asserting the need for human agency in confronting the crises we face. In the early 2020s, Corona, Climate, Chronic Emergency and How to Blow Up a Pipeline elaborated on this with essential contributions to debates on climate strategy following the insurgency of Extinction Rebellion and school climate strikes. Coauthored with Wim Carton, Overshoot and The Long Heat then offered masterful accounts of the ideological and technological bases of the march toward climate catastrophe.
More recently, Malm’s impassioned 2025 work, The Destruction of Palestine Is the Destruction of the Earth, places Israel’s genocide in Palestine in its proper historical setting, locating it in the context of British empire and enduring expansion of the fossil economy.
Malm, like Rooney, is no terrorist. In fact, it is the power of his ideas and the clarity of his expression that make him particularly dangerous for the British government. It clearly fears that Malm — like Rooney, Palestine Action, and Just Stop Oil (JSO) — will expose their inexcusable negligence on the most consequential questions of our time.
This episode raises a sobering question not just for the Marxist left, but for anyone in Britain committed to freedom of speech and political expression, and anyone who might expect to publicly criticize any government failing to act on genocide and climate collapse in the coming years: If Burnham’s government is prepared to ban Malm from entering the country, how many of its own citizens would it gladly deprive of their political freedoms if it had the opportunity?
This is an instructive moment. The only real difference between Burnham’s Labour and his predecessor Keir Starmer’s rule lies in the world of vibes and affect. Burnham says he identifies with ordinary people’s problems, names neoliberalism as an enemy, and shares your cultural tastes, perhaps evoking some combination of hope, nostalgia, and northern English pride.
But his government shares with Starmer’s an inability to confront the precipitous decline in living standards, an enthusiasm for growing the destructive defense and AI industries, and ongoing material support for Israel’s genocide in Gaza.
It leaves untouched the massive intensification of state repression of peaceful protest introduced under the last Tory government (in response to Extinction Rebellion and JSO), which was extended to Palestine Action by Starmer’s government.
Even worse than Starmer’s, Burnham’s government has abandoned Labour’s hard-won commitment to stop new fossil fuel production in the North Sea.
Each of these positions undermines the medium- to long-term viability of human civilization as we know it. The banning of Malm is an insight into how ostensibly center-left governments will deal with political dissent as they fail to address the crises in the years to come.
The Marxist left, within and outside the UK, is not only a legitimate political tradition that must be protected from repression on principle. It is the political tradition offering the strongest insights and most vibrant debate on the nature of the crises we face and how to overcome them. Its repression is an assault on everyone.
We should express our solidarity with Andreas Malm and Sally Rooney. But this situation also raises wider demands: for the de-proscription of Palestine Action and the repealing of anti-protest legislation. And, more materially, for an end to the UK’s practical support for Israel’s genocide in Palestine and to fossil fuel production in the North Sea.
Each of these claims are basic expressions of humanity and should be uncontroversial to state out loud in Britain today. It is the moral responsibility of anybody in the public sphere to express them. Burnham’s government rejects them all, and for this deserves our unrelenting opposition.

Kamala Harris Has Her Eye on Today’s Gubernatorial Races
The former vice president reminds The Nation that, even if government is divided in DC, “a governor, as the chief executive of a state, can actually make things happen.”
Today’s midterms will mark the end of one election cycle and the beginning of another. As soon as the votes from 2026 are counted, the 2028 presidential race will take center stage. But that’s just a formality.
For all intents and purposes, the 2028 contest began during the course of the midterm campaign. Several dozen prospective contenders for the Democratic nomination hit the midterm trail to boost their national profiles—campaigning in states across the country and positioning themselves as allies of the candidates who could flip control of Congress and check President Trump in the last two years of his term.
Most of these 2028 hopefuls zeroed in on Senate races, which grabbed the spotlight in final weeks of the 2026 campaign. Nobody doubts the importance of these contests, whether in Michigan, which saw a chaotic close to the race between progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Trump Republican Mike Rogers, or in Texas, where Democratic James Talarico could become the first Democratic senator from the state in more than three decades.
But the front-runner in several surveys that tested the strength of 2026 Democratic presidential prospects has placed an emphasis on today’s gubernatorial races, which will define the direction of states across the country.
That prospect is former vice president Kamala Harris, who, in a national Harvard-Harris poll released one week ago, garnered 34 percent support among likely Democratic presidential primary and voters—16 points ahead of the second-place finisher, California Governor Gavin Newsom. It was the same story in two other polls that were released in October—one for the Financial Times and one by the Echelon Insights firm—both of which gave the 2024 Democratic presidential nominee a clear lead.
Harris—whose 75,017,613 vote total in 2024 was the highest in history for any candidate except for the Republican who narrowly beat her that year, Donald Trump (77,302,580), and for the Democrat with whom she served as vice president, Joe Biden (81,283,501) in 2020—told The Nation that she has not decided whether to mount a new bid for the presidency. That’s a genuine response, as is Harris’s insistence that the top factor in making that decision will be her family. But she has little doubt that she could do the job, as someone with significant White House experience who recalls that she has “spent a lot of time with foreign leaders, thinking about America’s responsibility and role globally, as well as our responsibility as a government to our own people.”
To a greater extent than many prominent political figures, Harris thinks about the duties of executives—in Washington and in statehouses across the country. So while Harris made plenty of 2026 campaign appearances with Senate candidates—including El-Sayed in Michigan, late-surging Mississippi Senate candidate Scott Colom, and Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff—she also focused on some of the 36 gubernatorial races that will be decided today.
For Democrats, the chance to win control of statehouses is especially important. Even if they secure majorities in the House and Senate, they will still have to operate with divided government at the federal level—given that Trump is still in the White House. Democratic governors and legislatures can move far more immediately and far more effectively to address economic concerns, expand access to healthcare, invest in education, regulate data centers and artificial intelligence, and protect the rights of women and the LGBTQ+ community. They can also defend democracy by moving to address gerrymandering and to defend against voter suppression in the run-up to the 2028 election.
This understanding led Harris to Milwaukee, Wisconsin, in the days before the midterm election, where she campaigned with David Crowley, the Milwaukee County Executive who this year is the Democratic nominee to replace outgoing Democratic Governor Tony Evers.
Harris appeared on October 26 with Crowley—who’s in a tight race with MAGA Republican US Representative Tom Tiffany—at a packed Democratic campaign headquarters in a neighborhood on Milwaukee’s northwest side and then at a huge “Women for Crowley” event in a downtown hotel. As always, Harris came prepared, with plenty of insights regarding the Democrat she was supporting and plenty to digs at the Republican he was opposing. And the crowds loved it.
Harris has her share of critics, and there are certainly Democrats who would rather she sit out the 2028 race. But her fans are ardent, and they have been out in force this fall as she hit the trail on behalf of Democratic candidates from Michigan to Mississippi to New Hampshire and Georgia. That was certainly the case in Milwaukee, where Harris was greeted by enthusiastic crowds of Democrats who held cameras aloft, waved posters, and cheered her every remark.
“She’s a huge mentor of mine,” declared Crowley.
For her part, Harris was effusive in her praise of the candidate, whom she described to The Nation as someone who is “in it for all the right reasons.”
“He is a true public servant,” she said of Crowley, who grew up in a Milwaukee neighborhood that is one of the poorest in the country. “He has had the experience of being hungry and knowing that you can’t assume that the very basic needs that you have will be fulfilled—without the government playing its part to help those in need, at a time when they need it most.”
In the closing days of a campaign where candidates on both sides of the partisan aisle are talking about affordability, Harris recognized Crowley’s authenticity.
“It’s not lip service. It is a lived experience for him—in a way that he sees the pain that people are experiencing right now. There’s a whole lot of pain right now. It is about affordability of the basic needs that people have. And that pain is compounded with a real legitimate belief [on the part of so many Americans] that their needs are unimportant, as compared to the powerful and the rich.”
Crowley, she said, “gets it. He understands what the priority should be.”
