https://jacobin.com/2026/11/brazil-hilto.title: A Fight for Workers’ Rights Turned the Tide in Brazil
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/brazil-hilto.author: Cruz Bonlarron Martínez
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/brazil-hilto.text:
A Fight for Workers’ Rights Turned the Tide in Brazil
Erika Hilton, one of Brazil’s first trans legislators, has brought new energy to the Brazilian left. The socialist congresswoman helped lead the fight to establish a 40-hour workweek that also gave a vital boost to Lula’s presidential campaign.
As Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva celebrated his historic victory over far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro on Sunday, he embraced trans congresswoman Erika Hilton and kissed her on the cheek in celebration. The video circulated on social media, with many users pointing to it as evidence of Brazil’s acceptance of trans identity and the key role that the LGBTQ+ community plays within Lula’s coalition.
It is important to note that Hilton and other LGBTQ+ politicians are more than simply a piece of a diverse coalition. They are the force behind a piece of legislation that will reduce the Brazilian workweek from forty-four to forty hours, a historic achievement that contributed to Lula’s victory and helped keep fascism at bay.
Life Beyond Work
One day in 2023, after finishing his shift, a pharmacy assistant in Rio de Janeiro called Rick Azevedo decided to record a video railing against the six-day work schedule to which much of the Brazilian working class are subject, including a disproportionate number of black workers. In the video, he referred to the 6 x 1, the colloquial name for this work regime, as a “modern form of slavery” and asked when the working class was going to make a revolution to put an end to it.
Azevedo went on to note that if he, as a single man, had no time to do anything, he could only imagine how bad things are for others with kids. He ended the video with a call to revolt, warning that if ordinary workers like him did not organize behind the issue, things would never change. He originally archived the video, but after his manager called him in to work early the next day, he decided to post it on TikTok during his shift.
The video quickly went viral, with thousands of interactions shortly after it was posted. Azevedo, who already had a following on TikTok for posts about pop culture and Beyoncé Knowles, received messages from others who felt the same way. In response, he founded the social movement Vida Além do Trabalho (VAT, “Life Beyond Work”), organizing first through live streams and WhatsApp groups, then through petitions to change the law.
Azevedo, who had spent much of his life jumping from job to job but never finding enough time to finish formal university studies, became a movement leader overnight. The movement soon spread to other states and crowdfunded a protest in São Paulo to organize around the issue, gaining the attention of Erika Hilton, a rising star in the Socialism and Liberty Party (PSOL). Because of his newfound popularity, Azevedo decided to run for Rio’s City Council in 2024 with PSOL’s support, further popularizing the movement and solidifying his alliance with Erika Hilton.
The Fight in Congress
After the initial 2024 protests and news of Azevedo’s election in Rio, calls to change the workweek gained momentum and were taken up by some of Brazil’s progressive members of Congress. However, under Brazilian law, a change of this kind could not be made through a simple legislative process; it required an amendment to the Brazilian Constitution.
In Brazil, a constitutional amendment requires one-third of members in both houses to sign on. This seemed very hard to achieve at the time because many of those in Congress belonged to right-wing and center-right parties that initially opposed the change.
In February 2025, Hilton got 234 members of Congress to sign on to the constitutional amendment proposal, well over the third needed, allowing her to bring the amendment up for formal debate in Congress. The initial proposal also proved to be quite ambitious, calling for a thirty-six-hour workweek spread over four days without any cut to pay, which would have transformed Brazil’s labor regulations into some of the most progressive in Latin America.
The thirty-six-hour workweek met opposition from sectors on the center and Right who chose to side with capital and oppose it. Azevedo’s VAT movement and the Brazilian labor movement mobilized around the demand on May 1, and President Lula made the end of the 6 x 1 work schedule a centerpiece in his May Day address in 2025.
Lula stated that this change was necessary to build a balance between workers’ professional lives and their well-being. But despite the pressure, the legislation sat in Congress for the rest of 2025. In April 2026, the president sent his own proposal to Congress to keep the issue in the media cycle and continue putting pressure on the lower chamber.
The End of 6 x 1
The combination of pressure from above and below worked, and in May the proposal finally passed the lower chamber and moved to the Senate. By this point, the reform had been modified so that it would establish a forty-hour workweek with two days off instead of the four-day workweek Hilton had initially proposed.
The timing now meant that labor reform would be a key part of the national debate in Brazil’s presidential election. The right-wing candidate Flávio Bolsonaro was a sitting senator at the time, and he felt obliged to support the proposed constitutional change for fear of losing working-class voters. This essentially meant conceding that the Right had been wrong to oppose the labor reform.
After the first round of elections on October 4, it seemed that Bolsonaro’s compromise might have sufficed to shore up support for his candidacy, as he topped the polls and his far-right Liberal Party made significant gains in both houses of Congress. However, Rick Azevedo was elected to Congress on the same night, and Erika Hilton became the female deputy with the highest number of votes in Brazilian history: 1,596,472. This demonstrated how the fight for a shorter workweek connected with diverse sectors of the Brazilian electorate.
On October 14, a week after the first round of the election, the Brazilian Senate voted 75–1 to end the forty-four-hour workweek. This promised a change to the lives of sixteen million Brazilians who previously had only one day off a week. Although the legislation that eventually passed was less ambitious than Hilton’s original proposal, it still lowered the work week to forty hours with two days off. This promises to empower millions of workers by making Brazil into one of the few countries in Latin America, a region where businesses are notorious for exploiting workers, to have a forty-hour week.
Winning the Culture Wars
The debate around the forty-hour week became a key space for Lula’s campaign to regain momentum after it initially fell behind Bolsonaro in the first round, shifting the focus to what was at stake for the Brazilian working class and the possibility of future reforms. The issue forced the Right to concede that Lula and his coalition had the best interests of workers at heart.
The debate also revealed the hypocrisy of the Right’s homophobic and transphobic rhetoric around the family, with a gay man and a trans woman leading the fight for working-class families to be able to spend more time together, get an education, and watch their children grow. Now, as Lula enters his fourth (and surely final) term, the global left should watch closely to learn how to take back the narrative from the Right and connect working-class interests with the diverse forms of oppression that workers face.

https://gothamist.com/news/trump-adminis.title: Trump administration sends election monitors to NYC, NJ
https://gothamist.com/news/trump-adminis.author: Catalina Gonella
https://gothamist.com/news/trump-adminis.text:
The United States Department of Justice said Tuesday it’s sending election monitors to polling sites in Manhattan and Brooklyn in New York, and three counties in New Jersey.
It’s the first time the DOJ is sending election monitors to all 50 states, according to the federal agency. The Trump administration has previously said it planned to deploy about 1,000 monitors nationwide, but hadn’t announced specific locations.
The DOJ said election monitors would be in Manhattan and Brooklyn as well as Westchester, Albany and Erie counties in New York. In New Jersey, they’ll be monitoring polls at Middlesex, Bergen and Union counties. Portions of Union County are in the 7th Congressional District, where Republican Tom Kean Jr. is hoping to fend off a challenge from Rebecca Bennett. The race is considered among the most competitive in the country as Democrats try to take control of the House.
Local Democratic leaders, including New York Attorney General Letitia James, have issued statements in recent weeks, urging voters not to be intimidated by federal authorities near the polls and warning that election interference and voter intimidation are illegal.
James said in a statement last week that while it is normal for the DOJ to send election monitors to polling sites, they can't demand identification from voters, interfere with poll workers or engage in political activity near the polls. She said if poll workers encounter people identifying as DOJ monitors without advance notice, they should contact county election officials.
The DOJ said the monitors would include workers from its Civil Rights Division, U.S. Attorney’s Offices and Office of Personnel Management observers.
New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill said during last week’s installment of WNYC’s “Ask Governor Sherrill” call-in show that state officials have been working to ensure those running elections throughout the state know how to protect voters’ rights.
“We have been briefing all of the poll workers, all the municipalities and the counties to make sure that they understand all their rights and that they are alerting us,” she said. “If there are any concerns at their polling place, we will be in court very, very quickly to shut down any attempt to interfere with our elections.”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: An expert’s guide to Pierre-Auguste Renoir: five must-read books on the French Impressionist
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: José da Silva
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
• Click here for more reading lists on the world's greatest artists
The French Impressionist Pierre-Auguste Renoir is a surprisingly divisive artist, from some of his peers denigrating him to the so-called Renoir Sucks at Painting movement a decade ago and a critic recently labelling him “the chocolate boxiest” of the Impressionists. But the recently opened exhibition Renoir and Love at the National Gallery in London (which debuted at the Musée d’Orsay in Paris earlier this year and will travel to Boston in 2027) has had—for the most part—rave reviews and robust ticket sales. Its co-curator Christopher Riopelle, who is also the author of Renoir: The Great Bathers (1990), has selected five key books for anyone wanting to go beyond first impressions.
Renoir, My Father (1962) by Jean Renoir
“Father and son, both artistic geniuses—a rare combination. That the great cineaste Jean Renoir should have penned an idiosyncratic, anecdote-filled life of the father is more than we deserve. Moreover, it is a film-maker’s biography, countless scenes set up visually, in flowing time. No surprise to learn that the loving son wrote it in far-off Hollywood!”
Renoir’s Portraits: Impressions of an Age (1997) by Colin B. Bailey
“Colin B. Bailey is our leading Renoir scholar. It is invidious to choose which of his several publications to include; I settle on this study of 69 portraits. Bulging with new information, it is every bit as indispensable to social historians as to art historians. As Renoir studies resurge, let us hope it returns to print.”
Renoir in the 20th Century (2010) with essays by Roger Benjamin, Claudia Einecke, Guy Cogeval, Isabelle Gaëtan, Emmanuelle Héran, John House, Virgine Journiac, Martha Lucy, Laurence Madeline, Monique Nonne and Sylvie Patry
“Late Renoir: Marmite. But the period includes among its admirers Henri Matisse, Pablo Picasso and the collector Albert C. Barnes. Sylvie Patry guides us through the final two decades with concision, deep respect and an unfailing eye for bravura painting. More than that, she demonstrates why the allusive Classicism of the late works played a key role in Modernism.”
Renoir in the Barnes Foundation (2012) by Martha Lucy and John House
“The Renoir scholar John House wrote this assessment of the largest and greatest of all Renoir collections with a passionate and utterly engaged eye. Martha Lucy was with him all the way; it’s as if we eavesdrop on a wickedly clever conversation between receptive student and brilliant, probing master.”
Auguste Renoir: Lettres choisies (2026), edited by Augustin de Butler and Anne Distel
“At last, a meticulous scholarly edition of 314 key Renoir letters tracing his career from 1865 to 1919. Helped in shaping by the consummate Renoir scholar Anne Distel, finally we can ‘hear’ the master’s voice. The wit is clear but so, too, the anxiety. Let us have a translation soon, to stand beside the newly translated Claude Monet letters.”
• Renoir and Love, National Gallery, London, until 31 January 2027; Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, 28 February 2027-13 June 2027

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/mckinney-det.title: Another Detroit Socialist Is Heading to Congress
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/mckinney-det.author: Donavan McKinney, Sara Wexler
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/mckinney-det.text:
Another Detroit Socialist Is Heading to Congress
Donavan McKinney, a Democratic Socialists of America–endorsed candidate for the US House in Detroit, is set to win his general election today. Jacobin spoke to him before Election Day about why he’s running and what he hopes to accomplish in office.
- Interview by
- Sara Wexler
In 2018, the election of two democratic socialists to the House of Representatives marked the beginning of a new political era. The socialist freshmen, both endorsed by the recently reinvigorated Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), were Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez from New York City and Rashida Tlaib, representing Michigan’s Twelfth Congressional District in Detroit.
Eight years later, DSA boasts more than 120,000 members and politicians in elected offices across the country. And after a wave of Democratic primary victories earlier this year, democratic socialists are set to significantly grow their foothold in Congress in today’s general election.
Among the likely socialist victors is Donavan McKinney, who is expected to win easily in Michigan’s deep-blue Thirteenth District in Detroit and join Tlaib in representing the Motor City in the House. Jacobin spoke to him about why he’s running and how growing up working class in Detroit shaped his politics.
- Sara Wexler Why are you running for Congress?
- Donavan McKinney I’m running to bring the urgency that this moment demands. Right now, I represent the poorest state house district in Michigan: $14,000 is the median income. If you divide that up by twelve months, that’s a little over $1,200 a month. And the average rents in our neighborhoods, if you’re lucky, start at $1,300. So that’s all your money down the drain, and you’ve got to worry about the increase in the price of gas and groceries, and insurance costs, whether it’s health insurance or auto insurance. We have some of the highest auto insurance rates in the country. Then childcare costs as well and so many day-to-day expenses. I’m running to represent one of the five poorest congressional districts in the country. What I’m going through on the state level is the same thing. [Being in Congress will mean representing] bigger communities, a lot more people. However, it’s the same narrative — the same story: “I just don’t have enough resources to make ends meet.” So for me, this is about meeting the moment, getting people in these positions who are going to put working families first and put our district first.
- Sara Wexler Can you tell me about your campaign platform? What priorities are you running on?
- Donavan McKinney Universal childcare, Medicare for All, and getting big corporate money out of politics. First, I talk about universal childcare a lot as a state legislator. I coled the movement for Pre-K for all. We have pretty much universal pre-K in Michigan now because of our advocacy and the advocacy of many others. We want to expand that to childcare across the board; we’ll take the fight to Washington, DC, for universal childcare. For my wife and I, that’s the biggest expense in our day-to-day lives, because we have three beautiful children — two boys, four and two, and a baby girl who just turned one. We pay more for childcare for one of our children than we do for our whole mortgage. And you’ve got to think about how impoverished my district is. If we’re living paycheck to paycheck off of childcare alone, I don’t know how everybody else is getting through it. Second, Medicare for All: I’m a big believer because of my mom and what she had to go through. When I was an undergrad at the University of Michigan, I got a call from my mom panicking because she was rushed to the hospital emergency room and they had to do emergency brain surgery. She comes to find out that she had brain tumors growing. And at the time, the only way she could get health care was through her employer; she was working at the time, but her employer didn’t offer it. So she was uninsured. And they did the emergency surgery, but guess what? She got that big six-figure bill for that procedure, and she didn’t have any way to pay it. They put her on a payment plan, but I had to go work three jobs at the time while I was a full-time student to make sure that she got the care she needed. By the grace of God, the Affordable Care Act (ACA) kicked in not too long after that, and she was able to afford health care. But I’m a big believer in Medicare for All, because she had preexisting conditions. Whether you have a preexisting condition or not, you deserve health care. That’s why I’m a big proponent of Medicare for All. There [are so many problems] when it comes to ACA premiums, as well as my seniors on fixed incomes, rubbing pennies together to try to figure out if they should have food on their table for the day or pay more out of pocket for their doctor’s visits and skyrocketing costs when it comes to lifesaving prescription drugs. The third thing I talked about is getting money out of politics. I’ve led that initiative here at the state level. I’ve introduced that legislation two times since I’ve been in office, in back-to-back terms. Each term, we got more and more people. I think the first term we had fewer than ten people sign on. This time around, when we introduced it last year in the state legislature, I think we had thirty or forty people sign on. Now, if you look at every Democrat who’s running for state legislative office here in Michigan, they signed on to the Michiganders for Money Out of Politics initiative. We couldn’t get a hearing in the state house. So organizations and people on the ground decided to take back our power over legislation and create a ballot initiative. They collected six hundred thousand signatures across the state, and that initiative will be on the November 3 ballot. I’m excited about it, because it targets monopoly utility companies, our public utilities, as well as our insurance companies — health insurance companies and auto insurance — which give a lot of money to state legislators to really bend the needle toward them instead of working people. I’m looking to do the same thing federally, to sign onto the legislation of Congresswoman Summer Lee and Senator Bernie Sanders, which gets rid of all that dark super PAC money, as well as to overturn Citizens United. Those are my big three pillars.
- Sara Wexler You grew up working class in Detroit. Can you tell me a bit about your background and how that shaped your politics?
- Donavan McKinney I was born and grew up in Detroit, raised with my mom, my grandmother, and my younger brother. We moved thirteen times across the city; I spent the vast majority of my life in northeast Detroit, which I now represent in the state legislature. And if the general election goes well, I’ll be representing it in the halls of Congress. Like I said, we moved thirteen times. We stayed in cars, shelters, sometimes out in the street. We didn’t know where our next meal was going to come from, but there was no shortage of love and prayers that got us through those tough times. I remember what my grandmother told me growing up. She told me two things that I still live by today. Number one is count your blessings, because you woke up this morning when a lot of people didn’t. You have a roof over your head, clothes on your back, food on your table, and — we live in Detroit, the Motor City — a car to drive. Because our transit system isn’t that good yet, but we’re working on it; that’s something we’re going to take to DC to work on. But you’re able-bodied, you’ve got your mental health, you’ve got your faculties, things we take for granted day in and day out. Number two, she always used to say, “In life, there will always be people better off than you. There will always be people worse off than you, but never fight the urge to give.” And I put that quote on my first piece of literature when I first ran for state representative ten years ago, back in 2016 when I was just a bushy-tailed kid coming out of college, just trying to figure out life. I still live by those two principles today — they’re my North Star. That’s why I’m so passionate about working people and about the service, because that’s what’s forgotten in politics. [I like to say], politics is about the service of the people and bringing humanity and love and leading with your heart back into the politics, which [currently] is so divisive. There’s a lot of hatred, a lot of negativity, and we try to lead with love.
- Sara Wexler It seems like when you were growing up, people’s needs weren’t being met, and the affordability crisis was worsening, regardless of whether Democrats or Republicans were in power. What do you make of this?
- Donavan McKinney A lot of people I’ve talked to view the Democrats and the Republicans very similarly when it comes to economics. I do believe that the Democratic Party is the party of the people. I have seen the Democrats do a lot more than the Republicans in terms of [helping the] working class. But I’m a big believer in the Scripture. Scripture talks about how you can’t serve two masters. What is happening, especially now, is that the Dems are serving the corporate oligarchs, same as the Republicans. You’re either going to have to do what’s best and serve the interests of working people, or you’re going to serve the interests of just a few and increase the wealth of those who are taking advantage of regular working people. For me, we follow what we preach. That’s what people want to see. They want to see receipts. So look at our campaign: we ran a campaign that was people powered. We didn’t take a cent of corporate PAC money or AIPAC [American Israel Public Affairs Committee] money. A lot of our money came from individual people across our district, across our state, across our country, who believe in a different style of politics. Leading up to the primary, our average donation on ActBlue was around $30 or $32, something like that — tens of thousands of people just donating to a vision. I’m forever grateful for it, because we were outspent. My opponent [in the primary], the current congressman, had his own wealth. He made his money off of pharmaceuticals, and so he had his own money to put in. But he also took money from ICE [Immigration and Customs Enforcement] contractors and AIPAC as well as other corporate PACs, crypto, all of that — DTE, our monopoly utility — and just lying on our name, putting a lot of ads out. I’m very grateful, by the grace of God, that people were really waking up and realizing, “You know what? Donovan is better for the job.” We’re bringing a message that resonates with people and brings folks together.
- Sara Wexler Before running for office, you worked for Service Employees International Union (SEIU) Healthcare Michigan, which is the state’s largest health care union. How has your experience with labor organizing informed your politics?
- Donavan McKinney I tell this story a lot about my grandfather. My grandfather passed away late last year during the campaign cycle. I’m trying to not be emotional, because the man taught me a lot. When I was a kid, he used to bring me to the union meetings a lot. He worked at Ford Motor Company in the Detroit metro region and was part of the United Auto Workers (UAW) for forty-two years. One of the most interesting things about my grandfather is that during those forty-two years, he never missed a day of work. I asked him at his retirement party some years ago, “Granddad, how did you do it?” He told me one thing that stood out, which was that he took pride in what he was doing. He knew that, with his bare hands, he was helping change a life or a family’s life. But more important, he knew that not only the union had his back, but that Ford Motor Company had his back. But fast-forward to the year 2026, that work that he had and that salary that he made — that dollar isn’t stretching as far. And these corporations have gotten greedier. Take, for instance, what happened at the Poletown plant in my district, which is on the border of Detroit and Hamtramck. It’s a General Motors factory plant. It’s nicknamed “Factory Zero.” It was the first factory in America, and the first factory in America to be net zero. It was really green, really environmentally friendly and forward-thinking around that. Earlier this year, they cut over a thousand jobs, all union jobs. They cut everybody’s jobs, and then, just a few months later, replaced them with robots. I talk about it in the union halls a lot; I talk about how much it’s bullsh–t and how, at the end of the day, nobody has our back but working people ourselves. We need to start electing folks with the right type of mindset and, more importantly, with the lived experience that [leads them to prioritize working people] over these greedy corporations.
- Sara Wexler That leads nicely into my next question. You’re running as a democratic socialist. What does that mean to you?
- Donavan McKinney I define politics as the redistribution of resources. That’s it; it’s black and white. If you’re in these positions of power and influence, if you’re not trying to figure out ways to bring home as many resources as possible back to your communities and the people you represent, then I need you to get up out of here. That’s what led me to run for Congress in the first place, because I felt like our current congressman wasn’t meeting the moment. We’re going to be able to pick up the phone and do constituent service work, because I understand what it’s like being on the phone trying to get somebody to answer to help when you’re in dire need. My current congressman is known for not picking up the phone, not doing the real constituent work of the job. Half the battle is showing up. The other half is trying to figure out resources to improve the quality of life of the people you represent. So in terms of democratic socialism, I’m a big believer in Dr Martin Luther King’s teachings. And Tupac [Shakur] said it best: “They got money for wars but can’t feed the poor.” You’re telling me we’re spending money for a war that nobody wants — a billion dollars a day in Iran. And you’re also telling me that, with H.R. 1 [the One Big Beautiful Bill Act], the Republican trifecta cut health care and food assistance for the most vulnerable populations across our country. And I thought Republicans didn’t believe in red tape: I thought they believed in slim government and lean government and achieving efficiency in government. But they want to hurt people in order to give a tax break to the wealthiest top 1-percent earners of our country. They’re telling people, “We want you to get recertified every six months for your health care. But we DOGEd government, and we know that you’re not going to get recertified in time because we don’t have the caseworkers to certify you in the right amount of time. Because of the savings we’re going to have on the back end from folks not being able to recertify, we’re going to give a tax break to the ultrawealthy.” That’s not the America I want to live in; that’s not the America people in my community want to live in, or anyone who I know wants to live in. It’s up to us Democrats to level the playing field and right the ship, so to speak. I’m going to push hard as hell and advocate for the poor folks in my communities. A lot of my community is struggling and they’re looking for somebody that’s going to fight for them, and that’s my job.
- Sara Wexler As you mentioned, you were able to oust the incumbent Democrat in your primary. I’m wondering what role different organizations, DSA for instance, have played in your campaign.
- Donavan McKinney I was quoted earlier in the campaign, and I said, “We’re building the biggest and baddest coalition in the country,” which is true. I’ve even had members of Congress call me because they’re like, “Yo, how did you do this?” We have some of the most established folks and even the most conservative Democrats endorsing our campaign, as well as all-the-way-to-the-left DSA types endorsing our campaign. I don’t know if it was just because of me or also because of how bad the incumbent was, but it’s because we’re speaking values. We’re leading with our heart, and we’re following what we’re preaching. We brought together faith leaders, elected officials from the federal, state, county, and local levels, community block club leaders, and unions. I was told I was the only nonincumbent the AFL-CIO endorsed on the federal level when it came to the Democratic primary. So we had the unions; we had groups like Justice Democrats and DSA and so many other great folks coming together and realizing that we deserve better. That was our campaign message: We deserve better. I’m so grateful because I couldn’t have done it without this coalition. I couldn’t have done it without people coming together and realizing that their voices matter and that they have the power to make a difference in our politics and change the trajectory of our country. We’re going to continue that movement as we get sworn in in January. It’s the inside-outside strategy that Dr King talked about. You need people on the outside agitating, advocating, but you also need people on the inside who are willing to listen, willing to really put those words to paper and move legislation very swiftly in this moment, with the urgency that it demands.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Italy set to create restitution panel for Nazi-looted art
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: James Imam
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Italy’s parliament is considering legislation that would, for the first time, establish a formal process for restituting art and cultural property seized by the Nazis and Italian authorities from victims of racial persecution during the Holocaust era.
Introduced by a lawmaker from Brothers of Italy, the party led by the country’s prime minister Giorgia Meloni, the proposal has been hailed by as “an act of civilisation” by representatives of heirs of those whose property was stolen, and would bring Italy in line with Germany, Austria, France, the Netherlands, the UK and Switzerland, the latest European country to establish its own restitution mechanisms.
The bill grants the government powers to establish a five-member committee to examine the provenance of works that were confiscated, looted or sold under duress as a result of racial persecution between 1933 and 1945. The committee would assess individual cases and issue decisions on restitution to the original owners, their heirs or—if no living heirs are identified—the broader Jewish community in Italy.
If enacted, the bill, which is currently being examined by the lower house’s culture committee, would give the government six months to establish the restitution system.
“Introducing this bill does not merely mean finally bringing Italy into line with the highest international standards... but means, first and foremost, fulfilling a historic duty,” Federico Mollicone, a key Meloni ally who introduced the bill in March, tells The Art Newspaper.
“We are not merely talking about property claims, but about restoring human dignity, memory and the fundamental principles of our constitution,” says Mollicone, who is the president of the culture commission in Italy’s lower house of parliament.
Seized works in state museums
State-sponsored looting, confiscation and forced sale of Jewish-owned art and cultural heritage became increasingly commonplace following the fascist dictator Benito Mussolini’s 1938 introduction of racial laws that prohibited Jewish books, excluded Jews from public office and introduced limits on Jewish property ownership. The dispossessions increased from 1943, when Italian and occupying German Nazi forces began arresting and deporting Jews to concentration camps.
Some of the seized works subsequently entered the collections of Italian museums, where four publicly known disputed works are currently displayed, according to Katharina Hüls-Valenti, an expert in provenance research at Parma University. They include Edouard Manet’s Portrait de M. Arnaud à cheval (1875), which Hüls-Valenti says was sold under duress in 1935 by its owners, the family of German painter Max Liebermann, and donated to the Galleria d’Arte Moderna in Milan in 1958. Hüls-Valenti says that Liebermann’s heirs had sought restitution but had encountered resistance from the museum.
Asked to respond to those allegations, Paola Zatti, a curator at the Galleria d’Arte Moderna, said in a statement to The Art Newspaper: “The painting was sold by Liebermann’s wife in 1935 (incidentally, to a Jewish antiques dealer), but there is no evidence that she was forced to do so.”
Zatti added that, in accord with a lawyer representing Liebermann’s heirs in Germany, the museum had agreed to display a label explaining the work’s ownership history. The text, Zatti said, “clearly highlights the tragic moment when the work was sold by its Jewish owners” and helps visitors appreciate the “circumstances under which [the work] left Germany”.
Another painting, Cristo portacroce (around 1508-09) by Girolamo da Romano, was requisitioned by France’s pro-Nazi Vichy government in 1941 from the family of Federico Gentili di Giuseppe, an Italian Jewish businessman and art collector living in Paris. It was auctioned to a private collector and then bought by Milan’s Pinacoteca di Brera museum in 1998. Following a request by the heirs, US authorities seized the work while it was on loan to a Florida museum in 2011.
The real number of Holocaust-era seizures currently held by museums, Hüls-Valenti suggests, could be closer to dozens. “We really don’t know for sure,” she says. “Better research is required.”
Italy endorsed the 1998 Washington Principles, which established guidelines for the restitution of Nazi-looted art. A 2001 enquiry led by Tina Anselmi, a former Italian government minister, found evidence of systematic expropriation from Jews. It found evidence of 7,847 seizure warrants issued up to April 1945 for property including houses and land, businesses, bank deposits, insurance policies, jewellery, paintings and furniture.
Despite the report’s findings, Italy, a global leader in securing the restitution of its own national heritage, has been slower than other European countries to seek justice for dispossessed Jews. France created a commission for restitutions and compensation in 1999. The UK established the Spoliation Advisory Panel in 2000 to evaluate claims to works held by British national institutions.
Delay due to several factors
“Italy is obviously a central country in the world of art... and yet on this issue of the Holocaust restitution it had barely scratched the surface in addressing it,” says Gideon Taylor, the president of World Jewish Restitution Organisation (WJRO).
Experts point to various reasons for the delay in Italy’s response, including a national reluctance to confront the country’s fascist past, insufficient political will to prioritise the restitution of Jewish-owned cultural heritage, and a lack of transparency about provenance in museums. They say poor cataloguing has contributed to an assumption that few works would be affected by a law.
Complicating matters, Italian law recognises works held in Italian museums as inalienable parts of the national heritage. The bill addresses this hurdle by indicating that the final restitution decision would automatically remove the work from the public domain. Further, restituted works would no longer be subject to the protections of Italy’s heritage code, meaning they could permanently leave the country. The bill also indicates that existing statutes of limitations would not prevent restitutions.
The commission would accept claims from legitimate owners, their descendants or heirs, and the Union of Italian Jewish Communities (UCEI) or individual Jewish communities. It would include a member nominated by Italy’s art police and have to rule within 180 days of a claim. The bill is intended to help heirs seeking restitution from both public and private collections.
Italy’s parliament adopted the bill following the submission of a report evaluating the country’s restitutions record commissioned by the WJRO and written by the lawyer Lorenzo Casini, a former chief of staff at the culture ministry who now heads a public research institution in Lucca. It was written with the support of six leading experts, including Hüls-Valenti, the Parma professor.
“Museums don’t necessarily hide their works, but there isn’t full understanding of just how important transparency is and how helpful it would be for all these works to come to light,” Casini says. “Besides addressing the tragic wounds left by looting and filling the legislative gap in Italy, the law is specifically designed to bring those artworks to light.”
Speaking to parliament’s culture commission in June, Casini praised the bill but suggested areas for improvement, proposing widening the commission’s remit from art to other cultural heritage—including manuscripts, books, archives and ceremonial objects—and advising that the commission and researchers would require additional funds to carry out their work.
“The next step could hopefully be to seek funding once the law has been passed,” Casini tells The Art Newspaper.
Federico Mollicone says lawmakers will “ensure” the culture ministry’s upcoming funding plans include “adequate resources to support research projects on provenance, the digitisation of archives, and the training of dedicated experts”. He highlights culture minister Alessandro Giuli’s “strong commitment to this issue”.
He also predicts the bill will have a smooth passage into law, noting that there is “wide political consensus” on redressing injustices from racial persecution. Brothers of Italy has roots in the post-fascist parties that rose from the ashes of the Second World War.
“Our goal is to complete the parliamentary review and pass the bill in the coming months,” Mollicone says. “We want to bring this historic reform to a successful conclusion within this legislative session.” A general election is due to take place before the end of next year, with analysts suggesting it may be brought forward to the spring.
Paolo Gnignati, UCEI’s head of legal affairs, says the bill’s arrival in parliament is significant. “The regulations on restitution are something that can be meaningful to specific individuals because they have financial and personal implications,” he says. “But they are also, fundamentally, an act of civilisation.”

https://gothamist.com/news/floyd-bennet-.title: Floyd Bennett Field gets $10M for project to reopen historic hangars
https://gothamist.com/news/floyd-bennet-.author: Rosemary Misdary
https://gothamist.com/news/floyd-bennet-.text:
The historic hangars at Floyd Bennett Field are getting closer to reopening to the public for the first time in nearly a century.
Gov. Kathy Hochul committed $10 million in funding on Monday for the first phase of a two-part plan to transform the shuttered hangars at New York City’s first commercial airport into a public space that can host educational programming as well as cultural events.
The redevelopment will reopen hangars 3 and 4 to the public for the first time in nearly a century.
“These haven't been open to the public in nearly a century,” said Anastasia Yankopoulos, director of development and capital projects at Jamaica Bay Rockaway Parks Conservancy.
“People being able to step on the same ground where famous aviators of the golden era were, like, fixing their planes, that’s the biggest excitement.”
The first phase of construction on hangars 3 and 4 includes building renewable energy sources onsite, the conservancy said. The plan includes solar power on the roof and geothermal energy in the lawn in front of the buildings. The structures will also get bathrooms and other upgrades for use as a large events space such as concerts.
The conservancy plans to break ground in early 2028, after the National Park Service finishes improvements to the building exteriors. The total time of construction is estimated to span one year for the first phase. The conservancy is fundraising for the project.
“This money from the governor was such a huge boost to get this project to where it needs to be,” said Elizabeth Stoehr, deputy director of the Jamaica Bay Rockaway Parks Conservancy.
The second phase, which could begin shortly after, would further build out the space with an observation terrace and an area for purchasing food and beverages. Hangar 3 is slated to support park activities such as kayaking and biking.
Hangar 4 will host research projects with the Science and Resilience Center of Jamaica Bay, which is restoring West Pond. The structure will house labs, classrooms, meeting rooms and a workshop. In total, the redevelopment will add approximately 50,000 square feet for public use.
“The very fabric of the building, the very bricks, the very concrete were sentinels of this incredible aviation history and this idea that real innovation happened there,” Stoehr said. “It is thrilling that we get to work in this space that has such historical significance.”
In their present condition, hangars 3 and 4 are not accessible to the public or acceptable for use. Since the airfield was decommissioned, the hangars have not had much usage.
“The hangars have never been appropriately programmed and used to their full potential,” Yankopoulos said.
Floyd Bennett Field is a defunct airport in the Marine Park section of southeast Brooklyn, located on Jamaica Bay. The airstrip was opened in 1931 after roughly three years of construction and a cost of approximately $4.5 million. In 1933, Floyd Bennett Field had more than double the flights of Newark Airport, and was the second-busiest airport in America.
During World War II, the airfield became a naval base until 1970. The Coast Guard continued to use the facility for its helicopters until 1998.
In 1974, the airstrip reopened as part of Gateway National Recreation Area and managed by the National Park Service. While the flights no longer take off from the airfield, the New York City Police Department uses the runways as a helicopter base and another runway is reserved for radio-controlled craft enthusiasts. The current facility also has a campground and hosts astronomy events.
The surviving original structures are listed in the National Register of Historic Places. According to the National Park Service, many famous aviators and historic flights took-off from Floyd Bennett Field, including Amelia Earhart, John Glenn and Howard Hughes.
The airport is named after Floyd Bennett, a navy pilot who was the first to fly over the North Pole. Bennett died at the age of 37 from pneumonia shortly after a mission to rescue a stranded crew during World War I.
This story has been updated to correct the spelling of Floyd Bennett.

https://citylimits.org/opinion-washingto.title: Opinion: Washington is Making It Harder for People Like My Grandparents to Keep Their Health Insurance. I Won’t Let That Happen.
https://citylimits.org/opinion-washingto.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/opinion-washingto.text:
Share This Article
“As the federal government abandons the people it is meant to serve, New York City is leaning in to protect public goods like health coverage.”
A few years ago, I was working in a doctor’s office scheduling colonoscopies and endoscopies—screenings that can detect cancer early, when it is most treatable. Each appointment I booked felt like a small act of prevention against a disease that has claimed the lives of so many.
One day the doctor stepped into our office with new instructions: Stop scheduling appointments for patients insured through Medicaid. The reimbursement process was too slow and cumbersome, he said. It simply wasn’t worth the hassle.
The room went quiet. We were handed a list of Medicaid-allied insurance carriers we were to no longer accept. As I scanned the list, my heart dropped. On it was the plan that covered my grandparents.
If my own grandparents called to book a cancer screening, I was expected to turn them away.
After that, I was determined to do something that would serve everyone in my community, not just those who can afford it. I wanted to help others who, like my grandparents, have been abandoned by our broken healthcare system.
Problems like this inspired me to work at the New York City Health Department. I’ve joined a new team of highly trained community health workers with a mission to help all New Yorkers access health insurance and other services they deserve. The new Health and Affordability Resource Team, or HART for short, is designed to protect struggling New Yorkers at risk of falling through the ever-widening holes in our country’s social safety net.
Created by the Health Department together with Mayor Zohran Mamdani, HART deploys dozens of community health workers like me into the neighborhoods where we’re needed most, and where many of us are from. 
Through neighborhood outreach in 13 languages, we accompany people through each step of the process, from screening and applications to enrollment and follow-ups. Our primary goal is connecting people to health coverage and other essential benefits, housing stability and eviction prevention resources, and financial assistance for hospital bills.
We’re specially trained to help New Yorkers navigate the latest federal cuts to Medicaid and SNAP, including expanded work requirements and red tape that put as many as 900,000 New Yorkers at risk. These are people who could lose their health insurance—not because they don’t qualify, but because the federal government has made keeping it prohibitively complicated and confusing.
We’re not going to stand for that. Because as the federal government abandons the people it is meant to serve, New York City is leaning in to protect public goods like health coverage.
Years after leaving my job at the cancer screening clinic, it hit me: this wasn’t a one-time decision or one bad provider. It was an entrenched, systemic problem. The cards have been stacked against so many New Yorkers who deserve the care they are being denied.
People are sorted not by their medical need, but by how quickly and conveniently a payment arrives. And the patients who can least afford to miss a cancer screening are the ones being quietly refused. Many will never know why.
That day in the doctor’s office, I could have looked away. I had a steady job and the decision wasn’t up to me. But once you see people losing critical health care like that, you carry it with you.
I left that job and went back to school, this time for public health. I wanted to understand not just how a system fails people, but how it can be redesigned so that it improves people’s lives at scale. I am continuing my studies to receive a master’s in public health, learning about program design and evaluation.
As I’ve studied, I continued working alongside New Yorkers. I held a case management role supporting people with disabilities who needed home health aides. That work taught me what the paperwork could not: Navigating benefits and approvals is exhausting for anyone, and for people already managing a disability or a chronic illness, it can be overwhelming. I have sat with clients as they navigated hurdles that never should have been there.
Today with the Health Department, I’m building on what I’ve learned in classrooms and through my lived experience to help others understand and navigate the barriers in their lives.
As part of the Health and Affordability Resource Team, I get to take meaningful action every day to make life better for my fellow New Yorkers. And now, if my grandparents were to call, there are many ways I can assist them, too.
Jasmine Taylor is a community health worker on the Health and Affordability Resource Team at the NYC Health Department.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/midterms-def.title: Trumpism Is Running Out of Gas
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/midterms-def.author: Luke Savage
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/midterms-def.text:
Trumpism Is Running Out of Gas
A look at the polls and Donald Trump’s rhetoric on the midterms campaign trail suggests that MAGA may be exhausted and about to suffer a significant body blow.
I have no special insight into what the exact outcome of this yearʼs midterm elections is going to be. It would be absolutely astonishing if Democrats failed to take the House, and the latest NY/Sienna poll has the Democrats leading in all seven of the races that will determine control of the Senate. This includes nonnegligible edges in both Texas and Kansas, the latter of which hasnʼt elected a Democratic senator since the early 1930s.
In Michigan, which has been getting a great deal of attention for obvious reasons, Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed boasts a double digit lead, and several key gubernatorial races look to be leaning the same way. Donald Trumpʼs approval rating, meanwhile, is catastrophically low and has been dropping steadily. If Democrats donʼt make considerable gains across the board tonight, it will mean major polling companies got things badly wrong.
For other reasons that are less strictly related to polling, however, it has increasingly seemed to me that Trumpism is out of gas and may soon be on its last legs.
To reiterate something that cannot be repeated enough: Trump has never been particularly popular. So it was wrongheaded for shocked liberal commentators to throw up their hands and declare the country lost, both in 2016 and 2024. In order to consolidate its hold on the countryʼs politics, the Trump project ultimately needed to mobilize a larger popular coalition — something it has consistently proven unable to do.
In his second term especially, in fact, Trump has often seemed indifferent to public opinion and has looked visibly unconcerned when it comes to selling the administrationʼs direction to voters. (I wrote about this back in April specifically in relation to the US-Israeli attack on Iran, though there are certainly other examples.)
Beyond all this, Iʼve been struck by the nature of Trumpʼs midterm campaigning itself.
CNN recently published an interesting piece in which various reporters reflect on Trump’s rallies theyʼve been attending. Hereʼs how the piece opens:
Ballrooms. Cognitive tests. The male physique. As President Donald Trump closes out the midterm election season with a sprint through ruby red America, his message to voters has veered into some unexpected places. More than ever before, his stops have been remarkable because theyʼre about one thing: Trump himself. His message to voters is to pretend heʼs on the ballot, no matter how unpopular heʼs become. Concerns about the direction of the country, or the cost of living, are mostly shoved to the side.
Indeed, the substance of Trumpʼs speeches speaks to a political project that is increasingly exhausted and running on fumes.
When Trumpism has been politically strongest, its tenor has been insurgent, and it has at least tried to operate in some kind of populist register. It has successfully tapped into generalized anger toward the political class and rightly or wrongly (usually the latter) convinced at least some nontraditional GOP voters it will bring genuine heterodoxy to government. It has, albeit with deep incoherence, attacked the global trade consensus and hinted it will put an end to unpopular wars. It has promised jobs and reindustrialization. It has hit cost-of-living issues hard, even when engaging in more conventional right-wing messaging about immigration and culture war issues.
Trumpism has always been profoundly ugly. But here, again, it has found its greatest political success when able to democratize the ugliness somewhat. Its many appeals to racism and sexism have delivered politically when integrated into a larger narrative of hedonism — elect me and you, too, will have license to be nasty and say all the unsayable words again — and national renewal.
Here, for example, is an excerpt from Trumpʼs 2016 speech to the Republican National Convention:
America is a nation of believers, dreamers, and strivers that is being led by a group of censors, critics, and cynics. Remember: all of the people telling you that you canʼt have the country you want are the same people telling you that I wouldnʼt be standing here tonight. No longer can we rely on those elites in media, and politics, who will say anything to keep a rigged system in place. . . . My opponent asks her supporters to recite a three-word loyalty pledge. It reads: “Iʼm With Her.ˮ I choose to recite a different pledge. My pledge reads: “IʼM WITH YOU — THE AMERICAN PEOPLE.ˮ I am your voice.
The contrast between the above and how Trump has been speaking more recently is striking. The rank ugliness that has defined Trump-era conservatism from the beginning remains. Alongside the usual stand-up comedy, however, his midterm campaigning has also featured many moments like these, from the CNN piece:
The moment that stood out in Perry, Georgia, on October 24 was Trumpʼs assertion that the United States is “making hundreds and hundreds of billions, trillions of dollarsˮ in oil at a time when people are facing high prices at the pump. Appearing to recognize the disconnect, the president acknowledged his aides had advised him not to mention gas prices and oil. “My people said, ‘please donʼt mention that, sir!ʼˮ he said. Trump said the media would later report that “President Trump is talking about all the money we are making while people are suffering at the pump,ˮ in a kind of self-fulfilling prophecy. “I donʼt give a damn! Iʼm going to say it. Weʼre making a freaking fortune!ˮ he thundered.
At both stops on October 27, Trump dangled $5,000 checks for Americans if Republicans win control of the House and Senate. In Corpus Christi, he invited voters to spend their cash payment at Mar-a-Lago — before quipping they wouldnʼt be able to afford it. “You could even come to Mar-a-Lago,ˮ Trump said. “The problem is that for $5,000, the most youʼll be able to buy is a hamburger and maybe a small dessert. Iʼm not even sure you could buy that. No, donʼt go there. Thatʼs not a good place if youʼre price conscious.ˮ
Whatever he happens to be talking about — his war with Iran, the cost of living, his redecoration of the White House — Trumpʼs messaging, both on the campaign trail and off, has increasingly resembled the above. Thereʼs no hint of a populist undertone here. Thereʼs not even half-hearted attempt to sell the administrationʼs war with Iran nor any message about the cost of living beyond an emblematically cheeky assurance that everything is actually fine. When Trumpism has been most confident and politically robust, it has categorically not looked or sounded like this.
That, to say nothing of the polls, suggests to me that MAGA may really and truly be exhausted and about to suffer a significant body blow. Should that indeed happen, Trump may still be in a position to inflict plenty more harm — but will in all likelihood serve out the remainder of his time in office as a deeply unpopular and fatally compromised figure.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: New York Studio School revamp unearths long-forgotten murals
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Julie Belcove
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Back in 1907, Gertrude Vanderbilt Whitney established her sculpture studio in a converted stable and hayloft on MacDougal Alley in the heart of Manhattan’s Greenwich Village. The heiress and artist then proceeded to procure four neighbouring brownstones one by one, with the Lincoln Memorial sculptor Daniel Chester French being the last holdout.
The five buildings that now comprise 8 West 8th Street are some of the New York art world’s most storied. It was here that Whitney promoted US artists at a time when they were widely denigrated, and where she opened the Whitney Museum of American Art in 1931. After the museum relocated uptown, the nascent New York Studio School (NYSS) moved into the compound in 1967.
Over the past century Edward Hopper sketched, John Cage lectured and Philip Guston taught within these walls. Countless other greats practised, exhibited or, in the case of Marianne Faithfull, lived in what is now a National Historic Landmark. “This building has been the incubator for American art for 120 years,” says the artist Matthew Ritchie, sitting in a bare-bones conference room on a warm September afternoon. It has also been sorely in need of a makeover at least since he was a student here in the 1990s.
Leaks and hazards
When Ritchie was named the school’s director last year, the roof and studio skylights—coveted by students for their diffused natural light—leaked, the nearly century-old cloth-wrapped wiring had deteriorated dangerously and wheelchair access was extremely limited. His priority was renovation. The first phase—including doubling the public exhibition space and creating a new accessible lecture and performance hall in wood with stepped seating—is set to be completed this autumn, and phase two will begin in the spring.
Prior to Ritchie’s arrival, the school had obtained public grants for the necessary work, but they required matching funds and their expiration date was fast approaching. He quickly marshalled forces. The board agreed to donate the required money, he says, and the school tapped Matthew Baird of Baird Architects to helm the overhaul.
Ritchie and Baird’s history of collaboration dates back 17 years and across two other local institutions. In 2009, they teamed up to consider the effects of rising sea levels on the built environment as part of the interdisciplinary Rising Currents project at the Museum of Modern Art. Just a few years later, they put their theories into practice after Hurricane Sandy tore through the city, its storm surge flooding much of downtown. Ritchie was on the board of the beloved alternative art space The Kitchen when it enlisted Baird to rehabilitate its waterlogged lobby and black-box theatre.
The architect’s sensitive execution on that project—he preserved visual evidence of flood damage, for example—made him an obvious choice for the NYSS project, which presented a similar challenge. “You have this really cool building that’s got this patina of great artists that have moved through it,” Baird says. “How do you not erase that?”
Buried treasure
Thanks to Baird and Ritchie’s handle-with-care edict, the construction crew was on the lookout for treasures buried beneath layers of plasterboard. The artist Cecily Brown had told Ritchie that she painted her first mural on a school wall when she was a student in the 1990s but could not remember where. And the school archives held numerous photos of murals Whitney had commissioned from the artist Robert E. Locher for the original carriage house.
Sure enough, the crew uncovered the work of both artists within a 24-hour period. Brown’s piece—featuring disembodied penises, two of them appearing to kiss—is in the newly expanded gallery space on the main floor. To prevent it from potentially distracting from exhibitions, the design team installed a shallow cabinet in front of the mural.
Ritchie jokes that the set-up resembles a gabinetto segreto, or secret room, the most famous of which was a locked vault of erotic artefacts from Pompeii and Herculaneum. “Who doesn’t want a Cecily Brown mural? And then, who doesn’t want pornography in your brand-new public gallery?” he says with a laugh. “It’s the perfect combination.”
Workers discovered the two Locher murals where a bathroom and a hallway leading to it will be built. Intended to be viewed in the candlelight of Whitney’s dining room, one is a glimmering green, the other a trompe l’oeil image of doric columns. Baird tweaked the layout but not the location of the restroom. “Now it will be the most historic bathroom in New York,” Ritchie says.
A less fortuitous surprise: the beams beneath Robert Winthrop Chanler’s flame-motif fireplace in Whitney’s original second-floor studio were cracking, requiring emergency shoring up to stop the ceiling from collapse—together with the priceless fireplace. “This is the urgency of renovation,” Ritchie says. “You can wait too long, and then you lose it all.”
Super-tight deadlines
Because of the grant deadlines for the first phase of the project, Baird needed to work at warp speed, condensing three years of planning, permitting, bidding and execution into one. Owing to New York City’s complex building code, he approached the $2.2m renovation as “100 small projects” rather than gutting the 59,000 sq. ft building. The landmark-restoration specialist Jonathan Raible is overseeing the new roof.
In addition to enhancing the first floor’s public spaces, Baird rewired the building, renovated the wreck of a kitchen and improved accessibility by adding a wheelchair lift to the performance hall. “You can’t have a public programme if you don’t provide correct facilities for the public,” Ritchie says. “You’re not really welcoming them.”
Climbing the narrow staircases to the maze of studios where the school’s 27 full-time, in-person students work, Baird speaks enthusiastically about the second phase of renovations, which will include a student coffee bar. In keeping with his preservationist instincts, he plans to relamp with LED bulbs the elegant Fresnel recessed box lighting that Whitney installed for evenly washed walls, and he hopes to restore the system of baffles that modulated direct light in the studios as well as undertake other restoration while safeguarding the landmark’s character.
Ritchie already has his eye on another, likely longer-term fix for the school: free tuition. “That would require a very large endowment from extremely generous single or multiple donors,” he says, giving his best impression of a silver-tongued salesman, “which we’re eagerly awaiting with an entirely unique naming opportunity.”

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: Mamdani Administration Plans To Close 2 Small Harlem Schools, Move UWS School
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Alex Zimmerman, Chalkbeat
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
This story was originally published by Chalkbeat. Sign up for their newsletters at ckbe.at/newsletters.
Education officials are proposing to shutter two of New York City’s smallest schools, the first formal closure plans this academic year as Mayor Zohran Mamdani grapples with a growing number of underenrolled schools.
Two Harlem schools are on the chopping block: The Urban Assembly School for Global Commerce, a high school that serves 112 students, and School of Earth Exploration and Discovery Harlem, which serves just 40 children, making it the city’s smallest middle school. Both schools would close at the end of this school year.
Officials also plan to move The Center School, an Upper West Side school serving grades 5-8, to address overcrowding on a campus it shares with a popular elementary school. A plan to relocate the school to a different site last school year fell apart amid intense backlash.
All three Manhattan proposals are expected to come before the Panel for Educational Policy for a vote on Dec. 16.
The city is also gearing up to close a Bronx middle school, I.S. 224, Chalkbeat has learned, though the Education Department has not yet formally proposed it.
The Mamdani administration is facing growing pressure to close or consolidate schools as K-12 enrollment in the nation’s largest school district has plunged in the last 12 years by about 19%, or roughly 187,000 students. Declining headcounts have led to a glut of underenrolled schools that struggle to offer a full range of programs.
It remains to be seen whether these initial proposals represent the beginning of a larger push to merge or close underenrolled schools. Chancellor Kamar Samuels has indicated that addressing small campuses is top of mind and doing so could help reduce costs and expand academic offerings for students on campuses that are increasingly struggling to provide the basics.
“If a school is more underenrolled, it’s more likely not to offer the advanced classes that you need,” Samuels said earlier this year. “It may not offer the level of enrichment that you want to see.”
But Samuels has not shared a detailed roadmap for addressing the problem and has instead pointed to working groups in five of the city’s 32 local districts that are charged with coming up with community-driven plans on enrollment among a host of other issues.
Here’s what to know about the Education Department’s three proposals.
Closure Proposal: School of Earth Exploration and Discovery Harlem
City officials say SEED Harlem has gotten too small to be sustainable. Enrollment has plunged 68% since the 2022-23 school year, and it enrolled just six sixth graders this year.
It is also underperforming, with just 21% of students proficient in reading and in math, according to state tests, roughly half the average in District 5.
The school illustrates one of the central problems with tiny campuses: They are simultaneously expensive to operate and struggle to offer a full range of programs. SEED Harlem spent $93,000 per student last year, nearly four times the city average even as it has been forced to cancel partnerships with outside community organizations and scale back enrichment programs, officials said.
The school serves a vulnerable student population. Nearly all of the school’s students come from low-income families, and half have a disability. Just over half the school’s students are Black, and 44% are Latino.
Closure Proposal: The Urban Assembly School for Global Commerce
The proposed closure of Global Commerce, which Chalkbeat first reported last month, comes as the school has shed nearly a third of its students since the 2021-22 school year. It now enrolls 112 students.
Launched 13 years ago as part of former Mayor Michael Bloomberg’s push to open small themed high schools, the campus has been forced to end its career and technical education programs in supply chain management and marketing. With few staff on hand, its principal and assistant principal have stepped in to teach special education and some of its remaining career and technical programming, city documents show.
Like SEED, the school serves a high-need population: Nearly all of the school’s students come from low-income families. More than 90% of the school’s students are Black or Latino.
The Education Department also cited performance concerns. Just 20% of students met a city benchmark for advanced or career-oriented coursework, compared with 63% across Manhattan.
Despite the school’s challenges, the closure proposal has been gut-wrenching for students and staff, physical education teacher Gilbert Schuerch said.
“The amount of students I’ve held in my arms today,” he wrote on Substack after the closure was announced to the community, “and the number of tears shed — from me and the kids — has only reaffirmed how special this place has become to me and the kids.”
Relocation Proposal: The Center School
Facing overcrowding in its current building on West 84th Street, city officials are proposing to move the school 1.5 miles north to a campus at West 109th Street that houses P.S. 165. Officials say the move will help The Center School and P.S. 9, the coveted elementary school that currently shares its building, shrink class sizes under a state mandate.
The school faced a different relocation proposal last school year to a building on West 61st Street that houses P.S. 191. Families pushed back against the move for a variety of reasons, including insufficient community engagement and because they said the new location would not be able to adequately accommodate the school’s theater program.
The school, which served 247 students last year, is relatively affluent: About 23% come from low-income families, 55% are white, and about 27% are Black or Latino.
Officials plan to upgrade the theater space at the new campus, though they acknowledged the stage is smaller and shallower.
Last year’s proposal to move The Center School also involved eliminating the middle school grades at P.S. 191. Separately, the city proposed to eliminate the middle school grades at Manhattan School for Children and close the Community Action School. Those proposals were withdrawn last school year. An Education Department spokesperson did not say if they are still under consideration.
“NYCPS remains committed to meaningful engagement with communities before issuing any proposals,” Education Department spokesperson Dominique Ellison said in a statement.
Alex Zimmerman is a senior reporter for Chalkbeat New York, covering NYC public schools. Contact Alex at azimmerman@chalkbeat.org.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/03/trum.title: Trump Scrambles to Halt Military Aid to Israel to Deprive El-Sayed of a Talking Point
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/03/trum.author: Nick Turse
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/03/trum.text:
The United States will stop providing $4 billion in annual aid to Israel starting next year, President Donald Trump claimed in an Election Day interview. While the U.S. will continue to sell arms to its closest Middle East ally, Trump’s announcement — should it actually hold true — could represent a seismic shift in American foreign policy.
Still questions remain and experts are dubious that the claim is what it seems.
Trump told Fox News during a phone call on Tuesday that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had approached him with the idea years ago. He did not state specifically why he waited to announce the decision in the midst of a midterm vote in which his party is expected to lose its lock on Congress, but noted that U.S. aid to Israel has become a Democratic talking point, singling out Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed. “The left uses the $4 billion payment — that everybody knows about, it’s no secret — as a signal of unfairness,” said Trump.
An August 2026 Fox News poll found 55 percent of Michigan voters oppose continued military assistance to Israel, including 70 percent of Democrats, 66 percent of Independents, and 35 percent of Republicans.
U.S. public support for Israel has fallen since the Gaza war began in 2023, particularly among Democrats, as Netanyahu’s government has slaughtered civilians with impunity. Almost 75,000 Gazans have been killed and nearly 176,000 wounded, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Health in Gaza. A recent U.N. report said, “Israeli authorities and forces continue to commit genocidal acts with the genocidal intent to destroy, in whole or in part, the Palestinians in Gaza.”
Amid the slaughter, sympathy for Israel among all Americans fell from roughly 50 percent to 36, while sympathy for Palestinians rose to 41 percent, according to a February Gallup poll. Among Democrats, support for Israel plummeted from more than 50 percent in 2001 to roughly 17 percent this year. October 2026 polling from the Institute for Middle East Understanding’s D.C.-based IMEU Policy Project and YouGov found a majority of voters in six key swing states — Georgia, Iowa, Maine, North Carolina, Ohio, and Texas — support halting the transfer of bombs to Israel.
“You can consider it barter. You can consider military aid or cash,” Trump said. “Look, we give them $4 billion of things and money, and they don’t need it. And I was approached by Bibi Netanyahu, and we’ve been talking about it for a couple of years because it’s a lot of money.”
Experts cautioned not to take Trump at his word, especially as his administration pushes a pending $1.15 trillion National Defense Authorization Act that would embed Israeli technology within the Pentagon’s programs and supply chain.
“President Trump is a serial liar who has announced over $20 billion in weapons giveaways to Israel since taking office and launched a war at Israel’s request that has already cost every U.S. household over $2,000 — the equivalent of $262 billion,” said Hamid Bendaas, IMEU Policy Project’s communications director. “He and other politicians realize our taxpayer funding for Israel is a liability. That’s why he and his allies in Congress are at this very moment trying to advance legislation to conceal support for Israel by integrating Israeli weapons companies into the Pentagon. This is a bait and switch that would result in Americans funding Israeli weapons makers in record amounts.”
Others expressed skepticism about Trump‘s claim of an immediate end of annual aid in 2027. “It’s not plausible there will be a total cut-off starting January 1,” said Josh Paul, who spent more than 11 years as the director of congressional and public affairs at the State Department bureau that oversees arms transfers to foreign nations before resigning in 2023 over U.S. military assistance to Israel, noting that funding is baked into existing and pending legislation. “My guess is that he was speaking off the cuff with the next 10-year memorandum of understanding between the U.S. and Israel in mind, but did so in a way that is at best inaccurate or imprecise.”
A decade ago, President Barack Obama signed an unprecedented MOU with Israel to give its military $38 billion between 2019 and 2028, amounting to almost $4 billion a year.
Paul was hopeful, however that Trump’s statement would allow Republicans license to join Democratic colleagues in paring down future funding. He said it was a recognition of the bipartisan demand by the American people for an end to that military aid.
Trump’s announcement did not address the proposal in the National Defense Authorization Act, which would inextricably link the U.S. armed forces and the Israeli military, giving Israel leverage over the Pentagon.
“Initial reporting on Trump’s statement omits a crucial fact: that the National Defense Authorization Act contains a provision intended to protect U.S. tax dollars flowing to Israel from the massive shift in U.S. public opinion against funding Israeli aggression,” Annelle Sheline, who served as a foreign affairs officer in the State Department’s Bureau of Democracy, Human Rights, and Labor, told The Intercept. “The provision would move U.S. funding out of security assistance under the purview of the State Department — which carries legal provisions like the Leahy Laws, transparency requirements, and an annual congressional vote — into the Pentagon procurement process, which has none of these.”
Sheline added, “Insulated from public opinion and away from public visibility, U.S. funding to Israel is likely to grow exponentially.”
With his popularity in free fall in the U.S., Trump teased the possibility of decamping for Israel and taking Netanyahu’s job as the Israeli prime minister battles for his political life after an inconclusive election last week. “In fact, if people ever got tired of me in the U.S., I’ll move to Israel, become prime minister,” Trump declared during his Fox appearance.
The White House did not immediately respond to requests for further details.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
