https://apache.be/2026/11/04/adoptiedien.title: “Adoptiedienst wrikte Nepalese kinderen los van hun families”
https://apache.be/2026/11/04/adoptiedien.author: Kasper Nollet
https://apache.be/2026/11/04/adoptiedien.text:
Een Vlaamse adoptiedienst voerde in de jaren 90 bewust adopties uit op Nepalese kinderen met families, onder het valse voorwendsel dat er een risico bestond op kinderarbeid. Toezichthouder Kind en Gezin was daarvan op de hoogte en greep niet in. Dat schrijft onderzoeker Hari Prasad Sacré, die zelf in die periode geadopteerd werd uit Nepal, in een gastbijdrage op apache.be op basis van interne documenten die ook Apache kon inkijken.
In het kort
- Tussen 1992 en 2000 bracht het Vlaamse adoptiebureau Interadoptie zeven kinderen uit Nepal naar Vlaanderen.
- Inspectieverslagen en correspondentie tussen Interadoptie en Kind en Gezin (vandaag het agentschap Opgroeien) tonen aan dat Interadoptie bewust niet-verweesde kinderen uitkoos ter adoptie, schrijft adoptieonderzoeker Hari Prasad Sacré in een gastbijdrage op apache.be.
- De kinderen werden gescheiden van hun familie onder het valse voorwendsel dat ze behoed moesten worden voor kinderarbeid in de Nepalese tapijtenindustrie.
- Kind en Gezin wist volgens Sacré af van de mistoestanden, maar greep niet in. Zijn gastbijdrage komt op een moment dat er veel kritiek is op hoe Vlaanderen het onderzoek naar de historische wantoestanden in de adoptiesector voert.
Tussen 1992 en 2000 vonden in totaal zeven adopties plaats in Nepal die georganiseerd werden door de Vlaamse adoptiedienst Interadoptie. Adoptieonderzoeker en taalpedagoog Hari Prasad Sacré was een van die zeven adoptiekinderen.
“De Vlaamse adoptiedienst Interadoptie haalde kinderen uit Nepal om hen zogezegd te redden van kinderarbeid in de tapijtfabrieken. Maar hun broers en zussen bleven in Nepal, en geen van hen werd ooit een tapijtkind”, schrijft hij in een gastbijdrage op apache.be. Kind en Gezin, de dienst die destijds toezag op interlandelijke adopties, was daar volgens Sacré van op de hoogte. Toch greep de overheidsorganisatie niet in.
“De juridische en ethische kaders uit de jaren 90 zijn heel anders dan vandaag. Als we de praktijk van vroeger toetsen aan de kennis en normen die we vandaag hanteren, zouden deze adopties wellicht niet hebben plaatsgevonden”, reageert Dries Cludts, woordvoerder van Opgroeien, het agentschap dat in 2019 ontstond uit de fusie van Agentschap Jongerenwelzijn, Kind en Gezin en een deel van het Vlaams Agentschap voor Personen met een Handicap.
Eind april 2026 besliste de Vlaamse Regering om interlandelijke adopties definitief stop te zetten. In 2027 zal er nieuwe wetgeving in voege treden.
De beslissing van de regering kwam er na jaren van kritiek op het systeem. In verschillende dossiers bleek dat achtergrondinformatie niet klopte of dat documenten vervalst waren. Soms was er zelfs sprake van kinderhandel.
Een kind uit het binnenland adopteren blijft wel nog mogelijk, al gaat het daar om een zeer beperkte groep en zijn de voorwaarden verstrengd.
Tapijtindustrie als voorwendsel
In 1992 vat Interadoptie zijn activiteiten in Nepal aan op vraag van Vlaamse kandidaat-adoptieouders “die absoluut een Nepalees kindje wilden adopteren”, staat in een inspectieverslag uit 1993. Om aan hun verzoek tegemoet te komen, zou Interadoptie daarvoor samenwerken met het Nepalese staatsadoptiebureau Bal Mandir. Interadoptie schakelde een Nepalese bemiddelaar in, een vrouw met de naam S.S.
In een brief uit 1994 aan Kind en Gezin schrijft Interadoptie dat het bewust kiest voor niet-verweesde kinderen of voor kinderen die worden achtergelaten in ziekenhuizen
In een brief uit 1994 aan Kind en Gezin schrijft Interadoptie dat het bewust kiest voor niet-verweesde kinderen of voor kinderen die worden achtergelaten in ziekenhuizen. Uit een inspectieverslag van datzelfde jaar van Kind en Gezin staat te lezen hoe Interadoptie die keuze motiveert.
De adoptiedienst zou geconfronteerd worden met “het feit dat de kinderen in de weeshuizen dikwijls een beter leven hebben dan de kinderen die bij hun ouders verblijven”. Zogenoemde ‘tapijtkinderen’ zouden al vanaf 6 jaar tewerkgesteld worden in tapijtfabrieken. “Om die reden en in het belang van het kind opteert de adoptiedienst ervoor om geen kinderen uit weeshuizen te adopteren maar wel kinderen die het risico lopen om in zo'n tapijtfabriek te worden tewerkgesteld”, klinkt het in het inspectieverslag.
De kwestie van kinderarbeid in Nepal in die periode is reëel. “Maar de adoptiedienst gebruikte het beeld van de tapijtkinderen en kinderarbeid om kinderen los te wrikken van functionerende families met een slinkse retoriek”, schrijft Sacré. “Nepalese gezinnen worden in dat beeld neergezet als een risico-omgeving.”
De adoptiedienst slaagt er volgens hem zo in om de logica dat een kind bij zijn familie hoort volledig om te draaien. “Het gezegde ‘in het belang van het kind’ sluit elk kritisch gesprek uit. Wie dat argument inroept, maakt tegenspraak moeilijk. Wie kan er tegen zijn dat een kind niet in een fabriek moet gaan werken?”
Hij wijst erop dat een kind pas in aanmerking komt voor adoptie in het buitenland als zorg in de eigen familie of gemeenschap onmogelijk is. “De Speciale VN-rapporteur voor de verkoop van kinderen rekent het negeren van dat principe tot de praktijken die van een adoptie een verkoop van kinderen maken.”
De impact op de kinderen en hun families in Nepal is groot, schrijft Sacré. “Wij, Nepalees geadopteerden, kennen elkaar. Van zes van ons ken ik het verhaal en de families. Telkens gaat het om kinderen die werden weggehaald uit families waar ze nog ouders, grootouders, broers en zussen hadden. Die broers en zussen bleven in Nepal. Geen van hen kwam ooit in een tapijtfabriek terecht. Het risico waarvan wij gered moesten worden, was nooit een reëel gevaar in hun leven.”
Kind en Gezin op de hoogte
Na zeven adopties stopte Interadoptie in 2000 met adopties uit Nepal. Het is niet duidelijk waarom. Volgens een inspectieverslag uit 1993 begon de samenwerking met Nepal “op vraag van kandidaat-adoptanten […], die absoluut een Nepalees kindje wilden adopteren”. Toen dat koppel na zes maanden nog geen toewijzing had, wilde het toch vertrekken. “De verantwoordelijke van de adoptiedienst kon hen niet tegenhouden.”
“Kind en Gezin wist van bij het begin van de risico’s in Nepal”, schrijft Hari Prasad Sacré
“Kind en Gezin wist van bij het begin van de risico’s in Nepal”, concludeert Sacré. “Het is een schoolvoorbeeld van wat het Vlaamse expertenpanel rond transnationale adoptie in 2021 vaststelde, namelijk dat het systeem vraaggestuurd was. Niet de nood van een kind in Nepal, maar de wens van Vlaamse adoptanten zette de samenwerking met Nepal in gang.”
“Opgroeien erkent dat vragen over adoptie en afstamming voor betrokkenen erg gevoelig kunnen zijn. Daarom vinden we het belangrijk dat iedereen die daar behoefte aan heeft zijn of haar verhaal kan delen”, reageert de woordvoerder van agentschap Opgroeien.
Hij zegt dat het agentschap deze adopties vandaag wellicht zou hebben afgekeurd. “De juridische en ethische kaders uit de jaren 90 zijn heel anders dan vandaag.” Intussen heeft de Vlaamse Regering beslist om interlandelijke adoptie stop te zetten, beklemtoont hij. “Dat besluit past binnen de fundamenteel veranderde kijk op interlandelijke adoptie.”
Vragen bij onafhankelijk onderzoek
De gastbijdrage van Sacré komt op een moment dat er grote kritiek is op de manier waarop Vlaanderen het onderzoek naar de historische wantoestanden in de adoptiesector voert. Critici beschuldigen het Vlaams Centrum voor Adoptie (VCA), dat in 2023 de opdracht kreeg om wantoestanden te onderzoeken, van belangenvermenging.
Critici beschuldigen het Vlaams Centrum voor Adoptie, dat in 2023 de opdracht kreeg om wantoestanden te onderzoeken, van belangenvermenging
Enkele van de medewerkers van de voormalige adoptiediensten zijn immers ondergebracht in een adviesraad van het Vlaams Centrum voor Adoptie. Ook vinden critici het een probleem dat het VCA nog contact onderhoudt met partnerorganisaties die zelf betrokken waren bij omstreden adoptiepraktijken. Verschillende geadopteerden deden bij Apache al hun verhaal over hun ervaringen met het VCA-onderzoek.
Bovendien hebben enkele van de onderzoekers die werden ingeschakeld als onafhankelijke experts kritiek op de werkwijze van VCA. Drie academici haakten inmiddels al af omdat ze niet akkoord zijn met onder meer een verplichte geheimhoudinsclausule en een gebrek aan inspraak.
Een van de belangrijkste vragen waarmee veel geadopteerden vandaag zitten, is waarom het de overheid aan moed ontbreekt om voormalige adoptiediensten verantwoordelijk te stellen voor hun daden, zegt Sacré aan Apache.
Hari Prasad Sacré is blij met het voortschrijdend inzicht van het departement Opgroeien. “Dat deze adopties in de huidige regelgeving afgekeurd zouden worden is een mooie eerste stap van erkenning. Maar de levens van ons en onze families zijn onomkeerbaar getekend door de falende kaders van de jaren 90. Welke herstelmaatregelen plaatst de overheid hier tegenover?”

https://citylimits.org/new-latino-democr.title: New Latino Democrats Group Aims to Build Political Power Across Five Boroughs
https://citylimits.org/new-latino-democr.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/new-latino-democr.text:
Share This Article
The new club aims to increase Latino representation in local politics, develop future leaders and strengthen community involvement across New York City, founder Jamey Battle said.
After years of participating in Democratic clubs, women’s organizations and professional networks, Jamey Battle said she often found herself asking the same question.
“I kept thinking, where are the other Latinos?” said Battle, who previously worked in the New York State Assembly and for a lobbying firm. “How can I bring them into this space? How can I get us involved in this political movement?”
Rather than continuing to search for Latino representation within existing political organizations, Battle decided to help create that space, centered on Latino voices and experiences.
Last month, Latino Democrats of New York City (LDNYC) celebrated its official launch as a 501(c)(4). Founded in October 2025 as a volunteer organizing group, LDNYC now has nearly 200 members, according to a press release.
The club aims to increase Latino representation in local politics, develop future leaders and strengthen community involvement across New York City’s five boroughs.
“I came up with the idea for Latino Democrats about a year ago. I texted my vice president, Evelyn Norris Pez, and we reached out to people in the network that we knew that shared two values: integrity and community centeredness,” said Battle, the group’s president.
“I finally came to a realization of, why am I spending so much time trying to have Latinos fit into a space that was never made for us, that isn’t led for us by us, and that doesn’t serve us?”
The group celebrated its new nonprofit status on Oct. 21 with an inaugural “Primera Noche” reception at Lighthouse Rooftop in Long Island City, Queens.
The evening brought together elected officials, community leaders, organizers and supporters for a celebration featuring speeches, award presentations and conversations about Latino political participation.
Attendees included Claire Valdez, who will head to Congress in January to represent Brooklyn and Queens’ 7th District; Brian Romero, newly elected to the State Assembly in Woodside and Jackson Heights; plus Queens Assembly members Catalina Cruz and Steven Raga, among others.
Throughout the reception, speakers shared personal stories about their families, careers and the experiences that shaped their involvement in public service.
One recalled growing up with a Salvadoran mother who arrived in the United States undocumented at age 12, and described hearing family stories about workplace exploitation, wage theft, policing and immigration enforcement—experiences that they said continue to shape their approach to community advocacy.
In New York State, Latinos account for 2.2 million eligible voters, making them the largest ethnic and racial group after white voters, according to the Pew Research Center.
For Battle, the group’s launch marks an opportunity to bring more Latino New Yorkers into political spaces and develop a stronger network of community leaders.
It comes as Democrats celebrate sweeping wins across the country in Tuesday’s midterm election, including victories for several candidates Latino Democrats NYC endorsed.
“I’m really excited for the next few years, really mobilizing and energizing the Latino community in New York City and building political power for all Latino communities in New York City,” Battle said.

https://gothamist.com/news/strand-bookst.title: Strand Bookstore admits it took a pandemic loan despite being ineligible
https://gothamist.com/news/strand-bookst.author: Sonia Rao
https://gothamist.com/news/strand-bookst.text:
Strand Bookstore in Union Square acknowledged it accepted a pandemic-era Paycheck Protection Program loan for which it was not eligible, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia announced on Tuesday. The office stated that the bookstore would pay nearly $1.5 million to account for the error.
The Strand is owned by Nancy Bass Wyden, who is married to Oregon Sen. Ron Wyden. The U.S. Attorney’s Office said The Strand was ineligible when it applied in February 2021 for a loan of more than $930,000, as federal law prohibited businesses controlled by a member of Congress or their spouse from receiving the second round of PPP funding.
“The Paycheck Protection Program was created to save American jobs, not to enrich those who aren’t eligible for taxpayer-funded relief,” U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro said in a statement. “No one gets a pass when it comes to defrauding the American taxpayer.”
A spokesperson for The Strand described the application as an honest mistake, saying that neither the bookstore’s accountant nor the bank handling the loan were aware of the law barring a congressman’s spouse from receiving a PPP loan. The funds were returned as soon as The Strand became aware of the issue, according to the spokesperson.
The store has not responded to an inquiry to clarify whether it paid the original $932,350 loan amount or the new, higher sum announced by the U.S. Attorney's Office.
Ron Wyden, a Democrat, has been outspoken in his criticism of President Donald Trump, who appointed Pirro to her position in May 2025.
The Strand, which is known for the “18 miles of books” housed in its flagship store, has been open about its financial struggles in the past. In March 2021, responding to worker complaints of mismanaged funds, a Strand spokesperson told New York magazine that limited sales and a PPP loan were the only things keeping staff members paid in a period of struggle.
In December 2024, the Strand’s 110 unionized employees went on strike amid tense contract negotiations to demand they make more than New York City’s minimum wage of $16 an hour. Both parties reached a tentative agreement to raise the base pay rate by 50 cents an hour and grant employees a raise of $1.50 an hour in their fourth year working at the store.
Nancy Bass Wyden's grandfather, Ben Bass, founded the bookstore at its original Greenwich Village location in 1927. It moved 30 years later to its current location on East 12th Street and Broadway.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/04/will.title: Lesson From Lansing: To Win in Swing Districts, Fight Data Centers
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/04/will.author: Matt Sledge
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/04/will.text:
When progressive Will Lawrence beat two moderates in a Michigan congressional primary earlier this year, some Democrats were worried about his ability to win one of the nation’s most evenly divided districts.
Early Wednesday morning, Lawrence claimed victory over Republican Rep. Tom Barrett. (National news organizations such as The Associated Press had not called the race as of Wednesday morning.)
A national swing in favor of Democrats helped him — but so did a campaign that leaned heavily on opposition to data centers to 
situate Lawrence as a populist instead of an extremist.
Data centers were on voters’ minds everywhere, but they rarely dominated a race as much as the 7th Congressional District of Michigan. Lawrence vocally opposed data center construction almost as soon as he began running last year. A series of proposed hyperscale developments in and around Lansing pushed the issue into the limelight.
A month and a half before the election, Lawrence announced a data center platform calling for a moratorium on new development, environmental regulations, and a national jobs program to replace work taken away by artificial intelligence.
As progressives take stock of the 2026 midterms, Lawrence’s approach points one way forward for their wing of the Democratic Party. Lawrence’s opponent tried to turn his time as an environmental activist into a liability, but in an interview with The Intercept, Lawrence said his background primed him to come down on the same side as the public on a red-hot issue like data centers.
“I fought against Wall Street landlords trying to kick people out of their homes. I fought against oil companies who are polluting our air and water,” he told The Intercept in an interview last month. “So for me, this was not the first time that I’ve stood on the line against a corporate behemoth like this.”
From Sunrise to Congress
Lawrence is a co-founder of the Sunrise Movement, which had one of its most famous moments when its youth activists marched into the office of then-House Speaker Nancy Pelosi to push for the Green New Deal with Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., by their side in 2018.
Data centers and AI were remote issues for voters then, but they were starting to bubble up in the public consciousness by the time Lawrence announced his run for Congress in August 2025.
Two months later, one of his first moves as a candidate was to visit public meetings in two small townships in Michigan to express his opposition to proposed data center developments.
As a former member of the Democratic Socialists of America, he drew skepticism from many observers over his ability to win the primary in a district that narrowly voted for Donald Trump in 2024. They were equally skeptical of his ability to beat Barrett, a Republican who tried to play up his moderate bona fides in the race’s final weeks. Barrett was one of a handful of Republicans to vote in favor of a resolution to end the Iran war, for instance.
Lawrence had some major liabilities in a purple district, including tweets where he wrote “fuck the nuclear-family home” and told then-Democratic Sen. Joe Manchin in a song to “hurry up and die.”
While Barrett leaned on those posts and Lawrence’s time with the DSA to cast his opponent as an extremist, the young progressive had a card up his sleeves in the form of the data center issue.
It is the rare cause that leaps across party lines to unite Republicans and Democrats who are just as worried about water sources drying up and ceaseless buzzing sounds.
At an October 5 city council meeting in the quaint town of Mason, where a developer has proposed a hyperscale data center on a plot of picturesque farmland, Democrats and Republicans alike said they were outraged. Some residents said they would sell their house and leave town if the development is built.
In a sign of how politically charged the issue has become, many of the speakers were candidates for office angling for votes. Lawrence had dropped by himself a few weeks before. His first television ad centered on his opposition to the Mason project.
Karl Sime, a Mason resident who crisscrossed the area on behalf of Democratic candidates, told The Intercept last month that “100 percent” of voters were angry about the data center proposed for the swath of farmland just outside city limits.
“Sometimes they’ll just say it unprovoked,” he said. “You can see the body language just dramatically change into anger.”
Republican Countermoves
Lawrence was hardly the only candidate who tried to tap into opposition to data centers. Some Republicans tried to catch the wave as well.
Barrett voted for the One Big Beautiful Bill, which included tax breaks that could benefit rural data center developers. But as the danger he faced in the election became clear, he proposed legislation in Congress that would ban local officials from signing non-disclosure agreements with developers and would allow local communities to set regulations on data centers without federal interference.
Some voters said they wanted to see candidates take a harder stance in favor of regulation, however. At the City Council meeting last month, Doug DeLind said he was left shaking his head at neighbors who had yard signs opposing data centers and supporting Barrett.
DeLind, a sculptor who lives near the proposed data center, said that Barrett’s position was that “we’re going to leave it up to the local communities, but we’re not going to provide any federal protection or any guidelines to what a data center can do.”
Although Mason faces a more imminent possibility of a massive data center, Americans across the country are worried about having one in their backyard. Multiple surveys showed a remarkable shift in public opinion on the subject over the past year. Half of Americans oppose a data center being built within 3 miles of their house, according to a recent Politico poll.
In recent months, data centers became a signature issue for Democrats with progressive pasts trying to recast themselves as populists. Sherrod Brown, the party’s Senate candidate in Ohio, and Texas gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa also staked their campaigns on opposition to data centers. Both won.
“The playbook was listening to voters. I think voters across ideologies were speaking with one voice, and I think their opponents were some of the people most willing to silence voters and accept industry cash instead,” said Alex Bores, who became a national figure by arguing for stricter AI regulations during a failed New York congressional primary bid earlier this year.
As candidates ran away from data centers, the artificial intelligence industry’s most powerful super PAC stopped intervening in close races. An Intercept analysis found that the well-funded Leading the Future super PAC network, which is aligned with OpenAI, largely stopped spending in competitive general election races.
It lost in the one state where it did place a big bet, South Carolina. Incumbent Sen. Darline Graham, a Republican, fell to challenger Annie Andrews.
Bores, who now leads a pro-AI regulation group called Who Decides, said he was not surprised to see candidates increasingly market themselves as AI skeptics.
“I think it’s overdue. I think candidates and elected officials are catching up to where the electorate is, across parties,” Bores told The Intercept. “It is remarkable the agreement that voters have around wanting guardrails to protect us from the most powerful and fastest moving technology of our lifetime. Democracy is sometimes slow, but only so much.”
This story was supported by a grant from the Tarbell Center for AI Journalism.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.

The 1956 Hungarian Uprising Was a Working-Class Revolt
Seventy years ago today, Soviet forces crushed the Hungarian uprising that had electrified Eastern Europe. Latter-day conservative narratives distort the true history of the 1956 revolution and the crucial role of workers’ councils in driving it forward.
On October 23, 1956, tens of thousands of Hungarians took to the streets of Budapest. What began as a demonstration led largely by students rapidly became a popular uprising against the country’s Stalinist government.
Within days, the authority of the Hungarian Communist Party had crumbled, Soviet troops had been forced to withdraw, and workers across the country were establishing their own councils to organize production and exercise political power.
The Soviet leadership called it a “counterrevolution,” while Western governments celebrated it as a “revolt against communism.” Both interpretations obscured something fundamental: the Hungarian Revolution was driven by workers and ordinary people who wanted to free themselves from a system that claimed to represent their interests.
The uprising was ultimately crushed by Soviet military intervention on November 4. Thousands were killed; hundreds were executed in the repression that followed; and some two hundred thousand Hungarians fled the country. Yet the revolution remains one of the twentieth century’s most important challenges to authoritarian rule in the name of socialism.
For the international Left, its significance is difficult to overstate. As the Hungarian Marxist philosopher G. M. Tamás observed, Eastern Europe was precisely where socialism had supposedly been put into practice. What, then, were we to make of workers rising en masse against a self-proclaimed socialist government?
The answer begins with the contradictions of the Hungarian state itself — and with the people who dared to challenge it.
The Crisis of Stalinist Hungary
By the mid-1950s, Hungary was a country of roughly ten million people still recovering from the devastation of World War II. Following the defeat of Nazi Germany, it had been incorporated into the Soviet sphere of influence. Its economy was reorganized around state ownership, central planning, and rapid industrialization, while political power was concentrated in the hands of a Communist Party modeled on the ruling party in Joseph Stalin’s Soviet Union.
Under the leadership of Mátyás Rákosi, the party pursued an especially brutal version of this model. Heavy industry received priority over consumer goods, agriculture was subjected to forced collectivization, and living standards were sacrificed to ambitious production targets. The secret police, known as the State Protection Authority (ÁVH), became the instrument of a pervasive system of surveillance, intimidation, and repression.
The government justified these policies on the grounds that they were necessary for building socialism. But workers had little control over their workplaces, peasants faced coercive agricultural policies, and ordinary citizens had virtually no say in political decisions. Although the state owned the factories, that did not mean power was in the hands of the people who worked in those factories.
From a critical political-economic perspective, this exposed a deeper contradiction. The state mobilized society for rapid industrial accumulation while subordinating workers to the demands of production. The bureaucracy determined what was produced, how resources were allocated, and how much people were expected to sacrifice. The facade was socialist, but the relationship between rulers and ruled remained profoundly authoritarian.
The New Course
The unexpected death of Stalin in 1953 opened a small space for change. Under pressure from Moscow, Rákosi was replaced as prime minister by Imre Nagy, a reform-minded Communist who recognized that the existing economic model was unsustainable. The new government introduced economic and political reforms, known as the “New Course,” which promised to reduce the emphasis on heavy industry, improve living standards, expand consumer production, and ease political repression.
The reforms generated widespread hopes. Forced labor camps were closed, restrictions on private enterprise were relaxed, and peasants received greater freedom to cultivate their land. But the success of the reform program was far from guaranteed. Rákosi retained control of the party apparatus, and powerful Stalinist factions opposed Nagy’s attempts to change course. In 1955, with Soviet support, Nagy’s opponents accused him of “right-wing deviation” and had him removed from office.
His dismissal signaled that the state would not tolerate even limited reform when it threatened the authority of the party bureaucracy. The following year, Nikita Khrushchev’s denunciation of Stalin’s crimes at the Soviet Communist Party’s Twentieth Congress further undermined the regime’s legitimacy. If Moscow now acknowledged the terror and injustice of Stalin’s rule, what did that mean for the Hungarian leaders who had faithfully reproduced his methods?
Students, intellectuals, writers, and increasingly workers began demanding answers. By October 1956, Hungary was like a tinderbox waiting to explode.
A Revolution Takes Shape
The immediate spark came on October 23. Students gathered in Budapest to demand political reform, the return of Imre Nagy to government, the withdrawal of Soviet troops, and greater national independence. Their demands also encompassed changes to workplace conditions, including opposition to the unpopular piece-rate system that tied workers’ wages to production quotas.
The demonstration grew dramatically as people joined the march through the capital. By evening, a vast crowd had assembled outside parliament. Elsewhere, demonstrators pulled down a monumental statue of Stalin, an unmistakable declaration that the old order had lost its authority.
The turning point came when demonstrators gathered outside the Hungarian Radio headquarters, hoping to broadcast their demands. ÁVH security forces opened fire, killing and wounding people. The violent response by the government transformed a mass demonstration into an armed uprising. Weapons were seized, police vehicles were set ablaze, and insurgents began confronting the state’s armed forces.
The following day, Soviet troops entered Budapest, but their intervention failed to restore order. Some Hungarian soldiers refused to fight the insurgents; others defected or handed over weapons. Nagy returned to the premiership as the authorities struggled to regain control.
What had begun as a protest against political repression was becoming something much more radical. The uprising spread beyond the capital to industrial towns, provincial centers, and rural communities. Factories stopped working, local revolutionary committees appeared, and workers began organizing independently of the party and the state.
Workers’ Councils
This is where the conventional Cold War story becomes inadequate. The revolution cannot be understood simply as a national revolt against Soviet occupation, nor as an uprising orchestrated by anti-communist politicians. Its most consequential development was the emergence of independent working-class organization.
Across Hungary, workers established revolutionary councils, elected by their colleagues and answerable to them. These bodies coordinated strikes, organized supplies, represented workers in negotiations, and increasingly asserted authority over factories and local institutions. They were not merely trade unions demanding higher wages. In many cases, they challenged the state’s right to govern workplaces and society without popular consent.
Historical estimates suggest that more than two thousand workers’ councils were established during the revolution, involving more than 28,000 members. Their demands varied, but recurring themes included the withdrawal of Soviet troops, political freedoms, the release of prisoners, and genuine worker participation in economic decision-making.
For a brief moment, the factory floor became a site of political power. Workers who had supposedly constituted the ruling class discovered that they could organize production and articulate political demands without the supervision of party officials.
The revolution was not ideologically uniform. It brought together students, industrial workers, peasants, intellectuals, reform Communists, and supporters of different political traditions. Nor did all its participants share the same vision of Hungary’s future. But the workers’ councils gave the uprising a distinctive social character that neither the Soviet leadership nor its Western adversaries could comfortably accommodate.
Beyond Budapest
The working-class dimension of the revolution was particularly evident in Budapest’s industrial districts and in provincial manufacturing centers. Workers in Csepel, Újpest, and Kőbánya joined the resistance, while industrial towns such as Miskolc, Ózd, and Dunapentele (which had been renamed Sztálinváros under the Stalinist regime) became important sites of revolutionary activity.
These developments matter because the revolution is often remembered primarily through images of street fighting in Budapest. Yet the uprising spread through the networks of industrial production, workplaces, and communities that underpinned the Hungarian economy.
In Dunapentele, workers insisted that their town was socialist precisely because its inhabitants were workers and power belonged in their hands. They declared their intention to defend it against both fascist excesses and Soviet troops. Their statement captured the central contradiction of 1956: they were not necessarily rejecting the ideal of socialism but rejecting a political order that invoked socialism to justify its own domination.
Peter Fryer was a correspondent for the Daily Worker, the official newspaper of the Communist Party of Great Britain. He witnessed the uprising and described the devastation inflicted on Budapest by Soviet forces. Working-class districts suffered particularly heavily. Fryer’s reports challenged the official Communist account of a fascist conspiracy and helped expose the reality of the intervention to readers abroad.
Workers’ participation was not limited to the construction of councils or the organization of strikes. They also formed a substantial part of the armed resistance. Fighting was particularly intense in industrial neighborhoods, where insurgents used their knowledge of local streets and buildings to resist a much-better-equipped military force.
Young workers were especially prominent. Many had grown up under the Communist regime, experienced its workplace discipline and political restrictions, and reached adulthood with little memory of the prewar order. The motivation behind their revolt cannot be reduced to nostalgia for the old Hungary. They were challenging the society in which they had actually lived.
The distinction is crucial. The revolution did contain nationalist and anti-communist currents, and some participants sought a restoration of political arrangements from before the war. But these currents do not explain the independent organization of workers across the country, nor do they justify the Soviet claim that military intervention was necessary to defeat a fascist counterrevolution. The revolution’s social diversity should not obscure its central achievement: ordinary people began to exercise political power for themselves.
The Soviet Counterattack
By late October, the uprising had forced the government into a series of concessions. Nagy announced a coalition government and, under mounting pressure, moved toward political pluralism. On October 28, the government declared a ceasefire and acknowledged the revolutionary movement. The prospect of Soviet withdrawal appeared increasingly real.
But the Soviet leadership faced a dilemma. Allowing Hungary to break decisively from Moscow’s control risked destabilizing the entire Soviet bloc. The danger was not merely that another government might leave the Warsaw Pact. It was that a successful revolution organized from below might inspire workers elsewhere to challenge their own rulers.
The crisis also unfolded against a wider international backdrop. Western powers were unwilling to risk a direct military confrontation with the Soviet Union, while the Suez crisis was exposing the limits of Western claims to defend freedom and national sovereignty. Hungary’s fate would ultimately be decided by the balance of power between states, not by the rhetoric of either superpower.
On November 1, Nagy announced Hungary’s withdrawal from the Warsaw Pact and appealed for international recognition of the country’s neutrality. Meanwhile, Moscow had already begun preparing a second military intervention. In the early hours of November 4, Soviet forces launched Operation Whirlwind, attacking Budapest and other centers of resistance.
This time the assault was overwhelming. Some 58,000 Soviet troops advanced against a revolution that lacked the military resources to withstand a prolonged offensive. Hungarian army units were rapidly disarmed or neutralized, while workers and insurgents continued fighting in several areas.
Nagy broadcasted a desperate appeal for help announcing that Soviet forces had attacked the capital and were attempting to overthrow the government. He subsequently sought refuge in the Yugoslav embassy, but was later arrested. In 1958, following a secret trial, he was executed alongside other leaders of the revolution, including Pál Maléter.
By November 11, the main centers of armed resistance had been crushed. More than 2,500 people had died during the revolution. The workers’ councils, however, did not immediately disappear. Their continued existence forced the new authorities to confront a problem that military victory alone could not resolve: how to govern a population that had demonstrated such open hostility to the regime.
Defeat and the Consolidation of Kádár’s Rule
While Soviet tanks were reentering Hungary, a new Soviet-friendly government, led by János Kádár, was formed. However, the new government initially faced widespread opposition. Factories remained closed, transport services were disrupted, and workers organized strikes against the Soviet intervention. The Central Workers’ Council of Greater Budapest, established in November, became a focal point for efforts to coordinate resistance and negotiate with the authorities.
The government responded with a mixture of concessions and repression. Kádár’s representatives negotiated with workers’ leaders, seeking to persuade them to resume production. But when negotiations failed to break the resistance, the authorities turned decisively toward coercion.
On December 9, the headquarters of the Central Workers’ Council was raided and prominent activists were arrested. Martial law was imposed, strikes were criminalized, and imprisonment and execution became instruments of political control. By early 1957, organized resistance was increasingly difficult to sustain. Many young workers fled Hungary, while those who remained faced the prospect of prison, dismissal, or forced submission.
The repression was followed by a longer process of political consolidation. Kádár rebuilt the Communist Party (now renamed the Hungarian Socialist Workers’ Party, MSZMP) and sought to win the acquiescence of a population exhausted by conflict.
Over time, his government developed a more pragmatic approach to economic management and everyday life. Compared with the brutalities of the Rákosi period, Kádár’s Hungary eventually became associated with relative material security and a degree of private autonomy.
But these accommodations rested on the defeat of independent political organization. Workers could enjoy certain improvements in living standards, provided they did not seek to reclaim the political power they had briefly exercised in 1956.
The revolution therefore left a complicated legacy. Its defeat did not mean that Hungarian society returned unchanged to the prerevolutionary order. The authorities had learned that permanent mobilization, relentless austerity, and indiscriminate terror could undermine the stability they sought to secure. The memory of 1956 placed limits on the state’s room for maneuver, even as it tried to erase the revolution’s independent working-class character.
The Legacy of 1956 Today
The struggle over the meaning of 1956 did not end with the defeat of the revolution. In contemporary Hungary, its memory remains contested. Following the democratic transition in 1989–90, political commemorations have often emphasized themes of national independence and resistance to Soviet domination that primarily resonate with the emphasis of right-wing political parties on national sovereignty.
Under Viktor Orbán’s sixteen-year rule, the state invested heavily in creating an institutionally revisionist memory culture in Hungary, presenting the revolution as a reactionary struggle for “national sovereignty.” However, this picture is utterly detached from the reality of what was happening on the ground in 1956. While reactionary forces sought to co-opt the revolutionary movement at the time, as often happens in mass politics, the struggle did not lose its principled socialist character.
The interpretation that stresses the issue of national sovereignty obscures the revolution’s equally important challenge to domestic authoritarianism and the power of political elites. The workers’ councils should remind us that we cannot separate opposition to foreign domination from the question of who exercises power within society. The revolution was not simply a nation asserting its independence; it was also a population challenging a ruling class that claimed to represent it.
The lesson extends well beyond Hungary. At a time when authoritarian movements are gaining ground across Europe and elsewhere, 1956 challenges the assumption that political alternatives must be confined to a choice between authoritarian state control and the existing capitalist order. It also offers a warning to the Left: governments cannot claim to represent working people while denying them the freedom to organize independently, challenge political authority, and determine the conditions under which they live and work.
The legacy of 1956 is therefore neither simply nationalist nor merely anti-communist. It is a reminder that emancipation cannot be imposed from above, whether in the name of socialism, national security, or economic progress.
The Hungarian workers who challenged their rulers demonstrated that democracy means more than choosing between competing elites. It also means the collective capacity of ordinary people to shape their own lives. This crucial class aspect is often excluded from today’s discourse: many commentators attempt to draw parallels with the war in Ukraine, which often reduces this pivotal socialist revolution to merely a struggle for national sovereignty.
What 1956 Means for the Left
The Hungarian Revolution was neither a vindication of liberal capitalism nor the reactionary conspiracy portrayed by Soviet propaganda. It was a heterogeneous popular uprising whose most radical expression lay in the independent organization of workers.
That distinction remains politically important. If socialism means only state ownership, central planning, and rule by a party claiming exclusive authority to represent the working class, then the Hungarian workers’ revolt poses an uncomfortable question: What happens when the people supposedly represented by the state rise up against it?
We cannot find the answer by dismissing the revolution as an aberration or by ignoring the political diversity of its participants. It requires taking seriously the experience of workers who challenged bureaucratic control, organized their workplaces, and demanded the right to determine their own future.
The councils did not offer a complete blueprint for a socialist society. They operated under extraordinary circumstances, and their political projects were neither uniform nor free of contradictions. But they demonstrated that opposition to Stalinism could emerge from a desire for greater democracy and collective control, rather than simply a wish to restore capitalism.
For the Left, the lesson is not that the revolution should be claimed uncritically by any particular tradition. It is that socialism cannot be reduced to the power of the state, and workers cannot be treated as passive beneficiaries of policies devised in their name. Emancipation requires their active participation in shaping economic and political life.
In 1956, Hungarian workers confronted a regime that claimed to have abolished exploitation while denying them meaningful control over their labor and society. Their defeat exposed the violence required to preserve that contradiction. It also revealed the possibility of another kind of politics — one rooted in collective self-organization, political freedom, and the struggle against domination.
The Soviet tanks crushed the revolution. They could not entirely extinguish its challenge to the meaning of socialism. For anyone on the Left still committed to a society governed democratically by those who create its wealth, that challenge remains unfinished.

A 17th-century Dutch painting looted from France during the Second World War has been recovered by the Musée des Beaux-Arts d’Orléans. The painting, Willem Cornelisz Duyster’s Un Buveur (The Drinker), was stolen from Orleans’s Musée Paul Fourché following a Nazi attack on the city in 1940.
The Musée des Beaux-Arts was able to locate the painting thanks to an inventive poster campaign that placed “Wanted” in Wild West-style capital letters over images of artworks stolen from the museum. These were widely shared on social media, the museum’s website, and in various news outlets. Un Buveur was found by a community member in Orléans who took it upon himself to search for the missing works by sifting through online auctions—he found the painting in the catalog for an October 17 sale at the Gloggner auction house in Lucerne. The auction’s listing was initially thought to be a study for Duyster’s work, but after the museum contacted the auction house, researchers confirmed it as the original.
Un Buveur‘s owner purchased the painting at a London auction house in the 1990s, and “immediately proposed to restitute the painting” upon learning of its shaky provenance. “It was pretty natural for him to return it,” said Olivia Voisin, director of the Musée des Beaux-Arts, “Because he felt that he had been able to enjoy it for 35 years, and it was time for it to go home.”
424 paintings are still missing from the Musée des Beaux-Arts d’Orléans. They include works by Édouard Manet, Hans Holbein the Younger, Anthony van Dyck, Lorenzo Costa, and one painting attributed to Raphael’s workshop. In the years since the “Wanted” campaign started, three other paintings have also been recovered.

https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.title: ‘I put a smoke bomb in a road cone and stuck it on my head’: Delton Barrett’s best photograph
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.author: Interview by Chris Broughton
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.text:
I grew up on New Providence in the Bahamas, and still live on the south side of the island. After leaving school, I worked with my dad in construction, and that’s where I started taking photos. For the first couple of years, I used my flip phone, playing with images of nature and flowers on the sites we were working on, but in 2010 I bought my first DSLR (digital single-lens reflex) camera and started teaching myself about photography.
I started doing a lot of landscapes. I tended to shoot at sunrise or sunset, and became interested in taking photos of people in vacant spaces. Because I didn’t have a model, I used a tripod and a timer to include myself in these very fantasy-looking naturescapes.
This shot came about on a day when I woke up feeling I needed to try out something new. I took three or four different outfits to the western part of the island along with a few props, one of which was this cone. I often keep random items I find, sometimes incorporating them into images.
The road I was on leads to a dead end, so cars don’t drive along it much. It was a pretty safe space – I almost felt like I was in my own back yard. I’d been playing with ideas, and putting the cone on my head was the last one I tried that day. I just liked the way it looked but, as you can imagine, it was quite suffocating.
Then I remembered I had a smoke bomb in the car and it just happened to fit into the tip of the cone. Looking back, it’s a wonder I survived. I’d tried many shots and was getting tired. But it occurred to me that this shot really did look like someone losing their mind, going ballistic. The way I’m gripping the cone makes it unclear whether I’m trying to throw it off or hold it on. Perhaps I’m trapped inside, perhaps I’m in there intentionally because there’s something I don’t want to see.
Either way, there’s some kind of struggle happening. Maybe the smoke is giving a signal, calling people nearby for help, like: “Hey, something’s up here!” I call the image Stop the Madness. We pass people every day who give off signs that they are struggling, or not in their right mind. Maybe we walk past, maybe we help.
The island inspires me a lot. It’s the only backdrop I’ve ever really known. In 2024, I went to Madrid, which is highly developed compared with the Bahamas. When I came back to Nassau after, I thought: “Wow, we have so much more colour, so much more green.” I hadn’t really understood that until then. As an artist and photographer, what stimulates me are my surroundings. The beaches are a five-minute drive away – my images tend to have seas or a sunset or some type of bush involved. I use the elements around me to express my ideas.
Some of my images are manipulated to fit the concept or tell the story I want. If I need a seagull to be in a precise spot, for example, I won’t spend all day waiting for that to happen. One of my favourites shows me standing on top of the sea opposite another version of me in a different costume – and our fingers are almost touching, like in Michelangelo’s Creation of Adam. It’s an image I’d thought about for a long time, so when everything came together it was like a mother who’d waited nine months to have her baby. But often a scene is perfect as it is – all I need to do is frame it and adjust the lighting and maybe the contrast. That’s all that was needed for Stop the Madness.
Delton Barrett’s CV
Born: Manchester, Jamaica, 1991
 
High point: My first solo show in 2018 at D’Aguilar Art Foundation in Nassau. The Bahamas has been a lasting high point. It set the sail for me to continue to create great images that can inspire others in a way I’d also want to be inspired
 
Top tip: Create what makes you feel. Sit with your ideas and think about them until you’ve found the right way to execute them. We can become so excited in photographing the idea that we miss out the small details that make the image worth taking in the moment. In a nutshell I would say: “Take the pressure off shooting and focus more on what you want to shoot and how you want it to feel”

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: ‘We’re in Charge’: What the Blue Wave Means for New York City
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Claudia Irizarry Aponte
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
At an Election Day eve party at a bowling alley in Williamsburg on Monday night, Gov. Kathy Hochul laid out her dream scenario for the midterms.
The event, headlined by the statewide Democratic ticket, predicted a blue wave of voter unrest that would catapult two New Yorkers to the top of the House and the Senate and provide a check on the second administration of President Donald Trump.
“I cannot wait when I call up Hakeem Jeffries and say, ‘Mr. Speaker, I kind of need a few more billions of dollars for New York,’” Hochul said. “Then I call Chuck Schumer: ‘Mr. Majority Leader, I need a few more billions of dollars for New York State.’”
“Get used to it, America,” added Hochul. “Because we’re in charge.”
Hochul got her wish. Democrats captured Congress in a seismic realignment of the electoral map, gaining at least seven Senate seats and more than two dozen House seats, including a crucial pickup in the New York suburbs, with critical funding for the five boroughs on the line.
Now, there is renewed hope that federal dollars will flow for infrastructure projects like the $16 billion Gateway Program, the Penn Station overhaul and the Second Avenue Subway, and that Republican cuts to health care and food stamps might be softened.
Meanwhile, a new crop of state legislators on the left flank of the party — the Democratic Socialists of America doubled its representation in Albany — is eager to hold the governor’s feet to the fire on signature issues like taxing the rich, expanding childcare and raising the minimum wage.
Grace Mauser, the DSA’s local co-chair, said its contingent in the Legislature and its base will push the governor harder for a progressive income tax and higher taxes on the ultra-wealthy. Hochul thanked Mamdani Tuesday night for his support — and now the democratic socialists want to see her deliver.
MORE: How Every Neighborhood in New York City Voted for Governor
“I’m hopeful that Hochul has seen the energy, the excitement that can come from the masses of people who want and deserve a better government, and she takes those lessons and brings them to Albany, and is braver than she has been in past years in terms of standing up for working class New Yorkers,” Mauser said.
Other leaders of the Democratic party’s left echoed DSA’s demands.
“As soon as we’re done here we’re going right back into the state budget fight,” Jasmine Gripper, the co-executive director of the Working Families Party, told The City Reporter. “We will only accept a budget that is equitable and taxes the ultra-rich so that working families can thrive and children have what they need.”
As voters delivered strong results for Democrats in New York and elsewhere, politicos gathered at the Midtown Hilton for Hochul’s election night party were positively giddy at the prospect of two of their own leading both chambers of Congress.
“Before this night is over, we are going to say the words out loud ‘Speaker Jeffries takes the gavel,’” Sen. Kristen Gillibrand said Tuesday.
The previous night, at the Democratic unity event, Jeffries vowed to use his perch as Speaker to tackle Americans’ high cost of living and hold members of Trump’s cabinet accountable, name-checking Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and vowing to “stop this reckless and costly war of choice over in Iran.”
“Here in New York, and all across the country, we’re gonna run these MAGA extremists out of town,” he said.
House Democrats are musing over how they will use their majority to grill key members of the Trump administration under oath and slash Immigration Customs and Enforcement funding.
MORE: Mamdani Ballot Proposals on Public Space, Street Safety and More Pass in NYC
“Everything” is on the table, U.S. Rep. Grace Meng of Queens told The City Reporter. “We have to act fast. This is a mandate, not just a promotion or a change in title, but people want to see Democrats move fast and to hold the administration accountable.”
U.S. Rep.-elect Micah Lasher of Manhattan said that he talks to his predecessor Jerrold Nadler, the top Democrat on the powerful judiciary committee, “every day” about how to use the levers of Congress to reverse the worst of the Trump administration’s impacts on New Yorkers.
“We’re going to have robust oversight powers, and we need to use them, to shine a white hot light on the grift and the graft of this administration.”
For Hochul, Tuesday night was an opportunity to vindicate herself after she was partly blamed for Democrats’ poor showing in the 2022 midterms — the first time she ran at the top of the Democratic ticket — a year that cost state Democrats five House seats and the party its slim House majority.
Hochul spent the last few weeks of the race criss-crossing the state and in New York City touting her record, palling around with left-wing standard-bearers Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, and boosting Hudson Valley House candidate Cait Conley.

https://www.propublica.org/article/vermo.title: Vermont Was Supposed to Get an Audit of Its Lake Champlain Cleanup. It Never Happened.
https://www.propublica.org/article/vermo.author: Jonathan Mingle
https://www.propublica.org/article/vermo.text:
This summer, Vermont’s Clean Water Board celebrated a milestone: Over the past decade, the state has invested nearly a billion dollars to clean up its polluted streams, rivers and lakes. The vast majority of that money has gone toward Lake Champlain.
“I think that’s something to be extremely proud of,” said Douglas Farnham, the board’s chair.
Vermont was supposed to get an independent evaluation of what it has gotten for all that money. But that study was never done.
A decade ago, Vermont lawmakers mandated that the board submit an audit from an outside environmental consultant to determine whether the projects the state had invested in to improve water quality were working. The audit also was meant to examine whether the state’s agriculture and natural resource agencies are doing enough to enforce water quality regulations on farms, which are the biggest source of phosphorus in Lake Champlain.
Do You Live Near Lake Champlain? Help Seven Days and ProPublica Investigate Algae Blooms.
Seven Days and ProPublica have teamed up to investigate the cleanup of Lake Champlain. Have you been affected by this issue? We’d like to hear from you.
Lake Champlain has been overloaded with phosphorus-laden runoff from farms, roads and urban sewers for decades. That pollution fuels potentially toxic blue-green algae blooms that have raised health concerns and hurt the state’s tourism industry. Under sustained pressure from citizens, environmental advocates and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, Vermont’s leaders embarked on an ambitious initiative to improve the lake’s water quality, enshrined in the state’s landmark 2015 Clean Water Act.
Now, halfway through a 20-year cleanup effort mandated by the EPA, some lawmakers worry they don’t have enough information to ensure that the state is pursuing the most cost-effective cleanup strategies.
When lawmakers approved the clean water law, they took the major step of establishing a fund to pay for the cleanup and a board to administer it. Since 2016, Vermont has disbursed $928 million — $755 million in state funding and $173 million in local and federal dollars — on water quality projects and programs. That’s nearly as much as what Vermont has spent on paving and resurfacing state highways over the past decade.
As part of the law, the legislature also required the board’s leaders to provide it with a full program audit by January 2021.
But the board received no responses to an initial request for proposals in 2020. Lawmakers extended the deadline to 2023. Yet again, no outside firms bid on the audit.
Farnham said the board received informal feedback from some firms that the audit’s scope was too broad and complex. He reported back to fellow board members that he and Julie Moore, secretary of the Vermont Agency of Natural Resources, had asked legislators what to do next but didn’t receive any clear suggestions.
The board never issued a new request or revisited the matter (until Seven Days and ProPublica recently asked about it), and Vermont’s legislature never followed up to narrow the scope.
Former state Rep. David Deen, who sponsored the clean water law and retired in 2018, said he was dismayed to learn that the audit never happened.
“Personally, I find it amazing that they haven’t done that audit and that somebody in the legislature did not hold them to account to conduct that audit,” he said.
Rep. Amy Sheldon, the longtime chair of the House Committee on Environment, recalled hearing about the audit challenges but noted that it’s difficult for the legislature to follow up because Vermont’s lawmakers don’t have staff. In the other chamber, former state Sen. Chris Bray, who chaired the natural resources committee until 2025, said he did not recall hearing about the missing audit.
In an interview, Farnham acknowledged that an outside audit would be helpful. But he said the board already has robust tools for assessing progress through a yearly performance report compiled by the Vermont Department of Environmental Conservation, which coordinates and tracks most of the state’s clean water spending.
“We’ve got enough eyes coming at it from different angles that I think that mutes the need for that comprehensive audit,” he said.
The annual reporting process has improved greatly since the audit was mandated, and the DEC’s website “provides a lot of transparency,” about how the state is spending clean water money and the results, said Emily Bird, director of the department’s Water Investment Division.
But some current and former state officials say that approach isn’t a substitute for an audit to determine whether Vermont is getting adequate and cost-effective returns on its huge water quality investments.
The last independent assessment of clean water spending was a 2019 report from the state auditor. It found that a disproportionate amount of money was being spent on wastewater treatment plants, which contributed by far the smallest share of phosphorus pollution, instead of targeting bigger sources such as agriculture.
That mismatch persists seven years later. Agriculture is the largest source of phosphorus runoff, yet agricultural water quality programs receive less than a third of the total clean water funding in the current budget.
“I’d like to think they’re getting something done,” said Doug Hoffer, state auditor since 2013, referring to state agencies and legislators. “But the only way to know that is to hire someone who is independent to study that. And it’s really concerning that hasn’t been done. It really raises questions about accountability on both sides.”
An audit would do a few key things that the department’s performance reports do not, Tee Thomas, a former water finance director for the state of Vermont who now runs her own environmental consulting firm, noted via email. The reports rely on models for how effective each type of project is at reducing phosphorus. An audit would analyze water quality monitoring data from rivers and lakes to check those estimates. It would also scrutinize how well Vermont has managed projects and whether it’s gotten results, she said.
The Clean Water Fund gets, on average, $25 million to $30 million each year from the state’s rooms and meals tax, a surcharge applied to some property transfers and deposit money that consumers pay on cans and bottles. That money is paired with between $6 million and $12 million from the state’s annual capital bill, which finances infrastructure projects. The funds have gone to programs and projects to restore wetlands, expand natural buffers around fields, shore up rural roads against erosion, upgrade stormwater drains and improve manure storage on dairy farms.
The state treasurer in 2017 estimated that the cost of Vermont’s 20-year initiative would be $2.3 billion.
But finding that money could be difficult as state government spending outpaces tax revenue and cooling housing and tourism markets squeeze clean water funding sources.
Without the audit, the governor and legislators responsible for coming up with the next billion dollars’ worth of projects may not have a clear understanding of what Vermonters have gotten for the last billion, lawmakers said.
Jane Kitchel, who as longtime chair of the state Senate’s Committee on Appropriations was known for her encyclopedic knowledge of the Vermont budget, noted that a billion dollars is a significant sum for the small state. Had she not retired from the body two years ago, she said, reviving the audit “would be one of the things I’d put on my to-do list.”
The next legislative session starts in January. State Sen. Anne Watson, who chairs the Committee on Natural Resources and Energy and serves on the Committee on Appropriations, told Seven Days and ProPublica that she would likely discuss whether to revive the audit with her colleagues.
“If we value having a clean lake,” she said, “then we need to put our resources toward places that are going to make a difference, and it’s unclear to me right now that what we’re doing is effective.”

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Abdul El-Sayed Triumphed. Trump and Islamophobia Lost.
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: John Nichols
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
On Tuesday night, Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed became the first Muslim ever elected to the United States Senate—delivering the most direct and profound of the many rebukes that Republican President Donald Trump suffered as the American people thunderously transformed the country’s electoral and political landscape.
Yes, voters handed Democrats control of both chambers of Congress, creating a vital check on Trump’s presidency that substantially disempowers him in the last two years of his second term.
Yes, Republicans experienced substantial setbacks in states such as Iowa, Ohio, Kansas, South Carolina, and Texas, where Trump won with ease just two years ago—confirming the American public’s fundamental break with a historically unpopular, and now unmistakably lame-duck, president.
Yes, unprecedented wins in gubernatorial and legislative races have given Democrats the ability to turn states into laboratories of democracy that counter Trump’s pro-corporate agenda on everything from AI regulation to monopoly power, labor rights, and access to healthcare.
But the election of El-Sayed—a progressive, pro-labor, anti-racist doctor who advocated for Medicare for All, boldly called out genocide in Gaza and Trump’s war in Iran, and proudly defended his Muslim faith—struck a blow in the heart of the relentless Islamophobia that has long been a core part of the president’s political identity.
Trump did everything in his power to defeat the American-born son of immigrants from Egypt. He labeled El-Sayed a “jihadist” and “a Muslim Brotherhood guy,” and claimed that the Democrat “would be the only senator that will have to go through a metal detector before he’s allowed to go into the Senate.”
“We’ll have a hundred senators, and most of them will go directly [into the chamber],” said Trump, who at an October rally invited Republicans to laugh along with his bigotry. “We’re gonna have to get a special metal detector for Abdul.”
El-Sayed’s winning campaign against Republican Mike Rogers countered Trump’s hateful rhetoric with the most inspiring and reconciling statement of the midterms—a digital ad where El-Sayed spoke of his faith, saying:
My name is Abdul, it means “servant.”
I pray every day.
I reflect on my role in this life, on this earth.
How we leave it better than we found it.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
To serve God.
To serve our neighbors.
All across Michigan, families pray.
They feel hopeless.
Faith is a thing there’s just too little of in Washington.
We don’t have faith in our future.
We don’t have faith that we can actually fix things.
So yeah, we need a few more people of faith in Washington.
I’m Abdul El Sayed, man of faith, that’s a good thing, and I approve this message.
Michiganders heard the worst of Donald Trump’s Islamophobic hate-mongering. And they heard the best of Abdul El-Sayed’s faith-based hope. They chose hope, and sent a Muslim man of faith to the United States Senate.
So it was, early on Wednesday morning, that Abdul El-Sayed finished his campaign by saying, “to all the parents who struggled to explain to their kids why the president openly mocks someone for their name or how they pray, let them know tomorrow that the bad guys lost.”
