https://gothamist.com/news/rain-in-nyc-a.title: Rain in NYC and NJ will end weeks-long stretch of beautiful weather
https://gothamist.com/news/rain-in-nyc-a.author: Catalina Gonella
https://gothamist.com/news/rain-in-nyc-a.text:
It’s about to rain on New York City’s good weather parade.
Nearly three weeks of beautiful, clear-skied, mild weather days are coming to an end as a weather system moving through the area Thursday and Friday will bring cloudy skies and rainfall, according to the National Weather Service.
Local weather account New York Metro Weather, gives a daily weather vibes rating on X from 0 to 10. The account's been doling out 8s, 9,s and 10s from Oct. 19 through Nov. 3, with Wednesday receiving a 7 — an indication of the vibe shift to come.
John Homenuk, who runs the account, said that’s due to a persistent high pressure system that’s hung out over the area which no storm has yet been able to push away.
“When you have a stretch like this, it really is enjoyable,” he said. “It's not just one or two days and you have to kinda force yourself outside to go do something, you know? You have some options and the forecast is good for a while. So it's really nice, and you get to spend quite a bit of time outside. ”
Conditions are expected to stay dry through Wednesday with temperatures approaching 70 degrees in some parts of the city, but the National Weather Service predicts cloudy skies by the evening. A low pressure weather system approaching the area will likely bring showers in the first half of Thursday, which will be mostly cloudy with a high near 74, according to the National Weather Service.
Homenuk said he doesn’t expect “anything crazy” but the system will bring more humidity to the area and slightly cooler temperatures this weekend.
Things get a little more bleak Friday, with showers and possible thunderstorms after 1 p.m., and a high near 70 degrees, according to the NWS. The total rainfall will likely be under half an inch, which helps the area get closer to normal for the season after getting just half the normal amount of rain for October, NWS meteorologist John Murray said.
“ It could potentially be some heavy rain at times, it is possible Friday and into Friday night,” he said. “Could have some minor flooding here and there especially in your poor drainage, low-lying areas.”
But nothing lasts forever, even cold November rain. Conditions will be drier through Saturday and Sunday, though the chances of rain won’t be completely gone, and temperatures will remain unseasonably warm throughout the weekend, Murray said.

https://www.theguardian.com/news/ng-inte.title: Lab-grown meat was supposed to save the world. What happened?
https://www.theguardian.com/news/ng-inte.author: Erin Somers
https://www.theguardian.com/news/ng-inte.text:
On 5 August 2013, a man and a woman ate a burger. Not just any burger: a world-historic burger, made from cattle cells grown in a laboratory by Mark Post, a professor of vascular physiology at Maastricht University in the Netherlands. The burger had taken two years to produce and cost €250,000 (about £210,000 at the time), money furnished by the Google co-founder Sergey Brin. Now it was being tasted in public for the first time at Riverside Studios in London, at an event attended by 200 members of the press and livestreamed to thousands.
To make this particular burger, Post had extracted stem cells from the shoulder muscle of a living cow, then cultivated them in plastic containers filled with a nutrient-rich supplement called foetal bovine serum, which is derived from cow foetuses. The cells eventually became 20,000 strands of tissue, which in turn became a single 140g patty. Post believed that beef produced this way had the potential to dramatically reduce greenhouse-gas emissions and slow the climate crisis. Raising cattle for consumption requires massive amounts of land and water – and massive amounts of feed grown at a high environmental cost. He projected that global demand for meat would soon outstrip our ability to produce it the old-fashioned way, at which point our food systems would become unsustainable. But that didn’t have to mean a mass recalibration of our consumption habits or a global shift away from red meat. Post and his team had found another way.
Standing at a blond-wood island on an otherwise empty soundstage, Post lifted the kind of stainless-steel cloche usually found on a room service cart to reveal his creation. The raw patty sat in a petri dish on a bare plate, where it shone wetly under the studio lights. With the ITV London anchor Nina Hossain presiding, a Cornish chef named Richard McGeown pan-fried the burger in sunflower oil and butter for two volunteer tasters: Josh Schonwald, the Chicago-based author of The Taste of Tomorrow: Dispatches from the Future of Food, and Hanni Rützler, an Austrian nutrition scientist. So precious was this meat that they were given just the one burger to share between them. It was served deconstructed, alongside a sesame-seed bun, lettuce and tomato – showmanship to sell the burger a bit, give it context. The patty itself was reddish brown, flat and perfectly circular. When Schonwald and Rützler cut it, the burger did not bleed.
The two of them ate with forks and knives, passing the plate, sawing off thoughtful bites. Chewing slowly. Afterwards, they rendered their verdicts. “I would say it is somewhere on the spectrum between a Boca Burger and McDonald’s,” Schonwald told a reporter from NBC. “The absence of fat makes a big difference. It has the texture, which I was not expecting. It was like an animal-protein cake.” Rützler noted the burger’s blandness to a reporter from Science. “There is room for improvement here,” she said. At the end of the event, about €113,000 worth of burger remained uneaten. But none of this stopped Post from predicting that meat cultivated in a lab would become a consumer product within the decade.
The event – the theatrical reveal, the PR spectacle – triggered a kind of gold rush. One hundred and forty companies sprang up in six continents, trying to replicate what Post had done with beef across a range of other species: chicken, pork, fish, even quail. Investment to the tune of $3bn (£2.2bn) flooded into the sector. True believers claimed that cellular agriculture would not only fight the climate crisis and global food insecurity but also slow the spread of zoonotic disease and antibiotic resistance. A company called Upside Foods touted its plans to “set the new standard for meat” and to “make meat a force of good in the world”. A company called Vow created an enormous woolly mammoth meatball, though no one was allowed to eat it, since the DNA came from a fossil and the company didn’t know whether it was actually fit for human consumption. The thinktank RethinkX predicted that cultivated meat would decimate the US beef industry by 2030, reducing demand for the conventional variety by a whopping 70%. As the organisation wrote, “We are already on the cusp of the deepest, fastest, most consequential disruption in food and agricultural production since the first domestication of plants and animals 10,000 years ago.”
And yet, despite the frenzy, the meat itself never arrived. The challenges were numerous. There was the exorbitant upfront cost of building manufacturing facilities and the daunting amounts of energy required to run them. There was the difficulty of producing sufficient quantities of the stuff, at a price point low enough for people to buy. There was the lack of a highly skilled workforce trained to operate the new technology. There were rounds and rounds of inspections by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the US Department of Agriculture (USDA). There was even, occasionally, the unwanted appearance of rodent DNA in research samples, which happened to the companies Upside and Eat Just. After peaking in 2021, investment began to fall off. In 2023, the industry raised a measly $177m globally.
But it wasn’t only venture capitalists who had started to grow sceptical of cultivated meat. The technology soon became a target of conservatives. The state governments of Florida, Alabama, Mississippi, Indiana, Montana, Nebraska and Texas moved in quick succession to legislate against cultivated meat, passing laws that banned its sale, production, or both. The Florida governor Ron DeSantis made a media event out of signing that state’s law, posing for pictures in front of a blood-stained cutting board piled high with steaks. “Take your fake lab-grown meat elsewhere,” he said. “We’re not doing that in the state of Florida.” In 2024, the industrial biotech consultant Joel Stone told the New York Times that, if he had to put odds on it, the likelihood of the industry producing even 10% of the meat supply in the foreseeable future “would be zero”. Today, cultivated meat is available for purchase at just one store in the world: Huber’s Butchery in Singapore, where customers can buy packages of lab-grown chicken shreds from a manufacturer called GOOD Meat.
These developments were inconvenient for me, a person who became obsessed with the prospect of tasting cell-grown meat just as the possibility of ever doing so seemed to recede before my eyes. I was enthralled by the story of the meat, which seemed to contain so much of what defined this era of American life: dubious techno-optimism, bombastic culture-war posturing, carnival oddities like the mammoth meatball. It presented a snarl of competing motives, a mix of altruism and cold-blooded striving for capital (nothing can ever exist just for the common good; it has to make someone a billionaire). There was also the fact that I had been a vegetarian for almost 20 years.
The last meat I ever ate was a hotdog at Shea Stadium in New York in 2007. I don’t remember how it tasted – probably like every other hotdog I had eaten before. I washed it down with an exorbitantly priced but very cold Budweiser in one of those metal bottles. I quit eating meat after that, not because the hotdog had been disgusting but because I didn’t like the sensation of the inevitable bad bite, the periodic tangle with gristle or tendon or bone. Then my abstention grew into habit, and the habit was reinforced by other concerns: the catastrophic environmental consequences of industrial meat production; the creeping doubt, as I grow older, that I’m necessarily higher in the cosmic order than a chicken or a cow. But cultivated meat raised a compelling question. If you could subtract some of the downsides – make meat less destructive, engineer away its aesthetic flaws – what reason would there be not to eat it?
This question had begun to feel moot as the potential of cultivated meat grew less and less promising. But just when it seemed as though Post’s vision would never be realised, encouraging news emerged from a surprising place: North Carolina. In May 2024, when many of his peers were fleeing the sector, Jeff Bezos granted $30m through his Earth Fund to establish the Bezos Center for Sustainable Protein at North Carolina State University, an initiative dedicated to developing “dietary proteins that are environmentally friendly, healthy, tasty and affordable”. The donation cemented the state’s status as a new global centre of the cultivated-meat industry. The Bezos Center would join the North Carolina Biotechnology Center, an economic development organisation for the life sciences in Research Triangle Park.
On the commercial side of things, Believer Meats, an Israeli company producing cultivated chicken, had recently broken ground on a 200,000 sq ft manufacturing plant in Wilson, North Carolina. The plant would be the largest cultivated-meat facility in the world – capable, the company claimed, of producing 9.5m kilos of engineered chicken per year.
In September 2025, Believer received a “no questions” letter from the FDA, indicating that the agency did not encounter safety concerns in its inspection of the company’s products. “We are proud to be commercialising in this state, creating high-quality manufacturing jobs and enabling us to realise our vision to lead food innovations that care for the planet,” said Believer’s then CEO, a man named (for real) Gustavo Burger, in a press release celebrating the milestone. I got in touch with the company shortly after. In a Zoom meeting with Heather Hudson, Believer’s chief product and growth officer, and Rodrigo Lavall, from sales and marketing, the two dangled the possibility of a ribbon-cutting ceremony. They could tentatively plan something and invite me down to visit.
The whole thing felt a bit Wonka-ish. No one from the press had been allowed inside the factory yet. Only a few professionals in the field had even toured it. Why should I get the golden ticket? But I tried not to question my good fortune. Excited by the prospect of exclusive access, I started planning a trip to the Triangle. If lab-grown meat had a future, I might find it there. Maybe, I thought, I’d even get to taste it.
On a mild day in early December, I arrived at NC State’s sprawling campus, home to about 40,000 students. I expected it to be lively, teeming with kids, but it was eerily dead. Rohan Shirwaiker, the friendly, bespectacled director of the Bezos Center, met me in a pristine building where I didn’t see a single student. Everyone, he explained, had gone home for the holidays.
The Bezos Center aims to address, as its website puts it, the “critical barriers and gaps” still dogging cultivated meat. The process has changed as the industry scales up. It’s no longer Post labouring over a single burger in his lab for years at a time. Cultivation now takes place in sterile factories that look more like breweries, with cells grown not in culture dishes but in giant, stainless-steel bioreactors. Producers have also moved away from feeding the cells with foetal bovine serum, which is expensive and requires harvesting cow blood from slaughterhouses (not exactly a good look for a cruelty-free alternative meat product). The industry now relies on what is referred to as “serum-free media”, or SFM, proprietary compounds that vary from company to company. Still, the basic science remains the same: in one typical version of the process, stem cells are harvested from a living animal via needle biopsy, then nourished in solutions containing glucose, vitamins, fats, minerals, proteins and amino acids, which are swished around inside a reactor to ensure an even diffusion of nutrients. In these conditions, the cells divide, multiply and differentiate just as they would inside an animal. They are ready for harvesting when they reach the desired density: roughly within two to eight weeks, depending on the species being cultivated.
But what also remains is one of the industry’s fundamental challenges. You cannot simply grow a steak – yank it out of the reactor and slap it on the table at a restaurant – because a steak contains multiple kinds of tissue. At the moment, muscle and fat can only be cultivated separately, and typically they do not form solid matter but a semisolid slurry that must be taken from the reactors, washed, combined with other ingredients for flavour and texture, and extruded or 3D-printed into something you would recognise as meat: a burger or a nugget or a meatball or a fillet. Some companies are trying to circumnavigate the slurry stage by building scaffolding inside reactors for cells to cling to, producing a firmer product. (Certain types of cells don’t like floating in a tank all free like that. Tissue, I’m told, wants to adhere to bone.)
The cost of all this has come way down since Schonwald called Post’s burger an “animal-protein cake”, but right now, cultivated meat is far more expensive than the real thing. At Huber’s, in Singapore, the ominously named GOOD Meat 3, which contains only 3% chicken cells, sells for $5.62 (£4.20) per 110g serving. Meanwhile, chicken at my local supermarket, containing 100% animal cells, starts at $3.49 per 450g.
Shirwaiker took me on a tour of the Bezos Center’s brand new protein lab, which was still being set up. It was spacious and filled with light, lined with 3D printers and a humming but empty stainless-steel fridge. The printers, in particular, were huge and impressive. But the lab was still in the early phases of assembly; cables dangled from the ceiling, waiting for equipment that had yet to be delivered.
As Shirwaiker and I walked back to his office, we discussed the day’s shocking headline: while I was travelling to North Carolina from my home in upstate New York, news broke that Believer Meats was being sued for $34m by Gray Construction, the firm that built its hulking factory in Wilson. Believer had recently defaulted on an agreement to pay Gray an instalment of $22m. Maybe I should have seen it coming: after her initial enthusiasm, Hudson, my contact at Believer, had ghosted me in the days leading up to my trip.
I asked Shirwaiker what all this meant. He was as surprised as I was. He thought that the plant was so close to opening that the staff just needed to turn on the lights and boot up the chicken vats. No one knows yet what happened at Believer, he told me. It was unclear whether the company would survive.
Before I left the Bezos Center, Shirwaiker introduced me to the concept of the Gartner Hype Cycle. To me, it had the ring of an old concept, a framework invented in the mid-20th century by an economist or a professor. But no: it was formulated in 1995 by a woman named Jackie Fenn, who worked at the consultancy firm Gartner. Its purpose, according to a YouTube video made by the company, is to help you – a savvy investor, the video assumes – “understand the real risks and opportunities of an innovation so you can avoid adopting something too early, giving up too soon, adopting too late, or hanging on too long”.
Shirwaiker showed me a chart to illustrate. The x-axis was time, and the y-axis was visibility. The cycle begins with an “innovation trigger”, when a new technology is introduced to great fanfare, then arcs upward toward the “peak of inflated expectations” as excitement mounts. But this rise is inevitably followed by a dramatic fall, when investors realise how difficult it’s going to be to actually commercialise the innovation. Later comes a gentler climb up the “slope of enlightenment”, when second- and third-generation products emerge, until, finally, we reach the “plateau of productivity”, the slow, unflashy development of the technology. If Post’s burger was the innovation trigger, I asked Shirwaiker, where were we now? He circled the deep valley in the middle of the chart: the “trough of disillusionment”.
Before leaving campus, I tried Hudson again. I let her know that I was in the area and asked if I should “stop by”, as though the Believer facility were a conveniently located coffee shop rather than a meat factory in a rural area. I immediately received an auto-response that her email account was no longer active. Then I thought, what the hell, and decided to drive out to Wilson, about 45 minutes from Raleigh. I’ll go to see what’s up, I figured. I’ll talk to someone face-to-face, have some sort of confrontation with a person overseeing the plant – maybe even Hudson herself.
Rural North Carolina felt enormous, flat and empty. The landscape was almost featureless; huge swaths of nothing streamed by, and then I hit factories. Believer was located among a loose cluster of manufacturing facilities. To get there, I had to turn off a main strip containing a Chick-fil-A, a Bojangles, a McDonald’s and a Best-N-Burgers. At one point, I yielded to the flashing lights of what I thought was an emergency vehicle, only to find, as it passed, that it was a pickup truck towing a meat smoker. I was surrounded by the stuff. I thought of Post’s prediction that demand for meat would soon outstrip our ability to produce it. Sometimes it seems that this will happen tomorrow.
What I found when I got to Believer was grimmer than I expected. Not a chipper-then-confused-then-annoyed desk clerk wondering who this was showing up at a meat factory without an appointment, but no one at all. The facility was deserted, gated: a royal-blue cube under a pale late-autumn sky, millions of dollars of groundbreaking technology locked inside.
There is a widespread feeling in the US that everything is a hoax or a Ponzi scheme, and this feeling is only reinforced by the news. The news that self-driving taxis, when they become confused, are actually operated remotely from the Philippines. The news that the mysterious invention that could scan your blood for any number of disorders was an era-defining scam. The news that the crypto entrepreneur who pledged to secure the longtime survival of the human race was actually stealing $8bn of his customers’ money to fund his polycule in the Bahamas. I became paranoid, standing in front of the abandoned car park, that cultivated meat was just another lie, or a semi-lie, or a bluff. That the reason the meat was so difficult to get my hands on was that it did not exist. The possible implosion of Believer was disappointing not just because it represented a setback in the quest to reduce our carbon emissions and fortify our food systems against climate collapse, but because it seemed to confirm that we live in a cheap, mendacious world, where what passes for progress almost always turns out to be a confidence game.
The morning after my reconnaissance mission, more news broke: Believer was declaring bankruptcy and would shutter the factory in Wilson before it printed a single chicken strip.
I had timed my trip to North Carolina to coincide with the first annual Global Forum for Plant-Based and Alternative Proteins, held at the North Carolina Biotechnology Center. This was how I found myself cloistered among the faithful as their meat dreams unravelled in real time. All the local industry players were in attendance, and more had flown in from around the world. We were sitting together in NCBiotech’s blandly carpeted lecture hall for the opening session, listening to optimistic remarks about international collaboration, an opaque joke about an extruder, a shout-out to “Ian in the back from the insect side”, all the while knowing that the industry’s biggest gambit yet had just failed. With Believer gone bust, I hoped to salvage a glimmer of optimism for the industry from the day’s proceedings – or, at the very least, an honest assessment of what had gone wrong.
During a break in the programme, everyone filed out and congregated in the atrium. We were in the trough of disillusionment, but we were also in the divot of gossip. We were in the furrow of hanging around outside the auditorium talking excitedly. We were in the ravine of wanting to know what the hell had happened. I was surrounded by guys in crisp button-ups and thermal gilets and navy-blue blazers. There were not a ton of women present. All around me, speculation began to fly.
“There was a time about three or four years ago, post-pandemic, the money was so easy to come by. All you had to do was put a pitch deck together, and VCs would throw money at you.”
“They have a pretty star list of investors.”
“Yeah. That doesn’t guarantee a success.”
“They got the building up. The building is ready to, like, turn on.”
“It’s probably gonna be a liquidation. Again, we’re all assuming. We don’t know what the heck’s going on.”
“There’s got to be some news out of Israel.”
Later, we heard from venture capitalists who had no choice but to address the news head on. “I mean, elephant in the room: Believer Meats just down the road basically went out of business,” said Steve Simitzis, from Replicator VC, a firm that invests in early-stage food-tech companies. “I don’t have any information about it, but I would speculate that building factories around technology that isn’t ready at scale is probably a cause.” Well, duh, I thought. The VCs on the panel saw Believer as a cautionary tale. Don’t scale too quickly. Lower costs. Make something consumers actually want to eat. All these observations were sensible, even obvious, and yet wasn’t it also the case that the VCs themselves had put pressure on companies like Believer to expand rapidly in order to provide the returns they sought?
In the afternoon, we all tried to rally for a tasting of products by food startups. At last, I was sampling things. I drank some kind of fizzy peach tea. It was not immediately obvious to me what the innovation was, so I asked the young guy handing out the cans about it. It’s supposed to be refreshing, he said. Like after a run you can drink one and it won’t make you puke. Curiously, though, there was no cultivated meat on offer. The Research Triangle may be an industry hub, but the product did not seem to be available here. The product was still a prototype, or the product was too expensive to give out as samples. The closest thing on hand was plant-based vegan meat. I tried wheat-based turkey and wheat-based pepperoni from a company called The BE Hive. I tried “some kind of pulled meat”, as the person wheeling it out from the kitchen described it, from a company called Delight Soy. It had a stringy texture and was an orangish brown. I tried a fungi-and-soy-based salmon substitute from a company called Juicy Marbles. This one was very close to tasting like salmon. They had got something right, everyone around me agreed. To our wonder and dismay, Juicy Marbles had nailed the fishiness. Probably algae in there, someone remarked. We nodded. Yes, probably algae.
The experience was nauseating, though the cube of salmon tasted good. Or rather, it would have tasted good if you could isolate taste from the other senses. Like, if you didn’t see the morsel of fake fish, or feel it in your mouth, or smell its oily smell. And if you didn’t also know that it was synthetic. The knowing added a layer of queasiness. The idea that they would infuse soy with an unappealing smell for verisimilitude – a cloying, marine smell, like the hold of a fishing boat.
So all it would take for this thing to be palatable would be to experience it in a sensory vacuum and preferably context-free, or immediately after a blow to the head that wipes out everything you know about it. Then it would be pretty nice.
In January, a few weeks after my trip to the Research Triangle, a man ate a chicken sandwich. He ate two, actually: one made with conventional chicken and one made with a cultivated fillet. In a video of his visit to the Upside Foods factory in California, he stands next to a vat of swirling chicken cells. The cells are foamy, the cheerful yellow of Campbell’s broth. The man’s name is Jimmy Donaldson, though he’s known more widely as the YouTube sensation MrBeast, and he thinks that cell-grown meat has a lot of advantages. “These chickens don’t get diseases,” says MrBeast. “So then you don’t have to worry about a disease spreading on the farm and then you eating a sick chicken.” When it’s time to try to guess which sandwich is which, he can’t do it. “I honestly can’t tell,” he says, before guessing wrong.
Watching the video on my phone, it irked me that MrBeast had tasted the meat. That should have been me standing next to the churning chicken water. For months I’d been trying to find cultivated meat on the east coast; I had even considered buying it from Singapore on the grey market. Nothing panned out. Finally, Rohan Shirwaiker sent me details for a public tasting in the Bay Area held by Mission Barns, another partner of the Bezos Center. It would take place at the supermarket Berkeley Bowl West, which had previously sold a limited run of the company’s meatballs.
On a Friday in February, I flew out to San Francisco and got a cab over to the Mission Barns office, which was located in SoMa, on a desolate and unlovely block of warehouses. Not many Waymos swooping by out there, but at least it felt appropriately industrial, with the office upstairs and bioreactors below. Not that I got to see them: when I asked, I was gently rebuffed with the excuse that the company was in the process of moving to a larger facility in Alameda. I felt the ambient paranoia I’d experienced in North Carolina start to kick in again. After the collapse of Believer, Mission Barns seemed like one of the American companies closest to having its products on grocery-store shelves. At the end of last year, it received USDA approval for its cultivated pork fat. At the time of my visit, its products included bacon, pepperoni, meatballs and a couple varieties of sausage.
Bianca Lê, a smiley, put-together Australian and the then head of external affairs at Mission Barns, took me up to the company’s third-floor office, which contained a large kitchen on one side. As we sat at the wooden island, she told me about the origin of the cells for all of the company’s cultivated fat: a single Yorkshire pig named Dawn who was still, according to the company’s marketing materials, “happily roaming free” in an animal sanctuary in upstate New York, not far from where I live. Dawn reminded me of Dolly the sheep – a mascot for something much larger than herself. One wants to picture her soulful.
“Can I ask how Dawn was selected?” I said, hoping to hear something about Dawn as a superior specimen, the fattest, happiest, healthiest, smartest pig in the US.
“Yeah, honestly, it’s not that interesting of a story,” said Lê. “It’s just that she was available.”
The Mission Barns cultivation process takes about two weeks. At the end, they drain the bioreactors until they are left with just the fat slurry. “It’s white, it’s semisolid, it’s really pasty,” Lê said. That slurry is then combined with plant protein to create the final product, which typically contains less than 10% of animal cells per serving. I tried to understand how they got the fat out of one container and into the next, miming a large scoop or shovel, but this part was a secret. The company’s ultimate goal, Lê told me, wasn’t even to sell products but to license the system itself.
Mission Barns’s then CEO, Cecilia Chang, appeared: another smiley, put-together Australian. As she joined us at the counter, I asked her about the biggest challenges the company faces. “The timeline on being able to get costs down fast enough to get to a point of profitability,” she said. “The technology is there, but investors have really aggressive timelines.” Chang also mentioned a newer hurdle: the distrust of food science stoked by Donald Trump’s secretary of health and human services, Robert F Kennedy Jr. Still, the industry was trying to look at Kennedy’s Make America Healthy Again movement as an opportunity rather than as a disaster. After all, MAHA is focused on protein; Kennedy’s new, inverted food pyramid features steak at the very top. And, although the movement broadly disdains processed foods, Chang told me, it may appreciate that cell-cultivated meat is usually organic and antibiotic-free. I recalled the lay wisdom of MrBeast: “These chickens don’t get diseases.”
As we chatted, Zachary Tyndall, Mission Barns’s product-development and culinary manager, prepared some meat for me in a frying pan. Tyndall is a former chef who once worked at the three-Michelin-star restaurant Noma, an apprenticeship that seemed unnecessary for the level of cooking involved here. He used a spatula to roll a single meatball around in a pan. The meat was a pale, pinkish beige, like real pork. It’s not that different from cooking conventional meat, he told me, though maybe a little bit quicker, since the company’s meatballs are precooked and only need reheating. It smelled savoury, like food, and indeed, it was food. I’ll give it that.
I received my meatball on a tastefully speckled earthenware plate. Though nearly delirious with excitement, I tried to zoom out for a second and glimpse the situation with objectivity. I was looking at a single small meatball in the middle of a plate in a chilly, industrial office thousands of miles away from home. This was what I had elected to pursue over the course of months with single-minded determination. With all eyes on me, I used the fork to cut it in half and took a bite.
The taste. The taste was not terrible. It was seasoned, oregano-heavy. It even had a kick. Everyone was watching as I chewed, so I feigned deep consideration, the way you do when the waiter brings you a sample of wine at a restaurant. “Hmm,” I mused. I am contemplating the tasting notes, my face said. I am weighing the mouthfeel. I tasted the salami too, which looked exactly like regular salami. It tasted like salty paper. Salty paper with a kick – they’re good about putting in the kick. I could not find much to say to Chang and Lê about the meat, though I tried. The phrase “blandly inoffensive” came to mind. The word “anticlimax” came to mind. This was what I had come all this way for? To eat something that felt like mushy cardboard in my mouth?
“It’s good,” I managed to tell them. Then, suddenly, the nausea hit, a taste of vomit in the back of my throat. It was the Juicy Marbles effect again. The problem was not the flavour, not the texture, but the knowing. The Knowing. Knowing about the fat tank, about the sticky white substance. The envisioning of the scoop. The knowing about Dawn, an ordinary pig who was available, and the extraction process that took her cells. Earlier, I’d thought this feeling was triggered entirely by Juicy Marbles’s ersatz fish odour, by its inherent artificiality. I hoped it would be different with the cultivated meat, which was, in the end, an actual animal product, at least in part. But no. If anything, it was worse.
The next day at Berkeley Bowl West, a large grocery store across the Bay, I watched a couple of dozen customers line up to taste the meatballs. Lê explained that Mission Barns has a fanbase, people who follow the company’s progress and register for events in advance. Here, a new contingent of the public revealed itself to me: my fellow cultivated-meat-curious. They were young and slightly goth. They were gen-Z vegans with lip rings and huge black trousers that flapped in the wind. Aside from these devotees, the crowd was made up mostly of people who happened to be at the grocery store for other reasons: Saturday shoppers, parents with kids in tow, people in athleisure. It was a warm and sunny February morning, a good day for a free sample. Passersby queued up, mildly interested.
Previous tastings had drawn protesters. In 2024, the week before the Florida cultivated-meat ban went into effect, Upside Foods hosted the Freedom of Food pop-up, a tasting on a Miami rooftop that was pitched as a protest of the new law. A chef from Caja Caliente, a restaurant in Coral Gables, made chicken tostadas with chipotle crema while a group of conventional-meat zealots parked a van in front of the venue’s entrance. The van was affixed with a huge LED screen displaying criticism of lab-grown meat. No long-term health studies, it read. Secret chemical formulas.
But nothing like that happened in Berkeley. Tyndall stood at a hot plate, gamely rolling the meatballs around a pan and placing them into small bamboo trays. As the samples were distributed, I made myself eat another one to see if my reaction would be the same as the day before. Instantly, I was clobbered by the Knowing, but around me, muffled sounds of approval rose from the crowd. A few people told me, shrugging, that the texture seemed right. A child, maybe two years old, accepted a meatball from her dad. She ate it happily, bobbing around like little kids do, with no objection.
A woman in a fleece jacket walked around asking tasters to fill out a survey on an iPad. She was an independent researcher conducting a study on consumer acceptance of cultivated meat for Tufts University. After the science, this is one of the biggest challenges to the product’s long-term success. Do people actually want to try it? Do they want to incorporate it into their diets? According to a report published last year by the Good Food Institute, a nonprofit dedicated to promoting alternative proteins, only 18% of Americans find cell-cultivated meat extremely or very appealing, and almost 60% say they are somewhat or very unlikely to buy it. Interest typically decreases with age and increases with educational attainment, which tracked with my own observations. The goth college students were the most excited by the meatballs, but even they were muted in their praise. No one said “I love it” or “Hell yeah” or declared it a triumph. I did not hear the word “yum”.
The days of cultivated meat as a possible panacea for the climate crisis are long gone. Many of the industry’s biggest players – the ones still in business, anyway – are now embracing a more modest role in our food system. Since I tried its meatballs earlier this year, Mission Barns has announced a new strategy: it is pivoting from retail to wholesale and developing new products that will combine plant protein with conventional pork fat – to be replaced by their own, cultivated fat only once they’ve achieved a certain scale. Elsewhere, cellular agriculture is being used to create exclusive novelty items that could be fairly described as Frankenmeat, whereby their freakiness and limited availability are not liabilities but rather the selling points. Vow, the Australian company behind the mammoth meatball, has also developed a variety of Japanese quail foie gras as part of its objective to craft meats “unconstrained” by “the limits of nature”. Why, one might wonder? No real reason, except that they can. This, at least, feels like a more fitting use for cultivation technology and a more honest reflection of the ecosystem that has financed it.
This isn’t to say that engineered food needs to be virtuous to justify its existence. Before I left Berkeley Bowl West, Dixon gave me a tour of the store’s produce section, which was filled with the inordinate splendour of California. There must have been 20 varieties of crazy-looking mushrooms. She insisted I take two sumo citrus oranges – the ones with the bump on top – back home with me. Sumos aren’t naturally occurring; they were created in the 1970s by Japanese scientists who crossbred two citrus hybrids in a bid to produce a more flavourful, seedless fruit that might sell better than existing varieties.
I peeled a sumo and ate it as I walked through Berkeley. The afternoon was hot and windy, but the orange was sweet, hydrating, refreshing. Enormous and delicious. It was one shade paler than a traffic cone, with a palm-filling heft. It was perfect: a perfect example of an orange. A miracle, really, how it had just been handed to me.
A longer version of this piece appeared in the September edition of Harper’s

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/05/b.title: Election Recap: Street Safety and Transit Won Big Across the Empire State on Tuesday
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/05/b.author: Dave Colon
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/05/b.text:
New York backers of mass transit, livable streets and cities won big on Tuesday, as Democrats vanquished foes of congestion pricing, sent street safety champions to Congress and re-elected a governor who has enthusiastically embraced transit.
Congestion pricing’s mightiest haters turn out to be extremely meek
Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman and U.S. Rep. Mike Lawler (R-Hudson Valley for a couple more months) made a big show of opposing congestion pricing. Blakeman promised to end the toll and attacked the MTA throughout his campaign. Lawler, for his part, spent the past few years lying and whining about the same toll.
Neither politician survived Tuesday’s wave. Blakeman couldn’t even find enough voters in Nassau County who were mad enough about congestion pricing to lift him to victory on his home turf, and Lawler conceded to his opponent Cait Conley before midnight — even before election workers in Westchester County could hand-count a quarter-million ballots in the Democratic stronghold.
Elected officials should remember this fact about congestion pricing: fewer than 300,000 people drive cars into Manhattan’s Central Business District every single day from around this vast metropolitan area. There are simply not enough drivers whose opposition to congestion pricing would propel you to higher office.
Gov. Hochul, America’s transit champion, must build Nassau County II
In 2023, Gov. Hochul dreamed of solving New York State’s housing crisis by upzoning certain parts of the New York City metropolitan region that had spent decades refusing to build new homes. Her commendable ambition died on the rocks of her own inexperience and the catchy but evil chant, “Local control, not Hochul control.”
But that was three years ago. Get ready to learn Hochul control, not local control. In addition to trouncing Bruce Blakeman across the Empire State, America’s most prominent Bills fan won Nassau County — her opponent’s home and a longstanding metonym for NIMBYism.
If there was ever a time to go big on transit-oriented development and finding a way to fit one million more people into Nassau, this is the time to push it through. Nearly 80 percent of New York State voters support the construction of multifamily housing around transit stops.
Furthermore, Hochul now has time to fulfill an impressive slate of pending projects, including the Interborough Express, the second phase of the Second Avenue Subway, the 125th Street crosstown subway, Penn Access and the joint city-state plan to speed up buses. Hochul will oversee the creation of one more MTA capital plan during her new term, when the agency publishes its 2030-2034 five-year plan. She’ll be responsible for the headache of funding that plan, too.
Southern Brooklyn gets the blues
Recent election cycles have seen southern Brooklyn going increasingly Republican, as Democrats wrote off the region and conservatives made inroads among immigrant populations frustrated by crime or prices. But, as in so many states across the country, Republicans managed to completely alienate those voters by rewarding these them with ICE raids and tariffs that made their lives here harder and more expensive.
Republican State Sen. Steve Chan and Assembly members Lester Chang, Alec Brook-Krasny and Michael Novakhov all lost to Democratic challengers in districts that encompass neighborhoods including Bensonhurst, Sunset Park, Bay Ridge, Midwood and Sheepshead Bay.
Streetsblog readers may remember Novakhov as the pol who essentially defended speeding after a recidivist speeder struck and killed a mom and two children on Ocean Parkway. He later signed on to the “Stop Super Speeder” bill that passed in Albany earlier this year.
It’s a bird! It’s a plane! It’s a supermajority!
In January, Democrats will control at least 46 out of 63 seats in the state Senate, giving them a historically comfortable supermajority in the upper chamber of the legislature. That provides a big cushion if legislators want to override Hochul’s veto on any of their priorities, and leaves room for defections from bills that certain members might find unpalatable.
For Streetsblog purposes, the supermajority will include two new street safety champions into the senate: Nyack Mayor Joe Rand and Dutchess County Legislator Lisa Kaul. Both stressed their livable streets bonafides in office and on the campaign trail. Rand wants to make his district more walkable and bikeable and also wants better MTA operations west of the Hudson Valley, while Kaul has talked about dragging the New York State Department of Transportation’s attitude out of the car-centric thinking of the 1950s and 1960s.
The safe streets route to Congress
With the formality of the election out of the way, New York’s Congressional delegation will add at least three new members with a real interest in street safety. Micah Lasher told Streetsblog in June that he believes the federal government should make street safety a condition for getting transportation funding, and locally he said that he welcomed the 72nd Street bike lane proposal.
Brad Lander is an extremely well-known quantity on street safety. As a City Council member, he devised the Dangerous Vehicle Abatement Program in order to give the city’s automated camera enforcement some teeth, and constantly provided oversight of the city’s failure to properly implement it. Lander supported the Ninth Street protected bike lane, the redesign of Fourth Avenue and answered the Dave Colon Open Challenge in 2025. In Washington, he’ll push to create a 50-50 split between highway and transit funding for surface transportation rather than the current 80-20 split towards highways.
The pair will head to the capital with Claire Valdez, who will succeed Nydia Velázquez in Congress and penned an ambitious vision for federal involvement in transportation for Streetsblog. Valdez wants to pursue ideas like funding the QueensLink, giving more federal money to cycling infrastructure, sending money from the FHWA directly to cities instead of routing the money through state DOTs and directing more federal money to mass transit accessibility projects.
U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, meanwhile, seems poised to run for higher office — either the senate or presidency. Ocasio-Cortez talked about changing the 80-20 split, and a lot more, on a bike ride with Streetsblog earlier this year:
Mamdani voters delivered for Hochul
Gov. Hochul ran up the score big time in New York City, capturing 76 percent of Gotham’s vote. Even though he wasn’t on the ballot this time, Mayor Mamdani can claim some credit.
Analyst Michael Lange found that in the Mamdani-friendly Commie Corridor, Hochul’s vote share rose by 38 percent, compared to 18 percent in the rest of the city.
Two of Mamdani’s big campaign promises, free buses and universal childcare, will require state help to come to fruition. That means Hochul must either raise taxes or find a couple billion dollars in the state’s couch cushions.
Between the Assembly and state Senate, Mamdani and the Democratic Socialists of America sent 11 legislators to Albany to support the mayor’s agenda. Next year, Hochul and Mamdani will find out what each can get out of the other when neither has to worry about an election.
Mamdani’s show of force also had some closer-to-home implications: All five of ballot initiatives passed, including Proposal 1 to speed up outdoor dining approvals and Proposal 3 to clear bureaucratic hoops that slow bike lane and bus lane implementation.
Dave Colon is a reporter from Long Beach, a barrier island off of the coast of Long Island that you can bike to from the city. It’s a real nice ride. He’s previously been the editor of Brokelyn, a reporter at Gothamist, a freelance reporter and delivered freshly baked bread by bike.
The driver, Timothy McVey, 41, of Staten Island, turned himself in at the 62nd Precinct station house and was booked for failure to yield and failure to exercise due care

https://gothamist.com/news/even-in-defea.title: Even in defeat, a reclusive NJ Republican remained secluded to the last vote
https://gothamist.com/news/even-in-defea.author: David Brand
https://gothamist.com/news/even-in-defea.text:
Tom Kean went out quietly.
It was a familiar posture for the two-term Republican member of Congress.
Kean spent his election night party holed up in a swanky Basking Ridge hotel and banquet hall, banishing reporters from Gothamist and four other news outlets to the covered stone portico outside where a trickle of Republican Party officials passed through on their way into the gathering.
Many stopped near the wooden front doors to muse about their party’s chances. But their moods chilled as the temperature outside dropped and the election results rolled in. By 9:45 p.m., a steady flow of Kean supporters began leaving, muttering words like “depressing,” “grim” and “sad” to describe the mood.
Polls suggested that Republicans would face a tough election considered a referendum on President Donald Trump, whose favorability ratings have plummeted in New Jersey amid skyrocketing prices and an unpopular war with Iran. The polls proved correct, as Democratic challenger Rebecca Bennett defeated Kean to represent New Jersey’s 7th Congressional District.
Kean delivered a brief speech thanking his supporters and campaign staff, according to seven attendees. But former Morris County Executive Dick Kamin clarified, “It wasn’t a concession.”
Still, reporters couldn’t see or even hear it. Kean’s campaign did not provide access to a stream or recording of the closed-door meeting when asked after polls closed Tuesday.
The closed-door event mirrored the incumbent Republican’s public posturing throughout his four years in office.
Kean, the scion of a Jersey political dynasty, steadfastly refused to talk with the media during his two terms, at times greeting reporters’ persistent questioning with stone-faced silence.
Nor did Kean talk much with constituents. He did not hold town halls in the district, which spans a large swath of North Jersey from the edge of Staten Island to the Pennsylvania border, and he shunned most public appearances.
In March, he took an abrupt leave of absence from Congress, vanishing with no explanation and missing over 100 votes.
After months of speculation, Kean reemerged and returned to work in late June, explaining that he had been receiving treatment for serious depression.
Kean’s friends and supporters stood by him Tuesday, even as polls forecasted a loss.
Connie Wygara, a retiree serving on the Tewksbury school board, conceded that Kean was a “low-key” figure but said he nonetheless won victories for the district, like an increase to the State and Local Tax deduction, despite opposition from many other Republicans.
Business consultant Jacqui Cleary of Westfield described herself as a longtime friend of Kean’s and said she thought he did enough to connect with voters.
“He’s a thinker, and he keeps things brief,” Cleary said. “And so I'm okay with him being low-key. He's effective in what he does.”
And Ruth Dilley, a retired school paraprofessional and Kean supporter from Readington Township, said she was unbothered by his low profile.
“Everyone’s personality is different," Dilley said.

https://hellgatenyc.com/barn-owls-upper-.title: Evicted Upper West Side Barn Owls Are Doing OK—For Now
https://hellgatenyc.com/barn-owls-upper-.author: Hell Gate
https://hellgatenyc.com/barn-owls-upper-.text:
Despite an unceremonious, sudden, and possibly illegal eviction, it seems like the young barn owls of upper Manhattan will be OK.   
A parliament of barn owls had been nested in a hole in the roof of the rickety water tower of an Upper West Side apartment building—but late last week, birders noticed workers doing construction on the roof of the water tower, destroying the nest that the owls had built.  
Birder David Lei told Hell Gate that the fledglings being raised in the disrupted nest began roosting out in the open on nearby buildings last week, which was unusual, he explained. 
"That owl should have been roosting in a more sheltered location, like on an air conditioner windowsill, something like that," Lei said. "But it was out in the open, fully exposed. Songbirds had been bothering it during the day, just natural behavior. But you know, a hawk could have seen it and attacked it."
Lei said that management at 15 West 75th Street had told the residents that they were doing "scheduled maintenance" on the water tower. The building's management did not respond to Hell Gate's request for comment by publication time, but we will update this story if they do.

https://taz.de/Nadeln-und-Naegel-in-Hall.title: Nadeln und Nägel in Halloween-Bonbons: Die wirkliche Gefahr
https://taz.de/Nadeln-und-Naegel-in-Hall.author: Ambros Waibel und Valérie Catil
https://taz.de/Nadeln-und-Naegel-in-Hall.text:
Nadeln und Nägel in Halloween-Bonbons: Die wirkliche Gefahr
Fälle von manipulierten Süßigkeiten an Halloween ängstigen. Wie ist der Stand der Ermittlungen? Und ist vom Süßen oder Sauren in Zukunft abzuraten?
Wie bei anderen religiösen Festen spielen Lebensmittel eine große Rolle bei Halloween. Während Nikolaus und Weihnachten eher im privaten Kreis gefeiert werden, ist das gemeinschaftliche Ostereiersuchen, etwa in Zoos und Freizeitparks, inzwischen weit verbreitet. Halloween unterscheidet sich durch eine besondere Geste und Sozialität, wenn überhaupt dann noch mit den Sternsingern zu vergleichen.
Die Geschenke kommen von Privatleuten und sind damit keiner Kontrolle unterworfen. Wenn Halloween ist, sind es die Schwachen, die Kinder, die Fordernden sind und nicht die ewig gegängelten Bittsteller. Es erinnert an Fasching und Karneval, an die temporär verkehrte Welt.
Kinder fordern, Kinder treten allein in eine (fremde) Erwachsenensphäre, Kinder nehmen Geschenke von Fremden an und sind im Dunklen allein unterwegs. Die englischsprachige Maxime „Never Take Candy from a Stranger“, also „Nimm niemals Süßigkeiten eines Unbekannten an“, ist für einen Tag ausgesetzt.
Es ist naheliegend, dass Halloween damit genug Projektionsfläche bietet für reale Ängste und popkulturelle, sogenannte „Poisoned Candy“-Mythen. Diese „Poisoned Candy“-Mythen sind ein hartnäckiges Phänomen, das jährlich an Halloween wieder aufflackert, unabhängig davon, ob die Fälle echt sind oder nicht: Demnach sollen an Halloween verteilte Süßigkeiten mit gefährlichen Gegenständen wie Nadeln oder Rasierklingen versehen oder gar vergiftet worden sein, um gezielt Kinder zu verletzen. Und ein Blick in die aktuellen Nachrichten lehrt, dass das sehr wirklich werden kann.
Ermittlergruppe in Österreich
Ein Großteil dieser Fälle konnte in der Vergangenheit widerlegt werden. Manchmal enttarnte man sie als Form der Massenhysterie. In anderen Fällen entstand dieses Gerücht, wenn ein Kind unerwartet starb, nachdem es zufällig eine Süßigkeit gegessen hatte, und ein Schuldiger gesucht wurde.
Bekannt ist auch der Fall eines Vaters aus den USA, der 1974 Zyankali in Brausepäckchen mischte, um die Lebensversicherung seines achtjährigen Sohnes zu kassieren – und sich dabei vom „Poisoned Candy“-Mythos inspirieren ließ.
Oder aber es handelte sich lediglich um eine versehentliche Kontamination, wie es in Rheinland-Pfalz dieses Jahr geschehen ist, oder um einen Produktionsfehler, bei dem etwa ein Metallgegenstand in eine Verpackung geraten war. Urteile des Bundesgerichtshofes unterscheiden hier übrigens zwischen „arteigenen“ und „artfremden“ Fremdkörpern. Der Verbraucher könne eine völlige Gefahrlosigkeit nicht erwarten.
Meldungen zu am Halloween-Wochenende in die Hände von Kindern gekommenen manipulierten Süßigkeiten kommen aus deutschen und österreichischen Bundesländern. In Wien wurde die Ermittlergruppe „Treat“ des österreichischen Bundeskriminalamts gebildet. Für Deutschland teilte das BKA auf taz-Anfrage mit, dass ihnen das Phänomen „grundsätzlich bekannt“ sei, die Verantwortlichkeit jedoch bei den Landeskriminalämtern liege.
Der Holzspieß im Schokoriegel
Das LKA NRW sprach auf Anfrage von 24 gemeldeten Fällen. Verletzte habe es keine gegeben. Erkenntnisse darüber, wer dahinterstecken könnte, gebe es nicht. „Über Tätergruppen oder Motive zu spekulieren“, heißt es weiter, sei deshalb „unseriös“.
Das LKA Bayern spricht von 25 gemeldeten Fällen – ebenfalls ohne Verletzungen. 2 Fälle wurden in Hamburg, 3 in Brandenburg gemeldet, 9 in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, wobei sich ein Kind leicht verletzt haben soll. Auch die anderen Bundesländer verzeichneten Fälle.
In einem Fall im thüringischen Landkreis Hildburghausen hat sich inzwischen herausgestellt, dass ein neun Jahre altes Mädchen den Gegenstand, einen Holzspieß, selbst in einen Schokoriegel gesteckt hat. Wieso das Kind dies gemacht habe, sei bisher nicht bekannt, sagte eine Sprecherin der Polizei der dpa. Der Vater des Mädchens hatte eine vorherige Anzeige bei der Polizei zurückgenommen. Auch in Bayern gibt es mittlerweile 2 Fälle, in denen Kinder eingeräumt haben, Süßigkeiten selbst mit Gegenständen präpariert zu haben.
Auch aus Ungarn und Kanada werden Fälle gemeldet. Es kam bisher zu leichten Verletzungen im Mund bei Kindern, die Polizei rät zur Vorsicht, warnt aber auch vor Panik.
Sadismus und Halloween
Was aber könnten, unseriös gefragt, mögliche Motive sein für das Verteilen von manipulierten Süßigkeiten, dieses „feige und hinterhältige Verbrechen“, wie es der österreichische Innenminister Gerhard Karner (ÖVP) nannte?
Lisa Natter von der kriminologischen Forschungsgruppe beim Bayerischen Landeskriminalamt (BLKA) sagte auf dpa-Anfrage, den Begriff „Halloween Sadism“, habe der US-Soziologe Joel Best bereits in den 1980er Jahren geprägt.
„Er hat das als moderne urbane Legende untersucht, die als wahr erzählt wird und auch gesellschaftliche Ängste ausdrückt, deren tatsächliches Ausmaß aber häufig durch empirische Belege nicht gedeckt ist“, erklärte Natter. Wichtig sei dabei: Einzelne Fälle – wie jetzt in Deutschland, aber auch zum Beispiel in Österreich, Irland, Dänemark und Norwegen – würden damit nicht bestritten. „Es zeigt sich vielmehr, dass die Erzählungen als Resonanzraum für allgemeinere gesellschaftliche Ängste dienen.“
Die Polizei Essen sagte der Süddeutsche Zeitung, man gehe von mehreren Tätern aus, die Anregungen im Internet gefunden haben könnten. Auch über soziale Medien koordinierte Aktionen seien möglich. Über Ermittlungserfolge sei aber nichts bekannt, viele Verfahren seien wieder eingestellt worden.
Das Auto ist die Gefahr
Und trotzdem ist Halloween kein völlig harmloses Fest. Auch in diesem Jahr wurden Kinder und Jugendliche mit Reizgas verletzt, mit Messern und Schreckschusswaffen bedroht und beleidigt. Auch hier ist die Motivlage diffus.
Eine konkrete Gefahr gibt es am Ende aber doch: Das Risiko für Fußgänger durch ein Auto getötet zu werden, ist an Halloween ohnehin schon erhöht. Für Kinder bis 17 Jahren, das zeigte eine 2018 veröffentlichte Studie, ist es in den USA an diesem Tag dreimal höher als an anderen Tagen.
Noch gefährdeter sind Kinder von 4 bis 8 Jahren. Für sie ist das Risiko sogar 10-mal so hoch. In Niedersachsen etwa wurde ein siebenjähriges Mädchen beim Halloween-Spaziergang von einem Auto erfasst und schwer verletzt.
Achtsam sein auf den Straßen ist das Motto. Und wie bei anderen frohen Festen bleibt am Ende die Erkenntnis, dass man sich den Spaß an Halloween nicht nehmen lassen soll. Wer daran denkt, dass ein Weihnachtsbaum Feuer fangen kann und es sogar bei der Ostereiersuche zu tödlichen Unfällen kommt, wird das Risiko für Kinder an Halloween nicht kleinreden und schon gar nicht ausschließen – aber zu einer abgewogenen Einschätzung kommen können.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. So viele unterstützen freiwillig und regelmäßig. Noch nicht dabei? Werden Sie jetzt Teil der Community! Jetzt unterstützen

https://gothamist.com/news/brooklyn-fire.title: Brooklyn fire kills 6 people, injures 7 others in Sunset Park, officials said
https://gothamist.com/news/brooklyn-fire.author: Brittany Kriegstein
https://gothamist.com/news/brooklyn-fire.text:
Six people were killed and seven others were injured after a fire ripped through a two-story home in Sunset Park early Thursday morning, police and fire officials said.
Fire department officials said they received calls about the blaze around 1:40 a.m., and found an intense fire burning on multiple floors of the home on 58th Street and 7th Avenue in Brooklyn. It took more than 200 first responders and almost three hours to bring it under control.
Four people were pronounced dead at the scene, according to the FDNY and NYPD, while two more people died after they were taken to a local hospital with critical injuries. Both agencies said they did not immediately have identifying information for any of the victims.
Four other civilians were also hospitalized — one with serious but non-life threatening injuries, and the others with minor injuries, officials said. The three firefighters were also being treated for minor injuries, according to the department.
Officials said a lithium-ion battery was found at the scene, but it’s too early to tell whether it caused the fire.
Fire marshals on Thursday morning were looking closely at what appeared to be a charred stand up scooter that firefighters brought outside the house, along with debris that firefighters were shoveling through the home’s blown-out windows.
Luis Ramos, 54, who said he lived across the street from the fire, said the house looked like “a bonfire that was out of control” where flames were “coming out of everywhere,” including the roof, windows and door.
“Whoever was in there, they didn’t even have time to get out,” he said, adding that he witnessed a body that was black and charred. “There wasn’t a spot in that building that didn’t have a flame coming out.”
Ramos said he felt for the family who lived there, especially with Thanksgiving coming in a few weeks. “Instead of, you know, of happiness, they gotta bury their family members.”
Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who spoke at the scene of the fire on Thursday morning, said helping people recover from this fire will take time and resources.
"Because we know that fires are not only devastating in the moment, but also they displace New Yorkers from their home,” he said. “And they require help and support not just from their community, but from the city at large."
Mamdani said the Red Cross has moved all the displaced people into hotels.
Jimmy Juoguo, a neighbor, said the fire was very scary.
“It’s so sad because even we [didn’t] know each other, but it’s six people, it’s too much,” he said.
The incident comes less than a week after four family members, including 11-year-old Zion Maine, died when a lithium ion battery caught fire in the Bronx.
This is a developing story and has been updated with new information.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/france-polic.title: France’s Police Unions Are Throwing Their Weight Around
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/france-polic.author: Harrison Stetler
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/france-polic.text:
France’s Police Unions Are Throwing Their Weight Around
Amid protests in France, police unions are pushing for wage hikes and special legal privileges to cash in on the political capital they’ve built under Emmanuel Macron’s rule.
“The proportionate use of force should never be an obstacle to the job of restoring order,” French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez wrote in a September 30 message to police chiefs. High schoolers across the country had only just launched a wave of campus blockages over poor learning conditions, in demonstrations that would soon morph into a full-fledged social crisis. In an October 6 government questions session, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu dismissed as “slander” any claims of systemic violence in policing and crowd-control tactics.
In the weeks since then, little has punctured the pressure for similar deference to the police. Certainly not the persistence of intense protests — and, in some cases, rioting — which have instead strengthened the reflex among France’s political class to celebrate muscular policing as the lone rampart against disorder. Nor have the numerous examples of people, often minors, being maimed or otherwise severely injured by the arsenal of “nonlethal” weapons at the police’s disposal.
Then again, political authorities have ample reason to be wary. “I accuse!” wrote Fabien Vanhemelryk in a statement published after the most intense day of protests and looting on October 17, reprising the famous declaration from Émile Zola’s 1898 public letter on the Dreyfus affair. For Vanhemelryk — leader of France’s largest police union by membership, the hard-right Alliance Police Nationale — the deepening crisis was the result of “years of permissiveness, political cowardice, and concessions.”
From the police’s point of view, the turbulence of recent weeks will most likely stand as a reminder that the state’s reliance on them gives them leverage. As Emmanuel Macron’s presidency enters its twilight, police unions are waging their own offensive, demanding salary increases and bonuses and looking to secure a raft of other pet projects. They hope to reap the rewards of their importance not only within the powerful Interior Ministry but also in the practice of government that has come to define Macron’s near-decade in office, as policing has become a key crutch during critical periods of political and social tension.
It’s an understatement to say that French organized labor has seen better days. Police unions offer perhaps the most notable exception. But the Interior Ministry is not your average employer, and police unions aren’t your average professional constituency.
Material Demands, Symbolic Rewards
In a dramatic show of force this past September 15, upward of ten thousand off-duty police officers descended Paris’s Champs-Élysées to the National Assembly, with protesters hauling dummy coffins along the capital’s central artery in protest of low wages and strenuous work conditions. The demonstration was called by the hard-right Alliance Police Nationale and UN1TÉ, the two largest unions among rank-and-file officers. They are pushing for some €500 million in new funding, allowing for salary increases and bonuses in addition to around a thousand new hires.
The Interior Ministry has already been among the winners of the Macron years in financing terms.
In 2023, police unions won special carve-outs in Macron’s unpopular increase in the pension age to sixty-four, a reform suspended during last winter’s budget negotiations in parliament. Adopted in 2023 and designed to extend over five years, a special budgeting law earmarked €15 billion extra funding to the Interior Ministry, adding to the baseline annual appropriations, which rose from some €22 billion in 2022 to over €34 billion in 2026. (Compare that to the €4 billion in low-rate loans to local authorities for school renovations, which the government rolled out in late October as a concession to student protests.)
Still, with Macronist Premier Lecornu vying for tens of billions of euros worth of savings for the 2027 budget, Interior Minister Nuñez can only go so far in his attempt to satisfy police unions’ demands.
But the police want more than just financial concessions. In a controversial bill currently awaiting final approval from parliament, police unions hope to claim a strategic win in one of their long-running campaigns: erecting legal shields to protect police officers who use their firearms from investigation and eventual criminal scrutiny.
The title of the proposed law calls it a “presumption of legitimate defense,” but to the bill’s critics it’s better known as the “permit to kill.” According to the legislation, which sailed through the lower-house National Assembly in July, police who use their firearms “are presumed to have acted” in accordance with the law, unless evidence can be shown to justify an investigation. To critics, that amounts to a tautology opening major holes in the rule of law, hamstringing oversight by putting the onus on victims of police violence to prove possible wrongdoing.
For Laurent Bonelli, a sociologist of security policy, the government finds itself in a genuine structural dilemma, caught between stretched resources, an acquired dependence on stiff policing in moments of social unrest, and palpable frustration among average troopers.
“There’s only so much money to give, so what can be done?” Bonelli told Jacobin. “That’s where symbolic rewards come in. And a classic example of that is this bill on so-called legitimate self-defense.”
Presumed Guilty
Will a “legitimate defense” bill be rolled into an eventual postcrisis compromise for a police force exhausted as this fall’s social unrest stretches on? The current push for greater immunity for the police first gained momentum during a series of events not wholly unlike the current one. Over summer 2023, the fatal police shooting of seventeen-year-old Nahel Merzouk in the Paris suburb of Nanterre kicked off days of protests and rioting that fanned accusations of systemic racism and violence among the police.
In several respects, the Nahel crisis provided the template for this fall’s conflict over law and order. In an incendiary public declaration that summer, the Alliance Police Nationale and UNSA police unions referred to rioters as “wild hordes” and “pests,” demanding a swift restoration of order. In less-than-veiled threats to political authorities, they also called for “concrete measures of legal protection” for the officer responsible for Merzouk’s killing.
While the legislation does not make an explicit principle of police irresponsibility, Nathalie Tehio, president of the Ligue des droits de l’Homme, warns that the greater risk is in raising the threshold needed to obtain an investigation into police wrongdoing. “So long as the [use of a firearm] is presumed to be legal, there will quite simply be no investigation,” she told Jacobin. “What that means is that the victim, or the family of the victim, will have to bring proof to the contrary.”
Shielding police from scrutiny has been a leitmotif of security policy for some time. During Macron’s first term, his government tried to ban the filming and photographing of active-duty police officers. Legislation approved this past spring authorizes turning off video cameras during temporary police custody, a change that legal observers fear could weaken oversight over interrogation practices. The law also sought to anonymize the identities of police officers appearing in judicial proceedings, though that was struck down by the Constitutional Council.
All signs are pointing toward what Tehio called the “construction of police immunity.” The contrast could not be more striking when compared to the evolution of the law as it applies for everyone else.
One piece of legislation to emerge out of this fall’s social crisis is the “rioters-pay” law, which is currently being fast-tracked through parliament thanks to consensus support between the Macronist center and the far right. The bill stipulates legal responsibility — and potential financial liabilities — for individuals accused of having “wittingly participated” in a grouping that including acts of rioting and vandalism. A presumption of guilt, you might say, for participating in demonstrations that turn awry.
Magical Solutions
One-upmanship between the police forces and political authorities eager to satisfy a critical arm of the state is a dynamic that long predates Macron’s presidency.
Part of this power is due to the nature of the force itself. France’s National Police is rigidly centralized, making it practically immune to local control and oversight. Concrete practices have also helped drill in the clientelist influence of police unions with a staunch ideological bent. “Comanagement,” granting unions considerable say over things like internal promotions, hardens their influence over the workforce — and marks the Interior Ministry off from many other state administrations.
One immediate bugbear among the lower echelons is that superiors were granted a considerable salary increase this year. Police unions are looking to shore up support among their bases before public sector workers hold professional elections in December, with the police counting among the most unionized workforces in the country.
But the greatest leverage that hard-line police unions have is structural, drawing on their position as a critical state service in a society on edge. Macron and his predecessors have long developed a dependence on muscular policing to contain conflicts over political decisions, whether the labor law reforms of the mid-2010s, the 2023 pension drive, or the anger with the education system that erupted these last few weeks. From enforcing immigration law to handling more quotidian social problems like drug use and extreme mental health cases, the “forces of order,” as France’s police are often called, offer a one-size-fits-all solution.
“To many in the political class, the police has come to appear as something of a magic solution for resolving the consequences of an increasingly unequal society,” said Bonelli, the sociologist. “It should come as little surprise that the police as an institution would try to capitalize on its weight in the ongoing battles within the state itself.”
Tensions over policing are so fraught that it’s barely ever asked whether an institution that separates itself so dramatically from the surrounding society is acting in its own best interests.
“Promising impunity is in reality to abandon the police — which is indeed in need of many urgent reforms — to those who are pushing for permanent confrontation with the general public,” the minority Interior Ministry branch of the national Confédération Générale du Travail (CGT) union warned in a January press release, when the government threw its support behind the “legitimate defense” law.
Doubts like these are increasingly inaudible, however, as a radicalized majority goes on the offensive. In doing so, they’re also pulling back the veil on what is starting to look to many like a state within the state.
