Trump im Magageddon
Nach dem Verlust der Mehrheiten in beiden Kammern des Kongresses wetzen Trumps einstige Vertraute bereits die Messer.
Der Staub lichtet sich, und der Blick auf die Wahlen in den USA offenbart ein politisches Jahrhundertbeben. Die Demokraten gewinnen beide Parlamentskammern und konnten sogar in republikanischen Hochburgen Erfolge erzielen. Die Strategie der Republikaner, auf Trump-Loyalisten zu setzen, ist gescheitert. Und so werden sich in den kommenden Monaten weite Teile der US-Rechten von Trump distanzieren.
Den Startschuss gab sein Vizepräsident J.D. Vance. Mit beinahe übermenschlicher Geschwindigkeit fiel er noch am Wahlabend Trump in den Rücken. Auf X postete er eine verblüffend realistische Analyse über die Gründe für die Niederlage: der Iran-Krieg, hohe Lebenshaltungskosten und die Beziehung zu Israel. Da brachte es auch nichts, den Rassismus-Regler im Wahlkampf auf »volle Pulle« aufzudrehen – die Preise an der Tankställe und in den Supermärkten blieben dieselben, und die Menschen haben das bemerkt, und jeder macht Trump dafür verantwortlich. Es wird interessant sein, was dies auch für die zukünftigen Beziehungen zu Israel bedeutet.
Und so beginnt das Maga-Schiff zu sinken, während die ersten Ratten von Bord springen. Damit für Vance der mediale Vorteil einer Vizepräsidentschaft für eine eigene Präsidentschaftskandidatur nicht zum Nachteil wird, beginnt dieser jetzt, vermehrt Trump zu kritisieren.
Der Präsident könnte dabei Opfer seines eigenen Prinzips werden, das er 2015 im Vorwahlkampf in einem Kommentar zum vorherigen republikanischen Präsidentschaftskandidaten John McCain auf den Punkt gebracht hat: »Er hat verloren, danach habe ich ihn nie mehr so sehr gemocht. Denn ich mag keine Verlierer.« Der ambitioniertere Teil seiner Weggefährten wird sich daran ein Beispiel nehmen.
Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf
Bei uns muss niemand zahlen, um informiert zu sein. Klingt nach einem schlechten Geschäftsmodell? Ist es auch. Aber uns sind unabhängiger Journalismus und Teilhabe für alle wichtiger als Profit. Journalismus kostet trotzdem Geld: Recherche, Druck und all die Menschen, die ihn machen. Deshalb sind wir auf dich angewiesen. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro.
Spende einmalig oder regelmäßig, jeder Betrag zählt. Damit nd bleibt.

https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/n.title: Where to start with: John Berger
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/n.author: Henry Eliot
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/n.text:
John Berger was born a hundred years ago today. He was an artist, critic, novelist, poet, polemicist and playwright who made impassioned, idiosyncratic, fiercely attentive and deeply humane contributions to a swathe of artistic and intellectual disciplines across six decades. In fact, the diversity of his output can make it “difficult to grasp,” as Geoff Dyer observes, in his introduction to the Selected Essays. “Even admirers tend to know him in only one or two of his many incarnations.”
I hope the recommendations below provide a somewhat representative handle on Berger’s range. I have limited myself to books he assembled himself, which means I haven’t allowed myself to include anthologies, such as the excellent Understanding a Photograph, edited by Dyer, or Tom Overton’s collections Landscapes and Portraits, or the recent selection Across a Frontier, chosen by the similarly interdisciplinary critic, photographer and novelist Teju Cole.
There are many ways to approach Berger, but wherever you choose to start, you will be encountering, as Susan Sontag said of him, “a wonderful artist and thinker”.
The entry point
Berger is best remembered for Ways of Seeing, his 1972 BBC television series and accompanying Penguin paperback. Radically, he combined art and social criticism, discussing artworks in relation to advertising, mass reproduction, the female nude, the male gaze and social status. The book’s format is equally revolutionary: the text appears to begin on the front cover, and three of the seven chapters are made up of images only. Ways of Seeing is a sui generis design classic and a swift introduction to Berger’s enduring preoccupations with art, sex and politics.
The prizewinner
The same year that Ways of Seeing was published, Berger won the fourth Booker prize with G. (1972). The novel itself has been somewhat overshadowed by Berger’s acceptance speech, in which he pilloried the sponsor Booker McConnell Ltd for their “extensive trading interests” in the Caribbean, announcing that he would be donating half his prize money to the British Black Panther movement. This experimental novel follows a young man (G) and his vigorous sex life as he travels across Europe on the eve of the first world war. G is mostly oblivious – but inextricably connected to – the world-historical events taking place around him.
The quiet masterpiece
Another excellent place to start would be A Fortunate Man (1967), the first collaboration between Berger and the Swiss photographer Jean Mohr. It is a deceptively simple portrait of a country GP in the Forest of Dean, told through stark photography and haunting prose. Word and image interweave to powerful effect: the minutiae of one man’s vocation reflect compellingly on the whole of society. Berger and Mohr became close friends working on this project and collaborated several times over the following 50 years.
The one for writers
One of Berger’s lesser-known titles is Photocopies (1996), which presents a series of exquisite prose vignettes, titled as if they were photographs. Berger captures real moments, reproducing them – photocopying them – with pinpoint attention to detail. The book has an air of delicate stillness: it is a masterclass in clarity and an inspiration for prose stylists.
The one for artists
Ways of Seeing may have made his name, but much of Berger’s best art criticism is collected in About Looking (1980), which includes essays on Turner, Giacometti, Magritte, Francis Bacon and Walt Disney. It also includes his famous essay Why Look at Animals?, which considers the fact that we rarely interact with animals today, despite living in a world full of animal imagery.
The best on photography
Berger’s third collaboration with Mohr was Another Way of Telling (1982), a revelatory investigation into the art of photography. Despite its diffident subtitle – “A Possible Theory of Photography” – this landmark work stands alongside those of Walter Benjamin, Roland Barthes and Susan Sontag. A photograph is “a meeting place,” writes Berger, “where the interests of the photographer, the photographed, the viewer and those who are using the photography are often contradictory”.
The best on politics
To some extent, everything Berger wrote was political; he was always concerned with the human experience in relation to society. One topic he wrote about repeatedly was migration, most memorably in A Seventh Man (1975), another remarkable collaboration with Mohr. This galvanising book intimately documents the experience of migrant labourers seeking work in western Europe in the early 1970s, but it remains soberingly topical today.
The one that will make you cry
G. may have won the Booker prize, but To the Wedding (1995) is Berger’s greatest novel. Through fragments of conversations, songs and silences, we follow a mother and father, estranged for many years, travelling across Europe to the wedding of their daughter Ninon. It’s both a heartbreaking story and a triumphantly optimistic celebration of love and life. Colum McCann calls it “one of the greatest and most honest love stories of our time.”
The one that deserves more attention
The wonderful Here Is Where We Meet (2005) is fiction – or is it? In 8½ chapters, “John” has a series of encounters with people who are dead: he meets his mother sitting on a park bench in Lisbon, he meets his childhood mentor in Krakow market, he stands above the grave of Jorge Luis Borges in Geneva. This is Berger at his most playful, seamlessly blending novel, essay, criticism, memoir and travelogue. It’s a brilliant, unclassifiable achievement.
The one to carry in your pocket
“This is a book I carry with me everywhere,” writes the actor and director Simon McBurney, in his new introduction to And Our Faces, My Heart, Brief as Photos (1984). “It fits into the inside pocket of my jacket, a little larger than a passport.” This slim, numinous work contains scraps and scenes about mortality, art, sex and belonging. It is organised into two halves – “Once”, about time, and “Here”, about space – and manages to condense a lifetime’s wisdom into little more than a hundred pages.
- Henry Eliot edited the 2026 Bloomsbury reissues of John Berger’s work. He is the author of five books, including The Penguin Classics Book

https://hyperallergic.com/long-lost-geor.title: Long-Lost Georgia O’Keeffe Landscape Goes to Auction
https://hyperallergic.com/long-lost-geor.author: Rhea Nayyar
https://hyperallergic.com/long-lost-geor.text:
Long-Lost Georgia O’Keeffe Landscape Goes to Auction
Her painting “Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I” was stashed in an East Village closet for decades. Now it might sell for up to $3 million.
You think you know everything, and then all of a sudden, a virtually unknown Georgia O'Keeffe landscape emerges into the art history canon after spending decades boxed up in a New York City apartment closet. Just shy of a century old, O'Keeffe's long-lost “Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I” (1930) is slated to go under the hammer at Christie's 20th Century Evening sale on November 17.
Painted just one year after O'Keeffe's first visit to New Mexico, the rediscovered landscape work depicting Lobo Peak is likely one of three iterations the artist completed; the second in the series is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art's collection, and the third now resides in a private collection after having once belonged to David and Peggy Rockefeller.
Considered an important early work documenting O'Keeffe's growing love affair with the high desert, the artist's depiction incorporates her signature undulating contours and near-anatomical landscape features that seamlessly fuse a high-contrast palette of saturated earth tones.
So, what was it doing at the back of a closet in an East Village apartment for the last four decades?

https://www.propublica.org/article/afrif.title: Trump’s State Department Is Giving $1 Million to Controversial Group to Study Crimes Against White South Africans
https://www.propublica.org/article/afrif.author: Sharon Lerner, Anna Maria Barry-Jester
https://www.propublica.org/article/afrif.text:
After slashing funding for programs that documented atrocities and protected human rights abroad, President Donald Trump’s State Department is now granting one of its first new human rights awards to a controversial South African organization that promotes the disputed notion that white farmers are a violently targeted, persecuted group, according to multiple sources knowledgeable about the funding.
The group expected to receive the nearly $1 million award, AfriForum, is a nonprofit that advocates on behalf of Afrikaners, a subset of South Africa’s white population. The organization says its members, who have a “God-given calling,” fight for Afrikaner interests and self-governance. The money will be used to “document hateful rhetoric and violent acts” against Afrikaners and other minority populations in the country.
The new award comes from a State Department bureau tasked with promoting democracy and human rights internationally. Until last year, those funds were mainly spent in poor and authoritarian nations — to fight corruption in the Democratic Republic of Congo, for example, or combat child exploitation and sexual abuse in Afghanistan. Since Trump returned to office, his appointees have transformed the bureau, gutting its staff, canceling programs and reorienting some of its funding toward conservative causes in Europe.
Samuel Samson, who was appointed as a deputy assistant secretary to the State Department bureau by Trump, has claimed the U.S. has a “civilizational” connection to Afrikaners, who descend primarily from Dutch migrants and predominantly speak Afrikaans. Samson, who has met with far-right leaders in Europe since joining the administration last year, has framed the U.S. government’s financial support for Afrikaners as grounded in “a common heritage, a common culture, a common way of life, shared history and ultimately a common anthropology.”
Samuel Samson Speaks at Lex Libertas Event
There’s a long shared political history between Afrikaner groups and white nationalists in the U.S., said Audie Klotz, a political science professor at Syracuse University who has studied those connections. But, she said, “There’s no heritage connection here. It’s pure scientific racism. In the history of U.S. immigration, there’s no direct connection between South Africa and the United States.”
AfriForum met with the Trump administration in February 2025 to plead for help. The group told officials that Afrikaners are subject to racial discrimination and murders that are more frequent and asked the administration to “act strongly against hate speech that incites violence” against them, according to a statement.
South Africa is plagued by high rates of violence, and some Afrikaners have been tortured and murdered. But independent researchers have found those killings represent a tiny fraction of murders across the country, whose victims are disproportionately people living in poor urban areas, where residents are predominantly Black. Official government statistics, and two formal inquiries into the matter, do not reveal a pattern of targeted violence against Afrikaners.
But Trump subscribes to the idea that white farmers face a “genocide” and has cited disproportionate violence against them as a reason for punishing Africa’s wealthiest nation. In February 2025, he issued an executive order that cut off hundreds of millions of dollars of aid to South Africa and welcomed Afrikaners to the U.S. as refugees. Since then, the administration has opened the doors to more than 16,000 white South Africans while halting virtually all other immigration. Officials recently told Congress they plan to invite as many as 17,500 Afrikaner refugees to the U.S. in 2027.
AfriForum did not respond to specific questions for this story but said that “our understanding is that the allocation has not yet been finalised. Should the allocation indeed be awarded to AfriForum, we will make a public announcement in this regard.”
The new award is the administration’s latest show of support for the Afrikaner cause. The white South African group governed the nation for decades under a brutal system of segregation known as apartheid, which kept the Black majority an impoverished underclass until the system was dismantled in 1994. Now, with Black South Africans governing the country, white people — of which Afrikaners are the majority — remain one of the wealthiest segments of the population.
The support has caused dismay among several former high-level diplomats, who spoke to ProPublica anonymously because they fear retribution from the administration.
Two former senior U.S. officials responsible for Africa policy said that they would never have met with AfriForum, let alone funded the group, because it was considered to be politically extreme and not credible. They described the organization as cherry-picking crime statistics to create a misleading narrative. “We would certainly not have funded what we would see as a racially incendiary initiative,” said one of the officials.
The decision to direct money toward the group comes after the Trump administration halted programs that advocated for the end of violence in African countries such as Sudan, where the Biden administration determined in 2025 that there was a genocide, calling it “the world’s largest humanitarian catastrophe.”
“It’s offensive to provide funding solely to this one group after we’ve cut off funding in countries undergoing real documented crises,” said David Jandura, who managed the Africa portfolio for the State Department’s human rights bureau for several years and lost his job during the mass layoffs in 2025.
Congress has also raised questions about how the award was made. A Senate aide to Democrats told ProPublica that despite repeated requests to State Department officials, they had not received a briefing outlining the recipients of funds earmarked for democracy and human rights, which they described as “highly unusual.”
“The Trump Administration proceeded with funding fringe right-wing causes internationally despite objections from Congress,” said Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, a New Hampshire Democrat and ranking member of the Senate Committee on Foreign Relations, who described the lack of transparency as “unacceptable.”
In response to a series of questions about the AfriForum funding, a senior State Department official wrote in an email that the department does not comment on funding deliberations and that they routinely keep Congress informed of their actions, consulting extensively on this year’s programming. “The Administration has been clear about its concern about the abhorrent race-based discrimination and violence in South Africa,” the unnamed official wrote. “Human rights protections do not depend on a person’s income or ethnicity.”
In July, ProPublica revealed that the State Department originally intended to give the $1 million research award to Lex Libertas, a small organization founded last year by a former AfriForum executive named Ernst Roets. Trump officials later expanded the potential awardees to a small pool of handpicked organizations. The plan drew outrage from Congress over the content of the award as well as plans to bypass the typical competitive bidding process. After ProPublica’s reporting, the State Department released an open call for the funding opportunity, offering $986,500 to a nonprofit organization to “create a comprehensive record of violence affecting Afrikaner and other South African minority populations.” It’s this grant that is now being awarded to AfriForum.
Both AfriForum and Lex Libertas advocate for Afrikaner rights and have developed relationships with the Trump administration. Trump’s ambassador to South Africa, L. Brent Bozell III, visited AfriForum’s headquarters in September, praising the organization for its neighborhood watch programs while criticizing the South African government for not enacting policies requested by the Trump administration. AfriForum has also met with Trump officials in Washington, D.C., drawing public criticism from South African President Cyril Ramaphosa. And in September, Roets met with administration officials.
AfriForum was founded 20 years ago and, with some 300,000 members, claims to be the biggest civil rights organization in South Africa. It says it aims to “establish self-dependence and growing self-governance” and provides some local civic services, such as garbage collection and systems for reporting pot holes and broken traffic lights. The group has said it distances itself from “white supremacist and extremist groups” and that it disagrees with Trump’s assertion that white South African farmers are experiencing a “white genocide.” But it has also said the South African government is “targeting the continued existence of Afrikaners” through racial legislation and the downplaying of farm murders, among other things. Academics and former U.S. diplomats have repudiated some of the ideas the group promotes as racist.
It unsuccessfully challenged a ban on the “gratuitous display” of the national flag flown during apartheid, which a South African court has found to be a form of hate speech. And while the group’s leader, Kallie Kriel, has said apartheid “was wrong,” he has also said it did not constitute “a crime against humanity” as the U.N. has determined, on the grounds that not enough people were killed during that time.
AfriForum has been focusing on farm attacks since at least 2009. In 2018, during Trump’s first presidency, Kriel and Roets, who was then his deputy, met with government officials in Washington, D.C., about the issue, and Roets spoke about it with Tucker Carlson on Fox News, as the chyron below him announced in all caps, “White farmers brutally murdered every week in SouthAfrica.”
Additional research on crimes against white South Africans is an unnecessary and confusing use of U.S. taxpayer dollars, said Carolyn Holmes, a professor at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, who studies democracy in southern Africa. Holmes noted that AfriForum already produces annual reports on crimes against farming communities. “These data already exist,” she said. “You don’t need a new study. You don’t even need a far-right study, we have those.”
The U.S. support offers more than a financial boost to the organization. “For some time, AfriForum has been campaigning for recognition of their claim that white people face discrimination and persecution,” said Alex Dyzenhaus, a lecturer in international relations and African politics at the University of St. Andrews. “Before, they were only getting the Tucker Carlsons and the far right of the news ecosystem. Now they have the U.S. government on their side.”
The Trump administration has made the plight of white, rural South Africans a key foreign policy issue. In addition to the early executive order, Trump held a contentious meeting with Ramaphosa in the White House last year where Trump claimed white farmers were being executed. The administration has also considered an ad campaign focused on encouraging more Afrikaners to come to the U.S.
In September, Roets of Lex Libertas met with the White House to discuss what he sees as the crisis facing the Afrikaner community and, along with the New York Young Republican Club, placed 3,000 white crosses on the National Mall to commemorate South African farm murders.
Roets declined to answer specific questions from ProPublica but, in a text message, described the murders of several Afrikaners that he knew personally. He also wrote, “I see the suffering of black people in South Africa, I am deeply moved by it, and I spend every day of my life campaigning to make things better for us all.”
Appearing at a press conference for the Lex Libertas event, Samson, the State Department official, showcased the sharp shift the administration has made in U.S. relations with South Africa. While apartheid has been understood globally as a symbol of racist oppression, Samson described the current South African government as having discriminatory “race-based” policies and a cautionary tale for the rest of the world.
At the end of apartheid, in 1994, South Africa was a “flourishing, prosperous society,” Samson said. Since then, the country has gone to “ruin.” He blamed the fall on a “radical ideological leftist movement that wears human rights, that wears tolerance and inclusivity, as a skin suit to advance their Marxist communist worldview.”
Part of the Trump administration’s solution to this perceived crisis, he said, was to provide the research funding.

https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.title: Kamala Harris on Expanding Democratic Power in the South
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.author: John Nichols
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
Kamala Harris on Expanding Democratic Power in the South
A conversation with the former vice president about the fight for Democrats in the too-long-neglected South.
Kamala Harris made a big return to the campaign trail in the fall of 2026, heading to such battleground states as Michigan, where she boosted US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, and Georgia, where she campaigned with Senator Jon Ossoff and gubernatorial candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms. But Harris also visited places that rarely see former vice presidents, such as Columbus, Mississippi, where she appeared in a packed high-school gymnasium on behalf of Democratic Senate candidate Scott Colom. This campaigning, which she referred to as her “freedom tour,” has also taken the 2024 Democratic presidential nominee to Arkansas and Louisiana. Harris says she hasn’t decided whether to run for president again in 2028. But no matter what her own next step may be, she tells The Nation, she’s committed to boosting Democratic prospects in the too-long-neglected South.
—John Nichols
John Nichols:  Let’s talk about the fight for Democrats in the South.
Kamala Harris: One of my favorite subjects.
JN: You have been appearing at party events and with candidates across the region.
KH: And for my book tour. The publisher [of the book, 107 Days] was like, “Well, we don’t normally do a lot of book tours in the South.” And I was like, “Well, we’re going to do that, and people will come.” And they did—often a thousand people.
JN: There has been a lasting debate within the Democratic Party about how to approach deep-red states. A lot of strategists make the mistake of arguing, usually behind closed doors, “Let’s just write them off.”
KH: That is a mistake…. There are people in the South who have profound needs for the things the Democratic Party says we stand for: affordable healthcare, affordable childcare, a meaningful job that leads to the ability to have opportunity for your children. The dignity of all people—equality, fairness.
That point being number one.
The other point I would raise is that if you look at what’s happening demographically in the country, there is a reverse migration happening toward the South—both in terms of families who, historically, were from the South as well as a lot of young families, because it’s more affordable. And the South, you know, in terms of topography, is beautiful.
Popular

JN: There’s also a political side to this. In several Southern states in 2024, you ran as well as or better than you did in several Northern states that were historically identified as more competitive. There’s a base to build from in the South, right?
KH: That’s right. And I feel so strongly that you have to be able to do battle, instead of sitting back and implicitly accepting the notion that you can’t win there. You certainly won’t win if you don’t do battle. And that requires, as we know, being present. And it requires an investment. And that is part of the failure [for national Democrats], which is a failure to invest in the infrastructure that would allow us to win. And then it becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy.
Then what do we do? We abandon the people of those states who want clean drinking water? Who want the freedoms we say we fight for? Who want Medicaid, because their rural hospitals are shutting down because of a lack of federal funding? Who, as I was saying in Mississippi, know they deserve better? And who know it doesn’t have to be that way?
Well, the Democratic Party’s got to get hip to that, too: It doesn’t have to be that way.
JN: When Democrats aren’t hip to that, it narrows the party’s path to governing majorities, right?
KH: That’s my point—absolutely right. It’s about: Are we gonna play small ball?
Look, everything worthwhile requires investment. And investment, by its very nature, includes planting some seeds for a return that might be a little ways down the road but will be well worth the investment.
JN: There may also be an opening now, because of widespread disdain for the GOP administration. Have you been surprised by the implosion of Trump’s approval ratings this year?
KH: I’m not surprised. I say it publicly because I mean it: This is the most callous, corrupt, and incompetent presidential administration we’ve ever experienced.… What has happened also is [Trump] has created a party—and they’ve allowed it—in his own image. This is not Ronald Reagan’s party. That’s so cliché; everybody says it. But he has created a party in his own image, including the callous nature. So am I surprised about that? No.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: Brooklyn Asylum Seeker Breaks 30-Day Hunger Strike in ICE Detention in Georgia
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Gwynne Hogan
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
A Russian asylum seeker who lives in Brooklyn ended a monthlong hunger strike in a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention facility in Georgia on Wednesday.
Andrei Gerdiukov, who’s been in ICE detention since February, and the group of 10 strikers were demanding their releases — or in his case, at least a transfer to a facility in New York so he can be closer to his wife.
He and the other remaining hunger strikers broke their fast Wednesday, 30 days after they stopped eating on Oct. 6, according to Polina Chertushkina, 27, Gerdiukov’s wife, who spoke with him over the phone.
“His hands and legs were shaking,” Chertushkina said Gerdiukov told her, as he took his first bites of a pastry, his first solid food in a month. Chertushkina lost more than 30 pounds over the course of the month, she said.
Andrei Gerdiukov, 31, was among dozens of detainees at the Folkston D. Ray James ICE processing center in Georgia who launched a hunger strike last month. As the weeks dragged on, the strike dwindled to 11 participants, including Gerdiukov, who were then sent to another ICE detention center across the street.
In recent days, the remaining participants have been threatened with being force fed, Gerdiukov told The City Reporter in a phone call from the facility earlier in the week when the fast was ongoing
“I cannot sleep at all because of hunger,” he said.
“We’re waiting for them to start force feeding,” Gerdiukov said. “They told us every day.”
“I can see my ribs,” he said.
A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security didn’t immediately return a request for comment.
As the Trump administration has detained historic numbers of people as part of its mass deportation agenda, detainees across the country have turned to hunger strikes to protest the conditions of their confinement. The Guardian has reported on how ICE has force fed hunger strikers with the approval of federal courts. Force feeding is a practice widely condemned by human rights groups as a form of torture.
Gerdiukov has been in ICE detention since Feb. 22, when he and his wife were pulled over by Border Patrol agents during a traffic stop while they were on vacation in Florida with another Russian asylum-seeking couple.
All four were arrested, and the men were held in ICE detention while the women were released under orders of supervision, Chertushkina said in an interview.
In the months since, Gerdiukov has tried to win his freedom in every way he could think of. He tried to get bond in immigration court and filed a habeas corpus petition. He was denied bond and then ordered removed, a decision he’s appealing. His habeas corpus petition seeking release is still pending before a federal judge in Georgia, seven months after he filed.
He and other detainees raised grievances about food, lack of medical care and poor conditions at the facility. He and his wife requested a transfer through formal channels, reaching out to their local Congressmember Yvette Clarke (D-Brooklyn), whose office also requested he be transferred on their behalf, according to correspondence shared with The City Reporter. None of it went anywhere, he said.
“We tried every legal process. Every issue we tried to solve it here, but they didn’t listen to us,” he said. “They leave us only one choice, that’s to protest, hunger strike.”
Chertushkina said that staff approached Gerdiukov this week offering to transfer him to another facility in Georgia, but not one closer to New York. Now that the strike was over she wasn’t sure what they would do.
“Maybe other people can forget about it,” she said. “Everything will be as it was before.”
Fleeing Putin’s Russia
The couple entered the United States seeking asylum in 2024, after fleeing Russia ahead of the landslide re-election of President Vladimir Putin.
They were caught by Russian police distributing pamphlets in favor of the opposition and arrested, Chertushkina said in an interview, and Gerdiukov was beaten up.
When they were released and told to return the next week, they understood that to mean they would be put in prison if they didn’t get out of the country. They bought plane tickets right away.
“We came home, and we understood, we have to leave Russia. You have another choice, or we will be in prison,” Chertushkina said.
The couple settled in Midwood, Brooklyn, applied for asylum, got work authorization and were going through deportation proceedings, immigration court records show. Gerdiukov was working as a handyman, while Chertushkina was teaching English to Russians, Belarusians and Ukrainians in Southern Brooklyn, she said. They were settling into life in New York City.
“Everybody was very kind. In New York City I feel a lot of people support immigrants, and I thought all Americans were like New Yorkers,” Gerdiukov said. “But I was wrong. Right now, I can see the difference.”
When they decided to go on vacation with their Russian friends, they thought with their asylum claims and deportation cases pending, they were not at risk of arrest by ICE or border patrol.
“They gave me all [the] documents, I thought I was legal,” Gerdiukov said. “I brought it with me. I have nothing to hide. I’m clear.”
All four of the Russians were arrested by border patrol. The women were released on orders of supervision, which means Chertushkina cannot leave the state to visit her husband in detention.
The two men were handed off together to ICE custody and spent a week at Alligator Alcatraz before they were sent to Folkston. Gerdiukov’s friend, Andrei Mikhailov, is also partaking in the hunger strike at Folkston, while Chertushkina and Mikhailov’s wife, Ksenia Volkova, have been advocating for their detained husbands, calling elected officials and reporters across the country.
Spokespeople for Rep. Clark, Senator Kirsten Gillibrand, Senator Chuck Schumer and Governor Kathy Hochul haven’t returned requests for comment.
Gerdiukov has already faced retaliation for his protest, disciplinary records shared with The City Reporter show. He was cited with the “prohibited acts” of “engaging in group demonstration” and “conduct that disrupts” after staff said he helped orchestrate a video call with other detainees that was put online and published by several media outlets “to generate public and media attention.”
After the charges, Gerdiukov spent two weeks in solitary confinement, he and his wife said.
When Gerdiukov spoke to The City Reporter earlier in the week, he said he felt weak, exhausted and hungry all the time. Still, he said the separation from his wife hurts most.
“I’m trying not to think about that,” he said. “It’s the hardest part.”

https://taz.de/DFB-Kader-von-Juergen-Klo.title: DFB-Kader von Jürgen Klopp: Manchmal ist die Form entscheidend
https://taz.de/DFB-Kader-von-Juergen-Klo.author: Frank Hellmann
https://taz.de/DFB-Kader-von-Juergen-Klo.text:
DFB-Kader von Jürgen Klopp: Manchmal ist die Form entscheidend
Der Nationalmannschafts-Kader von Bundestrainer Klopp ist für die nächsten Aufgaben etwas konventioneller aufgestellt. So gehört nun auch Niclas Füllkrug dazu.
Vergleichsweise locker hat Jürgen Klopp auf seinem Barhocker gewirkt, als er sich am Donnerstag auf dem DFB-Campus zum Interview in die Umkleidekabine setzte. Fragen stellte statt einer Journalistenschar nur Pressesprecherin Franziska Wülle für den verbandseigenen TV-Sender. Trotz aller Lässigkeit versicherte der Bundestrainer, es sei ihm schwergefallen, für die letzten Nations-League-Gruppenspiele gegen Serbien in Belgrad (13. November) und gegen die Niederlande in Berlin (16. November) seinen 24-köpfigen Kader zu nominieren, „weil – und das ist eigentlich die gute Nachricht – es wieder mehr Spieler verdient hätten, dabei zu sein. Aber so soll es sein.“
Gleichzeitig bewies der 59-Jährige, dass er nicht dogmatisch vorgeht. Es wimmelt in der Bundesliga nicht an klassischen Mittelstürmern mit verlässlichen Quoten. Wenn einer wie Niclas Füllkrug in Bundesliga und DFB-Pokal in zehn Spielen zwölfmal trifft, muss er wieder in den Kreis der Besten zurückkehren. „Er hat unterschiedlichste Tore geschossen. Er hat einen unglaublichen Einfluss bei Werder Bremen“, lobte Klopp.
Obwohl der 33-Jährige an der Weser seinen dritten Frühling erlebt, hatte der Bundestrainer zwischenzeitlich den Eindruck erweckt, eine Rückkehr mache aus Altersgründen keinen Sinn. Ein Missverständnis. „Ich bin jetzt nicht mit all meinen Aussagen, die ich in Halbzeit-Interviews getroffen habe, so glücklich“, räumte der 59-Jährige ein.
Klopp erzählte, er habe Füllkrug nach seinem Auftritt im ZDF-Sportstudio kontaktiert. „Es war eine Freude, die Entscheidung zu treffen, und es war auch eine Freude, sie ihm mitzuteilen.“ Wäre morgen die Europameisterschaft, würde er „Fülle“ sofort mitnehmen, denn: „Manchmal schlägt Form alles andere …“
„Bunter Mix“
Klopps Aufgebot vereint Perspektive mit Pragmatismus. „Wir haben in der Mannschaft einen bunten Mix aus sehr jung und durchaus erfahren dabei.“ Zwar fehlen logischerweise viele der Überraschungsgäste aus dem Frühherbst – etwa Mika Baur oder Bambasé Conté –, aber immer noch sind 13 Akteure dabei, die keine Verantwortung für die WM-Blamage in Nordamerika trugen. Mit zwei Siegen soll noch das Nations-League-Viertelfinale im März 2027 erreicht werden. Das wäre auch wichtig, um in der Qualifikation für die EM 2028 nicht gegen einen Großen wie Spanien oder Frankreich spielen zu müssen.
Das geht im Tor los, wo „Marc-Andre ter Stegen als Nummer eins in die Spiele geht“. Es gehe auf dieser Schlüsselposition um „große Stabilität“, und der Schlussmann von Ajax Amsterdam habe „die meiste Erfahrung“. Vertreter sind Alexander Nübel und Jonas Urbig. In der Innenverteidigung sind Jonathan Tah und Nico Schlotterbeck als eingespieltes Gespann gesetzt, als Back-up gelten Waldemar Anton, Malick Thiaw und überraschend Finn Jeltsch, von dem Klopp „langfristig“ so viel hält, dass er den 20-Jährigen vom VfB Stuttgart gerne mal rechts probieren würde. „Er ist ein sehr dynamischer, schlauer Kerl.“
In der Zentrale setzt Klopp mit Kapitän Joshua Kimmich, Aleksandar Pavlović und Tom Bischof auf einen „kleinen Bayern-Block“. In diesem Mannschaftsteil brauche es „Physis mit technischen Fähigkeiten – und ein bisschen Torgefahr wäre auch nicht schlecht“.
Dafür steht Überraschungsgast Wael Moyha. „Es gibt nicht viele 17-Jährige, die in der Bundesliga spielen, das allein ist schon ein herausragendes Merkmal“, sagte der Bundestrainer, der mit Moyha „drei Gespräche“ führte, die alle „top“ gewesen seien. Klopp sagte, man habe sich mit der Familie darauf geeinigt, „dass wir ihn einfach mal mitnehmen zum Sehen“.
Im Sturm habe er sich für die Freiburger Entdeckung Derry Scherhant und Said El Mala entschieden, weil dieser auf einer neuen Position in Köln „das Spielfeld auf einer neuen Position kennenlerne“. Der Frankfurter Younes Ebnoutalib habe ihn als „positive Überraschung im ersten Camp überzeugt“. Ungeachtet der Unruhe um seine Person ist auch Lennart Karl dabei, den Klopp als „Toptalent“ pries.

Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. https://gothamist.com/news/dsny-worker-a.title: DSNY worker arrested for killing a woman in Brooklyn while driving a garbage truck
https://gothamist.com/news/dsny-worker-a.author: Brittany Kriegstein
https://gothamist.com/news/dsny-worker-a.text:
A Staten Island man on Wednesday was arrested for striking and killing a woman in Brooklyn while driving a Department of Sanitation garbage truck last week, according to the NYPD.
Timothy A. Mcvey, 41, was charged with failure to yield to a pedestrian and failure to exercise due care, the NYPD said.
Siobhan Lynch, 30, of Brooklyn, was crossing the parkway at Cropsey Avenue around 6:35 p.m. on Oct. 28 when the garbage truck, heading east, turned right onto the parkway and hit her, police said.
Emergency services took Lynch to NYU Langone Hospital, where she was pronounced dead. Mcvey stayed at the scene, police said.
“This is a terrible tragedy, and our thoughts are with the family of the victim,” Department of Sanitation spokesperson Joshua Goodman told Gothamist in an email last week.
Information on Mcvey’s attorney was not immediately available.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120368.title: Mietenwahnsinn | Habersaathstraße: Dauerlauf gegen Entmietung in Berlins Mitte
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120368.author: David Rojas Kienzle
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120368.text:
- Berlin
- Mietenwahnsinn
Habersaathstraße: Dauerlauf gegen Entmietung in Berlins Mitte
Räumungen, zerstörte Wohnungen, kein Wasser: Die letzten Bewohner der Habersaathstraße 40–48 hoffen auf das Landgericht und die neue Bezirkspolitik.
»Man muss sich arrangieren«, sagt Daniel Diekmann zu seiner Wohnsituation. Im Gespräch mit »nd« sitzt er auf einem Stuhl im Treppenhaus der Habersaathstraße 48 im Hochparterre. Dort, wo eigentlich vier Wohnungstüren sein müssten, sind riesige Sperrholzplatten in der Wand verschraubt, aus den Fugen quillt Bauschaum. »Die Platten sind fast schon eine Verbesserung«, kommentiert Diekmann ironisch. Vorher habe man ja nie wissen können, ob hinter den aufgebrochenen Türen nicht jemand lauere.
Diekmann hat noch eine Wohnung. Damit ist er einer der letzten verbliebenen Mieter im ehemaligen Schwesternwohnheim der Charité im Bezirk Mitte. Seit August 2023 gibt es kein Warmwasser mehr im Haus. Im November 2025 wurde die Fernwärmeversorgung abgestellt, nachdem der Vermieter den Vertrag nicht verlängert hatte. Und seit dem 22. Januar 2026 hat Diekmann kein fließendes Wasser mehr in seiner Wohnung. Damals stürmte eine Gruppe Vermummter das Haus und zerschlug in leer stehenden Wohnungen Armaturen, Toiletten, Waschbecken und Badewannen. Wasser lief durch das ganze Haus. Danach ließ der Eigentümer die Türen zu den dann unbewohnbaren Wohnungen mit den Sperrholzplatten verrammeln. Seither versorgt sich Diekmann mit kaltem Wasser aus Kanistern, die er in seine Wohnung trägt. Nachdem die Heizung abgestellt worden war, bot der Vermieter Ölradiatoren als Ersatz an. Aber die will Diekmann nicht, wegen der hohen Stromkosten.
Zuletzt machte die Räumung des Aufgangs Nummer 44 Schlagzeilen. Am 13. Oktober 2026 wurde das Haus unter Begleitung eines großen Polizeiaufgebots geräumt und Wohnungen wie zuvor im Aufgang 48 mit Spanplatten zugesperrt. Eine Bewohnerin, gegen die kein Räumungstitel vorlag, wurde dabei über Stunden eingesperrt und musste am Ende von der Feuerwehr mit einer Drehleiter befreit werden. Schritt für Schritt wird das Gebäude so unbewohnbar gemacht.
Die im Aufgang der Hausnummer 48 verrammelten und zerstörten Wohnungen wurden schon ein Jahr zuvor, im Oktober 2025 geräumt. Zuvor wohnten zahlreiche ehemalige Obdachlose im Gebäudekomplex. Sie hatten Ende 2021 Wohnungen besetzt, die schon damals lange leer standen. Nach einem Deal zwischen Eigentümer und Bezirk konnten die Besetzer*innen lange bleiben.
Früher wurde das 1984 gebaute Gebäude mit mehreren Aufgängen und mehr als 100 Wohnungen wegen seiner bunten Fassade Papageienplatte genannt. Heute ist die Fassade weiß, mit Ausnahme einzelner Flächen in Pink und Grün. Manche Fenster sind wie die Türen von innen mit Platten verschraubt. Im dritten Stock sind die Scheiben aus den Fenstern geschlagen und mit Plastikfolie verhängt.
Der katastrophale Zustand des Gebäudes ist Folge der heftigen Auseinandersetzungen um den Wohnblock. Unter der Ägide des berühmt-berüchtigten SPD-Finanzsenators Thilo Sarrazin wurde das damals landeseigene Gebäude 2006 für rund 2,2 Millionen Euro privatisiert und danach energetisch saniert. 2017 kaufte die Arcadia Estates Habersaathstraße 40–48 GmbH das Gebäude für rund den zehnfachen Preis. Der neue Eigentümer will das Gebäude abreißen und an seiner Stelle neu bauen. Doch dafür müssen die Mieter ausziehen, denn solange es gültige Mietverträge gibt, kann nicht abgerissen werden.
Ab 2018 bekamen Mieter*innen sogenannte Verwertungskündigungen. Diese sind nur rechtens, wenn dem Eigentümer durch die Fortsetzung des Mietverhältnisses »erhebliche wirtschaftliche Nachteile« entstehen. Aber nicht alle Mieter*innen haben ihre Wohnungen verlassen. Vom Vermieter angestrengte Klagen scheiterten vor der Justiz. Der Ausspruch einer Richterin – »Eine Wohnung ist kein Aktienpaket« – in einer Verhandlung 2023 ist mittlerweile zum geflügelten Wort geworden.
»Wir haben seit 2018 alle Prozesse vor dem Amtsgericht gewonnen«, sagt Diekmann. Am 15. Dezember geht es in die nächste Runde. Dann werden vor dem Landgericht die Berufungsverhandlungen in einem Prozessmarathon abgehandelt. Für die letzten fünf noch bestehenden Mietverhältnisse sind kurze 30 Minuten pro Verhandlung angesetzt. »Wir sind seit drei Monaten dabei, die Prozesse vorzubereiten«, sagt Diekmann. Er ist sich sicher, dass die Urteile zugunsten der Mieter*innen Bestand haben werden. »Natürlich gehen wir davon aus, dass wir gewinnen.«
Die Klagen haben über die Einzelfälle Bedeutung für das Haus. Auf eine Einwohneranfrage von Diekmann teilte das Bezirksamt im September 2026 mit, dass die zuletzt im Dezember 2025 verlängerte Abrissgenehmigung widerrufen werde, sollte das Landgericht die bisherigen Urteile bestätigen. Dann wären die Pläne der Arcadia Estates hinfällig.
Damit würde der Bezirk eine lange bestehende Forderung erfüllen, die nicht nur von den Mieter*innen aufgestellt wird. Denn die Zustände im Haus und das Agieren des Vermieters bewegen viele in der Hauptstadt. Sowohl die Berliner Linke als auch der Berliner Mieterverein fordern vom Bezirk, einen Treuhänder einzusetzen, der das Haus anstelle des aktuellen Eigentümers verwaltet. Aber der Bezirk hält das nicht für möglich. Da die entsprechenden Voraussetzungen nicht vorlägen, bestünden dazu keine Überlegungen, teilte der Bezirk im September auf eine parlamentarische Anfrage mit.
Auch bei kleineren Schritten, wie der Wiederherstellung der Fernwärmeversorgung, sieht der Bezirk keinen Handlungsspielraum. »Nur im Fall der drohenden Unbewohnbarkeit einer Wohnung und der erfolglosen Aufforderung an den Vermieter, seinen Pflichten nachzukommen« sei die bezirkliche Wohnungsaufsicht befugt, die Bewohnbarkeit anstelle des Vermieters wiederherzustellen, heißt es in der Antwort. »Im Fall der Habersaathstraße hat der Vermieter der Wohnungsaufsicht bereits vor Eintreten des Endes der Fernwärmeversorgung glaubhaft versichert, über Ölradiatoren die Wärmeversorgung zu gewährleisten.«
»Dieses ganze Zögern und Zaudern, davon haben die Leute die Schnauze voll«, sagt Diekmann. Ihm ist es wichtig, die politische Dimension der Auseinandersetzung zu betonen. »Es ging hier nie nur um meine Wohnung, es ging hier immer ums große Ganze.« Der Kampf um die Habersaathstraße, der seit der Privatisierung 2006 geführt werde, stehe exemplarisch für ganz Berlin und den Ausverkauf der Stadt. »Das ist ein Kampf um günstigen Wohnraum. Es gibt kein Recht auf Spekulation, es gibt kein Recht auf maximale Rendite.«
Diekmann macht sich leise Hoffnungen auf einen Wechsel in der Zuständigkeit des Amtes des Baustadtrats und das Engagement der Linken, die nach den Wahlen im September die Mehrheit stellt. Ihm ist es wichtig, dass auch die neu in das Bezirksparlament gewählten Abgeordneten genau über den Kampf um die Habersaathstraße Bescheid wissen und das Problem kennen. »So ein Leuchtturmkampf wie hier muss dann erklärt werden«, sagt er. Er ist sich aber sicher: »Es wird hier keinen Abriss geben.«

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: One museum visit a month could improve health, new report finds
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Joe Ware
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Visiting a museum or art gallery for just one hour a month could significantly improve people's physical and mental health, according to a new report which calls for cultural engagement to become as routine as exercise and healthy eating.
The research, commissioned by the charity Art Fund in partnership with University College London professor Daisy Fancourt, recommends that people spend at least 60 minutes with art in museums and galleries every month.
However, the survey of 2,000 UK adults found that 89% fail to meet this proposed target, equivalent to an estimated 49.5 million people.
The report, “The Recommended Dose of Art: A Prescription for Health and Wellbeing”, draws together scientific evidence suggesting that regular cultural engagement can reduce stress, improve cognitive health and potentially extend life expectancy.
Previous studies have shown that regular museum and gallery visits could nearly halve the risk of developing depression over the following decade. Other studies have linked cultural participation with reduced dementia risk and lower levels of loneliness.
Viewing original artworks in galleries was also associated with a 22% greater reduction in the stress hormone cortisol compared with viewing reproductions.
Fancourt, whose book Art Cure on the scientific benefits of art came out earlier this year, says regular engagement with art should be considered a health-promoting behaviour alongside exercise, a balanced diet and spending time outdoors.
“Guidelines like eating our 5-a-day of fruit and vegetables and getting our 10,000 steps have proven effective in helping us to prioritise other health-promoting behaviours in our busy lives,” she says in a statement. “Adding regular arts engagement to this list could be a simple and joyful way of investing further in our health and wellbeing.”
But the findings also raise questions about whether Britain's struggling museums have the resources to encourage more frequent visits. Jenny Waldman, the director of Art Fund, tells The Art Newspaper that the research strengthens the case for sustained public investment in museums, including protecting free admission at national institutions and supporting local and regional collections.
“We want to see sustained, long-term public investment across the museum sector, so that all museums have the resources to care for their collections and welcome the widest possible audiences,” she says.
Waldman acknowledged that removing admission charges alone would not overcome barriers to visiting museums, including accessibility and the resources available to institutions.
She says Art Fund's research among museum directors found that 36% of museums had reduced their opening hours because of insufficient funding and staffing.
“If we want museums to play a greater role in supporting public health, we must invest in the sector and give them the means to do so,” she adds.
Waldman also points to international developments, including Greece's introduction of arts prescribing into its national healthcare system and growing recognition of cultural organisations as public health assets. She also notes efforts closer to home: “Scotland's Chief Medical Officer, Sir Gregor Smith, recently published a report recognising arts organisations as important public health assets and calling for arts and culture to be embedded more widely in Scotland's approach to public health.”

https://hyperallergic.com/doris-salcedo-.author: Hyperallergic

Doris Salcedo Traces the Shape of Memory
The Colombian artist reflects on the state’s attempts to erase history, and the people’s continued refusal. Also: How should artists decide whether to participate in documenta 16?
In the face of decades of violence and erasure in Colombia, artist Doris Salcedo has made memory her medium. Senior Editor Valentina Di Liscia writes that her poignant sculptures evoke the victims of the devastating guerrilla conflicts “not by simply remembering or looking back, but by delicately articulating the contours of their absence.” Recently, the Colombian government drew ire for removing LGBTQ+, leftist, and feminist objects from the Museo Nacional in Bogotá, later reinstalled after public protests. Di Liscia spoke with Salcedo about the significance of that resistance, the generational wounds of political violence, and how Colombian artists are building paths forward, as they always have.
Meanwhile, artists around the world are grappling with the upcoming edition of the embattled documenta. Two anonymous artists who participated in the last iteration write candidly about the vicious attacks they endured from German media and politicians for opposing the genocide in Palestine. Their practical advice is for artists who are on the fence about showing their work at documenta 16, but it’s also an essential guide to navigating institutional networks that seek to quash meaningful political dissent, the very kernel of artmaking and creativity.
Today, we also report on an investigation into an Israeli airstrike in Lebanon that killed artist Ali Cherri’s parents in 2024, an overdue step toward justice, and the sentencing of Daniel Sikkema, who was found guilty of ordering the murder of his husband, gallerist Brent Sikkema.
More below, including glimmers of hope from the midterms — Claire Valdez will be your artist in Congress, after all.
—Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor, books
Doris Salcedo on Colombia’s Refusal to Forget
On October 15, dozens of objects were removed from display at the Museo Nacional in Bogotá under the orders of the country’s far-right president, Abelardo de la Espriella. Among them were artworks and materials related to LGBTQ+ and feminist movements; the country’s 2016 peace agreement with the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC); and the campaigns of left-wing leaders Carlos Pizarro and Bernardo Jaramillo Ossa, both assassinated in the 1990s, whom de la Espriella has called “terrorists.” The objects were reinstated within two weeks by a court order, but the incident roiled the nation: Hundreds took to the streets in protest and faced police repression.

https://www.propublica.org/article/safes.title: SafeSport Will Now Alert Schools, Clubs if Coaches Sanctioned for Abuse Continue to Work With Kids
https://www.propublica.org/article/safes.author: Molly Hensley-Clancy
https://www.propublica.org/article/safes.text:
The U.S. Center for SafeSport is taking steps to stop coaches banned over allegations of sexual abuse from working with children, part of an initiative that the organization said it is launching because of reporting by ProPublica and The Washington Post about gaps in the child protection system in youth sports.
Charged by Congress with investigating allegations of sexual abuse in sports, SafeSport has the power to suspend or permanently bar coaches from contact with athletes and place their names on a public disciplinary list. But the center has authority only over the country’s national sports governing bodies, which are overseen by the U.S. Olympic and Paralympic Committee. Elementary and high schools, colleges and many independent youth sports leagues are not required to follow SafeSport’s bans, though some opt to do so. Parents and other caregivers only know if a coach has been sanctioned if they check the list.
SafeSport’s new initiative encourages people to find and report banned coaches who are continuing to work with children, SafeSport said, with a publicity initiative that includes a video with its CEO.
It is also launching a new “internal process” to notify schools and other organizations that coaches are on the SafeSport list. Hilary Nemchik, SafeSport’s vice president of external affairs, said the organization would send a form letter when it learned coaches were still working with kids, either as a result of its own investigation or in response to a report.
“When SafeSport imposes a sanction for abuse or misconduct, the community should be aware,” Benita Fitzgerald Mosley, SafeSport’s CEO, said in a statement. “Someone could be on the SafeSport Database for abuse but go on to work at a school or coach for a league outside of our jurisdiction.”
ProPublica and The Post discovered several coaches who had been banned by SafeSport but continued to work with children. One story highlighted the case of a volleyball coach, Ryan Richardson, who SafeSport found to have committed sexual misconduct with a minor but who has continued coaching teenage girls in the Rio Grande Valley in Texas. An independent volleyball league allowed Richardson to coach at several of its tournaments even after his name appeared on SafeSport’s database. Videos posted online showed Richardson on the sidelines.
The reporting showed that Richardson continued coaching in part by allowing a former assistant, Gavin Rudder, to take over the volleyball club after Richardson was banned by USA Volleyball, the sport’s governing body, in 2024. ProPublica and The Post found that Rudder allowed Richardson to coach the teams for years after the ban, a violation of the SafeSport code.
After the story was published, SafeSport added Rudder’s name to its public database, listing him as temporarily restricted from unsupervised coaching or training.
Rudder is currently listed as the coach at Weslaco High School, near McAllen. Abel Aguilar, the Weslaco district’s deputy superintendent, said in an email that the district “does not comment on personnel matters.”
In a text message, Rudder said the SafeSport ban “has nothing to do with high school volleyball” and that he had not “done anything wrong.” He said he was no longer associated with Richardson’s club volleyball team following the end of the 2026 season.
Read More
Richardson has not responded to requests for comment on ProPublica and The Post’s reporting. When he was first suspended in 2024 by Lone Star Region Volleyball, the organization overseeing volleyball in South Texas, Richardson told the local news website MyRGV that complaints about him were an effort to “retaliate and defame someone’s character,” and said he “would never do anything to risk the physical or mental wellbeing of these strong young ladies.”
In announcing the changes, SafeSport also nodded to a bipartisan inquiry into a major youth sports organization launched last month by the powerful House Energy and Commerce Committee, which also oversees SafeSport.
The lawmakers said they were launching a probe of the Amateur Athletic Union after ProPublica and The Post reported that the nonprofit does not follow SafeSport bans and has become a haven for coaches who are banned for abuse. The committee asked AAU President Jo Mirza for details on its child safety policies and training, setting a deadline of Oct. 21.
Committee representatives this week didn’t respond to questions about the status of the investigation. The AAU, which has said in a statement that it is “committed to protecting its athletes through comprehensive protection policies overseen by our Compliance Department,” said it would “cooperate fully” with any inquiry.

https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.title: Women Are the Real Story of the Midterm Elections
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.author: Michele Goodwin
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
Women Are the Real Story of the Midterm Elections
In a rebuke of the Trump administration and its cataclysmic decisions and policies, voters elected record numbers of women into office.
The 2026 midterms were historic. The Democrats prevailed, taking control over both the House and the Senate and gaining five governor’s offices. Pundits and political analysts will spend the coming days, weeks, and months analyzing the election results, examining why Americans voted as they did. But what message did voters send?
Two messages are clear. First, the 2026 midterms were a resounding, blistering rebuke of the Trump administration and its cataclysmic decisions and policies. The administration has blatantly abused the powers of the executive branch, mishandled foreign affairs, slashed essential programs that helped the poorest Americans and farmers, disregarded and destroyed beloved institutions and sites, and gutted essential environmental regulations, to say nothing of its grifting, bullying, and attacks on women in power and through its disastrous policies and actions.
On one hand, in just two years, the Trump administration has undone decades of American progress. On the other, America was already failing so many of its people and Trump only intensified their suffering.
Despite promises in 2024 of making Americans better off or “great again,” the Trump administration failed its working- and middle-class constituents. Its erratic and arbitrary financial policies, including unlawful tariffs and baffling war in Iran continue to hurt American families, dramatically raising the costs of gas across the country. In the outer regions of Alaska, gas prices exceeded $25 per gallon. The high costs of food now make it difficult for Americans to feed their families. And despite Trump supporters’ rallying around tougher immigration laws in 2024, the mass detention of their neighbors and community members and the murdering of their fellow Americans by ICE agents were not part of their agenda.
Trump’s exploitation of office is at a breaking point. At every turn, he has financially benefited during this term in office, trampling the Emoluments Clause and presidential norms. The president has hawked not only Bibles and sneakers but literally hundreds of items. Visit the so-called Trump Store—an online bazaar, selling everything from branded footballs, honey, hoodies, roasted coffee, vests, shot glasses, candles, cookies, jellybeans, and chocolates. There is no arms-length dealing here. Trump is selling a pricey “Presidential Gold Aurum Note” and a “President Donald J. Trump ‘We The People’ Silver Medallion” and one in gold too. He’s also faced accusations of selling access to the White House.
Yet the midterms were not only about fighting back against an administration that shows little regard for the concerns of Americans. The second message they delivered was about women claiming their space and expanding political leadership. In a historic showing, pro-choice women leaders across the country secured House and Senate seats and prevailed in gubernatorial races—a powerful response to both Trump’s policies and the Supreme Court’s overturning of Roe v. Wade.
Keep in mind, since January 2025 when Donald Trump took office for a second term, his administration has targeted women with political harassment, pulling grants that focused on women’s health, demoting women leaders in the military, firing scores of Black women in government positions, and seeking to disenfranchise women voters through the SAVE Act, which “would make it harder to vote for 69 million women.” The National Partnership for Women and Families issued a report shortly after Trump returned to the White House, identifying “35 ways the Trump Administration has harmed women and families in its first 100 days.” That list has only grown since then.
Trump has frozen family-planning funding—gutting programs that provided breast cancer screenings, contraception, and STI testing. The administration has revoked efforts to raise the minimum wage, which would directly affect women workers, many of whom are the main provider and head of their household. Rather than prioritizing family leave or childcare initiatives, this administration decimated the Department of Education and invested in war, while turning its keys over to the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE). According to congressional oversight letters, the administration canceled minority health grants, diverting the money to “support things like treatment for erectile dysfunction in the name of family values.” Trump also terminated the federal diversity, equity, inclusion, and accessibility offices, which tracked gender disparities.
Voters responded by electing record numbers of women into office. In Georgia, Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta, made history by becoming the state’s first woman governor, and the first Black woman to ever be elected governor in US history. Bottoms beat out Rick Jackson, an anti-abortion billionaire who invested $200 million of his personal resources in the campaign. Audio recordings of Jackson surfaced where he was heard expressing “support for further restrictions beyond Georgia’s current six-week abortion law,” which ProPublica investigations have found contributed to the preventable deaths of women in the state.
In Ohio, Dr. Amy Acton resoundingly defeated Vivek Ramaswamy, who describes himself as “unapologetically pro-life.” Ramaswamy, a Trump loyalist, ran deeply disturbing, disgraceful ads against Acton, featuring her estranged mother calling her a liar. Notably, Acton was raped as a child by her stepfather. Nevertheless, Ramaswamy doubled down—as did Vice President JD Vance and Donald Trump, who criticized Republicans who urged Ramaswamy to not run the ad.
In a stunning victory, Representative Gina Hinojosa (D-Austin) defeated Governor Greg Abbott, becoming the first Latina governor of Texas. Hinojosa, who campaigned on the vision that “this is our last best chance to take back Texas for the people,” has shared her personal story of pregnancy loss. In contrast, Abbott played a critical role in rolling back reproductive freedom in Texas. The state was the first to implement an extreme abortion ban, nine months before Roe was overturned. And now in Texas doctors risk 99 years of incarceration, $100,000 fines, and the possibility of losing their licenses to practice medicine if they violate the state’s total abortion ban.
Deb Haaland, the former US secretary of the interior, will be New Mexico’s next governor. She will be the first Indigenous woman governor in US history. In Minnesota, a state that has felt the devastating brunt of Trump’s domestic immigration policies, voters have elected Senator Amy Klobuchar as their next governor. Klobuchar has consistently criticized the US Supreme Court’s overturning of Roe v. Wade. And, in Illinois, Lieutenant Governor Juliana Stratton has been elected to the Senate. Stratton helped spearhead in the state the ratification of the Equal Rights Amendment, which would prohibit sex discrimination.
As Trump’s lame-duck presidency comes into clear view, Americans are rejecting policies that keep them vulnerable and threaten their future, entangle them in wars, and make a mockery of the rule of law. There is a momentum building with historic wins across the nation, including in Texas, Ohio, and Iowa. As the Democrats return to power in Washington, DC, they should look not only to rebuild what was lost but to lay the groundwork for a third Reconstruction.

https://taz.de/Flughaefen-europaweit/!62.title: Flughäfen europaweit: Bombendrohungen gegen Passagierflugzeuge
https://taz.de/Flughaefen-europaweit/!62.text:
Flughäfen europaweit: Bombendrohungen gegen Passagierflugzeuge
Erneut gibt es mehrere Bombendrohungen gegen Flugzeuge in Europa. Die Hintergründe sind bisher nicht bekannt.
dpa | Zum zweiten Mal in dieser Woche sind mehrere europäische Flüge von Bombendrohungen betroffen. Wegen einer Bombendrohung ist unter anderem ein Linienflug zwischen Dublin und Rom nach Frankreich umgeleitet worden. Die Maschine landete am Militärflughafen Évreux, wie das Amt des französischen Premierministers mitteilte. Die 151 Passagiere und 6 Crew-Mitglieder würden in Sicherheit gebracht. Sprengstoffexperten seien nun im Einsatz. Évreux liegt etwa 100 Kilometer nordwestlich der französischen Hauptstadt Paris. Bereits am Dienstag hatte es Bombendrohungen gegen kommerzielle Flüge in Europa gegeben.
Zwischenfälle gab es zudem in Italien: Nach anonymen Hinweisen auf einem mutmaßlichen Bombenalarm an Bord eines Finnair-Fliegers aus Helsinki, der gegen 9.30 Uhr von Kampfjets der italienischen Luftwaffe eskortiert am Flughafen Rom-Fiumicino landete, leiteten Sprengstoffexperten der Polizei die vorgesehenen Sicherheitskontrollen ein. Diese dauern weiterhin an, wie die Nachrichtenagentur Ansa meldete.
Eine Maschine, die am Morgen am Airport Mailand-Malpensa gestartet war, wurde nach Angaben der Agentur Ansa wegen einer während des Fluges eingegangenen Bombendrohung nach Wien umgeleitet und landete dort. Ein österreichischer Polizeisprecher bestätigte die Landung auf Anfrage. Zuvor sei in Polen eine E-Mail mit einer Bombendrohung eingegangen. In Wien wurde jedoch keine Gefährdung festgestellt. Das Flugzeug sei mittlerweile unterwegs nach Warschau, hieß es. Der Sprecher sprach von einer „abstrakten“ Drohung und verwies auf ähnliche Vorfälle in der jüngsten Vergangenheit.
Auch in Dänemark, Tschechien, Bulgarien und Rumänien
Am Flughafen Kopenhagen gab es Drohungen gegen zwei Flüge. Bei der Durchsuchung der Flugzeuge sei aber nichts Verdächtiges gefunden, teilte die Polizei der Nachrichtenagentur Ritzau mit: „Nach unserer Einschätzung besteht beziehungsweise bestand keine Gefahr für Passagiere oder andere Personen, die sich am Flughafen aufhalten.“ Um welche Flüge es sich handelte, wollte ein Sprecher demnach nicht sagen.
Mehrere Bombendrohungen haben auch den Flugverkehr in Prag beeinträchtigt. Man habe Warnungen über improvisierte Sprengsätze an Bord von vier Flugzeugen erhalten, teilte die tschechische Polizei bei X mit. Nach der Landung auf dem internationalen Václav-Havel-Flughafen würden die Maschinen von Spezialisten durchsucht. Gleichwohl stufe man die Relevanz der Drohungen als niedrig ein.
Drei Maschinen der Gesellschaft Ryanair bekamen auf dem Weg nach Bulgarien Bombendrohungen, berichtete die bulgarische Nachrichtenagentur BTA unter Berufung auf das Verkehrsministerium in Sofia. Eine Maschine aus London wurde auf den Flughafen Plowdiw umgeleitet. Die zwei weiteren Flugzeuge – aus Kopenhagen und Madrid – landeten planmäßig in Sofia. Einen ähnlichen Fall gab es im Nachbarland Rumänien: Eine Maschine der Gesellschaft Wizz Air bekam auf ihrem Flug von Mailand nach Bukarest eine Bombendrohung, landete aber sicher und planmäßig in Rumäniens Hauptstadt, berichtete die rumänische Nachrichtenagentur Mediafax. Der Inlandsgeheimdienst SRI untersuche nunmehr das Flugzeug, hieß es.

https://gothamist.com/news/mamdani-pledg.title: Mamdani pledged support for NYC street vendors. Now they’re facing a crackdown.
https://gothamist.com/news/mamdani-pledg.author: Liam Quigley
https://gothamist.com/news/mamdani-pledg.text:
Mayor Zohran Mamdani has pledged to support street vendors, but under his administration tickets for people illegally hawking trinkets and merch have reached new highs, data shows.
Tickets issued by Parks Enforcement Patrol for unlawful vending reached 2,237 by the end of September, jumping 671 tickets — or 43% — from the same time in 2025.
Data shows parks officers are also issuing many more tickets for the relatively obscure offense of “unattended personal belongings.” In 2025, parks enforcement officers issued just 55 such tickets. They’ve issued 429 summonses for unattended belongings so far this year.
The trend comes after Mamdani created an office of street vendor services in March, which is led by longtime vendor advocate Carina Kaufman-Gutierrez. "Our street vendors are not a problem to solve, they are a community to support," Mamdani said at the time.
“This increase reflects several factors, including higher park attendance, increased vending activity and events in parks, and additional PEP staff on patrol," said Jeremy M. Edwards, deputy press secretary of the parks department.
The department will continue to work with vendors to ensure they understand the rules and regulations, he added.
The mayor’s office did not return a request for comment about the expanded enforcement.
Licensed Vendor John Golden said he’s getting slapped with violations for unattended personal belongings even though he has a license to sell merchandise at City Hall Park. Data shows he’s been hit with at least three violations.
“They give us the tickets and tell us to go fight in court, and we beat them, and they still come back. It’s harassment,” he said.
He said understood that unlicensed vendors are just trying to earn a living, but was frustrated he was also being caught in the crackdown.
“I understand that unlicensed guys gotta make money 'cause they got a family to feed too... I'd rather see you come out and work in the streets than rob and steal,” he said.
Parks enforcement patrol officers have issued 98 tickets for unattended personal belongings so far this year at City Hall Park.
DC37 Local 983 President Joe Puleo, who represents the roughly 350 parks enforcement officers in the city, said his members are addressing a problem that surged after the pandemic.
“ If you don't address it, it's just gonna get worse and worse,” he said. ”Foot traffic equals dollar signs.”
The City Council passed a bill last year ending jail time and criminal charges for breaking street vending rules.
Data shows Parks Enforcement Patrol officers have issued more tickets overall compared to last year. PEP officers typically crack down on unleashed dogs, drinking or smoking in parks, unlicensed operation of pedicabs and public urination.
Parks officers issued 6,591 tickets through September of 2026 according to city data, a surge of 59% compared to the same period last year.
Mayor Eric Adams banished vendors from the Brooklyn Bridge near City Hall Park in 2023, citing crowding concerns.
Mamdani has long supported efforts to increase the number of permits issued to street vendors. He filmed an early viral video for his campaign at a halal cart. He called vendors “the heart of New York City” in a tweet in December, shortly before taking office.
A press release on Kaufman-Gutierrez's appointment in March said she would "reduce unnecessary penalties and advance fair enforcement."
The city will begin distributing 10,500 new vending licenses in January.
