https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: ‘It’s kind of a melting pot’: how one US city transformed a highway into a leafy oasis
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Carl Smith
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Passing through the Mojave desert on State Route 14, going by landscapes Hollywood uses to represent alien planets, a driver might not expect to find a walkable, tree-lined boulevard.
 
But there are nine beautiful, leafy blocks on West Lancaster Boulevard, a piece of what used to be Highway 14. They were redeveloped as part of a mixed-use urban streetscape in the city of Lancaster, California in 2010.
 
The BLVD, as it’s been rebranded, is home to 250 public and private enterprises, from banks, tattoo shops and restaurants to museums, a performing arts centre and a public library. City Hall is just a block south.
 
The city invested $11.5m (£8.5m) to transform a busy thoroughfare into an inviting public space. The three lanes in the centre of the former five-lane road were replaced by a series of tree-lined ramblas – Spanish for “avenue” and “watercourse,” because dry stream beds served as streets in early cities.
The redesign was planned and funded by the city of redevelopment agency. Within four years of completion, it had generated more than $270m in economic output, attracted $130m in investment, created hundreds of jobs and prompted the building or renovation of hundreds of housing units, according to the city.
 
The revitalisation has also created more intangible benefits, residents say.. The city centre the feels like a gathering space, they said — somewhere where they can feel like part of a community.
John Elford, the manager of Lancaster public library, was a reference librarian when construction began. Customers were angry about the disruption, and many complained about a major city centre thoroughfare being torn apart.
 
“Suddenly it was all done, and they had the grand opening,” Elford says. “Everybody loved it and the complaints stopped.”
The more beautiful and walkable space encouraged people to get out of their cars, he says. People who hadn’t visited the library began to wander in. Their questions began to change. Instead of asking for a specific title, visitors wanted to know where the fiction or non-fiction sections could be found. They started spending time in the library, perusing books or reading quietly.
 
The change has made the library feel more like a community space that all residents can share, Elford says. In the past, encounters with homeless patrons sometimes drove other visitors away from the library. But Elford says people have come to know their unhoused neighbours, and sometimes witness their transformations through contact with the library’s social workers.
 
“They start to get to know that person without actually introducing themselves to them,” he says.
Property and business owners went into partnership with the city in 2013 to create the BLVD Association, a property-based improvement district — a defined area where businesses work together as caretakers and promoters with funding from city taxes.
 
In 2016, the association launched an ambassador programme, hiring representatives to walk the BLVD and assist visitors and businesses. Brian Morris Jr has seen occasional problems with begging or break-ins during his six months on the job, but not enough to keep the area from feeling safe and livable, he says.
Nicole Stevens runs Pretty Little Poppy Marketplace, a business focused on selling wares from local vendors. She has lived in Lancaster since 1993, and has a long perspective on how its “main street” has changed. The reimagining has brought small businesses and families together, she says. “I’ve enjoyed being able to bring my boy down here.”
 
Alex Arreola, a cashier and marketer at the Sassy Bird restaurant, says he’s become friends with residents and business owners because it’s easy and pleasant to just walk around. “A lot of cities don’t have this walkable spot,” he says. “It’s a big benefit, the best place in Lancaster right now.”
Lancaster opened a museum on the BLVD in 2012 to house exhibits and education highlighting the history, art and culture of California’s Antelope Valley. Kim Calderwood, the museum’s art programme manager, grew up in California City, about 40 miles from Lancaster.
 
The Burns Pharmacy, which is still open, was the only place on Lancaster Boulevard that she recalls visiting with her family as a child. She was excited by the area’s transformation, from more foliage to all the businesses and restaurants targeting a younger clientele.
 
It’s a common occurrence for people to discover the museum in the course of rambling on the BLVD, including Lancaster residents. “They’ll say: ‘I was wondering what this place was,’” Calderwood says. “‘I didn’t realise we had a museum here.’”
 
Nanette Rushing, the owner of Nantiquez Vintage Flair, also works in a museum of sorts. Exhibits are for sale: an Oscar de la Renta dress, rhinestone jewelery, a fringed buckskin mountain suit. She staged estate sales and sold items she collected in stores that belonged to other people before she came to the BLVD 10 years ago.
“This street dictates a lot of things, from food to music to art,” she says. “It’s kind of a melting pot, and we can always have more of that up here. I’m glad to be a part of it.”
As sunset approached, Lancaster resident Frazier Farrell walked past a farmer’s market on one of the ramblas. A booth for cemetery plots sat between one with dried fruit and nuts and a large display of fresh produce.
 
The BLVD is a popular place with younger residents, he says. They can drift between bars, the theatre, restaurants or standup comedy. The museum where Calderwood works has an open mic night and figure drawing classes. Farrell has been a student and model. He often encounters friends when he visits the district and has made new ones among the business owners.
 
Calderwood says the main complaint she hears is about the slow speed limits in the district. “I’m definitely biased towards this sort of city planning,” she says. “It’s just not something that we get out here, or pretty much any other place I’ve lived.”
A version of this article was originally published in Governing.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Guillaume Cerutti named president of the Palace of Versailles
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Alexandre Crochet
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
After eight months without a president, the Palace of Versailles finally has a new leader. Guillaume Cerutti, 60, has been named the president of the prestigious institution, according to the newspaper Politico. A graduate of France’s elite École nationale d’administration (ENA) and a former senior civil servant in the finance ministry, he succeeds Christophe Leribault, who was appointed president and director of the Louvre in February following the abrupt departure of Laurence des Cars.
The appointment marks Cerutti’s return to public service after two decades in the private sector. In a twist of fate, he is following in the footsteps of his former mentor, Jean-Jacques Aillagon, who headed the Palace and National Estate of Versailles from 2007 to 2011. Cerutti worked closely with Aillagon for many years, first at the Centre Pompidou, where Aillagon was the president from 1996 to 2002, and later as his chief of staff when Aillagon became France’s culture minister in 2002. “Having worked alongside Guillaume [Cerutti] for decades, I know he has all the experience and qualities needed to lead Versailles,” Aillagon told Le Monde.
Cerutti went on to put his management skills to work in the art market, becoming head of Sotheby’s France in 2007. In 2015, he was poached by François Pinault, who appointed him president of Christie’s operations in Europe, the Middle East, Russia and India. Just months later, he was promoted to global chief executive of the auction house. At both Sotheby’s and Christie’s, Cerutti built a reputation as a formidable cost-cutter. He also proved adept at steering Christie’s through difficult market conditions.
His next move within the Pinault empire, however, was less successful. In January 2025, Cerutti was appointed president of the Pinault Collection, which oversees the Palazzo Grassi and Punta della Dogana in Venice, as well as the Bourse de Commerce in Paris. Once again, he was following in the footsteps of Aillagon, who had held the same position in the 2010s. But, as Le Monde reports, Cerutti’s efforts to impose the kind of financial discipline he had introduced at Christie’s, coupled with his wish to slow the pace of acquisitions, brought him into conflict with Pinault, who was used to running his collection on his own terms. Barely a year later, Cerutti was forced to step down.
He now assumes one of the most coveted positions in French cultural life, taking charge of a historic palace, museum and gardens that welcomed 8.4 million visitors in 2025 and employ around 1,000 people. His extensive connections in the worlds of business, culture and politics could prove particularly valuable as Versailles faces mounting budgetary pressures and an ever-greater need to secure support from wealthy patrons.
- This article was originally published in The Art Newspaper France

https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: My childhood was one of survival and resilience. How can I model a joyful life for my kids? | Leading questions
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: Eleanor Gordon-Smith
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
I’m a child of first-generation immigrants and have always carried a story of survival and resilience. My parents were part of a “lost generation” who sacrificed a lot to put us all through university. There was a very defined path for success, some of which I followed and some not. I married outside of race; I made work choices for financial stability. I don’t know how to enjoy things that other people seem to. Hobbies, travelling, home renovations … I look at those like “what is the point?”
I want to say it’s because my upbringing was not full of leisure activities; my parents only allowed us to focus on academic topics. Now that I’m a mother though, I wonder how I can role model some of this “living well for its own sake” for my children. It’s hard to find simple joys actually joyful. Growing up, everything needed to be “applied” towards something, and it feels that mentality is informing everything I do. Any advice on how to break free and live in the moment?
Eleanor says: Sometimes the means take over the end. Like a strangler fig. We start out doing something as a way of achieving something else we value – as a means to an end. But over time, it takes up so much of our schedule and mental prioritisation that it starts to twist and wrap around the things we actually value. It crowds them out, competes for vital nutrients, until it wins. It becomes the thing we value for its own sake; the means become the end.
It happens with money. We start trying to get money for the good life it’ll bring, but over time we’ll throw parts of a good life on a pyre for the sake of getting more money.
And it happens with hard work.
Your parents decided to sacrifice, work hard, give things up. The original reason to do that was as a means to a better life. That’s why it’s worth making the mammoth sacrifices immigrant families make: leaving the place and people they knew, working hard in a new country, sometimes in multiple jobs or new languages. Nobody thinks it is worth doing these things because they are a temple to worship for their own sake. It is worth doing these so that life will be better for the generation after you. It is a means to an end – that things will be better for your kids.
Over time, though, the means can become the end. The organising mythos can become that we work hard to work hard; that it is the thing worth valuing for its own sake.
To think that way is to let the real value get strangled. Exactly like you said, everything growing up needed to be towards something. Couldn’t your quality of life, and your child’s, be what you were all working towards? Wasn’t a better life the point?
You asked how to break free.
Start with the feeling, not the activities. Don’t approach leisure as if it also needs a defined path. Other people might find joy in travel and home renovations, but you don’t have to. The first (only?) question is: what ignites a feeling of joy in you?
It can take time to get back in touch with your own reactions to things. Like finding the mind-muscle connection to a disused part of your body, if you’re long out of touch with asking “Do I enjoy this?” you may have to ask many times before you can detect the answer.
So don’t start with the hope that things will deliver joy and in-the-moment immersion right away. It might not feel like that at first. You can start in an exploratory way instead. Fieldwork. How does this make me feel? What can I detect in myself?
The joys that come to you might be totally specific to you. Some people feed crows. Some people dance disco. Some people preserve weeds. Making more room for enjoyment in your life is also the task of making more room for your actual self – how you actually feel, what you actually like. When you’re slow and still enough to ask what you truthfully feel about something, you’re already living more in the moment.
Your parents sacrificed a lot for you, and you’ve worked hard to honour that. You can cash in some of the hard-earned chips – be the person for whom life could be better – without feeling like it’s wrong. The point wasn’t to accumulate chips for the chips’ sake. Don’t let the means become the end.
The reader’s letter has been edited.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Rare Altdorfer landscape previously unknown to scholars to be auctioned next month
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Catherine Hickley
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
A rare landscape by the German Renaissance artist Albrecht Altdorfer will be offered at auction at Sotheby’s Old Masters Evening Sale in London on 9 December, with an estimated price of between £3m and £5m.
The painting of a thickly wooded landscape and a rainbow against a densely clouded sky, dating from around 1520, surfaced in a Swiss private collection. It was previously unknown to Altdorfer scholars and does not feature in the artist’s catalogue raisonné. It is one of only three known oil landscapes by Altdorfer, who is considered one of the first landscape artists. The other two are both in museums—one is in Munich’s Alte Pinakothek, and the other in London’s National Gallery.
“To add to the known body of work of one of the great masters of the Northern Renaissance is one of the most exciting discoveries imaginable in our field,” says George Gordon, the chairman of Sotheby’s Worldwide Old Masters Department.
The current owner of the painting inherited it from his father, who purchased it in 1957 from the collection of a noble Austrian family, the House of Harrach. Painted on parchment, it was later glued to a wooden panel support. It is the smallest of Altdorfer’s known landscapes. A distant castle perches on a rocky outcrop beyond the rain-wettened forest and undergrowth that dominates the painting, which is signed.
Altdorfer was born in 1480 in Regensburg in southern Germany, spent most of his career there, also working as a politician, and died in the city in 1538. His densely wooded landscapes are drawn from the mixed deciduous and evergreen forests either side of the Danube downstream from Regensburg, Gordon says.
He says it was difficult to give a price estimate for the painting because no Altdorfer work has been offered on the market since 1980, when the National Gallery paid the reported sum of £2.4m for Christ Taking Leave of His Mother (around 1520). It was one of the highest prices ever paid for a work of art at that time.
“We don’t really know what it’s worth because it’s many decades since an Altdorfer last came to the market,” Gordon says. “It could fetch more than our estimate. I think it’s quite likely that museums will be interested.”
Sotheby’s will exhibit the painting in New York from 7-19 November and in London from 4-9 December.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Seeing Trump and his acolytes lose so spectacularly is powerful schadenfreude for millions across the globe
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Rebecca Shaw
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
The last couple of days have been very bad for Donald Trump. Of course, in Trump’s usual style, he is denying that the Republican loss at the midterms has anything to do with him – but we all know it does. While I fear the Democrats will not use this decisive moment to exercise some ambition and take meaningful action, the goings-on of the last couple of days have been undeniably fun to watch.
Seeing so many conservatives lose in such a spectacular way has blessed millions across the globe with powerful schadenfreude. It is a much needed moment of relief, an experience of positivity to rejuvenate our ailing nervous systems (or whatever biology does). Sometimes you just need to see some terrible people have a terrible time. For me, it’s just been the icing on a cake I’ve been dining out on for the last couple of months: watching Trump supporters watch Trump describing other men’s bodies in detail.
I’m talking about the hardcore Donald Trump fans, the ones dedicated enough to still place themselves on the public-facing side of his campaign. The ones doing the real work: standing behind him on international television. They are the ones who love him the most. These hard-working, hardline, gun-toting, red-blooded American men and women (the two genders) were recently forced to stand behind Trump and smile and applaud as he described Republican senator John Husted in ways that would not be out of place in a Heated Rivalry novel:
“I examined his ass … and then I looked at his shoulders. I looked at his feet. I looked at his hand. I looked at his jawline. Studied him. He’s got a jawline.”
In even more wonderful news, in this instance, sex did not sell – Trump’s man crush suffered a crushing defeat in the midterms. But Trump is still president, and we don’t know where things will go from here. We have to find humour where we can in this world, and to me, the fact that in order for these Maga people to stand strong behind their man, they must appear to enjoy him sexually objectifying strong men, is really funny. It couldn’t be more satisfying. These are people who have spent years insisting on the narrowest, straightest possible definition of masculinity. They have the strongest opinions about what a man is, how a man should behave, what he should wear, who he should love, and presumably how much interest he should or should not show in another man’s juicy ass.
At a rally in Oklahoma last month, these same people stood there as Trump randomly talked about “big, strong, handsome Oklahoma studs” he had seen outside, and brought a couple of them on stage to examine, as if they were horses. I like to imagine his supporters being privately mortified, and questioning everything about themselves as they stood there. And the tests of their loyalty just keep getting better: in addition to his ongoing tour of man-meat monologues, last week Trump came out and said football was boring – in front of a crowd of Trump supporters who undoubtedly mostly love football. In a country struggling to afford fuel and groceries, where many find comfort in the sport, I find his bald-faced indifference to the people who idolise him extremely funny.
Of course, all of this has led to many jokes about Trump “being gay” or his “alleged dementia revealing he is bisexual”. His penchant for musical theatre and his laser focus on beautifying his ballroom with gilded gold or whatever have only added fuel to the fire. (I do think the world would be a much better place if he had followed his true calling of becoming a Mr Hollywood type entertainment reporter, standing on the red carpet making cutting remarks about celebrity outfits with Joan Rivers. Alas, we have this version.) But it’s not actually about love for other humans at all: it’s a total inability to stop treating them as objects for his amusement. I also suspect, in a way I find unfortunately relatable to me, that he got laughs for it once and now doesn’t know when to stop doing callbacks.
Trump’s supporters have spent years deriding men who aren’t as cartoonishly masculine as they would like. Now they have to stand behind a soft-handed, lame-duck president who thinks football is boring, and who can’t stop talking about spectacularly built men and ballrooms. They have been clapping and smiling and hopefully dying a bit inside.
I don’t know what Trump will be like from this point forward, or what parts of the anatomy he might move on to over the next two years. I do know that these people have already seen what years of this man and his party has done, how pathetic he is, the horrible things that have happened under his watch. Yet they’ve continued to show up. I suspect many of them will continue to stand with him long after the midterms. I hope for a better future, but in the meantime I’m going to get even more satisfaction out of pointing and laughing at them now – it was already fun before Trump got kicked in his not-supple, not-sexy ass.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Charles Dickens’s writing chalet and Hastings Castle added to list of English heritage sites at risk
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Maev Kennedy
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The cabin where Charles Dickens spent the last day of his life, the home in Stratford-upon-Avon of William Shakespeare’s daughter Susanna and the castle built by William the Conqueror high on the cliffs above the town of Hastings are among 197 buildings and sites added to Historic England’s Heritage at Risk Register today (5 November).
The list identifies sites such as buildings, parks, battlefields and shipwrecks that are threatened by decay, neglect or inappropriate development. There are now 4,991 entries on the register, all of which are labelled as of national importance. This encompasses 197 sites that were added this year.
The miniature Swiss chalet which became the writing retreat of Charles Dickens was a Christmas gift to the author in 1864, arrived flat packed in 94 pieces, and was put together by a theatre carpenter after Dickens and his house guests failed. Dickens placed it at the furthest end of the garden, reached by a tunnel he built under the road at his last home, Gad’s Hill, near Rochester in Kent. He spent much of 9 June 1870 working in the chalet on The Mystery of Edwin Drood, before returning to the house where he died that night, aged just 58.The house, now a school, and tunnel survive, but the chalet was moved in the 1960s to the garden of Eastgate House in Rochester, where it is now too fragile for public access.
Hall’s Croft, an imposing timber-framed building dating from 1613, was the home of Susanna Shakespeare and her husband John Hall. After many uses, and residents including the playwright George Bernard Shaw and the bestselling Victorian romantic novelist Marie Corelli, it was acquired by the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust and opened to the public in 1951. It had already been closed for several years for extensive conservation work when, in October 2025, a car reversed into the facade and caused further serious damage. The playwright Ken Ludwig has donated £1m to the work but major fundraising will still be needed.
Hastings Castle was one of the first three such sites built by William the Conqueror after his victory in the famous battle—and is depicted in the Bayeux Tapestry. The site, with a sweeping view across a stretch of the coast, has a long history, with remains of an Iron Age fort having been discovered there. The castle’s commanding site has made it very vulnerable to storms and coastal erosion and there have already been urgent works to stabilise its ruins. Future plans for the site include the creation of a new visitor centre and cafe.
Along with the sites that have been added this year there is good news: 85 sites for which solutions have been found, and which have now been removed from the register. They include the storm-lashed Newlyn Harbour in Cornwall and a little hut in the Gloucestershire garden of Edward Jenner, in which, in 1796, he performed the first-ever vaccinations.
A pair of elegant Georgian houses in east London, built around 1715 and Grade II* listed, had an unusual saviour: Tottenham Hotspur Football Club, which has converted them—with help from the Lottery Heritage Fund—into artists studios, gallery spaces, and a cafe. The space is run by Sarabande Foundation, which was founded by the late fashion designer Lee Alexander McQueen.
Rescue grants available include the Heritage at Risk Capital Fund and the Places of Worship Renewal Fund, both funded by the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport and administered by Historic England, and the Countryside Stewardship Heritage Service.
The UK’s heritage minister Baroness Twycross said in a statement that the register has a crucial role in identifying historic places in need of support. “Every part of the UK is bursting with history, so it is vital we protect the heritage sites at the heart of communities which help tell the stories of our nation.”
Claudia Kenyatta and Emma Squire, the joint chief executives of Historic England, said the most effective way of protecting the sites was to bring them back into use.“The sites saved and removed from the Register this year show what can be achieved when partners and communities work together to deliver positive lasting change.”

https://taz.de/Nachruf-auf-Autor-Joseph-.title: Nachruf auf Autor Joseph von Westphalen: Der Sterbesalat
https://taz.de/Nachruf-auf-Autor-Joseph-.author: Klaus Bittermann
https://taz.de/Nachruf-auf-Autor-Joseph-.text:
Nachruf auf Autor Joseph von Westphalen: Der Sterbesalat
Joseph von Westphalen konnte mit dem Montblanc-Füller umgehen wie Errol Flynn mit dem Degen. Nun ist der Romanautor und begnadete Polemiker gestorben.
Es war schon lange still um ihn geworden. Dabei hatten wir in den Neunzigern und Nullerjahren häufig und manchmal stundenlang telefoniert. Er erzählte von seinen neuen Entdeckungen alter Jazz- und Bluesstücke, von neuen Romanen, an denen er gerade arbeitete und die meistens mit einer neuen Amour fou zu tun hatten, der Joseph von Westphalen immer wieder verfiel. Vor allem in seinem letzten großen Roman „Der Liebessalat“, den er nur schrieb in der Hoffnung, dass das Buch in die Hände einer unbekannten Schönen fiele, die er auf einer seiner Lesungen gesehen hatte.
Westphalen schrieb also nicht aus Gründen des Ruhms und des Ehrgeizes, sondern aus dem einzigen Motiv, das die Mühe lohnt, ein Buch zu schreiben. Ohne die von ihm begehrte Frau, die schon eine fast mystische Aura verbreitet, wäre er „im Handumdrehen verhungert, verblödet, verrottet“, schrieb er.
Ihm war das Lächerliche durchaus bewusst, das hinter der schmachtenden Liebe zum Vorschein kommt und sich nicht selten als klebriges Selbstmitleid entpuppt. Das heißt, er stellte sich auch selbst infrage, wozu ein Breton in seinem Frauenanbetungsroman „Nadja“ nicht fähig gewesen wäre. Insofern hatte Westphalen mehr mit Balzac zu tun, der ebenfalls auf verschwenderische Weise der Liebe seinen Tribut zollte.
Ein besessener Vielschreiber
1945 in der Oberpfalz geboren, studierte er in München Literaturwissenschaften, war kurze Zeit von den Maoisten fasziniert und veröffentlichte schon bald im Haffmans Verlag, in dem fast die gesamte Riege der Neuen Frankfurter Schule erschien. Mit seinen Duckwitz-Romanen „Im diplomatischen Dienst“ landete er bei Hoffmann & Campe einen großen Erfolg. Westphalen war ein besessener Vielschreiber, der in mehreren Verlagen gleichzeitig veröffentlichte.
Dabei sorgte er im Kulturbetrieb immer wieder für Aufregung, weil er auch ein begnadeter Polemiker war, der kein Blatt vor dem Mund nahm, wenn er Neigungen zum Mainstream und zur allgemeinen Verblödung feststellte. Dies war vor allem während der Wiedervereinigungseuphorie der Fall. 1990, nicht lange nach dem Fall der Mauer, erschien ein Pamphlet mit dem Titel „Von deutscher Bulimie. Diagnose einer Freßgier“, wobei ihm die Vergeblichkeit seiner Kritik an der deutschen Einheit natürlich bewusst war.
Jahre, nachdem die Zeit Monika Maron und ihn zu einem wöchentlichen Ost-West-Dialog eingeladen hatte, bedauerte er seine „Beißhemmung“ gegenüber der „maulig-mopsigen Zonnentussi-Art meiner Briefpartnerin“, der er viel zu geduldig den Westen zu erklären versuchte, „als gälte es, eine misstrauische Behörde zu besänftigen“. Er schreckte vor Beleidigungen nicht zurück, die er allerdings immer mit hinreißender Verve begründete.
Als 1998 die Anthologie mit Bestsellerverrissen „Sorge dich nicht, lese!“ in der Edition Tiamat erschien und das Scherz-Verlagsimperium sich in seiner den Titel betreffenden Urheberrechtsehre verletzt fühlte, weil man glaubte, der jahrelang Platz 1 der Spiegel-Bestsellerliste belegende Ratgeber „Sorge dich nicht, lebe!“ von Dale Carnegie müsse vor unzulässiger Kritik mit einer einstweiligen Verfügung geschützt werden, ließ es sich Joseph von Westphalen nicht nehmen, unter dem Titel „Sorge dich nicht, zahle!“ eine furiose Anklage in der Süddeutschen Zeitung zu verfassen.
Beinahe ein Verlagsruin
Er forderte den Scherz-Verlag auf, die angedrohte Strafe bei Zuwiderhandlung von 10.000 Mark fallenzulassen, Scherz solle sich vielmehr entschuldigen und als Wiedergutmachung die Restauflage aufkaufen. Tatsächlich brachte der Artikel Westphalens Scherz dazu, die Klage aus Imagegründen zurückzuziehen. Der Verlagsruin war abgewendet. Mit seiner Montblanc-Feder wusste er so elegant umzugehen wie Errol Flynn mit dem Degen.
Anfang dieses Jahres verfasste Westphalen einen Nachruf auf seinen Freund Ulrich Enzensberger („es ist wirklich fürchterlich mit dieser Sterberei“) in der Süddeutschen. Ein Anlass, wieder mit ihm in Kontakt zu treten. Postwendend kam eine lange Mail, dass er wie eigentlich immer dabei sei, einen Roman zu schreiben, aber da er mit ihm „keine Frauen mehr beeindrucken“ wolle, fehle der Druck, aber der Impuls, einer bewunderten Frau bis ans Ende der Welt zu folgen, sei noch da.
Der Roman bleibt unvollendet, denn der literarische Freigeist und Husar Joseph von Westphalen ist mit 81 Jahren in München gestorben.
Klaus Bittermann ist der Verleger der Edition Tiamat.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Christie’s first Abu Dhabi art auction makes $8.9m
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Razmig Bedirian
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Christie’s first fine-art auction in Abu Dhabi has realised more than $8.9m, with several works fetching six figures and surpassing their original estimates.
The auction, titled Mawasim, was held last week (1 November) at The Abu Dhabi Edition. It marked the 20th anniversary of Christie’s first auction in the United Arab Emirates.
Topping the sale was Variations on the Hexagon (2006) by Monir Shahroudy Farmanfarmaian. The work was estimated between $150,000 and $250,000. It sold for $844,800, after almost seven minutes of bidding.
The mirror mosaic panel was commissioned for the opening of the Jameel Gallery at the Victoria and Albert Museum.
“It is a magnificent work of exceptional historical significance,” said Ridha Moumni, chairman of Christie’s Middle East and Africa.
“Farmanfarmaian is undoubtedly one of the most talented female artists in the region. This particular work, however, is especially spectacular.”
Other works that led the sale included Fahrelnissa Zeid’s Composition (1948-1949), which fetched $524,800. Her Endless Thoughts, painted in the late 1970s, sold for $486,400.
Ali Banisadr’s Homo Deus (2018), meanwhile, sold for $512,000, as did Faisel Laibi Sahi’s Baghdad Café (The Coffee Shop) (2016), which set a record for the artist. The painting, which measures six metres in length, is the largest by the Iraqi painter to go under the hammer.
Mahmoud Saïd’s Portrait de Princesse Fadia (Portrait of Princess Fadia)(1952) was sold for $486,400. Paul Guiragossian’s Noces (Wedding), an oil-on-masonite work created between 1958 and 1959, fetched $486,400. The sale marked a record for the medium for the artist, as did Samia Halaby’s Yesterday (1978), which sold for $358,400. The painting is a prime example of Halaby’s work from the 70s, when she developed her idiosyncratic approach to geometric abstraction.
Overall, Christie’s announced nine auction records, including for Jellal Ben Abdallah, whose Les Musiciennes (The Female Musicians) (1973) sold for $204,800 against an estimate between $100,000 and $150,000. Juliana Seraphim’s Femme Fleur (Flower Woman) (1973) also set a record, selling for $83,200. It had been estimated between $25,000 and $35,000.
Mawasim also marked the auction debut for several artists, including Nabil Kanso, Rami Farook, Fatma Lootah and Afra Al Dhaheri.
Moumni said that the fine-art auction of modern and contemporary works from the Middle East and North Africa was “the strongest results since 2015.
“It sends a very strong signal to the market and underscores the growing demand for art from the [region],” he said. “The results also demonstrate the significant presence of artists of Iranian origin in the market. We witnessed particularly spirited bidding for these artists, which was very exciting to see.”
Works by Emirati artists, such as Najat Makki and Hassan Sharif, have also “performed exceptionally well,” Moumni said.
Makki’s Emirates of Love (2025) sold for $28,160, whereas a painting from Sharif’s celebrated Press Conference series sold for $83,200.
“We were delighted to see works by all these UAE artists supported by both local and international collectors,” Moumni said. “There is still work to be done in further developing their market value, but the results were a truly wonderful surprise and a testament to the vitality of the UAE’s creative art scene.”
The auction, Moumni said, attracted a “healthy mix” of private collectors and institutional buyers. Interestingly, 30 per cent of participants were Generation Z and the millennial generations. There were also several first-time bidders.
“Thirty-seven per cent of participants were new to Christie’s, representing an encouraging expansion of our collector base,” Moumni said.
Sunday’s auction was the climactic conclusion to a week-long exhibition at The Abu Dhabi Edition, which presented the works featured in the Mawasim auction. The works came from private as well as institutional collections, such as from the Dalloul Collection and the Trad family collection in Beirut and the Barjeel Art Foundation in Sharjah.
Christie’s first auction in the UAE was held in 2006 in Dubai, at a time when the city’s arts scene was at a pivotal moment. New galleries and institutions were opening up and the city was preparing to host the DIFC Gulf Art Fair, which would then be rebranded at Art Dubai.
As a 20th anniversary auction, Mawasim was held in Abu Dhabi during a similar landmark moment. The UAE capital is preparing to host its first Frieze in November and the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi is meanwhile gearing up for its December opening.
“It was particularly important for us to present this anniversary auction here in Abu Dhabi, a city that is home to some of the region’s most significant museums, with several more important cultural institutions set to open in the coming years.”

https://taz.de/Harsche-Kritik-am-Bundesk.title: Kritik am Kanzler: Merz' No-Show bei der COP
https://taz.de/Harsche-Kritik-am-Bundesk.author: Kai Schöneberg
https://taz.de/Harsche-Kritik-am-Bundesk.text:
Kritik am Kanzler: Merz' No-Show bei der COP
Bundeskanzler Merz fährt nicht zur UN-Klimakonferenz in die Türkei. Die Reaktionen von Umweltverbänden, Grünen und Linken sind vernichtend.
„Blamage“, „verheerendes Signal“, „absoluter Tabubruch“: Umweltverbände, Grüne und Linke haben mit vernichtender Kritik auf die Ankündigung von Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz (CDU) reagiert, nicht zur UN-Klimakonferenz (COP) in die Türkei zu reisen. Der Kanzler bedanke sich für die Einladung, doch „aufgrund anderweitiger Verpflichtungen“ sei es ihm aber nicht möglich, teilzunehmen, hatte ein Regierungssprecher am Mittwoch in Berlin gesagt.
Die UN-Klimakonferenz beginnt am kommenden Montag in Antalya. Sie gilt als wichtigstes globales Forum zur Linderung der globalen Klimakrise. In den vergangenen fünf Jahren hatten die deutschen Kanzler*innen stets an der COP teilgenommen. Merz war auch im vergangenen Jahr im brasilianischen Belém.
Damals hatte er allerdings vor allem mit einer abwertenden Bemerkung über den COP-Austragungsort („Wer von euch würde denn gerne hierbleiben?“) Furore gemacht. Diesmal war seine Absage aufgrund verschiedener Andeutungen bereits erwartet worden. Für Donnerstagabend kündigten Klimaschutzorganisationen eine Aktion im Berliner Regierungsviertel an.
Luisa Neubauer von Fridays for Future kritisierte, mit seinem Fernbleiben lasse der Kanzler „demonstrativ“ junge Menschen in der Klimakrise im Stich. „Ehrlicher könnte Friedrich Merz nicht zeigen, wie wenig er sich um die Klimakrise schert“, erklärte der Klimaexperte der Linksfraktion im Bundestag, Fabian Fahl.
Greenpeace fordert „Zeitenwende“ in der Klimapolitik
Angesichts der Dramatik der Klimakrise müsse Merz persönlich auf der UN-Konferenz eine „Zeitenwende“ in der deutschen Klimapolitik ankündigen, die zurzeit nicht auf Kurs sei, forderte Martin Kaiser von Greenpeace Deutschland.
„Der Kanzler hat noch im August gesagt, er werde alles tun, um den Klimawandel zurückzudrängen“, sagte Grünen-Fraktionschefin Katharina Dröge. „Nun nimmt er sich nicht mal die Zeit, an der wichtigsten Entscheidungsplattform für die globale Klimapolitik teilzunehmen.“
Mehr Einsatz von der Bundesregierung beim Klimaschutz forderten am Donnerstag Brot für die Welt und die Diakonie Katastrophenhilfe. Deutschland müsse seine Zusagen zur Klimafinanzierung einhalten. Zwar habe die die Regierung 6 Milliarden Euro für Klimaschutz und Anpassung im Globalen Süden versprochen, aber im vergangenen Jahr nur 4,7 bereitgestellt.
Wie klimapolitisch und ökonomisch geboten ein Ausstieg aus fossilen Energieträgern ist, zeigte eine Analyse des Öko-Instituts im Auftrag des WWF. Danach sank zwar die Menge der Energieimporte in die EU in den vergangenen zehn Jahren um zehn Prozent. Die Kosten für Gas, Öl und Kohle stiegen aber um ein Drittel: Sie lagen 2025, also noch vor den Kostensteigerungen durch den Iran-Krieg, nach Abzug der Exporteinnahmen bei 296 Milliarden Euro. Öl- und Gasimporte machten dabei knapp 90 Prozent der europäischen Importrechnung aus. Die aktuellen Preisschwankungen zeigten erneut, „wie wichtig es auch für unsere Wirtschaft und geopolitische Sicherheit ist, sich aus der Abhängigkeit von fossilen Energien zu befreien“.
