https://www.artnews.com/art-news/market/.title: Georgia O’Keeffe Painting Found in Closet After 40 Years Heads to Christie’s With $ 3 M. Est.
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/market/.author: Harrison Jacobs
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/market/.text:
When Christie’s holds its 20th Century Evening Sale in two weeks, one painting will hit the block with a curious story. The Georgia O’Keeffe painting Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I (1930) only recently resurfaced after nearly 40 years out of the public eye.
Per the New York Post, the painting was found by a Rhode Island woman when she was helping her elderly aunt clear her East Village apartment. According to the 65-year-old woman, who the Post names only by her middle name, Betsy, she found the painting at the back of a closet under a row of fur coats.
“I thought, wow, that’s that’s pretty wild,” she told the Post. “I wondered, ‘Is there any way I can keep this?’ … But once we started exploring what the value of the piece was, I realized that it’s worth more than my house.”
According to the woman, her aunt told her in 2022 off-handedly that there was an O’Keeffe painting in the closet as they prepped the house for home health aides. However, Betsy didn’t actually find the work until a few weeks ago when her aunt was put into hospice at age 98.
The aunt, who has since died, was once a Foreign Services worker. She recieved the painting as a graduation gift from her mother in 1963, when she purchased it from The Downtown Gallery on 51st Street for $3,800. As Betsy tells it, the painting hung in the apartment until the 1980s, when she noticed a guest “eyeing it a bit too closely.”
“I think she was fully aware of its value … she recognized that it was an expression of her financial position,” Betsy said.
The painting has since become a bit of an oddity for Betsy and her family, who says she hung it up “for chuckles.” “The men in the family who’ve seen this have commented, there seems to be a number of ‘vaginas’ in the picture,” she said
The painting carries a $2 million to $3 million estimate, and a portion of the proceeds will be donated to an unnamed educaiton institution. The rest will go towards Betsy and her family “for things like paying off the mortgage.” Fair enough.
In a lot essay, Christie’s described the painting as an “important early work” that is “likely the first iteration in a series of three works depicting Lobo Peak, north of Taos Pueblo.” One of the other such works is in the collection of MoMA, while the other is in an unamed private collection.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: Hochul Made Big Gains in NYC’s Blue Wave — Except in These Neighborhoods
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Kennedy Sessions, Haidee Chu
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
Almost 2 million New Yorkers cast their ballots in this year’s gubernatorial election, 218,453 more than in 2022. The increase in voters helped Democratic incumbent Gov. Kathy Hochul safely secure another term, as she trounced Republican Bruce Blakeman in New York City, 76% to 24% with 97% of scanners counted.
Nationwide, Democrats rode an historic blue tsunami to control of the House and Senate. That lifted the party in New York City too, as many of its blue neighborhoods got bluer — and some of its red ones went blue too. Hochul gained votes in 92% of neighborhoods in the city compared with her 2022 effort.
In that election, Hochul beat Republican Lee Zeldin, 69% to 30% in New York City, but lost some 675,000 votes compared with Andrew Cuomo’s haul in 2018 — hemorrhaging voters in many neighborhoods.
Hochul’s biggest advance in 2026 was in South Williamsburg. There, she gained 45 percentage points over the 2022 election. Other notable neighborhoods that saw a blue swing were Borough Park, Bronx Park, Queensboro Hill and Sunset Park.
Hochul did lose ground in a handful of neighborhoods, however — nearly all of them in Manhattan, in areas among the most exposed to the new pied-a-terre tax. The contentious city tax targeting luxury second homes was announced by Hochul and Mayor Zohran Mamdani in April, signed into law in May and has since faced multiple legal challenges.
The governor lost seven percentage points in Carnegie Hill in Manhattan’s Upper East Side compared to her last showing in 2022 — the most of any neighborhood. Tribeca followed with a five percentage point decrease. The vast majority of these neighborhoods that inched toward the right nonetheless turned out overwhelmingly for Hochul overall.
Here are four more takeaways from the gubernatorial general election data:
Hochul Flipped These Neighborhoods
Hochul flipped 22 neighborhoods from red to blue from 2022, according to Board of Elections data. Besides South Williamsburg, some of the biggest leftward shifts came in Queensboro Hill, Sunset Park and Bensonhurst, where Hochul saw a 20 percentage point jump from 2022.
Not one neighborhood in the city flipped from Democrat to Republican.
Did Mamdani Voters Turn Out?
Ahead of the 2025 mayoral primary, then-candidate Zohran Mamdani urged New Yorkers to register to vote, drawing thousands of new voters to the polls. According to the Board of Election records, those same voters who registered last year came out in droves to cast their ballots in this year’s general election at a rate that almost matched the number of voters who registered in 2024, a presidential election year.
Voters who registered as part of Mamdani’s 2025 wave were just as likely, or more likely, to turn out this year as voters who registered ahead of the last three presidential elections. They were 6% of the overall 2026 electorate.
Millennials Beat Gen X in Voter Turnout
Millennials, born between 1981 and 1996, made up the second-largest voting group this election — beating Gen Xers, born between 1965 and 1980, voter records show. Younger neighborhoods also overwhelmingly voted for Hochul, according to CUNY’s Center for Urban Research. Overall, Hochul gained seven percentage-points compared to the 2022 election in districts where more than a quarter of voters are under 30.
Millennials accounted for 27% of the general election voters, or 528,809 votes, while Baby Boomers, born between 1946 and 1964, were the largest voting group, edging out millennials by just two percentage points. Gen Xers cast 25% of the total ballots.
Hochul Gained Most in Asian and Latino Neighborhoods
Hochul made inroads across all racial and ethnic groups — but especially in Asian and Latino neighborhoods. Compared with the 2022 gubernatorial race, the governor picked up 11 and seven percentage points in election districts where at least 40% of the vote-eligible population is Asian and Latino respectively, according to the Center for Urban Research.
Notably, nearly all the Latino neighborhoods that made a strong showing for Trump in 2024 voted for Hochul, and many of the Asian neighborhoods trending that way did the same. Overall, Hochul won 73.08% of votes in neighborhoods where more than half the population is foreign-born, according to Documented.

https://www.propublica.org/article/misso.title: Missouri Voters Just Made It Much Harder for Lawmakers to Overturn Citizen-Led Initiatives
https://www.propublica.org/article/misso.author: Jeremy Kohler
https://www.propublica.org/article/misso.text:
Across the country on Tuesday, voters delivered a wave of Democratic victories, flipping seats in Congress as well as state legislatures, and weakening a number of Republican majorities.
Missouri was no exception. Democrats made significant gains in the state House, picking up 16 seats, though Republicans still hold every statewide office and maintain control of the legislature.
Nonetheless, the election was more than just a rebuke of President Donald Trump. It reflected a long-simmering frustration with Missouri politicians who, time and again, have sought to override the will of voters — a practice that has intensified under years of Republican control. What’s more, voters went beyond weakening the Republican majority. They approved a constitutional amendment that curtailed the powers of the legislature and shifted more authority directly to the people.
Amendment 6, approved by a decisive margin, sharply limits the legislature’s ability to overturn laws and constitutional amendments enacted through citizen initiatives, and its ability to revive laws voters rejected through referendums.
Missouri Republicans have only themselves to blame, according to political observers who have watched the conflict between lawmakers and voters intensify. They resisted a voter-approved Medicaid expansion, repealed paid sick leave protections and sought to reverse abortion rights. They sometimes packaged their efforts with unrelated culture-war provisions, like limiting healthcare for transgender minors, that were intended to appeal to conservative voters.
Then they tried to persuade voters this summer to surrender some of their own power by changing the constitution to make it harder to pass initiatives in the first place. Voters rejected that proposal by more than a 4-to-1 margin.
“I think the people of Missouri are trying to wrest control back from our legislature because our legislature at this point does not seem to really be representing the majority view in the state,” said Jayne Woods, a professor at the University of Missouri law school who has written about the tension between direct democracy and legislative power.
Benjamin Singer is the co-founder and executive director of the Respect Missouri Voters campaign, which helped organize the push for Amendment 6. He said the frustration stretched back decades, including periods when Democrats controlled the legislature. He said when the campaign began organizing in late 2024, many volunteers were still angry about lawmakers’ decision in 2011 to weaken restrictions on puppy mills that voters had approved just a year earlier.
The campaign, he said, had already built a substantial volunteer operation before Republican lawmakers moved in 2025 to undo voter-approved measures that were intended to mandate paid sick leave and protect abortion rights. Respect Missouri Voters ultimately gathered enough signatures to put Amendment 6 on the ballot, seeking not only to protect the initiative process but to strengthen the electorate’s power over the legislature.
With the passage of that amendment, lawmakers now must get 80% support in both the House and Senate before they can propose changing or repealing measures enacted through citizen initiatives, or move to revive laws voters rejected through referendums. Even then, voters must approve any change in a statewide election. The restriction applies to measures voters have approved since 2010, including the constitutional amendment protecting abortion rights that voters approved in 2024.
Republican lawmakers put a measure on Tuesday’s ballot to restore abortion restrictions, but voters rejected that, too. With the passage of Amendment 6, abortion opponents don’t have a clear path to try again.
Amendment 6 also strengthens the referendum process. In addition to restricting lawmakers’ ability to reenact laws similar to those voters have rejected, the amendment explicitly protects the right of citizens to enact laws and constitutional amendments with a simple statewide majority, rejecting the higher threshold Republican lawmakers had sought to impose earlier this year. And it safeguards the power of Missouri’s courts to rewrite misleading ballot language, a power that Republican officials have repeatedly tried to strip away.
The result, political observers said, could make the legislature less consequential than it once was. Republicans still have the votes to pass most laws, but when voters reject those laws at the ballot box or enact their own measures or constitutional amendments through citizen initiatives, lawmakers will now face significant obstacles to overriding them.
Denny Hoskins, the secretary of state and one of Amendment 6’s most prominent Republican opponents, acknowledged how profoundly it would change the balance of power. Before the election, he told the Missouri Independent that if the amendment passed, “it will basically cut our legislature off at the knees as far as being able to pass laws to reduce crime and cut taxes.”
In text messages on Wednesday, Hoskins said that Amendment 6 weakens the legislature and governor “regardless of party” and predicted that it would be challenged in court. He said that “giving power back to the people” might be a great slogan but that the amendment’s sponsors “have no idea what this actually will do.”
Hoskins himself had tried to keep Amendment 6 off the ballot. In August, he refused to certify the initiative petition, arguing that it violated constitutional restrictions on ballot measures. He also rejected a separate petition seeking a statewide referendum on a newly gerrymandered congressional map that Republican lawmakers, working at Trump’s behest, had approved to give their party another seat in Congress.
The Missouri Supreme Court overruled him in both cases, ordering that the measures appear on the ballot. The court found Hoskins in contempt when he sought to use the map in spite of its ruling. Hoskins backed down and the justices did not have him arrested.
On Tuesday, voters rejected the map too. With Amendment 6 now in place — and Democrats significantly bolstering their numbers in the House — Republican lawmakers aren’t likely to gather enough support to override the voters’ rejection of their map.
Travis Crum, a law professor at Washington University in St. Louis and an expert on voting rights and election law, said he knew of no other state with a restriction quite like Missouri’s 80% threshold. But he said the amendment was understandable given the legislature’s repeated attempts to reverse voter-approved policies and its unsuccessful effort this summer to make citizen initiatives harder to pass.
“I think that there’s just been this boiling frustration with how the legislature has ignored the initiative process and then sort of tried to rewrite it to its own ends,” he said.
John Hancock, a former Missouri Republican Party chair and longtime GOP consultant, acknowledged that Republican lawmakers had brought some of the backlash on themselves. But he warned that Amendment 6 could make Missouri a magnet for well-financed out-of-state interest groups seeking to enact laws through ballot initiatives — possibly on taxation or gun policy.
That concern about wealthy outside interests was also central to the Republican-backed proposal to restrict citizen initiatives that voters rejected in August. Gov. Mike Kehoe had spent months warning voters about out-of-state special interests trying to rewrite the state constitution, even while a campaign supporting his proposal to phase out the state income tax benefited from funding from a Delaware nonprofit with undisclosed donors.
Woods said the defeat suggested voters weren’t persuaded by that argument. Regardless of who finances an initiative campaign, she noted, Missourians are the ones organizing, gathering support and ultimately deciding whether to approve the measures.
“I think that the people of the state pretty resoundingly said, ‘No, we don’t believe that that’s true,’” Woods said. “‘We believe this is our citizens who are doing this. This is what we want as citizens.’”

https://taz.de/Fuehrerschein-soll-billig.title: Führerschein soll billiger werden: Nicht aus Nettigkeit zur Jugend
https://taz.de/Fuehrerschein-soll-billig.author: Marco Mueller
https://taz.de/Fuehrerschein-soll-billig.text:
Führerschein soll billiger werden : Nicht aus Nettigkeit zur Jugend
Die Führerscheinreform soll den Lappen bis zu 1.000 Euro billiger machen. Wer braucht sowas, wenn man sich Wohnung und den Wocheneinkauf kaum leisten kann?
I ch bin gerne Beifahrer, liebe es mich von meinen Freund*innen durch die Welt kutschieren zu lassen. Und in absehbarer Zeit habe ich auch nicht vor, etwas an meinem Beifahrerdasein zu ändern. In Berlin komme ich mit dem Fahrrad und den Öffis ohnehin problemlos von A nach B und bin dazu noch schneller als mit dem Auto.
Die Möglichkeit hätte ich an sich trotzdem gerne. Wer weiß? Vielleicht möchte ich mich irgendwann in den ländlichen Peripherien des schönen Berliner Umlands niederlassen – und da braucht man, oh Wunder, einen Führerschein. Denn den 5-Minuten-Takt der Berliner U-Bahnen gibt es dort nicht. Der Zugang zum Führerschein bleibt mir und vielen anderen GenZler*innen bei einem durchschnittlichen Preis von 3.400 Euro pro Führerschein jedoch weitestgehend verwehrt.
Ohne finanzielle Unterstützung der Eltern, dem Sparkonto von Omi oder Opi, einem Lottogewinn oder Frühverschuldung ist es beinahe unmöglich, sich den Führerschein während der Lehre oder des Studiums leisten zu können. Aber das könnte sich jetzt ändern.
taz debatte
Die taz ist eine unabhängige, linke und meinungsstarke Tageszeitung. In unseren Kommentaren, Essays und Debattentexten streiten wir seit der Gründung der taz im Jahr 1979. Oft können und wollen wir uns nicht auf eine Meinung einigen. Deshalb finden sich hier teils komplett gegenläufige Positionen – allesamt Teil des sehr breiten linken Meinungsspektrums.
Nicht der Führerschein bereitet Sorge, sondern der Einkauf
Denn im Bundestag wird über die Führerscheinreform abgestimmt. Die soll vor allem das bürokratische Prozedere vereinfachen und so einen günstigeren Führerschein liefern. Üben mit Mama oder Papa auf dem Beifahrersitz ist auch eingeplant. Was dem Staat zu teuer ist, können jetzt die Eltern übernehmen. Bis zu 1.000 Euro soll man so sparen, sagt Verkehrsminister Bilger. Steuergeld kostet das alles keinen Cent.
Vor allem für junge Menschen vom Land ist ein günstigerer Führerschein wichtig und gut. Für den Großteil der GenZler*innen ist es aber nicht der Führerschein, der Sorgen macht, sondern die Lebensmittelpreise, das alltägliche Leben, das Bierchen, das man sich mal gönnen will.
Dass der Führerschein und damit die Möglichkeit, etwa mit dem Auto einkaufen zu fahren, ab nächstem Jahr also günstiger sein soll, ist für jene Menschen ziemlich egal, die erstmal gucken müssen, ob sie sich den nächsten Einkauf leisten können. Und auch für Menschen in der Stadt wären andere Reformen – wie die kostenlose Nutzung des ÖPNV oder der Ausbau von Fahrradwegen – sinnvoller.
Da hilft auch kein soziales Framing. Wie das vom ehemaligen Verkehrsminister Patrick Schnieder (CDU), der von Mobilität als „Teil der öffentlichen Daseinsvorsorge“, die „kein Privileg“ sein dürfe, spricht. Denn die Führerscheinreform ist bei Weitem keine Sozialreform.
Sozialer Aspekt nur vorgeschoben
Auch weil nicht alle von ihr profitieren werden: Beifahren darf nur, wer seit sieben Jahren ununterbrochen den Führerschein hat, höchstens einen Punkt in Flensburg kassiert hat und das Ganze unentgeltlich macht – im eigenen, passend versicherten Auto. Ein Teil der Ersparnis bekommt also, wer ohnehin ein Familienauto vor der Tür stehen hat. Und nur weil man sich den Führerschein mit der Reform eher leisten kann, heißt das nicht, dass es beim Auto, Sprit oder der Versicherung auch so ist.
Stattdessen dienen diese Reformen der Autoindustrie. Kein Wunder: Die deutsche PKW-Industrie steckt derzeit in ihrer mitunter größten Krise. In Dagobert Ducks Augen glitzern die Dollarzeichen, in Merz’ Augen wahrscheinlich der Dieselverbrenner.
Dass die Bundesregierung nicht aus Nettigkeit und sozialem Anspruch handelt, zeigte sich dieser Tage recht deutlich. Etwa als verkündet wurde, dass rund jeder dritte Wohngeldhaushalt durch die Wohngeldreform seinen Anspruch verlieren könnte – vor allem Rentner*innen. Wohnen, anders als der Führerschein, darf wohl ein Privileg bleiben.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. So viele unterstützen freiwillig und regelmäßig. Noch nicht dabei? Werden Sie jetzt Teil der Community! Jetzt unterstützen

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/05/midt.title: “Dead Man Walking”: Officials Say Hegseth Has to Go
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/05/midt.author: Nick Turse
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/05/midt.text:
In the run-up to the midterm election, seen by many as a referendum on the Iran war, Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth unveiled FORTRESS America — a project to allow U.S. military bases to survive a 90-day siege. But following the landslide Democratic victory, it’s Hegseth who finds himself increasingly besieged within his own fortress, the Pentagon, and on Capitol Hill where he stands on the brink of bipartisan impeachment.
In the wake of an election rout that handed Democrats firm control of the House and the Senate, Hegseth is in the crosshairs of lawmakers whom he has treated with contempt for two years, as he has withheld basic information from Congress and purged bipartisan-backed senior military leaders. “One of the first things we’re going to do in the majority, we’re going to run Pete Hegseth out of town,” Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., who is now in line to be speaker of the House, announced at a campaign rally just before Election Day. Asked about the self-styled War Secretary on Wednesday, Jeffries replied: “Is Pete Hegseth still around?”
As the blue wave crested on Tuesday, storm clouds stacked up on Hegseth’s horizon. “We’re going to go after Hegseth,” Rep. Rosa DeLauro, D-Conn., in line to return to the helm of the powerful House Appropriations Committee, announced after cruising to victory on Tuesday. “LAWYER UP,” Rep. Robert Garcia of California, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, posted on X. Both will be joined in the House by Democrat Nancy Lacore, a former Navy admiral who was fired by Hegseth, who declared victory in a traditionally red district in South Carolina.
By Wednesday evening, sentiment within the Pentagon suggested that Hegseth’s days are numbered, with names of potential replacements already being bandied about. “Dead man walking,” said one official. A former defense official agreed: “They pinned the failure in Iran on him. Now it’s only a matter of time.” Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, with support from Democrats, is slated to take aim at Hegseth as soon as next week with eight articles of impeachment for high crimes and misdemeanors.
With Hegseth increasingly under fire within the ranks, at the Pentagon, and on Capitol Hill, and with rumors swirling that the White House may cut him loose in the face of the staggering electoral defeat, The Intercept spoke with six current and former defense officials as well as additional sources on Capitol Hill, most on the condition of anonymity in order to speak freely. Hegseth has, they said, undermined the rule of law; irreparably harmed the U.S. military through purges of top commanders and those who refuse to pledge fealty; pursued relentless leak investigations; spurred religious extremism; and diminished the department he leads due to an almost endless raft of scandals, culture-war clownishness, and senseless policies.
One of the officials, Wes J. Bryant — until last year a senior targeting adviser and policy analyst at the Pentagon — gave voice to Massie’s more technical articles of impeachment which indict Hegseth for extrajudicial killings and waging unlawful war, among other crimes. “He is conducting state terrorism. He is 100 percent a war criminal. He needs to be prosecuted,” said Bryant, who was pushed out of his Pentagon job for blowing the whistle on Hegseth’s efforts to undermine protections for civilians.
Hegseth — a former Army National Guard officer turned Fox News host turned secretary of war — came into office amid a firestorm of scandal from his confirmation process, including a swirl of allegations of financial mismanagement at veterans’ nonprofits where he once worked, excessive drinking and public drunkenness, marital infidelity, and sexual assault.
His reign at the Pentagon has been no less tumultuous and marked by a string of appalling episodes of both major importance and more symbolic disgrace, beginning with Signal-gate — the texting of secret war plans that put troops in harm’s way — and follow-on digital security lapses. The Pentagon’s own inspector general concluded last December that “Hegseth violated security protocols and endangered U.S. troops and objectives by using a personal device to share sensitive operational details on the unclassified messaging app Signal.”
Those scandals, however, turned out to be the high point of his tenure. Since then, Hegseth has been under perpetual fire for his purge of top military leaders — many of them women and minorities; an inability to defeat Yemen’s Houthis in 2025 or win the Iran war in 2026; a strike on an elementary school in Minab, Iran, that killed more than 150 civilians, most of them children; his campaign of extrajudicial killings in attacks on so-called drug boats; overlapping efforts to weaken transparency, scuttle accountability, hobble military justice, and undercut protections for civilians in conflict; openly advocating for offering enemies “no quarter,” a war crime; his installation of a Pentagon makeup studio at taxpayer expense; an unnatural and immature fixation with violence; an obsession with troops’ testosterone levels, a censorship campaign that replaced the Pentagon press corps with cheerleading influencers, among other distractions, dysfunctions, and tantrums.
Pentagon press secretary Kingsley Wilson and other top spokespersons did not respond to detailed questions and repeated requests for comment.
The Heat on Hegseth
In April, Rep. Yassamin Ansari, D-Ariz., filed six articles of impeachment against Hegseth, including violations of the law of armed conflict and targeting of civilians, abuse of power, and obstructing congressional oversight. “Impeach Pete Hegseth,” Ansari wrote in a quote tweet of a Hegseth post on X on Wednesday.
In September, Massie was poised to force a vote to impeach Hegseth on eight charges. As the initiative gained bipartisan momentum, House Speaker Mike Johnson decided to punt and dismissed members of the House before the scheduled vote. But Massie, who was defeated in a GOP primary in May — the most expensive House primary in history — remains committed to ousting Hegseth and plans to force a vote on the measure.
“I give it better than a 50 percent chance of passing,” Massie told Roll Call just prior to Election Day, expressing confidence that all Democrats and some Republicans would join his effort. On Wednesday night, Massie took to X to double down on his commitment. “There is one contingency in which I won’t reintroduce the articles of impeachment,” he wrote. “Hegseth resigns.”
Massie’s office did not return a request for comment.
In the wake of Tuesday’s stunning electoral landslide, a senior Hill staffer told The Intercept that he believed mounting anger might cause top outgoing Republicans to vote to impeach Hegseth. “There are very angry senior Republicans in the national security space who honestly pin a lot of their election losses on him. They are furious,” he said. “They need some place to put their anger. So they’re asking themselves, ‘What is even the harm in voting to impeach Hegseth?”
“Democratic leadership wants to focus on people’s everyday lives and affordability, not impeaching Hegseth. But here we are. We are going to vote on impeachment because of Tom Massie. It’s happening,” said the senior staffer. “This reckoning is coming whether we want it or not. So why not?”
California Democrat Ro Khanna, who serves on the House Armed Services Committee and has repeatedly sparred with Hegseth during hearings, told The Intercept that he supports impeachment and thinks its odds of succeeding are “decent.” Rep. Adam Smith of Washington, the top Democrat on that committee, vowed on Wednesday to conduct aggressive Pentagon oversight and backed efforts to impeach Hegseth. “Going after the corruption, and going after the lack of transparency,” Smith told the Seattle Times of his plans to hold the department accountable while expressing support for Massie’s impeachment push.
In 250 years, the House has impeached just two Cabinet secretaries: William Belknap, the secretary of war, in 1876; and Alejandro Mayorkas, the secretary of homeland security, in 2024. In both cases, the Senate did not convict. Should Massie’s impeachment measure succeed in the House, it would likely die in the Senate, where Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., would have no incentive to bring it to a vote, said a congressional staffer for a member on the Armed Services Committee.
But some pundits predict Hegseth may not survive next week, much less the month or the year.
Trump was asked Wednesday afternoon whether he was considering replacing Hegseth, and he told reporters, “No, I think he’s doing a very good job.” One former Pentagon official called such public support from Trump “the kiss of death.” Another current defense official agreed. “He may lose his top cover,” said that official, using military slang for protection from above. The president, the official said, “always loves you right up until he throws you under the bus.”
As Republicans make sense of their loss, many are pointing to the Iran war, including Vice President JD Vance. “The reason we lost is the war,” he wrote on X. A Republican staffer on Capitol Hill said Hegseth “could easily become the president’s fall guy.” The senior staffer agreed, saying Hegseth “might be purged, himself, to avoid additional embarrassment.”
“If Hegseth does stay and he survives this moment, Oversight is going to come crashing down on his head,” said the senior staffer on Wednesday. “Will Hegseth continue to obstruct? Yes. But wait until the subpoenas start.”
Congressional committees have broad investigative powers, including the authority to subpoena administration officials to testify under oath and compel them to turn over documents. Smith said Hegseth and Deputy Secretary of Defense Steve Feinberg would be first on the list to testify. “We haven’t gotten a report back from the Minab girls’ school strike. How come we haven’t gotten clarity on the strike in Kuwait that killed six service members? How come they haven’t told us what the true cost is that’s been absorbed by all of our bases that have been destroyed in the Middle East?” Smith said to the Seattle Times. “There’s a host of issues we could dive into.”
Another staffer said renewed scrutiny of abuses of war powers like the boat strikes, especially the initial double-tap attack first disclosed by The Intercept; the secret memorandum by the Office of Legal Counsel laying out the legal rationale for the strikes; and the hidden costs, U.S. casualties, civilian casualties, and destruction of U.S. bases during the Iran war, would open a Pandora’s box for Hegseth.
In the Senate, Democrats have floated Hegseth’s removal as the price for cooperation on key legislation in the lame-duck session. Their Republican colleagues have also increasingly soured on Hegseth as he has purged top military commanders with whom they have strong ties. “They see Hegseth as the next Kristi Noem,” said one Capitol Hill source, referencing the former secretary of homeland security who was demoted this year to special envoy for the newly founded Shield of the Americas coalition after influential Republican senators turned against her.
On Tuesday, Sen. Thom Tillis of North Carolina, a Republican who is retiring, warned Hegseth of a coming “reckoning” in the lame-duck session. “He is one of the reasons why we don’t have the funding or guarantee for defense that we need,” he said. “I think after the election, we need to determine whether or not he’s the best person to bring those needs to Congress.”
Antipathy to Hegseth also extends far beyond the Beltway. Just 32 percent of voters approve of the way he is handling his job, while 57 percent disapprove, according to a Quinnipiac University poll in September. It was his lowest approval ever and historically dismal. (Fifty percent approved and only 13 percent disapproved of Trump’s first Secretary of Defense, James Mattis, late in his tenure in 2018.) Hegseth is even less popular in military circles. Sixty-four percent of active-duty service members, veterans, and military families disapprove of Hegseth, according to a recent poll conducted by Common Defense, a grassroots veterans organization. Last month, a Politico poll found that 63 percent of Democratic midterm voters would support impeaching the Pentagon chief.
Enemies Within
The war secretary is also under withering fire within the Pentagon, according to the current and former officials. They say Hegseth is reviled across the building by officers biding their time, waiting for him to flame out or be pushed out.
Derided in the Pentagon and the ranks by a variety of monikers such as “No Tab Pete,” a reference to his lack of prestigious military qualification patches such as the Ranger tab; “Whiskey Pete”; and “Dumb McNamara,” a reference to the Vietnam War-era Defense Secretary Robert McNamara, responsible for unfathomable death and suffering; Hegseth has been excoriated within his department for unhinged behavior — especially his relentless purge of top brass and high-ranking officials, which insiders see as an attempt to root out dissenting viewpoints, racial minorities, and women.
To enforce strict discipline, tamp down scandals, keep basic information from the American people and cow dissent, Hegseth has unleashed unrelenting polygraph tests of officials, even senior leaders. Several officials would not respond to questions citing this reason. One likened their situation to life under a totalitarian regime. Hegseth’s minions have also engaged in browbeating “leaky” offices. These efforts have generated further ill will throughout the Pentagon and the wider defense establishment. “The more good people he forces out of the military, the more the resentment grows,” said a current official.
Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia — who served as director for strategy, plans and policy on the Joint Staff assisting Joint Chiefs chair Gen. Dan Caine — was recently ousted. “She’s gonna have big problems, said Trump, who apparently thought the male general was a woman. “We’re very much looking for leakers.” Sylvia replaced Lt. Gen. Joseph McGee, whom Hegseth forced out last year. While not naming Sylvia, Pentagon mouthpiece Sean Parnell issued a social media broadside. “Following an extensive Air Force OSI investigation, the Department took necessary personnel action to protect sensitive information,” he crowed on X. “We vowed to find you, and we meant it.”
Other casualties of Hegseth’s campaign include Gen. Charles “CQ” Brown Jr. (chair of the Joint Chiefs of Staff), Adm. Lisa Franchetti (chief of Naval Operations), Gen. David Allvin (Air Force chief of staff), Adm. Linda Fagan (commandant of the Coast Guard), Lt. Gen. Jennifer Short (senior military assistant to the Secretary of Defense), Vice Adm. Shoshana Chatfield (U.S. military representative to the NATO Military Committee), and Lacore, the former vice admiral and Navy Reserve chief, now likely representative-elect, among others.
The officials said that Hegseth’s efforts to remake the military have done grave damage to the armed forces. “When you put people on polygraphs and fire a bunch of people who question the status quo and consistently shut down the conversation, then you absolutely lose the best leaders,” said a former field grade officer who served in Hegseth’s Pentagon. “You’re strangling initiative and creating a culture of yes men and yes women.”
Officials repeatedly lamented long-term harm to the Pentagon, whenever Hegseth leaves the helm. “He’s purging a generation of great leaders of the military, and it’s going to take a generation to recover from it,” said Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., a former Navy combat pilot who has been targeted by Hegseth. The former field grade officer echoed this. “If you’re doing it right, the talent selection is being done ten years out,” the source said, noting that promotions are a long-term process. “It’s about years down the road. And these people are being fired and forced out. We’re losing them. That’s generational impact that’s harming the force.”
In his September “state of the force” address to more than 500 junior officers and enlisted troops, Hegseth announced, “We are no longer the Woke Department or the Weak Department. Simple translation of that: No fatties. No trannies. No beardos. No weirdos. No wimps. No radicals.” He added, “The ideological clowns are out. The patriotic cowboys are in — with testosterone testing on top.”
Several officials drew connections between Hegseth’s fixation on manliness and testosterone with his childish fixation on “lethality,” his glorification of violence, and bloodlust. “‘Maximum lethality, not tepid legality,’” said one official quoting a Hegseth line. “That kind of language and the very, very real killing of civilians — and the posting online of what are outright snuff films, the narco-boat strikes, is evidence of a sickness of his mind.”
The real-world effects of Hegseth’s lethality obsession have been devastating. His Pentagon has gutted its premier center devoted to preventing civilian casualties in war zones. He also removed constraints on military commanders, “letting his preferred generals do anything they want,” said one of the former defense officials. This resulted, for example, in significantly more civilian casualties during attacks on Yemen’s Houthi government in 2025, while failing to achieve military objectives. The Pentagon’s own accounting of civilian casualties found that U.S. attacks killed 153 civilians and wounded almost 250 during the campaign of air and naval strikes, code-named Operation Rough Rider. A current official told The Intercept these were “lowball numbers.” At least 238 civilians were killed and 467 injured, according to the Yemen Data Project.
Several sources drew special attention to Hegseth’s effort — ultimately blocked by Trump — to livestream the firing squad execution of Nidal Hasan, who killed 13 people when he opened fire at Fort Hood in 2009. “This obsession with performative violence is a hallmark of fascist dictatorships,” said Bryant. Hegseth’s lethality doctrine, he continued, “is not only in line with the glorification of and reveling in violence and killing that defines him but is juvenile and ignorant from an operational and policy standpoint, as killing and lethality is only one relatively small aspect of what the military does.”
Officials also keyed in on Hegseth’s stilted version of violent Christianity. One former official pointed to Hegseth’s monthly Pentagon prayer services as sowing dissent within the building. “I would never go to that shit,” said a current official, drawing specific attention to a March service in which Hegseth quoted Psalm 3, praying for God to “break the teeth of the ungodly,” and asking God to back troops’ “overwhelming violence of action against those who deserve no mercy.” That official said Hegseth’s Christianity was an “abomination” and “an affront to the teachings of Jesus Christ.”
Bryant, a retired Air Force Special Operations targeting specialist and co-author of “Hunting the Caliphate: America’s War on ISIS and the Dawn of the Strike Cell,” likened Hegseth’s interpretation of Christianity to the puritanical brand of religion practiced by America’s enemies during the war on terror. “His so-called war on woke is actually a far-right Christian nationalist crusade. His skewed version of Christianity is as extreme as the sharia of ISIS and the Taliban are to Islam. And that’s what he is infusing into, and proliferating across, the force.”
Hegseth has been quick to smear everyone from veterans serving in Congress to members of the press as treasonous, calling rigorous reporting on the military “fundamentally anti-American.” He added: “It’s sick. It’s a national betrayal. It’s treason, actually.” Hegseth frequently tries to paint criticism of his department as smearing troops to foster an us-them divide between the military and the American people they serve.
During his September state of the force address, Hegseth cast troops as superior to those in the civilian world. “See, the Ivy League faculty lounges, they’ll never understand you, and that’s OK, because they could never, ever do what you do. The media will mischaracterize you, and that’s OK. Because deep down they know you’re the real reason they live free. They envy you because you do real things every single day,” said Hegseth, an Ivy League-educated millionaire who used to work for Fox News. “Lethality is your calling card. … The outside world can’t understand this, so stay true to this department. You don’t want to look like civilians, because you are different, you are set apart. You are warriors.” He added, “You are the real 1 percent.”
Several officials said Hegseth’s effort to cast the armed forces as superior to the rest of the American people was antithetical to military values and especially alarming under an administration that has dispatched troops to American cities and threatens to do so, again. “The worst thing would be if we deploy the military in the streets of cities like they did last year in California. I’m talking about where the military is violently interacting with our citizenry,” said the former field grade officer. “You’ve paved the way for a more obedient military and then you have guys and gals with the guns having to decide whether orders — from the president that we elected and the secretary of defense that he’s appointed — are lawful. It’s dangerous.”
Bryant, who served as branch chief of civilian harm assessments at the Pentagon, pointed out that Hegseth’s dichotomy embraces the elitism that he claims to despise. “Our military, just as our government, is meant to be not only for the people but of the people,” he told The Intercept. “When we look at fascist military regimes, now and in history, another hallmark is this strict separation of soldier or warrior class from the civilian population. It is fundamentally anti-American and it is dangerous.”
All six officials, in one way or another, assailed Hegseth as juvenile, embarrassing, and unserious. “Imagine any other SecDef talking about packing the Pentagon with ‘patriotic cowboys,’” said one of the former officials. “Any one of them would have been run out of town.” A current official said Hegseth was unequivocally the “worst SecDef in memory” and that Massie’s impeachment vote couldn’t come soon enough. That official said it would take years to undo the harm Hegseth has done to the military but whether he was removed by impeachment, was fired by Trump, or quit under duress, the first step was ridding the Pentagon of his presence. “Hegseth,” he said “has got to go.”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: French authorities investigate claim of fraud over Picasso plates and medallions on sale
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Vincent Noce
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
A criminal investigation amid a family crisis casts a dark shadow over the illustrious history of the French studio Ateliers Hugo, which produced jewellery and silverware created by major artists of the 20th century. According to a legal source, the court of Aix-en-Provence in the south of France has opened an investigation following a complaint by the Picasso family.
On 10 March, Paloma Ruiz-Picasso, representing the nine heirs of the Spanish artist, filed a complaint alleging “fraud, counterfeiting, forgery and concealment of these felonies”. The file does not name the alleged perpetrators, and their identity is not presently known. The following month the Picasso family published a formal warning in the Gazette Drouot, titled “Hugo silverware”. It urged “all art market professionals and buyers to exercise the utmost vigilance”, following the appearance of what it described as “a large number” of illegitimate silver plates and gold medallions, valued at millions of euros.
The title refers to Ateliers Hugo, a goldsmith based in Aix-en-Provence. It was founded in 1933 by François Hugo (1899-1981), the great-grandson of the famous French author Victor Hugo. In 1955 Pablo Picasso, who since 1947 had created a variety of ceramics in Vallauris on the French Riviera, commissioned François Hugo to produce plates and dishes from similar designs in fine metals, using the traditional technique of repoussé. Later, the workshop reduced them into medallions and earrings. With the help of his brother, the painter Jean Hugo, who introduced him to artistic circles, François made jewellery designed by Salvador Dalí, Max Ernst, André Derain, Jean Arp, Jean Dubuffet, Roberto Matta, Jean Lurçat and Dorothea Tanning. In 1975, his son Pierre Hugo (1947-2023) took over the company. Pierre was followed by his son Nicolas (born 1989).
Members of the Picasso family and their lawyer, Jean-Jacques Neuer, who filed the complaint, declined to comment to The Art Newspaper. But their complaint alleges that “it has been discovered that the moulds of Picasso’s works were reused for unauthorised productions of silver and gold pieces, followed by duplicates, some of them bearing three times the same number, and unnumbered specimens”.
According to a source close to the investigation, the Picasso Administration, which represents the family, says it has discovered at least 17 complete or almost complete suspicious collections, amounting to hundreds of pieces. The first red flag was raised by the Museum of Old and New Art (Mona), a private Australian museum in Tasmania. According to this source, in May 2023 the museum informed the Picasso Administration of its doubts over plates it had bought at Sotheby’s in London. An auction catalogue of 13 October 2021 describes a “complete set of 24 silver plates” bearing the signature of the artist, completed with an additional “unnumbered proof of Visage aux mains”. The pieces were “accompanied by a certificate of authenticity issued by Pierre Hugo”. The lot was sold for £1.4m. Sotheby’s declined to comment for this story.
According to the legal files, the seller was the British dealer Mark Maurice, from a now dissolved gallery named Masterpiece. The source close to the investigation says the dealer allegedly produced documents showing that he had commissioned a set of plates and a set of medallions from the Ateliers Hugo between 2017 and 2020. Mark Maurice indicated he was “unable to respond” to The Art Newspaper’s inquiries “due to strict non-disclosure agreements in place”.
In summer 2023 the ceramics museum in Vallauris, Musée Magnelli, exhibited another collection of 24 silver plates as well as gold medallions attributed to Picasso.
According to the legal files, the Picasso Administration protested, having found that they bore no number, mark or punch, as legally required. Nicolas Hugo acknowledges these facts, but tells The Art Newspaper that the works exhibited at Musée Magnelli were so-called “author’s copies, made for the exhibition, duly indicating in the catalogue that they were not for sale”. He adds that he “recovered them and had them melted after the show”. Representatives for the museum did not respond to a request for comment.
In June 2023, as reported in the legal files, the French branch of the auction house Bonhams made a request to the Picasso Administration for the right to reproduce silverware for a catalogue. The auction house was planning a sale of 95 lots from the Ateliers Hugo collection, including works by Ernst, Derain and Cocteau, valued between €400 and €50,000 each. The most valuable were 59 pieces, “made by” or “after” Picasso.
Works withdrawn from Bonhams sale
On 26 September 2023 Bonhams was informed by the Picasso Administration that these pieces were considered to be “unauthorised” editions. The auction house then decided to “delay the whole sale”, just two days before it was due to take place. Nicolas Hugo acknowledges he “did initiate, in the wake of good results obtained at Bonhams UK, this sale of pieces”, produced, he says, by his “father and grandfather”. But, he adds, “When we were informed by dealers of the presence of possible duplicates, I agreed to withdraw the sale and collaborated with the Picasso Administration to identify them.”
Bonhams declined to comment, but according to the source close to the investigation, the lots attributed to Picasso were sequestered when a British financial company, Suros Capital, tried to recover them as collateral for a €256,000 loan. A spokesperson for Suros confirmed the operation to The Art Newspaper, adding that “it was secured against not only the Picasso pieces, but a range of assets which are progressively realised, so the company expects to recover the loan in full”.
In November 2023, according to the source close to the investigation, a representative for Bonhams France informed the Picasso Administration that a Spanish collector contacted the auction house to sell 24 silver plates, estimated at £900,000. Again, the auction house refused on the basis of Picasso Administration’s doubts about the objects’ authenticity. In the legal files, the Picasso Administration claims the same collector had sold another set of 24 silver plates and one of 24 gold medallions in private sales through Bonhams in London in 2022. Neither the British auction house nor the Spanish collector made any comment.
The rights to reproduce the items disappeared with [my father and grandfather], so I have never minted any of Picasso’s creations Nicolas Hugo, Ateliers Hugo
Nicolas Hugo, who says he has not been interviewed by the investigators, claims he has no knowledge of the proceedings and “is unaware of the content of the complaint” issued by the Picasso Administration. But, he says: “The criminal investigation can only deal with facts related to the time of my father and grandfather, therefore falling under the statute of limitations and concerning persons now deceased.” He adds that “the rights to reproduce the items disappeared with them, so I have never minted any of Picasso’s creations”, and he does not have the legal status of a goldsmith. However, he says: “I have signed some certificates of authenticity, but only to confirm my father’s own signature.”
In interviews with The Art Newspaper, Nicolas Hugo describes himself as a “self-taught art dealer”. When he was around 20 years old, he started to work as an assistant in galleries in Paris, before moving to London. He is now an agent for several artists and a curator. In 2022, the French magazine Les Hardis described him as a “mix of British and Saint-Germain-des-Prés charm”. “My father became very ill in 2018,” he told the magazine. “I had an epiphany. I decided to take over the workshop. I immersed myself completely,” and started to train in manufacturing jewels.
“From 2019,” he tells The Art Newspaper, “I became involved in the history of his workshop and helped my father to showcase this heritage, for memorial and commercial reasons. I set up exhibitions in places like Barcelona or Vallauris and initiated this sale of the fonds d’atelier at Bonhams Paris. I have not taken over my father’s company and was not his partner.”
Ateliers Hugo in limbo
Nicolas Hugo says: “There have been some duplicates on the market, dating from my father’s period, but I have no idea who had made them in the workshop.” He says he has “no idea who put a collection on sale at Sotheby’s in 2021” and knows “nothing of the three sets proposed by this Spanish collector to Bonhams in 2022 and 2023”.
The criminal investigation is still at the preliminary phase. It comes at a time when the company is already in limbo. Pierre Hugo died in October 2023 and his five children have turned down his inheritance. Nicolas Hugo’s brothers and sisters declined to comment to The Art Newspaper due to the ongoing investigation.
However, sources close to the case say that Pierre Hugo’s heirs’ inheritance came with a €2.5m tax debt. According to these sources, three of the Hugo siblings said in police interviews they were “not at all” aware of the conduct of the workshop by their brother Nicolas, who had succeeded their ailing father in 2019. The sources said the three Hugo siblings were on alert after learning that Bonhams Paris declined to sell the collection from the Ateliers Hugo in September 2023. According to the same sources, when Pierre Hugo died a month later, the three siblings went to the workshop and took 21 moulds of plates that they decided to hand over to the Picasso Administration. Three moulds from the set were missing and they did not find those for the medallions.
According to these sources, the three Hugo siblings explained to the investigators that, “knowing that the rights of reproduction were extinct, they wanted to be sure this would be respected”. The siblings also asserted that they “did not want in any way to be implicated in these operations and made it clear to the Picasso Administration”, according to the sources.

https://citylimits.org/opinion-dcs-newes.title: Opinion: DC’s Newest Bosses Are From New York. They Must Deliver the IBX.
https://citylimits.org/opinion-dcs-newes.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/opinion-dcs-newes.text:
Share This Article
“New York’s civic and business leaders remain pessimistic about relying on the federal government’s support to bring the IBX to life; this is exactly the moment we need commitment from this Congress.”
We learned Tuesday evening that the Democrats will take control of the U.S. House and Senate. And it appears leaders of both chambers will be not only New Yorkers but Brooklynites—at no other time in U.S. history have both chambers been led by New Yorkers.
As a rent-stabilized Queens resident and member of Queens Community Board 5, I am calling on this new federal government to make an unwavering and comprehensive commitment to the construction of the Interborough Express (IBX). Strong federal support is the last remaining key to building the IBX. Our city cannot miss this opportunity.
The IBX is perhaps the most significant American public transit project in generations, establishing a new, non-Manhattan-oriented spine connecting the Brooklyn Army Terminal in Bay Ridge to Jackson Heights, Queens. This corridor would serve 160,000-plus weekday riders and connect nearly 1 million residents across some of the most transit-starved neighborhoods in New York City. Notably, my neighborhood may stand to benefit the most: bringing our district three to four new rail stations with connections to 16 more subway lines, up from our current one, the M train.
This new Congress comes at the heels of the draft environmental impact statement’s (DEIS) publication, a make-or-break moment for the IBX. Simultaneously, New York’s civic and business leaders remain pessimistic about relying on the federal government’s support to bring the IBX to life; this is exactly the moment we need commitment from this Congress.
New York now has the leverage to steward a century-long vision through the next two years of solvable engineering challenges, financial hurdles, and bureaucratic speed bumps with executive dedication and robust public collaboration. During this crucial phase, this Congress can show both New Yorkers and Americans what a serious government can do: deliver modern marvels that materially improve all of our lives, something generations past regularly enjoyed.
This leadership must take several forms.
First, it must courageously fund the IBX. New Yorkers cannot afford delays due to MTA funding deficits, and the federal government must readily fill in gaps should they arrive. Simply put, we must secure bigger checks from this government. We deserve the investment.
Although we are working toward 50 percent federal support for the IBX through the Federal Transit Administration’s New Starts program, these grants can cover up to 60 percent. An extra 10 percent, roughly $550 million, offers capital flexibility the MTA can direct quicker as the project progresses.
Similarly, mechanisms like the Transportation Infrastructure Finance and Innovation Act’s low-interest loans, greater congestion mitigation and air quality (CMAQ) grants, and expanded formula funding flexibility already have and must continue supporting nimble and adaptive budgets. Completing the IBX shouldn’t require innovative public financing—we have all the tools. We just need a Congress committed to them.
This political leadership must also embody bureaucratic excellence for the IBX. This can look like easing red-tape and ensuring smooth, synchronized partnership between federal and MTA leaders. It is already taking shape in notable ways. Federal funding is right now supporting design and engineering prerequisites for IBX transfers.
Given the highly competitive pool of New Start grant monies, however, this federal government must also classify the IBX under federal dashboard streamlining initiatives to prioritize its review, ensuring that federal agencies respond quickly to environmental impact assessments. Further, this federal government can issue swift Federal Railroad Administration regulatory waivers, protecting the IBX from freight regulatory disputes.
Ultimately, I am calling on this federal government to be nonstop cheerleaders for the IBX. It is through the constant drumming of support that the IBX can fulfill and expand its promise; Gov. Kathy Hochul, Mayor Zohran Mamdani, community boards, and countless New Yorkers are already exemplifying this.
Likewise, U.S. Sen. Chuck Schumer and Congressman Hakeem Jeffries must routinely visit station sites, organize public forums, and champion the IBX throughout the media. Setting this tone has real economic value, too. The sooner the IBX is operational, the sooner both its broad economic multipliers compound and increase while its overall per-rider costs decrease.
Delivering the IBX is not only an easy political homerun for their constituencies, but with their new leadership roles, the Democrats can take significant ownership of the IBX’s success.
Take this opportunity, Sen.Schumer and Congressman Jeffries. Remind the people what America is capable of. Imagine! Congress’s two Brooklyn leaders delivering our city the promise of the IBX. Show us that the mandate you received Tuesday night can work, that neighborly politics can deliver. Show us that the government can make our lives better. We deserve it.
I cannot wait to share IBX rides with my neighbors. I cannot wait for the IBX to connect me to new neighbors. I cannot wait to look into the future knowing the IBX will be there. What I’m asking of our Congress here is to step up. We need your help. We are so so close.
Gentry Fitch is a rent-stabilized tenant of Ridgewood, Queens and member of Queens Community Board 5. The views represented here are solely his own and do not reflect the views of QCB5.

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/05/s.title: Sunset Park Blaze Kills 6 As Lithium-ion Battery Fire Crisis Rages On
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/05/s.author: Sophia Lebowitz
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/05/s.text:
The fire left lives and homes ruined. Photo: Sophia Lebowitz
Six Brooklynites were killed in an early morning fire that engulfed an entire wooden row house — and authorities are investigating whether the blaze is linked to this year’s 68 percent rise in fires sparked or intensified by highly flammable lithium-ion batteries.
It took smoke-eaters three hours on Thursday to extinguish the 1:40 a.m. fire, which sent flames shooting out of every window. When the smoke cleared, four people were dead on the scene and two died later in the hospital. Four others remain hospitalized, officials said at a press briefing.
Fire marshals are still investigating, but early reports linked the fire to a lithium-ion battery, though it is unclear if the battery sparked the blaze or was simply consumed by it. Two burnt-out electric bike frames were spotted outside the building on Thursday.
The Sunset Park incident comes weeks after a family of four was wiped out in the Bronx when an e-bike caught fire in their apartment.
The story behind the story
After a peak in deaths associated with the batteries in 2023, officials were quick to pass legislation banning the sale of uncertified lithium-ion batteries and e-bikes, but they are still easy to obtain online on sites like Facebook Marketplace. In addition, after-market modifications make batteries unstable.
Many batteries bought during the pandemic — when the delivery industry fueled by e-bikes boomed — are nearing the end of their useable life. The decay of lithium-ion batteries is one reason why there have been fewer deaths this year from fires, even as there have been more blazes, because more fires are occurring outside of homes when batteries are discarded.
So far this year there have been 406 fires determined by FDNY to be caused by the batteries compared to 241 last year. But, the largest increase is in non-structural fires, up to 252 from 100, meaning blazes that occur outside of a home or business. Through mid-October, as Streetsblog reported exclusively, there were 87 lithium-ion fires in garbage trucks, up from 55 in all of last year, according to the Department of Sanitation.
“There’s no comprehensive plan to deal with the battery life cycles,” Baruch Herzfeld, who co-founded the battery charging company Popwheels, told Streetsblog last month. “There’s a fictitious belief that battery fires don’t happen unless batteries are charging. People are basing their safety guidelines on something that’s not true.”
The city’s efforts to promote outdoor battery storage and charging have largely fallen flat. After a successful pilot in 2024, the city has yet to install any public charging infrastructure and companies who provide battery subscription services are hindered by a web of ever-changing safety regulations that make it nearly impossible to grow. As of last month, the city hadn’t approved any permits that would allow landlords or business owners to set up charging cabinets on the sidewalk. The application will now be streamlined since New Yorkers overwhelmingly passed the mayor’s charter revision ballot proposals on Tuesday.
Sunset Park is filled with e-bikes — on the street, inside restaurants, within the gates of the many row houses, inside apartments. Elected officials want to see outdoor charging options.
“We have had multiple trainings from FDNY that ask people, do not store your battery inside, and also do not charge when you are sleeping. So that has been an ongoing issue,” said Council Member Susan Zhuang (D-Sunset Park) at the scene on Thursday. “I am going to look and see if we can set up some stations so people can just charge outdoors, that will be helpful to the community. It’s not just the delivery people that use the bikes, it’s everyone.”
A neighbor who has lived on the block for 42 years told Streetsblog she lives in fear of battery fires.
“I am angry as hell right now. We need control of these lithium batteries coming from China,” said Rukmin DeGaray. “They are no good for neighborhoods; they shouldn’t be allowed in any building that people live in. They just blow up and these old wooden buildings, they go up like lightning.”
The driver, Timothy McVey, 41, of Staten Island, turned himself in at the 62nd Precinct station house and was booked for failure to yield and failure to exercise due care

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: We Stomped All Over the Patriarchy on Tuesday Night
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Amy Littlefield
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
We Stomped All Over the Patriarchy on Tuesday Night
Almost everywhere, abortion rights initiatives won, and pro-choice candidates prevailed. Even in Idaho, where they didn’t, women are taking heart.
I’ve always wondered what smashing the patriarchy really feels like, and on Tuesday night, we found out.
Up until then, the patriarchy had been on quite the winning streak, so much so that a newly surfaced rape allegation against the sitting president was hardly a news story. Then, on Tuesday, we got to watch a child sexual abuse survivor defeat the Republican challenger who called her a liar in the Ohio governor’s race. We got to see Max Miller, an Ohio Republican whose ex-wife accused him of holding a gun to her head while she changed their toddler’s diaper, lose his seat in a former Republican stronghold. We got to see Texans elect a Democratic Latina governor from Brownsville, Gina Hinojosa, who ran an ad about her decision to carry a nonviable pregnancy to term—and used that horrific ordeal to defend the right of Texans to choose. A Tennessee woman denied an abortion under the state’s ban won a state House seat; Virginia, Missouri, and Nevada voted to protect or expand abortion rights; and Maine Senator Susan Collin was ousted in large part because of her vote to confirm accused attempted rapist Brett Kavanaugh, to the Supreme Court.
But there were exceptions to the trend, including the success of anti-trans ballot initiatives and the defeat of an abortion rights initiative in Idaho, a state that, in the midst of the blue tsunami felt, as Idaho-based reporter Kelcie Moseley-Morris put it to me, like an “island of sadness.”
Related Articles
“It was a great night in this nation for a rebuke” of patriarchy, Melanie Folwell, executive director of the ballot initiative campaign Idahoans United for Women and Families, told me. “But here in Idaho, where we had two of the wealthiest, most powerful patriarchies in the world—the Catholic Church and the Mormon Church—and then the supermajority Idaho GOP, my God, patriarchy won the day.”
Proposition 1 would have enshrined in Idaho statutes a right to abortion up until viability. But 56 percent of voters chose instead to keep the state’s near-total abortion ban. It was a gutting loss in a state where more than a third of the state’s ob-gyns have left or stopped practicing since the ban took effect, and where the campaign shared harrowing stories of women traveling to terminate nonviable pregnancies, getting med-flighted to neighboring states while miscarrying, or bleeding out while doctors whose colleagues have fled the state scrambled to save them. “I feel like the women and families and doctors were so brave telling their stories,” Suzanne Gallus, a Catholic mom of seven who knocked 1,289 doors to support Prop 1, told me. “For people to just ignore all that is especially hard to take.”
Folwell said the campaign faced uniquely strong headwinds, including an influx of new Republican residents that have turned the state into one of the country’s reddest and a convoluted explanation of the meaning of a “yes” or “no” vote that was attached to the ballot by the Republican secretary of state. The Mormon and Catholic churches donated a combined $1.3 million to an anti-abortion PAC that ran a barrage of ads in the final weeks of the campaign claiming that the proposition’s “fine print” would redefine fetal viability to exclude premature newborns who needed oxygen, allow “late-term abortion on demand,” and let minors get abortions without parental consent. The claims were false; the initiative didn’t repeal the state’s existing parental consent laws, and it would have allowed the state to ban abortion after fetal viability except in medical emergencies. But the ads forced canvassers like Suzanne Gallus, a Catholic mom of seven, to have uncomfortably technical conversations about fetal viability at the doors.
“For crying out loud, I’m not a doctor; I’m not a lawyer,” Gallus told me. “I know how to explain that, but then you’re getting into the weeds, and when you get into the weeds like that, I think you do more damage than you do good.”
Folwell said the initiative also suffered crucially from a lack of support from national organizations who balked at the fact that it could be repealed by the Republican legislature. The dozen or so abortion ballot initiatives that have passed since the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in states ranging from Ohio and Arizona to Virginia and Vermont have all been more enduring constitutional amendments, not statutory provisions, but Idaho does not allow voters to initiate constitutional amendments.
“There was a lot—from national groups— a lot of gnashing of teeth about, ‘Oh, well, it could just be statutorily overturned,’ before it was even won, and a lack of investment and care because of this silly gamesmanship about what’s next, rather than focusing on tangible movement-building and wins to get things done,” Folwell told me. “And I’m [feeling] pretty crappy about it.”
But Folwell felt proud of the 2,500 or so volunteers who powered her campaign.
“The most important story out of all of this is the degree to which there are thousands and thousands of women in this state who feel less alone,” Folwell said, her voice breaking. “And that’s from people who survived something terrible to people who found community in advocacy, and that all has meaning.”
“They may have been let down in myriad ways by people in the state and outside the state, but they showed up for each other.”
Among those who showed up was Whitney Montgomery, the daughter of the architect of Idaho’s abortion ban. Montgomery drew audible gasps during a Prop 1 rally when she revealed that she was the daughter of David Ripley, who has built his anti-abortion lobbyist career on an origin story about his objections to his ex-wife’s abortion. Montgomery’s childhood memories of her dad include his stint in jail for failing to pay child support to her mother—whom he divorced before later marrying the woman who had the abortion.
“I have spent years trying to understand how someone can dedicate his life to ‘saving babies’ while ignoring one of his own,” Montgomery wrote in an op-ed for the Post Register about her decision to support Prop 1. “By his own public admission, he was a cruel and abusive husband to many of his wives. As a child, I remember hiding in a bathroom with a phone nearby, ready to call 911 if things got worse.”
I interviewed Montgomery on election night, after she had just voted at her son’s elementary school; she’d brought her 3- and 6-year-olds to the polls as part of a family tradition, and that night, they were going to make Barack Obama’s chili recipe. Montgomery conceived through IVF, another reason she objects to the agenda of her father’s political party, which opposes it. When I told her that her decision to stand up to her father—who has admitted being a “jackass” to the wife who had the abortion—felt like a symbol of the stakes for this entire election, she agreed.
“It comes down to punishing women and having that control,” Montgomery said. “He feels like he was wronged by a woman, and now it’s this punishment to women’s health.
“It’s wild.”
(David Ripley didn’t respond to my calls for comment for this article. I did speak to his fourth wife, Wendy, at 10:15 am on Election Day. She told me her husband was still asleep. They’d had a late night; among other things, they were fending off teenagers from the nearby high school who kept stealing their anti–Prop 1 yard signs.)

“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
But outside of Idaho, women won the day, and even from the island of sadness, Montgomery felt like she was part of it.
“It was a sad night for Idaho but I’m so happy for the rest of the country and the progress that is being made,” Montgomery texted me on Wednesday. “I truly believe this fight is not over. It’s just the beginning.”
Indeed, Folwell’s critique about a lack of investment from national groups who saw Idaho as a lost cause echoed what I heard in 2021 from abortion rights advocates in Texas, who felt under-resourced, isolated, and ignored as they fought a Republican legislature that banned abortion at six weeks. To see Texas turn blue on Tuesday after the most highly invested-in Senate race in history, to see a new Democratic attorney general–elect pledge to drop lawsuits against out-of-state abortion providers, while a pro-choice Latina takes the governor’s office is a reminder that all progress is incremental, until it’s not. Before a wave grows big enough to smash the patriarchy, it starts with ripples too small to detect.
Gallus said she would keep making those ripples with the women she’d met through the campaign.
“Cultivating these little seeds here and there is really important when you’re in a place that is very extreme, because this is our home,” Gallus told me in an emotional interview on Wednesday.
“If Texas can do this, then maybe we can, too; it’s just going to take longer.”
