Elections in a Genocidal State Are Not Democratic
The defining feature of Israeli “democracy,” including its elections last week, is its operation according to a Jewish supremacist logic, intensifying the discrimination, oppression, apartheid, mass violence, and genocide against Palestinians.
The recent Israeli elections are a grotesque spectacle. They are grotesque because Israel is a state perpetrating genocide against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip, cheered on by most of its Jewish citizens. They are grotesque because they peddle the lie of democracy in a state subjecting millions of Palestinians in the West Bank and the Gaza Strip to a brutal military occupation for nearly six decades, without basic rights, dispossessing them to settle more than 750,000 Jews in crude violation of basic international law. And they are grotesque because they promote the illusion, both within and outside Israel, that nearly two million Palestinian citizens of Israel somehow hold the key to saving the state from itself. A genocide state and society, however, will do what a genocide state and society does: destroy the people it considers its enemies, especially those it sees as the enemy within.
These elections, in other words, should trigger alarm and open our eyes: we have not seen the worst of Israel’s genocidal assault against Palestinians, against all Palestinians under Israeli rule.
Instead we are drowned in reporting about the Israeli election results as a divide between a bloc led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu against a bloc opposing him, averting our gaze from the obvious and overwhelming majority bloc of ninety-three mandates (out of 120) that support Jewish supremacy and genocide. That very real majority includes the opposition party Yachad (in English: “Together”) that two former Israeli prime ministers lead, Yair Lapid and Naftali Bennett, the latter of whom on October 12, 2023, shouted at a Sky News anchor: “Are you seriously asking me about Palestinian civilians? What is wrong with you? We’re fighting Nazis.”
Supporters of Jewish supremacy and genocide on the anti-Netanyahu side also include Avigdor Lieberman, a far-right politician and leader of the Yisrael Beiteinu (“Israel Is Our Home”) party who, as defense minister in April 2018, praised an Israeli sniper who had shot an unarmed Palestinian man during the Great March of Return in Gaza. A soldier nearby caught the sniper’s war crime on video. As the Palestinian man falls to the ground, either the shooter or the soldier recording the act says in Hebrew, “Wow. What a video! Yes! That son of a b-tch.” Lieberman had this to say about the sniper: “He deserves a medal.”
So much change awaits us with Bennet and Lieberman. But the greatest promise for something new comes from Gadi Eisenkot, former Israeli army chief of staff and leader of Yashar (in English: “Straight”), the main opposition party. Yes, the same Eisenkot who in 2008, as a general and chief of Northern Command, explained the Dahiya Doctrine, his method of mass murder of civilians in Beirut two years earlier:
What happened in the Dahiya quarter of Beirut in 2006 will happen in every village from which Israel is fired on. . . . We will apply disproportionate force on it and cause great damage and destruction there. From our standpoint, these are not civilian villages, they are military bases. . . . This is not a recommendation. This is a plan. And it has been approved.
Planned, approved, and implemented — and then, also morphed into the Gaza doctrine, already well before October 2023, and back again to Lebanon in the last two years for more of that “great damage and destruction” that we can expect in the unlikely event of an Eisenkot-led, post-Netanyahu Israel.
It is, however, that longtime leader of Israel’s opposition, Yair Lapid, the poster boy of Israeli secular liberalism, who perhaps most signifies the danger of Israel’s genocide now escalating further. Lapid rose to political prominence in Israel’s elections in January 2013. Palestinian political parties then received eleven mandates, significantly less than the unprecedented success in the form of nineteen mandates that they won in the recent elections. Netanyahu was the sitting prime minister then too, and his Likud party gained thirty-one mandates in 2013 (it secured twenty-seven now). Lapid’s party then, Yesh Atid (in English: “There is a Future”), trailed behind with nineteen.
It was thus clear that any challenge to Netanyahu would require a coalition with Palestinian parties. But Lapid quickly clarified that such a scenario is “off the table.” Lapid proceeded to delegitimize all Palestinian political parties and, by implication, more than 1.6 million Palestinian citizens of Israel then, 20 percent of the state’s citizens. Lapid had promised his voters, in the name of his party then, a future, a different future. Clearly he assumed that all his voters were Jews, and that the Israeli future he envisioned belonged to them and them alone.
All Israeli governments since then, including the one led by Lapid in 2022, operated according to this Jewish supremacist logic, intensifying the discrimination, oppression, apartheid, mass violence, and, after October 2023, genocide against Palestinians. This is the defining feature of the charade of Israeli democracy: the extremely violent urge to eliminate Palestinians that Netanyahu, Lapid, Bennet, Eisenkot, and Lieberman share, together with the vast majority of Israeli Jews who voted for them in the past and now.
Par for the Course
This should surprise no one who knows anything about the Israeli state. In 2018, the Knesset (Israeli parliament) passed the Jewish Nation-State Law — one of the state’s basic laws, which function as a de facto constitution — that relegates Palestinian citizens to second-class status. Then, in May 2021, as many Israeli Palestinians came out to protest an attack on Palestinians in occupied East Jerusalem and a related Israeli attack on Gaza, the Israeli police responded with massive repression and violence, arresting hundreds. The situation deteriorated quickly, as Jewish and Palestinian citizens clashed across Israel — in some places, as in Haifa, with Jewish citizens attacking Palestinian citizens on the streets and, aided by the police, breaking into houses of Palestinians and attacking them there.
The attack on Israeli Palestinians intensified significantly in the weeks following the Hamas-led attack on Israel on October 7, 2023, and Israel’s subsequent genocidal assault on Gaza: Israeli police arrested over 250 Israeli Palestinian for any expression of identification with Palestinians in Gaza, with then–Israeli Police Commissioner Yaakov “Kobi” Shabtai threatening to expel them to Gaza. A large-scale poll among Israeli Jews a year and a half later, in March 2025, confirmed that many of them would approve of such action: 56 percent supported the expulsion of all Israeli Palestinians. Itamar Ben-Gvir, the far-right settler who serves as Israeli minister of national security, compounded Shabtai’s threat by distributing thousands of weapons to Israeli Jews to form hundreds of civilian “self-defense” units within Israel and in the occupied West Bank.
Israeli media and society added fuel to this fire, with Israeli journalists calling for large-scale killing and destruction in Gaza, as David Mizrahi Wertheim did already on October 7 when he suggested on social media to “turn the [Gaza] Strip into a slaughterhouse.. . . . we are facing human animals.” As Israeli American Pennsylvania State University sociologist Tamir Sorek has shown, this crude dehumanization and bloodlust persisted well beyond the days following October 7. A bit more than two months later, on December 26, 2023, former soccer star and TV commentator Danny Neuman said that “in Gaza, without exception, they are all terrorists, sons of dogs. They must be exterminated, all of them killed.” On February 8, 2025, to take another example, Kinneret Barashi, a lawyer and a television host, tweeted that “every trace of the murderous mutations in Gaza must be erased, from the delivery rooms to the last elderly person in Gaza.” The list goes on and on.
The Israeli elections, in other words, took place in the context of Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza, in an Israeli society immersed in genocidal discourse, and with Palestinian citizens considered second-class and suspected as dangerous. Netanyahu amplified this discourse on election day when he raised the false charge that Palestinian political parties are “stealing the elections.” As the success of Palestinian political parties became clear, he said that they were plotting the destruction of the Jewish state and, without evidence, that Qatar and Turkey somehow bribed Palestinians to vote.
While many Israeli Jewish politicians in the anti-Netanyahu camp reject these accusations, they nevertheless reproduce their rationale by calling to create a Zionist government without Palestinian political parties. It may happen that the Jewish religious Orthodox and ultra-Orthodox parties agree to join a coalition led by Eisenkot, even though they fiercely oppose his plan to recruit them into the Israeli army. Alternatively, a “unity government” with both Eisenkot and Netanyahu might emerge, even though Eisenkot has promised he would not go down that path.
What is highly unlikely to happen, in any case, is a government that would challenge Netanyahu’s dangerous anti-Palestinian discourse by including Palestinian politicians as equals, not to mention that Eisenkot is committed to continue Israel’s violent occupation and settler policies in the West Bank and Gaza Strip.
An exclusionary political discourse depicting millions of citizens as essentially disloyal should raise alarm wherever and whenever it emerges. In the case of the Israeli state that is perpetrating genocide in Gaza, such a discourse, advanced by the prime minister, points both to the abysmal failure of governments, the United Nations, and the international legal system to stop Israel’s ongoing genocide and to the acute danger of its looming escalation and spread beyond Gaza.
Looking at the history of twentieth-century genocides gives a horrific indication of what might await Israeli Palestinians. The Ottoman Empire destroyed Armenian communities and murdered around a million and a half Armenian citizens during World War I on the baseless charge that their loyalty lay with the Russian enemy. In 1994, the Hutu-controlled Rwanda state murdered about eight hundred thousand Tutsis and their Hutu supporters following the invasion in 1990 of the Rwanda Patriotic Front, a Tutsi armed force that sought to topple the government.
Israel’s genocide in Gaza has already led to a murderous and destructive escalation of Israeli state and settler violence in the occupied West Bank, with Israeli leaders now speaking explicitly about treating Palestinians in the West Bank like Palestinians in Gaza. Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz, for instance, referred to the killing and injuring of Israeli soldiers by two Palestinian gunmen outside Hebron on October 23, saying that “every clan neighborhood in Hebron from which the terrorists emerged today will be evacuated of its residents.. . . . Just like in Gaza, just like in Lebanon.” Netanyahu spoke even more directly: “We will act to destroy this place,” also announcing plans for the largest Israeli military operation in the entire West Bank since 1967. “The [Israel Defense Forces are] prepared to carry it out, and we will determine the timing, but it is on the way.”
Israel’s election results in the context of the genocide in Gaza, the intent of Israeli leaders to expand it to the occupied West Bank, and the widespread genocidal discourse among Israeli Jews together place all Palestinians under Israeli rule, including Israeli Palestinians, in great danger. The record performance of Palestinian political parties has rendered them, in the eyes of many Israeli Jews in both blocs, particularly problematic in the way they undermine, if not outright threaten, the dominance of Jews in the Israeli state.
The sixteen years of the Israeli siege on Gaza before 2023 — the longest siege in modern history — provided clear indications of the impending genocide. To paraphrase Netanyahu, it was on its way. Those who recognize and oppose genocide when the perpetrators declare it openly, in our faces, should resist the temptation to treat the Israeli elections — election in a genocide state — as anything other than a warning sign of even worse to come.

The Glimchers Can’t Keep Up the Pace
The mega gallery is struggling, Ebony L. Haynes joins Marian Goodman Gallery, longtime Manifesta director steps down, and more in Art Movements.
Art Movements, published every Thursday afternoon, is a roundup of must-know news, appointments, awards, and other happenings in today’s chaotic art world.
Rich People Problems
The beleaguered Pace Gallery is in the news again, this time after its United Kingdom tax filings revealed that it lost $5.4 million last year and has a $19.2 million debt-for-equity swap in the works with its US parent company. The filings also outlined plans made in 2025 to cut costs and reduce full-time positions.
The reports come in the wake of an abrupt downsizing over the summer, when the gallery laid off 50 workers and slashed 50 artists from its roster in one fell swoop. (Multiple Pace employees told Hyperallergic that they learned of the cuts only when the New York Times broke the story in early June; one artist said the gallery demonstrated "a callous breach of trust.") Additionally, Pace closed its Hong Kong gallery last October after 12 years and is still looking for a smaller space for its London outpost, which put its 8,600-square-foot location on the rental market in June.
Ebony L. Haynes Departs Zwirner
Nine months after Marian Goodman's passing at age 97, her namesake gallery has appointed Ebony L. Haynes as its inaugural senior director and global head of curatorial affairs. Haynes steps into the role after six years at David Zwirner, where she founded and led 52 Walker as a space run entirely by Black staffers. Under her leadership, the Tribeca gallery exhibited work by artists including Arthur Jafa, Cauleen Smith, Pope.L, and Gordon Matta-Clark. Marian Goodman Gallery also announced Rose Lord and Junette Teng, two of its longtime partners, as co-presidents.
What Else Happened?
- Estrellita B. Brodsky, Michael Govan, and Hank Willis Thomas received the annual Cultural Leadership Awards from the American Federation of Arts (AFA).
- Hedwig Fijen stepped down as director of Manifesta after 33 years at the biennial's helm. Emilia van Lynden and Catherine Nichols, appointed general director and artistic director, respectively, will jointly organize the next edition in 2028.
- Ade Omotosho, former assistant curator at the Dallas Museum of Art, was named associate curator at the Studio Museum in Harlem.
- Nolan Jimbo, former assistant curator at the Museum of Contemporary Art, Chicago, was appointed Arnhold associate curator at the Whitney Museum of American Art.
- Ido Radon won the Betty Bowen Award, which includes a solo show at the Seattle Art Museum in 2028.
- The Sundance Institute Cultural Impact Residency was awarded to documentary filmmakers Sara Chishti and Amin Pakparvar; fiction writer-directors Gabby Beans, Lydia Matata, and Rippin Sindher; and fiction film and episodic writers Pedro Eiras and Makisa Francis.
- The Vilcek Foundation awarded a total of $212,000 to 12 nonprofits across the United States, including the Japanese American National Museum in Los Angeles and Rhode Island Latino Arts. See the full list here.
Wildcard: A Blue Wave in Brooklyn
It has indeed been a beautiful week in the neighborhood. Brad Lander spent Halloween in a house costume made by his daughter, Rose, days before securing New York District 10’s House seat in the midterm elections on Tuesday; Queens-based organizer and artist Claire Valdez also won her race, becoming the first Native person to represent the state in Congress.
As one commenter observed, you gotta dress for the job you want!

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Trabalhadores cobram juros baixos e fim da autonomia do Banco Central em Porto Alegre
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Redação
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
Representantes do movimento sindical e trabalhadores reuniram-se na terça-feira (3), na Esquina Democrática, no Centro Histórico de Porto Alegre, para realizar o ato “Juros Baixos Já! Fim da Autonomia do Banco Central!”. A mobilização convocada pela Central Única dos Trabalhadores no Rio Grande do Sul (Cut-RS) questionou os impactos da atual política monetária sobre o crédito, o consumo popular, os investimentos públicos e a geração de empregos.
Os manifestantes defenderam a revogação da autonomia formal do Banco Central, estabelecida pela Lei Complementar nº 179/2021. Segundo eles, a definição da taxa básica de juros (Selic) deve estar subordinada ao projeto de desenvolvimento econômico e às decisões das urnas, e não aos interesses das instituições financeiras privadas.
Tentam impor o programa derrotado nas urnas, denuncia liderança sindical
Durante a manifestação, lideranças do movimento sindical discursaram em cima do carro de som e denunciaram o que consideram uma tentativa da mídia e do mercado financeiro de travar o orçamento público e forçar o governo a aplicar um programa de austeridade fiscal via juros elevados.
“Eles querem corte nas políticas públicas e no gasto público. O nosso problema real é o juro alto. É um juro que causa o endividamento das famílias e que rende à política econômica ao sistema financeiro”, afirmou Ísis Garcia, diretora do Sindicato dos Bancários de Porto Alegre e Região (SindBancários).
A deputada estadual Sofia Cavedon (PT) também criticou a política monetária e defendeu mudanças na condução econômica do país. “Governo Lula, presidente Lula candidato, foi muito cobrado pelo endividamento das famílias. E nós sabemos que o endividamento das famílias vem da política desastrosa de Temer e Bolsonaro e da autonomia do Banco Central, com juros altos, em cima de uma política anacrônica de que juros altos é que seguram a inflação”, afirmou.
“Nós temos caminho. Nós temos outro caminho: é o caminho do investimento, do desenvolvimento, é o caminho da previsão, do estabelecimento de metas para uma inflação adequada e juros no mesmo nível adequado a isso”, completou a deputada.
Cavedon ainda afirmou que as forças políticas contrárias ao governo não devem avançar por meio de uma política econômica recessiva. “Por isso, eles não vão ganhar a eleição no tapetão, em política econômica recessiva, na política econômica do tesouraço, da motosserra que Lula denunciou que Flávio Bolsonaro queria imitar o Milei. Por isso, eles perderam a eleição nesse Brasil. Por isso, essa luta nas ruas tem que tomar a juventude”, declarou.
O presidente da Central Única dos Trabalhadores do Rio Grande do Sul (Cut-RS), Amarildo Cenci, apresentou o ato como um espaço para discutir as questões da taxa de juros. “E a gente está aqui para dizer basta a essa exorbitante, criminosa taxa de juros no Brasil”, declarou.
“E nós, povo brasileiro, trabalhadores e trabalhadoras, centrais sindicais, movimentos sociais, nós queremos que essa taxa de juro injustificada baixe, venha pela metade pelo menos, para que esse dinheiro que rentabiliza os banqueiros, ele seja para desenvolver o nosso país e ter alcançar mais direitos para nossa população”, complementou Cenci.
Impacto direto no bolso e no desenvolvimento
De acordo com as entidades organizadoras, o Brasil voltou a ocupar posições de topo nos rankings mundiais de juros reais, com reflexos graves na vida da população. Elas apontam que a alta dos juros encarece o parcelamento do consumo básico e o crédito pessoal e dificulta a renegociação de dívidas das famílias trabalhadoras.
As entidades também avaliam que os juros elevados dificultam o acesso de pequenos empreendedores a financiamentos para expandir a produção, travando a criação de novas vagas de trabalho. Criticam ainda o custo elevado da taxa Selic, que, segundo elas, drena bilhões de reais do orçamento da União para o pagamento de juros da dívida interna, comprometendo verbas da saúde, educação e infraestrutura.
O movimento sindical prometeu manter a mobilização nas ruas e pressionar o Congresso Nacional e as autoridades monetárias por uma guinada na condução da política econômica do país.

https://gothamist.com/news/feds-accuse-f.title: Feds accuse former FBI agent of Brooklyn hit and run, leaving victim on a bench
https://gothamist.com/news/feds-accuse-f.author: Charles Lane
https://gothamist.com/news/feds-accuse-f.text:
A former FBI special agent hit a man in a Brooklyn crosswalk with his government car February, then dragged him unconscious onto a bench and left him there without calling for help, federal prosecutors alleged in an indictment unsealed Thursday.
Andrew Reyes, 30, of Brooklyn, was arrested Thursday morning and charged with violating the man’s civil rights as an FBI agent by moving him and driving off without getting him help. He also faces charges with lying to investigators about the crash, prosecutors said.
The crash happened around 6:20 a.m. on Feb. 3 at Ocean Parkway and Beverley Road in Kensington, according to the indictment. Prosecutors said Reyes was driving his FBI-issued Chevrolet Impala north in the southbound lane of Ocean Parkway, emergency lights on, when he went through a red light at Beverley Road.
The charges come nine months after the crash, and the court papers don’t say why Reyes’ emergency lights were on, how the victim is doing now or how investigators tied the crash to Reyes. Prosecutors have not identified the man, whom they described in a release as “severely injured.”
Reyes got out of his car after striking the man, dragged him from the street across the sidewalk and onto a bench, then went back for the man’s bag and set it next to him, according to the indictment. He then drove off with his emergency lights still on, prosecutors said. He did not call for medical help or report the crash to the FBI, according to the indictment.
On May 1, agents from the Justice Department’s Office of the Inspector General asked Reyes whether he had ever hit someone with his FBI car and not reported it, according to the indictment. He said he had not, prosecutors alleged.
“The defendant’s alleged conduct demonstrated a shocking disregard for human life and his sworn oath to uphold the law,” Joseph Nocella Jr., the U.S. attorney for the Eastern District of New York, said in a statement.
Reyes had been an FBI agent since about 2023 and was assigned to the bureau’s New York Field Office, according to court records. Prosecutors described him as a former agent but did not say when he left the FBI.
He was scheduled to be arraigned Thursday afternoon before a federal magistrate judge. His attorney declined to comment.
If convicted, he faces up to 10 years in prison, prosecutors said.

An annual report published by the Themed Entertainment Association (TEA)—a nonprofit trade association that represents creators, developers, designers, and producers in the visitor attractions and immersive experiences industry in forty countries—has found that institutions cross China ranked as the world’s most-visited museums in 2025.
According to Ocula, TEA recorded 161.4 million visits across its global top twenty museums in 2025, an increase of 5.4 percent from the same institutions in 2024. Chinese museums held twelve of the top twenty spots. Beijing’s Palace Museum was the most popular, with nineteen million visits—an increase of 11.8 percent from the previous year.
TEA also found that Gen-Z accounted for more than half of museum visits across China, attributed to an increased focus on technology in these museums, including immersive and AI-focused exhibitions.
By contrast, visitor numbers for Washington, D.C.’s federal museums declined steeply following the US government shutdown, which lasted forty-three days. Visits to the National Gallery of Art, for instance, fell to 2.8 million in 2025, a decrease of 28.9 percent. Similarly, attendance at the Smithsonian Institution’s National Museum of Natural History and National Museum of American History declined by 15.4 percent and 14.3 percent, respectively.
Unlike federally funded institutions, privately funded ones saw increases in attendance, including the Museum of Modern Art in New York and the Art Institute of Chicago, the latter of which had an increase of 13.3 percent. The only American museum to break into the top twenty was the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York, whose visitor numbers increased by 4.5 percent to 5.98 million.
Outside of China, the most visited institution was the Musée d’Louvre in Paris. As the fourth most-attended museum globally, it attracted 9.05 million visitors in 2025. Also of note is the National Museum of Korea, which saw its year-on-year visitorship increase 68.3 percent, the top 20’s biggest percentage increase.

https://www.humanite.fr/social-et-econom.title: Le 5 novembre, le gouvernement rêvait d’un essoufflement, 1,6 million de personnes lui ont répondu : récit d’une manifestation historique
https://www.humanite.fr/social-et-econom.author: Cyprien Boganda,Hélène May,Naïm Sakhi,Tom Demars-Granja,Elisabeth Fleury,Lisa Guillemin,Axel Nodinot
https://www.humanite.fr/social-et-econom.text:
Les chiffres sont records. Selon la CGT, 1,6 million de personnes ont manifesté jeudi 5 novembre contre la vie chère, à l’appel de l’intersyndicale au grand complet. Un désaveu pour l’exécutif, qui misait (en vain) sur un essoufflement. À travers le pays, entre assemblées générales, piquets de grève et cortèges syndicaux, récit d’une journée historique.
Une page d’histoire est peut-être en train de s’écrire sous nos yeux, à coups de slogans tantôt enragés tantôt rêveurs : jamais la France n’avait été secouée par un mouvement social d’une telle ampleur à six mois d’une élection présidentielle. Après avoir parié sur une rentrée sans histoire puis tenté d’éteindre la flambée de colère naissante en y apportant des réponses sectorielles, l’exécutif mise désormais sur son extinction.
Pas sûr que la rue valide ce scénario : jeudi 5 novembre, 1,6 million de personnes (étudiants, travailleurs du public et du privé, retraités, lycéens…) ont battu le pavé ou débrayé aux quatre coins du pays, renvoyant le spectre de l’essoufflement au statut de fantasme gouvernemental.
9 h 30, rue d’Aubervilliers (Paris) : « Un seul jour sans travailler, c’est du pain en moins pour nos enfants »
Ils ne sont pas bien nombreux – une vingtaine tout au plus –, mais leur détermination vaut celle d’une petite armée. Arrivés tôt ce matin dans l’aube froide, loin des caméras de télé et de l’agitation, des salariés d’Altice Technical Services, filiale du groupe de Patrick Drahi vendu à la découpe, avalent un thé devant le siège social de leur boîte. Ils font grève pour la cinquième fois depuis cet été, mais la décision n’a pas été facile à prendre. Pas surprenant, quand on est payé 1 600 euros net par mois. « Même un seul jour sans travailler, c’est du pain en moins dans la bouche de nos enfants », résume Abdel Ennanat, délégué Unsa.
D’autant que, depuis l’annonce du rachat de SFR par ses concurrents, les heures supplémentaires ou le travail le samedi qui permettaient jusque-là d’étoffer les fiches de paie, se sont envolés. Résultat, « on court pour finir à temps, on travaille la boule au ventre et on est dans le flou total, sans savoir comment on va s’en sortir, renchérit Kaïs, un jeune homme filiforme, appuyé contre la porte d’entrée. On est concernés à fond par le mouvement contre la vie chère. J’ai beau habiter chez ma mère, et ne pas payer de loyer, à la fin du mois, il ne me reste rien, alors que, tous les jours, on se lève et on travaille. »

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/market/.title: Two More Vienna Galleries Close, Citing ‘No New Collectors’ and ‘Challenging’ Financial Landscape
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/market/.author: Brian Boucher
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/market/.text:
Two more galleries in Vienna are closing or changing their models amid market challenges, reports the Art Newspaper (TAN).
Zeller van Almsick and Exile cite high costs and unreliable sales. This development comes after Zurich’s Eva Presenhuber is closing the Vienna outpost she has operated since 2022, as she told ARTnews in October, and Emanuel Layr changing his operating model.
Exile is calling it quits after some 18 years, with founder Christian Siekmeier telling TAN that “there are simply no new collectors emerging.” The gallery was founded in Berlin in 2008 and moved to Vienna after a decade, showing older generations including Alvin Baltrop and Nathalie du Pasquier as well as younger artists such as David Gruber and Katharina Marszewski.
Zeller van Almsick is shuttering after a decade. “There is no point in sugarcoating the fact that the past two years have been financially extremely challenging,” cofounder Magdalena Zeller told TAN. The gallery showed younger Austrian artists including Dejan Dukic, Carsten Fock, and Bianca Phos.
Layr, meanwhile, will go nomadic, while keeping a smaller, by-appointment showroom in the capital, as the founder revealed in September. “The gallery model as we know it is increasingly reaching its limits,” said Layr, who mounted his first show in 2011, at the time, while also saying that “financial reasons played no part” in the decision. The gallery’s roster includes such well-known artists as Julien Bismuth, Lili Reynaud-Dewar, and Leah Ke Yi Zheng.
He now tells TAN, “It’s harder to sell some things, costs are getting higher, then there’s a big art fair coming and taking another €100,000. I had to be more realistic, and think, ‘How much profit do I get? How much does the artist get?’”
These troubles come despite the fact that the city, whose metro area is home to 2.9 million, is rich with both historical and contemporary art institutions, as Art in America’s Emily Watlington wrote in 2025 after a dozen visits, calling it “Europe’s best art city.” But Zeller tells TAN that there is “a significant gap” between the city’s cultural heft and the level of activity among its collectors.
In a contrasting signal of the local market’s potential, a number of top Vienna galleries have banded together to launch a new fair, Astoria Artshow, which had its inaugural outing in September. That followed troubles at both the Spark Art Fair Vienna and Vienna Contemporary.
Longtime contemporary art collector Eva Frey tells TAN that there are not enough collectors in her age cohort (over 70) to sustain the city’s galleries. At the same time, she says there are not enough collectors in the 45 to 55 range, formerly the principal group supporting contemporary art, who are “established in a profession.”

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: After the ‘Blue Tsunami’: Dems Await Mamdani and Hochul in Puerto Rico as Taxes Take Center Stage
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Katie Honan, Claudia Irizarry Aponte
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico — The “blue tsunami” celebrations swelled onto the beaches of San Juan on Wednesday, less than a day after Democrats regained control of the House and Senate and Gov. Kathy Hochul easily won reelection.
The annual SOMOS convention, held by the New York Democrats in Puerto Rico after every Election Day, has seen the ebbs and flows of politics.
“Two years ago, this looked like a funeral,” outgoing Rep. Nydia Velazquez told The City Reporter at the conference’s opening reception, remembering President Donald Trump’s 2024 reelection. “Two years ago, we were here agonizing. And tonight, we are celebrating.”
Democrats routed their Republican opponents across the country, which state Attorney General Letitia James, who also waltzed to victory on Tuesday , said was “about a course correction.”
“It’s a rejection of all the chaos, confusion, and corruption,“ she told The City Reporter.
The other contrast to 2024: New York City is now led by a socialist, Zohran Mamdani, whose historic mayoral election and win seemed far off two years ago. He’s now riding some of the highest favorability numbers of any mayor in decades and has used his popularity to help elect members of the Democratic Socialists of America to Congress and the state Legislature — doubling the number of members heading up to Albany next year, from eight to 16.
When Mamdani and Hochul visited SOMOS last year, he was a freshly elected phenomenon while she was facing a potentially difficult reelection battle.
While Mamdani made an early endorsement of Hochul this year and barnstormed with her across the city, she is now the target of his next campaign: for higher taxes on the wealthiest people and corporations.
MORE: Hochul Made Big Gains in NYC’s Blue Wave — Except in These Neighborhoods
Grace Mausser, co-chair of the DSA’s New York chapter, said a more progressive tax structure is a top priority — and she hopes Mamdani was able to persuade Hochul during their time together on the trail.
“The wealthy elite don’t necessarily like Zohran, large businesses in the real estate industry don’t necessarily like Zohran. A lot of those special interests are allies of Hochul,” Mauser said.
Both Hochul and Mamdani are set to arrive in San Juan later this week for SOMOS.
State Sen. Zellnor Myrie (D–Brooklyn) told The City Reporter conversations around more progressive taxes will start happening over the next few weeks.
The governor has been reluctant to say whether she’ll push for a tax on the rich, although groups like the DSA and newly-elected state lawmakers have made it a priority.
“There’s a philosophical question about who has the mandate. And the governor just won by 20 points — that is a mandate by any person’s stretch,” Myrie said.
“But there were also very spirited primaries where voters chose them as well,” Myrie said of the new legislators. “And that is also a mandate.”

https://taz.de/Freie-Waehler-nach-Aiwang.title: Freie Wähler nach Aiwanger: Gesicht gesucht
https://taz.de/Freie-Waehler-nach-Aiwang.author: Dominik Baur
https://taz.de/Freie-Waehler-nach-Aiwang.text:
Freie Wähler nach Aiwanger: Gesicht gesucht
Die Freien Wähler brauchen einen Nachfolger für den verstorbenen Hubert Aiwanger. Und noch einen. Und noch einen … Keine leichte Sache.
Und jetzt? Nach dem ersten Schock stellt sich in Bayern die Frage, wie es ohne Hubert Aiwanger weitergeht. Eine Frage, die natürlich vor allem die Freien Wähler selbst beschäftigt. Während Ministerpräsident Markus Söder (CSU) Trauerbeflaggung an staatlichen Dienstgebäuden angeordnet hat und im Prinz-Carl-Palais ein Kondolenzbuch auslegen lässt und die Staatsanwaltschaft in Berlin ein mögliches Fremdverschulden beim Tod des stellvertretenden bayerischen Ministerpräsidenten und Freie-Wähler-Chefs ausschließt, muss dessen Partei Zukunftspläne für die Zeit danach schmieden – etwas, wovon sie bis Mittwochabend noch getrost annehmen konnte, dass es in sehr weiter Ferne liege.
Aiwanger war am Mittwoch völlig unerwartet während eines Berlin-Aufenthalts gestorben. In der Hauptstadt wollte er unter anderem ein neues Parteibüro eröffnen. Wegen Unwohlseins hatte er sich bei dem Termin kurzfristig vertreten lassen. Am frühen Abend wurde er in seinem Hotelzimmer leblos aufgefunden.
Aiwanger war nicht nur bayerischer Vize-Ministerpräsident, Wirtschaftsminister und Landtagsabgeordneter, sondern auch Chef der Freien Wähler sowohl auf bayerischer als auch auf Bundesebene. Beim Parteitag am 14. November in Geiselwind wollte sich Aiwanger als Bundesvorsitzender bestätigen lassen. Der Parteitag wurde nun verschoben. Dabei ist die Neubesetzung dieses Amtes keine die wohl leichteste Übung für die Freien Wähler.
Eigentlich drei Parteien
Wobei man eigentlich von drei verschiedenen Parteien spricht, wenn man von den Freien Wählern spricht. Da sind zum einen die Freien Wähler auf der kommunalen Ebene. Sie sind eine über Jahrzehnte gewachsene politische Kraft, die ihre Starke aus Persönlichkeiten vor Ort zieht. Auf dem Land stellen sie in Bayern zahlreiche Landräte, Bürgermeister, Gemeinderäte. Bei den jüngsten Kommunalwahlen im März schnitten sie besonders gut ab – im Gegensatz zur CSU, die vor allem in den Stichwahlen viele Landratsämter und Rathäuser verlor. An der Stärke der Freien Wähler auf kommunaler Ebene dürfte sich kaum etwas ändern.
Daneben gibt es noch die Freien Wähler auf Bundesebene – eine Splitterpartei, die in der Bundespolitik eine zu vernachlässigende Größe ist. Dann aber ist da noch die Landespartei – gewissermaßen das Lebenswerk Aiwangers. Mit 37 Abgeordneten sitzt sie im Bayerischen Landtag, mit vier Ministern und einem Staatssekretär im Kabinett. Für sie wiegt Aiwangers Tod politisch am schwersten.
Aiwanger war der starke Mann der Freien Wähler im Landtag, seit 2018 auch in der Staatsregierung. Im Wirtschaftsministerium wird erst mal Staatssekretär Tobias Gotthardt die Geschäfte übernehmen. Am Wochenende wollen sich die Vorstände der Bundes- und der Landespartei sowie die Landtagsfraktion zusammensetzen, um das weitere Vorgehen zu besprechen.
Schwierige Suche nach Schwergewichten
Derzeit gibt es keine Anzeichen dafür, wer Aiwanger in welcher Position nachfolgt. Gotthardt wäre zwar fachlich gesehen eine naheliegende Lösung für die Neubesetzung des Wirtschaftsministeriums, gilt aber nicht als besonderes Schwergewicht der Partei. Wobei sich die Frage stellt, wer das neben Aiwanger überhaupt tut.
Zumindest Fraktionschef Florian Streibl könnte man dies zuschreiben. Er dürfte in jedem Fall eine wichtige Rolle bei der Suche nach Nachfolgern spielen. Ob er selbst an einem Wechsel in die Regierung oder dem Parteivorsitz interessiert ist, ist nicht bekannt. Als besonders ehrgeizig gilt der 37-jährige Digitalminister Fabian Mehring, dem nachgesagt wird, sich jedes Amt zuzutrauen. Zur ersten Reihe der Freien Wähler gehören auch Kultusministerin Anna Stolz und Umweltminister Thorsten Glauber. Bekannte Gesichter der Partei sind zudem Stolz’ Vorgänger Michael Piazolo und der stellvertretende Landtagspräsident Alexander Hold. Ersterem fehlt allerdings als Städter und Professor die in der Partei so wichtige Bierzelttauglichkeit, Zweiterer engagiert sich gerade wieder verstärkt außerhalb der Politik – als Fernsehrichter auf Sat1.
Streibl beschrieb Aiwanger am Donnerstag nicht nur als „Ausnahme-Politiker“, sondern auch als „das Gesicht der Freien Wähler“. Anwärter, die Aiwanger in dieser entscheidenden Funktion nachfolgen könnten, hat die Partei derzeit freilich nicht.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. So viele unterstützen freiwillig und regelmäßig. Noch nicht dabei? Werden Sie jetzt Teil der Community! Jetzt unterstützen

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Actually, Democrats Don’t Have to Sacrifice Trans People or Immigrants to Win
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Elie Mystal
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Actually, Democrats Don’t Have to Sacrifice Trans People or Immigrants to Win
For two years, leading Democratic factions have insisted that the party must abandon key populations to win. Tuesday proved them wrong.
In Muncie, Indiana, Republican Representative Victoria Spartz lost her deep-red district to J.D. Ford, an openly gay Democrat who loudly and proudly supports trans rights. In Maine, Republican Senator Susan Collins lost to Democrat Troy Jackson, a logger who does not have Nazi tattoos or a history of violence toward women or a backlog of homophobic comments on Reddit. In Michigan, Muslim doctor Abdul El-Sayed defeated a Republican who was endorsed by a pro-Israel Democrat who lost the primary to him, while never wavering from his defense of Palestinian rights. In Minnesota, Peggy Flanagan, a citizen of the White Earth Nation, defeated a former NFL reporter while running explicitly on “dismantling ICE,” the paramilitary organization that is responsible for the murder of some of her neighbors and constituents. And in Alabama, Allison Montgomery won a state House race, becoming the first transgender legislator in Alabama.
For the past two years, we have been repeatedly told that to win elections, Democrats must abandon their principles. We’ve been told to throw certain groups under the bus. We’ve been told that AIPAC is an insurmountable force. We’ve been told to demonize immigrants. We’ve been told to embrace a form of masculinity that is toxic. We’ve been told that if we don’t do these things, Democrats cannot win anywhere outside New York and California.
No, no, no, and no. Tuesday night showed that having principles is a feature, not a bug. Tuesday night illustrated that Democrats can win anywhere. Tuesday night proved that no group needs to be left behind in order for the coalition to rise.
The Democrats are not the Republicans: There’s no ring you have to kiss or cult leader you have to praise to be part of the group. While the Democrats certainly had a national legislative agenda (that they’ll now be expected to deliver), I’d say the things that bind the current party together are not policies so much as principles. Decency, accountability, fairness, dignity. Donald Trump has debased the Republican Party to the point that the thing that marks you as a “liberal” is not where you stand on the marginal tax rate on incomes over $1,000,000 but where you stand on whether rape is a crime that should be prosecuted.
Having strong principles helped Democrats everywhere. Authentically standing up for those principles helped Democrats everywhere. Standing 10-toes down for what you believe helped Democrats even in races they lost. Just look at Angie Nixon, the DSA-backed candidate who came within striking distance of winning her Senate race in Florida. Nixon received almost no support from the Democratic National Committee, which wrote Florida off as a lost cause, and yet she almost pulled it out. She didn’t have to campaign on policing where kids go to the bathroom or promise to send bombs to Israel to get this close to the upset of the night. The difference between Nixon winning and Nixon losing was establishment Democrats seeing her potential earlier and giving her some money, not Nixon selling out her ideals to the first tech-bro billionaire willing to cut her a check.
Tuesday was a historically good night for candidates of color and women, but I must admit that the victory that was most gratifying to me was Jackson’s up in Maine. I’m one of those people who jumped off the Graham Platner bandwagon so hard when I saw his “Totenkopf” tattoo that I sprained several ankle ligaments. My tolerance for Nazi-aligned body art… does not exist. I got into a lot of fights with the lefty-boy commentariat who told me to overlook the tattoo, and essentially assured me that Platner embossed himself with Nazi insignia as a youthful indiscretion. I got into even more fights with people as Platner’s disgusting history of Reddit homophobia came out. By the time the allegations of sexual assault showed up, I was telling my Maine friends to write in “literally any black bear” instead of voting for Platner.
Through it all, I was told that Platner’s Marine-honed masculinity was the key to defeating Susan Collins and winning the Senate. I was told that I was being elitist for expecting a “perfect” candidate, as if my request of “maybe don’t nominate the guy who posts homophobic slurs and gets a Nazi tattoo” was some sort of impossible purity test from the egghead left. I was told I was out of touch with regular Maine voters, as if any of these pundits were in touch with rural Mainers who have to shovel snow off their roofs to keep their ceilings from caving in.
All of those political know-it-alls were dead wrong. Troy Jackson, it turns out, is every bit as “manly” as Platner without having committed assault. He’s every bit as “salt-of-the-earth” without being a bigot online. He’s not a guy I will probably agree with on a lot of things, but, by all accounts, he seems to be a decent person. And this year, in this election, that was enough.
I hope the pollster-industrial-complex learns that lesson from this election. No, Democrats don’t have to sacrifice trans children on the altar of the megachurch because J.C. (James Carville) told them to. No, Democrats don’t have to take testosterone supplements and treat consent as optional to prove they can win the locker room. No, Democrats don’t have to ignore suffering in Gaza. No, Democrats don’t have to mass deport their neighbors. No, Democrats don’t have to act like Republicans to win Republican districts.
Democrats won this election by having principles. If they also govern that way, things will work out just fine.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120369.title: Automobil-Industrie | Kretschmers Plan für »Auto-Union« stößt auf Skepsis
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120369.author: Hendrik Lasch
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120369.text:
- Wirtschaft und Umwelt
- Automobil-Industrie
Kretschmers Plan für »Auto-Union« stößt auf Skepsis
Debatte über Rettungsplan für Zwickauer VW-Werk im Landtag: Auch Koalitionspartner SPD warnt vor Eingriffen in die Tarifautonomie.
Der Plan zur Gründung einer neuen »Auto-Union« in Sachsen, mit der Ministerpräsident Michael Kretschmer (CDU) das bedrohte VW-Werk in Zwickau retten will, ist im Landtag auf verhaltene Reaktionen gestoßen. Insbesondere Aspekte wie die von Kretschmer ins Spiel gebrachten Lohnsenkungen und längeren Arbeitszeiten für die Beschäftigten stießen auf viel Kritik.
Susanne Schaper, Vorsitzende der Linksfraktion im Landtag, sprach von einem »Plan, bei dem die Beschäftigten zahlen und alle anderen hoffen sollen«. Henning Homann, Fraktionschef der mitregierenden SPD, warnte den Koalitionspartner CDU vor Eingriffen in Tarifautonomie und Mitbestimmung: »Um uns an Ihrer Seite zu haben, muss das gewährleistet sein.« Zur Niedriglohnpolitik früherer sächsischer Landesregierungen werde es »mit uns keine Rückkehr geben«.
Kretschmer hatte in der von der Linksfraktion beantragten Debatte seinen Vorstoß zur Rettung des 8000 Mitarbeiter zählenden Werkes verteidigt. Die Lage der deutschen Automobilindustrie sei »in höchstem Maße dramatisch«, sagte er; auch im VW-Konzern hätten »nicht alle Werke eine Zukunft«. Nach Angaben des Konzernvorstands ist das Zwickauer Werk ab 2031 nicht mehr wettbewerbsfähig ausgelastet; es drohe die Schließung. Angesichts dessen müsse »Sachsen sein Schicksal selbst in die Hand nehmen«, sagte Kretschmer und betonte, die Beschäftigten in Zwickau wollten »weiter hochwertige Autos bauen«.
Nach den Plänen Kretschmers soll das Zwickauer Werk von einer neuen Gesellschaft übernommen und wettbewerbsfähig gemacht werden, etwa durch Innovationen wie den Einsatz humanoider Roboter, aber auch durch neue Modelle bei der Entlohnung und den Ausstieg aus dem VW-Tarifmodell. In Rede steht etwa unbezahlte Samstagsarbeit. Ziel müsse sein, bei den Lohnkosten mit Standorten wie Mladá Boleslav (Tschechien) oder Poznań (Polen) konkurrieren zu können. Die Beschäftigten sollten »auch weiter Tariflöhne« erhalten, betonte der CDU-Politiker; es brauche aber mehr Flexibilität.
Die Gewerkschaft hatte diesen Aspekt von Kretschmers Vorschlag umgehend zurückgewiesen. Es sei zwar wichtig, dass sich die Landesregierung an den Bemühungen zur Rettung des Werkes beteilige, sagte Jan Otto, Bezirksleiter der IG Metall in Berlin, Brandenburg und Sachsen. Allerdings seien »längere Arbeitszeiten und Lohndrückerei dafür das völlig falsche Instrument«. Sein Zwickauer Kollege Thomas Knabel ergänzte, man wehre sich »gegen alle Versuche, die Beschäftigten zum Teil des Problems bei Volkswagen zu erklären«.
Auch im Landtag gab es Gegenwind. Der BSW-Abgeordnete Bernd Rudolph erklärte, die Beschäftigten hätten »ihren Beitrag längst geleistet«; das Zwickauer Werk erfülle die Kostenvorgaben des Konzerns. Der Grünen-Politiker Wolfram Günther merkte an, VW habe ohnehin bereits Tarifverträge gekündigt, was finanzielle Einschnitte für die Mitarbeiter zur Folge habe.
Schaper kritisierte, dass Kretschmer etwa bei den Milliarden-Boni für das Management keine Abstriche vorsehe, und rechnete vor, selbst eine Halbierung der Löhne würde jedes einzelne Auto nur fünf Prozent preiswerter machen. In Anspielung auf das Logo der historischen Auto-Union, das aus vier ineinander verschlungenen Ringen bestand, sagte die Linke-Politikerin, Kretschmer habe einen fünften Ring hinzugefügt: »einen Gürtel, den die Mitarbeiter enger schnallen sollen«.
Der CDU-Politiker bezieht sich mit dem Begriff »Auto-Union« auf ein Konstrukt, das 1932 ins Leben gerufen worden war, um die von der Pleite bedrohten sächsischen Fahrzeughersteller Horch, DKW, Wanderer und Audi zu retten. Der Name ist historisch belastet, weil die Auto-Union Teil der NS-Rüstungsindustrie wurde und Tausende KZ-Häftlinge sowie Zwangsarbeiter ausbeutete.
Initiator für die Gründung kurz vor dem Machtantritt der Nazis war die damalige sächsische Staatsbank. Diese sei, betonte Wolfram Günther, auch größter Anteilseigner gewesen und habe zunächst 75, später über 90 Prozent des Aktienkapitals gehalten. Bei Kretschmers Überlegungen sei dagegen »völlig unklar, wer mit welchem Geld reingehen« solle, kritisierte der Grünen-Politiker. Der Ministerpräsident hatte in der Debatte zuvor betont, man spreche »nicht darüber, dass wir das Unternehmen übernehmen oder uns daran beteiligen wollen«.
Generell ließen Kretschmers Überlegungen noch zu viele Fragen offen, merkte auch Rudolph an. Zu klären sei, wer die Investoren seien, welche Fahrzeuge gebaut werden und woher die Aufträge kommen sollten und welche Rolle dem VW-Konzern zugedacht werde. Erst, wenn ein konkretes industriepolitisches Konzept vorliege, könne über Bedingungen etwa für die Belegschaft verhandelt und »wenn nötig auch über eine Beteiligung des Freistaats nachgedacht« werden, sagte der BSW-Abgeordnete.
Ohnehin liege das Problem tiefer, sagte SPD-Fraktionschef Homann. In Europa gebe es in der Automobilindustrie Überkapazitäten für eine halbe Million Autos. »Kern der Bemühungen« müsse es daher sein, neue, wettbewerbsfähige Modelle auf den Markt zu bringen. Homann fügte hinzu: »Das ist die Aufgabe des Konzerns, nicht von Ministerien oder Staatskanzleien.«
Kein Milliardär im Rücken
Andere Medien haben Konzerne oder Milliardäre im Rücken. Wir haben die nd.Genossenschaft und Leser*innen wie dich. Das macht uns unabhängig und genau das wollen wir bleiben. Aber es heißt auch: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro.
Du kannst direkt hier spenden, einmalig oder regelmäßig, damit nd bleibt.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/midterms-dem.title: After the Midterms, the Left Has a Huge Opportunity to Seize
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/midterms-dem.author: Eric Blanc
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/midterms-dem.text:
After the Midterms, the Left Has a Huge Opportunity to Seize
In 2008, Barack Obama won a landslide victory and enormous mandate, only to quickly squander it. Today the Democratic establishment is far more delegitimized, and the Left is far stronger. History doesn’t have to repeat itself.
This week’s midterm results were a historic victory for working people and a devastating blow to Trumpism. After so much cruelty and darkness, millions of people have gotten to experience the joy of defeating the far right.
We’re entering an unusually fluid political moment, with enormous opportunities, formidable opponents, and no ready-made road map. Here are my initial thoughts about how we got here and what we should do now.
1. America Is Not a Deeply Right-Wing Country
Remember when centrist pundits insisted Trump’s 2024 victory meant America had become permanently conservative? That narrative hasn’t aged well. Roughly 70 percent of young voters backed Democrats in this election, with the margin among young people swinging by about 32 points since 2024.
Millions of Americans are angry at an economic and political system that keeps failing them. There’s an enormous opening for an alternative that can actually deliver.
2. Economic Populism Is Becoming More Central to Democrats
Democrats of every political stripe won, so it would be silly for any faction to claim a national mandate for its entire program. But a striking and novel feature of this election nationwide was the growing Democratic emphasis on corporate greed, billionaire power, and a rigged economic system — not just affordability, but the fight against those making our lives unaffordable. The old centrist, Third Way assumption that Democrats can only win by “running to the center” is increasingly out of step with the party’s own campaigns, at least when it comes to economics.
As one observer put it, the closing Democratic message across swing states and districts focused on “taking on corporate greed, endless war, and billionaire control of politics” — the kind of platform Bernie Sanders popularized in 2016 and Zohran Mamdani ran on in 2025. This shift remains very uneven, and it’s unclear how far mainstream Democratic politicians will go in actually confronting big business, unless forced by organized pressure from below. But their promises nevertheless raise expectations, and organized working people can fight to hold them to those promises.
3. Learn From Texas
James Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton in a state Donald Trump won by nearly 14 points in 2024. He ran on an essentially Bernie-lite economic platform, arguing that “Republicans and Democrats alike sold the false gospel of trickle-down economics.” As he declared in his victory speech: “We just sent a message to every billionaire megadonor, every trillionaire megadonor, every corrupt defender of this broken political system: in this state, in this country, power belongs to the people.”
Texas’s new Democratic governor, Gina Hinojosa, has been similarly explicit: “The one fight in this country is about economic power, and populism is about economic power.” And she’s right that centering bread-and-butter demands and broad fights against the economic elite is more effective than leaning into the culture war. As Hinojosa explained to The New York Times: “I have seen so many Democrats grandstand on culture-war issues, only to vote with corporate interests, and none of us are better for it.”
4. Socialists and Berniecrats Proved Their Electoral Viability
Abdul El-Sayed easily won Michigan’s Senate race despite a viciously racist campaign against him and Haley Stevens’s treachery. Angie Nixon came within three points of winning in Florida, and over fifty Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) candidates won nationwide. William Lawrence, a Sunrise Movement cofounder who ran against corporate power and Big Tech, defeated Republican incumbent Tom Barrett in Michigan. Scores of other leftists and economic populists scored impressive victories.
The Left has come extraordinarily far since 2016, and there’s no reason to assume its recent successes have exhausted its potential.
5. You Can’t Separate Performance From Money
It’s true that moderate Democrats have a short-term advantage in certain relatively conservative statewide races, especially during backlash elections after decades of bipartisan neoliberalism. But part of their apparent electoral advantage in those areas reflects the huge differences in campaign spending and institutional support. I found that economic populist Senate campaigns in 2026 tended to face a much larger Republican spending advantage than their more moderate Democratic counterparts.
Chuck Schumer and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee poured millions into establishment candidates who lost badly, while Angie Nixon received no comparable backing and nearly won in Florida. While centrist pundits like Matt Yglesias are claiming that leftists and populist candidates systematically underperformed compared to those they claim are “moderates,” any serious comparison of electoral performance has to take these disparities into account, as well as the genuinely anti-billionaire emphasis of candidates like Talarico.
And there’s a deeper strategic point here: our side has to run to win, but we also have to run to deliver big. That requires generally pushing for politicians prepared to enact ambitious reforms, like Zohran in New York City, even if taking some electoral risks is sometimes necessary in the process. So, while good campaigns have to read their local terrain and adjust accordingly, the biggest risk overall is staying with the same Democratic politics that got us into this mess in the first place.
6. AIPAC and Israel Suffered a Major Political Defeat
El-Sayed won despite extraordinary spending against him, including nearly $30 million from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) during the Democratic primary. Talarico and similar Democrats also publicly rejected AIPAC money. The old assumption that Democratic candidates must obediently support Israel to remain electorally viable is crumbling, finally.
7. There’s a Growing Constituency for Taking On the Artificial Intelligence Oligarchs
Voters across the country backed ballot measures restricting or blocking data center development. Voters sided against data centers in forty-three of forty-four measures, including six decided earlier in the year. The billionaire owners of these companies were among the elites quickest to accommodate Trump; we need to make challenging their power a central part of our agenda.
8. This Election Was a Repudiation of Donald Trump, Not a Vindication of Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries
The same Democratic leaders who failed to mount a serious fight against Trump’s authoritarian offensive are now trying to claim credit for his defeat. Their political timidity, ties to the billionaires, and low ambitions make them profoundly unsuited for the fights ahead.
Democrats need new congressional leadership willing to confront Trump and champion transformative change. And the close races in supposedly unwinnable states should convince the party to stop writing off large parts of the country. Competing there consistently will require a bold program and much more organizing between elections.
9. The Democratic Party’s Future Is Unusually Fluid
The most significant thing about Haley Stevens’s disgraceful endorsement of Republican Mike Rogers is that much of the Democratic establishment continued backing El-Sayed, however reluctantly. Sections of Barack Obama’s political orbit are clearly trying to accommodate the Left.
The balance of power inside the Democratic Party is changing, and its future direction is up for grabs. Socialists should take advantage of every opening for cooperation while continuing to build independent strength.
10. We Need a New New Deal
Without having any illusions that Democrats on their own will do the right thing, we should also acknowledge that there are no timeless formulas for what comes next. Whatever clues we can find from history are most likely to be found in the 1930s.
Franklin Delano Roosevelt, like some of the smarter mainstream Democratic politicians around today, was fundamentally a political opportunist, but he could read which way the winds were blowing. The Great Depression, militant strikes, pressure from the Left, and the growing power of organized labor helped push his administration and a wing of establishment Democrats toward Social Security, the Wagner Act, and a more confrontational stance toward big business. Crucially, those transformational victories involved both independent working-class mobilization and alliances with reformers inside the Democratic Party.
The lessons of the 1930s can hardly be reduced to a rule against ever working with liberal Democrats. We need concrete analyses of concrete situations to assess which compromises are needed, which fights to pick, and which alliances to make or break. A new New Deal is possible and necessary. And winning it is the precondition for any further advance toward economic democracy.
11. Celebrating MAGA’s Defeat Is Not “Libbing Out”
Yesterday I saw plenty of joking from radicals online that it was ok for one night to “lib out,” i.e. celebrate Democratic wins against Republicans. The implication here is that there’s something not properly socialist about being excited about and engaged with such wins. But this misses something crucial: socialists should be unapologetically part of the broad fight against MAGA, including in electoral battles.
And contrary to what some far-left DSA leaders seem to believe, if Democrats now fail to deliver, the main beneficiary will likely be an emboldened far right. Our most immediate task is to organize enough independent working-class power to make the anti-MAGA (i.e., Democratic) coalition succeed in meeting workers’ urgent needs, rather than lob critiques from the sidelines about how betrayal and disappointment are inevitable.
12) The Biggest Danger Is Repeating the Disastrous Missed Opportunity of 2006–8
Like last night, anger at George W. Bush’s presidency propelled Democrats to congressional majorities in 2006, culminating in Obama’s historic landslide in 2008. Democrats had a huge mandate and large congressional majorities.
But Obama’s centrism and demobilization of his base squandered much of that opportunity. Millions who had hoped for fundamental change quickly grew disillusioned. Republicans won sixty-three House seats in 2010, and eight years after Obama’s first victory, Trump entered the White House.
The stakes today are even higher, and our crisis much deeper. Everything depends on breaking the destructive doom loop of Democratic victories, dashed hopes, and increasingly reactionary Republican comebacks. The good news is that the Democratic establishment is far more delegitimized than in 2008, and the Left is far stronger. History doesn’t have to repeat itself.
13) Congress Needs to Go on the Offensive Immediately
Ro Khanna got it right when he said on Election Day:
When we win, we need America’s next New Deal.
Medicare for All.
$25 living wage.
End the Iran War.
Zero aid [to] Israel.
Tax the billionaires.
Make Trump Hoover if he vetoes it.
Democrats should polarize the country around popular legislation that would materially improve people’s lives.
They should fight to repeal the roughly $900 billion in looming Medicaid cuts, protect Affordable Care Act affordability, and save threatened rural hospitals. They should redirect money from Immigration and Customs Enforcement and endless war toward jobs, health care, and public investment. And they need to start fighting now to end the filibuster — part of a wider fight against minoritarian veto points that will eventually have to tackle the Supreme Court, statehood for Puerto Rico and Washington, DC, and other long-needed democratic reforms. We can’t allow appeals to bipartisanship or institutional norms to become another excuse for suicidal inaction. It’s good to investigate and prosecute Trump, his goons, and his corrupt billionaire buddies, but the centerpiece of this Congress should be an ambitious economic agenda that makes the stakes of 2028 clear.
14. AOC Needs to Run for President in 2028
The victories of El-Sayed and other left populists show there’s a real path to winning the White House in 2028. No less important, without Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez in the race, an ambitious anti-billionaire agenda is far less likely to dominate the Democratic primaries.
There are genuine risks to running her for president, but the biggest risk is nominating another centrist without the determination or mandate to transform the country. Even if AOC loses the nomination, her campaign would generate massive grassroots power and help move the entire party toward a program capable of meeting this moment.
15. We Need Big Organizing
All of our organizations, from unions to Sunrise to Indivisible to DSA and beyond, have a historic opening for growth if we can pivot away from our routines, our online self-selection, and our excessively small goals. We have an opening for on-the-ground left organizing at an unprecedented scale in contemporary America.
By 2028, we need our unions to be on the offensive against corporations that bent the knee to Trump, and we need them to set the ambitious goal of organizing a million new workers every year under a new Democratic administration and forcing through labor law reform. DSA should aim to become a mass organization of at least half a million members, much more deeply rooted in the broader working class. That means moving beyond insular, self-marginalizing politics, turning instead to scaling up mass campaigns capable of involving our nonactivist neighbors, coworkers, and friends.
The obstacles ahead remain enormous: billionaires, corporate Democrats, a hostile Supreme Court, and a Republican Party determined to sabotage any transformative agenda. We need organized movements capable of forcing recalcitrant Democrats to fight, winning and defending reforms against elite resistance, and keeping up the pressure long after Election Day.
There’s still an enormous amount of work ahead. But after two years of darkness, we’ve won an extraordinary victory. The future is unwritten. Let’s make the most of it.

https://hyperallergic.com/at-moma-brancu.title: At MoMA, Brancusi Is Lost in Space
https://hyperallergic.com/at-moma-brancu.author: Aruna D’Souza
https://hyperallergic.com/at-moma-brancu.text:
At MoMA, Brancusi Is Lost in Space
The artist’s work is glorious and resonant, but the Museum of Modern Art has a space problem, or an elegance problem, or a crowd mitigation problem.
Let’s get one thing out of the way first: For all my weariness about how canonical dead White men are STILL. CONSISTENTLY. CENTERED in museum exhibitions — even after said museums have publicly taken pains to expand collections, hire curators with broad expertise and interests, and invite new audiences into their spaces — I have ZERO complaints about putting on a Constantin Brancusi exhibition. Even in fall 2026, when the city’s three major museums have turned themselves over to Brancusi, Lichtenstein, and Pollock simultaneously. (I will go to my grave insisting that it should have been a Krasner show.)
That said, the work of this particular canonical dead White man is glorious, and continues to resonate with contemporary artists: His name has come up consistently in interviews with sculptors this past year, whether Rodney McMillian or Martin Puryear or a number of others I’ve talked to. Brancusi: The Artist and His Studio at the Museum of Modern Art is a great reminder of why. More than a survey, it demonstrates the importance of this artist’s atelier as a place of creation, of exhibition, and of sociability, and includes his drawings, photographs, films, tools, and even some of the record albums he owned — reminders of the legendary dinner parties he used to throw there.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/colunist.title: Listas de boicote e o convite ao diálogo
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/colunist.author: Bares pela Democracia
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/colunist.text:
Assim como nas eleições de 2022, após a extrema-direita perder mais uma em 2026, começaram a aparecer listas de boicotes a bares e outros comércios que apoiaram a candidatura do Lula. Um perfil no X, em especial, pegou a ideia e a identidade visual do projeto Sleeping Giants, mudou seu nome para Sleeping Zap e, obviamente, aplicou de uma forma toda torta.
Divulgaram uma lista requentada da eleição anterior com alguns locais que nem existem mais e tentaram provocar marcas a retirar seu patrocínio a artistas e portais que, na interpretação deles, são de esquerda. Até o Luciano Huck foi denunciado, para se ter ideia do nível da paranoia.
Ainda que seja uma tática que, como já ficou demonstrado antes, esfria e some, deve-se ter atenção. Porque não se trata de um boicote a grandes empresas, como já aconteceu com o Magazine Luiza, ou quando a própria esquerda o fez contra Riachuelo, Havan e afins. São pequenos locais que podem sofrer consequências financeiras sérias, levando ao fechamento de suas portas e demissões, ou seja, é uma iniciativa irresponsável que advoga contra os trabalhadores, incluídos os pequenos empresários. Assim como a demissão de pessoas que votaram no PT.
Além deste tipo de perseguição, há a violência física. Ao longo dessa eleição, a violência política foi alarmante, com inúmeros relatos de agressões vindas do lado bolsonarista, que resultaram até em morte, e que podem se voltar após o período eleitoral contra as pessoas que frequentam e trabalham em determinado estabelecimento. Temos ainda um governo municipal e estadual que também são de extrema-direita, que incentivam a violência quando não são eles próprios a praticá-la. É colocado um alvo em nossas costas.
O que também já vimos acontecer foi a formação de uma rede de solidariedade inversa, na qual a lista do boicote se transformou em um guia de locais a serem obrigatoriamente visitados. De toda forma, o mapeamento, a identificação e a perseguição a indivíduos e estabelecimentos associados à esquerda no Brasil possuem raízes históricas profundas. Podemos citar dois episódios que marcam a nossa sociedade até hoje: a Constituição de 1937, que instituiu o Estado Novo, e o início da militarização da polícia.
A Ditadura Vargas cumpriu a cartilha básica das ditaduras ao concentrar o poder no Executivo, suprimir direitos da população, censurar a imprensa, extinguir partidos, prender e matar opositores. Conforme consta no texto de introdução àquela constituição, a justificativa foi atender ao estado de apreensão criado no país pela infiltração comunista, tudo muito bem arquitetado pelo que ficou conhecido como Plano Cohen.
Sobre a militarização da polícia, ela aconteceu no ano de 1969, auge da Ditadura Militar, implantada também sob a desculpa do medo do comunismo. O que aconteceu foi que, até aquele ano, o policiamento de rua era feito por agentes de caráter civil, como é a Polícia ou a Guarda Civil atualmente. A PM ficava nos quartéis, sem contato com a população, sendo acionada apenas em casos que ficaram registrados em seu brasão, que conta com 19 estrelas que representam, por exemplo, a atuação no combate à Coluna Prestes, Guerra do Paraguai, Canudos, Revolta da Chibata, repressão à greve operária de 1917 e a “Contrarrevolução de 1964”.
Como bem sintetiza esta matéria do Outras Palavras: “A Polícia Militar paulista ostenta como atos heroicos e marcos históricos da corporação a atuação em atividades de clara repressão ao próprio povo”. Então, a partir de 1969, esta foi a polícia escolhida para atuar nas ruas com os cidadãos. A ideia de que há um inimigo interno a ser combatido, que são historicamente as pessoas de esquerda, passou a fazer parte do funcionamento comum da segurança pública brasileira. Encerrada a ditadura, restou à PM identificar outro inimigo, focando no controle social baseado no genocídio da juventude negra.
Portanto, não é novidade o mapeamento e perseguição de pessoas de esquerda, o que ainda habita o imaginário dos órgãos de segurança. Policiais militares, guardas civis, seguranças do metrô e de locais públicos privatizados, como o Anhangabaú, estiveram envolvidos em ocorrências de agressões e impedimento de campanhas políticas da esquerda no primeiro e no segundo turno. Assistimos, mais uma vez, a força policial atirando bombas e gás de pimenta por motivos eleitorais.
Tudo isso acontece pelas lentes do bolsonarismo, mas não só. Ao longo dos períodos de ditadura em que a política de Estado era não se discutir política, formaram-se ao mesmo tempo grupos conscientes da situação, que foram usados como desculpa para o endurecimento do regime, e parte da população que acreditava no discurso oficial ou passou a desacreditar das instituições. É o inverso da despolitização: é a política imposta sob uma ótica que detém uma máquina de propaganda por trás dela.
É o que ocorre com a fábrica de fake news organizada no governo Bolsonaro pelo gabinete do ódio e que, nestas eleições, mostrou a sua cara mais nefasta com o apoio explícito de governos estrangeiros, em especial dos EUA, e as redes sociais. Some-se a isso o histórico ódio ao petismo propagado pelas grandes mídias brasileiras e pronto: temos o anticomunismo 2.0.
Ninguém passa ileso às décadas de propaganda anticomunista, inúmeras matérias e editoriais diários durante todos os anos de governo petista, alertando sobre os extremos perigos do socialismo a ser implantado. A diferença é que esse cruzamento entre interesses de países conectados às big techs atinge um patamar de controle social que nenhuma ditadura na história imaginou ter.
Mesmo com esse time todo, somado ao mercado financeiro lutando contra, Lula saiu vencedor desta eleição em um movimento histórico do povo brasileiro que influenciou o mundo todo. Sim, é possível combater e vencer as máquinas de ódio.
Mais do que isso, o que ficou claro foi que a frente de esquerda deve ser ampla e aberta ao diálogo. Nem todo eleitor do Flávio Bolsonaro é fascista, como deu para perceber nas inúmeras conversas que tivemos que ter para virar votos. Pesquisas da época das manifestações pelo impeachment de Dilma Rousseff indicavam que apesar da maioria das pessoas que estavam ali se dizerem de direita, elas concordavam com serviços públicos gratuitos, como saúde e educação, que são pautas da esquerda.
Vimos agora que a desinformação pode ser combatida com troca de ideias. Há uma grande parcela de pessoas que podemos disputar nesse imaginário anticomunista delirante, e não há como ignorar os 56 milhões de votos em Bolsonaro e a composição do Congresso.
Que nós, frequentadores e trabalhadores de locais que se propõem a conversar, possamos usar essas eleições e os seus efeitos em uma permanente luta anticapitalista. Contra uma campanha de boicote, devemos abrir uma campanha de diálogo. Nos bares sempre haverá democracia.
*Luiz Guilherme Ferreira é advogado, dono de bar e integrante do Bares Pela Democracia. Atuou na luta pelo Parque Augusta, onde é conselheiro atualmente, e nas ocupações artísticas Casa Amarela e Ouvidor 63, além de outras pautas sobre direito à cidade.
*Este é um artigo de opinião e não necessariamente representa a linha editorial do Brasil do Fato
