https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ra.title: Rana Hadid on Taking the Zaha Hadid Foundation Into the Future
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ra.author: Hikmat Mohammed
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ra.text:
Last October 31 marked what would have been Iraqi architect Zaha Hadid’s 76th birthday, as well as the 10-year anniversary of her death. Rana Hadid, Hadid’s niece and chair of the trustees of the Zaha Hadid Foundation, said that the time is right for a proper celebration of her aunt’s legacy.
Last week, the Zaha Hadid Foundation reopened its doors at 10 Bowling Green Lane in Clerkenwell, the architect’s former headquarters. Meanwhile at the Architectural Association’s campus on Bedford Square, the foundation, together with the architecture school and the Serpentine, held a two-day symposium in Hadid’s honor. Titled “89 Degrees of Zaha Hadid,” the event celebrated her legacy, including talks on her beginnings in Baghdad and Beirut, her student years at the Architectural Association, and generally grand nature of projects and personality. (One talk is titled “Would they call me a diva if I were a guy?: Being Zaha.”)
Rana, who was present at the symposium, told ARTnews that she raised her hand during some talk correct misconceptions. “I get really upset when I hear things that are not true. We all have our own perceptions of how things happen, and after someone dies, it becomes very easy to change it,” said Rana. She took over as chairman and trustee of the Zaha Hadid Foundation in 2025 from Brian Clarke, artist and Hadid’s close collaborator, who died in July last year. Earlier, in 2020, the foundation settled a four-year legal and personal battle over the architect’s $133 million estate.
“When Zaha passed away, I discovered that I was an executor and trustee of her estate. She had never told me that I was either of these, and straight after her passing, we just had to deal with all of the legal matters.”
The Zaha Hadid Foundation encompasses 300,000 objects from the late architect’s life, from paintings, architectural models, sketchbooks, letters and even her wardrobe (which includes Comme des Garçons and Yohji Yamamoto pieces).
“Our greatest asset is the archive she left behind, and it goes beyond architecture. We can see the way that Zaha thought and how her methodology evolved, resulting in her designs and architecture,” said Rana, revealing that although she doesn’t necessarily believe in a 10-year plan for the future, the next two years are enough to keep her busy with international retrospectives in the works at major institutions. She added that there has been “huge interest” in Hadid’s paintings and wardrobe. An exhibition titled “Zaha Hadid: Visionary Museum Designs” will open next year at the Sir John Soane’s Museum in London, running from March 24 to June 20, 2027.
Rana wants Hadid’s archive to travel beyond the UK just like her architecture. The foundation has been offered exhibitions in Iraq and other countries in the Middle East. “We will be going to Iraq,” said Rana, who grew up in Beirut. She’s never visited Iraq, but said she still “feels Iraqi.”
“Zaha was first and foremost always Iraqi; she always credited the Iraqi part in her for who she was. She had a huge pride of place for Iraq,” said Rana. She recounted how Hadid used to make “the best leg of lamb, the Iraqi way, simmering over a fire for almost 20 hours” with rice. The Iraqi dialect would slip into her Arabic, too, with colloquialism like “Shaku maku?” (What’s there? What’s not there?)
Hadid’s exuberance was well documented, and to honor a decade of her death, Rana had to think like her late aunt, which is what inspired the two-day symposium.
“Zaha was really big on birthdays and she’d always like to make a big thing about her birthday. She would always say to me, ‘I hated surprises and I hate someone throwing me a surprise birthday party, so I may as well assume it, invite everyone and be in control,’” said Rana. A great number of Hadid’s friends and admirers attended the symposium, from Hans Ulrich Obrist and Deyan Sudjic to Aric Chen and Francesco Vezzoli.
“Symbolically, it’s been a very rough 10 years with legal disputes, and we’ve only been a foundation for four years,” explained Rana. “To turn Zaha’s office of 35 years into a foundation was very important to her because it was a former Victorian schoolhouse—and now people can come to learn and it serves everyone.”
The newly refurbished headquarters includes galleries, a learning space, lecture hall and collection display. The spaces will be used to host exhibitions, talks, workshops and creative residencies—the space has been inaugurated with an exhibition, “Zaha Hadid: Architecture of Performance,” curated by Catherine Howe and Libby Sellers, tracing the stage and set designs Hadid imagined for contemporary dance, classical opera and pop music.
Rana describes the Zaha Hadid Foundation as a platform for Hadid’s connections: “We’ve inherited a lot of friends, supporters and clients who became friends and family. Zaha had this amazing way of connecting with people and people loved her—without all of their help, we wouldn’t be here today.

https://taz.de/Demokratische-Sozialisten.title: Demokratische Sozialisten in den USA: Die andere „rote Welle“ bei den Midterms
https://taz.de/Demokratische-Sozialisten.author: Leon Holly
https://taz.de/Demokratische-Sozialisten.text:
Demokratische Sozialisten in den USA: Die andere „rote Welle“ bei den Midterms
Bei den Midterm-Wahlen konnten die Democratic Socialists of America viele Erfolge verbuchen. Was bedeutet das für die Zukunft der Demokraten?
Einer der größten Siege der Demokratischen Sozialisten bei den Midterms in den USA könnte ausgerechnet eine Niederlage sein. Im Rennen um einen Senatsposten in Florida verlor die Sozialistin Angie Nixon nur extrem knapp, mit 48 Prozent der Stimmen. Das ist bemerkenswert, weil es sich um Florida handelt, das Heartland der rechten Exilkubaner, wo Donald Trump bei der Wahl 2024 mit gewaltigem Abstand gewinnen konnte.
Nixon ist Mitglied der Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). Die Organisation setzt sich, wie der Name verrät, für einen demokratischen Sozialismus ein. Bei den Vorwahlen der Demokraten in Florida hatte sich die 42-Jährige Schwarze Frau gegen ihren Establishment-Konkurrenten durchsetzen können.
Nixon kam dem Sieg am Dienstag ganz nah, obwohl die republikanische Wahlkampfmaschine finanziell deutlich besser geschmiert war. Das nationale Establishment der Demokraten hatte sich erst spät für Nixon ausgesprochen – ob ihr das allerdings ein Hindernis war, lässt sich angesichts der wenig begeisternden Führung in Washington debattieren.
Noch vor wenigen Monaten sind Menschen verlacht worden, die behauptet hatten, eine Sozialistin dürfe sich im konservativen Florida ernste Hoffnungen auf einen Senatssitz machen. Die Midterms haben jedoch beweisen, dass Kandidaten der DSA sehr wohl auch jenseits der progressiven Metropolen Erfolg haben können.
Zwei Drittel der Rennen erfolgreich
Laut ihrem eigenen Wahlmonitor hat die DSA bei den für die Demokraten erfolgreichen Wahlen 222 Kandidaten unterstützt– auf allen Ebenen, von der nationalen, über die bundesstaatliche bis zur lokalen. Stand Donnerstagnachmittag konnten rund zwei Drittel dieser Kandidaten die Wahl für sich entscheiden. In 38 Rennen steht das Ergebnis noch aus.
Wie bereits der Fall Nixon andeutet, geht es hier nicht nur um tiefblaue Landstriche, sondern auch um Swing-Bezirke. So konnte etwa die Sozialistin Ashley Herrmann in ihrem Bezirk den Republikanern einen Sitz für Floridas Repräsentantenhaus abtrotzen. Diese Siege widerlegen die Behauptung der Zentristen in der Partei, dass ein demokratisch-sozialistisches Angebot nur in progressiven Städten, nicht aber in konservativeren Regionen verfangen kann.
Auch in New York City konnte die DSA Erfolge verbuchen. Drei linke Kandidaten, die vom sozialistischen Bürgermeister Zohran Mamdani unterstützt wurden, und von denen zwei DSA-Mitglieder sind, konnten Sitze im nationalen Unterhaus erringen. Gleiches gilt für die DSA-unterstützten Donavan McKinney in Michigan und Chris Rabb in Pennsylvania.
In Colorados Hauptstadt Denver konnte Melat Kiros den Wettkampf für das House für sich entscheiden – die 29-Jährige ist nicht nur selbst Mitglied der DSA, sondern auch die erste Schwarze Frau, die aus Colorado in den US-Kongress gewählt wurde. In der Hauptstadt Washington DC wird künftig eine sozialistische Bürgermeisterin regieren, und auch die DSA-Bürgermeisterkandidatin in Los Angeles hat zum aktuellen Stand der Auszählungen gute Chancen auf das Amt.
Über 130.000 Mitglieder
Die DSA wurden 1982 von dem Professor und Schriftsteller Michael Harrington gegründet. Sie sind eine unabhängige Organisation, die nicht direkt mit der Demokratischen Partei verbunden ist. Aus ihrer Mitgliedschaft rekrutieren sich jedoch Kandidatinnen und Unterstützer, die sich an den Vorwahlen innerhalb der Demokraten beteiligen.
Doch auch innerhalb der DSA gibt es Mitglieder, welche die Teilnahme an Wahlen und den Weg durch die Demokratische Partei kritisch sehen. Diese Fraktion möchte die Ressourcen lieber in den Aufbau einer unabhängigen Bewegung oder einer sozialistischen Partei stecken. Nach den Erfolgen der letzten Jahre haben die DSA heute laut eigenen Angaben über 130.000 Mitglieder.
Selbst an Orten, wo am Dienstag keine DSA-Kandidaten auf den Wahlzetteln standen, kann man ihre Handschrift erkennen – bzw. den Druck, den Wahlerfolge wie Mamdanis in New York ausgeübt haben. Im Wahlkampf der Demokraten rückte der Fokus ab von der „Bewahrung der Demokratie“, wie noch unter Präsidentschaftskandidatin Kamala Harris. Dafür wetterten die Progressiven James Talarico in Texas oder Abdul El-Sayed gegen die Korruption der Trump-Regierung, die oligarchischen Verhältnisse in Washington, den Krieg gegen Iran, und versprachen eine Verbesserung der Lebensstandards der arbeitenden Bevölkerung.
„Sozialistinnen und Sozialisten waren in den USA seit einem Jahrhundert nicht mehr so stark“, schreibt der US-Leiter der Rosa-Luxemburg-Stiftung Stefan Liebich in einer Analyse. Die damalige Bewegung organisierte nicht nur die Industriearbeiterschaft, sondern protestierte auch gegen den Eintritt der USA in den Ersten Weltkrieg, worauf die Regierung mit Repression und Haftstrafen reagierte. Zum Niedergang der Sozialisten trug weiter bei, dass Präsident Roosevelt Teile ihres Programms in seine New-Deal-Agenda aufnahm, bis der Neoliberalismus à la Reagan diese zaghaften sozialdemokratischen Errungenschaften zerschlug.
Unter anderen Vorzeichen beeinflusst die DSA jetzt erneut das demokratische Programm. Es sind die engagierten Basis-Mitglieder, die das Plädoyer für eine linke Wirtschaftspolitik ins Land und in die Wahlkämpfe tragen.
Nach den Wahlergebnissen gehe die Linke jetzt gestärkt in den Kampf um die weitere Ausrichtung der Demokraten, schreibt Liebich. Auch mit Blick auf die nächsten Wahlen 2028: Da ist mit der New Yorker Repräsentantin Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez mittlerweile sogar eine DSA-Frau als Präsidentschaftskandidatin im Gespräch.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.title: The Midterms Are Over, and We Won. Now It’s Time to Till the Democratic Soil
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.author: Zephyr Teachout
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
The Midterms Are Over, and We Won. Now It’s Time to Till the Democratic Soil
To renew the promise of self-government, we must create a politics beyond opposing Trump.
With the midterms over, we must now turn to the hard work of tending the democratic soil. Such work is not easy, and it will be tempting to train our attention instead on the polling about 2028, on Trump’s latest atrocities, on worrying about whether our country will survive.
These temptations are old ones. Thousands of years ago, the Greek statesman Demosthenes scolded Athenians for being “content to run round and ask one another, ‘Is there any news today?’” about Philip, King of Macedon, the great threat. He mocked the daily dialogue: “‘Is Philip dead?’ you ask. ‘No, indeed; but he is ill.’” Demosthenes begged the Athenians to see that “this Philip has not grown great through his own unaided strength so much as through our carelessness.” If Athenians kept up at this anxious gossip, he cautioned, they “will soon raise up a second Philip.”
Trump has become our modern-day Philip. His gross destruction of institutions and almost gleeful corruption, his desire to slander opponents and his naked venality, make his actions different in kind from those of other presidents. He flaunts his abuses like a peacock displaying its feathers. “Drain the swamp,” he crows, while accepting a jet from Qatar. “Leakers should be shot,” he shouts at a campaign rally.
“Is he ill?” we ask. “Are his poll numbers down?” Even if you are not embedded in Kalshi and Polymarket, you are likely tempted by the prognostications. But this obsession risks distracting us. Trump’s extremity only means we have greater responsibilities than we might want. As Wendell Berry said to Bill Moyers in 2013, “We don’t have a right to ask whether we’re going to succeed or not. The only question we have a right to ask is: ‘What’s the right thing to do? What does this earth require of us if we want to continue to live on it?’” If we don’t want to raise up a second Philip, there are at least three things people who believe in the promise of self-government should be doing today to till the democratic soil.
First, we must engage in local politics. We can yell at an inert Congress all we want, but if we are careless about our local democratic institutions, congresspeople will only become more untethered from our concerns—after all, the average representative theoretically hears from more than 700,000 people. From Arendt to Brandeis to Tocqueville, the greatest theorists of American democracy have pointed to the townships and local and regional politics as the places where the art of collective action amid difference is learned. It is where we develop the ability to laugh and feel compassion even as we fiercely disagree, tolerating opposing—even hated—ideas without breaking apart. In cities and towns, the public creates democracy tethered to human life.
The most riveting and inspiring actions today are happening locally, with local resistance against ICE and true left-right, MAGA-socialist-independent alliances forming in opposition to AI companies and surveillance tools like Flock cameras. Amid the decay, we see an extraordinary—and successful—uprising of political courage. In the first quarter of 2026, local opposition blocked or delayed at least 75 AI data-center projects, and the number of grassroots anti-data-center groups has been growing exponentially, from under 150 in spring 2025 to over 800 now. People are setting aside their differences to fight against a dictated industrial policy of building sprawling water-and-energy-gobbling server farms that communities don’t want.
Second, we need to build a national anti-corruption movement, one that is separate from the political parties. That anti-corruption movement must demand to investigate Trump’s corrupt deals with law firms and big companies, to be sure, but it must do far more. It must fight to overturn Buckley v. Valeo and Citizens United, the Supreme Court’s catastrophic rulings on campaign finances, as well as the court’s decision to bless lobbyists giving Rolex watches to governors. And it must reclaim our understanding of human nature from the view of it that has dominated American politics for half a century.
The economics revolution of the 1970s taught judges, policymakers, and politicians that to be human is to be Homo economicus—essentially, profit-maximizers whose behavior should be “nudged” in certain directions by laws that appeal to our self-interest. This vision of the person as inherently devoid of empathy feeds a politics of paranoia and mistrust of others. A society with a thin and suspicious understanding of the person will collapse on itself. We must expect courage and compassion from each other, and ourselves. When Aristotle warned against corrupt constitutions, he feared the radical breaking of a shared public life. He described the fundamental threat of corruption as that of the selfishness of rulers. We must renew from within.
Finally, we should use both national and local tools to take on the pinnacle of antidemocratic power: corporate monopolies. Not only are they destroying our food, land, and farmers, but the huge tech companies—the biggest monopolies today—are embedding isolation in every action we take, feeding each of us different content and, increasingly, assigning us different prices and different wages. Megacorporations like UnitedHealthcare are gobbling up independent medical practices and corrupting doctor’s offices by taking decisions away from primary-care providers. Massive monopolies have sucked the soul out of cities and rural areas across America and are driving the epidemic of loneliness and powerlessness.
What does the future require of us if we want to continue to live in it together? Our country is teetering between possibilities. To truly fight corruption, we need to recover democratic power and, with it, democratic responsibility. We cannot renew ourselves unless we build local institutions, learn to love each other through our bitterness, and, instead of asking which Democrat will save us in 2028, ask what the soil needs, and whether we are willing to get blisters on our hands to tend it.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120369.title: Fußball | Tür auf für den Torjäger: Niclas Füllkrug darf wieder ran
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120369.author: Frank Hellmann, Frankfurt am Main
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120369.text:
- Sport
- Fußball
Tür auf für den Torjäger: Niclas Füllkrug darf wieder ran
Bundestrainer Jürgen Klopp beweist mit der Rückholaktion des 33 Jahre alten Mittelstürmers, dass die Form ein wichtiger Gradmesser bleibt.
Vergleichsweise locker hat Jürgen Klopp auf seinem Barhocker gewirkt, als er sich am Donnerstag auf dem DFB-Campus zum Interview in die Umkleidekabine setzte. Fragen stellte nur Pressesprecherin Franziska Wülle für den verbandseigenen TV-Sender und nicht eine Journalistenschar im überfüllten Medienraum. Trotzdem versicherte der Bundestrainer mit den Deutschland-Trikots als Requisite im Rücken, es sei ihm ganz schön schwergefallen, für die letzten Nations-League-Gruppenspiele gegen Serbien in Belgrad (13. November) und gegen die Niederlande in Berlin (16. November) seinen 24-köpfigen Kader zu nominieren, »weil – und das ist eigentlich die gute Nachricht – es wieder mehr Spieler verdient hätten, dabei zu sein. Aber so soll es sein.«
Zugleich bewies der 59-Jährige, dass er nicht dogmatisch vorgeht. Es wimmelt in der Bundesliga seit geraumer Zeit nicht von klassischen Mittelstürmern mit verlässlichen Quoten. Wenn dann einer wie Niclas Füllkrug in Bundesliga und DFB-Pokal in zehn Spielen allein zwölfmal trifft, muss er wieder in den Kreis der Besten zurückkehren. »Er hat unterschiedlichste Tore geschossen. Er hat einen unglaublichen Einfluss bei Werder Bremen«, lobte Klopp.
Obwohl der 33-Jährige in seiner Wohlfühloase an der Weser seinen dritten Frühling erlebt, hatte der Bundestrainer zwischendurch den Eindruck erweckt, eine Rückkehr mache aus Altersgründen keinen Sinn. Ein Missverständnis. »Ich bin jetzt nicht mit all meinen Aussagen, die ich in Halbzeit-Interviews getroffen habe, so glücklich«, räumte der 59-Jährige ein.
Klopp ergänzte, dass er den zuletzt im Juni 2025 in der Nations-League-Finalrunde gegen Frankreich eingesetzten Torjäger nach seinem Auftritt im ZDF-Sportstudio kontaktiert habe. »Es war eine Freude, die Entscheidung zu treffen, und es war auch eine Freude, sie ihm mitzuteilen.« Wäre morgen die Europameisterschaft, würde er »Fülle« sofort mitnehmen, denn: »Manchmal schlägt Form alles andere.«
Sein aktuelles Aufgebot vereint Perspektive mit Pragmatismus. »Wir haben in der Mannschaft einen bunten Mix aus sehr jung und durchaus erfahren dabei.« Zwar fehlen logischerweise viele der Überraschungsgäste aus dem Frühherbst – von Mika Baur bis Bambasé Conté – , aber immer noch sind 13 Akteure dabei, die keine Verantwortung für die WM-Blamage in Nordamerika trugen.
Auffällig, dass der Bundestrainer sich für den November-Doppelpack ein tragfähiges Gerüst zusammengebaut hat, um mit zwei Siegen noch das Nations-League-Viertelfinale im März 2027 zu erreichen. Wäre nebenbei auch wichtig, um in der Qualifikation für die EM 2028 in Großbritannien nicht gegen einen Großen wie Spanien oder Frankreich spielen zu müssen.
Das geht im Tor los, wo »Marc-Andre ter Stegen als Nummer eins in die Spiele geht«. Es gehe auf dieser Schlüsselposition um »große Stabilität«, und der Schlussmann von Ajax Amsterdam bringe nun mal »die meiste Erfahrung« mit. Vertreter sind Alexander Nübel und Jonas Urbig – für Finn Dahmen und Noah Atubolu war daher kein Platz. In der Innenverteidigung sind Jonathan Tah und Nico Schlotterbeck als eingespieltes Gespann gesetzt, als Backup gelten Waldemar Anton, Malick Thiaw und überraschend Finn Jeltsch, von dem Klopp »langfristig« so viel hält, dass er den 20-Jährigen vom VfB Stuttgart gerne mal rechts probieren würde. »Er ist ein sehr dynamischer, schlauer Kerl.«
In der schwarz-rot-goldenen Herzkammer setzt Klopp mit Kapitän Joshua Kimmich, Aleksandar Pavlovic und Tom Bischof auf einen »kleinen Bayern-Block«. Dazu komme mit dem Dortmunder Felix Nmecha eine »Maschine«, wie Klopp sagte: »Er macht ein paar Dinge, wo wir uns wirklich fragen, wo kann das noch hinführen.« In diesem Mannschaftsteil brauche es »Physis mit technischen Fähigkeiten – und ein bisschen Torgefahr wäre auch nicht schlecht.«
Dafür steht Wael Moyha, der als blutjunger Überraschungsgast dazukommt. »Es gibt nicht viele 17-Jährige, die in der Bundesliga spielen, das allein ist schon ein herausragendes Merkmal«, sagte der Bundestrainer, der mit dem Jungspund »drei Gespräche« geführt habe, die alle »top« gewesen seien. Klopp flapsig: »Ich war mit 17 nicht so selbstbewusst, aber ich war auch nicht so gut mit 17.« Man habe sich mit der Familie darauf geeinigt, ihn einfach mal mitzunehmen – »zum Sehen«.
Im Sturm habe er sich für die Freiburger Entdeckung Derry Scherhant und Said El Mala entschieden, weil dieser das Spielfeld auf einer neuen Position in Köln kennenlerne. Der Frankfurter Younes Ebnoutalib habe ihn als »positive Überraschung im ersten Camp überzeugt«.
Ungeachtet der Unruhe um seine Person ist auch Lennart Karl dabei, den Klopp als »Toptalent« pries. Dagegen sind andere Offensivkräfte durchs Rüttelsieb gerauscht. Neben Karim Adeyemi vom FC Barcelona auch Nick Woltemade, der in der WM-Qualifikation noch als Hoffnungsträger galt. Der gebürtige Bremer bekam auch einen Anruf, in dem Klopp dem 24-jährigen sagte, dass der Wechsel zu Juventus Turin sicher nicht verkehrt sei, aber ihm fehle gerade »ein bisschen die Torgefahr«. Ganz im Gegensatz zu Niclas Füllkrug.
Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf
Bei uns muss niemand zahlen, um informiert zu sein. Klingt nach einem schlechten Geschäftsmodell? Ist es auch. Aber uns sind unabhängiger Journalismus und Teilhabe für alle wichtiger als Profit. Journalismus kostet trotzdem Geld: Recherche, Druck und all die Menschen, die ihn machen. Deshalb sind wir auf dich angewiesen. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro.
Spende einmalig oder regelmäßig, jeder Betrag zählt. Damit nd bleibt.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/colunist.title: Permanências e transformações na histórica virada de Lula
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/colunist.author: Observatório das Metrópoles
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/colunist.text:
A virada de Lula no dia 25 de outubro de 2026 reforça uma ideia às vezes esquecida: a política com “P” maiúsculo, ou a grande política, se faz também desafiando probabilidades e tendências consolidadas, em vez de simplesmente se conformar a elas. Agora, é preciso que essa ideia não volte ao esquecimento depois da eleição, mas se torne uma referência para o governo reeleito. Uma leitura atenta dos registros da virada histórica no segundo turno pode contribuir para isso.
Há quase quinze anos, o cientista político André Singer identificou como característica central do lulismo o encontro entre a imagem de um líder político de origem popular, Lula, e uma fração de classe específica, o subproletariado, entendido como um numeroso contingente da população historicamente submetido à extrema pobreza e precariedade das condições de trabalho e moradia. Esse encontro teria sido impulsionado, sobretudo, pelas políticas de combate à miséria e à fome implementadas após a eleição presidencial de 2002, quando a base eleitoral petista ainda apresentava uma composição mais marcadamente de classe média.
O cruzamento dos resultados das duas últimas eleições presidenciais com mais de 150 variáveis e indicadores econômicos, sociais, políticos e ambientais produzidos para os 5.570 municípios brasileiros pelo grupo Dependência, Urbanização e Política nas Cidades (DePoliCi), do INCT Observatório das Metrópoles, reafirma a atualidade da tese de Singer. A análise, desenvolvida com base no relatório de pesquisa “A Urbanização Dependente nos Municípios e Regiões”, que será lançado no dia 12 de novembro no site do INCT Observatório das Metrópoles, mostra que, em 2022, quanto maior era a proporção de trabalhadores de um município com remuneração inferior ao valor da cesta básica calculada pelo Departamento Intersindical de Estatística e Estudos Socioeconômicos (DIEESE), maior tendia a ser o percentual de votos válidos obtidos por Lula. Também há associações positivas entre o voto lulista e a precarização do trabalho (medida pela participação de ocupados sem vínculo formal ou por conta própria), bem como a presença de pessoas pretas, pardas e indígenas na população local. Em sentido inverso, o PIB per capita municipal apresentou associação negativa com o desempenho do candidato petista. Um índice sintético de vulnerabilidade, construído a partir dessas quatro dimensões da desigualdade, também se associou fortemente à votação em Lula, tanto em 2022 quanto em 2026. Essas relações, porém, descrevem padrões territoriais e não permitem inferir como votou cada indivíduo.
Tais clivagens também aparecem na divisão ocupacional. No universo de 14 regiões metropolitanas (Belém, Fortaleza, Recife, Salvador, Belo Horizonte, Vitória, Rio de Janeiro, São Paulo, Campinas, Baixada Santista, Curitiba, Porto Alegre, Goiânia e Distrito Federal), os municípios com maior participação de ocupações do topo da hierarquia profissional, particularmente dirigentes e gerentes, tenderam a registrar proporções maiores de votos nos adversários de Lula. Em contrapartida, os que têm maior presença relativa de trabalhadores em ocupações elementares, de serviços e em parte das atividades manuais tenderam a apresentar melhor desempenho petista. Não se trata de uma divisão homogênea, pois diferentes frações ocupacionais e regiões metropolitanas apresentam exceções e nuances importantes. Mesmo assim, a tendência se confirma também em escalas mais locais, como a dos bairros. No Rio de Janeiro, por exemplo, algumas das maiores favelas, como Rocinha, Vidigal e Complexo do Alemão, estão entre os bairros com maior proporção de votação petista no segundo turno.
Contudo, a permanência dessas clivagens convive com transformações decisivas, que ajudam a compreender as flutuações das preferências eleitorais e as reviravoltas recentes. De um lado, o padrão geral mostrou expressiva estabilidade nas quatro votações realizadas nos primeiros e segundos turnos de 2022 e 2026, como demonstra a Figura 3. A vulnerabilidade, a precarização e a presença de trabalhadores com remuneração extremamente baixa continuaram positivamente associadas à votação lulista; já a integração dos municípios aos circuitos mais internacionalizados de acumulação e o PIB per capita mantiveram associações negativas.
Por outro lado, como explicar uma virada tão expressiva entre os turnos de 2026, inclusive o fato de 213 municípios terem passado da liderança de Flávio Bolsonaro à de Lula como candidato mais votado? A resposta exige olhar para duas mudanças na dinâmica da disputa: o grau de participação da população nas eleições e a ampliação relativa do voto petista em territórios nos quais ele tradicionalmente encontrava maior resistência, conforme já havia sido indicado em outro texto recente.
No contexto de permanência das grandes clivagens de classe, o primeiro fator foi a participação eleitoral. Depois de um primeiro turno relativamente morno em termos de campanha de rua, a reação à possibilidade de vitória de Flávio Bolsonaro foi acompanhada de intensa mobilização petista nas ruas e nas redes. Os resultados são compatíveis com a hipótese de que essa movimentação contribuiu para ampliar o comparecimento às urnas, embora os dados territoriais, isoladamente, não permitam medir seu efeito causal. O segundo turno de 2026 registrou o menor índice de alienação eleitoral (soma das abstenções, dos votos brancos e dos votos nulos em relação ao eleitorado apto) de toda a série das eleições presidenciais iniciada em 2002. Depois de atingir 28,83% em 2018, o indicador recuou para 24,23% em 2022 e chegou a 21,84% em 2026, uma redução de quase sete pontos percentuais em oito anos. Em números absolutos, foram aproximadamente 34,7 milhões de eleitores que deixaram de comparecer às urnas ou optaram por votos brancos e nulos, contra 42,5 milhões em 2018. Trata-se de uma reversão expressiva do crescimento da alienação eleitoral observado em parte importante da série histórica recente.
Essa queda, porém, não foi maior onde Lula é mais forte. Entre os dois turnos de 2026, a abstenção caiu 2,4 pontos percentuais nos municípios menos vulneráveis e 0,6 nos mais vulneráveis, além de ter subido na região Norte. O que mudou em relação a 2022 foi o padrão, já que naquele ano a abstenção aumentou do primeiro para o segundo turno, sobretudo nos municípios mais vulneráveis (coeficiente de 0,40 com o índice de vulnerabilidade), enquanto que em 2026 essa associação diminuiu (0,26), como mostram as Figuras 6 e 7.
O segundo fator, não menos importante, foi a ampliação relativa do voto petista em territórios onde ele é historicamente mais fraco, isto é, nos municípios menos vulneráveis e mais populosos, especialmente no Sudeste. É significativo que os municípios mais vulneráveis, situados nos quatro decís superiores do índice de vulnerabilidade, não tenham alcançado o máximo de votação lulista no segundo turno de 2026, mas no de 2022. A vitória mais recente, portanto, não decorreu simplesmente de um aumento uniforme do apoio nas bases populares. Houve também mudanças nas associações ocupacionais, já que áreas com maior presença de profissionais de nível superior, e sobretudo de técnicos de nível médio e trabalhadores administrativos, apresentaram uma inclinação relativamente mais favorável ao PT do que em 2022, ainda que a clivagem geral de classe tenha permanecido.
Há, entretanto, movimentos na direção contrária que precisam ser considerados. Áreas com maior participação de trabalhadores da agropecuária e de operadores de máquinas passaram a apresentar associações menos favoráveis ao voto lulista, enquanto os territórios com maior presença de dirigentes e gerentes continuaram fortemente refratários ao PT. Além disso, os municípios em que a agropecuária constitui a atividade econômica de maior valor adicionado vêm registrando retrações importantes na proporção do voto em Lula. Essas tendências lembram que a ampliação da coalizão eleitoral não ocorreu de maneira uniforme entre os distintos segmentos da classe trabalhadora e entre as atividades econômicas.
Assim, foi a combinação entre o aumento do comparecimento, com menos abstenção diferencial nos municípios mais vulneráveis do que em 2022, e avanços substantivos da votação petista em territórios menos propensos a essa preferência que ajudou a produzir a virada histórica. A mobilização popular nas ruas e nas redes mostrou a possibilidade de contrariar tendências políticas persistentes, inclusive a expansão da alienação eleitoral, sem que as grandes clivagens sociais do voto tenham desaparecido.
Como ensinou Antonio Gramsci, construir hegemonia exige conquistar apoio e direção política para além dos limites imediatos do próprio grupo social. Resta saber se a condução do novo governo será capaz de transformar a energia eleitoral em uma articulação política mais abrangente, preservando as conquistas voltadas ao subproletariado identificado por Singer, mas dialogando também com outras camadas da classe trabalhadora brasileira, inclusive as vinculadas à agropecuária, onde o apoio petista perdeu intensidade, e à indústria de transformação, onde isso ocorreu no primeiro turno, sem deixar de demarcar as diferenças de interesse que a separam, ou deveriam separar, das classes dominantes. A eleição mostrou que as estruturas sociais condicionam a política, mas não encerram suas possibilidades. O desafio agora é fazer dessa abertura uma orientação duradoura de governo, para além do que Singer chamou de pacto conservador e reformismo fraco.
*Erick Omena é professor do IPPUR/UFRJ e coordenador do Grupo Dependência, Urbanização e Política nas Cidades (DePoliCi), sediado no núcleo Rio de Janeiro do INCT Observatório das Metrópoles.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/5.title: Top US civil rights official resigns
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/5.text:
Top US civil rights official resigns
New Democratic Congress expected to probe Trump Justice Department civil rights office’s handling of Epstein files and ICE killings.
As President Donald Trump’s administration prepares for a flurry of congressional investigations into shootings by immigration agents and the Jeffrey Epstein files, the top official in charge of the United States Department of Justice’s civil rights division has resigned.
US Attorney General Todd Blanche on Thursday confirmed Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon’s departure in a post on social media.
“Today, I accepted the resignation of Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon,” Blanche wrote on X. “She has defended the civil liberties of every American and enforced the law without fear or favor.”
A top Trump ally, Dhillon was confirmed to her role in April 2025 and has overseen a dramatic overhaul of the Justice Department’s civil rights division, which is tasked with enforcing anti-discrimination laws. Hundreds of former Justice Department officials penned a letter last December decrying the “destruction” of the agency division under Trump.
Dhillon is the first high-ranking official to resign from the Trump administration since US Democrats swept both chambers of the US Congress in the country’s pivotal midterm elections on Tuesday.
Democratic congressman Robert Garcia, who will likely become the new chair of the powerful House of Representatives Committee on Oversight and Accountability, pledged on Wednesday to take on four major investigations, including abuses of power by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents and the Epstein files.
Dhillon reportedly told her staff earlier this year that her office, which has typically been charged with investigating law enforcement killings by police officers, would not be looking into the fatal shootings of two US citizens – Renee Good and Alex Pretti – who were gunned down by ICE agents in Minneapolis.
In May, Garcia accused the administration of continuing to shield Trump from scrutiny related to unreleased documents tied to the Epstein investigation
During a closed-door hearing in which Blanche’s predecessor, Pam Bondi, was asked by lawmakers about the case, the California Democrat Garcia alleged Dhillon repeatedly intervened to block questions about the president’s connection to the release of the files.
The Justice Department referred Al Jazeera to Blanche’s social media post when asked when Dhillon submitted her resignation. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.title: On HBO's “The Gilded Age,” Ben Ahlers is New York high society’s man of the hour
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.author: Sonia Rao
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.text:
A few years ago, actor Ben Ahlers came home to his Bushwick apartment building after a night out and heard music playing through a neighbor’s front door. As he got closer, he realized that he recognized the sound of the furiously moving strings: It was the orchestral theme to “The Gilded Age,” in which he plays inventor Jack Trotter. The HBO period series, set in late 19th-century New York City, was Ahlers’ big break.
Ahlers told Gothamist in a recent interview that he hadn’t expected an overlap between Bushwick night owls and people who watch “The Gilded Age.” But that expectation shifted as the soapy drama about New York high society exploded in popularity. With the series now back for a fourth season, Ahlers said he isn’t even surprised anymore by “bald Long Island dads” coming up to him to confess that their wives converted them into fans.
The actor, who played Happy Loman earlier this year in the Broadway revival of “Death of a Salesman,” is adapting to his growing fame at the same time his “Gilded Age” character adjusts to newfound wealth. It wasn’t common for working-class Americans in the late 19th century to rise quickly in rank, and yet that’s exactly happens when Jack, a former footman, makes a small fortune patenting and selling an efficient alarm clock (a feat inspiring legions of “Gilded Age” fans to refer to Ahlers as “Clock Twink” online; more on that later).
“Jack made a lot of money very quickly, and as exciting as that is … a whole new world opens up to him that he’s completely unfamiliar with and alone in,” Ahlers said. “I am hopeful and nervous and excited to watch him navigate this world while trying to keep the lovable playfulness and purity that got him to the table in the first place.”
The money is a miracle to Jack, who uses some of it to buy a furnished townhouse. But in the fourth season, it becomes abundantly clear that he still feels most at home with the servants he once worked with at the Van Rhijn household. He swings by the Van Rhijns’s downstairs kitchen — “Gilded Age” creator Julian Fellowes channels another of his works, “Downton Abbey” with this upstairs/downstairs dynamic — to regale his friends with the tale of how he struggled to eat an artichoke while dining with richer folks.
In real life, Ahlers still doesn’t know how to eat a whole artichoke: “I did the best I could,” he said. Filming the kitchen debrief reminded him of what it felt like to return home to small-town Iowa during his first few years at the University of Michigan, when he was still “fresh off the hog truck.” He was a former high school athlete studying musical theater alongside classmates who had attended performing arts academies, a contrast he described as “both really intimidating and really, really exhilarating.”
Ahlers left Michigan during his senior year, moving to New York to appear in what turned out to be a short-lived NBC drama called “The Village.” He spent time in Los Angeles and Vancouver after the show was canceled, but returned to New York in January 2020 to begin preparing for the supporting role he had just booked on “The Gilded Age.”
Production was set to begin March 3, 2020. That did not happen. When the cast finally regrouped to shoot that fall, with the pandemic raging on, “we were all confused and scared and doubtful, and there was this sort of existential weight,” Ahlers said. Playing Jack, a happy-go-lucky footman chasing a pipe dream, inspired him to keep going. He dove in deep, even taking classes with the Horological Society of New York ahead of the second season to better understand clockmaking. Earlier this year, he co-hosted the society’s gala.
“To be able to step into the world of Jack, who had so much optimism and so much playfulness, reminded me of that part of myself,” he said. “It’s not like I had to tap into a past memory of when I was optimistic. It was as if Jack called me into that space.”
The entire experience of working on “The Gilded Age” has been surreal for Ahlers, who said “if 17-year-old Ben in Iowa was given a glimpse into what I’m doing, he wouldn’t believe it.” And he definitely wouldn’t know how to respond to “Clock Twink.”
As an adult, Ahlers isn’t sure what to make of the cheeky nickname, either. (A “twink” is gay slang for a boyish-looking man with a slender build. It should be noted that, as someone who stands 6-foot-2 and clearly once played high school football, he doesn’t really strike you as a twink in real life.) The actor is flattered by all the attention, of course, but recognizes that a good portion of the fandom — such as the Long Islanders converting their husbands to “Gilded Age” watchers — probably aren’t participating in the “Clock Twink” and “Railroad Daddy” discourse online.
“What’s so difficult about tracking that experience is that so much of the interaction exists on the internet,” Ahlers said. “Depending on what day of the week it is, the internet sometimes feels like the only real thing in the world — and also just this hologram of meaninglessness. It’s very difficult to have a realistic understanding of … how people feel about me apart from the handful engaging with it online.”
It’s not so unlike the uncertainty Jack feels as a newer guest at lavish salons and dinner parties, knowing that he was recently serving people at these very events. Are they truly accepting of his brand new status? Are they gossiping behind his back? In the end, he doesn’t seem to care — he has his inventor brain and the support of his found family.
“To have Jack as the backbone of my career over the last seven years, with all of the volatility and this massive transition that we’re going through as a collective … has been really cool,” Ahlers said. “Jack has this steady, optimistic positivity and an awareness that allows him to roll with the punches. He’s given me more than I’ve given him.”

The Paul Hamlyn Foundation on November 4 named the ten artists and composers who have received the organization’s 2026 Awards for Artists. The honors, presented annually, are England’s largest of their kind, with each winner receiving £75,000 (roughly $101,000). The funding arrives with no strings attached. “It is a privilege each year to reaffirm our commitment to the arts through the giving of Awards for Artists,” said Jane Hamlyn, chair of the visual arts judging panel, in a statement. “Many artists find their creativity diminished when resources are scarce, but we hope these awards can provide the recipients with the freedom they need to grow and develop.”
As has been typical in recent years, the recipients were divided evenly between visual artists and composers. The prevailing artists this year are sculptor Linda Bell, known for her large-scale, interactive works; installation artist Racheal Crowther, who explores issues of care and control; multidisciplinary artist Rory Pilgrim, whose work centers the experience of marginalized populations within a larger political and social framework; multidisciplinary artist Georgina Starr, who investigates the ethereal and the transient; and painter and installation artist Hayley Tompkins, whose work embodies feeling and sendation.
Composers Olivia Chaney, Bushra El-Turk, Charlotte Keeffe, Daudi Matsiko, and Ayanna Witter Johnson round out the cohort.Established in 1994, the awards have gone through several iterations: Since 2007, they have been presented in aid of UK-based artists and composers who are at what the foundation describes as “critical” points in their respective careers: There are no age limits associated with the prizes. The organization to date has distributed nearly £13 million among 377 artists and composers, including Larry Achiampong, Black Obsidian Sound System (B.O.S.S.), Phyllida Barlow, Sonia Boyce, Jeremy Deller, Gustav Metzger, and Yinka Shonibare.

https://www.humanite.fr/politique/auster.title: 5 novembre : quand 1,6 million de manifestants battent le pavé, Matignon n’a que des rustines à proposer
https://www.humanite.fr/politique/auster.author: Stéphane Guérard
https://www.humanite.fr/politique/auster.text:
Sonné par la démonstration de force des syndicats et organisations de jeunesse, le premier ministre a convoqué les organisations patronales et de travailleurs pour parler salaires et pouvoir d’achat, lundi 9 novembre, tout en poursuivant ses coups de rabot austéritaires.
Quand ça ne veut pas… Jeudi 5 novembre, les colères sociales ont battu massivement le pavé partout en France. Ni la tentative de pourrissement des mobilisations lycéennes depuis la rentrée des vacances d’automne, ni les changements de dernière minute des parcours de cortège, ni le déploiement sécuritaire annoncé, Raid et BRI compris, par un ministre de l’Intérieur toujours alarmiste, ni les mesurettes censées soulager le pouvoir d’achat n’y ont rien changé.
Dès la mi-journée, l’exécutif s’est aligné sur le niveau de mobilisation annoncé par la CGT, reconnaissant de fait sa défaite. Finalement, la centrale de Sophie Binet revendique 1,6 million de participants...

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/st.title: Stolen Picasso Prints Found Under Pile of Clothes in French Riviera Apartment
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/st.author: Alex Greenberger
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/st.text:
Six stolen prints by Pablo Picasso have been safely recovered from an apartment in the French Riviera, where, according to investigators, the works were stowed beneath a pile of clothes and toolboxes, not too far from the restaurant from which they were pilfered.
The theft happened almost exactly one month before French investigators found the prints, which regularly hang in the restaurant L’Amandier, located in Mougins, the village where Picasso famously resided at the time of his death in 1973.
At around 2 a.m. on October 1, two men, both wearing gloves and masks, entered the restaurant through a door and stole the prints in under a minute. In the morning, the restaurant’s owner, Matthieu Autant, discovered the works were missing and proceeded alert local authorities, which assigned the task of retrieving the stolen art to officers in nearby Cannes.
La Libre, a Belgian outlet, reported that the prints were worth the equivalent of a little more than $112,000—not much, as far as Picassos go. But, speaking to the French publication Le Monde, lieutenant colonel Guillaume Plaidy said that the works “were not easy works to sell,” all the more so because lacked the know-how required to find a buyer for these works. Instead, these men were “known more for drug and weapons offenses,” Plaidy said.
Still, Plaidy added, “We had to act quickly: Works like these carry a high risk of being resold and never returning to the art market.”
On November 3, 40 gendarmes searched two apartments and found the works in the process. Seven men, all aged between 18 and 30, were subsequently arrested. Those men include three burglars and four accomplices, per Le Monde.
Though the theft of the prints may be relatively minor, it gained notice because it comes at a moment of heightened attention to art theft in Europe. Following the storied Louvre heist of 2025, works have been stolen from institutions ranging from the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer, France, to the Magnani Rocca Foundation, near Parma, Italy.
Within France, the quick recovery of the Picasso prints seemed to inspire hope. Leisa Paoli, head of the Female Artists Museum of Mougins, said, “We are delighted to be able to recover them; I thought they might have already left the country.”
Autant, the owner of L’Amandier, seemed both relieved and a little exasperated. He told the channel France 2, “We may have to rethink the security arrangements.”

https://taz.de/Die-US-Demokraten-nach-de.title: Die US-Demokraten nach den Midterms: Gewonnen, und jetzt?
https://taz.de/Die-US-Demokraten-nach-de.author: Bernd Pickert
https://taz.de/Die-US-Demokraten-nach-de.text:
Die US-Demokraten nach den Midterms: Gewonnen, und jetzt?
Den US-Demokraten steht nach dem Erfolg bei den Midterms ein Richtungskampf bevor: Kompromiss oder Attacke?
Noch ist die Zeit nicht vorbei, in der Social-Media-Feeds von US-Demokraten vor allem aus Videos von Siegesreden vor jubelnden Anhängern oder lustigen Memes bestehen, jedenfalls aber vom Enthusiasmus eines Wahlsiegs geprägt sind, den so selbst die kühnsten Optimist*innen nicht hatten erwarten können.
Aber in den Jubel mischen sich die ersten ernsthaften Diskussionen darüber, wie die demokratische Performance im neuen Kongress eigentlich aussehen soll, der sich am 3. Januar 2027 konstituiert. Und auch, ob die beiden bisherigen Fraktionsführer, Senator Chuck Schumer und der Abgeordnete Hakeem Jeffries, beide aus New York, eigentlich wirklich die richtigen sind, um die neue Macht zu kanalisieren.
Die Gruppe „Indivisible“, bekannt als Organisatoren der großen landesweiten „No Kings“-Proteste, postete schon am Mittwoch auf Bluesky eine Kachel gegen Schumer als neuem Senatsführer. „Gestern haben die Wähler klargestellt, dass sie eine neue Generation demokratischer Kämpfer wollen. Wir brauchen einen Anführer im Senat, der in der Lage ist, diesen Kampf zu führen. Es ist Zeit, eine neue Führung zu wählen“, heißt es in dem Post.
Tatsächlich hat Schumer seit geraumer Zeit den Ärger vieler progressiver demokratischer Anhänger auf sich gezogen. Spätestens, als er im März 2025 dafür sorgte, dass ein republikanischer Übergangshaushalt im Senat auch mit demokratischen Stimmen verabschiedet wurde, galt er in progressiven Kreisen als feige und opportunistisch. Das Gleiche wiederholte sich im November letzten Jahres.
Schlechtere Umfragewerte als Trump
In nationalen Umfragen geben gerade einmal 25 Prozent der Befragten Schumer eine positive Bewertung: Das ist deutlich unter den historisch schlechten Umfragewerten von Präsident Trump.
Dazu kommt: Die Demokratische Partei und die politisch-ideologische Zusammensetzung ihrer gewählten Kandidat*innen haben sich verändert, seit Schumer 1980 erstmals ins Repräsentantenhaus und 1998 in den Senat gewählt wurde. Schumer, Sohn einer jüdischen New Yorker Familie, verstand sich lange öffentlich als Shomer Yisrael, als Schutzengel Israels. Er ist einer jener demokratischen Politiker, deren Wahlkämpfe über Jahrzehnte von der pro-israelischen Lobby-Organisation AIPAC unterstützt wurden. Neu gewählte Senatoren wie Abdul El-Sayed, der Shootingstar aus Michigan, haben Teile ihres Wahlkampfes darauf aufgebaut, eben gerade kein Geld von der AIPAC anzunehmen.
Aber nicht nur ideologische Grundfragen müssen Schumer und Jeffries womöglich neu beantworten. Auch wie die neue Kongressmehrheit taktisch agieren will, steht zur Diskussion. Kooperation mit der Regierung suchen, um etwa eine Erhöhung des Mindestlohnes oder Verbesserungen bei Medicare durchzusetzen, ohne von Trump per Veto gestoppt zu werden – oder kompromisslose Opposition mit Untersuchungsausschüssen bis hin zu Amtsenthebungsverfahren? „Wir können gleichzeitig spazieren gehen und Kaugummi kauen“, zitierte Jeffries nach der Wahl zu dieser Frage eine US-Redensart.
Aber ob das funktioniert in einem Jahr, in dem sich unterschiedlichste Flügel der Partei auf das Präsidentschaftswahljahr 2028 vorbereiten? Spätestens die zweite Jahreshälfte 2027 wird von den bevorstehenden Vorwahlen geprägt sein. Bis ein*e Kandidat*in gefunden ist, hinter dem oder der sich die Partei versammelt, ist die Kongressführung die einzige, die die Demokraten haben. Und das kann ganz schön haarig werden.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: Peru airport officials discover 3,000 tarantulas smuggled inside dirty socks
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Agence France-Presse
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
More than 3,000 tarantulas were seized at an airport in Lima on their way to Germany, Peruvian authorities said.
The spiders were hidden inside dirty socks contained in three suitcases carried by two Germans and a Polish citizen, the National Forestry and Wildlife Service (SERFOR) told Agence France-Presse on Thursday.
They were spotted after agents noticed some unusual wriggling inside the luggage during a routine customs inspection at Jorge Chávez international airport. “We noticed that some of them were moving. There were small ones and large ones,” said Cora Suarez, a SERFOR wildlife control technician.
One tarantula can sell for about €500 ($560) in Europe, Suarez said, meaning the wildlife trafficking scheme would be potentially worth €1.5m for just one trip.
The hidden arachnids, which came from several regions of Peru, were found in varying stages of development, from eggs and hatchlings to adults, Suarez said.
The Europeans accused of smuggling the tarantulas were detained by police specialising in environmental crimes and will face criminal proceedings, SERFOR said.
Illegal wildlife trafficking is a highly lucrative criminal activity that generates around $20bn annually worldwide, according to Interpol.
Such trafficking is among the primary causes of the loss of biodiversity on the planet.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Presidente do Paraguai vai ao Senado se defender de impeachment nesta sexta (6)
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Redação
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
O presidente de direita do Paraguai, Santiago Peña, vai prestar depoimento aos senadores no processo de impeachment contra ele nesta sexta-feira (6), a partir das 10h. Em sessão realizada na noite desta quinta-feira, o Senado recebeu a denúncia contra o mandatário.
Peña é alvo de pedido de impeachment em resposta à crise aberta com o fechamento do Ueno Bank, instituição financeira ligada a ex-sócios comerciais do presidente, que deixou congeladas as economias de centenas de milhares de paraguaios.
O presidente apresentou um pedido de renúncia no início da tarde desta quinta, mas o pedido não foi aceito pela Câmara dos Deputados, cuja sessão de análise foi esvaziada pelo próprio Partido Colorado, ao qual Peña é filiado.
O presidente da Casa, o deputado governista Raúl Latorre, convocou duas sessões seguidas: a primeira para votar a acusação contra Peña e, logo depois, outra para tratar do pedido contra o vice-presidente, Pedro Alliana. O pedido contra Alliana foi arquivado, mas o de Peña foi aceito e encaminhado ao Senado.
Do lado de fora do Congresso paraguaio, centenas de manigfestantes exigem o impeachment de Peña.
No Senado, os parlamentares designados como procuradores votaram pela aceitação integral da denúncia contra o presidente Santiago Peña. O presidente do Casa, Basilio ‘Bachi’ Núñez, determinou a notificação dele e convocou oficialmente uma sessão extraordinária para esta sexta-feira, às 10h.
Nesta sessão, o presidente deverá comparecer perante o plenário do Senado para apresentar sua defesa e submeter as provas de sua inocência. Os próprios senadores vão julgar Peña.
Nas redes sociais, Peña fez uma publicação afirmando que vai comparecer à sessão.
“Diante da continuidade do processo de impeachment, vou comparecer e exercer meu direito à defesa. Farei isso com argumentos e provas, respeitando a Constituição e as instituições da República. Mesmo que já tenham antecipado sua decisão, vou exercer esse direito. Não por uma questão de orgulho pessoal, mas porque prestar contas e dar explicações também é uma responsabilidade perante o povo paraguaio”, escreveu na rede social X.
Entenda
A quebra do banco digital Ueno Bank mergulhou o Paraguai em uma crise financeira e política. Em dois dias, o colapso levou centenas de pessoas às ruas da capital, Assunção, derrubou o presidente do Banco Central do Paraguai (BCP), deixou grandes redes varejistas praticamente sem vendas e fez o Congresso correr para mudar a lei e acelerar a devolução do dinheiro bloqueado dos clientes.
O Ueno tem 2,9 milhões de clientes, cerca de 40% da população paraguaia, e processa perto de 3 milhões de transações por dia. Por ele passam dois terços dos pagamentos eletrônicos das grandes redes de varejo, e a Associação de Importadores e Comerciantes do Paraguai (Asimcopar) já alerta para uma semiparalisação do mercado.
Os manifestantes reivindicam a devolução integral dos depósitos, incluindo os recursos do Instituto de Previdência Social (IPS) e das caixas de aposentadoria aplicados no banco. Os protestos também cobram responsabilidades do presidente Santiago Peña, que foi acionista do grupo controlador do banco até 2025.

https://www.artforum.com/news/georgia-ok.author: Polly Watson
https://www.artforum.com/news/georgia-ok.text:

An early Georgia O’Keeffe work discovered in a closet in Manhattan’s East Village in 2022 is bound for the auction block. O’Keeffe’s Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I, 1930, is estimated to get $3 million at Christie’s November 17 evening sale in New York. The painting is thought to be the first in a series of three depicting New Mexico’s Lobo peak: The second is held by the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, and the third is in a private collection.
Painted in the artist’s typical flat style, in hues of green, tan, and brown, the ten-by-twenty-four-inch canvas depicts the desert hills near O’Keefe’s longtime home, an enduring subject for her. Unknown but for a 1931 photograph and a mention in the appendix of the artist’s catalogue raisonné, the work turned up in the New York apartment of a now-deceased elderly retiree. The woman, a world-ranked bridge master who had traveled widely with the Foreign Service, casually mentioned to her visiting niece that there was an O’Keeffe in the hall closet, whereupon said niece uncovered the work from beneath a pile of fur coats and noted its unmistakable “OK” signature.
The painting was a graduation present, purchased from O’Keeffe’s Manhattan dealer, the Downtown Gallery, in April 1963 for $3,800. It hung in the apartment of its owner until 1980s, when, after noting a visitor player eyeing it a bit too closely, the woman put it back in its original packing crate and placed it in the closet, where it remained until she mentioned it to her niece.
“I wondered, ‘Is there any way I can keep this?’” the niece, identified only as Betsy, told the New York Post. “But once we started exploring what the value of the piece was, I realized that it’s worth more than my house.”
“Rediscoveries are rare in the well-established market for academically researched and highly revered historic American artists,” Tylee Abbott, Christie’s international director, told the Post.
Also rare for most people is the chance to lay hands on a work of this caliber—even for a day.
“For chuckles, I hung it up on the wall of my house for an afternoon,” Betsy told the Post, “just to say I had a Georgia O’Keeffe in my house.”

https://gothamist.com/news/better-days-a.title: Better days ahead for NYC commuters with Democrats in control of Congress, MTA chair says
https://gothamist.com/news/better-days-a.author: Stephen Nessen, Ramsey Khalifeh
https://gothamist.com/news/better-days-a.text:
MTA Chair Janno Lieber said Thursday that he’s optimistic the end of the “anti-city” movement has arrived and that more federal funding for public transportation projects is on the horizon after Democrats won control of Congress in the midterm election.
Since President Donald Trump took office in 2025, his administration has repeatedly withheld funding from New York and the MTA. The Trump administration attempted to shut down congestion pricing, threatened to pull funding for the Second Avenue Subway extension project and took over the redesign of Penn Station.
“Obviously, having a Democratic Congress led by two New Yorkers and with the Senate Appropriations Subcommittee led by (Sen.) Kirsten Gillibrand, we are hopeful that we can do much, much better than that historical short-changing,” Lieber said during a special appearance on WNYC’s On The Way.
He was referring to Rep. Hakeem Jeffries and Sen. Chuck Schumer, who are frontrunners to serve as House speaker and Senate majority leader, respectively.
“I think we have more confidence that the existing projects will be funded, and we would like to now start pursuing money for new big projects,” Lieber said.
“But the bigger issue is is a mandate in Congress right now to stop this anti-city campaign that has been in effect in Congress and in Washington for the last couple of years,” Lieber added.
Lieber will speak about the future of mass transit in New York in a special event at WNYC’s The Greene Space on Nov. 17.
One pool of funding MTA officials are seeking to tap is the Surface Transportation Reauthorization bill, which expired in September. Some $256 million went to the MTA through former President Joe Biden’s infrastructure bill. Lieber said he’ll be looking to the Democratic Congress to reauthorize that money to fund vital accessibility signal upgrade projects.
The MTA has other major projects in the works that will require further federal funding, like the extension of the Second Avenue Subway west across 125th Street and building the Interborough Express, a light rail line connecting Brooklyn and Queens together that is only half-funded.
Tom Wright, the president of the Regional Plan Association, said with new pro-transit New York representatives headed to Washington, securing funding for bigger projects should be a priority.
“If through the new Congress there is money for mass transit, the IBX ought to be at the front of the line because it is such an excellent project,” Wright said. “And I think that that's what our delegation needs to be focused on.”

https://citylimits.org/it-reflects-every.title: ‘It Reflects Everyone’: The Country’s Tallest Mural Spans the Length of This NYCHA Building
https://citylimits.org/it-reflects-every.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/it-reflects-every.text:
Share This Article
Towering at 307 feet, Dominican artist Angurria completed the piece in just 22 days, spending up to nine hours a day on a scaffold lift. “I grew up in Los Alcarrizos painting the people of my neighborhood,” he told City Limits. “In the South Bronx I found the same pride, the same strength, the same families.”
When Nestor Omar García, a Dominican artist widely known as “Angurria,” began painting a gargantuan mural—covering all 29 stories of a public housing development in the South Bronx—one of the first faces to come to life on the empty canvas was a young child, wearing headphones and perched atop a woman’s shoulders.
Tanya Pedler, president of the New York City Housing Authority (NYCHA) development’s resident association, who has a 7-year-old son who is autistic, told City Limits it’s her favorite part of the piece.
“We have a lot of children in this neighborhood that suffer from sensory processing disorders,” she said, “and I wanted to make sure our special needs community was represented.”
Towering at 307 feet tall, the mural, titled “Un MAR de Gente / From Every Shore,” is the largest in the country, according to organizers—and Angurria completed it in just 22 days. 
He used a scaffold elevator—often spending eight to nine hours on the lift each day—and help from two assistants to paint the southwest facing side of Morrisania Air Rights, a public housing development built in 1980 using air rights over Metro-North rail tracks in the South Bronx.
The complex is home to some 1,950 residents, who played a role in deciding what the record-breaking mural should include. “I hope that it reflects everyone who not only lives in the Bronx, but all these children who are here today,” Angurria said at the .
One of the only challenges, Angurria said, was the wind. “When it’s windy, the lift moves maybe two or three meters,” he said. “That was very difficult, but only for us. Everyone was so kind here.”
“This was an incredible experience for me,” Angurria told City Limits. “I grew up in Los Alcarrizos painting the people of my neighborhood, and in the South Bronx I found the same pride, the same strength, the same families.”
ArtBridge, a New York City-based nonprofit that transforms urban infrastructure like construction scaffolding into canvases for public art, commissioned Angurria to complete the mural.
They worked with another nonprofit group called Public Housing Community Fund (PHCF), created by the NYCHA in 2016 to facilitate design, construction and resident input for public projects that are funded by private donors. The M·A·C VIVA GLAM Fund awarded ArtBridge a $165,000 grant to support the mural.
Pedler said she reached out to the PHCF about a year ago, saying, “we needed to have a mural here, because the walls were a little hideous.”
“They connected us to ArtBridge, and this whole process was quite quick,” Pedler told City Limits. “We started talking about this last winter, and it’s completed before the year is out.”
A Jamaican immigrant who was raised in Queens after her family immigrated in 1989, Pedler also spent time in the city’s foster care system. She described how her past experiences with instability now inspire her to seek improvements for her neighbors, or help others who are struggling—with being a teenage mom, for instance, or transitioning to their first home in public housing, like she once did.
She’d previously collaborated with PHCF on other improvements at Morrisania Air Rights, like when she called on the city in 2022 to renovate the development’s playground, which several residents said was too dangerous for children to use because of unmanageable drug and criminal activity.
Former Mayor Eric Adams visited the playground in 2022, and it’s since received about $1 million in investments, largely through federal funding secured by Congressman Ritchie Torres in 2024. About $750,000 of that is being used to install a sensory playground and garden at the public housing development.
“This is a welcome sign that no matter who you are, or where you’re from, or what language you speak, or what God you worship, you are welcome right here in the Boogie Down Bronx,” Torres said at a ribbon cutting for the mural on Oct. 27.
After ArtBridge commissioned the mural, Pedler said she went to events in the borough, hung up flyers and shared information on social media about ways residents could influence details in the design, including identities that were important to them. The nonprofits, along with Angurria, then held workshops with residents to gather insight on themes and imagery they’d like to see in the art.
“The residents came out, young and old,” Pedler said. “They wanted to make sure that their voices were heard, and I’m grateful for them because we wouldn’t have this beautiful masterpiece if it wasn’t for them.”
Pedler also noted a particular request from 13-year-old resident Hawa Batchilly, who asked for more representation of Black and brown Muslim girls in their community. Of the finished mural, Batchilly said “it shows me that Muslim girls are all allowed to be here.”
“Children deserve beauty, representation, and a chance to believe that something extraordinary can happen where they live,” Pedler said.
Pedler’s message for other public housing residents, and especially other tenant association leaders, is “to dream and dream big.”
“Our residents look up and see stories that reflect our mothers, grandmothers, and children,” Pedler said. “Whether your roots are American, Jamaican, Honduran, Mexican, Dominican, Panamanian, African or whatsoever else, you belong in this story.”
