https://hyperallergic.com/its-time-to-ta.title: It’s Time to Talk About Classism in the Art World
https://hyperallergic.com/its-time-to-ta.author: Melissa Holbrook Pierson
https://hyperallergic.com/its-time-to-ta.text:
It’s Time to Talk About Classism in the Art World
In his memoiristic new book, photographer Mark Alice Durant weaves his personal experiences into a larger rebuke of the economic inequality that governs the art world.
For something that determines so much — about the art we make, the art we get to see or not, the art that may never be made at all — the issue of class is rarely discussed in the art world. Breaking the silence, artist and writer Mark Alice Durant speaks up in his memoir-cum-rebuke, Confessions of a Working Class Artist (2026). It reads both like a Künstlerroman and an updated version of the seminal guide for the aspiring artist, Rainer Maria Rilke’s Letters to a Young Poet (1929), for our dystopian neo-Gilded Age.
For Durant, also the author of the moving photographic memoir Summer of the White Fox, and After (2024) and publisher at Saint Lucy Books, which released both titles, choosing to become an artist was an act of self-exile. He writes that he psychically uprooted himself from the working-class precincts of Boston where he grew up as well as from his extended family, with the exception of his mother, unusually open-minded and supportive of her son. Perhaps she saw herself in his youthful gift of a framed reproduction of Jules Breton’s 1884 painting of a field worker, “The Song of the Lark.” After deciding on this path, Durant writes, “I could never return home on some level.”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Ex-husband of Brent Sikkema sentenced to life in prison over murder-for-hire killing
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Gabriella Angeleti
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The former husband of the late New York art dealer Brent Sikkema, Daniel Sikkema, aged 56, has been sentenced to life imprisonment for organising Sikkema’s murder in 2024. A federal court in Manhattan handed down the sentence on Wednesday (4 November).
In May 2026, after a two-week trial, Daniel Sikkema was convicted on charges of murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire and conspiracy to commit murder in a foreign country. In addition to life imprisonment, he was sentenced to five years of supervised release.
Brent Sikkema, who was aged 75 at the time of his murder, was found stabbed to death at his home in the Jardim Botânico neighbourhood of Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, on 15 January 2024. According to prosecutors, Daniel Sikkema began planning the murder in 2023 in the midst of his divorce from the dealer, with whom he had been married for around 15 years and shared a son.
As the couple’s divorce proceedings became more acrimonious, Daniel Sikkema, who holds dual US and Cuban citizenship, recruited the Cuban national, Alejandro Triana Prevez, as the hitman. On the night of the murder, Prevez entered the late Sikkema’s residence and stabbed him 18 times. Prevez subsequently received $5,000 from Daniel Sikkema and was promised further payments.
Prosecutors said Daniel Sikkema made 11 payments to Prevez and Prevez’s partner in Cuba, using the identities of unwitting friends, employees and family members to conceal the transactions. Prevez was arrested by Brazilian authorities four days after the murder at a gas station on the side of the highway in the state of Minas Gerais, around 600 miles from Rio de Janeiro. He had stolen cash and jewellery in his possession. His case is being handled separately by a Brazilian court.
Brent Sikkema was born in 1948 in Morrison, Illinois, and studied at the San Francisco Art Institute before beginning his career. In the early 1990s, he founded Wooster Gardens in SoHo, moving the gallery to Chelsea in 1999. The business became Sikkema Jenkins & Co in 2003 following the involvement of Michael Jenkins and Meg Malloy.
The gallery is now known as Sikkema Malloy Jenkins and continues to operate in Chelsea. It has championed the work of artists including Kara Walker, Vik Muniz, Sheila Hicks, Jeffrey Gibson and Arturo Herrera. A representative for Sikkema Malloy Jenkins told The Art Newspaper that the gallery will not be providing any statement regarding the conviction or sentencing.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/sw.title: Sweden Returns Benin Bronze Trove to Nigeria, Indigenous Remains to Bolivia
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/sw.author: Tessa Solomon
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/sw.text:
The Swedish government is set to return 40 sacred artifacts from the Kingdom of Benin to Nigeria, marking one of the largest repatriations of the so-called Benin Bronzes.
Nigerian media report that the artworks are expected to be received by a delegation from the Benin Palace in Lagos today, a development that Oba Ewuare II, the monarch of Benin, described as years in the making. Since ascending to the throne, Ewuare has advocated fiercely for the return of bronze sculptures, ceremonial objects, and ivory carvings—collectively known as the Benin Bronzes—from museum and private collections worldwide, with considerable success.
“We have been trying, through my grandfather’s efforts, to bring back our artifacts,” Ewuare said in a statement. “My grandfather succeeded, my father succeeded more, and I think now history is obvious to everybody. We are doing our best to triple and triple all those efforts of our forefathers.”
The Kingdom of Benin was looted of roughly 5,000 royal and religious objects in 1897 by British forces on a punitive expedition through what is now Nigeria. Dispersed through illicit channels among museums and private collections worldwide, the artifacts have become emblematic of efforts by formerly colonized countries to reclaim their cultural heritage, as well as the broader—and often contentious—debate over the ethics of ethnographic collections. In recent years, public sympathies have seemingly shifted toward formerly colonized countries, prompting a wave of repatriations. Museums across the United States, as well as institutions in the Netherlands, Germany, and Switzerland, have returned Benin Bronzes and other ethnographic objects to their countries of origin.
The Swedish government also announced today that it will return 77 objects belonging to the Kallawaya people, including human remains, to the Archaeological Museum in La Paz, Bolivia. The remains were taken out of Bolivia illegally and remained in the collection of the World Culture Museum until 2023, when the Swedish government announced their transfer of ownership.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/05/abdu.title: Abdul El-Sayed Won His Senate Seat With a Mandate on Palestine. Can He Deliver?
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/05/abdu.author: Jonah Valdez
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/05/abdu.text:
One senator out of the 100 who will fill the upper chamber of the 120th Congress was elected to his seat on a loud campaign promise to end U.S. complicity in Israel’s genocide in Gaza.
Abdul El-Sayed will walk into a newfound Democratic majority after animating his base with pro-Palestine pledges seldom heard from a U.S. Senate contender. As a first-term senator, he’ll lack seniority on the committees to which he’s assigned. And although his critiques of the U.S. relationship with Israel have proven overwhelmingly popular in public opinion surveys and among voters at the polls, the same can’t be said for most of his soon-to-be colleagues.
“It’s going to be a fight,” said Beth Miller, political advocacy director for Jewish Voice for Peace Action, which supported El-Sayed’s campaign. “The Democratic establishment, when it’s in control, has not taken measures in support of Palestine in the past. And so this is about making sure that now they finally start listening to what the overwhelming majority of their bases say.”
El-Sayed’s run marked the first time the Jewish-led, anti-Zionist group backed a Senate campaign. Pro-Palestine lobbying groups like JVP Action have been pushing for legislation to block weapons transfers to Israel for years, aligning themselves with a small but growing number of left-leaning House members. The group helped author the Block the Bombs Act, introduced by Delia Ramirez, D-Ill., which netted 82 co-sponsors and became a pro-Palestine litmus test in some Democratic primary campaigns.
Building consensus around a single bill in the Senate is harder, but the upper chamber offers stronger levers to pull. Senators can force votes called Joint Resolutions of Disapproval that would block foreign security assistance, such as weapons sales to Israel. Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., has exercised this option repeatedly throughout the genocide in Gaza to try and block the sale of certain bombs, firearms, and other military equipment to Israel. While his resolutions failed in the Republican-controlled Senate, the most recent ones drew support from wide majorities of Democrats — soon to be the party in power.
Yet with the looming threat that Democrats might actually be able to pass legislation, El-Sayed would find himself under pressure from the likely Senate majority leader, Chuck Schumer, who has long maintained the support of the pro-Israel lobby, to fall in line with party priorities.
“The question is, ‘Who does he want to be?’ Does he want to be someone like Bernie, who is willing to sometimes stand up to leadership?” said Hamid Bendaas, communications director for the Institute for Middle East Understanding Policy Project, which also backed El-Sayed’s run. “It’s hard to do that as a freshman and someone who’s just getting in there.”
Bendaas expressed confidence that the Michigan senator would be a champion of pro-Palestine legislation, but he noted that El-Sayed would have to balance his priorities, especially after running a campaign focused on economic populism and providing universal healthcare through Medicare for All.
Shifting Winds
There is a tension revealed by the dilemma facing Sen.-elect El-Sayed: While a growing share of Americans — and an overwhelming majority of Democrats — disapprove of the U.S. spending billions of dollars on aid to Israel, voters’ clear No. 1 concern in the 2026 election cycle was the cost of living and their own economic precarity.
Some pundits have encouraged pro-Palestine candidates like El-Sayed to put their anti-genocide principles aside, arguing that more moderate Democrats performed better on Tuesday night. They compare El-Sayed’s 7-percentage-point defeat of Mike Rogers to James Talarico’s 12-point win over Ken Paxton in Texas — and some have already asked Talarico to defy his new colleague.
But on the campaign trail, El-Sayed often connected the issues of a high cost of living and outsized U.S. spending on aid to Israel. “We ought to be spending our money here, to build schools and provide healthcare and child care here, rather than sending our money abroad to a foreign government that’s done terrible things with our money,” he said in a September interview with Bloomberg TV. El-Sayed’s approach made him the target of nearly $40 million in outside spending from the super PAC for the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, which supported widespread anti-Arab and Islamophobic attacks and accusations of antisemitism in an attempt to keep a vocal critic of Israel out of the Senate.
“None of it mattered,” said Yousef Munayyer, a senior fellow at the Arab Center Washington D.C. who likened the gravity of El-Sayed’s win to that of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. “And this is not the Commie Corridor. This is a swing state. A lot of taboos here have been shattered, and people are going to learn from this and be emboldened now.”
In addition to bringing joint resolutions to block future weapons transfers — like the Trump administration’s planned sale of $2.8 billion in 2,000-pound bombs to Israel — El-Sayed could introduce resolutions citing the Foreign Assistance Act; Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., used one to demand a State Department report on Israeli detention of Palestinian children and Israeli military and settler killings of American citizens in the West Bank. He would also be able to introduce amendments to the Pentagon’s annual spending bill that carves out billions of dollars in joint U.S.–Israel weapons research. (The Senate is currently sitting on this year’s $1.15 trillion National Defense Authorization Act, which would even more deeply enmesh Israeli technology within the Pentagon’s programs and supply chain.)
Munayyer, the former head of the U.S. Campaign for Palestinian Rights, said that despite the uncertainty over whether moderate Democrats will be willing to link arms with progressives next session, El-Sayed’s win creates an environment ripe for accountability over Israel.
“You have a climate now where there’s going to be a lot less intimidation felt by people who had previously been hesitant to speak out on these issues because they thought it was political suicide,” he said.
Even Republicans are beginning to feel the shifting winds. On the morning of Election Day, President Donald Trump made a surprise announcement on Fox News that the U.S. would halt the annual $4 billion in military aid to Israel. The move would only cut off one path for Israel to get weapons from the U.S. — still allowing direct weapons sales to Israel from U.S. companies and weapons development and sharing with the Pentagon — and Trump said it was made in agreement with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who had been previewing it for months. Tactically, Trump said the goal was to take a “talking point” away from Democrats. He cited El-Sayed by name.
While ballots were still being counted on Wednesday, Vice President JD Vance, an expected 2028 presidential contender, posted on X an early post-mortem of the massive GOP losses across the country. He wrote that the party could bring back “voters who had abandoned us” if they “End the war” in Iran and “Change our relationship to Israel.”
Such recognition from the Trump White House is new territory for U.S. politics, Munayyer said.
“We are about to witness, in my view, something we have never seen before in American politics,” Munayyer said. “A robust debate in the presidential primary campaigns in both parties, where the question of the U.S.-Israel relationship is going to come up time and again. That’s never happened before, and it’s gonna be seismic.”
The question is whether Democrats will stay on top of the wave. If Schumer, a staunch supporter of Israel, remains in charge of the Senate majority, he’ll have power over appointments to key committees — giving him the opportunity to curb the influence of a figure like El-Sayed.
“I don’t think that Democrats want to have a messy fight about this stuff when the base is largely in agreement on it,” Munayyer said. But while Senate Democrats have evolved on the issue of Israel and Palestine — even Sanders expressed far weaker critiques of the Israeli state a few years ago — it’s one thing to be the dissenting party when you’re in the minority. It’s another to wield serious power.
Constant Pressure
El-Sayed is perhaps the most vocal supporter of Palestinian rights of any U.S. senator elected since James Abourezk of South Dakota, who in the late 1970s became the first Arab American to serve in the Senate. Abourezk frequently advocated for a Palestinian state and was an early critic of the pro-Israel lobby. After his time in Congress, he founded the American-Arab Anti-Discrimination Committee.
El-Sayed, now the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate, frequently referred to Israel on the campaign trail as an “ethnostate” and said he opposes any nation that organizes its government by ethnicity and religion. In an appearance on ABC News, El-Sayed argued Israel was not a U.S. ally. Two days before the election, he spent a large portion of his sit-down with “60 Minutes” calling for Palestinians’ right of self-determination and repudiated the question of whether Israel had a right to exist. In his victory speech, he criticized attempts by pro-Israel critics to conflate advocacy for Palestinians rights as “hate.”
Even so, in the lead-up to the general election, El-Sayed started being subjected to pressure from some on the pro-Palestine left. Critics chastised his decision to stump with former Vice President Kamala Harris over her complicity in the Biden administration’s support for the genocide in Gaza. Similar ire was directed at his partnership with former President Barack Obama, who has yet to name or condemn the genocide and governed over U.S. wars in the Middle East that saw the United States kill thousands of civilians.
Advocates for Palestinian rights, however, told The Intercept they recognized the utility in El-Sayed’s campaigning with the highest-profile members of the Democratic Party, and they counted it as a success that he earned their support. But they said they were not pinning all their hopes on a single individual.
On top of all the other calcified interests and long-standing political biases that shape the U.S. Senate, there’s the influence of the sprawling U.S. weapons industry, with manufacturing giants like Lockheed Martin and Boeing lobbying for their interests and showering politicians in campaign cash. That industry wants to keep profiting off the genocide in Gaza, said JVP Action’s Miller, and El-Sayed alone is not enough to stop that.
“This is not gonna be that one man comes into the Senate and changes everything,” she said. “This is that one person has been elected with a mandate that has demonstrated where the masses of people are at on this issue, and now we have to keep fighting harder than ever before.”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

https://taz.de/Debatte-im-Bundestag/!622.author: Anna Lehmann
https://taz.de/Debatte-im-Bundestag/!622.text:
Debatte im Bundestag : Pflegesystem bleibt Pflegefall
Im Bundestag wurde in erster Lesung über die Pflegereform debattiert. Klar wurde wieder, woran es im System mangelt: an Solidarität mit den Pflegenden.
I st doch schön, wenn im männlich geprägten Bundestag mal eine Debatte geführt wird, bei der alle Redner:innen, bis auf zwei, weiblich sind. So wie an diesem Donnerstag. Bezeichnend war allerdings, dass es dabei um die Pflegereform ging, die der Bundestag in erster Lesung debattierte. Das spricht für sich und zeigt, woran es im Pflegesystem mangelt: an Solidarität, und zwar unter den Geschlechtern, aber auch in der Gesellschaft.
Der jetzt in den Bundestag eingebrachte Gesetzentwurf gleicht diese Unwucht leider nicht aus. Pflege ist ein Thema, das fast alle Mitglieder unserer alternden Gesellschaft in irgendeiner Form betrifft oder betreffen wird – sei es, weil sie Angehörige haben, die darauf angewiesen sind, oder weil sie selbst betroffen sind. Doch die Hauptlast der Arbeit tragen Frauen, sie sind das Rückgrat des Pflegesystems, in den Heimen, bei den Diensten, aber auch zu Hause. Dort werden 86 Prozent der Pflegebedürftigen umsorgt und meist sind es die Mütter und Töchter, die für die pflegebedürftigen Kinder oder Eltern einkaufen, sie waschen oder die Windeln wechseln.
Auch die finanzielle Last ist ungleich verteilt, und zwar zu Ungunsten der gesetzlich Versicherten. In der gesetzlichen Pflegeversicherung kommen für eine Leistungsempfängerin aktuell rund 12 Versicherte auf, in der privaten sind es hingegen 22.
taz debatte
Die taz ist eine unabhängige, linke und meinungsstarke Tageszeitung. In unseren Kommentaren, Essays und Debattentexten streiten wir seit der Gründung der taz im Jahr 1979. Oft können und wollen wir uns nicht auf eine Meinung einigen. Deshalb finden sich hier teils komplett gegenläufige Positionen – allesamt Teil des sehr breiten linken Meinungsspektrums.
Trotz kräftigen Zuschusses aus dem Bundeshaushalt reicht das Geld schon derzeit nicht aus, und die Lücke wird in den kommenden Jahren wachsen. Es ist deshalb grundsätzlich geboten, die Pflege zu reformieren und finanziell nachhaltig aufzustellen. Doch allein mit Einsparungen, wie sie die Regierung plant, ist es nicht getan. Diese könnten die Pflege sogar verteuern. Denn sie treffen eben vor allem jene, die dafür sorgen, dass das System überhaupt noch funktioniert. Wenn die Verhinderungspflege gestrichen wird, die es den Angehörigen ermöglicht, mal eine Auszeit zu nehmen, dann steigt der Druck auf sie. Entweder beantragen die Kinder dann doch einen Heimplatz für den dementen Vater – was insgesamt teurer ist – oder sie werden selbst zu Pflegefällen.
Auch den Entlastungsbeitrag zu streichen, der Menschen im Pflegegrad I ermöglicht, selbstständig zu bleiben, wird nach hinten losgehen. Was bringt es der betagten Seniorin, wenn der Putzhelfer nicht mehr kommt, aber die Pflegekasse einen Berater schickt, der ihr erläutert, wie sie ihre Fenster wieder selbst putzt und ihr Tipps zum Erklimmen der Leiter gibt?
Wenn die Koalition die Pflege stärken will, muss sie jene stärken, die hilfebedürftige Menschen unterstützen oder pflegen. Umsonst ist das nicht. Ein Ausgleich zwischen privater und gesetzlicher Pflegeversicherung ist deshalb geboten. Und eine Debatte in der Gesellschaft, wie viel uns Solidarität und Zusammenhalt wert sind.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. So viele unterstützen freiwillig und regelmäßig. Noch nicht dabei? Werden Sie jetzt Teil der Community! Jetzt unterstützen

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120369.title: Wahre Freunde | Tiger und Bär machen weiter
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120369.author: Christof Meueler
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120369.text:
- Kultur
- Wahre Freunde
Tiger und Bär machen weiter
Fürchtet euch nicht! Janosch ist gestorben, doch seine beiden wichtigsten Figuren sind unsterblich freundlich.
Vor langer Zeit, vor fast einem Vierteljahrhundert, sang die Hamburger Band Blumfeld ein schönes Lied: »Alles macht weiter«. Es war eine Weiterentwicklung eines noch älteren Gedichts des Kölner Schriftstellers Rolf-Dieter Brinkmann. Blumfeld sangen: »Alles macht weiter / die Zeit und ihr Garten / der Baum vor dem Fenster / das Hoffen und Warten (…) / die Einsamkeit in der Menge / die glücklichen Stunden / Phantasien und Pläne / Planten un Blomen / Enten und Schwäne …«
Man müsste es nun ergänzen um »Kleiner Tiger und Kleiner Bär«, die wichtigsten Helden aus den Kinderbüchern von Janosch, der eigentlich Horst Eckert hieß. Denn die beiden machen auf jeden Fall weiter, auch wenn ihr Autor an diesem Dienstag gestorben ist; er wurde 95 Jahre alt. Das Weitermachen in der Fantasie schaffen nur die wenigsten literarischen Figuren. »›Jawohl‹, sagte der kleine Bär, ›ich bin stark wie ein Bär und du bist stark wie ein Tiger. Das reicht‹«, heißt es im Trickfilm ihrer bekanntesten Geschichte »Oh, wie schön ist Panama«.
Und einmal mehr irrt Kulturstaatsminister Wolfram Weimer, als er verkündete: »Mit Horst Eckert verlieren wir alle auch ein Stück Kindheitsgeschichte.« Wir haben nichts verloren, denn Kleiner Tiger und Kleiner Bär machen ja weiter. Der Trick ist, dass sie keine Angst haben und sehr freundlich, friedlich und gemütlich sind. Auch aus dem Grund, weil ihr Autor von seinem Vater regelmäßig verdroschen wurde. Und wer das jemals erlebt hat, will das nicht mehr sehen oder fühlen. Deshalb ziehen die beiden furchtlos durch die Landschaft. Das berühmteste Zitat lautet: »›Wie gut‹, sagte der kleine Tiger, ›wenn man einen Freund hat, der ein Floß bauen kann. Dann braucht man sich vor nichts zu fürchten.‹«
Sie wollen zu Fuß nach Panama, aber niemand kann ihnen sagen, wie man da richtig hinkommt, und so laufen sie im Kreis und freuen sich, als sie wieder zu Hause sind. Auf dem Sofa ist es auch sehr schön. Jeden Tag fängt der Kleine Bär Fische und der Kleine Tiger sammelt im Wald Pilze. Der Kleine Bär brät den Fisch mit Salz, Pfeffer, Zitrone und Zwiebeln – eigentlich täglich. Variante: Geschmorte Pilze. Dazu gibt es Wasser, das hier »Gänsewein« genannt wird. Nur als der Kleine Tiger krank ist, darf er sich etwas wünschen: Forellen mit Mandelkernsoße und Semmelbröseln. Dazu fehlen aber die Zutaten, also gibt es Kraftbrühe mit Petersilie.
Es ist diese lässige Laxheit, die die Janosch-Bücher auszeichnet, sie sind meilenweit entfernt von der heutigen Leistungsoptimierung in Kindergarten und Grundschule, wo die Kinder immerzu etwas lernen sollen, um die anderen neoliberalistisch zu übertrumpfen. Tiger und Bär aber sind souverän-solidarische Kumpels. Sind sie vielleicht queere Pioniere, so wie Ernie und Bert? Wenn der Bär angelt, fühlt sich der Tiger einsam. Und der Bär wird eifersüchtig, als der Tiger mit dem Kleinen Schweinchen abhängt und sogar zu ihm zieht. Doch sie können das gemeinsam lösen. Ja, sie sind voll die Lieben. Und Blumfeld singen: »Alles macht weiter wie bisher / die Zeit vergeht und steht doch still / die Vögel ziehen übers Meer / und der Wind weht, wohin er will.«
Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf
Bei uns muss niemand zahlen, um informiert zu sein. Klingt nach einem schlechten Geschäftsmodell? Ist es auch. Aber uns sind unabhängiger Journalismus und Teilhabe für alle wichtiger als Profit. Journalismus kostet trotzdem Geld: Recherche, Druck und all die Menschen, die ihn machen. Deshalb sind wir auf dich angewiesen. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro.
Spende einmalig oder regelmäßig, jeder Betrag zählt. Damit nd bleibt.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Maya Yang
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Donald Trump signed a proclamation on Thursday that he says will prevent future administrations from changing his design of the Oval Office and Cabinet Room, spaces which he declared as national monuments that should be preserved.
In the days since his party suffered historic defeats in the midterm elections, the president has seemingly turned his attention to the many renovation projects he has begun across the nation’s capital. Sitting behind the Resolute Desk on Thursday, Trump declared the Oval Office a “national monument”.
“I’m going to be signing a document which will make them into a landmark for the ages,” he told reporters in the gold-covered Oval Office.
According to the president, the proclamation would ensure the West Wing rooms would not be “touched by anybody, destroyed, ripped down by stupid people, in order to build something in a slightly different shape”.
“I just thought it was very important that nobody be allowed to come and take it down and try and do something with it,” he said.
“Every once in a while they’ll look and they’ll say, oh, maybe what we’ll do is we’ll put some glass up that’s a little bit better or something, and I say no, you’re not going to do anything. We’re going to leave this as it is,” he continued.
“If anyone ever decides to come and start knocking down walls, you’ll call me wherever I may be, and I will come back here and I will make sure it never happens.”
Since returning to office, Trump has embarked on a series of White House “beautification” projects, most notably the demolition of the East Wing to make way for a $600m ballroom, as well the building of a permanent granite helipad on the South Lawn.
Speaking to reporters from the Oval Office, the president defended his wider renovation work at the White House, saying the building’s exterior had suffered from years of deterioration. He pointed to cracked windows, damaged stonework and broken decorative features, saying he had paid for repairs and hired skilled workers to restore them.
“When you looked at that wall one year ago, it was badly damaged from years of service,” he said, adding that exterior columns had also been in “horrible shape”.
On the desk next to where he signed the proclamation was a red baseball cap emblazoned with the word “Veto” – an explicit reminder of his threat to block the legislative priorities and bills passed by the new Democratic-controlled Congress next year.
Democrats made significant gains in several traditionally Republican states where Trump had previously won, including Texas, Kansas, South Carolina and Iowa, by campaigning on issues including affordability and tackling corruption, while also securing control of Congress.
Trump’s opulent redesign of the Oval Office has drawn criticism, including from former president Barack Obama, who recently joked that “he’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory. Just gold everywhere.”
Obama’s remark prompted a coordinated response from the White House, with treasury secretary Scott Bessent appearing to hit back by dining at a Cheesecake Factory.
In a final appeal ahead of the midterm elections, Trump held a press conference highlighting the delayed results of his $14m renovation of the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool, while blaming Joe Biden for the algae that had accumulated in its waters.
“This was in the Biden era … Look, it’s not an easy thing. The algae is brutal. It forms easily. All you saw was dirt and filth and paper and everything else for years,” Trump said on Monday.
Two days later, as the scale of his party’s staggering losses came into focus, Trump led a media tour of the White House Ballroom construction site, where he marveled at the renovations to come.
“The whole thing is a miracle,” he said.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Do Paraguai ao Brasil: como falta de regulação em bancos digitais deixa mais pobres em risco
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: José Bernardes
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
A crise política e financeira no Paraguai — que deixou metade da população do país sem acesso a cerca de US$ 850 milhões em recursos públicos e fundos previdenciários — aconteceu devido a fraudes de um banco digital, o Ueno. O episódio guarda semelhanças com o escândalo do Banco Master no Brasil. Pressionado, o presidente Santiago Peña, que sofre um processo de impeachment, tentou renunciar. Peña foi acionista do grupo controlador do Ueno até março de 2025.
Ao Conexão BdF, da Rádio Brasil de Fato, a economista Marilane Teixeira, professora e pesquisadora do Centro de Estudos Sindicais e de Economia do Trabalho (Cesit) do Instituto de Economia da Unicamp, pondera que, diante do cenário, há uma oportunidade para repensar os modelos de bancarização atuais. “[Os bancos digitais] ampliam a sua presença em um contexto em que oferecem muitas facilidades. Portanto, é fácil captar a sociedade, a opinião pública, principalmente as pessoas mais simples, que estão, às vezes, mais expostas a algum nível de vulnerabilidade, oferecendo menores taxas”, explica.
Essa expansão, continua Teixeira, se dá em um ambiente de pouca regulação. “Muitas vezes, você abre uma conta sem nenhum tipo de burocracia. Oferecem rendimentos que, depois, objetivamente não têm lastro, que não se sustentam. E há pouca fiscalização sobre a atuação desses bancos”, destaca.
A economista destaca que, tanto no caso do Paraguai, como no Brasil com o Banco Master e o Will Bank, as principais vítimas são pessoas mais pobres, que dependem desses recursos e se sustentam com suas economias. “É um momento para repensar um pouco como esses sistemas operam e ampliar o nível de regulação, de controle e de fiscalização. E aí o Congresso brasileiro tem um papel muito importante”, ressalta.
Para ela, o momento também exige retomar o debate sobre a importância da atuação do Banco Central nesses casos. “O BC tem obrigação de atuar para garantir transparência e fiscalização das operações que são feitas por essas instituições”, resume.
Para ouvir e assistir
O jornal Conexão BdF vai ao ar em duas edições, de segunda a sexta-feira: a primeira às 12h e a segunda às 17h, na Rádio Brasil de Fato, 98.9 FM na Grande São Paulo, com transmissão simultânea também pelo YouTube do Brasil de Fato.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/6.title: Turkiye’s parliament ratifies Mecca defence agreement
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/6.text:
Turkiye’s parliament ratifies Mecca defence agreement
Parliament’s approval lays the groundwork for further Turkish involvement in Saudi Arabia’s conflict with the Houthis.
Turkiye’s parliament has ratified a defence pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan that includes a collective defence clause, committing NATO’s second-largest military to the group’s aid in case of attack.
The ratification on Thursday comes as Riyadh continues to face attacks by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis.
Turkiye first signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement in August and sent it to parliament for ratification last month.
Article 1 of a bill approving the pact was adopted by the Turkish parliament on Wednesday.
But afterwards, Deputy Parliament Speaker Celal Adan adjourned the session until Thursday afternoon, the Anadolu news agency reported.
After parliament returned to session, lawmakers continued to debate the other articles in the pact.
The agreement ultimately passed with 279 votes in favour and 119 against, with 398 of the chamber’s 592 lawmakers taking part in the vote.
The pact contains 16 articles, according to a document submitted to the Turkish parliament, seen by the Reuters news agency.
In Article 1 of the accord, the signatories shall use “all necessary means” to eliminate threats to one another’s territorial integrity. Article 1 can be invoked in case of an attack on any member state.
Once the first article is invoked, the document lays out provisions for what follows.
“In the event one of the parties is subjected to an armed attack or military aggression by another country or group of countries, the parties shall immediately provide assistance to the party under attack, utilising the full range of mutual assistance measures available to them,” says Article 2 of the pact.
This key clause mirrors Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty, the document that established the NATO military alliance. NATO’s Article 5 establishes that an attack on one member is treated as an attack on all.
Given that Turkiye is a member of both NATO and the Mecca pact, critics have raised questions about whether the country’s government might face a conflict of interest in allocating its military resources.
Turkish officials, however, have dismissed such concerns as unfounded.
Other articles in the Mecca pact concern a mutual agreement to increase defence industry cooperation and military coordination, with the aim of deterring threats.
Those articles, in part, commit member states to conducting joint training, pursuing technological innovation and sharing logistics and intelligence resources.
The draft approved by Turkish lawmakers commits member countries to the pact for 10 years, after which point they may withdraw.
It also leaves open the possibility of other countries joining, with the approval of the pact’s existing members. Syria’s government has already expressed interest.
Despite Thursday’s parliamentary ratification, it is not a foregone conclusion that Turkish troops would be deployed to Saudi Arabia amid the Houthi attacks.
Experts say any Turkish troop deployment would also require other legislative processes.
Turkiye’s Defence Minister Yasar Guler said in October that the scope of potential support for Saudi Arabia would be determined after ratification.
“We absolutely do not foresee entering into any conflict with the Houthis,” Turkish media reported Guler as saying. Instead, Turkish support “would be to strengthen deterrence”.
Tensions between Saudi Arabia and Yemen had abated somewhat following a 2022 ceasefire. But the Houthis have escalated their attacks on Saudi Arabia in recent months, notably launching a series of deadly strikes on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh.
The region also remains embroiled in the US-Israel war on Iran, which has contributed to cross-border tensions.
On Thursday, Saudi Arabia announced it had intercepted a drone in the region of Medina. Riyadh has accused the Houthis several times of targeting Mecca and Medina, two holy cities in Islam, an accusation the Iran-backed group systematically rejects.

Just two months after Metropolitan Museum of Art’s Costume Institute canceled its planned spring 2027 John Galliano show in response to a firestorm of criticism, the New York institution has set tongues wagging with the announcement of that show’s replacement. Titled “extraORDINARY: Fashion and the Poetics of the Everyday,” the group exhibition will feature familiar garments such as puffer jackets and jeans, and humble materials including Bubble Wrap and paper, all reimagined as high fashion.
The new exhibition opens May 9, 2027 days after the museum’s annual Met Gala fundraiser, and slots into the space originally reserved for the Galliano show. That exhibition was scrapped after the museum received pushback from donors and others over the designer’s past antisemitic and anti-Asian comments. Andrew Bolton, the curator in charge of the Costume Institute, told the New York Times there had been no plan B in place at the time of the cancellation, and that the new show was meant to follow on from this year’s exhibition, “Costume Art.” Among the garments expected to go on view are Marc Jacobs’s 1990s grunge collection for Perry Ellis, and the Calvin Klein jeans worn by Brooke Shields in her infamous 1980 ad for the brand.
Anna Wintour, the global editorial director of Vogue and Met board member who typically chairs the Met Gala, was nowhere mentioned as an architect of the exhibition. Wintour had championed Galliano, known for his boundary-pushing, highly feminine designs. Page Six reports that she is expected to helm the 2027 fundraiser, as usual.
News of the replacement show was greeted with considerably less fanfare than that of Galliano’s planned exhibition.
“If you think you know your everyday outfit of T-shirt and jeans, just wait ’til you see it in the Met!” chirped Artnet News’s Min Chen with more than a hint of sarcasm, while Artnews’s Alex Greenberger characterized it flatly as “unlikely to rile up anybody.”
The Costume Institute’s annual exhibition has historically been the theme for the Met Gala, with attendees dressing to impress. With “extraORDINARY: Fashion,” the museum has sparked a question that has likely not arisen before: “So, is everyone going to wear jeans to the Met Gala now?” queried Cosmopolitan.

Entre craintes et espoirs, le cortège parisien a envoyé avec force le message du nécessaire rassemblement à gauche lors de la manifestation du 5 novembre contre la vie chère.
Virginie, la cinquantaine, est auxiliaire de puériculture dans une crèche associative à Paris. Ces derniers samedis, elle les a tous passés avec les lycéens. Elle a respiré du gaz lacrymogène. S’est fait confisquer ses lunettes de piscine. À cru perdre son compagnon dans une charge policière.

https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.title: Bowling, burgers and civilian housing: Life on the Fort Hamilton Army installation
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.author: James Ramsay
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.text:
This column originally appeared in the Looped In NYC newsletter. Sign up here.
Back in the spring, when people across the city were making summer vacation plans and debating where to find the best beach along a commuter rail line, I started hearing murmurs in my neck of southern Brooklyn about one specific priority: Everyone was jockeying for a seasonal membership at the pool club on the Fort Hamilton Army installation.
We didn’t bite — we’re a beach family — but the idea of getting a little R&R on a military compound happened to be a familiar thrill. I grew up about 10 miles south of a major Marine Corps base in Southern California, and my hockey coach, an active-duty sergeant, used to bring us on base for parties on their beach, which was essentially empty.
So the “Looped In” team decided last week to cross through the gates of Fort Hamilton — passports in hand — to see what else a civilian can get up to on base, and the answer is: a lot, starting with renting a home.
“We have approximately 212 leases, and of that, probably 40% are what we call ‘waterfall’ residents,” said Tony Mercante, the administrator in charge of the privatized housing on the installation.
“Waterfall residents” — cool code name — refers to the civilians who live on base, and at rates that are pretty competitive compared to the city’s median rent.
For $3,800 a month, Mercante said, you can get a 1,700-square-foot three-bedroom garden apartment, complete with a washer/dryer hookup, a dishwasher, a garbage disposal, most utilities included and one parking spot.
“This is a very idyllic installation,” he added. “When you come through those gates, we basically have no crime. It's a tiny, self-contained community where a lot of people know each other.”
“Idyllic” is a more-or-less fair descriptor. Walking around Fort Hamilton, a 176-acre rolling plot at the foot of the Verrazzano Bridge, feels like being on a Hollywood backlot version of an American suburb. The trees are tall and mature, the roads are windy, the SUVs actually obey the speed limit. There’s a chapel, a Post Office, a gas station and a Burger King.
But “self-contained” isn’t the same thing as “trapped.”
Garrison Command Sgt. Major Eric Riding, who moved to Fort Hamilton about a year ago from Fort Sam Houston in Texas, said the access to the city has been incredible.
“You walk out about a block and a half, you're on the [R train],” Riding said. “I think the public transportation in this city is the best I've ever seen, and I've been all over.” (He said he’s going with his family to see the Rockettes this Christmas; the R train can get them right there!)
Susan Blair, the chief of public affairs for Fort Hamilton, told us the installation’s relatively small size — and its location within the largest city in the country — means it actually relies on local civilians to keep it up and running.
“When you go to a base like Fort Bragg or Fort Hood, the entire surrounding community almost relies on the base — the base supports a lot of the economy. Where it's almost the inverse here,” she said.
And the outside community has plenty of ways to support the base’s economy, hence the private apartments, the pool club, the clubhouse bar (where Thursdays at 4 p.m. are reportedly bumpin'), the wedding and events venue space, the Harbor Defense Museum and not least, the bowling alley. (Civilians looking to visit the installation unescorted are required to fill out background check forms and submit them in-person or via fax 24-48 hours prior to visits.)
Stephen Ramosa, who lives next door in Bensonhurst, said he started working at the Fort Hamilton Bowling Center about a year ago and sees a mix of civilian bowlers and servicemembers and their families.
“ We have a senior league Tuesday mornings. That's the one that I run, and they're pretty chill,” he said. “They're pretty old, and they still bowl better than me.”
Things we didn’t see on our tour: tanks, humvees, helicopters, firearms or any kind of weaponry that wasn’t a historical artifact. Blair said that Fort Hamilton was used as a staging ground for law enforcement after 9/11, but generally, much of its significance now is related to its history.
“One of the unique things about Fort Hamilton is it's one of two bases where a Revolutionary War battle was actually fought,” Blair said.
In August of 1776, British troops landed on the beach outside what’s now Fort Hamilton and kicked off one of the largest battles of the war, one that ended with General George Washington retreating up to Manhattan.
“We did not win that one,” Blair said. “But we won the big thing.”

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/tr.title: Trump Convenes Final Review for Triumphal Arch, Seeks Immediate Start on Construction
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/tr.author: Tessa Solomon
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/tr.text:
President Donald Trump’s planned 250-foot-tall triumphal arch could win approval as soon as Thursday, after he bulldozed a mountain of opposition to secure a final review by a federal commission. Approval would clear the way for construction to begin immediately, though a federal judge could still block the project, as some on Capitol Hill hope.
Washington, D.C., media reported that the Trump-allied National Capital Planning Commission began reviewing plans for the arch on Thursday afternoon, just two days after Republicans lost control of the Senate and the House of Representatives in seismic midterm elections. The commission is expected to approve the plans following lengthy public testimony. Meanwhile, the project’s opponents have called on the federal courts to halt it before construction can begin.
“The Court should not allow this lawless project to evade scrutiny,” Brian Schwalb and Jay Jones, the attorneys general of D.C. and Virginia, respectively, wrote in a joint court filing on Wednesday, as reported by the Washington Post.
The structure would rise at Memorial Circle, between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery, to a height that critics say would cast shadows over the surrounding memorial landscape at various times of day. In recent weeks, the president has reimagined the project as a “military complex,” complete with a sniper’s nest.
Trump first announced plans for the triumphal arch more than a year ago, presenting it as a necessary tribute to the nation’s 250th anniversary. A project of this magnitude would traditionally require congressional approval, which the president has not sought. D.C. lawmakers, historic preservationists, and veterans’ groups argue that the project has been illegally advanced and threatens the site’s solemn character.
In a lawsuit filed last month, the Arlington County Board argued that the arch would “directly obstruct[ing] the line of sight between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery that was deliberately created to symbolize the nation’s post-Civil War reunification.”
The Trump administration maintains that the arch is authorized by century-old plans approved by Congress to commemorate the nation’s reunification after the Civil War. Critics, however, have pointed out that the lawmakers’ plans called for a pair of columns, not a triumphal arch of the kind the president has likened to France’s Arc de Triomphe, “but better, more beautiful actually, much more beautiful.”
Mark Paoletta, a White House official who was appointed commission chairman in August, reportedly said on Thursday that the empty space at Memorial Circle “dishonors our veterans and leaves a key monumental gateway to Arlington that Congress authorized uncompleted.” He added that it was a “national disgrace” that such a landmark was not already standing, praising the president’s “historic vision.”
The Arlington County Board’s lawsuit, which names the National Park Service, as a defendant, accuses the administration and its official of failing to consider the arch’s potential risks to regional flight paths and its impact on emergency services.
“Using the Arch to store large stockpiles of ammunition and as a staging point for drones and snipers, so close to commuters and tourists, will dramatically worsen these public-safety harms and the risk of accidents,” the lawsuit warns.

https://taz.de/Schlecht-gefuellte-Gasspe.title: Schlecht gefüllte Gasspeicher: Die Naivität hat die Seiten gewechselt
https://taz.de/Schlecht-gefuellte-Gasspe.author: Patrick Graichen
https://taz.de/Schlecht-gefuellte-Gasspe.text:
Schlecht gefüllte Gasspeicher: Die Naivität hat die Seiten gewechselt
In der Bonner Republik galten Grüne und Linke, die auf Erneuerbare setzten, als naiv. Angesichts knapper Gasvorräte sind es nun die Konservativen.
E s ist November, es wird zusehends nasskalt, und Sankt Martin steht vor der Tür. Während für Eltern mit kleinen Kindern jetzt die Saison der Laternenumzüge beginnt, startet energiewirtschaftlich eine andere: die Saison des Gas-Ausspeicherns. Leider haben wir da ein Problem: Die deutschen Gasspeicher sind nur zu 60 Prozent gefüllt – so niedrig wie noch nie zu dieser Jahreszeit. Noch dazu hat der Gaspreis an der Börse die Marke von 100 Euro durchbrochen – wie zuletzt Ende 2022. Es wird also ein teurer Winter, und falls es im Januar richtig kalt wird, kann es an einzelnen Tagen sogar knapp werden mit dem Gas.
Man fragt sich, wie das passieren konnte: innerhalb von vier Jahren die zweite Energiepreiskrise? Und obendrein nur halb volle Speicher?!? Es ist, als ob der Kanzler und die zuständige Ministerin im März 2026, nach Trumps Angriff auf den Iran, die Augen verschlossen hätten vor der Realität. Statt sich der Lehren von 2022 zu besinnen, die Gasspeicher zu befüllen und Alternativen zu teurem Gas und Öl voranzutreiben, wurde das Gegenteil getan – auf den Gasmarkt vertraut, die Wärmepumpenförderung gekürzt und die Erneuerbaren ausgebremst.
Bei der Ursachenforschung für dieses schwer erklärliche Verhalten landet man bei der Identitätskrise der deutschen Konservativen. Der ehemalige Zeit-Chefredakteur Roger de Weck hat den kulturkämpferischen Impuls in seinem gerade erschienenen Band „Glanz und Elend der Konservativen“ als Kernproblem der heutigen Konservativen beschrieben. Ich will dem noch eine Facette hinzufügen: eine neue geo- und energiepolitische Naivität.
Kolumne Energie für alle
Jede*r braucht Energie. Der Umstieg auf Sonne, Wind und Co. kann sie klimafreundlicher, demokratischer und billiger machen. Doch die fossile Lobby kämpft hartnäckig ums Überleben. Wie Energiepolitik funktioniert, erklärt hier regelmäßig Patrick Graichen. Er war Wirtschaftsstaatssekretär unter Robert Habeck und Mitgründer des Thinktanks Agora Energiewende. Heute ist er Berater, Aufsichtsrat und Blogger.
Das war früher anders. In meiner Jugend – lang ist’s her, es waren die 1980er Jahre in der Bonner Republik und Helmut Kohl war der ewige Kanzler – war es jedenfalls so, dass wir, die grün und links tickende Jugend, als die Naiven galten. Wir würden das mit der Geopolitik nicht verstehen und vor den Bedrohungen durch „den Russen“ die Augen verschließen. Zudem seien wir mit unseren Träumereien von grünen Technologien weltfremd, mit Solar- und Windenergie könne man keine Industrienation versorgen.
Konservative träumen von der Kernfusion
Heute sind die Rollen vertauscht: Erst war es die Gasabhängigkeit von Putin, dann die von Trump – in beiden Fällen versicherten Konservative, dass man sich keine Sorgen machen müsse. Bis dann die Gaspreise explodierten. Das magische Denken gilt auch für die Energietechnologien: Während Wind- und Solarenergie inzwischen weltweit über 80 Prozent der neu zugebauten Energieträger ausmachen, träumen deutsche Konservative von neuen, sündhaft teuren Atomkraftwerken oder gar Fusionsreaktoren. Zudem glauben sie, mit dem Aus vom Verbrenner-Aus im Jahr 2035(!) die deutsche Autoindustrie zu retten, während gleichzeitig das E-Auto in Europa und China seinen Siegeszug antritt.
Die Naivität, so scheint es, hat die Seiten gewechselt: Die Weltfremden versammeln sich jetzt bei FAZ und Welt, und Sie, liebe taz-Leser:innen, sind die neuen Realisten… erstaunlich das alles, wie so vieles in diesen Zeiten!
Leider hilft diese Erkenntnis für den Winter nur bedingt. Schauen Sie deshalb schon mal nach den warmen Pullis. Und wenn Sie oder Ihre Freunde im Keller eine Öl- oder Gasheizung haben: Jetzt ist der richtige Zeitpunkt, sich Angebote für eine Wärmepumpe einzuholen und den KfW-Antrag einzureichen – schon im Februar sinken die Fördersätze wieder. In jedem Fall: Bleiben Sie stabil im grauen November!
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. So viele unterstützen freiwillig und regelmäßig. Noch nicht dabei? Werden Sie jetzt Teil der Community! Jetzt unterstützen

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120369.title: Pflegereform | Korrekturen unverzichtbar
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120369.author: Ulrike Henning
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120369.text:
- Kommentare
- Pflegereform
Korrekturen unverzichtbar
Das Pflegeneuordnungsgesetz bringt absehbar keine Entlastung für die Familien und auch nicht mehr Wahlmöglichkeiten. Im Gegenteil. Ein Kommentar
Immerhin wurde in Sachen Pflegefinanzierung eingesehen, dass Lückenstopferei mit Darlehen vom Bund keine nachhaltige Idee ist. Die Rückzahlung soll also laut dem Pflegeneuordnungsgesetz (PNOG) erst ab 2035 erfolgen. Aber dieser Aufschub löst keines der Probleme in der Versorgung wirklich. Vielmehr schafft das Gesetz neue Probleme. Nun wird etwa von der CDU eingewandt, dass im parlamentarischen Verfahren noch nachgebessert werden soll.
Aber eine Lawine von hektischen Reaktionen ist längst losgetreten: Pflegebedürftige und solche in spe drängeln sich um Begutachtungstermine noch in diesem Jahr, damit sie 2027 unter Bestandsschutz fallen. Noch gravierender dürfte sein, wenn mit Blick auf Kündigungsfristen schon jetzt ambulante Dienste Personal abbauen, weil ab Januar einiges nicht mehr finanziert wird. Denn auch wenn das Gesetz noch nachgebessert werden sollte, in Kraft treten wird es am 1. Januar. Übergangsfristen scheinen unvermeidlich.
Sicher ist, dass der jetzt vorliegende Gesetzentwurf die häusliche Pflege erst einmal nicht stärken wird. Und das, obwohl überall herumgetutet wird, dass die Angehörigen der Pflegedienst der Nation seien. Die Versorgung dürfte komplexer und für Pflegebedürftige noch unverständlicher werden. Was unter diesen Vorzeichen von der sinnvollen Idee für mehr Prävention übrig bleibt, ist die große Frage.
Nicht übersehen werden darf ein weiterer Skandal. Erneut und immer noch halten sich Bund und Länder bei den Finanzfragen raus: Weder ist die Rückzahlung von Pandemiekosten in Milliardenhöhe an die Versicherung vorgesehen, noch steht die Übernahme der Heim-Investitionskosten durch die Länder auf der Tagesordnung.
Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf
Bei uns muss niemand zahlen, um informiert zu sein. Klingt nach einem schlechten Geschäftsmodell? Ist es auch. Aber uns sind unabhängiger Journalismus und Teilhabe für alle wichtiger als Profit. https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Alabama, Florida and Indiana carry out executions on same day
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Guardian staff and agency
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Alabama, Florida and Indiana all carried out executions on Thursday in an unusual instance of three states administering the death penalty on the same day.
In a record-tying 19th execution of the year, Florida executed Jesse Guardado via a three-drug lethal injection. Guardado had pleaded guilty to fatally stabbing a 75-year-old woman inside her Walton county home in 2004 before stealing her jewelry box, $80 and other valuables to buy drugs. The woman had helped him get a job and housing.
Hours earlier, Indiana executed a man for killing two children in a house fire in 2010. And in Alabama, a man died by injection Thursday evening for his conviction in a fatal home robbery.
The death penalty in the US has faced renewed scrutiny since the September failed execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee, although courts have rejected efforts to halt other executions after she survived two massive doses of pentobarbital.
Thursday’s executions were taking place the same day California’s governor, Gavin Newsom, announced he would commute all 548 death sentences in his state, saying that he believed “state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values”.
Newsom’s announcement was a sharp contrast with Florida, where outgoing Republican governor Ron DeSantis has made aggressive use of the death penalty like few other governors. His state has carried out more than half of the 34 executions so far this year in the US.
It is the second time since August that three states were set to carry out executions on a single day, although it remains unusual. Prior to this year, the last time it happened was 2010.
In Indiana on Thursday, Jeffrey Weisheit, 50, was pronounced dead at 12.45am at the state prison in Michigan City, said Noelle Russell, spokesperson at the state’s department of correction.
She said he had no final words. He had acknowledged killing his girlfriend’s two children in a house fire in the Evansville area in 2010 but had hoped that governor Mike Braun would grant clemency and change his sentence to life in prison. Braun declined.
In Alabama, Michael Taylor died by lethal injection. In 1991, when he was 19, he beat two people, aged 83 and 79, to death with a metal bar during a robbery in their home in Gadsden.
Death penalty opponents had urged Alabama’s Republican governor, Kay Ivey, to reduce Taylor’s sentence to life in prison, but she declined.
Esther Brown of Project Hope to Abolish the Death Penalty said: “If the state kills Michael, it is not the 19-year-old who made the worst mistake of his life whom it kills. But the mature, well-respected, God-fearing man sitting in that cell today.”
The state went forward with plans to execute Taylor, 54, by lethal injection after a judge declared a nitrogen gas method unconstitutional. His attorneys objected to the last-minute switch to lethal injection since he selected nitrogen gas as his method several years ago, but a judge ruled against Taylor.
Alabama executed murderer Kenneth Smith in 2024 by nitrogen asphyxiation, in an episode that witnesses found excruciating, after previously failing to succeed in its attempt to kill him using lethal injection.
Meanwhile, in Indiana earlier on Thursday, lawyers failed to persuade the state governor to allow Weisheit to undergo brain scans to assess a history of head injuries and mental health problems. They had asked for a life sentence.
Weisheit’s last objection centered on the state’s planned use of lethal drugs purchased from a pharmacy that is facing a disciplinary hearing next week in front of the Indiana pharmacy board, the state regulatory agency.
The execution provided “long-awaited justice for Alyssa Lynch and her brother Caleb, two innocent children whose lives were stolen in an act of unspeakable cruelty”, Indiana attorney general Todd Rokita said.
The Associated Press contributed reporting

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: ‘Refém da taxa de juros’: para economista, mercado cobra austeridade mas lucra com a dívida
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: José Bernardes
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
Pressionado por setores do mercado financeiro, o governo Lula pode anunciar algum modelo de ajuste fiscal. O ministro da Fazenda, Dario Durigan, reuniu-se com o presidente reeleito e, em seguida, declarou que “não há fórmula mágica” para o equilíbrio das contas públicas e que o governo vai conseguir equilibrar compromissos fiscais e de campanha.
Segundo Durigan, eles não discutiram medidas específicas. “Como a gente está dizendo em avançar, ter superávit nos próximos anos, estamos necessariamente falando em reforçar as regras vigentes hoje de modo que a gente garanta a valorização de políticas públicas de maneira sustentável”, afirmou.
A economista Marilane Teixeira, professora e pesquisadora do Centro de Estudos Sindicais e de Economia do Trabalho (Cesit) do Instituto de Economia da Unicamp, avalia que a ideia de que há um gasto excessivo desconsidera o arcabouço fiscal criado em 2023. “As despesas reais, descontando a inflação, não podem superar 70% das receitas. Você já vem fazendo uma política de austeridade, você não está ampliando, você está vinculando os gastos à receita”, explica ao Conexão BdF, da Rádio Brasil de Fato.
O ajuste fiscal, destaca a professora, foi o que mais contribuiu para a polarização do primeiro para o segundo turno, justamente porque o plano de Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) falava em cortes drásticos, que afetariam programas sociais. “Existe um problema central que é fazer o ajuste fiscal sem mexer em alguns pressupostos, como taxa de juros, interesses do sistema financeiro, etc”, pondera.
Segundo a economista, não é possível “mexer no gasto porque isso pode gerar recessão na economia. Isso pode resultar em um problema muito maior”. Marilane Teixeira ressalta que os juros são o problema fundamental atual dessa balança de interesses. “A gente tem praticamente 52% da dívida pública a uma remuneração com taxas flutuantes, a Selic, por exemplo. Ou seja, do ponto de vista do sistema financeiro, é uma hipocrisia eles cobrarem política de austeridade, quando são eles os maiores beneficiados pelas altas taxas de juros”, critica.
Teixeira aponta que é exatamente nesse contexto que se dá o artigo de André Lara Rezende, um dos responsáveis pelo Plano Real. “A proposta que o Lara fez foi o seguinte: ‘Vamos desindexar, vamos definir um teto para remuneração desses papéis da dívida pública.’ E aí houve reação. É claro que isso não é uma coisa fácil de fazer de forma abrupta. Mas, sim, de uma forma progressiva”, pontua. “O governo poderia renegociar a dívida em condições mais favoráveis e não ficaria refém do mercado financeiro”, afirma.
Para ouvir e assistir
O jornal Conexão BdF vai ao ar em duas edições, de segunda a sexta-feira: a primeira às 12h e a segunda às 17h, na Rádio Brasil de Fato, 98.9 FM na Grande São Paulo, com transmissão simultânea também pelo YouTube do Brasil de Fato.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/6.title: Trump met Russian envoy after he appeared with Melania Trump and Ukrainians
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/6.text:
Trump met Russian envoy after he appeared with Melania Trump and Ukrainians
Trump again said a major Russia-Ukraine deal is ‘very close’, but gave no specifics.
US President Donald Trump has said that a deal between Russia and Ukraine may be imminent, following a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin’s special envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, at the White House.
“I think we’re going to be very close to settling Russia-Ukraine,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office on Thursday, while declining to disclose details of his conversation with Dmitriev.
“There’s going to be an agreement. It’s going to be a big agreement, and it’s going to involve more than Ukraine,” Trump said, adding that the effort could include “all of Europe”.
Trump has frequently predicted that an agreement to end Europe’s deadliest conflict since World War II was close. Negotiations have, however, picked up in recent weeks.
Trump said he did not meet the Ukrainian delegation on Thursday.
The meeting between the US president and Dmitriev came after a diplomatic gathering hosted by First Lady Melania Trump, which brought Russian and Ukrainian representatives together to mark and build on the localised six-day truce she helped broker in the southern Ukrainian city of Oleshky in October. The US president did not attend the event.
The temporary ceasefire ran from October 27 to November 1 and allowed for the evacuation of nearly 800 civilians from the besieged, Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in Ukraine’s Kherson region, as well as the delivery of critical food and medical supplies.
Senior officials from both countries attended on Thursday, including Dmitriev; Yana Lantratova, Russia’s human rights commissioner; David Arakhamia, leader of the Servant of the People party in Ukraine’s parliament; and Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine’s parliamentary human rights commissioner.
Melania Trump also spoke at the event, which the White House described as “the first time in American history that a First Lady has personally brought representatives of two nations at war to the White House for diplomacy”.
“Together, we can create something more enduring than a temporary ceasefire,” she said, urging both sides to see the humanitarian truce in Oleshky “as a spark in a world of darkness”.
The first lady presented Putin’s and Zelenskyy’s representatives with large white envelopes and asked them to deliver her personal letters to each leader. Dmitriev presented her with a painting by an 11-year-old girl, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy sent her the Order of Princess Olga, a Ukrainian award recognising her role in the ceasefire.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/pa.title: Paris Court Orders Sotheby’s to Return Nazi-Looted Pissarro Painting to Jewish Heirs
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/pa.author: Brian Boucher
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/pa.text:
A Paris court has ordered the restitution of a painting by Camille Pissarro, allegedly seized by the Nazis during World War II, to the descendants of Jewish banker and art collector Salomon Flavian, reports Le Figaro. A group of his heirs sued Sotheby’s in Paris in September, saying they were improperly left out of an agreement struck with other members of their family
The case concerns the French Impressionist’s 1902 canvas Darse de pêche et bassin Duquesne, Dieppe, après-midi ensoleillée (Fishing dock and Duquesne basin, Dieppe, sunny afternoon), showing the port city in western France.
Sotheby’s London sold the painting in 2024 for £1.2 million ($1.5 million at the time). The auctioneer indicated that the work was being offered “pursuant to a settlement between the current owner and heirs of Salomon Flavian,” whose collection the Nazis seized in Paris in 1941. The house’s lawyers maintained in court that the heirs’ consent was gained through Mondex Corporation, which specializes in the recovery of art and other assets looted during World War II, reported the Art Newspaper. But seven plaintiffs maintained in court in September that only two relatives, Gilles and Nicholas Flavian, had signed the agreement and that the rest had not been consulted, per the newspaper.
In its Thursday decision, the court nullified all sales since the initial seizure of the painting, and ordered the return of the work. It concluded that the Flavian family established that Salomon had owned the painting, that it had been confiscated by the Germans, and that he had taken steps to recover his assets after the war. The court ordered Sotheby’s to inform the family of the identity of the buyer in the 2024 sale, or be fined €1,000 ($1,123) per day thereafter, reports Le Figaro, noting that the judgment applies immediately, even in the event of an appeal.
In an email to ARTnews, Mondex Corporation consultant James Palmer said that an appeal will be filed “forthwith.” Palmer argued that the archives of dealer Paul Rosenberg and the 1939 Pissarro catalogue raisonné “both clearly identify [British artist and collector] Edward Le Bas as the owner of the painting from 1939 to the early 1950s.” This means the painting could not have been seized from Flavian during the 1940s, he says.
“Of great importance is the fact that France currently lacks a formal restitution framework, which disadvantages both the state and claimants,” he added, contrasting France with existing adjudication bodies in the UK, Germany, Austria, Switzerland, and the Netherlands, which, he said, “operate on a crucial general principle: that the benefit of the doubt is presumed in the claimant’s favor unless there is evidence to the contrary.”
Regarding Le Bas’s ownership, he continued, “These crucial facts were not commented upon by the court in its decision and can therefore be presumed to have been given no significant consideration, which is a flaw in the judicial assessment of the case. We are confident that when the vast amount of complex provenance research evidence is properly understood and considered that the court of appeal will reach a different conclusion.”

https://taz.de/Klimaberichterstattung-in.title: Klimaberichterstattung in der ARD: Wenn niemand die Klimasau sieht
https://taz.de/Klimaberichterstattung-in.author: Nick Reimer
https://taz.de/Klimaberichterstattung-in.text:
Klimaberichterstattung in der ARD: Wenn niemand die Klimasau sieht
Die ARD lehnt einen Imagefilm ab. Etwa weil sie darin schlecht wegkommt? Der Anteil ihrer Berichterstattung über das Klimaproblem sank zuletzt.
Filmpremiere im Rosa-Luxemburg-Gymnasium in Berlin-Pankow: „Wir schauen hin“ heißt der Streifen, in dem der Schauspieler Matthias Matschke die personifizierte Klimasau spielt. Ein bisschen Überschwemmung hier, ein bisschen Feuer da – und die Bienen gibt es auch nicht mehr, denn jetzt gibt es Artensterben. Vielleicht 250 Schüler sind an diesem Donnerstagvormittag zur Premiere gekommen, und die erleben, wie die Klimasau Matschke wütet. Weil sie ja kann, wie Matschke sagt: „Im Alltag oder in den Medien, da komm ich ja kaum vor.“
Interessanter als der 35-Sekunden-Spot ist seine Geschichte: Seit dem Jahr 2020 kämpft der Verein „Klima vor acht“ für eine bessere Berichterstattung über die Klimakrise im Fernsehen. Der Name entstand durch einen Sendeplatz: „An einem ganz normalen Tag kann man im öffentlich-rechtlichen Fernsehen bis zu sieben Schalten zur Börse sehen“, sagt Friederike Mayer, die Vorsitzende des Vereins. Das gipfelt schließlich in der Sendung „Börse vor acht“. Meyer: „Der Sendeplatz vor der ‚Tagesschau‘ hat eine große Reichweite.“ Allerdings hätten die wenigsten Deutschen ein Aktiendepot, während die Klimakrise alle betreffe. Deshalb forderte die Initiative eine adäquate Sendung: „Klima vor acht“ und sammelte dafür 30.000 Unterschriften.
Die ARD lehnte eine solche damals ab mit der Begründung, sich nicht in den Dienst von Aktivisten stellen zu wollen. Stattdessen führte die ARD „Sprüche vor acht“ ein, offensichtlich eine Provokation. Tatsächlich aber haben die Aktivisten recht: Die Berichterstattung über die Erderhitzung und das Artensterben ist im Fernsehen deutlich unterrepräsentiert. „Klimathemen spielen in 1,8 Prozent der Sendezeit der vier großen Sender eine Rolle, bei der Biodiversität sind es sogar nur 0,2 Prozent“, sagt die Schauspielerin Maria Furtwängler – zu sehen etwa als „Tatort“-Kommissarin Charlotte Lindholm in der ARD. Mit ihrer MaLisa-Stiftung hatte sie 2023 ARD, ZDF, RTL und ProSiebenSat1 untersucht, Furtwängler engagiert sich stark für den Artenschutz.
Die Zahlen decken sich mit jenen, die der Verein „Klima vor acht“ für die Öffentlich-Rechtlichen erhebt: Seit 2021 bilanziert er jede Sendeminute, in der das Wort „Klima“ vorkommt, zieht allerdings irrelevante Begriffe wie „Investitionsklima“ oder „Klimaanlage“ wieder ab. „Unsere Daten zeigen: Die Berichterstattung ist geringer geworden“, erklärt Mayer. Tatsächlich ergab die Auswertung des ersten Halbjahres 2026: Der Anteil einer Berichterstattung über das Klimaproblem lag in der ARD und beim ZDF bei unter 1 Prozent.
Verein produziert selbst Sendungen
Um das zu ändern, hatte der Verein selbst angefangen, geeignete Filme für einen Sendeplatz „Klima vor acht“ herzustellen. Die drei- bis fünfminütigen Folgen der Pilotstaffel beschäftigten sich beispielsweise mit der Rolle der Moore, mit dem Erneuerbare-Energien-Gesetz, dem Grönlandeis oder der Attributionsforschung – also jener Wissenschaft, die betrachtet, wie der Klimawandel bereits auf unser Wetter wirkt. 2021 kooperierte der Verein mit dem Privatsender RTL und entwickelte das Format „Klima Update“, das zweimal pro Woche nach den Hauptnachrichten von „RTL aktuell“ ausgestrahlt wurde. 2022 wurde die Sendung für den Adolf-Grimme-Preis 2022 nominiert.
„Im Alltag oder in den Medien, da komm ich ja kaum vor“, sagt die Klimasau Matthias Matsche im Premierenfilm. Der sollte eigentlich vor der „Tagesschau“ in der ARD laufen – als bezahlter Werbespot. Der Verein hatte dafür anderthalb Jahre lang Spenden gesammelt, die notwendigen 135.000 Euro waren in diesem Jahr zusammengekommen. Allerdings lehnte die ARD Media GmbH nun eine Ausstrahlung ab: Begründung: Es handele sich bei dem Spot nicht um zulässige Werbung. Gemäß dem Medienstaatsvertrag müsse Werbung den Zweck erfüllen, entweder den Absatz von Produkten zu fördern oder aber das Image eines Unternehmens zu verbessern. Beides sah die ARD Media im Fall des „Wir schauen hin“-Spots nicht erfüllt. Auch die neue EmpCo-Richtlinie führte die ARD als Ablehnungsgrund an: Mit ihr will die EU-Kommission falsche Umweltaussagen in der Werbung verhindern.
Friederike Mayer sieht beides anders und verweist auf einen Imagefilm der Deutschen Telekom: „Die Kampagne lautete ‚Augen auf gegen Hass‘ und lief genau an der Stelle, an der wir den Sendeplatz buchen wollten“. Bei ihren Arbeiten an dem „Wir schauen hin“-Film habe sich der Verein an ebenjenem Imagefilm der Telekom orientiert. Zudem würden keine produktbezogenen Umweltaussagen gemacht, „die EmpCo ist also irrelevant“. Die Vereinsvorsitzende: „Wir haben jetzt einen Medienanwalt beauftragt, gerichtlich gegen die Ablehnung durch die ARD Media vorzugehen.“
